C h a p t e r   1
Common Diseases
ACUTE FEVER
The overall mean oral temperature for healthy adult individuals is 36.8 ± 0.4°C, with 
a nadir at 6 AM and a peak at 4–6 PM. A morning temperature of greater than 37.2°C 
and an evening temperature of greater than 37.7°C is often considered as fever. Fever 
may be continuous, intermittent or remittent. However, with frequent self-medication 
with antipyretics, classic patterns are not generally seen.

It is important to work towards finding the cause of fever. A meticulous history of 
chronology of symptoms, any associated focal symptom(s), exposure to infectious 
agents and occupational history may be useful. A thorough physical examination 
repeated on a regular basis may provide potentially diagnostic clues such as rash, 
lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, abdominal tenderness, altered 
sensorium, neck stiffness and lung crepts (Fig. 1.1 and see Tables 1.2–1.5). Drug fever 
should be considered when the cause of fever is elusive.

The cause of fever may be from a large range of diagnoses. If the history and physical 
examination suggest that it is likely to be more than a simple upper respiratory infection 
(URI) or viral fever, investigations are indicated. The extent and focus of diagnostic 
workup will depend on the extent and pace of illness, diagnostic possibilities and the 
immune status of the host. If there are no clinical clues, the workup should include a 
complete haemogram with erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), smear for malarial 
parasite, blood culture, Widal test and urine analysis including urine culture. If the 
febrile illness is prolonged beyond 2 weeks, an X-ray chest is indicated even in the 
absence of respiratory symptoms. Any abnormal fluid collection should be sampled. 
Ultrasonography is needed in some cases of acute fever such as in amoebic liver abscess.

Routine use of antipyretics in low-grade fever is not justified. This may mask important 
clinical indications. However, in acute febrile illnesses suggestive of viral or bacterial 
cause, fever should be symptomatically treated.

Chapter 1  Common Diseases    3
And/Or if fever does not come down after 2 hours:
Tab. Ibuprofen 400–600 mg 8 hourly.
Specific: Antibiotics/antimalarials depending on the cause suggested by clinical and 
laboratory evaluation
Outcome
In most cases of fever, either the patient may recover spontaneously or a diagnosis is 
reached after repeated clinical evaluation and investigations. If no diagnosis is reached 
in up to 3 weeks, the patient is said to be having fever of unknown origin (FUO) and 
should be managed accordingly.
Patient education
	
l Self-medication and over-medication should be avoided. 
	
l Avoid injectable Paracetamol/non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
	
l Antibiotics should be taken only on advice of a physician. 
	
l Avoid covering the patient having high fever with blanket, etc. 
	
l Plenty of fluids should be taken. Stay in cool environment. Washing/sponging of 
face and limbs should be done repeatedly.
References
	 1.	 Fever. In: Loscalzo J, Kasper DL, Longo DL, et al. (eds), Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine. 
21st ed. New York: McGraw Hill Company Inc.; 2022, pp. 130–133.
	 2.	 Clinical approach to patient with suspected infection. In: Firth J, Conlon C, Cox T (eds), Oxford 
Textbook of Medicine. 6th ed. Oxford University Press; 2020.
FEVER IN CHILDREN
There is a diurnal variation in normal body temperature such that it is higher in the 
evening than in the morning. However, significant fever in children is defined as a 
rectal temperature of >38°C, oral temperature of >37.5°C or an axillary temperature 
of >37.2°C. 
Hyperpyrexia:  Fever greater than 41.5°C is called hyperpyrexia and warrants 
aggressive antipyretic therapy because of risk of irreversible organ damage.
Fever of unknown origin:  It is defined as fever greater than 38.3°C on multiple 
occasions, in the absence of an identified cause after reasonable investigations for 
likely aetiologies and after ruling out self-limiting fever. The investigations may be 
conducted in the outpatient or inpatient setting over a duration of 2–3 weeks without 
rigid time-based criteria.
Nosocomial FUO:  This refers to hospitalized patients receiving acute care in whom 
infection or fever was absent on admission but in whom a fever of 38.3°C or more 
occurs on several occasions. Multiple readings of more than 38.3°C in a patient with 
less than 500 neutrophils/mm3 are labelled as neutropenic FUO.

text:
Assessing fever in young children is challenging due to:
	
l The child is not able to communicate his/her symptoms; practitioners rely on 
observations and concerns of parents.
	
l Rapidly changing clinical pictures make quick decisions challenging.
	
l Child behaviour may not reflect illness severity; alert children may deteriorate 
rapidly, while quiet ones may become more active post-treatment.
Documentation of fever
	
l Oral temperature is accurate provided no hot/cold drinks have been consumed in 
the preceding 20 minutes. Axillary temperatures are the least accurate and rectal 
thermometers are uncomfortable, especially in older children. Their use should be 
restricted to children younger than 6 months. Ear tympanic membrane thermometers 
are an accurate reflection of inner body temperature. 
	
l Digital thermometers may measure temperature within a few seconds and are 
accurate. Liquid crystal strips applied to the forehead for recording temperature are 
not accurate.
	
l Temperature can also be measured by infrared thermometry using a hand-held 
device. These devices are preferred for screening and should be checked for medical 
certification before being used to monitor temperature.
Identify severity of illness in children with fever in under-5-year children 
(Table 1.1).
Table 1.1.  Identifying severity of illness in children with fever in under-5-year children.
Low risk

6    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Find a cause
	
l Try to find the cause/focus of infection by careful history and physical examination.
	
l Short-duration fevers (less than 2 weeks) are usually due to infections. Look for any 
characteristic feature suggesting involvement of a particular system. Character of the 
fever (such as relapsing, Pel–Ebstein, step ladder, etc.) may give a clue to the cause. 
Heat hyperpyrexia, dehydration fever, allergy to drug (drug fever) and haemolytic 
crisis are less common causes of short fevers.
There are three major categories of children presenting with fever; see respective 
sections for their management:
	 1.	Fever due to infection without localized signs (Table 1.2)
	 2.	Fever due to infection with localized signs (Table 1.3)
	 3.	Fever with rash (Table 1.4)
Additional causes for fever lasting longer than 7 days (Table 1.5) are the following:
	
l Long-duration fevers lasting more than 2 weeks should be investigated for 
infections, malignancies, connective tissue disorders, autoimmune diseases and 
metabolic causes.
	
l Appropriate laboratory investigations such as total and differential leucocyte 
count, peripheral smear, urinalysis, serological tests, radiological investigations, 
and cultures of blood and body fluids are carried out as indicated by the signs and 
symptoms related with fever (for details of inflammatory markers, see Appendix II).
Children with any one of the following conditions must be seen immediately: 
age <3 months, fever >40.6°C, crying inconsolably, crying when moved/touched, 
difficult to awaken, stiff neck, purple/red spots present on the skin, breathing 
difficult and does not get better even after clearing of nasal passages, drooling of

text:
l Assure parents and explain that low-grade fever need not be treated with antipyretics.
	
l Give more fluids. Give additional 12% for every 1°C rise in body temperature above 
the baseline.
	
l Dress in only one layer of light clothing. Do not cover with blankets during rigors.
	
l Place in a cool and airy environment (21–22°C).
	
l Sponging: Sponge with lukewarm water (not cold during summer or hot during 
winter) in children with febrile delirium, febrile seizure and fever >41.1°C. Sponging 
should be done over the entire body (head to toe) and not just over the forehead. 
Give paracetamol 30 minutes before sponging to avoid shivering during sponging. 
Until paracetamol has taken effect, sponging will cause shivering, which may 
ultimately increase the temperature. Continue this till the body temperature comes 
down to 38°C. Note: Alcohol-based rub should not be used.
	
l Heat stroke requires immediate and aggressive cold water sponging.
	
l The body may be massaged gently so that the cutaneous vessels dilate and body 
heat is dissipated.
	
l For children younger than 3 months: Identify the low-risk febrile infant as per 
Table 1.6. These children can be managed on an outpatient basis.
	
l Hospitalize if the child appears toxic or does not fulfil the criteria in Tables 1.1 and 1.6.
In children older than 3 months:
	
l Rectal temperatures <39°C need not be treated. 
	
l Temperatures >39°C need administration of antipyretics.

Tab./Syr. Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg/dose; dose can be repeated at 8-hourly intervals.
Note: Efficacy is similar to that of Paracetamol. Effects last for 6–8 hours compared

(Caution: Aspirin should NOT be used for the risk of Reye’s syndrome.) Specific 
treatment for the cause of fever should be simultaneously undertaken. (For details of 
management of malaria, dengue, chikungunya, enteric fever and tuberculosis [TB], 
see respective sections below, and for management of COVID-19, see ‘Influenza-Like 
Illness (ILI)/Severe Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI)/COVID-19’ in Chapter 5.)
Monitoring
Close monitoring of all children, especially young febrile infants, is essential.
Patient education
	
l Estimating a child’s temperature by feeling the child’s skin is not accurate. 
	
l Explain to the parents the correct method of measuring temperature and cleaning 
of the device. Do not measure the temperature in a child’s mouth if he/she has 
consumed a hot or cold food or drink in the last 30 minutes.
	
l Clean the thermometer with cool water and soap. Rinse with water.
	
l Emphasize adequate fluid intake, rest and appropriate use of antipyretics.
	
l Recognize red flag signs and report to a doctor immediately:
	– Oral, rectal, ear or forehead temperature of 104°F (40°C) or higher
	– Armpit temperature of 103°F (39.4°C) or higher
	– A seizure caused by a fever
	– Fevers that keep coming back (even if they last only a few hours)
	– A fever as well as an ongoing medical problem, such as heart disease, cancer, 
lupus or sickle cell anaemia
	– A fever as well as a new skin rash
References
	 1.	 Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management. NICE Guideline [NG143]. November 
2019, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng143/resources/support-for-education-and-learning-
educational-resource-traffic-light-table-pdf-6960664333 [accessed December 15, 2023].
	 2.	 The Johns Hopkins Hospital, Kleinman K, McDaniel L, Molloy M. The Harriet Lane Handbook: 
The Johns Hopkins Hospital. 22nd ed. 2020.
	 3.	 Fever. In: Hay WW, Levin MJ, Deterding RR, Abzug MJ (eds), Current Paediatric Diagnosis 
and Treatment. 24th ed. New York: Lange Medical Books; 2018.
	 4.	 Mahajan P, Batra P, Thakur N, et al. Consensus guidelines on evaluation and management of the 
febrile child presenting to the emergency department. Indian Pediatr. 2017;54:652–660.
FEVER OF UNKNOWN ORIGIN
FUO is defined as the presence of fever of 38.3ºC (>101ºF) or more recorded on several 
occasions, evolving over 2–3 weeks without an exact diagnosis even after detailed

Chapter 1  Common Diseases    11
investigations and after excluding self-limiting fever. It is usually an uncommon 
presentation of common diseases. The diagnosis of FUO with respect to time cutoff 
depends on the age of the child, immune status of the child, travel history and history 
of hospitalization. In endemic areas, elicit travel history for infections like malaria, 
rickettsial diseases, viral haemorrhagic fever, leptospirosis or kala-azar.
FUO are classified into few main categories along with common causes in each 
of these categories.
	 1.	Classic FUO: It corresponds to the previous definition except that instead of 
1 week of investigations, it requires up to three outpatient visits or 3 days in 
the hospital, viz. TB, abscesses, bacterial endocarditis, visceral leishmaniasis, 
non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, Hodgkin’s lymphoma, acute leukaemia and systemic 
lupus erythematosus. As mentioned above, the cutoff time period is not rigid and 
the diagnosis of FUO should be kept irrespective of rigid time-based cutoffs. 
	 2.	Nosocomial FUO: It refers to fever of >38.3°C on several occasions that develops 
after admission in a hospitalized patient and is elusive to diagnose. In children who 
are in ICU, FUO could result from postoperative collection (abscess, haematoma, 
foreign bodies), infected prostheses, infected catheters, Clostridium difficile colitis, 
deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, stroke and drug fever. In those who 
are not in the ICU, the causes can be similar, but the children are less ill. 
	 3.	Immunodeficiency-associated FUO
	
a.	HIV-related FUO: Fever can be a result of opportunistic infections, viz. TB, 
cryptococcosis, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and bacterial pneumonia. 
These need to be investigated by special tests including cultures and molecular 
diagnostics.
	
b.	Neutropenic FUO: It refers to fever for 5 days in a patient who has a neutrophil 
count of less than 500/mm3 or is expected to fall to this level in 1–2 days, 
after appropriate empirical antibiotics. The causes could be Gram-negative 
bacterial, staphylococcal, and central venous catheter infections, invasive fungal 
infections, dental abscesses, perianal infections, cytomegalovirus and herpes 
simplex virus infections. In children who have undergone haematopoietic stem 
cell transplant or organ transplant, fever should be taken as a red alert sign. This 
may herald graft-versus-host disease, graft rejection, relapse of malignancy or 
immune reconstitution apart from opportunistic infections.
If the patient does not fit into any of the above-mentioned definitions, he/she 
should be referred to a specialist for investigations and management.
SALIENT FEATURE
	
l Prolonged unexplained fever, often with no localizing clue on history, physical 
examination and basic laboratory investigations
Diagnostic evaluation
A detailed clinical history and repeated and meticulous physical examination are 
valuable in providing potentially diagnostic clues to the cause of fever in these patients.

12    Standard Treatment Guidelines
No single algorithmic approach to diagnosis can be recommended for all patients with 
FUO and the diagnostic approach needs to be individualized.
A complete haemogram including peripheral blood smear for malarial parasite, 
serum biochemistry, particularly liver function tests (LFTs), a tuberculin test, 
blood culture (two sets) and an X-ray of chest should be done in every patient with 
prolonged fever. Other investigations which are often helpful include ESR, C-reactive 
protein (CRP), tests related to collagen vascular disease, an ultrasonography of the 
abdomen to localize intra-abdominal foci of infections and a contrast-enhanced 
computed tomography (CECT) of the chest and abdomen in detecting mediastinal 
lymph nodes and parenchymal lung abnormalities not seen on conventional chest 
X-ray. Furthermore, diagnostic approach should take into consideration the diagnostic 
clues from the evaluation of history, results of repeated physical examination, basic 
investigations and any investigation done prior to this episode. If any abnormal or 
doubtful lesion is detected, fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)/biopsy should be 
obtained. The availability of newer serological tests and polymerase chain reaction 
(PCR)–based molecular tests offers advantage to detect microbial infections. These 
need to be individualized as per the availability and local infection trends.

Treatment will be based on the specific cause of fever. Thorough investigations 
generally yield a specific cause of fever in about 90% of patients. Sometimes evaluation 
may need discontinuation of all drugs being taken by the patient to rule out drug fever 
as the cause of FUO.
Symptomatic treatment for fever (for details, see Fever): Sponging with 
lukewarm water may be done if fever produces discomfort. The emphasis in patients 
with classic FUO is on continued observation and examination. (Caution: Avoid 
‘shotgun’ trials. Empirical therapies consisting of therapeutic trials commonly used in 
patients with FUO are antibiotics, antitubercular treatment [ATT] and corticosteroids.)
Note: A young child younger than 3 years who is toxic looking should be hospitalized 
for fever workup. Parenteral antibiotics may be indicated in young infants (younger 
than 2 months) after risk stratification (for details, see Sepsis). Stable-looking children 
younger than 3 years may be started on empirical antibiotics (oral) after obtaining blood 
culture and urine culture if there is laboratory evidence of infection and/or inflammation 
with persistent fever.
If a therapeutic trial is started on the basis of clinical evaluation and inability to 
reach a definitive diagnosis, the following principles must be kept in mind:
	
l Give only one set of trial at a given time.
	
l The doses of drugs and period of therapeutic trial must be adequate.
	
l The patient must be followed closely for response.
The ability of glucocorticoids and NSAIDs to mask fever while permitting the 
spread of infection dictates that their use should be avoided unless infection has been 
largely ruled out.

In about 10% of cases, no cause may be diagnosed despite thorough evaluation. In such 
cases, if the patient is well preserved, just a close clinical and investigative follow-up 
may be enough to look for any PDCs which may be evolving or appear later in the 
course of disease. However, if the patient is sick or is deteriorating and no diagnosis is 
reached, an appropriate empirical therapeutic trial is justified.
Patient education
	
l Self-medication should be avoided.
	
l Antibiotics should be taken only on the advice of a physician.
	
l Avoid covering the patient with high fever with a blanket, etc. 
	
l Plenty of fluids should be taken. Stay in a cool environment. Washing/sponging of 
face and limbs should be done repeatedly.

DIZZINESS AND VERTIGO
The term dizziness is used for light-headedness, faintness, spinning, giddiness, 
confusion and blackouts. Vertigo can be classified into four main categories based on 
a patient’s history: vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium and light-headedness. Patients 
frequently use the term ‘dizziness’ to encompass these sensations. They often struggle 
to articulate the nature of their symptoms, but they can more reliably pinpoint the 
timing and triggers. Episodic vertigo triggered by head movement might be attributed to 
benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, while vertigo accompanied by unilateral hearing 
loss could indicate Ménière’s disease. On the other hand, episodic vertigo without any 
discernible trigger may signal vestibular neuritis.
The primary focus during evaluation is to determine whether the underlying cause 
is peripheral or central. Vertigo may result from diseases of the inner ear or disturbances 
of the vestibular centres or pathways in the central nervous system (e.g. Ménière’s 
disease, arteriosclerosis of cerebral vessels, brain lesion, head injury, motion sickness, 
or large and rapid variations in barometric pressure).​ Peripheral aetiologies are typically 
benign, while central causes often necessitate urgent intervention and treatment.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patients experience a perception of self-motion when at rest or distorted self-
motion during regular head movement.
	
l Depending on the underlying cause/condition, it may be associated with nausea 
and vomiting, or accompanied by other symptoms and signs (e.g. headaches and 
visual symptoms).
	
l The HINTS (head-impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) examination distinguishes 
peripheral from central aetiologies. The physical examination involves orthostatic 
blood pressure measurement, cardiac and neurological assessment, nystagmus 
evaluation and the Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre. 
	
l Observing the patient’s gait and conducting a Romberg’s test is essential. An 
unsteady gait prompts assessment for peripheral neuropathy. A positive Romberg’s 
test indicates abnormalities in proprioception receptors or their pathway.
	
l Laboratory testing and imaging are not required if no neurological abnormality 
is found on examination.
	
l The diagnostic approach uses the timing of the symptom, the triggers that provoke 
the symptom and a targeted examination. The responses categorize dizziness into 
three clinical scenarios: triggered episodic, spontaneous episodic or continuous 
vestibular.

Chapter 1  Common Diseases    17
	
l Episodic triggered symptoms involve brief episodes of intermittent dizziness 
triggered (seconds to hours) by head motion; they may indicate benign 
paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). Dizziness from orthostatic hypotension 
occurs with movement to the upright position. 
	
l Episodic symptoms occurring spontaneously without an apparent trigger and 
lasting from seconds to days may be indicative of conditions such as Ménière’s 
disease, vestibular migraine or psychiatric disorders. Conversely, continuous 
vestibular symptoms persisting for days to weeks might be linked to traumatic or 
toxic exposure. Classic vestibular symptoms include enduring dizziness or vertigo 
accompanied by nausea, vomiting, nystagmus, gait instability and intolerance to 
head motion.
	
l In cases where there is no history of trauma or exposures, and medications 
associated with dizziness are ruled out, the presentation is more consistent with 
vestibular neuritis or central aetiologies. It is worth noting that central causes 
can also present with movement-triggered patterns. Additionally, elderly patients 
may be more susceptible to adverse effects from medications, emphasizing the 
importance of considering medication-related issues in this population.
	
l Axioms for defining a dizzy spell as vestibular: If the patient in a significant 
spell does not have spontaneous labyrinthine nystagmus, and also if the dizziness 
has been non-episodic and continuous for 2–3 months, then this dizziness cannot 
be vestibular.

l BPPV responds well to canalith repositioning procedures like the Epley’s 
manoeuvre. Pharmacological treatment has no role in the treatment of BPPV as it 
may increase the risk of falls.
	
l Managing Ménière’s disease involves salt restriction and diuretics. 
	
l Vestibular neuritis: Reassurance and explanation are essential, in combination with 
symptomatic treatment for the first few days with a combination of antihistamine, 
antiemetic or benzodiazepine and vestibular rehabilitation.

Reassure the patient and in cases where positional vertigo cannot be ruled out, advise 
the patient to take complete rest with minimal movements only.

SYNCOPE
Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness, with rapid onset and quick recovery, 
and associated with loss of postural tone, mainly because of decreased or cessation of 
cerebral perfusion. It accounts for 1–3% of emergency room visits and 1% of hospital 
admission. Increased incidence is seen after the age of 70 years. Incidence is twice 
common in cardiac patients than in non-cardiac patients. It leads to physical injury (30% 
of patients admitted to emergency, among whom 5% have major trauma). Recurrence 
is common: ≥1 episode during their lifetime reported by approximate 20% of adults.
SALIENT FEATURES
l	 Black-out of vision, sweating, giddiness, light-headedness and palpitation 
are common prodromal symptoms. Classification of syncope is shown in 
Figure 1.3. Vasovagal syncope is the commonest type occurring at all ages and is 
characterized by sudden onset and rapid recovery without any neurological deficit.
l	 Rule out cardiac cause if it is associated with palpitation and/or exertions. Sitting 
and supine syncope are more likely due to cardiac cause. Although uncommon, 
vasovagal syncope has been reported during sleep, while driving or in supine and 
sitting positions.
l	 Age >54 years, <3 episodes of syncope and duration of warning symptoms 
<6 seconds favour the syncope due to AV block or ventricular tachycardia.

Chapter 1  Common Diseases    19
l	 Hot, crowded, closed space, prolonged standing, fasting and summer season are 
commonly associated circumstances.
l	 In case of prolonged loss of consciousness or delayed recovery, consider other 
differentials.
l	 Physical examination should include the following: supine and standing BP and 
pulse measurement – orthostatic hypotension (fall in systolic BP ≥20 mmHg or 
diastolic BP ≥10 mmHg on standing).
l	 Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome: There occurs significant elevation of 
heart rate (>30 bpm) in upright position, without change in blood pressure, in the 
absence of medications, dehydration, prolonged bed rest, neuropathy or substantial 
weight loss.
l	 Cardiac murmur and neurological deficit are seen and psychiatric evaluation 
should be performed in pseudo-syncope.
l	 ECG is mandatory in all cases, and if required cardiac studies including ECHO 
and Holter monitoring (in case of recurrent severe unexplained syncope with ECG 
features suggesting arrhythmic syncope) should be performed to confirm cardiac 
causes – structural or rhythm related. 
	
	
Other testing should be guided by history and physical examination: CBC, 
electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose (rarely helpful if asymptomatic or 
presenting hours later), BNP level, cardiac enzymes (only if history suggestive of 
MI), D-dimer (for pulmonary embolism [PE] workup), urine pregnancy and urine 
drug screen, neuroimaging, EEG only if indicated, lung scan or helical CT scan of 
the chest if concern for pulmonary embolism.
l	 Autonomic testing is performed in suspected neurodegenerative disease or in 
selected patients.

l Careful evaluation of history and event from the patient as well from witnesses is 
more important for diagnosis than physical examination.
	
l Elicit history including the following important points: body position during event, 
triggers, prodromal symptoms, circumstances, duration of loss of consciousness, 
recovery time and previous similar episodes.
	
l Check for orthostatic hypotension.
	
l Treatment decisions are based on the type of syncope and risk stratification. Risk 
stratification (based on mortality and risk of recurrence) is important to identify the 
need of admission.
Orthostatic and vasovagal syncope

l Education regarding identification and avoidance of triggers (such as if the patient 
faints while blood is being drawn, draw the blood sample in lying down position)

20    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l In patients with orthostatic hypotension, education regarding lifestyle manoeuvres 
(to avoid triggers and situations, explain the risk of recurrence), adequate hydration 
and salt intake, reduction/discontinuation of hypotensive therapy, support stockings, 
head-up tilt sleeping depending on the clinical severity.
	
l Counter-pressure manoeuvres to stop a vasovagal syncopal episode, or at least delay 
it long enough that one can lie down with the feet elevated
	– Tensing the arms with clenched fists, leg pumping and leg-crossing
	– Standing with crossed legs and clenching of the buttocks
	– Intense gripping of the hands (a rubber ball or similar object as hard as possible) 
and tensing of the arms (gripping one hand with the other while simultaneously 
moving both arms away from the body)
	– Tilt training (stand in tilt position with support of wall for 30–60 minutes daily; 
gradually increase the time for standing in tilt position; it should be omitted 
immediately if the patient experiences presyncope symptoms)
	
l Orthostatic training
	– Use of elastic compression stockings, which are worn on the feet and lower legs
	– Contraction of the leg muscles before and while standing: leg-crossing and 
pressing knee with each other, squatting position, lying down with leg elevation
	– Avoiding immediate standing position; rising to stand slowly and in stages

JAUNDICE
Jaundice is defined as yellow discolouration of the skin, sclera and tissues caused 
by increased levels of circulating bilirubin. Jaundice in adults can be an indicator 
of significant underlying disease. Common causes of jaundice in clinical practice 
include acute viral hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, chronic hepatitis/cirrhosis, gallstones 
and malignancy of the gallbladder/pancreas or extrahepatic biliary system. Chronic 
haemolytic anaemias are less common and usually present in childhood or sometimes 
in young adults. It is caused by elevated serum bilirubin levels in the unconjugated 
(indirect) or conjugated (direct) form for clinical purposes (Fig. 1.5). This classification, 
along with findings from the history, physical examination and initial laboratory testing, 
is used to narrow the diagnostic possibilities and guide the subsequent evaluation. 
Initial differentiation between the three types of jaundice by appropriate clinical history, 
examination and investigations including full blood counts, LFTs, viral markers, 
ultrasound examination of the liver and biliary tract and, if indicated, CT scan of the 
abdomen/endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).

Chapter 19.

ACUTE VIRAL HEPATITIS
Acute viral hepatitis is caused by hepatitis viruses A and E (faeco-oral transmission) or B, 
C and D (parenteral, sexual, perinatal transmission). Viral hepatitis, caused by hepatitis 
viruses A–E, remains a major public health problem in India. Hepatitis A and E are water 
and foodborne infections that are often the cause of sporadic or outbreaks of hepatitis in 
India. All types of viral hepatitis produce clinically similar illnesses. These range from 
asymptomatic and inapparent to fulminant and fatal acute infections common to all 
types, whereas in case of blood-borne types (HBV, hepatitis C virus [HCV], and HDV), 
the presentation may vary from subclinical persistent infections to rapidly progressive 
chronic liver disease with cirrhosis and even hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). 
Hepatitis A virus (HAV) and hepatitis E virus (HEV) are important causes of acute 
viral hepatitis and acute liver failure (ALF). HAV infection causes severe disease in adults, 
and HEV may cause more ALF in pregnant women and is responsible for 10–30% of 
acute hepatitis and 5–15% of ALF cases in India. Overall, HEV accounts for 10–40% of 
acute hepatitis and 15–45% of ALF. Population prevalence of chronic HBV infection in 
India is around 3–4%, with a higher prevalence in high-risk groups. Anti-HCV antibody 
prevalence in the general population is estimated to be around 1% with higher prevalence 
among high-risk groups. Chronic HBV infection accounts for 40–50% of cases of HCC 
and 20–30% of cases of cirrhosis in India. Chronic HCV infection accounts for 12–32% 
of cases of HCC and 12–20% of cases of cirrhosis. High-risk groups for HBV are IV 
drug users, persons born in endemic areas, men who have sex with men, recipients of 
multiple blood transfusions, patients undergoing haemodialysis, heterosexual persons 
with multiple partners or a history of sexually transmitted disease, household contacts 
or sexual partners of HBV carriers and health care workers exposed to infected blood 
or bodily fluids. Early identification of persons with chronic HBV or HCV infection 
enables them to receive the necessary care and treatment to prevent or delay progression 
of liver disease. Also transmission can be reduced through counselling on risk behaviours 
and provision of prevention commodities (such as sterile needles and syringes) and 
hepatitis B vaccination (for details, see Immunoprophylaxis in Appendix II).
Hepatitis A infection
It is an outbreak-prone disease with an incubation period of around 4 weeks. Person-
to-person spread of HAV is enhanced by poor personal hygiene and overcrowding. 
Excretion in the stool occurs for 7–14 days after the onset of the clinical illness and is 
diagnostic of an acute HAV infection. No carrier state has been identified. Inactivated 
attenuated vaccine, which is safe, immunogenic and effective, is available.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The most common clinical consequence of infection with hepatitis A virus (HAV) 
is an illness characterized by onset with a prodromal phase (nausea, vomiting, 
anorexia, fever, dull aching pain in the upper right abdomen) followed by icteric 
phase (appearance of jaundice in 3–7 days of onset, associated with improvement

Chapter 1  Common Diseases    25
	 in nausea and return of appetite) followed by convalescent phase, when jaundice 
gradually settles.
	
l Physical examination findings are jaundice and hepatomegaly and may be 
associated with right upper quadrant pain and discomfort.
	
l In acute hepatitis with clinical jaundice, the serum bilirubin levels are greater 
than 3 mg/dL and serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is more than 200 U/L. 
Anti-HAV IgM antibodies indicate acute infection and are generally detectable 
5–10 days before the onset of symptoms and can persist for up to 6 months. IgG 
antibodies against HAV become the predominant antibody during convalescence 
and remain detectable indefinitely. Anti-HAV total antibodies (IgG and IgM) 
or specific IgG (but anti-HAV IgM negative) indicate immunity to hepatitis A 
because of either past infection or vaccination.
	
l Sometimes relapsing hepatitis is seen in acute HAV.

l Acute hepatitis treatment is supportive. IV fluids are given as required in case of 
uncontrolled nausea and vomiting.
	
l There is no role for antiviral drugs in the therapy for HAV infection. Virtually all 
previously healthy patients with hepatitis A recover completely with no clinical 
sequelae. Rarely ALF can occur, which needs to be managed in specialist centres. 
	
l Repeat LFT at weekly interval and the patient can resume activity when the enzyme 
levels come down to less than 3–5 times normal. 
Hepatitis E infection
Cases of hepatitis E are not clinically distinguishable from other types of acute viral 
hepatitis. Diagnosis is strongly suspected in appropriate epidemiological settings, e.g. 
occurrence of several cases in localities in known disease-endemic areas, in settings 
with risk of water contamination, in case of severe disease in pregnant women and if 
hepatitis A has been excluded. Acute sporadic hepatitis by HEV is more common in 
adults than in children.
	
l Definitive diagnosis of hepatitis E infection is based on the detection of specific IgM 
antibodies to the virus in blood. In acute hepatitis with clinical jaundice, the serum 
bilirubin levels are greater than 3 mg/dL and serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 
is more than 200 U/L.
	
l There is no specific treatment capable of altering the course of acute hepatitis E. 
As the disease is usually self-limiting, hospitalization is generally not required. 
Hospitalization is required for people with ALF and symptomatic pregnant women.
	
l Immunosuppressed people, especially post-transplant recipients, can develop chronic 
hepatitis E which is defined as persistence of HEV RNA in blood or stool for more 
than 3 months; refer these patients to a higher centre for specific treatment. This is

26    Standard Treatment Guidelines
more often seen in developed countries where HEV infection by zoonotic genotype 
(GT3/4) of the virus is common unlike in developing countries where human 
genotypes of virus GT 1 and 2 are predominant.
	
l During prodromal phase, adequate intake of fluids should be maintained. Once the 
appetite improves, the patient should be advised to take a normal diet (fat restriction 
or giving high carbohydrate has no advantage).
Hepatitis B infection
	
l The spectrum of clinical manifestations of HBV infection varies in both acute 
and chronic diseases. During the acute phase, manifestations range from 
subclinical or anicteric hepatitis to icteric hepatitis and, in some cases, ALF. The 
incubation period for HBV varies from 30 to 180 days. Chronicity develops in 
<5% of immunocompetent adults after acute HBV infection. In chronic phase, 
manifestations range from an asymptomatic carrier state to chronic hepatitis, 
cirrhosis and HCC. Reactivation of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) can present with 
hepatitis flares, which if severe can lead to acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF). 
Extrahepatic manifestations can also occur with both acute and chronic infections.
	
l HBV and HCV co-infections may result in an accelerated disease course. Patients 
tested for HBV and HCV should also be tested for HIV due to the common modes 
of transmission and TB. 
Acute hepatitis 
Approximately 70% of patients with acute HBV infection have subclinical or anicteric 
hepatitis, while 30% develop icteric hepatitis. The disease may be more severe in 
patients co-infected with other hepatitis viruses or with underlying liver disease.
Fulminant hepatitis B is unusual (seen in 0.1–0.5% of patients). A serum sickness–like 
syndrome manifested as fever, skin rashes, arthralgia and arthritis, which usually subsides 
with the onset of jaundice, may develop during the prodromal period, followed by 
constitutional symptoms, anorexia, nausea, jaundice and right upper quadrant discomfort. 
The symptoms and jaundice generally disappear after 1–3 months, but some patients have 
prolonged fatigue even after normalization of serum aminotransferase concentrations.
	
l The complete eradication of HBV rarely occurs after recovery from acute HBV 
infection and that latent infection can maintain the T-cell response for decades 
following clinical recovery, thereby keeping the virus under control. The virus 
persists in hepatic cells as integrated DNA and covalently closed circular (ccc) DNA 
reservoir, maintaining a lifelong presence.
	
l The rate of progression from acute to CHB in immunocompetent persons is 
determined primarily by the age at infection. The rate is approximately 90% for 
a perinatally acquired infection, 20–50% for infections between the age of 1 and 
5 years, and less than 5% for an adult-acquired infection.
Treatment (acute hepatitis)
	 1.	Treatment for acute HBV is mainly supportive. In addition, appropriate measures 
should be taken to prevent infection in exposed contacts.

Chapter 1  Common Diseases    27
	 2.	Indications for hospitalization are severe prodromal symptoms causing 
dehydration, presence of early signs of hepatic encephalopathy (e.g. altered 
sensorium, disturbed sleep pattern, flapping tremors) and decreased liver span 
on examination. Also consider hospitalization in patients who are older, have 
significant comorbidities or cannot tolerate oral intake.
	 3.	Refer to a tertiary care centre in case of ALF and severe cases such as those who 
develop coagulopathy (international normalized ratio [INR] >1.5) and prolonged 
jaundice (>4–6 weeks).
	 4.	If the patient develops ascites and/or encephalopathy within 4 weeks of 
development of jaundice, reactivation of chronic HBV is likely and he/she should 
be referred to tertiary centres.
(See also Appendix II for immunoprophylaxis.)
Chronic hepatitis B
	
l Many patients with chronic HBV are asymptomatic (unless they have decompensated 
cirrhosis or have extrahepatic manifestations), while others have non-specific 
symptoms such as fatigue. Some patients experience exacerbations of the infection 
(reactivation of chronic HBV infection) which may be asymptomatic, or present like 
acute hepatitis illness or, if severe, like ACLF.
	
l Physical examination may be normal, or there may be stigmata of chronic liver 
disease. Jaundice, splenomegaly, ascites, peripheral oedema, upper gastrointestinal 
bleed and encephalopathy may be present in patients with decompensated cirrhosis. 
	
l Laboratory tests may be normal, but most patients have a mild to moderate elevation 
in serum AST and ALT (>10 × ULN during acute hepatitis flare due to reactivation 
of chronic HBV infection). Hypersplenism (decreased haemoglobin, white blood cell 
and/or platelet counts) or impaired hepatic synthetic function (hypoalbuminaemia 
and/or prolonged prothrombin time/INR) indicates cirrhosis.
	
l The two major extrahepatic complications of chronic HBV are polyarteritis nodosa 
and glomerular disease.
	
l CHB infection is defined as the persistence of HBsAg for more than 6 months. 
Workup of such patients should include the following: virological tests (HBsAg 
[qualitative], HBeAg, anti-HBe, HBV DNA quantification), LFTs, ultrasound upper 
abdomen and non-invasive measures to assess liver fibrosis (e.g. liver elastography, 
AST to Platelet Ratio Index [APRI]).

Treatment of CHB is by nucleoside/nucleotide analogue (NUC) regimens and is 
lifelong in most cases. The main goal of treatment of CHB is to suppress HBV 
replication. Decisions to start and stop antivirals is based on HBsAg positive status, 
ALT levels, HBV DNA levels and fibrosis level of the liver and everyone infected does 
not require treatment. It is best to refer patients to specialist centres for their follow-up 
based on treatment guidelines. Such patients also need surveillance for HCC.

28    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Screening for Hepatitis B to be done for the following groups:
	
l Antenatal screening of pregnant women for hepatitis B
	
l High-risk groups – spouses, siblings and family members of HBsAg-positive patients
	
l Opportunistic screening for HBV and HCV of patients visiting health care facilities 
	
l Health care workers following a needlestick injury
Hepatitis C infection
	
l HCV causes both acute and chronic hepatitis. Acute hepatitis is often clinically mild 
and marked by fluctuating elevations of serum ALT and AST levels. It is extremely 
rare to find acute life-threatening HCV infection; usually seen in patients with chronic 
kidney disease requiring haemodialysis or patients requiring frequent bold transfusions.
	
l Spontaneous clearance of acute HCV infection occurs within 6 months of infection 
in 15–45% of infected individuals in the absence of treatment. Almost all the 
remaining 55–85% of persons will harbour HCV for the rest of their lives (if not 
treated) and are considered to have chronic HCV infection. If left untreated, chronic 
HCV infection can cause liver cirrhosis, liver failure and HCC. Early detection and 
treatment can prevent serious liver damage and improve long-term health.
	
l The standard method of diagnosis is by detection of anti-HCV antibody. All antibody 
HCV-positive patients should be referred for HCV RNA testing. A total of 60–70% 
of anti-HCV-positive treatment-naïve patients will have HCV RNA, i.e. viraemia. 
	
l All patients with viraemia of all age groups including children older than 3 years 
regardless of the stage of the disease with any amount of HCV RNA should be 
initiated on treatment with all oral direct-acting antivirals (DAA). The standard 
duration of treatment is 12 weeks. 
	
l No on-treatment testing for HCV genotype/HCV RNA is needed, and 12 weeks after 
stoppage of treatment, HCV RNA test is done to check for a sustained virological 
response (SVR). 
	
l About 96–97% of patients, irrespective of genotype, attain SVR with the current 
DAA strategy.
Patient education
	
l Instruct the caregivers to report and hospitalize the patient if there is alteration in 
the behaviour or sensorium of the patient.
	
l There is no need to isolate the patient.
	
l The patient should avoid taking alcohol for 4–6 months after recovery.
	
l Advise patients to drink plenty of fluids and take a diet rich in fruits, fibre, lean 
proteins (such as fish) and food rich in natural sugars. 
	
l The spouse of the patient with acute viral hepatitis B should use barrier method to 
prevent sexual transmission and be vaccinated against hepatitis B.
	
l Family screening for HBV infection (by testing for HBsAg, total-HBc and anti-
HBs titres) is mandatory. Educate patients and their families on food hygiene and 
proper sanitation facilities, such as access to safe drinking water, consumption of 
hygienically cooked fresh food and proper disposal of excreta particularly from 
persons with viral hepatitis.

l Advise avoidance of unnecessary percutaneous injection (through the use of 
alternative non-percutaneous routes of drug administration, such as oral or topical 
applications), promotion of the use of disposable single-use (auto-disable) syringes 
and safe disposal of used needles and other sharps.
	
l Provide vaccination for HBV and HAV (see details in Chapter 19 in the section 
‘Immunization Schedule’ and Immunoprophylaxis in Appendix II).
See also ‘Neonatal Jaundice’ and ‘Acute Viral Hepatitis’ in Chapter 19.

TUBERCULOSIS
TB is one of the most prevalent chronic infections in our country and is responsible for 
high morbidity and mortality. It is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and afflicts 
the lungs most commonly. In about 20% of cases, extrapulmonary involvement is seen. 
Tubercular lymphadenopathy is the commonest form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis 
(EPTB). TB is a notifiable disease. All cases of TB, irrespective of the method of 
diagnosis (microbiologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed), initiation of treatment 
(whether on treatment or not), source of treatment (government or non-government), 
type of patients (TB or drug-resistant tuberculosis [DR-TB]) and type of regimen used 
for treatment (daily or intermittent), should be notified to local/district/state health 
authorities, through various means of notification. The patient can be notified in real 
time through web-based case notification site www.nikshay.gov.in. from both public 
and private sectors. Pharmacists and chemists dispensing anti-TB drugs, laboratories 
diagnosing TB cases, medical practitioners, clinics, hospitals and nursing homes also 
need to notify.

30    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Pulmonary TB refers to disease involving lung parenchyma. It usually presents with 
fever, malaise, chronic cough with sputum production, anorexia and weight loss.
	
l Sometimes chest pain and haemoptysis may be the presenting symptoms.
	
l Extrapulmonary TB refers to disease involving sites other than lung parenchyma 
and lymph nodes are the commonest site. It presents most commonly as 
prolonged fever and cervical, mediastinal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy. 
	
l Abdominal TB may present as ascites, chronic abdominal pain, diarrhoea, 
recurrent subacute intestinal obstruction, etc.
	
l CNS TB presents as irritability, headache, vomiting, chronic meningitis, seizures 
or focal neurological deficits, and altered sensorium.
	
l Skeletal TB may present as Pott’s spine, tuberculous osteomyelitis and 
monoarticular arthritis. 
	
l Tubercular constrictive pericarditis presents with oedema/ascites. 
	
l Symptoms of genitourinary TB include tubo-ovarian masses, secondary 
amenorrhoea in women, chronic epididymo-orchitis in men and painless 
haematuria in both the sexes. Diagnostic algorithm is given in Figure 1.6.
	
l Presumptive pulmonary TB refers to a person with any of the symptoms and 
signs suggestive of TB including cough >2 weeks, fever >2 weeks, significant 
weight loss, haemoptysis and any abnormality in chest radiograph. (Exception: 
Cough of any duration is significant in HIV-positive individuals and people with 
contacts of microbiologically confirmed TB.) Diagnostic algorithm is shown in 
Figure 1.6. For screening of key population, see ‘Contact Investigation’.
	
l Presumptive paediatric TB refers to children with persistent fever and/or cough for 
>2 weeks, loss of weight/no weight gain and/or history of contact with infectious 
TB cases within the last 2 years. Diagnostic algorithm is shown in Figure 1.7. 
	
l Presumptive extrapulmonary TB refers to the presence of organ-specific 
symptoms and signs such as lymphadenopathy, pain and swelling in joints, neck 
stiffness and disorientation, and/or constitutional symptoms such as significant 
weight loss, persistent fever >2 weeks and night sweats (Fig. 1.8). Diagnostic 
algorithm for TB lymphadenitis is given in Figure 1.9.
	
l Presumptive DR-TB refers to the patient who is eligible for Rifampicin-resistant 
screening at the time of diagnosis Or/and during the course of treatment for 
drug-sensitive (DS)-TB or H mono/poly regimen. This includes all notified 
patients with TB (public and private), follow-up positive on microscopy including 
treatment failures on standard first-line treatment and all oral H mono/poly 
regimen, and any clinical non-responder including paediatric patients.
	
l All efforts should be undertaken for microbiological confirmation of the diagnosis 
in patients with presumptive TB. Acceptable methods for microbiological diagnosis 
are sputum smear microscopy for AFB, culture (solid [LJ] media, automated 
liquid culture systems) and rapid molecular diagnostic tests for MTB complex and 
detection of Rif and INH resistance, nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), and 
Xpert MTB/Rif testing using the GeneXpert Truenat and line probe assay (LPA).

Chapter 1  Common Diseases    31
	
l Probable TB cases are patients with TB without microbiological confirmation 
(smear microscopy, culture and molecular diagnosis) but with strong clinical 
and other evidence (e.g. X-ray, fine needle aspiration cytology [FNAC], 
histopathology) and treated. For patients with presumptive TB found to be 
negative on rapid molecular test, an attempt should be made to obtain culture on 
an appropriate specimen.
	
l Definitive diagnosis is made by microbiological confirmation – demonstrating the 
bacilli (ZN stain, LED microscopy, fluorescent stain); bacilli growth on solid LJ 
culture and liquid culture and by molecular tests including CB-NAAT tests (Gene 
Xpert MTB/Rif, Xpert Ultra, Truenat and Truenat Ultra) and line probe tests, 
in sputum or bronchial secretions. For a comprehensive diagnostic approach, 
diagnostic algorithms for TB in adults (Fig. 1.6) and children (Fig. 1.7) are used.
	
l A positive NAAT provides useful confirmation but a negative test does not 
always rule out TB. NAAT does not replace the role of routine AFB smear 
and culture. Gene Xpert Ultra is an advanced version of the Gene Xpert with 
better TB detection capabilities and more definitive identification of Rifampicin 
susceptibility and resistance​. Gene Ultra can be used as an alternative to Gene 
Xpert for initial testing in patients with signs or symptoms of TB. It is important 
to note that CB-NAAT may remain positive for several years after therapy and 
should not be utilized for follow-up; caution should be exercised when using it to 
diagnose relapse.
	
l Chest radiograph merely localizes the site of pathology and does not define 
an aetiology. The radiological signs to suggest TB are the presence of miliary 
shadows or fibrocavitary shadows on a chest X-ray. Chest X-ray where available 
could be used as a screening test only. Any abnormality in chest X-ray should be 
further evaluated for TB including microbiological confirmation. In the absence of 
microbiological confirmation, careful clinical assessment for TB diagnosis should 
be done. Diagnosis of TB based on X-ray is termed clinically diagnosed TB.
	
l Tests not recommended in the diagnosis of TB in adults are tuberculin skin test/
Mantoux’s test, serology (IgM, IgG, IgA antibodies against MTB antigens banned 
in India), serum ADA, conventional TB-PCR tests and IGRA.
	
l NAAT (sputum-BAL, gastric lavage without food particles, pleural fluid, ascitic 
fluid, CSF, FNAC/biopsy material from lymph node and other tissues) is the 
preferred first diagnostic test in children, people living with HIV (PLHIV), all 
MDR close contacts, all retreatment smear-negative cases and extrapulmonary 
TB. Diagnostic algorithm for TB in children is given in Figure 1.7.
	
l Standardized tuberculin skin test (TST) and IGRA may be used as complementary 
tests in children in combination with microbiological tests, history of contact, 
radiology and symptoms.
	
l Definitive diagnosis of extrapulmonary TB is made on the basis of microscopy/
culture and drug sensitivity testing (DST)/NAAT/molecular test/histopathological 
examination of the appropriate specimens from the presumed sites of involvement 
(Fig. 1.8).

32    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Extrapulmonary TB is paucibacillary. Negative microbiology does not rule out 
TB. Obtaining a biopsy sample is difficult but should be attempted. The sample 
should be divided into two parts (pathology and microbiology). ​Sensitivity of 
Xpert is low when performed on other body fluids (pleural, ascitic, synovial)​. It 
should not be performed on peripheral blood​. ADA is useful for the diagnosis of 
tubercular effusions (pleural, pericardial, ascetic):
	– ADA >70 units/L: High likelihood of TB. Empirical ATT​ can be initiated.
	– ADA 40–70 units/L: May or may not be tubercular. Clinical judgement is needed.
	– ADA <40 units/L: Less likelihood of being TB. Strongly consider alternative 
diagnoses​.
	
l Although ultrasonography and radiological examination of the system involved 
are useful investigations. CT scan is rarely necessary and is not cost and radiation 
effective. Chest CT scan, however, may offer an opportunity for CT-guided 
biopsy for tissue diagnosis.
	
l Tests for latent TB infection (LTBI) include the following: tuberculin skin tests 
(Mantoux test​) or interferon gamma release assay​ (QuantiFERON TB Gold​, 
T-SPOT TB test​) and C-spot TB test​. Screen high-risk groups for LTBI, rule out 
active TB and initiate TPT. A positive QuantiFERON TB Gold in high prevalence 
area means LTBI but the patient does need to be started on TB preventive 
therapy (TPT), whereas an HIV-positive asymptomatic patient with positive 
QuantiFERON TB Gold test needs to be started on TPT.
	
l All patients with newly diagnosed TB or those currently on treatment should also be 
tested for COVID-19. All COVID-19 cases should be screened for TB symptoms.
	
l Universal DST is a component of the End TB Strategy; more than 70% of drug-
resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) cases globally remain undetected. Xpert and 
Xpert XDR play a key role in prompt identification of drug resistance. LPA is 
technically more difficult but is being performed in several laboratories now and 
should be used when necessary. Conventional DST remains the only option for 
newer drugs (linezolid, bedaquiline, delamanid).

Once a decision to treat TB has been taken, it is important to define and document 
the disease in order to prescribe the correct therapy and for the purpose of reporting 
(Table 1.7).

l Assess the nutritional status. Manage malnutrition, if identified as per guidelines, 
and provide a linkage for extranutritional support with high-protein diet. However, 
routine use of vitamin supplements is not required.
	
l Advise rest depending on the patient’s symptoms.

Non-specific: Tab. Paracetamol 500 mg 6–8 hourly is given till fever resolves.

40    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Review treatment regimen
The treatment regimen should be reviewed in relation to medical history, contacts and 
all DST reports. If any resistance appears that was not present or evident previously, 
the patients should be managed as DR-TB or MDR-TB with a new regimen, and 
rapid action should be taken to ensure that adequate infection control measures are 
implemented.
Assessment of patients when treatment failure is suspected
Any patient not clinically responding to therapy after several weeks should be 
considered as being at risk for failure. In particular, patients should be considered as 
being at a high risk for treatment failure if they had at least 3 months of full adherence 
to what was deemed to be an effective treatment regimen with quality-assured drugs, 
but show evidence of active disease – clinical, radiographic or bacteriological (DST or 
culture) – or reappearance of disease. The following steps are recommended in such 
a situation:
	
l Confirm treatment: The treatment card should be reviewed to confirm that the 
patient has fully adhered to treatment.
	
l Look for undetected comorbidities: Some undetected comorbidities mimic 
treatment failure through clinical and chest radiographic deterioration that occurs 
simultaneously with repeated culture-negative and smear-negative results. These 
comorbidities (e.g. non TB mycobacteria [NTM], fungal or lung infections or a 
pulmonary malignancy) should be diagnosed and treated appropriately. Illnesses 
that may decrease absorption of medicines (e.g. chronic diarrhoea) or may result in 
immune suppression (e.g. HIV infection) should also be excluded. 
	
l Review the bacteriological data: A single positive culture in the presence of an 
otherwise good clinical response can be caused by a laboratory contaminant or error. 
In such cases, subsequent cultures that are negative help to prove that the apparently 
positive result did not reflect treatment failure. Positive smears with negative 
cultures may be caused by the presence of dead bacilli and thus do not necessarily 
indicate treatment failure.
	
l Review the DST: If there is evidence of acquired resistance to any drug, treatment 
failure is likely and a new regimen for DR-TB may need to be started promptly.
	
l Review CXR: If comparison of CXR at baseline and at the current time shows no 
improvement or deterioration of the CXR image, this may indicate failure of TB 
treatment.
	
l Review treatment regimen: The treatment regimen should be reviewed in relation 
to medical history, contacts and all DST reports. If any resistance appears that 
was not present or evident previously, the patients should be managed as DR-TB 
or MDR-TB with a new regimen, and rapid action should be taken to ensure that 
adequate infection control measures are implemented.
	
l Consider malabsorption. In rare cases, genetic reasons mean that one or more drugs 
are not well absorbed, leading to suboptimal blood levels, suboptimal effect of the 
drug and potential development of drug resistance. Therapeutic drug monitoring

Chapter 1  Common Diseases    41
can help to evaluate the drug level in the blood and, eventually, to adjust the dose. 
Absorption of drugs is reduced in severely ill patients admitted to the critical care 
department with conditions such as central nervous system TB or acute respiratory 
distress syndrome (ARDS). In such cases, intravenous anti-TB treatment should be 
considered until the situation improves and a nasogastric tube can be used.
Treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis
	
l Diagnosing DR-TB relies on bacteriological assessments, as there are no specific 
clinical patterns indicating drug resistance. Epidemiological markers, particularly 
a thorough patient history, are crucial for assessing the likelihood of DR-TB. This 
includes details like contact with known or suspected multidrug-resistant (MDR) 
cases, drug and dose history, and treatment adherence. A lack of response to 
treatment may suggest a drug-resistant strain, but non-response can also stem from 
factors such as misdiagnosis, poor adherence, associated immunodeficiency like 
HIV, paradoxical upgrading reactions or concurrent infections.
	
l Integrated DR-TB algorithms for adults and children are given in Figures 1.10 and 
1.11, respectively. All patients considered to have ‘probable’ MDR-TB should be 
presented to and discussed with a DR-TB Centre (DR-TBC) Committee followed 
by a decision to treat which ought to be made in consultation with the paediatrician.
	
l If the NAAT/line probe assay (LPA) reveals RR/MDR-TB or if LPA reveals H mono 
resistance, refer to District DR-TB Centre (DDR-TBC) with a family member for 
further management without further delay. The treatment initiation of the patients 
following results of NAAT and FL LPA on standard regimens, i.e. either shorter MDR-
TB regimen or all-oral longer regimen or H mono/poly DR-TB regimen, could be 
undertaken by the physicians at the DDR-TBC. The first-line treatment will be stopped 
and the appropriate standard DR-TB regimen will be initiated at the DDR-TBC.
	
l A shorter oral Bedaquiline-containing MDR/RR-TB regimen of 9–11 months’ 
duration is recommended in eligible patients with confirmed MDR/RR-TB who have 
not been exposed to treatment with second-line TB medicines used in this regimen for 
more than 1 month, and in whom resistance to fluoroquinolones has been excluded.
	
l All-oral longer regimen comprises of 18–20 months of treatment with 6–8 months 
of intensive phase (IP) and 12 months of CP. Monthly follow-up culture should be 
done from the third month onwards. After 6 months, review and start CP if the fifth- 
or fourth-month (consider fourth-month culture result if fifth-month culture result is 
not available at the end of 6-month treatment) liquid culture is negative, respectively. 
If fourth- or fifth-month culture remains positive, extend treatment by 1 month. 
Extension beyond 1 month is decided on the sputum culture of fifth or sixth and sixth 
or seventh months. The IP can be extended up to a maximum of 2 months after which 
the patient is considered as failed for the regimen and re-evaluated for individualized 
all-oral longer regimen. The total duration of CP is 12 months. H mono/poly regimen 
is of 6-month duration without any IP or CP. Monthly follow-up smear should be 
done from the third month onward. If certain EPTB conditions and if any resistance 
to fluoroquinolone (FQ) or INH (Z) are detected or if smear at the fourth month is 
positive, the duration of treatment needs to be extended to 9 months.

44    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Treatment in special situations
Pregnant women  and lactating mothers
	
l Test all women of child-bearing age for pregnancy as part of the pre-treatment 
evaluation and while on treatment if there is a history of amenorrhoea of any duration.
	
l First-line ATT are safe in pregnancy except Streptomycin which is absolutely 
contraindicated during the entire pregnancy. Pregnant women and lactating mothers 
should receive full course of TB. After ruling out active TB in the infant, give 6 months 
of INH preventer therapy and BCG vaccination to the baby. Give Pyridoxine 10 mg/
kg to the mother and the infant. Breastfeeding can be continued even when mother is 
on treatment for TB but the mother should continue to practice cough hygiene.
	
l Ethionamide (Eto) is contraindicated during the first 32 weeks of pregnancy. The 
shorter oral Bedaquiline-containing MDR/RR-TB regimen cannot be administered in 
pregnant women before 32 weeks due to Eto-led potential teratogenicity in the first 
trimester and risk of hypothyroidism in the infant in the second trimester. Beyond 
32 weeks, the choice of regimen needs to be a consultative decision between the 
obstetrician and the physician at the N/DDR-TBC. Longer oral M/XDR-TB regimen 
can be designed to avoid known toxicities until better safety profiles are established.
Women on oral contraceptives
Switch over to alternate methods of contraception, i.e. condoms/diaphragm, intrauterine 
device (IUD) or depot medroxyprogesterone, as per preference of the patient and 
eligibility.
Patients with renal disease
	
l All patients with active TB (pulmonary or extrapulmonary) should receive standard 
ATT with modifications where appropriate. Exclude chronic kidney disease (CKD). 
In patients undergoing dialysis, give ATT immediately after haemodialysis to avoid 
premature drug removal or alternatively give 4–6 hours before dialysis.
	
l There is no change in the dose of INH and Rifampicin. Reduce the doses of 
Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide in cases of severe renal failure. Increase the dose 
interval to 3 times weekly for Ethambutol (15 mg/kg), Pyrazinamide (25 mg/kg) and 
aminoglycosides in patients with CKD stages 4 and 5. Also, administer Pyridoxine 
in patients receiving INH. Avoid aminoglycosides. If streptomycin must be used, 
give 15 mg/kg or 3 times per week to a maximum of 1 g per dose with monitoring of 
serum drug levels. In patients on rifampicin, adjust the dose of immunosuppressants 
in post–renal transplant patients. 
	
l Double the corticosteroid dose in patients receiving rifampicin. In case of DR-TB in 
patients with mild renal impairment, reduce the dose of aminoglycosides. 
	
l In severe liver failure, discontinue aminoglycosides and replace with other potent 
non-nephrotoxic ATT with dose or interval adjustment as appropriate in case of 
ethambutol, quinolones, cycloserine and PAS. Second-line drugs which might require 
a dose or interval adjustment in the presence of mild to moderate renal impairment 
are E and Lfx. In the presence of severe renal impairment, Lfx can be replaced with 
normal-dose Mfx (200/400 mg based on the patients’ weight).

l No dosage adjustments are required in patients with mild to moderate renal 
impairment (dosing is not established in severe renal impairment; use with caution).
Patient with hepatic disease
Give the standard ATT regimen to patients with hepatitis virus carriage, past history 
of acute hepatitis and current excessive alcohol consumption. Anticipate hepatotoxic 
reactions to ATT in these patients. Get LFTs done at the start of treatment in unstable 
or advanced liver disease. Use lesser hepatotoxic drugs in case of severe liver disorder 
in consultation with the specialist. Monitor clinically (and LFT, if possible) in case of 
pre-existing liver disease during treatment. If the serum ALT level is more than three 
times normal before initiation of ATT, consider the following regimen:

9 months of INH and rifampicin, plus ethambutol (until or unless INH susceptibility 
is documented)

of 6–9 months of rifampicin

ethambutol

DR-TB in patients with pre-existing liver disease
Pyrazinamide, PAS and ethionamide are potentially hepatotoxic drugs. Hepatitis occurs 
rarely with FQs. Higher potential for hepatotoxicity is seen in elderly, alcoholics and 
those with pre-existing liver disease. In mild hepatotoxicity, most second-line ATT are 
safe; however, avoid pyrazinamide and ethionamide. Rule out other causes of hepatitis 
(viral hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, non-TB drug-induced hepatitis). If the patient 
develops hepatitis on second-line ATT, further management should be as in patients 
with non-MDR-TB. Monitor strictly monthly LFT in patients with MDR-TB having 
deranged LFT at the time of pre-treatment evaluation and while on treatment. In patients 
with pre-existing liver disease with persistently abnormal liver function test, a shorter 
oral MDR/RR-TB regimen will be avoided due to the presence of H(h), Eto and Z.
Patients with seizure disorders
	
l Determine whether the seizure disorder is under control and whether the patient 
is taking antiseizure medication. If the seizures are not under control, initiation 
or adjustment of antiseizure medications will be needed prior to the start of TB 
treatment, especially DR-TB. TB might itself involve the central nervous system 
and may cause seizures. However, when seizures present for the first time during 
anti-TB treatment, they are likely to be the result of an adverse effect of one of the 
anti-TB drugs. Consider drug interactions with INH and rifampicin. Avoid high dose 
of INH in patients with active seizure disorder as it carries a high risk of seizures.

46    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l For at-risk patients on INH, consider prophylactic oral Pyridoxine 10–25 mg/kg, 
and for patients on Cycloserine, Pyridoxine 25 mg for every 250 mg of Cycloserine 
daily. The optimal dose in children is not established. Eto and FQ have been 
associated with seizures and hence should be used carefully amongst MDR/RR-TB 
patients with history of seizures. Though the seizure is not common with Bdq, it 
should also be considered while assessing the causality assessment. Anti-seizure 
drugs may have drug interactions with FQ. Hence close monitoring of serum levels 
of anti-epileptic drugs should be done.
Patients with HIV/AIDS (PLHIV)
	
l Refer all patients diagnosed with TB cases to the nearest ICTC for HIV counselling 
and testing. The presentation of MDR/RR-TB in the PLHIV does not differ from 
that of DS-TB. Early diagnosis of DR-TB and HIV, prompt initiation of appropriate 
second-line anti-TB drugs and ART, sound patient support and infection control 
measures are essential components in the management of DR-TB in PLHIV.
	
l The shorter or longer oral MDR-TB regimen can be used in PLHIV, including in those 
who are receiving ART. In PLHIV with pulmonary MDR/RR-TB, additive toxicities 
or drug–drug interactions between anti-TB and ART medicines potentially overlap, e.g. 
Mfx and Cfz or Efavirenz and Bdq; Ritonavir may potentially increase the risk of Bdq-
related adverse events and hence combined use should be avoided or used with caution. 
	
l All HIV-TB co-infection should receive TB treatment with daily regimen as in 
HIV-negative patients with TB. Start ATT first and then start ART as soon as TB 
treatment is tolerated between 2 weeks and 2 months irrespective of CD4 counts. 
In EPTB, start ART after 2 weeks of initiation of ATT in all patients irrespective 
of CD4 counts (as soon as the patient is stabilized, special attention to monitoring 
hepatotoxicity).
	
l In case of DR-TB, start second-line anti-TB drugs first, followed by ART as soon as 
second-line anti-TB drugs are tolerated. Generally, this should be within the first 2 weeks 
of initiating DR-TB treatment (for details, see the section ‘HIV and AIDS’ in Chapter 7).
	
l Adjustments to regimen:  ART medical officer and physician of N/DDR-TBC 
collaborate closely to decide on the ART regimen composition to adjust to the 
shorter oral Bedaquiline-containing MDR/RR-TB regimen. However, regimen 
modification may be considered on a case-by-case basis in longer oral M/XDR-TB 
regimen based on drug–drug interactions and synergistic side effects between the 
component drugs of both regimens.
	
l Dolutegravir (DTG)–based regimen (with NRTI) is the preferred first-line 
regimen for patients with TB-HIV coinfection. The drugs used are Dolutegravir 
Plus Tenofovir Plus Lamivudine. As Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer, the 
coadministration of Rifampicin with Dolutegravir can reduce the bioavailability of 
DTG; therefore, the dose of DTG is doubled to 50 mg twice a day.
	
l When a patient is already on 2 NRTIs + 1 NNRTI (EFV)–based regimen ([AZT 
or TDF or ABC] + 3TC + EFV) has to be given 2HREZ + 4HRE–based ATT 
for the newly detected TB, the same ART regimen can be continued without any 
modification.

l Occasionally, patients with HIV-related TB may experience a temporary exacerbation 
of symptoms, signs or radiographic manifestation of TB after beginning TB treatment. 
This paradoxical reaction occurs in HIV-infected patients with active TB and is 
thought to be a result of immune restitution due to the simultaneous administration 
of ART and TB medication (IRIS syndrome). Symptoms and signs may include high 
fever, lymphadenopathy, expanding intrathoracic lesions and worsening of chest 
radiographic findings. The diagnosis of a paradoxical reaction should be made only 
after a thorough evaluation has excluded other aetiologies, particularly where TB 
treatment has failed. For severe paradoxical reactions, Prednisone (1–2 mg/kg for 
1–2 weeks, and then gradually decreasing doses) may be used.
	
l Patients with DR-TB and HIV may suffer from severe wasting, diarrhoeal diseases 
and malabsorption syndromes. Wherever possible, provide socioeconomics and 
nutritional support to patients with DR-TB living with HIV.

Psychiatric illness
	
l For patients with DR-TB with a concurrent psychiatric illness, evaluation and 
treatment should be done by the psychiatrist before the start of treatment for DR-
TB to establish a baseline for comparison if new psychiatric symptoms develop 
while the patient is on treatment. There is a high baseline incidence of depression 
and anxiety in patients with MDR/RR-TB, often connected with the chronicity and 
socioeconomic stress factors related to the disease. Undertake a formal consultation 
with the psychiatrist available at a DR-TBC or linked to the same.
	
l H(h), FQ and Eto are associated with psychosis. Pyridoxine prophylaxis may 
minimize the risk of neurological and psychiatric adverse events. When any 
patient on DR-TB treatment develops psychosis, rule out other aetiologies such as 
psychosocial stresses, depression, hypothyroidism, illicit drug and alcohol use.

	 4.	All patients at high risk of hepatitis should have baseline LFTs, and should be

	 5.	Monitoring and management of side effects: ATT is usually well tolerated; 
however, poor management of adverse effects increases the risk of treatment 
interruption and LTFU liver failure which may result in death or permanent 
morbidity. However, some patients can develop GI intolerance, vomiting, etc., for 
which only symptomatic therapy is required. The commonest major side effect with 
ATT is drug-induced hepatitis. The easily recognizable symptom of high-coloured 
urine in a patient with jaundice is masked due to discolouration of urine because of 
rifampicin. Suspect hepatitis if vomiting is persistent and associated with anorexia. 
	
l Clinically, icterus may be evident. If there is AST or ALT elevation <5× ULN, 
with normal bilirubin in an asymptomatic patient, continue with all the drugs, 
and monitor clinical symptoms, ALT/AST and bilirubin levels every 2 weeks 
till resolution.
	
l In case of AST/ALT elevation ≥5× UNL with normal bilirubin or AST or ALT 
elevation ≥3× UNL accompanied by bilirubin ≥2× UNL OR a symptomatic 
patient, stop all hepatotoxic drugs, and refer to a higher centre for evaluation. 
In most patients, the drugs can be reintroduced after the hepatitis has resolved. 
Once the enzyme level improves, reintroduce the remaining drugs, one at a 
time with the least hepatotoxic agents first, while monitoring liver function by 
testing enzymes every 7 days (sequential reintroduction involves starting with 
Rifampicin at 10 mg/kg, followed by Isoniazid at 5 mg/kg, and Pyrazinamide at 
25 mg/kg Or incremental reintroduction begins with Rifampicin at 150 mg/day, 
with a gradual dose increase by day 11. Isoniazid is then introduced at 100 mg/
day by day 8, with a gradual increase by day 11. Finally, Pyrazinamide is added 
at 500 mg/day on day 15, with a gradual increase by day 18). If the most likely 
agent is not essential, do not reintroduce. If ATT hepatitis is severe (liver failure, 
coagulopathy or altered sensorium), avoid reintroduction of Pyrazinamide.
	
l If AST and ALT decrease to ≤2× UNL, restart full doses of withheld drugs in 
the allocated regimen gradually in the order of R and Z.
	
l Monitor AST and AST every 3 days after each reintroduction to ensure no 
deterioration before reintroducing the next drug. If either of R or Z cannot be

l Perform viral serology to rule out other aetiologies of hepatitis, if available, 
especially to hepatitis A, B and C, and investigate for alcohol use and address

l Pyrazinamide-induced arthralgia or arthritis usually responds suitably to 
analgesic therapy. If there is severe arthralgia, lower the dose or discontinue the 
suspected agent if this can be done without compromising the regimen. Drug 
rash and hypersensitivity is a major side effect in which case the patient needs 
to be referred to a higher centre. Patients with peripheral neuropathy due to 
INH, Lzd, Cs, H, Am, FQ, rarely Eto, E should receive daily pyridoxine for its

with individual drug to determine the likely offending drug. Do not reintroduce 
rifampicin in patients who develop thrombocytopenia. Hyperuricaemia can occur

emergence of resistance, particularly to Rifampicin. It is the duty of the prescriber 
to ensure appropriate and complete treatment in all cases and report all ADRs to
