Recording and reporting
Documentation of the following in the TB treatment card (paper-based recording 
form) at the time of initiation of treatment is a pre-requisite for all including private 
practitioners:
	
l Details of the patient
	
l Drugs administered with their dosages
	
l Follow-up investigation results
	
l Monitoring adherence to treatment
	
l Recording adverse events
	
l Recording treatment outcomes
	
l The original TB treatment card is kept at the Peripheral Health Institution and 
updated fortnightly. A duplicate treatment card is given to the treatment supporter 
for documentation of daily events. The treatment supporter should be trained on how 
to record the treatment card. 
	
l Details on the patient’s HIV status are not included in the treatment supporter’s copy 
to maintain confidentiality.
	
l The data are entered in Nikshay on a regular basis by statistical assistants at the 
nodal DR-TB centre and senior DR-TB TB-HIV supervisors at the district DR-
TB centre. From Nikshay, the information on ADRs is directly communicated to 
Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI) through a connecting bridge called 
VigiFlow.
	
l X-rays should be retained until treatment completion, and a drawing of the X-ray 
picture with comments should be entered in the remarks column. 
	
l There should be a provision to check correct categorization and drug dosages. A 
dosage table based on the patient’s weight could be printed on the card to ensure 
correct dosage for the child.
Patient education
	
l Explain to the patient that TB is completely curable if treated earlier with complete 
treatment. But if untreated or partially treated, it turns to complications, DR-TB and 
death. Medication with proper dosage, proper duration and by a proper health care 
worker is highly successful. Early disappearance of symptoms during treatment is 
not a sign of cure. Emphasize the importance of adherence to treatment and periodic 
follow-up for sputum conversion and for drug side effects are the forerunner of 
successful treatment. ‘MDR-TB is man-made’ which is difficult to treat and costly.
	
l Free TB treatment is available for patients in the private sector and those 
practitioners registered with Private Practitioner Support Agency (PPSA). It is now 
mandatory to report all diagnosed case of TB before prescribing treatment.
	
l Smoking of tobacco adversely affects the treatment outcome and, therefore, counsel 
to quit smoking and refer to the smoking cessation clinic and protect from passive 
smoking. The environment of the patient has to be smoke free at home/office and at 
clinic. Check smoking status of the patient with TB at every interaction. 
	
l Alcohol abuse: Elicit history of addiction to alcohol and if found alcoholic, advise to 
strictly refrain from alcohol as it would increase the chances of the patient developing 
hepatitis (jaundice), irregularity in drug intake and adverse treatment outcome.

58    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l ADRs (gastric upset, swelling of joints, yellow conjunctiva, etc.) during treatment are 
usual and the patient should approach a medical officer before stopping medication.
	
l Rifampicin colours the urine as well as other body secretions orange-red. The patient 
must be warned about this to avoid unnecessary alarm. He/she should also be advised 
to take anti-TB medicines, particularly Rifampicin and INH, on an empty stomach 
and not to take any meals for about 1 hour afterwards for good absorption of the drug.
	
l Advise the patient or the primary caregiver regarding the probable side effects and 
explain when to contact the treating doctor. If the patient vomits within half hour of 
the dose, repeat the dose.
	
l Importance of screening symptomatic contacts and children younger than 6 years: 
Encourage patients to bring symptomatic adult contacts and all children aged 6 years 
and younger for screening at health facility for early detection of cases among them 
and appropriate treatment and chemoprophylaxis for eligible children.
	
l Proper sputum disposal and personal hygiene (covering the mouth while coughing) 
should be explained for infectious patients. TB is an infectious communicable 
disease and spreads on coughing (droplet infection) and contact.
	
l Address all fears of the patient and/or the caregiver regarding the disease as this 
disease has a lot of social stigma.
	
l Emphasize on storage condition of Ethambutol as it is a hygroscopic drug which 
tends to crumble, if not properly stored, particularly during rainy season.

SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Malaria is an acute and chronic protozoan illness characterized by paroxysms 
of fever, chills, sweats, fatigue, anaemia and splenomegaly. In atypical cases, 
classical symptoms may not manifest.
	
l Falciparum malaria (severe and complicated malaria): Severe manifestations can 
develop over a short span of 12–24 hours and it is associated in varying degrees 
with the following clinical signs:
	– Cerebral: Mental clouding, coma, convulsions, delirium, occasionally localizing 
signs, hyperpyrexia (>42°C), shock, bleeding manifestation, haematocrit <15% 
or Hb <5 g/dL, hypoglycaemia, oliguria, anuria, acute respiratory distress 
syndrome (ARDS), macroscopic haemoglobinuria and jaundice.
	
l In children, febrile convulsions, repeated vomiting and dehydration are common 
if the temperature is high due to any cause. Therefore, these symptoms are not 
necessarily indicative of severe malaria. Manage children with these symptoms as 
severe malaria in routine programme situations and confirm diagnosis of malaria 
at the earliest.
	
l Diagnosis is made by the presence of protozoa in the blood in thick and thin 
smear slides. Thick smear is used for easy detection of parasite and thin smear 
for identification of species. Note that blood films may be negative even in a 
severe attack because of sequestration of parasites in the deep capillaries. Rapid 
diagnostic kits (RDK) monovalent (for P. falciparum) or bivalent (for both 
P. vivax and P. falciparum) can be used for detection where microscopy results 
are not obtainable within 24 hours of sample collection.
Treatment of malaria
	 1.	All fever cases suspected to be malaria after ruling out other common causes 
should be investigated by microscopy or rapid diagnostic test (RDT). In all 
confirmed cases, start treatment and the first dose is always given in the presence 
of the health volunteer/worker.
	 2.	Patients with uncomplicated malaria can be managed at the primary level but 
patients with severe malaria with complications should be admitted and managed 
in a hospital where facilities for detailed investigations and blood transfusion exist.
	 3.	P. vivax cases should be treated with chloroquine for 3 days and Primaquine for 
14 days for prevention of relapse. 
	
	Note: Primaquine is contraindicated in pregnant women, infants and patients 
with known glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency (For drugs 
causing G6PD deficiency, see Appendix VII). Instruct patients to report back in 
case of haematuria or high-coloured urine/cyanosis or blue colouration of the 
lips. Stop Primaquine in such cases and manage as for anaemia.

combination therapy (ACT). This should be accompanied by single dose 
primaquine on day 2. Monotherapy with oral artemisinin derivatives is banned 
in India.
	 5.	Pregnant women with uncomplicated P. falciparum should be treated as follows:
l	First trimester: Quinine
l	Second and third trimesters: ACT
	 6.	All cases of mixed infection should be treated as P. falciparum.
	 7.	In cases where parasitological diagnosis is not possible due to non-availability 
of either timely microscopy or RDT, treat suspected malaria cases with the 
full course of chloroquine, till the results of microscopy are received. Once the 
parasitological diagnosis is available, appropriate treatment as per the species 
should be administered.
	 8.	Presumptive treatment with chloroquine is no more recommended.
	 9.	Suspect resistance if, in spite of full treatment with no history of vomiting 
and diarrhoea, the patient does not respond within 72 hours, clinically and 
parasitologically.
	10.	In patients not responding to ACT, treat with oral Quinine with Tetracycline/
Doxycycline. Report to the concerned District Malaria/State Malaria 
Officer/ROHFW for initiation of therapeutic efficacy studies.

Treatment of severe malaria (consider as an emergency)
Severe malaria is an emergency and treatment should be given as per severity and 
associated complications which can best be decided by the treating physician as 
microscopic evidence may be negative for asexual parasites and partial treatment. Pregnant 
women with severe malaria in any trimester can be treated with artemisinin derivatives.
Inj. Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg IV or IM given on admission (time = 0 hour), then at 12 and 
24 hours, and then once a day.
(Caution: Care should be taken to dilute artesunate powder in 5% sodium bicarbonate 
provided in the pack only.) 
Or
Inj. Artemether 3.2 mg/kg IM given on admission and then 1.6 mg/kg/day.
Or
Inj. Arteether 150 mg IM daily for 3 days in adults only (not recommended for 
children).
Or
Inj. Quinine: 20 mg/kg on admission (IV infusion in 5% dextrose/dextrose saline over 
a period of 4 hours or divided IM injection) followed by maintenance dose of 10 mg/kg 
8 hourly. The infusion rate should not exceed 5 mg/kg/h. Do not give loading dose of 
Quinine, i.e. 20 mg/kg, on admission if the patient has already received quinine or if 
the clinician feels inappropriate. NEVER GIVE BOLUS INJECTION OF QUININE. 
If parenteral quinine therapy needs to be continued beyond 48 hours, reduce dose to 7 
mg/kg 8 hourly.
Note: The parenteral treatment in severe and complicated malaria cases should be given 
for a minimum of 48 hours once started (irrespective of the patient’s ability to tolerate 
oral medication earlier than 48 hours) followed by a full course of oral area-specific 
ACT for 3 days.

Once the patient can tolerate oral therapy or after at least 24 hours of parenteral 
therapy, further follow-up treatment is as follows:
	
l In patients receiving artemisinin derivatives and quinine, give a full course of 
oral ACT. However, avoid ACT containing mefloquine in cerebral malaria due to 
neuropsychiatric complications associated with it.
	
l As per WHO recommendations, parenteral artesunate is the treatment of choice in 
all trimesters of pregnancy. If Artemisinin derivatives (artesunate or artemether) are 
not available, parenteral quinine may be given to save the life of the mother.
	
l Treat severe malaria due to P. vivax like severe P. falciparum malaria. Give 
primaquine for 14 days for prevention of relapse after the patient recovers from acute 
illness and after delivery in case of pregnant patients.
Do not give corticosteroids, intravenous mannitol, heparin, anticoagulants, 
adrenaline or overhydrate.
Monitoring 
Monitor core temperature (preferably rectal), respiratory rate and depth, pulse, blood 
pressure and level of consciousness every 4 hours; record urine output, and look for the 
appearance of brown or black urine (haemoglobinuria) or oliguria; monitor therapeutic 
response, both clinical and parasitological, by regular observation and blood films; 
carry out regular laboratory evaluation of haematocrit or haemoglobin, glucose, urea 
or creatinine and electrolytes; avoid drugs that increase the risk for gastrointestinal 
bleeding (aspirin, corticosteroids).
Supportive treatment
Treat fever, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte imbalance, hypotension, renal failure, anaemia 
and convulsions appropriately (for details, see respective sections).
Chemoprophylaxis
Chemoprophylaxis should be administered only in selective groups in high P. falciparum 
(Pf) endemic areas. Encourage the use of personal protection measures including 
insecticide-treated bed nets (ITN)/long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLIN) for pregnant 
women and other vulnerable population including travellers for longer stay. However, for 
longer stay of military and para-military forces in high Pf endemic areas, the practice of 
chemoprophylaxis should be followed wherever appropriate, e.g. troops on night patrol 
duty, and decisions of their medical administrative authority should be followed.
Short-term chemoprophylaxis (up to 6 weeks)
Tab. Doxycycline 100 mg once daily for adults and 1.5 mg/kg once daily for children. 
(Caution: It is contraindicated in children younger than 8 years, pregnant and lactating 
mothers.) Start it 2 days before travel and continue for 4 weeks after leaving the 
malarious area.

Chemoprophylaxis for longer stay (more than 6 weeks)
Tab. Mefloquine 5 mg/kg up to 250 mg weekly for adults and administer 2 weeks 
before, during and 4 weeks after exposure. Note: Mefloquine is contraindicated in 
individuals with a history of convulsions, neuropsychiatric problems and cardiac

Patient education
	
l Take measures to stop mosquito breeding and for protection from mosquitoes, e.g. 
mosquito nets, repellents, long sleeves and long trousers. 
	
l Report fever without any other signs and symptoms to the nearest health facility. 
	
l All tablets for the day should be taken together with plenty of water after food. Do 
not take them on an empty stomach. In high fever, bring down the fever first. If 
chloroquine syrup is not available for children, crush the tablet and give with honey 
or thick syrup.
	
l If vomiting occurs within 45 minutes of chloroquine intake, repeat the dose of 
chloroquine.
	
l Watch for side effects of drugs prescribed. Chloroquine may cause nausea, vomiting 
and diarrhoea, mild headache and skin allergy/rash. Chloroquine, primaquine and 
sulphadoxine + pyrimethamine should not be given if the patient is suffering from 
G6PD deficiency.
	
l Report back if haematuria or high-coloured urine and cyanosis develop; in such case, 
stop primaquine immediately.
	
l If there is no improvement after 48 hours or if the condition worsens and in case of 
occurrence of cerebral malaria symptoms, seek medical help immediately.

DENGUE
Dengue is the most important emerging tropical viral disease of human beings in the 
world today. Aedes aegypti, a daytime mosquito, is the principal vector in India and 
countries of South-east Asian region, mostly seen in the rainy season or in months 
following the rainy season. All cases of suspected, probable and confirmed dengue 
fever should be reported to the local/district/state health authorities and municipal 
health officer of the concerned municipality every week/daily during the transmission

period in a prescribed format, as it is a notifiable disease. Laboratory confirmation is 
not necessary before notification, but it should be obtained.
SALIENT FEATURES
• Dengue has a wide clinical spectrum that includes both severe and non-severe 
clinical manifestations. After the incubation period (4–10 days), the illness begins 
abruptly and is followed by the three phases – febrile, critical and recovery.
• Dengue fever (DF) is an acute febrile illness of 2–7 days’ duration with two or 
more of the following manifestations: headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia/
arthralgia and rash, followed by a critical phase (2–3 days) when the patient is 
afebrile (temperature drops to 37.5–38°C) and is at risk of developing severe 
dengue (presenting with haemorrhagic manifestations – petechiae, mucosal 
membrane bleeding [e.g. nose and gums], positive tourniquet test and leucopenia) 
followed by recovery phase (2–3 days). Massive vaginal bleeding (in women 
of child-bearing age) and gastrointestinal bleeding may occur during the 
critical phase. Some patients with severe shock, multiple organ involvement 
and other complications may experience a longer convalescence period. The 
patient may develop pulmonary oedema due to fluid overload during this phase, 
especially if the fluid replacement rate is not reviewed and revised periodically.
• Dengue laboratory diagnosis is not necessary for clinical management except in 
atypical cases or when carrying out differential diagnosis with other infectious 
diseases.
• A diagnosis of dengue infection in the first 5 days of illness is confirmed by 
detecting NS1 antigen by ELISA or detecting dengue viral antigen by PCR. After 
5 days of the onset of illness, the IgM antibodies can be detected by IgM capture 
ELISA. Other methods which provide confirmatory diagnosis are isolation of 
virus (virus culture + VE) from serum, plasma or leucocytes and demonstration 
of seroconversion or fourfold rise in titre of IgG antibodies in paired sera 
collected 2 weeks apart; however, these are performed in the referral centres 
only. Detection of NS1 antigen by ELISA in early infection and detection of 
IgM antibodies by IgM capture ELISA remain the mainstay of diagnosis. RDTs 
(card test, etc.) have a variable sensitivity and specificity and should not be used 
for confirmation of diagnosis. Send the blood samples of suspected dengue cases 
to Sentinel Surveillance Hospital (SSH) for testing by ELISA. While collecting 
sample, mention the day of onset of fever and the day of sample collection to guide 
the laboratory for the type of test to be performed (NSI for samples collected from 
days 1 to 5 and IgM [MAC-ELISA] after day 5).
• Progressive leucopenia is followed by a rapid decrease in platelet count in parallel 
with a rising haematocrit compared with the baseline. In the absence of the patient’s 
baseline, age-specific population haematocrit levels could be used as a surrogate 
during the critical phase. The degree of increase above the baseline haematocrit 
often reflects the severity of plasma leakage. Additional tests should be considered as 
indicated (and if available) – liver function test, glucose, serum electrolytes, urea and 
creatinine, bicarbonate or lactate, cardiac enzymes, ECG and urine-specific gravity.

• Co-infection of dengue has been reported with COVID-19 and it is difficult 
to distinguish symptoms and signs because of their overlapping initial clinical 
presentations and laboratory parameters (see ‘Influenza-Like Illness (ILI)/Severe 
Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI)/COVID-19’ in Chapter 5, Fig. 5.5 and Table 
5.5). A high index of suspicion should be kept to identify dengue and COVID-19 
co-infections in patients presenting with an acute febrile illness.
Note: The tourniquet test is performed by inflating a blood pressure cuff to a point 
midway between the systolic and diastolic pressures for 5 minutes. A test is considered 
positive when 10 or more petechiae per 2.5 cm2 are observed. The test may be negative 
or mildly positive during the phase of profound shock.

l Dengue fever has an unpredictable course. Therefore, monitoring for warning signs 
and other clinical parameters is crucial to recognizing progression to the critical phase. 
	 Warning signs of severe dengue are abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent 
vomiting, red spots or patches on the skin, passage of black stools, bleeding into the 
skin or from the nose or gums, heavy menstrual/vaginal bleeding, sweating, cold 
skin, drowsiness, mental confusion or seizures, difficulty in breathing, clinical fluid 
accumulation, liver enlargement >2 cm and laboratory sign (increase in haematocrit 
concurrent with rapid decrease of platelet count). A patient can progress from dengue 
to severe dengue and, depending on the stage of the disease when the patient reports, 
a mixed picture can be seen. 
	
l Individuals at high a risk for severe dengue include infants and children (age <10 
years), particularly those with malnutrition, elderly (age >65 years), obese or 
pregnant, and those with haemolytic diseases like glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase 
deficiency, thalassaemia and other hemoglobinopathies. Additionally, individuals with 
congenital heart disease, chronic conditions such as diabetes mellitus, hypertension, 
obstructive lung diseases, cardiovascular diseases, chronic renal failure and chronic 
liver disease are at an elevated risk. Patients undergoing long-term steroid or NSAID 
treatment also fall into the high-risk category for severe dengue.
	
l Depending on the clinical manifestations and other circumstances, patients with 
dengue without warning signs may be sent home; patients with dengue with 
warning signs, coexisting conditions or social circumstances may be referred for 
in-hospital management; patients with severe dengue require emergency treatment 
and urgent referral. Admission during the febrile period should be reserved for those 
who are unable to manage adequate oral hydration at home, infants and those with 
coexisting conditions.

The goals of fluid resuscitation are:
	
l Improving central and peripheral circulation, i.e. decreasing tachycardia, improving 
BP and pulse volume, warm and pink extremities, a capillary refill time <2 seconds, 
decrease in haematocrit
	
l Improving end-organ perfusion, i.e. achieving a stable conscious level (more alert 
or less restless), resolving bowel/abdominal symptoms and urine output ≥0.5 mL/
kg/h or decreasing metabolic acidosis
Treatment of hypotensive shock
	
l For all patients (infants, children and adults), initiate intravenous fluid resuscitation 
with crystalloid or colloid solution at 20 mL/kg as a bolus given over 15–30 minutes 
to bring the patient out of shock as quickly as possible. Colloids are the preferred 
choice if the BP has to be restored urgently (in patients with pulse pressure less 
than 10 mmHg). Consider intra-osseous route if peripheral venous access cannot 
be obtained.
	
l Initiate IV fluid resuscitation under close supervision, evaluate the patient’s response 
and avoid the development of pulmonary oedema. These fluids should not contain 
glucose.
	
l If the patient improves, give a crystalloid/colloid solution of 10 mL/kg/h for 1 hour, 
and then reduce gradually following fluid resuscitation given in Figures 1.8 and 1.9 
depending on the patient’s response.
	
l Stop/reduce intravenous fluids when any of the following signs are present: signs of 
cessation of plasma leakage, stable BP, and fall of pulse rate and peripheral perfusion 
haematocrit in the presence of a good pulse volume apyrexia (without the use of 
antipyretics) for more than 24–48 hours, resolving bowel/abdominal symptoms and 
improving urine output.
Treatment of haemorrhagic complications
Give 5–10 mL/kg of fresh packed red cells or 10–20 mL/kg fresh whole blood (see 
respective section for details). 
	
l In patients with profound thrombocytopenia, ensure strict bed rest and protect 
from trauma. Do not give intramuscular injections. Platelet counts are unreliable 
to predict bleeding. Prophylactic platelet transfusion is not superior to supportive 
care in confirmed dengue infection and thrombocytopenia (≤20,000 platelets/µL 
without persistent bleeding). There is no need to give prophylactic platelets even at 
<20,000/mm3.
	
l Prophylactic platelet transfusion may be given at the level of <10,000/mm3 in 
the absence of bleeding manifestations. Platelet transfusion may also be given in 
prolonged shock. In case of systemic massive bleeding, platelet transfusion may

72    Standard Treatment Guidelines
be needed in addition to red cell transfusion. Figure 1.17 depicts algorithm for 
management of severe bleeding.
	
l Standard dose for adults is 5–6 units of random donor platelets (RDP) or 1 unit of 
apheresis platelets (AP). (For details, see Appendix XIII.)
Monitoring
	
l Monitor for alertness and comfort levels, vital signs and peripheral perfusion every 
15–30 minutes until the patient is out of shock, and then 1–2 hourly. Monitor those 
receiving higher IV fluids more frequently for fluid overload. Review the patient 
at least 4 times per day and prescribe only intravenous fluids for a maximum of 
6 hours at a time.
	
l Monitor urine output each hour until the patient is out of shock, and then every 
1–2 hours (an acceptable urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/h). Keep a detailed record 
of all fluid intake and output.
	
l Monitor haematocrit before and after fluid boluses until stable, and then 4–6 hourly.
	
l For children without shock, nurses should check the child’s vital signs (temperature, 
pulse and blood pressure) at least 4 times per day and the haematocrit once daily, 
and a doctor should review the patient at least once daily.

l Hepatic involvement is commonly associated with preexisting conditions like viral 
hepatitis, cirrhosis of the liver and hepatomegaly due to some other cause. 
	
l The AST/ALT level may be very high; PT may be prolonged. Hepatic 
encephalopathy may be present due to severe liver failure. Low albumin may be 
associated with severe dengue shock syndrome and bleeding.
	 1.	Start with hepatic failure regimen.
	 2.	Provide appropriate fluid and blood transfusion.
	 3.	If PT is prolonged, IV Vitamin K1 may be initiated.
Dengue myocarditis
	
l Acute myocarditis (rare) (contributes to the development of dengue shock syndrome 
[DSS]). More in the presence of CAD, hypertension, diabetes and valvular heart 
disease
	
l Patients on Aspirin and other antiplatelet agents are at risk for severe bleeding
	
l Management of shock with IV fluids is challenging (myocardial dysfunction). The 
patient may develop pulmonary oedema due to improper fluid management
Dengue in diabetes
	
l There may be severe complications in DF when target organs are involved like 
diabetic retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy, vasculopathy, cardiomyopathy and 
hypertension. 
	
l Due to dengue infection, the blood sugar may become uncontrolled, which may 
sometimes require Insulin therapy for better management.

74    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) may develop during DSS and may cause acute kidney 
injury (AKI) if fluid therapy is not initiated in time.
Treatment of complications
Fluid overload with large pleural effusions and ascites is a common cause of acute 
respiratory distress and failure in severe dengue. Other causes of respiratory distress 
include acute pulmonary oedema, severe metabolic acidosis from severe shock and 
ARDS. Both hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia may occur, even in the absence of 
diabetes mellitus and/or hypoglycaemic agents.
Dengue in pregnancy 
	
l Complications of dengue depend on different stages of pregnancy such as early, late, 
peripartum or postpartum. It carries an increased risk of bleeding, foetal complications, 
low birth weight and premature birth. The risk of vertical transmission increases during 
pregnancy. It must be carefully differentiated from preeclampsia. An overlap of signs 
and symptoms, including thrombocytopenia, capillary leak, impaired liver function, 
ascites and decreased urine output, may make this clinically challenging. 
	
l Pregnant women with dengue fever respond well to the usual therapy of fluids, rest 
and antipyretics. Early recognition and the institution of appropriate treatment is 
the key. 
	
l If the mother acquires infection in the peripartum period, evaluate newborns for 
dengue with serial platelet counts and serological studies.
Patient education
	
l Since this disease can rapidly become very serious and lead to a medical emergency, 
carefully watch for danger signs and immediately report to a doctor. Do not wait.
	
l The complications usually appear between the third and fifth days of illness.
	
l Watch the patient for 2 days after the fever disappears for critical phase features. 
Arthralgia may continue longer but eventually resolves with no sequelae.
	
l Give large amounts of fluids (water, coconut water, soups, milk and juices) along with 
normal diet. Adequate oral fluid intake may reduce the number of hospitalizations. 
Give small amounts of oral fluids frequently for those with nausea and anorexia.
	
l All vector control efforts should be directed against the breeding of mosquitoes and 
prevent mosquito bites by using appropriate full-sleeved clothing, repellent creams, 
bed nets, etc., while sleeping during daytime. Efforts should be intensified before 
the transmission season (during and after the rainy season) and during epidemics.
	
l Check thoroughly all outdoor containers filled with water for Aedes breeding and 
apply antilarval insecticides wherever needed.
	
l Avoid antiadult vector control measures like indoor space spray and fogging as 
routine. These need to be carried out selectively in areas wherever needed. Also 
avoid these measures in areas and households reporting COVID-19 cases as the 
insecticide used for fogging may induce uneasiness for the breathing of the patients.

CHIKUNGUNYA
Chikungunya is caused by an arbovirus and transmitted by A. aegypti mosquito. It 
resembles dengue fever, and is rarely life-threatening. After an incubation period of 
4–7 days, symptoms last for 3–7 days. Severe cases of chikungunya can occur in the 
elderly, in the very young (newborns) and in those who are immunocompromised. It is 
not necessary to confirm the diagnosis of each and every suspected chikungunya case 
in an outbreak situation. Chikungunya virus infection is diagnosed by detecting IgM 
antibodies by IgM capture ELISA after 5 days of the onset of illness. However, IgM 
antibodies may persist and may be detected for months and hence clinical correlation is 
important. In less than 5 days of the onset of illness, PCR may be performed to detect 
chikungunya nucleic acid for confirmation of diagnosis. Other methods of diagnosis 
include isolation of virus from blood in cell lines or demonstration of seroconversion or 
fourfold rise in IgG antibodies in paired sera collected 2 weeks apart. 
Symptomatic treatment of the suspected chikungunya fever cases should be started 
immediately on the basis of epidemiological diagnosis of the disease. Laboratory 
confirmation of the suspected cases would be required to validate the clinical diagnosis 
of the suspected cases. Confirmation of few cases would be enough to identify the 
cause of fever outbreak.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occurs sudden onset of flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, headache, 
nausea, vomiting, severe joint pain (arthralgia) and rash. Rash may appear at 
the outset or several days into the illness; its development often coincides with 
defervescence, which takes place around day 2 or 3 of the disease. The rash is 
most intense on the trunk and limbs and may desquamate.
	
l Fever and arthralgia is the hallmark of chikungunya fever. Chikungunya fever 
follows three phases: acute phase (<3 weeks), subacute phase (3 weeks to 
3 months) and chronic phase (>3 months). Usually it is a self-limiting illness but 
may progress to subacute or chronic phase.

76    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Migratory polyarthritis usually affects the small joints. The joints of the 
extremities in particular become swollen and painful to touch. Joint pain is often 
debilitating and varies in duration. Residual arthritis, with morning stiffness, 
swelling and pain on movement, may persist for weeks or months after recovery. 
	
l Although rare, the infection can result in meningoencephalitis, especially in 
newborns and those with pre-existing medical conditions. 
	
l Pregnant women can pass the virus to their foetus. 
	
l Haemorrhage is rare and all but a few patients recover within 3–5 days.

There is no specific treatment and is same as for dengue (for details, see the section 
‘Dengue’). Most cases recover fully but in some cases, joint pain may persist for several 
months. Treatment is mainly supportive, directed primarily at relieving the symptoms:
	 1.	Take adequate oral fluid intake.
	 2.	Control fever with paracetamol 500 mg 6 hourly (maximum 3 g/day).
	 3.	Use joint pain cold compresses for involved painful joints. Avoid hot fomentation 
in acute stages. Perform movement and mild exercises. Use optimal analgesics 
Ibuprofen or diclofenac.
Refer to a higher centre if there occur fever >5 days, intractable joint pain, altered 
sensorium, reduced urine output, bleeding, incessant vomiting and jaundice. Refer 
sooner at extremes of age, pregnancy and significant comorbid illness.
Dengue fever and chikungunya outbreaks evolve quickly, requiring emergency actions to 
immediately control infected mosquitoes in order to interrupt or reduce transmission and 
to reduce or eliminate the breeding sites of the vector mosquito, A. aegypti.

TYPHOID OR ENTERIC FEVER
The term ‘enteric fever’ is a collective term that refers to both typhoid and paratyphoid 
fever, and ‘typhoid’ and ‘enteric fever’ are often used interchangeably. Enteric fever 
is characterized by severe systemic illness with fever and abdominal pain. It is caused 
by Salmonella typhi and paratyphi. S. typhi causes a variety of illnesses including 
asymptomatic carriage, gastroenteritis, enteric fever, etc.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The onset of fever is typically gradual and continuous (temperature up to 
40°C) with constitutional symptoms like malaise, anorexia, lethargy, headache,

Chapter 1  Common Diseases    77
	 constipation or diarrhoea (pea-soup stool), which may be associated with 
abdominal pain and tenderness, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly and/or change in 
mentation. Usually, the patient is sick and toxic looking with a coated tongue and 
has a soft splenomegaly. Typhoid fever can present atypically in young infants as 
an acute febrile illness with shock and hypothermia.
	
l Examination may reveal a toxic look, and bradycardia relative to the height of the 
fever may be noted. Complete blood counts in most cases with typhoid fever are 
normal. Leucopenia or pancytopenia is seen in 10–25% of cases. Leucocytosis 
might indicate conditions like intestinal perforation or other diagnoses such as 
pyogenic infection or leptospirosis. Mild normochromic or hypochromic anaemia, 
slight thrombocytopenia and a mild increase in liver transaminases, accompanied 
by a normal bilirubin, and raised CRP, are seen.
	
l Blood culture is confirmatory which isolates the organism and assesses 
antimicrobial sensitivity. This process typically takes 2–3 days for results, 
necessitating empirical antimicrobial treatment in the interim. A negative blood 
culture does not rule out enteric fever, as factors such as antibiotic pre-treatment, 
low sample volume and a low circulating bacterial load in the blood contribute 
to this reduced sensitivity. While bone marrow culture offers a higher yield, it is 
seldom conducted. Alternative cultures from faeces, urine or bile aspirate may be 
performed, but a positive result may indicate chronic faecal carriage rather than 
acute infection.
	
l In the acute phase of illness, serological tests like the Widal test and newer rapid 
diagnostic test are not conclusive. The Widal test gauges antibodies against O 
and H antigens of S. typhi and S. paratyphi A. A single measurement during the 
acute phase may yield false-negative or false-positive results. Level of 1 in 160 
dilution or more is taken as a positive test. Other commercially available point-of-
care RDTs identify IgM antibodies against S. typhi antigens, but are not accurate 
enough to be considered reliable for diagnosis.
	
l Complications like hepatitis, peritonitis, meningitis, pneumonitis and myocarditis 
can occur, usually after the first week.

l For individuals in endemic regions and returning travellers, exclude malaria and 
dengue fever. Additionally, contemplate other potential causes based on local disease 
patterns such as scrub and murine typhus, leptospirosis, brucellosis, influenza, 
chikungunya, COVID-19 and other viral conditions.
	
l Severe disease usually manifests in the second or third week of illness characterized 
by persistent fever, escalating weakness, anaemia, weight loss, prolonged vomiting 
or altered mental state. Delayed treatment, the virulence of the bacterial strain and 
host-related factors contribute to the severity of the disease.
	
l In-patient treatment is recommended if the patient is very sick, is not accepting 
orally with inadequate urine output, has altered sensorium/drowsiness or is having

78    Standard Treatment Guidelines
very high pyrexia particularly in the second week of illness when the risk of 
complications increases or if the complications have already ensued. 
	
l Refer to a hospital immediately for appropriate management if any of the red flags 
are present:
	– In adults, two or more Quick Sepsis-related Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) 
criteria – altered mental status, respiratory rate ≥22 breaths/min or systolic blood 
pressure ≤100 mmHg – on initial examination may indicate a risk of severe sepsis. 
	– In children, looking sick and toxic, inability to take oral medication, 
persistent vomiting, signs of severe dehydration, abdominal distension with 
or without tenderness, jaundice, drowsiness or altered consciousness, signs of 
gastrointestinal bleeding, signs of haemodynamic shock (such as mottled skin 
and reduced capillary return), seizures or any sign of severe disease as per the 
Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) algorithm may indicate a 
risk of severe sepsis.

Adequate nutrition and hydration should be maintained ensuring adequate intake either 
orally or with intravenous fluids (in severely ill).

1.	Manage fever (see Fever).
	 2.	Antipyretics can cause precipitous fall in temperature and even shock in enteric 
fever. They should be used judiciously. Therefore, hydrotherapy is preferred for 
fever management in such patients. 
	 3.	Specific therapy:  Multidrug resistance is prevalent among S. typhi. Empirical

Moreover, the escalating resistance to fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins 
presents a mounting challenge. Most S. typhi and S. paratyphi isolates remain 
susceptible to azithromycin and ceftriaxone, although resistant isolates have 
been reported.

Assessment of response to therapy
	
l The toxic look of the patient decreases and appetite starts returning in 72–96 hours

l Small frequent feeds should continue. Give plenty of oral fluids and compensate for

ACUTE RHEUMATIC FEVER
Rheumatic fever is a multisystem inflammatory disease that occurs as a delayed 
sequelae (2–6 weeks) to group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis. It is 
commonly a disease of childhood between the ages of 5 and 15 years. The disorder is 
largely self-limited and resolves without sequelae but chronic and progressive damage 
to heart valves leads to rheumatic heart disease (RHD).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The major clinical manifestations of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) are carditis 
and arthritis, followed in descending frequency by chorea (with a female 
predominance), subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum (uncommon 
but specific of ARF). 
	
l Diagnosis of initial episode of rheumatic fever is based on the presence of two 
major or one major plus two minor Jones criteria in addition to evidence of recent 
streptococcal infection (positive throat culture or rapid antigen test, or elevated or 
increasing Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titre [>333 units for children and >250 units 
for adults, raised anti-DNAse B titre], positive throat swab or recent scarlet fever). 
	– Two major manifestations or one major plus two minor manifestations or 
three minor manifestations plus supportive evidence of antecedent Group A 
Streptococcus (GAS) infection should be present. 
	– Jones criteria cannot be strictly applied in indolent carditis, when chorea is the only 
major manifestation and in some cases with recurrent attack of rheumatic fever.
	
l Major criteria include the following: carditis (clinical and/or subclinical), 
arthritis (monopolyarthritis or polyarthritis or polyarthralgia), chorea (movement 
disorder), subcutaneous nodules (rare) and erythema marginatum (rare). 
	
l Minor criteria include the following: fever (≥38.5°C), arthralgia, elevated acute 
phase reactants (ESR ≥30 mm and/or CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL) and prolonged PR 
interval (unless carditis is a major criterion).
	
l ARF diagnosis (subsequent episode): Patients with a history of ARF or RHD 
are at a high risk for recurrent attacks if re-infected with group A streptococci. 
Presumptive diagnosis of ARF recurrence is made when a reliable past history 
of ARF or established RHD is present, and in the face of documented group A 
streptococcal infection, two major, one major and two minor, or three minor 
manifestations, or when minor manifestations alone are present; however, exclude 
other more likely causes of the clinical presentation.
	
l Perform echocardiography with Doppler in all cases of confirmed and suspected 
ARF.
	
l RHD most frequently affects mitral and aortic valves. Isolated aortic valve 
involvement is rare and tricuspid and pulmonary valve involvement is unusual. 
	
l Specific criteria for Doppler findings in rheumatic valvulitis are the following: 
(i) mitral regurgitation (all four) – seen in ≥2 views, jet length ≥2 cm, peak 
velocity >3 m/s, pansystolic; and (ii) aortic regurgitation (all four) – seen in ≥2 
views, jet length ≥1 cm, peak velocity >3 m/s, pandiastolic.
	
l Complications of RHD are cardiac failure and infective endocarditis.

Chapter 1  Common Diseases    83
Treatment (acute rheumatic fever)
Hospitalization is needed for moderate-to-severe carditis, severe arthritis or chorea.

l Rest is individualized according to symptoms. For arthritis, rest for 2 weeks is 
adequate. Carditis without congestive heart failure (CHF) needs 4–6 weeks of rest. 
In cases of CHF, rest must be continued till the CHF is controlled. 
	
l Appropriate diet is a must for a growing child with cardiac involvement.
	
l In severe CHF, salt restriction, fluid restriction and upright posture are 
recommended. 
	
l Protect the patient from getting injured in chorea.

1.	All patients with acute rheumatic fever should be treated as if they have group 
A streptococci infection whether or not the organism is actually recovered from 
culture:
	
	Inj. Benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU single IM after test dose
	
	In children: 1.2 MU (>27 kg), 0.6 MU (<27 kg) IM single injection
	
	Or
	
	Oral Penicillin V 500 mg twice daily for 10 days
	
	In children: 125–250 mg twice daily for 10 days
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Azithromycin 12.5 mg/kg/day once daily for 5 days
	
	Or
	
	Cap. Cephalexin 15–20 mg/kg/dose twice a day for 10 days
	 2.	In arthritis and mild carditis without CHF
	
	Tab. Aspirin 6–8 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 2–3 weeks; taper doses once 
symptoms resolve. In children: 50–70 mg/kg/day for 3–5 days followed by 
50 mg/kg/day for 3 weeks followed by half the dose daily for another 4–6 weeks 
to be given after meals. (Caution: Avoid gastric irritants, allow frequent feeding, 
medicine must not be taken on an empty stomach, and monitor for tinnitus, 
deafness and respiratory alkalosis/acidosis.)
	
	If there is no response in 4 days, rule out other conditions like chronic 
inflammatory and myeloproliferative disorders before switching over to steroids.
	 3.	In carditis with cardiomegaly and/or with CHF
	
	Tab. Prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day, maximum 80 mg/day till ESR normalizes – usually 
2–3 weeks, then half the dose for 2–3 weeks followed by tapering of the dose by 
5 mg/24 hours every 2–3 days. 
	
	On tapering of Prednisolone, start Aspirin 50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 
6 weeks. Start aspirin 50–75 mg/kg/day simultaneously, to complete total 12 weeks 
to prevent rebound of disease activity. (Caution: Monitor blood pressure and blood 
sugar.)
	
		
If there is no response to oral steroid therapy, start Inj. Methyl prednisolone 
30 mg/kg/day for 3 days.

84    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
		
Laboratory and clinical rebound may occur 2–3 weeks after cessation of 
Aspirin therapy but usually resolves spontaneously. 
	
		
For treatment of HF, see Cardiac failure in Chapter 3. 
	 4.	In chorea
	
	Mild chorea is treated with a quiet environment and sedatives like oral 
phenobarbitone or diazepam. If there is no response, give 
	
	Tab. Haloperidol 0.25–0.5 mg/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses for 2–4 weeks after 
clinical improvement.
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Sodium valproate 15 mg/kg/day for 2–4 weeks after clinical improvement.
	
	Or 
	
	Tab. Carbamazepine 7–20 mg/kg/day for 2–4 weeks after clinical improvement.
Resistant cases can be treated with plasmapheresis or pimozide. 
Assessment of response and monitoring
	
l If there are laboratory features of rheumatic activity (ESR, CRP, ASO), anti-
inflammatory drugs must also be given.
	
l In acute rheumatic fever, observe for appearance of valvular lesions (most common 
in the first 4 weeks of disease; for details, see Chapter 3) and in RHD for effort 
intolerance, signs and symptoms of CHF and echocardiographic studies of cardiac 
functions.
	
l Usually joint pains disappear within 24–48 hours, tachycardia settles, pericardial 
friction rub, if present, disappears and gradually ESR comes to normal. In 
established cardiac lesions with CHF not controlled by medical management, the 
patient should be referred to a higher centre for surgical intervention.
	
l Monitor blood levels of salicylates. 
	
l Watch for salicylate toxicity (ototoxicity, hyperventilation and metabolic acidosis). 
	
l Follow up the patient for response to fever and decrease in acute phase reactants, 
and to reduce salicylates or taper steroids. 
	
l Perform echocardiography for monitoring complications of carditis.
	
l Termination of anti-inflammatory therapy may be followed by the reappearance 
of clinical manifestation. It is usually not treated unless clinical manifestations are 
severe; reinstate aspirin or steroids in such cases.
For secondary prevention (for prevention of recurrences)
Inj. Benzathine penicillin 1,200,000 units (if weight >27 kg) or 600,000 units (if weight

Duration of prophylaxis
Duration of secondary prevention is individualized.
	 1.	Rheumatic fever with carditis and residual valvular involvement: For 10 years 
or until 40 years or lifelong
	 2.	Rheumatic fever with carditis and no residual valvular involvement: For 
10 years or up to 21 years, whichever is later
	 3.	Rheumatic fever without carditis: For 5 years or until 21 years, whichever is later
Patient/parent education
	
l Provide early and adequate treatment of sore throat. 
	
l Patients with RHD should avoid contact with sore throat cases and if possible 
environmental modifications, e.g. avoid overcrowding.
	
l Explain consequences of rheumatic fever and ensure monitoring to rule out residual 
valvular involvement and compliance with prophylaxis.
	
l Patients with valvular involvement should report to a cardiologist for evaluation and 
further management. 
	
l Explain the importance of prophylaxis against rheumatic carditis as detailed earlier.

Emergencies
CARDIOPULMONARY RESUSCITATION (CPR)
Treat cardiac arrest or airway obstruction as a medical emergency and obtain expert 
help immediately.
CPR consists of a series of lifesaving actions by which oxygenated blood supply to 
brain and vital organs is maintained, and this improves the chances of survival after 
cardiac arrest.
The ‘Chain of Survival’ refers to the chain of events that must occur in rapid succession 
to maximize the chances of survival from sudden cardiac arrest (CA). A strong Chain of 
Survival can improve chances of survival and recovery for victims of CA.
Chain of Survival (Adult)
a. In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (IHCA)
	
l Surveillance, prevention and treatment of pre-arrest conditions
	
l Immediate recognition of CA and activation of emergency response
	
l Early CPR with an emphasis on chest compressions
	
l Rapid defibrillation
	
l Basic and advanced emergency medical service
	
l Effective Advanced Life Support & post-cardiac arrest care (multidisciplinary) in 
view of the recent pandemic of the novel coronavirus disease (COVID-19) has been 
modified (Fig. 2.1).
b. Out of the Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA)
	
l Immediate recognition of CA and activation of emergency response
	
l Early CPR
	
l Rapid defibrillation (automated external defibrillator [AED])
	
l Effective Advanced Life Support and post cardiac arrest care.
Chain of Survival (Paediatric)
	
l Prevention of arrest (e.g. early recognition and treatment of respiratory condition)
	
l Early bystander CPR
	
l Rapid activation of emergency response system
	
l Effective Advanced Life Support and post-cardiac arrest care.

In adults, CA is often sudden and due to a cardiac cause whereas in children it is not 
sudden but mostly secondary to respiratory failure, sepsis, shock or airway obstruction 
(including foreign-body aspiration), submersion and neurological disease. Beyond 1 year 
of age, injuries are the leading cause of death. Therefore, prompt identification and 
management of these conditions is essential to minimize paediatric CA.
CPR in COVID-19 Patients 
CPR in COVID-19 patients needs special considerations as it involves competing interests 
of providing timely and high-quality resuscitation to patients while simultaneously 
protecting the rescuers from transmission of infection to the rescuer during aerosol-
generating procedures involved in CPR (such as chest compressions, positive pressure

88    Standard Treatment Guidelines
ventilation and establishment of an advanced airway) as viral particles remain suspended 
in the air with a half-life of approximately 1 hour. Second, resuscitation efforts require 
numerous providers to work in close proximity to one another and the patient. Finally, 
these are high-stress emergent events in which the immediate needs of the patient 
requiring resuscitation may result in lapses in infection control practices.
Diagnosis of Cardiopulmonary Arrest
1. Unresponsive
Gently tap the victim and ask loudly, ‘Are you okay’? Call the victim’s name, if you 
know it. If the victim is responsive, he or she will answer, move, or moan. Quickly 
check to see if there are any injuries or if he or she needs medical assistance. If the 
victim is unresponsive and not breathing (or only gasping), begin CPR.
2. Cardiac arrest
	 i.	Absence of definite pulse for 10 seconds in major arteries (carotid or femoral in 
older children and femoral or brachial in infants as carotid is difficult to palpate 
due to short neck).
	 ii.	Ventricular fibrillation/pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT)/asystole/pulseless 
electrical activity (PEA) on ECG.
3. Respiratory arrest
Absence of respiration on looking (absent chest movements) for 10 seconds or agonal 
gasps.
Levels of CPR
There are two levels of CPR: 
	 1.	BLS (basic life support): It includes three links of chain of survival, i.e. 
immediate recognition and activation of emergency response, early CPR and rapid 
defibrillation using AED. It is called Basic as it can be initiated without additional 
equipment. Skill and speed are most essential. The steps of BLS survey include:
	
l Verify scene safety
	
l Check for responsiveness, breathing and carotid pulse
	
l Call for help/activation of emergency medical services (EMS)
	
l Providing chest compression and breathing
	
l Using AED 
	 2.	ACLS (advanced cardiac life support): Use of equipment and drugs and 
advanced interventions to restore effective oxygenation and ventilation, and return 
of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) with intact neurological functions. Underlying 
principles are:
	
l Use a systematic approach, based on airway, breathing and circulation (i.e. the 
ABCDEs) to assess and treat the acutely ill patient
	
l Undertake a complete initial assessment and re-assess regularly

l Always assess the effects of treatment or other interventions 
	
l Always correct life-threatening abnormalities before moving on to the next part 
of assessment 
	
l Recognize the circumstances when additional help is required and ask for it promptly 
	
l Use all members of the multidisciplinary team 
	
l Communicate effectively
	
l The underlying aim of the initial interventions should be seen as a “holding 
measure” that keeps the patient alive and produces some clinical improvement, 
in order that definitive treatment may be initiated
	
l Remember that it often takes a few minutes for resuscitative measures to have 
an effect
BASIC LIFE SUPPORT (BLS)
BLS can be provided as a lone rescuer or as a multirescuer team. Depending on the 
level of skills, confidence and availability of equipment (Bag mask device, AED, 
etc.), BLS can be given as: 
	
l Hands only CPR: Chest compressions at the rate of 100–120/minute (usually OHCA)
	
l 30:2 CPR: Single rescuer/two rescuers (usually OHCA)
	
l Multirescuer team (usually IHCA)
(A) Airway
	
l After delivery of 30 compressions, open the airway and deliver 2 rescue breaths in 
case of lone rescuer.
	
l Clear airway by cleaning blood, secretions, foreign particles (suction, if available).
	
l Prevent posterior displacement of tongue due to muscle relaxation during CPA, by 
head tilt and chin lift or jaw thrust (may use an airway if available).
	– Head tilt: Put a hand at forehead and tilt head back to sniffing or neutral position 
in an infant and little more in older children and adults.
	
(Caution: In a patient with suspected cervical spine injury, head tilt should be 
avoided.)
	– Chin lift: Put finger of other hand under bony part of lower jaw at chin and lift 
chin upward.
	– Jaw thrust: Place 2–3 fingers under each side of lower jaw at its angle and lift 
jaw upward with the elbow resting on the surface on which the victim is lying.
(B) Breathing
While maintaining an open airway, observe for breathing within 5–10 seconds while 
taking pulse.
Key points:
	
l 2 breaths after 30 compressions
	
l Each breath given over 1 second
	
l Visible chest rise with each breath

l Do not hyperventilate
	
l Can be delivered by:
	– Mouth to mouth
	– Mouth to nose
	– Pocket mask (Barrier Device)
	– Bag Mask Device (AMBU)
Note: Avoid excessive ventilation, with enough volume to produce visible chest rise. 
It applies to all forms of ventilation during, CPR, including mouth to mouth/nose/
mask/airway breath (may use bag and mask, if available). Inhale and then make a seal 
around the mouth and nose together in an infant and seal mouth only in older children 
and adults (nose pinched with the hand used for head tilt) to exhale smoothly. Avoid 
delivering breaths that are too large or too forceful. Once advanced airway is in place, 
continue chest compressions at the rate of 100–120/min.
Combination of ventilation and chest compression
	
l If both cardiac and respiratory arrest – Compression:ventilation = 30:2 in adults, 
children and infants with one rescuer and 15:2 with 2 rescuers. 
	
l Compression only CPR, if unable or unwilling to provide rescue breaths, although 
the best method of CPR is compression coordinated with ventilations.
Key Points – BLS
	
l Verify the scene safety.
	
l Check the responsiveness. Gently tap the victim and ask loudly, ‘Are you okay?’ 
Call the victim’s name, if you know it. If the victim is responsive, he or she will 
answer, move, or moan. Quickly check to see if there are any injuries or if he or 
she needs medical assistance. If the victim is unresponsive and not breathing (or 
only gasping), begin CPR. 
	
l Activate the EMS and obtain an AED, if one is nearby. 
	
l Assess the victim for normal breathing and a pulse. Position the victim supine on 
a firm flat surface with the head level with the heart. To assess the need for CPR, 
the lay rescuer should assume that CA is present, if the victim is unresponsive and 
not breathing or only gasping. 
	
l If no definite pulse in 10 seconds then begin CPR starting with high quality chest 
compressions as early as possible.
	
l Continue this cycle of 30 compressions and 2 breaths for approximately 
2 minutes before rotating if two rescuers are available.
	
l Rescuer should stand or kneel at the side of the patient so that his hips are at level 
with the victim’s chest.

provide hands-only compressions only CPR for adult victim who suddenly collapses 
with an emphasis on ‘Push Hard and Fast’ on the centre of the chest and continue 
hands-only CPR until an AED arrives and is ready to use. In hospital, one rescuer

The contraindications to CPR include a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order or any 
other advanced directive indicating a person’s desire to not be resuscitated in the event 
of cardiac arrest, as per current legal provisions. A relative contraindication exists if 
the treating physician determines that resuscitation would be medically futile. In cancer 
patients, factors such as the stage of the neoplastic disease, the cause of the cardiac 
arrest and the patient’s preference should be considered when deciding whether or not 
to perform CPR.
CPR in special circumstances
Accidental electrical shock: Rescuer should ensure his/her own safety and ascertain 
that the patient is no longer in contact with the electrical source. For safe removal of 
the patient before starting CPR use, switch off electricity supply. Non-conducting, 
non-metallic grapples or rods can be used, and equipment should be grounded.
Drowning: Place the patient horizontally on a firm surface, such as a surfboard or float 
for effective compression. Rescue breathing may be started in shallow water.
Traumatic cardiac arrest: Highest priority should be airway opening manoeuvres and a 
brief period of external ventilation after clearing the airway since airway obstruction is 
the most likely treatable cause of arrest. To minimize cervical spine injury, administer jaw 
thrust, but not head tilt or chin lift. Immediate needle decompression is lifesaving in case 
of cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax. Most patients with traumatic CA have 
severe hypovolaemia due to excessive blood loss (hence only chest compression may be 
ineffective without correction of underlying cause) or have non-survivable brain injuries.
In an infant, compress the sternum with two fingers placed just below the 
intermammary line. Two fingers (index, middle) to compress sternum by at least 4 cm 
at the rate of at least 100/min and do not lift the finger when compression is released. 
Two thumb-encircling hands technique can also be used.

ADVANCED CARDIAC LIFE SUPPORT (ACLS) 
The management of CA is highlighted in the ACLS algorithms (Figs 2.5 and 2.6).
Primary Assessment
The ABCDE’s of the Primary Assessment are as follows:
(A) Airway
	
l Assess and manage airway using advanced airway (supraglottic advanced airway or 
endotracheal [ET] intubation), if needed. 
	
l Waveform capnography to confirm and monitor ET tube placement.
	
l Secure the advanced airway device so it does not dislodge, especially in patients who 
are at risk for movement. Secure the ET tube with tape or a commercial device. Do 
not use devices to secure the airway devices that are circumferential.
(B) Breathing 
	
l Give bag-mask ventilation at the rate of 8–10 breaths/min with continuous chest 
compressions, provide supplemental oxygen and avoid excessive ventilation. 
Monitor the adequacy of ventilation and oxygenation 
	
l Achieve SpO2 > 94%
	
l If bag-mask ventilation is adequate, defer the insertion of an advanced airway until 
it becomes essential (patient fails to respond to initial CPR or until spontaneous 
circulation returns).
	
l Monitor ventilation adequacy – clinical criteria (chest rise, cyanosis), continuous 
waveform capnography and oxygen saturation
(C) Circulation
	
l Obtain IV/IO access, attach ECG leads, identify and monitor arrhythmias, give fluids 
if needed, and use defibrillation if appropriate. 
	
l Do not interrupt compressions and delay shock for accessing vascular access, drug 
delivery, advanced airway placement. 
	
l Monitor CPR quality
	
l Continuous waveform capnography 
	
l Intra-arterial pressure (IAP)

l Give appropriate medications to manage rhythm (e.g. Amiodarone, Lidocaine) 
and blood pressure (e.g. dopamine or epinephrine [use with caution as it increases 
myocardial oxygen demand])
	
	Inj. Epinephrine
	
	Indication: During ACLS, epinephrine can be given in three ways: intravenous, 
intraosseous and endotracheal tube. Dose and route: Intravenous push/IO: 1 mg 
epinephrine IV is given every 3–5 minutes. When given intravenously, always 
follow the IV push with a 20 mL normal saline flush.
	
	Inj. Amiodarone
	
	Indication: Amiodarone should only be used after defibrillation/cardioversion and 
epinephrine have failed to convert VT/VF. Dose and route: 300 mg IV/IO push; if 
no conversion 150 mg IV/IO push. After conversion Infusion #1 360 mg IV over 6 
hours (1 mg/min) followed by infusion #2 540 mg IV over 18 hours (0.5 mg/min). 
(Caution: Dilute with D5W and give with an in-line filter. Infusions exceeding 2 
hours must be administered in glass or polyolefin bottles containing D5W with 
maximum cumulative dose of 2.2 g in a 24-hour period).
	
	Inj. Lidocaine
	
	Lidocaine is used as a replacement for amiodarone if it is not available. Dose and 
route: Initial dose of 1–1.5 mg/kg IV or IO. If pVT or VF persists the lidocaine may be 
repeated at 0.5–0.75 mg/kg over 5- to 10-minute intervals (maximum dose 3 mg/kg).
	
	Inj. Magnesium sulphate
	
	It can be used during cardiac arrest primarily to treat Torsade de pointes that is 
caused by a low serum magnesium level. Dose and route: An initial dose of 1–2 g 
IV or IO diluted in at least 10 mL of normal saline. Give the dose over 5 minutes.
	
	Inj. Naloxone
	
	Indication: For all victims of narcotic overdose or poisoning and newborn 
resuscitation (if mother has been given Morphine or Pethidine during labour) 
who have a definite pulse but no normal breathing or only gasping. For details, 
see Opioid intoxication in Chapter 15. Dose and route: 0.4 mg/kg IV IM or 2 mg 
intranasal (IN); may repeat after 4 minutes.
	
	Inj. Glucose 
	
	Indication: Hypoglycaemia. Dose and route: 0.5–1 g/kg IV and maintain blood 
sugar around 140–180 mg/dL. For diabetics with symptomatic hypoglycaemia 
who are able to follow command and swallow safely, administer oral glucose in 
the form of food or liquids containing sugar.
(D) Disability
	
l Check neurological function (responsiveness, consciousness level, pupils – size, 
equality and reaction to light); check for reversible drug-induced causes of depressed 
consciousness. Assess the patient’s consciousness level using either the AVPU (Alert, 
Voice, Painful, Unresponsive) or Glasgow Coma Scale (see Table 2.10 in section 
on coma).

l Measure the blood glucose using a rapid glucose meter or stick method to exclude

(E) Exposure
	
l Look for trauma, bleeding, unusual signs, alert bracelets, pacemaker, medication

ROSC is resumption of sustained perfusing cardiac activity associated with significant 
respiratory effort after cardiac arrest. ROSC is indicated by: 
	
l Breathing, coughing, or movement and a palpable pulse or a measurable blood pressure
	
l Sudden sustained increase in PETCO2 > 40 mmHg
	
l Spontaneous arterial pressure waves in IAP monitoring

l Review the results of laboratory or radiological investigations.
	
l Check that important routine medications are prescribed and being administered.
	
l Consider which level of care is required by the patient (e.g. ward, high 
dependence unit [HDU], ICU).
	
l Make complete entries in the patient’s notes of your finding, assessment and 
treatment. Record the patient’s response to therapy.
	
l Consider definitive treatment of the patient’s underlying condition.
	
l Communicate effectively with the patient’s family and friends during and after 
CPR.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    107
Post-resuscitation care 
Immediate management of post-cardiac care after the return of spontaneous circulation 
can improve survival rates and functional recovery in the patient. It should be provided 
by multidisciplinary management with neurologic and physiologic assessment 
monitoring in critical care unit:
	 1.	Optimize cardiopulmonary function and systemic perfusion, especially perfusion 
in the brain. 
	 2.	Titrate oxygen administration to maintain arterial saturation ≥94%. Use continuous 
waveform capnography to confirm and monitor the correct placement of the ET 
tube, if needed. Avoid hyperventilation.
	 3.	Identify and treat hypotension. If SBP < 90 mmHg, treat shock with fluids: IV or 
IO bolus of 1–2 L normal saline or Ringer’s lactate And Epinephrine IV infusion 
at a dose of 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min, Or Norepinephrine IV infusion at a dose of 
0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min Or Dopamine IV infusion at a dose of 5–10 mcg/kg/min.
	 4.	Try to identify the treatable causes of the arrest. Institute measures to prevent 
recurrence. 
	 5.	Obtain serial ABG samples. Provide adequate mechanical ventilation to minimize 
lung injury. 
	 6.	Look for and treat seizures. Do serial 12-lead ECG and cardiac biomarkers for 
the detection of acute coronary syndromes. If ST-elevation myocardial infarction 
(STEMI) is detected, EMS personnel should transport the patient to an appropriate 
facility quickly to reduce time to treatment. 
	 7.	Emergency coronary angiography for patients with elevated ST and 
haemodynamically or electrically unstable patients without ST elevation for whom 
a cardiovascular lesion is suspected.
	 8.	If STEMI or acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is not detected, determine 
the patient’s ability to follow commands. If the patient is unable to follow the 
commands or respond in a meaningful way, the high-performance team should 
initiate targeted temperature management (TTM). Maintain temperature to optimize 
neurological recovery, fluid and electrolyte balance between 32°C–36°C and then 
maintain it constantly for at least 24 hours. Avoid hyperthermia. Do not actively 
rewarm haemodynamically stable patients who spontaneously develop a mild 
degree of hypothermia (>33°C [91.5°F]) after resuscitation from cardiac arrest. 
	 9.	Anticipate and treat and prevent multiple organ dysfunction. Avoid excessive 
ventilation and hyperoxia. 
	10.	Once TTM has been initiated, or if the patient is responsive and able to follow 
commands, transfer the patient to appropriate critical care unit.
Maternal cardiac arrest 
To relieve aortocaval compression during chest compressions and optimize the quality of 
CPR, it is reasonable to perform manual left uterine displacement in the supine position 
first. Left uterine displacement can be performed from either the patient’s left side with 
the two-handed technique or the patient’s right side with the one-handed technique,

108    Standard Treatment Guidelines
depending on the positioning of the resuscitation team. If this technique is unsuccessful, 
and an appropriate wedge is readily available, then providers may consider placing the patient 
in a left-lateral tilt of 27°-30°, using a firm wedge to support the pelvis and thorax.
In nonsurvivable maternal trauma or prolonged maternal pulselessness, do not 
delay in performing perimortem caesarean delivery (PMCD). Consider PMCD at 
4 minutes after the onset of maternal cardiac arrest or resuscitative efforts (for the 
unwitnessed arrest, if there is no maternal ROSC).
Termination of CPR
The resuscitation team must make a conscientious and competent effort to give patients 
a trial of CPR and ACLS. The final decision to stop efforts can never be as simple as 
an isolated time interval. 
	
l Decision to cease CPR efforts depends on many factors:
	– Time from collapse to CPR
	– Time from collapse to 1st defibrillation
	– Co-morbidities
	– Pre-arrest state
	– Initial arrest rhythm
	– Response to resuscitative measures
	
l If all of the following criteria are present, consider termination of resuscitation:
	– Arrest not witnessed by emergency medical services personnel 
	– No return of spontaneous circulation (before transport)
	– No AED shock was delivered (before transport)
	
l If any criteria are missing, continue resuscitation and transport.
	
l In patients arriving to the emergency department after having suffered prehospital 
traumatic cardiac arrest, resuscitation may be discontinued after 20 minutes in adults 
and at least 30 minutes of unsuccessful resuscitative efforts in children, including 
CPR, if there are no signs of life (absent vital signs or other signs of life have been 
confirmed) and any of the following:
	– No cardiac motion observed by Focused Assessment using Sonography for 
Trauma (FAST)
	– Cardiac monitoring reveals:
	
■Asystole
	
■No organized cardiac rhythm
	– Injuries are obviously incompatible with life (e.g. decapitation)
	– Signs of prolonged death: Rigor mortis, livor mortis, algor mortis or decomposition.
	
Otherwise, consider terminating resuscitative effort when no reversible cause is 
identifiable and the patient fails to respond to the BLS and ACLS surveys.
	
l When not to cease CPR efforts:
	– Hypothermia till temperature >34°C
	– Poisoning till antidote given
	– Some reversible condition identified.

ANAPHYLAXIS
It is a generalized severe life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction characterized by 
hypotension, peripheral circulatory collapse and respiratory difficulty in the form 
of stridor and dyspnoea. Anaphylaxis can occur due to food, insect stings, inhaled/
ingested allergens or drugs (Table 2.2). Symptoms may occur instantaneously or within 
a few minutes after an intravenous injection of the offending agent. Less frequent 
triggers encompass latex, tick bites, exercise (with or without food), cold temperatures, 
radiocontrast agents, immunization (rare) and unidentified causes (idiopathic). 
In food allergies, anaphylaxis typically manifests within 1–2 hours of ingestion. 
Onset can be rapid, occurring within 30 minutes, or delayed by several hours, as 
observed in conditions like mammalian meat allergy and food-dependent exercise-
induced anaphylaxis, where symptoms often arise during physical activity.

110    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Anaphylactic reactions to stings and injected medications, including radiocontrast 
agents and vaccines, generally manifest within 5–30 minutes but may also exhibit 
delayed onset. While anaphylaxis to oral medications is possible, it is less common 
compared to reactions to injected medications.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Any acute onset illness with typical skin features (urticarial rash or erythema/
flushing, and/or angioedema), PLUS involvement of respiratory and/or 
cardiovascular and/or persistent severe gastrointestinal symptoms.
	 Or
	 Any acute onset of hypotension or bronchospasm or upper airway obstruction where 
anaphylaxis is considered possible, even if typical skin features are not present.
	
l Sudden onset and rapid progression of symptoms. Onset usually occurs in 
minutes but depends upon the trigger. Patient can deteriorate over a brief period 
of time (½ to 3 hours). However, skin or mucosal changes alone are not a sign of 
anaphylactic reaction.
	
l Cardiovascular collapse (hypotension) is the most common periarrest manifestation.
	
l Gastrointestinal signs and symptoms include abdominal pain, vomiting and 
diarrhoea.
	
l Differential diagnosis to be considered since failure to identify other conditions 
can be fatal are angioedema, severe, near-fatal asthma, vasovagal reactions and 
ACE inhibitors.

Treatment (Immediate treatment)
Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis. Treatment depends on severity. Severe anaphylactoid 
reaction is a life-threatening emergency. Effective treatment is based on general life 
support principles: airway, breathing, circulation and prompt diagnosis and rapid 
supplementation of appropriate therapy (Fig. 2.7).
Do not delay treatment for lack of complete history or definite diagnosis.
	 1.	Remove allergen (if still present), stay with the person, call for assistance and 
locate adrenaline injector.
	 2.	Lay the person flat and do NOT allow him/her to stand or walk.
	
l If unconscious or pregnant, place in recovery position – on the left side if 
pregnant, as shown below
	
l If breathing is difficult allow them to sit with legs outstretched
	
l Hold young children flat, not upright
	 3.	Call for an ambulance early and shift the patient to the emergency department, if 
not in hospital. Always give Adrenaline FIRST, then asthma reliever, if someone 
with known asthma and allergy to food, insects or medication has SUDDEN 
BREATHING DIFFICULTY (including wheeze, persistent cough or hoarse voice) 
even if there are no skin symptoms.
	 4.	Start CPR, at any time if person is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
	
	(For details, see Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation given earlier.)
	 5.	If inadequate response after two to three adrenaline doses, or deterioration of 
patient, start IV adrenaline infusion (to be given by staff trained in its use or in 
liaison with an emergency/critical care specialist).
	
	(Caution: IV boluses of adrenaline are NOT recommended without specialised 
training as they may increase the risk of cardiac arrhythmia.)
	 6.	Establish one or preferably two wide-bore intravenous lines in adults and 
hypotensive children. Commence rapid fluid resuscitation with normal saline.
	 7.	If the only manifestation of anaphylaxis is urticaria or angioedema, initial IM dose 
of Adrenaline and Inj. Ranitidine 1 mg/kg diluted in 5% dextrose to a total volume 
of 20 mL and injected IV over 5 minutes. H2 antihistamines do not relieve upper 
or lower airway obstruction or shock. If no progression occurs, the patient can be 
kept under observation for at least 12 hours and then discharged.
	
	Notes:
	
l Antihistamines have no role in treating or preventing respiratory or 
cardiovascular symptoms of anaphylaxis. Diphenhydramine or Cetirizine relives 
itch and hives only. Do not use oral sedating antihistamines as side effects 
(drowsiness or lethargy) may mimic some signs of anaphylaxis and parenteral 
Promethazine worsens hypotension and causes muscle necrosis.
	
l The benefit of corticosteroids in anaphylaxis is unproven. Inj. Hydrocortisone 
2–6 mg/kg or Dexamethasone 0.1–0.4 mg/kg IV early in the course of therapy. 
Beneficial effects are delayed by at least 4–6 hours. Do not use steroids as first-
line measure in place of Adrenaline.
	
l Management of anaphylaxis in pregnant women is the same as for non-
pregnant women. Adrenaline should be the first line treatment for anaphylaxis

Follow-up and monitoring
A good prognosis is expected if Adrenaline is administered immediately; however, 
outcomes are worse with a delay of more than 30 minutes in its administration. 
Observe vital signs frequently and if possible monitor electrocardiogram and pulse 
oximetry. Observe patient for at least 6 hours after last dose of Adrenaline as relapse, 
protracted and/or biphasic reactions may occur and with instructions to return to 
hospital, if symptoms return. Admit patients who have suffered a severe anaphylactoid 
reaction, protracted anaphylaxis (e.g. required repeated doses of Adrenaline or IV fluid 
resuscitation), OR have a history of asthma or severe/protracted anaphylaxis, or have 
other concomitant illness (e.g. asthma, history or arrhythmia), or stay in remote place 
cannot return to hospital, if symptoms return, for up to 24 hours. Patients who remain 
clinically unstable after initial resuscitation should be admitted to an intensive care unit.
Record all details of the event and report to appropriate authorities.
Discharge care
All patients who have experienced anaphylaxis should be sent home with the following:
