BURNS
Burns are a major preventable cause of morbidity and mortality. They can be due to 
a variety of causes, namely thermal (flame and dry heat; scalds from hot liquids), 
electrical, chemical and radiation. The depth of a thermal burn injury depends on the 
temperature of the burning agent and the duration of contact. For electrical burns, the 
damage depends on a number of factors like voltage, resistance of various tissues, 
type of current (alternating or direct), amperage, etc. For a chemical burn, the depth of 
injury depends upon the nature (e.g. acid, alkali, etc.) and concentration of chemical 
apart from duration of its contact with body tissues. Radiation burns have become rare 
because of improved technology of delivering radiation to patients and stringent safety 
measures in nuclear reactors.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    115
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Depending on the depth, burns have been classified into four degrees (see 
below). The deeper the burn wound and the larger the burned area, greater is the 
morbidity and mortality.
	
l Early complications include shock, toxaemia, sloughing of mucous membranes-
gastrointestinal tract and respiratory tract inhalation injuries, acute renal failure, 
and haematemesis (Curling ulcer), pain, anxiety, fluid loss and dehydration, local 
tissue oedema and infection. Burns involving face, nose, mouth or neck may 
obstruct the airway and circumferential burns on the chest may cause breathing 
problem.
	
l Late complications include protein losing enteropathy, secondary haemorrhage, 
hypertrophic scar/keloid and contracture especially burns to areas of the body 
with flexion creases. 
	
l Circumferential burns of arms, legs, fingers or toes may put the survival of the 
extremity at risk.

The treatment of burns depends on the depth of injury and the extent of affected body 
surface area (BSA) involved. The severity of the burn determines the type of treatment 
as well as the place of treatment. Depending on the extent of burning of layers of skin 
and tissue, burns are classified into first-, second-, third- and fourth-degree burns as given 
below. The deeper the burn and the larger the burned area, the more serious the burn.
First-degree burns are burns of the epidermis (e.g. sunburn), are characterized by 
redness, dryness, pain, itching and minor swelling. Peeling occurs as it heals in up 
to 5 days without scarring. Need home care and need a moisturizing cream and oral 
antihistaminic for itching. However, if a larger area is involved on hands, feet, face, 
groin, buttocks or a major joint, seek medical attention.
Second-degree burns are superficial (involving papillary dermis)/deep partial-
thickness (involving reticular layer) burns that involve epidermis and part of the 
dermis as well. The former are pink and moist in appearance and painful. There can be 
blister formation if overlying epidermis is intact. It usually heals in 10–21 days with 
epithelialization from sweat and sebaceous glands without scarring. Deep dermal burns 
are waxy white in colour and take up to 6 weeks to heal with hypertrophic scarring. 
They are also at risk of conversion to still deeper burns due to infection and drying.
If the burned area is larger or covers the hands, feet, face, groin, buttocks or a major 
joint, treat it as a major burn and get medical help immediately.
First and second-degree burns are also called partial thickness burns because, given 
proper treatment by dressings, they can heal on their own.
Third-degree burns involve epidermis and whole of dermis and hence, there is no 
chance of healing (except by contracture formation) without surgical intervention in the

116    Standard Treatment Guidelines
form of skin grafting. The burnt skin is tough, dry, inelastic, translucent and parchment-
like with thrombosed veins visible underneath (an eschar). Blisters do not form, and 
these burns are painless because of complete destruction of all nerve endings.
Fourth-degree burns involve the subcutaneous tissues and even musculotendinous 
and neurovascular structures and the bones as well. Electrical burns are very commonly 
fourth degree and have a great morbidity and mortality.
Third- and fourth-degree burns come under the category of full-thickness burns as they 
need surgical intervention for the wound healing and patient’s recovery.
Assessment and triage of patients suffering from burns in emergency department are 
shown in Figure 2.8 and burns classification based on severity (Table 2.3).
Assess the severity of burns and burn extent estimation
The total body surface area (TBSA) burnt can be assessed by various methods. Wallace 
‘Rule of Nine’ is the most commonly used method to estimate the area in adults and 
children (Fig. 2.9). Infants and toddlers have a bigger head while their lower extremities 
are smaller. Lynch and Blocker’s ‘Rule of 5’ is used for them. Head and neck (20%), 
anterior and posterior trunk 20% each while all the four extremities are 10% each. For 
scattered burns, ‘rule of palm’ (also called ‘Rule of hand’) is used where the palmar 
surface of patient’s own hand is equal to 1% of TBSA. 
The severity of a burn determines whether the patient can be treated on an out-patient 
basis or needs admission in a general hospital or at a specialized burn center. Patients 
with burns can be traditionally divided into three categories based on the severity of 
their burns: minor, moderate and critical (Table 2.3).
Causes of death in burn patients 
A burn patient may die due to primary neurogenic shock, electrocution (ventricular 
fibrillation/cardiac asystole), secondary hypovolemic shock, acute Curling’s ulcer 
(haemorrhagic shock), asphyxia due to inhalation of smoke and carbon monoxide 
(CO), carbon dioxide etc., laryngeal edema, acute renal failure, associated head 
and other injuries, tetanus, burn wound toxaemia and sepsis, cachexia, anaemia and 
hypoproteinemia, etc.
First-aid at the site of injury/accident
For all thermal burns, the slogan is ‘Pour water on burns.’ The aim is to take the victim 
away from the scene of fire and smoke, extinguish the burning clothes, etc. and bring 
the temperature of skin to at least normal body temperature (37°C).
	 1.	Stop the burning process by removing clothing and irrigating the burns.
	 2.	Extinguish flames by allowing the patient to roll on the ground, or by applying a 
blanket, or by using water or other fire-extinguishing liquids.
	 3.	Instead of running, it is better to roll and try to extinguish fire.

For major burns, call for emergency medical assistance (Emergency Medical Services 
[EMS] 1092/102/108). Until an emergency unit arrives, follow these steps:
	 1.	Check for signs that the person is alive such as a heartbeat, breathing, coughing or 
movement. If such signs do not exist, begin CPR (see section on Cardiopulmonary 
Resuscitation). Look for evidence of respiratory distress and smoke inhalation 
injury, a common cause of death in the acute burn victim. Laryngeal oedema can 
develop suddenly and unexpectedly.
	 2.	Remove rings, bracelets and other potentially constricting articles. 
	 3.	Do not remove burnt clothing adherent to skin. However, do ensure that the victim 
is no longer in contact with burning materials or exposed to smoke or heat.
	 4.	Do not immerse victims with critical large burns in cold water. Doing so may cause 
shock. Avoid hypothermia: keep the person with the burn as warm as possible.
	 5.	If the area of the burn is large, after it has been doused with cool water, apply clean 
wraps about the burned area (or the whole patient) to prevent systemic heat loss 
and hypothermia. Hypothermia is a particular risk in young children. Do not cover 
patient with a blanket.
Transportation
	
l Transportation of burn victims should be done as quickly as possible in ACLS 
ambulance (Emergency Medical Services [EMS] 1092/102/108), so that the “golden 
period” of resuscitation is not wasted.
	
l At the site of injury, make all attempts to maintain the airway.
	
l Always rule out head injury, cervical spinal injury, other limb injury before 
transportation; if any of these is present, shift with adequate precaution in the form 
of cervical brace, limb splint, etc. 
	
l Keep patients well covered during transportation, especially infants and children to 
avoid excessive heat loss and resulting hypothermia.
Note: Do not give anything by mouth except in minor burns.
Immediate resuscitation and care in hospital
	
l Clear the airway and rule out respiratory tract injury (inhalation injury) in patients 
with a history of being trapped in a closed space, facial burns, singeing of eyebrows/

Moderate to Severe Burns
1. Fluid resuscitation
	 i.	Rapid, aggressive fluid resuscitation to reconstitute intravascular volume and 
maintain end-organ perfusion. A simple way to calculate prognosis of the patient 
is to sum the age of the patient and the percentage of burn. If it is close to 100, the 
mortality is close to 100%. Early fluid resuscitation may be initiated in patients 
with burned area of 15% TBSA or higher and children with a burned area of 10% 
TBSA or higher and in case of patients with a smaller burned area depending on 
the general condition.
	 ii.	Isotonic crystalloid resuscitation preparations fluids (Ringer’s lactate) to be infused 
through a wide-bore cannula long line/venesection at the rate of 4 mL/kg/% burns 
area (Parkland Formula). If Ringer’s lactate is not available, then normal saline 
(NS) can be used. Half of the volume calculated is infused in the first 8 hours after 
the injury and the rest is infused in the next 16 hours (for details, see respective 
section on fluid and electrolyte imbalance in adults and children).
	
	Note: No role of colloids in first 24 hours.
	iii.	Monitoring of fluid resuscitation: Insert indwelling Foley catheter. Monitor 
hourly urine output and maintain 1 mL/kg body weight/hour. Adjust infusion 
rate (increased or decreased) based on urine output, hydration and other clinical 
parameters of the patient. Any formula for fluid calculations is a guideline only 
to start the treatment. Monitor haemoglobin, hematocrit, serum electrolytes, KFT 
and blood sugar daily or as per requirement. and manage accordingly. Gradually 
decrease intravenous fluids while increasing oral fluids (preferably ORS) as bowel 
activity returns. During this switch period, watch the patient for vomiting, paralytic 
ileus, abdominal distention, return of bowel sounds and passage of stools, especially 
patients with co-morbidities or multiple trauma, raised central venous pressure.

2. Pain relief
	 i.	For minor burns, oral Paracetamol in appropriate dosages can be given. For others, 
injectable Paracetamol, Tramadol or Pentazocine be prescribed by IV route as 
needed in the presence of shock. Inj. Paracetamol Or Inj. Tramadol 50 mg or Inj. 
Pentazocine 30 mg (for severe pain 45–60 mg) IM or IV (in children over 1 year 
– 1 mg/kg IM or SC; by IV up to 500 mcg/kg) every 3–4 hours when necessary. 
(Caution: Their absorption from the muscle is erratic and multiple doses may get 
absorbed when the patient recovers from shock.)
	 ii.	Correct hypovolemia and hypoxia before administering narcotic analgesics.
	iii.	For minor burns, apply cold compresses using fresh running water; avoid ice cold water.
3.	Systemic antibiotics
	
All the burn wounds are sterile to begin with. A burn wound provides a large, warm, 
moist and protein-rich medium for growth of microorganisms from endogenous 
and exogenous sources. The patient is also more susceptible to infection due to a 
depressed immune system. Most cases of minor burns, if taken care of properly, can 
be managed by application of local antimicrobials on the wound without the need 
of systemic antibiotics at all. Prolonged and haphazard use of antibiotics leads to 
development of drug resistance with consequent risks to patient.
	 i.	Administer systemic antibiotics on the day of burn to all moderate and critical burn 
patients. Send wound swabs regularly for culture-sensitivity examination based on 
patient showing development of symptom and signs of systemic sepsis, and adjust 
appropriate systemic antibiotics in maximal doses accordingly. 
	
	Inj. Ampicillin 500 mg 6 hourly IV.
	
	In children: 50–100 mg/kg in 4 divided doses for 7–10 days.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV or IM once a day (or in equally divided doses twice a 
day)
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Ciprofloxacin (infusion 100 mg/50 mL), 500 mg 2 times a day for 7 days.
	 ii.	Switch to appropriate antibiotics (amikacin, tobramycin), piperacillin-tazobactam, 
meropenem, imipenem, etc. according to culture sensitivity results.
	
	Bacteria generally isolated from the burn wound are Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, 
Escherichia coli, S. aureus, S. faecalis, Proteus and Acinetobacter, etc. After 
3–4 weeks, the burn wounds may show fungal infections and appropriate wound 
cultures need to be done and antifungal therapy instituted.

i.	 In case of airway burns, keep endotracheal tube ready by bedside
	
ii.	 Place nasogastric tube in major burns
	 iii.	 Place urinary catheter in all major burns and record hourly urine output. 
Titrate the fluid infusion to maintain urine output as mentioned above. Monitor

Burns of special sites
Burns of hands
Treat burns of hands with special care to preserve function. 
	 1.	Cover each finger with a separate tulle gauze after application of antimicrobial 
cream, and separate them with gauze to prevent the formation of syndactyly.
	 2.	The fingers are dressed in functional position and whole hand and upper extremity 
elevated to prevent oedema and start finger movement within the dressing itself.
	 3.	At least once a day, remove the gloves, bathe the hands, inspect the burn and then 
reapply silver sulfadiazine and the gloves.
	 4.	For full-thickness burns, consider early excision of eschar and skin grafting.
	 5.	Consult a specialist after healthy granulation tissue appears for further treatment.
Burns of face, head and neck
	 1.	Burns of head and neck are very important because of several reasons. Face has 
various specialized sensory organs (e.g. eyes, nose, ears, etc.) and aerodigestive 
orifices. These are critical to function and survival. Burns involving respiratory 
tract (inhalational burns) threatens the very survival of the patient. The face is a 
mirror of individual’s personality, and any disfigurement tremendously affects the 
victim psychologically.
	 2.	Cheeks, lips and forehead burns may undergo hypertrophic, atrophic and 
depigmented scarring following burns. However, timely assessment, diagnosis 
and splinting can prevent much of the deformation associated with burns. Areas to 
be watched are lips and nasolabial folds, do not hesitate to quickly shave of these 
areas and provide full thickness skin graft so that contracting bands are minimized.

	 3.	Open dressing (exposure method), repeated cleaning, local antibiotic ointment 
application, early pressure garment, chin strap, face mask application. Proper face 
mask with lateral pull from circumoral area markedly reduces deformity in this 
area. Cleanse the burnt area gently with a mild antibacterial soap solution, then 
dab it dry. Clip hair short if necessary. Apply triple antibiotic ophthalmic ointment 
(Neosporin, polymyxin, and bacitracin) after applying non-stick tulle gauze. 
	 4.	Use of eye ointment helps prevent skin ointment from inadvertently entering and 
harming the eye. Assess corneal status early, as ensuing facial oedema closes the 
eyes. 
	 5.	Generalized facial oedema typically increases gradually, peaking within 3 days 
before decreasing. Therefore, position the patient with their head elevated.
Burns of eyelid 
	 1.	In case of full-thickness eyelid burns, exposure keratitis, corneal perforation and 
ultimately loss of vision are to be prevented by applying plenty of ophthalmic 
antibiotic ointment and using pad and bandage. If a corneal injury is present, 
atropine eye ointment (a mydriatic agent, 1%) should also be added to prevent 
ciliary spasm and iridocyclitic adhesions. 
	 2.	Ointments should be put repeatedly to prevent adhesions forming between 
conjunctival surfaces. 
	 3.	All corneal injuries should be covered (patched). Intense periorbital edema in the 
early postoperative period serves the same purpose. Skin grafting should be done 
early to prevent loss of vision.
	 4.	In case of full-thickness eyelid burns and if these burns are a part of extensive 
burns to the rest of the body, perform tarsorrhaphy to preserve the cornea. 
	 5.	The common post burn sequelae of the eyelids are ectropion (commonest), loss 
of eyelid and symblepharon. An eyelid ectropion can lead to exposure keratitis, 
corneal ulceration and ultimately loss of vision. 
	 6.	Definitive treatment is skin graft over raw area, till the time grafting is done protect 
cornea with ointment, pad and bandage. Symblepharon occurs commonly after 
acid burns, evaluate whether the eye has vision or not. These cases have variable 
degrees of conjunctival loss which makes reconstruction very complicated.
Burns of perineum and external genitalia
The areas are special because not only they are difficult to dress but also because of 
lot of microbial contamination from gut bacteria. Thus, they need admission and are 
managed by exposure method with coverage of the patient as a whole with a cradle to 
protect the burn areas.
Scalds
Scalds may result from drinking extremely hot fluids or some irritant chemicals. In such 
cases, the inner side of the mouth and throat becomes red and swollen. Give cold water to 
drink or ice, followed by milk or egg emulsion to drink and refer the patient to a hospital.

124    Standard Treatment Guidelines
BURNS OF SPECIAL TYPES
Electrical burns and chemical burns come under the category of special types because of 
several reasons starting from their different first aid, clinical appearances, intravenous 
fluid therapy, surgical requirements, complications and prognosis/outcome, etc.
Electrical burns
These have been arbitrarily divided into low tension (<1000 volts, e.g. domestic voltage 
which is 220 volts in India) or high tension (>1000 volts; e.g. transmission cables and 
electric trains and metro where it is 25000 volts).
	 1.	Electrical injuries may not be readily apparent. It may vary from just a tingling 
sensation to gangrene of extremities (muscle necrosis) to instant death due 
to cardiac arrhythmias (ventricular fibrillation or asystole). There may be 
strong muscular contractions leading to fractures and pain, seizures and loss of 
consciousness, etc. 
	 2.	All electrical burns need admission for at least 24 hours for observation. 
Since the cutaneous burns are less compared to deeper burns, the intravenous 
fluid requirements cannot be calculated using formulae for thermal burns. 
Myoglobinuria and haemoglobinuria due to muscle necrosis are very common 
and may lead to acute kidney injury (acute renal failure), if preventive steps 
are not taken. Thus, the desired urine output is double the amount for thermal 
burns to flush out these pigments. Additionally, sodium bicarbonate (50 mL of 
7.5% solution as a bolus) and mannitol (25 g initially) are given and repeated 
as necessary. The aim is to have a urinary pH above 6.5 and a serum pH from 
7.40–7.45.
	 3.	Requirement for fasciotomies of various muscle compartments in upper and lower 
extremities, surgical debridement of dead and necrotic skinc, muscles and even 
amputations (sometimes multiple) are far more common compared to thermal burn 
injuries. Most electrical burn wounds need skin grafting or skin flap cover to close 
the wound.
	 4.	The risk of tetanus and gas gangrene is also greater and needs appropriate 
preventive and therapeutic steps. In electrical burns, intramuscular human tetanus 
immunoglobulin (TIG) 250/500 IU may be given for passive protection for patients 
with wounds grossly contaminated with soil.
First-aid for electrical burns at the accident site
	 1.	Call for emergency help immediately.
	 2.	Turn off the source of electricity if possible. The dictum is ‘rescuer should not 
become the next casualty’. If not, move the source away from both rescuer and the 
injured person using a dry, nonconducting object made of cardboard, plastic or wood 
to separate the ‘live’ wire from the victim. Do not use metal or anything which is wet. 
	 3.	Begin CPR, if the person shows no signs of circulation, such as breathing, coughing 
or movement.

or a clean cloth. Do not use a blanket or towel. 
	
	Do NOT pour water.
	 5.	In some patients with burns, there may be associated injuries such as head injury, 
spinal injury, or long bone fractures, especially if there is a history of falling from 
a height or violent muscular jactitation. It is important to transport these patients 
carefully, taking appropriate measures to prevent complications such as tongue fall,

(For details, see section First-aid at the site of injury/accident earlier.)
Treatment is as for thermal burns as per the percentage of burns described above and 
treat internal injury as appropriate. Consider fasciotomy to prevent gangrene. Get ECG 
to rule out cardiac conduction abnormalities. 
Chemical burns
A large number of chemicals can cause cutaneous burn injuries. They are not only 
accidental but also homicidal and suicidal. Chemical burns are caused by contact with 
household or industrial chemicals in a liquid, solid, or gas form or natural foods. The 
chemicals may be acids, alkalis, oxidants and vesicants, etc. 
	 1.	Identify the chemical that was involved. Common acidic household compounds 
are acetic acid, hydrochloric acid or sulphuric acid or bases like ammonia.
	 2.	The chemical burn is characterized by discolouration of skin with clear line of 
demarcation. It is brown or black with sulphuric acid and yellow with nitric 
acid. The trickle marks are the special features. There is absence of blisters. The 
chemical substance may be present over the surface and the clothings. 
	 3.	The acid burn victim suffers from severe pain and burning. In case of acid attack 
(homicide vitriolage), the corrosives may enter in the eyes and cause corneal 
damage, ocular adnexa and even deeper tissues with permanent loss of vision.
	 4.	Treatment for chemical burns to the eyes is similar to first aid for chemical burns 
in other areas. The eyes must be constantly and continuously washed with running 
water for about an hour for acids and for 2 hours for alkalis until the patient can be 
seen by an ophthalmologist.
(For details, see Chemical Injuries to Eyes in the following text.)
First aid in case of chemical burns
All chemical burn victims should be rushed to the nearest specialized medical care 
units at the earliest. However, a good first aid at the accident site is more important than 
reaching the hospital at the earliest.
	 1.	Remove smeared clothing
	 2.	Removal of metallic ornaments in and around acid burn area. 
	 3. 	Manual removal of solid chemicals with forceps or no touch technique.

126    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 4.	The principle of first aid is ‘dilution’. With a very few exceptions, diluting it by pouring 
water decreases the depth of injury. For acid burns, the area should be kept under 
running tap water for at least 30–60 minutes while for alkalis, it should be 1–2 hours.
	 5.	Thoroughly wash the burn site with running tap water. In case of acid: irrigate 
with water for 30–60 minutes or until the pain stops and in case of alkali for up to 
1–2 hours or until the pain stops. (Caution: Uninvolved areas should not come in 
contact with this effluent fluid. Also, the first-aid provider should safeguard himself 
from contact with chemicals.) No attempt should be made to search for an antidote, 
as this can waste precious time and the reaction is exothermic, with the endpoint 
being unknown. 
	 6.	Do not try to neutralize the chemical as it may cause exothermic reaction and more 
damage. The rescuer must be careful not to cause harm to himself/herself. 
	 7.	The alkalis are more dangerous than acids! If the burn occurs in an industrial 
setting, the workers must know the chemical(s) used, their antidotes to be made 
available in the factory and all this information supplied to the clinician on 
reaching the medical facility. 
	 8.	Remove chemicals from the scene or cap the source of chemical as many chemical 
may cause inhalation injury due to toxic chemical vapours.
	 9.	Victims with chemical burns of eye (see section on Injuries to eyes in the following text).
Management in the hospital
	 1.	Copious washing to continue till litmus test is negative. 
	 2.	Assess and manage chemical inhalation burns.
	 3.	Treatment of burn area as above. 
	 4.	Early excision is preferred for early and better recovery. These burns heal with bad 
scars and deformities of face and neck. These may require secondary surgeries for 
correction of deformities.
	 5.	Psychological support at every stage of management is an essential part of 
treatment and rehabilitation to get back to society.
Care of Healed Burn Wound
The depth of the burn and the surface involved influence the duration of the healing 
phase. Without infection, superficial burns heal rapidly. Burn scars undergo maturation, 
at first being red, raised and uncomfortable. They frequently become hypertrophic and 
form keloids. They flatten, soften and fade with time, but the process is unpredictable 
and can take up two years or more.
	 1.	All these actions are to be taken till the wounds mature, usually a period of 
1–2 years or rarely more. All patients are advised to protect newly regenerated 
neoepithelium from minor and major trauma till it becomes strong enough. It 
should be lubricated and massaged with bland oils (e.g. coconut oil and creams/
moisturizers twice daily after a bath as it tends to become dry and crack. Protect 
from sun light lest it should hyperpigment). 
	 2.	Many patients complain of itching in healed areas and need antihistaminic drugs 
at bedtime.

	 3.	All patients need psychological support. 
	 4.	Exercises and splinting (static and dynamic) to maintain full range of joint motion 
and prevent development of contractures. 
	 5.	To prevent hypertrophic scarring, customized pressure garments need to be worn 
almost 24 hours a day.
Post burn Sequelae
Despite best of modern treatment, a burn patient may be left with a large number of 
sequelae in the form of scars, contractures, loss of body parts (e.g. pinna, amputations), 
chronic non-healing scar ulcers, development of malignancy, etc. 
	 1.	Multiple plastic surgical reconstructive operations are required over a period of several 
years for their improvement so that the patient can successfully return to society.
	 2.	In children the scars cannot expand to keep pace with the growth of the child and 
may lead to contractures. Arrange for early surgical release of contractures before 
they interfere with growth. 
	 3.	Burn scars on the face lead to cosmetic deformity, ectropion and contractures about 
the lips. Ectropion can lead to exposure keratitis and blindness and lip deformity 
restricts eating and mouth care. Consider specialized care for these patients as skin 
grafting is often not sufficient to correct facial deformity. 
Recorrection and rehabilitation
	 1.	Splinting and physiotherapy prevents the majority of contractures particularly of 
hands and knees. 
	 2.	Surgical correction for contractures to restore optimum position. 
	 3.	Use of compression garment and sometimes excision and grafting followed by 
compression therapy helps in reducing hypertrophy and itching. 
	 4.	Provide psychological support and rehabilitation. 
Patient education
	
l Provide psychological support to the patient and relatives about the extent of burns, 
possible outcome and complications.
	
l Educate parents about prevention of accidents and burns in future by taking 
necessary preventive steps at home.
	
l Transport of patients to healthcare centre should be done at the earliest.
	
l The wound should be covered with a clean cloth and teach home management of 
burns. Once all wounds have healed – advise for massage with oil or moisturizer, active 
physiotherapy, cervical collar, splints and pressure garments.
	
l Inform the relatives about the medicolegal aspects of the injury and importance 
of evidence and dying declaration by the patient in case of homicidal burns or 
suspected dowry deaths.
	
l Deformities can be prevented by appropriate postoperative management such as 
postoperative lubrication, massage and pressure garments.
	
l Appropriate surgical management of the post burn defect and deformities is also 
possible, however, timely reconstruction of lost organ is desired.

SHOCK
Shock is a state of acute circulatory failure that leads to tissue hypoxaemia. Early 
recognition and treatment of shock, regardless of aetiology, decreases mortality and 
improves outcome.
SALIENT FEATURES
Shock is a progressive disorder which, if untreated, can lead to severe haemodynamic 
and metabolic deterioration, finally causing multiorgan failure. Stages of shock can 
be arbitrarily classified as: 
	
l Early compensated shock: Vital organ function is maintained by intrinsic 
compensatory mechanisms. Blood pressure is usually normal, there is increasing 
tachycardia and hypotension. The skin is cold and clammy, increased capillary refill 
time (>3 sec). If there is delay in treatment, it may lead to decompensated shock.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    129
	
l Decompensated shock: There is a fall in blood pressure and cardiac output. Features 
of peripheral poor perfusion are compounded with manifestations of vital organ 
impairment. Patients may have alteration of mentation (impaired cerebral perfusion), 
oliguria (renal hypoperfusion) and myocardial ischaemia (coronary flow 
impairment). Patient has acrocyanosis, cold and damp extremities and a pale look. 
If untreated, it can progress to an irreversible state of shock. 
	
l Irreversible shock: It is a term applied to the clinical situation in which even 
haemodynamic correction does not halt the progressive organ failure.

130    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Treatment (Stepwise management)
Fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone of shock resuscitation, although the choice and 
amount of fluid may vary based on the aetiology of shock.
	 1.	Immediately start oxygen therapy 4–6 L/min.
	 2.	Initial volume expansion measures. Venous access should be restored as early as 
possible (within 3–5 min). Peripheral veins should be tried first. If unable to do so, 
then central veins like jugular/femoral can be used. Establish 2 wide bore IV lines 
and infuse crystalloids.
	 3.	If venous access cannot be achieved in a short period, intraosseous infusion can be 
given into the bone marrow by putting a bone marrow needle.
	 4.	Nature of fluids: Normal saline/Ringer’s lactate (crystalloids) can be used initially 
in all types of hypovolaemic/haemorrhagic shocks. Colloids are used in conditions 
with capillary leaks, burns, dengue fever, nephrotic shock. Whole blood can be 
used as replacement in cases of trauma and haemorrhagic shock; packed cells are 
used in burn patients.
	 5.	Volume of fluids: Boluses of 20 mL/kg should be pushed in 5–7 minutes to 
restore blood volume quickly through three-way cannula. Features of recovery, 
i.e. warm skin and improved capillary filling time appear very quickly after fluid 
replacement. If these do not appear, give a second bolus.
	 6.	In case no improvement is seen and facilities for monitoring CVP are not 
available and there are no features of over-hydration (increased work of breathing, 
pulmonary crepitations, hepatomegaly, gallop rhythm), give another bolus and start 
inotrope (Table 2.5). If facilities for CVP are available, modify fluid therapy and 
inotropes according to CVP as given in Figure 2.10.

Monitoring
Assess and tailor for maintenance fluid requirements depending on the clinical 
condition. The aim is to improve peripheral perfusion. Monitor pulse rate, respiratory

aetiology
Use of inotropes
Inotropes are used to increase myocardial contractility. These are given as continuous 
intravenous infusions preferably with an infusion pump. Initial therapy is undertaken 
with either dopamine or dobutamine. If no response, more potent agents like adrenaline 
and noradrenaline can be used. Dose of dopamine/dobutamine generally required is 
5–10 mcg/kg/min, can be augmented to 20 mcg/kg/min (Table 2.4).

132    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Preparation of catecholamine infusions in infants and children can be done 
by following formula:
For Dopamine and Dobutamine, 6 × body weight in kg is the dose added to sufficient 
diluent to create a total volume of 100 mL. 1 mL/h of this fluid will deliver 1 mcg/kg/min. 
For adrenaline, 0.6 × body weight in kg is used in a similar diluent to deliver 0.1 mcg/kg/
min. Response to inotropes is measured in the same way as after fluid push. If a patient 
shows better peripheral perfusion, i.e. improved capillary filling time and warm extremities 
and blood pressure reaches within normal range, inotropes can be maintained for few hours, 
till underlying condition shows features of reversal. If the patient does not show signs of 
improvement, refer to a tertiary level centre where facilities for ventilation are available.
Metabolic corrections
Metabolic acidosis as a consequence of tissue ischaemia is the most important 
secondary complication. Correction is indicated only when marked acidosis (pH <7.2) 
is present. Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg can be used initially but subsequent doses 
should be based on base deficit (mEq = body weight in kg × base deficit × 0.3).
Ventilatory support may be required in critically sick patients showing signs of 
ventilatory fatigue/failure.
Cardiogenic shock
Cardiogenic shock is best viewed as pump failure and common causes are acute 
myocardial infarction in adults and dysrhythmias in children. Classic acute coronary 
syndrome symptoms and signs are combined with altered mental status, hypotension, 
arrhythmia, diminished pulses, dyspnoea, peripheral oedema, jugular venous distension 
and orthopnoea. Immediate treatment is same as mentioned above, ECG should be 
ordered within 10 minutes of presentation. However, invasive monitoring and advanced 
life support systems are required, refer to a tertiary level centre after initial resuscitation 
(see section on arrhythmia, myocardial infarction for specific treatment).
For anaphylactic shock, see section on Anaphylaxis.
Haemorrhagic shock
	 1.	Restore vascular volume as quickly as possible: Insert two peripheral IV lines 
(2 catheters 16G in adults)
	 2.	Replacement of lost blood with crystalloids 1.5:1 volume and colloids on a 1:1 
volume basis until blood transfusion threshold is met
	 3.	Control bleeding (compression, tourniquet, surgical haemostasis)
	 4.	Determine blood group
	 5.	Transfuse blood
Septic shock
Septic shock is a consequence of bacteraemia most commonly by gram-negative 
organisms, but gram-positive and viral infections can also cause it. It follows trimodal

FLUID AND ELECTROLYTE IMBALANCE AND 
REPLACEMENT (IN ADULTS)
Disturbances in fluid and electrolyte balance occur in a wide spectrum of diseases, 
are not confined to any particular field of medicine and are common following burns, 
trauma and major surgery.
Electrolyte abnormalities can cause cardiac arrhythmias or cardiopulmonary arrest. 
Life-threatening arrhythmias are associated most commonly with potassium disorders, 
particularly hyperkalaemia, and less commonly with disorders of serum calcium and 
magnesium. In some cases, therapy for life-threatening electrolyte disorders should start 
before laboratory results become available. The electrolyte values for definitions have been 
chosen as a guide to clinical decision-making. The precise values that trigger treatment 
decisions depend on the patient’s clinical condition and rate of change of electrolyte values.
The conventional and easy method of evaluating disturbances in fluid and 
electrolyte balance is the frequent measurement of the concentration of serum 
electrolytes. It is crucial to remember that intracellular and extracellular electrolytes 
are normally constant, and that major shifts in and out of ‘compartments’ can occur in 
disease with minimal changes in serum electrolyte. Compositional changes also involve 
disturbances in acid-base balance.

inadequate water intake or excessive water losses.

l Identify and treat the underlying cause. 
	
l Replace water deficit as assessed by degree of dehydration over a period of 48 hours

Over-rapid correction may lead to cerebral oedema. (Caution: Sodium-free solutions

HYPONATRAEMIA
Hyponatraemia is defined when plasma [Na+] <135 mEq/L. It is the most common 
disorder of body fluid and electrolyte balance. It occurs in up to 30% of hospitalized 
patients and can lead to a wide spectrum of clinical symptoms, from subtle 
(nausea without vomiting, confusion, headache) to severe or even life-threatening 
(cardiorespiratory distress, somnolence, seizures). Severe symptoms of hyponatraemia 
are caused by brain oedema and increased intracranial pressure. 
Causes of hyponatraemia are those associated with a reduced, normal or increased 
extracellular fluid volume. It can be hypovolemic hyponatraemia such as diarrhoea, 
vomiting, heat stroke where there is sodium loss as well as excess water loss. It 
can be euvolemic like SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone), 
hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency and hypervolemic hyponatraemia like 
cirrhosis of liver, congestive cardiac failure and nephrotic syndrome where excessive 
water retention causes dilutional hyponatraemia.

Treatment is required when plasma [Na+] <125 mEq/L.
	 1.	For hypovolemic hyponatremia, NS infusion to correct volume loss as well as 
hypertonic saline (3% saline) to be infused very slowly, e.g. rate of correction of 
plasma [Na+] is 0.5 mEq/L/h to avoid osmotic demyelinating syndrome (central 
pontine myelinolysis).
	 2.	Treatment of euvolemic hyponatraemia is fluid restriction and 3% saline infusion 
as above.
	 3.	For hypervolemic hyponatraemia fluid restriction, diuretics and tolvaptan 
15–30 mg once daily may be given. The correction of hyponatraemia is up to 
plasma [Na+] 130 mEq/L.

HYPOKALAEMIA 
It is defined as serum potassium <3.5 mEq/L. Clinical symptoms include muscle 
weakness, hypotonia, respiratory difficulty, paralytic ileus, leg cramps. ECG changes 
include ST depression, T-wave flattening/inversion, U waves and arrhythmias. Pulseless 
electrical activity or asystole may develop.

l Identify and treat the underlying cause. 
	
l Correct the deficit with potassium supplements at 40 mEq/L of fluids. The amount 
of fluid is dictated by the hydration status of the child. Potassium chloride may be 
given orally (15 mL = 20 mEq). Intravenous correction with KCl (0.5–1 mEq/kg 
over 1 hour) is required when patient is unable to take orally, serum potassium is 
<2.5 mEq/L, has respiratory paralysis, or in the presence of arrhythmia.
	
l Correct the potassium deficit over a period of 24 hours.
	
l Potassium-rich foods such as banana or fruit juice may be advised on a long-term 
basis, especially in undernourished children.
HYPERKALAEMIA
It is defined as serum potassium >5.5 mEq/L. Symptoms include paraesthesias, 
weakness, ascending paralysis, respiratory failure and tetany. ECG changes are 
characteristic including high-peaked T waves, prolonged PR interval, widened QRS 
complex, heart blocks and arrhythmias in that order. It is life-threatening and can cause 
sudden death, requires immediate therapy.

Exclude pseudohyperkalaemia due to lab error, haemolysis, leucocytosis, thrombocytosis, 
repeated clenching of fist during phlebotomy and traumatic venipuncture.
	 1.	Mild hyperkalaemia: (Serum K+ 5.5–6 mEq/L.) Stop the potassium intake and 
offending drugs such as potassium-sparing diuretics, ACEI, NSAIDs, recheck 
potassium levels. Consider correction of acidosis and intravascular volume.

136    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Diuretics – Inj. Frusemide 40–80 mg IV and Kayexalate 15–30 g in 50–100 mL of 
20% Sorbitol orally or by retention enema. 
	 2.	Moderate hyperkalaemia: (Serum K+ 6–7 mEq/L or peaked T waves.) Administer 
a glucose insulin infusion (0.5 g/kg glucose with 0.3 U regular insulin/g glucose, 
over 1 hour; close monitoring of glucose every 30–60 minutes) and/or a sodium 
bicarbonate infusion (2 mEq/kg over 5–10 min), in addition to the measures 
already mentioned above. Can be repeated 4–6 hourly. Note: Do not give sodium 
bicarbonate simultaneously with calcium in the same IV line or at the same time.
	 3.	Severe hyperkalaemia: (Serum K+ >7 mEq/L or ECG changes apart from tall 
T waves.) Urgently administer intravenous 10% calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/kg over 
5–10 minutes. This immediately reverses the cardiac effects of hyperkalaemia. This 
should be followed up with measures for moderate hyperkalaemia. Intravenous 
Salbutamol (4 mcg/kg in 5 mL water) or nebulized Salbutamol (2.5–5.0 mg) 
given over 15–20 minutes also acts rapidly to lower serum K+. Dialysis has to be 
done in case hyperkalamia is refractory to therapy as in renal failure. Consider 
Hydrocortisone 1–2 mg/kg IV to consider if suspicion of adrenal insufficiency (like 
associated shock, hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis).
	 4.	Monitoring of the therapy should be done with ECG and serum potassium levels 
after 1–2 h of initial intervention following which frequency can be reduced 
depending on the potassium levels and reversibility of the cause.
	 5.	After emergency management and stabilization of hyperkalaemia, the patient should 
be hospitalized. Once the potassium level is restored to normal, discontinue potassium-
lowering therapies and monitor serum potassium level daily. Further work-up should 
be initiated to determine the inciting cause and to prevent future episodes.
Common causes of hyperkalaemia include:
	
l Chronic kidney disease
	
l Diabetes ketoacidosis
	
l Congestive heart failure
	
l Medications: K+-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory 
drugs, potassium supplements, penicillin derivatives, succinylcholine, heparin 
therapy (especially in patients with other risk factors), β-blockers.
Less common causes can include:
	
l Massive injury resulting in muscle damage
	
l Burns over large parts of the body
	
l High-volume blood transfusions
	
l HIV and certain other infections
	
l Alcoholism or heavy drug use that breaks down muscle fibres, releasing potassium.

Prevention of electrolyte disorders
Identify and treat life-threatening electrolyte abnormalities before cardiac arrest 
occurs. Remove any precipitating factors (e.g. drugs) and monitor electrolyte values 
to prevent recurrence of the abnormality. Monitor renal function in patients at risk of 
electrolyte disorders (e.g. chronic kidney disease, cardiac failure). In haemodialysis 
patients, review the dialysis prescription regularly to avoid inappropriate electrolyte 
shifts during treatment.
For hypocalcaemia and hypercalcaemia, see Chapter 11.
VOLUME CHANGES: VOLUME DEFICIT
I. Obvious causes
Vomiting, diarrhoea, intestinal fistulae, nasogastric suction, fluid loss following 
burns, sequestration of fluid in soft tissue injuries and infections, diuretics, renal 
disease/adrenal insufficiency.
II. Less obvious causes
Unsuspected inadequate fluid intake, fluid loss through excessive sweating as in high 
fever, hot humid temperature, haemodialysis, haemofiltration from surgical incisions 
and in diseases like tetanus.

The first principle is to restore circulating volume through infusion of intravenous fluids. 
Once this is satisfactorily achieved, disturbances in electrolytes and acid-base balance, if 
present, need to be rectified. Various fluids used for volume replacement are given below.
A. Replacement fluids
	 1.	Replacement fluids are used to replace abnormal loss of blood, plasma or other 
extracellular fluids as first line treatment for hypovolaemia in: 
a.	 Treatment of patients with established hypovolaemia, e.g. haemorrhagic shock. 
b.	Maintenance of normovolaemia in patients with ongoing fluid losses, 
e.g. surgical blood loss.
	 2.	Intravenous replacement fluids are the first line of treatment for hypovolaemia. 
Initial treatment with these fluids may be lifesaving and provides some time to 
control bleeding and obtain blood for transfusion if it becomes necessary.
	 3.	Crystalloid maintenance fluids, which contain dextrose, are not suitable for use 
as replacement fluids. Only crystalloid solutions with a similar concentration of 
sodium to plasma (NS or balanced salt) solutions (Ringer’s lactate or Hartmann’s 
solutions) are effective as replacement fluids. These should be available in all 
hospitals where intravenous replacement fluids are used. Fluid and electrolyte 
requirements in adults and children are shown in Table 2.6.
	 4.	Crystalloids should be infused in a volume at least 1.5:1 ratio in order to correct 
hypovolaemia.

138    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 5.	All colloid solutions (albumins, dextran, gelatins and hydroxyethyl starch 
solutions) are replacement fluids. However, they have not been shown to be 
superior to crystalloids in resuscitation.
	 6.	Colloid solutions should be infused in a volume equal to the blood volume deficit.
	 7.	Plasma should never be used as a replacement fluid.
	 8.	Plain water should never be infused intravenously. It will cause haemolysis and 
will probably be fatal.
	 9.	In addition to the intravenous route, the intraosseous, oral, rectal or subcutaneous 
routes can be used for the administration of fluids, blood and certain drugs. 
However, with the exception of intraosseous route, other routes are generally 
unsuitable in severely hypovolaemic patients.
	10.	Rectal fluids are administered through a plastic or rubber enema tube which is 
inserted into the rectum and connected to a bag or bottle of fluid. The fluid rate can 
be controlled by using a drip giving set, if necessary. The fluids used need not be 
sterile. A safe and effective solution for a rectal rehydration is 1 L of clean drinking 
water with a teaspoon of table salt.
	11.	Subcutaneous fluids: Occasionally, when other routes of administration of fluids 
are unavailable, a subcutaneous infusion can be used. A cannula or needle is 
inserted into the subcutaneous tissue (the abdominal wall is a preferred site) and 
sterile fluids are administered in a conventional manner. Do not give Dextrose-
containing solutions subcutaneously as they can cause sloughing of tissues.
	12.	Oral and nasogastric fluids: Oral rehydration can often be used in mildly 
hypovolaemic patients if the oral route is not contraindicated. Do not use if:
–	 The patient is unconscious.
–	 The patient has gastrointestinal lesions or reduced gut motility, e.g. obstruction.
–	 General anaesthesia and surgery are planned imminently.

B. Maintenance fluids
Maintenance fluids are fluids used to replace the normal physiological loss that occurs 
in a patient through skin, lung, faeces and urine. Since a considerable proportion of 
the loss is water, maintenance fluids are mainly composed of water in the form of a 
dextrose solution. Some electrolytes may also be included in these solutions.
All maintenance solutions are crystalloid solutions. Some examples of crystalloids 
that are suitable as maintenance fluids are 50% dextrose and 4% dextrose in sodium 
chloride 0.18%.
VOLUME EXCESS
Volume excess is often iatrogenic when the fluid intake has consistently exceeded the 
output. Excessive intravenous infusions of saline and blood transfusions are important 
causes of hypervolaemia. Renal insufficiency, congestive heart failure, liver disease and 
other causes of sodium retention or excessive sodium administration can all produce 
increase in extracellular fluid content and hypervolaemia.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Oedema, ascites, pleural effusion, neck veins full, pulmonary congestion, 
hyperdynamic circulation with tachycardia, warm skin and a bounding pulse. 
	
l Increase in the systolic pressure and pulse pressure. 
	
l CVP >12 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) >20 mmHg in 
the presence of pulmonary oedema.

In cases of moderate volume excess, salt restriction, restriction of fluid intake and 
the use of frusemide as a diuretic. Fulminant pulmonary oedema secondary to 
overhydration from overtransfusion of blood or fluids is more appropriately dealt 
with by phlebotomy in stages so that PCWP (pulmonary capillary wedge pressure) is 
reduced below 15 mmHg. Rarely, ultrafiltration (dialysis) may be required.

SEPSIS
Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host 
response to infection. Sepsis is a clinical syndrome associated with invasion of blood 
stream by microorganisms and is shaped by pathogen factors and host factors (e.g. sex, 
race and other genetic determinants, age, comorbidities, environment) with characteristics 
that evolve over time. It may be associated with infection at specific sites (e.g. lungs, 
urinary tract, gastrointestinal tract) or there may be no clear originating focus. In 
hospital settings, gram negative infections predominate with Escherichia coli, Klebsiella 
pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa being the most common pathogens.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Infection: A suspected or proven infection caused by any pathogen, or a clinical 
syndrome associated with a high probability of infection. Evidence of infection 
includes positive findings on clinical examination, imaging or laboratory tests (e.g. 
leucocytes in a normally sterile body fluid, perforated viscus, chest radiograph 
consistent with pneumonia, petechial or purpuric rash, or purpura fulminans) or a 
positive culture, tissue stain, or polymerase chain reaction test.
	
l Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host 
response to infection. 
	
l Sepsis: Organ system dysfunctions are assessed with an increase in the Sequential 
Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score ≥2 points consequent to the infection. 
The baseline SOFA score can be assumed to be zero in patients not known to have 
preexisting organ dysfunction (Table 2.7). A SOFA score ≥2 is associated with an 
in-hospital mortality greater than 10%. Failure to meet 2 or more quick SOFA or 
SOFA criteria should not lead to a deferral of investigation or treatment of infection 
or to a delay in any other aspect of care deemed necessary.
	 Septic shock is a subset of sepsis particularly associated with profound circulatory, 
cellular and metabolic abnormalities posing a greater risk of mortality than with 
sepsis alone. Patients with septic shock can be clinically identified by a persisting 
hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg and having a 
serum lactate level >2 mmol/L (18 mg/dL) despite adequate volume resuscitation. 
Sepsis with cardiovascular dysfunction persisting after at least 40 mL/kg of fluid 
resuscitation in 1 hour.

142    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Refractory septic shock: Fluid refractory septic shock – shock persisting 
after ≥60 mL/kg of fluid resuscitation. Catecholamine-resistant septic shock – 
shock persists despite treatment with catecholamines (i.e. dopamine or adrenaline 
[epinephrine] infusion, or both, or noradrenaline [norepinephrine] infusion).
	
l The initial clinical presentation of sepsis in children may be non-specific 
(especially in younger age groups).
	
l Severe sepsis is redundant now and Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome 
(SIRS) being nonspecific is no longer used to define sepsis.

Progression to organ failure and shock is often rapid. Goals and principles of treatment 
in septic shock are: 
	
l Early recognition and treatment. When sepsis is suspected on clinical grounds, start 
investigations and treatment for sepsis, including fluid resuscitation.
	
l Early and adequate antibiotics – start antibiotics in proper dosage and spectrum as 
early as possible,
	
l Source control – early identification of the source of infection, and treat with 
antimicrobial therapy, surgery, or both
	
l Early hemodynamic resuscitation and continued support – resuscitate the patient, 
using supportive measures to correct hypoxia, hypotension, and impaired tissue 
oxygenation (hypoperfusion)
	
l Maintain adequate organ system function, guided by cardiovascular monitoring, and 
interrupt the progression to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS)
Non-pharmacological (immediate)
	 1.	Care of airway and breathing as given in section on CPR.
	 2.	After initial assessment, a central venous catheter (CVC) should be inserted in 
patients with septic shock.
	 3.	If hypoperfusion exists, early restoration of perfusion prevents or limit multiple 
organ dysfunction as well as reduce mortality. Treatment of multiorgan failure in 
sepsis is primarily supportive. Correct metabolic abnormalities, if any.
	 4.	First priority is source control and obtaining cultures. Cultures should be obtained 
prior to administration of antibiotics when feasible.
	 5.	Removal or drainage of a focal source of infection. Indwelling intravenous catheter, 
Foley’s catheter, etc. should be replaced if considered as a source.
	 6.	Maintain body temperature between 36.5°C and 37.5°C (97.5–99.5°F)
	 7.	Target-glucose <180 mg/dL. Bicarbonate not recommended when pH >7.15.
	 8.	Mechanical ventilation: Target-a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg of ideal body weight, 
plateau pressure of <30 cm H2O, PEEP – increase with FiO2 as per ARDSnet 
protocol. Prone over supine position in patients with sepsis-induced ARDS and 
Pa/FiO2 ratio <150.

	 9.	An initial brief history and examination, as well as laboratory, microbiologic 
(including blood cultures), and imaging studies are often obtained simultaneously 
while access is being established and the airway stabilized.
	10.	Quickly obtain the following laboratory investigations (within 45 minutes of 
presentation) but should not delay the administration of fluids and antibiotics: 
Complete blood counts with differential, chemistries, liver function tests, and 
coagulation studies including D-dimer level, ABG analysis, urinalysis. 
	11.	Early blood culture (two sets of blood cultures aerobic and anaerobic cultures 
drawn from two separate sites before antimicrobial administration). Avoid drawing 
blood for cultures through an indwelling or central intravascular catheter whenever 
possible, since ports are frequently colonized with skin flora. 
	12.	Microbiologic cultures from suspected sources (e.g. sputum, urine, intravascular 
catheter, wound or surgical site, body fluids) from readily accessible sites.
	13.	Imaging targeted at the suspected site of infection is warranted (e.g. chest 
radiography, computed tomography of chest and/or abdomen).
	14.	General care of skin, orodental hygiene and nutrition supplementation should be 
taken care of, in prolonged severe sepsis.

1.	Oxygen therapy – 2–4 L/min with catheter/mask (to keep SaO2 >95%).
	 2.	Intravenous fluids – to be guided by haemodynamic status. 30 mL/kg of IV 
crystalloid fluid (NS or balanced salt solution) within the first 3 hours of sepsis 
presentation. If in shock, aggressive fluid therapy and drugs as mentioned in 
section on shock to maintain urinary output at more than 1 mL/kg/h (see section 
on Shock). Consider 4% albumin in refractory hypotension.
	 3.	In patients who remain hypotensive despite adequate fluid resuscitation, give 
norepinephrine 2–12 mcg/min (no true maximum dose) to maintain mean arterial 
pressure (MAP) of 65 mmHg. Avoid dopamine. Add epinephrine, if norepinephrine 
is inadequate, and vasopressin (up to 0.03) if not at target MAP or to taper 
norepinephrine. 
	 4.	Consider inotropes in low cardiac output states, i.e. septic cardiomyopathy, which 
can be common in these patients.
	 5.	No steroids unless refractory septic shock in which fluids and vasopressors fail to 
achieve haemodynamic stability.
	 6.	Packed RBC/blood transfusion indicated in patients only when haemoglobin 
<7 g/dL.
	 7.	Assess and restore end-organ perfusion.
	 8.	Antibiotics: Begin broad spectrum, empiric antibiotic therapy within 1 hour in 
septic shock after taking samples for culture from blood and other relevant sites. 
Choice of antibiotics depends on suspected organism and that penetrate in adequate 
concentrations into tissues presumed to be the source of infection.

Follow-up and monitoring
Continuous monitoring of pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure, capillary filling time, 
urinary output and neurological status should be done for early detection of septic shock 
or multiorgan failure. Patients should be referred to tertiary level centre, if very sick or 
shows no signs of improvement after initial therapy.
Therapeutic endpoints of resuscitation of septic shock in children:
	
l Normalization of the heart rate
	
l Capillary refill of <2 seconds
	
l Well-felt dorsalis pedis pulses with no differential between peripheral and central 
pulses
	
l Warm extremities
	
l Normal range of systolic pressure and pulse pressure
	
l Urine output >1 mL/kg/h
	
l Return to baseline mental status tone and posture
	
l Normal range respiratory rate
	
l Other endpoints that have been widely used in adults and may logically apply 
to children include central venous pressure of 8–12 mmHg. Resuscitation of the 
circulation should target a central or mixed venous oxyhaemoglobin saturation 
(ScvO2 or SvO2, respectively) of ≥70%. Other common goals include a central 
venous pressure (CVP) 8–12 mmHg, a mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥65 mmHg, 
and a urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg per hour.

Ventilation
	
l Start supplemental oxygen if the peripheral SpO2 is < 92% and maintain SpO2 not 
higher than 96%.
	
l In patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (acute respiratory distress 
syndrome [ARDS]) despite conventional oxygen therapy, high flow nasal canula 
(HFNC) is preferred over conventional oxygen therapy and non-invasive positive 
pressure ventilation (NIPPV). If HFNC is not available and there is no urgent 
indication for endotracheal intubation, give a trial of NIPPV with close monitoring 
and short-interval assessment for worsening of respiratory failure.
	
l Closely monitor patients receiving NIPPV or HFNC for worsening of respiratory 
status and consider early intubation in a controlled setting, if worsening occurs.

l In mechanically ventilated adults with COVID-19 and ARDS, low Vt ventilation 
(Vt 4–8 mL/kg of predicted body weight) is recommended over higher tidal volumes 
(Vt >8 mL/kg) targeting plateau pressure (Pplat) of <30 cm H2O. Avoid frequent 
disconnection of ventilator circuit, nebulization or metered dose inhaler.
	
l For mechanically ventilated adults with COVID-19 and moderate to severe ARDS, 
higher positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) strategy is used over a lower PEEP 
strategy. If a higher PEEP strategy (i.e. PEEP > 10 cm H2O) is used, monitor patients 
for barotrauma. Intermittent boluses of neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) to 
facilitate protective lung ventilation. Continuous NMBA infusion for up to 48 hours 
in case of persistent ventilator dyssynchrony or the need for ongoing deep sedation, 
prone ventilation, or persistently high plateau pressures. Daily assessment for weaning 
and early extubation; enteral nutrition within 24 hours, achieve full feeds by 48 hours.
	
l Inhaled pulmonary vasodilator is suggested as a rescue therapy in case of severe 
ARDS, and hypoxemia despite optimizing ventilation and other rescue strategies.
	
l ECMO, if available in case of refractory hypoxemia despite optimizing ventilation, 
use of rescue therapies, and proning.

and duration based on clinical severity) and pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis and 
therapeutic anticoagulation in severely ill or critical patients.

guidance from the Government.

STRIDOR
Stridor is a harsh sound produced by turbulent air flow due to obstruction the larynx, 
trachea and bronchi.
	
l Inspiratory stridor is a low-pitched sound which is produced in supraglottis and 
tracheal tissues.
	
l Expiratory stridor is a high-pitched sound which is produced in lower respiratory 
tract like bronchi and bronchioles.
	
l Biphasic stridor is produced in the rigid walls of rima glottidis, subglottis and 
trachea.
Common causes of stridor are as follows:
A. Congenital
	 1.	Nasal causes such as choanal atresia, septum deformities, alar collapse
	 2.	Craniofacial anomalies like Pierre Robin syndrome, Apert syndromes
	 3.	Macroglossia due to Down’s syndrome and Beckwith’s syndrome 
	 4.	Congenital laryngeal abnormalities like laryngomalacia, laryngeal webs, laryngeal 
cysts, laryngeal clefts, vocal cord paralysis
	 5.	Subglottic stenosis
	 6.	Tracheal stenosis and tracheomalacia
B. Acquired
	 1.	In children
	
l Acute: Foreign body aspiration, airway burns, bacterial tracheitis, epiglottitis, 
anaphylaxis, croup, peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess
	
l Chronic: Vocal cord paralysis, laryngeal spasm, neoplasms
	 2.	In adults 
	
l Croup 
	
l Allergies 
	
l Angioneurotic oedema
	
l Laryngeal trauma
	
l Laryngeal tumours
	
l Ludwig’s angina

It is an acute infection of the larynx and trachea and is usually caused by viruses. In 
children, it may lead to respiratory obstruction. It usually presents in second year of 
life. The child presents with barking cough, stridor, low-grade fever, hoarse voice. The 
symptoms are often increased at night. Assessment and management of croup is given 
in Table 2.9.

l Avoid upsetting the child 
	
l Leave child with parent in a comfortable position.

154    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Do NOT insert tongue depressor, since this may precipitate complete obstruction.
	
l Do NOT attempt IV access or blood tests.
	
l Do NOT ask for a chest or lateral neck X-ray.
	
l Do NOT force an oxygen mask over face.
	
l Do NOT leave the child unsupervised.
	
l Maintain airway by positioning the patient in a lateral position with neck slightly 
extended.
	
l Gentle suction of secretions, if required.
	
l Oxygen by Ventimask/hood at the rate of 4–6 L/min.
	
l With the supportive and specific therapy, need for endotracheal intubation/
tracheostomy may arise rarely. In case, the patient is deteriorating steadily despite 
therapy, elective intubation/tracheostomy should be done to prevent respiratory 
failure.

l No role of antibiotics in uncomplicated croup as it has a viral aetiology. Antitussives 
(codeine) have no proven effect on the course or severity of croup and interfere with 
the assessments due to sedation. Effect of humidified air on the severity of croup 
has not been proven.
	
l Observe for 4 hours post-adrenaline. If good improvement, consider discharge once 
stridor free at rest with instructions to parents to monitor at home and come back to 
the hospital if there is worsening of symptoms. If deterioration after improvement, 
give further doses of adrenaline and consider admission/transfer as appropriate. If no 
improvement, reconsider diagnosis such as acute upper airway obstruction.
B. ACUTE EPIGLOTTITIS
Acute epiglottitis is usually caused by Streptococcus pyogenes and Haemophilus 
influenzae type b (Hib). It is potentially a life-threatening condition. The widespread 
use of the Hib vaccine has significantly reduced the incidence of epiglottitis caused 
by Hib. Lateral X-ray of soft tissue neck may show swollen epiglottis (thumb sign). It 
is a medical emergency; airway and specific therapy must be introduced aggressively.

1.	Non-pharmacological treatment as above in acute laryngotracheitis.
	 2.	Allow the child to remain in its favoured position and usually the child is 
comfortable in a sitting position (Tripod sign). The child should be admitted 
or referred to a tertiary care centre where someone skilled in intubation and 
tracheostomy is available with PICU.
	
	Give humidified oxygen and administer IV antibiotics when airway is secured.
	 3.	Inj. Cefotaxime 100 mg/kg/day divided into 3 doses. 
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day (maximum dose 4 g/day) in 2 divided doses. 
	
	If cephalosporins are not available, Tab. Chloramphenicol 500 mg 6 hourly.
	
	In Children 100 mg/kg/day divided into 6 hourly doses.

C. DIPHTHERIA
It is usually seen in non-immunized children or partially immunized children.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The most common presentation is fever, toxaemia and sore throat with greyish 
white patch on the tonsils and/or pharynx which bleeds on removal of membrane 
and toxaemia.
	
l May present as hoarseness, stridor but laryngeal examination may show a 
membrane-like structure (pseudomembrane), removal of which leads to bleeding. 
	
l Large cervical lymph nodes (bull’s neck appearance).
	
l Common complications are palatal palsy, III nerve palsy, polyneuritis and 
myocarditis.
	
l Confirmation of the diagnosis on Albert’s or Neisser’s stain of the material from 
beneath the membrane reveals club shaped organisms in palisades or as individual 
cells at sharp angles to each other giving a ‘Chinese-letter’ pattern.
	
l For culture, transport to the laboratory in non-nutritive, moisture reducing 
selective transport medium. Diphtheria bacilli grow fairly quickly on selective 
media such as Loeffler’s slant and Tellurite agar.

1.	Supportive treatment as above in acute laryngitis.
	 2.	Immediately refer the child to infectious diseases hospital under supervision and 
oxygen therapy without waiting for smear results. In an immunized patient or 
in mild disease or where the diagnosis is doubtful, treatment may be deferred 
for a couple of hours till smear results are available. In case the child cannot be 
transferred, droplet isolation (separation of patient beds by 1 metre and use of 
surgical mask within 1 metre of the patient) till three consecutive throat cultures 
are negative should be done and following measures should be taken immediately:
	 3.	Inj. Diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) diluted 1:20 in isotonic saline and given at a 
rate of 1 mL/min 20,000–40,000 IU, IV (after test dose) for pharyngeal and 
laryngeal involvements with disease present for <48 hours; 40,000–60,000 IU for 
nasopharyngeal infections; 80,000–100,000 IU for diffuse involvement that has 
been present for >3 days/neck oedema/tachycardia/collapse/breathlessness.
	
	DAT test dose – place one drop of a 1:10 dilution of DAT on the conjunctival sac 
Or Scratch skin test 0.02 mL of 1:100 dilution is placed on a scratch (procedure 
consists of placing 1 drop of a 1:100 dilution of DAT on the skin and then making a 
0.64-cm (1/4-inch) scratch through the drop) Or intradermal skin test 0.02 mL of a 
1:100 dilution of the DAT is given as an intradermal injection. Read intradermal skin 
test after 20 minutes. A control test using 0.9% sodium chloride injection facilitates 
interpretation of the results. A positive reaction is defined as signs of conjunctivitis 
or tearing or more than 3 mm of erythema at the site of intradermal injection. 
Keep resuscitation kit ready since negative intradermal, scratch or conjunctival

156    Standard Treatment Guidelines
sensitivity test does not completely rules out systemic sensitivity. When the skin or 
conjunctival test is positive or a doubtful reaction occurs, the risk of administering 
diphtheria antitoxin should be weighed against the risk of withholding it, If 
diphtheria antitoxin must be used, desensitization should be performed.
	
	Note: Store DAT injection in dark between 2° and 8°C. DO NOT FREEZE.
	 4.	Inj. Crystalline penicillin 1–1.5 lakh units/kg/day divided into 4 doses for 14 days.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Procaine penicillin 300,000 units in children <10 kg and 600,000 units in 
children >10 kg IM once a day for 14 days.
	
	Or
	
	If hypersensitive to penicillin, Syr. Erythromycin 40–50 mg/kg/day divided into 
4 doses for 14 days.
	
	Rifampicin and clindamycin can be used in patients allergic to penicillin.
	 5.	IV saline infusion over 60 minutes.
Confirm eradication of the organism by two consecutive negative cultures after 
treatment is completed.
Monitoring and follow-up
	 1.	Watch the child for altered sensorium, degree of stridor, pulse rate, respiratory rate 
and for other features of respiratory distress like intercostal recession, etc.
	 2.	Laryngeal examination should not be done until facilities for intubation are 
available because it might lead to sudden respiratory arrest. 
	 3.	If child develops stridor at rest, hospitalize immediately.
	 4.	Increasing respiratory distress with alteration of sensorium or cyanosis may be an 
indication for intubation.
Treatment of close contacts (all household members and those in direct contact of 
oral secretions of the patient)
	 1.	Take throat sample for culture
	 2.	Antibiotics irrespective of immune status. Inj. Benzathine penicillin 600,000 units 
(<6 years) and 1,200,000 units (>6 years) single dose IM Or oral Erythromycin 
40 mg/kg/day (maximum 1 g/day) for 7–10 days.
	 3.	Complete immunization schedule in unimmunized contacts. Administer booster 
dose of the vaccine (DPT in those below 7 and Tdap in those above 7 years) in 
contact who have received primary immunization but no toxoid in the past 5 years.
Patient education
	
l Advise bed rest for at least 2–3 weeks due to risk of myocarditis.
	
l Avoid overuse and misuse of voice.
	
l If stridor worsens or is noticed at rest, the patient should immediately report to the 
nearest health facility.
	
l Children with diphtheria should be completely immunized after recovery of 
the current episode and contact to be immunized immediately (see section on 
Immunization in Chapter 19).
	
l Those who present late for immunization should be given 3 doses of the trivalent 
vaccine at 4–8 weeks interval and a booster dose 6–12 months after the third dose. The

Chapter 2  Emergencies    157
second booster is not required if the first booster was given after 4 years; if the first 
booster was given before 4 years the second booster is given between 4 and 6 years. 
	
l Those individuals unimmunized till 7 years should be given two doses of the 
Td vaccine and 1 dose of Tdap vaccine at 0, 4–8 weeks and 6–12.

TRAUMA
Injury and trauma, often used interchangeably, represent a major health problem 
worldwide. Injuries cause nearly 16,000 daily deaths globally, constituting 12% of the 
global disease burden. Road traffic injuries contribute significantly, comprising 22.8% of 
injury-related deaths. Lower- and middle-income countries, including India, contribute 
to 90% of injury mortality, highlighting global outcome disparities in trauma between 
high-, lower-, and middle-income nations. Injuries particularly impact the productive 
youth, causing excess mortality and significant disability, ranking as the third leading 
cause of mortality and the primary cause of death among 1 to 40-year-olds.
Accidental injury is a major cause of mortality and morbidity in India, with the 
country accounting for 1% of global vehicles but contributing to 6% of total road 
accidents. The World Health Organization (WHO) projects a concerning rise in road 
accidents in India, foreseeing 546,000 deaths and 15,314,000 disability-adjusted life 
years lost by 2030.
Pre-Hospital Care
Airway management: If patient has a reduced conscious level and patient’s 
airway reflexes are absent, consider using a supraglottic device (laryngeal 
mask airway, proseal, i-gel, etc.). Use basic airway manoeuvres such as inserting 
Guedel’s airway and bag-and-mask ventilation if the patient’s airway reflexes are 
present or supraglottic device placement is not possible. 
Chest trauma: Clinically assess for presence of pneumothorax for the purpose of triage 
or intervention. In patients with an open pneumothorax, cover the open pneumothorax 
with a simple occlusive dressing and observe for the development of a tension 
pneumothorax. 
Haemorrhage: 
	
l Use simple dressings (sterile gauze pads) with direct pressure to control external 
haemorrhage. In patients with major limb trauma use a tourniquet or bandage roll, rubber 
tubing, crepe bandage, if direct pressure has failed to control life-threatening haemorrhage.

158    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l If active bleeding is suspected from a pelvic fracture after blunt high-energy trauma: 
Apply a pelvic binder.
	
l Inj. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min followed by 1 g over 8 hours as soon as 
possible in patients with major trauma and active or suspected active bleeding. 
Note: Do not use intravenous tranexamic acid more than 3 hours after injury in 
patients with major trauma.
	
l Use peripheral intravenous access, titrate volume resuscitation with Ringer’s lactate 
or Normal saline to maintain a palpable central pulse (carotid or femoral). 
	
l Minimize ongoing heat loss in patients with major trauma. Use blankets for reducing 
heat loss. 
Pain management: Assess pain regularly in patients with major trauma using a pain 
assessment scale. For patients with major trauma, after medical consultation Morphine 
IV and adjust dose as needed to achieve adequate pain relief.
Spine trauma: Carry out full in-line spinal immobilization by placing two blocks on 
either side of the head. Intravenous fluid bottles can also be used to prevent movement. 
Fractures: Do not irrigate open fractures of the long bones, hindfoot or midfoot. Use 
saline soaked dressing covered with an occlusive layer. In patients with suspected long 
bone fractures of the legs, apply a rigid or malleable splint or adjacent leg as a splint if 
the suspected fracture is above the knee.
INTITIAL MANAGEMENT AND CARE OF 
A TRAUMA PATIENT
An individual brought with history of trauma can have injury to one or multiple areas 
of the body, some of which could be life threatening. Therefore, one should adopt a 
system to quickly evaluate the patient, investigate and treat in order to save life and 
salvage function.
	
l The primary objective in individual management of a patient with trauma is to first 
recognize and treat injuries that are life threatening. This has been called the primary 
survey. The primary survey is conducted simultaneously along with the resuscitation 
measures (horizontal and not vertical chain of actions).
	
l Assessment of non-life-threatening injuries or injuries which can wait follows the 
primary survey and resuscitation of vital functions. This is known as the secondary 
survey. A detailed head-to-toe, front-to-back examination is done in secondary 
survey. The patients back is examined by logrolling keeping in mind that he/she 
might have spinal injury, which might worsen while examination.
1. PRIMARY SURVEY
Shout and talk to the patient as soon as you take over care from pre-hospital paramedics, 
police, or relatives. This maneuver will help you to broadly assess two things:
	
l Airway Patency or airway not threatened.
	
l Alertness on AVPU Scale (Alert, responding to verbal stimulus, painful stimulus, 
Unresponsive), anything less than Alert should alert the physician.

I.  Triage: Sorting of patients according to salvageability and available resources
The principle of Triage is based on the need for treatment and the available resources 
when encountered with a large number of patients requiring treatment as in mass 
casualty situations. Triage is performed at the site of injury, at the hospital and for 
transfer to a tertiary care level (Fig. 2.12). The injured should be evaluated for 
	
l Life-threatening injuries involving the airway, circulation and central nervous 
system
	
l Serious but not immediately life-threatening trauma, such as hemorrhage, 
fractures and soft-tissue injuries
	
l Patients not requiring immediate attention. On the basis of the severity of injuries, 
the casualties are separated into priority groups

Priority I (immediate resuscitation [Red]): Casualties requiring immediate 
resuscitation and urgent surgery, e.g.
	
l Multiple system injury

Priority II (potentially life-threatening injuries [YELLOW]): Cases requiring

These are as follows:

l Second: Abdominal haemorrhage
	
l Third: Pelvic haemorrhage
	
l Fourth: Extremity haemorrhage
