THORACIC TRAUMA
Thoracic trauma is responsible for one-fourth of civilian trauma deaths. Two-thirds 
of these deaths occur after reaching the hospital. Deaths can be prevented by prompt 
transportation, diagnosis and correct management.
Most thoracic traumas do not require thoracotomy but rather simple life-saving 
manoeuvres of airway control, rapid infusion of fluids and tube thoracostomy are 
needed. The trauma can be penetrating or blunt.
Blunt trauma causes injury to the chest by the following mechanisms:
	 1.	Direct blow, e.g. rib fracture.
	 2.	Deceleration injury, e.g. pulmonary contusion.
	 3.	Compression injury, e.g. cardiac and diaphragm injury.
SALIENT FEATURES
Chest pain and shortness of breath. Careful physical examination of the patient 
is important especially in the management of patient with equivocal radiological 
investigation.

(a) Resuscitation. Assess the patency of airway, breathing and circulation. Ensure 
the patency of the airway and adequacy of ventilation. Insert two 16G intravenous 
cannulae and start resuscitation with crystalloid. If haemothorax or pneumothorax 
are suspected in a patient with acute respiratory distress, chest tube should be 
inserted through the fourth/fifth intercostal space in the mid to anterior axillary line 
on the affected side without waiting for chest radiography.
(b) Quick assessment of injuries and their management 
1. Chest wall
	(a)	Rib fracture can vary from simple fracture to fracture with haemo-pneumothorax, 
to severe multiple fractures with flail chest and internal injuries. In case of 
simple fractures, pain with inspiration and localized tenderness and occasional 
localized crepitus on examination are present. Diagnosis is confirmed with a

Chapter 2  Emergencies    167
chest X-ray, anteroposterior view. Exclude other intrathoracic injuries; if found, 
refer immediately to a higher centre for underlying lung injuries. Patients are 
treated with adequate analgesic drugs, muscle relaxants. Strapping of ribs is no 
longer done as it affects deep breathing. In cases of multiple fractures, intercostal 
nerve blocks or epidural analgesia is required to ensure adequate pain relief and 
ventilation. Elderly patients need admission for pain relief, ventilation assistance 
and observation.
	(b)	Flail chest occurs due to unilateral fracture of 2 or more ribs, both anteriorly and 
posteriorly; and bilateral anterior or costochondral fracture of more than 4 ribs 
causes a paradoxical respiratory motion. It leads to hypoventilation, atelectasis, 
hypercapnia and inadequate ventilation (RR > 40/min, pO2 < 60 mmHg with 60% 
FiO2). It requires immediate endotracheal intubation and ventilatory support.
2. Pleural space
	(a)	Haemothorax should be suspected in cases of penetrating or severe blunt thoracic 
injury. It is classified according to the amount of blood collected inside the 
pleural cavity and more importantly rate of bleeding after evacuation. In 85% 
of the patients with haemothorax, only tube thoracostomy is required. After tube 
thoracostomy if the rate of continuing haemorrhage is more than 100–200 mL/h 
for 3 consecutive hours or the haemorrhagic output exceeds 1000 mL in 24 hours, 
thoracotomy should be performed.
	(b)	Pneumothorax is a true surgical emergency requiring immediate diagnosis and 
chest tube insertion. Subcutaneous emphysema, absent breath sounds, mediastinal 
shift and acute respiratory distress warrant immediate chest tube insertion without 
waiting for a chest X-ray examination. Sucking chest wounds, which allow air to 
pass in and out of the pleural cavity, should promptly be treated by closure of the 
wound (initially sealing with large pads and later with suturing) and concomitant 
tube thoracostomy. Simple pneumothorax (without tension) should also be 
managed by chest tube insertion but only after documentation by chest X-ray.
3. Lung injury
	(a)	Pulmonary parenchymal injury can be effectively managed non-operatively, 
but about 15% of penetrating lung injury requires thoracotomy for control of 
haemorrhage. Approximately 80–90% of pulmonary injuries requiring operation 
can be managed by simple suturing or stapling of the involved segments. Only 
10–20% of cases require anatomical lung resection. 
	(b)	Pulmonary contusion in most patients with flail chest can also appear without 
any evidence of rib fracture (particularly in children). Treatment is often delayed 
because clinical and X-ray findings may not appear until 12–24 hours after injury.
	(c)	Clinical findings are loose, copious, blood-tinged secretions, chest pain, restlessness, 
and laboured respiration. X-ray changes consist of patchy parenchymal opacification 
or diffuse peribronchial densities.

168    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	(d)	Management involves careful pulmonary support and clearing of secretions with 
ventilatory support if ABG cannot be maintained in a physiologic range. Positive 
end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) is a useful adjunct in the management of those 
requiring ventilation. Fluid overload should be avoided.
4. Trachea and bronchus
Tracheobronchial injuries should be suspected when there is a massive air leak or when 
the lung does not readily expand after chest tube placement. In most patients having 
pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumo-mediastinum and haemoptysis, 
diagnosis may require tracheobronchoscopy. When diagnosis is confirmed, thoracotomy 
and primary repair is advised.
5. Heart and pericardium
Cardiac tamponade can occur both from blunt and penetrating cardiac trauma. Tamponade 
in blunt trauma is often due to myocardial rupture or coronary artery laceration. Patient 
presents with chest pain, distended neck veins, shock and cyanosis. Treatment includes 
immediate thoracotomy, pericardial decompression and repair of injuries.
6. Oesophagus
Anatomically, the oesophagus is well protected and perforation from external wounds 
is relatively infrequent. The most common symptom of oesophageal perforation is 
pain; fever develops within hours in most patients. Regurgitation of food, hoarseness, 
dysphagia or respiratory distress may be present. Physical findings include shock, local 
tenderness, subcutaneous emphysema in suprasternal notch and neck or Hamman’s 
sign. X-ray findings on plain chest films include evidence of foreign body or missile 
and mediastinal widening or air. Contrast studies (Urografin, not barium) confirm 
the diagnosis. Treatment consists of early recognition (24–48 hours), closure of 
oesophageal perforation and pleural drainage. Old perforation may require advanced 
surgical management and should be referred to a specialized centre.

SPINAL TRAUMA
After circulatory stabilization and before transfer from the emergency room, rule out 
or confirm spinal injury that should be cleared by clinical examination or imaging, if 
available. 
Assessment for spinal injury 
	
l On arrival at the hospital, use a prioritizing sequence to assess people with suspected 
trauma, for example ABCDE: Airway with in-line spinal immobilization, Breathing, 
Circulation, Disability (neurological), Exposure and environment. Protect the

Chapter 2  Emergencies    169
person’s cervical spine with manual in-line spinal immobilization avoiding moving 
the remainder of the spine, particularly during any airway intervention at all stages 
of the assessment
	
l History and thorough clinical examination for spinal injury including the functions 
associated with it must be carried out. 
	
l The spine is supposed to be stable, unless any of the following 5 criteria are present: 
impaired consciousness, neurologic deficit (paraparesis or quadriparesis), spinal pain 
or paraspinal tenderness (myogelosis, i.e. area of hard or stiff muscle), intoxication, 
trauma in the extremities. 
	
l Assume the presence of a spinal injury in unconscious patients until evidence to the 
contrary is found. 
	
l Carry out full in-line spinal immobilization if polytrauma with suspected traumatic 
brain injury or if this assessment cannot be done. 
Assessment of Cervical Spine
	
l Assess whether the person is at high, low or no risk for cervical spine injury using 
the Canadian C-spine rule as follows: 
–	The person is at high risk, if they have at least one of the following high-risk 
factors: age 65 years or older, dangerous mechanism of injury (fall from a height 
of greater than 1 metre or 5 steps, axial load to the head, e.g. diving, high-speed 
motor vehicle collision, rollover motor accident, ejection from a motor vehicle, 
accident involving motorized recreational vehicles, bicycle collision, horse riding 
accidents), paraesthesia in the upper or lower limbs.
–	The person is at low risk, if they have at least one of the following low-risk 
factors: involved in a minor rear-end motor vehicle collision, comfortable in a 
sitting position, ambulatory at any time since the injury, no midline cervical spine 
tenderness, delayed onset of neck pain. 
–	The person remains at low risk, if they are unable to actively rotate their neck 
45º to the left and right (the range of the neck can only be assessed safely if the 
person is at low risk and there are no high-risk factors).
–	The person has no risk, if they have one of the above low-risk factors and are able 
to actively rotate their neck 45º to the left and right. 
Assessment of Thoracic or Lumbosacral Spine 
	
l Assess the person with suspected thoracic or lumbosacral spine injury using these 
factors: 
–	Age 65 years or older and reported pain in the thoracic or lumbosacral spine, 
dangerous mechanism of injury (fall from a height of greater than 3 metres, 
axial load to the head or base of the spine, e.g. falls landing on feet or buttocks, 
high-speed motor vehicle collision, rollover motor accident, lap belt restraint 
only, ejection from a motor vehicle, accident involving motorized recreational 
vehicles, bicycle collision, horse riding accidents, pre-existing spinal pathology,

170    Standard Treatment Guidelines
or known or at risk of osteoporosis, e.g. steroid use, suspected spinal fracture in 
another region of the spine) 
–	Abnormal neurological symptoms (paraesthesia or weakness or numbness), on 
examination: Abnormal neurological signs (motor or sensory deficit)
–	New deformity or bony midline tenderness (on palpation) 
–	Bony midline tenderness (on percussion) 
–	Midline or midback or low back pain (on coughing) 
–	On mobilization (sit, stand, step, assess walking): Pain or abnormal neurological 
symptoms (stop if this occurs). 
–	Do not carry out or maintain full in-line spinal immobilization in people if they 
have low-risk factors for cervical spine injury and are pain free and are able to 
actively rotate their neck 45º left and right and in the absence of any above factors.
Procedure for spinal immobilization
	
l Let the patient find a position where they are comfortable with manual in-line 
spinal immobilization. Manually stabilize the head with the spine in-line using the 
following stepwise approach: 
	– Fit an appropriately sized semi-rigid collar unless contraindicated by a 
compromised airway, known spinal deformities, such as ankylosing spondylitis 
(in these cases, keep the spine in the person’s current position). 
	– Reassess the airway after applying the collar.
	– Place and secure the person on a stretcher. 
	Radiological investigations
	
l Urgent diagnostic imaging (CT) if there is suspicion of spinal injury associated 
with abnormal neurological signs or symptoms and interpretation immediately by 
a healthcare professional with training and skills in this area after stabilization. 
Cervical spine X-ray should be considered if CT is not available with caution of a 
high false-negative rate. MRI should be done if there is a neurological abnormality 
which could be attributable to spinal cord injury. 
	
l Perform an X-ray as the first-line investigation for people with suspected spinal 
column injury without abnormal neurological signs or symptoms in the thoracic 
or lumbosacral regions (T1–L3). Perform CT if the X-ray is abnormal or there are 
clinical signs or symptoms of a spinal column injury. If a new spinal column fracture 
is confirmed, image the rest of the spinal column. 
	
l Do not use medications like Methylprednisolone, Nimodipine, Naloxone, aimed at 
providing neuroprotection and prevention of secondary deterioration, in the acute 
stage after acute traumatic spinal cord injury. Do not use medications in the acute 
stage after traumatic spinal cord injury to prevent neuropathic pain from developing 
in the chronic stage.
HEAD INJURY
Head injuries are a frequent form of injuries in cities. A systematic approach is required 
to differentiate trivial injury from severe forms which may be life-threatening or may 
lead to neurological sequelae.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    171
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patients with head trauma may present with a variety of symptoms, including 
headache, amnesia, impaired level of consciousness, disorientation or confusion, 
vomiting, loss of consciousness, blurred vision or seizures.
	
l Symptoms and signs of severe forms may appear immediately as in concussions or 
contusions or may appear after a few minutes to hours as in acute subdural haematoma.

l The management of head injury patients should be guided by clinical assessments 
and protocols based on the Glasgow Coma Scale and Score (GCS) (see Table 2.9 in 
section on Coma).
	
l Patients with history of unconsciousness at any time since injury, amnesia for the 
incident or subsequent events, severe and persistent headache, nausea, vomiting, 
bleeding from nose/ear, seizures or presence of black eye, suspected fracture of 
skull and haematoma of scalp indicate severe form of head injury and require 
hospitalization.
	
l An important goal of stabilization is to avoid secondary injury to the traumatized 
brain from hypoxia, hypotension, hyperthermia or raised intracranial pressure.
	
l A structured approach to the assessment of airway, breathing, circulation and 
disability (ABCD) to be followed.
Minor head injury (GCS 13–15)
A patient who is alert and has only one or more symptoms of headache, faintness, 
nausea, a single vomiting, difficulty with concentration or slight blurring of vision, 
may have scalp bruising or laceration should be kept under observation for a few 
hours and then sent home with proper instructions to the family members about red 
flag signs – loss of consciousness at any time, focal neurological deficit, retrograde or 
anterograde amnesia, persistent headache, repeated vomiting or seizures post injury. 
Decision for X-ray skull and CT scan depends on degree of trauma to the rest of body 
and skull, in addition to the worsening of symptoms and signs.
Minor head trauma (GCS 14 or 15) asymptomatic patients may be discharged 
home to the care of reliable parents or guardians. Written instructions describing 
warning signs to watch for (e.g. worsening headache, persistent vomiting, difficulty 
in awakening), who to contact in such a case and when to return for follow-up, should 
be provided.
Moderate head injury (GCS 9–12)
Patients with brief loss of consciousness at time of injury but currently alert or 
responds to voice, may be drowsy, have two or more episodes of vomiting, persistent 
headache, up to one single brief (<2 minutes) convulsion occurring immediately 
after the impact, may have a large scalp bruise, haematoma or laceration but normal 
examination otherwise. If no neurological deterioration on history from the patient/

172    Standard Treatment Guidelines
parents and ambulance, observe in the Emergency Department for a period of 4 hours 
with 30 minutely neurological observations (conscious state, PR, RR, BP, pupils’ size 
and reactivity and limb power). 
The patient may be discharged, if there is improvement at 24 hours to normal 
conscious state and no further vomiting (patient should be able to tolerate oral fluids 
in the hospital) and with full written and verbal instructions to patient and their 
caregiver to report back immediately in case of red flag signs as above.
A persistent headache, large scalp haematoma or possible penetrating wound may 
need CT scan, if not already performed. If the patient is still drowsy or vomiting at 4 
hours, progressive focal neurological signs, a seizure without full recovery or there is 
any deterioration during this time, consult with a neurosurgeon regarding admission 
and further investigation.
Severe head injury (GCS 8 or less)
Patients with suspected open or depressed skull fracture, haemotympanum, periorbital 
bruising (panda eyes), cerebrospinal fluid leakage from ear or nose, postauricular 
bruising (battle’s sign), persistent confusion, behavioural change, post-traumatic 
seizures, coma, focal neurological signs, and features of raised intracranial pressure 
require immediate attention and should be admitted to the hospital. A CT scan should be 
done in all such cases and treated as follows:
	 1.	Check and maintain airway and breathing (see section on Cardiopulmonary 
Resuscitation)
	 2.	Check circulation by pulse volume, rate, blood pressure
	 3.	Establish IV access
	 4.	IV fluids according to volume loss: Crystalloids such as NS (0.9%) is a fluid of 
choice. Colloid can be given if required to treat hypovolaemia due to major blood 
loss (see section on Shock)
	 5.	Check for and stabilize extracranial injuries
	 6.	A head injury may be accompanied by a cervical injury. If spinal injuries are 
excluded, then transfer the patient in side position with head down, to a tertiary 
care centre where neurosurgical interventions are available
	 7.	If spinal injury is suspected then transfer the patient on a hard board, place two 
sandbags on either side of the head
	 8.	Assessment by GCS may be used to prognosticate or follow a patient of head injury 
for improvement/deterioration of neurological status. Patients with Glasgow Coma 
Scale score 8 or less or with deterioration of level of consciousness should be 
transferred to a centre where facilities for neurosurgical interventions are available. 
Over 85% of patients with aggregate score of 3 or 4 die within 24 hours while score 
of 11 or more indicates death in only 5–10%
	 9.	A subdural haematoma, epidural haematoma or large intracerebral haematoma may 
require surgical intervention and must immediately be attended to by a neurosurgeon
	10.	Hyperthermia, hypoxia and hypercarbia exacerbate intracranial pressure, so does an 
awkward head position like acute flexion. These conditions must be appropriately 
treated, if necessary, by mechanical ventilation

Chapter 2  Emergencies    173
	11.	In case of raised intracranial pressure, particularly with signs of transtentorial 
herniation (pupil widening, decerebrate rigidity, extensor reaction to painful 
stimulus, progressive clouded consciousness), give Inj. Mannitol (20%) 0.25–1 g 
IV over 30–60 minutes every 3–4 hours
12. Do not administer glucocorticoids in traumatic brain injury
	
	Monitoring of patients with a head injury, who warrant admission, should have 
neurological observations carried out at least in the following frequency starting 
after initial assessment in the emergency department:
	
l Half hourly for 2 hours
	
l Hourly for 4 hours
	
l Two hourly for 6 hours
	
l Four hourly thereafter until agreed to be no longer necessary 
	
l Perform a monitoring CT scan in case of neurologic deterioration
Post-traumatic seizures
Patients with impact seizures or an isolated post-traumatic seizure shortly after the injury, 
but whose neurological examination and imaging are normal, are at low risk of further 
complications and may be discharged. Factors increasing the risk of post-traumatic 
seizures may include younger age, severe head trauma (GCS ≤8), cerebral edema, subdural 
haematoma, and open or depressed skull fractures. Prophylactic antiseizure medicine for 
post-traumatic seizures in paediatric head trauma patients is not proven effective.
	 1.	The acute treatment of post-traumatic seizures is identical to that of acute seizures 
occurring in other contexts (See Chapter 9).
	 2.	Observe for neurological deterioration such as agitation or abnormal behaviour, 
a sustained (for at least 30 minutes) drop of 1 point in GCS score (greater weight 
given to a drop of 1 point in the motor response score of the GCS), any drop of 3 or 
more points in the eye-opening or verbal response scores of the GCS, or 2 or more 
points in the motor response score, development of severe or increasing headache 
or persisting vomiting, new or evolving neurological symptoms or signs such as 
pupil inequality or asymmetry of limb or facial movement.
	 3.	Obtain an immediate CT scan and reassess and manage the patient’s clinical condition 
appropriately. In a patient who has had a normal CT scan but has not achieved GCS 
equal to 15 after 24 hours’ observation, obtain another CT scan or MRI scanning.
Note: Do not discharge until patient achieves GCS equal to 15 or normal consciousness in 
infants and young children as assessed by GCS paediatric version (see section on coma). 
Patients admitted after a head injury may be discharged after resolution of all significant 
symptoms and signs providing they have suitable supervision arrangements at home.
Patient education
	
l The majority of patients with minor head injury who do not exhibit intracranial 
pathology, their symptoms will resolve quickly.

174    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l A guarded prognosis in severe head injury is given but some children and young adults 
show remarkable recoveries despite low score on Glasgow Coma Scale (Table 2.9).
	
l Give verbal and printed discharge advice with contact details of the hospital at 
the time of discharge to patients with any degree of head injury, and their families 
and carers to report back in case of persistent/increasing headache, vomiting, and 
deterioration of level of consciousness or appearance of any focal motor weakness.
	
l Headache: If patient complains of headache, give paracetamol as and when 
required. If no relief for 24 hours, consult/report back to doctor. 
	
l Vomiting: Patient may have vomited once but if vomiting continues, report back 
to the doctor. 
	
l Drowsiness: Immediately after the head injury patients may be sleepy. There is no 
need to keep the patients awake if they want to sleep. If patients do go to sleep, wake 
them every ½ to 1 hour to check their condition and their reaction to familiar things. 
One should do this until they are no longer drowsy and have been awake and alert 
for a few hours.
	
l Amnesia: Patients should be examined for amnesia by asking about current location/
surroundings/known face identifications, etc. If the patient is very young, look for 
his/her behaviour/reactions/approaches, etc.
	
l If there is any difficulty waking the child, report to the nearest emergency 
department or call an ambulance if patient’s behaviour is very different to their 
normal behaviour. 
	
l Patients with a more severe head injury admitted for up to 72 hours should be 
assessed for intensive rehabilitation.
	
l While counselling, families focus on injury prevention (falls, sports-related injuries, 
injuries involving the use of a bicycle, motor vehicles, especially as a pedestrian).

COMA
A coma is defined as a prolonged period of unconsciousness and lack of reaction to 
stimulus. Patients in coma cannot be aroused.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    175
SALIENT FEATURES
The following causes affect the functions of reticular-activating system and its 
connections with cerebrum.
	
l Structural damage to brain (haemorrhage, tumours, trauma, localized infections, 
meningitis, stroke). 
	
l Metabolic disturbances (ischaemia, anoxia, uraemia, diabetes), respiratory/
hepatic/renal failure, dyselectrolytaemia, endocrinopathies, drugs like opiates, 
barbiturates, benzodiazepines, antidepressants and cyanide. 
	
l Abnormal electrical activity – periodic lateralized epileptiform discharge (PLED).

l The immediate goal in acute coma is the prevention of further nervous system damage.
	
l Hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypoxia, hypercapnia, and 
hyperthermia should be corrected rapidly and assiduously.
	
l An oropharyngeal airway is adequate to keep the pharynx open in drowsy patients 
who are breathing normally.
	
l Tracheal intubation is indicated if there is apnoea, upper airway obstruction, 
hypoventilation or emesis or if the patient is liable to aspirate because of coma.
	
l Mechanical ventilation is required if there is hypoventilation or if there is an 
intracranial mass and a need to induce hypocapnia (PCO2 25–30) in order to lower 
intracranial pressure.
	
l Establish intravenous access and draw blood samples for biochemical and other 
investigations.

1.	Inj. Glucose (25 or 50%) 50 g IV. 
	 2.	Inj. Thiamine 100 mg IV. 
	 3.	If opiate overdose is suspected, give Inj. Naloxone 0.8 mg IV. If the response is 
inadequate, double the dose every 15 minutes (for details, see section on Opioid 
Intoxication).
	 4.	If benzodiazepine overdose is suspected, give Inj. Flumazenil 200 mcg IV slowly. 
If no response, repeat 100–200 mcg after 1 minute. If required, give maximum dose 
of 1 mg or give as IV infusion of 100–400 mcg/h, if drowsiness recurs. 
	 5.	If focal neurological deficit or signs of herniation/decerebration/decortication 
occur, CT scan, EEG and neurologic consultation are required. 
	 6.	If no clear aetiology and no herniation, CSF examination should be done to rule 
out infective meningitis.
	 7.	If signs of raised intracranial tension (papilloedema, convulsions, decerebrate 
posture indicating herniation) occurs: 
	 i.	 Avoid giving free fluid (glucose solution) intravenously.
	ii.	 Inj. Frusemide 40 mg IV to maintain adequate urine output of 30–50 mL/h.
	iii.	 Inj. Mannitol 1.0 g/kg IV over 10 minutes followed by 0.25g/kg 6–8 hourly.

FRACTURES
A fracture is a break in the structural continuity of a bone. It is termed as an open 
(compound) fracture if there is a concomitant wound through which the fracture 
haematoma communicates to the environment. If the fracture does not communicate 
to the environment, it is called closed fracture.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Pain, swelling, tenderness, loss of function, deformity, shortening, crepitus, 
abnormal mobility and loss of transmitted movement, singularly or in combination.
	
l Diagnosis to be based on the above clinical features; however, purposeful 
manipulation of limb to be AVOIDED to elicit signs like crepitus and abnormal 
mobility of the fracture site.

Emergency care of fractures at the site of accident (First aid)
	
l All trauma patients with a cervical spinal column injury or with a mechanism 
of injury having the potential to cause cervical spinal injury and all head injury 
patients who are unresponsive should be immobilized at the scene and expeditiously 
transported to nearest hospital using one of several available methods – a 
combination of a rigid cervical collar and supportive blocks on a backboard with 
straps. In case of patient needing airway management, then one health care worker 
from the head end side of the patient should provide in-line immobilization with the 
clasped hand under the head and forearms on both sides straddling and supporting 
the head to prevent movements of cervical spine. After urgent airway management, 
as soon as possible, the cervical collar should be placed while the assessment and 
management of breathing and circulation is being carried on. The collar should be 
removed once the patient has been examined by a competent person and finds the 
cervical spine painless and non-tender in a well oriented and conscious patient. In 
case of tenderness or in an unresponsive head injury patient, the collar must be kept 
till X-rays Cervical Spine AP, Lateral and Open mouth AP views or CT/MRI are 
done to rule out cervical spine injury. CT scan or MRI done in a head injury patient 
should include screening of the cervical spine in all suspected cases.

178    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l If injury to the spine is suspected, carefully move the person from the site 
of accident in one piece like a log of wood without any twisting or flexion. 
(For details, see section on Spinal Trauma.)
	
l If injury to limbs is suspected, give temporary immobilization (splintage) after 
grossly correcting the deformation without moving or manipulating using any 
available immobilization device like wooden stick/an umbrella/a folded magazine 
or newspaper, otherwise a fractured lower limb can be temporarily supported and 
tied with opposite lower limb for splintage and before transferring the patient; 
and a fractured upper limb can be splinted by supporting it on the chest wall and 
wrapping any cloth piece around it. Take a note of the colour of the finger or toes 
before applying splintage.
	
l If the patient has an open fracture with excessive bleeding, avoid tying any 
circumferential tourniquet to any part of the limb to stop bleeding (unless the 
bleeding is life-threatening) as the ligature can be more injurious to the distal 
circulation of the limb. If at all a tourniquet is to be applied, the exact time of 
application should be noted and written on the limb of the patient as well as 
informed to the attendants accompanying the patient to the hospital for onward 
transmission of this information to the concerned doctors. Most of the bleeding 
wounds can be controlled by digital pressure and in case of larger sized wounds, 
sterile dressing pads should be used to cover the wound secured by bandages tied 
over the splint so that direct tourniquet effect on the limb is avoided.
Care of patient in the emergency department
The general aim of early fracture management is to control haemorrhage and 
management of shock, provide pain relief, prevent ischaemia-reperfusion injury and 
remove potential sources of contamination (foreign body and non-viable tissues). 
Suspected cases of fracture on arrival in the emergency department should be assessed 
for the neurovascular status, by assessment of distal peripheral pulses and active 
movements of the limb fingers and toes. Movements of joints may be gently assessed 
if a conscious patient actively performs the movements. Confirm fracture by X-ray and 
document findings.
	(a)	Open fractures: Table 2.11 depicts open fracture classification.
	 1.	 Perform debridement:
	
l immediately for highly contaminated open fractures
	
l within 12 hours of injury for high‑energy open fractures (likely Gustilo–
Anderson classification type IIIA or type IIIB) that are not highly contaminated.
	
l within 24 hours of injury for all other open fractures management
	 2.	 Fluid resuscitation, tetanus and antibiotic prophylaxis and arrangement of blood 
should simultaneously be initiated as the patient is prepared for an emergency 
debridement under anaesthesia-immediately for highly contaminated open 
fractures. 
	 3.	 Open grade 1 fractures with innocuous small wound less than 1 cm should also 
be operated under anaesthesia at the earliest by enlarging the skin wound for 
proper debridement.

	 4.	 All open fractures should be adequately immobilized by an appropriate external 
fixator. 
	
	   Do not irrigate open fractures of the long bones, hindfoot or midfoot in the 
emergency department without anaesthesia outside the operating theatre. Apply 
a saline-soaked dressing covered with an occlusive layer (if not already applied) 
for open fractures in the emergency department before debridement. Administer 
prophylactic intravenous antibiotics immediately to people with open fractures 
if not already given. Do not base the decision whether to perform limb salvage 
or amputation on an injury severity tool score. Perform emergency amputation 
when a limb is the source of uncontrollable life-threatening bleeding, or a limb 
is salvageable but attempted preservation would pose an unacceptable risk to 
the person’s life, or a limb is deemed unsalvageable after orthopaedic and, if 
available, an additional plastic surgeon’s assessment. 
	(b)	Vascular injury: Use hard signs (lack of palpable pulse, continued blood loss 
or expanding haematoma) to diagnose vascular injury. Do not rely on capillary 
return or Doppler signal to exclude vascular injury. Perform immediate surgical 
exploration if hard signs of vascular injury persist after any necessary restoration of 
limb alignment and joint reduction. Do not delay revascularization for angiography 
in people with complex fractures.
	(c)	Compartment syndrome: In people with fractures of the tibia, maintain awareness 
of compartment syndrome for 48 hours after injury or fixation by regularly 
assessing and recording clinical symptoms and signs in hospital. (For details, see 
section on Compartment Syndrome.)
	(d)	Patient with fracture in an extremity: Splint the limb with either Cramer wire 
(a malleable metallic support) or a slab or goose splint (thin layers of wood 
adhered to cloth) or a Thomas splint (for femoral fractures) or Bohler Braun splint 
(for fractures around the knee or leg bones fractures); include the proximal and the 
distal joint of the fractured segment of the limb in splintage (Table 2.12). Surgeon 
to rule out neurovascular injuries. Any open wound or crush injuries of hands 
and feet are dressed before application of splintage. Do NOT apply tourniquet or 
sutures. Keep tips of the fingers/toes exposed. The definitive treatment should be 
provided by an orthopaedic surgeon after radiological examination.

Compartment syndrome 
Injuries around elbow and knee are prone to compartment syndrome. Intense pain and 
stretch pain on stretching muscles of the compartment in the initial phase is diagnostic. 
Distal pulse may still be present, and paraesthesia and paralysis are late signs. 
	
l Keep a high index of suspicion and refer immediately to a higher centre for releasing 
compartment by incising fascial septum to reduce the pressure and re-establish circulation.

PELVIC FRACTURES
Classification
Pelvic fractures are generally divided into two types based on amount of energy 
involved:
	 i.	Low energy fractures resulting in isolated fractures of individual bones of pelvis 
without disruption of pelvic ring.
	 ii.	High energy fractures generally producing pelvic ring disruption.
Evaluation
	
l Evaluate the patient with attention to ABC of trauma care (i.e. airway and breathing, 
circulation). 
	
l Conduct a primary survey and note baseline vital signs and neurological status.
	
l Assess pelvic stability, very carefully, by pushing anterior-superior iliac spines 
towards each other and then apart (preferably perform this manoeuvre once only).
	
l Perform perineal and digital rectal examination for any wounds of open fracture.
	
l Secondary detailed survey is carried out once the patient’s condition is stable and 
X-rays, CT and other relevant investigations are done. 
	 Note: Do not log roll people with suspected pelvic fractures before pelvic imaging 
unless an occult penetrating injury is suspected in a person with haemodynamic 
instability or when log rolling is needed to clear the airway (e.g. suction is 
ineffective in a person who is vomiting). When log rolling, pay particular attention 
to haemodynamic stability.

1.	As a primary aid, the pelvis can be quickly and temporarily stabilized by wrapping 
a sheet tightly around it. Isolated stable pelvic bone fractures are treated by bedrest 
(for symptomatic duration) and analgesics, followed by gradual mobilization and 
weight bearing.
	 2.	Severe ecchymosis around pelvis, urinary retention, bleeding per urethral meatus 
or externally rotated or short limbs, abdominal tenderness and guarding, inability 
to stand or even to sit and other associated fractures suggest relatively severe life-
threatening injury. If active bleeding is suspected from a pelvic fracture following 
blunt high‑energy trauma, apply a pelvic binder. Refer immediately to a higher

Chapter 2  Emergencies    185
centre with a pelvic binder at two large calibre catheters (minimum of 16-gauge) 
with ongoing intravenous fluids. 
	
	Note: Do not pass a catheter without a specialist guide if there is bleeding at the 
meatus and do not perform compression distraction test in unstable injuries.
	 3.	Treatment of unstable pelvic ring disruptions (Fig. 2.13) includes:
	
l Volume replacement (see section on Shock).
	
l Control haemorrhage: Apply pressure dressing for conspicuous external bleeding. 
or pelvic binder tied over trochanter and binding the legs in internal rotation. 
Open pelvic fracture wounds can be packed to control bleeding. Apply external 
fixator as a resuscitative measure in patients with demonstrable haemodynamic 
instability after an initial fluid bolus. Remove pelvic binder as soon as possible 
within 24 hours of application if there is no pelvic fracture, or a pelvic fracture is 
identified as mechanically stable, or the binder is not controlling the mechanical 
stability of the fracture or there is no further bleeding or coagulation is normal.
	
l Inj. Tranexamic acid should be administered shortly after injury.
	
l In case of unstable pelvic injury, immediate anterior external fixation (AEF) 
applied within 20–30 minutes. The anterior fixator contributes to haemostasis 
by maintaining a reduced pelvic volume, allowing tamponade, by decreasing 
bony motion at the fracture site, and allowing clots to stabilize.
	
l In the emergency setting, the pelvic C-clamp also stabilizes pelvic ring injuries 
and controls haemorrhage. With an assembly time of approximately 10 minutes, 
the C-clamp stops bleeding by applying compression indirectly to fracture 
surfaces and the veins of the presacral plexus. In contrast to other tools available 
for compression of pelvic ring injuries, the C-clamp allows for unrestricted 
access to the abdomen, pelvis, and proximal femur. These properties make the 
C-clamp ideal to be used intraoperatively to obtain compression of the posterior 
pelvic ring. These clamps have been used therapeutically in haemodynamically 
unstable patients, and prophylactically in stable patients with unstable pelvic-
ring disruptions. Mechanically and technically, a posterior device is better than 
an anterior one. In experienced hands, the posterior device is faster and safer to 
apply, and its position can be easily modified to allow access to the abdomen 
for the general surgeon. C-clamp application cannot only be difficult but also 
dangerous in cases of comminuted sacral fractures: neurovascular injury can 
occur due to crushing of the sacrum. 
	
l Urological management: Catheterize the urinary bladder to document urinary 
output as a crucial determinant of adequate volume resuscitation. Blood at 
urethral meatus/inability to void urine/perineal haematoma/high riding prostate 
indicate urethral injury. Microscopic haematuria indicates bladder contusion.
Further management is required in consultation with general surgeon.
Gastrointestinal injuries: Concomitant small bowel/large bowel/rectal/anal tears or 
perforation can occur. Peritoneal lavage and abdominal CT are required to exclude GI 
trauma with close pelvis fractures (for details, see section on Trauma).

URETHRAL INJURIES
Urethra is a narrow fibromuscular tube that conducts urine and semen from the bladder 
and ejaculatory ducts in a male and conducts only urine in a female. It is about 20 cm 
in male and shorter 5 cm only in female. The male urethra is divided into anterior and 
posterior segment. The posterior urethra comprises prostatic and membranous parts 
whereas the anterior urethra includes the bulbar and penile sections. An anterior urethral 
injury constitutes 10% of total urethral injury often resulting from blunt straddle or 
penetrating trauma, placement of penile constriction bands or iatrogenic injuries from 
instrumentation. Posterior urethral injuries constitute the major bulk of urethral injuries. 
They are usually associated with some other injuries.
Common causes include pelvic bone fractures, particularly bilateral pubic rami 
fractures, and blunt or penetrating perineal injuries leading to perineal hematomas. In 
contemporary terms, urethral injuries associated with pelvic fractures are now referred 
to as pelvic fracture urethral injuries (PFUI). Urethral injuries are more prevalent in 
males due to the longer and less mobile nature of their urethra. Risk factors include 
straddle fractures and diastasis of the sacroiliac joint. The bulbomembranous urethra is 
more vulnerable and is injured more frequently.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Presence of blood at meatus along with a palpable urinary bladder, and inability 
to pass urine. The blood at meatus indicates posterior urethral injury; however, 
quantity of blood at the meatus does not necessarily correspond to the severity 
of the injury.
	
l Perineal haematoma, especially expanding haematoma due to extravasation of urine.
	
l Floating prostate on per rectal examination.
	
l For diagnosis, a high degree of suspicion of urethral injuries based on the type of 
injuries and sign and symptoms of the patient is required.
	
l The retrograde urethrography (RGU), if feasible, must be performed prior to any 
intervention to determine the type (stretching, contusion, partial, or complete), 
location (anterior or posterior urethra) and any associated urinary bladder injuries.

The urethral injury is usually associated with pelvic injuries and/or a part of other 
physical injuries. Assess thoroughly to rule out other vital and life-threatening injuries 
such as vascular and airways injuries and manage as below:
	 1.	Co-ordinate with other specialists, usually trauma, critical care and orthopaedic 
specialists, as these patients often have multiple injuries. Correct life-threatening 
injuries first. 
	 2.	In case of minor injuries such as stretching injury, no treatment is required. Wait 
and watch, if any sign of deterioration, manage accordingly.
	 3.	In case of contusion to the urethra, no treatment is required. Depending upon the 
extent of contusion, simply urethral catheterization/suprapubic catheterization may 
be required. Always use a simple self-retaining rubber catheter (Foley’s catheter) 
of appropriate size.
	 4.	In case of anterior urethral injury, immediate repair with minimum debridement 
and tension-free spatulated anastomosis should be done if specialist care services 
are available. Otherwise, urethral cathedral alignment with suprapubic urinary 
diversion followed by delayed repair after 3–12 months is a good option. The other 
non-urethral injuries would heal by 12 months.
	
	Note: Do not do emergency repair of defects longer than 2 cm in the bulbar urethra 
and longer than 1.5 cm in the penile urethra.
	 5.	In case of posterior urethral injuries rule out extravasation of urine by retrograde 
urethrography (RGU). If no extravasation, simple urethral catheterization followed 
by cystogram to rule out urinary bladder/urinary bladder neck injuries.
	
l If there are injuries to the membranous urethra, suprapubic catheterization 
followed by delayed repair after 3–12 months or suprapubic catheterization with 
endoscopic aligning catheterization followed by early urethral repair.
	
l Open placement of suprapubic catheter should be done in case of suspected 
urinary bladder injuries or bladder neck injuries or in case of rectal and vascular 
injuries or as part of other orthopaedic procedures.
	
l The other non-urethral injuries would heal by 12 months. See also Pelvic 
fractures above.
	 6.	In cases of suspected urinary bladder injuries, bladder neck injuries, or other 
associated injuries, it is advisable to perform open placement of a suprapubic 
catheter during orthopedic procedures. Catheterization is discouraged to mitigate 
the risk of converting partial injuries into complete ones. Catheterization also 
increases the potential for infecting pelvic hematomas. However, with the 
availability of experienced personnel, a cautious attempt at Foley catheter insertion 
can be made. Any resistance encountered during the process should prompt 
consideration of RGU. In instances of hemodynamic instability, suprapubic 
catheterization (SPC), guided by ultrasound or performed openly, is recommended.
Definitive urethral management: Definitive management options include immediate 
intervention (within 48 hours), delayed primary repair (2 days to 2 weeks), or deferred 
repair (more than 3 months). To guide the course of action:

	 1.	Radiological assessment: Utilize RGU or micturating cystourethrography (MCU) 
for accurate assessment of stricture length. MRI for estimating distraction defect 
length, degree of prostatic displacement and identifying the presence or absence 
of false passages.
	 2.	Functional evaluation: Document erectile function, as poor erectile function correlates 
with an increased risk of urethral stricture due to compromised blood supply. These 
comprehensive assessments help tailor the definitive urethral management strategy 
based on accurate information about the nature and extent of the injury.
