CARBON MONOXIDE
The most important and common source of carbon monoxide (CO) exposure is smoke 
inhalation. Heating systems in rooms that are not properly ventilated (e.g. gas, wood, 
kerosene heaters and stoves and brick ovens) and petrol engine exhaust fumes can cause 
such exposure. Diesel fumes produce very little carbon monoxide.
SALIENT FEATURES
Low-level poisoning
	
l Early features: Low-level exposure may produce no abnormal physical signs. 
Symptoms are likely to be mild and may include nausea, subjective weakness, 
headache and poor concentration/memory.
	
l Late features: Some patients develop symptoms later, perhaps after several weeks 
of apparent recovery from the incident. This late stage is more common in those 
aged over 40. Neurological or neuropsychiatric features including disorientation, 
apathy, irritability, inability to concentrate, personality change, parkinsonism, 
parietal lobe lesions and memory loss. Encephalopathy develops 2–6 weeks after 
the initial acute intoxication. Urinary incontinence and/or faecal incontinence and 
disturbance of gait are common. 
	
l Chronic poisoning is often unsuspected and unrecognized, and features may 
appear non-specific, e.g. headache, nausea and flu-like symptoms, vertigo, 
alteration in consciousness and subjective feeling of weakness. They are most 
common in winter as that is when fires are used and ventilation is restricted. 
Suspected if more than one person in a household has such symptoms that do not 
appear to be due to a viral infection. There may be black, sooty marks near a fire.
High-level poisoning
	
l The above symptoms may be more severe. Tachycardia and tachypnoea, dizziness 
and ataxia, angina, hypotension, arrhythmias, agitation, seizures, impairment of 
consciousness and respiratory failure; cerebral oedema and metabolic acidosis 
may develop. In addition, personality change, poor performance on the mini-
mental state examination may also be seen.
	
l Oxygen saturation levels are usually normal. ECG changes, metabolic acidosis, 
raised TLC and amylase and raised SGOT and SGPT in severe cases. A raised 
carboxyhaemoglobin level is definitive diagnostic investigation. However, it can 
be misleading as the levels start falling as soon as the patient is removed from the 
site of exposure. Symmetrical and diffuse low-density lesions in globus pallidus, 
cortical lesions on CT scan are characteristic.

Prehospital
Remove the patient promptly from the source of exposure and immediately institute 
oxygen therapy with a non-rebreather mask.

222    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Hospital
	 1.	Perform intubation for the comatose patient or, if necessary, for airway protection, 
and provide 100% oxygen therapy and may be required for 24 hours.
	 2.	Early blood samples may provide a much more accurate correlation between 
carboxyhaemoglobin (HbCO) and clinical status; however, do not delay oxygen 
administration to acquire them. 
	 3.	Institute cardiac monitoring. Measure pulse oximetry gap, the difference between 
the saturation as measured by pulse oximetry and one measured directly by 
arterial blood gas is equal to the HbCO level. Most of the point of care blood gas 
analyzer will give carboxyhemoglobin level. Measure the HbCO concentration as 
an emergency if there is suspicion of carbon monoxide poisoning. HbCO of 30% 
indicates severe exposure but much lower concentrations do not exclude significant 
poisoning and the relationship between HbCO and severity of poisoning and 
clinical outcome is poor.
	 4.	In uncomplicated intoxications, venous HbCO levels and oxygen therapy are likely 
to be sufficient. 
	 5.	Evaluate patients with significant cardiovascular disease and initial HbCO 
levels above 15% for myocardial ischaemia and infarction and treat accordingly 
(for details, see Chapter 4).
	 6.	Consider immediate transfer of patients with levels above 40% or cardiovascular 
or neurologic impairment to a hyperbaric facility if feasible. Persistent impairment 
after 4 hours of normobaric oxygen therapy necessitates transfer to a hyperbaric centre.
	 7.	Calculate a gross estimate of the necessary duration of therapy using the initial 
level and half-life of 30–90 minutes at 100% oxygen.
	 8.	Pregnant patients with lower HbCO (above 15%) should be considered for 
hyperbaric treatment. Continue treatment even after carbon monoxide is no longer 
found in the blood.
	 9.	Inj. Mannitol 1g/kg intravenously over 20 minutes if cerebral oedema is suspected. 
Follow-up and monitoring
	
l Acidosis generally improves with oxygen therapy. Do not aggressively treat acidosis 
with a pH above 7.15. Monitor the heart rhythm and blood gases for 4–6 hours. In 
patients who fail to improve clinically, consider other toxic inhalants or thermal 
inhalation injury.
	
l Asymptomatic patients with HbCO levels below 10% may be discharged. Admit 
patients with histories of lung or vascular diseases, young children and pregnant 
women without symptoms for observation in a monitored setting (CCU/ICU) and 
evaluate acid-base status. 
	
l Refer patients with cerebral oedema with raised ICP to a neurosurgical ICU setting. 
Cardiac arrest, coma, metabolic acidosis and high HbCO levels are associated with 
poor outcome. 
	
l Neuropsychiatric testing may have prognostic efficacy in determining delayed 
sequelae.

Patient education
	
l If treatment is timely, most people will be able to recover from carbon monoxide 
poisoning.
	
l Discuss the possibility of delayed neurologic complications, although they are much 
more common in severe intoxication.
	
l During the weeks following treatment, explain to the patient to report any changes 
in vision, coordination, or behaviour to doctor. 
	
l Minimize physical activity for 2–4 weeks.
	
l Advise patients to stop smoking.
OLEANDER POISONING
Ingestion of oleander seeds or leaves is a common cause of accidental poisoning 
worldwide, particularly among children. Poisoning by pila kaner or yellow oleander 
(Cerebrathevetia) and Nerium oleander (white oleander) is frequent in south India. 
The kernels of the seed are most toxic with the lethal dose being 8–10 seeds. These 
plants contain several glycosides, which resemble digitoxin.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The patient develops skin rashes, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, 
pupillary dilatation, tingling and numbness, restlessness, bradycardia, arrhythmias, 
hypotension and nervous system toxicity. Hyperkalaemia is common. Depression, 
loss of appetite, and visual halos are usually only seen in chronic overdose cases.
	
l ECG shows sinus bradycardia, AV blocks, ST-T changes, prolongation of PR 
interval, AV dissociation and ventricular ectopic. In severe cases, ventricular 
tachycardia and fibrillation can occur.

1.	Provide support to safeguard airway, breathing and circulation.
	 2.	Monitor vital signs, including temperature, pulse, breathing rate, blood pressure 
and cardiac monitoring.
	 3.	Activated charcoal, if patient reports within 1 hour of ingestion.
	 4.	Correct fluid, electrolyte and acid-base disturbances (for details, see respective 
sections).
	 5.	For bradycardia give atropine and pacing (for details, see section on Chapter 3).
	 6.	For ventricular tachyarrhythmias, give Lidocaine (for details, see Chapter 3).
	 7.	For life-threatening poisoning, Digoxin-specific Fab antibody fragments are useful.

Methanol is commonly found in home chemicals, industrial chemicals, varnishes, 
paints, dies and used as denaturant in ethanol. Poisoning can be accidental or may

224    Standard Treatment Guidelines
be consumed by chronic alcoholics deprived of their alcoholic beverage of choice, 
suicidal ingestion of methanol containing products and unintended consumption of such 
products by children. Methanol is cheap and may be used to fortify illicit spirits. Toxic 
dose is 15–30 mL of 40% methanol. Symptoms of toxicity appear within 12–24 hours 
due to accumulation of toxic metabolite, formic acid/formate which is responsible for 
the metabolic acidosis and end-organ toxicity. 
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Methanol typically induces nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and mild CNS 
depression initially. After 12–24 hours depending upon consumption there is 
metabolic acidosis, visual disturbance (difficulty in vision, pupillary dilation, 
retinal oedema and optic disc hyperaemia) due to formation of formic acid. At 
later stages, seizures, coma and respiratory failure may develop.
	
l An electrocardiogram, basic metabolic panel, complete blood count, transaminases, 
lipase, pregnancy status, serum or urine ketones, lactate. Toxic ethanol level is 
confirmatory if available. Rule out salicylate toxicity especially when evaluating a 
patient with metabolic acidosis.
	
l High anion gap metabolic acidosis may appear later, observe patient presenting 
with normal acid-base status early after ingestion for a minimum of 12 hours with 
serial basic metabolic panels every 2–4 hours to monitor for the development of 
metabolic acidosis and an elevated anion gap. Measure osmolar gap (OG) for 
further risk stratification in the early presenting patient using formula: Serum 
osmolality = [2(Na) + BUN/1.6 + Glucose/18 + Ethanol/4.6].
	
l OG = measured serum osmolality − calculated osmolality. A normal osmol gap is 
<10 mOsm/kg. An osmolar gap of >10 is suggestive of toxic alcohol (methanol, 
ethylene glycol, etc.) ingestion.

Admit in ICU as these patients are at risk of developing hypotension, tachycardia, 
hypoglycaemia, CNS and respiratory depression. Start treatment without delay on 
suspicion of methanol or ethylene glycol intoxication. With prompt diagnosis and 
treatment, patients often recover. Retinal toxicity and basal ganglia toxicity may result 
in permanent symptoms. Significant morbidity and mortality can occur when patients 
present late, or diagnosis is not recognized in a timely fashion.
The treatment of both alcohols is the same, and differentiating which of the two 
toxic alcohols is responsible is not necessary before implementing treatment.
	 1.	Maintain airway, breathing and circulation (see section on CPR in Chapter 2).
	 2.	Gastric lavage if patient reports within 30 minutes of consumption or who have 
ingested large amounts of methanol while maintaining a normal mental status. Do 
not use activated charcoal.
	 3.	Sodium bicarbonate 50 mg intravenously every 4 hours if pH <7.35 or bicarbonate 
<15 mEq/L.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    225
	 4.	If methanol level >20 mg/dL, osmolar gap >10 mOsm/kg H2O, bicarbonate 
<15 mmol/L or if there is evidence of retinal toxicity, give Inj. Fomepizole loading 
dose 15 mg/kg IV as soon as possible, subsequent dose 10 mg/kg every 12 hours 
for 48 hours. After 48 hours, 15 mg/kg 12 hourly (higher maintenance dose due 
to autoinduction) until serum level of Methanol is <20 mg/dL and resolution of 
metabolic acidosis and symptoms.
	
	Or
	
	If Fomepizole not available. Ethanol 10% empirical loading dose of 8 mL/kg IV 
over 30–60 minutes, followed by maintenance dose of 1–2 mL/kg per hour.
	
	Ethanol 50% oral empirical loading dose of 2 mL/kg followed by 0.2–0.4 mL/kg 
per hour. Maintenance dosing is doubled during dialysis.
	
	When treating with ethanol the goal therapeutic serum concentration is a range of 
80–120 mg/dL. Loading dose is calculated using the product of the goal plasma 
concentration (C = 100 mg/dL), the volume of distribution of ethanol (V = 0.6 L/kg), 
and the patient’s weight. Maintenance dosing is then based on elimination rate. 
Close monitoring of serum ethanol concentrations is essential in order to achieve 
a value within the recommended range.
	
	(Caution: Adverse effects include hypoglycaemia, headache, nausea, dizziness but 
not sedation, pancreatitis, and local phlebitis. Check serum glucose levels frequently, 
at least every 2 hours and maintain sugar levels between 100 and 150 mg/dL.)
	 5.	Haemodialysis in severe ethylene glycol and methanol poisoning, if serum 
methanol levels >50 mg/dL. Other indications of hemodialysis are metabolic 
acidosis, significant electrolyte disturbance unresponsive to conventional treatment, 
CNS, visual or fundoscopy abnormalities, renal failure and in case of consumption 
of lethal dose of 1g/kg or >30 mL of methanol. During dialysis, Fomepizole needs 
to be dosed every four rather than every 12 hours.
	 6.	Inj. Folinic acid (Leucovorin) 1 mg/kg (maximum dose 50 mg) every 4–6 hours 
until metabolic acidosis resolves. If Folinic acid is not immediately available, folic 
acid can be substituted at the same dose. 
	 7.	In comatosed alcoholic patients, give Inj. Thiamine 100 mg IV every 6 hours and 
50 mg of Pyridoxine every 6 hours. Consult specialist if signs of optic injury or 
neurological deficit persists.
DHATURA POISONING
Datura stramonium (thorn apple) grows in India at high altitudes. The seeds and fruits 
are the most poisonous parts of the plant with hyoscine, hyoscyamine and traces of 
atropine as the active principles. The dried leaves and dried seeds are used in India as 
a substitute for stramonium and belladonna. The drug is commonly used in India for 
criminal purposes.

226    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Peripheral effects are predominant and result from anticholinergic 
(parasympatholytic) action. Central effects involve initial stimulation of the CNS, 
with excitement and restlessness followed by subsequent depression, delirium 
and coma.
	
l Within half an hour of taking the poison, gastric irritation starts. The patient 
complains of a bitter taste, dry mouth and throat, burning pain in the stomach 
and difficulty in swallowing and talking. This is followed by giddiness, ataxia, 
incoordination of muscles, a peculiar, flushed appearance of the face, dry hot 
skin, rise in temperature, diplopia, dilated pupils with loss of accommodation, 
reddening of the conjunctiva and drowsiness. Sometimes, an erythematous rash 
appears all over the body.
	
l Usually a full, bounding pulse which later becomes weak and irregular. 
	
l Muttering delirium, tries to run away from the bed, picks at bed clothes, tries 
to pull imaginary threads from the tips of his fingers and develops dreadful 
hallucinations of sight and hearing. The condition may pass on to stupor, 
convulsions, coma and sometimes death from respiratory failure. Death may 
occur within 4–24 hours.

1.	The stomach is washed out with 1:10,000 potassium permanganate solution or 5% 
tannic acid solution. 
	 2.	In severe life-threatening poisoning, Inj. Physostigmine 1–2 mg IM or IV repeated 
after half an hour, if necessary. Watch for side effects: bradycardia, heart block, 
excessive secretions.
	 3.	Inj. Pilocarpine nitrate 6–15 mg injected subcutaneously.
	 4.	Inj. Diazepam may be given for convulsions (see section on Status Epilepticus).
	 5.	For delirium, chloral hydrate, Inj. Paraldehyde or any short-acting barbiturate is 
usually given. (Caution: Morphine is contraindicated.)
OPIOID INTOXICATION
Opioid overdose can be a medical emergency and is usually accidental. It can result 
from incorrect estimation of dose or erratic pattern of use in which person has lost 
previous tolerance to drug. Often caused by combined use with other CNS depressants, 
e.g. alcohol or sedative hypnotics or consumption of cough syrups containing codeine, 
lomotil and opiate-containing analgesics.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression (respiratory rate <8/minutes) and CNS 
depression, decreased gastrointestinal motility, analgesia, nausea and vomiting, 
slurred speech, hypotension, bradycardia and seizures.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    227
Treatment (Immediate admission in intensive care unit [ICU])
	 1.	Establish adequate airway and respiration. Oxygen inhalation and IV fluids. If 
facilities are available, give artificial ventilation.
	 2.	Activated charcoal 1 g/kg suspended in water if ingestion of large doses of oral 
opioids is suspected and presents within 4 hours of ingestion and after protecting 
the airway.
	
	Or
	
	Gastric lavage to remove any remaining drug if presents within 1 hour of 
consumption.
	 3. 	In stable/conscious patients, administer naloxone first (activated charcoal can be 
delayed), as patient’s sensorium may deteriorate rapidly – 
	
	Inj. Naloxone 0.01 mg/kg in neonates; 0.1 mg/kg IV in children up to 5 years and 
2 mg in older children and adults; response seen in 1–2 min; if needed repeat every 
2–3 minutes up to 10 mg. If no response to 10 mg, it is unlikely due to opioids 
except in case of buprenorphine or suspect another diagnosis. Titrate dose relative 
to the patient’s symptoms to ameliorate the respiratory depression but not provoke 
a severe withdrawal state. 
	
	If the patient is a chronic opioid user start with lower doses to avoid withdrawal 
reaction. If successful, continue 2/3rd of the wake-up dose every hour IV until 
the opioid has been cleared (at least for 24 hours for heroin and 72 hours for 
methadone overdose). Babies born to opioid-abusing mothers may experience 
intoxication, overdose or withdrawal.
	 4.	Always consider possible polysubstance overdose. A patient successfully treated 
with naloxone may wake up briefly only to succumb to a subsequent overdose 
from another slower acting drugs, e.g. sedative-hypnotic taken simultaneously. 
Give Inj. Flumazenil 0.2 mg/min (maximum 3 mg in an hour). only when there is 
confirmed benzodiazepine overdose. (Caution: It might precipitate seizures and 
increase intracranial pressure.)
	 5.	Supportive measures for respiration, hypotension with pressor agents and cardiac 
arrhythmia.
	 6.	Body warmth to be maintained with hot water bottles.
	 7.	If convulsions are present, Inj. Diazepam 10 mg IV and repeated as required 
(for details, see section on Status Epilepticus).
	 8.	The patient should not be made to walk forcibly in opium poisoning, as it is 
frequently done, but attempts should be made to keep him awake, by flicking a wet 
towel on the face.

ANIMAL BITES
Animal bites pose a major public health problem; the most important are arising from 
bites from snakes, dogs, cats and monkeys. Prompt medical treatment with appropriate 
anti-venom is required for poisonous snake bites (details given in following section). 
Rabies is a significant health concern following bite by warm blooded animals 
especially dog, cat and monkey.
DOG BITES (RABIES)
Rabies can be transmitted by rabid animal bites or licks on abraded skin or intact 
mucosa. All warm blooded animals can suffer from rabies and transmit the disease. In 
India, rabies is mainly transmitted by bite or lick of a rabid dog or cat. Animals which 
can transmit rabies are monkey, horse, sheep, goat, mongoose, jackal, fox, hyena and 
bat. Exposure to rodents, rabbits and hares seldom, if requires specific anti-rabies 
treatment. Bat rabies has not been conclusively reported from India as yet.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The incubation period for rabies is typically 2–3 months but may vary from 1 week 
to 1 year, dependent upon factors such as the location of virus entry and viral load. 
Prodromal symptoms such as headache, malaise, sore throat and fever last about 
3–4 days. Pain and tingling at the bitten site. 
	
l Stage of excitation – patient is intolerant to noise, bright light or a cold draught. 
Hydrophobia is a characteristic symptom of rabies. Aerophobia may be present. 
Examination shows increased reflexes, dilatation of pupils, increased sweating, 
lacrimation and salivation. Mental changes include fear of death, anger, irritability 
and depression. Convulsions may occur resulting in death. 
	
l The last stage is that of paralysis and coma. The total duration of illness lasts for 
2–3 days.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    229
A. Treatment (Post-exposure)
The WHO recommended classification (Table 2.16) of animal bite for post-exposure 
treatment should be followed. Every instance of human exposure to a suspected rabid 
or wild animal must be treated as a category III, considered as a ‘medical emergency’ 
and the ‘life-saving’ post-exposure prophylaxis must be provided immediately.
The post-exposure treatment is a three-pronged approach. All three carry equal 
importance and should be done simultaneously:
	 1.	Management of wound: Immediate washing of the wound or scratch is a priority. 
Wound toilet must be done even if several hours or days have elapsed. The wound 
is immediately flushed and washed with plenty of soap and water (avoid direct 
touching of wounds with bare hands). Punctured wounds should be irrigated with 
the help of catheters. After thorough washing and drying the wound(s), apply 70% 
alcohol or povidone-iodine.

a Exposure to domestic rodents, squirrel, hare and rabbits does not routinely require PEP.
b Stop PEP, if trained professional has confirmed that the animal (dog or cat only) remains healthy throughout an 
observation period of 10 days. The treatment may be modified if dog or cat involved remains healthy throughout 
the observation period of 10 days by converting post-exposure prophylaxis to pre-exposure vaccination by 
skipping the vaccine dose on day 14 and administering it on day 28 while using Essen Schedule. While using 
ID administration, complete course of vaccination should be given irrespective of the status of the animal. If a 
suspect animal cannot be captured and tested, then a full course of prophylaxis should be completed.
	 A history of rabies vaccination in an animal is not always a guarantee that the biting animal is not rabid. 
Elicit appropriate documentation of vaccination status of dog/cat and proper history before deciding to defer 
post-exposure prophylaxis after bite by vaccinated dog/cat. 
	 Institute PEP immediately irrespective of whether the bite was provoked or unprovoked.

230    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
	Note: The application of irritants (like chillies, oil, turmeric, lime, salt, betal leaves, 
herbs, etc.) is unnecessary and damaging.
	
	Do not suture bite wounds immediately. If suturing is required, it should be done 
after thorough wound washing and infiltration of rabies immunoglobulin in the 
depth and around the wound(s). Suturing should be delayed by a few hours to 
allow the diffusion of antibodies into the tissues. Minimum loose sutures should 
be applied to arrest bleeding in life-threatening situations.
	
	Dog bite requiring closure and deeper bites are considered high risk for infection, 
hence antibiotic prophylaxis may be considered with Amoxicillin/clavulanate 
875/125 mg every 12 hours Or Clindamycin 300 mg 3 times per day plus 
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice per day Or Doxycycline 100 mg twice per day.
	
	Tetanus vaccination may be given if it has been more than 5 years since the patient 
has been immunized (for details see Immunization in Chapter 19).
	 2.	Passive immunization with rabies immunoglobulin (RIG): Local infiltration of 
RIG in category III rabies and in both category II and III exposures in immune 
compromised (HIV/ AIDS, patients on chemotherapy, steroid therapy, cancer 
patients, etc.) – RIG should be infiltered in the depth and around the wound even 
if the lesion has begun to heal followed by administration of antirabies vaccine. 
RIG is not required in individuals who have received complete post-exposure 
prophylaxis (PEP) or pre-exposure prophylaxis in the past.
	
	Antirabies vaccine (ARV) should be administered regardless of the availability of 
RIG.
	
	RIG is administered only once, preferably at or as soon as possible after initiation 
of post-exposure vaccination. It is not indicated beyond the seventh day, i.e. 
when three doses of rabies vaccine have been given to the patient. (Caution: RIG 
should never be administered in the same syringe or at the same anatomical site as 
vaccine.)
	
	A new rabies monoclonal antibody (mAb) is now available for use and is a safer 
alternative to RIG. The dose is 3.3 IU/kg thus easier to inject with less pain and 
with minimal risk of allergic reactions. Like RIG, it can be given upto 7th day of 
initiation of antirabies vaccination.
Doses of rabies immunoglobulin (RIG)
	
	Human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) 20 IU/kg (maximum 1500 IU), 
available in concentration of 150 IU/mL. SHOULD NEVER BE INJECTED 
INTRAVENOUSLY. The antirabies sera should always be brought to room 
temperature (25–30°C) before use.
	
	Or
	
	Equine antirabies serum (ERIG) 40 IU/kg (maximum 3000 IU), available in 
concentration of 300 IU/mL, given as a single dose within 24 hours of bite, i.e. 
day 0 along with the first dose of anti-rabies vaccine. If RIG was not administered

Chapter 2  Emergencies    231
when ARV was begun, RIG can be administered up to seventh day after 
administration of the first dose of vaccine.
	
	Infiltrate as much of the calculated dose of RIG as is anatomically feasible into 
and around the wound(s). Avoid multiple needle injections into the wound(s). Must 
not exceed the total recommended dose of RIG as it may reduce the efficacy of the 
vaccine. 
	
	If the calculated dose of RIG is insufficient to cover infiltration in all wounds, 
sterile saline can be used to dilute 2 or 3 fold to permit thorough infiltration. 
Infected bite wound is no contraindication to infiltration of immunoglobulin.
	
	Keep animal bite victim under observation for at least ½ hour after administration 
of ERIG (be ready for management of reactions, if occurs). There is no need to 
admit the patient.
	 3.	Active immunization with antirabies vaccine (ARV):
	
l Start PEP at the earliest in category II and III exposure. Evaluate people who 
present for treatment even months or years after a possible rabies exposure and 
treat as if the event has occurred recently. The vaccination status of the suspect 
animal should not be the deciding factor when considering to initiate PEP.
	
l There is no contraindication to PEP. Give rabies PEP in pregnancy, lactation, 
infancy, old age and concurrent illness in the event of an exposure according 
to the category of exposure. People taking chloroquine for malaria treatment 
or prophylaxis may have a reduced response to ID rabies vaccination. These 
patients should receive the rabies vaccine intramuscularly.
	
l Currently available Cell Culture Vaccines (CCVs) and purified duck embryo 
vaccine (PDEV) can be administered by IM regimen and CCVs approved for 
ID use can be administered by ID regimen.
Intramuscular schedule (Essen regimen). Five doses (1-1-1-1-1) on days 0, 3, 7, 14, 
21. The day 0 is the day of initiation of vaccine. The dose of vaccine per injection is 2.5 
IU/dose/mL for cell culture vaccines (Human Diploid Cell Vaccine [HDCV], Liquid 
[Adsorbed], HDCV and Purified Chick Embryo Cell Vaccine [PCECV] and 0.5 mL or 
1 mL for Purified Vero Cell Rabies Vaccine [PVRV], irrespective of age and weight 
of individual. Preferable site is deltoid; anterolateral thigh in children (Caution: Must 
NOT be given into gluteus muscle).
Intradermal (ID) schedule. Use vaccines approved by DCGI for ID route for PPE. A 
dose of 0.1 mL of vaccine, irrespective of reconstituted volume (0.5 mL or 1 mL for IM 
route), is administered per ID site as per. Thai Red Cross Schedule (2-2-2-0-2) and 
on two sites per visit (one on each deltoid area, an inch above the insertion of deltoid 
muscle) on days 0, 3, 7 and 28. The day 0 is the date of first dose administration of 
anti-rabies vaccine and may not be the date of rabies exposure/animal bite.
Note: Correct ID injection should result in a raised papule with an orange peel 
appearance. If a papule is not observed, the needle should be withdrawn and vaccine 
re-administered correctly nearby.

232    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l The intradermal route is preferred as it reduces cost but must not be used in case of 
immunocompromised patients, individuals receiving long-term corticosteroids or 
other immunosuppressive therapy or chloroquine. As far as possible, vaccination 
schedules should be completed in the stipulated time; however, there is no need to 
restart the series, if the doses are not given on the exact schedule, as variations of a 
few days are unlikely to affect the response to vaccination. 
	
l Switching over in the rabies vaccine product and/or the route of administration 
should only be allowed in unavoidable circumstances to ensure completion of a 
PEP schedule. PEP need not be restarted, and the schedule of the new administration 
route should be adopted.
	
l Vaccinated persons should be kept under medical supervision for at least 15–20 
minutes following vaccination. Mild systemic adverse events following immunization 
(AEFI) include headache, malaise, nausea and fever. Symptomatic treatment may be 
needed. Minor and transient erythema, pain and/or swelling may occur at the site of 
injection, particularly following intradermal administration. Serious AEFIs mainly of 
allergic or neurological nature rarely occur. Previous reaction to any component of 
a vaccine is a contraindication to the use of the same vaccine for PEP or PrEP (Pre-
exposure prophylaxis), and the vaccine product should be changed.
Storage and handling of ARV
Antirabies vaccine should be kept and transported at a temperature range of 
+2°C to 8°C. Liquid (adsorbed) rabies vaccines should never be frozen. While using 
ID administration, store vaccine vial at 2–8º C after reconstitution and protect from 
sunlight. Use total content of the vial as soon as possible, but at the maximum within 
8 hours. Discard all unused vaccine after 8 hours of reconstitution. Intradermal PrEP 
should be given to enough individuals in the same session so that opened vials are used 
within 6–8 h to avoid wastage.
B. Post-exposure prophylaxis of immune-compromised patients (HIV/AIDS 
patients, patients on chemotherapy, steroid therapy, cancer patients, etc.) should be 
managed by proper and thorough wound management and antisepsis accompanied 
by local infiltration of rabies immunoglobulin followed by complete course of anti-
rabies vaccination by IM route in both category II and III exposures. Preferably, if 
the facilities are available, anti-rabies antibody estimation should be done 14 days 
after the completion of course of vaccination to assess the need of additional doses of 
vaccine.
C. Post-exposure treatment of persons previously vaccinated
If re-exposed persons who have previously received and documented full pre- or 
post-exposure prophylaxis (either by IM or ID route) with a cell-culture vaccine should 
receive intradermal administration of PEP: one-site ID vaccine administration on days 
0 and 3 Or four-site ID vaccine administration on day 0 only; Or one-site intramuscular 
administration of an entire vaccine vial on days 0 and 3. Proper wound toilet should be 
done. Treatment with RIG is not required.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    233
People without documentation of previous PEP equivalent to PrEP or complete PrEP 
should receive a full PEP, including RIG, if indicated.
D. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)
Indications: In people with occupational exposure such as Laboratory staff working 
with rabies virus, veterinarians, animal handlers and wildlife officers, travel or 
residence in an endemic setting with limited access to timely, adequate PEP. PrEP 
should be given at least 7 days before. PrEP obviates administration of RIG after a 
bite. One full dose of vaccine intramuscularly (1-0-1-0-1) or 0.1 mL intra-dermally 
(1-0-1-0-1) on days 0, 7, 21/28).
Laboratory staff and others at high continuing risk of exposure should have their 
neutralizing antibody titre checked every 1–2 years period after the primary 
vaccination. If it is less than 0.5 IU/mL, a booster dose of vaccine should be given. 
Periodic booster injections are recommended as an added precaution only for people 
whose occupation places them at continual or frequent risk of exposure; antibody 
monitoring, if available, is preferred.
Patient education
	
l Dog bite (categories II and III) is an emergency and as a general rule rabies 
post-exposure treatment should not be delayed or deferred.
	
l Immediate washing with plenty of water and soap or only water if soap is not 
available and disinfecting with alcohol/iodine.
	
l Complete the course of post or pre-exposure prophylaxis.
	
l Education on dog behaviour and bite prevention for both children and adults is 
essential. Training and socialization of dogs to children from the time they are 
puppies is important. Training makes a dog more confident and less likely to bite 
out of fear. Pets should have regular veterinary visits to stay updated on vaccines 
and to improve health. Pets that are in pain or sick are more likely to bite. Neutering 
dogs has been shown to decrease bites. Do not leave young children alone with pets.

INSECT AND ARACHNID BITES AND 
STINGS CAUSING SKIN DISEASES
Mosquitoes and other biting flies
Most insect bites and stings cause small reactions that are confined to the area of 
the bite (localized reactions). They can usually be treated at home. Besides being 
vectors of several most important parasitic diseases, including malaria, leishmaniasis, 
onchocerciasis and filariasis, mosquitoes and other biting flies can induce florid local 
lesions in susceptible persons (for details see respective sections).
Bees, wasps, hornets and ant (Hymenoptera spp.)
First aid
Sting removal most essential – inspect the sting site and if sting present remove the sting 
and the venomous sac immediately by scraping it out, either with fingernails or using 
something with a hard edge, such as a bank card. (Caution: Avoid using tweezers or 
anything else that could puncture or squeeze the venom sack and make symptoms worse.)
Honey bees can only sting once, because they leave their stingers behind them. Wasps 
and hornets do not usually leave the sting behind, so could sting again so leave the 
room calmly.
Most insect bites and stings cause itching and swelling that usually clears up within 
several hours. The level of swelling caused by a sting can often be startling. The 
swelling caused by a local reaction may decrease within a few hours, but it can take a 
few days to fully resolve.
For minor bites and stings:
	 1.	Wash the affected area with soap and water.
	 2.	Place a cold compress (a flannel or cloth cooled with cold water) over the affected 
area to reduce swelling for at least 10 minutes.
	
	Do not burst the blister or scratch the area because it can become infected.
If the bite or sting is painful or swollen:
	 3.	Topical administration of ice pack or calamine lotion for symptomatic relief. Some 
natural products and essential oils (honey, aloe vera gel, lavender oil, rosemary oil, 
calamine lotion) applied locally have a role in reducing swelling, however, apple 
cider vinegar, baking soda may be harmful. No clinical research to support use of 
toothpaste.
	 4.	Systemic antihistamines and analgesics can be given to relieve pruritus or pain.
	 5.	Systemic corticosteroids may be appropriate, if there are severe side effects.
For severe reaction
	 1.	Any person who collapses or who complains of wheezing, feeling of anxiety or 
faintness, generalized itching or tightness in the chest within approximately 1 hour

Chapter 2  Emergencies    235
of being stung by an insect should be treated as having anaphylactic shock. If 
possible get ECG done.
	 2.	Inj. Adrenaline 1 mg (as hydrogen tartrate) 0.5–1.0 mL IM injection of Adrenaline 
(1:1000 solution) repeated every 15–20 minutes, if required.
	 3.	All patients should be observed at least for 24 hours for recurrent anaphylaxis.
	
	(For details, see section on Anaphylaxis.)
Patient education
Explain tips to avoid insect stings:
	
l Avoid wearing bright colours, scented perfume or hair sprays.
	
l Bees and wasps only sting humans to protect their hive. Therefore, do not disturb 
their hive.
	
l Bees and wasps are slow fliers – walk away from them by walking quickly.
SCORPION STING/BITE
Clinical effects of the envenomation and outcome depends upon the species of 
the scorpion and lethality and dose of venom injected at the time of sting and time 
elapsed between sting and hospitalization. Severe effects are seen in first victim than 
envenomed by same scorpion to subsequent victim. 
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l On the basis of clinical manifestations at the time of arrival to hospital and 
according to severity they are graded in 4 grades: 
	
l Grade 1: Severe excruciating local pain at the sting site radiating along with 
corresponding dermatomes, mild local oedema at the sting site without systemic 
involvement.
	
l Grade 2: Signs and symptoms of autonomic storm. Vomiting, salivation, sweating, 
priapism and bradycardia are early diagnostic signs. Sweating and salivation persist 
for 6–13 hours. Increased oral secretions and bronchorrhoea in the early cholinergic 
and prolonged sympathetic stimulation can worsen respiratory compromise.
	
l Grade 3: Cold extremities, tachycardia, hypotension or hypertension with pulmonary 
oedema (respiratory rate >24 per minute, basal rales or crackles in lungs).
	
l Grade 4: Tachycardia, hypotension with or without pulmonary oedema with warm 
extremities (warm shock). 
	
l ‘TAP sign’: Sudden tap at and around the site of sting induces severe pain and 
withdrawal is diagnostic sign of sting. Severe pain without systemic involvement 
is suggestive of benign or dry sting by venomous species.

The clinical manifestations and severity of the symptoms vary among patients; 
individualize management of scorpion stings. Time lapse between the sting and

determines the outcome. Furthermore, frequent patient monitoring allows earlier 
recognition of the life-threatening problems of scorpion envenomation. Management

Chapter 2  Emergencies    237
A. First aid
	
l Move the patient away from the scorpion
	
l Assess and stabilize the patient’s airway and vital signs – pulse oximetry, heart rate, 
blood pressure and respiratory rate. Use invasive monitoring for patients who are 
unstable haemodynamically
	
l Administer oxygen
	
l Administer intravenous fluids to help prevent hypovolaemia from vomiting, diarrhoea, 
sweating, hypersalivation and insensible water loss from a tropical environment
B. Local treatment
	 1.	Immobilize the affected part in a functional position below the level of the heart. 
Calm the patient.
	 2.	Use ice bags to reduce pain and to slow the absorption of venom; most effective 
during the first 2 hours following the sting.
	 3.	If there is any delay in transferring patient to a health facility, apply a 
lymphatic-venous compression wrap 1 inch proximal to the sting site. 
(Caution: Do not stop the arterial flow. Remove this wrap only when the provider 
is ready to administer systemic support.) 
	 4.	Antiscorpion venom (ASV), if available, 3 vials IV stat and 1–2 vials 2–4 hourly 
without skin test, administered as early as possible.
	 5.	In children with hypotension, tachycardia (which may rise to 180–230 beats per 
minute), air hunger, warm extremities, or cardiogenic shock, give Dobutamine at 
a dose of 5–15 mcg/kg/minute (for details see Shock given earlier).
C. Wound care
	 1.	Apply a topical or local anaesthetic agent to the wound. 
	 2.	Administer local wound care and topical antibiotic to the wound.
	 3.	Administer Inj. Tetanus toxoid Or Tetanus and diphtheria toxoids (Td) 0.5 mL 
IM immediately and a booster injection in previously immunized individuals. 
Administer tetanus immune globulin to patients not immunized against Clostridium 
tetani.
	 4.	Administer systemic antibiotics, if signs of secondary infection occur.
D. Supportive care
	 1.	Pain management – In case of severe pain, Tab. Paracetamol 500 mg as and when 
necessary.
	 2.	Fluid management – Encourage oral fluids whenever feasible. If tachypnoea 
and altered sensorium, give N/5 saline infusion. Balance the fluid requirements 
carefully. In children with pulmonary oedema, CVP monitoring is essential. 
	 3.	Systemic treatment is instituted by directing supportive care toward the organ 
specifically affected by the venom (Fig. 2.13)
	 4.	Perform intubation and institute mechanical ventilation with end-tidal carbon 
dioxide monitoring for patients in respiratory distress.

238    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
	Note: Dopamine aggravates the myocardial damage through catecholamine-like 
actions; Inotropic medications, such as digitalis, have little effect and should be 
avoided.
	 5.	In case of severe muscle spasms, give Inj. Diazepam Or Lorazepam Or Midazolam 
continuous infusion for severe nervous system excitation.
	 6.	If the heart rate is less than 50 beats per minute and hypotension is present without 
hypovolemia, administer atropine to counter venom-induced parasympathomimetic 
effects.
Note: Exercise caution when using narcotics for a patient with an unsecured airway. 
The use of steroids to decrease shock and oedema is of unproven benefit.
Monitoring
	
l Monitor blood pressure, pulse rate and respiration every 30 minutes for 3 hours, 
every hour for next 6 hours and later every 4 hours till improvement. General time 
guidelines for the disappearance of symptoms after antivenom administration are 
as follows:
	
l Severe neurologic symptoms reverse in 15–30 minutes. Mild-to-moderate neurologic 
symptoms reverse in 45–90 minutes.
	
l In the first hour, local pain abates. In 6–12 hours, agitation, sweating, and 
hyperglycaemia abate. In 6–24 hours, cardiorespiratory symptoms abate.
Patient education
	
l In endemic areas of venomous sting, vigorously shake and check for scorpion in 
clothing, beddings, shoes, package without blindly putting hands. Sandal does not 
prevent sting. 
	
l Pesticides may be used to kill scorpions.
	
l At times of opening the school thoroughly clean and wash the tables and rooms 
(roof, walls and floor) and take care while opening the school bag.
	
l Do not sit touching to mud walls. 
	
l False ceiling under loose tiles of roof and bamboo cot with scrupulous use of 
mosquito net protects from scorpion sting.
References

SNAKE BITE
Snake bite is an acute, life-threatening, time-limiting medical emergency preventable public 
health hazard and a neglected tropical disease. Although the total number of bites in India 
may be more than 5–6 lakhs, only less than 30% are venomous bites. Non-fatal bites may 
be as high as 1.4 million per year as per Million Death Study. The poisonous snakes found

Chapter 2  Emergencies    239
in India belong to the families Elapidae and Viperidae. The most common Indian elapids are 
Naja naja (Indian Cobra) and Bungarus caeruleus (Indian Krait). Among Viperidae, Daboia 
russelii (Russell’s viper) and Echis carinatus (saw-scaled viper) are prevalent.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patient can present in the four clinical syndromes or in combination, i.e. 
progressive weakness (neuroparalytic/neurotoxic), bleeding (vasculotoxic/ 
haemotoxic), myotoxic and painful progressive swelling (Table 2.17). Examine 
the bite site and look for fang marks or any signs of local envenomation. Fang 
mark or their patterns have no role to determine whether the biting species 
was venomous or non-venomous or amount of venom injected, severity of 
systemic poisoning and nature of poisoning – Elapidae or viperidae venom, 
etc. Some species like Krait may leave no bite marks.
	
l Dry Bite: Snake bites are not always accompanied by the injection of venom (dry 
bites). Symptoms due to anxiety and sympathetic over-activity may be present. 
Differentiate from symptoms and signs of envenomation listed in Table 2.17 and 
Figure 2.14. Redness, increased temperature, persistent bleeding and tenderness 
locally. However, local swelling can be present in these patients due to tight ligature.
	
l Occult Snake Bite: Krait bite victims often present in the early morning with 
descending paralysis with no local signs and no bite marks. Suspect in case of
	– Snake bite victim wakes up in the midnight to 5 AM in the morning with 
severe epigastric/umbilical pain with vomiting persisting for 3–4 hours and 
followed by typical neuroparalytic symptoms within next 4–6 hours. There 
may not be any history of snake bite.
	– Unexplained respiratory distress in children in the presence of bilateral ptosis 
or sudden onset of acute flaccid paralysis (locked-in syndrome).
	– Sometimes patients may present with throat pain, chest pain or joint pain also.
	
l The important early diagnostic criteria of systemic viper poisoning are 
blood-stained sputum and non-clotting of blood. The early signs of an elapid 
envenomation are ptosis and glossopharyngeal palsy.
First-Aid Measures 
Shift the victim to the nearest health facility (PHC with bed or hospital) IMMEDIATELY 
after providing first-aid to a health facility where optimal medical care with antisnake 
venom (ASV) is available, close observation and definite treatment can be provided. 
At the Community or Village Level 
	 1.	Check history of snake bite and look for obvious evidence of a bite (fang puncture 
marks, local pain, bleeding, swelling of the bitten part, breathing difficulty, 
abdominal pain, vomiting, etc.). 
	 2.	Reassure the patient as around 70% of all snake bites are from non-venomous 
species and there is treatment for venomous snake bite.

	 3.	Immobilize the limb in the same way as a fractured limb (splint should extend the 
entire length of the limb, immobilizing all of the joints of the limb) in the recovery 
position (prone, on the left side) with airway protected.
	 4.	Use bandages or cloth to hold the splints (wooden stick), but do NOT block the 
blood supply or apply pressure.
	 5.	Nil by mouth till victim reaches a medical health facility.
	 6.	Arrange transport of the patient to medical care as quickly and passively as 
possible by vehicle ambulance (toll free no. 102/108/etc.), boat, bicycle, motorbike, 
stretcher, etc., whichever is readily available. If ambulance is not available, 
motorbike may be a feasible alternative for rural India, but third person should hold 
the patient sitting behind.
	 7.	Victim must not run or drive himself to reach a Health facility. 
	 8.	If possible PHC medical officer should accompany the patient to inform the doctor 
or referral doctor of the progress, manifestation of the new symptoms and facilitate 
resuscitation on the way.
	 9.	Remove shoes, rings, watches, jewellery and tight clothing from the bitten area. 
	10.	Leave the blisters undisturbed. 
Important Don’ts
	 1.	Do NOT attempt to kill/catch the snake. 
	 2.	Discard traditional first-aid methods (black stones, scarification) and alternative 
medical/herbal therapy.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    241
	 3.	Do NOT wash wound and interfere with the bite wound (incisions, suction, rubbing, 
massage, tattooing, application of herbs or chemicals, cryotherapy and cautery). 
	 4.	Do NOT apply or inject antisnake venom (ASV) locally. 
	 5.	Do NOT tie tourniquets as they may cause gangrenous limbs. 
	 6.	If victim is expected to reach the hospital in more than 30 minutes but less than 
3 hours, crepe bandage may be applied by qualified medical personnel till the 
patient is shifted to the hospital. The bandage is wrapped over the bitten area as 
well as the entire limb with the limb placed in a splint. It should be capable of 
admitting a finger beneath it. 
Treatment (Fig. 2.15)
At A Healthcare Facility
	 1.	Admit all victims of confirmed or suspected snake bite and observe for at least 
24 hours for signs of envenomation.
	 2.	Provide first-aid measures, supportive measures immediately before referring to a 
higher centre. 
	 3.	Administer ASV therapy as soon as there is evidence of envenomation before 
referring to a higher centre.
	 4.	Refer patients presenting with neuroparalytic symptoms immediately to a higher 
facility for intensive monitoring after giving Atropine + Neostigmine (AN) injection.
Critical or Non-Critical Arrival 
	 1.	Assess circulation, airway and breathing and deal with any life-threatening 
symptoms on presentation as below:
	
	Vasculotoxic patients presenting with bleeding from multiple orifices with 
hypotension, reduced urine output, obtunded mentation (drowsy, confused) and 
cold extremities need urgent attention and ICU care for volume replacement, pressor 
support, dialysis and infusion of blood and blood products (see the following sections). 
	
	Neuroparalytic patients presenting with respiratory paralysis, tachypnoea 
or bradypnoea or paradoxical respiration (only moving abdomen), obtunded 
mentation and peripheral skeletal muscle paralysis need urgent ventilator 
management with endotracheal intubation, ventilation bag or ventilator assistance. 
	
	Other patients can be evaluated to decide the severity of their illness.
	 2.	Establish large-bore intravenous access and start NS slow infusion. 
	 3.	Test for the presence of a pulse distal to the tourniquet. If the pulse is absent
	 4.	In case of a clinically confirmed venomous bite, remove tourniquet only in the 
presence of a doctor by the side of the patient after starting loading dose of ASV 
and keep Atropine Neostigmine injection ready. 
	 5.	In case of multiple ligatures/tourniquets/pressure immobilization, all the ligatures 
can be released in Emergency Room EXCEPT the most proximal one, which should 
only be released after admission and all preparations for handling the complications 
and to start ASV. Sudden removal can lead to a massive surge of venom leading to

	 6.	Carry out a medical assessment including history and physical examination and 
every 1–2 hourly and record bite site local swelling, painful tender and enlarged 
local lymph glands, persistent bleeding from the bite wound, blood pressure, pulse 
rate, bleeding (gums, nose, vomit, stool or urine), level of consciousness, drooping 
eyelids and other signs of paralysis. The Glasgow Coma Scale cannot be used

Chapter 2  Emergencies    243
to assess the level of consciousness of patients paralyzed by neurotoxic venom. 
Bilateral dilated, poorly or a non-reacting pupil is not a sign of brain dead in elapid 
envenoming. Patient with Elapidae bites, especially Krait bite, may present with 
locked in syndrome (LIS) as patient is conscious but unable to communicate, open 
eyes, or move any limb due to quadriplegia and anarthria. Patients retain vertical 
eye movement, facilitating non-verbal communication. In complete LIS, the patient 
cannot communicate in any form. These patients can be saved with high index of 
suspicion by referring to a centre with ventilator support. Confirmatory tests such 
as EEG, cerebral blood flow and nerve conduction velocities are recommended to 
avoid misdiagnosis of coma or brain death. With ventilation and intensive care, 
spontaneous recovery after synthesis of new neuromuscular junction and vesicle 
happens after few days. Duration can vary from 30 hours to 6 days (krait bite takes 
longer to recover).
	 7.	To identify impending respiratory failure, bedside lung function test in adults, namely 
	
l Single breath count: Number of digits counted in one exhalation – normal >30 
	
l Breath-holding time: Breath held in inspiration – normal > 45 sec
	
l Ability to complete one sentence in one breath.
	
l Cry in a child whether loud or husky can help in identifying impending 
respiratory failure. 
	 8.	Check for and monitor 20 minutes whole blood clotting test (20 WBCT) every hour 
for first 3 hours and every 6 hours for remaining 24 hours.
	 9.	Check distal pulses and monitor if there is presence of gross swelling. The presence 
of a pulse does not rule out compartment syndrome. 
	10.	Examine snake carefully the snake, if brought, and identify, if possible. Take one 
smart phone photograph of the snake, dead or alive, if available, for confirmation 
by an expert.
	11.	Look for life-threatening complications such as acute kidney injury, hypotension, 
parotid swelling, conjunctival oedema, subconjunctival haemorrhage, renal failure, 
acute respiratory distress syndrome (leaking syndrome) and refractory shock and 
manage accordingly.
Non-critical arrival and critical patients after stabilization
Determine the time elapsed since the snake bite. Obtain a brief medical history (date of 
last tetanus immunization, use of any medication, history of allergy etc.)

1.	Simple bedside examination: Measure limb circumference 10 cm proximally to 
the bite and repeat every 2–4 hourly, single breath count – 1001, 1002…., breath 
holding time and chest expansion measurement and look for drooping of upper 
eyelids. Keep on monitoring the patient and repeat all above, every 1–2 hour.
	 2.	Bedside tests: BT, CT and 20 WBCT.
	 3.	20-minute whole blood clotting test (20 WBCT) (Result should be written as 
Clotted/Not clotted; not as Positive/Negative)

244    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Place 2 mL of freshly sampled venous blood in a small glass vessel and leave 
undisturbed for 20 minutes at ambient temperature. Gently tilt the test tube to see if the 
blood is still liquid (do not shake); the patient has hypofibrinogenaemia (‘incoagulable 
blood’) as a result of venom-induced consumption coagulopathy. If blood clot is formed 
and signs and symptoms of neurotoxic envenomation present, classify as neurotoxic 
envenomation. If clotted (but diagnosis is not confirmed), carry out the test every 1 hour 
from admission for 3 hours and then 6-hourly for 24 hours. If the test is non-clotting, 
repeat 6 hours after administration of loading dose of ASV. Based on the repeat test 
results, a decision can be made regarding the need for additional doses of ASV.
(Caution: Use new, clean, dry test tube only; strictly avoid plastic tube as it interferes 
with Hangman factor and becomes incoagulable.)
If there is any doubt, repeat the test in duplicate, including a ‘control’ (blood from a 
healthy person). If negative, the test should be carried out every 30 minutes from 
admission for 3 hours and then hourly after that to ascertain if repeat dose of antivenom 
is indicated.
Early clues that a patient has severe envenoming:
	
l Rapid early extension of local swelling from the site of the bite. In Cobra bite on 
finger, necrosis may start in few minutes.
	
l Early tender enlargement of local lymph nodes, indicating spread of venom in the 
lymphatic system.
	
l Visible signs of neurological impairment such as ptosis, muscular weakness, 
respiratory distress or respiratory arrest. 
	
l Early spontaneous systemic bleeding especially bleeding from the gums, bite site, 
haematuria, haemoptysis, epistaxis or ecchymoses. 
	
l Unconsciousness either with or without respiratory arrest.
	
l Passage of dark brown/black urine. The snake has been identified as a very 
venomous one, i.e. Cobra, Russell’s viper.
Observe every case of alleged snake bite for at least 24 hours before discharging for:
	 a.	Pulse rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure and WBC count every hour for 
3–4 hours and every 4 hours for remaining 48 hours.
	 b.	Blood urea, creatinine, WBC count. 
	 c.	Urine output, urine for RBCs (in case of Viper bite). 
	 d.	Vomiting, diarrhoea, abnormal bleeds. 
	 e.	Extent of local swelling and necrosis. ECG, ABG analysis, BT, CT, PTT (to be 
repeated 6 hourly, if abnormal).
1. Antisnake Venom Therapy

l If antisnake venom (ASV) is indicated, i.e. signs and symptoms of systemic 
envenomation with or without evidence of laboratory tests, administer FULL dose 
without any delay. Do NOT give incomplete dose. Do NOT wait for any test report.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    245
	
l There are no absolute contraindications to ASV but do not routinely administer 
ASV to any patient claiming to have bitten by a snake without signs and symptoms 
of envenoming. However, at the same time do not delay or withhold ASV on the 
grounds of anaphylactic reaction to a deserving case. 
	
l ASV not indicated in purely local swelling, and a normal WBCT, even if accompanied 
by a bite mark from an apparently venomous snake or non-progressive swelling a 
number of hours old. However, rapid development of swelling involving more than 
half of the bitten limb (in the absence of a tourniquet) and severe swelling after bites 
on the digits (toes and fingers) indicates bite with envenoming requiring ASV.
Antisnake Venom (ASV): Antisnake venom is produced in both lyophilized form (less 
rigid cold chain and longer shelf life) and liquid form (less preferable as cold chain is 
crucial). Reconstitute ASV supplied in dry powder form by diluting in 10 mL of distilled 
water/NS. Mixing is done by swirling and not by vigorous shaking. (Caution: Do not 
use, if reconstituted solution is opaque to any extent.) Total dose is diluted in 10 mL/kg 
0.9% Saline or 5% Dextrose and given as an infusion over 1 hour. The patient should be 
closely monitored.
Dose of ASV for neuroparalytic snake bite: ASV 10 vials stat as infusion over 
30 minutes followed by the second dose of 10 vials after 1 hour if no improvement 
within the first hour.
Dose of ASV for vasculotoxic snake bite: Low-dose infusion therapy is as effective 
as high-dose intermittent bolus therapy and also saves scarce ASV doses.
Low-dose infusion therapy: 10 vials for Russel’s viper or 6 vials for Saw-scaled 
viper as stat as infusion over 30 minutes followed by 2 vials every 6 hours as infusion 
in 100 mL of NS till clotting time normalizes or for 3 days whichever is earlier. 
OR
High-dose intermittent bolus therapy: 10 vials of polyvalent ASV stat over 30 minutes as 
infusion, followed by 6 vials 6 hourly as bolus therapy till clotting time normalizes.
No ASV for Sea snake, confirmed Green Pit viper snake bite even if with signs of 
envenomation as available ASV do not contain antibodies against them.
2. Prophylactic Epinephrine (Adrenaline)
Give prophylactic Epinephrine 0.25 mg of 0.1% solution by subcutaneous injection 
(In children 0.005 mg/kg of 0.1% solution) except in known hypertensive and 
if patient presents with BP more than 140/90 in adult victims or patients with 
cardiovascular disease and draw Epinephrine in readiness in two syringes before 
ASV is administered. 
Monitoring of Patients and Precautions During ASV Administration
	 1.	Give ASV only by the IV route and slowly with the physician at the bed side 
during the initial period to intervene immediately at the first sign of any reaction. 
Observe all patients carefully every 5 minutes for the first 30 minutes and then at 
15 minutes for 2 hours for manifestation of a reaction.

246    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 2.	NEVER give ASV by IM route and do NOT inject the ASV locally at the bite 
site. NO ASV test dose or skin/conjunctival hypersensitivity testing as it has no 
predictive value in detecting anaphylactoid or late serum reactions.
	 3.	Take all aseptic precautions before starting ASV to prevent any pyrogenic reactions 
to ASV.
	 4.	At the earliest sign of an adverse reaction, suspend temporarily. (For details of 
management of ASV reaction, see below.)
	 5.	Maintain a strict intake output chart and note colour of urine to detect acute kidney 
injury early. 
	 6.	Pregnant women and children including newborns and small children are 
treated in exactly the same way as other victims including ASV dose independent 
of the body weight in children, but the total volume is restricted to 5 mL/kg and 
given more slowly to prevent fluid overload.
	 7.	ASV dosage in victims requiring life-saving surgery such as in intracranial 
bleeding – before surgery, restore coagulation to avoid catastrophic bleeding and 
higher initial dose of ASV (up to 30 vials) can be administered.
Repeat Dose of ASV
Vasculotoxic/haemotoxic envenomation: Repeat clotting test every 6 hours until 
coagulation is restored (time required for liver to replace clotting factors). Administer 
ASV every 6 hours until coagulation is restored (maximum 30 vials). In patients who 
continue to bleed briskly, repeat ASV within 1–2 hours. If coagulation abnormality 
persists even after 30 vials, give fresh frozen plasma (FFP) or cryoprecipitate 
(fibrinogen, factor VIII), fresh whole blood, if both FFP and cryoprecipitate are not 
available. No further ASV.
Neuroparalytic/neurotoxic envenomation: Repeat ASV (maximum 20 vials) when 
there are worsening neurotoxic or cardiovascular signs even after 1–2 hours. Adverse 
antisnake venom (ASV) reactions.
Early ASV and Pyrogenic Reaction
Early anaphylactic reaction (starts with itching, urticaria, dry cough, nausea and 
vomiting, abdominal colic, diarrhoea, tachycardia) and occurs within 10–180 minutes 
of start of therapy and often progresses to cause hypotension, angioedema and shock. 
Pyrogenic reaction: Usually occurs 1–2 hours after ASV includes fever, chills and rigors. 
	 1.	Stop ASV temporarily.
	 2.	Oxygen administration
	 3.	Start fresh IV NS infusion with a new IV set.
	 4.	Administer Epinephrine (adrenaline) (1 in 1,000 solution, 0.5 mg [i.e. 0.5 mL] in 
adults intramuscular over deltoid or over thigh; in children 0.01 mg/kg). Repeat 
every 5–10 minutes if symptoms persist.
	 5.	Administer Inj. Chlorpheniramine maleate 10 mg (in children: 0.2 mg/kg) IV. 
	 6.	In case of fever, Paracetamol and other cooling procedures (tepid sponging and 
fanning). No need to stop ASV.

	 7.	Once the patient has recovered, re-start ASV slowly for 10–15 minutes keeping 
the patient under close observation. The rate of infusion can be increased gradually 
in the absence of a reaction until the full starting dose has been administered 
(~over an hour). 
	 8.	In case of persistent shock, normal saline bolus and adrenaline infusions can be given.
Note: Role of hydrocortisone in managing early ASV reaction is not proved.
Late (serum sickness like) reactions: Develops 1–12 days post ASV (fever, vomiting, 
recurring urticaria, arthralgia, myalgia, lymphadenopathy and nephritis). 
Administer Prednisolone (0.7 mg/kg/day) for 5–7 days, with or without oral 
Chlorpheniramine maleate (0.25 mg/kg/day).
Management of Neurotoxic (Neuroparalytic) Envenomation 
Antisnake venom treatment alone cannot be relied upon to save the life of a patient with 
bulbar and respiratory paralysis. In addition, administer:
	 1.	Oxygen 
	 2.	Assisted ventilation – insert endotracheal tube with the help of the 
anaesthesiologist, if available, or by a trained medical personnel or use laryngeal 
mask airway (LMA) or assist ventilation manually by anaesthetic bag or 
mechanical ventilator. 
	 3.	Administer Atropine and Neostigmine (AN). Give one dose of ‘AN’ injection as 
below before transferring to the higher centre. 
	 4.	Initial dose of ASV is administered over 1 hour. If ASV not available or if no 
improvement after the initial dose, refer to a higher facility.
Atropine Neostigmine (AN) Challenge Test and Dosage	
 
In all cases of neurotoxic envenomation, the ‘AN challenge Test’ is administered. Do 
not give AN in case of confirmed Krait bite.
	 1.	Inj. Atropine 0.6 mg followed by neostigmine 1.5 mg IV stat and repeat dose of 
neostigmine 0.5 mg with atropine every 30 minutes for 5 doses (In children: Inj. 
Atropine 0.05 mg/kg followed by Inj. Neostigmine 0.04 mg/kg) and repeat dose 
0.01 mg/kg every 30 minutes for 5 doses).
	 2.	Thereafter to be given as tapering dose at 1 hour, 2 hour, 6 hours and 12 hours. 
	 3.	Observe the patient closely for 1 hour to determine if the neostigmine is effective. 
	
	Positive response to ‘AN’ trial is measured as 50% or more recovery of the ptosis 
in 1 hour.
	
	Stop AN dosage schedule if: Complete recovery from neuroparalysis. Carefully 
watch patients for recurrence. Patient shows side effects in the form of fasciculation 
or bradycardia.
	
	No improvement after 3 doses of AN indicates Krait bite. Give Inj. Calcium gluconate 
10 mL IV (In children: 1–2 mL/kg [1:1 dilution] slowly over 5–10 minutes every 6 
hourly and continue till neuroparalysis recovers which may last for 5–7 days).

248    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Management of Vasculotoxic Envenomation
	 1.	Strict bed rest to avoid even minor trauma. 
	 2.	Screen for haematuria, haemoglobinuria and myoglobinuria by Dipstick method. 
Centrifuged urine showing pink colour indicates haemoglobinuria, clear 
supernatant (RBCs settle down as deposit) and myoglobinuria. 
	 3.	Closely monitor urine output and maintain 1 mL/kg/h urine output.
	 4.	If the patient is bleeding severely irrespective of full dose of ASV or is already 
seriously anaemic, give transfusion of blood or fresh frozen plasma or transfer 
where facility is available. 
	 5.	Prompt recognition of organ dysfunction and immediate intervention to reverse 
organ impairment. 
In Case of Shock, Myocardial Damage 
If the patient has intravascular volume depletion (i.e. supine or postural hypotension, 
or empty neck veins):
	 1.	Establish intravenous access.
	 2.	Give fluid challenge: 2 L of isotonic saline over 1 hour or until the jugular venous 
pressure/central venous pressure rises to 8–10 cm above the sternal angle (with the 
patient propped up at 45°). 
	 3.	Observe the patient closely. Stop fluid challenge immediately, if pulmonary oedema 
develops.
	 4.	If urine output does not improve or dipstick positive for blood give a trial of 
forced alkaline diuresis (FAD) within first 24 hours of the bite to avoid pigment 
nephropathy leading to acute tubular necrosis (ATN). Delayed FAD has no role. 
If patient responds to first cycle, continue for 3 cycles. FAD converts oliguria 
into polyuria and avoid ATN and acute kidney injury needing dialysis in more than 
75% patients. 
	
	If there is no response to furosemide discontinue FAD and refer patient 
immediately to a higher centre for dialysis. 
	 5.	Detection and management of hyperkalaemia
	
	Hyperkalaemia (>7 mmol/l or hyperkalaemic ECG changes – tall peaked T waves, 
prolonged P-R interval, absent P wave, wide QRS complexes)
	
i.	 Give 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate intravenously over 2 minutes (with 
ECG monitoring if possible) repeated up to 3 times.
	
ii.	 Give 50 mL of 50% dextrose with 10 units of soluble insulin intravenously.
	
iii.	 Sodium bicarbonate 40 mL of 8.4% by slow intravenous infusion and 
Salbutamol aerosol by inhaler may also be used.
	
iv.	 Diuretic
	
v.	 Hemodialysis
	 6.	Management of severe acidosis
	
	If the patient is hypotensive and profoundly acidotic (deep sighing ‘Kussmaul’ 
respirations, very low plasma bicarbonate levels or very low pH <7.10, administer 
sodium bicarbonate)

i.	 Calculate bicarbonate deficit
	
ii.	 Administer 2–3 ampoules (40 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate equivalent 
to 1 mmol/mL) in 55 dextrose water or half of the calculated deficit 
can be replaced in 3–4 hours. (Caution: Intravenous bicarbonate may 
precipitate profound hypocalcaemia and seizures, especially in patients with 
rhabdomyolysis.)
	
iii.	 Severe acidosis in snake bite is usually associated with acute renal failure. 
Volume expansion by sodium bicarbonate can cause fluid overload. If no 
clinical improvement, dialysis is indicated.
	 7.	Indications for dialysis 
	
l Absolute value of blood urea >130 mg/dL (27 mmol/L) (BUN 100 mg/dL), 
Sr. Creatinine >4 mg/dL (500 μmol/L) Or evidence of hypercatabolism in the 
form of daily rise in blood urea 30 mg/dL (BUN > 15), Sr. Creatinine >1 mg/dL, 
Sr. Potassium >1 mEq/L and fall in bicarbonate >2 mmol/L 
	
l Fluid overload leading to pulmonary oedema
	
l Hyperkalaemia (>7 mmol/L or hyperkalaemic ECG changes – tall peaked 
T waves, prolonged P-R interval, absent P wave, wide QRS complexes)
	
l Unresponsive to conservative management.
	
l Uraemic complications – encephalopathy, pericarditis.
	
	Haemodialysis is preferable in cases of hypotension or hyperkalaemia. Peritoneal 
dialysis can be performed at a secondary health care centre. Continuous renal 
replacement therapy and intermittent haemodialysis are equivalent in patients 
with severe sepsis and acute renal failure because they achieve similar short-term 
survival rates.
	
	Continuous therapy is recommended to facilitate management of fluid balance 
in haemodynamically unstable patients. An efficient dose for continuous renal 
replacement therapy would be 20–25 mL/kg/h of effluent generation.
 	8.	In shock, infusion of isotonic crystalloids or albumin, with boluses of up to 
20 mL/kg for crystalloids (or albumin equivalent) over 5–10 minutes titrated 
to reversing hypotension, increasing urine output, and attaining normal capillary 
refill, peripheral pulses, and level of consciousness without inducing lung 
crepitations or hepatomegaly. 
	
	If hepatomegaly or rales develop, initiate inotropic support with dopamine or 
dobutamine. 
	 9.	In sepsis, noradrenaline is the inotropic agent of choice. Treat patients with 
hypotension associated with bradycardia with atropine.
	10.	For coagulopathy (prolonged CT, PT, aPTT), administer fresh frozen plasma 
(FFP) infusion. Early FFP administration (<6–8 h) post-bite is less likely to be 
effective. Administer 10–15 mL/kg of FFP over 30–60 min within 4 hours of ASV 
administration. The aim should be a return of coagulation function, as defined by 
an INR of <2.0, at 6 h after ASV administration was commenced. Non-response to 
FFP can occur with use of FFP that has low activity of FV and FVIII, because of 
either poor storage or premature thawing (> 24 hours) prior to administration.

250    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
	Maintain PCV of 30%, measure serial PCV every 4–6 hours depending upon 
bleeding severity. If PCV <30, give blood transfusion/PCV transfusion. 
	
	Note: Avoid intramuscular injections.
	
	Do NOT give Heparin or Antifibrinolytic agents in venom-induced thrombosis. 
Severe Local Envenoming
	 1.	Give prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics for cellulitis after completion of the 
first 10 vials of ASV:
	
	Inj. Amoxicillin + clavulanic acid 1.2 g IV thrice daily for the first 7 days and then 
switch to oral therapy with Tab. Amoxicillin + clavulanic acid 625 mg 3 times a 
day for further 3–7 days; in children: 100 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses IV; for oral 
therapy, the dose is 50 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses. 
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV twice daily (in children: 100 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses) 
for 7 days.
	 2.	Inj. Metronidazole 400 mg IV infusion thrice daily for 7 days (In children: 
30 mg/kg/day in 3–4 divided doses). 
Recovery phase marked by 
	
l Normalization of blood pressure. Within 15–30 minutes bleeding stops, though 
coagulation disturbances may take up to 6 hours to normalize. 
	
l Neurotoxic envenoming of the postsynaptic type (Cobra bites) begins to improve 
within the first 30 minutes, but patients may require 24–48 hours for full recovery. 
Envenoming with Kraits, Russel’s Viper and sea snakes usually takes a considerable 
time to improve. Recovery of respiratory muscles is reflected by improvement of 
neck flexors where flexing the neck against gravity indicates timing to wean off 
ventilation.
	
l Nausea, headache and generalized aches and pains may disappear very quickly. 
	
l In shock patients, BP may increase within the first 30–60 minutes and arrhythmias 
such as sinus bradycardia may resolve. 
	
l Active haemolysis and rhabdomyolysis may cease within a few hours and the urine 
returns to its normal colour. However, red colour urine may persist for several days 
in spite of adequate ASV treatment; does not require further ASV.
	
l Patient in deep coma recovers fully, if no hypoxic brain damage. 
	
l Autonomic dysfunctions (including hypertension) are transient and do not need 
treatment. 
Other Measures
	 1.	Clean the bitten site with povidone-iodine solution, but do not apply any dressings. 
	 2.	Leave blisters alone. Allow them to break spontaneously and heal. If there is 
local necrosis, excise and apply saline dressings. Surgical decompression may be 
necessary in some cases.

Surgical Procedures in Snake Bite
Debridement of necrotic tissue – wait for 5–7 days before commencing debridement of 
necrotic tissue in order to specify the line of demarcation between viable and non-viable 
tissue. Refer patients requiring skin grafting and amputation of a necrotic digit/limb to 
a surgeon after completion of ASV treatment. 
Compartmental Syndrome (5 ‘P’)
	
l Occurs in viper/sometimes cobra bite due to progressive local swelling and cellulitis. 
May be aggravated by tourniquet. 
	
l Diagnosed by 5 Ps – Pain (severe), Pallor, Paraesthesia, Pulselessness, Paralysis or 
weakness of compartment muscle.
Criteria for fasciotomy in snake bite limb
Clinical evidence of an intracompartmental syndrome and if intracompartmental 
pressure >40 mmHg of NS (in adults) or vascular Doppler showing absent distal flow. 
Bedside compartment pressure measurement procedure (Fig. 2.16) – Insert a 16 no. 
needle in the suspected compartment at a depth of 1 cm and connect to a simple tubing

252    Standard Treatment Guidelines
irrigated with NS. Measure rise in the saline column in the tubing. Timely fasciotomy 
after correction of haemostatic abnormalities (with ASV or without clotting factors) 
decreases the need for repeated dialysis.
Early treatment with fasciotomy after correction of coagulopathy (antisnake 
venom and blood products) remains the best way of preventing irreversible muscle 
damage.
Discharge and Follow-Up
	
l If no symptoms and signs develop after 24 hours, the patient can be discharged. 
	
l Keep the patient under observation for 48 hours, if ASV was infused with advise 
to return to the emergency, in case of worsening of symptoms/signs (bleeding, 
worsening of pain and swelling at the bite site, difficulty in breathing, altered 
sensorium, reduced/increased urine output, etc.). 
	
l Explain about the signs/symptoms of serum sickness (fever, joint pain, joint 
swelling) which may manifest after 5–10 days. 
	
l Wait for 5–7 days before commencing a debridement of necrotic. 
Instructions while Referring
	
l Inform the need for referral to the patient and/caregiver. 
	
l Give prior intimation to the receiving centre. Send with a referral note with details 
of treatment given and clinical status at the time of referral.
	
l Arrange for an ambulance preferably equipped with transport ventilator. Do NOT 
waste time to get an ideal ambulance. If ventilator is not available, use a tight-fitting 
face mask connected to an anaesthetic (Ambu) bag. 
	
l During transfer, continue life-supporting measures, insert nasogastric tube and 
provide airway support, if required.
	
l If ASV is not available at first contact centre, transfer to the nearest health facility 
where ASV is available confirmed by telephone.
	
l Transfer, if required, only after completion of ASV infusion to a higher health 
facility where mechanical ventilator and dialysis facilities are available.
	Victims who arrive late
Some victims arrive after the bite, often after several days, usually with acute kidney 
injury. 
	 1.	Determine the current venom activity such as bleeding.
	 2.	Perform a 20 WBCT and determine if any coagulopathy is present. If coagulopathy 
is present, administer ASV. If no coagulopathy is evident, assess the case for 
evidence for one or other complications and consequences. For secondary 
complications of snake bite provide appropriate supportive measures.
	 3.	In the case of neurotoxic envenoming (ptosis, respiratory failure, etc.), administer 
one dose of 8–10 vials of ASV. However, at this stage it is likely that all the venom 
is bound, and patient requires respiratory support. There is no need for ASV if 
ptosis is the only symptom and it is not progressing.

Chapter 2  Emergencies    253
Snake bites again (repeated bite)
If a patient has been bitten by a poisonous snake and received ASV earlier and comes 
back with features of repeat snake bite, consider as a fresh case and treat accordingly 
irrespective of the interval between the snake bite. However, care should be taken while 
administering ASV, since he/she has been sensitized.
Patient education
	
l If discharged within 24 hours, advise the patient to return if there is any worsening of 
symptoms such as bleeding, pain or swelling at the site of bite, difficulty in breathing 
and altered sensorium.
	
l Also explain to the patient about serum sickness which may manifest after 5–10 days.
After snake bite: Do’s and Don’ts given as below:
Do’s 
	
l Seek medical help right away.
	
l Call ambulance and transfer patient to a medical health facility. Arrange transport 
of the patient to medical care as quickly, safely and passively as possible by vehicle 
ambulance (toll free no. 102/108/etc.), boat, bicycle, motorbike, stretcher, etc. 
	
l Keep the person calm. Reassure them that bites can be effectively treated in an 
emergency room. Restrict movement and keep the affected area below heart level 
to reduce the flow of venom.
	
l Remove any rings or constricting items, because the affected area may swell.
	
l Create a loose splint (it should be capable of inserting one finger beneath) to help 
restrict movement of the area.
	
l Ideally the patient should lie in the recovery position (prone, on the left side) with 
his/her airway protected to minimize the risk of aspiration of vomitus. 
	
l Monitor the person’s vital signs – temperature, pulse, rate of breathing, and blood 
pressure – if possible. If there are signs of shock (such as paleness), lay the person 
flat, raise the feet about a foot and cover the person with a blanket.
Don’ts
	
l Do NOT waste time in traditional first-aid methods.
	
l Do NOT allow the person to become over-exerted. If necessary, carry the person 
to safety.
	
l Do NOT apply a tourniquet. Do NOT block the blood supply or apply pressure.
	
l Do NOT apply cold compresses to snake bite.
	
l Do NOT cut into snake bite with a knife or razor.
	
l Do NOT try to suck out the venom by mouth or wash the wound.
	
l Do NOT give the person stimulants or pain medications unless a doctor tells you 
to do so.
	
l Do NOT give the person anything by mouth.
	
l Do NOT raise the site of the bite above the level of the person’s heart.
	
l Do NOT attempt to kill or catch the snake as this may be dangerous. Bring in the 
dead snake only if this can be done safely. Do NOT waste time hunting for the snake,

254    Standard Treatment Guidelines
and do NOT risk another bite if it is not easy to kill the snake, and do NOT risk 
another bite if it is not easy to kill the snake (better to omit). Be careful of the head 
when transporting it – a snake can actually bite for several hours after it is dead 
(from a reflex).
	
l For prevention of snake bites
	– Identify major situational sources of bites; walk at night with sturdy footwear 
and use a torch. 
	– When walking, walk with a heavy step as snakes can detect vibration and will 
move away.
	– Carry a stick when grass cutting or picking fruit or vegetables or clearing the base 
of trees. Use the stick to move the grass or leaves first. Give the snake a chance to 
move away. If collecting grass that has previously been cut and placed in a pile, 
disturb the grass with the stick before picking the grass up.
	– Keep checking the ground ahead while cutting crops like millet, which are often 
harvested at head height and concentration is fixed away from the ground.
	– Pay close attention to the leaves and sticks on the ground when wood collecting.
	– Keep animal feed and rubbish away from your house. They attract rats and snakes 
will follow.
	– Try to avoid sleeping on the ground.
	– Keep plants away from your doors and windows. Snakes like cover, and plants 
help them climb up and into windows.
	– During trekking, etc. through forests or mountains, stay on clearly marked tracks. 
Do not step or reach into an area where you cannot see the ground. Wear boots, 
long-sleeved shirts and long pants.
