Cardiovascular Diseases
HYPERTENSION
Hypertension (HT) stands as a prominent global cause of annual mortality, contributing 
to as much as 30% of myocardial infarctions. High BP is the leading modifiable risk 
factor for morbidity and mortality worldwide. An estimated 46% of adults with HT are 
unaware that they have the condition. One of the global targets for non-communicable 
diseases (NCDs) is to reduce the prevalence of HT by 33% between 2010 and 
2030. Despite the rising prevalence of HT, a significant number of patients remain 
underdiagnosed and undertreated. Opportunistic screening for HT in adults either as 
a systematic programme or as an opportunistic exercise during visits to health care 
providers can help identify HT earlier. HT is usually asymptomatic and discovered 
on routine measurement of blood pressure (BP). Secondary HT presents as a part of a 
symptom complex as in renovascular or renal parenchymal disease, connective tissue 
disorders (systemic lupus erythematosus [SLE], scleroderma, etc.), coarctation of aorta, 
acromegaly, Cushing’s disease and other glucocorticoid excess states including chronic 
steroid therapy, obstructive uropathy, phaeochromocytoma, primary aldosteronism and 
other mineralocorticoid excess states, obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome and thyroid 
or parathyroid disease.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Non-specific symptoms are fatigue, headache and epistaxis.
	
l Uncontrolled hypertension can lead to target organ damage (TOD) such as coronary 
artery disease (CAD), left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), cerebrovascular 
accidents (CVA), transient ischaemic attacks (TIA), retinopathy, lower extremity 
arterial disease, aortic dilation, aneurysm, dissection and renal dysfunction.
	
l Associated risk factors are age >55 years in males and >65 years in 
females, smoking, diabetes mellitus, microalbuminuria or GFR <60 mL/min, 
hyperlipidaemia, family history, obesity, sedentary lifestyle and ethnic group.
	
l Routine laboratory tests recommended before initiating therapy include fundoscopy 
and 12-lead electrocardiogram; urinalysis, urinary albumin excretion or albumin/
creatinine ratio, blood glucose and haematocrit; serum potassium, creatinine (or the 
corresponding estimated GFR) and calcium; and a lipid profile (after a 9- to 12-hour 
fast) that includes high-density lipoprotein, cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein 
cholesterol and triglycerides.

256    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l More extensive testing for identifiable causes is not indicated generally unless 
BP control is not achieved or secondary hypertension is suspected (clinical clues 
include snoring/daytime sleepiness, abrupt onset of hypertension, hypertension onset 
<40 years of age, accelerated/malignant hypertension, abrupt loss of BP control in a 
patient with prior BP control, resistant or refractory hypertension).
	
l Specific tests are performed by indication such as chest X-ray (fluid overload), ECHO 
(aortic dissection, heart failure or ischaemia), troponin, CK-MB (in suspected cardiac 
involvement, e.g. acute chest pain or acute heart failure) and N-terminal pro–B-type 
natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), renal ultrasound (renal impairment or suspected 
renal artery stenosis).
Diagnosis of hypertension
Inadequate BP measurement methodology or use of inaccurate BP-measuring devices 
can lead to overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment, or underdiagnosis and exposure 
to preventable cardiovascular disease (CVD).
	
l Diagnosis based on office BP (OBP) should be made after at least two to three separate 
office visits at 1 to 4-week intervals (depending on the BP level and CVD risk).
	
l Confirm diagnosis by home-based blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) or 
ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), if possible. BP readings vary by 
measurement technique; diagnostic criteria are specific to the technique. Use an 
average threshold of 140/90 mmHg for office diagnosis of HT, but 135/85 mmHg 
for home and 130/80 mmHg for 24-hour ambulatory monitoring.
	 For grading of HT, see Table 3.1. 
	
l Single BP reading for diagnosis is considered if the measurement is 180/110 mmHg 
or higher with evidence of CVD requiring immediate treatment. Otherwise, the 
patient should be reassessed every 1–4 weeks to confirm BP elevations.
White-coat HT: It is defined as an elevated Office BP (≥130/80 mmHg) despite a 
normal out-of-office BP (at home or daytime ambulatory BP). Conditions in which 
white-coat HT is more common are the following: grade I HT on office BP measurement 
or marked Office BP elevation without hypertension-mediated organ damage (HMOD). 
Routine drug treatment is not indicated.
Masked HT: It is defined as BP that is normal in the office but elevated on out-of-office 
BP measurements usually due to poorly controlled nocturnal BP.
Classification of OBP, definitions of HT grade and management of HT are shown in 
Table 3.1 and Figure 3.1.
Precautions to be taken while measuring BP
	
l The auscultatory method of BP measurement with a properly calibrated and 
validated instrument should be used.
	
l BP should be measured using an appropriate-size cuff, bladder length 80% of arm 
circumference and width 40% of arm length, in both upper limbs and at least one 
lower limb in both supine and erect posture.

Treatment approach in a patient with HT is given as follows:
	 1.	Evaluate cardiovascular risk and any HT-mediated organ damage. 
	 2.	Lifestyle modifications are essential for managing HT, and optimal treatment starts 
with diet and exercise.
	 3.	Evaluate 3–6 months after lifestyle intervention in patients with grade 1 HT and 
no comorbidities for initiation of antihypertensive drug therapy.
	 4.	Initiate antihypertensive drug therapy immediately in patients with comorbidities 
or grade 2 HT including patients with masked HT and when BP is uncontrolled/
not on-treatment target BP (>130/80 mmHg in high-risk patients with conditions 
such as diabetes, chronic kidney disease [CKD; eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and/or 
urine albumin:creatinine ratio ≥300 mg/g], post-renal transplantation, heart failure 
with reduced or preserved ejection fraction, known CVD, peripheral arterial disease 
and/or ≥10% 10-year atherosclerotic CVD [ASCVD] risk).
	 5.	First-line therapy consists of one of four antihypertensive classes – thiazide 
diuretics, calcium channel blockers (CCB), angiotensin-converting enzyme 
inhibitors (ACEI) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) – unless there is a 
comorbidity consideration favouring the use of another drug from a different drug 
class (described as below). 
	 6.	Start with a single antihypertensive in patients with low-risk grade 1 HT or in 
patients aged 80 years or older. Otherwise, low-dose combination therapy should 
be initiated, most often an ACEI or ARB combined with a dihydropyridine CCB. 
	 7.	Start therapy with lower doses of drugs and change doses or add drugs at a slower 
rate in elderly patients. 
	 8.	Increase to full-dose treatment before adding a third antihypertensive, usually 
a thiazide-like diuretic if not already selected. If full-dose treatment with three 
medications is ineffective, add spironolactone. Beta-blockers are not recommended 
unless indicated for other medical conditions. 
	 9.	At each step, optimize the medication dose, check adherence to the current regimen 
and evaluate lifestyle factors that may contribute to elevated BP. At each step, also 
confirm that the blood pressure measurement is accurate with home or ambulatory 
readings. 
	10.	The dose of drugs can be increased, or a new drug added at approximately 2- to 
4-week intervals. This frequency can be faster or slower depending on the clinical 
circumstances of the patient and the judgment of the practitioner.
	11.	Monitor BP regularly (usually every 4–6 weeks) and adjust medication doses as 
needed to achieve target BP.
	12.	After starting medication, target BP should be <140/90 mmHg within 3 months, 
and after 3 months, reduce the target to <130/80 mmHg in patients younger than 
65 years.

Hypertension in pregnancy 
Alpha-methyldopa, beta-blockers and vasodilators are preferred medications for safety 
of the foetus. ACEI and ARBs are contraindicated (for details, see the section ‘Pre-
eclampsia’ in Chapter 15).
Hypertension in children and adolescents
In children and adolescents, HT is defined as BP that is, on repeated measurement, at the 
95th percentile or greater adjusted for age, height and gender. The fifth Korotkoff sound 
is used to define DBP. Rule out secondary causes of HT such as Cushing’s diseases, 
phaeochromocytoma, kidney disease and coarctation of the aorta. 
Lifestyle interventions are strongly recommended, with pharmacological therapy 
instituted for higher levels of BP or if there is insufficient response to lifestyle 
modification. Choices of antihypertensive drugs are similar in children and adults, but 
effective doses for children are often smaller and should be adjusted carefully.

Malignant hypertension 
Patients presenting with BP 220/130 mmHg and evidence of vascular damage like 
papilloedema and deranged renal function should be referred to a tertiary care centre.
Note: Do not attempt excessive, rapid and uncontrolled reduction of BP in hypertensive 
urgencies with IV drugs or oral or sublingual nifedipine as it may precipitate renal, 
cerebral or coronary ischaemia. The initial goal in hypertensive emergencies is to reduce 
mean arterial BP by no more than 25% (within minutes to 1 hour), and then, if stable, to 
160/100 to 110 mmHg within the next 2–6 hours. If the patient is clinically stable and 
the initial level of reduced BP is well tolerated, aim for further gradual reductions of BP 
towards a normal BP over the next 24–48 hours. 
Resistant hypertension
Resistant HT is the failure to reach goal BP in patients who are adhering to full doses of 
an appropriate three-drug regimen that includes a long-acting CCB, ACEI or ARB), and 
a diuretic (maximum or maximally tolerated dose). Patients who achieve target BP with 
≥4 antihypertensive drugs are also considered to have refractory HT.

264    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Older adults and patients who are obese or diabetic, or have peripheral artery 
disease and obstructive sleep apnoea are more prone to develop resistant HT. Check as 
below and refer these patients to a HT specialist:
	
l Rule out white-coat HT and inaccurate BP measurement. 
	
l Screen for secondary HT and associated disorders such as obstructive sleep apnoea 
and endocrine causes.
	
l Identify and correct medication nonadherence, salt intake, alcohol intake and 
inadequate doses or inappropriate antihypertensive combinations, concomitant 
intake of NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, cyclosporine, antidepressants especially 
monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors, cocaine, amphetamines, other illicit drugs, 
tobacco, some over-the-counter dietary supplements and medicines (e.g. liquorice 
and cough syrups), etc.

1.	To assess BP control, it is essential to assess the effectiveness of lifestyle 
modifications and drug treatments, to identify HMOD and necessary risk factor 
modifications, and to check adherence.
	 2.	Initial physician visits (including virtual care visits) should take place every month 
or even more frequently, depending on HT grade, CVD risk, previous unsuccessful 
attempts to achieve BP control and other factors suggesting antihypertensive 
treatment difficulties.
	 3.	After the end of the titration phase, when BP is controlled, less frequent visits may be 
necessary, followed by annual visits to maintain physician–patient relationship and 
monitor adherence to treatment plans. In cases where BP control was challenging 
or for high-risk patients, more frequent visits may be necessary for continued 
monitoring.
Patient education
	
l Explain regular BP monitoring at home for adequate BP control and explain 
the consequences of uncontrolled HT and the need for a long-term control with 
medication.
	
l Hypertensive urgencies may occur in patients with chronic HT in a number of 
situations: Non-adherence to therapy, after sudden withdrawal of beta-blocker or 
clonidine therapy, after ingestion of a large quantity of salt, or due to anxiety
	
l Emphasise the importance of treatment adherence as it is a major cause of poor BP 
control. Recheck annually individuals with normal BP readings as well as those 
with white-coat HT. Monitor BP every 3–6 months for patients with elevated BP. 
Follow patients with stage 1 HT who do not initially qualify for drug therapy every 
3–6 months. 
	
l Advise regarding control of other risk factors like diabetes and hyperlipidaemia.
	
l Emphasize to patients not to stop taking their antihypertensive medications without 
consulting their health care provider. Even if the BP is close to the normal range, 
sudden discontinuation of medication can lead to a rebound increase in BP.

ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME
Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) refers to a group of clinical symptoms compatible with 
acute myocardial ischaemia and covers the spectrum of clinical conditions ranging from 
unstable angina (UA) to non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) to 
ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
Myocardial ischaemia is caused by critical obstruction in coronary arteries due 
to atherosclerosis, embolism or vasospasm. Patients presenting with suspected ACS

MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION (MI)
The term MI is used when there is evidence of myocardial necrosis in a clinical setting 
consistent with myocardial ischaemia. Sudden death may be the first manifestation in a 
significant number of patients. Some patients may be asymptomatic and may be detected 
on routine ECG.
SALIENT FEATURES
Any one of the following criteria meets the diagnosis:
	
l Chest pain starts abruptly, often severe, crushing, heavy or ‘band-like’ in 
nature and not greatly affected by breathing or changing position. It persists 
for over 20 minutes with constant intensity, widespread in the retrosternal area, 
possibly radiating to the arms (usually to the left arm), back, neck or jaw. In 
some patients, it may resemble the symptoms of acute abdomen (pain begins 
in the upper abdomen accompanied by nausea). Elderly patients and patients 
with diabetes may, in particular, present with a feeling of general malaise and a 
feeling of heaviness, sweating and nausea without chest pain. The pain may be 
the first occurrence of angina pain or it may be a known symptom of previously 
diagnosed stable angina which is worsening (over days to a few weeks) and is 
suggestive of UA. Bradycardia and hypotension often manifest as dizziness or 
fainting in inferior myocardial damage. Other clinical manifestations include 
acute pulmonary oedema, loss of consciousness and sudden death.
	
l Detection of rise and/or fall of cardiac biomarkers (preferably troponin) with at 
least one value above the 99th percentile of the upper reference limit, together 
with evidence of myocardial ischaemia with at least one of the following 
symptoms of ischaemia.
	
l ECG changes are indicative of new ischaemia, new ST-T changes (STEMI) or 
>2 mm in men or >1.5 mm in women in leads V2–V3, or ST elevation >1 mm in at 
least two other contiguous leads (contiguous leads refer to lead groups, i.e. lateral 
leads I, aVL; inferior leads II, III and aVF; anterior leads V1–V6) and new left 
bundle branch block (LBBB). Development of pathological Q waves in the ECG.
	
l ECG can be normal in the first 6 hours even in frank heart attacks. Cardiac 
biomarkers (trop-I, trop-T) rise in 3–8 hours with a gradual fall in up to 
10 days and CK-MB rises in 4–6 hours with a rapid fall over 50–70 hours; 
serial evaluation every 6–8 hours for 24 hours is recommended. If the troponin 
concentration is normal 12 hours after the onset of chest pain, ACS is unlikely.
	
l There is imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or new regional 
wall motion abnormality.
Pre-hospital care
	
l A 12-lead ECG is obtained immediately at the first point of care and again on arrival 
at hospital. Serial ECG recordings are obtained if the pain continues, particularly

Chapter 3  Cardiovascular Diseases    269
when ECG changes are not noted in the initial recordings or changes are evident in 
the repeated recordings. Differentiate from non-ischaemic causes when interpreting 
ECG. The alleviation of chest pain subsequent to Nitroglycerin (glyceryl trinitrate) 
administration may be misleading and should not serve as a diagnostic measure. It 
is recommended to obtain another 12-lead ECG if symptom relief ensues following 
Nitroglycerin administration. The complete normalization of ST-segment elevation 
after nitroglycerin administration, coupled with the alleviation of symptoms, 
suggests coronary spasm, with or without associated myocardial infarction. In such 
instances, early coronary angiography (within 24 hours) is recommended. For cases 
involving recurrent episodes of ST-segment elevation or chest pain, immediate 
angiography is necessary.
	
l Administer 162–325 mg of Aspirin (chewed) plus Clopidogrel 300 mg orally to 
patients with chest pain suspected of having STEMI as soon as possible unless 
contraindicated or already taken by the patient and atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 
for plaque stabilization. 
	
l Notify receiving hospital activation of the catheterization laboratory for patients with 
a STEMI identified on pre-hospital; obtain ECG.
	
l Minimize pre-hospital delay. The goal of transport time is to keep total ischaemic time 
(door-to-device [D2D] time) within 90–120 minutes.
Treatment (preferably in CCU)

Diagnosis should be made as soon as possible (within 20 minutes of arrival in the 
hospital). Admit in the CCU (if available); administer supplementary oxygen 4–6 L/min 
for the first few hours in patients with respiratory distress and oxygen saturation ≤94%; 
ensure bed rest; ensure IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry; 
avoid visitors and outside influences, e.g. radio, newspapers; advise therapeutic lifestyle 
changes; modify diet; and restrict sodium intake.
Pharmacological (the first 24 hours)
	 1.	Inj. Morphine 2–4 mg IV, repeated 4–6 hourly, if needed.
	 2.	Tab. Aspirin (non-enteric coated) 150–325 mg PO is administered as soon as possible 
on admission, if not taken earlier.
	 3.	Tab. Clopidogrel 300 mg stat and 75 mg/day for maintenance.
	 4. 	Tab. Nitroglycerin 0.3–0.6 mg or Tab. Isosorbide 5–10 mg sublingual.
	 5.	Confirm MI by cardiac enzymes estimation and ECG.
	 6.	Thrombolysis vs. Primary PCI: Consult first with the cardiologist on call at the PCI 
centre regarding the feasibility of primary PCI or the antithrombotic medication. 
	
	Perform thrombolysis within 6–12 hours of symptom onset (best results if 
administered within 1–2 hours of symptom onset) in case symptom duration is short 
(<3 hours), the patient is haemodynamically stable, primary PCI is not available or 
transport time to a PCI-capable hospital is too long.

270    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
	Thrombolytic agents as below are preferred; however, cost may be a hindrance: 
	
	Inj. Tenecteplase 30–50 mg IV bolus Or Alteplase 15 mg IV bolus, 0.75 mg/kg 
over 30 minutes, 0.5 mg/kg over 60 minutes (total dose not to exceed 100 mg) Or 
Reteplase 10 units IV, two doses at an interval of 30 minutes
	
	Or Inj. Streptokinase 1.5 million units IV as loading dose over 60 minutes.
	
	The sign of successful thrombolysis is ST-segment resolution >50% in the lead with 
the highest elevation within 90 minutes of the start of thrombolytic therapy.
	
	Or
	
	Primary PCI may be done as an alternative to thrombolysis with a goal of door-to-
balloon time <90 minutes, if fibrinolytics contraindicated, with failed fibrinolytics 
(rescue PCI), cardiogenic shock or uncertain diagnosis of STEMI.
	 7.	Perform close monitoring as mortality is maximum in the first 24 hours.
	 8.	Provide adequate analgesia.
	 9.	Limit physical activities at least for 12 hours.
	10.	Do not use prophylactic antiarrhythmics but they should be readily available.
	11.	Inj. Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously 12 hourly or Inj. Dalteparin 120 IU/kg 
subcutaneously 12 hourly; reduce dose in patients older than 75 years (–25%) and 
in renal failure Or Inj. Heparin (unfractionated Heparin 5000 units IV 6 hourly) for 
72 hours (more useful with thrombolytics). (Caution: If the patient is on Warfarin, 
do not start Heparin until international normalized ratio (INR) reduces to near the 
lower limit of the target range. If INR is too high, administer vitamin K1 1–3 mg IV.)
	12.	Inj. Nitroglycerin as in angina if pain is continuing and there is no hypotension and 
bradycardia/excessive tachycardia for 24–48 hours and if there are concerns about 
switching to oral Nitroglycerin. Do not use Nitroglycerin as a substitute for narcotic 
analgesics that are often required in patients with acute MI.
	13.	If there is no contraindication, give Inj. Metoprolol 2 mg IV every 2 minutes for three 
injections; if it is well tolerated, followed by 50 mg PO started 15 minutes after the 
last IV dose and given every 12 hours for 48 hours and then 100 mg once a day.
	14.	If there is no hypotension or contraindications and uncomplicated MI, give 
Tab. Enalapril 5 mg 2 times a day orally.
	15.	Measure serum lipids, electrolytes and magnesium levels. In case of hyperlipidaemia, 
give Tab. Atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 40 mg once daily.
	
	After the first 24 hours:
	16.	Continue Aspirin, beta-blockers, Nitroglycerin, Heparin, ACEI and analgesia 
(if required).
	17.	Observe and treat any complication – high-dose Aspirin if pericarditis, diuretics 
if HF; defibrillation if haemodynamic compromise in AF, atropine if heart block/
bradycardia and intra-aortic balloon if severe hypotension.

Indications for angiography/angioplasty
	
l Urgent angiography/angioplasty with a goal door-to-balloon time of 90 minutes 
in case of ischaemic episodes (spontaneous/provoked) and preserved LV systolic 
function; interval coronary angiography within a few days after successful 
thrombolysis
Indications for urgent surgery
	
l Failed PCI with persistent chest pain or haemodynamic instability
	
l Persistent or refractory ischaemia in a patient who is not a candidate for catheter 
intervention
	
l Cardiogenic shock and coronary anatomy not amenable to PCI
	
l Mechanical abnormality leading to pulmonary oedema/hypotension, e.g. papillary 
muscle rupture or acute ventricular septal defect
	
l Life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias in the presence of ≥50% left main stenosis 
and/or triple-vessel disease
Indications for temporary pacing
	
l Sinus bradycardia unresponsive to drugs, Mobitz type II atrioventricular (AV) block, 
third-degree AV block, bilateral bundle branch block (BBB), newly acquired BBB, 
and bifascicular or trifascicular block
Discharge from hospital
Stable patients with a low risk of complications may be candidates for early discharge 
such as patients with STEMI managed with fibrinolysis, with an uncomplicated 
course after at least 5 days of heparin infusion or discharge on enoxaparin for 2 days 
(therapeutic dose). However, the duration of hospitalization in patients treated with 
reperfusion therapy may be determined by other needs, such as patient education or 
titration of medications to optimum doses. Non-invasive testing (subthreshold treadmill 
test [TMT]) for ischaemia should be performed before discharge to assess the presence 
and extent of inducible ischaemia in patients with STEMI who have not had coronary 
angiography and do not have high-risk clinical features for which coronary angiography 
would be warranted. Exercise testing early after STEMI may also be performed to 
assess functional capacity and ability to perform work at home/work; evaluate efficacy 
of current medical regimen and titrate accordingly; perform risk stratification for future.
Long-term management (secondary prevention)
	
l Complete smoking cessation – at every visit, ask about smoking and assist the patient 
in quitting.
	
l Initiate or maintain lifestyle modification – weight control, increased physical activity, 
alcohol moderation, sodium reduction and emphasis on increased consumption of 
fresh fruits, vegetables and low-fat dairy products. Minimize the intake of trans fats, 
red meat and processed meats, refined carbohydrates and sugar/sweetened beverages.

272    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l BP control goal is <140/90 or 130/80 mmHg, if the patient has diabetes or chronic 
kidney disease.
	
l Maintain LDL-C <100 mg/L (for very high-risk patients, an LDL-C <70 mg/dL); 
if TG are ≥200 mg/dL, non-HDL-C should be <130 mg/dL, whereas non–HDL-C 
should be <100 mg/dL for very high-risk patients with lifestyle modification, diet 
and hypolipidaemic agents. 
	
l Physical activity should be performed for 30 minutes 7 days/week (minimum 5 days/
week).
	
l Weight management goal is to maintain body mass index of 18.5–24.9 kg/m2 and 
waist circumference of <40 inches for men and <35 inches for women.
	
l Aspirin, beta-blockers, ACEI and statins (selected patients) are given for an indefinite 
period. In those who do not tolerate aspirin, give Tab. Clopidogrel 75 mg/day. For 
patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting, aspirin (110–325 mg) should be 
started within 6 hours after surgery to reduce saphenous vein graft closure.
	
l Warfarin is given for compelling indication for anticoagulant therapy, such as AF, 
prosthetic heart valve, LV thrombus or concomitant venous thromboembolic disease. 
Use of Warfarin in conjunction with Aspirin and/or clopidogrel is associated with an 
increased risk of bleeding; therefore, monitor closely.
	
l Obtain ECG and echocardiogram after 6 weeks to assess for need of automated 
implantable cardioverter defibrillator (AICD) in indicated patients.
Patient education
	
l Counsel the patient to comply with medication, stop smoking, reduce weight, 
regularly exercise (20-minute brisk walk at least 3 times a week) and restrict fat 
intake to control serum lipids.
	
l Ask family members of patients experiencing STEMI to immediately activate the 
Emergency Response Team when symptoms appear (unresponsive to nitroglycerin or 
new-onset chest pain manifesting as heaviness, burning and discomfort, with heaviness 
or pain often precipitated by physical or mental exertion; neurological changes – 
alteration in level of consciousness, seizures, symptoms of stroke; significant acute 
change in pain, fluid status or skin colour) and advise them to take CPR training and 
familiarize themselves with the use of an automated external defibrillator (AED).

CARDIOMYOPATHY
It refers to any structural or functional abnormality of the ventricular myocardium, 
excluding congenital/valvular heart defects, vascular (systemic/pulmonary) and nodal or 
conductive system diseases. The commonest type of cardiomyopathy is usually caused by 
ischaemia and characterized by ventricular dilatation and systolic dysfunction. The other 
important causes include alcohol, endocrinopathies (diabetes, thyrotoxicosis), myocarditis, 
genetic or idiopathic.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occur features of biventricular failure resulting in dyspnoea, orthopnoea 
and peripheral oedema. 
	
l Diagnosis is clinical, supported by ECG, chest X-ray and echocardiography. 
	
l The presentation of hypertrophic cardiomyopathies is quite variable and 
may include dyspnoea, chest pain, syncope or presyncope, abnormal 
electrocardiographic findings or abnormal cardiac examination findings.

Most cases of dilated cardiomyopathy present as HF, and, thus, the same treatment is 
used for both conditions (see respective sections). Treat any underlying treatable cause.
	
l Address fluid retention as a cause of worsening shortness of breath.
	
l Respiratory failure or cardiac arrest is a medical emergency.
	
l Prompt evaluation is necessary in patients with a history of syncope.

HF is defined as inadequate cardiac output to meet the perfusion of the body under 
normal filling pressures. It is a clinical syndrome of inadequate cardiac output resulting 
in fluid retention in the lungs, abdominal organs and peripheral tissue. Common causes 
include CAD, hypertensive heart disease, cardiomyopathy, valvular heart disease and

	 1.	Systolic failure: The left ventricle loses its strength and ability to contract 
normally. The heart cannot pump enough blood into circulation. 
	 2.	Diastolic failure (or diastolic dysfunction): The left ventricle loses its ability to 
relax normally (because the muscle has become thick and stiff). The heart cannot

274    Standard Treatment Guidelines
properly fill with blood during the resting period between each beat or fills with 
elevated pressure.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Dyspnoea, poor effort tolerance, peripheral oedema, decreased urine output 
(cyanosis may or may not be present)
	
l Raised jugular venous pressure (JVP), S3 summation gallop and bilateral basal 
crepitations
	
l Profuse pink frothy sputum in severe cases
	
l Tender hepatomegaly and ascites

1.	Since it is a syndrome, appropriate examination and investigations like chest 
X-ray, ECG, ABG and echocardiography should be done to identify the cause. 
Measurement of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or N-terminal pro–B-type 
natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) should be done to establish the diagnosis, 
prognosis or disease severity. (BNP <35 ng/L and/or NT-proBNP <125 ng/L in 
ambulatory patients and BNP <100 ng/L and NT-proBNP <300 ng/L in hospitalized 
patients rules out HF.)
	 2.	Evaluate and record the severity of clinical disease, functional limitation and the 
ability to perform typical daily activities using the New York Heart Association 
(NYHA) functional class (Table 3.2) or 6-minute walk test.
	 3.	The treatment is based on four progressive stages of HF; progression from 
one stage to the next is associated with reduced 5-year survival and increased 
plasma natriuretic peptide concentrations. Interventions at each stage are aimed 
at modifying risk factors (stage A), treating structural heart disease (stage B) and 
reducing morbidity and mortality (stages C and D).
	 4.	Recognizing and control of HT, lipid abnormality, diabetes mellitus and other 
conditions (smoking, alcohol) that may lead to HF is important in all stages.
Table 3.2.  Criteria for NYHA functional classiﬁcation in patients with HF.
Class I
No limitation of physical activity. Ordinary physical activity does not cause undue 
fatigue, palpitation or dyspnoea.
Class II
Slight limitation of physical activity. Comfortable at rest, but ordinary physical 
activity results in fatigue, palpitations or dyspnoea.
Class III
IIIA: Marked limitation of physical activity. Comfortable at rest, but less than 
ordinary activity causes fatigue, palpitation or dyspnoea.
IIIB: Marked limitation of physical activity. Comfortable at rest, but minimal exertion 
causes fatigue, palpitation or dyspnoea.
Class IV
Unable to carry on any physical activity without discomfort. Symptoms of cardiac 
insufficiency present at rest. If any physical activity is undertaken, discomfort is increased.
HF, heart failure; NYHA, New York Heart Association.

	Stage A: It includes at-risk patients (HT, lipid disorders, obesity, diabetes mellitus, 
tobacco use) who are asymptomatic without structural heart disease. Long-term 
management of these risk factors reduces the risk of incident HF. 
	
	Stage B: It includes patients with structural heart disease who are asymptomatic; 
it includes NYHA class I (no limitations on physical activity). It is also called 
asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD). 
	
	In patients with stage B HF with or without a recent or remote history of MI or 
ACS and reduced ejection fraction, ACEIs or ARBs should be used to prevent 
symptomatic HF. ACEIs and beta-blockers should be used in all patients with a 
reduced ejection fraction to reduce mortality. To prevent symptomatic HF and 
cardiovascular events, statin should be used.
	
	Tab. Enalapril 2.5–20 mg/day as a single or two divided doses or Tab. Lisinopril 
2.5–20 mg/day as a single daily dose may be given. 
	
	If the patient is intolerant of ACEIs for reasons other than hyperkalaemia or renal 
insufficiency, start with Tab. Losartan 50 mg once daily; increase to 100 mg in 
1–2 divided doses or Telmisartan 20–40 mg/day. 
	
	Stage C: It includes patients with structural heart disease who are currently 
symptomatic or have a history of HF symptoms and includes NYHA classes I, 
II (slight limitation of physical activity), III (marked limitation) and IV (unable to 
engage in physical activity without symptoms, or symptoms that occur at rest). 
	
	In addition to interventions for patients with stage A and B HF, diuretics should be 
used if there is a history of fluid retention and monitor for electrolyte abnormalities 
and dehydration. Give Tab. Torsemide 5–10 mg twice daily with evening dose 
before 4 PM.
	
	In patients with NYHA class II–IV HF who have an ejection fraction of 35% 
or less, give Tab. Spironolactone 25–200 mg daily (Caution: Monitor for 
hyperkalaemia and renal insufficiency) and Tab. Metoprolol-XR 12.5–200 mg or 
Bisoprolol 2.5–5 mg Or Carvedilol 3.125–25 mg twice a day.
	
	Stage D: It includes patients with refractory HF who require specialized 
interventions (NYHA class IV); refer to a cardiologist.
ACUTE HEART FAILURE

l Restrict physical activity and advise bed rest in propped-up position with a back rest. 
	
l Oxygen inhalation – give high-flow oxygen 5–6 L/min through facemask or 60% 
venturi mask.
	
l Restrict dietary sodium (2–3 g/day; no added salt in cooking and no table salt). 
	
l Restrict fluid depending on urine output and other conditions. Restrict daily fluid intake 
to <2 L in patients with severe hyponatraemia (serum sodium <130 mEq/L) and in all 
patients demonstrating fluid retention that is difficult to control despite high doses of 
diuretic and sodium restriction.

276    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Identify and treat precipitating factors – arrhythmias, fluid overload, thyroid disease, 
infection, anaemia, pregnancy, pulmonary embolism (PE), dietary or medical 
non-compliance, recent addition of negative inotropic drugs (verapamil, nifedipine, 
diltiazem, beta-blockers) or initiation of medicines that increase sodium levels 
(steroids, thiazolidinediones, NSAIDs).
	
l Closely monitor renal function, weight and urine output during diuretic therapy.
	
l Perform dialysis or ultrafiltration or mechanical fluid removal (ascitic tap, paracentesis, 
etc.) for patients with confirmed diuretic resistance (as dose escalation beyond a 
person’s previously recognized dose ceiling or a dose approaching the maximum 
recommended daily dose without incremental improvement in diuresis). 
	
l Discontinue drugs with negative inotropic action (high-dose beta-blockers, calcium 
antagonists, etc.). 
	
l Do not routinely give opiates and sodium nitroprusside, inotropes or vasopressor to 
people with acute HF.

Treatment consists of a judicious use of vasodilators, diuretics and inotropic support.
	 1.	In severe/acute cases, give Inj. Frusemide 40–80 mg IV stat and repeat after 
2–3 hours. Individualize the maximum dose up to 200 mg/day. Maintenance dose is 
40 mg IV 12 hourly till clinical improvement is seen.
	
	High dose of Frusemide infusion, i.e. 10 mg/h undiluted and 1 mg/h as continuous 
infusion, can be used in a refractory patient. 
	 2.	Tab. Enalapril 2.5–20 mg/day may be given as a single or two divided doses or Tab. 
Lisinopril 2.5–20 mg/day is given as a single daily dose.
	
	If the patient is intolerant of ACE inhibitors for reasons other than hyperkalaemia or 
renal insufficiency, start with Tab. Losartan 50 mg once daily; increase to 100 mg in 
1–2 divided doses or Telmisartan 20–40 mg/day.
	 3.	Tab. Spironolactone 25–50 mg daily may be used in combination with above.
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Torsemide 5–10 mg is given twice daily with evening dose before 4 PM.
	 4.	Tab. Isosorbide mononitrate 60 mg/day preferably as a slow-release preparation 
is given at night. In NYHA classes II and III, if ACEI/aldosterone antagonists are 
contraindicated, Isosorbide mononitrate with Hydralazine has added mortality benefit 
over other drugs.
	 5.	In NYHA classes II, III and IV and AF, give Tab. Digoxin 0.5 mg on the first day 
followed by 0.25 mg/day. Monitor for digitalis toxicity. Therapeutic digoxin levels 
are present at trough levels of 1.5–2 ng/mL. 
	 6.	Tab. Carvedilol 3.125 mg per day may be given in single or two divided doses; 
dose is doubled every 4–6 weeks (maximum dose 25 mg). It is useful if persistent 
tachycardia, idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, reduced ejection fraction (<40%); 
dose should be doubled, if required, only after 2 weeks.
	 7. 	Inj. Heparin 5000 units is given 12 hourly SC if the patient is bedridden.

	 8.	In all patients with HF and chronic or documented paroxysmal, persistent or 
long-standing AF or a history of systemic or pulmonary emboli including stroke or 
TIA, symptomatic or asymptomatic ischaemic cardiomyopathy and documented 
recent large anterior MI or with LV thrombus, unless contraindicated, give Tab.

In case of refractory failure and for management of the underlying cause, refer the 
patient to a higher centre for cardiac resynchronization therapy.
Monitoring 
Clinical evaluation at each follow-up visit should include:
	
l Functional capacity and activity level
	
l Changes in body weight
	
l Patient understanding of and compliance with dietary sodium restriction
	
l Patient understanding of and compliance with medical regimen
	
l History of arrhythmia, syncope, presyncope, palpitation
	
l Adherence and response to therapeutic interventions
	
l The presence or absence of exacerbating factors for HF, including worsening 
ischaemic heart disease, HT and new or worsening valvular disease
	
l Re-evaluation of electrolytes and renal function is done at least every 6 months in 
clinically stable patients and more frequently following changes in therapy or with 
evidence of change in volume status.
Patient education
	
l Explain the need to control salt intake, stay physically active and follow regular 
compliance with medication. 
	
l Patients discharged from the hospital should be seen in 1–2 weeks and every 
1–3 months thereafter.
	
l Advise to contact the physician if there occur symptoms of digitalis toxicity, e.g. 
anorexia, nausea and vomiting or worsening of HF. 
	
l Diuretics should be taken in the morning and if two doses a day are required, the 
second dose should be given before 4 PM.
	
l Explain the need for lifestyle changes – alcohol moderation; cessation of smoking; 
management of dyslipidaemia, diabetes, HT and ischaemic heart disease; weight 
reduction in obese patients; and physical activity.

VENOUS THROMBOSIS
The presence of thrombus within a superficial or deep vein and the associated 
vessel wall inflammatory response is called thrombophlebitis. Superficial vein 
thrombosis does not confer an increased risk of PE. Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) 
is diagnosed only in 50% of the clinical cases and approximately 45% of femoral and 
iliac deep venous thromboses embolize to the lungs known as PE. The incidence of 
thrombophlebitis increases with age. The risk factors include stasis, vascular injury, a 
hypercoagulable state and pregnancy.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Unilateral leg swelling, pain, leg tenderness, erythema, palpable cord, 
increased skin turgor, distention of superficial veins, pedal oedema, chronic 
stasis dermatitis; insensitive Homans’ sign (increased pain or resistance with 
dorsiflexion of foot); sudden chest pain or dyspnoea if presenting with PE
	
l D-dimer, specific factor levels in heritable causes (e.g. factor V Leiden, proteins 
C and S, ATIII), antiphospholipid antibodies, lupus anticoagulant; diagnosis 
established by the presence of risk factors, clinical evidence of DVT and 
confirmation on duplex ultrasonography

Superficial thrombophlebitis or lower extremity DVT can be managed as an outpatient; 
heat, elevation of the limb and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are 
helpful.

Treat as inpatient in case of proximal DVT or suspected PE; high comorbid risk for 
bleeding; active bleeding; history of non-compliance; allergy to LMWH, heparin, 
or pork products; and comorbidities that complicate outpatient therapy – active 
malignancy, infection or stroke.
	 1.	Inj. Unfractionated heparin bolus of 80 units/kg followed by infusion of 18 units/kg/h 
adjusted to activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) of 1.5–2 times control for at 
least 5 days. (Caution: Heparin-associated thrombocytopenia [HAT] with platelet 
count <150,000/mm3 occurs in 5–10% of patients receiving unfractionated heparin 
secondary to heparin-dependent antibodies.)
	
	Or
	
	Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH): The dose depends on the product and is 
adjusted for renal insufficiency for at least 5 days, such as Inj. Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg

Or give Dalteparin 200 IU/kg 12 hourly subcutaneous injection.
	 2.	Tab. Warfarin is started at a dose of 5 mg/day. Monitoring of the INR is started 
on the third day and maintained at target prothrombin time (PT) to 1.3–1.5 times 
control or INR of 2–3 for 6 months. (Caution: Consider concomitant drugs for

Give overlap of LMWH and Warfarin for 3–4 days to achieve target INR; then

If Warfarin is contraindicated, give Inj. heparin 5000–10000 units subcutaneously

Majority of patients have resolution of symptoms and recanalization of thrombosis.

PULMONARY EMBOLISM/INFARCTION
PE is defined as occlusion of a major pulmonary artery branch by a blood clot 
originating from the venous system of the body. Predisposing factors for PE are 
surgery, immobilization, trauma, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, postpartum, cancer, 
chemotherapy, stroke and indwelling venous catheter.

present with a full-blown acute cor pulmonale.

cough, crepitations, rhonchi and occasionally pleural rub or signs of collapse

raised JVP, hepatomegaly, pedal oedema and cyanosis.
	
l ECG changes seen are S1, Q3T3 pattern in 10% of patients, S wave in lead I, 
Q wave and inverted T wave in lead III. Incomplete RBBB or right ventricular 
ischaemia is present.

INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS
Bacterial endocarditis is a life-threatening infectious disease that occurs in relatively 
young patients with underlying rheumatic diseases and congenital heart diseases (CHD). 
The blood culture is negative in a high proportion of cases; the diagnosis is often delayed, 
and the mortality is substantial. There occurs infection of the endothelial surface of the 
heart with its attendant complications. Acute bacterial endocarditis (ABE) is usually 
caused by S. aureus, group A haemolytic streptococci, pneumococci or gonococci. 
Subacute bacterial endocarditis (SABE) is usually caused by S. viridans or other 
streptococci, and rarely by other organisms. Prosthetic valvular endocarditis (PVE) 
develops in 2–3% of patients within 1 year, more in the aortic valve than in the mitral 
valve and least with porcine valves. Early onset infections (<2 months) are caused by 
resistant S. epidermidis, coliforms, Candida, etc. while late infections are caused by 
low-virulence organisms. ABE may affect normal valves, especially in intravenous drug 
addicts, while SABE complicates deformed/damaged valves or CHD.

Major criteria
	
l Positive blood culture

cultures
	– Persistently positive blood culture: Blood cultures (≥2) drawn more than 
12 hours apart, or all of three or a majority of four or more separate blood 
cultures, with the first and last drawn at least 1 hour apart
	– Single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetii or anti-phase I IgG antibody 
titre >1:800
	
l Evidence of endocardial involvement: Oscillating intracardiac mass, abscess, new

Minor criteria
	
l Predisposition: Predisposing heart condition or intravenous drug use

ACUTE PERICARDITIS
It refers to inflammation of the pericardium, which may be acute or chronic and may result 
in pericardial effusion. It may be caused by viruses, bacteria, mycobacteria, connective 
tissue disorders, uraemia, MI, malignancies, radiation and trauma. Most cases of acute 
pericarditis in immunocompetent patients are due to viral infection or are idiopathic.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patient presents with retrosternal or left-sided chest pain that is relieved by sitting 
and leaning forward and intensified by lying supine, dyspnoea, friction rub (high 
pitched, scratching), tamponade and serial ECG changes. Cardiac tamponade 
accompanies 10–15% of patients with acute pericarditis.
	
l Classic diagnostic quartet of cardiac tamponade is tachycardia, hypotension, 
jugular vein distension and pulsus paradoxus (augmented decrease >10 mmHg 
in systolic pressure with inspiration).
	
l ECG shows widespread ST elevation with upward concavity.
	
l X-ray shows increased transcardiac diameter, intact cardiophrenic angels, pencil 
line and lateral cardiac borders with narrow pedicle – money bag appearance 
when pericarditis turning into effusion. Absence of pericardial fluid in ECHO 
does not exclude acute pericarditis.

1.	Tab. Aspirin 650 mg orally every 3–4 hours followed by gradual tapering every 
2–3 days for a treatment period of 3–4 weeks
	
	Or

symptom resolution; may be continued for days or weeks for recurrent or incessant

	 4.	Anticoagulants not to be used except in the case of prosthetic valves when Heparin 
may be used
	 5.	Treatment of primary disease causing pericarditis

recurrent pericarditis.

Pericardial effusion occurs when pericarditis leads to accumulation of fluid in the

ARRHYTHMIA
Cardiac arrhythmia refers to an abnormality of the heart rhythm – excessively fast 
(tachyarrhythmia) or excessively slow (bradyarrhythmia) which may be in a regular or 
irregular rhythm. Both fast and slow arrhythmias can lead to cardiac arrest, seen most 
commonly with tachyarrhythmia.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Presenting symptoms are palpitations, anxiety, light-headedness, angina, 
syncope or near syncope, and hypotension, and the condition may lead to cardiac 
compromise.

the ejection fraction [EF], poorer the prognosis)

Holter monitoring (if no abnormality seen in ECG on presentation).

It refers to any heart rhythm with a rate more than 100 beats/min. It may be 
supraventricular or ventricular type.
SUPRAVENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is the generic term used for paroxysmal, regular, 
supraventricular tachyarrhythmias. The tachycardia may be due to an atrioventricular 
nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT), AV reentrant tachycardia (AVRT), junctional 
tachycardia or atrial tachycardia. Pregnancy may precipitate SVT. It may be 
asymptomatic or symptomatic.

beats/min; P wave may be buried in QRS or follow QRS complex.

VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA
Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is wide QRS tachycardia originating in the ventricles due 
to reentry, triggered activity or automaticity. CAD is the most common cause. Persons 
of all ages are affected but VT is more common in older individuals. VT followed by 
ventricular fibrillation is the usual cause of sudden death.

l Signs and symptoms depend on the rate and duration of VT and extent of 
underlying heart disease, if any. The patient may present with syncope, cardiac 
arrest, dyspnoea, palpitations and chest discomfort or angina.

are present. If the rate of consecutive ventricular beats is >100/min, it is called 
accelerated idioventricular rhythm which is a benign condition, usually occurring

l In sustained VT, VT persists for >30 seconds; in non-sustained VT, VT persists 
for three beats to 30 seconds.

beats, uniformity of QRS wave in the V leads (concordance) and a frontal plane 
QRS axis ≥30 (extreme axis deviation or north-west axis).

ATRIAL FIBRILLATION
AF is the most common arrhythmia. It is characterized by sustained rapid irregular 
atrial rhythm, mostly associated with an underlying heart disease, e.g. rheumatic heart 
disease, coronary heart disease and HT. Other non-cardiac causes include thyrotoxicosis 
and alcohol ingestion.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l AF usually presents with severe palpitation, chest discomfort, weakness, 
breathlessness and sometimes signs/symptoms of arterial embolic phenomenon 
like stroke and acute limb ischaemia.
	
l Diagnosis requires confirmation by ECG – irregularly irregular rhythm with or 
without fast ventricular rate.

l Management depends on the pattern of presentation – paroxysmal, persistent or 
permanent and underlying conditions. 
	
l No therapy is needed for paroxysmal AF unless severe symptoms develop such as 
hypotension, HF and angina pectoris. 
	
l In case of recurrent paroxysmal AF with minimal or no symptoms, treat with 
anticoagulants and rate control as needed. 
	
l If the patient is haemodynamically unstable, electrical cardioversion using 200 J is 
the treatment of choice.
	
l In patients with disabling symptoms, in addition to rate control and anticoagulants, 
antiarrhythmic agents may also be required. Consider AF ablation if antiarrhythmic 
drugs fail.

Reassurance, oxygen inhalation, propped-up position, if the patient is dyspnoeic

The aim of pharmacological treatment is rate control, prevention of thromboembolism 
and correction of rhythm disturbance.

	 3.	For prevention of the risk of embolism, NOAC or Warfarin can be used depending 
on the CHA2DS2-VASc score.
BRADYARRHYTHMIAS AND BLOCKS
Bradyarrhythmia is defined as a heart rate of <60/min in other than well-trained 
athletes. Bradycardia is generally classified into three categories – sinus node 
dysfunction (SND, mostly age related), AV block and conduction disorders. SND is 
most often related to age-dependent progressive fibrosis of the sinus nodal tissue and 
surrounding atrial myocardium.

l Symptomatic bradycardia is defined as a documented bradyarrhythmia that is 
directly responsible for development of the clinical manifestations of syncope 
or presyncope, transient dizziness or light-headedness, heart failure symptoms 
or confusional states resulting from cerebral hypoperfusion attributable to slow 
heart rate. 
	
l Clinical presentation depends on disparate electrophysiological manifestations, 
ventricular rates, transience of these abnormalities, overall medical conditions and 
medications. The severity of clinical manifestations generally correlates with the 
heart rate or the pause duration.

Blood Diseases
BLEEDING DISORDERS
Bleeding disorders (BD) encompass distinct disease entities characterized by excessive 
bleeding tendencies, often associated with unique haemostatic and/or genetic 
abnormalities, each presenting with distinct symptoms and treatment approaches. These 
disorders can arise from various factors, such as genetic mutations affecting clotting 
factor production, deficiencies in platelets, or dysfunctional blood vessels. Mild to 
moderate bleeding disorders (MBD) may not manifest clearly at diagnosis, becoming 
evident later or after significant haemostatic challenges. Examples include mild 
haemophilia A and B, and some platelet function defects. Severe bleeding disorders 
(SBD) entail organ or life-threatening bleeding requiring hospitalization, often with 
early onset. Examples include complete deficiencies of specific clotting factors or co-
factors. Bleeding of unknown cause (BUC) refers to cases with mild to severe bleeding 
phenotypes not attributable to known abnormalities even after extensive investigation.
Major issues to be determined during bleeding
	
l Is haemostatic capacity reduced or is there a non-haematological cause for bleeding?
	
l If haemostatic capacity is reduced, is it due to a heritable defect with late clinical 
onset or is it the result of a newly acquired defect?
	
l If newly acquired, is it due to an anticoagulant drug?
	
l If not due to reduced haemostatic capacity, then what are the likely circumstances 
that resulted in abnormal bleeding?
History and clinical examination
In assessing a patient’s bleeding disorder, a thorough history and clinical examination 
are essential. Key considerations include the patient’s lifelong bleeding history, 
previous encounters with surgery or dental procedures, and whether the symptom is 
isolated. Understanding the type of bleeding problem, such as mucocutaneous, easy 
bruising, spontaneous, or post-traumatic bleeding, aids in diagnosis. Menstrual history 
can provide valuable insights, with menorrhagia having a low positive predictive value 
but the absence of it suggesting a lower likelihood of a bleeding disorder. Systemic 
inquiry and examination for signs of systemic disease, vascular lesions and preoperative 
history are crucial, as they help exclude acquired conditions and identify clinically

298    Standard Treatment Guidelines
significant bleeding risks, including those related to anticoagulant therapy, the most 
common cause of acquired bleeding disorders.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Suspect
	– Vascular and platelet disorders – prolonged bleeding from cuts, purpura and 
mucosal bleeding
	– Coagulation disorders – if delayed bleeding after injury or deeper bleeding into 
joints, muscles and abdomen or chest 
	
l Laboratory investigations include complete haemogram with peripheral smear, 
PT, APTT, Vitamin K, KFT, LFT, immunoglobins, factor assays and platelet 
function tests depending on type of bleeding. 
	
l The PT (normal 11–14 sec) can be prolonged by oral anticoagulant therapy 
(typically warfarin), Vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, disseminated 
intravascular coagulation (DIC), Factor VII deficiency.
	
l Prolonged APTT is seen in DIC, dilutional coagulopathy (massive blood 
transfusion), severe and moderate deficiencies of factors VIII, IX, or XI, 
antiphospholipid antibodies (known as lupus anticoagulant activity), contact 
factor deficiency (including factor XII and prekallikrein). Unfractionated heparin 
(LMWH has minimal effect at therapeutic levels).
	
l Normal PT and APTT do not exclude moderate factor deficiency. LMWH, vWD, 
platelet abnormality or very rare factor deficiency such as factor XII, vWD often 
missed because PT, APTT and platelet count are normal. If history suggestive of 
vWD then plasma level of vWF must be measured. The bleeding time is not a 
reliable test and is rarely performed.
	
l Fibrinogen is low in DIC and liver disease.
Approach to treatment
Management typically involves a combination of medication, blood transfusions and 
lifestyle modifications to prevent and control bleeding episodes based on the criteria 
defining a bleeding symptoms as insignificant (trivial) or significant (non-trivial) or 
true bleeding. A distinctive bleeding history is a prerequisite for the diagnosis of any 
bleeding disorder and should guide further laboratory investigations.

PLATELET DISORDERS
Disorders of primary haemostasis involve platelet plug formation, which relies on 
functional platelets, vWF for platelet adhesion and normal vessel constriction.
Platelet disorders fall under two broad groups:
	 1.	Quantitative (platelet count) disorders, as either low platelet count (thrombocytopenia) 
or high platelet count (thrombocytosis)
	 2.	Qualitative, affecting the functionality of platelets, even when their numbers are 
normal (thrombasthenia)
These two can easily be separated in a patient with superficial ‘platelet-related’ 
bleeding by doing a blood platelet count in CBC, along with peripheral smear for 
platelets. These disorders, inherited or acquired, often result in bleeding, with common 
causes including thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction. Thrombocytopenia 
may stem from various factors like decreased production, increased destruction via 
immune or nonimmune mechanisms, or consumption due to coagulation activation, as 
seen in conditions like ITP, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and disseminated 
intravascular coagulation.
Acquired platelet function disorders may arise from drug use (e.g. Aspirin, 
NSAIDs), uraemia, paraproteins, myelodysplastic, or myeloproliferative disorders. 
Bleeding can also result from vessel inflammation, malformations, or connective 
tissue abnormalities, as seen in conditions like Henoch–Schönlein purpura, vasculitis 
associated with paraproteins or cryoglobulins, systemic lupus erythematosus, or 
hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, characterized by capillary malformations often 
visible in oral and nasal cavities, leading to bleeding episodes, particularly from the 
nose and gastrointestinal tract.
THROMBOCYTOPENIA
Normal platelet count in blood ranges between 150,000 and 400,000/mm3. Normally, 
all this quantity is not required; there is a great buffer in this – a person with a count 
of 100,000/mm3 or lesser is unlikely to bleed clinically provided there is no other 
compounding abnormalities contributing to bleeding. With platelet count <20 × 10/L 
there is often easy bruising, petechial haemorrhages and more serious bleeding can occur.
Low platelet counts suggest either reduced production or increased destruction 
of platelets in the bone marrow, the site of their production. When there is reduced 
platelet production, bone marrow examination shows reduced megakaryocytes as seen 
in aplastic anaemia and marrow infiltration by malignancy. On the other hand, if the 
bone marrow shows increased megakaryocytes, it implies a compensatory reaction to 
an underlying increased destruction of platelets, as occurs in autoimmune idiopathic 
thrombocytopenic purpura (AITP), hypersplenism and disseminated intravascular

thrombocytopenia. An accelerated rate of fall in platelet count can be an ominous 
sign. 
Note: Remember, an innocuous-looking superficial bleed may complicate into serious, 
life-threatening intracranial bleed. Institute all the general measures for resuscitation, 
support and recovery.
Asymptomatic thrombocytopenia
	 1.	The majority of patients with chronic thrombocytopenia with no clinical bleeding 
and in good clinical condition may not require active/aggressive medical 
intervention, and are often kept under follow-up. Patients with thrombocytopenia 
who are asymptomatic will require decision for active treatment based on the:
	
l severity of thrombocytopenia
	
l rapidity of progress of thrombocytopenia 
	
l any involvement of other arms of haemostasis such as coagulation factor defects 
or thrombolytic defects 
	
l other systemic conditions 
	
l other drugs being administered 
	
l vulnerabilities such as pregnancy or neonates/infants
	 2.	All efforts should be made to arrive at the primary cause of thrombocytopenia, so 
as to accord appropriate treatments regardless of the platelet count.
	 3.	Platelet transfusion can be considered as supportive, symptomatic treatment 
to ameliorate the risk of serious systemic bleeds from the severely low platelet 
counts. It is mainly indicated when thrombocytopenia is due to inadequate 
platelet production in the bone marrow such as in aplastic anaemias, cancer 
chemotherapies and some infective conditions. It is not of much benefit in the 
immune thrombocytopenias from increased peripheral destruction. Platelet counts 
less than 20,000/mm3 generally herald a high risk of bleeding.
Platelet transfusion
	
l Platelets for transfusion can be sourced from a random donor or a single donor.
	
l Random donor platelets are separated from the regularly donated blood by 
differential centrifugation.
	
l A bag of random donor platelet raises an adult recipient's platelet count by about 
10,000/mm3. Generally, six bags are donated to bring the platelet counts to a safe 
level.

304    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Single donor platelet is six to eight times more potent and hence a single bag is 
effective in an adult. Also, single donor platelets are safer and likely less immunogenic.
	
l Check the response to transfusion by doing platelet count, 45 minutes after transfusion.
	
l This will be poor in conditions accompanied by excessive destruction of platelets 
such as idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) and DIC.
	
l Platelets are stored at room temperature (22°C) on an agitator. NEVER refrigerate 
platelet bags. Once issued from the blood bank, they should be transfused rapidly 
(generally within 10 minutes).
(For details, see Appendix XIV.)
Autoimmune idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (AITP)
AITP is often of autoimmune pathology, but no systemic immune disease symptoms 
accompany. It can be encountered at any age, but is more frequent in young women and 
children. Clinical hallmarks of this disease are as follows:
	
l There are isolated bleeding symptoms consistent with thrombocytopenia and without 
constitutional or systemic symptoms (significant weight loss, bone pain, night 
sweats, other organ system involvement).
	
l Bleeding commonly presents on the skin as petechiae or ecchymosis, and may also 
occur from mucosal surfaces such as the eyes, oral cavity, gums and genitourinary 
tract (resulting in haematuria), or during menstruation in women (manifesting as 
menorrhagia).
	
l Bleeding is more likely when ITP is acute, as compared with chronic ITP.
	
l Absence of splenomegaly is characteristic of AITP.
	
l Laboratory investigations reveal thrombocytopenia below the reference range, 
usually less than 100,000/mm3.
	
l Antibodies against self-antigens of platelets can be detected in nearly 50% of 
patients with AITP.
	
l Presence of concomitant anaemia is not unusual, indicating significant overt or 
covert loss of blood from bleeding leading to iron deficiency. The conditional folate 
or vitamin B12 deficiency further contributes to anaemia. Furthermore, women, who 
commonly are anaemic, may suffer more. 
	
l This anaemia is of iron-deficiency origin (at times, compounded by folate/vitamin 
B12 deficiency), and must be treated with appropriate supplementation after 
checking CBC and serum ferritin (SF).
	
l Rarely, the anaemia may also be autoimmune, when the condition is known by the 
name of Evan syndrome.
	
l Bone marrow examination may not be necessary if the clinical context is strong. 
Else it may be done to rule out for any platelet production defects or bone marrow 
infiltrative disorders.
	
l Test for HBsAg, HCV, HIV and iron deficiency.
	
l Routine use of anti-platelet, anti-phospholipid and anti-nuclear antibodies, 
thrombopoietin levels or platelet parameters on automated analysers is not recommended 
unless one suspects systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or similar disorder.

The goal of all treatment strategies is to achieve a platelet count that is associated with 
adequate haemostasis rather than a normal range platelet count. 
	
l The decision to treat depends on the severity of bleeding, anticipated surgical 
procedures, medication side effects and health-related quality of life. 
	
l Treatment is indicated in adults if platelet count is <20,000 or 20,000–50,0000/mm3 
with wet purpura. 
	
l Treatment is not indicated if platelet count is >50,000/mm3 and if the patient is 
stable.
	
l Treatment options in adult AITP include those given below:
	 1.	Tab. Prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day is given till response or 4–6 weeks, followed by 
slow tapering based on response.
	 2.	Steroid-sparing immunosuppressive agents such as Cyclophosphamide or 
Azathioprine are substituted for long-term treatment in chronic ITP. Children with 
acute AITP respond much better, and with longer remissions, whereas adults may 
be more prone to progressing to a chronic state.
	 3.	In case of acute AITP, Inj. Normal Human Immunoglobulin (IVIG) 400 mg/kg 
daily for 5 days IV is given. It is preferred but is much more expensive. In children, 
0.8–1.0 g/kg as single dose can be used in conjunction with corticosteroids, if a 
more rapid increase in platelet count is required.
	 4.	Inj. Anti-D 50–75 mcg/kg single dose IV can be used in Rh-positive, non-
splenectomized patients.
	 5.	Give supportive treatments in the form of supplemental folic acid 5 mg daily 
and iron supplementation in deficient patients and institute the general measures 
enunciated above.
	
	Note: Failure with one therapy may still be followed by response to other therapy.
	 6.	Splenectomy is more likely to be required in adults, after exhausting all other 
medical modalities of treatment and if steroid is ineffective after 3–6 months. In 
children, splenectomy or other intervention with potentially serious complications 
should be delayed as long as possible, less warranted by severe disease 
unresponsive to other measures or due to quality-of-life considerations. 
	 7.	Pneumococcal vaccination should be a prerequisite before subjecting to 
splenectomy. (The spleen innately protects against encapsulated bacterial infections 
like those caused by pneumococcus. The vaccination is typically administered 
2–3 weeks before surgery.)
	 8.	In case of relapsed ITP (platelet count <30,000/mm3), Rituximab, a monoclonal 
antibody to CD20, or TPO receptor agonists (Romiplostim) may be considered.
Immune thrombocytopenia is not uncommon in systemic disorders.
Secondary ITP (HIV-associated): Treat underlying HIV infection with anti-retroviral 
therapy prior to other treatment options unless there is clinically significant bleeding 
(for details, see Chapter 7).
Secondary ITP (HCV-associated): Treat with anti-viral therapy with interferon if there 
are no contraindications. Monitor platelet count closely due to risk of worsening of

306    Standard Treatment Guidelines
thrombocytopenia attributable to interferon. If treatment is required, initial management 
should be with IVIG as above.
Secondary ITP (MMR-related): Children with a history of immune thrombocytopenia 
who are not immunized should receive their scheduled first MMR vaccine.
In children with either non-vaccine- or vaccine-related ITP, check vaccine titres. If 
the child displays full immunity, no further MMR vaccine should be given. If the 
child does not have adequate immunity, then the child should be re-immunized at 
the recommended age.
ITP in pregnancy: Pregnant patients requiring treatment should receive either 
corticosteroids or IVIG. Mode of delivery should be based on obstetric indications. 
Transfusing platelets in ITP is not useful as these are rapidly destroyed, but platelet 
concentrates may be transfused in life-threatening bleeding before specific therapy 
takes effect.
PLATELET FUNCTION DEFECTS
If clinical presentation suggests platelet defect but platelet counts are normal, suspect 
platelet dysfunction. Bleeding time is prolonged in most cases in the presence of 
normal platelet count in blood. Platelet function defects are complex spanning from 
defects of adhesion (von Willebrand disease [vWD], Bernard–Soulier syndrome) to 
defects in aggregation (Glanzmann thrombasthenia) and defects in secretory granules 
(grey platelet syndrome). The term thrombasthenia means weak platelets. Glanzmann 
thrombasthenia (GT) is one of several inherited disorders of platelet function, which 
also include Bernard–Soulier syndrome, as well as deficiencies of platelet adhesion, 
aggregation and secretion. These are hereditary in nature, and quite infrequent but with 
lifelong liability. vWD remains the commonest hereditary coagulation effect, presenting 
like any other platelet pathology with superficial bleeds and accounting for significant 
cases with puberty menorrhagia in young women. vWD has specific treatment available 
in the form of von Willebrand factor (vWF) concentrated as an injection, to be used on 
demand or on regular replacement basis to prevent bleeds.
More commonly, the platelet functions are deranged from acquired causes like the 
drugs (Aspirin, Clopidogrel, Dipyridamole, Glycoprotein Ib/IIa inhibitors such as 
Abciximab, NSAIDs, alcohol) or systemic diseases (uraemia, paraproteinaemias, DIC 
products, etc.).
Liver-related dysfunctions include alcohol dependency, viral hepatitis infections, 
myeloma, myeloproliferative disorders and macroglobulinaemia. 
Testing for platelet function confirms the specific defects. However, such facilities are 
not easily available in the country.

l If active bleeding occurs, transfuse platelets.
	
l Administer specific drugs/agents as in case of vWD.

Chapter 4  Blood Diseases    307
	
l Administer non-specific agents to help haemostasis, like local thrombin preparations, 
anti-fibrinolytics like tranexamic acid and epsilon-aminocaproic acid (EACA).
	
l Follow the general measures listed at the beginning of this chapter.
von Willebrand disease (vWD)
Desmopressin (DDAVP) promotes release of stored VWF and raises levels 3- to 10-
fold. Peak effects are achieved 30 and 90 minutes after intravenous and intranasal 
delivery, respectively. The usual parenteral dose is 0.3 mcg/kg infused intravenously 
in approximately 50 mL of normal saline over approximately 30 minutes. The dose 
of the highly concentrated intranasal preparation is 150 mcg for children weighing 
less than 50 kg and 300 mcg for larger children and adults. It is important to note that 
highly concentrated products (e.g. Stimate®) deliver 150 mcg per spray, a much higher 
concentration than that used to treat enuresis.
After a diagnosis of vWD, a DDAVP challenge is recommended to evaluate VWF 
response. VWF and FVIII levels should be assessed before and at various intervals – 
1 and 4 hours after DDAVP administration. A three-fold increase in VWF and FVIII 
levels to at least 30 IU/dL (30%) is typically considered adequate for dental procedures, 
minor surgery, or treating epistaxis or menorrhagia. (Caution: DDAVP is generally safe 
but can cause side effects like facial flushing, headache, tachycardia, light-headedness 
and mild hypotension, with more serious risks including severe hyponatraemia and 
seizures. Caution is advised in patients with a history of coronary artery disease or in 
older adults, and monitoring for tachyphylaxis with repeated DDAVP administration is 
necessary, considering the potential for reduced effectiveness over time.)
In type 1 vWD, DDAVP is usually effective, while type 3 patients typically do 
not respond. The response in type 2 vWD varies: type 2A patients may benefit from 
DDAVP, whereas type 2M patients typically do not. DDAVP is contraindicated in 
type 2B vWD due to transient thrombocytopenia from mutant VWF release. In type 
2N vWD, DDAVP increases FVIII levels but only transiently, making it suitable for 
situations requiring short-term FVIII elevation.
COAGULATION DISORDERS
Coagulation disorders are broadly divided into disorders of haemostasis and disorders 
of thrombosis, and a small intermediate group involves both the disorders. Disorders 
of haemostasis commonly result from platelet defects (vide supra) or clotting factor 
defects. The latter, again, can be hereditary or acquired, and are reflected in one or more 
of the following laboratory parameters:
	
l Prolonged prothrombin time: In liver failure, vitamin K deficiency, oral 
anticoagulants, DIC
	
l Prolonged activated prothrombin time (aPTT): Haemophilia, liver failure, DIC
	
l Prolonged thrombin time: Heparin, DIC
Hereditary defects are usually single-factor defects, whereas acquired ones are 
generally multi-factor derangements.

308    Standard Treatment Guidelines
As a prototype of hereditary coagulation disorders, haemophilia stands out, with 
its conspicuous clinical presentation and excellent treatments options.
Patients may present with any of the following:
	
l Excessive bleeding after any dental procedure like tooth extraction
	
l Excessive bleeding after any surgery/circumcision
	
l Repeated joint swelling after sports injuries
	
l Haematoma or infection after intramuscular injections
HAEMOPHILIA
Haemophilia is a hereditary or congenital bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency 
or lack of clotting factor VIII or factor IX. Clotting factor VIII and IX are essential 
proteins involved in the blood clotting process, resulting in two separate disorders 
called haemophilia A and haemophilia B, respectively. In about one-third of cases with 
haemophilia, there is no family history but the disease results from a new heritable 
mutation in the haemophilia gene located on X chromosome.
The severity of haemophilia tends to parallel the degree of loss of function of 
the corresponding haemophilia gene, categorized as severe, moderate or mild with 
blood clotting factor levels of <1%, 1–5% and >5–40%, respectively. Acquired 
deficiencies stem from decreased synthesis due to liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, 
or drug interference, consumption from conditions like DIC, or accelerated clearance 
due to paraproteins, amyloid, or autoantibodies. Fibrinogen disorders include 
congenital absence or low levels (afibrinogenemia, hypofibrinogenemia) and acquired 
abnormalities like decreased synthesis, increased consumption, or inhibitors interfering 
with fibrin polymerization. Factor XIII deficiency, whether congenital or acquired, 
impairs cross-linking and can manifest in bleeding, with severe cases marked by 
umbilical stump bleeding, intracranial haemorrhage, recurrent soft-tissue haemorrhages 
and miscarriages in females.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Most commonly, bleeding is in large joints (80%) and in deep muscles (15%). 
Infrequent bleeds can occur anywhere and may be life-threatening in the absence 
of treatment.
	
l The bleeding can be spontaneous especially in severe haemophilia, or after minor/
major trauma or surgical interventions. 
	
l The diagnosis is laboratory based and it is mandatory to characterize the type, 
haemophilia A or haemophilia B, for the appropriate treatment.
	
l Diagnosis of haemophilia can be confirmed only in good haematology labs 
dealing in haemostasis.

l Treatment revolves around administration of the missing clotting factor VII or IX 
as the case may be.

Chapter 4  Blood Diseases    309
	
l Clotting factor replacement in haemophilia requires regular replacement, so as to 
prevent/reduce possibility of any bleed. This is called regular replacement therapy 
(RRT) – sometimes erroneously called prophylaxis therapy.
	
l On demand clotting factor is administered only when there is a clinical bleed.
For full (100%) correction, the dose to be administered is:
	 1.	Factor VIII as 50 IU/kg IV 12 hourly
	 2.	Factor IX as 100 IU/kg IV 24 hourly
	
	Often, only half of this dose may be required in most emergency bleeds.
	 3.	Antibodies to the external clotting factor protein may develop, and this eventually 
reacts and nullifies the administered clotting factors. This may be suspected when 
the patient's response to treatment goes down. These are known as haemophilia 
inhibitors and make the body resistant to the benefits of clotting factor. For such 
situations, other bypassing agents or activated factor VII is required for treatment. 
Refer such cases to specialists.
	
	Note: The clotting factors for treatment traditionally come from donated plasma, 
thereby bringing risk of transfusion-transmitted infections such as hepatitis B and 
C, and HIV. Vaccinate patients with haemophilia against hepatitis B. Whereas 
newer clotting factors come with recombinant technology and do not have these 
risks. Also, the newer technologies are giving longer half-life clotting factors. 
Newer clotting factors using bispecific monoclonal antibodies like the Emicizumab 
are available and gene therapy is in the pipeline.
	 4.	Supportive care, in addition to clotting factors, from various specialists such as 
physiotherapists, orthopaedists, psychologists and social support, is crucial to 
address different aspects of the condition and improve the overall quality of life 
for individuals with these disorders.
	 5.	Take general measures listed at the beginning of this chapter.
Specific issues
Bleeding issues in females encompass heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB), ovulation 
bleeding and prolonged bleeding after miscarriage or postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). 
Up to 20% of women with HMB may have underlying conditions like von Willebrand 
disease (vWD) or platelet function disorders. Risk assessment for bleeding disorders 
is crucial in all cases of excessive bleeding, especially in PPH cases where uterine 
atony is common. Isolated severe HMB since menarche or acute episodes of HMB or 
ovulation bleeding requiring hospital admission also warrants full investigations for 
bleeding disorders. 
A comprehensive history, family background and consideration of clotting factor 
levels are essential for diagnosis, particularly as hormonal changes during pregnancy 
can mask bleeding disorder symptoms. Multidisciplinary management involving 
gynaecologists is key, with combination therapies often necessary for effective treatment, 
along with vigilant monitoring for iron deficiency (screening total iron binding capacity 
and/or Ferritin, even when haemoglobin is normal) in reproductive-aged women.

310    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Some cases previously labelled as bleeders of unknown cause may now be 
diagnosed through advancements in molecular characterization and laboratory 
technologies.
Patient Education
	
l Emphasize the connection between bleeding history, laboratory/genetic testing 
and future bleeding risk, guiding personalized approaches. Adults with uncertain 
bleeding history and normal screening tests should minimize drugs affecting 
haemostasis and be reassured about manageable bleeds with tranexamic acid and 
local procedures; caution regarding thrombosis risk in moderate bleeding disorders 
is necessary, potentially requiring antithrombotic agents. 
	
l Second-stage investigations are advised for high-risk surgeries, with detailed 
information on available treatments including antifibrinolytics, desmopressin, 
platelet transfusion and replacement therapies. 
	
l Give instructions for preventing or managing spontaneous bleeds and at-risk 
situations like dental procedures, trauma, with pedigree investigation and genetic 
tests recommended by ISHBT for accurate diagnosis and appropriate management, 
including antifibrinolytics or Desmopressin use.
