SICKLE CELL DISEASE (SCD)
Sickle cell anaemia is a constituent of the group of inherited disorders known as 
SCD which is an inherited disorder of haemoglobin. Sickle cell haemoglobinopathy 
is a hereditary genetic mutation in the haemoglobin gene, and is characterized by 
the presence of sickle-shaped RBCs in blood. This comprises sickle cell anaemias 
(HbSS and compound heterozygous states) and sickle cell trait (AS) along with SCD 
interacting with thalassaemic disorders (HbS-Thal).
The incidence of sickle cell haemoglobinopathy varies between 5% and 40% in 
India with a high number of cases from Gujarat, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, Odisha

Chapter 4  Blood Diseases    311
and Madhya Pradesh and is particularly prevalent in many tribes (Bhils, Madias, 
Pawaras, Pardhans and Otkars) and certain castes of Hindus (agharia, chasa, kulita, 
etc.) practicing consanguineous marriage. Co-inheritance of the sickle gene with 
β-thalassaemia, HbD Punjab and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) 
deficiency has also been reported from India. 
The Government of India under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare and 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs has launched the National Sickle Cell Elimination Mission 
(2023) with the goal to eliminate SCD as a public health problem in India before 2047 
by using multi-pronged strategies, to improve accessibility to affordable and quality 
health care to all patients with SCD and to lower the prevalence through awareness, 
change of practices and screening interventions.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Persons with sickle cell traits remain practically asymptomatic throughout their 
life, whereas most with sickle cell disease become symptomatic from the second 
half of infancy.
	
l Sickle cell disease in a steady state is manifested as mild anaemia, haemolytic 
jaundice and hepatomegaly with or without splenomegaly. Splenomegaly may 
undergo auto-infarction and become non-palpable. 
	
l Acute manifestations are painful crisis or vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC), acute 
chest syndrome, splenic sequestration crisis, aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19 
infection), haemolytic crisis, sickle cell hepatopathy (acute hepatic sequestration 
and acute intrahepatic cholestasis), avascular necrosis of femoral and humeral 
head, osteomyelitis, hand–foot syndrome (dactylitis), priapism, stroke and splenic 
infarction with ensuing increased rate of infection with pneumococcus and other 
capsulated organisms. 
	
l In addition, various chronic organ changes include growth retardation, gallstones, 
pulmonary hypertension, retinopathy, leg ulcer, chronic renal failure, iron 
overload following repeated transfusion, etc.
	
l Sudden death may occur due to splenic sequestration crisis, acute chest syndrome 
and stroke. Other causes of death are acute painful crisis, sepsis, aplastic crisis, 
falciparum malaria, hepatopathy, pulmonary hypertension and progressive renal 
damage culminating in end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Death may also occur 
during pregnancy and delivery.
	
l Screen patients with clinical features suggestive of sickle cell disease in 
communities known to have a high prevalence or with a family history of the 
disorder with sickle cell slide test and haemoglobin electrophoresis using cation 
exchange high-performance liquid chromatography (CE-HPLC)/automated 
capillary zone electrophoresis is done.

SCD in a steady state is managed by daily folic acid (1 mg/day) supplementation and 
avoidance of precipitating factors for crisis. Blood transfusion and hydroxyurea (HU)

312    Standard Treatment Guidelines
are the only two disease-modifying measures. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation 
(HSCT) is the only approved curative therapy which is available only in select centres. 
Recently gene therapy trials have shown promising results.
Pain Management 
	 1.	Resting of the affected part (limb) comfortably and massaging it gently can be 
helpful. 
	 2.	Keep well hydrated orally 
	 3.	Analgesics: 90% of painful episodes can be managed at home or at the PHC with 
Paracetamol, Diclofenac orally or suppositories and Tramadol.
	
l For mild pain: Tab. Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg every 6 hours
	
l For moderate pain: Tab. Paracetamol every 6 hours plus Diclofenac 1 mg/kg every 
8 hours
	
l For severe pain: Tab. Paracetamol 10–15 mg /kg plus Diclofenac 1 mg/kg and Tab. 
Tramadol 50–100 mg orally every 4–6 hours for adults older than 17 years.
If the patient is not responding to the above-mentioned treatment, refer him or her 
to a hospital.
For severe pain unrelieved by above-mentioned oral medicines in children, give 
Diclofenac suppository 0.5 mg/kg. If suppository is not available, Inj. Paracetamol 
5–7 mg/kg infusion over a period of 1 hour or Inj. Diclofenac 0.5 mg/kg IM or IV 
is given.
If pain is not relieved, add Inj. Tramadol hydrochloride 1 mg/kg IV in a total volume 
of 4 mL.
Hospital Care for Severe SCD Pain
Pain in a crisis is usually quite severe and requires immediate treatment. The first dose 
of an analgesic must be given within 30 minutes of the arrival of the patient at the 
health facility. Build trust by believing that the patient is in pain and show him or her 
that you are there to help. Empathetic body language is essential.
Children Younger than 5 years
The site of pain changes with age; a child younger than 3 years might keep crying 
without respite. Check for any swelling of the foot and fingers at the site that is hurting. 
	 1.	Since children younger than 3 years are more prone to some infections, 
all the vaccines from birth to 2 years and after 2 years must be taken. 
Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) before 2 years of age and pneumococcal 
polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) after 2 years of age must be taken.
	 2.	Infection in SCD is prevented by the use of oral penicillin 65 mg twice a day till 
12 months, 125 mg twice a day for children younger than 2 years, and 250 mg twice 
a day for children between 2 and 5 years or Amoxicillin 20 mg/kg/day. Penicillin

Chapter 4  Blood Diseases    313
should be continued lifelong if a patient has had a splenectomy. Alternatively, if a 
patient is allergic to Penicillin, Azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day is given.
	 3.	Assess risk of stroke by transcranial Doppler as early as 2 years of age. Regular 
blood transfusion can decrease the risk of stroke.
Children Aged 5–10 years
The site of pain changes to large joints like the elbows, ankles, knees and wrists. Lack 
of oxygen supply can cause blood to collect in the spleen and liver. First, the spleen 
increases in size; the patient looks pale and ill, and may go into shock in a few hours. 
	 1.	Initiate IV fluid immediately followed by blood transfusion. If blood is 
not available, start IV fluids and refer the patient to a higher health facility 
immediately. Avoid over-transfusion.
	 2.	If the patient has suffered two serious health events involving enlargement of the 
spleen, splenectomy may be advised. Repeated attacks and complications of an 
enlarged spleen may result in death. Long-term antibiotics be prescribed following 
splenectomy.
	 3.	Respiratory exercise using spirometer every day, from 5 year onwards, helps to 
improve breathing.
	 4.	Flu and typhoid vaccination is administered every year.
Aged 10–18 years
	
l Pain might shift to the backbone and chest (ribs) in addition to long joints. Pain in 
the hips should be taken seriously and treated early to avoid serious complications 
later in life.
	
l Acute chest syndrome (ACS): Chest pain with difficulty in breathing is quite 
common at this age.
	
l Puberty and physiological and sexual development may be delayed, leading to 
psychological and emotional issues. It is important to reassure the patient that these 
delays are temporary and can be resolved.
	
l If vaccination is not already given, give pneumococcal, flu and typhoid vaccines 
every year till 18 years of age. Continue zinc supplementation.
Vaso-Occlusive Crisis (VOC) or Acute Painful Crisis or Hand–Foot 
Syndrome
	 1.	Hospitalize moderate-to-severe cases.
	 2.	Provide oxygen inhalation in case of oxygen saturation <95%.
	 3.	Administer oral or intravenous fluid.
	 4.	For pain relief, NSAIDs and/or opioids, e.g. Inj. tramadol 50–100 mg IM two to 
three times daily and Inj. ketorolac 30–60 mg IM stat followed by 15–30 mg 6–8 
hourly; if morphine is not available or diclofenac, paracetamol or combination with 
tramadol for 5–7 days.
	 5.	Administer an antibiotic for infection, if warranted.

314    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Fever 
Fever in patients with SCD must be taken seriously as death from sepsis is common. 
Admit the patient if the temperature is >100.0°F, and treat as follows:
	 1.	Immediate evaluation with history and physical examination, CBC and, if 
available, blood culture, and urine culture when urinary tract infection is suspected
	 2.	Inj. Ceftriaxone plus Cloxacillin with or without Gentamicin IV and oral 
Azithromycin.
Hydroxyurea (HU) is indicated in patients with repeated painful crisis (three 
times or more in the last 12 months), in patients with repeated blood transfusion for 
symptomatic anaemia (two times or more in the last 12 months), in patients with history 
of ACS, for infants older than 9 months and children irrespective of their clinical 
condition, as an alternative to repeated blood transfusion, and for prevention of stroke 
and chronic kidney disease in patients on erythropoietin.
Tab. Hydroxyurea 10 mg/kg/day; dose is increased intermittently to a maximum 
up to 35 mg/kg/day in case of no response. (Caution: Do not prescribe HU without 
confirmation of genotype in pregnancy, lactating women, patients with advanced 
hepatic and renal disease, and patients with myelosuppression.) HU treatment will 
take 3–6 months to show results. Do not change the dosage; lack of response benefit is 
due to an irregular or improper dosage. HU should be continued during hospitalization 
unless there are other complications.
Monitor CBC every 3 months, LFT and renal function after 2–4 weeks of starting 
therapy with HU. Stop HU if the absolute neutrophil count <2000/mm3, platelet 
count <80,000/mm3 and Hb <5 g/dL. HU can be restarted at a lower dosage after 
haematological recovery. (Refer to a concerned specialist.) 
Keep a record of baseline haemoglobin level and maintaining this level of 
haemoglobin is enough and there is no need to increase this level with unnecessary 
and harmful transfusions. 
Blood Transfusion 
Blood transfusion is indicated in case of splenic sequestration crisis, hyper-haemolytic 
crisis, aplastic crisis, ACS and pregnancy (haemoglobin level <7.0 g/dL), before 
surgery to raise the haemoglobin level up to 10 g/dL or if the Hb drops 2 g% or more 
from the usual or baseline Hb. 
	
l Never raise haemoglobin beyond 10 g/dL. 
	
l Simple transfusion is given in anaemia, aplastic crisis and splenic sequestration with 
severe anaemia. Exchange or simple transfusion can be given in symptomatic ACS, 
hepatic sequestration, intra-hepatic cholestasis, multi-organ failure and stroke. In 
ACS with <90% oxygen saturation, give only exchange transfusion. 
	
l Lifelong transfusions are planned in patients with a high risk of stroke. 
	
l Exchange transfusion can be life-saving in ACS, stroke, priapism and refractory 
VOC not responding to standard therapy.

Acute Chest Syndrome
It is characterized by fever, tachypnoea, dyspnoea, pulmonary infiltrate in X-ray, 
leucocytosis and fall of Hb and oxygen saturation <95%. 
	 1.	Hospitalize the patient and start oxygen immediately.
	 2.	Administer analgesics to control pain as mentioned earlier.
	 3.	Administer antibiotics covering atypical organisms and pneumococci. Administer 
Tab. Azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily Or Inj. Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV Or IM 
once a day (or in equally divided doses twice a day) for adults.
	 4.	Use Albuterol nebulizer as required
	 5.	Perform simple or exchange transfusion.
	 6.	Judiciously use IV fluid to avoid fluid overload.
	 7.	Perform spirometry for prevention.
Stroke
	 1.	Perform simple or exchange transfusion to maintain HbS concentration <30%. 
	 2.	For secondary prevention of stroke, consider prophylactic blood transfusion every 
3–4 weeks.
	 3.	If there is evidence of iron overload (SF >1000 ng/mL), administer iron chelators 
like deferasirox (DFX) 20 mg/kg/day (maximum dose 40 mg/kg).
	 4.	Monitor with CBC, SGOT, SGPT, urea, creatinine monthly and SF quarterly: 
Adjust dose every 3–6 months, by 5–10 mg/kg, based on SF trends.
Priapism: Analgesics, IV fluid, exchange transfusion, corporal aspiration and 
epinephrine irrigation
Avascular necrosis of femoral head: Pain relief and avoidance of weight bearing
Hepatopathy: Like splenic sequestration – hydration, rest, close observation, referral 
for simple or exchange transfusion
Leg ulcer: Leg elevation, occlusive zinc oxide dressing, skin grafting
Referral to a higher centre
Refer to a higher centre in case of severe VOC and ACS not responding to available 
treatment, ophthalmic complications, renal failure, avascular necrosis needing femoral 
head decompression and hip replacement, stroke, and priapism not responding to 
analgesics and hydration.
SCD & Pregnancy
Pregnancy in patients with SCD possesses special challenges in terms of increased 
foetal and maternal morbidity and mortality. Monitor and conduct delivery in the 
institution with the following precautions:
	 1.	Iron supplementation like that in normal pregnancy unless evidence of iron 
overload (SF >1000 ng/mL)

316    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 2.	Haemoglobin and urine examination monthly
	 3.	Tab. Folic acid 5 mg/day
	 4.	NSAID use only between 12th and 28th weeks
	 5.	Tab. Aspirin 75 mg daily to reduce risk of pre-eclampsia
	 6.	Avoid Pethidine and general anaesthesia during delivery (an anaesthetic assessment 
in the third trimester is warranted)
	 7.	Blood transfusion if >2 g drop in haemoglobin from baseline
Postpartum care
	 1.	Maintain maternal oxygen saturation greater than 94% and adequate hydration 
based on fluid balance until discharge.
	 2.	Low-molecular-weight heparin should be administered while in the hospital 
and 7 days post-discharge following vaginal delivery or for a period of 6 weeks 
following caesarean section.
	 3.	Acute crisis and other complications of SCD remain a risk in the puerperium.
	 4.	Perform early testing for SCD in the baby if the partner is a carrier or affected.
	 5.	Advise contraceptives.
Acute painful crisis during pregnancy
Painful crisis is the most frequent complication of SCD during pregnancy. 
	 1.	Assess rapidly for medical complications requiring interventions such as ACS, 
sepsis or dehydration and precipitating factors.
	 2.	Initial investigations should include full blood count, reticulocyte count and renal 
function. 
	 3.	Other investigations should be done depending on the clinical scenario but may 
include blood cultures, chest X-ray, urine culture and liver function tests. 
	 4.	Initial analgesia should be given within 30 minutes of arriving at the hospital and 
effective analgesia should be achieved within 1 hour. Analgesic ladder should 
be used, starting with paracetamol for mild pain, NSAIDs for mild to moderate 
pain between 12 and 28 weeks of gestation, weak opioids for moderate pain and 
stronger opiates such as morphine for severe pain.
	 5.	Monitor at 20-minute intervals for pain severity, respiratory rate and sedation. 
	 6.	Refer to a higher centre in case of severe VOC and ACS not responding to 
available treatment, ophthalmic complications, renal failure, avascular necrosis 
needing femoral head decompression and hip replacement, stroke, and priapism 
not responding to analgesics and hydration.

l Educate patients to avoid precipitating factors of painful crisis such as excess 
physical and mental exertion, exposure to excess cold and heat, and exposure to fava 
beans and to infection; and ensuring intake of plenty of fluid
	
l Public education for testing before marriage, partner testing and prenatal diagnosis
	
l Avoidance of consanguineous marriage

THALASSAEMIA
It is a group of heterogenetically inherited disorders that result from a reduced rate of 
synthesis of α- or β-chains of haemoglobin leading to thalassaemia major, minor or 
intermedia. β-thalassaemia is common and the most important type encountered across 
India. Four percent of Indians are thalassaemia carriers and around 12,000 people 
with thalassaemia major are born annually. Those with the trait of β-thalassaemia 
(thalassaemia minor) are clinically asymptomatic or can present with mild anaemia 
which may not require any specific treatment. The clinical severity of β-thalassaemia 
intermedia lies between trait and homozygous and the principle of management is 
similar to that of β-thalassaemia major. RBC transfusion requirements of these patients 
are smaller, and selected patients may benefit from therapeutic splenectomy. Patients 
seeking clinical care are typically those with severe or intermediate β-thalassemia, 
needing regular red cell transfusions.
β-THALASSAEMIA INTERMEDIA
The clinical presentation of β-thalassaemia intermedia or non-transfusion-dependent 
thalassemia (NTDT) lies between trait and severe form of homozygous state. Anaemia 
and its complications are observed after 2 years of age. The diagnosis is based on 
clinical manifestations and not on laboratory parameters; however, genetic mutation 
analysis (presence of silent/mild β-thalassaemia mutation or co-inheritance of genetic 
modifiers) may help in early diagnosis of NTDT.

The clinical presentation of β-thalassaemia intermedia or non-transfusion-dependent 
thalassemia (NTDT) lies between trait and severe form of homozygous state. Anaemia 
and its complications are observed after 2 years of age. The diagnosis is based on 
clinical manifestations and not on laboratory parameters; however, genetic mutation

1.	Folic acid supplementation and HU are the mainstay of therapy in NTDT. 
	 2.	HU initiated at the dose of 10 mg/kg/day may be increased by 5 mg/kg/day 
every 4–8 weeks to the maximum tolerated dose of 25 mg/kg/day. Increase 
in Hb of about 1.0–2.5 g/dL is expected with reduction in complications like 
extramedullary haematopoiesis, leg ulcers, thrombosis, pulmonary hypertension 
and osteoporosis.
	 3.	NTDT may require infrequent blood transfusion or intermittent regular transfusions 
during special conditions like growth/puberty failure, pregnancy, infections, 
pathological fractures, splenomegaly/hypersplenism and persistently Hb <7 g/dL 
despite on the maximum tolerated dose of HU. In such situations, the principle of 
management is similar to that of β-thalassemia major.
β-THALASSAEMIA MAJOR
β-thalassaemia major, also known as transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (TDT), is a 
severe form of thalassaemia requiring regular blood transfusions to maintain normal 
haemoglobin level.
The clinical presentation of β-thalassaemia major in early infancy includes 
failure to thrive, loss of appetite, irritability, recurrent bouts of fever and intercurrent 
infections. Usually, diagnosis is made between 3 and 24 months of age. If diagnosis is 
not made early or chronic transfusion therapy is not initiated, the child may land into 
complications of anaemia – jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, growth retardation, skeletal 
changes, thalassaemia facies and early death. Chronic transfusion regimen has its own 
complications like infections including hepatitis B and C, HIV, iron overload leading 
to endocrinopathies, and liver and heart failure.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patients may present with haemolytic anaemia, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly 
sometimes with leg ulcers and pigment stones in the gallbladder.
	
l Severe anaemia becomes apparent at 3–6 months after birth.
	
l Expansion of bone leads to thalassaemia facies–frontal bossing, malar 
prominence (maxilla is enlarged) and malocclusion of teeth.
	
l Microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with low MCV and MCH–peripheral blood 
smear may show target cells with anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, nucleated red cell, 
reticulocytes and fragmented RBCs.
	
l Diagnosis is confirmed by HPLC/capillary zone electrophoresis.
	
β-thalassaemia (major): HbA, 0–5%; HbA2, 2%; HbF, 80–98%
	
β-thalassaemia (intermedia): HbA2, variable; HbF, 20–70%; HbA, 20–50%
	
β-thalassaemia (trait): HbA, ≥90%; HbA2, >3.5%; HbF, 0–2%

1.  Transfusion therapy
The objectives of the treatment are to prevent chronic hypoxia, bone marrow 
hyperplasia, growth retardation, splenomegaly and hypervolaemia.
	
l Transfusion is initiated after confirming the diagnosis of thalassaemia major and Hb 
<7 g/dL on two occasions more than 2 weeks apart without any other co-existing 
factors to cause anaemia.
	
l Leucoreduced packed red cell transfusion 15–20 mL/kg body weight is done at 
the rate of 5 mL/kg/h over 3–4 hours every 2–4 weeks (1–3 units in one sitting 
depending on weight of the patient and volume of blood bag). Transfusion rate 
should be limited to 1–3 mL/kg in patients with cardiac failure.
	
l If washed red cells are present in patients with repeated severe reactions despite 
leucoreduction or patients with immunoglobin A (IgA) deficiency, transfuse them 
within 24 hours and do not use them as a substitute for leucoreduction. 
	
l Do not transfuse first-degree relative donor’s blood to avoid later GVHD during 
bone marrow transplantation.
	
l Perform ABO and Rh (C, c, D, E, e) and Kell-compatible blood transfusion to avoid 
alloimmunization against these antigens.
	
l Warming blood to room temperature before transfusion is NOT indicated in 
patients with thalassaemia. Avoid pre-medication with Paracetamol, anti-allergic or 
Frusemide and restrict it to only in conditions when it is absolutely necessary.
	
l Maintain pre-transfusion Hb between 9.5 and 10.5 g/dL. In patients with cardiac 
failure, maintain pre-transfusion Hb level at 11–12 g/dL with frequent transfusions.
	
l NAAT tested blood from non-remunerated donors reduces the risk of transfusion-
transmitted infections like hepatitis B and C and HIV.
2.  Iron chelation
	
l Iron overload from repeated transfusions is inevitable. Hence, iron chelation therapy 
is supplemented if the SF level is >1000 ng/dL. Iron chelators like DFX are required. 
	
l MRI T2* is a better non-invasive modality to measure liver iron concentration 
and cardiac iron overload. Usually, it is advised once a year after 8 years of age. 
With MRI T2*, the target should be to keep cardiac T2* values >20 and liver iron 
concentration <2 g/dw of the liver.
	
l First-time iron chelation is initiated when the SF value crosses 1000 ng/dL. Target 
should be to keep it around 500 ng/mL with adequate uninterrupted iron chelation.
	
l With MRI T2*, the target should be to keep cardiac T2* values >20 and liver iron 
concentration <2 g/dw of the liver.
	
l DFX is the drug of choice for iron chelation in thalassaemia. Initial dose is 20 mg/
kg/day that can be escalated up to the maximum dose of 40 mg/kg depending on 
iron over load and tolerability. DFX can be dissolved in 100–200 mL water or juice 
(apple/orange) in a non-metallic (glass) container; given 30 minutes before food. The 
most common side effects are skin rashes and loose motions. Monitor CBC, SGOT, 
SGPT, urea and creatinine monthly. If creatinine level is above normal or liver

enzymes raise by >5 ULN, reduce the dose or withdraw. This may be re-challenged 
under strict monitoring after values return to the normal level. Film-coated tablets 
(FCT) of DFX, 14–28 mg/kg swallowed have lesser side effects. 
	 Or 
	 Tab. Deferiprone (DFP) 75–100 mg/kg is given in two to four divided doses after 
meals. (Caution: The colour of urine becomes reddish. DFP is a good chelator 
of iron from the heart. For associated nausea and vomiting, give antacids and/or 
anti-emetics. For patients developing arthralgia on DFP, give short-term low-dose 
NSAIDs, reduce the dose or withdraw the drug if it persists. The most serious side 
effects [1–2%] are neutropenia and/or thrombocytopenia. Monitor CBC every 2–3 
weeks. Stop DFP if WBC count is <3000, neutrophils are <1000 or platelets are 
<100,000. If cytopenia is due to any other cause (e.g. fever/infection), the drug may 
be restarted with low dose after the counts become normal. Never re-challenge with 
DFP if at any point if the neutrophil count reduces to <500 ng/mL.)
	 Or
	 Inj. Deferoxamine (DFO) 20–40 mg/kg subcutaneous is given over 12 hours with 
portable infusion pump in home settings. (Caution: Avoid >30 mg/kg before 
completion of puberty. The dose of 50–60 mg/kg can be given by slow intravenous 
infusion over 24 hours continuously in highly iron-overloaded patients or patients 
suffering from cardiac complications due to high iron overload in the heart. Addition 
of vitamin C 2–3 mg/kg orally after 2 weeks of initiation of DFO therapy increases 
iron excretion. Vitamin C is contraindicated in associated cardiac problems. The 
side effects of DFO include skin reactions, induration at the injection site, growth 
retardation, Yersinia enterocolitica infection and visual or hearing impairment. 
	
Annual auditory and visual consultation is required to monitor ophthalmic toxicity 
and ototoxicity. In case of any drug-induced impairment, reduce the dose or 
withdraw the drug.)
	 Maintain target SF around 500 ng/mL with adequate uninterrupted iron chelation. 
Measure SF after 10–12 blood transfusions and then every 3 months. SF trend is a 
better indicator of iron chelation than a single value. SF values may be falsely high 
during infection and inflammatory conditions and low in vitamin C deficiency.
Patients who are highly iron overloaded, having cardiac, liver or endocrine 
complications, or unable to tolerate full dose of one chelator, a combination of two 
of the available three chelators (DFX and DFP) may be given. DFO + DFP is a better 
combination to chelate iron from the heart. In some patients in whom iron overload is 
persistently high in spite of dual iron chelation, a triple-drug combination has also been 
tried. The dose of each drug in combination therapy depends on various factors like iron 
overload, organ damage and drug toxicity. Combination therapy should be prescribed 
only by experts in the management of thalassaemia.
3.  Splenectomy
The spleen is invariably enlarged in patients with NTDT due to persistent anaemia. 
Patients with TDT if maintained on Hb >10 g/dL do not suffer from splenomegaly.

Mild splenomegaly can be reduced with hypertransfusion regimen with more 
frequent transfusions to maintain pre-transfusion Hb around 11 g/dL. Splenectomy 
is indicated if massive splenomegaly is present with a possible risk of rupture, PRBC 
requirement increases >200–220 mL/kg/year or hypersplenism is present (diagnosed 
with cytopenia).
Splenectomy should not be performed before the age of 5 years. HiB, 
pneumococcal, meningococcal and influenza vaccination should be given at least 
2 weeks before surgery. All these vaccines can be given on the same day at different 
sites. Repeat HiB, meningococcal and pneumococcal vaccines after 3–5 years and flu 
vaccine annually. Post-splenectomy penicillin prophylaxis should be given lifelong. 
Amoxycillin or Erythromycin can be given to those who cannot tolerate penicillin. 
Splenectomy increases the risk of thrombosis, pulmonary hypertension and fulminant 
infections. Low-dose aspirin can be prescribed in patients with platelet count >500,000 
mm3 to reduce the risk of thromboembolism.
4.  Diet and supplements
	
l Avoid iron-rich foods like mutton, leafy vegetables, spinach, jaggery, beetroot, 
pomegranate and packed foods containing iron. Fish, white of egg and limited 
quantity of chicken can be taken. Avoid citrus fruits with meals but these can be 
taken 2 hours after food.
	
l Milk products and soya products can be taken liberally. Tea immediately after meals 
reduces dietary iron absorption from the gut.
	
l Tab. Folic acid 1–5 mg/day.
	
l Calcium, vitamin D and zinc supplements as per requirement.
5.  Permanent cure
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is the established therapy for permanent 
cure. Greater than 90% successful transplant can be envisaged in adequately transfused 
and chelated patients younger than 7 years with the liver <5 cm below the costal margin 
and 100% HLA-matched donor. With newer improved techniques, 75–85% success is 
expected in older patients also. In India, successful HSCT in thalassaemia has been done 
in the age group of 20–25 years. HSCT should be discussed with parents at an early 
stage. Financial support is available for non-affording families from various quarters like 
corporate social responsibility (CSR), PM/CM relief funds and NGOs. 
Gene therapy by gene insertion (Zynteglo) has been approved by the US FDA; 
however, not yet available in India and the cost is a limiting factor. Patients with TDT 
between the ages of 4 and 35 years who do not have HLA-matched donor available 
can benefit from this. New platforms using CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing have shown 
remarkable results in 44 patients with TDT. No gene editing–related adverse events 
have been reported till date.
Note: Patients with thalassaemia can live a near-normal life with dignity and achieve 
any position provided they maintain pre-transfusion Hb near 10 g/dL and SF around 
500 ng/mL under strict guidance of a thalassaemiologist.

Patient education
	
l Educate parents on prevention.
	
l Parents of patients with thalassaemia are obligatory thalassaemia carriers. They 
should be informed about the autosomal recessive nature of the disease and advised 
to undergo prenatal diagnosis of thalassaemia at 10 weeks of gestation in every 
future pregnancy.
	
l Guide parents that siblings of patients with thalassaemia have 1 in 4, uncles/aunts, 
1 in 8 and cousins, 1 in 16 chance of being a thalassaemia carrier. 
	
l To prevent new thalassaemia births in their extended family, test thalassaemia carrier 
status before marriage and avoid marriages between two carriers. Marriage after 
HbA2-haemoglobin matching instead of horoscope matching should be taken up in 
the society for counselling and informed decision making.
	
l If the marriage cannot be avoided or is already solemnized, both partners should 
be screened for thalassaemia carrier status by Hb HPLC before pregnancy or 
immediately after conception followed by genetic counselling and antenatal 
diagnosis if required. If a foetus is found to be suffering from homozygous 
thalassaemia, the pregnancy can be terminated as per the government rules; if it is 
found to be healthy or in a carrier state, then it can be allowed to continue.

Respiratory Diseases
PNEUMONIA
Pneumonia is an inflammation in alveolar tissue, most often caused by a microbial 
agent. Inhalation is the commonest route of infection. The most frequent pneumonia is 
the community acquired pneumonia (CAP), most commonly caused by Streptococcus 
pneumoniae (typical) and less frequently by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Haemophilus 
influenzae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus or Legionella pneumophila 
(atypical). Hospital-acquired pneumonia is likely to be caused by Gram-negative bacilli 
and S. aureus. Aspiration pneumonia, usually seen in patients with neuromuscular 
disorders or in ICU care, is polymicrobial including anaerobes. Age is an important 
predictor of the infectious agent.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Acute-onset fever, productive cough, chest pain, shortness of breath and 
(in some cases) pleuritic chest pain; systemic symptoms like headache, body ache 
and delirium are more severe with atypical pneumonia.
	
l New focal signs are seen on physical examination of the chest. 
	
l In contrast, the elderly patients differ in their presentation. The classic symptoms 
and signs of pneumonia are less likely and non-specific features, especially 
confusion, are more common. Also, absence of fever is more common compared 
with in younger patients.
	
l The atypical pneumonia syndrome is characterized by a more gradual onset, a dry 
cough, shortness of breath and a prominence of extrapulmonary symptoms (headache, 
myalgias, fatigue, sore throat, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea) and abnormalities on 
chest X-ray despite minimal signs of pulmonary involvement (other than rales).
	
l The ‘primary atypical pneumonia’ caused by M. pneumoniae results in a violent, 
episodic cough with small mucoid sputum preceded by fever with or without 
chills and may be accompanied by profound weakness.
	
l Diagnosis is by new chest radiographic evidence of pneumonic consolidation 
which is at least segmental or present in more than one lobe and is not known to 
be previously present for which there is no other explanation.
	
l Confirmation of the aetiological diagnosis is by blood culture/sputum culture 
and/or molecular diagnostic methods.
	
l Urea and electrolytes are done to gauge the severity assessment; C-reactive protein 
(CRP), full blood count and liver function tests are done as a baseline measure.

l CURB-65 score aids in determining the initial severity and planning of treatment 
of pneumonia (Fig. 5.1). It is essential to interpret the CURB-65 score alongside 
clinical judgment for all patients.
	
l CAP in the elderly: Pneumonia in the elderly presents several distinct prognostic 
factors for mortality. These include aspects such as the severity of pneumonia, 
inadequate response to infection and reduced functional capacity. However, 
traditional prognostic tools like CAP scores and biomarkers hold diminished 
predictive value in this demographic. Thus, there is a pressing need to adhere to 
established guidelines. Additionally, it is important to identify and address issues such 
as nutritional status, appropriate fluid management, maintaining functional ability 
and implementing therapies to manage comorbidities in these vulnerable individuals
	
l Antibiotics are the mainstay of treatment – initial choice depends on the setting in 
which infection was acquired, age, clinical presentation, pattern of abnormality on 
chest X-ray, result of staining of sputum or other infected body fluids and current 
pattern of susceptibility of pathogens to antimicrobial agents. The choice of antibiotic 
may be modified based on clinical response, sputum culture and sensitivity report.
Plan A: Outpatient treatment: Previously healthy and no risk factors for 
drug-resistant S. pneumoniae (DRSP) infection:
Cap. Azithromycin 500 mg once daily Or Cap. Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily, for 
minimum 5 days
Or
Cap. Doxycycline 200 mg loading dose, and then 100 mg once daily for 5 days
Or
Cap Amoxycillin 500 mg thrice daily for minimum 5 days
Plan B: Presence of comorbidities, such as chronic heart, lung, liver or renal disease; 
diabetes mellitus; pregnancy; alcoholism; malignancies; asplenia; immunosuppressing 
conditions or use of immunosuppressant drugs; use of antimicrobials within the 
previous 3 months (in which case an alternative from a different class should be 
selected); or other risks for DRSP infection:
Tab. Amoxicillin–Clavulanate 2 g 2 times daily Or Inj. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV/IM once 
daily Or Tab. Cefpodoxime 200 mg twice daily Or Inj. Cefuroxime 500 mg IM/IV 
2 times daily for 10 days.
Or
Cap. Azithromycin 500 mg once daily Or Cap. Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for 
10 days Or Cap. Doxycycline 200 mg loading dose, and then 100 mg once daily for 
10 days

ASTHMA
Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder associated with variable airflow obstruction 
and bronchial hyperresponsiveness which is reversible spontaneously or with treatment. 
It can begin at any age but most often has its roots in early childhood.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Presenting features include classic triad of recurrent cough, wheeze and 
breathlessness which vary over time and in intensity; however, all the three may 
not be present.
	
l Clinical symptoms may be increased due to upper respiratory viral infections, 
exercise, exposure to smoke, dust, acid reflux, obesity, cold air, cold food or 
various allergens. 
	
l Diagnosis is clinical and reversible airway obstruction is demonstrated on 
pulmonary function tests (Fig. 5.2). An increase in FEV1 after inhaling a 
bronchodilator by >200 mL and >12% of the pre-bronchodilator value is termed 
as significant bronchodilator reversibility.

Figure 5.2.  Diagnosis of asthma.

l For every patient, assessment of asthma should include the assessment of asthma 
control; treatment issues, particularly inhaler technique and adherence; and any 
comorbidities that could contribute to symptom burden and quality of life. Asthma 
can be broadly classified into well controlled, partly controlled and uncontrolled on 
the basis of the Asthma Control Questionnaire.
	
l Risk factors for asthma exacerbations include high short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) 
use, obesity, chronic rhinosinusitis, gastro oesophageal reflux disease (GERD), 
smoking, incorrect inhaler technique, low FEV1, higher blood eosinophil count, 
elevated fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) and low birth weight.
	
l Based on the severity, asthma can be:
	– Mild asthma: Asthma that is well controlled with low-intensity treatment, i.e. 
as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)–formoterol or low-dose ICS 
plus as-needed SABA
	– Moderate asthma: Asthma that is well controlled with low- or medium-dose 
ICS–long-acting bronchodilator (LABA)
	– Severe asthma: Asthma that remains uncontrolled despite optimized treatment 
with high-dose ICS–LABA

Wherever possible, identify and avoid the trigger factor(s), stop smoking and do regular 
breathing exercises, e.g. ‘Pranayama’ and physical activity and weight loss.

Goals of long-term asthma care 
	 1.	Freedom from symptoms, including nocturnal cough, acute attacks and emergency 
doctor/hospital visits, frequent school absenteeism, adverse drug effects.
	 2.	Normal daily activities and sports participation, growth charts, peak expiratory 
flow/spirometry.
Acute exacerbation of asthma (Fig. 5.3)
	
l Good response is defined as the patient feeling well with minimal or no dyspnoea, 
marked improvement in heart rate and respiratory rate, and little or no rhonchi on 
auscultation with oxygen saturation greater than 95% at room air. If response is 
sustained for the next 3–4 hours, patients showing good response may be sent home 
on inhaled or oral bronchodilators for 7–10 days.
	
l If the response is partial or the patient is on maintenance treatment with high-
dose inhaled steroids or attended emergency room in the last 72 hours, add Tab. 
Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day maximum 60 mg/day for 3–5 days to re-establish control. 
(Caution: Resist overuse of oral steroid as an alternative to daily inhaled preventer 
therapy.) Call the patient again for reassessment after 1 week or early if symptoms 
are not getting controlled or worsening.
	
l Patients not showing any response or poor response should be treated as 
moderate-to-severe acute asthma.

332    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Life-threatening asthma
Treatment of a life-threatening episode should be immediate and no time should be 
spent on detailed clinical history.
	 1.	Oxygen inhalation 4 L/min to maintain SpO2 >90%.
	 2.	Inj. Terbutaline 10 mcg/kg subcutaneously or IV (maximum 40 mcg/day).
	 3.	Inhaled Salbutamol/Terbutaline preferably by nebulizer (as discussed above).
	 4.	Ipratropium Bromide 250 mcg by nebulizer with Salbutamol.
	 5.	Inj. Hydrocortisone 10 mg/kg IV.
	 6.	Inj. Aminophylline 5 mg/kg bolus slowly followed by 0.8–1.2 mg/kg/h slow 
infusion (if the patient has received theophylline preparation in the last 72 hours, 
reduce bolus dose to 2.5 mg/kg).
	 7.	Inj. Magnesium sulphate 40 mg/kg in 50 mL 5% dextrose as slow infusion over 
30 minutes can be considered.
	 8.	If there is no response, get arterial blood gas analysis and X-ray chest and serum 
electrolytes. Intubate the patient if there is no or poor respiratory effort and 
increased carbon dioxide with respiratory acidosis. Transfer to the intensive care 
unit as early as possible.
Notes:
	
l Do not give antibiotics routinely. Antibiotics are required only if there is a 
consolidation, high-grade fever or polymorphonuclear leucocytosis.
	
l Mere presence of crackles is not an evidence of pneumonia and does not warrant 
antibiotics.
	
l Mucolytics and cough syrups are not helpful.
	
l Avoid sedation in acute asthma.
	
l Non-sedating antihistaminics may be used if associated allergic rhinitis is present.
Monitoring 
Hospitalized children should be assessed by a nurse every 3 hours even when 
improving or every 6 hours when stable and by a doctor at least once a day. Monitor 
respiratory rate and signs of impending respiratory failure. Check oxygen therapy 
periodically. 
Discharge
Consider discharge if a child is stable and able to take medications orally, does not need 
oxygen and is on 4–6 hourly salbutamol inhalation.
Long-term management of asthma
Long-term asthma management depends on severity over a period of time. Assess 
severity of asthma on the basis of the frequency of symptoms including disturbance 
of sleep, effect on day-to-day activity of the patient and need for medication, 
hospital visit and hospitalization and pulmonary function tests (PFTs) by spirometer 
(Table 5.1).

Treatment of chronic asthma
Principles of asthma treatment
	 1.	Use rescue medication (SABA) for symptoms of dyspnoea, wheezing and chest 
tightness at any stage.
	 2.	Begin anti-inflammatory medication (inhaled ICS preferred) when symptoms occur 
two or more times a week.
	 3.	Do not use LABA bronchodilators as solo treatment. Never use LABA without ICS.
	 4.	Adding LABA to ICS is the preferred approach when step-up therapy is needed.
	 5.	Medium- or high-dose ICS may be necessary to control persistent symptoms, but 
risk more systemic absorption.
	 6.	Sustained-released theophylline is a bronchodilator with weak anti-inflammatory 
properties and frequent side effects.
	 7.	The use of a spacer device is recommended when metered-dose inhaler (MDI) 
canisters are used to reduce oropharyngeal deposition and reduce systemic 
absorption. In children younger than 4 years, MDI with spacer with facemask; for 
children older than 4 years, MDI with spacer; for patients older than 12 years, MDI 
may be used directly or dry powder inhaler is as effective; and for elderly patients, 
MDI with spacer; however, some may prefer dry powder inhaler.
	 8.	Reassess inhaler technique as part of clinical assessment and review treatment 
plan with current clinical control criteria. If the patient is unable to use a device 
satisfactorily, an alternative should be found.

Follow-up and modification in treatment
	
l Monitoring is necessary as asthma is a variable disease. Treatment has to be adjusted 
periodically in response to loss of control as indicated by worsening symptoms or 
development of an exacerbation.
	
l Call the patient every 4–12 weeks after starting treatment, thereafter every 3–12 
months (in pregnancy, review every 4–6 weeks) depending on the patient’s initial 
level of control, response to treatment and ability/understanding to engage in self-
management of action plan. In case of acute exacerbation, review visit within 1 week 
depending on the patient’s initial level of control and response to treatment. On each 
visit, examine the patient; look for adverse effects of the drugs and record height 
and weight in children. Measure peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR)/PFTs and record 
the assessed status of disease.
	 Note: To date, there is no good-quality evidence that vitamin D supplementation 
leads to improved asthma control or fewer exacerbations.
Stepping down in well-controlled asthma
	
l Step down the medications if control is sustained for at least 3 months and choose 
an appropriate time (no respiratory infection, patient not travelling, not pregnant). 
Follow a gradual stepwise reduction in treatment. 
	
l When deciding which drug to step down first and at what rate, the severity of 
asthma, the side effects of treatment, the beneficial effect achieved and the patients’ 
preference should all be taken into account.

Rescue therapy of flare-ups (acute exacerbation)
Parents/patients should be trained to identify acute exacerbations.
	 1.	Identify acute exacerbation by increase in cough, wheeze and breathlessness (assess 
whether the patient is able to speak sentences or only words).
	 2.	Measure PEFR (if feasible); if decreased by 15% from the baseline, administer 
Salbutamol by MDI with spacer with or without facemask, 1 puff at a time, repeated 
every 2–4 minutes up to a maximum of 10–20 puffs with monitoring of symptoms.
	
	If symptoms are relieved and PEFR is increased at the end of inhalation, continue 
on Salbutamol/Terbutaline 2 puffs every 4–6 hours and plan a visit to treating 
physician.
	
	If there is PEFR or FEV1 <60% best, no improvement or partial improvement 
after 48 hours or symptoms of life-threatening attack (severe distress, difficulty in 
speech, feeding, cyanosis, exhaustion) at any time, refer the patient immediately to 
a hospital and during transportation continue inhaled Salbutamol/Terbutaline and 
give a dose of prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg if can be given orally for 5–7 days.
	 3.	Consider alternative causes of acute breathlessness (heart failure, upper airway 
dysfunction, foreign body or pulmonary embolism).
	 4.	In patients who experience exacerbation on exercise, give 2 puffs of SABA 20 
minutes before exercise. Encourage swimming and yoga. Practice nose breathing 
and slow deep breathing during exercise. Notify the teacher/coach about the child’s 
condition and advise the need for inhaled medication prior to activity.
	 5.	In case of seasonal asthma, initiate daily preventer regime weeks prior to the 
anticipated onset of symptoms and continue throughout the season.
Patient/parent education
	
l Explain the nature and pathogenesis of asthma in simple language and inform the 
patient that it is a chronic and recurrent condition and severity may change over a 
period of time.

338    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Emphasize that there is a wide spectrum of severity of asthma and that most patients 
can lead an active and normal life.
	
l Inform on the reversible nature of the illness, and that asthma can be controlled but 
may need continuous therapy and regular follow-up.
	
l Provide written asthma action plan to patients as appropriate for their level of 
asthma control and health literacy, so that they know how to recognize and respond 
to worsening asthma.
	
l Emphasize that the drugs used ‘control’ asthma but do not ‘cure’ asthma. Reassure 
parents that a majority of children outgrow their symptoms and can lead active, 
normal lives.
	
l Ask to maintain a record of daily symptoms such as cough, coryza, wheeze and 
breathlessness. A record of sleep disturbances, absence from school due to illness 
and medication is required to keep the patient symptom free.
	
l Clear myths and misconceptions regarding inhaled therapy and emphasize merits of 
the inhaled route. Provide information that inhalers are not habit-forming, and are 
safe and better than tablets or syrup.
	
l Counsel regarding approximate time taken to note improvement and emphasize the 
need for compliance with the prescribed preventer drugs as continuous preventer 
drugs may be required for certain grades of asthma.
	
l Patients/parents should be trained to identify acute exacerbations and initiate rescue 
plan as above.
	
l Environmental control to avoid precipitating factors is very important.
	– The patient/parents should avoid dusting (wet mopping is preferred) when 
children are around.
	– Avoid using carpets, stuffed toys, open bookshelves, smoking and chemical 
sprays in the house. Mosquito nets should be preferred over repellents. Animal 
dander may persist for a few months after the pet is given away. Therefore, 
improvement in asthma may not be immediately evident.
	
l The role of diet in the precipitation of asthma symptoms is overemphasized; 
providing a general list of food items that should be avoided to all patients is 
irrational. In fact, Food with chemicals like preservatives/colouring agents and 
common food allergens such as nuts, eggs, chocolates and sea food should be 
avoided if food allergy is suspected.
	
l Discuss the usage and maintenance of the inhaler device selected.
	
l Check adherence and watch patients using their inhalers and correct errors at every 
opportunity. It is best to use MDI with spacers; however, if low-dose steroids are being 
given, then dry powder inhaler can also be used. MDI must be shaken well before 
inhalation. If inhaler has not been used for a week or more, it should be shaken well and 
one puff released into the air. It is then attached to spacer (commercial/indigenous made 
from plastic bottle) and the patient is asked to inhale 3–4 times slowly and deeply just 
when the drug is released by activation of MDI. Do not rush. If ‘mist’ comes out from 
the top of the inhaler or the sides of the mouth, the process should be started again. This 
escaping mist indicates incorrect technique.

CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE (COPD)
COPD is a common preventable and treatable disease; however, widespread under-
diagnosis and misdiagnosis often result in patients either not receiving any treatment 
or receiving incorrect treatment. Achieving a timely and accurate diagnosis of COPD 
can exert a profoundly positive influence on public health. COPD is characterized 
by chronic respiratory symptoms (dyspnoea, cough, sputum production and/or 
exacerbations) due to abnormalities of the airways (bronchitis, bronchiolitis) and/
or alveoli (emphysema) that cause persistent, often progressive, airflow obstruction. 
The main environmental exposures leading to COPD are tobacco smoking and the 
inhalation of toxic particles and gases from household and outdoor air pollution and 
occupational dust, vapours, fumes, gases and other chemicals as well as host factors 
such as genetics, developmental abnormalities, low birth weight, prematurity and 
childhood respiratory infections.
Exacerbations and comorbidities contribute to the overall severity in individual 
patients. The most important aetiology is inhalation of smoke, mostly from 
bidi/cigarette (80% of smokers get it), the other factors being air pollution, infections 
and genetic. Recognizing that factors beyond tobacco smoking play a role in COPD, 
that its onset can occur in early life impacting young individuals and that precursor 
conditions (pre-COPD, PRISm [Preserved Ratio Impaired Spirometry; FEV1 
<80% predicted and a FEV1/forced vital capacity {FVC} ratio of 0·70 or higher]) 
exist unveils new possibilities for preventing, diagnosing early and intervening 
therapeutically in a timely and effective manner.

340    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Shortness of breath, limitations in physical activity and/or coughing, with or 
without the production of sputum.
	
l Acute respiratory events marked by intensified respiratory symptoms, known as 
exacerbations, are present, necessitating particular preventive and therapeutic 
interventions.
	
l Forced spirometry showing the presence of a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 
<0.7 is mandatory to establish the diagnosis of COPD.
	
l Chronic cough, often overlooked by patients with COPD, may initially be 
intermittent but can become a daily occurrence throughout the day. It may be 
productive or unproductive. Significant airflow obstruction can occur without a 
cough, and syncope or rib fractures may result from prolonged coughing spells 
in severe COPD cases.
	
l Patients with COPD often experience intermittent sputum production, and 
chronic bronchitis is traditionally defined as regular sputum production for 3 or 
more months in 2 consecutive years. Sputum production can be intermittent, and 
large volumes may indicate underlying bronchiectasis. Purulent sputum suggests 
increased inflammatory mediators, potentially indicating a bacterial exacerbation, 
although the association is relatively weak.

A COPD management programme includes four components: assess and monitor the 
disease; reduce risk factors; manage stable COPD, manage and prevent exacerbations; 
actively identify comorbidities and assess the impact of the disease on the patient’s 
overall health.
The spirometric classification of severity of airflow limitation is divided into four grades 
based on post-bronchodilator FEV1 using the fixed ratio FEV1/FVC <0.70, as follows:
	
l GOLD 1 (mild; FEV1 ≥ 80% predicted)
	
l GOLD 2 (moderate; 50% ≤ FEV1, <80% predicted)
	
l GOLD 3 (severe; 30% ≤ FEV1, <50% predicted)
	
l GOLD 4 (very severe; FEV1 <30% predicted)
Modified MRC Dyspnoea Scale (0–4) is a commonly used tool to assess the severity 
of breathlessness in individuals:
	
l Grade 0: Breathlessness only with strenuous exercise
	
l Grade 1: Breathless when hurrying on the level or walking up a slight hill
	
l Grade 2: Walks slower than people of the same age on the level because of 
breathlessness or has to stop for breath when walking at own pace on the level
	
l Grade 3: Stops for breath after walking approximately 100 yards or after a few 
minutes on the level
	
l Grade 4: Too breathless to leave the house or breathless when dressing or 
undressing

The treatment depends on ABE classification of COPD which is determined by 
symptoms (COPD assessment test [CAT] or modified Medical Research Council 
[mMRC]) and exacerbations in the preceding year.
Acute exacerbation is an acute event characterized by a worsening of the patients’ 
respiratory symptoms that is beyond normal day-to-day variation. Signs of severity 
include use of accessory respiratory muscles, paradoxical chest wall movements, 
worsening or new-onset central cyanosis, development of peripheral oedema, 
haemodynamic instability and deteriorated mental status. Acute exacerbation is 
commonly precipitated by viral upper respiratory infections.

l Cessation of smoking, avoiding inhalation of smoke from other sources (home 
or occupational), chest physiotherapy to help expectoration of sputum, postural 
drainage of sputum and adequate hydration

Treatment as below depending on the presentation.
A.  Stable COPD
	 1.	Group A COPD: mMRC 0–1, CAT <10 with 0 or 1 moderate exacerbation 
not leading to hospital admission. It is treated with a bronchodilator (LABA or 
LAMA).
	 2.	Group B COPD: mMRC ≥2, CAT ≥10 with 0 or 1 moderate exacerbation not 
leading to hospital admission. It is treated with a combination of LABA + LAMA.
	 3.	Group E COPD: ≥2 moderate exacerbations or ≥1 moderate exacerbation 
leading to hospital admission. It is treated with a combination of LABA + LAMA. 
Consider LABA + LAMA + ICS if absolute blood eosinophil count (eos) ≥300 
cells/µL. Single inhaler therapy is preferred as it offers greater convenience and 
efficacy compared to multiple inhalers.
Note: Mucolytics have no proven benefit. Antitussives and respiratory stimulants 
are not recommended. Alpha-1 antitrypsin augmentation is not recommended unless 
COPD is related to its deficiency. Statins are not recommended for prevention of 
exacerbations. Theophylline exerts a small bronchodilator effect in stable COPD and 
associated with modest symptomatic benefits. Leukotriene modifiers have not been 
tested adequately in COPD patients.
B.  Follow-up
	 1.	Review response (dyspnoea/exacerbation), assess inhaler technique, possible 
interfering co-morbidities and adherence to treatment non-pharmacological 
approaches including pulmonary rehabilitation and self-management education. 
	 2.	If response to initial treatment is appropriate, maintain it.

342    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 3.	If response (dyspnoea) is not adequate, adjust therapy. 
	
l Escalate from LABA or LAMA to LABA plus LAMA.
	
l Switch inhaler device and medicines irrespective of the ABE assessment at 
diagnosis. 
	 4.	Consider de-escalation of ICS if pneumonia or other significant side effects. Do not 
de-escalate if blood eos ≥300 as it is associated with development of exacerbation. 
	 5.	Ensure maintenance of exercise programme and physical activity, adequate sleep 
and health diet. If not appropriate consider self-management education with written 
action plan and pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) programme (described below) and/
or maintenance exercise programme post PR, stress management techniques.
	 6.	Follow-up management may also include investigation (and treatment) of other 
causes of dyspnoea.
C.  Exacerbation 
In case of exacerbation adjust therapy. 
	 1.	Escalate from LABA or LAMA to LABA plus LAMA if eos is <300. If eos >100 
on LABA + LAMA, add ICS.
	 2.	If eos is >300 LABA + LAMA + ICS.
	 3.	In patients with chronic bronchitis, severe to very severe COPD (if FEV1 <50%) 
and a history of exacerbations consider Roflumilast. 
	 4.	Antibiotics are not routinely recommended for all COPD exacerbations. Mild 
exacerbation may respond to increased bronchodilator and steroids. Antibiotics are 
required if there is increase in sputum volume, purulence and dyspnoea and in case 
of the patient requiring ventilatory (invasive or non-invasive) or haemodynamic 
support. Oral/parenteral antibiotics are given as per local antibiogram. If sensitive, 
Amoxycillin 500 mg + Clavulanic acid 125 mg 3 times a day for 7–10 days. 
	
	Long-term Azithromycin use is preferred in former smokers who experience 
exacerbations despite appropriate therapy, as it has been shown to reduce 
exacerbations over a 1-year period. (Caution: It is associated with development 
of antimicrobial resistance and impaired hearing.)
	 5.	Ensure that self-management education with written action plan includes avoidance 
of aggravating factors and monitoring/management of worsening symptoms. Also, 
ensure the maintenance of an exercise program and physical activity, adequate 
sleep, and a healthy diet. Self-management education should also include guidance 
on pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) programmes and/or maintenance exercise 
programmes post-PR, as well as stress management techniques.

Supplemental oxygen
Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) is recommended for individuals with COPD 
who consistently have a persistent arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) of ≤55 mmHg or 
an oxygen saturation (SaO2) of ≤88% while at rest Or PaO2 >55 but <60 mmHg 
(>7.3 kPa but <8 kPa) with right heart failure or erythrocytosis. This therapeutic 
approach involves the continuous administration of supplemental oxygen, typically 
for a minimum of 15 hours/day, with the objective of improving oxygen saturation 
(to keep SaO2 >90%). Recheck in 60–90 days if supplemental oxygen is effective and 
whether still indicated and alleviating associated symptoms. LTOT aims to enhance 
the quality of life, alleviate breathlessness and mitigate the risk of complications in 
individuals with chronic respiratory diseases. Essential components for successful 
LTOT management include regular monitoring and strict adherence to prescribed 
oxygen levels.
Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV)
	
l Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV) may improve hospitalization-
free survival in select patients after recent hospitalization, especially those with 
pronounced daytime persistent hypercapnia (PaCO2 >53 mmHg).
	
l In patients with severe chronic hypercapnia and a history of hospitalization for acute 
respiratory failure, long-term non-invasive ventilation be considered.
	
l All patients with advanced COPD should be provided with end of life and palliative 
care support to optimize symptom control and allow patients and their families to 
make informed decisions about future management. For details see Palliative care 
in Chapter 8.
	
l Provide nutritional supplementation in malnourished COPD patients as it may 
improve muscle strength and overall health status.
	
l Fatigue can be managed by self-management education, pulmonary rehabilitation, 
nutritional support and mind-body interventions.
Pulmonary Rehabilitation Programme
Pulmonary rehabilitation, self-management and integrated care are vital components in 
managing COPD. They help improve outcomes and quality of life for individuals living 
with COPD and reduce hospitalizations and emergency department visits.

344    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Pulmonary rehabilitation programmes focus on improving exercise capacity, 
reducing symptoms and enhancing quality of life through structured exercise 
training, education and behavioural interventions. 
	
l Self-management strategies empower patients to better cope with their condition by 
providing tools and skills to monitor symptoms, manage exacerbations and adhere 
to treatment plans. 
	
l Integrated care involves coordinating healthcare services across different providers 
and settings to ensure comprehensive and patient-centred care, aiming to optimize 
outcomes and minimize the burden of COPD on individuals and healthcare systems.
Vaccination
	
l Influenza vaccination every year and pneumococcal vaccinations (one dose of 
PCV20 or PCV15 followed by PPSV23) decrease the incidence of lower respiratory 
tract infections.
	
l RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) vaccine is recommended for patients over 60 years 
of age and/or with chronic heart or lung disease.
	
l Tdap vaccination protects against pertussis if not vaccinated in adolescence.
	
l Zoster vaccine is recommended to protect against shingles in COPD patients over 
50 years of age.
Patient education
	
l Exercise training programmes improve exercise tolerance and dyspnoea.
	
l Explain about the importance of total cessation of smoking and its benefit not only 
during the acute stage but also during the long-term recovery of lung functions. 
	
l Emphasize on the correct inhaler technique. (For details, see the section ‘Asthma’.)
	
l Engaging in pulmonary rehabilitation, which combines exercise training with condition-
specific education, enhances exercise capacity, alleviates symptoms and improves the 
overall quality of life for individuals with COPD, regardless of the severity grade.

BRONCHIECTASIS
Bronchiectasis is caused by permanent abnormal dilatation of one or more 
bronchi/bronchioles due to destruction of ciliated epithelium, elastic and muscular 
tissue. The destructive process may be initiated by primary microbial infection 
(necrotizing pneumonia, tuberculosis, aspergillosis, etc.) or obstruction (foreign body, 
tumour, lymph node, etc.) resulting in stasis and secondary infection.

l Bronchiectasis has an insidious onset with chronic persistent productive cough, 
increasing volume, change of colour of sputum and purulence due to recurrent 
infection.
	
l The next common symptoms are haemoptysis, breathlessness and pleuritic chest 
pain. The patient may present with symptoms due to complication (cor pulmonale 
or respiratory failure) such as swelling of feet, bluish coloration of the skin and 
breathlessness.
	
l Signs such as clubbing of fingers and presence of course, fixed and leathery 
crepitation are the hallmark of the disease.
	
l X-ray chest may be normal or may show tram-track shadows, hyperinflation/air 
trapping and multiple ring-like shadow. Increased TLC count and presence of

secretion
	
l Graded exercise
	
l Routine deep breathing exercises
	
l Maintenance of good nutrition

Monitoring and follow-up
Observe for the improvement in amount and colour of sputum and constitutional 
symptoms. If there is no clinical response and sputum culture report is available, change 
the antibiotic accordingly. If bronchospasm is not relieved by MDI, nebulization should 
be done.
Refer to a higher centre in case of uncontrolled or life-threatening haemoptysis, 
frequent exacerbation, localized disease (for surgery) and presence of complications 
such as respiratory failure or cor pulmonale.
Surgery is indicated in case of uncontrolled haemoptysis and if the disease is localized 
to one lobe. Emergency surgical resection may be necessary for life-threatening 
haemoptysis but embolization of appropriate bronchial artery is usually attempted first.
Long-term mucoactive treatment (≥3 months) is given to adult patients with 
bronchiectasis who have difficulty in expectorating sputum and poor quality of life 
and in whom standard airway clearance techniques have failed to control symptoms. 
Antibiotics may be given for 14 days. If Pseudomonas is isolated, eradication with 
antibiotics is recommended. Prolonged oral or nebulized antibiotics should be 
attempted for recurrent (three or more) exacerbations per year.
Patient education
Emphasize on stopping smoking, annual vaccination against Pneumococcus in high-risk 
cases, prompt treatment of upper respiratory tract infections, physiotherapy and early 
antibiotic treatment if there is change in colour of sputum.

Lung abscess is defined as a localized area of destruction of lung parenchyma 
characterized by suppuration and necrosis, mostly due to bacterial infection. It is classified 
into ‘acute’ or ‘chronic’ based on symptoms’ duration (<4–6 or ≥4–6 weeks, respectively).
Lung abscess is characterized as ‘primary’ when it appears after lung infection 
in a previously healthy person or in patients prone to aspiration of nasopharyngeal 
or oropharyngeal material (e.g. alcoholics, drug addicts), in patients with a reduced 
level of consciousness, comatose patients or after epileptic seizures. Mixed microbial

348    Standard Treatment Guidelines
flora, including anaerobic bacteria and microaerophilic streptococci, are involved 
in the formation of abscesses related to the aspiration of gastric contents. Abscess 
formation may occur secondarily in cases of mechanical bronchial obstruction caused 
by endobronchial mass, a foreign body or extraluminal compression, septic pulmonary 
emboli due to infective endocarditis, contamination of bullae or bronchiectasis.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Clinical findings depend on the nature of the infections. Most cases are due to 
mixed infections, whereas dominant pathogens isolated are anaerobic bacteria 
found in normal oral and upper intestinal microbial flora.
	
l Lung abscesses caused by anaerobic or mixed bacteria present with non-specific 
symptoms and signs, e.g. fever, night sweats, dull chest pain, fatigue, anorexia, 
weight loss and productive cough with foetid sputum or sometimes bloody sputum.
	
l Physical examination includes fever, poor dentition and gingival disease, anaemia, 
clubbing, tachycardia, tachypnoea and abnormal findings consistent with lung 
parenchymal infection, pleural fluid and amphoric or cavernous breath sound on 
auscultation.
	
l Anaemia of chronic disease and leucocytosis are usually present.
	
l Diagnosis is based on radiological findings revealing cavitation with an air–fluid 
level. Typically the cavity wall is thick and irregular, and a surrounding pulmonary 
infiltrate is often present. Documenting anaerobic infection is usually difficult.
	
l Computed tomography (CT) is more sensitive than chest radiography, as it is 
useful to detect small cavities, provide evidence for obstructing endobronchial 
lesions and again distinguish lung abscess from hydropneumothorax.
	
l Although there is frequent contamination by normal respiratory flora, but sputum 
cultures have been proven to be useful in diagnosing lung abscesses caused by 
aerobic pathogens such as Klebsiella, Staphylococcus and Pseudomonas.
	
l Fibreoptic bronchoscopy with quantitative cultures of samples obtained by 
protected specimen brush or broncho-alveolar lavage (BAL) or transthoracic 
needle aspiration is usually required for targeted antimicrobial treatment.

1.	Avoid procedures such as nasogastric feeding tube, sedation, lying flat on the bed 
while sleeping, reflux and frequent choking. 
	 2.	Measures such as semi-recumbent or upright position, reduction of stomach volume 
with suction or metoclopramide, neutralization of gastric acid with H2 blockers 
and antacids should be taken. 
	 3.	Chest physiotherapy for drainage of pus.
	 4.	Empirical therapy with broad-spectrum antibiotics followed by antibiotics as per 
microbiological documentation by cultures.
	
	Inj. Clindamycin 600 mg intravenous every 8 hours followed by 150–300 mg 
6 hourly orally.

	Or 
	
	Inj. Amoxicillin–Clavulanate Or Ampicillin–Sulbactam Or Piperacillin + 
Tazobactam combined with Metronidazole. 
	
	Note: Avoid monotherapy with Metronidazole due to inadequate coverage for 
aerobic and microaerophilic streptococci.
	
	In MRSA, give Inj. Linezolid 600 mg IV twice daily followed by oral administration 
after clinical improvement Or Inj. Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV twice daily. 
Monitoring and follow-up
	
l The appropriate duration is minimum of 2–3 weeks of antibiotic therapy depending 
on the clinical and radiographic response of the patient. Treat the patient at least 
until fever, putrid sputum and abscess fluid have resolved. Treatment interval may 
be prolonged to several months (>2 months), especially when the initial lesion is of 
a large size (maximum diameter >6 cm).	
	
l Refer the patient to a tertiary care centre in case of persistence of bacteraemia or high-
grade fever after 72 hours, haemoptysis (moderate/massive), absence of change in 
sputum production/character or changes in the radiographic images over 7–10 days for 
bronchoscopy, CT-guided percutaneous drainage or cardiothoracic surgical intervention.
	
l Surgical resection of necrotic segments of the lung is helpful if the response to 
antibiotic is poor, for large abscesses or ventilation–perfusion scans suggesting little 
residual lung function and airway obstruction limiting drainage.
	
l Consider the possibility of malignancy or unusual microorganisms in case of slow 
resolution. Investigate a thick-walled lung abscess to rule out malignancy.
Patient education
	
l The symptoms of a lung abscess are similar to the symptoms of other lung conditions 
including pneumonia and tuberculosis. The most noticeable symptom of a lung 
abscess is productive cough, which may be bloody or pus-like with a foul odour.
	
l Most lung abscess can be treated with a course of antibiotics. Chronic abscess or 
untreated abscess could lead to fatal complications (e.g. empyema, pneumatocele, 
bronchopleural fistula).
	
l Alcoholism, compromised immune system, malignancy, HIV and autoimmune 
diseases are common predisposing factors.

PLEURAL EFFUSION
A pleural effusion is an abnormal amount of fluid around the lung. Pleural effusions 
can result from many medical conditions.

350    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Dyspnoea, dry and non-productive cough, fever, pleuritic chest pain, decreased 
or absent breath sounds, dullness on percussion, and stony dull, decreased vocal 
resonance.
	
l Elevated white cell count and/or C-reactive protein (CRP) and blood culture are 
performed. Diagnosis is confirmed by chest X-ray and diagnostic thoracocentesis 
(20–50 mL of pleural fluid). Types of pleural fluid are exudates and transudates.
	
l Exudates have at least one and transudates have none of the following criteria:
	
i.	 Pleural fluid/total serum protein ratio >0.5
	
ii.	 Pleural fluid/serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) ratio >0.6
	 iii.	 Pleural fluid LDH >2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH 
	– Transudate: Congestive cardiac failure, cirrhosis of the liver, nephrotic 
syndrome, myxoedema, peritoneal dialysis, hypoproteinaemia, atelectasis
	– Exudates: Infectious diseases – tuberculosis, other bacterial, viral, fungal, 
parasitic; malignant diseases – bronchogenic carcinoma; metastatic disease 
(mesothelioma, lymphomas), pulmonary embolism, rheumatoid arthritis, 
systemic lupus erythematosus; gastrointestinal disease – oesophageal 
perforation; pancreatic disease – amoebic liver abscess, uraemia, 
chylothorax, haemothorax, traumatic; drug-induced – Nitrofurantoin, 
Dantrolene, Amiodarone, Methotrexate, etc.
	
l In tubercular pleural effusion, pleural fluid is straw-coloured effusion with 
lymphocyte predominance, protein >3 g/dL (exudative), and adenosine deaminase 
(ADA) level >40 units/L. 
	
l Ultrasound chest may be done to detect small amounts of fluids, loculation and 
septation. Percutaneous pleural biopsy is done if malignancy or tuberculosis is 
suspected and in case of undiagnosed exudative pleural effusion.

l Treatment is based on the underlying condition (tuberculosis/heart failure/nephritic 
syndrome/liver cirrhosis). (See respective sections for details.)
	
l For large pleural effusion causing breathlessness, perform therapeutic thoracocentesis. 
Not more than 1 L of pleural fluid should be removed to prevent post-thoracocentesis 
shock and re-expansion pulmonary oedema in one sitting. Stop the procedure if the 
patient develops cough or chest pain. (Caution: Complications can include pain, 
pneumothorax, haemorrhage and subcutaneous emphysema (do check X-ray after the 
procedure and be prepared to manage any complications that may arise.)
For para-pneumonic effusion
	 1.	Give appropriate antibiotics where possible. Antibiotic choice should be guided 
by bacterial culture results and sensitivity. Penicillins, penicillins combined with 
b-lactamase inhibitors, metronidazole and cephalosporins penetrate the pleural 
space well.

	Note: Avoid aminoglycosides; intrapleural antibiotics are not recommended. 
Switch to oral therapy once there is clinical and objective evidence of improvement 
in sepsis. Prolonged courses of antibiotics may be necessary and can often be 
administered as an outpatient after discharge.
	
		
In case of poor clinical progress during treatment with antibiotics alone, promptly 
review and perform repeat pleural fluid sampling and probably chest tube drainage.
	 2.	Urgent drainage of para-pneumonic effusions is done if frankly purulent fluid, a 
pleural fluid pH of less than 7.2, loculated effusions, and bacteria on Gram stain 
or culture are seen. Chest tube should be removed when pleural fluid drainage is 
less than 50 mL for 24 hours and draining fluid becomes clear yellow. 
	
	(Caution: Complications of chest tube drainage are pain, pneumothorax, 
haemorrhage and subcutaneous emphysema.)
	 3.	In case there is no clinical or radiological improvement with declining pleural fluid 
drainage, perform a pleural space ultrasound examination or chest CT scan to look 
for pleural fluid loculations and ensure proper tube placement. 
	
	Note: Drainage failure is a consequence of misplacement of the chest tube, tube 
malfunction and loculations.
Monitoring and follow-up
	
l All patients with empyema and pleural infection require outpatient follow-up with a 
repeat chest X-ray and inflammatory markers within 4 weeks following discharge and 
continued outpatient care may be required for several months depending on progress.
	
l Early referral to a thoracic surgeon is done in patients with pleural effusions that 
are uncontrollable, failure of chest tube drainage and antibiotics. Refer to a higher 
centre in case of pleural effusion recurrence due to a malignancy despite drainage; 
refer for pleural sclerosis with instillation of a sclerosing agent occasionally into the 
pleural cavity through a tube thoracostomy or surgery.
Patient education
	
l The long-term survival of patients with pleural infection is good if prompt treatment 
is initiated.
	
l Advise patients to return for prompt medical attention if recurrent symptoms develop 
since late relapse of pleural infection is well recognized.
	
l Advise patients with pleural infection to take adequate nutrition.

PNEUMOTHORAX
Pneumothorax is the presence of air in the pleural cavity resulting in collapse of a part 
of or the whole lung. A primary pneumothorax occurs without an apparent cause and 
in the absence of significant lung disease, while a secondary pneumothorax occurs in 
the presence of existing lung pathology. Tension pneumothorax develops occasionally 
and is a medical emergency. Unless reversed by effective treatment, these sequelae 
can progress and cause death. Catamenial pneumothorax is a rare condition in which 
women experience pneumothorax at the onset of menstrual period. 
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The major symptoms of a spontaneous pneumothorax are the sudden onset of 
chest pain and/or shortness of breath. The pain may be either dull or sharp or 
stabbing. It begins suddenly and is worsened by breathing deeply or coughing. 
	
l On examination, hyper-resonant percussion note and absent or reduced breath 
sounds are seen. 
	
l The most accurate diagnostic test is a chest X-ray, which will show air collected 
around the outside surface of the lung.

1.	First-line treatment of pneumothoraces depends on a combination of clinical 
features and size/type of pneumothorax. It may include observation with 
supplemental oxygen therapy, percutaneous aspiration of the air in the pleural 
space, insertion of a chest drain and, in some patients, video-assisted thoracoscopy 
(VATS) or thoracostomy.
	 2.	In patients who have no significant underlying lung disease, a small spontaneous 
pneumothorax resolves without treatment and these patients require only 
monitoring. Patients with a small primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) 
without breathlessness may be discharged with early outpatient review along with 
clear written advice to return in the event of worsening breathlessness.
	 3.	In tension pneumothorax and in larger pneumothorax, or when there are marked 
symptoms, urgent needle decompression followed by a chest tube connected to 
a one-way valve system is required. Needle decompression is required before 
transport to the hospital, and can be performed by an emergency medical technician 
or other trained professional. The needle or cannula is left in place until a chest 
tube can be inserted.
	 4.	Occasionally, surgical intervention involving pleurodesis or pleurectomy is required 
when tube drainage is unsuccessful or as a preventive measure in case of repeated 
episodes.
Patient education
	
l Advise the patient to return to the hospital if increasing breathlessness develops. 
	
l All patients should be followed up by respiratory physicians until full resolution.

Chapter 5  Respiratory Diseases    353
	
l Air travel should be avoided until full resolution.
	
l Diving should be permanently avoided unless the patient has undergone bilateral 
surgical pleurectomy and has normal lung function and chest CT scan postoperatively.
