INFLUENZA-LIKE ILLNESS (ILI)/SEVERE ACUTE 
RESPIRATORY INFECTION (SARI)/COVID-19
SARIs are most often viral infections that cause flu-like symptoms (first reported in 
2003) causing substantial mortality and morbidity. SARI is associated with a large 
number of different viral agents, notably influenza A and B viruses, parainfluenza 
viruses, coronavirus, respiratory syncytial viruses (RSV), metapneumovirus, 
adenoviruses (AV) and rhinoviruses. Influenza, in particular, is a very common and 
sometimes a serious infection with an epidemiological picture marked by seasonal 
peaks in winter months. Three-quarters of the infection is asymptomatic and 
complications are more severe among well-recognized high-risk groups. Antigenic drift 
and shift in the viruses potentiate local and regional outbreaks and global pandemics 
(recently COVID-19) mostly due to travel from affected countries.
Rarely, animal coronavirus can evolve and infect people and then spread between 
people as seen with Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS) and severe acute 
respiratory syndrome (SARS). All viruses, including SARS-CoV-2, change over time. 
Variants of SARS-CoV-2 may result in changes in transmissibility, clinical presentation 
and severity.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The case definitions for influenza-like illness (ILI) and severe acute respiratory 
infection (SARI) are not necessarily intended to capture all cases but to describe 
trends over time.
	
l ILI case definition: It is an acute respiratory infection (ARI) with measured fever 
of >38°C and cough, with onset within the last 10 days.

Epidemiological criteria
	
l Residing or working or travelling to or working in any health care setting in 
an area with a high risk of transmission of virus any time within 14 days prior 
to symptom onset
	
l SARI case definition: An ARI with history of fever or measured temperature 
≥38°C and cough; onset within the last ~10 days; and requiring hospitalization
B.	SARI may present with mild, moderate or severe illness; the latter includes severe 
pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), sepsis and septic shock 
(Table 5.4).
Probable case
A.	A patient who meets clinical criteria above AND is a contact of a probable or 
confirmed case, or linked to a COVID-19 cluster
B.	A suspect case with chest imaging showing findings suggestive of COVID-19 disease
C.	A person with recent onset of anosmia (loss of smell) or ageusia (loss of taste) in 
the absence of any other identified cause
D.	Death, not otherwise explained, in an adult with respiratory distress preceding 
death AND was a contact of a probable or confirmed case or linked to a COVID-
case cluster
Confirmed case
A.	A person with a positive nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) including RT-
PCR or any other similar test approved by the ICMR.
B.	A person with a positive SARS-CoV-2 antigen-RDT AND meeting either the 
probable case definition or the suspect criteria OR
C.	An asymptomatic person with a positive SARS-CoV-2 antigen-RDT who is a 
contact of a probable or confirmed case
	
l Asymptomatic person not meeting epidemiological criteria with a positive SARS-
CoV-2 antigen-RDT2 (to be confirmed with NAAT).
	
l Additional neurological manifestations reported include dizziness, agitation, 
weakness, seizures, or findings suggestive of stroke including trouble with speech 
or vision, sensory loss or problems with balance in standing or walking. Older 
people and immunosuppressed patients in particular may present with atypical 
symptoms such as fatigue, reduced alertness, reduced mobility, diarrhoea, loss of 
appetite, confusion and absence of fever.
	
l Routine investigations including haematological, biochemical, radiological and 
microbiological tests as necessary. Biomarkers associated with COVID-19 severity 
might be useful in estimating severity and predicting prognosis. Hyperinflammation 
plays an important role in COVID-19 disease progression, and an inflammatory 
cytokine storm can increase the severity. (For details, see Appendix X.)
	
l Dual infections with other respiratory infections (viral, bacterial and fungal) have 
been found in patients with COVID-19; test as appropriate. Blood cultures, when 
required, shall be collected before initiation of antimicrobial therapy to rule out 
bacterial causes of pneumonia and sepsis.

l COVID screening for all patients with diagnosed TB and TB screening for all 
patients with COVID, ILI and SARI should be conducted. 
	
l Maintain a high index of suspicion for prevalent epidemic prone diseases and 
clinical presentation (e.g. dengue, malaria, chikungunya, seasonal influenza, 
leptospirosis, scrub typhus) particularly during the rainy and post-rainy season.
	
l The clinical features of both COVID-19 and dengue are overlapping. Figure 5.5 
and Table 5.5 depict the salient features of common infections and COVID and 
diagnostic methods.
	
l Collection of sample for SARS-CoV-2: Collect following samples using 
appropriate PPE for specimen collection (droplet, airborne and contact 
precautions for upper respiratory tract [URT] specimens; airborne precautions 
using full PPE for lower respiratory tract [LRT] specimens) for NAAT. If NAAT 
is unavailable or has a prolonged turnaround time, antigen testing should be 
considered for LRT samples, especially in situations in which these samples are 
readily accessible, such as in mechanically ventilated patients. Avoid sputum 
induction owing to increased risk of aerosol transmission. A single negative URT 
sample does not exclude the diagnosis, and additional URT and LRT samples 
should be collected. Collect paired serum sample in case repetitive negative 
NAAT/RT-PCR results are present. One specimen is taken in the acute phase 
and one in the convalescent phase 2–4 weeks later. SARS-CoV-2 antibody 
tests are not recommended for diagnosis of current infection with COVID-19. 
In hospitalized patients with confirmed COVID-19, repeated samples can 
be collected, as clinically indicated, but are not indicated for release from 
COVID-19 precautions.

The guiding principles of treatment are:
	 I.	Screening and triage is done at the first point of contact in a health facility for early 
recognition of suspected patients with COVID-19 and rapid implementation of 
source control measures (Table 5.6).
	 II.	Early identification of those with severe manifestations (Table 5.4) is done 
for immediate optimized supportive care treatments and safe, rapid admission 
(or referral) to intensive care unit (Fig. 5.6 for adults and Figs. 5.7 and 5.8 for 
children). After initial assessment, management and stabilization, refer the patient 
to appropriate COVID-19 care destination: within the health facility (critical care 
unit or ward); to a different health facility; community facility; or home, according 
to the patient’s medical needs and established COVID-19 care pathways.
	
		
For those with mild and moderate illness, hospitalization may not be required 
unless there is concern for rapid deterioration. However, isolation is necessary for all 
suspect or confirmed cases to contain virus transmission. Counsel patients with mild 
COVID-19 about signs and symptoms of complications (such as light-headedness, 
difficulty breathing, chest pain and dehydration) that should prompt urgent care.

Sepsis
Adults: Acute life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to suspected or 
proven infection, with organ dysfunction.
Signs of organ dysfunction include altered mental status, difficult or fast breathing, low oxygen saturation, 
reduced urine output, fast heart rate, weak pulse, cold extremities or low blood pressure, skin mottling, or 
laboratory evidence of coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, acidosis, high lactate or hyperbilirubinaemia.
A change of 2 in sequential organ failure assessment score (SOFA) score is used to define organ 
dysfunction.
Children: Suspected or proven infection and ≥2 age-based SIRS criteria, of which one must be 
abnormal temperature or white blood cell count.
Septic shock
Adults: Persisting hypotension despite volume resuscitation, requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 
mmHg and serum lactate level >2 mmol/L. 
Children: Any hypotension (SBP <5th centile or >2 SD below normal for age) or two to three of the 
following: altered mental state; tachycardia or bradycardia (HR <90 or >160 bpm in infants and HR <70 
or >150 bpm in children); prolonged capillary refill (>2 s) or warm vasodilation with bounding pulses; 
tachypnoea; mottled skin or petechial or purpuric rash; increased lactate; oliguria; hyperthermia or 
hypothermia.

(prevention dose adjusted for weight).
Use of steroids
•	 Systemic corticosteroids recommended in patients with severe and critical COVID-19 when SpO2 falls 
below 92%. The timing of initiation of systemic corticosteroids is important. Steroid initiation 7 days or more 
after symptom onset may be more beneficial than treatment initiated within 7 days of treatment onset. 
Systemic corticosteroids can be administered both orally and intravenously. Administer intravenously in 
critically-ill patients who are unable to absorb any nutrients or medications due to intestinal dysfunction. 
The once daily dexamethasone formulation may increase adherence. A dose of 6 mg of dexamethasone is 
equivalent (in terms of glucocorticoid effect) to 32 mg of methylprednisolone (8 mg every 6 hours or 16 mg 
every 12 hours) or 40 mg of prednisone, or 150 mg of hydrocortisone (50 mg every 8 hours). Monitor 
glucose levels in patients with severe and critical COVID-19, regardless of the diabetic status of the patient 
(for details see Chapter 11).
Updated risk rate for hospital admission
•	 Updated risk rates for hospital admission in non-severe COVID reflect the current trends of COVID-19 virus 
variants causing less severe disease and heightened immunity due to vaccination. This results in lower 
risks of severe illness and death for most patients:
	 –	 High risk (6% hospitalization rate): Individuals who are immunosuppressed remain at a higher risk if 
they contract COVID-19.
	 –	 Moderate risk (3% hospitalization rate): This category includes people older than 65 years; individuals 
with conditions like obesity, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, kidney or liver disease, 
cancer; people with disabilities; and those with comorbidities of chronic disease.
	 –	 Low risk (0.5% hospitalization rate): Individuals not falling into the high- or moderate-risk categories 
are considered to be at low risk of hospitalization, with most people falling into this category.
	 	 The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends nirmatrelvir–ritonavir for individuals at high and 
moderate risk of hospitalization. In cases where nirmatrelvir–ritonavir is not available for high-risk 
patients, molnupiravir or remdesivir can be considered as an alternative.
•	 Tocilizumab (off-label) to be used ONLY in severe and critically-ill patients meeting following criteria:
	 – Moderate to severe disease
	 – Significantly raised inflammatory markers (CRP ≥75 mg/L)
	 – Not improving in terms of oxygen requirement even after 24–48 hours of administration of steroids
	 – Rule out active bacterial/fungal/tuberculous infection at the time of administration of Tocilizumab. The 
recommended dose is single dose of 8 mg/kg (with a maximum dose of 800 mg) in 100 mL NS over 
1 hour. 
•	 Ivermectin is advised only in the context of clinical trials for severe or critical patients with COVID-19.

	1.	Give supplemental oxygen therapy immediately to any patient with emergency 
signs during resuscitation to target SpO2 ≥94% and to any patient without 
emergency signs and hypoxaemia (i.e. stable patient with hypoxaemia) to target 
SpO2 >90% or ≥92–95% in pregnant women.
	 	In children with emergency signs (obstructed or absent breathing, severe 
respiratory distress, central cyanosis, shock, coma or convulsions), oxygen 
therapy is performed during resuscitation to target SpO2 ≥94%.
	 	Use precautions when handling contaminated oxygen interfaces of patients with 
infection (Appendix II).
	2.	Use conservative fluid management in patients with SARI when there is no 
evidence of shock and treat cautiously with intravenous fluids, as aggressive 
fluid resuscitation may worsen oxygenation, especially in settings in which 
there is limited availability of mechanical ventilation.
	3.	Antibiotic therapy or prophylaxis should NOT be used in patients with mild or 
moderate COVID-19 unless signs and symptoms of a bacterial infection exist. 
Obtain sputum and blood culture samples as well as pneumococcal urinary 
antigen testing before starting antibiotics. Stop antibiotics in patients who were 
started on antibiotic treatment on admission when representative cultures as well 
as urinary antigen tests show no signs of involvement of bacterial pathogens 
after 48 hours. For patients with secondary bacterial respiratory infection, 
follow respective guidelines for sepsis and hospital-acquired and ventilator-
associated pneumonia.
	 	Note: High CRP levels do not necessarily indicate that the pneumonia is due to 
bacteria; rather, they indicate COVID-19 inflammatory response; CBC could 
be high because of high-dose steroids.
	4.	Tailor management according to comorbid condition(s) and the patient’s clinical 
presenting symptoms (see Chapter 6 for GI symptoms and Chapter 9 for stroke), 
especially diabetes (see Chapter 11 for management of diabetes in COVID-19). 
Continue or modify previous medical therapy according to the patient’s clinical 
condition. Do not stop antihypertensive medicines routinely. Continue ARB or 
ACEI if the patient is on these medicines except when there are other reasons to stop 
these (e.g. hyperkalaemia, hypotension or acute deterioration in renal function).
	 	For details of management of suspected or confirmed COVID in pregnancy see 
Chapter 15.
	5.	Communicate early and proactively with the patient and family and provide 
support and prognostic information. Understand the patient’s values and 
preferences regarding life-sustaining interventions.
	
V.	 Manage hypoxaemic respiratory failure and ARDS despite standard oxygen 
therapy delivered via a face mask with reservoir bag (flow rates of 10–15 L/min, 
to maintain minimum FiO2 0.60–0.95). Hypoxaemic respiratory failure in ARDS 
commonly results from intrapulmonary ventilation–perfusion mismatch or shunt 
and usually requires mechanical ventilation.
	 VI.	 Management of septic shock (see details in Chapter 2).

368    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	VII.	 Monitor patients with COVID-19 for signs or symptoms suggestive of 
thromboembolism, such as stroke, deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary 
embolism or acute coronary syndrome. If these are clinically suspected, proceed 
immediately with appropriate diagnostic and management pathways.
	VIII.	 Evaluate patients presenting with rapidly developing neurological symptoms 
suggestive of stroke as soon as possible and standard stroke protocols should be 
followed including systemic thrombolysis and/or intra-arterial thrombectomy, 
if indicated. Signs and symptoms of stroke can include weakness of limbs or 
face, sensory loss, speech difficulties, impairment of vision, ataxia, confusion 
or decreased consciousness. (For details, see Chapter 9.)
	 IX.	 Implement interventions (Table 5.7) to prevent complications associated with 
critical illness.
	
X.	 There is no specific anti-SARS-CoV-2 treatment for patients with suspected or 
confirmed SARS-CoV at present. Unlicensed treatments should be administered 
only in the context of ethically approved clinical trials or the Monitored Emergency 
Use of Unregistered Interventions Framework (MEURI), with strict monitoring.
	 XI.	 Manage any underlying cause of delirium by monitoring oxygenation and fluid 
status, correcting metabolic or endocrine abnormalities, addressing coinfections, 
minimizing the use of medications that may cause or worsen delirium and 
maintaining normal sleep cycles as much as possible. 
	
1.	 In patients receiving invasive ventilation, minimize continuous or intermittent 
sedation, targeting specific titration endpoints (light sedation unless 
contraindicated) or with daily interruption of continuous sedative infusions, 
to reduce delirium. 
	
2.	 Use calming communication strategies and reorient the patients experiencing 
agitation (marked restlessness or excessive motor activity, often accompanied 
by anxiety). Use minimum effective doses of antipsychotic medications at the 
lowest frequency and for the shortest duration possible, with doses adjusted 
according to age, medical comorbidities and degree of distress. Lorazepam 
can be added in the lowest dose and for the shortest duration in severely 
agitated patients. (For details, see Chapter 15.)
	 XII.	 In case of new anxiety and depressive symptoms, promptly identify and 
assess for anxiety and depressive symptoms and initiate psychosocial support 
strategies and first-line interventions, for their management. 
	
	 	
In case of sleep problems, advice sleep hygiene (including avoiding the 
use of psychostimulants such as caffeine, nicotine or alcohol) and stress 
management (including relaxation techniques and mindfulness practices). (For 
details, see Chapter 15.)
	 XIII.	 Discharge on clinical resolution taking into account the patient’s condition, 
disease experience and other factors. RT-PCR (after resolution of symptoms) 
testing is not required for discharge or release from home isolation.

370    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 XIV.	 At the time of discharge, counsel all patients (and their caregivers) to monitor 
for resolution of signs and symptoms and to seek care if any one or more of 
these persist, or the patient develops a new or changing symptom, including 
acute life-threatening complications, such as pulmonary embolism, myocardial 
infarction, dysrhythmias, myopericarditis and heart failure, stroke, seizures 
and encephalitis for which they should seek emergency care. Screen for

Dengue co-infection with COVID
Clinical presentation of dengue and COVID overlaps. In case of dengue without 
warning signs, Salicylates and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) 
should be avoided as these may predispose to mucosal bleeds. Both COVID-19 
and dengue infection are accompanied by coagulopathy and vasculopathy with 
coagulopathy being predominant in the former, leading to the use of low-molecular-
weight heparin (LMWH) in moderate to severe COVID-19 cases. Follow national 
guidelines for clinical management of dengue fever for most co-infection cases.
	
l Monitor closely fluid status in dengue co-infection depending on haemodynamic 
status of the patient and degree of severity. Monitor the patient for warning signs, 
along with haematocrit and platelet counts, hospitalize patients with warning 
signs and give intravenous fluids (crystalloids – Ringer’s lactate or normal 
saline infusion – are preferred). For details, see Chapter 1. In the presence of 
COVID-19, be careful with aggressive fluid administration as it leads to worsening 
of oxygenation. Aggressive fluid resuscitation is recommended for patients with 
COVID-19 in shock for initial resuscitation. 
	
l Use LMWH carefully when platelet count decreases to less than 1 lakh, withhold 
LMWH based on clinical condition of the patient and perform close monitoring with 
D-dimer. In case of co-infection with active bleeding, stop LMWH immediately.
	
l Use of corticosteroids: Give dexamethasone as per COVID-19 management 
guidelines after dengue viraemic stage, i.e. 5/6 days of dengue illness. Tocilizumab, 
antivirals and other supportive management to be used as per national management 
guidelines for COVID-19 management.

Clinical specimens: Nasopharyngeal swab, throat swab, nasal swab, wash or

COVID-19-ASSOCIATED MUCORMYCOSIS (CAM)
Mucormycosis, a fungal infection, is known to occur in patients with low immunity such 
as those with diabetes, post-transplant and those with cancer. Mucormycosis, if uncared 
for, may turn fatal. A sudden surge has been observed in COVID-19 pandemic and is a 
notifiable disease under the Epidemic Diseases Act (1897). Suspect mucormycosis in 
patients with COVID-19, patients with diabetes or immunosuppressed individuals. It 
may occur during COVID-19 infection or a few weeks after recovery from COVID-19.
SALIENT FEATURES
In patients with COVID-19 illness (active/recovering/post-discharge), the common 
presentation is rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis (ROCM) as follows:
	
l Initially – nasal blockade or congestion, nasal discharge (bloody or brown/black), 
local pain, one-sided facial pain or numbness or swelling, headache, orbital pain, 
toothache, loosening of maxillary teeth, jaw involvement 
	
l Blurred or double vision with pain, paraesthesia, fever, skin lesion, thrombosis 
and necrosis (eschar)

Chapter 5  Respiratory Diseases    375
	
l Pulmonary mucormycosis: Fever, cough, chest pain, pleural effusion, 
haemoptysis, worsening of respiratory symptoms
	
l Laboratory testing: CBC/ESR/FBS, PPBS, HbA1C/LFT/RFT with electrolytes/
HIV, HbsAg/CSF (if indicated).
	
l Suspected patients should undergo appropriate radio-imaging study: MRI – PNS 
with brain contrast study for ROCM, plain CT thorax for pulmonary mucormycosis
	
l Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis: Consult ENT surgeon for endoscopic 
collection of debrided tissue/biopsy – KOH mount and microscopy, 
histopathology of debrided tissue (presence of ribbon-like aseptate hyphae 5–15 
µm thick that branch at right angles). Do not wait for culture results to initiate 
therapy as mucormycosis is an emergency.
	
l Pulmonary mucormycosis: Perform broncho-alveolar lavage (BAL); mini BAL; 
non-bronchoscopic lavage; transbronchial biopsy; CT-guided biopsy from the lung 
– process for microscopy and culture; chest X-ray and/or HRCT – reverse halo sign, 
thick-walled cavity (differentiate from COVID-associated pulmonary aspergillosis), 
multiple nodules, pleural effusion; galactomannan and beta-d-glucan tests.

Mucormycosis is a medical emergency; maintain a high index of suspicion. Timely 
initiation of treatment reduces mortality. Multidisciplinary team approach is required 
with infectious disease specialist, microbiologist, histopathologist, intensivist, ENT 
specialist, ophthalmologist, neurologist, dentist, surgeons (maxillofacial/plastic), 
radiologists, etc. See Figure 5.9 for the management of mucormycosis.

DYSPEPSIA
Dyspepsia is a common symptom with an extensive differential diagnosis and a 
heterogeneous pathophysiology. It is a syndrome of chronic or recurrent abdominal 
pain or discomfort in the upper abdomen with bloating, anorexia, early satiety, 
belching or regurgitation, nausea and heartburn. The symptoms of dyspepsia overlap 
significantly with those associated with peptic ulcer disease (PUD), gastro-oesophageal 
reflux disease (GERD), other functional disorders such as epigastric pain syndrome 
and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), malignancy, adverse effects of medications, 
pancreatitis, biliary tract disease, vascular disease and motility disorders.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Dyspepsia according to Rome IV criteria is defined as one or more of the 
following conditions: (i) post-prandial fullness, (ii) early satiety and inability 
to finish a normal-sized meal, and (iii) epigastric pain or burning which is 
unexplained after routine clinical evaluation. It may be organic due to acid peptic 
disorders, upper gastrointestinal (GI) malignancy, pancreatitis, gastroparesis, 
diabetes, hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, medications (non-steroidal anti-
inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs]) or functional.

Chapter 6  Gastrointestinal Diseases    381
	
l Physical examination reveals epigastric tenderness on muscle tensing (Carnett’s 
sign). Functional dyspepsia is classified as ‘ulcer-like dyspepsia’ (upper 
abdominal pain related to food intake), ‘dysmotility type’ (nausea, vomiting, 
belching, early satiety, bloating) or ‘non-specific dyspepsia’. Functional dyspepsia 
requires exclusion of other organic causes of dyspepsia. Approximately 20–25% 
of patients with dyspepsia have an underlying organic cause. However, up to 
75–80% of patients have functional dyspepsia with no underlying cause on 
diagnostic evaluation.

The goal is to identify alarm features and rule out organic dyspepsia by history and

following indications:

GASTRO-OESOPHAGEAL REFLUX DISEASE (GERD)
Some degree of reflux is physiological. Physiological reflux episodes typically 
occur post-prandially, are short-lived, asymptomatic and rarely occur during sleep. 
Pathological reflux is associated with symptoms or mucosal injury and often occurs 
nocturnally.
GERD is a condition that develops when the reflux of stomach contents causes 
troublesome symptoms and/or complications. The spectrum of clinical presentations 
of GERD ranges from typical oesophageal symptoms of heartburn and regurgitation to 
an assortment of extraoesophageal manifestations including respiratory and laryngeal 
symptoms. GERD can be classified relative to the presence or absence of erosions; 
GERD symptoms without erosions on endoscopic examination constitute non-erosive 
reflux disease (NERD), whereas GERD symptoms with erosions constitute erosive 
oesophagitis. Dyspepsia is a chronic or recurrent pain or discomfort centred in the upper 
abdomen; patients with predominant or frequent (more than once a week) heartburn or 
acid regurgitation should be considered to have GERD until proven otherwise.

384    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Classic symptoms of GERD are heartburn (pyrosis) and regurgitation. Other 
symptoms of GERD include dysphagia, chest pain, water brash, globus sensation, 
odynophagia, extra-oesophageal symptoms (e.g. chronic cough, hoarseness, 
wheezing) and, infrequently, nausea.
	
l The diagnosis of GERD can often be based on clinical symptoms alone in patients 
with classic symptoms such as heartburn and/or regurgitation.
	
l In patients without classic symptoms, other disorders need to be excluded before 
attributing the symptoms to GERD. As an example, unexplained chest pain should be 
evaluated with an electrocardiogram and exercise stress test prior to a GI evaluation.
	
l Upper endoscopy is indicated in patients with suspected GERD to evaluate alarm 
features (new onset of dyspepsia in a patient aged ≥60 years, evidence of GI bleeding 
[haematemesis, melaena, haematochezia, occult blood in stool], iron-deficiency 
anaemia, anorexia, unexplained weight loss, dysphagia, odynophagia, persistent 
vomiting, GI cancer in a first-degree relative) or abnormal imaging.
	
l In patients with suspected GERD with chest pain and/or dysphagia and a normal 
upper endoscopy, an oesophageal manometry should be performed to exclude an 
oesophageal motility disorder.
	
l Ambulatory pH monitoring can be used to confirm the diagnosis of GERD in those 
with persistent symptoms (whether typical or atypical, particularly if a trial of twice-
daily PPI has failed) or to monitor the adequacy of treatment in those with continued 
symptoms.

l The core principles of GERD management are lifestyle interventions, reduction of 
oesophageal luminal acid either by local acid neutralization or by suppression of 
gastric acid secretion using medical treatment, or, rarely, antireflux surgery.
	
l Identify alarm features and rule out organic causes by history and upper GI 
endoscopic examination in case of one or more alarm features. 
	
l The primary goals of treatment are to relieve symptoms, improve the patient’s 
health-related quality of life, heal oesophagitis, prevent symptom recurrence and 
prevent or treat GERD-associated complications in the most cost-effective manner. 
	
l The management of GERD follows a stepwise approach.

l ‘Lifestyle modification’ like weight reduction if obese, elimination of fatty foods 
and avoiding alcohol, smoking and excessive consumption of tea/coffee, chocolate, 
citrus juice, etc; patients with post-prandial symptoms to take small, frequent meals 
and avoid large meals
	
l Elevation of head end of the bed and early dinner (2–3 hours before sleep) in patients 
with nocturnal GERD

Follow-up of patients on PPIs.
	
l If relief is obtained, taper down to a lower dose that controls the patient’s symptoms. 
If there is no relief, perform upper endoscopy with biopsies, if not done earlier.

386    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l In patients requiring long-term therapy (erosive oesophagitis and Barrett’s 
oesophagus), PPIs should be administered in the lowest effective dose, including 
on-demand or intermittent therapy. (Caution: Avoid PPI overuse. Long-term 
therapy with PPIs increases the risk of hypergastrinaemia, pneumonia, Clostridium

to a higher centre. Refractory heartburn is defined as symptoms of reflux of gastric 
content that do not respond to a double dose of a PPI given for at least 8 weeks.

before undergoing any tests such as aspirin/NSAIDs, iron, potassium, quinidine,

PEPTIC ULCER
Peptic ulcer is an acid–pepsin–related ulceration of mucosa of the stomach and 
duodenum. The two most common types of peptic ulcer are called ‘gastric ulcers’ and 
‘duodenal ulcers’. The most common causes of PUD are H. pylori infection and use 
of NSAIDs. A peptic ulcer is a defect in the gastric or duodenal mucosa that extends 
through the muscularis mucosa into the deeper layers of the wall. Peptic ulcers may 
present with dyspeptic or other GI symptoms or may be initially asymptomatic and then 
present with complications such as haemorrhage or perforation.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Approximately two-thirds of peptic ulcers are asymptomatic. Patients with 
silent peptic ulcers may later present with ulcer-related complications such as 
haemorrhage or perforation. Most patients with bleeding peptic ulcers present 
without antecedent dyspepsia or other heralding GI symptoms. Older adults and 
individuals on NSAIDs are more likely to be asymptomatic from their ulcers and 
later present with ulcer complications.
	
l Upper abdominal pain or discomfort is the most prominent symptom in patients 
with peptic ulcers. The ‘classic’ pain of duodenal ulcers occurs 2–5 hours after a 
meal when acid is secreted in the absence of a food buffer, and at night (between 
about 11 PM and 2 AM) when the circadian pattern of acid secretion is maximal. 
Patients with peptic ulcers, and particularly pyloric channel ulcers, may have 
food-provoked symptoms (epigastric pain that worsens with eating, post-prandial 
belching and epigastric fullness, early satiety, fatty food intolerance, nausea and 
occasional vomiting) due to visceral sensitization and gastroduodenal dysmotility. 
Symptoms are recurrent and periodic. 
	
l Complications include upper GI bleed, perforation and gastric outlet obstruction. 
A total of 95% of duodenal ulcers and 60% of gastric ulcers are related to H. 
pylori infection and remaining related to NSAID intake. 
	
l The diagnosis of peptic ulcer disease is suspected in patients with dyspepsia, 
especially in patients on NSAID or with a history of H. pylori infection. H. pylori 
infection may be diagnosed by non-invasive urea breath test or stool antigen 
assay. Occasionally, peptic ulcers may be diagnosed or suspected based on 
contrast imaging performed for evaluation of abdominal pain. The diagnosis of 
peptic ulcer disease is definitively established by direct visualization of the ulcer 
on upper endoscopy. Figure 6.1 depicts the approach to diagnosis of gastric and 
peptic ulcer.

presentation. The initial management of a stable patient with dyspepsia differs

390    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Timing of repeat endoscopy in gastric and duodenal ulcers
Patients with duodenal ulcers who have been treated do not need further endoscopy 
unless symptoms persist at 4 weeks or recur.
In patients with gastric ulcers, the decision to perform surveillance endoscopy 
should be individualized. Surveillance endoscopy (with biopsies of the ulcer if still 
present) should be performed after 8–12 weeks of antisecretory therapy in patients with 
gastric ulcers and any one of the following: symptoms despite medical therapy, unclear 
aetiology, giant gastric ulcer (>2 cm), biopsies not performed or inadequate sampling on 
the index upper endoscopy, ulcer appearing suspicious for malignancy on index upper 
endoscopy (mass lesion, elevated irregular ulcer borders or abnormal adjacent mucosal 
folds), patients with bleeding ulcers at initial presentation who show signs of continued 
bleeding and risk factors for gastric cancer.
Prevention of recurrence
	
l Carefully assess the need for aspirin and NSAIDs in patients with a history of PUD. 
	
l Confirm eradication of infection in patients treated for H. pylori, 4 or more weeks 
after the completion of therapy.
	
l Limit maintenance antisecretory therapy to high-risk subgroups of patients with 
PUD (refractory peptic ulcer; H. pylori–negative; NSAID – ulcer disease, giant 
[>2 cm] ulcer, age >50 years or multiple comorbidities; failure of H. pylori 
eradication; frequently recurrent peptic ulcers [>2 documented recurrences a year, 
continued NSAID use]).

l Emphasize to the patient that successful eradication depends on full compliance 
with the treatment. 
	
l Patients should avoid frequent use of unsupervised painkillers. If these are required 
on a long-term basis, a safer drug in the lowest doses should be taken in consultation 
with a doctor.
	
l Instruct patients to report to the physician urgently if vomiting of blood or passage of

is frequent vomiting or symptoms of GI bleed.
	
l There is no role of bland diet or drinking cold milk in the treatment of peptic ulcer.

VOMITING
Nausea is the unpleasant feeling that one is going to vomit. Vomiting is the forceful 
expulsion of the gastric contents due to involuntary contraction of abdominal 
musculature and simultaneous relaxation of gastric fundus and lower oesophageal 
sphincter. Regurgitation is spitting up of the gastric contents without associated nausea 
or forceful contraction of abdominal musculature. 
Causes of vomiting
	(a)	Central (due to stimulation of vomiting centre) – neurological diseases, raised 
intracranial pressure, vestibular system disorders, drugs and toxins, any acute 
severe pain, toxic or metabolic disorders like ketoacidosis, systemic infections, 
radiation exposure, pregnancy and psychogenic vomiting
	(b)	Peripheral – obstructive lesion of GIT, acute gastritis or gastroenteritis, severe 
upper GI bleed (UGIB), etc.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Excessive vomiting causes loss of salt and water and exhaustion while chronic 
recurrent vomiting prevents eating and causes starvation. Severe nausea and 
retching may result in upper GI bleed by causing Mallory–Weiss tear in the 
oesophagus/cardia of the stomach. 
	
l A detailed history and clinical examination usually give a clue to the cause of 
acute vomiting. For chronic and recurrent vomiting, investigation should be 
done to exclude a local cause in the GIT, evidence of raised intracranial tension 
(ICT) or presence of any other neurological condition. Psychogenic vomiting is 
diagnosed by exclusion of organic causes only.

l Acute gastroenteritis is usually self-limiting. Advise the patient to take sips of cold 
water/ORS. 
	
l Prevent motion sickness by avoiding heavy meals before travel. 
	
l Give rest to the injured part to prevent severe pain.

1.	Treat the underlying cause (medically or surgically) as appropriate.
	 2.	Hospitalize the patient to give IV fluids, if dehydrated. Start oral fluids as soon as 
the patient can tolerate. Give appropriate analgesics, if the patient has severe pain.

	In pregnancy, avoid all drugs, if possible. See the section ‘Nausea and Vomiting in

CONSTIPATION
Constipation is a symptom, not a disease. Different patients have different perceptions 
of symptoms. The commonest cause of constipation is habitual; the important 
contributory factors are insufficient dietary fibre, physical inactivity, suppression 
of defaecatory urges occurring at inconvenient moments, prolonged travel, etc. 
Constipation may also occur following an attack of diarrhoea after taking a purgative 
and this needs no treatment.

Chapter 6  Gastrointestinal Diseases    393
Primary constipation, or functional constipation, is classified into three subtypes: 
normal transit constipation, slow transit constipation and disorders of defecation. Risk 
factors and groups at risk are infants and children, age >55 years, recent abdominal or 
perianal/pelvic surgery, inadequate fibre diet, less fluid intake, drugs causing constipation, 
known comorbidities (neurological and structural abnormalities) and terminally ill 
patients. Recent onset or severe symptoms of constipation are usually due to secondary 
causes such as neurological, hormonal, colonic, malignancy and depression. 
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Symptoms of constipation include hard stools, excessive straining, infrequent 
bowel movements (<3 per week), a sense of incomplete evacuation or the use 
of manual manoeuvres to facilitate defecation. Symptoms which last >3 months 
are considered chronic.
	
l According to Rome IV criteria for constipation, a patient must have experienced 
two or more of the following symptoms over the preceding 3 months: 
	– Fewer than three bowel movements (BM) per week, straining
	– Hard stool in more than 25% of BMs
	– A sense of incomplete evacuation in more than 25% of BMs
	– Excessive straining in more than 25% of BMs
	– A need for manual manoeuvres (digital evacuation, support of the pelvic floor) 
to facilitate more than 25% of BM
	– Sensation of anorectal obstruction/blockage more than 25% BM
	– Fewer than three SBM per week
	– Loose stools are rarely present without the use of laxatives
	– Insufficient criteria for irritable bowel syndrome
	 Note: Opioid-induced constipation [OIC] should not be diagnosed as functional 
constipation [FC] because it is challenging to distinguish between opioid side 
effects and other causes of constipation.
	
l The initial evaluation of patients who present with chronic constipation should 
include a history, physical examination and laboratory studies to identify 
secondary causes of constipation and alarm features that warrant additional 
evaluation for organic disease. Alarm features include the following:
	– Haematochezia or haem-positive stool
	– Iron-deficiency anaemia
	– Clinically significant weight loss (>5% of the usual body weight over 6–12 
months)
	– New onset of unexplained constipation
	– Obstructive symptoms
	– Family history of colorectal cancer or IBD
	
l Colonoscopy should be done in patients with alarm features and in patients 
aged ≥45 years with constipation who have not previously had a colonoscopy 
to exclude organic disease. Additional evaluation (e.g. abdominal CT) may be 
required based on symptoms.

Habitual constipation 
A graded approach to treatment is based on non-pharmacological treatment followed 
by pharmacological treatment. Constipation in patients without alarm features can be 
managed with fibre and osmotic or stimulant laxatives.

1.	Provide reassurance – since many patients with normal stools and in pregnancy 
imagine that they are constipated.
	 2.	Stop or reduce medications that cause constipation.
	 3.	Advise a high-fibre diet (25 g of fibre) and fluid supplementation (up to 1.5–2.0 
L/day) with decrease in consumption of caffeinated drinks. Also advise a gradual 
increase in fibre (either as standardized supplements or incorporated in the diet) 
and adequate fluid intake. Bulk-forming agents like ‘ispaghula husk’ or ‘psyllium 
seeds’ also help to relieve mild constipation.
	 4.	Advise retraining of bowels (avoiding suppression of urge to defaecate, making a 
regular habit). The optimal time to have a bowel movement typically is soon after 
waking and/or 30 minutes after meals when colonic activity is the greatest.
	 5.	Advise regular physical exercise such as walking for 0.5–1 hour daily and 
abdominal exercises.

Usually required for moderate to severe constipation
The second step in the graded approach is to add osmotic laxatives followed 
by stimulant laxatives, enemas and prokinetic drugs

IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME
IBS refers to a group of GI symptoms associated with lower bowel that occurs in the 
absence of organic disease. It is not a psychiatric or psychological disorder. However, 
psychological factors or coexisting psychological conditions may play a role in 
the persistence and perceived severity of abdominal symptoms and contribute to 
impairment of quality of life and excessive use of health care services.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l A positive diagnosis of IBS is made using Rome IV criteria: recurrent abdominal 
pain at least 1 day/week in the last 3 months associated with two or more of the 
following: 
	– Related to defaecation (may be increased or unchanged by defaecation)
	– Associated with a change in stool frequency
	– Associated with a change in stool form or appearance
	
l The supportive symptoms of IBS include altered stool frequency, altered stool 
form, altered stool passage (straining and/or urgency), mucorrhoea, abdominal 
bloating or subjective distention.
	
l IBS is classified into four subtypes: IBS with predominant constipation (IBS-C), IBS 
with predominant diarrhoea (IBS-D), IBS with mixed bowel habits (IBS-M) or IBS 
unsubtyped (IBS-U). 
	
l Diagnosis made generally by history (primary presenting symptoms [pattern of 
pain], precipitating factors, alarm features and other associated gastrointestinal 
and extra-gastrointestinal symptoms) and physical examination is normal. 
Figure 6.3 depicts the diagnostic approach to IBS. 
	
l Urgent colonoscopy is indicated in the presence of red flag signs: nocturnal 
symptoms, rectal bleeding, onset after the age of 50 years, weight loss, family 
history of colon cancer, faecal soiling, fever and anaemia.

l Establish a positive patient–physician relationship, with the patient’s symptoms and 
distress being accepted as real and accepting the impact of symptoms. Identify and help

Indications for hospitalization
These include patients with clinical signs of dehydration, especially young children 
or elderly, those with suspected cholera, immunosuppressed patients and those with 
severe systemic symptoms.
Role of probiotics and antidiarrhoeals
Probiotics are live microbes which impart health benefits and some strains of probiotics 
have been found to be effective in reducing the severity and duration of acute 
infectious diarrhoea as an adjunct more in children than in adults; however, there is 
no consensus on their cost-effectiveness for routine use since diarrhoea is self-limiting 
and requires no treatment other than rehydration therapy. Species of Lactobacillus and 
Bifidobacterium, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, some species of E. coli and Bacillus are 
commonly used as probiotics. The optimal dose of probiotics depends on the strain 
and product.
Antidiarrhoeals and antiemetics have no benefits in acute or persistent diarrhoea. 
There is inadequate evidence for the use of the adsorbents kaolin/pectin, activated 
charcoal or racecadotril.

causes a slight increase in the frequency of stools due to increased gastrocolic reflex. 
	
l They should report to the physician if they are not able to retain any fluid taken 
orally and develop significant decrease in urine output.
	
l Promote prevention of acute diarrhoea through adequate hand washing, safe food 
preparation, access to clean water and vaccinations.

GI MANIFESTATIONS OF CORONAVIRUS DISEASE 2019 
(COVID-19)
GI manifestations of COVID have been reported in 10–60% of patients with 
COVID-19, with variable onset and severity. The majority of COVID-19-associated 
GI symptoms are mild and self-limiting and include diarrhoea, anorexia, nausea, 
vomiting and abdominal pain/discomfort lasting for 5–14 days and do not require 
further diagnostic investigations specific to the GI system. 
	 1.	Provide supportive care and symptomatic treatment with oxygen, optimal 
hydration, electrolyte correction and antiemetics as necessary. Avoid NSAIDs and 
unnecessary antibiotics.
	 2.	A minority of patients may present with an acute abdomen with aetiologies such 
as acute appendicitis, acute pancreatitis, intestinal obstruction, bowel ischaemia, 
haemoperitoneum or abdominal compartment syndrome. An abdominal computed 
tomography (CT) scan and angiogram may be required in select patients. The 
usefulness of stool RT-PCR, peritoneal biopsies and peritoneal fluid RNA tests in 
management is limited.
	 3.	Supportive and symptomatic care is the mainstay of therapy. However, a minority 
of patients may require surgical or endoscopic treatment for acute abdomen and 
GI bleeding.
	 4.	Standard supportive care activities and surgical procedures should be performed 
with appropriate personal protective equipment and infection control measures to 
prevent transmission of infection (see Appendix II).
Nutrition: Patients with COVID disease may have reduced oral intake due to the 
severity of their disease or as a side effect of the medicines used for treatment. A number 
of medications used in patients with COVID-19 (such as Favipiravir, Oseltamivir, 
Remdesivir, Tocilizumab, steroids, Budesonide) have documented GI side effects.
	 1.	In severe disease, enteral nutrition is important for maintaining gut mucosal 
integrity. Nutritional assessment by a specialist should be done, and a high-calorie, 
immunomodulatory diet should be administered. Administer parenteral/enteral 
feeding in patients with mechanically ventilated, nasogastric or nasojejunal tube 
insertion. Commence enteral feeding early following improvement of the clinical 
condition.
	 2.	The presence of comorbidities (including pre-existing digestive disorders – IBD, 
GI malignancies) is associated with poor clinical outcome in COVID-19 due to 
interruptions of endoscopic/surgical services leading to delays in the diagnosis and 
treatment.
Reference
	 1.	 Kariyawasam JC, Jayarajah U, Riza R, Abeysuriya V, Seneviratne SL. Gastrointestinal 
manifestations in COVID-19. Trans R Soc Trop Med Hyg. 2021;115(12):1362–1388.

CHRONIC DIARRHOEA
A patient is diagnosed as having chronic diarrhoea if he/she continues to have diarrhoea 
for more than 4 weeks. The important causes of malabsorption in India include tropical 
sprue, coeliac disease, tuberculosis and chronic pancreatitis (CP). 
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l It may be classified as small bowel diarrhoea (low-frequency, bulky, greasy, frothy, 
foul-smelling stools associated with lot of flatulence indicating malabsorption) 
or large bowel diarrhoea (high-frequency, low-volume, loose/watery stools with 
rectal symptoms – urgency, frequency and pain during defaecation).
Treatment (to be treated by a specialist)
It can be planned only after a proper diagnosis is made. Use of anticholinergics or 
non-specific antidiarrhoeal agents should be discouraged in the absence of proper 
diagnosis. Treatment of tropical sprue is discussed next.
	
l Obtain a careful detailed history and screening blood tests to exclude anaemia and 
coeliac disease, as well as stool tests for inflammation and blood. If symptoms 
persist despite normal first-line investigations and treatment, then refer to a specialist 
for further investigations. Indications for referral include anyone of the following:
	– Alarm features (onset after age 50 years, rectal bleeding or melaena, nocturnal 
pain or diarrhoea, progressive abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss, fever 
or other systemic symptoms, laboratory abnormalities [iron-deficiency anaemia, 
elevated C-reactive protein or faecal calprotectin] or family history of IBD or 
colorectal cancer)
	– Severe diarrhoea, suspected IBD, or inconclusive diagnosis after initial evaluation 
	
l Refer to a gastroenterologist for diagnosis and long-term management for the 
underlying cause (e.g. IBD, CP). Tests for malabsorption include faecal fat excretion 
study, d-xylose absorption, small bowel contrast studies and mucosal biopsy, and 
structural and functional evaluation of the pancreas. Diagnosis of ulcerative colitis 
(UC) is confirmed by colonic endoscopy and mucosal biopsy. Colonoscopy is 
performed to exclude colorectal cancer in patients with altered bowel habits with 
or without rectal bleeding. Faecal calprotectin is performed to exclude colonic 
inflammation in those suspected with IBS and younger than 40 years.

and malabsorption of nutrients. It occurs in residents of or visitors to the tropics. The 
exact cause of tropical sprue is unknown, but it is usually triggered by an intestinal 
microbial infection. Villous destruction and demonstrable nutrient malabsorption occur 
in varying degrees. Folate, vitamin B12, and iron deficiencies are the most common 
nutrient deficiencies. The differential diagnosis of tropical sprue includes infection,

text:
406    Standard Treatment Guidelines
coeliac disease, intestinal scleroderma, small bowel bacterial overgrowth, blind loop 
syndrome, lymphoma and tropical pancreatitis. Diagnosis is made by small bowel 
barium study (mucosal oedema, flocculation and clumping of barium and jejunal 
mucosal biopsy (reveals varying degree of mucosal atrophy). Without treatment, 
tropical sprue runs a relapsing course and can result in severe malnutrition.

condition: Coeliac Disease (Coeliac sprue or Gluten-sensitive Enteropathy)
text:
Advise the patient to drink plenty of oral fluids. Advise him/her to avoid fatty food and 
dairy products and take otherwise a balanced diet. These nutrients should be introduced 
gradually once the patient has been on regular pharmacological treatment.

condition: Coeliac Disease (Coeliac sprue or Gluten-sensitive Enteropathy)
text:
1.	Treat the underlying cause as appropriate.
	 2.	Administer a combination of antibiotics and folic acid to patients for 3–6 months. 
	
	Tab. Norfloxacin 400 mg 2 times a day
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Ciprofloxacin 500 mg 2 times a day
	
	Or
	
	Cap. Doxycycline 100 mg 2 times a day
	
	Or
	
	If the above-mentioned drugs are contraindicated, Tab. Cotrimoxazole 960 mg 
2 times a day
	 3.	For anaerobic infections, Tab. Tinidazole 2 g orally as single dose with food
	 4.	Tab. Folic acid 5 mg 2 times a day for 3–6 months’ duration depending on the 
patient’s response; other minor nutrient supplements given if there is evidence of 
specific deficiency
	 5.	Tab. Vitamin B12 500–1000 mcg once daily
Monitoring and follow-up
Assess patients’ responses by improvement of symptoms, weight gain and correction 
of anaemia. The duration of treatment depends on the duration of symptoms. Give a 
second course of antibiotics if the patients have a partial improvement in symptoms 
or early recurrence (<3 months). Patients with no improvement in symptoms after 
two courses of antibiotic therapy or progressive symptoms should be evaluated for 
alternative diagnoses. Coeliac disease and lactose intolerance are commonly associated 
with malabsorption.
COELIAC DISEASE (COELIAC SPRUE OR GLUTEN-
SENSITIVE ENTEROPATHY)
Coeliac disease is a chronic disorder of the digestive tract that results in an inability 
to tolerate gluten. It can present with a variety of GI symptoms (e.g. diarrhoea, 
steatorrhoea, weight loss, bloating, flatulence, abdominal pain) and also non-GI

Chapter 6  Gastrointestinal Diseases    407
abnormalities (e.g. abnormal liver function tests, iron-deficiency anaemia, bone 
disease, skin disorders). However, many individuals with coeliac disease may have no 
symptoms at all.
Diagnostic approach
	
l Testing for coeliac disease should be performed in adults with suggestive GI or 
extraintestinal signs/symptoms of coeliac disease. Extraintestinal signs/symptoms of 
coeliac disease include unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia, folate or vitamin B12 
deficiency, persistent elevation in serum aminotransferases, dermatitis herpetiformis, 
fatigue, recurrent headaches, recurrent foetal loss, low-birth-weight offspring, 
reduced fertility, persistent aphthous stomatitis, dental enamel hypoplasia, metabolic 
bone disease and premature osteoporosis, idiopathic peripheral neuropathy or non-
hereditary cerebellar ataxia.
	
l Testing for coeliac disease should ideally be performed while patients are on a gluten-
containing diet. The testing approach varies based on the probability of coeliac disease.
	– Individuals with a low probability of coeliac disease: Evaluation begins with 
serological testing. Patients with positive serological testing should undergo an 
upper endoscopy with small bowel biopsy to diagnose coeliac disease.
	– Individuals with a high probability of coeliac disease: Both serological testing 
and small bowel biopsy (regardless of coeliac-specific serology results) should 
be performed.
	
l Serological tests: Serological tests include immunoglobulin A (IgA) anti-tissue 
transglutaminase (tTG) antibody is the preferred test for detection of coeliac disease 
in adults. In addition, total IgA levels should also be measured. In patients with IgA 
deficiency, deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP) IgG should be done.
	
l Biopsy: The diagnosis of coeliac disease is established by the presence of increased 
intraepithelial lymphocytes with crypt hyperplasia (Marsh type 2) alone, or in 
conjunction with villous atrophy (Marsh type 3) on small bowel biopsy in a patient 
with positive coeliac serology. However, villous atrophy can be patchy and may also 
be present in a variety of other disorders that should be considered in appropriate 
clinical settings. Sometimes, positive serology is not associated with the presence 
of villous atrophy. Instead, the duodenal mucosa may be normal or show only an 
intraepithelial lymphocytosis and a diagnosis of active coeliac disease cannot be 
made. This intriguing subset of patients is labelled as having ‘potential coeliac 
disease’. Refer potential coeliacs to a specialist centre.
	
l Treatment: The treatment for coeliac disease is primarily a gluten-free diet, which 
requires significant patient education, motivation and follow-up. Review the original 
diagnosis to exclude an alternative diagnosis if symptoms persist or recur.
LACTOSE INTOLERANCE
There are four types: primary, secondary, developmental and congenital. Primary 
lactose intolerance occurs as the amount of lactase declines as people age. Secondary

408    Standard Treatment Guidelines
lactose intolerance can be caused by infection, coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel 
disease (IBD), or other diseases.
SALIENT FEATURE
	
l Common symptoms include abdominal pain and bloating, excessive flatus and 
watery stool following the ingestion of foods containing lactose.
	
l A diagnosis of lactose intolerance can usually be made clinically with a careful 
history supported by dietary manipulation, i.e. removal of lactose from the diet.
	
l Removal of lactose from the diet along with lactase supplementation can be 
done for 2–4 weeks to see whether this improves the symptoms. Symptoms 
usually resolve in 2–3 days on removal of lactose from the diet and resolution 
of symptoms on withdrawal of lactose from the diet confirms the diagnosis. If 
necessary, diagnosis can be confirmed by using a breath hydrogen or lactose 
tolerance test.

1.	Treatment consists primarily of avoiding lactose-containing foods such as milk and 
dairy products such as cheese and yogurt. Alternatives to milk for lactose-intolerant 
individuals include products such as soy milk. The degree of lactose malabsorption 
varies greatly; however, most patients can tolerate up to 350 mL of milk daily without 
symptoms and respond to gradual re-introduction of lactose as per lactose intolerance.
	 2.	Supplement calcium and vitamin D in lactose-intolerant patients. 
	 3.	Lactase enzyme supplements can be taken throughout the day whenever lactose is 
ingested. 
Patient education
	
l Advise a well-balanced diet including all major and minor nutrients to maintain nutrition. 
	
l Patients should be advised to follow proper hygienic measures regarding eating habits.
	
l Patients are asked to come back for review if there is no clinical improvement in 
3–4 weeks of treatment. 
	
l Travellers to the tropics should be aware of the tropical sprue and take steps to limit 
exposure to enteric pathogens. If protracted diarrhoea occurs, they should report to 
a medical doctor promptly.
	
l Most people with lactose intolerance can tolerate some milk products without 
symptoms such as low-fat milk products; skim milk may be better tolerated than 
whole-milk products. Gradual introduction of milk products into diet can improve 
symptoms as well as smaller servings of dairy are less likely to cause GI problems. 
Drinking milk with other foods lessens the symptoms of lactose intolerance as it 
slows the digestive process.
	
l Educate patients about the hidden sources of lactose in food products such as bread 
and baked goods, processed breakfast cereals, instant potatoes, candies, dressings 
and mixes for pancakes and biscuits.

ULCERATIVE COLITIS
Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the large bowel, 
characterized by relapsing and remitting episodes of inflammation limited to the 
mucosal layer of the colon occurring in genetically susceptible individuals often 
modified by environmental triggers. The symptoms of UC may vary depending on 
the extent of involvement of the rectum and colon and the extent often involves more 
proximal portions of the colon in a continuous fashion. 
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patients may present in acute stage with bloody diarrhoea that may last for 
weeks to months; associated symptoms include colicky abdominal pain, urgency 
and tenesmus. Patients may have systemic symptoms of low to moderate fever, 
backache, arthralgias and weight loss. 
	
l The diagnosis of UC is based on the presence of chronic diarrhoea for more than 
4 weeks and evidence of chronic colitis on endoscopy and biopsy. 
	
l Different types of UC depending on the affected area of the colon are proctocolitis, 
proctosigmoiditis, left-sided colitis, pancolitis and acute severe colitis.
	
l Acute disease is graded as mild (<4 stools/day without intermittent small 
amounts of blood, no fever, no tachycardia, normal Hb, ESR, CRP), moderate 
to severe (>6 stools/day with blood, fever >37.5°C, heart rate > 90/min, anaemia 
with Hb level <75% of normal and ESR >30 mm/h, elevated CRP, faecal 
calprotectin >150–200) and fulminant (>10 stools/day with continuous blood, 
fever >37.5°C, heart rate >90/min, transfusion required for anaemia, ESR >30 
mm/h, CRP elevated, faecal calprotectin >150–200). During remission, the 
patient may be asymptomatic or (formed stool, no blood, no urgency, CRP and 
ESR normal, FC <150–200) may have extraintestinal symptoms.

410    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Abdominal imaging is not required for the diagnosis of UC but may be performed 
in patients who present with symptoms of colitis.
	
l Extent of involvement of the colon should be determined for deciding the mode 
of treatment and prognostication.
	
l Extent of colonic involvement is best determined by colonoscopy and segmental 
biopsy. However, full-length colonoscopy should be withheld in patients with 
severe active disease.

The course of UC typically consists of intermittent exacerbations alternating with 
periods of complete symptomatic remission. However, a small percentage of patients 
may have continuing symptoms and are unable to achieve remission. The aim of the 
treatment is induction of remission in acute stage and then maintenance of remission.

There is no specific dietary restriction but patients may avoid any food which causes 
discomfort.

Topical treatment is more effective than oral therapy for induction and maintenance of 
remission in patients with ulcerative proctitis and left-sided colitis.
A.  Mild active UC
Rectal 5-aminosalicylate therapies at a dose of 1 g/day for induction of remission.
Or
Prednisolone phosphate enema, 20 mg in 100 mL saline 1–2 times a day 
Or 
Hydrocortisone enema 100–125 mg in 100 mL saline 1–2 times a day (to be prepared fresh) 
Or 
Hydrocortisone foam 125 mg 1–2 times a day
Distal/left colonic involvement
Combine rectal mesalamine with Tab. Mesalamine 2.4–3.6 g/day in divided doses
If disease limited to rectum
Prednisolone phosphate enema, 20 mg in 100 mL saline 1–2 times a day
Or
Hydrocortisone enema 100–125 mg in 100 mL saline 1–2 times a day (to be prepared 
fresh)
Or
Hydrocortisone foam 125 mg 1–2 times a day

Chapter 6  Gastrointestinal Diseases    411
B.  Moderate to severe or extensive acute disease
	 1.	Start (1) as above
	 2.	Tab. Prednisolone 20–60 mg/day in single or divided doses
Note: While systemic glucocorticoids were once the mainstay of therapy, there are a 
growing number of effective biological agents for moderate to severe UC, including 
anti–tumour necrosis factor (TNF) therapy, anti-integrin therapy and others. There 
are limited data comparing one induction strategy with another, and treatment is 
individualized. Referral to a specialist is warranted.
Follow-up:  If the symptoms do not improve or worsen, hospitalize the patient.
C.  Acute severe disease with systemic symptoms (requires hospitalization 
under the care of specialist)
	 1.	Inj. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV 4 times a day
	 2.	Patient to be kept ‘nil by mouth’ and given adequate intravenous fluids and electrolytes.
	 3.	Blood transfusion to be given as per requirement.
	 4.	Patient switched over to oral steroids and aminosalicylates to be started as in A(1) 
after 5 days, when the patient is allowed to take orally.
Once remission is induced, steroids are tapered slowly over 4–6 weeks’ period. For 
acute attack, there is no use of giving steroids for more than 12 weeks.
If the patient fails to respond to steroids, refer him/her to a gastroenterologist for 
immunosuppressive therapy or surgery.
Follow-up:  Close clinical/biochemical/radiological monitoring is required for any 
complications like toxic megacolon/perforation.
D.  Maintenance of remission
	 1.	Any of the drugs used in A(1) should be given lifelong.
	 2.	Corticosteroid use on a daily basis beyond 3 months is not desirable. Azathioprine/ 
6-Mercaptopurine should be used in patients with steroid-dependent disease. 
	 3.	The choice of maintenance therapy depends primarily on the specific agent used to 
achieve remission, and it also depends on patient preferences, clinician preferences 
and cost.

Complications associated with UC include severe bleeding, toxic megacolon, 
perforation, strictures, and the development of dysplasia and colorectal cancer. Toxic 
megacolon is characterized by colonic diameter ≥6 cm or caecal diameter >9 cm and 
the presence of systemic toxicity. Patients with fulminant colitis are at a high risk of 
developing toxic megacolon and consequent perforation of the colon.
Surgical
	
l Indications for emergency surgery are colonic perforation, life-threatening massive 
bleeding and toxic megacolon. Urgent surgery is required in patients who develop

412    Standard Treatment Guidelines
acute fulminant colitis characterized by more than 10 stools/day, continuous 
bleeding, abdominal pain, distension and acute, severe toxic symptoms including 
fever and anorexia.
	
l Refer patients with acute fulminant colitis refractory to medical treatment (failure 
of glucocorticoid therapy) to a specialist for treatment with a biological agent, 
infliximab or another anti-TNF agent.
	
l Surgery is an important treatment option for patients with UC, especially for patients 
with large bowel obstruction, steroid-dependent disease, cancer or high-grade 
dysplasia.
Patient education
	
l Patients should be followed up at 6-month interval and maintenance treatment 
should be continued. 
	
l Screening and subsequent surveillance colonoscopy to assess for dysplasia in 
individuals with UC of extent greater than the rectum should start 8 years after 
diagnosis. Surveillance colonoscopies in patients with UC should be performed 
at 1- to 3-year intervals. Patients with UC and primary sclerosing cholangitis 
(PSC) should undergo a screening colonoscopy at the time of diagnosis of UC and 
surveillance annually thereafter.
	
l Patients should be explained about chronic nature of the disease and continuation 
of maintenance treatment for life along with regular follow-up and risk of colonic 
cancer after 10 years of onset of disease.

AMOEBIC LIVER ABSCESS (ALA)
Liver abscess is the commonest extraintestinal form of amoebiasis, caused by 
E. histolytica. In endemic areas, it usually affects young individuals, more commonly 
chronic alcoholics. Females are only rarely affected. The most important complication 
is abscess rupture.

Chapter 6  Gastrointestinal Diseases    413
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Presenting symptoms include acute fever and right upper quadrant abdominal 
pain which may be dull ache or pleuritic in nature. 
	
l ALA is less common in elderly and is more likely to be chronic in presentation 
with low abdominal pain, intermittent fever and general symptoms. Jaundice is 
uncommon. 
	
l Complications include rupture of abscess into the pleural, pericardial or rarely 
peritoneal cavity. 
	
l Elevated blood counts/ESR/serum alkaline phosphatase, one or more hypoechoic 
lesions in the liver on ultrasonography and positive test for antibodies to 
E. histolytica in high titre help in the diagnosis. Examination of pus of the 
parasite is usually negative.

1.	Tab. Metronidazole 800 mg 3 times a day for 7–10 days. If the patient is very toxic, 
Inj. Metronidazole 500 mg given 8 hourly until the patient improves (switch over 
to oral therapy whenever possible)
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Tinidazole 2 g as a single dose with food for 3–5 days (in children: 50 mg/kg 
[up to 2 g]) (Caution: Close monitoring is recommended when treatment duration 
exceeds 3 days.)
	 2.	Since the parasites can persist in the intestine in 40–60% of patients, treatment with 
a Nitroimidazole to always be followed with a luminal agent 
	
	Tab. Paromomycin 25–30 mg/kg/day orally in 3 divided doses for 7 days 
	
	Or 
	
	Tab. Diiodohydroxyquin 650 mg orally 3 times daily for 20 days for adults; 
	
	in children: 30–40 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses for 20 days 
	
	Or 
	
	Tab. Diloxanide furoate 500 mg orally 3 times daily for 10 days for adults; 
	
	in children: 20 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses for 10 days
Indications for aspiration of amoebic liver abscess
	 1.	Doubt about possibility of pyogenic abscess
	 2.	No improvement with medical treatment
	 3.	Impending rupture of abscess – abscess very close to the surface of the liver
	 4.	Large left lobe abscess, to prevent rupture into the pericardium

l Monitor the patient for resolution of symptoms with medical treatment and aspirate, 
if there is any indication. 
	
l Abscess cavity may persist for several weeks even after cure of infection. Therefore, 
frequent ultrasonographic examinations are unnecessary unless the patient develops 
symptoms; these may be repeated after 4–6 weeks after the patient becomes 
asymptomatic. 
	
l After treatment with Metronidazole, Tab. Diloxanide furoate 500 mg 3 times a day 
for 1 week may be given, especially if the patient is in a non-endemic area.
Patient education
	
l Avoid taking alcohol specifically on treatment with metronidazole. 
	
l Stress the need for maintaining hygiene regarding food intake to prevent enteric 
infections.
Reference
	 1.	 Amoebiasis and infection with free living ameba. In: Loscalzo J, Kasper DL, Longo DL, et al. 
(eds), Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine. 21st ed. New York: McGraw Hill Company 
Inc.; 2022, pp. 1714–1720.
PYOGENIC LIVER ABSCESS
Liver abscesses constitute 48% of all visceral abscesses. Pyogenic abscesses in the liver 
are usually caused by spread of infection from the peritoneum, abdominal viscera like 
appendicitis/diverticulitis/portal pyaemia or disease of the biliary tract. They are mostly 
caused by coliform organisms.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Fever is the most common symptom, associated with abdominal pain, toxaemia, 
symptoms of the associated problem like appendicular pain/mass, etc. Mostly 
abscesses are small and multiple. 
	
l Diagnostic investigations include full blood counts, USG of the abdomen, blood 
culture and examination of pus including culture. CT scan and MRI are seldom 
indicated.

Surgical
	
l Perform ultrasound or CT-guided percutaneous drainage of all suspected liver 
abscesses. Perform needle aspiration for small single abscess or with catheter 
placement; in other cases, or open surgical drainage, perform laparoscopic 
drainage for multiple/multilocular abscess, or drainage by endoscopic retrograde

Chapter 6  Gastrointestinal Diseases    415
cholangiopancreatography (ERCP for patients with previous biliary procedures 
whose infection communicates with the biliary tree). 
	
l All aspirate material should be sent for Gram stain and culture (both aerobic and 
anaerobic).

Initial empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic(s) should be commenced as soon as possible 
after collection of blood culture sample, prior to abscess aspiration. If the patient does 
not have sepsis and the aspiration can be done within several hours, then empirical 
antibiotic therapy should be withheld until immediately thereafter to increase the 
microbiological yield. The empirical regimen should cover streptococci, enteric Gram-
negative bacilli and anaerobes.
	 1.	Inj. Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV 2 times a day 
	 2.	Inj. Gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day IV in 3 divided doses 
	 3.	If source of abscess is intra-abdominal sepsis, add Inj. Metronidazole 500 mg IV 
3 times a day.

l Monitor for clinical improvement and modify the therapy based on culture 
sensitivity report.
	
l Abscess should always be drained.
	
l Surgery is considered if there is no improvement with medical treatment and 
percutaneous drainage in 4–7 days. Follow-up imaging is warranted only in the 
setting of persistent clinical symptoms or if drainage is not proceeding as expected.
Patient education
	
l Avoid drinking alcohol while on treatment with Metronidazole. 
	
l Stress the need for maintaining hygiene regarding food intake to prevent enteric 
infection.

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine. 21st ed. New York: McGraw Hill Company Inc.;

ACUTE PANCREATITIS
It refers to acute inflammation of the pancreas, usually caused by alcohol or gallstone 
migrating through the common bile duct. It is less commonly caused by trauma, 
infections like mumps, ascariasis and drugs like diuretic and Azathioprine.

416    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l It clinically presents as acute-onset, constant upper abdominal pain ‘penetrating 
through to the back’, and may be partially relieved by sitting with the trunk 
flexed and the knees drawn up. In severe cases, there is anorectal paralytic ileus, 
vomiting, abdominal distension, jaundice and fever.
	
l Diagnostic criteria: Two out of the following:
	a.	
Pancreatic type of abdominal pain
	b.	 Raised serum amylase/lipase (>3 times of upper limit of normal)
	c.	
Radiological evidence (diffuse/focal enlargement of the pancreas)
	
l Raised procalcitonin is a sensitive test for detection of pancreatitis. Serum lipase 
elevation is specific for pancreatitis. Ultrasonogram or CT scan further helps to 
confirm the diagnosis.
	
l Routine abdominal CT scan is not recommended at initial presentation in patients 
with acute pancreatitis unless there is diagnostic uncertainty because there is 
no evidence that CT improves clinical outcomes and the complete extent of 
pancreatic and peripancreatic necrosis may become clear only 72 hours after the 
onset of acute pancreatitis.
	
l At initial evaluation, the severity of acute pancreatitis should be assessed by 
clinical examination to assess for early fluid losses and organ failure (particularly 
cardiovascular, respiratory or renal compromise) and measurement of the 
systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) score.
	
l Severe acute pancreatitis is associated with persistent organ failure 
(cardiovascular, respiratory and/or renal) and high mortality.

In 85–90% of cases, the disease is self-limiting and subsides in 3–7 days with moderate 
fluid resuscitation, management of pain and nausea, and early oral feeding. There is no 
proven treatment of acute pancreatitis. Treatment is mainly supportive.

l Send blood for complete blood count, amylase, KFT, LFT, blood sugar, serum 
triglycerides and arterial blood gases. Repeat the test at 48 hours, or early if 
indicated. 
	
l In patients with mild pancreatitis, recovery generally occurs quickly, making it 
unnecessary to initiate supplemental nutrition. A soft diet can be started early 
(within 24 hours) as tolerated if the pain is decreasing and inflammatory markers 
are improving. Start with a low-residue, low-fat and soft diet, provided there is no 
evidence of ileus or significant nausea and/or vomiting.
	
l In patients with severe pancreatitis, enteral nutrition through a nasojejunal tube 
placed endoscopically or radiologically should be provided rather than initiating 
parenteral nutrition. If the target rate is not achieved within 48–72 hours and if

Chapter 6  Gastrointestinal Diseases    417
severe acute pancreatitis is not resolved, supplemental parenteral nutrition should 
be provided.
	
l Fats should be avoided until the acute phase settles.

The goals of initial management are fluid replacement, electrolyte balance, calorie 
support and prevention of local and systemic complications.
	 1.	Promptly transfer to an intensive care unit if there are signs that suggest that the 
pancreatitis is severe or is likely to become severe or in case of sustained organ failure.
	 2.	The only effective treatment in the first 24–48 hours after the diagnosis of 
acute pancreatitis is intravenous hydration. Significant third-space losses due 
to inflammatory collections, increased permeability of vasculature resulting in 
transudation of fluid from intravascular to extravascular compartment, nausea 
and vomiting and inability to ingest adequate amounts of fluids lead to increases 
in haematocrit blood urea nitrogen and creatinine, possible development of 
necrotizing pancreatic and peripancreatic necrosis and acute kidney injury. 
	
		
Moderate intravenous hydration (1.5 mL/kg/h with a 10-mL/kg bolus in 
patients with hypovolaemia) with goal-directed therapy for fluid management 
is done. Reassess fluid requirements at frequent intervals in the first 6 hours of 
admission and for the next 24–48 hours. 
	
		
Use of lactated Ringer’s solution in patients with acute pancreatitis may 
reduce hospital stay and ICU admissions. (Caution: In rare patients with acute 
pancreatitis due to hypercalcaemia, lactated Ringer’s is contraindicated because 
it contains 3 mEq/L calcium. In these patients, normal saline should be used for 
volume resuscitation.) 
	 3.	Avoid hydroxyethyl starch–containing fluids as there is no demonstrable mortality 
benefit and possible risk of multiple organ failure.
	 4.	Monitor haematocrit, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and lactate to assess volaemia 
and adequate tissue perfusion.
	 5.	Monitor electrolytes frequently in the first 48–72 hours and especially with 
aggressive fluid resuscitation. Hypocalcaemia should be corrected if ionized 
calcium is low or if there are signs of neuromuscular irritability (Chvostek’s or 
Trousseau’s sign). Low magnesium levels can also cause hypocalcaemia and 
should be corrected. 
	 6.	Monitor serum glucose levels hourly in patients with severe pancreatitis and treat 
hyperglycaemia (blood glucose greater than 180–200 mg/dL) as it can increase the 
risk of secondary pancreatic infections.
	 7.	Perform nasogastric tube aspiration if there is evidence of paralytic ileus, 
abdominal distension and vomiting. 
	 8.	Give Inj. Tramadol 50 mg IM repeated 6–8 hourly, if needed. 
	 9.	Give enteral nutrition as soon as the patient tolerates. Total parenteral nutrition 
(TPN) should be avoided.
	10.	Use of prophylactic antibiotics to prevent pancreatic infection is not recommended.

418    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	11.	Patients with moderately severe or severe acute pancreatitis, signs of sepsis or 
clinical deterioration 72 hours after initial presentation should undergo a contrast-
enhanced CT scan to assess the presence of pancreatic or extrapancreatic necrosis 
and local complications. Patients with persistent organ failure and extensive local 
complications should be managed by a specialist. Complications (to be managed by 
a specialist) include acute peripancreatic fluid collection, acute necrotic collection, 
pseudocyst, walled-off necrosis and haemorrhage.
	12.	Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) should be performed 
early in the course (within 24 hours of admission) for patients with gallstone 
pancreatitis and cholangitis. Other indications for ERCP include patients with 
common bile duct obstruction (visible stone on imaging), dilated common bile duct 
or increasing liver tests without cholangitis. Refer to specialists in such cases.
	13.	Cholecystectomy should be performed after recovery from acute pancreatitis in all 
operable patients with gallstone pancreatitis or biliary sludge.
Patient education
	
l Avoid alcohol, avoid fatty food and explain to the patient about the need of early 
gallbladder removal in patients with gallstone.
