CHRONIC PANCREATITIS
CP is characterized by chronic, progressive pancreatic inflammation and scarring, 
irreversibly damaging the pancreas, and resulting in loss of exocrine and endocrine 
function. The syndrome of CP results from exposure to risk factors (genetic and 
environmental). It is usually caused by chronic alcohol consumption or possibly 
malnutrition in tropics. Most patients with CP have more than one underlying aetiology. 
The causes of CP are toxic-metabolic (alcohol, smoking, hypertriglyceridaemia), 
idiopathic, genetic, autoimmune, recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis, and obstructive.

Chapter 6  Gastrointestinal Diseases    419
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Chronic pancreatitis typically presents as chronic unrelenting pain with episodic 
flares. 
	
l It is characterized by chronic diarrhoea due to malabsorption, upper abdominal 
pain and diabetes mellitus. 
	
l However, many of the clinical features take time to manifest and may be absent in 
the early stages of CP.
	
l Suspect CP in patients with chronic abdominal pain and/or a history of relapsing 
acute pancreatitis, symptoms of pancreatic exocrine (diarrhoea, steatorrhoea or weight 
loss) insufficiency, or pancreatogenic diabetes. Occasionally, patients with CP are 
asymptomatic and the diagnosis is suspected incidentally on imaging.
	
l Cross-sectional imaging with high-quality CT scan using multidetector 
technology and a pancreatic protocol, or MRI with magnetic resonance 
cholangiopancreatography are the best initial diagnostic tests.
	
l In patients with suspected CP, but inconclusive cross-sectional imaging, 
endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) or a direct pancreatic function test with secretin, if 
available, can be done.
	
l The most common complications of CP include metabolic consequences of 
exocrine insufficiency (particularly osteopenia and osteoporosis), pancreatogenic 
(type 3c) diabetes and opioid dependency due to the treatment of pain. Other 
less frequent complications include pseudocyst formation, bile duct or duodenal 
obstruction, pancreatic ascites or pancreatic pleural effusion, splenic vein 
thrombosis, arterial pseudoaneurysms, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, 
gastroparesis and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

The goals of treatment include pain management, correction of pancreatic insufficiency 
and management of complications.

It includes cessation of alcohol and smoking. Dietary modification includes small meals 
low in fat and sugar, use of ‘coconut oil’ as the source of fat and restriction of sugars/
refined carbohydrates if the patient has impaired glucose tolerance.

Prior to initiating therapy in a patient with CP who presents with abdominal pain, 
confirm that the symptoms are in fact due to CP and not an alternative aetiology, 
especially in the early stages of CP when abdominal pain may be significant, but 
characteristic and diagnostic imaging features may be absent.
	 1.	The majority of patients with pain due to CP require analgesics.

420    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
	Stepwise approach to treatment of pain should be taken for pain control. Begin with 
paracetamol and/or NSAIDs for the initial management of abdominal pain.
	
	Consider the use of antioxidant therapy (with selenium, ascorbic acid, β-carotene 
or Methionine) for CP with pain; it may reduce pain and can be considered for 
clinical use, especially early in the course of disease.
	
	Give Tab. Tramadol 50 mg twice a day only in patients in whom all other 
reasonable therapeutic options have been exhausted.
	
	In patients with pain requiring opioid therapy, adjunctive agents to minimize the 
use of opioid analgesia and treat coexisting depression can be used. Adjunctive 
agents include antidepressants or pregabalin or gabapentin. (For details, see chapter 
on palliative care).
	 2.	Patients with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency require pancreatic enzyme 
supplementation 40,000–50,000 USP units with each meal, and one-half that 
amount with snacks. The effectiveness is monitored clinically by an improvement 
in stool consistency, loss of visible fat in the stool, improvement in fat-soluble 
vitamin levels and gain in muscle strength and body weight. (Caution: Advise 
the patient to take the dose with the first bite of a meal. However, if consuming a 
meal takes more than 20 minutes, recommend taking half the number of capsules 
with the first bite and the other half in the middle of the meal to maximize 
digestion. If the non-enteric-coated preparation is chosen, add ranitidine or PPI 
to avoid acid denaturation of lipase. Although it is estimated that delivery of 
10% of normal pancreatic lipase output (approximately 90,000 USP units with 
each meal) can theoretically correct steatorrhoea and maldigestion, in practice, 
enzyme replacement therapy only rarely leads to normalization of digestion. The 
full 90,000 USP units (10% of the normal pancreatic enzyme output) may not be 
needed, as the remaining pancreas may still have some function and gastric lipase 
may compensate, but some patients may need more than 90,000 USP units.)
Diabetes management
Glucose intolerance occurs with some frequency in CP, but overt diabetes mellitus 
usually occurs late in the course of the disease. Monitor annual fasting glucose levels. 
Diabetes in patients with CP is usually insulin requiring but there is an increased risk of 
both treatment-related and spontaneous hypoglycaemia. Oral hypoglycaemic agents may 
be tried in these patients (for details, see the section ‘Diabetes Mellitus’ in Chapter 11).
Nutrition
	 1.	Restrict fat intake depending on the degree of the severity of fat malabsorption; 
generally, intake of 20 g/day or less is sufficient.
	 2.	Give pancreatic enzyme supplements for relief of the target symptoms or 
achievement of nutritional goals since residual pancreatic function is difficult 
to measure and changes with progression of the disease; the size and content of 
meals also vary. Pancreatic enzyme supplements come in various forms (including 
delayed release, enteric coated and non–enteric coated), which contain varying

Chapter 6  Gastrointestinal Diseases    421
concentrations of lipase, protease and amylase. Once the appropriate dose of 
pancreatic enzymes is determined, patients should be instructed on how to take the 
pancreatic enzymes. Enzymes should be taken with the first bite of a meal. 
	 3.	Vitamin D supplementation in patients with substantial steatorrhoea may require 
fat-soluble vitamin D analogues (calciferol).
	 4.	Vitamin E supplementation is required in patients with severe pancreatic 
insufficiency or cholestatic liver disease.
Endoscopic or surgical interventions
Refer patients with symptomatic, obstructed pancreatic duct or if there are peripancreatic 
collections for endoscopic or surgical drainage procedures through ERCP and/or EUS.
Surveillance for pancreatic cancer in certain types of CP
Screen high-risk groups for patients with pancreatic cancer using serum biomarker 
carbohydrate tumour-associated antigen (CA19.9) followed by EUS or MRI. High 
risk groups/patients are: smokers, CP, diabetes, obesity, intraductal papillary mucinous 
neoplasm, pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN), family history of pancreatic 
cancer and genetic features (p16/FAMM, BRCA2 and BRCA1/HBOC, STK11/Peutz–
Jeghers, MSH2, MLH1/HNPCC, APC/FAP mutations, PALB2 mutation, PRSS1/
SPINK1 mutations, p53/Li–Fraumeni).
Patient education
	
l Patients should be regularly followed up for appearance of any specific nutrient 
deficiency, especially deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins, and adequate supplements 
should be given, if required. 
	
l Patients should be explained about cessation of alcohol and smoking and may 
require behavioural therapy (for details, see Chapter 16).

GASTROINTESTINAL BLEEDING
GI bleeding can manifest in several forms and can be classified as overt (acute), 
occult (chronic) or obscure. Overt GI bleeding is visible and can present in the form 
of haematemesis, ‘coffee-ground’ emesis, melaena (black, tarry, sticky, foul-smelling 
stools) or haematochezia (presence of identifiable fresh/altered blood in stool). A 
minimum of 60 mL of blood is required in the stomach to produce melaena. Black 
stools may also be seen in patients taking some medications such as iron, charcoal or 
bismuth salts. Occult or chronic GI bleeding as a result of microscopic haemorrhage is 
not apparent and usually presents as positive faecal occult blood test (FOBT) with or

422    Standard Treatment Guidelines
without iron-deficiency anaemia. Obscure GI bleeding is recurrent bleeding when the 
source remains unidentified after upper endoscopy and colonoscopic evaluation and is 
usually from the small intestine. UGIB is defined as bleeding from any site from the 
pharynx to the duodenojejunal (DJ) flexure or up to the ligament of Treitz. Bleeding 
from the GI tract distal to the DJ flexure is called lower GI bleed (LGIB).
The most common causes of overt UGIB include PUD, oesophagogastric varices, 
erosive oesophagitis, Mallory–Weiss tear and neoplasms including gastric cancers. 
Chronic occult GI bleeding may occur anywhere in the GI tract, from the oral cavity to 
the anorectum. Causes of chronic occult GI bleeding can be broadly categorized into 
mass lesions, inflammatory, vascular and infectious. More common causes include 
colorectal cancer, severe oesophagitis, gastric or duodenal ulcers including from the 
use of aspirin and other NSAIDs, IBD, coeliac disease, vascular ectasias, diverticula 
and portal hypertensive gastropathy. Non-GI sources of blood loss such as haemoptysis 
and oropharyngeal bleeding can also cause a positive FOBT. The common causes of 
obscure GI bleeding are small bowel tumour, varices, diverticula and coeliac disease.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patient presents with occult or overt bleed or fresh blood. 
	
l Active bleed is indicated by the presence of fresh blood in vomitus, nasogastric 
tube aspirate, melaena and passage of fresh blood in stool.
	
l Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are the mainstay of diagnosis. Capsule endoscopy 
and deep enteroscopy are performed for diagnosis of obscure GI bleeding.
	
l A stepwise evaluation is followed to identify the cause of bleeding. The choice 
and sequence of procedures depends on clinical suspicion and symptoms. 
Patients with positive FOBT and no anaemia should first be investigated with a 
colonoscopy (upper endoscopy in case of upper GI symptoms), whereas patients 
with iron-deficiency anaemia require both upper endoscopy and colonoscopy.

Overt Upper GI Bleeding
Acute GI bleed is an emergency and needs active management.
Triage: Admit all patients with haemodynamic instability or active bleeding (manifested 
by haematemesis, bright red blood per nasogastric tube or haematochezia) to an ICU 
for resuscitation and close observation with BP, electrocardiographic monitoring and 
pulse oximetry.
I. Pre-endoscopic management (haemodynamic assessment and 
resuscitation)
	 1.	Begin immediate assessment of activity and severity of bleed and resuscitation as 
needed. 
	 2.	Maintain vital signs (blood pressure, airways, respiration, temperature).

Chapter 6  Gastrointestinal Diseases    423
	 3.	Insert a large-bore IV cannula and send the blood samples for Hb, TLC, platelets, 
coagulation profile, renal and liver function tests, blood grouping and cross-matching.
	 4.	Start IV fluids like normal saline/Ringer’s lactate/polymer from degraded gelatin.
	 5.	Administer blood transfusions if haemoglobin <7 g/dL or higher threshold if severe 
bleeding with hypotension. The transfusion target should be a haematocrit of 24% 
or a haemoglobin of 8 g/dL in case of variceal bleeding.
	 6.	Severity of GI bleed is assessed as mild (the patient has tachycardia but blood 
pressure is maintained), moderate (tachycardia with postural hypotension, 
tachypnoea, sweating, cold skin) and severe (hypotension and shock).
	 7.	Risk assessment: If Glasgow-Blatchford score ≤1, consider outpatient endoscopy 
and management. Erythromycin (as a prokinetic agent) and PPI may be considered. 
Patients with cirrhosis should receive vasoactive drugs and antibiotics.
Nasogastric or orogastric lavage is not required in patients with UGIB for 
diagnosis, prognosis, visualization, or therapeutic effect. 
II. Pharmacological treatment (pre-endoscopic immediate treatment)
	 1.	Inj. Rabeprazole 20 mg IV 6-hourly for 72 hours.
	 2.	Inj. Erythromycin 250 mg infusion 30–120 minutes before endoscopy to increase 
the diagnostic yield.
	 3.	If variceal bleed is suspected (chronic alcoholic, jaundice, splenomegaly, dilated 
abdominal veins, ascites, encephalopathy):
	
	Inj. octreotide 50 mcg IV immediately followed by 25 mcg/h infusion 
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Terlipressin 1–2 mg IV given 4–6 hourly
III. Endoscopic management
	 1.	Patients with UGIB should undergo early endoscopy within 24 hours of admission. 
Perform urgent endoscopy after resuscitation if the patient has severe bleeding with 
haemodynamic instability, and if there are any bleeding ulcers, varices and clots, and 
should be treated appropriately with thermocoagulation and sclerosant injection, clips, 
etc. In patients who are haemodynamically stable and without serious comorbidities, 
endoscopy should be performed as soon as possible in a non-emergent setting.
	 2.	Discharge from the emergency department without inpatient endoscopy may be 
considered in patients with urea nitrogen <18.2 mg/dL, haemoglobin ≥13 g/dL for 
men (12 g/dL for women), systolic blood pressure ≥110 mmHg, pulse <100 beats/
min and absence of melaena, syncope, cardiac failure and liver disease as they have 
<1% chance of requiring intervention.
	 3.	Patients receiving antiplatelet and anticoagulant (antithrombotic) medication in 
the management of cardiovascular disease are at a high risk of UGIB. In patients 
with the potential need for endoscopic therapy, if the situation allows, international 
normalized ratio (INR) should be corrected to <2.5, if possible before undertaking 
endoscopy, or time allowed to wane anticoagulant activity (usually over 1–2 days 
in the absence of renal disease for short-acting drugs).

424    Standard Treatment Guidelines
IV. Post-endoscopic management
	 1.	Patients who have ulcers with high-risk lesions (active bleeding, visible vessel, 
adherent clot) should receive high-dose parenteral PPIs for 72 hours followed by 
oral PPI using twice-daily oral PPIs through 14 days, followed by once-daily dose.
	 2.	Patients with cirrhosis should continue taking antibiotics for up to 7 days regardless 
of the bleeding source.
	 3.	Variceal bleeding should be treated with vasoactive drugs for up to 5 days.
	 4.	Patients at a low risk after endoscopy can be fed after 24 hours.
	 5.	Patients undergoing endoscopic haemostasis with high-risk stigmata should be 
hospitalized for at least 72 hours. 
	 6.	Certain high-risk patients with acute variceal bleed in cirrhosis (CTP-B with 
active spurt at endoscopy; CTP-C) require urgent pre-emptive TIPS and should be 
managed by specialists.
V. Long-term prevention of recurrent bleeding ulcers
	 1.	In case of H. pylori–associated bleeding ulcers, give H. pylori treatment (see the 
section ‘Peptic Ulcer’).
	 2.	In case of NSAID- and aspirin-associated bleeding, re-evaluate the need of 
NSAIDs. If cardiovascular risk outweighs the risk of bleeding, start with low-
dose aspirin soon after haemostasis is achieved. Early reintroduction of other 
antithrombotic drugs is also recommended after haemostasis is achieved to reduce 
thrombotic events and death.
	 3.	In patients on single or dual antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulants use PPI.
	 4.	In patients with idiopathic (non–H. pylori, non-NSAID) ulcers, use long-term 
antiulcer therapy (e.g. daily PPI).
	 5.	In patients with previous ulcer bleeding who require antiplatelet or anticoagulant 
therapy for cardiovascular prophylaxis, use PPI therapy.
Overt lower gastrointestinal bleeding
Acute LGIB may originate in the small bowel, colon, or rectum. Common causes 
of LGIB are diverticular disease, angiodysplasia or angiectasia, neoplasms, colitis 
including Crohn’s disease and UC, and benign anorectal lesions such as haemorrhoids, 
anal fissures and rectal ulcers.
	
l LGIB presents with haematochezia; however, bleeding from the right colon or the 
small intestine can present with melaena and bleeding from the left side of the colon 
tends to be bright red in colour. 
	
l It can present as an acute and life-threatening event.
	
l Chronic bleeding might manifest as iron-deficiency anaemia, faecal occult blood or 
intermittent scant haematochezia.

1.	In case of life-threatening bleeding, perform immediate volume resuscitation along 
with initial patient assessment.

Chapter 6  Gastrointestinal Diseases    425
	 2.	Perform colonoscopy for diagnosis for both acute and chronic bleeding.
	 3.	If colonoscopy fails or cannot be performed, perform angiography. The use of 
radioisotope scans is reserved for cases of unexplained intermittent bleeding when 
other methods have failed to detect the source. 
	 4.	To promote haemostasis, embolization or modern endoscopic techniques, such as 
injection therapy, thermocoagulation and mechanical devices, may be used.
	
	Surgery is performed in case of severe uncontrolled bleeding.

l Monitor pulse, blood pressure, urine output and severity and activity of bleed. The 
presence of identifiable blood/clots per rectum in a patient with UGIB indicates a 
severe ongoing bleed and need for very active management.
	
l Transfer the patient urgently (after starting the above-mentioned treatment) to a 
higher centre for further investigations and treatment in case of uncontrolled bleed, 
severe bleed, poor urine output and shock (see also Shock in Chapter 2).
Obscure gastrointestinal bleed
Obscure GI bleeding refers to recurrent bleeding with no identifiable source even 
on multiple diagnostic modalities including upper endoscopy, colonoscopy or small 
bowel radiography. It can be either overt or occult, depending on clinical presentation. 
Most cases of obscure GI bleeding are from the small intestine caused by vascular 
(angiodysplasia, telangiectasias), benign tumours, inflammatory lesions, Meckel’s 
diverticulum and medications.
Repeat endoscopy may be required in patients with initial negative colonoscopy 
and oesophagogastroduodenal endoscopy. Further evaluation with capsule endoscopy, 
CT/MR enteroclysis or Meckel’s scan as appropriate may be required.

TETANUS
It is an acute neurological disorder resulting from contamination of a wound (may be 
a trivial one) by an obligate anaerobic organism Clostridium tetani. People of all ages 
can get tetanus but the disease is particularly common and serious in newborn babies 
and their mothers when the mother is unprotected from tetanus. The average incubation 
period is 10 days ranging from 3 to 21 days depending on the injury site and the central 
nervous system. A shorter incubation period is associated with more severe disease, 
complications and a higher chance of death. In neonatal tetanus, symptoms usually 
appear in 7 days (range 4–14 days) after birth.
Tetanus can be categorized into the following four clinical types: (i) generalized, 
(ii) localized, (iii) cephalic and (iv) neonatal.
Neonatal tetanus is a form of generalized tetanus that occurs in newborns, resulting 
from infection due to the use of contaminated delivery instruments when dealing 
with the umbilical cord of newborns of unimmunized mothers. It is still common in 
developing countries and has a very poor prognosis.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Generalized tetanus, the most common form, usually starts with trismus or lockjaw 
followed by rigidity and violent, painful, generalized muscle spasms and seizures 
provoked by slightest stimulation. Generalized muscle spasms may compromise 
respiration. Fever and tachycardia may be present. Mentation is not impaired.
	
l Localized tetanus generally involves the extremity.
	
l Cephalic tetanus is a rare form of the disease that usually is associated with chronic 
otitis media or head trauma, and it has a poor prognosis.
	
l The presenting symptoms of neonatal tetanus include the inability to suck, poor 
feeding, irritability, rigidity, facial grimacing, severe spasms and opisthotonos. 
The neonate has the normal ability to suck and cry in the first 2 days of life, but 
loses this ability between days 3 and 28 and becomes rigid and has spasms.
	
l Prognosis and management depend on grade. Poor prognostic features are age >70 
years, heart rate >140/min, BP >140 mmHg, temperature >38.5°C and severe tetanus.

l In neonatal tetanus, poor prognostic features are pneumonia, recurrent apnoea, 
cyanosis and opisthotonos.
	
l Tetanus is diagnosed on the basis of clinical features and does not require 
laboratory confirmation.
	 1.	Grade I or mild: Muscle rigidity with few or no spasms.
	 2.	Grade II or moderate: Trismus, dysphagia, rigidity and short-lasting spasms are 
present.
	 3.	Grade III or severe: Frequent explosive spasms, autonomic dysfunction, 
particularly sympathetic over-activity, may be present.
	 4.	Grade IV or very severe: There occur features of grade III plus violent autonomic 
disturbances involving the CVS – severe hypo- or hypertension.
	
l Other presentations include local, cephalic (cranial nerves) or neonatal tetanus 
(within 2 weeks of life).
	
l Complications include respiratory failure, respiratory infections, barometric trauma 
due to prolonged ventilator support, persistent hypotension, labile hypertension, 
cardiac arrhythmia, sepsis and sudden death.
Treatment (medical emergency)
Tetanus is a medical emergency requiring:
	
l Hospitalization
	
l Immediate treatment with human tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG)
	
l Control of muscle spasms
	
l Aggressive wound care
	
l Antibiotics
Rule out seizures, meningitis and metabolic disorders, such as hypoglycaemia and 
hypocalcaemia in neonates.

l Admit in a quiet dark room/ICU with minimum tactile and auditory stimulation, 
cardiopulmonary monitoring, protection of airways/respiratory support 
(intubation/tracheostomy) with or without ventilation, and cleaning/exploration and 
debridement of wound.
	
l Maintain hydration and enteral/parenteral nutrition with a high-calorie and 
high-protein diet.
	
l Assess the wound type for appropriate care, considering cleanliness (clean or 
dirty) and depth (superficial or deep/penetrating). Dirty wounds, including those 
contaminated with dirt, faeces or saliva, pose a higher tetanus risk. Penetrating or 
puncture wounds may also carry an elevated risk.
	
l Clean all wounds thoroughly, removing dirt and foreign material, and debride 
necrotic tissue to minimize the risk of C. tetani proliferation.

1.	Inj. Crystalline penicillin 2 megaunits 6 hourly IV for 10 days.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Metronidazole 500 mg IV 8 hourly or 1 g 12 hourly.
	
	If a mixed infection is suspected, Cefazolin 1–2 g IV every 8 hours Or Cefuroxime 
2 g IV every 6 hours, Or Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV every 24 hours can be used. 
However, do not use antibiotics for prophylaxis against tetanus.
	 2.	Assess the need for administering Tetanus Immunoglobulin (TIG) for prophylaxis 
(in case of dirty wounds and in patients who either are unvaccinated or have not 
received a primary series of tetanus toxoid–containing vaccines).
	
	Inj. Human TIG (HTIG) 500 units IM.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Equine antiserum, 10,000 units IM after sensitivity test if Human TIG is not 
available. (Caution: Intradermal test dose of 0.1 mL in a 1:10 dilution should be 
administered prior to giving the full dose in order to evaluate for hypersensitivity 
reactions.)
	
	Note: Antiserum should be given before local manipulation of the wound with part 
of the dose infiltrated around the wound. HTIG should be administered at different 
sites than Tetanus toxoid.
	
	(Caution: Tetanus immunoglobulin does not produce natural immunity and a 
full course of immunization with Tetanus toxoid should be administered once the 
patient has recovered.)
	 3.	Begin or continue active immunization with an appropriate Tetanus Toxoid vaccine 
(i.e. DTaP, Tdap, Td), 0.5 mL IM at a separate site as soon as the person’s condition 
has stabilized as tetanus disease does not result in tetanus immunity and the person 
can be infected again. For those with an unknown tetanus vaccine history, assume 
no prior vaccination and administer 3-dose primary series.
Grade I tetanus: As above in the section ‘Non-pharmacological’:
	 1.	For control of muscle spasms, Tab. Diazepam 5–20 mg 3 times a day in mild 
tetanus; Inj. Diazepam 10–30 mg IV and repeated as needed every 1–4 hours can 
be given in increments of 5 mg, Or Lorazepam in 2-mg increments, titrated to 
achieve spasm control without excessive sedation and hypoventilation (high dosage 
up to 600 mg/day may be required). In children: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg every 2–6 hours; 
titrate upwards as needed. A continuous infusion of IV Midazolam can be given as 
it does not contain propylene glycol.
	
	Note: Patients with tetanus frequently exhibit tolerance to the sedative impact 
of benzodiazepines, often remaining awake and alert even with doses that would 
typically induce sedation or anaesthesia in other individuals. As these medications 
may be necessary for an extended duration, typically weeks, a gradual tapering is 
recommended to prevent withdrawal reactions.
	 2.	If spasms not controlled:
	
	Inj. Phenobarbitone 200 mg IM every 8–12 hours

Chapter 7  Infections – Bacterial, Viral and Parasitic Diseases     429
	
	Or 
	
	Inj. Chlorpromazine 50 mg IM in adults 4 times a day
	
	The ideal sedative and muscle relaxant schedule for each patient should be 
individualized. An objective goal is to decrease in rigidity is relaxation of 
abdominal muscles.
Grade II
	 1.	As above for Grade I
	 2.	Tracheostomy
	 3.	Inj. Magnesium sulphate 40 mg/kg IV loading dose followed by infusion of 
1.5 mg/h for patients ≤45 kg and 2 g/h for patients >45 kg to control muscle spasms
	
	(Caution: Monitor patellar reflex to avoid overdose. If areflexia develops, reduce 
dose.)
Grade III and Grade IV
	 1.	As above for Grade II
	 2.	Ventilator support
	 3.	Neuromuscular blocking agents when sedation alone is inadequate
	
	Inj. Pancuronium 2–4 mg IV
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Gallamine 20–40 mg IV
	 4.	In case of hypotension:
	
	Inj. Dopamine/Dobutamine 10–40 mcg/kg/min infusion titrated to maintain systolic 
BP of 100 mmHg.
	 5.	If bradyarrhythmias, Inj. Atropine 0.6–1.2 mg IV.
	 6.	If hypertension, see Chapter 3 for details.
Supportive care
	 1.	Early nutritional support is crucial due to the elevated energy demands in tetanus, with 
preference for enteral feeding. To prevent stress ulceration-related gastro-oesophageal 
haemorrhage, consider prophylactic treatment using sucralfate or acid blockers.
	 2.	Administer early thromboembolism prophylaxis with heparin, low-molecular-
weight heparin or other anticoagulants.
	 3.	Initiate physical therapy promptly after spasms cease, as patients with tetanus may 
experience prolonged muscle wasting and contractures leading to disability.
Patient education
	
l Tetanus is a preventable disease, but can be life-threatening when it occurs, It is 
most commonly acquired from a wound site and injuries of other tissues. Immunize 
all patients with tetanus toxoid during the convalescent period. If more than 5 years 
have elapsed since the last tetanus shot, a booster dose should be administered in 
the emergency department.
	
l Tetanus-prone wounds are wounds that have been present for longer than 6 hours; 
deep (>1 cm) wounds; grossly contaminated wounds; and wounds that are exposed 
to saliva or faeces, stellate, or ischaemic or infected (including abscesses, avulsions, 
punctures or crush injuries).

HIV AND AIDS
HIV has emerged as a global pandemic. It is transmitted from one infected person to 
another through penetrative sexual acts, both heterosexual and homosexual, through a 
contaminated blood transfusion or the sharing of needles and syringes, and from mother 
to child. Due to these restricted routes of transmission, the HIV epidemic was initially 
concentrated among high-risk groups. These ‘high-risk groups’, the population most 
vulnerable to HIV, are made up of sex workers (male and female), men having sex with 
men, transgenders and injecting drug users.
India has the second highest burden of HIV in the world with an estimated 2.47 
million people living with HIV in 2022; there were around 66,410 estimated annual 
new infections and 39,630 estimated annual AIDS-related deaths. India has a low 
prevalence of 0.2% with a higher prevalence concentrated only in those with high-risk 
behaviour. The availability of ART has dramatically changed the treatment outcome 
of patients with HIV infection and has significantly reduced the disease mortality. The 
‘Treat All’ policy was launched in 2017 with the aim to reduce the risk of infection and 
mortality related to HIV/AIDS.
SALIENT FEATURES
A case of HIV infection is defined as an individual with HIV infection irrespective of 
clinical stage (including severe or stage 4 clinical disease), confirmed by laboratory 
criteria. HIV infection is diagnosed based on laboratory criteria.
	
l Adults and children 18 months or older: All samples reactive in the first test 
should further undergo confirmatory second/third tests based on different 
principles/antigens using the same serum/plasma sample as that of the first test.
	 A testing strategy for diagnosis describes a sequence for the specific 
testing objective of diagnosis (as opposed to screening only), taking into 
consideration the presumed HIV prevalence in the population (for details 
see below).
	
l Clinically suspected or probable HIV infection using an AIDS-defining condition 
or HIV at any immunological stage in an adult or child requires confirmation of 
HIV infection by the best age-appropriate test.
	
l Clinical staging is used once HIV infection has been confirmed (Table 7.1). The 
clinical stage is useful for assessment at baseline (first diagnosis of HIV infection) 
or entry into long-term HIV care and in the follow-up of patients in care and 
treatment programmes.

l AIDS in adults and children is defined as the occurrence of life-threatening 
opportunistic infections (OIs), malignancies, neurological diseases and other 
specific illnesses in patients with HIV infection and CD4 counts <200 cells/mm3.
	
l Advanced HIV disease in adults, adolescents and children older than 5 years: 
For adults, adolescents and children 5 years or older, advanced HIV disease is 
defined as CD4 cell count <200 cells/mm3 or WHO stage 3 or 4 event.
	
l Advanced HIV disease in children younger than 5 years: All children younger 
than 5 years infected with HIV (who are not already receiving ART and clinically 
stable) are considered to have advanced disease.

Utility of CD4 measurement in the context of ‘Treat All’ and viral load as 
monitoring tool
Baseline CD4 is important to monitor treatment response, identify complications 
like immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), anticipate opportunistic 
infections (OI) infections, identify the need for OI prophylaxis and offer immunization 
advice. Serial CD4 measurements are more informative than individual values as they 
reflect trends over time. Where possible, these assessments should compare the same 
parameter. The CD4 measurement may be discontinued in a stable children living 
with HIV (CLHIV) older than 5 years on ART in whom regular viral load monitoring 
is advised.

434    Standard Treatment Guidelines
National Strategies and Algorithms for HIV Testing
Different rapid tests are available under the National AIDS Control Programme 
(NACP). The tests used should have a sensitivity of ≥99.5% and specificity of ≥98%. 
Window period represents the period between infection with HIV and the time when 
HIV antibodies can be detected in the blood (6–12 weeks). A blood test performed 
during the window period may yield a negative test result for HIV antibodies. These 
cases may require further testing after 12 weeks.
Objectives of Testing
	 1.	Transfusion and transplant safety
	 2.	Diagnosis of HIV infection in symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals
	 3.	Prevention of parent-to-child transmission (PTCT)
	 4.	For post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
	 5.	Epidemiological surveillance using unlinked anonymous HIV testing
	 6.	Research
HIV testing strategies (for adults/adolescents and children ≥18 months of age)
Confirmatory diagnosis of HIV infection is essential for ensuring access to care and 
treatment services. National HIV testing strategies enable the programme to screen 
for HIV or confirm the diagnosis of HIV at the nearest Integrated Counselling and 
Testing Centre (ICTC). In view of the low prevalence of HIV in India, it is necessary 
to use three different principles or antigen-based rapid tests to confirm the diagnosis. 
All samples reactive in the first test should further undergo confirmatory second/
third tests based on different principles/antigens using the same serum/plasma 
sample as the first test. The same blood sample is utilized for performing all the tests 
for identifying HIV antibodies. For indeterminate results, testing should be repeated on 
a second sample taken after 14–28 days.
A testing strategy for diagnosis describes a testing sequence for the specific 
testing objective of diagnosis (as opposed to screening only), taking into 
consideration the presumed HIV prevalence in the population. The national 
programme follows strategy I for screening and strategy II (A) for surveillance 
purposes, whereas it uses strategy II (B) and strategy III for diagnosis in symptomatic 
and asymptomatic persons, respectively. The following strategies should be used for 
HIV testing and diagnosis in adults and children older than 18 months:
	
l For clinically symptomatic individuals: The sample should be reactive with two 
different kits (strategy II (B).
	
l For clinically asymptomatic individuals: The sample should be reactive with three 
different kits (strategy III).
For clinically symptomatic individuals: A patient who is clinically symptomatic 
and suspected to have HIV infection/disease should be referred to the ICTC for 
confirmation of the diagnosis. In this case, the same blood sample is tested twice using

Chapter 7  Infections – Bacterial, Viral and Parasitic Diseases     435
kits with either different antigens or principles. The patient is declared HIV negative 
if the first test is non-reactive and HIV positive when both tests show reactive results. 
When there is discordance between the first two tests (first reactive and the second non-
reactive), a third test is done. If the third test is also negative, it is reported as negative. 
If the third test is reactive, it is reported as indeterminate and the individual is retested 
after 14–28 days, as shown in strategy II (B).
For clinically asymptomatic individuals: Confirmation of HIV diagnosis in 
asymptomatic individuals is done at an ICTC using three rapid tests of three different 
antigens or principles. The individual is considered HIV negative if the first test is non-
reactive and HIV positive when all three tests show reactive results. For indeterminate 
results, testing should be repeated on a second sample taken after 14–28 days, as shown 
in strategy III.
HIV testing (for infants/children younger than 18 months)
Maternal antibodies to HIV, transferred passively to the infant during pregnancy, 
usually persist for nearly 9–12 months in the infant. In some children, they may persist 
for as long as 18 months. Thus, during this period, children born to HIV-infected 
mothers will test positive for HIV antibodies regardless of their own infection status. A 
positive ELISA/rapid test that detects antibodies to HIV, therefore, does not necessarily 
indicate the presence of HIV infection in the infant/child. Rather, a positive ELISA/
rapid test indicates exposure to HIV. More reliable indicators of the HIV infection status 
of the infant are tests that detect HIV viral RNA or antigens.
Total nucleic acid (TNA) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test is performed on a 
dried blood spot (DBS) sample of the infant to detect viral nucleic acids for diagnosis 
of HIV-1 infection during infancy. This test is performed at 6 weeks of age or at the 
earliest opportunity when the infant and the mother come in contact with the health 
care system/workers. At and after 6 months of age, TNA PCR must be performed after 
screening for HIV antibodies. 
It is also important to take breastfeeding into consideration in the HIV testing 
algorithm. Since breast-fed children have an ongoing risk of HIV acquisition, they are 
tested (TNA PCR) 3 months after complete cessation of breastfeeding or 18 months 
of age, whichever is later, to reliably exclude HIV-1 infection. For more detailed 
information, refer to Chapter 2.1 on ‘HIV Exposure in Infants and Young Children’ and 
Annexure 1 and 1x of national guidelines for HIV care and treatment 2021.
Pre- and Post-Test HIV Counselling
A number of moral, legal, ethical and psychological issues are related to a positive 
HIV status; hence, any laboratory attempting to assess the HIV status of an individual 
should be conversant with these issues. Testing laboratories should ensure pre- and 
post-test counselling for every individual and confidentiality to be maintained while 
disclosing the results.

436    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Counselling is an integral part of prevention, diagnosis, management and support 
of people living with HIV/AIDS. All testing should follow five Cs of counselling: 
consent, confidentiality, counselling, correct test results and immediate connection 
to services for HIV prevention, treatment and care. Counselling aims to enable the 
person to take personal decisions related to HIV/AIDS, prevent the spread of infection 
by helping in change of behaviour and lifestyle and provide psychosocial support to 
individual and family. The spouses/partners of those with HIV-positive results and 
children of HIV-infected mothers should also be counselled and offered HIV testing. 
All persons found positive for HIV should be immediately linked to appropriate HIV 
care, support and treatment services. For more details, please refer to the national HIV 
Counselling and Testing Services (HCTS) guidelines, NACO, December 2016.
Components of pre-test counselling
	 1.	Assess risk and likelihood and meaning of positive, negative and indeterminate test 
results.
	 2.	Assess and educate regarding the understanding of HIV transmission and natural 
history, window period and differentiation between HIV infection and full-blown 
AIDS.
	 3.	Discuss confidentiality provisions and anonymous testing.
	 4.	Assess psychological stability, social support and impact of a positive result.
	 5.	Ensure follow-up and discuss risk reduction plan and referral to other services, if 
needed.
	 6.	Obtain informed consent for HIV antibody testing.
Components of post-test counselling
	 1.	The results of HIV testing should always be given in person and under all 
precautions of keeping confidentiality.
	 2.	Disclose test results and provide interpretation (positive, negative, indeterminate) 
in the context of that person’s risk of infection.
	 3.	If the test is negative, readdress and reinforce risk reduction plan especially 
regarding safer sexual practices. Discuss the need for repeat testing for those with 
recent (<6 months) exposure or ongoing risk behaviour.
	 4.	If the test is positive, counsel about the meaning of a positive HIV test; differentiate 
with full-blown AIDS and ways to avoid transmitting HIV to others. Assess need 
for psychological support and provide referrals for medical, psychological or social 
service, if necessary. Emphasize the importance of early clinical intervention and 
schedule follow-up visit to assess psychological status and to address partner 
notification issues.
PREVENTION OF PARENT-TO-CHILD 
TRANSMISSION (PPTCT) OF HIV
PTCT is a major route for transmission of new HIV infections in children. It contributes 
to about 4% of HIV infections in India. The Prevention of Parent to Child Transmission

condition: Prevention of Parent-to-Child Transmission (PPTCT) of HIV
text:
Chapter 7  Infections – Bacterial, Viral and Parasitic Diseases     437
(PPTCT) programme is being implemented under the NACP to achieve the goal of 
elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT). Children born to women living 
with HIV acquire HIV infection from their mother, during pregnancy, during labour/
delivery or through breastfeeding, which is largely preventable with appropriate 
intervention, by providing ART to mothers and antiretroviral prophylaxis to infants.
PPTCT of HIV under the NACP involves provision of free counselling and testing 
services, detection of HIV-positive status, and administration of ART to all HIV-positive 
pregnant women and ARV prophylaxis to their infants to prevent vertical transmission 
of HIV. 
The essential package of PPTCT services includes:
	
l Offer routine HIV counselling and testing to all pregnant women enrolled into 
antenatal care (ANC) with ‘opt out’ option.
	
l Ensure involvement of the spouse and other family members and move from an 
‘ANC-centric’ to a ‘family-centric’ approach.
	
l Provide lifelong ART, as per the national guidelines, to all pregnant and 
breastfeeding HIV-infected women regardless of CD4 count and clinical stage 
(Fig. 7.1).
	
l Provide care for associated conditions (like STI/RTI, TB and other OIs, 
hypertension, diabetes).
	
l Promote institutional deliveries of all HIV-infected pregnant women (ANMs/
ASHAs, community workers to accompany to institutions; reduction of stigma 
and discrimination among health care providers through sensitization and capacity 
building).
	
l Perform viral load testing at 32–36 weeks of gestation to determine the risk of HIV 
transmission to the baby.
	
l Provide ARV prophylaxis to infants as per the national guidelines.
	
l Provide nutrition counselling and psychosocial support to HIV-infected pregnant 
women (linkages with ANMs, ASHAs, community outreach workers, DLNs (district 
level networks) to advise them on the right foods to take and go to Anganwadi 
centres for nutritional support and to the district-level network of Positive People 
for peer counselling and psycho-social support).
	
l Provide counselling and support for initiation of exclusive breast-feeds within an 
hour of delivery as the preferred option and continue for 6 months. After 6 months, 
complementary feeding should be given along with breastfeeding. Mothers living 
with HIV should breastfeed for at least 12 months and may continue breastfeeding 
for up to 24 months or beyond, like the general population, while being fully 
supported for ART adherence. 
	
l Integrate follow-up of HIV-exposed infants into routine health care services 
including immunization.
	
l Ensure initiation of Co-trimoxazole prophylactic therapy (CPT) and early infant 
diagnosis (EID) using HIV TNA PCR at 6 weeks of age onwards as per the NACO 
EID guidelines.
	
l Strengthen community follow-up and outreach through local community networks 
to support HIV-positive pregnant women and their families.

Chapter 7  Infections – Bacterial, Viral and Parasitic Diseases     439
	
l Counselling for institutional delivery so that interventions for PPTCT can be undertaken
	
l Counselling on infant feeding practices and ARV prophylaxis for the child
	
l Safe obstetric practices
Interventions during labour and delivery
Under the cover of maternal ART, the care given to HIV-infected mothers and their 
babies is like the care given to uninfected mothers and their babies. Normal vaginal 
delivery is considered unless the woman has obstetric indications (like foetal distress, 
obstructed labour) for a caesarean section.
When delivering HIV-infected women, follow safe delivery techniques as below:
	
l Follow standard work precautions.
	
l Minimize vaginal examinations and use aseptic techniques.
	
l Avoid prolonged labour; consider oxytocin to shorten labour.
	
l Avoid artificial rupture of membranes.
	
l Use non-invasive foetal monitoring and avoid invasive procedures.
	
l Support perineum and avoid routine episiotomy.
	
l Avoid instrumental delivery as much as possible unless indicated. If indicated, low 
cavity outlet forceps is preferable to ventouse as it is generally associated with lower 
rates of foetal trauma than ventouse.
Care of the newborn during delivery
	
l Suctioning the newborn with a nasogastric tube should be avoided unless there is 
meconium staining of the liquor. If suctioning the baby is a must, then we need to 
keep the suction pressure below 100 mmHg pressure or use a bulb suction.
	
l Avoid milking the cord and delayed cord clamping. Perform early cord clamping 
after it stops pulsating and after giving the oxytocin injection immediately after 
delivery as part of active management of third stage of labour.
	
l Infants should be handled with gloves until all blood and maternal secretions have 
been washed off. Always cover the cord with gloved hands and gauze before cutting 
the cord to avoid blood splattering.
	
l Wipe and clean the baby’s mouth and nostrils as soon as the head is delivered.
	
l Initiate feeding within the first hour of birth according to the preferred and 
informed choice of the couple.
Infant ARV prophylaxis
In addition to maternal ART, the HIV-exposed infant must also be given prophylactic 
ARV drugs to further reduce chances of HIV transmission during the perinatal period 
and breastfeeding. The key factors for consideration when deciding the duration of 
prophylaxis are assessing the risk of the infant at delivery based on viral load test 
result available within 4 weeks prior to delivery and time to viral suppression with 
Dolutegravir (DTG) or non-DTG-based maternal ART regimens.
	
l Dual ARV prophylaxis for infants at a high risk of HIV transmission and a single-
drug ARV prophylaxis for infants at a low risk of HIV transmission is recommended.

Chapter 7  Infections – Bacterial, Viral and Parasitic Diseases     441
Immunization and vitamin A supplementation
Immunize all HIV-exposed children according to the National Immunization Schedule 
before HIV infection causes severe immune suppression (for details, see ‘Immunization 
Schedule’ in Chapter 19).
	
l HIV-exposed infants, like all other infants, should be given BCG at birth. If BCG 
has not been given at birth, or for neonates with HIV infection confirmed by early 
virological testing, BCG vaccination should be delayed until ART has been started 
and the infant confirmed to be immunologically stable (CD4 >25%). For children 
who are receiving ART, and have not received BCG earlier, it may be given once 
they are clinically well and immunologically stable (CD4% >25% for children 
younger than 5 years or CD4 count ≥200 cells/mm3 for those older than 5 years). 
	
l Severely immunocompromised HIV-infected infants, children, adolescents and 
young adults as defined above should not receive measles virus–containing vaccine, 
because vaccine-related pneumonia has been reported. An additional dose of measles-
containing vaccine should be administered to HIV-infected children receiving ART 
following immune reconstitution (CD4 count 20–25%). Likewise, a supplemental 
dose of measles-containing vaccine may be considered in HIV-exposed infants or 
soon after diagnosis of HIV infection in children older than 6 months who are not 
receiving ART and for whom the risk of measles is high, with the aim to provide 
partial protection till they are revaccinated.
	
l Rotavirus vaccine, though a live vaccine, is recommended for use in HIV-exposed 
infants due to their vulnerability to diarrhoea. Nevertheless, like all live vaccines, it 
should not be given in children with known severe immunodeficiency.
	
l Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) is given at 2, 4 and 6 months, with 
booster at 12–15 months. Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) should 
be administered at least 8 weeks after the last dose of PCV to children with HIV 
infection aged 2 years or older.
	
l Inactive Japanese encephalitis (JE) vaccine is safe for use in children with HIV infection. 
A reduced immune response may be seen in HIV-infected children. However, most 
children with immune recovery after ART develop a protective antibody response. A live 
attenuated JE vaccine is also now available. This should be avoided in children with HIV.
	
l Vitamin A supplementation should be as per the National Immunization Schedule.
	
l Check for seroconversion and give boosters as required especially for hepatitis B. A 
4-dose, double-quantity schedule for hepatitis B has been recommended in view of 
poor seroconversion with routine immunization.
Desirable vaccines not currently available through the national schedule include the 
following:
	
l Inactivated hepatitis A vaccine (2 doses 6 months apart between 12 and 23 months)
	
l Inactivated influenza vaccine (starting at 6 months of age, 2 doses 1 month apart; 
9 years and older, single dose; annual booster with single dose)
	
l Varicella vaccine: Administer the first dose at age 15–18 months and the second 
dose at age 4–6 years. Since this is a live attenuated vaccine, it is given only to 
asymptomatic children who are not severely immunocompromised.

442    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l A single dose of Hib is indicated in unimmunized children older than 5 years (those 
who have not completed the primary series and the 15-month booster of Hib earlier).
	
l Meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) should be administered 2 doses at 
least 8 weeks apart between 9 and 23 months of age, and a booster 2–5 years after 
the primary series.
	
l The 3-dose series of human papillomavirus vaccine; tetanus toxoid, reduced 
diphtheria toxoid and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine; and meningococcal 
conjugate vaccine all are indicated in HIV-infected adolescents.
	 Note: Since these children may not have an adequate response to vaccines, they may 
remain susceptible to infections despite having been immunized. Positive serological 
test results in these children are not always reliable markers of protection.
ASSESSMENT FOR INITIATION OF CO-TRIMOXAZOLE 
(CPT) PROPHYLAXIS AND ART
Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is an effective and proven strategy for reducing morbidity 
and mortality in children with HIV infection. It protects the infants and children 
not only from Pneumocystis jirovecii infection but also from malaria, diarrhoea due 
to Isospora and Cyclospora, toxoplasmosis and other bacterial diseases. All HIV-
exposed infants should get Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis from the age of 6 weeks. 
The recommended dose is 5 mg/kg/day as a single daily dose. Prior to starting CPT, 
evaluation must be done based on Figure 7.2.
Clinical staging can be used to guide when to start Co-trimoxazole. Indications 
for Co-trimoxazole (CPT) prophylaxis and duration of prophylaxis are shown in 
Tables 7.4–7.6.
Antiretroviral therapy
The goals of ART are:
	 1.	Clinical goals: Increased survival and improvement in quality of life
	 2.	Virological goals: Greatest possible sustained reduction in viral load
	 3.	Immunological goals: Immune reconstitution, which is both qualitative and quantitative
	 4.	Preventive goals: Reduction of HIV transmission by suppression of viral load
	 5.	Therapeutic goals: Rational sequencing of drugs in a fashion that achieves 
clinical, virological and immunological goals while maintaining future treatment 
options, limiting drug toxicity and facilitating adherence
Thorough assessment needed before starting ART and goals of this assessment
	 1.	Determine the clinical stage of HIV infection.
	 2.	Perform a detailed history and physical examination that focuses on past significant 
illness (especially related to HIV); identify current, ongoing HIV-associated illnesses 
or OIs that require treatment; and identify other coexisting medical conditions.
	 3.	Determine the need for OI prophylaxis.

	 4.	Perform laboratory investigations (Tables 7.7 and 7.8) – including a CD4 count – 
to determine the staging of the disease and to rule out the OIs and baseline safety 
parameters.
	 5.	Identify and manage other high-risk behaviours – injecting drug use, unprotected 
sex, etc.
Considerations before initiation of ART
All people with confirmed HIV infection should be referred to the ART centre for 
registration into HIV care, comprehensive clinical and laboratory evaluation to assess 
baseline status, treatment of pre-existing OIs, treatment preparedness, counselling and 
rapid ART initiation, preferably the same day unless contraindicated otherwise.

Baseline investigations – essential tests for all patients registering in HIV care at ART centre
•	 Haemogram/CBC
•	 Urine for routine and microscopic examination
•	 Fasting blood sugar
•	 Blood urea, serum creatinine
•	 Serum bilirubin, ALT (SGPT)
•	 VDRL

•	 X-ray chest PA view

specimen using nucleic acid amplification test (CBNAAT/Truenat) and/or other required investigations
•	 Complete liver function test (LFT) for those being initiated on antitubercular treatment (ATT) 
and for patients with hepatitis B or C co-infection
•	 Lipid profile (if available)
•	 Ultrasonography (USG) whole abdomen
•	 rK-39 strip test to confirm or rule out leishmaniasis (especially in patients with HIV infection who 
live in or travel to endemic areas, i.e. Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and West Bengal)
•	 Pregnancy test (if applicable)
•	 For women, cervical Pap smear or other method of cervical cancer screening (if available)
•	 For men having sex with men (MSM), anal Pap smear (if available)
Non-availability/non-feasibility of any of these tests should not delay the initiation of art.

health facility where the centre is located, with support from the state health department.

The following principles need to be kept in mind:
	
l The patient should be adequately prepared, and informed consent should be obtained 
from the patient or from the caregiver in case the patient is a minor, before initiating

l Treatment should be started based on the person’s informed decision and preparedness 
to initiate ART with information and understanding of the benefits of treatment, 
lifelong course of medication, issues related to adherence and positive prevention.
	
l A caregiver should be identified for each person to provide adequate support. 
Caregivers must be counselled and trained to support treatment adherence, follow-up 
visits and shared decision making.

symptom tool (current cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss) and those who do 
not have TB need to be started on tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT)/Isoniazid 
preventive therapy in addition to ART.
	
l ART should not be started in the presence of an active OI. In general, OIs should 
be treated or stabilized before commencing ART. Mycobacterium avium complex

450    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Patients starting on DTG should be monitored for blood glucose (6 monthly) and 
weight gain (on monthly visits). Appropriate physical activity should be advised to 
prevent weight gain.
	
l Guidance on laboratory investigations is mentioned in the laboratory investigations 
as described above.
Treatment failure to first-line and second-line ART
The working definitions of first-line and second-line ART regimens are as follows:
	
l First-line ART: First-line ART is the initial regimen prescribed for an ART-naive 
patient.
	
l Second-line ART: Second-line ART is the subsequent regimen used in sequence 
immediately after first-line therapy has failed.
	
l Third-line ART: Third-line ART is the subsequent regimen used in sequence 
immediately after second-line therapy has failed.
Substitution versus switch
Any change of ARVs prescribed should be carefully distinguished between substituting 
a drug within a given regimen and switching an entire ART regimen:
	
l Substitution: Substitution refers to replacement of ARV drug(s) in a virally 
suppressed PLHIV due to adverse effects of a drug, drug–drug interactions or 
programme policy. This does not indicate change of regimen due to treatment failure. 
Any substitution after 6 months should be preceded by viral load testing. This helps 
to understand whether a single drug substitution is enough (if plasma viral load 
<1000 copies/mL) or whether the patient must be checked for treatment failure (if 
plasma viral load ≥1000 copies/mL).
	
l Switch: Treatment failure refers to the loss of antiviral efficacy (plasma viral load 
≥1000 copies/mL) to the current regimen. When the regimen is changed because of 
ARV treatment failure, it is referred to as the switch of the entire regimen.
Monitoring: Broad principles and objective
All patients initiated on first-line ART need to be monitored carefully at every visit as 
per standard protocol on clinical and laboratory monitoring indicators. As emphasized 
earlier, a high index of suspicion is needed to detect first-line failure early.
Suspect the possibility of failure of the regimen whenever a patient is found to have:
	
l Increasing trend of plasma viral load (just around 1000 copies/mL)
	
l Static/declining trend in CD4 counts
	
l New clinical manifestations (symptoms and/or signs)/worsening of existing condition
	
l Issues related to undetected OIs, and suboptimal treatment adherence, which need 
to be addressed
Note: It is important to make appropriate pre-workup and timely referral to SACEP 
for evaluation of such patients following the SACEP guidelines. Once the patient 
has undergone viral load test and been evaluated by SACEP, if required, one of the

following possible decisions will be conveyed by the SACEP of Centres of Excellence 
(CoE)/Paediatric CoE (pCoE)/ART Plus centre to the referring ART centre:
	 1.	Switch to the ‘prescribed’ second-line or third-line ART.
	 2.	Regimen change is not required.
	 3.	Continue the current ART, reinforce adherence and re-evaluate.
	 4.	Evaluate for HIV-2.
Once the decision has been made to change the regimen, the decision will be 
communicated to the referring centre. The second-line ART can be initiated at the ART 
centre while for the third-line ART, initiation will be done at CoE/ART Plus Centre.
The objective of the second- and third-line ART is to prolong the survival of the 
PLHIV as much as possible with complete suppression of viral replication. This requires 
regular monitoring with viral load every 6 months for all patients on second/third-line ART.
Formulation of second-line ART for PLHIV failing first-line ART
Formulation of second-line ART is based on the following:
	
l First-line ART in adults and adolescents recommends a three-drug combination 
therapy from two classes of ARV drugs for initial treatment, i.e. 2NRTI + 1INSTI.
	
l Patients on 2NRTI + 1NNRTI (non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors) 
should be transitioned to INSTI-based regimen after viral load testing.
	
l Document all changes in drugs/regimen taken by a patient during the course of 
treatment to identify the most optimum regimen for the second/third-line regimen.

Monitoring of patients on second-line ART
	
l All patients on second-line ART need to undergo viral load testing every 6 months.
	
l The viral load algorithm shall be followed based on the result.
	
l Patients with unsuppressed viral load should undergo enhanced adherence counselling.
	
l Once optimum adherence is achieved for 3 consecutive months, repeat viral load 
test should be done.
Workup of patients with suspected second-line failure
	
l All cases with suspected second-line failure need to be thoroughly evaluated for 
treatment adherence and presence of any major OI. If adherence is good and there 
is no major OI, such patients with second-line treatment failure should be referred 
to CoE/ART Plus first electronically with the referral form containing the latest 
relevant reports and complete history of treatment.

be taken to improve adherence and/or treat OI. Such patients should be closely 
monitored clinically, immunologically and virologically. If no improvement is 
seen within 3 months, the case should be referred to CoE/ART Plus for further 
assessment.

text:
454    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l In view of the introduction of DTG and optimization of ART, initiation and 
dispensation of third-line ART is being decentralized to all the ART centres.
Initiation of third-line ART
	
l Third-line regimens should include new drugs with minimal risk of cross-resistance 
to previously used regimens such as INSTIs and second-generation NNRTIs and PIs.
	
l Under the national programme, it has been decided to provide INSTI (DTG) and a 
new boosted PI (Darunavir/Ritonavir). Accordingly, the regimen is DTG (50 mg) 1 
tablet once a day + Darunavir (600 mg) + Ritonavir (100 mg), 1 tablet each twice daily.
	
l As per WHO recommendations, in some cases, the existing NRTI backbone can also 
be continued for the possible retention of some ARV activity; however, it should be 
used judiciously for the possible risk of cumulative toxicities of NRTI backbone. 
Therefore, the third-line prescription must be a more balanced one for long-term 
management and acceptance.
	
l In cases with difficulty in assessment of second-line failure, complicated prior 
treatment regimens, patients referred from private, multi-NRTI exposed cases, any 
intolerance to third-line drugs, cases requiring these third-line drugs as alternate 
within the second-line ART or any other query, SACEP at CoE can obtain expert 
opinion from the National AIDS Clinical Expert Panel (NACEP) electronically, by 
addressing nacep.naco@gmail.com.
	
l The guidance given next should be utilized. Various scenarios that can be 
encountered while prescribing third-line regimen and respective guidance are 
provided in Table 7.15.
OCCUPATIONAL HIV EXPOSURE AND HIV 
POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS (PEP)
PEP refers to the comprehensive management given to minimize the risk of infection 
following potential exposure to blood-borne pathogens (HIV, HBV, HCV). This includes 
counselling, risk assessment, relevant laboratory investigations based on informed consent 
of the source and exposed person, first aid and, depending on the risk assessment, the 
provision of short term (4 weeks) of antiretroviral drugs, with follow-up and support. 
Administer the first dose as soon as possible after exposure, within 72 hours. Once 
commenced, the full PEP should be taken unless there are specific reasons to stop.
The following stepwise approach to occupational exposure is recommended:
Step 1: Management of exposure site – first aid immediately
Do not panic.
For skin – if the skin is broken after a needlestick or sharp instrument
Immediately wash the wound and surrounding skin with water and soap and rinse well. 
Do not scrub; do not use antiseptics or skin washes (bleach, chlorine, alcohol, betadine).
After a splash of blood or body fluids to unbroken skin
Wash the area immediately; do not use antiseptics.

For the eye
Irrigate the exposed eye immediately with water or normal saline. Sit in a chair, tilt the 
head back and ask a colleague to gently pour water or normal saline over the eye. If 
wearing contact lens, leave them in place while irrigating, as they form a barrier over 
the eye and will help protect it. Once the eye is cleaned, remove the contact lens and 
clean them in the normal manner. This will make them safe to wear again. Do not use 
soap or disinfectant on the eye.
For mouth
Spit the fluid out immediately; rinse the mouth thoroughly, using water or saline, and spit 
again. Repeat this process several times. Do not use soap or disinfectant in the mouth.

text:
456    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Step 2: Establish eligibility for PEP as soon as possible
A designated person/trained doctor must assess the risk of HIV and HBV transmission 
following an accidental exposure to blood (AEB). This evaluation must be made 
rapidly, to start any treatment as soon as possible after the accident. This assessment 
must be thorough (because not every AEB requires prophylactic treatment). 
The first dose of PEP should be administered ideally within 2 hours (but 
preferably within the first 72 hours) of exposure and the risk evaluated as soon as 
possible. If the risk is insignificant, PEP could be discontinued if already commenced. 
PEP needs to be started as soon as possible after the exposure and within 72 hours. In 
animal studies, initiating PEP within 12, 24 or 36 hours of exposure was more effective 
than initiating PEP 48 or 72 hours following exposure. Thus, PEP is more effective 
when given within 72 hours after exposure.
Two main factors determine the type of exposure and the HIV status of the source 
patient.
Assessing the severity of exposure and risk of transmission
Severity of occupational exposure for health care providers (HCP) can be categorized and 
described based on the amount of blood/fluid involved and the entry port (Table 7.16).
Assessing the HIV status of the source of exposure (Table 7.17)
A baseline rapid HIV testing of the source of exposure should be done before starting 
PEP, if possible. Informed consent should be obtained before testing of the source as 
per national HIV testing guidelines. Initiation of PEP, where indicated, should not be 
Table 7.16.  Categories of exposures.
Category of 
exposure
Definition and example
Mild exposure
Exposure to mucous membrane/non-intact skin with small volumes, 
contact with the eyes or mucous membranes or subcutaneous injections 
following small-bore needles
Moderate exposure
Exposure to mucous membrane with large volumes or percutaneous 
superficial exposure with solid needle, e.g. a superficial cut or needlestick 
injury penetrating glove
Severe exposure
Percutaneous exposure with large volume, e.g.:
•	 An accident with a high-calibre needle (>18 G) visibly contaminated 
with blood
•	 A deep wound (haemorrhagic wound and/or very painful); transmission 
of a significant volume of blood
•	 An accident with material that has previously been used intravenously 
or intra-arterially
Note: The wearing of gloves is one of the standard workplace precautions, but glove punctures do happen. 
  In case of an AEB with material such as discarded sharps/needles and dried contaminated blood, the transmission 
risk remains for a week for HIV; the risk remains more significant for HBV and HCV, as they survive longer than 
HIV outside the body.

shall be preferably initiated within 72 hours of exposure.
Assessment of the exposed individual
The exposed individual should have confidential counselling and assessment by an 
experienced physician. He/she should be assessed for pre-existing HIV infection (see 
Step 5) intended for people who are HIV negative at the time of their potential exposure 
to HIV. Exposed individuals who are known or discovered to be HIV positive should not 
receive PEP. They should be offered counselling and information on the prevention of 
transmission and referred for clinical and laboratory assessment for subsequent linkage 
to comprehensive HIV services. 
Besides the medical assessment, counselling (see Step 3) of exposed HCP is 
essential to allay fear and start PEP (if required) at the earliest.
Step 3: Counselling for PEP
For an informed consent, exposed persons (clients) should receive appropriate 
information about what PEP is and the risk and benefits of PEP. It should be clear 
that PEP is not mandatory. The client should understand details of the window period, 
baseline test, drugs that are used, their safety and efficacy, and issues related to these 
drugs during pregnancy and breastfeeding. He/she should be counselled on safe sexual 
practices till both baseline and 3-month HIV test are found to be negative. 
Psychological support: Many people will feel anxious after exposure. Every exposed 
person needs to be informed about the risks and the measures that can be taken. This 
will help to relieve part of the anxiety, but some may require further specialized 
psychological support.
Documentation on record is essential: Special leave from work, if required, should be 
considered for a period of, say, 2 weeks (initially), and then as required based on assessment 
of the exposed person’s mental state, side effects and requirements. For the recording and 
reporting framework, please refer to NACO operational guidelines for ART services. 
Step 4: Assessing need for PEP and prescribing PEP
Deciding on PEP regimen
The decision on the need for PEP for HIV (following an occupational exposure in 
health care worker) will depend on the exposure, the source person’s HIV status and

Chapter 7  Infections – Bacterial, Viral and Parasitic Diseases     459
Key considerations while prescribing PEP
	
l PEP should be started preferably within 72 hours of exposure.
	
l If HCP presents after 72 hours of exposure, PEP can still be used after counselling 
about its effectiveness.
	
l PEP should be made available in the emergency department, labour room, intensive 
care units and operation theatres (OTs).
	
l The exposed person should go to the designated clinic/officer, at the earliest, for a 
complete risk assessment, HIV counselling, testing and PEP.
	
l All hospital staff members must know whom to report to for PEP and where PEP 
drugs are available.
Expert opinion may be obtained for the following situations:
	
l Delay in reporting exposure (>72 hours)
	
l Unknown source (use of PEP should be decided on a case-by-case basis after 
considering the severity of exposure and the epidemiological likelihood of HIV 
transmission; do not delay PEP initiation if indicated)
	
l Source patient being on ART or possibly having HIV drug resistance (refer/consult 
as soon as possible)
	
l Major toxicity of PEP regimen (minor side effects may be managed symptomatically; 
refer to an expert for non-tolerance or non-adherence)
	
l Refer/consult if in doubt or complicated cases (e.g. major psychological problem)
PEP must be initiated as soon as possible, preferably within 72 hours.
Regimen for PEP
	
l As PEP for HIV has its greatest effect if begun within 2 hours of exposure, it is 
essential to act immediately. There is little benefit if more than 72 hours have 
lapsed but PEP can still be used if the health care worker presents after 72 hours of 
exposure. The prophylaxis needs to be continued for 28 days.
	
l Report exposure immediately to the appropriate authority.
	
l Never delay the start of therapy due to debate over regimen. In cases with exposure 
from the patient on ART, start the available three-drug regimens and seek opinion 
after that.

Step 5: Laboratory evaluation
	
l The reason for HIV testing soon after occupational exposure is to establish a 
‘baseline’ against which future test results can be compared. When offered HIV 
testing, the exposed person should receive standard pre-test counselling according 
to the national HIV testing and counselling guidelines and should give informed 
consent for testing. Confidentiality of the test result must be ensured.
	
l There are possibly different reasons for delaying HIV testing: the HCP may be unable 
to give informed consent immediately after the exposure due to anxiety or the exposure 
occurs outside working hours or in settings where HIV testing is not readily available. 
The HIV test may be done up to several days after the exposure, depending on the 
informed consent and with pre- and post-test counselling, ensuring confidentiality. 
	
l Do not delay PEP if HIV testing is not available. 
	
l HIV RNA testing by PCR during PEP has a very poor positive predictive value and 
should be strongly discouraged. Pregnancy testing should also be available, but its

Step 6: Follow-up of an exposed person
Whether or not PEP has been started, follow-up is indicated to monitor possible 
infections and to provide psychological support.
Clinical follow-up
	
l In addition, in the weeks following an AEB, the exposed person must be monitored 
for the eventual appearance of signs indicating an HIV seroconversion – acute 
fever, generalized lymphadenopathy, cutaneous eruption, pharyngitis, non-specific 
flu symptoms and ulcers of the mouth or genital area. These symptoms appear in 
50–70% of individuals with a primary (acute) HIV infection, almost always within 
3–6 weeks after exposure. When a primary (acute) infection is suspected, referral to 
an ART centre for an expert opinion should be arranged immediately.
	
l An exposed person should be advised to take precautions (e.g. avoid blood or tissue 
donations, breastfeeding, unprotected sexual relations or pregnancy) to prevent 
secondary transmission, especially during the first 3 months following exposure. 
Condom use is essential.
	
l Counselling regarding adherence and side effects should be provided and reinforced 
at every follow-up visit. If PEP is prescribed, the exposed HCP should be followed 
up every week with laboratory tests recommended as shown in Table 7.20; 
psychological support and mental health counselling are often required.

CO-INFECTION WITH TUBERCULOSIS AND HIV
PLHIV are 18 (15–21) times more likely to develop active TB disease than people 
without HIV. TB accelerates HIV disease progression and HIV paves the way for 
clinical TB and mycobacteraemia. TB is the most common OI in PLHIV. It is also 
well recognized that HIV and TB make a fatal combination with extremely high death 
rates. TB is a primary and leading cause of AIDS-related deaths among PLHIV. India 
accounted for an estimated 71,000 patients with incident TB among PLHIV in 2019. 
Early diagnosis, effective TB treatment, prompt linkage to HIV care and early initiation 
of ART and TPT are key factors for reducing the negative impact of TB in PLHIV.

464    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l All PLHIV should be regularly screened for TB during every visit to the ART 
centres using the four-symptom complex – current cough, fever, weight loss 
and	 night sweats among adults. In children, the four-symptom complex includes 
current cough, fever, poor weight gain and history of contact with a TB case.
	
l Confirmation is done by NAAT/other appropriate investigations for TB diagnosis. 
Sputum in adults; two samples are recommended – one on the spot and one early 
morning (day 2).
	
l Chest X-ray shows miliary pattern, hilar adenopathy, pleural effusion, focal 
infiltrates in upper and hilar regions, multilobar infiltrates, interstitial infiltrates and 
cavitation with severe immunosuppression. However, X-ray might appear normal.
	
l Atypical presentation is seen if there is severe immunosuppression.

HIV-TB coinfected patients
ART reduces the incidence and recurrence of TB, as well as case fatality rates. It also 
facilitates immunological reconstitution and decreases AIDS-defining illness and 
mortality. This benefit is seen across different ranges of CD4 counts.
All PLHIV diagnosed with active TB should be initiated on ART regardless of CD4 
count, after initiation of TB treatment in accordance with the National TB Elimination 
Programme (NTEP) guidelines (see Chapter 1). ART should be started as soon as 
possible, keeping in mind the time needed for acceptance of the diagnosis, counselling 
needs, pill burden, drug interactions/additive toxicities with antitubercular treatment 
(ATT) and TB-associated IRIS (TB-IRIS). The timing of initiation of ART in relation 
to ATT and the recommended ART regimens in HIV-TB cases in adults and adolescents 
are given in Table 7.22.

ART regimen in PLHIV receiving first-line (Rifampicin-containing) ATT
	
l DTG-based regimen (with NRTI backbone) is the preferred regimen for all PLHIV 
on first-line (Rifampicin-containing) ATT. However, Rifampicin (RIF) is a potent 
inducer of drug-metabolizing enzymes and drug transporters, and co-administration 
with DTG reduces bioavailability of DTG, which can be overcome by doubling the 
DTG dose to 50 mg twice daily. Therefore, patients on Rifampicin-containing ATT 
should receive an additional tablet of DTG 50 mg (at an interval of 12 hours with 
the regular dose of DTG) till the completion of ATT. Once the ATT is completed, 
additional tablet of DTG 50 mg should be stopped 2 weeks after stoppage of 
Rifampicin-containing treatment regimen.
	
l Rifampicin is a liver cytochrome enzyme inducer and suppresses bioavailability of 
PIs, thereby decreasing the efficacy of ART. Therefore, if a patient co-infected with 
HIV on first-line ATT needs to be co-administered boosted PI (ATV/r or LPV/r or 
DRV/r)–based ART regimen, Rifampicin should be replaced by Rifabutin for the 
entire course of ATT (Table 7.23).
Considerations in PLHIV already on ART at time of diagnosis of active TB
The following points should be considered in PLHIV if TB is diagnosed in patients 
already receiving ART:
	
l In PLHIV who are already on ART at the time of TB diagnosis, appropriate modification 
of ART/ATT needs to be done to maintain optimal efficacy of ATT as well as ART.
	
l When a patient on ART presents with active TB, there is a possibility of suspecting 
treatment (ART) failure. The NACO recommends the following guiding principles 
in this context: 
	– If an episode of TB occurs within the first 6 months of the initiation of ART, it 
should not be considered as failure of the treatment and IRIS should be suspected 
and managed accordingly. 
	– If an episode of TB develops more than 6 months after the initiation of ART, 
PLHIV should be assessed for the possibility of treatment failure (based on CD4 
counts and viral load) with special focus on adherence.
	– When a patient already on 2NRTI + 1NNRTI (EFV)–based regimen has to be 
given 2HREZ + 4HRE–based ATT for the newly detected TB, the same ART 
regimen can be continued without any modification.
	– When a patient already on 2NRTI + DTG–based regimen has to be given 2HREZ 
+ 4HRE–based ATT for the newly detected TB, the same ART regimen can be 
continued with one modification. Since co-administered Rifampicin reduces the 
bioavailability of DTG, this can be overcome by the additional tablet of DTG 
50 mg (at an interval of 12 hours with the regular dose of DTG) till the completion 
of ATT. Once the ATT is completed, the additional tablet of DTG 50 mg should be 
stopped 2 weeks after the stoppage of Rifampicin-containing treatment regimen.
	– When a patient already on 2NRTI + PI–based regimen develops TB, the ART 
regimen has to be modified if 2HREZ + 4HRE–based ATT is co-administered. 
There are two options as described in Table 7.24.
