IV. Toxoplasmosis 
Toxoplasmosis is a parasite that has a predilection for the brain.
Symptoms
Altered mental state (confusion, unusual behaviour), headache, fever, 
seizures, paralysis and coma. 
Presentation 
time frame
Acute-to-subacute over days to weeks.
CD4 count
<100.

Typical appearance on computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance 
imaging (MRI) scan as multiple contrast-enhancing lesions in the grey 
matter of the cortex or basal ganglia, often associated with oedema. 
Diagnosis is frequently presumptive on the basis of appearance on scan. 
If no response to appropriate empirical anti-toxoplasmosis therapy after 2 
weeks, then consider brain biopsy to rule out CNS lymphoma.
Preventive therapy 
(prophylaxis)
Indicated when CD4+ cell counts are below 350 (for primary PCP 
prophylaxis).
Preferred: TMP/SMX (1 double-strength every 12 h 3 times a week; or a 
single-strength or 1 double-strength tablet once a day). 
Stopping 
preventive therapy
CD4+ cell counts above 350 in 2 subsequent testings.

•	 Body weight ≤60 kg: Pyrimethamine 50 mg OD + Sulfadiazine 1000 mg 
QDS + Leucovorin 10–25 mg OD (can increase to 50 mg OD or BD).
•	 Body weight >60 kg: Pyrimethamine 75 mg OD + Sulfadiazine 1500 mg 
QDS + Leucovorin 10–25 mg OD (can increase to 50 mg OD or BD).
Corticosteroids may be used in the presence of significant cerebral oedema.
Alternative 
treatment
Pyrimethamine Plus Clindamycin 600 mg IV or PO QDS; preferred 
alternative for patients intolerant to Sulfadiazine or who do not respond to 
Pyrimethamine–Sulfadiazine.
TMP–SMX (TMP 5 mg/kg and SMX 25 mg/kg) (IV or PO) twice daily.

therapy
Pyrimethamine 25–50 mg OD + Sulfadiazine 2000–4000 mg PO daily (in 
2–4 divided doses) + Leucovorin 10–25 mg OD.
Stopping 
maintenance therapy
Patient who has successfully completed initial therapy, remains 
asymptomatic of signs and symptoms of Toxoplasma encephalitis and CD4 
count >200 cells/mm3 for >6 months in response to ART.

V. Cryptosporidiosis
Cryptosporidiosis is a parasite that infects the GI tract and can cause symptoms.
Symptoms 
Chronic diarrhoea with frequent watery stools, abdominal cramps, nausea, 
fatigue, weight loss, loss of appetite, vomiting, dehydration, electrolyte 
imbalance (especially sodium and potassium) and fever.
Presentation 
time frame
Acute to chronic presentation over days to weeks or months in some cases.
CD4 count
<100.

Stool examination for detection of acid-fast oocysts in the stool or biopsy of 
small intestine. A specific request for examination for cryptosporidiosis is 
required (special laboratory techniques are needed).
Preventative 
therapy 
(prophylaxis)
Because chronic cryptosporidiosis occurs primarily in persons with 
advanced immunodeficiency, initiation of ART before the PLHIV becomes 
severely immunosuppressed should prevent the disease.

There are no proven effective therapies.
•	 Aggressive oral and/or IV rehydration and replacement of electrolyte loss.
•	 Rapid ART initiation.
•	 Nitazoxanide 500–1000 mg oral twice daily with food for 14 days, Or 
Paromomycin 500 mg oral 4 times a day for 14–21 days.
Immune recovery induced by ART alone results in excellent clinical responses.
Maintenance 
therapy
There are no proven therapies that prevent cryptosporidiosis.

Tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT)
Ruling out active TB
Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for active TB with a clinical 
algorithm. The absence of all the four symptoms of current cough, night sweats, fever 
and weight loss (4S negative, i.e. 4S -ve) can identify a subset of adolescents and 
adults living with HIV who have a very low probability of having TB disease and who 
can be reliably initiated on TPT. CLHIV (older than 12 months) who do not report 
current cough, fever, poor weight gain and history of contact with a TB case (4S -ve) 
are unlikely to have active TB. CXR can not only pick up non-tuberculous pulmonary 
diseases like pneumonia (PCP) but can also help rule out active TB in certain situations. 
Test for TB infection (TST) may be of some use in CLHIV.
Eligibility for TPT
All adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB with a clinical 
algorithm. Those who do not report any one of the four symptoms of current cough, 
fever, weight loss and night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should, therefore, 
be assessed for IPT initiation. All CLHIV older than 12 months, who do not report 
with current cough, fever, poor weight gain and history of contact with a TB case, are 
unlikely to have active TB and should, therefore, be assessed for TPT initiation. Infants 
younger than 12 months living with HIV who are in contact with a person with TB and 
who are unlikely to have active TB on an appropriate clinical evaluation or according 
to national guidelines should receive TB preventive treatment. If there is any doubt 
about the TB status of a patient, TPT should be delayed. The regimen plan and dosing 
chart are provided in Table 7.28.

TB preventive treatment. Alternatively, the multivitamin/B-complex formulations 
with the requisite prophylactic dose of Pyridoxine available within the general health 
system may be considered.

RICKETTSIAL DISEASES (SCRUB TYPHUS)
An infectious disease syndrome caused by several rickettsial bacterial organisms are 
some of the most covert emerging and re-emerging diseases. Among the major groups 
of rickettsioses, commonly reported diseases in India are scrub typhus, murine flea-
borne typhus, Indian tick typhus and Q fever.
Scrub typhus is the commonest occurring rickettsial infection in India caused by 
Orientia tsutsugamushi. The infection is transmitted through the larval mites or ‘chiggers’ 
belonging to the family Trombiculidae. Only the larval stages take blood meal. Small 
rodents, particularly wild rats of subgenus Rattus, are natural hosts for scrub typhus. 
Rickettsial infections are generally incapacitating and difficult to diagnose; untreated 
cases have case fatality rates as high as 30–45% with multiple organ dysfunction, if not 
promptly diagnosed and appropriately treated. Elderly may have a more severe disease.
Scrub typhus can occur in areas where scrub vegetation consisting of low-lying 
trees and bushes is encountered, and also in habitats such as banks of rivers, rice fields, 
poorly maintained kitchen gardens and grassy lawns.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Acute undifferentiated febrile illness of 5 days or more with or without eschar 
should be suspected as a case of rickettsial infection (if eschar is present, fever 
of 5-day duration or more should be considered as scrub typhus).

l Other presenting features may be headache, rash (rash more often seen in fair 
persons; common in spotted fever) and lymphadenopathy. Rash usually becomes 
apparent after 3–5 days of the onset of symptoms. Initially rash is in the form of 
pink, blanching, discrete maculae which subsequently becomes maculopapular, 
petechial or haemorrhagic.
	
l The complications of scrub typhus usually develop after the first week of illness: 
multiorgan involvement like that of the liver, lung and kidney, acute respiratory 
distress, septic shock, myocarditis and meningoencephalitis.
	
l The differential diagnosis of dengue, malaria, pneumonia, leptospirosis and 
typhoid should be kept in mind. 
	
l Eschar is an early clinical manifestation and if present is a pathognomonic sign 
of scrub typhus. Eschars are painless, punched-out ulcers up to 1 cm in width, 
with a black necrotic centre (resembling the mark of a cigarette burn), which is 
surrounded by an erythematous margin. Usually a single eschar is found on the 
neck, axillae, chest, abdomen and groin, but multiple eschars have also been 
documented representing localized necrosis at the site of chigger bite. Eschar is 
pathognomonic but may be absent in a few patients. 
	
l Weil-Felix test (titre of 1:80) after 5–7 days of onset of fever and IgM and IgG 
ELISA are considered as possible infection. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and 
immunofluorescence assay (IFA) are confirmatory (Fig. 7.7).
	
l Additional diagnostic investigations to assess the severity of the other organ 
involvement include leucocytosis (WBC, count >11,000/μL later in the course 
of the disease (total lymphocyte count [TLC] often normal during early course 
of the disease), thrombocytopenia (i.e. <100,000/μL), raised ESR and CRP, and 
raised transaminase levels. Hyponatraemia and hypoalbuminaemia are seen in 
severe cases. Chest X-ray shows infiltrates, mostly bilateral.
	
l Routine blood cultures do not detect Rickettsia.

Approach to treatment
	
l Antibiotic therapy with doxycycline as below should be instituted on suspicion 
of rickettsial disease without waiting for laboratory confirmation of the rickettsial 
infection. Prior vaccination does not exclude typhus.
	
l Consider typhus (along with malaria and dengue) in febrile travellers returning from 
endemic areas. Rickettsial infections typically present within 2–14 days. Febrile 
illnesses presenting >18 days after travel are unlikely to be rickettsial. Rule out 
malaria, dengue and typhoid in fever cases of duration of 5 days or more.
	
l Assess disease severity and complications, if any, and refer to a secondary or tertiary 
centre in case of complications like acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute 
renal failure, meningoencephalitis and multiorgan dysfunction as appropriate after 
initiating doxycycline. In addition to the recommended management of pneumonia, 
treatment of scrub typhus (doxycycline) should be provided to the patient.
	
l Figure 7.5 depicts the management algorithm for rickettsial infections.

476    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Uncomplicated cases
Tab. Doxycycline 200 mg/day in 2 divided doses; continue until clinically improved 
and the patient is afebrile for at least 48 hours; the usual course is 5–7 days.
Note: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.
In children (older than 8 years and <45 kg: 5 mg/kg/day (maximum 200 mg/day) in 2 
divided doses.
In children ≤45 kg: 5 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (maximum of 200 mg/day); in 
children >45 kg: adult dose.
Or
Tab. Azithromycin 500 mg in a single dose for 5 days. Note: Azithromycin is a drug 
of choice in pregnant women.
In children: 10 mg/kg body weight for 5 days. If the clinical signs and symptoms 
persist, an alternative diagnosis should be considered.

Patient education
	
l Educate patients about vector control measures. 
–	Scrub typhus: Wear protective clothing and use insect repellents.
–	Endemic typhus: Practice ectoparasite and rodent control.
–	Epidemic typhus: Practice delousing and cleaning of clothing. Hot water washing 
and hot drying effectively kills ticks on cloths. 
	
l Travel advice (minimize exposure risks, vector avoidance) 
–	Pets should be protected with medications or tick collars and periodic deticking 
should be done.
–	Regular tick checks should be performed after spending time with tick-infested 
animals or in tick-infested habitats.
–	Perform prompt removal of attached ticks – take a bath soon after exposure; use 
proper technique of tick removal, i.e. use tweezers, grasp tick’s head as close to the 
skin surface as possible and gently pull upwards with constant pressure followed by 
washing with soap and water or alcohol or an iodine scrub. Ticks should neither be 
removed nor be crushed with bare fingers. Gasoline, nail polish, kerosene, petroleum 
jelly or lit matchsticks should not be used for tick removal. Incineration of ticks after 
removal, rather than flushing down the sewer system, is recommended.

478    Standard Treatment Guidelines
PARASITIC DISEASES – INTESTINAL PROTOZOAL 
INFECTIONS
Amoebiasis and giardiasis are the commonest intestinal protozoal infections. Patients 
with amoebiasis and giardiasis commonly present as asymptomatic carriers.
AMOEBIASIS (INTESTINAL)
Infection is caused by intestinal protozoa – Entamoeba histolytica. It usually spreads 
by infective cysts in stool which contaminate the food and drinking water.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Lower abdominal pain and mild diarrhoea develop gradually and may lead to 
full-blown dysentery. 
	
l There occur 0–12 stools per day with blood and mucus and little faecal matter. 
	
l Caecal involvement may mimic acute appendicitis. 
	
l Chronic form, i.e. amoebic colitis, can be confused with inflammatory bowel 
disease. Other form of chronicity may present as amoeboma. 
	
l Untreated or incompletely treated intestinal infection may result in amoebic liver 
abscess and involvement of other extraintestinal site. 
	
l Diagnosis is made by demonstration of cysts and/or trophozoites of E. histolytica 
in the stool.
Treatment (asymptomatic cyst passers)
	
l In nonendemic areas, Tab. Diloxanide furoate 500 mg 8 hourly for 10 days
Treatment (acute amoebic dysentery and chronic infections)
	 1.	Tab. Metronidazole 400–800 mg 8 hourly orally with food for 7 days
	
	In children, 15 mg/kg divided in 3 doses for 7 days
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Tinidazole (300 mg, 500 mg and 1 g) 2 g orally once a day for 3 days with 
food
	
	In children ≥3 years, 50 mg/kg (maximum dose 2 g/day) once a day for 3 days
	 2.	In non-endemic areas for intraluminal parasites, Tab. Diloxanide furoate 500 mg 
8 hourly for 10 days
	
	In children, 20 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses for 10 days
Fulminant amoebic colitis may occur and present with more severe diarrhoea, 
abdominal pain and fever leading to intestinal perforation.
For treatment of amoebic liver abscess, see Chapter 6.

Chapter 7  Infections – Bacterial, Viral and Parasitic Diseases     479
GIARDIASIS
It is an intestinal disease caused by protozoal parasite – Giardia lamblia. The disease 
spreads by direct faeco-oral transmission.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Acute giardiasis: Although diarrhoea is common, upper intestinal manifestations 
like abdominal pain, bloating, belching, flatus, nausea and vomiting may 
predominate. Duration is usually more than 1 week.
	
l Chronic giardiasis: History of one or more episodes of acute diarrhoea, increased 
flatus, loose stools, abdominal distension, borborygmi, eructation of foul-smelling 
gas and passage of foul-smelling flatus and weight loss. Symptoms could be 
intermittent, recurring and gradually debilitating; Severe disease may result in 
malabsorption, weight loss, growth retardation and dehydration. 
	
l Diagnosis is made by the demonstration of cysts and/or trophozoites of 
G. lamblia in the stools.

condition: Parasitic Diseases Parasitic Diseases – Intestinal Protozoal Infections
text:
Tab. Tinidazole 2 g as a single dose with food
In children (age >3 years), 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) as a single dose with food
Or
Tab. Metronidazole 400 mg every 8 hours for 7 days with food
In children, 15 mg/kg (maximum 250 mg per dose) divided in 3 doses for 7 days
Patient education
	
l These infections are spread by ingestion of food or water contaminated with cysts.
	
l Properly cooked food, use of clean drinking water, proper sanitation, good personal 
hygiene and hand washing with soap after defaecation and before meals may prevent 
infection.
	
l Infection can be minimized by avoiding eating unpeeled fruits and vegetables or 
any food eaten raw. 
	
l Side effects of medications are usually mild and transient and include nausea, 
vomiting, abdominal discomfort, metallic taste and a disulfiram-like reaction; 
therefore, avoid the use of alcohol during treatment for 3 days.

480    Standard Treatment Guidelines
WORM INFESTATION
The majority of worm infestations are asymptomatic.
Hookworm infestation
Infection is caused by Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus. The infective 
larvae penetrate through the skin, usually the foot, and travel through subcutaneous 
tissue to the intestines. The adult forms live in the jejunum and feed on blood, thus 
leading to chronic blood loss and anaemia.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Most of the affected individuals may be asymptomatic. Patients usually present 
with symptoms of anaemia (hypochromic microcytic). 
	
l Pruritic maculopapular dermatitis (ground itch) is present at the site of skin 
penetration by infective larvae. 
	
l Serpiginous tracts of subcutaneous migration are seen in previously sensitized 
hosts. 
	
l Mild transient pneumonitis occurs because of larvae migration through the lungs. 
	
l Intestinal manifestations include epigastric pain often with post-prandial 
accentuation and inflammatory diarrhoea. 
	
l Major consequences include progressive iron-deficiency anaemia and 
hypoproteinaemia leading to weakness, shortness of breath and skin depigmentation. 
	
l The condition is diagnosed by the demonstration of ova of A. duodenale and/or 
N. americanus in the stool and occult blood.

Tab. Albendazole 400 mg as a single dose.
(In children between 1 and 2 years of age, Syr. Albendazole 200 mg as a single dose. 
In children older than 2 years, Syr. Albendazole 400 mg as a single dose.)
Or
Tab. Mebendazole 100 mg 12 hourly for 3 days in children older than 2 years.
(Caution: It is contraindicated in children younger than 2 years.)
Or
Tab. Pyrantel pamoate (250 mg); Syr. (250 mg/5 mL) 10 mg/kg body weight (not to 
exceed 1 g/day) once daily for 3 days.
(Caution: It is not recommended in children younger than 1 year.)
In children older than 1 year, Susp. Pyrantel pamoate 10 mg/kg as a single dose.
For treatment of anaemia, see Anaemia in Chapter 1.

Chapter 7  Infections – Bacterial, Viral and Parasitic Diseases     481
Patient education
	
l Hookworm infestation occurs through skin penetration by the infective larvae.
	
l The disease can be prevented by the use of boots and gloves while working in the 
fields.
	
l Avoid playing barefoot in the fields.
	
l The deworming agents should not be used in pregnancy, lactation and along 
with alcohol.
	
l Side effects of these drugs are generally mild which may include nausea, abdominal 
pain, headache, dizziness, malaise and skin rash.
ASCARIASIS (ROUNDWORM INFESTATION)
Ascariasis is caused by Ascaris lumbricoides, the largest intestinal nematode parasite 
of humans reaching up to 40 cm in length. The worm is usually located in the small 
intestine. Infection spreads by orofaecal route.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Most infected individuals have low worm burden and are asymptomatic. 
	
l Features of pulmonary involvement because of larval migration include irritating 
non-productive cough, bronchospasm or pneumonitis and burning substernal 
discomfort aggravated by coughing or deep inspiration, dyspnoea, fever and 
eosinophilic pneumonitis. 
	
l There occur heavy intestinal infection pain in the abdomen and small bowel 
obstruction which may get complicated by perforation, intussusception or 
volvulus. Aberrant migration of a large worm may cause biliary colic, cholangitis, 
cholecystitis, pancreatitis and oral expulsion of the worm.

Tab. Albendazole 400 mg as a single dose. In heavy infestation, however, a 2–3 days’ 
course is indicated. (In children between 1 and 2 years of age, Syr. Albendazole 
200 mg as a single dose. In children older than 2 years, Syr. Albendazole 400 mg as a 
single dose.)
(Caution: It is contraindicated in pregnancy.)
Or
Tab. Mebendazole 100 mg 12 hourly for 3 days.
(Caution: It is contraindicated in children younger than 2 years.)
Or
Tab. Pyrantel pamoate 11 mg/kg as a single dose up to a maximum of 1 g; it can be 
used in pregnancy.
Or

482    Standard Treatment Guidelines
In children between 1 and 2 years: Albendazole Susp. (200 mg/5 mL) 200 mg as a single 
dose; in children older than 2 years: Syr./Tab. Albendazole 400 mg as a single dose.
Partial intestinal obstruction may be managed with nasogastric suction, IV fluid 
administration and instillation of Piperazine through nasogastric tube. Complete 
obstruction and other surgical complications require surgical referral for intervention.
Patient education
	
l Infection occurs mainly via faecally contaminated soil and via eggs borne on 
vegetables and food.
	
l Follow proper sanitation and good personal hygiene – hand washing with soap after 
defaecation and before meals may prevent infection.
	
l Infection can be minimized by avoiding unpeeled fruits and vegetables or any food 
eaten raw and use of clean drinking water.
ENTEROBIASIS
Infection is caused by Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm). Adult pinworm is around 
1 cm long and dwells in the lumen of the small and large intestine around the caecum 
area. The eggs are transmitted by hand-to-mouth passage.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Most pinworm infestations are asymptomatic. 
	
l The cardinal symptom is perianal pruritis because of deposition of eggs in the 
perianal area, which becomes worse at night due to migration of female worms. 
Excessive itching can lead to perianal excoriation and bacterial superinfection. 
Sometimes it is also associated with enuresis in children. 
	
l Heavy infection causes abdominal pain and weight loss. 
	
l Rarely, in females, vulvovaginitis and pelvic or peritoneal granulomas occur. 
	
l Eosinophilia is present. 
	
l Diagnosis is made by demonstration of the ova of E. vermicularis in perianal swabs, 
or a cellophane tape should be pressed against the perianal skin. In the morning, when 
the child gets up, eggs stick to the tape and can be examined under the microscope.

Tab. Albendazole 400 mg as a single dose. (In children 1–2 years: Syr. Albendazole 
200 mg as a single dose; in children older than 2 years: 400 mg as a single dose.)
Repeat treatment after 2 weeks.
Or
Tab. Mebendazole 100 mg as a single dose in adults and children older than 2 years.
(Caution: It is contraindicated in pregnancy and in children younger than 2 years.)
Or
Tab. Pyrantel pamoate 11 mg/kg body weight as a single dose.

Chapter 7  Infections – Bacterial, Viral and Parasitic Diseases     483
Assessment of response of worm infestation to therapy
	
l Clinical improvement
	
l Repeat stool, perianal swab examination for ova of E. vermicularis
	
l Absolute eosinophil count, haemoglobin and peripheral blood smear examination at 
monthly intervals for 3–6 months
	
l Serum albumin level in hookworm infection
Patient education
	
l Treatment of all family members is required to eliminate asymptomatic reservoirs of 
potential reinfection. Change underclothes daily and keep bed linen clean. 
	
l Follow proper sanitation and good personal hygiene, nail hygiene and clipping, and 
hand washing with soap after defaecation and before meals to prevent infection. 
Dispose of faeces properly.
	
l Infection can be minimized by avoidance of unpeeled fruits and vegetables or any 
food eaten raw, use of clean drinking water and avoidance of unhygienic handling 
by a person carrying ova in the fingernails.

LEISHMANIASIS
Leishmaniasis is caused by parasitic protozoa of the genus Leishmania. Humans are 
infected via the bite of phlebotomine sandflies, which breed in forest areas, caves 
or the burrows of small rodents. Of the four Indian states, namely Bihar, Jharkhand, 
West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh, Bihar alone contributes more than 60% of the kala-
azar (KA) cases. Kala-azar is a notifiable disease in all kala-azar endemic states of 
India. The elimination of kala-azar as a public health problem is defined as annual 
incidence of less than 1 case per 10,000 population at the block level.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There are four main types of disease: In cutaneous forms, skin ulcers usually form 
on exposed areas, such as the face, arms and legs. These usually heal within a 
few months leaving scars. Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis produces disseminated 
and chronic skin lesions resembling those of lepromatous leprosy. It is difficult 
to treat. In mucocutaneous forms, the lesions can partially or totally destroy the 
mucous membranes of the nose, mouth and throat cavities and surrounding tissues. 
Visceral leishmaniasis (VL), also known as kala-azar, is characterized by high

484    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 fever, substantial weight loss, swelling of the spleen and liver, and anaemia. If 
left untreated, the disease can have a fatality rate as high as 100% within 2 years.
	
l Physical signs usually depend on the duration of the disease. Early cases may 
present with asymptomatic splenomegaly. Late cases are generally wasted and 
febrile, and show hyperpigmentation of the face, hands and feet. 
	
l The spleen is generally massively enlarged; the liver is usually moderately 
enlarged and lymphadenopathy may be present.
	
l Complications include extreme wasting and intercurrent infections. If untreated, 
80–90% of patients die. 
	
l Diagnosis is suggested by clinical features, progressive pancytopenia and severe 
anaemia, hypergammaglobulinaemia and hypoalbuminaemia, and rapid dipstick 
test, confirmed by demonstration of Leishmania donovani (LD) bodies in the 
bone marrow/splenic/lymph node aspirate. (Measure potential risks and gains 
for each patient.) PCR assays with primers may prove useful. Most serological 
tests are non-specific. In endemic regions with limited laboratory access, rapid 
diagnostic test (RDT) (rK39 dipsticks) serological tests are used as the primary 
test to confirm the diagnosis in patients with a high clinical suspicion of VL.
	
l Diagnosis of post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) involves a patient from 
a KA-endemic area with multiple hypopigmented macules, papules, plaques or 
nodules, who is RDT positive, confirmed by a positive in slit-skin smear (SSS) 
or biopsy or PCR.
	
l The RDT is not useful in the diagnosis of relapse cases as it can remain positive 
for months or years after treatment of VL. For a relapse, parasitological 
confirmation is the gold standard.

Cold sponging, rest and high-protein diet
Pharmacological (visceral leishmaniasis)
	 1.	Tab. Paracetamol 500–1000 mg 6–8 hourly to reduce fever.
	 2.	Treatment of intercurrent infections.
	 3.	Inj. Liposomal Amphotericin B (LAMB) 10 mg/kg single dose IV over 2 hours 
after test dose across all age groups including paediatric, pregnant and elderly 
patients. Filter and dilute as per instructions. For test dose, start the infusion very 
slowly at 2 drops/min for a period of 10 minutes and observe the patient.
	
	If the patient tolerates the test dose well, then infuse the rest of the dose over a 
period of 2 hours or more. Monitor the patient closely in case of reaction. Stop 
infusion and treat as per protocol for anaphylaxis. (Note: Store at a cool and dry 
place at 2–25°C at all times.)

(Caution: It should NOT be used in children younger than 2 years, pregnancy,

Treatment with Miltefosine is provided as directly observed therapy (DOTS) with

If the patient is not responding to the first line of the drug, the drug was discontinued

Inj. Amphotericin B deoxycholate 1 mg/kg/day on alternate day for 15 doses through IV

Discharge and follow-up
	
l All patients who have completed the treatment with LAMB and had a good clinical 
response can be sent home. 
	
l Perform follow-up visit at 6 months (±2 weeks) after the end of treatment to ensure 
definite cure. Trace defaulters to treatment actively. Encourage discharged VL 
patients to report to the health facility on recurrence of symptoms or appearance of

Patient education
	
l There are three main forms of leishmaniases – visceral (also known as kala-azar 
and the most serious form of the disease), cutaneous (the most common) and 
mucocutaneous.
	
l People of all ages are at risk for infection if they live or travel where leishmaniasis 
is found. Leishmaniasis is usually more common in rural than in urban areas, but it 
is found in the outskirts of some cities. The disease is associated with malnutrition 
and a weak immune system.

l Poor housing and domestic sanitary conditions (such as a lack of waste management 
or open sewerage) may increase sandfly breeding and resting sites, as well as their 
access to humans. 
	
l Since the disease is transmitted by the bite of infected female phlebotomine 
sandflies, vector control helps to reduce or interrupt transmission of disease by 
controlling sandflies, especially in domestic conditions. Control methods include 
insecticide spray, use of insecticide-treated nets, environmental management and 
personal protection.

Tumours/Carcinoma and Palliative Care
SCREENING AND EARLY DIAGNOSIS OF CANCERS
Cancer represents a significant public health challenge in India, with its prevalence 
increasing due to factors such as extended life expectancy, demographic shifts, and 
the impact of tobacco and other risk elements. The predominant cancers in the country 
include oral, breast, cervical and lung cancer. Unfortunately, a large portion of cases 
are diagnosed and treated in advanced stages, leading to low survival rates and elevated 
mortality figures. The primary contributors to cancer cases in India are tobacco usage, 
infections and other preventable causes.
To address this issue, India has implemented the National Programme for 
Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke 
(NPCDCS). Furthermore, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) initiated 
the National Cancer Registry Programme in 1982 to furnish accurate data on cancer 
prevalence and incidence.
Approaches to Cancer Control include:
	 1.	Prevention
	 2.	Early detection
	 3.	Diagnosis and treatment
	 4.	Palliative care
Prevention: Prevention is a cornerstone of effective disease control initiatives. 
Globally, tobacco stands out as the primary cause of cancer. Therefore, the focus 
of prevention efforts, through initiatives like Tobacco Free Initiative (TFI), aims to 
diminish smoking rates and overall tobacco consumption. Additionally, secondary 
prevention strategies target specific cancers such as those affecting the uterine cervix, 
mouth and breast. Tertiary prevention involves enhancing and expanding therapeutic 
services, including pain management, to improve patient outcomes.
Early diagnosis: Early diagnosis plays a pivotal role in enhancing cancer prognosis 
by enabling timely intervention. Unfortunately, accessing cancer care often encounters 
delays, especially in resource-constrained environments and among vulnerable groups, 
leading to late-stage diagnoses. The repercussions of delayed or inaccessible cancer 
care include reduced chances of survival, heightened morbidity, increased health care 
expenses and, ultimately, preventable fatalities and disability due to cancer.

CANCER SCREENING TESTS
Cancer screening plays a pivotal role in early detection and prevention of various 
malignancies, aiming to identify the disease at its earliest, most treatable stage. 
Screening methods vary depending on the type of cancer but commonly involve non-
invasive procedures such as mammography for breast cancer, Pap smears for cervical 
cancer and colonoscopies for colorectal cancer. These screenings are particularly 
beneficial for individuals with known risk factors or those within certain age groups. 
However, it is essential to weigh the benefits of early detection against potential harms, 
such as false positives or overdiagnosis. The decision to undergo cancer screening 
should be based on informed discussions between individuals and their health care 
providers, considering individual risk factors, overall health and personal preferences.
Additional requirement for the decision to screen should be evidence supporting 
the effectiveness of early treatment and adequate facilities for diagnosis and treatment. 
Some of the effective screening tests which have been shown to reduce mortality due 
to cancer are given next.
BREAST CANCER
Mammography is the primary screening tool for breast cancer. In addition to 
mammograms, clinical breast examinations (CBE) and breast self-examinations (BSE) 
are recommended to enhance early detection efforts. The frequency and starting age 
for mammography screening may vary based on individual risk factors and medical 
guidelines. Women with a family history of breast cancer or other risk factors may be 
advised to start screening earlier or undergo more frequent screenings.
Clinical breast exams and regular breast self-examinations: CBE and regular 
BSE entail the routine examination of the breasts by health care providers or women 
themselves, aiming to detect any lumps, pain, changes in size or other abnormalities. 
CBE are typically recommended every 3 years for women in their 20s and 30s, and 
annually for women aged 40 years and older.
Breast self-examination: BSE encourages women to remain vigilant and promptly 
report any changes or concerns to their health care provider. Despite not directly 
reducing breast cancer deaths, this proactive approach aids in identifying potential 
issues early, thus contributing to timely diagnosis.
Mammography: For women aged 50–69 years, mammograms are advised every 
2 years for those at an average risk, and annually for those at a high risk. Additionally, 
women aged 40–49 years with a family history or other risk factors may undergo 
regular mammography, although the extent of benefit is not as firmly established. In 
cases of strong familial breast cancer, with or without confirmed BRCA mutations, 
it is recommended to undergo both annual MRI and annual mammography, either 
simultaneously or in alternation.

yields uncertainties or in specific clinical scenarios such as BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene

490    Standard Treatment Guidelines
mutations, other high-risk genetic variants, lobular cancers, suspicion of multifocality 
or multicentricity, and the presence of breast implants. However, MRI is not 
recommended for screening women at an average or intermediate risk for breast cancer.
For women aged 50–69 years, regular mammography (annually or biennially) 
is advised. In cases of strong familial breast cancer, regardless of BRCA mutation 
status, both annual MRI and mammography are recommended, either concurrently or 
alternately.
Ultrasound alone or combination with mammography in screening for breast 
cancer: Ultrasound, either alone or in combination with mammography, is utilized 
in breast cancer screening. Combined mammography and ultrasound screenings have 
demonstrated an enhanced detection rate, leading to improved sensitivity.
Further diagnostic assessments are determined based on clinical examination and 
imaging, including bilateral mammography and ultrasound of both breasts and regional 
lymph nodes. In symptomatic scenarios, two-dimensional digital mammography may 
also be used.
CERVICAL CANCER
In women aged 30 years or older, screening tests aim to detect preinvasive lesions. 
Human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, with greater sensitivity and specificity than 
visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or cytology, is recommended, with a transition 
to replace VIA with HPV DNA testing for primary screening. HPV DNA–based 
screening programmes are more impactful and cost-effective in reducing cervical 
cancer morbidity and mortality. Screening frequency varies based on age and results. 
If HPV DNA test is not available, then Pap smear should be done every 3–5 years. 
Screening with cytology is done every 3 years in woman aged 21–29 years. HPV DNA 
test combined with Pap smear in women 30–65 years done every 5 years. Women 
from the general population with a positive DNA test should be followed every 
2 years. Women living with HIV with a positive DNA test will be followed every year. 
Screening may not be needed for certain groups, such as those aged >65 years with 
normal results in the past 10 years or individuals with no cervical precancer, a total 
hysterectomy or HPV vaccination. Continue screening of women with a history of 
CIN2, 3 or adenocarcinoma after the age of 65 years. Screen sexually active girls and 
women if HIV positive.
Human papillomavirus testing: HPV testing is recommended in conjunction with 
Pap smears, especially for women aged 30 years and older. HPV is a major risk factor 
for cervical cancer. If the result is normal, the next screening is done after 5 years. 
Testing frequency may vary based on individual risk factors and health care provider 
recommendations. The cut-off level of HPV is ≥1.0 pg/mL.
Pap smear test: The Pap smear test is a widely used screening method to detect abnormal 
cells in the cervix which may turn into cancer. It is recommended for women starting 
in their 30s, and the frequency may vary based on individual risk factors and health 
guidelines. Cut-off level ASCUS+, atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance.

Cotesting: It refers to an HPV test along with the Pap test. If both of the results are 
normal, the next screening test should be done after 5 years.
Visual inspection with acetic acid or visual inspection with Lugol’s iodine (VILI): 
Inspection of the cervix is done after application of 1% acetic acid to detect pre-invasive 
lesions in women between 30 and 60 years of age (priority given to those between 30 
and 49 years of age) at least twice in a lifetime to begin with followed by colposcopy in 
VIA-positive cases in resource-limited settings. In Schiller’s test, application of Lugol’s 
iodine demarcates abnormal areas on the cervix. Rescreen negative cases after 3 years.
	
l Screen positives should be evaluated for confirmation of the diagnosis. HPV is 
positive in the primary screening test; a ‘screen and treat’ approach is used.
	
l When acetic acid is used, and no lesions are visible, eligibility criteria for ablative 
treatment (cryotherapy or thermo-coagulation) are assessed.
	
l Criteria include no suspicion of invasive cancer or glandular disease, a fully 
visible transformation zone and a type 1 transformation zone. Cryotherapy can be 
performed immediately, even before biopsy results.
	
l If the patient is screen-positive but VIA reveals an incompletely visualized 
transformation zone (type 2 or 3 TZ), referral for colposcopy and further evaluation 
with biopsy is recommended.
	
l The ‘screen–triage–treat’ approach is followed for women living with HIV, with 
annual follow-ups for those with HPV-positive and VIA-negative tests.
COLON AND RECTAL CANCER AND POLYPS
Colorectal cancer typically originates from precancerous polyps, which are abnormal 
growths found in the colon or rectum. Screening tests are effective in detecting these 
precancerous polyps, enabling their removal before they progress into cancer or early 
detection of colorectal cancer when treatment outcomes are most favourable.
Colonoscopy: Colonoscopy is often considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer 
screening. It is typically recommended for individuals aged 50 years and older, and the 
frequency may vary based on individual risk factors, family history and health care 
provider recommendations.
Faecal occult blood test (FOBT): FOBT is a non-invasive test that detects hidden 
blood in the stool, which can be an early sign of colorectal cancer. It may be 
recommended periodically, usually every 1–2 years, especially for individuals who are 
not opting for or are not suitable candidates for colonoscopy.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy: This procedure involves examining the lower part of the 
colon and rectum. It may be recommended periodically, usually every 5 years, as part 
of colorectal cancer screening.
Virtual colonoscopy (computed tomography colonography): While not as common 
as traditional colonoscopy, virtual colonoscopy may be considered as an alternative 
in some cases. Individuals with a family history of colorectal cancer or specific risk 
factors may receive tailored screening guidelines. This might involve earlier or more 
frequent testing, particularly for those with conditions such as inflammatory bowel

492    Standard Treatment Guidelines
disease (e.g. Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis), a family history of colorectal cancer 
or colorectal polyps, or a genetic syndrome such as familial adenomatous polyposis 
(FAP) or hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch’s syndrome).
LUNG CANCER
Screening is advised solely for asymptomatic adults deemed at high risk due to 
concerns about false-positive results and overdiagnosis. It is worth noting that repeated 
low-dose CT (LDCT) tests, despite their diagnostic utility, can potentially induce cancer 
in otherwise healthy individuals due to radiation exposure.
For individuals at an elevated risk of lung cancer, such as heavy smokers or those 
with prolonged occupational exposure to carcinogens, engaging in discussions with 
health care providers regarding the potential advantages and drawbacks of screening 
is crucial.
Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) is recommended for lung cancer 
screening in heavy smokers aged between 50 and 80 years who have a history of heavy 
smoking, currently smoke or have quit within the last 15 years.
OTHER SCREENING TESTS
Screening for ovarian, pancreatic, prostate, testicular and thyroid cancers has not 
demonstrated efficacy in reducing mortality associated with these types of cancers.
OVARIAN CANCER
Ovarian cancer is often referred to as the ‘silent killer’ because it tends to show few 
early symptoms, and by the time it is diagnosed, it may have reached an advanced 
stage. However, for women at a higher risk of ovarian cancer, such as those with 
a strong family history of the disease or known genetic mutations (e.g. BRCA1 or 
BRCA2), discussions with health care providers about individualized screening 
approaches may be considered. Screening methods for high-risk individuals might 
include transvaginal ultrasound and blood tests, but there is no universally agreed-
upon screening protocol due to the limitations and uncertainties associated with current 
screening methods.
CA-125 test: While the CA-125 test is a valuable tool for monitoring certain conditions 
and assessing the response to treatment, it is generally not recommended as a screening 
test for the general population. CA-125 is not specific to ovarian cancer and can be 
elevated in other conditions, such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids and certain non-
cancerous diseases of the abdomen or pelvis. Additionally, some individuals with 
ovarian cancer may have normal CA-125 levels. In certain cases, CA-125 testing 
may be used in conjunction with other diagnostic tools for individuals at a high risk 
for ovarian cancer due to family history or genetic predisposition. However, its use is 
generally not recommended for population-wide screening.

with prolonged occupational exposure to carcinogens, engaging in discussions with 
health care providers regarding the potential advantages and drawbacks of screening 
is crucial.
Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) is recommended for lung cancer 
screening in heavy smokers aged between 50 and 80 years who have a history of heavy 
smoking, currently smoke or have quit within the last 15 years.
OTHER SCREENING TESTS
Screening for ovarian, pancreatic, prostate, testicular and thyroid cancers has not 
demonstrated efficacy in reducing mortality associated with these types of cancers.
OVARIAN CANCER
Ovarian cancer is often referred to as the ‘silent killer’ because it tends to show few 
early symptoms, and by the time it is diagnosed, it may have reached an advanced 
stage. However, for women at a higher risk of ovarian cancer, such as those with 
a strong family history of the disease or known genetic mutations (e.g. BRCA1 or 
BRCA2), discussions with health care providers about individualized screening 
approaches may be considered. Screening methods for high-risk individuals might 
include transvaginal ultrasound and blood tests, but there is no universally agreed-
upon screening protocol due to the limitations and uncertainties associated with current 
screening methods.
CA-125 test: While the CA-125 test is a valuable tool for monitoring certain conditions 
and assessing the response to treatment, it is generally not recommended as a screening 
test for the general population. CA-125 is not specific to ovarian cancer and can be 
elevated in other conditions, such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids and certain non-
cancerous diseases of the abdomen or pelvis. Additionally, some individuals with 
ovarian cancer may have normal CA-125 levels. In certain cases, CA-125 testing 
may be used in conjunction with other diagnostic tools for individuals at a high risk 
for ovarian cancer due to family history or genetic predisposition. However, its use is 
generally not recommended for population-wide screening.

Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP): It is sometimes used as a tumour marker for certain types of 
cancer, primarily hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer) and certain types of testicular

or for individuals without specific risk factors or symptoms.
PROSTATE CANCER
Prostate cancer screening aims to detect the disease in asymptomatic individuals 
at an early, potentially more manageable stage. The primary screening tests for 
prostate cancer are the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test and the digital rectal 
examination (DRE), typically recommended for individuals aged 40–49 years after 
thorough discussion of the benefits and drawbacks with their health care provider.
PSA: PSA levels in the blood may rise due to various factors, including non-cancerous 
conditions such as prostatitis, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) as well as prostate 
cancer itself. It is important to recognize that prostate cancer often progresses slowly, 
and not all cases pose immediate harm. However, prostate cancer screening carries the 
risk of overdiagnosis and overtreatment, as some individuals may undergo unnecessary 
treatments with potential side effects.
ORAL CANCERS
Oral cancers primarily affect subsites including the lip, oral cavity, nasopharynx and 
pharynx. The prevalence of oral cancer is notably high in South Asia due to exposure 
to various risk factors. Squamous cell carcinomas (SCC) represent more than 90% of 
all cases of oral cancer. However, other malignant tumours can originate from different 
tissues such as epithelium, connective tissue, minor salivary glands, lymphoid tissue, 
and melanocytes, or metastasize from distant tumours.
	
l Several premalignant lesions, including leucoplakia, erythroplakia, oral lichen 
planus and oral submucous fibrosis, exist with varying potentials for malignant 
transformation. Among these, oral lichen planus is recognized as a potentially 
malignant disorder, presenting in six distinct subtypes: papular, reticular, plaque-like, 
atrophic, erosive and bullous. Atrophic and erosive subtypes carry a higher risk of 
malignant transformation compared with others.
	
l The most common risk factors associated with oral cancer include tobacco use, 
alcohol consumption, chewing of betel quid containing areca nut and exposure to 
radiation. Early diagnosis is critical and can be life-saving, as late-stage cases may 
progress to severe dysplasia, carcinoma in situ or SCC.
	
l Regular dental check-ups, self-examinations and awareness of risk factors are 
essential components of oral cancer prevention and early detection efforts in India. 
Individuals at a high risk, such as tobacco users, may benefit from more frequent 
screenings and comprehensive preventive measures.

hands to palpate or feel for any lumps or abnormalities in the oral cavity, neck and jaw. 
Skin examination is done in people with a new mole or a change to an existing mole.
Oral visual inspection (OVI) and counselling: OVI and counselling of at-risk

a biopsy may be performed to determine whether they are cancerous. Further diagnostic 
tests, such as imaging studies, may be recommended to assess the extent of the disease.
Approach to patients presenting with oral lesions
Patients exhibiting persistent tongue and/or jaw pain; a lump or thickening inside the 
mouth or lip; a white or red patch on the gums, tongue, tonsil or lining of the mouth; 
or a small, indurated ulcer resembling a common canker sore, along with difficulty 
swallowing or chewing, and difficulty moving the jaw or tongue should undergo the 
following assessment steps:
	 1.	Assess oral habits and lifestyle, focusing on the quantity, frequency and duration 
of tobacco use and alcohol consumption.
	 2.	Perform an extraoral examination of the head and neck region, checking for 
asymmetry, tenderness or swelling, and palpating lymph nodes in submandibular, 
neck and supraclavicular regions for size, number, tenderness and mobility. 
Examine the lips and perioral tissues for any abnormalities.
	 3.	Conduct a systematic oral examination of all oral tissues, with special attention 
to high-risk sites such as the lateral and ventral aspects of the tongue, floor of the 
mouth and the soft palate complex, to detect oral cancer and precancerous lesions 
like leucoplakia, erythroplakia, non-healing ulcers and oral submucous fibrosis. 
Identifying precursor lesions is crucial as they may regress with cessation of 
tobacco use. Early stage oral cancer is generally treatable.
	 4.	Inspect lesions, paying close attention to size, colour, texture and outline, with a 
focus on predominantly white, red and white, ulcerated and/or indurated lesions.
	 5.	Assess mucosal changes using toluidine blue staining or loss of fluorescence, which 
can indicate premalignant or malignant conditions. Identify satellite lesion sites and 
aid in selecting biopsy sites. Diagnostic biopsy should be performed on suspicious 
mucosal lesions persisting for more than 3 weeks after removing local irritants like 
trauma, infection or inflammation.
	 6.	Document findings appropriately, utilizing drawings and photographic records of 
clinically visible tumours for staging, decision making and follow-up.
	 7.	Conduct further tests such as sentinel lymph node biopsy, indirect/direct 
laryngoscopy, CT, MRI or PET as needed, following initial oral examination.

LUNG CANCER
Lung cancer has emerged as the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among men. 
It encompasses malignancies originating in the airways or pulmonary parenchyma,

496    Standard Treatment Guidelines
commonly referred to as bronchogenic carcinoma. The majority, about 95%, of lung 
cancers fall into two main categories: small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and non-small cell 
lung cancer (NSCLC). Distinguishing between these types is crucial for determining 
staging, treatment approaches and prognosis. Approximately 5% of lung malignancies 
are attributed to other cell types.
NSCLC represents a diverse group of diseases, and their molecular characterization 
is pivotal in guiding treatment decisions, in cases of both metastatic disease and 
recurrence following initial therapy.
Several environmental and lifestyle factors contribute to the development of lung 
cancer, with tobacco smoking, particularly cigarettes, being the primary risk factor. 
Second-hand smoke exposure is also a significant contributor. Additionally, exposure 
to asbestos, radon and wood burning smoke further elevates the risk. Certain pulmonary 
conditions associated with inflammation, such as pulmonary fibrosis, chronic 
obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and tuberculosis, 
have been linked to a notable increase in lung cancer incidence.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Most patients seek diagnostic evaluation due to symptoms suggestive of lung 
cancer or incidental findings on chest imaging. Unfortunately, many patients with 
clinical signs or symptoms related to lung cancer already have advanced disease 
on presentation.
	
l Always consider lung cancer in individuals, especially current or former smokers, 
presenting with new-onset cough or haemoptysis.
	
l Symptoms of lung cancer can arise from the tumour’s local effects, regional or 
distant spread, or unrelated metastatic effects (paraneoplastic syndromes).
	
l Clinical manifestations of lung cancer may include cough, haemoptysis, pleural 
disease (intrathoracic effects), as well as extrathoracic metastases (commonly in 
the liver, bone and brain) and paraneoplastic phenomena (such as hypercalcaemia, 
Cushing’s syndrome, hypercoagulability disorders and various neurological 
syndromes).
	
l Both NSCLC and SCLC may present with similar symptoms, making it 
challenging to distinguish between them based solely on clinical features. 
However, certain features, such as rapidly progressive symptoms and specific 
paraneoplastic syndromes (e.g. syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone), 
may suggest SCLC. Conversely, Pancoast’s syndrome and hypercalcaemia are 
more commonly associated with NSCLC.
	
l Histopathology, molecular characterization, and imaging techniques such as 
positron emission tomography (PET) and CT play critical roles in initial staging 
and identifying tumour involvement sites, especially in patients with NSCLC.
The primary objectives of the initial assessment of a patient suspected of having lung 
cancer include:
	
l Determining the clinical extent and stage of the disease

Chapter 8  Tumours/Carcinoma and Palliative Care    497
	
l Identifying the optimal target site and method for the initial tissue biopsy
	
l Characterizing the specific histological subtype of cancer
	
l Evaluating the presence of comorbidities, secondary complications and 
paraneoplastic syndromes that may impact treatment options and prognosis
	
l Considering the patient’s values and preferences, which play a role in guiding 
diagnostic and therapeutic decisions
	
l Refer suspected patients to a specialized centre for comprehensive management. 
	
l Treatment options vary and include:
	 1.	Surgical resection remains the optimal approach for achieving long-term survival 
and potential cure in patients with resectable NSCLC. The decision for surgical 
candidacy involves preoperative staging, assessment of performance status, and 
evaluation of concurrent comorbidities and pulmonary function to anticipate 
postoperative outcomes. Patients with stage I or II disease who are ineligible for 
surgery or decline the procedure may consider non-surgical local therapies.
	 2.	Immunotherapy serves as first-line treatment for patients with high levels of 
programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression (staining on at least 50% of tumour 
cells, regardless of intensity). Targeted therapies tailored to specific NSCLC 
subsets are available for individuals with mutations in the epidermal growth factor 
receptor (EGFR), B-Raf proto-oncogene (BRAF), EML4-anaplastic lymphoma 
kinase (ALK) fusion oncogene and c-ROS oncogene 1 (ROS1) fusions.
	 3.	Systemic chemotherapy remains the cornerstone of treatment for SCLC due to its 
widespread dissemination in most patients at presentation and its responsiveness 
to chemotherapy.
	
	Patients with limited-stage disease typically receive a combination of chemotherapy 
and radiation therapy. The extent of disease (stage) at presentation significantly 
impacts prognosis. Median survival for limited-stage disease ranges from 15 to 
20 months, with reported 5-year survival rates of 10–13%. Conversely, for extensive-
stage disease, median survival is 8–13 months, with 5-year survival rates of 1–2%.
Patient education
	
l Emphasize the prevention of cancer by discouraging smoking initiation and 
encouraging cessation among current smokers. There exists a direct correlation 
between the intensity of exposure to passive or second-hand smoke and the relative 
risk of lung cancer. While smoking cigars or a pipe also increases lung cancer risk, 
it may be comparatively lower than with cigarettes.
	
l Behavioural counselling and pharmacological interventions aid individuals in 
quitting smoking.
	
l For those who successfully quit smoking, the risk of developing lung cancer decreases, 
with the greatest benefits seen in those who cease smoking by age 30 years. Even if 
individuals struggle to quit entirely, promote harm reduction by encouraging them 
to decrease smoking, which can still lower their lung cancer risk or refer to Tobacco 
cessation clinic. Annual LDCT screening is required for asymptomatic smokers and 
former smokers aged 55–77 years who have a smoking history of 30 pack-years or 
more and either continue smoking or have quit within the past 15 years.

l Explain that lung cancer treatment, whether curative or palliative, often involves a 
multimodal approach incorporating surgery, radiotherapy and systemic therapy using 
cytotoxic chemotherapy or molecularly targeted agents.
	
l Educate patients about potential side effects and negative impacts on quality of life 
both during and after treatment.

CARCINOMA CERVIX
Cervical cancer is a significant contributor to cancer-related mortality among women 
globally, often ranking as the leading or second leading cause of death from cancer. 
Particularly in developing nations, it stands as the primary cause of cancer-related deaths 
among women. The disease primarily manifests in two main types: SCC (comprising 
approximately 85% of cases) and adenocarcinoma (representing the remaining 15%).
Precancerous conditions known as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and 
adenocarcinoma in situ precede the development of invasive cervical cancer. These 
conditions serve as precursors to SCC and invasive endocervical adenocarcinomas, 
respectively. If diagnosed, these precursor lesions can often be effectively treated with 
simple methods, leading to favourable outcomes.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Abnormal bleeding may manifest as postcoital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding 
or post-menopausal bleeding. Additionally, persistent vaginal discharge with 
an unpleasant odour, unresponsive to treatment, may occur. Pain and urinary 
symptoms typically occur in the later stages of the disease.
	
l Visible growth or ulcers on the cervix that are easily friable and bleed on touch 
may indicate cervical cancer. Diagnosis is confirmed through cervix biopsy.
	
l The initial evaluation of patients suspected of having invasive cervical cancer 
involves a comprehensive history and physical examination, along with 
laboratory tests including a complete blood count, urine analysis, kidney function 
tests and chest radiography. Additional imaging studies such as CT or MRI 
scans, intravenous pyelogram (IVP), cystoscopy or proctosigmoidoscopy may be 
performed. HIV testing, especially for younger patients at risk, is recommended 
following counselling and consent.
	
l The staging of cervical carcinoma involves a simple per speculum examination 
of the cervix by medical or paramedical personnel to detect any abnormalities. 
Staging is further determined through rectovaginal examination.

Cervical cancer staging: Staging of cervical cancer is conducted following a 
comprehensive clinical examination (Table 8.1).
Cervical cancer grading: Grading is performed by a histopathologist and comprises 
three grades: intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN1), moderate-grade lesions (CIN2) and 
high-grade lesions (CIN3).

Treatment options for cervical cancer vary depending primarily on the stage of the 
disease, including factors such as tumour size, depth of invasion and the presence of 
metastasis. The main treatment modalities include surgery and combined radiation 
therapy and chemotherapy.
Stages IA1
For stage IA1 cervical cancer diagnosed through punch or wedge biopsy, it is crucial to 
perform a cone biopsy to rule out more invasive disease. Cone biopsy can be performed 
using a knife, large loop or laser.
Following conization, the subsequent management options include:
	 1.	Extrafascial hysterectomy (abdominal/laparoscopic/robotic/vaginal) may be 
recommended if the cone biopsy specimen shows negative lymphovascular space 
invasion (LVSI). In such cases, the risk of lymph node involvement is low, eliminating 
the need for lymph node dissection. Preservation of the ovaries is feasible, especially 
in young women and when the histological type is not adenocarcinoma.
	 2.	Modified radical hysterectomy or trachelectomy (for fertility preservation) along 
with pelvic lymphadenectomy may be considered if LVSI is positive in the cone 
biopsy specimen (stage IIA).
	 3.	Repeat conization is advised if the cone margins are positive and fertility 
preservation is desired.
	 4.	Regular follow-up is recommended if fertility preservation is desired, LVSI is 
negative in the cone biopsy specimen and the cone margins are disease-free.
	 5.	Radical brachytherapy with low dose rate or high dose rate may also be a treatment 
option.
Stage IA2
The available treatment options include:
	 1.	Modified radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy involves the removal 
of the entire uterus, upper third of the vagina, bilateral parametria, medial half, 
uterosacral half and uterovesical ligaments.
	
l The decision regarding bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is discretionary and 
depends on the patient’s age and the histological type of the tumour.
	
l Lymph node removal, encompassing the common iliac, external iliac, internal 
iliac and obturator groups from both sides, is essential.

Stages IB and IIA
Comparable cure rates are achieved with radical surgery or radiotherapy for stage IB1 
and IIA1 cervical carcinoma. However, the long-term complication profiles differ 
between radiation therapy and surgery alone.
The selection of treatment depends on various factors, including the patient’s 
age, the desire to preserve ovarian function, comorbid conditions, any associated 
gynaecological conditions necessitating surgery, available facilities and expertise, and 
the patient’s preferences.
The treatment options include:
	 1.	Radical hysterectomy (type III) with pelvic node dissection, including assessment 
of para-aortic lymph nodes during surgery
	 2.	Radical trachelectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy, suitable for fertility 
preservation, particularly in stage IB1 with a tumour size less than 2 cm and 
negative lymph nodes
	 3.	Radical radiation therapy
Stages IB2 and IIA2
The treatment options include concomitant chemo-radiation (radiation therapy plus 
weekly Cisplatin) or radical hysterectomy and lymphadenectomy.
	 1.	Radical radiation therapy involves both external radiotherapy and brachytherapy.
	 2.	Weekly administration of Inj. Cisplatin at 40 mg/m2 ensures appropriate hydration 
during the external radiotherapy sessions.
	 3.	For those opting for radical hysterectomy (type III) and bilateral pelvic 
lymphadenectomy, the procedure involves the removal of the entire uterus, upper 
third of the vagina, bilateral parametria, uterosacral and uterovesical ligaments, as 
well as bilateral pelvic lymph nodes.
	 4.	The decision to perform bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is discretionary. Para-
aortic lymph node assessment is conducted during the surgical procedure.
Stages II2 and IIA2
	 1.	Treatment alternatives encompass concurrent chemo-radiation (involving radiation 
therapy along with weekly Cisplatin) or the option of radical hysterectomy and 
lymphadenectomy.

502    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 2.	Provide concurrent chemotherapy using weekly Cisplatin dosage of 40 mg/m2 
throughout the external radiation course, contingent on the presence of sufficient 
renal functions/creatinine clearance.
	 3.	For patients exhibiting positive common iliac or para-aortic nodes (up to 3 cm in 
maximum dimensions), consider extended-field radiation therapy, with or without 
concurrent chemotherapy.
Stages IIB and III
The primary treatment modality continues to be radiotherapy, with the addition of 
concurrent chemotherapy playing a crucial role in reducing metastasis and enhancing 
survival. It is recommended to incorporate concurrent chemotherapy, specifically 
Cisplatin at a weekly dose of 40 mg/m2, throughout the external radiation course, given 
the presence of sufficient renal function/creatinine clearance.
Stage IVA
The majority of patients in stage IVA typically exhibit a poor overall condition and 
extensive local disease in our context, making palliative radiation therapy/chemotherapy 
the preferred approach. Prominent symptoms, such as vaginal bleeding, profuse 
discharge and low backache attributed to local disease, can be effectively palliated.
A commonly used strategy involves hypofractionated palliative external beam 
radiation therapy, with the option of incorporating low dose rate/high dose rate (LDR/HDR) 
brachytherapy in select cases where patients respond favourably to the initial treatment.
For details of palliative chemotherapy, see the next sections.
Stage IVB
In cases of metastatic disease, patients are not amenable to a cure, and the primary 
objective of treatment is to manage symptoms and extend survival. Radiation therapy 
proves beneficial for palliating symptoms arising from central disease or symptomatic 
distant metastases, including skeletal metastases, enlarged para-aortic or supra-
clavicular nodes, and brain metastases. Palliative radiotherapy is administered using 
larger fractions over shorter durations compared with traditional radical treatment 
courses. Generally, individuals with a poor performance status are not considered 
suitable candidates for palliative chemotherapy.
In instances of invasive cervical carcinoma during pregnancy, palliative 
chemotherapy is typically used for extra-pelvic disease or recurrences, as well as for 
pelvic recurrences without prior irradiation. There is some evidence suggesting that 
palliative chemotherapy may offer relief from symptoms and/or contribute to prolonged 
survival in this particular scenario.
Choice of chemotherapy
	
l Combination therapies have demonstrated consistent improvements in response rates 
and progression-free survival (PFS), albeit without a significant impact on overall

used regimen involves paclitaxel in conjunction with either cisplatin or carboplatin. 
Another regimen explored in a randomized phase III trial is the combination of 
topotecan and Cisplatin, which exhibited superiority over single-agent Cisplatin in 
terms of response rate, PFS, and OS. However, it is not the preferred standard due to 
its unfavourable toxicity profile, marked by myelosuppression and gastrointestinal 
side effects.
	
l In a recent phase III trial, four platinum doublets were compared (Cisplatin 
combined with Paclitaxel, Topotecan, Gemcitabine and Vinorelbine). While no 
statistically significant differences in OS were observed, there was a trend favouring 
cisplatin–paclitaxel in terms of response rate, PFS and OS.
	
l Less commonly used second-line palliative chemotherapy agents encompass 
Vinorelbine, Bevacizumab, Irinotecan, Ifosfamide and 5-FU. The preferred choice 
for palliative chemotherapy regimens is paclitaxel plus carboplatin or single-agent 
cisplatin. In cases where peripheral neuropathy is a concern, Gemcitabine–platinum 
serves as an acceptable alternative. Many clinicians substitute Carboplatin for 
Cisplatin in various regimens. Typically, four to six cycles of chemotherapy are 
administered.
	
l For patients deemed unsuitable for palliative radiotherapy or chemotherapy, those 
experiencing symptoms should receive supportive and symptomatic care. Palliative 
care, including counselling and symptom management, should be initiated early in 
the course of metastatic disease. Referral to a palliative care team is advisable, if 
available, to ensure comprehensive care (for details, see the section ‘Palliative Care’).
Cervical cancer in pregnancy
The diagnosis of invasive cervical carcinoma coexisting with pregnancy occurs in 
approximately 3% of cases. The treatment approach and timing depend on several factors, 
including the stage of the disease, duration of the pregnancy and patient’s preferences.
	
l For patients diagnosed with carcinoma in situ of the cervix via cytology and 
colposcopy-directed biopsies, follow-up throughout the pregnancy is possible, and 
definitive treatment can be postponed until re-evaluation of the cervix at 6 weeks 
postpartum. When there is suspicion of microinvasive or invasive carcinoma, a 
biopsy should be performed for diagnosis even during pregnancy. Microinvasive 
carcinomas can be monitored throughout pregnancy.
	
l During the early stages of pregnancy (up to 20 weeks), treatment is deferred, 
and adequate surgery or radiotherapy can be administered based on the stage of 
the cancer. In the late second trimester, pregnancy can be carried to the period of 
viability; however, chemotherapy may be considered. If the foetus is delivered 
after viability, appropriate surgical treatment can be performed concurrently, or 
radiotherapy/chemo-radiotherapy can be initiated after a 2-week interval.
	
l In the third trimester, patients can undergo classical caesarean section delivery 
followed by surgery for operable cases or initiation of radiotherapy/chemo-
radiotherapy after a 2-week interval.

504    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Follow-up after primary therapy
Response evaluation
Regular physical examinations are essential within the first 2 years as the majority of 
patients who experience recurrences do so within this period following their therapy. 
These examinations should include nodal assessment, particularly of the supraclavicular 
region, rectovaginal examination and Pap smears at 2- to 3-month intervals during this 
period. Subsequently, examinations every 4–6 months are appropriate, with annual 
examinations recommended beyond 5 years. Any symptoms such as pain, vaginal 
bleeding or gastrointestinal/genitourinary dysfunction should be promptly investigated.
For patients at a high risk of recurrence, interval chest X-rays and abdominal–
pelvic CT scans should be considered, particularly during the first 2 years of post-
treatment. Additionally, CT scans or intravenous pyelograms (IVPs) following 
treatment may aid in diagnosing ureteral obstruction, whether pathological or treatment-
related, at potentially early stages.
Chemotherapy-induced anaemia
Patients often experience a decline in haemoglobin levels in the context of cancer, 
primarily attributed to factors such as prolonged vaginal bleeding, inadequate nutrition, 
advanced disease, bone marrow toxicities from treatment and insufficient supportive 
care. A diminished haemoglobin level during radiotherapy or chemo-radiotherapy is 
indicative of reduced local control and survival rates. Presently, there is insufficient 
evidence to advocate for the routine utilization of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.
Patient education
	
l Raise awareness within the community about risk factors such as early age at marriage, 
having multiple sex partners, experiencing multiple pregnancies and smoking.
	
l Stress the importance of regular screening with Pap smears and VIA to detect any 
abnormalities early.
	
l Encourage early reporting of suspicious symptoms such as postcoital bleeding, 
postmenopausal bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding and persistent vaginal discharge.
	
l Highlight the safety and effectiveness of the HPV vaccine as an option for 
preventing cervical cancer.

CARCINOMA BREAST
Breast cancer represents a potentially life-threatening malignancy that can develop in 
one or both breasts. It can manifest as either non-invasive or invasive forms.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Most breast cancers typically manifest as a palpable lump detected by the 
patient during self-examination or through routine physical examination and 
mammography. In some cases, thickening of the breast tissue may be observed. 
Paget’s disease of the nipple may present with noticeable skin changes, including 
erythema, crusting, scaling and discharge.
	
l A minority of patients with breast cancer may exhibit signs of metastatic disease, 
such as pathological fractures or pulmonary dysfunction.
	
l During examination, a distinct lump may be palpable. Advanced breast cancers 
may exhibit characteristics such as adherence of the lump to the chest wall or 
overlying skin, the presence of satellite nodules or skin ulcers. Fixed axillary 
lymph nodes may indicate tumour spread. Inflammatory breast cancer, known for 
its aggressive nature, often presents with diffuse inflammation and enlargement 
of the breast, sometimes without a palpable lump.
	
l The exact causes of breast cancer remain incompletely understood, but certain 
factors may increase the risk of developing the disease, including age (especially 
greater than 65 years) and inherited genetic mutations (such as BRCA1 and BRCA2).
	
l Indicators suggesting the potential presence of an inherited genetic mutation within 
a family include a history of breast cancer among multiple close relatives, as well 
as occurrences of other cancers, particularly ovarian and colon cancer. Additionally, 
factors such as nulliparity or late childbirth, early onset of menstruation, late 
menopause and hormone replacement therapy (especially combinations of 
oestrogen and progesterone) may be associated with an increased risk.
	
l Breast cancer is categorized based on disease advancement, including early stage, 
locally advanced and metastatic. Further classification is based on hormonal and 
HER2 receptor status, resulting in subtypes such as luminal A-like (ER- and 
PgR-positive, HER2-negative tumours), luminal B-like (ER- and/or PgR-positive, 
HER2- positive or -negative tumours), HER2 overexpressing (ER- and PgR-
negative, HER2-positive tumours) and basal-like (triple-negative tumours).
For details on screening for breast cancer, see earlier text.

506    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Evaluation of a breast lump (Fig. 8.1)
Assessment of a breast lump: The diagnosis of breast cancer relies on a 
comprehensive approach involving clinical examination, imaging and pathological 
assessment.
All women presenting with a breast lump should undergo a TRIPLE TEST, which 
includes:
	 1.	Clinical examination is conducted by a skilled clinician, preferably a breast 
surgeon.
	 2.	Bilateral imaging, typically comprising a bilateral mammogram and/or ultrasound/
MRI as deemed appropriate, is performed. MRI of the breast may be warranted in

	 3.	Histopathological or cytological confirmation is essential before initiating cancer-
directed treatment (such as surgery, chemotherapy or other systemic therapies). 
An exception may be made in cases requiring frozen section analysis for primary 
diagnosis.
	
	Core biopsy is preferred for cases planned for neoadjuvant therapy (to assess 
grading and receptor status) and for guided biopsies of non-palpable lesions, 
especially if mastectomy is considered. FNAC is an acceptable alternative for small 
lesions in operable breast cancers or if the patient cannot undergo core biopsy. 
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) evaluation is necessary prior to neoadjuvant therapy. 
In instances of discordance in the triple test results, further evaluation should be 
pursued.
	 4.	Observe simple cysts, whether solitary or multiple, and do not necessitate 
aspiration.

The primary treatments for breast cancer encompass surgery, radiation and systemic 
therapy, which includes endocrine therapy, chemotherapy and targeted therapy. 
Tailoring therapeutic approaches for patients with non-invasive or invasive breast 
cancer involves a complex and diverse array of options. There is no one-size-fits-all 
treatment, and a combination of treatments is typically necessary. Various factors, 
including the patient’s age, menopausal status (among women), cancer type (e.g. ductal 
vs. lobular), stage and hormone receptor status, influence the treatment choice. The 
final pathological diagnosis follows anatomical classification and the tumour, node, 
metastasis (TNM) staging system.
	 1.	Treatment planning involves collaboration among various specialists, including 
oncologists, surgeons, radiation oncologists and pathologists, to ensure 
comprehensive care tailored to the individual patient’s needs.
	 2.	Treatment of EBC involves a combination of local modalities (surgery, 
radiotherapy [RT]), systemic treatments (chemotherapy [ChT]), endocrine therapy 
(ET), molecularly targeted therapies, immunotherapy) and supportive measures, 
delivered in diverse sequences. The use of predictive biomarkers (i.e. ER, PgR, 
HER2, Ki-67 and approved gene expression signatures) is well established in 
aiding treatment recommendations.
	 3.	Surgical intervention, such as lumpectomy (breast-conserving surgery) or 
mastectomy, serves as the primary treatment for localized breast cancer, aiming 
to excise the tumor and surrounding tissue. The selection of the surgical approach 
depends on various factors including tumor size, location, characteristics and 
patient preference. Most women undergoing mastectomy should be offered 
immediate or delayed breast reconstruction, with the optimal technique determined 
through individualized discussions considering anatomical, treatment- and patient-
related factors and preferences.

508    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
	Evaluation of the axillary lymph nodes is critical to assess the extent of disease 
spread. Techniques such as sentinel lymph node biopsy or axillary lymph node 
dissection are employed for this purpose. The status of regional lymph nodes 
remains a significant prognostic indicator for long-term outcomes in early stage 
breast cancer. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is the standard staging approach 
for clinically negative axillary lymph nodes at diagnosis or after neoadjuvant 
chemotherapy.
	 4.	Adjuvant therapy, comprising chemotherapy, hormonal therapy and targeted 
therapy, may be recommended post-surgery to decrease the risk of disease 
recurrence and enhance outcomes. The selection of adjuvant therapy depends 
on tumor characteristics, hormone receptor status, HER2 status and patient 
comorbidities.
	 5.	Radiation therapy following breast-conserving surgery reduces the risk of local 
recurrence by targeting residual breast tissue and regional lymph nodes. It may 
also be indicated after mastectomy, especially in cases with axillary lymph node 
involvement. 
	
	Comprehensive locoregional radiation therapy, encompassing the chest wall 
and regional lymph nodes, improves outcomes, particularly for patients with 
axillary lymph node involvement. Modern locoregional radiation therapy, guided 
by CT-based planning, minimizes recurrence, particularly distant recurrence. 
Post-mastectomy radiation therapy can be administered after immediate breast 
reconstruction.
	 6.	Neoadjuvant therapy should commence promptly upon completion of diagnosis 
and staging, ideally within 2–4 weeks. Adjuvant systemic therapy should follow 
without undue delays, ideally within 4–6 weeks, as delayed administration 
beyond 12 weeks post-surgery may compromise efficacy. Consideration may be 
given to neoadjuvant use of the same chemotherapy regimen when indicated for 
adjuvant therapy.
	 7.	Endocrine/hormonal therapy should be employed in all patients with hormone 
receptor-positive breast cancer, unless contraindicated. Endocrine/hormonal 
therapy, such as selective estrogen receptor modulators (e.g. Tamoxifen) or 
aromatase inhibitors, forms the cornerstone of treatment for hormone receptor-
positive breast cancer. 
	
	The most common endocrine therapy (ET) used is:
	
	Tamoxifen 20 mg/day for about 5 years. In postmenopausal women with ER-
positive early invasive breast cancer who are not low risk, Tamoxifen 20 mg/day 
for 2–3 years followed by Exemestane 25 mg daily for the remaining 2–3 years 
Or Anastrozole 1 mg/day for at least 3 years Or Letrozole 2.5 mg/day for at least 
2 years.
	
	Patients receiving aromatase inhibitors (AIs) are at a high risk of fractures; 
therefore, they should receive prophylactic Tab. Alendronate 70 mg once a week 
along with Vitamin D3.
