	 8.	Targeted therapy, particularly for HER2-positive breast cancer, involves the use 
of drugs that specifically target HER2-positive cancer cells, such as trastuzumab 
(Herceptin) or pertuzumab, often in combination with chemotherapy or other 
treatments.
	 9.	For locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer, systemic therapy, including 
chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, targeted therapy, or combinations thereof, is 
administered to manage the disease and alleviate symptoms.
	10.	Metastatic breast cancer (MBC): In metastatic breast cancer (MBC), the cancer 
has spread beyond the breast to other parts of the body. Although MBC is presently 
incurable, recent treatment advances have improved median OS for individuals 
across various subtypes of metastatic disease.
	
l The primary objective in managing metastatic disease is to prolong survival, 
alleviate symptoms and improve the overall quality of life. Hence, the 
preferred therapeutic approaches are those with minimal toxicity and proven 
enhancements in OS.
	
l Systemic therapy is the standard of care in MBC but may be supplemented with 
locoregional treatments (LRTs) according to the disease status, visceral crisis 
and refractory status of the individual patient. Presence or absence of visceral 
crisis is determined by severe organ dysfunction through evaluation of signs, 
symptoms, laboratory studies and disease progression speed.
	
l Endocrine-based therapy is less toxic compared with chemotherapy. 
Consequently, the preferred first-line treatment for most patients with HR-
positive/HER2-negative disease and no visceral crisis involves endocrine 
therapy, either in combination with targeted therapy (preferred) or alone, 
especially when targeted therapy is unavailable, inaccessible or deemed 
inappropriate. Chemotherapy is reserved for patients with cancers refractory 
to endocrine therapy or those requiring a rapid treatment response for 
visceral crisis.
	11.	Recurrent breast cancer (advanced cancer): Most breast cancer recurrences 
manifest within the initial 2–3 years post-treatment, although some may occur 
years later. The choice of treatment depends on the recurrent cancer’s stage, 
hormone responsiveness and patient’s age. Approximately 10–20% of recurrent 
breast cancers are localized, while the majority present with metastases. 
Participation in clinical trials is encouraged for all patients with recurrent cancer.
Psychological support at any stage
Psychological support is vital at every stage. Research indicates that psychotherapy, group 
support or a combination thereof can alleviate pain and reduce stress. There is no evidence 
to suggest that confronting the realities of the condition leads to physical deterioration.

l Regular follow-up visits are advised every 3 months during the initial 3 years post-
treatment (every 6 months for low-risk early breast cancer), followed by visits every

510    Standard Treatment Guidelines
6 months from years 4 to 5, and annually thereafter. The frequency of visits can be 
adjusted based on the risk of relapse and patient preferences.
	
l Annual bilateral mammography (after breast-conserving therapy) or contralateral 
mammography (after mastectomy) is recommended, supplemented with ultrasound 
and breast MRI when necessary.
	
l Breast cancer survivors should participate in national screening programmes for 
other cancers.
	
l Routine laboratory tests (e.g. blood counts, routine chemistry, tumour marker 
assessment) or imaging are not recommended for asymptomatic patients.
	
l Symptom-directed investigations should be conducted as needed.
	
l Regular bone density assessments are advised for patients receiving AIs or 
undergoing ovarian function suppression (OFS).
	
l Asymptomatic patients who have undergone potentially cardiotoxic treatment should 
receive cardiac follow-up as clinically indicated, particularly those with normal 
cardiac function.
	
l For patients taking Tamoxifen, an annual gynaecological examination is 
recommended; however, routine transvaginal ultrasound is not recommended.
	
l Premature menopause, infertility and potential sexual dysfunction should be discussed 
and addressed with each patient before initiating adjuvant therapy, as appropriate.
	
l Premenopausal women contemplating pregnancy should be informed that available 
evidence suggests that pregnancy appears to be safe after breast cancer treatment.
	
l For women wishing to conceive, temporarily discontinuing adjuvant endocrine therapy 
after 18–30 months, with a wash-out period of 3 months, followed by attempts to 
conceive within a 2-year period before resuming ET, does not appear to adversely affect 
short-term breast cancer outcomes in lower-risk HER-positive, HER2-negative EBC.
Patient education
	
l Inform patients about the follow-up procedures outlined above.
	
l Discuss with patients that all breast surgeries will result in some degree of scarring, 
and the post-surgical appearance of the breast depends on the surgical technique 
used. A shared decision regarding breast reconstruction can be made.
	
l Explain potential side effects of radiation therapy, which may include fatigue, 
nausea, loss of appetite and skin changes such as burns or moisture build-up. 
Encourage patients to expose the treated skin to air to facilitate healing.
	
l Describe chemotherapy as a treatment regimen administered over a course of days, 
followed by a rest period lasting several weeks. The number of treatment cycles 
varies based on cancer type and response to the drugs.
	
l Highlight the purpose of adjuvant chemotherapy, which is to reduce the risk of 
cancer recurrence following surgery. It targets any remaining microscopic cancer 
cells that may not be detectable by scans or tests.
	
l Discuss potential side effects of chemotherapy, including lowered immunity, 
anaemia, nausea, vomiting, mouth sores and temporary hair loss. Assure patients 
that hair typically grows back within 3–6 months after treatment.

TESTICULAR TUMOURS
The precise cause of testicular cancer remains unknown, but certain risk factors have 
been identified, including undescended testicles, congenital anomalies (such as kidney 
or penile abnormalities) and a family or personal history of testicular cancer in one 
testicle. Germ cell tumours account for the majority (90–95%) of testicular cancers, 
although histological types can vary. The peak incidence occurs in the third decade of 
life for non-seminomas and in the fourth decade for pure seminomas.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occur painless unilateral scrotal mass, loss of testicular sensation, 
testicular pain, back or flank pain and epigastric lump due to pre- and para-aortic 
lymphadenopathy. However, gynaecomastia, haemoptysis and bone pain are rare.
	
l Testicular cancer diagnosis involves a comprehensive approach, including the 
patient’s medical history, physical examination, ultrasound imaging and blood 
tests to measure specific tumour markers. Additionally, a biopsy of testicular 
tissue may be performed for further evaluation. Scrotal ultrasound is utilized to 
confirm the presence of a testicular mass, determine its localization (intra- or 
extra-testicular) and simultaneously assess the opposite testis.
	
l Serum levels of tumour markers – alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), human chorionic 
gonadotropin (hCG) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) – are crucial for staging 
and prognostic assessment before and after orchidectomy.
	
l Furthermore, contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the chest, 
abdomen and pelvis is recommended for evaluating the status of retroperitoneal 
and mediastinal lymph nodes in all patients with biopsy-proven testicular 
malignancy. Bone scans and brain imaging are reserved for select patients with 
symptoms indicative of bone or brain involvement. PET–CT or bone scans should 
not be used for staging purposes.
	
l Orchidectomy, coupled with a thorough pathological examination of the testis, 
is imperative to confirm the diagnosis and delineate the local extension of the 
malignancy. In instances where there is an urgent, life-threatening scenario due to 
extensive metastasis, chemotherapy may need to commence before orchidectomy. 
FNAC is not recommended due to the potential risk of malignancy extension into 
the scrotal skin, thereby exacerbating the disease stage.

l Testicular tumours show excellent cure rates, owing to several key factors: 
meticulous staging on diagnosis; prompt initiation of appropriate treatment involving 
chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery; as well as rigorous follow-up and salvage 
therapies.
	
l Every individual presenting with a suspected testicular mass should undergo inguinal 
exploration with exteriorization of the testis within its tunics. If a malignant tumour 
is identified, orchidectomy with division of the spermatic cord at the internal 
inguinal ring is imperative.
	
l In cases where the diagnosis remains uncertain, a testicular biopsy (intraoperative 
enucleation of the intraparenchymal tumour) is performed for immediate histological 
examination of fresh tissue. For patients with disseminated disease and life-
threatening metastases, chemotherapy is initiated upfront, with orchidectomy 
potentially deferred until clinical stabilization is achieved.
Stage 1 tumour (lesion in testis but no evidence of lymph nodal involvement or distant 
metastasis)
	
l In case of both seminoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (NSGCT), 
long-term surveillance (for at least 5 years) is needed with serial CT scan imaging 
and measurement of tumour markers.
	
l If the patient is not willing for surveillance, then chemotherapy with PEB regimen 
(Cisplatin, Etoposide, Bleomycin) may be offered to patients with NSGCT Or nerve-
sparing retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy to patients unwilling for chemotherapy.
	
l Adjuvant treatment is not recommended for patients at very low risk.
Stage 2 tumour (testicular tumours with lymph nodal involvement)
	
l Seminoma: Radiotherapy
	
l NSGCT: With elevated tumour markers – chemotherapy And/or resection of residual 
tumour, if any
	
l Without elevated tumour markers – retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy And/or 
adjuvant chemotherapy (PEB regimen 2 cycles)
Stage 3 tumour (distant metastasis)
	
l Primary chemotherapy (PEB regimen 3–4 cycles) for both seminoma and NSGCT
Patient education
	
l Emphasize that follow-up care is essential because testicular cancer has the potential 
to recur. The majority of recurrences following curative therapy manifest within 
the initial 2 years; hence, surveillance should be particularly vigilant during this 
period. Late relapses, however, can occur beyond the 5-year mark, warranting yearly 
follow-up for life.
	
l The frequency and nature of examinations are contingent on the estimated risk 
of relapse, the selected treatment approach and the duration since completion of 
therapy. Accordingly, these parameters should be adjusted to accommodate such 
risks. For instance, follow-up physical examinations and tumour marker assessments

PALLIATIVE CARE
Palliative care is a specialized, patient-centred health care approach focused on 
improving the quality of life for individuals with serious illnesses. It emphasizes 
symptom relief and stress reduction, with effective pain management being a crucial 
aspect. Palliative care can be delivered through various means, including hospice care, 
in-patient care, outpatient care and home-based care, providing services directly to the 
patient’s doorstep. Hospice care, a form of palliative care, caters to patients with a life 
expectancy of 6 months or less, prioritizing comfort over life-prolonging therapies.
Palliative care addresses serious illness diagnoses, significant symptom burdens, 
psychosocial distress, decision-making support and increased assistance, involving a 
range of professionals such as physicians, nurses, support workers and volunteers. Early 
palliative care delivery reduces unnecessary hospital admissions and health service 
utilization. The National Programme for Palliative Care (NPPC) in India, launched in 
2012, aims to extend palliative care accessibility.
Applicable to a wide range of diseases, palliative care is not limited to specific treatment 
plans and can begin at the time of diagnosis, continuing throughout the illness course. 
Unlike hospice care, designed for terminal stages, palliative care is suitable for patients of 
any age and at any stage of a serious illness. It should be available long before the terminal 
stage. Pain and difficulty in breathing are common and serious symptoms in patients in 
palliative care, with opioids being essential for managing pain and alleviating distressing 
physical symptoms, ensuring early relief to uphold dignity and reduce suffering.
Principles and key elements of palliative care
The principles of palliative care should be integrated from the point of diagnosis in 
chronic conditions such as cancer. This aspect, often termed supportive care, should 
be an integral part of disease-specific treatment protocols. As the disease advances 
and curative interventions diminish, the significance of palliative care becomes more 
pronounced. In the terminal stages, palliative care extends to end-of-life support,

514    Standard Treatment Guidelines
including bereavement counselling and assistance for grieving family members 
following the patient’s passing.
	 1.	Holistic approach: Palliative care takes a holistic approach to addressing physical, 
emotional and spiritual aspects of suffering. It aims to enhance overall well-being 
and provide support to both patients and their families.
	 2.	Assessment of pain: Pain is subjective, and its impact varies among individuals. 
Palliative care professionals conduct thorough assessments to understand the 
nature, intensity and impact of pain on the patient’s life. This assessment helps 
tailor a personalized pain management plan.
	 3.	Multidisciplinary team: Palliative care teams typically include physicians, nurses, 
social workers, chaplains and other specialists working together to address the 
diverse needs of patients. The multidisciplinary approach ensures comprehensive 
care that goes beyond just managing physical pain.
	 4.	Medication management: Medications are a cornerstone of pain management 
in palliative care. Opioids, non-opioid analgesics and adjuvant medications may 
be prescribed based on the type and severity of pain. The goal is to find the right 
balance between pain relief and managing potential side effects.
	 5.	Non-pharmacological interventions: In addition to medications, non-
pharmacological interventions such as physical therapy, massage, acupuncture and 
relaxation techniques may be used to alleviate pain and enhance overall comfort.
	 6.	Communication and shared decision making: Open communication between 
health care providers and patients and their families is essential in palliative care. 
Shared decision making ensures that patients are actively involved in determining 
their pain management goals and preferences.
	 7.	Psychosocial support: Pain often has emotional and psychological components. 
Palliative care addresses these aspects through counselling, support groups and other 
psychosocial interventions to help patients cope with the emotional impact of pain.
	 8.	Advance care planning: Palliative care includes discussions about advance care 
planning, allowing patients to express their preferences regarding future medical 
decisions, including pain management, in case they become unable to communicate.
	 9.	Continuous assessment and adjustments: Pain management in palliative care is 
an ongoing process. The care team regularly reassesses pain levels, adjusts treatment 
plans and ensures that interventions align with the changing needs of the patient.
Palliative care guidelines
	
l The oncology team should follow recommended treatments for common symptoms.
	
l Address comorbid physical and psychosocial conditions with appropriate clinicians.
	
l Collaborate with palliative care specialists for complex concerns to enhance patients’ 
quality of life.
	
l Refer to mental health, social support, spiritual care and other services as needed.
	
l Consider collaboration with palliative care teams to identify additional community 
support.
	
l Provide primary palliative care, aligning anticancer treatments with patient goals 
and managing symptoms.

Chapter 8  Tumours/Carcinoma and Palliative Care    515
	
l Obtain informed consent for treatments from patients or surrogate decision makers 
for realistic understanding of options.
Physical aspects of care
Addressing physical symptoms is a key aspect of palliative care. Common symptoms 
include pain, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, cachexia, constipation, delirium, diarrhoea, 
dyspnoea, fatigue, sleep disturbances, insomnia, agitation, cough, fever, reflux 
disease, hiccups, ascites, pleural effusions, skin and wound care, pruritus, and urinary 
incontinence and retention.
This guideline focuses on a few common symptoms in the alleviation of which opioids 
and pain management play a crucial role.
Symptom management
	
l Conduct a thorough assessment of symptoms in all patients. For noncommunicative 
patients, assess symptom intensity using physical signs.
	
l Educate the patient/family/caregiver about the patient’s condition and the risk/benefit 
of treatment options.
	
l Provide emotional and psychosocial support for both the patient and the family/
caregiver(s) as an integral part of symptom management.
	
l When possible, prioritize palliative interventions that can address multiple symptoms 
as a general principle.
ANOREXIA/CACHEXIA
Cachexia, marked by physical wasting, is common in advanced cancer, often linked 
with anorexia. However, it can also occur independently due to inflammatory factors. 
Cachexia results in weakness, immune system impairment, metabolic dysfunction and 
other complications, affecting treatment outcomes and patient well-being. Unintentional 
weight loss is a common problem for the medically ill or frail elderly.
	 1.	For older adults, prescription appetite stimulants or high-calorie supplements are 
discouraged. Instead, optimize social supports, address medications interfering 
with eating, provide appealing food and clarify patient goals. While high-calorie 
supplements may increase weight, their impact on the quality of life, mood and 
survival remains inconclusive.
	 2.	During assessment, consider formal swallowing evaluation for dysphagia. Address 
conditions affecting food intake, such as dysgeusia, xerostomia, dental issues, 
hiccups, mucositis and depression.
	 3.	Social support, dietary counselling and feeding assistance are non-pharmacological 
options.
	 4.	Appetite stimulants like megestrol acetate may be considered for patients with a 
significant impact on their quality of life.

516    Standard Treatment Guidelines
DYSPNOEA
Dyspnoea is prevalent in most patients nearing the end of life and can pose significant 
discomfort, even if lung disease is not their primary diagnosis.
	 1.	Opioids have demonstrated efficacy in alleviating air hunger.
	 2.	Oxygen may benefit patients with hypoxia, but dyspnoea does not always correlate 
with oxygen saturation levels.
	 3.	Identifying and addressing underlying factors, like fluid overload, aligning with 
individual goals, can be beneficial when feasible.
URINARY INCONTINENCE
	 1.	Avoid indwelling urinary catheters for managing urinary incontinence. The bladder, 
especially with catheter use, is a common source of bacteraemia in post-acute and 
long-term care settings.
	 2.	Limit catheter use and duration, reserving them for specific indications like acute 
retention, outlet obstruction, aiding wound healing or end-of-life comfort when 
necessary.
PAIN MANAGEMENT
Pain, a subjective symptom, lacks an objective measurement; however, addressing it is 
crucial for enhancing the quality of life. No single assessment technique is universally 
applicable. Various assessment tools, including the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), 
Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), Verbal Rating Scale (VRS), Brief Pain Inventory (BPI), 
Critical Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT), Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia 
(PAINAID) and Integrated Palliative care Outcome Scale (IPOS), aid in evaluating 
pain. The choice of tool depends on individual circumstances.
	 1.	Obtain the patient’s pain score and goal, considering statements like ‘I can live with 
a pain of 2–3/10’, and determine whether the patient is opioid-naïve.
	 2.	Regularly assess pain in all terminally ill patients, including those with cognitive 
impairment.
	 3.	Utilize the cancer pain management ladder to guide pain management based on 
pain severity to minimize risks associated with opioids use:
	
l Step 1 – mild pain (non-opioids with or without adjuvants): Non-opioid 
analgesics such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or 
acetaminophen with or without adjuvants
	
l Step 2 – moderate pain (non-opioids plus weak opioids with or without 
adjuvants): Weak opioids (hydrocodone, codeine, tramadol) with or without 
non-opioid analgesics and with or without adjuvants
	
l Step 3 – severe and persistent pain (non-opioids plus strong opioids with 
or without adjuvants): Potent opioids (morphine, methadone, fentanyl, 
buprenorphine, tapentadol) with or without non-opioid analgesics, and with or 
without adjuvants
	
l Step 4: Nerve blocks, epidurals

	 4.	Educate patients about the purpose and extent of pain relief to achieve tolerable 
pain levels.
	 5.	Balance medication use (the optimum dosage) and side effects to prevent misuse 
or abuse while optimizing benefits. Opioid rotation may be considered to enhance 
analgesia and reduce side effects (see below).
NON-STEROIDAL ANTI-INFLAMMATORY (NSAIDS) DRUGS
	
l NSAIDs serve as the mainstay for treating mild to moderate somatic pain (e.g. bone, 
muscle, skin). They are also useful as adjuvants in certain cases, such as pain from 
bony cancer metastases.
	
l All NSAIDs offer analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic effects. Selection 
should consider dosing schedule, formulation (e.g. tablet, oral liquid, transdermal 
patch), cost, route of administration and contraindications if any. Acetaminophen 
(Paracetamol) is effective for mild to moderate pain alone or in combination, with a 
recommended dosage not exceeding 4000 mg every 24 hours in healthy individuals 
to minimize hepatotoxicity risk.
	
l Prolonged NSAID use warrants concomitant proton pump inhibitor therapy for 
gastroprotection.
ADJUVANTS
Adjuvants, a diverse group spanning various drug classes, aid in treating neuropathic 
and visceral pain conditions, and enhancing opioid analgesia. Also known as co-
analgesics, they include antidepressants (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants [TCAs], 
serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors [SNRIs]), anticonvulsants (e.g. 
Gabapentin, Pregabalin), topical anaesthetics (e.g. Lidocaine patch, Capsaicin), 
corticosteroids, bisphosphonates and cannabinoids. In bone pain, therapies involve 
radiation, steroids, NSAIDs, calcitonin and bisphosphonates.
	
l TCAs like amitriptyline and nortriptyline effectively address continuous dysesthesias 
(pins and needles). SNRIs such as Duloxetine and Venlafaxine, along with 
anticonvulsants like Gabapentin and Pregabalin, provide relief for lancinating pain 
(shooting, shock).
	
l Dosage of the commonly used adjuvants is given table 8.2. Gabapentin is titrated 
every 3–5 days, while pregabalin reaches maximum doses within a week.
	
l Topical anaesthetics like the lidocaine patch and therapies such as capsaicin are 
beneficial for localized and superficial neuropathic pain.
	
l In bone pain, therapies involve radiation, steroids, NSAIDs, calcitonin and 
bisphosphonates. Single-fraction palliative radiotherapy may also be used to address 
pain associated with bone metastases.
	
l Duloxetine, anticonvulsants or TCAs address painful diabetic neuropathy.
	
l NSAIDs may help in biliary colic, and octreotide aids intestinal obstruction pain.
	
l Haloperidol is a first-line treatment for nausea, vomiting, agitation, delirium and 
anxiety. SSRIs, like Fluoxetine, are primary for depressed mood or persistent

complex psychiatric illnesses such as psychotic or bipolar disorders to specialist

l Petroleum jelly can be applied to dress non-healing wounds, serving as a protective

NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL MANAGEMENT
Non-pharmacological approaches and integrative interventions serve as additional 
pain management options. Examples include cognitive behavioural therapy, relaxation, 
distraction, meditation, praying, aromatherapy, hypnosis, massage, application of hot 
or cold packs, repositioning, and use of supportive braces and art or music therapy. 
Peripheral therapies, like transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), 
acupuncture and acupressure, offer alternative strategies.
Peripheral nerve blocks effectively target localized pain and are safe, often 
reducing the need for medications. In cases of refractory pain, consult with pain 
management or palliative care specialists for palliative sedation, adhering to local 
institutional policies.
CULTURAL ASPECTS
Assess and adapt services, procedures and policies to ensure cultural and linguistic 
accessibility for diverse populations.
PSYCHOLOGICAL AND PSYCHIATRIC ASPECTS OF CARE
Addressing psychological aspects in serious illness is vital for quality palliative care. 
Regular assessment is crucial to detect and treat emotional distress, which often 
manifests as physical symptoms like pain, constipation, nausea and vertigo. Affective 
disorders negatively impact the patient’s quality of life. If physical symptoms persist,

Chapter 8  Tumours/Carcinoma and Palliative Care    519
investigating psychological or other causes is essential, and addressing the root causes 
of anxiety and depression is recommended.
AGGRESSION
Avoid using antipsychotics as the first choice for managing behavioural and 
psychological symptoms in dementia. Although aggression and challenging behaviours 
are common in dementia, antipsychotic medications offer limited benefits and pose 
risks such as oversedation, cognitive decline, falls, strokes and increased mortality.
Reserve the use of these drugs for cases where non-pharmacological measures 
fail, and there is an imminent threat to the patient or others. Identifying and addressing 
the root causes of behaviour changes can often eliminate the need for drug treatment.
INSOMNIA
Avoid prescribing benzodiazepines or other sedative–hypnotics as the primary 
treatment for insomnia, agitation or delirium in older adults. Extensive studies 
consistently reveal a significant increase in the risk of falls, hip fractures, motor 
vehicle accidents, leading to hospitalization, and death among older adults using these 
medications. Educate older patients, caregivers and providers about the harms of these 
medications.
Reserve the use of benzodiazepines for specific situations such as alcohol 
withdrawal symptoms/delirium tremens or severe generalized anxiety disorder 
unresponsive to alternative therapies.
Individualized treatment plans
Tailoring treatment plans, including dosing, to address patient needs, preferences 
and concerns is essential. Understanding pain nature, intensity and triggers is crucial. 
Consider unique aspects like medical history, cultural background and personal values 
in plan development. This approach acknowledges the absence of standardized dosages 
in pain treatment, presenting a significant challenge. Dosages must continually adapt, 
balancing desired effects and potential side effects.
PHARMACOLOGICAL MANAGEMENT OF PAIN WITH OPIOIDS
In managing pain pharmacologically with opioids for terminal illness, strong opioids 
are often necessary, especially for various pain subtypes such as visceral pain that may 
require multiple drugs.
Morphine and other opioids
Morphine is the preferred choice due to its cost-effectiveness and availability, making 
it clinically crucial in palliative care. Accessible in various forms, it is essential for 
patients with terminal dyspnoea or moderate/severe pain associated with acute, chronic 
or malignant conditions.

520    Standard Treatment Guidelines
When nearing the end of life, the benefits of opioid use may outweigh the risks 
for optimal symptom management. However, shared decision making is essential to 
reduce or eliminate opioids and avoid long-term complications. Close follow-up and 
re-evaluation are necessary, with dose reduction or discontinuation as needed.
Note: Opioids should not be the first-line treatment for chronic pain outside cancer, 
palliative and end-of-life care, except under specific circumstances with strict monitoring.
Administration routes
Oral: Morphine, a potent opioid analgesic, is available in various oral dosage forms. 
These formulations include Immediate-Release (IR) Tablets or Capsules (for rapid onset 
of pain relief), Extended-Release (ER/CR) Tablets or Capsules (for controlled release of 
morphine over an extended period, allowing for less frequent dosing), and oral solution 
for those who may have difficulty swallowing tablets or capsules.
Intravenous and subcutaneous: Intravenous opioids offer rapid pain relief, usually 
within an hour, and are preferred for severe, uncontrolled pain. Immediate-release 
oral morphine, on the other hand, takes effect in about 20 minutes but needs to be 
administered every 4 hours. Subcutaneous injections are preferred for patients who 
cannot swallow or use transdermal patches. Both routes provide the same dose and are 
equally well tolerated.
Rectal: Rectal morphine offers pain relief comparable to intravenous and subcutaneous 
administration but with a faster onset, although it may be unacceptable to some patients.
Epidural: Epidural administration shows similar efficacy to oral and subcutaneous 
morphine. While potential complications exist, such as CSF leak, spinal administration 
can benefit patients with severe side effects or inadequate pain control.
Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump with guard: Patients unable to take 
opioids orally or requiring significant doses may benefit from a PCA pump.
First-line maintenance
	
l Prefer oral dosing for mild to moderate pain, avoiding intravenous or rectal 
administration.
	
l For constant pain, prioritize round-the-clock over on-demand drug administration, 
aligning with pharmacokinetic characteristics.
	
l Prescribe oral morphine at 30–60 mg every 4–6 hours, with 5 mg oral IR Morphine 
as a rescue for breakthrough pain in patients on maintenance oral Morphine 
treatment.
	
l Adjust doses for a balance between pain control and side effects.
	
l Consider oral sustained-release Morphine or scheduled long-acting opioids for 
patients requiring multiple daily doses of short-acting opioids due to advanced and 
progressive disease.
	
l If pain remains inadequately controlled, review the analgesic strategy and seek 
specialist advice.

l Avoid transdermal patch formulations as the first line for patients suitable for oral 
opioids; consider subcutaneous opioids if requirements are unstable, prioritizing the 
lowest acquisition cost in both patch and subcutaneous deliveries.
	
l Exercise caution with Methadone due to its lengthy, unpredictable half-life.
	
l Utilize equianalgesic dosing tables and expert guidelines for initiating, monitoring 
and adjusting doses of oral and parenteral opioids.
Severe pain management
	
l Opioid-naive patients with moderate pain: Start Morphine IR at 10–15 mg orally. 
Reassess in 1 hour. If pain decreases by 50%, continue the same dose every 4 hours. 
If unchanged, repeat the dose, reassess and increase by 50%. Continue adjusting 
every hour until pain relief; once effective dose is determined, administer this dose 
every 4 hours.
	
l Severe pain score >6/10 in emergency: Prefer IV route; subcutaneous route if IV 
route is not available. Administer IV Morphine 2–5 mg every 15 minutes until pain 
decreases by 50% or the patient’s pain goal is achieved. Continue this effective 
dose every 4 hours. If pain persists, double the IV morphine dose; reassess every 
15 minutes until relief. Do not use IM route or long-acting forms like Fentanyl 
patch, MS Contin and OxyContin.
	
l Severe pain score ≥7 in patients on chronic opioids: Calculate total IV Morphine 
equivalents taken over the last 24 hours. Reassess in 15 minutes. If pain is relieved, 
continue this dose every 4 hours. If unrelieved, repeat the initial dose, reassess and, 
if necessary, give a double dose every 15 minutes until pain relief. Administer the 
dose that reduces pain by 50% every 4 hours.
	
l Continuous infusion: Calculate the 24-hour dose based on the effective dose during 
an acute pain crisis. Use 10% of the 24-hour dose for bolus (5 mg every 15 minutes). 
If on PCA, calculate the lockout period based on the effective hourly dose.
Breakthrough pain in patients who can take oral opioids
Breakthrough pain management in palliative care for patients on opioids involves 
addressing sudden, intense episodes of pain that occur despite the regular use of opioid 
medications. Recognize breakthrough pain by assessing its frequency, intensity and 
duration.
	
l Distinguish between predictable (occurring with certain activities) and unpredictable 
breakthrough pain.
	
l Ensure that the baseline opioid therapy is appropriately titrated for continuous pain 
control.
	
l Prescribe short-acting opioids for breakthrough pain, often administered in addition 
to the patient’s regular, long-acting opioid regimen.
	
l Use immediate-release opioids with a rapid onset of action.
	
l Individualize the breakthrough pain by dose based on the characteristics of the pain 
and the patient’s response.

522    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Consider starting with a percentage of the total daily opioid dose (e.g. 5–15% of the 
total daily opioid dose).
	
l Instruct patients on the proper use of breakthrough medication. Encourage them to 
take the breakthrough dose at the onset of pain or during activities that provoke pain.
	
l Consider scheduled or preventive dosing during periods when breakthrough pain is 
more likely to occur, such as before physical activities. Breakthrough pain may occur 
with the use of extended-release formulations or transdermal patches. Long-acting 
opioids reach a steady-state dose after about 20–24 hours (morphine and oxycodone) 
or 72 hours (transdermal fentanyl). Once a steady state is achieved, titration may 
occur following the same process.
	
l Utilize fast-onset formulations, such as sublingual, buccal or intranasal routes, for 
quicker relief.
	
l Educate patients and caregivers.
	
l Provide education on recognizing and managing breakthrough pain.
	
l Address concerns about opioid use and potential side effects.
	
l Explore the use of non-opioid medications, such as NSAIDs or adjuvant 
medications, to complement breakthrough pain management.
	
l Avoid offering fast-acting fentanyl as the first-line rescue medication.
	
l Seek a specialist’s advice if pain remains inadequately controlled despite 
optimization.
Ensure proper medication adherence
As any dosing alterations can lead to pain recurrence:
	
l Ensure medication adherence for effective pain management. Educate patients and 
caregivers on tailored adherence strategies. For example, consider specific needs 
of dying patients, balancing pain management with reduced consciousness levels. 
In contrast, in advanced cancer, opioids can be aggressively titrated for moderate/
severe pain.
	
l Address concerns about addiction, tolerance and side effects associated with opioids 
as these may lead to unfortunate under-treatment of pain. Addressing such barriers 
improves compliance and pain control.
	
l Provide verbal and written information on strong opioid treatment to improve 
compliance and pain control.
	
l Patients with cancer rarely develop tolerance to opioid analgesic effects (i.e. needing 
a higher dose for the same relief); increased requirements typically signify disease 
progression. Recognize pseudo-addiction behaviours stemming from inadequate 
pain control; providing written information enhances patients’ trust in their doctor.
	
l Similarly, addiction is rare; do not withhold opioids due to concerns about 
psychological dependence.
Switching opioids
Opioid switching may be necessary due to reasons such as cognitive decline, impaired 
swallowing, organ dysfunction or side effects. Dose conversion ratios differ, but

starting doses after switching should be lower than the equivalent original opioid due to 
incomplete cross-tolerance. Initiate the new opioid at a reduced dose, typically 25–50% 
of the newly calculated dose, and then titrate for optimal analgesia.
Balancing access and misuse
Strategies which can help minimize the risk of misuse and addiction are responsible 
prescribing practices, patient education and close monitoring. Identifying and 
addressing any signs of substance use disorder promptly is crucial. Doctors should be 
trained to address opioid side effects judiciously and avoid inappropriate morphine use 
for mild or chronic non-malignant pain.
	
l Controlled drug (CD) prescriptions must be handwritten, signed and dated, detailing 
patient information, drug name, strength, dose and quantity. If necessary, include 
the date of birth to differentiate between patients or a family member with similar 
names. Specify the name and form of the drug and indicate the total quantity in both 
words and figures. CD prescriptions are valid for 14 days and cannot be issued using 
the ‘repeat’ method.
	
l Injectable and fast-acting oral formulations of morphine must be available by 
prescription at all hospital-based clinics.
	
l Ensure that the prescription provides an ample supply of morphine, enabling patients 
or their families to obtain refills without facing excessively frequent, costly or 
burdensome travel requirements.
	
l Assess and minimize the risk of opioid dependence and misuse. Recognize 
concerning behaviours indicating opioid misuse and take additional precautions in 
areas with high crime rates to ensure opioid accessibility without burdening patients 
excessively.
	
  Indications of potential opioid misuse include adverse life consequences (such 
as job loss or relationship problems), concurrent substance abuse, drug-seeking 
behaviour (such as requesting early refills), non-cooperation with the opioid 
treatment plan (e.g. failure to follow up with the clinical team or refusal to use non-
opioid therapies), lack of reliability (self-adjusting drug doses, running out of stock 
prematurely) and loss of control over drug use (misplacement of prescriptions).
	
l Maximize opioid access for medical use while minimizing diversion risks. Store 
morphine securely, train personnel in safe handling, and maintain accurate records. 
Implement checks and balances for CDs, including patient records, transfers and 
stock management. Morphine should be securely stored in a robust, double-locked 
and securely anchored container or cabinet at all times. Additionally, maintaining 
records of the remaining supply, as well as documenting the amount dispensed to 
a patient and any quantity returned or wasted by the patient’s family, is essential.
	
l Record patients’ own CDs brought into the hospital at admission at the back of the 
CD register (CDR) or a separate register for that purpose and store in the CD cabinet.
	
l Record transfer of CDs at each point where a CD moves from the authorized 
possession of one person to another, by means of the signatures of both parties.

524    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Do not transfer CDs to another ward/department except when the CD is attached to 
the patient, e.g. syringe driver.
	
l Check the stock balance of all CDs at each change of shift with the minimum of a 
daily check.
	
l Use the handover checks as an opportunity to check that stock is sufficient and re-
order as required.
	
l Report any stock discrepancies immediately for investigation.
	
l Complete an incident form and notify the Pharmacy Services Manager.
	
l Dispose of expired medicines safely.
Prescribing in special situations
	
l Seek specialist advice for patients with renal or hepatic comorbidities, adjusting 
dosages to optimize pain relief and manage side effects. Fast-acting fentanyl is not 
recommended.
	
l For patients with renal failure, use caution with reduced dosages of morphine 
and fentanyl. Tramadol is not recommended. Consider low-dose subcutaneous or 
intravenous fentanyl or buprenorphine.
	
l In hepatic failure, use codeine cautiously with reduced dosages. Tramadol and 
Oxycodone require dose reduction, and methadone necessitates careful titration. 
Consider low-dose subcutaneous or intravenous fentanyl or buprenorphine.
	
l Tramadol is contraindicated in patients with a history of seizures; use cautiously with 
a history of substance abuse or psychiatric disorders.
ERRORS DUE TO OPIOID ADMINISTRATION
Errors in opioid administration can have serious consequences due to the potent effects 
of these medications on the central nervous system. Overdoses or incorrect dosages can 
lead to respiratory depression, coma and even death. Common causes or factors leading 
to errors in opioid administration can stem from various sources:
	
l Ineffective communication between health care providers, inadequate handovers or 
unclear prescription instructions can result in misinterpretation and dosing errors.
	
l Failure to tailor opioid doses to each patient’s unique characteristics, including 
medical history, pain intensity and tolerance, can lead to inadequate pain relief or 
excessive sedation.
	
l Insufficient monitoring of patients’ responses, vital signs and potential side effects 
can contribute to errors, as health care providers may overlook signs of opioid 
toxicity or inadequate pain control.
	
l Opioid dosages often require complex calculations, especially in patients with 
specific medical conditions. Errors can occur when calculating and administering 
these doses.
	
l Improper storage of opioids can compromise their efficacy and safety, leading 
to errors in dosing. Storing medications inappropriately may also contribute to 
diversion or misuse.

Chapter 8  Tumours/Carcinoma and Palliative Care    525
	
l Insufficient training of health care professionals in opioid administration, especially 
in specialized situations like PCA or epidurals, can contribute to errors.
MANAGEMENT OF OPIOID SIDE EFFECTS
Adherence to standardized protocols is essential for initiating and maintaining pain 
management. Management of some of the common side effects associated with opioid 
use is given next.
Constipation
The management of opioid-induced constipation involves a combination of lifestyle 
modifications, pharmacological interventions and, in some cases, consultation with 
health care providers. The key strategies are given next.

Increase dietary fibre intake through fruits, vegetables and whole grains.
	
l Maintain adequate fluid intake to prevent dehydration and promote bowel regularity.
	
l Encourage regular physical activity to stimulate bowel function.
	
l Establish a regular bowel schedule, attempting to have a bowel movement at the 
same time each day.
	
l Educate patients about the potential for opioid-induced constipation and the 
importance of early intervention.

Stool softeners and laxatives like polyethylene glycol, lactulose or senna can effectively 
relieve constipation. While there are multiple options available, a systematic review 
has shown no significant difference among them. Combining laxatives with diverse 
mechanisms may be advantageous for addressing stubborn constipation. Consider 
administering lactulose solution along with a senna preparation on a regular basis. If 
possible, consider gradual dose reduction or switching to alternative pain management 
strategies to reduce opioid-induced constipation.
Nausea
Some patients may experience nausea during the initial phases of opioid treatment. If 
nausea persists beyond this period, antiemetics, such as metoclopramide, can be offered. 
In cases where nausea remains unresolved, considerations may include switching 
opioids, adjusting the route of administration or reducing the dose to alleviate symptoms.
Orthostatic hypotension
Orthostatic hypotension, a potential side effect of opioid therapy, can be addressed 
through various strategies. Patients should be advised to rise slowly from a seated 
or lying position to minimize the risk. Adequate hydration is essential, and patients

526    Standard Treatment Guidelines
should maintain a consistent fluid intake. Compression stockings may be considered 
to improve venous return. Dose adjustment or medication review by a health care 
professional can also help mitigate orthostatic hypotension associated with opioid use.
Drowsiness
Drowsiness, sedation or impaired concentration may arise during the initiation or dose 
escalation of strong opioid treatment, often being transient. Patients should be cautioned 
about the impact on tasks requiring alertness, such as driving. Management steps include:
	
l Discontinue non-essential medications causing sedation, evaluate and treat other 
potential causes, and consider a 25% dose reduction in cases of persistent or 
moderate-to-severe sedation.
	
l Adjuvant therapies like a trial of Methylphenidate (5 mg orally daily) Or medications 
such as Risperidone, Olanzapine or Haloperidol for delirium can be explored.
	
l Switching opioids may also be considered.
Respiratory depression
Opioid-induced respiratory depression (OIRD) is a potentially lethal complication 
linked to opioid overdoses or concurrent use with depressants like sleep medication 
or alcohol. This risk exists for both patients with acute and chronic pain on opioid 
therapy and individuals misusing opioids. Combating respiratory depression involves 
co-treatment with non-opioid respiratory stimulants, preventing depression without 
compromising analgesic effects. Factors increasing OIRD risk include drug history, 
errors, opioid switching, concomitant medications and comorbid conditions (asthma, 
COPD, sleep apnoea, liver impairment and/or chronic kidney, pancreatitis, traumatic 
injury, skin ulcers, etc.).
	
l Although higher opioid doses are associated with a greater risk for overdose, the risk 
for overdose is also present in individuals taking lower opioid doses.
	
l Clinical signs of overdose include low respiratory rate (RR), with rapid-response 
interventions such as rescue breathing and naloxone administration in case RR is 
<6/min and loss of consciousness. For dying patients, an RR of 6–12/min is typical.
	
l Clinically significant respiratory depression with RR <6/min and loss of 
consciousness requires rapid interventions such as rescue breathing and naloxone 
administration. If the patient is arousable and RR >6/min, naloxone is not 
administered.
	
l Dosing, especially in PCA and epidurals, should be precise, and standing orders 
should cover naloxone administration.
	
l Regular monitoring of vital signs, pain scale and narcotic side effects is essential.
Opioid-induced hyperalgesia
Opioid-induced hyperalgesia is characterized by heightened pain sensitivity despite 
escalating opioid doses, often accompanied by widespread pain and allodynia (pain 
from typically non-painful stimuli). This phenomenon is more common with higher

Chapter 8  Tumours/Carcinoma and Palliative Care    527
doses of injectable morphine. Initial management involves reducing or discontinuing 
the current opioid dose, if possible, or transitioning to an opioid with fewer neurotoxic 
effects, such as fentanyl. It is essential to optimize non-opioid adjuncts. Consult a pain 
or palliative care specialist for further management.
PAEDIATRIC PALLIATIVE CARE (PPC)
Children are not little adults. While the definition and principles of palliative care 
in as above apply to the entire lifespan, PPC is distinct from adult palliative care, 
requiring unique attention to physical, developmental, psychosocial, ethical, spiritual 
and relational aspects specific to children.
Key differences include the uncertainty of prognosis, the need to integrate 
palliative care with intensive treatments, dual focus on growth and potential death, 
greater emotional burden for families and clinicians, continual developmental changes 
(physical, hormonal, cognitive, expressive and emotional), and varied information, 
recreational and educational needs, and modes of coping with stress.
Generalist clinicians with basic or intermediate palliative care training are often 
sufficient for most cases, analogous to general practitioners treating common infections 
without the need for specialists. Health systems should prioritize basic PPC training for 
general paediatricians, family doctors and paediatric nurse practitioners.
‘Palliative care plus’: preventing and relieving the suffering of children without 
a life-threatening illness
Acute and procedural pain and acute pain from traumatic injuries is often inadequately 
treated in children or not treated at all. ‘Palliative care plus’ extends its focus to 
alleviating pain in children without life-threatening illnesses, often addressing acute 
and procedural pain. Inadequate treatment of such pain not only causes unnecessary 
suffering but also leads to emotional distress, fear, agitation and a higher risk of chronic 
emotional sequelae. Examples of painful procedures include phlebotomy, injections, 
lumbar puncture, bone marrow aspirate, thoracentesis and dressing changes.
	
l Non-pharmacological techniques and topical analgesia can help minimize pain for 
quick and minimally invasive procedures, while more complex procedures may 
require systemic analgesia or opioids; for example, burn dressing changes require 
systemic analgesia medication while intraoperative and postoperative pain usually 
require an opioid.
	
l Various medications and treatments, such as paediatric formulations of Paracetamol, 
Ibuprofen, Morphine and Diazepam, as well as access to palliative cancer treatments, 
play crucial roles in managing pain in these cases.
	
l Morphine, though essential in palliative care, should not be the first-line treatment 
for chronic pain outside specific contexts, emphasizing careful monitoring and 
special circumstances.

HEADACHE
Headache is one of the most common symptoms for patients seeking medical care. 
Migraine is the second most common primary headache disorder in the world leading 
to significant loss of diseased-adjusted life years (DALY). Before diagnosing as 
primary headache, serious intracranial pathology should be ruled out by identifying 
red flag signs and symptoms. See Figure 9.1 for approach to management of headache. 
Meticulous clinical history and physical examination, an understanding of the 
typical features of primary headaches and application of International Classification 
of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3) diagnostic criteria can reduce the need for 
neuroimaging, lumbar puncture (LP) or other investigations. 
Approach to the history and physical examination of a patient presenting with 
headache for the first time or with a change in headache pattern should include:
	
l Onset of headache – new, old with increase in intensity or duration and/or change 
in character
	
l Headache type (pulsatile, throbbing, aching, thunderclap, head or neck trauma), duration 
of attacks (>4 hours, continuous/intermittent), frequency of headaches per month
	
l Pain location (unilateral, bilateral, associated neck pain, etc.)
	
l Headache-associated symptoms (nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, 
autonomic features like conjunctival injection, rhinorrhoea, etc.)
	
l Relationship of headache attacks with precipitating factors (stress, posture, cough, 
exertion, straining, neck movement, jaw pain, etc.)
	
l Identification of red flags (SNOOP10) (Fig. 9.1)
	
l Headache severity and effect on work and family activities
	
l Acute and preventive medications tried, response and side effects
	
l Presence of coexistent conditions that might influence treatment choice (insomnia, 
depression, anxiety, hypertension, asthma and history of heart disease or stroke)
The physical examination should incorporate the following elements:
	
l Screening neurological examination – mental status; cranial nerve examination; eye 
examination – pupils, eye movements, fundus examination, visual fields
	
l A focused neurological examination (e.g. lower cranial nerve examination in a 
patient with dysarthria or plantar responses in a patient with reflex asymmetry) in 
case of neurological symptoms or signs on screening examination

MIGRAINE
It is a benign and recurring syndrome of headache, nausea, vomiting and other 
neurological symptoms in various admixtures. Migraine headache is a common and 
potentially debilitating disorder. Treatment of acute migraine is challenging because 
of substantial non-response rate to medications and difficulty in predicting individual 
response to a specific agent or dose.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Migraine may or may not be preceded by a focal neurological phenomenon called 
‘aura’ most commonly experienced as visual alteration (flickering lights, spots, 
loss of vision). Aura may involve sensory symptoms (paraesthesia, numbness 
or motor weakness) or fully reversible dysphasic speech disturbance. Table 9.1 
depicts the criteria for classification of migraine disorders. Diagnoses of migraine 
can be refined based on the frequency of monthly migraine days (MMDs) and 
monthly headache days (MHDs); patients with fewer than 15 MMDs or MHDs 
have episodic migraine, and those with at least 15 MHDs, of which at least 8 are 
MMDs, have chronic migraine.
	
l Pain intensity may be mild (the patient is aware of a headache, but is able to 
continue daily routine with minimum alterations), moderate (the headache inhibits 
daily activities, but is not incapacitating) and severe (incapacitating headache). 
Visual analogue scale can be used for self-monitoring of the intensity of migraine.
	
l Rule out secondary headache when making a diagnosis of a primary headache 
disorder (Fig. 9.1). Look for warning signs for possible disorders other than primary 
headache in case of progressively worsening headache over time, sudden onset, red 
eyes, halos and unilateral visual symptoms. In most cases, a non-contrast CT is the 
best initial test. Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI might be appropriate in persons with 
a rapidly accelerating course of head injury or focal neurological findings. 
	
l Rare forms of migraine include basilar migraine with aura, hemiplegic migraine 
and retinal migraine. (Refer to a specialist for management.)

Identify and avoid trigger factors such as hunger, sunlight, tobacco, alcohol, foods 
(chocolate, cheese), strong odours or sprays, irregular sleep patterns, increased screen 
time and stress levels. Also assess menstrual cycle relationships in female patients. 
Maintain a healthy lifestyle. Address workplace ergonomics and give instruction in 
self-care of neck tension. Include hobbies and, if possible, exercise in the daily routine.

Goals
Instruct the patient to maintain a headache chart (includes frequency, duration, intensity 
of pain along with the need for abortive medications) for monitoring and self-awareness

of the headaches. Develop a written headache treatment plan for prevention and 
management of acute migraine to decrease headache frequency and decrease headache 
severity (headaches responding quickly to an abortive therapy); avoid medication 
overuse (limit treatment to an average of 2 headache days per week and consider 
preventive treatment for patients exceeding this limit).
The choice of acute migraine treatments depends on rapidity of onset, headache 
severity, associated symptoms (e.g. nausea/vomiting), disability, safety issues and 
patient preference. Acute treatment is most effective when given at the first sign of 
pain and when pain is mild. If a patient does not respond to 1–2 adequate doses of a 
given medication during a migraine episode, it is appropriate to try another medication.
Abortive therapy
	 1.	In case of mild-to-moderate migraine, i.e. occasional throbbing headaches, no 
major impairment of functioning:
	
	Tab. Ibuprofen 400 mg stat; if required, give 200–400 mg after 6 hours (maximum 
dose 1200 mg daily; do not exceed 2 days of use per week).
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Acetaminophen/Aspirin/caffeine (500 mg Aspirin component) once. Give an 
additional 500 mg if needed after 4 hours (maximum dose 4000 mg daily; do not 
exceed 3 days of use per week). 
	
	Or 
	
	Tab. Diclofenac 50 mg; if required, repeat after 8 hours.
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Indomethacin 25 mg stat; if required, repeat after 8 hours.
	
	If associated nausea and vomiting, Tab. Domperidone Or Metoclopramide 
10 mg stat.
	 2.	In patients with moderate-to-severe headache, or mild-to-severe headache with 
nausea or vomiting or rapid progression to severe headache or failure of first-line 
treatment as above; Choose a non-oral route of administration for severe nausea 
or vomiting.
	
	Tab. Sumatriptan 25–100 mg orally at onset, may repeat after 2 hours 
(maximum dose 200 mg daily)/Rizatriptan 5–10 mg once daily, may repeat after 
2 hours (maximum dose 30 mg daily). Intranasal preparations can also be used. 
Individuals may respond differently to different triptans. If a patient does not 
respond to one triptan, an alternative triptan may be offered.
	
	(Caution: If using two different formulations of a Triptan, use no more than two 
doses combined in 24 hours. Do not exceed 3 days of use per week. Do not take 
Triptans within 24 hours of any Ergotamine or vice versa. Use Rizatriptan 5 mg 
in patients receiving Propranolol with a maximum of 15 mg daily. Avoid or use 
with caution triptans in patients with coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular 
disease, uncontrolled hypertension and other vascular disorders and risk factors.)
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Diclofenac 75 mg IM at onset.

	If attack is not controlled by above, refer the patient with severe migraine to a

Hospital management of acute migraine
	 1.	Inj. Metoclopramide 10 mg IV. 
	 2.	Inj. Sumatriptan 6 mg SC, may repeat after 1 hour (maximum dose 12 mg daily).

	Or

	 3.	In severe headache unresponsive to other drugs, Inj. Sodium Valproate 500 mg IV

	Inj. Dexamethasone 4 mg IV 8 hourly for 2 days has limited evidence.
	
	Note: Opioid medications and butalbital/caffeine/aspirin are not recommended 
due to the high potential for the development of medication overuse headaches.
Prophylaxis
Consider prophylactic treatment in patients with migraine in any of the following 
situations:
	
l Attacks significantly interfering with patients’ daily routines despite acute treatment 
	
l Frequent attacks (two severe or disabling or four less disabling migraine attacks per 
month)
	
l Contraindication to, failure, or overuse of acute treatments, with overuse defined as: 
	– 10 or more days per month for ergot derivatives, triptans, opioids, combination 
analgesics and a combination of drugs from different classes that are not 
individually overused
	– 15 or more days per month for non-opioid analgesics, acetaminophen and NSAIDs 
including aspirin
	
l Adverse events with acute treatments 
	
l Patient preference
Prevention: Prevention should also be considered in the management of certain 
uncommon migraine subtypes, including hemiplegic migraine, migraine with brainstem 
aura and migraine with prolonged aura, and of those who have previously experienced 
a migrainous infarction, even if there is low attack frequency.

Prophylaxis treatment
In addition to the above non-pharmacological and pharmacological treatment of the 
acute episode, consider the following depending on comorbidity:
Tab. Propranolol 80–320 mg daily
Or
Tab. Amitriptyline 10–50 mg at bedtime
Or
Tab. Flunarizine 5–10 mg daily (preferable in patients with aura)
Or
Tab. Topiramate 50–200 mg daily for obese patients
Or
Tab. Sodium Valproate 50–100 mg/day Or Divalproate sodium 250–1000 mg/day
Note: There is insufficient evidence on the safety or efficacy of magnesium in migraine 
prophylaxis.
The goals of preventive therapy are:
	
l Fifty percent reduction in the frequency of days with headache or migraine
	
l Significant decrease in attack duration and/or attack severity as defined by the patient
	
l Improved response to acute treatment 
	
l Reduction in migraine-related disability and improvements in functioning in 
important areas of life 
	
l Improvements in health-related quality of life and reduction in psychological 
distress due to migraine
Start the chosen drug at a low dose and increase it slowly until therapeutic effect 
or side effects develop. Before considering failed treatment with a given migraine 
prevention medication, advance to the maximum recommended dose. A full therapeutic 
trial may take 2–6 months. If found to be effective, continue for at least 6 months and 
then slowly taper to assess its continued need. If headache recurs after discontinuation 
of prophylactic therapy, reinstate the medication regime for another 6 months’ trial. If 
several preventive drugs fail, refer to a specialist.
Advise the patient to keep and review a headache diary to monitor the effects of 
treatment on severity, frequency and disability. Diary entries should include day/time, 
headache severity, other symptoms (nausea, vomiting, photophobia), impact on usual 
activities, duration of attack, migraine triggers, prescribed medications including over-
the-counter (OTC) medication and response to medication and menstrual cycle day.
Menstrual migraine
Abortive therapy for menstrual migraine is the same as for non-menstrual migraine. 
Patients with frequent and severe attacks may benefit from short-term, perimenstrual use 
of long-lasting triptans, such as naratriptan and frovatriptan, during the perimenstrual 
phase (i.e. from day −2 to day +5 of menstruation). Patients receiving continuous 
preventive therapy and experiencing breakthrough menstrual migraine headaches may 
benefit from perimenstrual elevation of the dose of the preventive medication.

536    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Medication overuse headache (MOH)
Medication overuse headache is a state of daily or near-daily refractory headaches 
resulting from overuse of acute pain medicines by a patient with migraine. Potential 
triggers include OTC or prescribed symptomatic medications (all narcotics, analgesics, 
triptans, dihydroergotamine [DHE], benzodiazepines or decongestants) and caffeine in 
more than moderate amounts.
	 1.	Provide patient education.
	 2.	Stop overused medication; tapering may be required. It may take 2–6 weeks to 
resolve after elimination of medication overuse.
	 3.	Treat symptoms during withdrawal of overused medication.
	 4.	For headache frequency 15 or more days/month, treat with Prednisolone as above.
	 5.	Develop a written headache treatment plan that includes acute and prophylactic 
treatment.
Patient education
	
l Avoid precipitating factors like lack of sleep, glare, anxiety, hunger, foods like 
processed cheese, banana, chocolates, wine, etc. 
	
l Avoid overdose or frequent use of ergot preparation as these can cause hypertension 
and precipitate vascular disease. 
	
l Drug for acute migraine should be taken as early as possible at the onset.
	
l Regular, more than twice a week, or increasing consumption of analgesics over time 
are alarms that require attention.
	
l Advise behavioural intervention relaxation techniques and stress management 
techniques.

NEUROCYSTICERCOSIS (NCC)
This is the most common parasitic disease of the CNS worldwide produced by invasion 
of the CNS by the cystic stage (cysticercus) of pork tapeworm (Taenia solium) and is a 
common cause of seizures worldwide. Human beings acquire the disease when they ingest 
the food or water contaminated with the eggs of T. solium.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The clinical features depend on the site and number of cysts in the CNS, and the 
inflammatory response of the CNS. Neurocysticercosis can remain silent or present 
most commonly with headaches, seizures, encephalitis, meningitis, hydrocephalus or 
increased intracranial pressure.

Chapter 9  Central Nervous System Diseases    537
	
l Neurological, cognitive or personality disorder may be the presenting features 
and decreased visual acuity may be seen in ocular cysticercosis. 
	
l In spinal neurocysticercosis, cord compression, nerve root pain, transverse 
myelitis or meningitis are seen.
	
l Neuroimaging (CT/MRI) is the investigation of choice. The role of serological 
tests is currently as an adjunct to imaging techniques. A positive serological test 
(EITB, ELISA and dot blot assay) supports the diagnosis of NCC but a negative 
test does not exclude it.

The aim of therapy is to control symptoms, i.e. convulsions.
	 1.	Patients with multiple enhancing lesions and seizures should be initially treated 
with antiepileptic drugs, antiparasitic therapy and corticosteroids. However, 
corticosteroids should not be routinely used in patients with isolated calcified 
parenchymal neurocysticercosis (CPN) and perilesional oedema. 
	 2.	Antiepileptic drugs are needed for all patients with single enhanced lesions (SELs) 
and seizures along with antiparasitic drugs (Albendazole) with corticosteroids initiated 
prior to antiparasitic therapy. (For choice of antiepileptic drugs see Epilepsy below).
	 3.	Treat patients with calcified parenchymal lesions symptomatic therapy alone 
instead of antiparasitic drugs. 
	 4.	If there is no calcification, or SELs are present without risk factors for recurrent 
seizures and the patient is free of seizures for 2 years, treatment can be gradually 
discontinued. Risk factors for recurrent seizures include residual cystic lesions or 
calcifications on neuroimaging studies, breakthrough seizures or >2 seizures.

In live NCC cysts (one to five live cysts) and granuloma, cysticidal drugs accelerate 
the destruction of the parasites, resulting in faster resolution of the infection. Refer the 
patient to a physician or neurologist for supervised treatment with the following:
Tab. Albendazole 15 mg/kg/day (maximum 1200 mg/day) in 2 divided doses per 
day for 28 days, taken with fatty meals (Caution: Monitor for hepatotoxicity and 
leucopenia; in case of absolute neutropenia or elevation of transaminase >5 times the 
upper limits of normal, withhold albendazole until normalization of laboratory tests and 
consider alternative approaches [Praziquantel or no anthelminthics]). 
Note: Before administering Albendazole, 2–3 days’ priming is done with Tab. 
Prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 5–7 days. Absolute contraindications are ocular cyst [all 
patients with NCC should undergo a fundoscopic examination prior to initiation of 
Albendazole], intraventricular cysts, spinal medullary cysts, heavy cyst burden or 
calcified cysts or enhancing [degenerating cysts] or increased intracranial pressure [ICP].)
In patients with >2 viable parenchymal cysticerci, combine Albendazole with 
Praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day for 10–14 days.

538    Standard Treatment Guidelines
In patients with untreated hydrocephalus or diffuse cerebral oedema, manage 
elevated ICP alone and do not give antiparasitic treatment.
Subarachnoid cysts treat with antiparasitic drugs. Subarachnoid NCC does not 
respond well to single antiparasitic drugs at doses and durations used for parenchymal 
NCC. Optimal management may require chronic anti-inflammatory therapy, intensive 
antiparasitic therapy and surgical therapy (CSF diversion for hydrocephalus or 
minimally invasive surgical debulking).
Surgical treatment is indicated in case of ocular cysticercosis, ventricular cyst or 
hydrocephalus (antiparasitic therapy should be deferred until after surgical therapy.) 
Refer patients with refractory epilepsy and calcified parenchymal neurocysticercosis 
(CPN) for evaluation for surgical removal of seizure foci.
Monitoring 
	
l MRI should be repeated at least every 6 months until resolution of the cystic component.
	
l Retreat with antiparasitic therapy for parenchymal cystic lesions persisting for 
6 months after the end of the initial course of therapy. 
Pregnancy
Defer antihelminthic therapy until after delivery. However, pregnant patients with 
elevated ICP need to be aggressively managed as they would be if not pregnant. 
Corticosteroids can be used in pregnancy when necessary. For use of antiepileptic 
drugs, see the section ‘Epilepsy’. Methotrexate is teratogenic and should be avoided.
Patient education
	
l Neurocysticercosis is a preventable parasitic infection caused by larval cysts. 
Humans become infected after consuming under-cooked food or unpeeled fruits and 
vegetables, especially pork, or water contaminated with tapeworm eggs, or through 
poor hygiene practices. Food safety, improved sanitation and hygiene are all crucial 
to preventing the transmission of T. solium. Prolonged freezing or thorough cooking 
of pork kills the parasite.
	
l Personal hygiene and thorough washing and avoiding unpeeled fruits and vegetables 
in areas endemic for T. solium helps prevent ingestion of eggs.
	
l All members of a family of an index case of cysticercosis should be examined for 
the presence of eggs or signs of disease. 
(Also see the section ‘Neurocysticercosis’ in Chapter 19.)

EPILEPSY
Epilepsies are a group of disorders characterized by chronic, recurrent, paroxysmal 
changes in neurological function caused by abnormalities in the electrical activity of 
the brain. Each episode of neurological dysfunction is called a seizure.
Epilepsy is a disease of the brain defined by any of the following conditions:
	 1.	At least two unprovoked (or reflex) seizures occurring >24 hours apart
	 2.	One unprovoked (or reflex) seizure and a probability of further seizures similar to 
the general recurrence risk (at least 60%) after two unprovoked seizures, occurring 
over the next 10 years
	 3.	Diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome (as defined by cluster of features)
Isolated non-recurrent seizures may occur in otherwise healthy individuals for a variety 
of reasons, and under these circumstances, the individual is not said to have epilepsy.
SALIENT FEATURES
l	 A seizure (convulsion) is defined as a paroxysmal involuntary disturbance of brain 
function that may manifest as an impairment or loss of consciousness, abnormal 
motor activity, behavioural abnormalities, sensory disturbances or autonomic 
dysfunction. Some seizures are characterized by abnormal movements without 
loss or impairment of consciousness.
l	 Diagnosis should be made by a description of the seizure(s) from the patient and 
witnesses about frequency, symptoms during and following attacks, duration, 
circumstances and trigger factors, injury, tongue biting and incontinence.
l	 Diagnostically relevant factors are seizure types, age at onset (many epilepsies 
are age-specific), family history, past history of head injury, febrile convulsions, 
precipitating factors, e.g. photic stimulation, alcohol and other drug intake, and EEG 
for evidence of generalized or focal abnormality. There are better chances of detecting 
abnormalities if EEG is done soon after the seizure or within 48 hours. Abnormal 
EEG without seizures does not necessarily mean that a person has epilepsy.
l	 CT/MRI is performed for evidence of structural lesion. 
l	 Consider differential diagnosis of vasovagal syncope, non-epileptic attack 
disorder (pseudo-seizures), migraine, breath-holding spells, etc.

For immediate care during seizure, see the section ‘Status Epilepticus’. Long-term 
treatment is required for recurrent seizures. 
	
l Patients with first episode of seizures with no previous history of same or other 
types of seizures and in whom neurological and metabolic diseases are ruled out 
may be kept under observation and are not treated unless parents/patients are not

540    Standard Treatment Guidelines
willing to take the risk. However, patients presenting with status epilepticus (SE), 
partial seizures, Todd’s palsy, presence of neurological deficit, hemiparesis, mental 
retardation, cerebral palsy, strong family history of epilepsy and abnormal CT head 
and EEG have a higher risk of recurrence and can be put on long-term therapy after 
the first seizure.
	
l For alcohol withdrawal and metabolic or drug-related seizures, long-term treatment 
is considered only if there are recurrences suggestive of epilepsy.
	
l Treatment for seizures following head injury should be initiated after the first 
seizure; however, there is no role of prophylactic treatment for seizures after head 
injury. However, the duration of treatment depends on the risk of late epilepsy.
	
l Any seizure presenting after 20 years of age should be investigated for secondary 
causes of seizures.

The choice of antiseizure medication (ASM) should be based on seizure type, epilepsy 
syndrome (appropriate drug), affordability and availability of ASM.
Generalized tonic–clonic seizures and absence seizures
Tab. Valproic acid 15–40 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses increased by 200 mg at 3 days 
interval.
Or
Tab. Phenytoin 3–8 mg/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses or single night dose.
Or
Tab. Carbamazepine 10–30 mg/kg/day (600–1800 mg 3 times a day).
Or
Tab. Phenobarbitone 60–180 mg/day at night. In children: 5–8 mg/kg/day.
If seizures are not controlled with adequate dose of two first-line ASMs, refer to a 
tertiary care centre for addition of:
Tab. Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily; dose can be increased every 2 weeks 
(maximum 3000 mg/day) in adults and children older than 16 years.
In children: 1 to <6 months, 14 mg/kg/day; 6 months to <4 years, 20–50 mg/kg/day; 4 to 
<16 years, 20–60 mg/kg/day given in 2 divided doses. (Caution: Dosage adjustment is 
required in impaired renal function.)
Or
For absence seizures, add Tab. Lamotrigine 25–200 mg/day; start with 25–50 mg/day and 
slowly increase every 2 weeks to the maximum tolerated dose to achieve seizure control.
Focal onset seizures with preserved or impaired awareness, i.e. partial 
seizures (simple and complex partial seizures)
Tab. Carbamazepine 10–35 mg/kg/day (600–1800 mg 3 times a day).
Or
Tab. Valproic acid 15–40 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses increased by 200 mg at 3 days’ 
interval.

Principles of management
The aim of treatment is to control seizures with the most appropriate ASM without 
causing any significant side effects.
	
l Patient should preferably be controlled on a single drug (monotherapy).
	
l Start the drug with a low dose. If seizures recur, the dose can be increased after 
checking the compliance/drug levels.
	
l If seizures remain uncontrolled despite reaching the maximum dose of the first drug, 
add another drug as above and gradually reach the maximum dose of the second.
	
l If seizures are controlled by addition of a second drug, always try withdrawal of the 
first drug after few weeks of control of seizures.
	
l Combination therapy (polytherapy or adjunctive or ‘add-on’ therapy) can be 
considered when two attempts at monotherapy with ASMs have not resulted in 
seizure freedom. 
	
l If seizures continue despite trial with two ASMs, the patient should be referred to 
a specialist for evaluation and addition of second-line ASM such as Levetiracetam, 
Lacosamide and Lamotrigine.
	
l The formulation or brand of Phenytoin should preferably not be changed (variations 
in bioavailability or different pharmacokinetic profiles may increase the potential 
for reduced effect or excessive side effects). 
	
l Modified-release formulations offer ease of administration due to less frequent 
dosing and better compliance. These are costlier than regular formulations.
	
l Women with pregnancy prefer Levetiracetam Or Lamotrigine Or Carbamazepine.
Laboratory tests during ASM therapy
	
l Perform complete blood count, liver enzymes and renal functions before starting 
ASM.
	
l Perform serum calcium, alkaline phosphatase and other tests of bone metabolism 
every year for adults taking enzyme-inducing drug. 
	
l Asymptomatic minor abnormalities in blood test results are not necessarily an 
indication for changes in medication. 
	
l Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is not routinely indicated for management of 
epilepsy. Indications are the following: no response despite adequate dosage and 
compliance or detection of unsuspected poor compliance or ASM non-compliance in 
case of uncontrolled seizures; suspected drug toxicity; the patient being on multiple 
ASMs for adjustment of ASM dose while managing drug interactions; and during 
pregnancy, SE, or liver or kidney disease.

542    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Frequency of follow-up 
	
l People with epilepsy should maintain a seizure diary and have regular follow-up to 
ensure that the prescribed medication is taken as advised and to detect any adverse 
effects of ASM. This will also avoid a situation in which they continue to take 
treatment that is ineffective or poorly tolerated.
	
l The first follow-up may be undertaken anytime within 2–4 weeks of initiation of 
treatment. Subsequent follow-ups are undertaken at every 3–6 months, depending 
on the control of seizures and side effects.
	
l Review the seizure diary to assess efficacy tolerability and ensure ASM compliance. 
Lifestyle issues such as sleep, regular food intake, alcohol use, driving and 
pregnancy (if planned) should also be discussed.
	
l Review medication being taken by patients regularly, particularly for medicines 
with potential interactions with ASMs – certain ASMs (Phenytoin, Phenobarbitone, 
Carbamazepine, Oxcarbazepine) induce hepatic enzymes and induce metabolism, 
particularly of antitubercular drugs, antiretroviral agents, oral contraceptives and 
oral anticoagulants.
	
l Valproic acid inhibits hepatic enzymes and slows down metabolism of concomitant 
ASMs and other drugs causing toxicity requiring dose reduction.
(For seizures due to granuloma, see section on Neurocysticercosis)
Generalized absence and myoclonic seizures
Sodium valproate is the drug of first choice. Refer patient to a neurologist if patients 
who do not achieve adequate seizure control on sodium valproate or do not tolerate. 
The second choice depends on the seizure type and epilepsy syndrome.
Women with epilepsy (WWE) 
WWE who continue appropriate ASMs under proper supervision have more than 
90% chance of having a normal pregnancy and children. All WWE should be advised 
to plan their pregnancies using barrier contraception as some ASMs may make oral 
contraceptives ineffective. Pregnancy planning is vital as many antiseizure medications 
have the potential to affect foetal development and birth defects. The goal is optimal 
seizure control with minimum foetal exposure to AEDs. Any potential risk to the foetus 
should be balanced against the increase in risk of seizures. Non-adherence to ASM 
medication and alterations in ASM clearance are the major causes of breakthrough 
seizures. Pregnant women should continue to remain on their current ASM, as 
switching ASM can increase the risk of breakthrough seizures. Valproic acid should 
be avoided in women who can become pregnant. During pregnancy, plasma ASM 
concentrations may fluctuate due to physiological changes in absorption, increases in 
renal clearance, altered hepatic clearance, increases in plasma volume distribution and 
hepatic enzymatic induction from female sex steroid hormones. Most marked decline 
in blood levels is seen with phenytoin, phenobarbitone and newer ASMs such as 
levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, topiramate and zonisamide.
