All WWE in the reproductive age group, start:
	 1.	Tab. Folic acid (5 mg/day) at the time of starting ASM.
	 2.	Monotherapy with a single ASM at low dose is preferred. Regarding choice of 
ASM, there is no superiority for one ASM over the other with regard to foetal 
malformations. Nevertheless, valproic acid at higher doses carries a higher risk 
for neural tube defects. Levetiracetam and Carbamazepine are the preferred ASM 
for WWE. Seizures may remain unchanged in 50% of WWE or improve (25%) or 
even worsen (25%) during pregnancy.
	 3.	Continue ASMs in pregnancy. 
In a woman with an offspring with malformation in the previous pregnancy, 
carefully review the ASM therapy and, if necessary, change the ASM prior to the 
next pregnancy.
	 1.	Screen all pregnant WWE for foetal malformations by serum alpha-fetoprotein at 
16 weeks and by detailed ultrasound scanning by an experienced ultrasonologist 
at 18 weeks.
	 2.	If preterm labour is threatened in women taking enzyme-inducing ASMs, 
administer Betamethasone 48 mg over 48 hours.
	 3.	Give 2 doses of Vitamin K 10 mg IM at 34 and 36 weeks of pregnancy to all WWE, 
unless contraindicated.
	 4.	Give Vitamin K 1 mg IM at birth to all infants born to mothers taking ASMs.
During labour
	 1.	Continue ASMs during labour. If this cannot be tolerated orally, a parenteral 
alternative should be administered.
	 2.	Seizures during labour should be terminated as soon as possible.
	 3.	Inj. Lorazepam 4 mg IV or Diazepam. If seizures persist, manage as for SE. If 
seizures recur during labour, particularly after prolonged remission, consider 
other aetiological possibilities such as cortical vein thrombosis and eclampsia. 
Continuous foetal monitoring should be done in women at a high risk of a seizure 
in labour, and following an intrapartum seizure.
Note: Pethidine should be used with caution in WWE for analgesia in labour. 
Diamorphine should be used in preference to pethidine.
Postnatal period 
	 1.	If the ASM dose was increased in pregnancy, it should be reviewed within 10 days 
of delivery to avoid postpartum toxicity.
	 2.	WWE should be advised to continue their AEDs postnatally.
	 3.	Mothers should be well supported in the postnatal period to ensure that triggers of 
seizure deterioration such as sleep deprivation, stress and pain are minimized.
	 4.	Neonates born to WWE taking ASMs should be monitored for adverse effects 
associated with ASM exposure in utero. WWE who are taking ASMs in pregnancy 
should be encouraged to breast-feed.

be offered effective contraception to avoid unplanned pregnancies. Copper 
intrauterine devices (IUDs), the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system 
(LNG-IUS) and medroxyprogesterone acetate injections should be used as these

Age-dependent epileptic encephalopathies (ADEE)
These include early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, infantile spasms and Lennox–
Gastaut syndrome (LGS) with onset within 1 month, 4–12 months and 1–6 years, 
respectively. These are difficult to control and generally have associated mental defects.
West’s syndrome (infantile spasms, hyper-arrhythmia on EEG and mental 
retardation):
	 1.	Inj. ACTH 30–40 units/day for 3 weeks with tapering over the next 2 weeks.
	
	Or

over the next 2 weeks.
	 2.	Syr. Sodium valproate 15–40 mg/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses; continue for 
2–3 years after seizures are controlled.
	 3.	Tab. Clonazepam 0.01–0.03 mg/kg in 2–3 divided doses until seizures are controlled.
	 4.	Tab. Vigabatrin starting with a 50-mg/kg/day dose and increasing 50 mg/kg every

Lennox–Gastaut syndrome
For control of seizures, multiple drugs may be required and treatment should be best carried 
out at a specialized centre. Valproic acid and Clobazam should be used initially. Lamotrigine 
and Topiramate should be added in case of continuing seizures. Avoid Carbamazepine.
Discontinuing antiseizure drug (ASM) therapy
Withdrawal of ASM medication can be discussed with patients suffering from 
idiopathic epilepsy after 2 years’ seizure-free period. ASMs should be withdrawn 
over a period of 3–6 months or longer because abrupt withdrawal may cause SE. 
Withdraw one drug at a time in patients on multiple ASMs. If seizures recur during or 
after withdrawal, revert back to their ASM dose before reduction. Avoid withdrawal in 
certain epilepsy syndromes (e.g. juvenile myoclonic epilepsy) because of a high risk 
of relapse following withdrawal.
Surgery for epilepsy
Drug-resistant epilepsy is defined as ‘failure of adequate trials of two tolerated and 
appropriately chosen and used ASM schedules (whether as monotherapies or in 
combination) to achieve sustained seizure freedom’.

Before labelling seizures as intractable, it is essential to rule out errors in management that 
can mimic intractability. These errors include inadequate dosing, irrational polytherapy, 
inappropriate choice of ASM, or the presence of a non-epileptic attack disorder (NEAD). 
Every effort should be made to keep a seizure diary and see whether a specific ASM 
is actually helping or in some cases worsening the seizures, e.g. Carbamazepine/
Oxcarbazepine may worsen and sometimes even induce absence/myoclonic seizures. 
General principles of managing refractory epilepsy are as follows:
	 1.	Review the diagnosis and classification
	 2.	Review ASM currently and previously used
	 3.	Consider non-pharmacological treatments
	 4.	Address co-morbidities and lifestyle issues
	 5.	Optimize quality of life
Refer intractable epilepsy early to a tertiary centre for appropriate evaluation 
(including high-end MRI using standardized epilepsy protocols, video EEG, etc.) as well as 
to get guidance on management options like newer ASMs, the ketogenic diet and surgery.
Patient/parent education
	
l Important information for caregivers in case a person is found having a seizure 
(fit) or is unconscious after a seizure:
DO’S during seizure:
	– Put the person on one side and allow the fit to be over. The fit is usually over in 
1–2 minutes. Loosen the person’s clothes.
	– Inform his/her relatives and/or the treating doctor if any contact details are 
available in his/her pocket.
	– Rush the person to the nearby hospital/medical facility in case the fits do not stop 
or there are several fits one after the other or the patient remains unresponsive.
DON’TS during seizure:
	– Don’t put anything like a spoon, piece of wood or cloth in between the teeth or 
in the mouth or a key in the patient’s hands. Don’t put a shoe or onion in front 
of his/her nose.
	– Don’t forcibly stop his/her arms and legs from jerking.
	– Don’t give him/her anything to drink or eat. 
	– Don’t crowd around the person having a seizure.
	
l Most parents are initially frightened by the diagnosis of epilepsy and require support 
and accurate information. Anticipate and provide answers to questions, including 
inquiries about duration of the seizure disorder, side effects of medication and 
convulsions, aetiology, social and academic repercussions, and parental guilt.
	
l Provide information to parents and encourage them to maintain a seizure diary and 
treat the child as normally as possible. For most children with epilepsy, restriction 
of physical activity is unnecessary except that the child must be attended by a 
responsible adult while the child is bathing and swimming.

546    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Most children with epilepsy are well controlled on medication, have normal 
intelligence and can be expected to study in normal schools and lead normal lives. 
However, these children require careful monitoring, as learning disabilities are more 
common in children with epilepsy than in the general population.
	
l Cooperation and understanding among the parents, physician, teacher and child 
enhance the outlook for the patients with epilepsy.
	
l Counselling should also include first aid measures to be used if the seizure recurs.
	
l Patients should be instructed to avoid high-risk activities like swimming, driving, 
roof tops and fire places for at least 6 months after the last seizure.
	
l Explain that medications should be taken exactly as prescribed. Irregular intake of drugs 
or sudden stoppage can lead to SE and will also prolong the duration of the treatment.
	
l Advise the patient to report immediately in case of SE, if seizure frequency increases 
and if any intermittent illness develops, especially fever and behavioural problem.
	
l Young women on AED must consult doctor before conceiving.
	
l Explain possible long-term side effects of the AEDs: Phenytoin – gingival 
hypertrophy, hirsutism, acne, chloasma, coarsening of facial features, sedation and 
ataxia; Carbamazepine – sedation, ataxia and diplopia; Valproic acid – sedation, 
ataxia, diplopia and hair loss. Hepatotoxicity can occur in children.
	
l Explain special precautions to be taken with AEDs: In patients on valproic acid, frequent 
liver function test should be done at the beginning and the first 6 months of drug therapy.
	
l For prevention of gum hypertrophy, the patient should be advised to maintain good 
oral hygiene and frequent rinsing of the mouth.
	
l In patients on AEDs, explain possible risk of drug interactions, especially oral 
contraceptives and antitubercular drugs.

STATUS EPILEPTICUS
Status epilepticus (SE) is an emergency condition associated with a high morbidity 
and mortality if not treated early and effectively. However, about 12–30% of adult 
patients first present with SE as their first presentation. In patients with known epilepsy, 
the most common cause is a change in medication. SE can occur due to underlying 
metabolic disturbances, CNS infections, head trauma and hypoxia.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occur continuous convulsing seizures (CSE) lasting for more than 5 
minutes or two or more discrete seizures between which there is incomplete 
recovery of consciousness. Compensatory mechanisms start failing after 30 
minutes resulting in hypotension, decreased cerebral blood flow, normo- or 
hypoglycaemia, hypoxia and hyperpyrexia.
	
l Transient or early (0–30 minutes) physiological changes are hypertension, 
increased cerebral blood flow, hyperglycaemia, hyperkalaemia and lactic acidosis.
	
l Non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) is a change in mental status 
(change from baselines for at least 30 minutes) associated with ictal discharges 
on EEG.
	
l Refractory SE (RSE) is seizure activity that continues after first- and second-line 
AED therapies have failed. RSE can be generalized CSE (GCSE) or NCSE.

Non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE)
NCSE is less critical compared with convulsive status but requires ICU with facility for 
continuous EEG monitoring. General measures, investigation and treatment apply as

anticonvulsants may be tried.

Maintenance AED treatment following control of status epilepticus
Along with emergency treatment of GCSE and NCSE, maintenance AED therapy 
should be given to prevent recurrence of seizures.
	
l In patients known to have epilepsy, their usual AED should be maintained and dose 
adjustments may be carried depending on serum AED levels.
	
l In patients presenting for the first time as status, start AEDs to control status and 
then these can be continued as oral maintenance therapy.
Patient education
	
l Convulsive SE is a serious complication most often seen in patients with pre-existing 
epilepsy and is most often precipitated by missing or discontinuing medication or 
associated medical illness.
	
l If the patient continues to convulse for more than 5 minutes or does not regain 
consciousness after a seizure, he/she should be hospitalized.
	
l The patient should be transported in lateral position and the mouth should be cleared 
from secretions/frothing.

ACUTE BACTERIAL MENINGITIS
The three main pathogens, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae 
and Neisseria meningitidis, account for 75–80% of cases after the neonatal period. 
There has been a worldwide increase in infection with strains of S. pneumoniae 
resistant to penicillin and other beta-lactam antibiotics (second- and third-generation 
cephalosporins).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Two of the following features are present: fever with prominent headache, neck 
stiffness and altered mental status (lethargy to coma); marked CSF pleocytosis 
(100–10,000 WBC/μL [normal <5]) with 60% or greater polymorphonuclear 
leucocytes; growth of organism in culture; focal neurological signs; seizures; 
and papilloedema. 
	
l Infants, elderly and immunocompromised patients may show only mild 
behavioural changes with low-grade fever and little clinical evidence of 
meningeal inflammation. Examination findings that may indicate meningeal 
irritation include a positive Kernig’s sign, positive Brudzinski’s sign, neck 
stiffness and jolt accentuation of headache (i.e. worsening of headache by 
horizontal rotation of the head two to three times per second).

l Urgent LP and blood cultures should be sent before giving the first dose of 
antimicrobials. After CSF is obtained, the Gram stain results, WBC, RBC counts, 
glucose levels and protein levels should be evaluated immediately. Although no 
single measure is diagnostic, abnormal CSF findings are highly suggestive of 
meningitis and helpful in determining the likely aetiology. Table 9.3 depicts the 
typical CSF parameters in patients with meningitis. 
	
l Most cases of aseptic meningitis are viral and require supportive care. 
	
l In cases with focal findings, seizures, elderly, immunocompromised or clinical 
evidence of raised ICP, contrast-enhanced cranial computed tomography (CECT) 
should be done before LP.
	
l The CSF Gram stain result is positive in at least 60% of cases and CSF culture 
results are positive in approximately 75%. The likelihood of finding Gram stain or 
culture-positive CSF may decrease if antibiotics are administered before doing LP.

552    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Early in disease, 10–20% of patients have CSF cell counts less than 1000 cells/µl. 
Otherwise, cell counts less than 1000 cells/µl in a patient with a compatible clinical 
syndrome indicate partially treated meningitis, concurrent immunosuppression or a 
non-bacterial meningitis. 
	
l Blood cultures should be drawn before antimicrobial administration. Initiation of 
antimicrobials before LP decreases the yield of CSF culture, the likelihood of a low 
CSF glucose level and the degree of elevation of CSF protein.
	
l Petechial or purpuric rash suggests N. meningitidis, or, less often, Staphylococcus 
aureus, Pneumococcus or Rickettsia spp.
Treatment (hospitalize preferably in ICU)
The aetiologies of meningitis range in severity from benign and self-limited to life-
threatening with potentially severe morbidity. Bacterial meningitis is a medical 
emergency that requires prompt recognition and treatment.

l Maintain vitals and endotracheal intubation in patients with poor respiratory effort
	
l Elevation of the head to 30° and hyperventilation if evidence of raised ICP
Pharmacological (Fig. 9.3)
	 1.	Empirical antimicrobial should be initiated promptly if bacterial meningitis is 
suspected based on the patients’ age and underlying disease status. Do not delay 
empirical antibiotic treatment while awaiting diagnostic testing or transfers. Once 
Gram stain, culture and susceptibility tests are available, specific antimicrobial 
therapy targeting the pathogen should be administered (Table 9.4).

Patient education
	
l Make sure that all routine childhood immunizations are on time as per schedule. If not, 
ask patients to get vaccinations against flu, pneumonia and meningitis as appropriate.
	
l Early treatment of bacterial meningitis can prevent serious complications. Ask the 
patient to report to the doctor right away in case any member of the household has 
been around anyone who has meningitis.
	
l Explain to patients and caregivers that bacterial meningitis strikes very fast. It 
spreads quickly through the body and can cause severe long-term health problems 
and can even be fatal. So it is vital to get medical help right away. 
	
l Explain appropriate infection prevention and control precautions as common bacteria 
or viruses that can cause meningitis can spread through coughing, sneezing, kissing 
or sharing eating utensils, a toothbrush or a cigarette.
	
l Explain to the relative that in an unconscious patient, nothing should be administered 
orally until the patient recovers his/her level of consciousness.

TUBERCULOUS MENINGITIS
Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is a very critical disease and requires rapid diagnosis 
and treatment because of fatal outcome and permanent sequelae. A high index of 
clinical suspicion is absolutely essential especially if the patient presents with a clinical 
picture of meningoencephalitis. TBM must also be differentiated from other forms of 
acute and subacute meningitis, viral infections and cerebral abscess. Protracted course, 
diversity of underlying pathological mechanisms, variation of host immunity and 
virulence of M. tuberculosis make prediction of prognosis difficult. Prognosis is related 
directly to the clinical stage at diagnosis.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l TBM is a subacute disease comprising a prodromal phase of low-grade fever, 
malaise, headache, dizziness, vomiting and/or personality changes. It may persist 
for a few weeks, after which patients can develop more severe headache, altered 
mental status, stroke, hydrocephalus and cranial neuropathies. Seizures are 
uncommon manifestations of TBM in adults. However, seizures are commonly 
seen in children with TBM.

556    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Classic features of bacterial meningitis, such as stiff neck and fever, may be 
absent. Coma and death may occur without treatment.
	
l Neurological sequelae in survivors may include mental retardation in children, 
sensorineural hearing loss, hydrocephalus, cranial nerve palsies, stroke-associated 
lateralizing neurological deficits, seizures and coma.
	
l Classic neuroradiological features of TBM on MRI are basal meningeal 
enhancement, hydrocephalus.
	
l Send CSF samples to labs as soon as possible for examination of cells, proteins, 
sugar and cytology. Typically, the CSF is clear or slightly opalescent. There is a 
moderate degree of pleocytosis (usually less than 500 cells) with a predominant 
lymphocyte response. Biochemical examination reveals raised protein, usually 
less than 200 mg/dL. But in late cases and particularly when a spinal block 
develops, the protein content may be as high as 1–1.5 g/dL. Sugar is reduced to 
40 mg/dL or less. Smear positivity has been reported in less than 10% of samples.
	
l NAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF) is used as a preferential test for TBM. A negative 
Xpert MTB/RIF result on a CSF specimen does not rule out TBM. A diagnosis 
of tuberculous meningitis and decision to give antitubercular therapy are often 
made if a clinical syndrome is accompanied by a consistent CSF profile, evidence 
of tuberculosis elsewhere in the body or response to specific antimycobacterial 
therapy in the absence of evidence for other diagnosis.
	
l Criteria like the Lancet consensus scoring system and Thwaites system can 
be used for guiding diagnosis in cases with diagnostic dilemma and atypical 
symptoms.
	
l Bidirectional testing: All patients positive for TB should be tested for COVID-19 
and all COVID-19-positive patients should be tested for TB.
Treatment (hospitalize)
	 1.	Administer daily antitubercular therapy (ATT) standard daily first-line regimen 
with four first-line antitubercular drugs (RHZE) for 2 months. Do not extend 
IP in the daily regimen. Continuation phase (CP) in both new and previously 
treated cases with three drugs (RHE) for at least 10 months. Treatment duration 
may be increased in some cases as per the clinician’s decision. In case of optic 
neuritis, use streptomycin in place of ethambutol. Record protocol and duration 
of treatment at the time of initiation of ATT.
	
	(For details of therapy, see ‘Tuberculosis’ in Chapter 1.)
	 2.	Corticosteroid is indicated in HIV-negative patients and may be used in 
HIV-positive patients in case other life-threatening opportunistic infections are 
absent or in case of the impending or established spinal block and are given for 
4–6 weeks and tapered slowly over 2–6 weeks.
	
	Inj. Dexamethasone 8–16 mg/day IV in 3–4 divided doses in adults for 2 weeks.
	
	In children: 8 mg/day or 0.3–0.6 mg/kg/day. If not feasible, give oral Dexamethasone
	
	Or

	 3.	Urgent neurosurgical consultation and intervention (ventricular shunt) is performed

	 4.	If signs and symptoms of increased ICP are present, manage accordingly.

HERPES SIMPLEX ENCEPHALITIS
Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) is the most common cause of fatal sporadic acute 
encephalitis having a mortality of 70–80%, and leaves many survivors severely disabled 
without any significant predilection for age, sex, race or season.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The clinical hallmark of HSE is acute/subacute onset of fever, headache, 
altered consciousness and focal neurological symptoms/signs, especially 
personality/behaviour changes suggestive of a temporal lobe/frontal involvement. 
	
l CSF shows mononuclear pleocytosis (50–200 cell/mm3), mildly raised protein 
and normal or mildly decreased sugar. 
	
l The diagnosis is confirmed by CSF-PCR suggestive of HSV expression in 
CSF and contrast-enhanced MRI. EEG usually shows abnormality (slow 
waves/periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges [PLEDs]) localized to 
temporal/frontal lobes.

558    Standard Treatment Guidelines
A high index of suspicion is required and diagnosis should be considered in any 
patient with progressive deteriorating level of consciousness, fever, abnormal CSF and 
focal neurological signs in the absence of other causes.

Hospitalize the patient preferably in a set-up with ICU facilities.

l In patients with signs of increased ICP, raise the head end of patient by 30°, and 
perform ICP monitoring and hyperventilation in the intensive care unit.
	
l Maintain adequate hydration; however, in patients with syndrome of inappropriate 
ADH secretion (SIADH), restrict fluid intake. (Caution: Prevent dehydration.)

For seizures (see the section ‘Status Epilepticus’):
	 1.	Inj. Mannitol 20% 1 g/kg stat followed by 0.5 g/kg every 4–6 hours.
	
	Or
	
	Sol. Glycerol 30 mL 6 hourly orally.
	 2.	Start empirical treatment with Acyclovir in all cases at a very early stage or 
suspected of HSE pending confirmation of the diagnosis.
	
	Inj. Acyclovir 10 mg/kg 8 hourly for 10 days. The drug should be diluted to 
a concentration not exceeding 7 mg/mL and infused slowly over 60 minutes 
(can cause local phlebitis if extravasation occurs).
	
	If diagnosis of HSE is definite, give treatment for 21 days to prevent relapse. 
However, in a stable patient without documented evidence of HSE including 
negative CSF-PCR and a normal MRI, acyclovir can be discontinued after 5 days 
of presumptive treatment.
	
	Note: Role of steroids is controversial.
	
	Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is associated with HSE. Patients may have 
features like movement disorders, seizures, encephalopathy and sleep/autonomic/
language/behavioural abnormalities. These usually occur after the initial illness is 
resolved, so ruling out relapse of HSE by PCR is paramount.
Patient education
	
l Unlike most viral infections, this is treatable and the drug used is quite safe.
	
l If there is relapse of symptoms after resolution of initial illness, contact a neurologist 
for evaluation.
For treatment of acute meningoencephalitis in children, see Chapter 19.

JAPANESE ENCEPHALITIS
Japanese encephalitis (JE) is an acute viral infection of the CNS caused by JE virus 
which is a flavivirus. The virus is transmitted by the bite of infected Culex mosquitoes. 
Culex tritaeniorhynchus is the principal vector of the disease in South East Asia. The 
mosquito becomes infected by feeding on pigs and wild birds infected with the JE virus. 
The infected mosquitoes then transmit the virus to humans and animals during the 
feeding process. The transmission reaches its dead end in a human. The disease is not 
directly transmitted from person to person. The incubation period is usually 6–16 days 
(usually 4–6 days). JE is most commonly seen the age group of between 1 and 15 years.
The incubation period is between 4 and 14 days. In children, gastrointestinal 
pain and vomiting may be the dominant initial symptoms. Case fatality rates range 
from 10% to 35%. Neurological movement disorder (Parkinson’s features, dystonia, 
dyskinesia), seizures, focal weakness or mental retardation, psychiatric sequelae, and 
anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis are common among survivors.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Mild infections may occur without apparent symptoms other than fever with 
headache or may present with abrupt onset of headache, high fever, neck stiffness, 
stupor, disorientation, coma, tremors, convulsions (especially in infants) and 
paralysis. Focal neurological findings and rapidly changing central nervous 
system signs (e.g. hyperreflexia followed by hyporeflexia or plantar responses 
that change) are seen.
	
l Diagnosis of JE infections can be made by serological tests, such as 
haemagglutination inhibition test by demonstrating a fourfold rise in antibody 
(IgG) titres in paired sera or IgM antibody in serum and CSF. CSF pleocytosis 
(100–1000 leucocytes/μL) occurs; initially, it is polymorphonuclear but in a few 
days, it becomes predominantly lymphocytic.
	
l CT/MRI helps differentiating Japanese encephalitis from herpes simplex 
encephalitis and shows low-density non-enhancing areas in the thalamus, basal 
ganglia and brainstem.

There is no specific antiviral treatment for JE. Treatment of JE is supportive and 
symptomatic with mannitol, steroids, antiepileptic drugs and IV fluids.

560    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Patient education
	
l As JE is a mosquito-borne disease, measures should be taken to eliminate mosquito 
breeding sites and prevent mosquito bites (use of mosquito repellents, long-sleeved 
clothes, coils and vaporizers). 
	
l Travelers spending extensive time in JE endemic areas are recommended to get 
vaccinated before travel. 
	
l For non-immunized persons, vaccination is indicated mainly for persons spending 
30 days or more in a rural agricultural endemic area during the transmission season. 
	
l For initial immunization, usually two doses of JE vaccine are given, beginning with 
the first dose at 9 completed months followed by the second dose at 16–18 months. 
Two doses 3 months apart till 15 years of age are given in endemic districts only. 
For details, see ‘Immunization Schedule’ in Chapter 19.
	
l Common reported side effects include local reactions at the injection site and mild 
systemic symptoms such as headache, myalgia, gastrointestinal symptoms and fever.

STROKE
Stroke/cerebrovascular disease (CVD) refers to a rapidly developing clinical syndrome 
of focal or global loss of brain functions lasting for more than 24 hours or leading to 
death with no apparent cause other than that of vascular origin. Transient ischaemic 
attacks (TIAs) refer to when focal or global cerebral dysfunction disappears within 
24 hours. Most TIAs last for less than 30 minutes.
Stroke is not a homogeneous condition. There are clear pathological subtypes – 
cerebral infarction, primary intracerebral haemorrhage and subarachnoid haemorrhage with 
more than 100 potential underlying causes. Pre-hospital stroke identification and prompt 
transfer of the patient to a centre well equipped with stroke management is very important.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Presentation varies depending on the site of involvement – carotid circulation 
stroke presents with hemiplegia and/or aphasia. Vertebrobasilar insult produces 
dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, dizziness/crossed signs or coma.

Chapter 9  Central Nervous System Diseases    561
	
l The Face, Arm, Speech and Time (FAST) test is a simple approach to diagnose 
stroke. One or more of the following are present in 88% of all strokes and TIAs: 
face weakness, arm weakness and speech difficulty symptoms.
	
l Brief initial neurological examination is performed to determine the degree of 
neurological deficit using validated stroke scales like the NIHSS (NIH Stroke 
Scale).
	
l All patients should undergo urgent neuroimaging (NECT or MRI) to distinguish 
ischaemic stroke from intracranial haemorrhage (ICH), complete blood count, 
blood glucose, urea, serum creatinine, serum electrolytes, ECG and markers 
of cardiac ischaemia. Selected patients may require liver function tests, chest 
radiography, arterial blood gases, EEG, lumbar puncture, blood alcohol level, 
toxicology studies or pregnancy test.
	
l Assess cardiac status for associated coronary artery disease.
	
l Stroke can be a presenting symptom of COVID-19, and can happen in young 
people (younger than 45 years) without traditional stroke risk factors. Combined 
aetiologies and presentations among these patients are hypercoagulable state, 
vasculitis, cardiomyopathy and endothelial dysfunction. Stroke can also manifest 
in severely affected patients with COVID-19 as a multiorgan involvement. Tests 
are performed for SARS-CoV-2 and inflammatory markers [for details, see 
inflammatory markers (Appendix X)].

Transient ischaemic attack
	
l Consider patients presenting with transient symptoms suggestive of a 
cerebrovascular event to have had a TIA, unless neuroimaging reveals an alternative 
diagnosis (Fig. 9.4). Neuroimaging should be performed within 24 hours of symptom 
onset or as soon as possible in patients with delayed presentations.
	
l In patients who are first seen after fully resolved or with rapidly resolving 
neurological symptoms, determine the cause of stroke and then identify treatable 
causes that can reduce the risk of stroke (greatest in the first 7–14 days).
	
l In patients with a history of TIA, give Tab. Aspirin 150 or 300 mg daily Or 
Clopidogrel 75 mg once a day if allergic to aspirin.
Stroke (Best treated in a specialized stroke unit)
The overall goal is to minimize acute brain injury and maximize patient recovery. The 
window period for thrombolysis is 4.5 hours. Stroke management as given next should 
be provided throughout the patient care journey, while following strict infection control 
measures at all times to reduce spread of infection and to protect health care staff (see 
Appendix II) [see ‘Influenza-Like Illness (ILI)/Severe Acute Respiratory Infection 
(SARI)/COVID-19’ in Chapter 5].

Clinical suspicion symptoms may include episodes of neurological deficit, unilateral paresis, memory loss, headache,

Risk factors: Cigarette smoking, obesity, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, family history of coagulation 
disorder or recent TIA
Emergent evaluation (within 24 hours of symptom onset)
MRI (preferred) or non-contrast head CT, ECG, echocardiogram, blood glucose, serum electrolytes, lipids

Immediately following acute stroke
	
l Manage airway, breathing and circulation. Take precautions to avoid aspiration and 
ensure adequate oxygenation. Provide supplemental oxygen to maintain oxygen 
saturation >94%.
	
l Nil orally. A swallowing assessment (50 mL water swallow test) should be 
undertaken before starting eating or drinking. Testing the gag reflex is invalid as 
a test of swallowing. Assess patients with normal swallow for the most suitable 
posture and equipment to facilitate feeding. Consider nasogastric feeding in patients 
with abnormal swallow. Consider gastrostomy feeding for patients who are unable 
to tolerate nasogastric tube. Give only intravenous fluids (dextrose saline or normal 
saline) in patients with altered sensorium for at least 2–3 days.
	
l Perform urgent neurosurgical assessment for patients with large cerebellar infarcts 
with hydrocephalus and subarachnoid haemorrhage and for selected cases of cerebral 
haemorrhage.
	
l Establish time of symptom onset (last known normal).
	
l Acute elevation of BP is often transient and declines spontaneously. 
Hypotension/excessive BP reduction not recommended.
	
l Maintain blood glucose level between 140 and 180 mg/dL (avoiding both 
hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia). Manage elevated blood glucose 
>140 mg/dL with sliding scale insulin in the first week of stroke onset. Monitor 
for hypoglycaemia and accordingly administer 20% glucose (50 mL bolus). 
Dextrose-containing fluids in non-hypoglycaemics are not recommended. Excessive 
intravenous fluids are not recommended.
	
l Monitor temperature every 4 hours for at least the first 48 hours and preferably as 
long as the patient is in the ward. Treat even mild fever as elevation of temperature 
consistently worsens the neurological outcome from ischaemic insults.
	
l Correct hypovolaemia with intravenous normal saline. 
	
l Perform cardiac monitoring for at least the first 24 hours and correct cardiac 
arrhythmias.
	
l Tab. Aspirin at least 150 mg immediately after brain imaging has excluded 
intracranial haemorrhage (ICH; in patients with t-PA, delay Aspirin until after the 
24-hour post-thrombolysis). In patients with a large hemispheric infarct (malignant 
middle cerebral artery [MCA] territory infarct), delay Aspirin until surgery or 
decision is made not to operate. In patients with dysphagia, Aspirin may be given 
by enteral tube.
	
l Give subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) for preventing deep vein 
thrombosis (DVT) in immobilized patients and prothrombotic states unless bleeding 
risk is high. COVID-19-related cardiomyopathy adds risk of cardioembolic stroke; 
Heparin or Warfarin may be preferable.
Acute ischaemic stroke (cerebral infarction)
Immediate specific management of ischaemic stroke in patients presenting within 
a specific time window from symptom onset (usually within 4.5 hours), absence of

564    Standard Treatment Guidelines
contraindications such as recent surgery or bleeding disorders as below. The door-to-
needle time (time of bolus administration) should be within 60 minutes from hospital 
arrival. Selection of thrombolytic agents depends on factors such as patient eligibility, 
time window for treatment and the specific agent’s pharmacokinetics and safety profile, 
with alteplase (tPA) being the most commonly used due to extensive clinical evidence 
supporting its efficacy and safety in ischemic stroke.
	 1.	Start thrombolytic therapy with Inj. Alteplase 15 mg IV bolus, 0.75 mg/kg over 
30 minutes, 0.5 mg/kg over 60 minutes (total dose not to exceed 100 mg) Or 
Reteplase 10 units IV, two doses at an interval of 30 minutes Or Inj. Tenecteplase 
30–50 mg IV bolus Or rtPA 0.9 mg/kg (maximum dose 90 mg) infusion over 
60 minutes, with 10% of the dose given as a bolus over 1 minute in carefully 
selected patients fulfilling the criteria for thrombolysis treatment in specialist units.
	
		
Thrombectomy (clot retrieval treatment) increases the chance of a good outcome 
by more than 50% in selected cases of large vessel occlusion.
	
	Note: No benefit has been demonstrated for Heparin, corticosteroids, nimodipine 
or other calcium channel antagonists, barbiturates, plasma volume expanders or 
haemodilution techniques in mortality in patients with acute ischaemic attack.
	 2.	In ischaemic stroke, do not treat elevated blood pressure unless the patient is being 
considered for thrombolysis and is in hypertensive emergency. Lower BP carefully 
and maintain SBP <185 mmHg and DBP <110 mmHg before fibrinolytic therapy is 
initiated and maintained below 180/105 mmHg for at least the first 24 hours after 
intravenous rtPA treatment. 
	
	Withhold antihypertensive medication in patients with ischaemic stroke unless 
SBP is >220 mmHg or the mean arterial blood pressure (MAP) is >120 mmHg and 
lower BP by approximately 15% during the first 24 hours. Lower blood pressure 
slowly with the use of oral medications except in hypertensive emergency.
	
	Note: Sublingual use of antihypertensives is not recommended.
Monitoring
	
l Measure BP and perform neurological assessments every 15 minutes during and 
after IV rtPA infusion for 2 hours, then every 30 minutes for 6 hours and then hourly 
until 24 hours after IV rtPA treatment. If the patient develops severe headache, acute 
hypertension, nausea or vomiting or has a worsening neurological examination, 
discontinue the rtPA infusion if it is being administered and obtain emergent 
CT scan.
	
l Delay placement of nasogastric tubes, indwelling bladder catheters or intra-arterial 
pressure catheters if the patient can be safely managed without them.
	
l Obtain a follow-up CT or MRI scan at 24 hours after IV rtPA before starting 
anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents.
Intracranial haemorrhage
	
l If SBP is >220 mmHg or MAP is >150 mmHg (recorded twice, 2 or more minutes 
apart), then BP should be aggressively treated with parenteral antihypertensives

Chapter 9  Central Nervous System Diseases    565
(e.g. labetalol or nitroglycerin as below) with frequent BP monitoring. Target BP 
should be 160/90 or MAP of 110 mmHg. However, lowering SBP to less than 
140 mmHg in less than 6 hours is not recommended.
	
l Maintain SBP between 150 and 220 mmHg and without contraindication to acute 
BP treatment, acute lowering of SBP to 140 mmHg is safe.
Inj. Labetalol 10–20 mg IV over 1–2 minutes, may repeat once.
If blood pressure is not controlled or diastolic BP >140 mmHg, institute 
Nitroprusside 0.5–1.5 mcg/kg/min infusion increased in steps of 500 mcg/kg/min every 
5 minutes within a range of 0.5–0.8 mcg/kg/min. Stop if response is unsatisfactory with 
maximum dose in 10 minutes.
If SBP >180 mmHg or MAP >130 mmHg with (suspected) ICP elevation, maintain 
cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) at 60–80 mmHg, and lower BP with intravenous 
antihypertensives (bolus or infusion).
If SBP >180 mmHg or MAP >130 mmHg without evidence of ICP elevation, clinically 
evaluate the patient every 15 minutes, and control BP with intravenous antihypertensives 
(bolus or infusion) to maintain a MAP of 110 mmHg or SBP/DBP of 160/90 mmHg.
If systolic BP is <180 mmHg and diastolic BP is <105 mmHg, defer antihypertensive 
therapy. Overzealous treatment can convert ischaemic penumbra into an infarct. 
Low blood pressure:  Volume replenishment is the first line of approach. Isotonic 
saline or colloids can be used and monitored with the central venous pressure or 
pulmonary artery wedge pressure. If hypotension persists after correction of volume 
deficit, consider continuous infusions of pressors (Dopamine 2–20 mcg/kg/min), 
particularly for low systolic blood pressure, such as systolic BP <90 mmHg.
ICP monitoring and treatment
	 1.	Patients with a GCS score of ≤8, those with clinical evidence of transtentorial 
herniation or those with significant IVH or hydrocephalus might be considered for 
ICP monitoring and treatment. Maintain a CPP of 50–70 mmHg depending on the 
status of cerebral autoregulation.
	 2.	Perform ventricular drainage for hydrocephalus especially in patients with a 
decreased level of consciousness.
	 3.	Corticosteroids should not be administered for treatment of elevated ICP in ICH.
Note: Efficacy and safety of intraventricular administration of rtPA and endoscopic 
treatment of IVH is uncertain.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Patient presents with severe headache with vomiting, neck stiffness and altered sensorium, 
and non-contrast CT scan shows blood in the cisterns and CSF is uniformly blood stained.
Tab. Nimodipine 60 mg 4 hourly.
Immediately transfer the patient to a tertiary care centre with a neurosurgery set-up 
after securing patent airway and blood pressure and investigate for underlying cause 
and angiography to identify aneurysm.

566    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Surgical treatment in stroke
Surgery for ischaemic stroke may be required in select patients with MCA infarction 
(decompressive hemicraniectomy and be operated within a maximum of 48 hours). 
Patients with cerebellar haemorrhage who are deteriorating neurologically or who 
have brainstem compression and/or hydrocephalus from ventricular obstruction 
should undergo surgical removal of the haemorrhage as soon as possible; suboccipital 
craniectomy may be required in patients with large cerebellar infarct causing 
compression of the brainstem and altered consciousness; ventriculostomy is performed 
in symptomatic hydrocephalus.
Acute arterial dissection
Investigate with appropriate imaging (MRI and MR angiography) and in case of stroke 
secondary to arterial dissection, treat with either anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents. 
In selected patients, stenting may be indicated.
Cardioembolic stroke
Treat patients with a disabling ischaemic stroke who are in atrial fibrillation with Tab. 
Aspirin 300 mg for the first 2 weeks before starting anticoagulation with Tab. Warfarin.
In patients with prosthetic valves who have disabling cerebral infarction and who 
are at a significant risk of haemorrhage transformation, stop anticoagulants for 1 week 
and substitute with Tab. Aspirin 150–300 mg daily.
General early supportive care (supportive services to use protective 
precautions for COVID-related stroke)
Position
The patient is advised to undertake activities like sitting, standing or walking only 
with caution as early as possible preferably within 24 hours of the stroke onset. An 
occasional patient who deteriorates on assuming sitting or standing posture should be 
advised bedrest with frequent position changes to avoid bed sores and contractures, etc.
Early mobilization
Start passive full-range-of-motion exercises for paralysed limbs during the first 
24 hours. Refer all patients to a physiotherapist/rehabilitation team as soon as possible, 
preferably within 48 hours of admission.
Oral care
All patients with stroke should have an oral/dental assessment including dentures, 
signs of dental disease, etc., on or soon after admission. Follow an appropriate oral care 
protocol for every patient with stroke including frequency of oral care (twice per day 
or more), types of oral care products (toothpaste, floss and mouthwash) and specific 
management for patients with dysphagia or consult a dentist.

Chapter 9  Central Nervous System Diseases    567
Swallowing
Assess swallowing before the patient begins eating, drinking or receiving oral 
medications. Patients who cannot take solid food and liquids orally should receive 
nasogastric tube feedings to maintain hydration and nutrition while undergoing efforts 
to restore swallowing.
Nutrition
Determine nutritional status of every patient using a valid nutritional screening method 
within 48 hours of admission. Consider nutritional support in a malnourished patient. 
Routine use of nutritional supplements has not been shown to be beneficial.
Management of seizures
Treat even single seizure with IV loading dose of Levetiracetam/Sodium Valproate 
followed by orally for a period of at least 3 months. If needed, add Carbamazepine or 
Sodium Valproate. Treat SE (for details, see Epilepsy and Status Epilepticus as above). 
Note: Prophylactic antiseizure medication is not recommended.
Bladder care
Avoid an indwelling catheter as far as possible and if used, assess daily and remove as 
soon as possible. Intermittent catheterization should be used for urinary retention or 
incontinence.
Bowel care
Assess the patient with bowel incontinence for other causes of incontinence including 
impacted faeces with spurious diarrhoea. Perform drug review in patients with severe 
constipation to minimize the use of constipating drugs. Give advice on diet, fluid intake 
and exercise (as much as possible). Oral laxatives and rectal laxatives should be given 
only if severe problems remain.
Infections
Development of fever after stroke should prompt a search for pneumonia, urinary 
tract infection or DVT. Prophylactic administration of antibiotics is not recommended. 
Appropriate antibiotic therapy should be administered early (after taking relevant 
culture specimens).
Venous thromboembolism
Prophylaxis of deep vein thrombosis
	
l Early mobilization and optimal hydration should be maintained for all patients with 
acute stroke.
	
l In patients with paralysed legs (due to ischaemic stroke), give Inj. LMWH (with 
appropriate prophylactic doses as per the LMWH agent).

568    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Prevention of stroke in patients with stroke and transient ischaemic attack 
Evaluate all patients for modifiable risk factors within 1 week of onset including 
hypertension, diabetes mellitus, smoking, carotid artery stenosis (for those with 
non-disabling stroke), atrial fibrillation (AF) or other arrhythmias, and structural cardiac 
disease. In any patient in whom no risk factor is found, investigate for rare causes 
including antiphospholipid antibodies, proteins C and S, and anti-thrombin III.
Management of hypertension
If hypertension (≥140 systolic and ≥90 diastolic) persists for more than 2 weeks, treat 
hypertension and lifestyle modification (for details, see the section ‘Hypertension’ in 
Chapter 3). An optimal target for all patients is <130/80 mmHg.
Antiplatelet therapy
	
l All patients with ischaemic stroke or TIA should receive antiplatelet therapy unless 
there is an indication for anticoagulation.
	 Tab. Aspirin at least 150 mg once daily within 24 hours Or Tab. Clopidogrel 75 mg 
once daily Or extended-release Dipyridamole 200 mg added to Aspirin 50 mg twice 
daily is given. 
	 Note: For patients who have an ischaemic cerebrovascular event while taking 
Aspirin, increasing the dose of Aspirin provides no additional benefit. Combined 
aspirin–extended release Dipyridamole as well as clopidogrel is marginally more 
effective than Aspirin in preventing vascular events but increases the risk of 
haemorrhage and is not recommended unless there is indication for this therapy (i.e. 
coronary stent or acute coronary syndromes). Addition of a proton pump inhibitor 
should not be routine and should be considered only when there is dyspepsia or other 
significant risk of gastrointestinal bleeding with aspirin.
	
l In every patient with atrial fibrillation (valvular or non-valvular), unless 
contraindicated, start anticoagulation if he/she is likely to be compliant with the 
required monitoring and is not at a high risk for bleeding. Aspirin also provides 
some protection if there are constraints to the use of oral anticoagulation. 
(Note: Anticoagulation should not be used for patients in sinus rhythm unless 
cardiac embolism is suspected.)
	
l Consider anticoagulation for all patients who have ischaemic stroke associated 
with mitral valve disease or prosthetic heart valves or within 3 months of 
myocardial infarction. Do not start anticoagulation until brain imaging has excluded 
haemorrhage and 14 days have passed from the onset of a disabling ischaemic 
stroke (except when a demonstrable intracardiac thrombus is present). Tab. Warfarin 
5–7.5 mg/day is given for effective anticoagulation target; INR is 2.5 (range 2.0–3.0) 
except for mechanical cardiac valves (3.0: range 2.5–3.5).
Carotid intervention
Patients with TIA or non-disabling stroke and ipsilateral 70–99% internal carotid artery 
stenosis (measured by two concordant non-invasive imaging modalities or on a catheter 
angiogram) should be offered carotid endarterectomy. Stenting is performed in select

Chapter 9  Central Nervous System Diseases    569
symptomatic patients with moderate (50–69%) stenosis within 2 weeks of the stroke 
unless contraindicated. Note: Carotid intervention is not recommended for patients 
with mild (<50%) stenosis. All those with carotid stenosis should receive all secondary 
prevention measures whether or not they receive carotid intervention.
Lipid-lowering therapy
All patients with a history of TIA or ischaemic stroke should be treated with a statin 
if they have a total cholesterol of >200 mg/dL, or LDL cholesterol >100 mg/dL. The 
treatment goals should be a total cholesterol of <200 mg/dL and LDL cholesterol of 
<100 mg/dL (<70 mg/dL for very high-risk individuals). Treatment with statin therapy 
should be avoided or used with caution in patients with a history of haemorrhagic stroke.
Diabetes
Screen all patients for DM with testing of fasting plasma glucose, HBA1C, or an oral 
glucose tolerance test.
Obesity
Screen all patients with TIA or stroke for obesity with measurement of BMI.
Nutrition
Conduct a nutritional assessment for patients with a history of ischaemic stroke or 
TIA, looking for signs of overnutrition or undernutrition. Counsel patients to follow a 
Mediterranean-type diet instead of a low-fat diet. Routine supplementation with vitamins 
is not recommended. Reduce sodium intake to <2.4 g/day. Further reduction to <1.5 g/
day is also reasonable and is associated with even greater BP reduction.
Sleep apnoea
Consider a sleep study in suspected cases as there is a high prevalence of stroke in 
people with sleep apnoea.
Homocysteinaemia
Routine screening for hyperhomocysteinaemia among patients with a recent ischaemic 
stroke or TIA is not indicated.
Antiphospholipid antibody
Routine testing is not recommended for patients with ischaemic stroke or TIA who 
have no other manifestations of the antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and who have 
an alternative explanation for their ischaemic event, such as atherosclerosis, carotid 
stenosis or AF.
Rehabilitation (rehabilitative services should use protective precautions for 
COVID-related stroke)
Rehabilitation is beneficial when begun as early as possible and continued in the 
community as part of a well-coordinated (‘seamless’) multidisciplinary programme of 
accelerated hospital discharge and home-based resettlement to promote ongoing recovery.

570    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Patient education
	
l To educate patients, family members and caregivers about the identification of stroke 
symptoms and reporting to a hospital in the window period; to apprise patients, 
family members and caregivers about activation of emergency response team to 
speed up treatment of stroke
	
l Modification of lifestyle factors including physical activity, not smoking, avoiding 
environmental tobacco smoke, moderate alcohol consumption, maintaining a normal 
body weight and eating a low-fat diet high in fruits and vegetables; promotion of 
weight maintenance in patients with overweight/obesity who are unable to achieve 
recommended weight loss; sleep hygiene, sleep duration (>6 hours) and good quality 
of sleep
	
l Control of risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidaemia and 
cessation of cigarette smoking
	
l To advise weight loss which has been shown to improve cardiac features of 
metabolic syndrome, which has also been shown to improve insulin sensitivity; 
lower plasma glucose, plasma LDL-C and plasma triglycerides; raise HDL-C; lower 
BP; reduce inflammation; improve fibrinolysis; and improve endothelial function in 
patients with metabolic syndrome

ACUTE INFLAMMATORY DEMYELINATING 
NEUROPATHY/GUILLAIN–BARRÉ SYNDROME (GBS)
GBS is an acute, frequently severe, fulminant polyradiculoneuropathy usually presenting 
as ascending paralysis. It is presumed to have immune-mediated pathogenesis with 
lymphocytic infiltration of peripheral nerves and destruction of myelin for which no

Chapter 9  Central Nervous System Diseases    571
specific cause can be demonstrated, although it is commonly preceded by a viral or other 
infection – respiratory and gastrointestinal; it can reach nadir within 3 days to 4 weeks 
and the onset of symptoms follows a monophasic course with recovery. Several subtypes 
are recognized. COVID may have a varied neurological manifestation (including CNS – 
headache, encephalopathy and stroke; peripheral nervous system [PNS] – dysfunction of 
taste/smell, neuropathy]; and the muscular system – myalgia, myositis, rhabdomyolysis) 
which can emerge standalone or during the clinical course. A high index of suspicion 
for COVID-19 in patients presenting with new-onset neurological symptoms is required 
for an early diagnosis.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Diagnostic criteria for GBS are progressive motor weakness of more than one 
limb and partial or total areflexia. 
	
l Involvement of respiratory muscles is common and can be diagnosed by the 
presence of respiratory distress/shallow respiration, weak voice, inability to 
cough effectively and decreased inability to count in single breath. 
	
l Features strongly supportive of diagnosis are progression of symptoms up to 
4 weeks, relative symmetry, mild sensory signs or symptoms, facial nerve 
(50%) or other cranial nerve involvement, transient or absent bladder 
involvement, recovery 2–4 weeks after nadir, autonomous dysfunction and 
absence of fever at the onset; CSF features are elevation of proteins after the 
first week and cell count <10 mononuclear/mm; electrophysiological evidence 
of demyelination (prolonged F-wave, distal latencies, decreased conduction 
velocities, conduction block) is present.

Hospitalization is necessary for even mild cases for observation of progression of 
neurological deficit. 
Admit in ICU in case of one or more of the following: rapid progression of 
weakness, severe autonomic or swallowing dysfunction, evolving respiratory distress 
and Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score (EGRIS >4).

l General care includes care of the back, bowel, bladder, and pressure points.
	
l Physiotherapy should be instituted early.
	
l Ventilatory support should be provided in impending respiratory failure (required 
in ~30% of cases).

Treatment should be started at the earliest in case of one or more of the following: 
inability to walk >10 m independently, rapid progression of weakness, severe

572    Standard Treatment Guidelines
autonomic or swallowing dysfunction or respiratory insufficiency. Also it is not 
effective if started after ~2 weeks of first motor symptoms.
Mild cases: No specific therapy is needed (corticosteroids have no role).
Severe cases: As indicated by progressive weakness requiring assistance for walking 
(power grade 3 or less), involvement of respiratory/bulbar muscles, swallowing difficulty:
Inj. Human immunoglobulins 400 mg/kg day for 5 days (Caution: Contraindicated in 
patients with IgA deficiency)
Or
If facilities are available, Plasmapheresis 40–50 mL/kg for a total of 4–5 exchanges 
over 7–10 days
Monitoring
	
l All patients should be closely monitored for: (i) progression of motor weakness, 
(ii) involvement of respiratory/bulbar muscles, and (iii) autonomic disturbance, e.g. 
hypo/hypertension, cardiac arrhythmia and bladder/bowel control.
	
l Early complications include choking, cardiac arrhythmia, infections, DVT, pain, 
delirium, depression, urinary retention, constipation, corneal ulceration, dietary 
deficiency, hyponatraemia, pressure ulcers, compression neuropathy and limb 
contractures.
	
l Start rehabilitation programme early and manage long-term complaints such as 
fatigue, pain and stress.
Patient education
	
l Explain the natural course of the disease. It can progress to involve all the four 
limbs, respiration and swallowing. 
	
l Disability can be reduced with treatment and most patients achieve complete or 
nearly complete recovery. 
	
l Prognosis is bad in old age, rapidly progressive weakness, axonal form of GBS and 
delay in onset of treatment. 
	
l Role of physiotherapy should be stressed. 
	
l Provide psychological support.

DEMENTIA
Dementia is a progressive and largely irrevocable clinical syndrome characterized by a 
widespread impairment of mental cognitive function. The essential features of dementia 
are an acquired and persistent compromise in multiple cognitive domains that are severe 
enough to interfere with everyday functioning. Majority of dementias are degenerative 
and progressive. The deficiency of acetylcholine is the predominant neurochemical 
defect in Alzheimer’s disease. Vascular dementia is the second most common cause 
of dementia after Alzheimer’s disease. Rapidly progressive dementias, i.e. ‘affecting 
activities of daily living within 1 year of onset of symptoms’, need to be evaluated 
for correctable causes which include infectious, metabolic, vascular, autoimmune and 
neoplastic conditions.
SALIENT FEATURES
As the condition progresses, the patient can experience some or all of the following:
	
l There occur memory loss, language impairment, changes in personality, 
difficulties with activities of daily living, self-neglect, psychiatric symptoms 
(e.g. apathy, depression or psychosis) and out-of-character behaviour (e.g. 
aggression, sleep disturbance or disinhibited sexual behaviour; although the latter 
is not typically the presenting feature of Alzheimer’s disease but can be seen in 
frontotemporal dementia).
	
l A diagnosis of dementia should be made only after a comprehensive assessment 
including history, cognitive and mental state examination, physical examination 
and other appropriate investigations, and a review of medications in order 
to identify and minimize use of drugs that may adversely affect cognitive 
functioning.
	
l Perform a basic dementia screen at the time of presentation: routine haematology, 
biochemistry, thyroid function test, serum vitamin B12 and folate levels.
	
l Syphilis serology, HIV, CSF examination and EEG should be performed in 
selected cases and not as a routine investigation.
	
l MRI is the preferred modality to assist with early diagnosis and detect subcortical 
vascular changes, and to exclude other intracranial lesions. A specialist’s advice 
should be taken when interpreting scans in patients with learning disabilities.

Obtain history not only from the patient but also from someone who knows the patient 
well to:
	 1.	Establish the presence and characteristics of any substantial changes, and to 
categorize the cognitive behavioural syndrome (concerns should not be dismissed 
as ‘normal ageing’ without a proper assessment

574    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 2.	Investigate possible causes and contributing factors to arrive at a diagnosis
	 3.	Appropriately educate, communicate the findings and diagnosis, and ensure 
ongoing management, care and support (treatable causes of dementia should 
be ruled out before considering the diagnosis of degenerative dementia; the 
common treatable causes of dementias are alcoholic, endocrinal – hypothyroidism, 
metabolic, infective and dementia related to head trauma [subdural haematoma])
Note: Degenerative dementias are not curable, but the progression of dementia can be 
slowed down and quality of life can be improved by available treatment modalities. 
For optimal results, multiple modalities should be utilized including pharmacotherapy, 
behaviour management, psychotherapy, psychosocial treatment, support and education 
of families.

l Behavioural modification, scheduled toileting and prompt voiding reduce urinary 
incontinence.
	
l Reactivation of occupational rehabilitation
	– Memory training, maximal creative activity, improving sensory motor function, 
psychosocial functioning 
	
l Graded assistance, practice and positive reinforcement should be used to increase 
functional independence.
	
l Low lighting levels, music and simulated nature sounds may improve eating behaviour 
for persons with dementia, and intensive multimodality group training may improve 
activities of daily living, but these approaches lack conclusive supporting data.
Pharmacological (to be given by a specialist)
For cognitive deficits: For mild-to-moderate dementia (Mini-Mental State Examination 
[MMSE] score between 10 and 20):
Tab. Rivastigmine 1.5–6 mg/day in 2 divided doses (maximum dose 12 mg/day). If the 
patient is intolerant to oral therapy, Rivastigmine dermal patches in 5- and 10-cm sizes 
to be applied 12 hourly anywhere on the body surface (preferably back).
Or
Tab. Donepezil 5–10 mg/day as a single dose.
Start with the lowest dose and titrate to the maximum dose in 4–6 weeks’ time.
For severe dementia, add second-line drug:
Tab. Memantine hydrochloride 5–10 mg as a single dose. Start with 5 mg and increase 
to 10 mg after 4 weeks.
Note: New drugs Lecanemab and Aducanumab, both antibodies targeting amyloid in 
mild AD, are now available in some countries.

Chapter 9  Central Nervous System Diseases    575
Review after every 6 months by MMSE score and global, functional and behavioural 
assessment. Carer’s views on the patient’s condition at follow-up also should be sought.
For behavioural and psychotic symptoms in dementia (BPSD), treat agitation or 
psychosis with dementia and depression accordingly (for details, see ‘Schizophrenia 
and Acute Psychotic Disorder’ and ‘Depression’ in Chapter 16).
Note: Review medications being taken by patients before making diagnosis and 
avoid antiparkinsonian anticholinergics, tricyclic antidepressants, all conventional 
antipsychotics and clozapine, antispasmodics, antihistaminics, antimuscarinics and 
skeletal muscle relaxants.
Patient education
	
l Short-term programmes which are directed towards educating the family caregivers 
about dementia should be offered to improve the caregiver’s satisfaction.
	
l Intensive long-term education and support services should be offered to caregivers 
of the patient with dementia to delay time to nursing home placement.

PARKINSON’S DISEASE
Parkinson’s disease (PD) refers to the idiopathic form of parkinsonism. It affects 
1–2 per 1000 population older than 65 years. Pathologically, there is degeneration and 
depletion of the pigmented dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra pars compacta.

576    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The core features are bradykinesia, asymmetric-onset rigidity, rest tremors (pill-
rolling movements) and postural instability.
	
l There occurs difficulty in performing fine coordinated movements like writing, 
using hand tools and kitchen utensils, grooming, and doing and undoing buttons. 
	
l There occurs difficulty in rolling in bed and getting out of chairs or automobiles.
	
l There occurs gait difficulty with slowing, stooped posture, decreased or loss of arm 
swing and gait festination. Limb discomfort and stiffness may be an early symptom.
	
l Diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease remains clinical. As such, there is no role of 
investigations.
	
l It can occur in individuals younger than 50 years, also known as young-onset 
Parkinson’s disease (YOPD). In YOPD, MRI brain should be done to rule out 
other diseases like mass lesions, Wilson’s disease and stroke.

Perform neuropsychological assessment to diagnose PD dementia in all patients in the 
early stages of the disease using global cognitive measure (level I global cognitive test 
– MoCA/MMSE) and, in addition, more detailed testing of the main cognitive domains 
including memory, executive functions and instrumental functions. (Level II tests include 
at least two tests per domain for a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment.)

l Occupational and physiotherapy improves activities of daily living along with mood 
and mobility.
	
l Mindfulness practices, walking and cycling help to decrease stress, anxiety, sleep-
related problems and dementia in PD.
	
l Nutrition: A balanced diet with fibre supplement should be taken.

‘Early disease’ refers to PD in people who have disease <5 years and have not 
developed motor complications. ‘Late disease’ refers to PD in people on Levodopa who 
have developed motor complications.
Treatment should be started once the parkinsonian symptoms begin to impair the 
activities of daily living. Start with a low dose and gradually increase until the benefit 
or side effects occur.
Early PD
Any of the following can be given as monotherapy or in combination. The choice of 
the drug first prescribed should take into account clinical and lifestyle characteristics 
and patient preference.
	 1.	Tab Pramipexole 0.125–4 mg/day in 3 divided doses.
	
	Or

Chapter 9  Central Nervous System Diseases    577
	
	Tab. Ropinirole 6–24 mg/day in 3 divided doses. 
	
	Or 
	
	Tab. Piribedil 25–100 mg/day as a single dose or 2 divided doses.
	 2.	Tab. Rasagiline 0.5 mg once a day for 4 weeks, and then 1 mg once a day. 
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Safinamide 50 mg/day.
	 3.	For tremor-predominant PD, add:
	
	Tab. Trihexyphenidyl 6–20 mg in 3 divided doses.
	
	(Caution: Avoid anticholinergics in patients older than 65 years.)
	 4.	If symptoms worsen, add Tab. Levodopa plus Carbidopa (100–250 mg Levodopa) 
in divided dose as per requirement. (Caution: Do not combine with meals; give 
at least half an hour before meals and avoid a high-protein diet; modified-release 
levodopa preparations should not be used so as to delay the onset of motor 
complication in people with early PD.)
	 5.	Tab. Amantadine 100 mg twice or thrice daily. It is better for axial symptoms like 
gait instability. (Caution: Hallucinations and pedal oedema are the frequently 
encountered side effects. Evening dose should be given maximum by 5 PM to 
prevent hallucinations.)
Notes:
	
l The practice of withdrawing patients from their antiparkinsonian drugs (so-called 
drug holidays) to reduce motor complications should not be undertaken because of 
the risk of neuroleptic malignant like syndrome (NMS).
	
l Selegiline and apomorphine have a limited role in treatment. Co-enzyme Q10 and 
vitamin E should not be used as a neuroprotective therapy for people with PD.
Late PD
Most people with PD will develop, with time, motor complications and will eventually 
require Levodopa therapy + Dopamine agonists/COMT inhibitors, triple combination 
– levodopa + carbidopa + entacapone – and/or dopamine agonist.
Refer the patient to a neurologist if drug-induced dyskinesias or motor fluctuations 
occur and those with Parkinson’s plus syndrome (progressive supranuclear palsy, 
multisystem atrophy, etc.) for surgical interventions such as deep brain stimulation.
PD with dementia: About 20–30% of patients with PD may also have dementia and 
around 40% of patients with PD have associated mild-to-moderate depression which 
has a major impact on the quality of life; therefore, they should be treated appropriately. 
For details of management, see the section ‘Dementia’ and Depression. Patients with 
PD may experience agitation, hallucinations or delusions causing severe distress. Avoid 
antipsychotics as they can worsen the motor features of the condition, and cause severe 
antipsychotic sensitivity reactions in some patients.
Other associated problems: Screen and treat appropriately for sleep disturbance, fall risk 
and autonomic disturbances: urinary dysfunction, weight loss, dysphagia, constipation, 
erectile dysfunction, orthostatic hypotension, excessive sweating and sialorrhoea.

578    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Vitamin D deficiency: Vitamin D deficiency should be treated in patients with PD for 
optimal neurological function.
Fall prevention
Patients with PD are more likely to fall than their healthy age-matched peers. Consider 
an individualized multifactorial intervention programme for all people with fall or at 
risk of fall with the following specific components:
	
l Strength and balance training 
	
l Home hazard assessment and intervention 
	
l Vision assessment and referral 
	
l Medication review with modification/withdrawal
Patient education
	
l Provide all relevant information to patients and families regarding the disease, 
its prognosis and therapeutic options. Discussions should focus on therapeutic 
expectations, lifestyle modification and aids to overcome motor disability or limitation.
	
l Antiparkinsonian medication should not be withdrawn abruptly or allowed to fail 
suddenly due to poor absorption (e.g. gastroenteritis, abdominal surgery) to avoid 
the potential for acute akinesia or NMS.

MYASTHENIA GRAVIS
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is the most common primary disorder of neuromuscular 
transmission. It may begin at any age from infancy to very old age. Subtypes include 
congenital MG and generalized MG.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patients with MG seek medical attention for specific muscle weakness or 
dysfunction that typically worsens with activity and improves with rest. Ptosis or 
diplopia is the initial symptom in approximately two-thirds of patients; nearly all 
will develop both within 2 years and subsequently develop generalized weakness 
more noticeable in the upper limbs than in the lower limbs and often proximal. 
Difficulty in chewing, swallowing or talking is the initial symptom in one-sixth

Chapter 9  Central Nervous System Diseases    579
	 of patients and limb weakness in 10%. Dysphagia, choking or nasal regurgitation 
of liquids is present in more severe bulbar weakness. Head drop and neck pain 
occur due to neck weakness. Respiratory weakness may manifest with exertional 
dyspnoea or orthopnoea.
	
l Myasthenic weakness typically fluctuates during the day, usually being least in 
the morning and worsening as the day progresses, especially after prolonged use 
of affected muscles. Symptoms may also worsen with heat, infections, surgery or 
emotional stress, menstruation, pregnancy and the post-partum state.
	
l Ocular MG: Only ocular muscle weakness is present. The patient may have 
weakness of eye closure. Strength in all other facial, bulbar and limb muscles is 
normal.
	
l Impending myasthenic crisis: There occurs rapid clinical worsening of MG that, 
in the opinion of the treating physician, could lead to crisis (respiratory/bulbar) 
in the short term (days to weeks).
	
l Myasthenic crisis: It represents a serious, life-threatening, rapid worsening of 
MG and potential airway compromise from ventilatory or bulbar dysfunction. 
Precipitants include poor control of generalized disease, medical treatment 
for bulbar myasthenia, certain medicines (see below), systemic infection, 
especially of the respiratory tract, aspiration, surgery and emotional stress or hot 
environment in refractory myasthenia.
	
l Remission: The patient has no symptoms or signs of MG. Weakness of eyelid closure 
is accepted, but there is no weakness of any other muscle on careful examination.
	
l Refractory MG: Post intervention status (PIS) is unchanged or worse after 
corticosteroids and at least 2 other immunosuppressive (IS) agents, used in adequate 
doses for an adequate duration, with persistent symptoms or side effects that limit 
functioning, as defined by the patient and physician.
	
l Diagnostic procedures are ICE pack test, edrophonium chloride test, positive 
acetylcholine receptor antibodies and repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) showing 
decrementing response. CT thorax is done for thymoma/thymic hyperplasia.

l Stop any medicine that may be contributing to weakness (such as steroids, 
aminoglycosides, Quinolones, macrolides, tetracyclines, nalidixic acid, antimalarials, 
neuroleptics, phenytoin, carbamazepine, beta-blockers including topical timolol eye 
drops, labetalol, long-acting benzodiazepines, baclofen, botulinum toxin, iodinated 
contrast agent, neuromuscular blocking agents, e.g. lignocaine). Anticholinesterases 
can also lead to myasthenic crisis–like symptoms. Signs of excessive cholinergic 
activity are miosis, diarrhoea, salivation, abdominal cramps, seating and weakness.
	
l Treat any infection.
	
l Management approach (Fig. 9.5).
	 1.	Pyridostigmine is initiated as part of the initial treatment regimen for most patients 
with MG, with dosing adjusted according to symptom response. Discontinuation

580    Standard Treatment Guidelines
of Pyridostigmine can signal achievement of treatment goals and may guide the 
tapering of other therapies. 
	 2.	Corticosteroids or immunosuppressive (IS) therapy should be considered for 
patients who do not reach treatment goals with Pyridostigmine alone.
	 3.	Nonsteroidal IS agents like Azathioprine, Cyclosporine, Mycophenolate mofetil, 
Methotrexate and Tacrolimus are utilized when steroid side effects are significant, 
response to corticosteroids is inadequate, or there is symptom relapse on 
corticosteroid dose reduction.
	 Tab. Pyridostigmine 60–1500 mg daily (immediate-release preparation usually 
600 mg/day divided into 5 or 6 doses; sustained-release preparation 180–540 mg once 
or twice daily [separated by at least 6 hours]; the immediate-release tablets or oral 
solution in conjunction with the sustained-release tablets may be used for optimum 
control); titrate up to find the lowest effective dose. The duration of action varies; the 
onset of action is usually within 15–30 minutes and lasts for 3–4 hours.
	
Note: In case of overdosage with anticholinesterase medication (increased weakness 
and other side effects (diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, salivation, nausea), give 
Atropine/Diphenoxylate or Loperamide.
	 Tab. Prednisone 20 mg/day, with gradual escalation to avoid the early weakening 
that occurs in up to one-third of patients treated initially with a high-dose regimen. 
Then increase the dose stepwise (usually by 5 mg/day at 2- to 3-day intervals), 
until there is marked clinical improvement or a dose of 50–60 mg/day is reached.

(Caution: Prednisolone may either induce or exacerbate diabetes mellitus.)
Refer patients who are resistant to pyridostigmine with or without corticosteroids or

Ocular MG: When ophthalmoparesis or ptosis in ocular MG remains unresponsive 
to anticholinesterase agents and significantly affects the patient’s functionality or 
well-being, corticosteroids are typically the first-line immunosuppressants in ocular 
MG, with steroid-sparing agents potentially required if corticosteroids alone prove
