Tab. Prednisolone with 5 mg on alternate days for 3 doses and increase by 5 mg every 
3 doses until symptoms improve (maximum dose 50 mg on alternate days or 0.75 mg/
kg/alternate day). Titrate down, seeking the lowest effective dose, only after achieving 
remission (absence of symptoms and signs having withdrawn from pyridostigmine) 
for at least 2–3 months.
Non-steroidal immunosuppressive (IS) agents
Tab. Azathioprine (AZA) 50 mg/day initially; if it is well tolerated, increase gradually 
to 2–3 mg/kg or until the white blood count falls to 3000–4000/mL. The beneficial 
effect takes 3–6 months to begin and even longer to peak. 
Or
Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 2–2.5 g/day in divided twice daily doses Or 
Cyclosporine 4–5 mg/kg/day Or Tacrolimus 0.07–0.1 mg/kg/day given in 2 equally 
divided doses (to minimize side effects). (Caution: Monitor for hypertension and 
nephrotoxicity.) Once treatment goals are achieved, maintain the dose for 6 months to 
2 years, and then taper slowly to the minimal effective amount. Dosage adjustments 
should be made no more frequently than every 3–6 months.
In MG with life-threatening signs such as respiratory insufficiency or dysphagia, in 
preparation for surgery in patients with significant bulbar dysfunction, when a rapid 
response to treatment is needed, when other treatments are insufficiently effective and prior 
to beginning corticosteroids if deemed necessary to prevent or minimize exacerbations, 
refer to a physician or a centre with expertise in management of MG and ADD:
Inj. Immunoglobulin IV (IVIG) 1–2 g/kg over 2–5 days; action may last as long as 
30 days. (Caution: IVIG is contraindicated in hypercoagulable states, renal failure or 
hypersensitivity to immunoglobulin.) Consider IVIG as maintenance therapy for patients 
with refractory MG or for those in whom IS agents are relatively contraindicated. 
Or

582    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Plasma exchange (PLEX) 4–6 exchanges on alternate days; it has a rapid onset of action 
(3–10 days). (Caution: In patients with sepsis and hypotension, it may lead to increased 
bleeding and cardiac arrhythmias, and venous access complications.)
In severe treatment-resistant, MuSK antibody–positive MG, Inj. Rituximab 
375 mg/m2 IV in 4 weekly infusions, or 1 g IV on two occasions 2 weeks apart.
Impending and manifest myasthenic crises are emergent situations requiring aggressive 
management and supportive care. Admit patients with impending crisis and observe 
closely for respiratory and bulbar function, with the ability to transfer to an intensive care 
unit if it progresses to manifest crisis.
Single breath count (SBC) is a surrogate marker for the FVC and can be used as a 
method for monitoring. It requires the patient to take a breath and count slowly (i.e. at 
a speed of 2 numbers per second); an SBC less than 15 is a danger sign. PLEX and IVIg 
are employed as short-term therapies for impending and manifest myasthenic crises, 
especially in patients with notable respiratory or bulbar dysfunction. Corticosteroids or 
alternative IS agents are initiated concurrently to attain a lasting clinical improvement. 
Due to the potential transient exacerbation of myasthenic weakness by corticosteroids, 
it might be appropriate to delay their administration for several days after commencing 
PLEX or IVIg to allow for the beneficial effects of the latter treatments.

l Once patients reach treatment goals, corticosteroid doses should be gradually 
tapered; maintaining a low dose long term may help sustain treatment outcomes. 
	
l Similarly, for nonsteroidal IS agents, once treatment goals are attained and sustained 
for 6 months to 2 years, the IS dose should be tapered slowly to the minimum 
effective amount, with adjustments made no more frequently than every 3–6 months. 
	
l Tapering IS drugs carries the risk of relapse, particularly in symptomatic patients or 
after rapid tapering, necessitating potential dose adjustments. Maintaining some level 
of immunosuppression may be necessary for many years or even lifelong.
Surgical treatment
Thymectomy for MG in non-thymomatous MG or without detectable AChR antibodies 
is done to minimize the dose or duration of immunotherapy in case patients fail to 
respond to immunotherapy or experience intolerable side effects. In children, consider 
thymectomy in case of generalized AChR antibody-positive MG or when response 
to pyridostigmine and IS therapy is unsatisfactory. Thymectomy is not indicated in 
patients with MuSK, LRP4 or agrin antibodies.
MG in pregnancy
	 1.	Advise the patient to plan for pregnancy well in advance to allow time for 
optimization of myasthenic clinical status and to minimize risks to the foetus.

Chapter 9  Central Nervous System Diseases    583
	 2.	Reassure patients that if the condition is previously well controlled, they will 
remain stable throughout pregnancy. If worsening occurs, it is more likely during 
the first few months after delivery. 
	 3.	Oral pyridostigmine is the first-line treatment during pregnancy. Do not use 
IV cholinesterase inhibitors (ChEIs) as they may produce uterine contractions.
	 4.	Postpone thymectomy until after pregnancy as benefit is unlikely to occur during 
pregnancy.
	 5.	In the absence of a compelling indication, postpone diagnostic CT until after delivery.
	 6.	Prednisone is the immunosuppressive (IS) agent of choice during pregnancy. 
Patients who are not satisfactorily controlled with or cannot tolerate corticosteroids, 
Azathioprine and Cyclosporine can be administered in expectant mothers as they 
are safer than other ISs, although human risk cannot be ruled out.
	 7.	PLEX or IVIG is useful when a prompt, although temporary, response is required 
during pregnancy. Carefully consider both maternal and foetal issues, weighing 
the risks of these treatments against the requirement for use during pregnancy and 
their potential benefits.
	 8.	Encourage spontaneous vaginal delivery.
	 9.	Do not administer magnesium sulphate for management of eclampsia in MG 
because of its neuromuscular blocking effects; Barbiturates or Phenytoin usually 
provides adequate treatment.
	10.	Examine all babies born to mothers with myasthenia for evidence of transient 
myasthenic weakness with rapid access to neonatal critical care unit, even if the 
mother’s myasthenia is well controlled.
Patient education
	
l Effective treatment is available for this potentially fatal condition.
	
l Report immediately in case of red flag signs – rapid worsening of primary 
myasthenic symptoms, rapid progression of bulbar symptoms, increasing dose 
of pyridostigmine, tachypnoea, tachycardia, decreased forced vital capacity and 
respiratory infection.
	
l Do not discontinue medicines abruptly. Patients having surgery or experiencing 
other stresses need close monitoring and possibly changes in treatment to prevent 
myasthenic crisis.
	
l Review the full list of medications being taken by the patient as some medications 
are contraindicated in MG such as aminoglycoside and quinolone antibiotics, quinine 
and intravenous magnesium.

Genitourinary Diseases
NEPHROTIC SYNDROME
It is a clinical complex characterized by profuse proteinuria (>3.5 g/1.73 m2/24 hours), 
peripheral oedema and hypoalbuminaemia. Hyperlipidaemia and thrombotic disease 
may also be present. Majority of cases of nephrotic syndrome (NS) in adults are due to 
one of the following: minimal change disease (MCD), membranous glomerulopathy 
(MN), and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). Common secondary causes are 
diabetic nephropathy, amyloidosis and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Periorbital and generalized pitting oedema, transudative pleural effusion and 
ascites. Hypercoagulability predisposes these individuals to peripheral arterial or 
venous thrombosis, renal vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. 
	
l Proteinuria of >3.5 g/24 hours. Renal biopsy is indicated in all adults and 
children (except in children aged 6 months to 6 years) with nephrotic syndrome 
for establishing a definitive diagnosis, guiding therapy and estimating prognosis.

l Advise moderate salt restriction, usually 2 g/day (no cooking salt), and 
low-cholesterol diet.
	
l There is no consensus regarding the optimal protein in diet for these patients. High- 
protein diet is not recommended as it may hasten the progression of renal disease by 
increasing proteinuria. A protein intake of 0.8–1 g/kg/24 hours (plus grams of protein 
lost in urine) of mainly first-class proteins is recommended.
	
l Fluid restriction is usually not required unless the oedema is severe.

Non-specific treatment
	 1.	Depending on severity of oedema, give Tab. Frusemide 80–240 mg/day in 2 divided 
doses (8 a.m., 2 p.m.) Or Torsemide 10–100 mg once daily depending on the severity 
of oedema (start with 10–20 mg/day; titrate upward by approximately doubling the

Chapter 10  Genitourinary Diseases    585
dose until the desired response is achieved). The aim is to remove up to 1.0 kg/day 
of oedematous fluid. Excess fluid should be removed without inducing clinically 
significant plasma volume depletion (i.e. unexplained elevation in serum creatinine 
[SCr] or clinical manifestations of hypovolaemia).
	
	Other classes of diuretics may be used in combination with loop diuretics in case of 
inadequate response such as Tab. Spironolactone 100 mg Or Metolazone 5–20 mg 
once daily may be added.
	 2.	To reduce proteinuria, an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEI) or 
angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) should be used in maximum tolerated doses 
with regular monitoring of SCr and serum potassium:
	
	Tab. Ramipril 5–20 mg/day in one or two divided doses
	
	Or 
	
	Tab. Telmisartan 40–80 mg/day in a single daily dose
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Losartan 25–50 mg/day as a single dose
	
	If there is >30% rise in creatinine or potassium is >5.5 after initiating ACEI/ARBs, 
they should be stopped and restarted at a low dose once creatinine and potassium 
return to baseline.
	 3.	Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and proteinuria may benefit from 
SGLT2 inhibitors:
	
	Tab. Dapagliflozin 5–10 mg once daily Or Tab. Empagliflozin 10–25 mg once daily
	 4.	Hyperlipidaemia in patients with nephrotic syndrome along with other risk factors 
like diabetes mellitus, hypertension and cardiovascular diseases may require 
treatment with lipid-lowering therapy like statins
	 5.	Hypercoagulability, particularly in cases of membranous nephropathy should be 
treated with anticoagulant therapy.
	
	The risk of arterial or venous thrombotic events in both children and adults with NS 
is elevated compared to general population, particularly within the initial 6 months 
of diagnosis. Thrombosis is more prevalent in adults than in children and tends to 
be predominantly venous rather than arterial. A serum albumin of <2.5 g/dL is an 
indication for starting prophylactic anticoagulation in patients with NS.
Specific treatment of primary nephrotic syndromes
Minimal change disease
Tab. Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (maximum 80 mg/day) for 12–16 weeks and tapered 
slowly over the following 6 months. Up to 80–90% of adults experience remission under 
this treatment, although there is a relapse rate of 50–65% and approximately 10–25% of 
individuals may undergo repeated relapses. Monitor these patients for the presence of 
symptoms and proteinuria. Treatment of relapse is a shorter course of oral prednisolone 
with 1 month of full dose followed by tapering to cessation over the next 1 month.
For patients with frequent relapses who do not have steroid side effects, low-dose 
prednisolone (15 mg on alternate days) for prolonged periods may be given. If patients 
still relapse on such low doses, the dose may be increased.

586    Standard Treatment Guidelines
In patients with frequent relapses, glucocorticoid resistance or steroid-associated 
side effects, calcineurin inhibitors, such as tacrolimus, in combination with low-dose 
prednisolone, may be used. If patients continue to relapse even after tacrolimus therapy, 
then rituximab may be tried under specialist care.
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
FSGS is a histopathological finding of scarring (sclerosis) of glomeruli and damage to 
renal podocytes. It can be divided into two types:
	 1.	Primary/idiopathic FSGS
	 2.	Secondary FSGS due to the following:
	
l Drugs: Intravenous (IV) heroin, analgesics, pamidronate, lithium, anabolic steroids, 
doxorubicin
	
l Viruses: Hepatitis B and C, HIV, parvovirus B19, cytomegalovirus, SARS-CoV-2
	
l As an adaptive change secondary to- solitary kidney, renal agenesis, vesicoureteral 
reflux
	
l Haemodynamic causes in patients without decreased renal mass: Obesity 
(especially morbid obesity), sickle cell nephropathy
	
l Miscellaneous: Alport's syndrome, sarcoidosis, radiation nephritis
	 1.	Evaluate thoroughly to exclude secondary forms of FSGS.
	 2.	General measures like salt restriction, BP control and use of ACEI like ramipril 
should be used in all cases. 
	 3.	Specific treatment: Same as above for minimal change disease and should be 
considered only for idiopathic FSGS.
	
	In case of steroid-resistant FSGS:
Cap. Cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg/day (target through levels 100–175 ng/mL)
Or
Cap. Tacrolimus 0.05–0.1 mg/kg/day (target through levels 5–10 ng/mL)
The treatment may be given for at least 4–6 months. It may be continued for at 
least 12 months followed by slow tapering if there is partial or complete remission. 
However, response rate is poor.
Membranous nephropathy (MN)
It can be divided into primary and secondary MN.
	
l Primary (75–80%): Idiopathic, but attributed to the presence of one of the following 
antibodies – antibodies against phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R), antigen 
neural epidermal growth factor-like 1 (NELL), antibodies against thrombospondin 
(THSD7A), antibodies against neutral endopeptidase (NEP) and exostosin
	
l Secondary (20–25%)
	– Infections (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, malaria, human immunodeficiency 
virus, schistosomiasis)

Chapter 10  Genitourinary Diseases    587
	– Neoplasms (adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma of lungs and 
gastrointestinal tract, haematological malignancies)
	– Drugs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, anti–tumour necrosis factor-alpha 
inhibitors, penicillamine, probenecid)
	– Heavy metal poisoning (gold, mercury)
	– Autoimmune diseases (SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, IgG4-
related nephropathy)
	– Miscellaneous (haematopoietic stem cell transplant, graft-versus-host disease, 
diabetes mellitus)
	 1.	Secondary causes should be sought and treated appropriately in all cases of biopsy-
proven membranous nephropathy. 
	 2.	Control BP preferably with ACEIs at the maximum tolerated dose in all cases. 
	 3.	General measures include salt restriction, diuretics, treatment of dyslipidaemia and 
anticoagulation.
	 4.	Specific treatment with steroids or cytotoxics should be started when at least one 
of the following conditions is met:
	
l Urinary protein excretion persistently exceeds 4 g/day and remains at over 
50% of the baseline value and does not show progressive decline during 
antihypertensive and antiproteinuric therapy over a period of at least 6 months.
	
l Severe, disabling or life-threatening symptoms related to the nephrotic 
syndrome are present.
	
l Rise of SCr by 30% or more within 6–12 months from the time of diagnosis in 
the presence of eGFR is not less than 25–30 mL/min/1.73 m2 AND this change 
is not explained by superimposed complications.
Idiopathic membranous nephropathy may be categorized into low-risk, 
medium-risk and high-risk.
Low-risk: Proteinuria of <4 g/day; such cases have an excellent prognosis and 
steroids or cytotoxic drugs are not indicated.
Medium-risk: Proteinuria of 4–8 g/day are best treated by rituximab. If rituximab 
is not available, modified Ponticelli regimen is used (6 months): 
	– Months 1, 3 and 5: Methylprednisolone (1 g) daily for 3 days followed by oral 
prednisone (0.5 mg/kg/day) for 27 days
	– Months 2, 4 and 6: Cyclophosphamide orally 2–2.5 mg/kg/day for 30 days
	
To be given with appropriate pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) and antiviral 
prophylaxis (trimethoprim–sulphamethoxazole [TMP-SMZ] and valganciclovir) 
High-risk: Proteinuria >8 g/day and/or declining renal function; such cases are 
best treated by rituximab. 
Note: Steroids alone have no role in the treatment of membranous nephropathy. 
Overall 40% of cases respond spontaneously; 30–40% remit and relapse spontaneously; 
10–20% show progressive decline in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) over 10–15 years 
to end-stage renal disease (ESRD).

588    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)
Treatment depends on the cause of MPGN. Presence of hepatitis C and disorders of 
alternate complement pathway require specialized management. For idiopathic MPGN 
with nephrotic syndrome and progressive decline in kidney function, initial treatment 
with cyclophosphamide plus low-dose steroids is recommended. MPGN usually 
progresses to ESRD over 5–10 years.
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)
It needs aggressive management preferably by a specialist.
Inj. Methylprednisolone 0.75–1 g/day IV for 3 days followed by oral Prednisolone and 
Cyclophosphamide
In anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease, plasmapheresis should be 
done in combination with cyclophosphamide and steroids after confirmation on biopsy.
(For treatment of nephrotic syndrome in children, see Chapter 19.)

ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY
The term ‘acute kidney injury (AKI)’ has replaced the previously used term ‘acute 
renal failure’. It encompasses the entire spectrum of the syndrome from minor changes 
in markers of renal function to requirement for renal replacement therapy (RRT). 
It is accompanied by a significant decline in the renal excretory function occurring 
over hours or days detected clinically by a rise in plasma concentration of urea and 
creatinine. Most of the times, AKI is reversible; however, some decrease in GFR may 
remain for long term. AKI is a global problem and occurs in community; in hospitals 
where it is common in medical, surgical, paediatric and oncology wards; and in ICUs. 
Irrespective of its nature, AKI is a predictor of immediate and long-term adverse 
outcomes. Individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are especially susceptible 
to AKI which, in turn, may act as a promoter of progression of the underlying CKD.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The clinical picture is usually dominated by the primary condition, which causes 
AKI. Manifestations of uraemia like anorexia, nausea, vomiting, muscular 
cramps and signs of encephalopathy may appear later. Staging of AKI according 
to Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria is as follows:

l For purposes of diagnosis and management, AKI is divided into three categories:
	– Pre-renal due to renal hypoperfusion (55%)
	– Renal due to disease which involves renal parenchyma (40%)
	– Post-renal due to diseases causing urinary obstruction
	
l Complications of AKI include hyperkalaemia, intravascular volume overload, 
metabolic acidosis, infections, arrhythmias, pericardial effusion, pulmonary 
oedema and GI bleeding due to stress ulceration.

Determine the cause of AKI whenever possible promptly with special attention to 
reversible causes (Table 10.1). Then evaluate, stratify patients for risk of AKI according 
to their susceptibilities and exposures and manage patients according to stage and 
cause of AKI. Monitor patients at an increased risk for AKI to stage the severity with 
measurements of SCr and urine output. Individualize the frequency and duration of 
monitoring based on patient risk and clinical course.

590    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Stage-based management of AKI is as follows:
	
l Identify high-risk patients.
	
l Discontinue all nephrotoxic agents when possible.
	
l Ensure volume status and adequate perfusion pressure (mean arterial pressure 
[MAP] >65 mmHg).
	
l Consider functional haemodynamic monitoring.
	
l Monitor SCr and urine output.
	
l Avoid hypoglycaemia.
	
l Consider alternatives to radio-contrast procedures.
	
l Perform non-invasive diagnostic workup (priority of action over invasive diagnostic 
workup).
	
l Check for change in drug dosing (priority of action).
	
l Consider RRT.
	
l Consider ICU admission.
Indications of referral of patients to emergency department
	
l All patients with stage 2 or 3 AKI
	
l Patients with stage 1 AKI with unknown aetiology, comorbid conditions or who do 
not improve with simple interventions like fluid resuscitation
Prerenal AKI
	 1.	Replacement fluids to be tailored according to the composition of lost fluids, 
e.g. in haemorrhage; blood transfusion/packed RBCs. If blood transfusion is 
required, blood should be as fresh as possible, as longer-stored blood may lead 
to hyperkalaemia. In most other situations of hypovolaemia, buffered crystalloids 
like Ringer’s lactate are the fluid of choice. Normal saline (0.9%) is given in case 
of burns, pancreatitis and diabetic ketoacidosis.
	
	(Fluid intake = Urine output + fluid loss from other sources + insensible loss of fluid 
about 500 mL/day.) Estimate of the amount of fluid required based on hydration 
status of the patient as assessed by jugular vein distension and dry tongue, etc. 
	 2.	In patients with cirrhosis complicated by AKI, fluids should be administered slowly 
and titrated against jugular venous pressure (JVP). 
	 3.	Large-volume paracentesis should be accompanied by IV albumin.
Intrinsic AKI/renal AKI 
It should be managed by a specialist. Approach for treatment depends on the likely cause.
	
l Acute glomerulonephritis, vasculitis – glucocorticosteroids, cyclophosphamide and/
or plasmapheresis
	
l Allergic interstitial nephritis – withdrawal of the offending drug and glucocorticoids

l Malignant hypertension, toxaemia of pregnancy – aggressive control of blood pressures

Indications for RRT in AKI include:
	 1.	Uraemia/azotaemia (uraemic encephalopathy, uraemic pericarditis, uraemic

	 2.	Fluid overload: Oliguria resulting in clinically significant volume overload and

	 3.	Metabolic acidosis, refractory to medical management

592    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Prevention of acute poisoning/overdose of medicines: To prevent acute overdosage, 
doses of all essential medicines for the underlying disease should be adjusted according 
to the degree of renal impairment (see Appendix VII).
Prevention of AKI
Since there is no specific therapy for ischaemic or nephrotoxic AKI, prevention is very 
important and includes:
	 1.	Aggressively restore intravascular volume in case of losses, e.g. during surgery, 
trauma, burns, gastroenteritis. 
	 2.	Avoid/reduce the dose of nephrotoxic drugs appropriately. 
	 3.	Hypovolaemia should be avoided in patients receiving nephrotoxic drugs.

Small changes in kidney function in hospitalized patients are associated with significant 
changes in short- and long-term outcomes. Evaluate patients 3 months after AKI for 
resolution, new onset or worsening of pre-existing CKD. If patients have CKD, manage 
accordingly. If patients do not have CKD, consider them to be at an increased risk for 
CKD and care accordingly.
Patient education
	
l Tailor information appropriate to the person's individual needs about long-term 
treatment options, monitoring, self-management and support to people who have 
had AKI (and/or their parent or caregiver if appropriate) in collaboration with a 
multidisciplinary team. 
	
l Give information about future care to people needing RRT after discharge following 
AKI including information about the frequency and length of dialysis sessions and 
the preparation needed (such as having a fistula or peritoneal catheter).
	
l Discuss with the patients and the caregivers the risk of developing AKI, particularly 
the risk associated with conditions leading to dehydration (e.g. diarrhoea and 
vomiting) and drugs with nephrotoxic potential (including over-the-counter 
NSAIDs). People who are at risk of AKI, particularly those who have CKD with 
an eGFR less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, neurological or cognitive impairment or 
disability, may have limited access to fluids because of dependence on a caregiver.

CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE
CKD is defined as abnormality of kidney structure or function present for more than 3 
months. Presence of GFR of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, an albumin excretion rate 
of 30 mg/24 hours or greater and urine albumin–creatinine ratio (ACR) of 30 mg/g 
or greater for more than 3 months are diagnostic of CKD. End-stage renal disease 
with GFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m2 would result in death without RRT. The important 
underlying causes are diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic glomerulonephritis, 
chronic pyelonephritis, analgesic nephropathy and polycystic kidney disease.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The symptoms of uraemia develop gradually and late. They include fatigue, 
dyspnoea, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, ankle oedema, pruritis, purpura and 
neuromuscular disturbances. Nocturia may be present. CKD is nearly always 
asymptomatic in its early stages.
	
l Examination may show the presence of pallor, nail dystrophy, purpura, 
hypertension, cardiomegaly, heart failure (CHF), features of pulmonary oedema, 
pleural effusion and pericarditis with or without effusion.
	
l The abnormalities in blood urea and creatinine may be detected during evaluation 
of anaemia.
	
l CKD is classified into five stages based on GFR and three stages based on albumin 
excretion rate. Screening and monitoring tests are estimated GFR, microalbuminuria 
and proteinuria.
	
l KDIGO criteria for CKD based on GFR and albuminuria are shown in Table 10.2.
	
l Elevated blood urea and creatinine, hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, 
hyperkalaemia and a partially compensated metabolic acidosis are the frequently seen 
biochemical abnormalities. Peripheral smear shows a normocytic, normochromic 
anaemia and urinalysis usually reveals proteinuria and low-fixed specific gravity.
	
l Presence of shrunken kidneys on ultrasound suggests ESRD. Kidney biopsy should 
be considered if the kidneys are of normal size. A skeletal survey may show evidence 
of renal osteodystrophy. In certain diseases like diabetic nephropathy and polycystic 
kidney disease, kidney size may be normal or increased.

1.	Identification and management of associated factors precipitating acute or 
chronic renal failure, e.g. drugs, hypovolaemia, infections, obstructive uropathy, 
hypertension, HF, diabetes mellitus
	 2.	Detection and management of any life-threatening emergency, requiring urgent 
treatment, e.g. hyperkalaemia, pulmonary oedema, metabolic acidosis, uraemic 
encephalopathy or accelerated hypertension
	 3.	Identification of a specific cause of CKD and its treatment so as to delay the 
progress of CKD and intensive diabetic control

596    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Control of blood glucose levels in case of diabetes
Managing glycaemic levels in individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and CKD 
should involve lifestyle interventions, initial use of metformin combined with a 
sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) as the primary treatment, and the 
incorporation of supplementary pharmacological measures as necessary to achieve 
optimal glycaemic control.
Most patients with T2D, CKD and eGFR ≥30 mL/min per 1.73 m2 would benefit 
from treatment with both metformin and an SGLT2i. (For details of management of 
diabetes, see Chapter 11)
Treatment of volume overload
Many patients with CKD have volume overload especially in later stages of CKD. 
Salt restriction and loop diuretics like frusemide or torsemide must be prescribed to 
maintain volume balance. 
Treatment of anaemia
	 1.	Look for common aggravating causes of anaemia, e.g. GI blood loss, iron 
deficiency and chronic infections, and treat accordingly. Assess iron status of the 
patient before erythropoietin (EPO) therapy. 
	 2.	Provide iron supplementation to ensure adequate response to EPO. Liposomal iron 
has better absorption than traditional formulation. Inj. Iron Sucrose may be given 
(see section on Anaemia). 
	 3.	If haemoglobin is less than 10 g/dL, give Inj. Erythropoietin (EPO) 80–120 units/kg/
week subcutaneous (divided into 2–3 times a week) Or long-acting erythropoiesis-
stimulating agents (ESA) such as Inj. Darbepoetin alfa 0.45 mcg/kg IV (in 
patients undergoing dialysis) or subcutaneously once every 4 weeks or continuous 
erythropoietin receptor activator (CERA) once a month. These drugs have the 
advantage of less frequent injections and better compliance but at a higher cost. 
	
	Note: The target Hb should be 10–12 g/dL and the optimal rate of correction should 
be to increase haematocrit by 4–6% over a 4-week period. To evaluate anaemia 
in individuals with CKD, assess haemoglobin concentration as follows: when 
clinically necessary for those with GFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m2, annually for GFR 
30–59 mL/min/1.73 m2 and biannually for GFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2.
	 4.	Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor (HIF-PHI), also known 
as hypoxia-inducible factor stabilizers (HIF stabilizers), is a novel approach 
for managing renal anaemia. By stabilizing HIF, it stimulates erythropoiesis 
and increases haemoglobin levels in patients with CKD, offering a promising 
therapeutic strategy for addressing anaemia associated with renal dysfunction.

acid–base disturbances

	 2.	Tab. Calcium acetate/carbonate 1–2 g/day in divided doses with meals

Treatment of pericarditis
Uraemic pericarditis is an absolute indication for initiation or intensification of dialysis. 
Heparin-free dialysate should be used.
Treatment of bleeding diathesis
Usually, the problem arises when a patient with chronic renal failure needs to undergo 
some surgery. Before surgery, Inj. Vasopressin (DDAVP) 0.3 mcg/kg in 100 mL of 
saline over 30 minutes may be given.
Treatment of symptomatic hyperuricaemia
Tab. Allopurinol 100–200 mg/day is given preferably after food, and then adjusted 
according to plasma or urinary uric acid concentration.
Monitoring of CKD
	
l Persons with CKD should be assessed at frequent intervals. The exact frequency 
of GFR and ACR monitoring depends on the severity of CKD, the risk and rate of 
progression. As CKD stage advances, the patient should be seen at shorter intervals. 
	
l Patients should be referred for creation of an arteriovenous fistula at least 6 months 
before the expected time of start of dialysis. Early referral to nephrologist is 
associated with better outcomes for patients. 
	
l Factors associated with progression include cause of CKD, level of GFR, level 
of albuminuria, AKI, age, sex, race or ethnicity, elevated BP, hyperglycaemia, 
dyslipidaemia, smoking, obesity, history of cardiovascular disease, ongoing exposure 
to nephrotoxic agents and others. Small fluctuations in GFR are common and do not 
necessarily indicate progression.
Renal replacement therapy
The modalities of RRT include haemodialysis, continuous ambulatory peritoneal 
dialysis or renal transplantation; the choice depends on many factors – their availability, 
the patient’s preference and availability of potential donors. Only kidney transplantation 
offers the potential for nearly complete rehabilitation. The issue of RRT should be 
discussed with all patients with CKD especially those with irreversible and progressive 
disease. The pros and cons of all three modalities should be explained.

598    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Indications for dialysis 
	 1.	Development of complications that cannot be controlled by conservative and 
pharmacological means, i.e. fluid overload, pericarditis, refractory hyperkalaemia, 
severe metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy and progressive neuropathy attributable 
to uraemia
	 2.	Patients with eGFR <5 mL/min/1.73 m2 
	 3.	Patients with eGFR 5–15 mL/min/1.73 m2 having signs and symptoms due to 
ESRD (as eGFR declines below 10 mL/min/1.73 m2, most patients develop signs 
and symptoms of ESRD and require dialysis)
Other common indications of dialysis are declining appetite and nutritional status, 
fatigue and malaise, persistent volume overload and mild cognitive impairment.
Time of referral for kidney transplantation
Kidney transplantation is the treatment of choice for ESRD and offers the best long-
term outcomes.
Patients who opt for kidney transplantation and have no contraindications 
for transplantation should be referred to a transplant centre when eGFR is 
<30 mL/min/1.73 m2. Even though RRT will not be started at such a GFR, the proper 
evaluation of recipient and donor can be done and if the donor turns out to be unfit, 
other donors can be explored. Long-term outcomes are better when transplantation is 
done before receiving any dialysis or less than 6 months of dialysis rather than after 
long periods on dialysis.
Pre-transplantation evaluation
	
l Candidates for renal transplantation should undergo an extensive evaluation to 
identify factors that may have an adverse effect on outcome.
	
l Identify and treat all coexisting medical problems that may increase the morbidity 
and mortality rates of the surgical procedure and adversely impact the post-transplant 
course including social issues of the patient to determine conditions that may 
jeopardize the outcome of transplantation, such as financial and travel restraints or 
a pattern of non-compliance.
	
l All transplant candidates should undergo laboratory evaluation, infectious profile, 
diagnostic procedures, immunological evaluation and in select recipients special 
procedures as indicated. 
Pre-transplant surgical interventions
The medical workup may reveal circumstances that necessitate surgical intervention to 
prepare the patient for kidney transplantation. Such interventions may include native 
kidney nephrectomy or nephroureterectomy; reserved for specific indications such as large 
polycystic kidneys, significant proteinuria or chronic reflux disease.

In addition to the surgical transplantation procedure itself, management includes the 
following:
	 1.	Organ procurement: Identification of potential donors, assessment of donor 
suitability, determination of donor brain death, medical management of donor
	 2.	Lifelong immunosuppressive therapy to all kidney transplant recipients to prevent 
acute and chronic rejection
Anatomic complications of surgery are renal artery thrombosis, renal artery stenosis, 
urine leaks from disruption of the anastomosis, ureteral stenosis and obstruction 
(relatively late complications), and lymphocele.
Induction of immunosuppression
Kidney transplant recipients receive induction immunosuppressive therapy which 
includes antibodies like Basiliximab Or Rabbit antithymocytic globulin (rATG-
thymoglobulin) Or Alemtuzumab.
In patients at a high risk of rejection, rATG-thymoglobulin is indicated, while in patients 
at a low risk of rejection, either rATG-thymoglobulin or Basiliximab is indicated.
Maintenance immunosuppression
	 1.	Tab. Tacrolimus 0.12–0.2 mg/kg in 2 divided dosages
	 2.	Tab. Mycophenolate sodium 720 mg orally twice a day on an empty stomach, 
1 hour before or 2 hours after food intake or mycophenolate mofetil 2 mg/day 
	
	Or 
	
	Tab. Azathioprine 2.5 mg/kg/day
	 3.	Tab. Prednisolone started at 1 mg/kg/day for initial 3 days and then tapered to 
20 mg/day for the first week (the daily dose is then decreased by 5 mg every week 
so that it is 15 mg/day for 1 week, then 10 mg/day, then 5 mg/day for 1 month 
which is then continued)
 	
	Patients should be kept on long-term follow-up to look for indications of renal 
allograft dysfunction and other complications. The critical considerations in 
medical follow-up are rejection, nephrotoxicity of cyclosporine, tacrolimus and 
recurrence of native kidney disease.
Allograft dysfunction and rejection
Hyperacute rejection of the renal allograft may occur within hours of the transplant, 
and need nephrectomy.
Acute rejection appears within the first 6 months after transplantation (15% of cases).
Chronic rejection occurs more than 1 year after transplantation and is a major cause 
of allograft loss.

l Counsel patients and prepare the patient physically and psychologically for RRT, 
when ESRD is inevitable as most of these patients have varying reactions to illness 
from anger to depression.
	
l Explain the patient about prevention of rejection of transplant and other transplant 
complications, need for regular monitoring with lab tests and compliance with 
medications.

URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS (UTIs) 
UTI is defined as an infection of any part of the urinary tract. UTIs are common 
bacterial infections managed in general practice. They predominantly affect sexually 
active women, and are relatively uncommon in the first year of life and in the elderly.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Lower UTI includes infections of the urethra and bladder and can present with 
pain and burning during micturition, frequency of micturition, urgency, dysuria, 
pyuria or sometimes even haematuria. Fever is usually absent in lower UTI. Acute 
cystitis may present with suprapubic pain or discomfort. Presence of new onset of 
even one of the classic symptoms of acute uncomplicated cystitis with the absence 
of vaginal discharge or irritation has a positive predictive value of 90% for UTI.
	
l Upper UTI includes infections of the kidneys and ureters. The symptoms usually 
develop rapidly, sometimes within a few hours. In addition to symptoms of lower 
UTI, these patients may have high fever, chills, rigours and pain in the loins, 
nausea and vomiting. 
	
l UTIs in men are usually complicated. 
	
l Sometimes UTIs may be asymptomatic, and are detected accidentally when the 
urine is tested. Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ABU) is more common in pregnant 
women and the elderly. Untreated, ABU in midstream clean-catch urine in 
pregnancy can progress to upper UTI which can further lead to premature delivery 
and poor foetal outcome. After treatment of ABU, periodic (e.g. monthly) follow-up 
urine cultures are recommended.

Chapter 10  Genitourinary Diseases    601
	
l Urine – presence of >10 pus cells/hpf on microscopic examination, nitrites and 
leucocyte esterase on urine dipstick testing is an indicator of acute uncomplicated 
UTI. Urine culture is not indicated in uncomplicated UTI. It is recommended 
only for patients with suspected acute pyelonephritis, recurrent UTI, atypical 
symptoms and high local rates of resistance. A bacterial growth >103/mm3 
is diagnostic of acute uncomplicated cystitis. In asymptomatic patients, two 
consecutive urine specimens should be examined and >105/mm3 bacteria of 
a single species should be demonstrable in both specimens before therapy is 
instituted. The presence of bacteriuria of any degree in suprapubic aspirates or 
>102/mm3 in urine obtained by catheterization indicates infection.
Collection of urine sample: Collection of urine sample for culture should be from 
the midstream and should be preceded by adequate cleaning of the external genitalia 
avoiding any antiseptic washes. Patients with recurrent UTIs should undergo 
ultrasonography of the genitourinary tract and micturating cystourethrogram to detect 
underlying structural or functional abnormality.

General principles
	
l Except in acute uncomplicated cystitis in women, diagnosis must be confirmed 
before starting treatment with antibiotics and antimicrobial sensitivity should direct 
the therapy.
	
l Identify the predisposing factors and correct, if possible.
	
l Each course of treatment should be defined as failure or cure on the basis of symptoms.
	
l Uncomplicated lower UTIs (immunocompetent, no comorbidities, no known 
urological abnormalities, non-pregnant, premenopausal) generally respond to 
short courses of therapy (3–5 days’ therapy) and if symptoms are prolonged, 
then a 7-day course of antibiotics should be given. Upper UTIs and complicated 
lower UTIs (history of childhood UTI, immunocompromised, pre-adolescent or 
post-menopausal, pregnant, underlying metabolic disorder – diabetes mellitus, 
urological abnormalities – stones, stents, indwelling catheters, neurogenic bladder 
and polycystic kidney) require longer treatment.
	
l Recurrences (more than 2 weeks) after cessation of therapy nearly always represent 
reinfection.
	
l Community-acquired infections, particularly the first infections, are usually due to 
more antibiotic-sensitive strains.
	
l Upper UTI may need in-patient treatment. In hospitalized patients, those requiring 
instrumentation and having recurrent infections, antibiotic-resistant strains are the 
more likely causes of UTI.
	
l A urine culture is recommended for women with suspected acute pyelonephritis, 
women with symptoms that do not resolve or that recur within 2–4 weeks after the 
completion of treatment, and women who present with atypical symptoms.

If symptoms are severe, antibiotics may be started empirically after sending the urine 
samples. If symptoms are not severe, the antibiotics can be started as suggested by the 
culture and sensitivity report. 
	 1.	The choice of antibiotics depends on sensitivity reports; however, in the absence of 
sensitivity reports, antibiotics given in Table 10.3 may be used empirically. (Also 
see the section on Antimicrobial Stewardship).
	
	Adult males with UTI should receive a 10- to 14-day course of antibiotics. 
Outpatient regimens include a fluoroquinolone, trimethoprim–sulphamethoxazole 
(TMP-SMZ) or nitrofurantoin (should not be given if GFR <50).
	
	Inpatient treatment includes IV antimicrobial therapy with a third-generation 
cephalosporin, such as ceftriaxone; a fluoroquinolone, such as ciprofloxacin/
levofloxacin; or an aminoglycoside.
	 2.	Alkalinizing agents may be used with certain antibiotics like cotrimoxazole to 
prevent precipitation of crystals.
	 3.	Tab. Phenazopyridine 100–200 mg up to 3 times a day for the first 2–3 days as a 
urinary analgesic may be used to relieve dysuria.
Treatment of specific cases
Uncomplicated cystitis in women: Complete resolution of symptoms in females 
with uncomplicated cystitis may require approximately 5–6 days; give antibiotic 
therapy for at least a week.
UTIs in pregnancy: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy must be treated 
appropriately. The physiological changes associated with pregnancy increase the 
risk of serious infectious complications from symptomatic and asymptomatic UTIs 
even in healthy pregnant women. Consequently, treatment is indicated for pregnant 
women with asymptomatic bacteriuria as well as for those with symptomatic UTIs; 
antibiotic selection may differ, and regimens are typically more prolonged.
(Caution: Cotrimoxazole and fluoroquinolones are not recommended during 
pregnancy.) (For details, see Chapter 15.)
UTI in patients with diabetes: UTI in patients with diabetes is more common, 
is more serious and carries a worse outcome. Various impairments in the immune 
system, poor metabolic control and incomplete bladder emptying due to autonomic 
neuropathy may all contribute to the enhanced risk of UTI in these patients. Choice 
of therapy and duration of treatment depend on several factors, including presence 
of symptoms, severity of systemic symptoms, whether infection is localized in 
the bladder or also involves the kidney, presence of urological abnormalities, 
accompanying metabolic alterations and renal function.

Chapter 10  Genitourinary Diseases    603
UTIs in elderly: Treatment is not recommended for asymptomatic infections among 
the elderly, particularly men.
UTIs in catheterized patients: Need for treatment, and optimal type and duration of 
treatment for such patients with asymptomatic bacteriuria have not been established. 
Removal of the catheter with a short course of antibiotic may be appropriate. If 
the catheter cannot be removed, bacteriuria should be ignored unless the patient is 
symptomatic or at a high risk of developing bacteriuria.

604    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Prophylaxis
Suppressive antibiotics: These are indicated in patients with repeated infections with 
an underlying cause, till the underlying cause is removed or controlled, e.g. infants and 
children with vesicoureteric reflux till 3–5 years of age and elderly requiring prolonged 
catheterization. The recommended drugs are the same as above.
Antibiotics for prevention are recommended to women who have two or more 
episodes of infection within 6 months or three or more infections within 1 year. The 
recommended antimicrobials include daily or thrice-weekly administration of a single 
dose of TMP-SMZ (80/400 mg), TMP alone (100 mg) or nitrofurantoin (50 mg). 
Prophylaxis should be initiated only after bacteriuria has been eradicated with a 
full-dose treatment regimen. Same regimen can be used as a single dose after sexual 
intercourse in women in whom episodes of symptomatic UTIs are related to sexual 
intercourse. Frequent urine cultures are essential during this period.

Routine post-treatment urinalysis or urine cultures in asymptomatic patients are not 
necessary. In upper UTIs, fever and other symptoms normally subside within 2–3 days 
after starting the treatment. If symptoms do not subside within 5 days, underlying 
abnormalities like obstruction to the urinary tract, stones or collection of pus should 
be looked for. If the infection relapses after an initial treatment for 14 days, a 6-week 
treatment is recommended. 
Patient education
	
l To drink plenty of water 
	
l Not to control the urge to pass urine; to empty the bladder completely and very often 
	
l To empty the bladder after sexual intercourse
	
l Both the partners to clean the genitalia before and after sexual intercourse 
	
l To wipe from front to back during ablution

Hormonal Disorders
HYPOTHYROIDISM
Hypothyroidism can be classified into primary and secondary hypothyroidism. The 
most common cause of primary hypothyroidism is autoimmune thyroiditis, specifically 
Hashimoto's thyroiditis, where the body's immune system attacks and damages 
the thyroid gland. Other primary causes include iodine deficiency, thyroid surgery 
or radiation therapy, congenital abnormalities and certain medications. Iatrogenic 
causes include I131 therapy, antithyroid or lithium treatment and thyroidectomy. 
Secondary hypothyroidism occurs due to pituitary or hypothalamic disorders. Pituitary 
disorders such as tumours, trauma, or pituitary insufficiency can cause secondary 
hypothyroidism. Additionally, hypothalamic dysfunction or abnormalities affecting 
the hypothalamic-pituitary axis can also contribute to secondary hypothyroidism. 
Differentiating between primary and secondary causes of hypothyroidism is crucial for 
appropriate diagnosis and management strategies. Thyroid disease is the second most 
common endocrine disorder encountered in pregnant women after diabetes.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patient presents with weakness, tiredness, coarse dry skin, hoarse voice, facial 
puffiness, unexplained weight gain, intolerance to cold, constipation, irregular 
menses, infertility, recurrent abortion, cardiac enlargement and/or pericardial 
effusion, goitre with or without prolonged relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes.
	
l Myxoedema coma is a rare complication of severe hypothyroidism with signs of 
hypothermia, hypoventilation, hyponatraemia, hypoxia, hypercapnia and hypotension. 
In severe primary hypothyroidism, several cardiac manifestations can occur due 
to the impact of thyroid hormone deficiency on the cardiovascular system. The 
cardiac silhouette is enlarged largely due to effusion of fluid rich in protein and 
glycosaminoglycans into the pericardial sac, but the myocardium may also be dilated.
	
l Diagnosis is confirmed by low serum T3, T4, and raised serum TSH in primary 
hypothyroidism and low in secondary hypothyroidism. Thyroperoxidase (TPO) 
antibodies are present in 90–95% of patients with autoimmune hypothyroidism.
	
l Pregnancies in women with subclinical hypothyroidism are more likely to be 
complicated by placental abnormalities, low-birth-weight babies, preterm birth, 
cognitive and developmental abnormalities in foetus, hyperbilirubinaemia and 
respiratory distress in the newborn.

Overt hypothyroidism is increased in serum TSH (>10 mIU/L) as a result of decreased 
thyroxine and a negative feedback, while in subclinical hypothyroidism, serum TSH 
levels are mildly elevated (ranging from 4 to 10 mIU/L), but the thyroxine (T4) levels 
remain within the normal range.
Normally T4 and TSH are inversely related due to negative feedback mechanism. 
If both T4 and TSH are low or both are high, it suggests disease at the level of 
hypothalamus or pituitary. Refer these cases to a specialist.

Subclinical hypothyroidism with no symptoms, monitor these patients every 3–6 months 
in case TSH is 4.5–10 with a normal T4, and anti-thyroperoxidase (TPO) negative, or 
patients with positive anti-TPO but TSH <4.5. Treat if TSH is >10 or between 4.5 and 
10, if symptomatic/has goitre or is anti-TPO positive or >3 in pregnant patients, as per 
the trimester of pregnancy.
Tab. l-Thyroxine 50–100 mcg/day should be taken on an empty stomach in the 
morning. Dose should be adjusted based on TSH levels. Goal is normal TSH (lower half 
of the reference range). Measure TSH levels after 6–8 weeks of instituting therapy. Adjust 
by 12.5 or 25 mcg increments if TSH is high; decrement by same if TSH is suppressed.
Note: Thyroid hormones should not be used to treat symptoms suggestive 
of hypothyroidism without biochemical confirmation of the diagnosis. When full 
replacement is achieved, follow-up measurement should be conducted at annual 
intervals and later at 2–3 years’ interval. Ensure ongoing compliance.
Special treatment considerations in pregnant women
	
l A woman with hypothyroidism should be euthyroid prior to conception and during 
early pregnancy (affects foetal neuronal development).
	
l Check for TSH on the first antenatal visit. Total T4 is not reliable during pregnancy. 
Treat all overt patients with hypothyroidism with l-Thyroxine with a starting dose 
of 50 mcg/day or more in all patients with a TSH >2.5 mIU/L and low T4 in the 
first trimester or >3.0 mIU/L in the second trimester and 1.20 mcg/kg/day in newly 
diagnosed patients with subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH >2.5) with antibody 
positivity.
	
l In a patient with known hypothyroidism taking l-Thyroxine, increase dose by 30% on 
the first antenatal visit. Monitor TSH every 4–6 weeks until mid-gestation and at least 
once near 28 weeks’ gestation and titrate up the dose (target TSH <2.5) accordingly. 
After delivery, reassess TSH levels after 6 weeks to return to pre-pregnant dose. 
Breastfeeding is allowed in a mother with hypothyroidism on l-thyroxine.
Treatment considerations in elderly
	
l Elderly require less thyroxine (less by up to 20%), especially those with coronary 
artery disease (CAD). Starting dose is 12.5 mcg/day with similar increments every

2–3 months until TSH is normalized. Serum TSH is variable and has a higher range 
cut-off as the age progresses.
	
l In cases with hypothyroidism with low TSH, a suprathyroid cause is suspected 
and requires detailed investigations. Refer to a tertiary care centre. Assess 
the response clinically and by serum TSH (serum T4 in suprathyroid type) at 8-weekly 
intervals; once the euthyroid state is restored, follow-up at 6–12 months’ interval. 
	
l For patients with TSH levels between 5 and 10 but with normal T3/T4 levels and a 
goitre indicating euthyroidism, assess vitamin D3 levels as vitamin D3 deficiency 
may impair hormone biosynthesis.
Myxoedema coma
	 1.	Warm blankets, mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure
	 2.	Correction of metabolic disturbances and treatment of precipitating factors
	 3.	l-Thyroxine 500 mcg bolus, and then 50–100 mcg IV daily; if IV preparation 
not available, same dose via Ryle’s tube; once acute phase over, l-Thyroxine 
maintained as above
	 4.	Inj. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat, 25–50 mg 8 hourly
(Caution: Avoid sedatives.)
Patient education
l	l-Thyroxine should be taken as single daily dose, ideally on awakening, at least 30 
minutes before eating anything.
	
l Fibre and bran products (e.g. ispaghula husk) may impair absorption, as also 
cholestyramine, colestipol, iron sulphate, sucralfate, oral calcium and aluminium 
hydroxide. Metabolism of l-Thyroxine is increased by Phenytoin, Rifampicin and 
Carbamazepine.
	
l Explain to the patient that the treatment is lifelong. Do not modify the dose or stop 
treatment without consultation.
	
l Overtreatment may lead to decreased bone mineral density and adverse cardiac 
consequences.

HYPERTHYROIDISM
It classically occurs in Graves’ disease, which is characterized by diffuse goitre, 
ophthalmopathy (40%) and dermopathy (1–2%) in varying combinations. Other 
important causes are toxic multinodular goitre (MNG), toxic adenomas and side effects 
of certain medications – excess iodine and thyroid hormone, amiodarone, etc.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occur sweating, tremors, unexplained weight loss with good appetite, 
heat intolerance, wide pulse pressure, sinus tachycardia and atrial arrhythmias; 
worsening of angina or cardiac failure and sometimes diarrhoea may predominate 
in older patients.
	
l In Graves’ disease, goitre, ophthalmopathy and dermopathy are seen.
	
l Diagnosis is confirmed by low to undetectable serum TSH and increased 
serum T4 and T3. Antithyroid antibodies are elevated in Graves’ disease and 
lymphocytic thyroiditis but are not necessary for diagnosis; however, they can 
be used for monitoring the effects of antithyroid drugs in patients with Graves’ 
disease. Radionuclide uptake and scan distinguishes the high uptake of Graves’ 
disease from the low uptake of thyroiditis and provides other useful anatomic 
information.
Pre-treatment assessment
Assess smoking, thyroid size (either by sonography or by inspection and palpation), 
orbitopathy, FT4, FT3 and thyrotropin-binding immunoglobulin (TBII) before starting 
treatment with antithyroid drug (ATD) therapy.

A.  Pharmacological
	 1.	Adjunctive treatment – for adrenergic symptoms like sweating, tremor and 
tachycardia
	
	Tab. propranolol 40 mg gradually titrated up to 120 mg a day
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Atenolol 50–200 mg a day to be continued until the patient becomes euthyroid 
(with target pulse of 60–90 if blood pressure allows) 
	 2.	Tab. Carbimazole 10–20 mg every 8–12 hours; after euthyroid state achieved in 
6–8 weeks, once-daily dose.

	Or 
	
	Tab. Methimazole 10–40 mg once daily
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Propylthiouracil 100–150 mg every 8 hours
	
	(Caution: Periodically monitor thyroid function tests and prothrombin time during 
therapy. Measure alkaline phosphatase, ALT, AST and bilirubin if symptoms of 
hepatic dysfunction occur. Measure CBC with differential count if symptoms 
of infection – fever, severe sore throat, etc. – develop, stop the medication; dose 
modification is not needed in Methimazole, except when the patient is pregnant, 
in which case modification should be considered.)
	 3.	Review with serum TSH and T4 after 4–6 weeks’ treatment has been initiated. Once 
controlled, reduce to the smallest effective dose. Drugs are given for an average of 
2 years.
	 4.	In thyroiditis, symptomatic treatment usually is sufficient because the associated 
hyperthyroidism is transient.
	 5.	Definitive treatment is surgery/radioiodine ablation of thyroid tissue (for details, 
see thyroid swelling in Surgery section in Chapter 18).
B.  Surgery: Subtotal thyroidectomy in younger patients (younger than 30 years) in 
whom antithyroid therapy has been unsuccessful, in patients with very large goitre 
causing compressive symptoms and in those with severe ophthalmopathy
C.  Radioactive iodine (I131): Method of choice in the elderly, younger patients 
(completed family) with recurrent thyrotoxicosis following surgery or when surgery is 
refused/contraindicated. (Caution: Radioiodine should never be given in pregnancy. 
In women of child-bearing age, if radioiodine treatment is planned, a pregnancy test 
must always be carried out.)
Pregnancy
In pregnant women, surgery should not be performed in the first and third trimesters. 
Antithyroid drugs are less risky but may induce hypothyroidism in the foetus and should 
be used in the smallest necessary dose to keep serum TSH and T4 in upper normal range.
Propylthiouracil use should be restricted during or just prior to the first trimester 
and thyroid storm and in patients who experience minor side effects with Methimazole. 
Switch to Methimazole for the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. Methimazole 
is preferred following the first trimester of pregnancy. The usual maintenance 
dose is 200 mg/day. If >300 mg/day is required during the first trimester, subtotal 
thyroidectomy is indicated in the second trimester.
Avoid Propranolol as it can cause foetal growth retardation and neonatal respiratory 
depression.
Ophthalmopathy 
Refer to an ophthalmologist.
Initiate therapy in mild cases with elevation of the head at night, diuretics 
to decrease oedema, use of tinted sunglasses and 1% methylcellulose eyedrops

610    Standard Treatment Guidelines
to prevent drying and refer patients with severe and progressive exophthalmos to an 
ophthalmologist.
Toxic multinodular goitre
Radioactive iodine (I131) is the treatment of choice. Large doses are usually required. 
Treatment with antithyroid drugs is given till the patient is euthyroid. Surgery may be 
required for very large goitres.
Propranolol may be useful before and after radioactive iodine administration. 
Recent studies suggest a potential role for iodine in patients who have adverse reactions 
to ATD or contraindications for radioiodine or surgery. Sometimes iodine is used 
as a beneficial adjunct to ATD: 38 mg potassium iodide (KI) + 15 mg methimazole 
resulted in better control of hyperthyroidism and fewer adverse reactions than 30 mg 
methimazole alone.
(For details, also see Thyroid Nodule in Chapter 18.)
Thyrotoxic crisis or thyroid storm 
Refer to a tertiary care centre in case of life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism 
with fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice, delirium and coma; symptoms are usually 
precipitated by acute illness like stroke, infection, trauma and diabetic ketoacidosis 
(DKA), and in poorly controlled patients undergoing surgery or radioiodine treatment:
	 1.	Tab. Propylthiouracil 600 mg loading dose, and then 200–300 mg every 6 hours 
orally or through Ryle’s tube
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Carbimazole 15–25 mg 6 hourly
	 2.	One hour after the first dose of antithyroid drug, saturated solution of Potassium 
iodide (SSKI) 5 drops every 6 hours
	
	Or
	
	Lugol’s iodine 10 drops 3 times a day
	
	Or
	
	Sodium iodide 1 g IV slowly
	 3.	Tab. Propranolol 40–60 mg 4 hourly
	 4.	Inj. Dexamethasone 2 mg IV 6 hourly
	
	Continue iodides and dexamethasone until normal metabolic stage is achieved and 
provide supportive treatment like cooling, antipyretics, antibiotics for infection 
and IV fluids. Once euthyroid status is achieved, manage as already outlined.
Patient education
	
l To report to the doctor if fever or sore throat develops on antithyroid drugs, complete 
blood count should be done; discontinue ATD if TLC count <1500/mm3. 
	
l If allergic rash or drug sensitivity develops, give antihistamines and preferably 
change to another drug. If agranulocytosis, hepatitis, drug fever and arthralgias 
develop, preferably stop antithyroid treatment. 
	
l Iodide is useful in impending thyrotoxic crisis and patients with severe cardiac 
disease; it must be used only after antithyroid drugs have been given.

HYPOCALCAEMIA
Hypocalcaemia is a potentially life-threatening biochemical abnormality that carries 
risks for serious errors in diagnosis and treatment. It may be an asymptomatic 
laboratory finding or a life-threatening metabolic disturbance. Hypocalcaemia may 
be caused by hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency 
states, chronic renal failure (CRF), malabsorption syndrome and hypomagnesaemia. 
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The classic symptoms of hypocalcaemia are neuromuscular excitability in the 
form of muscle twitching, spasms, tingling and numbness. Carpopedal spasm 
is characteristic but in severe cases can progress to tetany, seizures and cardiac 
dysrhythmias. Positive Chvostek’s and Trousseau’s signs are characteristic. 
	
l ECG may reveal prolongation of the QT interval and marked QRS complex and 
ST-segment changes (like MI).
	
l Total serum calcium is <8.5 mg/dL (ionized calcium <4 mg/dL). In hypoalbumi­
naemia, add 1 mg/dL of calcium to the estimated level for every 1 g fall of 
albumin below 4 g/dL (corrected serum calcium). However, this threshold 
varies greatly and is dependent on the rate of fall. Hypomagnesaemia and 
hyperphosphataemia can induce hypocalcaemia.

Approach to treatment
	
l Children with any acute illness or condition affecting the input, distribution or output 
of electrolytes and/or fluid in the body are at risk of electrolyte abnormalities. 
	
l Critically abnormal test results should be reported and acted on in a timely manner. 
Errors in sample collection or processing may lead to inaccurate electrolyte values 
and it is essential to consider the clinical context.
	
l Serum electrolyte reference ranges vary and may differ among laboratories. Utilize 
age-appropriate normal ranges provided by your local pathology service.
	
l Investigate and correct any underlying cause of hypocalcaemia.

612    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Correct low magnesium levels first. Without replenishing magnesium first, any 
increase in calcium will be transient. 
	
l Parathyroid hormone and vitamin D levels should ideally be checked before 
initiating treatment for hypocalcaemia.
Severe hypocalcaemia
Severe hypocalcaemia (ionized calcium <1.9 mg/dL) is a medical emergency and/or 
symptomatic at any level below the reference range. 
	 1.	Calcium gluconate solution 20 mL of 10% over 10–15 minutes followed by 60–80 
mL of 10% solution in 1 L 5% dextrose (45 mEq/h elemental calcium)
	
	(Caution: Do not mix with bicarbonate solution as it may result in precipitation 
of calcium carbonate; calcium chloride can be used as an alternative to calcium 
gluconate, but it is more irritant to veins and should only be given via a central 
line.) ECG monitoring is recommended because dysrhythmias can occur if 
correction is too rapid.
	
		
Measure serum calcium every 4–6 hours and adjust rate. Aim is to 
maintain the total serum calcium concentration at 7–9 mg/dL. Note: Untreated 
hypomagnesaemia will often make hypocalcaemia refractory to therapy; therefore, 
correct magnesium levels first.
	 2.	If associated with hypomagnesaemia, Inj. Magnesium sulphate 1–2 g IV on day 
one followed by oral Magnesium oxide 600–1200 mg 3 times a day to replenish 
stores (to keep the ionized calcium above 2 mmol/L).
Asymptomatic/mild hypocalcaemia/maintenance treatment
Treat the underlying cause, if possible. Usually long-term treatment is required in 
conditions like hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism and chronic vitamin D 
deficiency states.
	 1.	Tab. Calcium carbonate (40% elemental calcium by weight) 1–2 g elemental 
calcium orally 3 times a day initially and subsequently maintenance dose of 0.5–1 g 
3 times a day.
	 2.	In CRF, calcium alone gives an inadequate response; correct concomitant 
hyperphosphataemia before instituting the following therapy:
	
	Vitamin D 50,000 IU orally each week for 8 weeks
	
	Or
	
	Calcitriol 0.25–1 mcg orally daily (dose can be increased every 4–7 days – more 
expensive but less toxic than vitamin D for hyperphosphataemia.
	 3.	Low-phosphate (low cereal) diet and phosphate-binding agents, e.g. aluminium 
hydroxide
Long-term follow-up (preferably by an endocrinologist): For patients commenced 
on 1-Alfacalcidol or Calcitriol, monitor adjusted serum calcium levels initially 
approximately 1 week post-discharge, and then if satisfactory at 1, 3 and then 6 months. 
Assess PTH and 24-hour urinary calcium within 2–4 weeks of starting treatment.

HYPERCALCAEMIA
The common causes are primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy; other causes 
include vitamin D toxicity, high bone turnover or renal failure. Hypercalcaemia is 
defined as total serum calcium concentration >10.5 mEq/L (or an elevation in ionized 
calcium >4.8 mg/dL).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Fatigue, depression, confusion, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, constipation, 
polyuria, short QT interval on ECG and occasionally cardiac arrhythmias. 
	
l Generally symptoms appear when serum Ca2+ >11.5–12.0 mg/dL; severe 
hypercalcaemia (>15–18 mg/dL) can result in death.

Treatment varies with severity and rate of rise of serum calcium levels. Severe 
hypercalcaemia is a medical emergency regardless of symptoms.

614    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic hypercalcaemia (calcium <12 mg/dL) 
does not require immediate treatment. 
	
l Serum calcium of 12–14 mg/dL may be well tolerated chronically and may not 
require immediate treatment. However, aggressive treatment is required for an acute 
rise to these concentrations as it may cause marked changes in sensorium.
	 1.	Perform rehydration infusion of 0.9% saline at 300–500 mL/h (saline diuresis) 
until fluid deficit is replaced and diuresis occurs (urine output ≥200–300 mL/h). 
Once adequate rehydration has occurred, the saline infusion rate is reduced to 
100–200 mL/h. Monitor for fluid overload in elderly and patients with renal 
impairment.
	 2.	Monitor electrolytes, especially potassium and magnesium, and replace accordingly.
	 3.	Haemodialysis is the treatment of choice to rapidly decrease serum calcium in 
patients with heart failure or renal failure. For extreme conditions, administer a 
chelating agent (e.g. 50 mmol PO4 over 8–12 hours or EDTA 10–15 mg/kg over 
4 hours).
	 4.	After rehydration, give:
	
	Inj. Zoledronic acid 4 mg over 15 minutes
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Pamidronate 30–90 mg (depending on severity of hypercalcaemia) at 20 mg/h 
Or ibandronic acid 2–4 mg 
	
	(Caution: Give more slowly and consider dose reduction in renal impairment. 
Monitor serum calcium response – will reach nadir at 2–4 days; it can cause 
hypocalcaemia if there is vitamin D deficiency or suppressed PTH. Role of oral 
phosphorus is limited.)
	
	And/or
	 5.	Give Inj. Salmon calcitonin 4 IU/kg and repeat measurement of serum calcium in 
several hours. If a hypocalcaemic response is noted, then repeat every 6–12 hours.
	 6.	Inj. Denosumab, 120 mg SC, in patients with hypercalcaemia of malignancy non-
responsive to bisphosphonates.
	 7.	Inj. Prednisone 40–100 mg IV in 4 divided doses.
	
	Glucocorticoids are also useful in the rare form of hypercalcaemia (in certain 
autoimmune disorders, where inactivating antibodies against the receptor mimic 
familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia [FHH]).
	 8.	Encourage early weight-bearing mobilization.
	 9.	Definitive treatment, wherever possible, is parathyroidectomy in primary 
hyperparathyroidism.
Patient education
	
l In patients with mild asymptomatic and moderate hypercalcaemia due to 
hyperparathyroidism, advise to keep active, avoid immobilization, drink adequate 
fluids (at least 6–8 glasses of water per day) and avoid thiazide diuretics, lithium, large 
doses of vitamin D or A and calcium supplements and calcium-containing antacids.
	
l Check serum calcium and albumin twice a year, renal function and urine calcium 
once a year, and bone density of distal radius once every 2 years.

DIABETES MELLITUS
Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a group of metabolic disorders characterized by 
hyperglycaemia. It is divided into two broad categories: Type 1 DM is characterized 
by insulin deficiency and occurs commonly early during childhood, and type 2 is 
DM characterized by variable degree of insulin resistance, impaired insulin secretion 
and increased hepatic glucose output. Other types of diabetes are gestational diabetes 
mellitus (GDM) and other specific types of diabetes due to other causes, e.g. monogenic 
diabetes syndromes (such as neonatal diabetes and maturity-onset diabetes of the 
young), diseases of the exocrine pancreas (such as cystic fibrosis and pancreatitis) and 
drug- or chemical-induced diabetes (such as with glucocorticoid use, in the treatment 
of HIV/AIDS or after organ transplantation). Early aggressive glycaemic control 
prevents or delays long-term microvascular complications (retinopathy, neuropathy, 
nephropathy) and macrovascular complications (carotid artery disease, CAD and 
peripheral arterial disease). Opportunistic screening for undiagnosed diabetes and 
prediabetes should be done for individuals presenting to healthcare settings for 
unrelated illness, family members of diabetes patients, antenatal care, dental care, 
overweight children and adolescents at onset of puberty. Additionally, community 
screening should be considered wherever feasible.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and unexplained weight loss occur in a patient 
with classic symptoms of hyperglycaemia or hyperglycaemic crisis – with a 
*random or casual plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL or **fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 
mg/dL or 2-hour plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL after a 75-g glucose load and 
HBA1C ≥ 6.5. In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycaemia, the result should 
be confirmed by repeat testing.
	
l Impaired fasting glucose (IFG) 100–125 mg/dL and impaired glucose tolerance 
(IGT) (2-hour plasma glucose 140–199 mg/dL, HBA1C between 5.7 and 
6.4) are considered ‘pre-diabetes’ and are risk factors for future diabetes and 
cardiovascular disease (CVD). Use of HbA1c as a sole diagnostic test for 
screening of diabetes/prediabetes is not recommended.
	
l Opportunistic screening for undiagnosed diabetes and pre-diabetes in asymptomatic 
adults and adolescents who are overweight or obese and have two or more risk 
factors for diabetes (hypertension, history of CVD, abnormal lipid profile, physical 
inactivity, women with a history of gestational diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome,

616    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 other clinical conditions associated with insulin resistance, e.g. severe obesity, 
acanthosis nigricans), family members of diabetes patients, antenatal care, dental 
care; and wherever feasible community screening may be done.
	
l For all people, testing should begin at the age of 45 years. If tests are normal, 
repeat testing should be carried out at a minimum of 3-year intervals. Test yearly 
those with pre-diabetes and risk status.
*Random/casual is defined as any time of day without regard to last meal.
**Fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 hours.
Pre-diabetes: Lifestyle modification is required in all patients with diabetes and pre-
diabetes for prevention and delay of diabetes.
	
l Screening for and managing modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease 
(CVD), such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking and alcohol consumption, 
should be done concurrently.
	
l Lifestyle modification: Efforts to reduce body weight by 5–10% are recommended 
for individuals who are overweight or obese. Increase moderate-intensity physical 
activity (such as brisk walking) to at least 1 hour daily if overweight or obese and at 
least half an hour daily if normal weight. Six to eight hours of sleep daily. Healthy 
lifestyle measures including diet and physical activity are equally important for 
non‑obese patients with pre-diabetes.
	
l Nutrition (reduced calorie meal plan with emphasis on overall quality of food 
consumed with an emphasis on whole grains, legumes, nuts, fruits and vegetables 
and minimal refined and processed foods)
	
l Children to be encouraged to take a well-balanced diet with adequate macronutrients and 
micronutrients as in case of normal children to ensure normal growth and development
	
l Metformin therapy for prevention of type 2 diabetes in those with pre-diabetes, 
especially for those with BMI ≥35 kg/m2, those younger than 60 years and women 
with prior GDM. Alternatively, alpha‑glucosidase inhibitors (AGIs) such as acarbose 
or voglibose may be initiated if metformin is not tolerated.
	 Note: Other pharmacological interventions with pioglitazones, orlistat, vitamin D, 
or bariatric surgery are not recommended.
Treatment of DM Type 1
Type 1 DM always requires lifelong insulin therapy in addition to dietary management 
(see below for insulin therapy).

Insulin therapy 
	 1. 	Start with insulin 0.3–0.5 unit/kg/day subcutaneously. Various types of insulins 
available are shown in Table 11.1.
	 2.	Basal bolus regimen: Manage all patients with type 1 diabetes preferentially with 
combined intermediate/long-acting (basal) and short-acting insulin (bolus). This

Chapter 11  Hormonal Disorders    617
consists of pre-meal short-acting insulin and bedtime intermediate/long-acting insulin 
not later than 22:00 hours. The initial total daily insulin dose is divided into 40–50% 
basal insulin; the rest is given as bolus insulin split equally before each meal. Adjust 
dose on an individual basis based on pre- and post-prandial glucose levels. 
	
	Or
	
	Pre-mixed insulin twice daily, i.e. a mixture of intermediate- or short-acting 
insulin, provides adequate control, when used with at least daily BG monitoring. 
One-third of the total insulin requirement is given as regular and two-thirds as 
intermediate-acting insulin. One-third of the total dose is used before dinner and 
two-thirds before breakfast.
	 3.	Insulin is given SC 30 minutes before meals.
	 4.	Insulin delivery devices: Various options are available which include syringes 
(U 40/U 100), prefilled pens, pen device with cartridges and insulin pump. In 
visually impaired patients, prefilled pens may be used.
	 5.	The abdominal wall is the common injection site. The back of the arm, the outer 
side of the thigh and the upper buttocks are also used for injection. Rotate injection

	 6.	Dose, type and timing of insulin are adjusted according to pre-prandial blood glucose 
(BG) levels (individualize goals). BG goal range before meals is 90–130 mg/dL and 
that at bedtime/overnight is 90–150 mg/dL, and HBA1C <7.5%. A lower goal (7.0%)

in children with frequent hypoglycaemia or hypoglycaemia unawareness.
	
	Measure post-prandial BG when there is a discrepancy between pre-prandial BG

	 7.	Increment of dose should not be more than 10% of the existing dose and dose

	 8.	Explain diabetes self-management and adjustment of insulin, dose based on

	 9.	Use insulin analogues in select cases when they are justified on clinical grounds, 
preferably under the guidance of a specialist. Patients must be properly trained for 
administration of SC injections. 
	10.	Explain features of hypoglycaemia to the patient and his/her attendant. Ensure

	11.	Patients with type 1 DM should measure glucose at least twice daily (pre-breakfast 
and pre-dinner). 
	12.	Explain about sick day management.
	13.	Refer patients with diabetes ketoacidosis to a higher centre.
Treatment of Type 2 DM
It is possible to control mild type 2 DM with non-pharmacological therapy 
(dietary control and exercise); however, moderate and severe forms will require, in 
addition, one or more oral hypoglycaemics and occasionally insulin therapy.
Non-pharmacological in pre-diabetes and mild DM
Lifestyle modification: Most patients with type 2 DM are, however, obese and should 
be put on dietary restrictions for weight reduction as above.

l Caloric distribution and carbohydrate, fat and protein counting
	– Carbohydrate intake should be 45–65% of total calories per day, protein 10–35% 
of total kcal/day (10% for those with nephropathy) and fat 20–35% (saturated fat 
<7% of total kcal/day and polyunsaturated fat 10% of kcal/day. Minimize the

intake of trans-fats). Complex carbohydrates should be preferred over refined 
products. Low glycaemic index (GI) and low glycaemic load (GL) foods should 
be preferred. Quantity of rice (GI: 73) should be limited as it has high GI; brown 
rice (GI: 68) should be preferred over white rice.
	– Diet rich in fruits, leafy vegetates, nuts, fibre, whole grains and unsaturated fat 
is preferred.
	– Follow meal planning, healthful eating and/or portion control and counting. 
A low-glycaemic-index diet may modestly improve hyperglycaemia. 
A low-carbohydrate-diet (<130 g/day) is not recommended in the treatment of 
overweight/obesity. Routine supplementation with antioxidants (vitamins E, C 
and carotene) is not advised.
	– Use of caloric sweeteners including sucrose is safe when consumed within the 
intake levels recommended by FDA.
	– Fibre intake should be 20–35 g/day and sodium 3,000 mg/day.
	– Oils with high monounsaturated fatty acid (MUFA) and polyunsaturated fatty 
acid (PUFA) should be used.
	
■Use of two or more vegetable oils is recommended in rotation.
	
■For non‑vegetarians, consumption of 100–200 g of fish/week is advised as 
good source of PUFA and for vegetarians vegetable oils (soybean/safflower/
sunflower), walnuts and flaxseeds are recommended.
	
■Avoid consumption of foods high in saturated fat (butter, coconut oil, margarine, 
ghee).
	
■Saturated fatty acids (SFAs) intake should be less than 10% of total calories/
day (<7% for individuals having high triglycerides).
	
■Use of partially hydrogenated vegetable oils (Vanaspati) as the cooking 
medium should be avoided.
	
■Reheating and refrying of cooking oils should be avoided.
	– However, individual dietary recommendations may vary based on factors such as 
overall health status, lipid profile and cardiovascular risk factors.
	 2.	Exercise: Perform regular physical exercise for 0.5–1 hour (for sedentary workers). 
Lifestyle modification of increasing physical activity in day-to-day work is 
also recommended: at least 150 minutes/week of moderate-intensity aerobic 
physical activity (50–70% of maximum heart rate) and/or at least 90 minutes/
week of vigorous aerobic exercise (>70% of maximum heart rate). The physical 
activity should be distributed over at least 3 days/week and with no more than 2 
consecutive days without physical activity. In the absence of contraindications, 
encourage resistance exercise three times a week. 
	 3.	Follow cessation and avoid all kinds of tobacco products.
	 4.	Control cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors – BP, dyslipidaemia and other 
related co-morbidities.

Metformin should be initiated in combination with lifestyle interventions at the time 
of diagnosis and should be continued as long as it is tolerated and not contraindicated;

620    Standard Treatment Guidelines
other OHAs, including insulin, should be added to Metformin. Metformin has the 
advantage of promoting mild weight loss in obese patients. Patients with fasting glucose 
200–250 mg/dL respond well. Treatment may be started with any of the following drugs 
and the dose individualized focusing on individualized target HbA1c for each patient 
based on: age, duration of diabetes, comorbidities, cost of therapy, hypoglycaemia risk, 
weight gain, durability and dose can be increased every 2–3 weeks as determined by 
BG response:
	 1.	Monotherapy: Administer Tab. metformin 500 mg once or twice a day in obese 
patients and increase the dose to 1000 mg 2 times a day with meals. Supplement 
vitamin B12 as needed in patients on long-term metformin. (Caution: If eGFR is
