	Or
	
	Tab. Glimepiride 1–8 mg/day once daily should be taken at the same time every 
day with breakfast Or Tab. Glipizide 2.5–40 mg/day before breakfast Or Tab. 
Glipizide ER 5–10 mg/day with breakfast Or Tab. Gliclazide MR 30–120 mg/day 
as single dose at breakfast time. (Caution: Modified release formulations [MR and 
ER] should be swallowed whole and not broken, chewed or crushed, as this would 
damage the modified release action.) 
	
	Or 
	
	Tab. Glyburide (glibenclamide) 1.25–20 mg/day should be administered with 
breakfast or with the first main meal.
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Pioglitazone initially should be given 15–30 mg, up to 45 mg usually once 
daily without regard to meals. (Caution: Do not administer in patients with 
active or with a history of severe osteoporosis and bladder cancer and those with 
uninvestigated haematuria. Before starting on pioglitazone, assess for risk factors 
for bladder cancer; review after 3–6 months and stop if there is no response.)
	 2.	Combination therapy: If goal is not achieved or maintained (HBA1C is >1.5 
above the target) in 3 months with monotherapy at maximal tolerated doses. In 
some cases, dual therapy may be indicated initially if it is considered unlikely that 
single agent therapy will achieve glucose targets. The following combination can 
be given:
	
l Sulphonylurea + Metformin
	
l Sulphonylurea + Thiazolidinedione (Pioglitazone, Rosiglitazone)
	
l Sulphonylurea + alpha-glucosidase inhibitor (AGI; acarbose)
	
l Metformin + DPP‑4 inhibitor (Vildagliptin/Sitagliptin/Teneligliptin/Linagliptin) 
or SGLT2 inhibitors (Canagliflozin, Dapagliflozin and Empagliflozin)
	
l If glucose targets are not achieved with two agents: start third oral agent‑AGI, 
DPP‑4 inhibitor, SGLT2 inhibitor, or TZDs (depending on second‑line agent 
used) or start insulin or glucagon‑like peptide 1 (GLP‑1) agonists.
	
l Patients not achieving glycaemic targets on three oral agents, consider GLP‑1 
agonists or insulin if glucose targets are not achieved with OHA. Exceptionally, 
addition of fourth agent may be considered.

l In the presence of IR, addition of TZDs may be considered.
	
l For patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), 
heart failure, diabetic kidney disease (DKD) or in need of weight reduction 
consider using SGLT2 inhibitors.
	
l If postprandial hypoglycaemia is the issue AGI, glinides or SGLT2 inhibitors 
may be considered.
	
l In elderly patients with increased risk of hypoglycaemia, use a DPP‑4 inhibitor

l Insulin: Add insulin or intensify insulin therapy in patients with primary 
(markedly symptomatic and/or elevated BG levels or HBA1C >8%) or 
secondary failure to oral agents after 3 months, often as single dose of 
intermediate-acting insulin 0.3–0.4 unit/kg/day either before breakfast or 
at bedtime in combination with Tab. metformin. Insulin is also required in 
situations like pregnancy, surgery and infection.
	
l Consider insulin as initial therapy in patients with:
	– Fasting plasma glucose >250–300 mg/dL or HBA1C >10% since more rapid 
glycaemic control will reduce glucose toxicity to islet cells, improve insulin 
secretion and possibly make OHAs more effective
	– Severe weight loss or lean patients
	– Underlying renal or hepatic disease, or acutely ill or hospitalized patients.
	– Therapeutic choice of regimen, preparation and delivery device should be 
made through a process of shared, informed decision making.
	– Initiate with once‑daily basal insulin, once‑daily premixed/co‑formulation 
insulin, or twice‑daily premixed insulin, either alone or in combination with 
or other OHAs, based upon patient’s age, clinical features, glucose profile,

in life threatening or organ/limb threatening clinical situations.
	– Analogue insulins may be used in preference to human insulins with possible 
lower risk of nocturnal and symptomatic hypoglycaemia; however, economic 
considerations must be taken into account.
	– Match timing of insulin and meals.
	– Counselling/education about SMBG and hypoglycaemia prevention, 
recognition and treatment are recommended to all patients initiating with 
insulin.
	– Provide guidance for adjusting insulin dose adjustments, administration, 
storage and other practical aspects.
	
l Titration using a self‑titration regimen (dose increases of 2–4 units every 3 days 
or biweekly) or with more frequent contact with a healthcare professional. 
Titration should be done at regular and short intervals to attain glycaemic goals 
without causing hypoglycaemia. Titration should be done to control FBG first, 
followed by prandial control of meal with highest glycaemic excursion in 
sequential order.

622    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Intensify insulin therapy if patients fail to achieve glycaemic goals even after 
optimal dose titration considering following options:
	– In patients on basal insulin: Switch to premix insulin twice daily or premix 
analogues twice or thrice‑daily
	– Switch to insulin co‑formulation based regimen
	– Add prandial insulin (basal plus or basal bolus) with largest meal of the day
	– Add GLP‑1 analogues
Individualize therapy: For patients who have been diagnosed with diabetes, consider 
a combination of metformin and one of the treatment options based on patients Age, 
BMI, CKD, duration of diabetes, established CVD, financial condition, glycaemic 
status and hypoglycaemia concern.
(For details, see section Insulin Therapy.)
Tests for glucose control
	
l Self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) is done three or more times daily for 
patients using multiple insulin injections or insulin pump therapy. It is needed more 
often than usual when adding another drug or modifying therapy, whereas in patients 
using less frequent insulin injections, noninsulin therapies or medical nutrition 
therapy (MNT) alone, SMBG may be less intensive. To achieve post-prandial 
glucose targets, post-prandial SMBG may be appropriate.
	 Note: Ensure that the patient knows correct SMBG technique and assess 
understanding about adjusting therapy using SMBG data at every follow-up visit.
	
l Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in conjunction with intensive insulin regimens 
may be required to lower HBA1C in selected adults (age ≥25 years) with type 1 
diabetes with frequent nocturnal hypoglycaemia and/or hypoglycaemia unawareness.
	
l Perform the HBA1C test at least two times a year in patients who are meeting 
treatment goals (and who have stable glycaemic control) and quarterly in patients 
whose therapy has changed or who are not meeting glycaemic goals (HBA1C is 
not very reliable in patients with haemoglobinopathies like sickle cell anaemia and 
thalassaemia).
	
l The following tests should be carried out once a year: lipid profile, serum creatinine, 
urine for microalbumin, ECG and dilated fundus examination. BP should be checked 
on every visit.
Glycaemic goals 
	
l Glycaemic control is fundamental to the management of diabetes, and glycaemic goals 
are shown in Table 11.2. Lowering HBA1C has been associated with a reduction of 
microvascular complications of diabetes and possibly macrovascular disease.
	
l Monitor people with diabetes for diabetes distress regularly and especially when 
treatment targets are not met and/or at the onset of diabetes complications.

Key concepts in setting glycaemic goals:
•	 HBA1C is the primary target for glycaemic control. Individualize and reassess glycaemic 
targets over time based on duration of diabetes, age/life expectancy, comorbid conditions, 
established vascular complications, patient preferences, resources and support available, etc.
•	 Certain populations (children, pregnant women and elderly) require special considerations
•	 Less intensive glycaemic goals (<8%) should be considered in patients in whom the glycaemic 
goal is not attained despite adequate trial of effective doses of multiple glucose-lowering 
agents including insulin, diabetes education and monitoring such as in patients who develop 
level 3 hypoglycaemia and who have limited life expectancy, advanced microvascular or 
macrovascular complications, extensive comorbid conditions or long-standing diabetes.
•	 Post-prandial glucose may be targeted if HBA1C goals are not met despite reaching 
pre-prandial glucose goals.
Metabolic surgery
Metabolic surgery may be considered for treatment of type 2 diabetes if BMI ≥40 kg/m2 
and in adults with BMI 35.0–39.9 kg/m2 who do not achieve durable weight loss and 
improvement in comorbidities (including hyperglycaemia) with reasonable non-surgical 
methods.
Diabetes Management in Patients with COVID-19
The presence of diabetes and poorly managed glucose levels in people with COVID-19 
have led to higher death rates and longer hospital stays. Regular monitoring of BS can 
help avoid complications caused by high or low blood glucose. Diabetic emergencies 
like DKA and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) are life-threatening but 
preventable. These complications can be precipitated by any infectious disease 
including COVID-19. Additionally, during COVID recovery, individuals with 
uncontrolled diabetes may face a heightened risk of mucormycosis (black fungus).
	
l A patient with normal initial glycaemic profile may develop stress hyperglycaemia 
during the course of illness, especially if COVID severity increases, due to 
glucocorticoids. Table 11.3 depicts insulin dosage for steroid-induced worsening of 
BG in people with or without diabetes.
	
l Initiate or optimize OHA (at admission: pre-meal BG 150–180 mg/dL and/or 
post-meal BG 200–250 mg/dL), in consultation with an endocrinologist/physician. 
(Caution: Metformin can lead to lactic acidosis in moderately and severely ill 
patients with hypoxia or haemodynamic instability; there is a risk of hypoglycaemia

624    Standard Treatment Guidelines
with sulphonylureas if poor oral intake and on insulin therapy; SGLT2 inhibitors 
can cause dehydration and euglycaemic ketoacidosis; pioglitazone can increase the 
risk of fluid retention and oedema and is contraindicated in patients with cardiac 
and renal dysfunction).
Patients with pre-existing diabetes
	 1.	Continue existing OHA and insulin in a patient with diabetes at admission. 
	 2.	Give basal–bolus insulin regiment as above.
	 3.	Administer IV insulin infusion, in patients with moderate to severe COVID with 
uncontrolled hyperglycaemia (pre-meal >300 mg/dL, post-meal >400 mg/dL) 
despite the use of basal–bolus insulin, critical illness, DKA or HHS. 
	
	Initiate IV infusion 0.05–0.1 unit/kg/h (infusion rate [units/hour] = BG level [mg/
dL]/100) and titrate infusion rate based on BG level, magnitude of BG change in 
previous hour, time of the day, insulin sensitivity, dietary status, etc. (Caution: 
Check ketone status before starting infusion; prepare 50 units of regular insulin 
in 50 mL normal saline [1 unit/mL]; before starting infusion, prime IV tubing by 
flushing 20 mL of the prepared solution and discard the unused insulin solution 
after 24 hours.)
	
	Target BG between 140 and 220 mg/dL depending on the risk of hypoglycaemia 
and monitor CBG 2–4 hourly. Switch to basal–bolus when the patient is on a 
consistent diet and stable doses, has euglycaemia and is haemodynamically stable 
for at least 24–48 hours.
	 4.	Monitor serum potassium in patients on IV insulin every 6 hours in patients with 
NPO status and every 12 hours in those who are accepting orally. (Caution: 
Overlap insulin infusion with basal–bolus insulin regimen for 60–120 minutes 
before stopping. Do not stop insulin infusion abruptly.)

Chapter 11  Hormonal Disorders    625
PREVENTION AND MANAGEMENT 
OF DIABETES COMPLICATIONS
Cardiovascular disease
CVD is the major cause of mortality and morbidity and attributes to direct and indirect 
costs of diabetes management. Emphasize on reducing cardiovascular risk factors, 
when possible, and clinicians should be alert for signs and symptoms of atherosclerosis.
1. Hypertension/blood pressure control
Screening and diagnosis: Measure standing blood pressure also at every routine 
clinical visit to assess both autonomic function and potential volume depletion. Confirm 
BP if ≥130 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥80 mmHg on a separate day.
Goal: It is to achieve systolic blood pressure <130 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure 
<80 mmHg.

condition: Prevention and Management of Diabetes Complications
text:
l In patients without albuminuria, any of the four classes of antihypertensives such as 
an ACE inhibitor, an angiotensin-receptor blocker (ARB), a thiazide-like diuretic or 
calcium channel blockers (CCBs) may be used depending on tolerability.
	
l Two or more agents at maximal doses may be required to achieve blood pressure 
targets. Administer one or more antihypertensive medications at bedtime.
	
l Monitor serum creatinine/estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and serum 
potassium levels if the patient is on ACEI or ARB or diuretics. (For details, see 
Hypertension section in Chapter 3.)
2. Dyslipidaemia/lipid management
Screening: Screen for lipid disorders at least annually and more often if needed. 
Assess patients with low-risk lipid values (LDL <100 mg/dL, HDL >50 mg/dL and 
triglycerides <150 mg/dL) every 2 years.
Treatment and goals
	
l Advise lifestyle modifications focusing on the reduction of saturated fat, trans-fat 
and cholesterol intake; weight loss (if indicated); and increased physical activity. 
	
l In individuals without overt CVD: The primary goal is an LDL <100 mg/dL 
(2.6 mmol/L). For those older than 40 years and those younger than 40 years but 
with other risk cardiovascular factors who do not achieve lipid goals with lifestyle 
modifications alone, statin therapy to achieve an LDL reduction of 30–40% 
regardless of baseline LDL levels is recommended.
	
l In individuals with overt CVD: All patients should be treated with a statin to achieve 
an LDL reduction of 30–40%. Lower triglycerides to <150 mg/dL (1.7 mmol/L) and 
raise HDL cholesterol to >40 mg/dL (1.0 mmol/L). In women, an HDL goal 10 mg/
dL higher (>50 mg/dL) should be considered.
	
l Statin therapy is contraindicated in pregnancy.

condition: Prevention and Management of Diabetes Complications
text:
626    Standard Treatment Guidelines
3. Antiplatelet agents
	
l In patients with a history of CVD, give Tab. Aspirin 75–162 mg/day to patients with 
diabetes with a history of CVD as a secondary prevention strategy Or Clopidogrel 
75 mg/day if aspirin is not tolerated. Dual antiplatelet therapy with both Aspirin and 
Clopidogrel for up to a year after an acute coronary syndrome can be used.
	
l In patients with type 1 and 2 diabetes at an increased cardiovascular risk, including 
those who are older than 50 years or women aged 60 years who have at least one 
additional risk factor (family history of CVD, hypertension, smoking, dyslipidaemia 
or albuminuria), give Tab. Aspirin 75–162 mg/day as a primary prevention strategy.
4. Smoking cessation
	
l Advise on quitting smoking at every visit.
	
l Include smoking cessation counselling and other forms of treatment as a routine 
component of diabetes care.
5. Coronary heart disease (CHD) screening and treatment
	
l In patients older than 55 years, with or without hypertension but with another 
cardiovascular risk factor (history of CVD, dyslipidaemia, microalbuminuria or 
smoking), consider an ACE inhibitor (if not contraindicated) to reduce the risk of 
cardiovascular events. 
	
l In patients with a prior myocardial infarction or in patients undergoing a 
major surgery, continue β-blockers for at least 2 years after the event. Avoid 
thiazolidinedione in patients with symptomatic heart failure. Avoid metformin in 
unstable or hospitalized patients with heart failure.
	
l In asymptomatic patients, routine screening for CAD is not recommended; treat 
risk factors.
6. Nephropathy screening and treatment
	
l Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and 
end-stage renal disease (ESRD) requiring renal replacement therapy. For details, 
see Chapter 10.
	
l Goal is to reduce the risk and/or slow the progression of nephropathy, and optimize 
glucose and blood pressure control.
Screening
	
l Perform an annual test for the presence of microalbuminuria in patients with type 1 
diabetes with diabetes duration of ≥5 years and in all patients with type 2 diabetes, 
starting at diagnosis and during pregnancy. Albuminuria is defined as a persistently 
increased urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio >30 mg/g in spot urine.
	
l Measure serum creatinine at least annually for the estimation of glomerular filtration 
rate (GFR) in all adults with diabetes regardless of the degree of urine albumin 
excretion. The serum creatinine alone should not be used as a measure of kidney 
function but instead should be used to estimate GFR and stage the level of CKD.

condition: Prevention and Management of Diabetes Complications
text:
Chapter 11  Hormonal Disorders    627
Treatment goal
	
l Start either ACEI or ARB in patients with modestly elevated (30–299 mg/24 hours, 
previously microalbuminuria) or higher levels (>300 mg/24 hours, previously 
macroalbuminuria) of urinary albumin excretion. (Caution: Monitor serum 
creatinine and potassium levels; ACEI or ARB is not recommended for primary 
prevention and in pregnant patients.) (For details, see Chapter 10.)
	
l SGLT2 inhibitors (Canagliflozin, Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin) provide both 
kidney and cardiovascular protection, and are safe in CKD irrespective of type 
2 diabetes. Continue with SGLT2 inhibitors, even if eGFR drops below 20 mL/
min/1.73 m², unless intolerance or initiation of kidney replacement therapy occurs. 
Evidence on SGLT2 inhibitors in kidney transplant recipients is limited.
	
l Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (such as Liraglutide [once daily] 
or Semaglutide [1 weekly subcutaneously, daily orally], Dulaglutide [once weekly], 
Albiglutide [once weekly], Exenatide [twice daily]) improve glycaemic control and 
reduce the progression of diabetic kidney disease.
	
l Individualize HBAIC target ranging from <6.5% to <8.0% in patients with diabetes 
and CKD not treated with dialysis.
	
l Non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor (nsMRA) antagonists (Spironolactone/
Eplerenone) may be used for cardiorenal protection in patients with an eGFR equal 
to or exceeding 25 mL/min/1.73 m2, maintaining normal serum potassium levels, 
and exhibiting albuminuria (30 mg/g or more [3 mg/mmol]), despite being on the 
maximum tolerated dose of an ACEI.
7. Retinopathy screening and treatment
Diabetic retinopathy (the most frequent cause of new cases of blindness in adults) 
is a highly specific vascular complication of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes and its 
prevalence is strongly related to the duration of diabetes. Also evaluate for glaucoma, 
cataracts and other disorders of the eye as they may occur earlier in people with 
diabetes. Optimal glycaemic and blood pressure control can substantially reduce the 
risk and progression of diabetic retinopathy. 
Screening
	
l An initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination is done by an ophthalmologist 
within 5 years in adults with type 1 diabetes and shortly after the onset of diabetes 
in those with type 2 diabetes. Examine every 2 years if there is no evidence of 
retinopathy for one or more eye examinations. If diabetic retinopathy is present, 
perform annual subsequent examinations for patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. 
If retinopathy is progressing or sight threatening, then examinations are required 
more frequently.
	
l In women with pre-existing diabetes planning pregnancy or who have become 
pregnant, conduct eye examination in the first trimester with close follow-up 
throughout and for 1 year postpartum.

condition: Prevention and Management of Diabetes Complications
text:
l Promptly refer patients with any level of macular oedema, severe non-proliferative 
diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) or any proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) to an 
ophthalmologist. For details, see Chapter 13.
	
l Laser therapy can reduce the risk of vision loss in patients with high-risk 
characteristics (HRCs).
Intensive diabetes management with the goal of achieving near normoglycaemia 
prevents and/or delays the onset of diabetic retinopathy. The presence of nephropathy 
is associated with retinopathy. High blood pressure is an established risk factor for the 
development of macular oedema and is associated with the presence of PDR. During 
pregnancy and 1 year postpartum, retinopathy may be transiently aggravated; laser 
photocoagulation surgery can minimize this risk.
8. Neuropathy screening and treatment 
Screening
	
l Screen all patients clinically for distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DPN) at diagnosis 
and at least annually thereafter. Note: Electrophysiological testing is rarely needed, 
except in situations in which the clinical features are atypical.
	
l Provide special foot care for insensate feet to decrease the risk of amputation.
	
l Perform simple inspection of insensate feet at 3- to 6-month intervals for either 
temperature or pinprick sensation (small-fibre function) and vibration sensation using 
a 128-Hz tuning fork (for large-fibre function). All patients should have annual 10-g 
monofilament testing to identify feet at risk for ulceration and amputation. Refer for 
special footwear, preventive specialist or podiatric care in case of an abnormality.
	
l Institute screening for autonomic neuropathy at the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes and 
5 years after the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes. (Note: Special electrophysiological 
testing for autonomic neuropathy is rarely needed and may not affect the 
management and outcomes.)
Foot care: Amputation and foot ulceration are the common consequences of diabetic 
neuropathy and major causes of morbidity and disability in people with diabetes. The 
presence of erythema, warmth or callus formation may indicate areas of tissue damage 
with impending breakdown. 
	
l Examine the patient’s feet at every encounter and annual comprehensive foot 
examination. Foot examination should include inspection of the skin, assessment 
of foot deformities, assessment of pulses in the legs and feet, and testing for loss of 
protective sensation (monofilament with at least one other assessment for pinprick, 
temperature, vibration). Assess for bony deformities, limitation in joint mobility and 
problems with gait and balance.
	
l Refer appropriately at the first sign of foot ulcer, patients with high-risk feet (patients 
on dialysis and those with Charcot foot or prior ulcers or amputation) and patients 
with symptoms of claudication or decreased or absent pedal pulses for ankle-brachial 
index for further vascular assessment as appropriate.

condition: Prevention and Management of Diabetes Complications
text:
Chapter 11  Hormonal Disorders    629
	
l Refer patients who smoke or who have a history of prior lower-extremity complications, 
loss of protective sensation, structural abnormalities or peripheral arterial disease to foot 
care specialists for ongoing preventive care and lifelong surveillance.
	
l Provide general preventive foot self-care education to all patients with diabetes.
	
l Advise patients with neuropathy or evidence of increased plantar pressures 
(erythema, warmth or calluses) to wear well-fitted walking shoes or athletic shoes 
that cushion the feet and redistribute pressure. 
	
l Advise use of extra wide or deep shoes or custom-moulded shoes in people with 
bony deformities such as prominent metatarsal heads, bunions and hammer toes. 
	
l Advise use of custom therapeutic footwear to reduce the risk of future foot ulcers 
in high-risk patients. Dressings (such as hydrocolloid) promote wound healing, 
controlling the exudate and protecting the wound.
Diabetic foot infections (DFIs)
DFIs are common and potentially serious complications of diabetes, particularly in 
individuals with poorly controlled blood sugar levels. These infections typically occur 
due to a combination of factors such as peripheral neuropathy, reduced blood flow to the 
feet (peripheral arterial disease) and impaired immune function. Minor injuries, cuts, or 
wounds on the feet can easily become infected and lead to more severe complications 
if left untreated.
	
l Prompt diagnosis and appropriate management of diabetic foot infections are crucial 
to prevent further tissue damage, ulceration and even amputation.
	
l Treatment may involve wound care, antibiotics to control infection and measures to 
improve blood sugar control and promote wound healing.
	
l Preventive measures such as regular foot inspections, proper foot hygiene and 
wearing appropriate footwear are essential to reduce the risk of DFIs.
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy
Elicit the symptoms of autonomic dysfunction carefully during the history and review 
of systems, particularly since many of these symptoms are potentially treatable. Major 
clinical manifestations include resting tachycardia, exercise intolerance, orthostatic 
hypotension, constipation, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, sudomotor dysfunction, 
impaired neurovascular function, ‘brittle diabetes’ and hypoglycaemic autonomic failure.
In patients with painful symptoms, give Tab. Gabapentin 300–1200 mg 3 times 
daily Or Carbamazepine 200–400 mg 3 times daily Or Pregabalin 100 mg 3 times 
daily Or Duloxetine 60–120 mg daily Or Tab. Imipramine 25–75 mg at bedtime Or 
Amitriptyline 10–75 mg at bedtime Or Nortriptyline 25–75 mg at bedtime Or Capsaicin 
cream 0.025–0.075% applied 3–4 times daily. Dose response may vary. Start with a 
lower dose and titrate upwards as required.
Patient education
	
l Explain the nature of the disease and potential complications arising due to poorly 
controlled diabetes.

630    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Stress upon the importance of lifestyle modifications and maintenance of normal 
weight, adhering to regular dietary schedule including counselling regarding the 
‘better’ food choices and diet portion control. Prolonged sitting should be interrupted 
every 30 minutes with short bouts of physical activity. Avoid fasting and feasting.
	
l Lifestyle modifications (regular exercise, quitting smoking and limiting alcohol 
intake) may have other beneficial effects (reduced cardiovascular complications). 
Provide counselling on smoking cessation and refer to Tobacco Cessation Clinic, 
if required.
	
l Advise the patient to always carry identification card carrying diagnosis, medication 
and contact numbers in emergency along with hypoglycaemia kit.
	
l Educate patients to match insulin and meal timing. Explain about the warning 
symptoms and signs of hypoglycaemia and need to take sweets/candies/drinks in 
such a situation. 
	
l Perform regular follow-up to monitor BP (quarterly), HBA1C testing (2–4 times/
year), eye examination (annual), foot examination (1–2 times/year by physician; daily 
by the patient), screening for diabetic nephropathy (annual) and lipid profile (annual). 
	
l Explain about sick day management.
	
l In patients with long-standing diabetes, give instructions for care of feet, choice of 
footwear and avoiding walking barefoot. Consider therapeutic footwear for patients 
at high risk for foot problems.
(See also Diabetes Mellitus in Chapters 15 and 19 and Diabetic Retinopathy in 
Chapter 13.)
DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS
Ketoacidosis is an acute complication of diabetes, usually occurring in type 1 
diabetes, but can also occur in type 2 diabetes, characterized by hyperglycaemia, 
hyperketonaemia and acidosis. Important precipitating factors include poor compliance 
to treatment/sudden stoppage of insulin, suboptimal insulin dose pre- or postoperatively 
and infections/stress.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occur nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, rapid deep breathing 
(Kussmaul’s sign) and altered sensorium. Sometimes the patient may present with 
a sudden onset of extremely high blood glucose (BG) levels (>700 mg/dL) and 
HbA1C of 12 or 14 with ketosis.
	
l Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstration of ketones in urine (or elevated levels 
in blood), hyperglycaemia (>250 mg/dL), low arterial pH, low bicarbonate 
(<15 mmol/L) and high anion gap (>16 mmol/L), high haematocrit and MCV, 
high triglycerides, hyperkalaemia and low phosphate.

Chapter 11  Hormonal Disorders    631
Treatment (admit in critical care unit)
Treatment includes confirmation of diagnosis and continuous monitoring of the 
response to treatment as follows:
	
l Suspect and confirm diagnosis; assess fluid loss and degree of acidosis. 
	
l Suspect and get complete blood counts, glucose, renal functions, electrolytes and 
arterial blood gases. 
	
l Evaluate and treat precipitating factor(s) – infection, insulin omission and other 
problems that may have precipitated ketoacidosis.
First hour
	 1.	If blood pressure is normal, replace fluids: 2–3 L of 0.9% saline or lactated 
Ringer’s solution over the first 1–3 hours (10–20 mL/kg/h).
	 2.	If shock and oligaemia persist, perform rapid infusion of normal saline until blood 
pressure rises to normal and subsequently continue with infusion, saline at the rate 
of 1 L/h.
	 3.	Give Inj. insulin (regular) 5–10 units/h IV infusion or Inj. insulin (regular) 20 units IM 
immediately followed by 5 units/h, 1–2 hours after starting fluid replacement therapy.
	 4.	Inj. Potassium chloride (KCl) 10–20 mmol (maximum 40 mmol) in each litre of 
IV fluid (maximum recommended rate is 0.5 mmol/kg/h) if serum K+ is not more 
than 5 mmol/L and urine output is adequate. If serum potassium is <3.3, correct 
potassium levels first to 3.3 and then start insulin. (For details, see Hypokalaemia 
in Chapters 2 and 19.)
	
		
Phosphate is not given routinely. If serum phosphate levels are <1.0 mg/dL, 
give 20–30 mEq/L of potassium phosphate added to IV fluids.
	 5.	Bicarbonate administration is not recommended except for treatment of life‑threatening 
hyperkalaemia. Inj. Sodium bicarbonate 50–100 mmol infused over 30–60 minutes.
	 6.	If infection/sepsis is suspected, start Inj. Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV 12 hourly after 
obtaining appropriate cultures of body fluids and treat the source of infection.
Second hour
	
l Continue IV normal saline 500 mL/h (use 0.45% saline if serum sodium 
>150 mmol/L). 
	
l Continue insulin infusion as above (if BG >250 mg/dL). 
	
l Continue IV infusion of KCl (rate of infusion adjusted according to serum level).
Third and fourth hours
	
l Continue as for second hour. Subsequently, give 0.45% saline at 250–500 mL/h.
	
l Observe for cognitive/neurological functions.
Fifth to eighth hours
	
l Normal saline infusion 250 mL/h (change to dextrose saline if BG <250 mg/dL)
	
l Neutralizing insulin (1 unit per 2 g of glucose infused) infusion to continue until 
ketonuria disappears

632    Standard Treatment Guidelines
After eight hours
	
l Continue IV fluids and insulin. 
	
l Change to subcutaneous insulin when ketones disappear, blood glucose is 200 mg, 
serum HCO3 >15 mEq/L, venous pH >7.3 and anion gap <12 mEq/L. Give dose 
0.5–0.8 unit/kg/day with half dose as basal insulin and half as bolus (short acting).
	
l Stop KCl infusion when plasma potassium levels are normal. 
	
l Change antibiotic if culture sensitivity report demands.
Patient education
	
l Explain about the importance of regular intake of insulin and diet as per requirement.
	
l To explain to the patient to be vigilant about recognizing any signs and symptoms of 
infection early on (such as symptoms like redness, warmth, swelling, or tenderness 
around any wounds or sores, any unusual discharge or odour; fever, chills, increased 
pain, or changes in skin colour or texture can also be indicators of an infection). 
If any symptoms occur, they should consult the physician promptly for timely 
treatment and optimal recovery.
NON-KETOTIC HYPEROSMOLAR COMA
It is characterized by profound dehydration due to sustained hyperglycaemic 
dehydration and hyperosmolarity, usually seen in elderly patients with type 2 diabetes, 
associated with stroke or sepsis.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Severe dehydration, altered sensorium and marked hyperglycaemia. There may 
be features of venous thrombosis due to hyperviscosity.
	
l Other features include focal neurological deficit and sepsis.
	
l The condition is diagnosed by finding very high blood glucose (BG >500–1000 
mg/dL), high plasma osmolality, acidosis and azotaemia, absence of ketosis or 
mild ketonaemia.
	
l Features like nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and Kussmaul’s respiration are 
characteristically absent.

1.	Normal saline or half-normal saline (0.45%) 2–3 L rapidly infused over 
2–3 hours (administration of 0.45% normal saline is indicated if serum sodium is 
>150 mEq/L)
	 2.	Inj. Insulin (regular) 5 units/h as IV infusion
	 3.	Potassium chloride and sodium bicarbonate infusion as per requirement and 
administered as in ketoacidosis
	 4.	Diagnosis and treatment of precipitating cause and prevention of recurrence 
(mortality is very high)

Chapter 11  Hormonal Disorders    633
HYPOGLYCAEMIA
Hypoglycaemia occurs due to increased utilization of glucose by the body (as during 
fasting or exercise or in alcoholics) or overdose of hypoglycaemic drug(s).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Symptoms may be due to sympathetic stimulation (like anxiety, profuse sweating, 
palpitation, tremors), neuroglycopenia (light-headedness, confusion/altered 
sensorium, convulsions, coma, focal neurological deficits) or general (weakness, 
hunger or blurred vision). Sometimes the patients may be asymptomatic, e.g. 
elderly patients with long-standing diabetes with autonomic neuropathy and 
cardiovascular diseases. Prolonged hypoglycaemia may result in permanent 
neurological deficits.
	
l Level 1 hypoglycaemia is characterized by blood glucose (BG) <70 mg/dL; 
level 2 hypoglycaemia (BG <54 mg/dL) is the threshold at which neuroglycopenic 
symptoms begin to occur and requires immediate action to resolve the 
hypoglycaemic event. Level 3 hypoglycaemia is a severe event characterized by 
altered mental and/or physical functioning that requires assistance from another 
person for recovery.

Immediate 
	 1.	If the patient presents with early signs and is conscious, follow the 15–15 rule – 
15 g of quick-acting oral glucose or carbohydrates (sweets/biscuits//honey/juice/
regular [not diet] soda) to raise BS and check it after 15 minutes. If it is still below 
70 mg/dL, repeat another serving. Once self-monitored BG returns to normal, 
for prevention of recurrence, ask the patient to consume a meal or snack. When 
treating hypoglycaemia, carbohydrate source choice is important. Avoid complex 
carbohydrates, or foods that contain fats and carbohydrates (chocolate), as they can 
slow the absorption of glucose. Also avoid overtreatment.
	 2.	If there is level 2 and 3 hypoglycaemia, and the patient with diabetes on treatment 
is unconscious and glucometer is not available, Inj. Glucose (25–50%) 50–100 mL 
infused rapidly IV.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Glucagon 1 mg IM or SC. If the patient is receiving long-acting insulin/
OHAs, continue IV infusion of 5% glucose with regular monitoring of blood 
glucose hourly. It is contraindicated in hypoglycaemia caused by sulphonylureas 
as glucagon stimulates insulin secretion.
Note: In case of doubt between hypoglycaemia and DKA, always choose to give 25% 
Dextrose because hypoglycaemia can be life-threatening, whereas slight rise in glucose 
in DKA will not alter the prognosis of the patient.

634    Standard Treatment Guidelines
On recovery, identify the cause and re-educate the patient to avoid future episodes. 
	
l Modify treatment in the event of hypoglycaemia occurring repeatedly at a particular 
time of the day or in the event of hypoglycaemia unawareness.
	
l Hypoglycaemia occurring in the setting of advanced kidney disease (CKD stage 4 
or 5) requires relatively longer observation for avoidance of recurrence even long 
after initial corrective measure are taken.
Note: Slow recovery from coma may be due to cerebral oedema, but may respond to 
IV Mannitol and forced ventilation with high inspired oxygen concentration.
Prevention of hypoglycaemia
Ask about symptomatic and asymptomatic hypoglycaemia at each encounter especially 
those at risk of hypoglycaemia:
	
l Identify high-risk patients – patients experiencing level 2 or level 3 hypoglycaemia 
event within the past 1 year, patients on insulin and/or insulin secretagogues, patients 
having other comorbidities and patients having HBA1C <7% documented within 
the past 6 months.
	
l Educate patients older than 65 years and their caregivers.
	
l Ask patients to report hypoglycaemic events and note reason for hypoglycaemia. 
Some common reasons are overdose of insulin or diabetes pills, skipping meals or 
not eating enough, delayed meals, exercising without eating and drinking alcohol.
	
l Re-evaluate treatment regimen in case of hypoglycaemia unawareness or one or 
more episodes of severe hypoglycaemia.
Patient education
	
l Explain about the symptoms of hypoglycaemia to the patient, caregiver and school 
personnel.
	
l Advise patients to keep an identification band with them at all times, including 
emergency contact numbers. Stress upon regular intake of meals along with 
hypoglycaemic agents and advise the patients to keep hypo kit with them all the time 
including in school, office and at home, to recognize signs of hypoglycaemia early 
and take sugar or any other sugar/glucose-containing snacks/drinks at the earliest.

	 5.	 Diabetes mellitus: complications. In: Loscalzo J, Kasper DL, Longo DL, et al. (eds), Harrison’s 
Principles of Internal Medicine. 21st ed. New York: McGraw Hill Company Inc.; 2022, 
pp. 3120–3128.
	 6.	 Chawla R, Madhu SV, Makkar BM, et al. RSSDI-ESI Clinical Practice Recommendations 
for the Management of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus 2020. https://rssdi.in/newwebsite/pdfdata/
Chawla2020_Article_RSSDI-ESIClinicalPracticeRecom.pdf [accessed March 15, 2024].
	 7.	 Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India. Clinical Guidance on Diagnosis and 
Management of Diabetes at COVID-19 Patient Management facility, Version 2.0. June 1, 2021.
	 8.	 Cardiovascular disease and risk management: standards of care in diabetes – 2024 Diabetes Care. 
2024;47(Suppl. 1):S179–S218.
ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY (AI) AND ADRENAL CRISIS
It is caused due to deficient production of glucocorticoids and/or mineralocorticoids 
and their resultant effect on the body. It can be due to defect in adrenals (primary AI 
due to Addison's disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia [CAH], congenital adrenal 
hypoplasia, adrenoleukodystrophy, adrenal haemorrhage in newborns or in fulminate 
infections [Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome]) or pituitary defect (secondary AI 
due to hypopituitarism, cessation of glucocorticoid therapy, pituitary–hypothalamic 
pathology including cranial irradiation).
AI may be permanent (Addison’s Disease, CAH) – discovered in childhood or 
because of complete surgical removal of the pituitary gland or surgical removal of the 
adrenals. Temporary AI is caused by some medications, infections and/or surgeries.
An adrenal crisis is a physiological event caused by an acute relative insufficiency 
of adrenal hormones. It may be precipitated by physiological stress in a susceptible 
patient. It should be considered in patients who have a history of known primary AI, 
hypopituitarism, or previously or currently being on prolonged steroid therapy. Adrenal 
crisis may also be the first presentation of an underlying disease or there may be a 
history suggestive of chronic hypoadrenalism.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Acute crisis: Fever, vomiting, dehydration, weakness, pain abdomen, altered 
sensorium, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, acidosis, hypotensive 
shock.
	
l Chronic insufficiency: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, unusual weakness, fatigue, 
hypotension, loss of weight, hypoglycaemia, hyperpigmentation, postural 
dizziness, hyponatraemia. 
	
l The optimal diagnostic test is the corticotropin stimulation test (250 mcg for 
adults and children older than or aged 2 years, 15 mcg/kg for infants and 125 
mcg for children younger than 2 years) IV; peak cortisol levels below 500 nmol/L 
(18 mcg/dL) (assay dependent) at 30 or 60 minutes indicate adrenal insufficiency. 
	
l A serum 8 a.m. cortisol level (or at the time of presentation in acute crisis): 
A value of >20 mcg/dL virtually excludes the diagnosis. A value of <3 mcg/dL is 
highly suggestive of hypoadrenalism. 
	
l Values from 3 to 18 mcg/dL are indeterminate and require an adrenocorticotropic 
hormone (ACTH) stimulation test for confirmation.

Acute crisis 
	 1.	Look for and treat the precipitating cause of illness. Exclude sepsis. In all cases of 
possible AI/crisis, ask for immediate blood glucose using a bedside glucometer, 
serum glucose, urea, sodium and potassium, and arterial or capillary acid–base.
	 2.	Maintain adequate intravascular volume guided by blood pressure: Sodium chloride 
0.9%, IV infusion 2–3 L should be infused initially depending on the volume status 
of the patient.
	 3.	Inj. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately prior to the availability of the results 
of diagnostic tests; then follow with 6 hourly (dose as per age). Change to oral 
maintenance therapy once the patient is stable as per the dose mentioned in chronic 
management.
	 4.	Monitor glucose levels closely and treat hypoglycaemia if present.
Chronic adrenal insufficiency (maintenance therapy)
	 1.	Tab. Hydrocortisone replacement dose (usually 30 mg/day) in the amount and at the 
times as prescribed. See sick day rules and prevention of adrenal crisis as below.
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Prednisone 5 mg daily; increase up to a maximum of 7.5 mg/day, if necessary.
	 2.	For patients who have primary AI and remain clinically symptomatic or 
hypotensive, Tab. Fludrocortisone 50–100 mcg daily.
	
		
Monitor response to therapy with symptoms, blood pressure and electrolytes. 
Prevention of adrenal crisis in a susceptible patient
	
l Patients on corticosteroids should wear an identification bracelet or card carrying the 
words ‘Adrenal insufficiency: In emergency give hydrocortisone at 2 mg/kg IM/IV’.
	
l The stress dose of hydrocortisone parenterally as above should also be given prior 
to surgery and in the initial day(s) post-surgery or general anaesthesia, following 
trauma (e.g. fracture/laceration requiring sutures), requiring intensive care in a 
patient with known AI. For elective procedures, the initial dose can be given at 
induction, with 6-hourly dosing continuing thereafter. Switch to oral steroids once 
the patient is stable and tolerating oral intake post-operatively.
	
l Give written instructions for sick days (“sick day rules”): During illness (flu, fever, 
etc.), increase the usual oral dose of steroids to double or triple for 1–3 days. Consult 
the doctor if the patient feels sick for more than 3 days.
	
l In case of vomiting or diarrhoea in a patient susceptible to adrenal crisis, consider 
to have incipient adrenal crisis, even if he/she is otherwise well as oral medicines 
are not reliably absorbed in this scenario. Observe these patients for ~4–6 hours in 
the Emergency Department.
Treatment during pregnancy
	
l Monitor pregnant patients with AI for clinical symptoms and signs of glucocorticoid 
over- and under-replacement (e.g. normal weight gain, fatigue, postural hypotension 
or hypertension, hyperglycaemia), with at least one review per trimester.

Chapter 11  Hormonal Disorders    637
	
l Adjust dose based on the individual clinical course; increase hydrocortisone dose, in 
particular during the third trimester. Hydrocortisone is preferred to cortisone acetate, 
prednisolone or prednisone. (Caution: Do not administer Dexamethasone.)
	
l Hydrocortisone stress dosing during the active phase of labour is similar to that used 
in major surgical stress.
Patient education
	
l All patients should wear a medic alert bracelet or carry a card mentioning disease 
and contact number in case of emergency. Also equip the patient with hydrocortisone 
injection kit to avert or treat adrenal crisis. 
	
l Explain sick day management and during times of severe ‘stress’, i.e. acute illness, 
surgery, trauma, etc. Start Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV and attend medical facility 
urgently. In case of minor stress, maintenance steroid dose should be doubled for 
the duration of illness and gradually tapered to the usual dose.
References
	 1.	 Disorders of the adrenal cortex. In: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine. Loscalzo J, 
Kasper DL, Longo DL, Fauci AS, Hauser SL, Jameson JL (eds), 21st ed. New York: McGraw 
Hill Company Inc., 2022, pp. 2955–2976.
	 2.	 Diagnosis and treatment of primary adrenal insufficiency: an Endocrine Society clinical practice 
guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2016;101(2):364–389.
CUSHING’S SYNDROME
Iatrogenic cause is the most common due to chronic glucocorticoid use. Endogenous 
causes are Cushing’s syndrome (CS) in pituitary tumour, adrenal tumour, nodular 
hyperplasia and ectopic ACTH producing tumour-like bronchial carcinoids. CS is 
a long-lasting condition that can be life-threatening because of its complications, 
including diabetes, hypertension and depression.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Clinical features include central obesity, diabetes, hypertension, hirsutism, 
depression, fragility of the skin, easy bruisability, purplish striae, proximal 
myopathy and hyperpigmentation.
	
l Investigations: Perform one of the four tests for initial screening of CS:
	(i)	 24-Hour urinary free cortisol (UFC) excretion increased above normal (3×) 
on two occasions
	(ii)	 Overnight Dexamethasone suppression (ODS) test (plasma cortisol 
>1.8 mcg/dL at 8–9 a.m. after 1 mg Dexamethasone at 11 p.m.)
	(iii)	 Midnight salivary cortisol >2 mcg/dL
	(iv)	 Longer low-dose Dexamethasone suppression test for 48 hours
	
l Plasma ACTH >15 pg/mL is referred to as ACTH-dependent CS; ACTH 
<5 pg/mL is referred to as ACTH-independent CS.

638    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Confirmation and localization of CS requires additional biochemical and 
radiological tests. Imaging includes CT/MRI of the pituitary or adrenals with or 
without different radio-nuclear imaging techniques.

1.	Treatment depends on the aetiology. Treatment goal is to normalize cortisol 
levels to eliminate the signs and symptoms of established CS and treat co-
morbidities (psychiatric disorders, diabetes, hypertension, hypokalaemia, 
infections, dyslipidaemia, osteoporosis and poor physical fitness) associated with 
hypercortisolism.
	 2.	Refer the patient to a specialist. Tab. Ketoconazole (400–1200 mg) can be used 
to reduce hypercortisolaemia rapidly till definite management is planned Or Tab. 
Mitotane 500–1000 mg/day in cases where surgery or other treatments have not 
been effective or are not feasible.
	 3.	For drug-induced CS, gradual tapering of equivalent doses of steroids is done till 
physiological resumption of the hypothalamo-pituitary axis (HPA).
	 4.	Refer CS due to pituitary secreting adenoma, due to ectopic ACTH-secreting 
adenoma or due to adrenal carcinoma to a higher centre.
Surgical: Initial resection of the primary lesion(s) underlying the syndrome is the 
curative treatment. In Cushing’s disease, the treatment of choice is selective removal of 
the pituitary corticotroph tumour, usually via an endoscopic trans-sphenoidal approach. 
In patients in whom surgery was not curative or who cannot undergo surgery, second-
line options include repeat trans-sphenoidal surgery, radiotherapy, medical therapy and 
bilateral adrenalectomy.
Adrenalectomy is performed in case of adrenal carcinoma or adenoma. After 
surgical remission, patients with hypocortisolaemia should receive glucocorticoid 
replacement and education about AI (see the section ‘Adrenal Insufficiency’).
Patient education
	
l Explain the course of illness and cause of the disease.
	
l Features of CS improve over a period of 2–12 months after treatment. However, 
annual lifelong testing for recurrence and education of patients and families about 
the clinical features of recurrence are required.
	
l Monitor blood pressure, glycaemic status, dyslipidaemia, ophthalmological 
examination and bone health.
References
	 1.	 Treatment of Cushing's syndrome: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline. J Clin 
Endocrinol Metab. 2015;100(8):2807–2831.
	 2.	 Disorder of the adrenal cortex. In: Loscalzo J, Kasper DL, Longo DL, et al. (eds), Harrison’s 
Principles of Internal Medicine. 21st ed. New York: McGraw Hill Company Inc.; 2022, pp. 
2955–2976.

Chapter 11  Hormonal Disorders    639
ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION
It refers to the inability to attain and maintain an erect penis with sufficient rigidity 
for vaginal penetration. Organic causes include neurogenic, vasculogenic or 
endocrinological causes as well as many systemic diseases and certain drugs.
Psychogenic factors are very important. Other important aetiological factors are DM, 
atherosclerosis and many drugs, especially antihypertensives. Besides a complete history, 
examination and routine investigations like complete blood count, plasma glucose and 
lipid profile, special investigations like serum prolactin, serum testosterone and plasma 
gonadotrophins, and at times vascular testing or psychological tests may be helpful.

1.	Consider the removal of drugs that may be associated with the problem. 
	 2.	A change in lifestyle or drugs may resolve the problem.
	 3.	Treat the underlying condition.
	 4.	Refer to a higher centre in case an organic disease or a medical condition is 
suspected as a cause, e.g. Peyronie’s disease. Refer to a urologist or an appropriate 
specialist if surgical intervention is needed, e.g. penile prostheses, vascular surgery 
and pelvic fractures.

Tab. Sildenafil 25–100 mg; the onset of action is within 60–90 minutes. 
Or
Tab. Tadalafil 5–10 mg; the onset of action is within 30 minutes.
Give lower initial doses in the elderly, patients with renal insufficiency or patients 
on drugs like Erythromycin, Cimetidine and Ketoconazole which may increase the 
serum concentration. (Caution: It is contraindicated with concomitant nitrate therapy, 
congestive heart failure and cardiomyopathy; cautiously use in CAD, borderline 
hypotension, hypovolaemia and patients on complex antihypertensive treatment.)
Or
Inj. Testosterone enanthate 100–200 mg IM every 1–2 weeks in low testosterone states.
Or
Intraurethral alprostadil (prostaglandin E1) semisolid pellets of 125–1000 mcg.
Or
Intracavernosal alprostadil self-injection 1–40 mcg.
Patient education
	
l Counsel and educate both partners about the causes, treatments and lifestyle changes 
related to erectile dysfunction (ED). This approach aims to reduce anxiety, stress 
and relationship concerns, promoting effective communication, mutual support 
and shared decision-making. Encourage partners to express their feelings and

640    Standard Treatment Guidelines
expectations in a supportive environment, and explore strategies together to enhance 
intimacy and maintain a healthy relationship.
	
l Explain the side effects of sildenafil and other drugs. Sildenafil can cause headache, 
facial flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion and transient altered colour vision.
References
	 1.	 Sexual dysfunction. In: Loscalzo J, Kasper DL, Longo DL, et al. (eds), Harrison’s Principles of 
Internal Medicine. 21st ed. New York: McGraw Hill Company Inc.; 2022, pp. 3055–3063.
	 2.	 Sexual dysfunction in men and women. In: Reed Larsen P, Kronenberg HM, Melmed S, Polonsky 
KS (eds), William’s Textbook of Endocrinology. 14th ed. WB Saunders; 2020, pp. 768–769.

ENT Diseases
ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA (AOM)
AOM is caused by inflammation of the mucous membrane lining the middle ear cleft 
(consisting of the Eustachian tube, tympanic cavity, mastoid antrum and mastoid 
air cells) produced by pus-forming organisms. It is common in children because of 
recurrent upper respiratory infection (URI) leading to ascending infection through the 
Eustachian tube.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Severe throbbing pain in the ear (rubbing, tugging or holding the ear may be 
a sign of pain), and excessive crying in children, fever, irritability, otorrhoea, 
anorexia, vomiting or lethargy, difficulty in hearing and rarely giddiness are 
present.
	
l It is often bilateral in children, preceded by upper respiratory tract infection.
	
l Congestion and bulging of the eardrum occurs leading to perforation and 
discharge. 
	
l Diagnosis of acute otitis media (AOM) is clinical in children who present with 
bulging of the tympanic membrane (TM) or new onset of otorrhoea not due to 
acute otitis externa and/or recent (less than 48 hours) onset of ear pain (holding, 
tugging, rubbing of the ear in a nonverbal child) or intense erythema of the TM. 
Diagnosis should not be made in children without middle ear effusion (MEE). 
Otoscopy should be used for the assessment of the TM. Pneumatic otoscopy is 
up to 94% sensitive and 90% specific for identifying MEE.

l Advise steam inhalation and to keep the ear clean in case of pus discharge. 
	
l Prevention: Encourage exclusive breastfeeding for at least 6 months. 
	
l Encourage avoidance of tobacco smoke exposure.
	
l Decongestants and antihistamines have an unproven role in symptom relief.

1.	For fever and pain, give Tab. Paracetamol 500 mg (in children 15 mg/kg/dose) as 
and when required (for details, see section on fever in Chapter 1).
	 2.	The decision to start with an antibiotic depends on the presence of risk factors, 
age of the child and severity of illness. For children aged 2 years with confirmed 
AOM, immediate antibiotic treatment is recommended in cases of severe disease 
(i.e. temperature >39°C [102.2°F] in the past 48 hours, significant otalgia or toxic 
appearance).
	
	In case the patient is not allergic to Penicillin, give Cap. Amoxycillin 80–90 mg/
kg/day in two divided doses for 5–7 days. In children, give 40–50 mg/kg in two 
divided doses for 7 days. In complicated cases and children younger than 2 years, 
a longer course, i.e. 10 days, is given.
	
	If the child has received Amoxicillin in the last 30 days or has a history of recurrent 
AOM unresponsive to Amoxicillin, give Amoxicillin 45 mg/kg/day plus Clavulanic 
acid 3.2 mg/kg/day (Amoxicillin to clavulanate ratio of 14:1) in two divided doses 
for 7 days.
	
	Reassess the patient if the caregiver reports that the child’s symptoms have 
worsened or failed to respond to the initial antibiotic treatment within 48–72 hours 
and determine whether a change in therapy is needed.
	
	If the initial treatment fails at 48–72 hours, give Inj. Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg/day IM 
or IV for 1–3 days (maximum 1 g/day) Or Clindamycin 30–40 mg/kg/day in three 
divided doses for 3 days with or without Ceftriaxone.
	
	If there is no improvement with the second-line treatment after 48–72 hours, then 
refer for tympanocentesis for culture of middle ear fluid.
	
	If the patient is allergic to penicillin, then:
	
	Tab. Azithromycin 500 mg on day 1, 250 mg on days 2–5
	
	In children: 10 mg/kg once on day 1, and then 5 mg/kg once a day from days 2–5, 
orally
	
	Or 
	
	Tab. Clarithromycin 1 g/day
	
	In children: 15 mg/kg/day in two doses 
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Clindamycin 1.8 g/day
	
	In children: 20–30 mg/kg/day in three doses
	
	Note: In lower-risk children older than 2 years with AOM and having non-severe 
OM or questionable diagnosis and in children aged 6 months to 2 years, defer 
antibiotics or ‘watchful waiting’ for 2–3 days with close follow-up. Prophylactic

Chapter 12  ENT Diseases    643
antibiotics do not reduce the frequency of AOM episodes in children with recurrent 
AOM.
	 3.	Xylometazoline HCl: 0.1% solution, one to two nasal drops in each nostril, one to 
two times daily 
	
	In children: 0.05% solution, one to two nasal drops in each nostril, one to two times 
daily
	
	Or
	
	Oxymetazoline: 0.05% solution, one to two nasal drops in each nostril, two times 
daily
	
	In children: 0.01% solution, one to two nasal drops in each nostril, two times daily
	 4.	In case of ear discharge (due to rupture of tympanic membrane), add ear drops 
Ciprofloxacin two drops three times a day.
	 5.	If symptoms of URI are present, add Tab. cetirizine 10 mg daily.
	
	Infants 8 weeks and younger are at a greater risk of severe sequelae from AOM, 
including sepsis, meningitis and mastoiditis.
Surgical treatment
Refer to an otolaryngologist for a surgical intervention:
	 1.	In case of persistent treatment failure and recurrent AOM
	 2.	In case of recurrent AOM (three episodes in 6 months or four episodes in 1 year 
with one episode in the preceding 6 months; evaluate adults with recurrent AOM 
[more than two episodes per year] or otitis media with effusion that persists for 
more than 6 weeks for mechanical Eustachian tube obstruction)
	 3.	In case of intense pain, bulging of the eardrum or persisting fever despite treatment
	 4.	In case of complications like acute mastoiditis, facial nerve palsy, labyrinthitis, 
meningitis, extradural empyema, lateral sinus thrombophlebitis, brain abscess and 
otitic hydrocephalus
Patient education
	
l Treat upper respiratory and sinus infections at the earliest.
	
l Counsel parents that fever and ear pain may persist for 48–72 hours after initiation of 
antibiotics. However, parents should seek care immediately if the child is vomiting 
or has a high fever, headache or pain behind the ear.
	
l Do not instil oil drops in ears.
References
	 1.	 Acute otitis media. In: Watkinson C, Clarke RW (eds), Scott Brown’s Otolaryngology and Head 
and Neck Surgery, vol. 2. 8th ed. Boca Raton, FL, USA: CRC Press; 2018, pp. 137–154.
	 2.	 Kliegman RM, St Geme J. Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics. 21st ed. Philadelphia, PA: Elsevier; 
2019.
	 3.	 Indian Academy of Pediatrics. Acute otitis media. Standard treatment guidelines; 2022.
	 4.	 Gaddey HL, Wright MT, Nelson TN. Otitis media: rapid evidence review. Am Fam Physician. 
2019;100(6):350–356.

644    Standard Treatment Guidelines
CHRONIC OTITIS MEDIA
(ACTIVE MUCOSAL OR TUBOTYMPANIC TYPE)
Chronic otitis media (COM) is characterized by the presence of a central perforation in 
the tympanic membrane. It may present as an active disease when infection may occur 
through the nasopharynx or through the perforation, thus causing ear discharge. In the 
inactive disease, the only presenting feature may be hearing loss.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Discharge: Intermittent, mucoid, copious purulent during acute exacerbation
	
l Hearing loss: Usually conductive type

Aural toilet by dry mopping or careful suction or by wicking (using a sterile cotton 
wick in external auditory canal)

condition: Chronic Otitis Media (Active Mucosal or Tubotympanic Type)
text:
1.	Ciprofloxacin HCl 0.3% w/v ear drops two to three drops or Ofloxacin ear drops 
three to four times daily for 2 weeks.
	 2.	When ear infection is associated with marked inflammation, combine with 
Prednisolone 0.5% + Lignocaine 2% + acetic acid 2% to be used as three to four 
drops three to four times daily for 2 weeks. (Caution: Avoid ear drops containing 
Chloramphenicol, Gentamicin, Streptomycin and Neomycin due to concerns for 
ototoxicity.)
	 3.	In case of profuse mucopurulent discharge and for any associated upper respiratory 
tract infection (URTI) and otitis externa, give systemic antibiotics.
	
	Cap. Amoxicillin 250–500 mg three times a day for 7 days
	
	In children: 20–40 mg/kg in three divided doses
	
	Or
	
	In case the patient has already received Amoxicillin in the past 1 month, then:
	
	Cap. Amoxicillin 250–500 mg plus Clavulanic acid 125 mg 8 hourly for 7 days
	
	The choice of antibiotic may be changed on the culture and sensitivity report of the 
pus if the patient does not respond.
Surgical treatment
Once the ear is dry and any local nidus of infection has been treated, refer the patient 
to an ENT surgeon for surgical management (myringoplasty).
Patient education
	
l Explain to the patient/parents to seek prompt consultation if pain, fever, drainage 
and/or increase in hearing loss occurs; consult immediately if a child has a fever,

Chapter 12  ENT Diseases    645
is unusually irritable or cannot sleep, frequently rubs or pulls his or her ears, has 
vomiting or diarrhoea or does not respond normally to sounds (does not startle when 
a door slams or pots clang).
	
l Explain to the patient not to allow water to enter the ear.
	
l Explain to the patient to take immediate treatment in case of URTI.
	
l Do not instil oil in the ear.
References
	 1.	 Chronic otitis media. In: Watkinson C, Clarke RW (eds), Scott Brown’s Otolaryngology and 
Head and Neck Surgery, vol. 2. 8th ed. Boca Raton, FL, USA: CRC Press; 2018, pp. 155–164.
	 2.	 Otitis Media. Clinical Practice Guidelines, American Academy of Paediatrics and endorsed by 
the American Academy of Family Physicians; 2019, https://www.aafp.org/patient-care/clinical-
recommendations/all/otitis-media.html [accessed December 15, 2023].
	 3.	 Rosario DC, Mendez MD. Chronic suppurative otitis. [Updated January 31, 2023]. In: StatPearls 
[Internet]. Treasure Island, FL: StatPearls Publishing; 2023, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/
NBK554592/ [accessed December 15, 2023].
OTITIS MEDIA WITH EFFUSION
It is characterized by the presence of non-purulent fluid in middle ear cleft which may 
be because of Eustachian tube dysfunction, unresolved otitis media or allergy.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Hearing loss – conductive type and tinnitus–is present.
	
l Otoscopy may show retraction of the drum or air–fluid level and air bubbles 
behind the drum.
	
l Diagnosis in children is based on clinical impression of the presence of middle 
ear fluid with pneumatic otoscopy.
	
l Tympanometry should be performed in patients with suspected otitis media with 
effusion (OME) for whom the diagnosis is uncertain on clinical examination.

l In most patients, watchful waiting for 3 months from the date of effusion onset (if 
known) or 3 months from the date of diagnosis (if onset is unknown) is done. 
	
l Do not give systemic antibiotics for treating otitis media with effusion (OME) unless 
there is associated URI or AOM.
	
l Do not give oral antibiotics, antihistamines, decongestants, systemic corticosteroids 
for treating OME. 
	
l Tympanostomy tubes or adenoidectomy, or both are recommended when surgery is 
performed for OME in a child aged 4 years or older.

Steam inhalation, Valsalva manoeuvre in the absence of throat infection

l Intranasal corticosteroids – Mometasone furoate or Fluticasone furoate spray twice 
daily in children with adenoidal enlargement not compromising the airway to a 
severe extent
	
l Systemic antibiotics indicated if there is associated URI or AOM
Surgical
Surgical measures may be necessary if patients do not respond to long-term 
pharmacological measures. Do not perform tympanostomy tube insertion in children 
with a single episode of OME of less than 3 months’ duration. Refer to a tertiary care 
centre for surgery which may include myringotomy with or without grommet insertion, 
or adenoidectomy.
Age-appropriate hearing testing should be done when OME persists for ≥3 months 
or at any time that language delay, learning problems, or a significant hearing loss is 
suspected in a child with OME or prior to tympanostomy tube insertion. Re-examine 
at 3- to 6-month intervals until the effusion is no longer present, significant hearing 
loss is identified or structural abnormalities of the eardrum or middle ear are suspected.
Patient education
	
l As above in COM
	
l Valsalva manoeuvre
References
	 1.	 Rosenfeld RM, Shin JJ, Schwartz SR, et al. Clinical practice guideline: otitis media with effusion 
executive summary (update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2016;154(2):201–214.
	 2.	 Chronic otitis media. In: Watkinson C, Clarke RW (eds), Scott Brown’s Otolaryngology and 
Head and Neck Surgery, vol. 2. 8th ed. 2018, pp. 155–164.
	 3.	 Clinical Practice Guidelines. Otitis Media with Effusion (Update). American Academy 
of Paediatrics and endorsed by the American Academy of Family Physicians; 2015, 
Clinical Practice Guideline: Otitis Media with Effusion (Update) - American Academy of 
Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS) (entnet.org) [accessed December 15, 
2023].
WAX
Wax (cerumen) is a mixture of the secretions of the ceruminous and pilosebaceous 
glands located in the cartilaginous portion of the external auditory canal.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Pain, hearing loss, tinnitus, occasionally vertigo and dry cough

1.	If pain is severe, Tab. Ibuprofen 400 mg SOS
	
	In children: 20 mg/kg/day divided into three doses
	 2.	Wax softener (Turpentine oil – 15%; Benzocaine – 2.7%; Chlorbutol – 5%; 
Paradichlorobenzene – 2%) three to four drops, three to four times daily for 3–4 
days before cleaning the ear when the wax is hard; follow this with removal by an 
otolaryngologist
	
	(Caution: If there is previous history of ear discharge or perforated drum, then 
instrumental manipulation with ring probe, hook or forceps and suction cleaning 
is advisable.)
Patient education
	
l Wax is a normal secretion and provides protection to the eardrum and should be 
removed only if it disturbs hearing. 
	
l Cleaning the ear with buds should be avoided as it can push the wax to the deeper 
canal. 
Reference
	 1.	 Diseases of the external ear. In: Logan Turner’s Diseases of the Nose, Throat and Ear. 
11th ed. Boca Raton, FL, USA: CRC Press; 2016.
OTOMYCOSIS
It is the fungal infection of the external auditory canal seen more commonly in tropical 
and subtropical climates. The fungi commonly found are Aspergillus niger and Candida 
albicans. Otomycosis may develop as a primary infection or as a mixed infection with 
bacteria.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Itching with or without pain, greyish-white fungal debris with or without black 
specks and ear blockage

Regular ear toilet – by suction/dry mopping/instrumentation – must be done prior to 
pharmacological treatment. No syringing should be done.

1.	Topical Clotrimazole as liquid 3-4 drops, 3-4 times a day to be instilled and 
continued for at least a week after clinical resolution of the infection

648    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 2.	Tab. Ibuprofen 400 mg as and when required
	
	In children: 20 mg/kg/day in three divided doses
	 3.	Tab. Cetirizine 10 mg once a day in case of significant itching in the ear
Patient education
	
l Ear should be kept dry; entry of water into the ear should be prevented. 
	
l The ear should not be plugged with cotton after eardrop instillation or bathing.
Reference
	 1.	 Otitis externa and otomycosis. In: Watkinson C, Clarke RW (eds), Scott Brown’s Otolaryngology 
and Head and Neck Surgery, vol. 2. 8th ed. 2018, pp. 953–958.
EXTERNAL EAR FURUNCULOSIS
It is due to staphylococcal infection of hair follicle in the outer cartilaginous part of 
the external auditory canal. It may be single or multiple. Abrasions facilitate infection, 
which is more common in patients with diabetes. Careful history and local examination 
help in differentiating the condition from mastoiditis.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Pain, tenderness, swelling, ear blockade
	
l Regional lymphadenitis and sometimes discharge

1.	10% Ichthammol in glycerine-soaked wick to be packed in the ear

SORE THROAT
A sore throat can be caused by a variety of factors, including viral infections, bacterial 
infections, allergies and environmental irritants. Viral infections are more common than 
bacterial infections and are usually caused by a cold or flu virus. 
Symptoms of a viral throat infection may include a sore throat, runny nose, cough 
and fever. These symptoms usually develop gradually and usually improve on their 
own within a week or so. Lymph nodes in the neck may be slightly enlarged and tender. 
Viral infections typically do not produce pus on the tonsils or throat.
Bacterial infections, on the other hand, are less common and are usually caused 
by Streptococcus bacteria. Symptoms of a bacterial throat infection may include a sore 
throat, swollen lymph nodes in the neck, fever and white patches on the tonsils. These 
symptoms usually develop suddenly, especially strep throat, and may be more severe 
than those of a viral infection. Bacterial infections often cause intense pain and difficulty 
swallowing. Bacterial infections, particularly strep throat, typically cause a high fever. 
Headaches are common in bacterial throat infections. Nausea and vomiting can occur, 
especially in children. Bacterial infections usually do not cause a significant cough. They 
may persist longer than viral infections, and symptoms might worsen without treatment.
The diagnosis of a viral infection is clinical based on symptoms and a physical 
examination. Specific viral tests are not routinely performed for common viral throat 
infections. In contrast, bacterial infections are diagnosed through a rapid strep test or a 
throat culture.
UPPER RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTION (URTI)
Acute pharyngitis (AP) in adults is one of the most common infectious diseases. Most 
AP cases are viral in origin and occur in the context of a common cold. Responsible 
viruses include rhinoviruses, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza, influenza and 
adenoviruses. URTI are generally benign and self-limited. Other less common causes 
of pharyngitis include allergies, trauma, cancer, reflux and certain toxins. More severe 
cases tend to be bacterial and may develop after an initial viral infection. The most 
common bacterial infection is group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus, which causes 
5–36% of cases of AP.

l Symptoms of acute infectious rhinosinusitis include nasal congestion, clear, watery 
rhinorrhoea initially, followed by mucopurulent nasal discharge, facial pain and 
pressure sensation, headache, olfactory disturbance, postnasal drainage and cough.

ACUTE RHINOSINUSITIS
Acute rhinosinusitis (ARS) is defined as symptomatic inflammation of the nasal cavity 
and paranasal sinuses lasting less than 4 weeks. The term ‘rhinosinusitis’ is preferred to 
‘sinusitis’ as sinus passages are contiguous with the nasal passages. The most common 
aetiology of ARS is a viral infection (rhinovirus, adenovirus, influenza virus and 
parainfluenza virus). The most common causes of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS) 
are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis. 
Fungal infection is rare, occurs in immunocompromised patients and should prompt urgent 
evaluation and referral to otolaryngology, neurosurgery and/or ophthalmology specialists.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Three “cardinal” symptoms that are most sensitive and specific for acute 
rhinosinusitis are purulent nasal drainage accompanied by either nasal obstruction 
or facial pain, pressure and fullness. In children, the same cardinal symptoms 
may be observed, and in addition to those, other symptoms may be present, 
such as irritability, lethargy, cough or vomiting. In the event of severe infection, 
deterioration of the general condition, fever greater than 39°C and periorbital or 
facial oedema may be present.
	
l Signs (may be seen but the absence of these does not exclude acute sinusitis): These 
include hyponasal speech indicating nasal obstruction, swelling, redness of the skin 
due to congestion of the capillaries (erythema) or abnormally large fluid volume 
(oedema) localized over the involved cheek bone or periorbital area, palpable 
cheek tenderness or percussion tenderness of the upper teeth, purulent drainage 
in the nose or posterior pharynx and signs of extra-sinus involvement (orbital or 
facial cellulitis, orbital protrusion, abnormalities of eye movement, neck stiffness 
indicating complications).
	
l Acute viral sinusitis (the common cold) is caused by or presumed to be caused 
by viral infection when symptoms or signs of acute rhinosinusitis are present for 
less than 10 days and the symptoms are not worsening.

persist for more than 3 weeks despite antibiotics or recur more than four times

ALLERGIC RHINITIS
Allergic rhinitis (AR) is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity of the mucous membrane of 
the nasal passage. It is very common, affecting 10–30% of adults and nearly 40% of

656    Standard Treatment Guidelines
children at some parts of their life. Almost 80% of patients with asthma have associated 
AR and around 50% of cases of AR have associated asthma. Common causes include:
	
l Allergens: Aeroallergens (both outdoor and indoor); dust, animal and insect 
allergens (house dust, house dust mites, cockroach and pet dander); and occupational 
allergens, including latex, can be significant, especially for healthcare professionals 
who may come into contact with latex gloves.
	
l Pollutants: These include indoor pollutants like biomass fuel, tobacco and gas 
pollutants; and outdoor pollutants like ozone, oxides of nitrogen and sulphur from 
diesel exhaust. 
	
l Drugs: These include aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs 
(NSAIDs).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Sneezing, itching, watery nasal discharge and a feeling of nasal obstruction are 
present.
	
l It may be associated with allergic conjunctivitis, atopic dermatitis and bronchial 
asthma.
	
l It can be divided into the following types:
	– Seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR/hay fever): Sneezing, itching, watery 
rhinorrhoea and conjunctivitis are prominent symptoms. 
	– Perennial allergic rhinitis (PAR): This differs from SAR as this is due to 
long-standing nasal mucosal congestion. In this condition, nasal discharge 
is more viscous and may be purulent. Usual symptoms are nasal blockage, 
postnasal discharge and hyposmia.
	
l Based on Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma (ARIA) classification 
according to symptom duration and severity, AR is divided into four types: 
	– Mild (normal sleep, no troublesome symptoms, no trouble with daily life, 
sports or leisure) 
	– Intermittent symptoms (<4 days a week or <4 weeks)
	– Persistent (>4 days a week and >4 weeks) 
	– Moderate to severe (troublesome symptoms interfering in daily life, sports and 
leisure, sleep disorder)
	
l Clinical diagnosis of AR is made when a history and physical examination is 
consistent with an allergic cause and one or more of the following symptoms are 
present: nasal congestion, runny nose, itchy nose or sneezing. Findings of AR 
consistent with an allergic cause include, but are not limited to, clear rhinorrhoea, 
nasal congestion, pale discolouration of the nasal mucosa, and red and watery eyes.
	
l Specific IgE (skin or blood) allergy testing should be done in patients who do 
not respond to empirical treatment, or when the diagnosis is uncertain, or when 
knowledge of the specific causative allergen is needed to target therapy.
	
l Sinonasal imaging is not needed routinely.

Managing the condition relies on a combination of patient education, self-monitoring, 
regular doctor visits, trigger avoidance and pharmacotherapy.

l Avoiding known allergens; environmental controls (e.g. removal of pets, the use of 
air filtration systems, washing of bed linen in hot water, keeping surroundings clean 
and maintaining low humidity with proper ventilation, sun drying, avoiding wall-
to-wall carpeting, pest control and reduction in relative humidity less than 50% to 
reduce house dust mite concentration in the environment)

l Seasonal AR is an allergic reaction to pollen from trees, grasses and weeds. This 
type of rhinitis occurs mainly in the spring and fall, when pollen counts from trees, 
grasses and weeds are high in the air.
	
l Perennial AR is caused by allergens that are present all year long. The primary 
causes of this type of rhinitis are allergies to dust mites, mould, animal dander and 
cockroach debris.
	
l The first and best option is to avoid contact with allergens. Other prevention tips are:
	– Do not touch or rub nose; wash hands often with soap and water; wash bed linens 
and pillowcases in hot water and detergent to reduce allergens; use dust mite–
proof covers for pillows, comforters, duvets, mattresses and box springs; keep 
windows closed during high pollen and mould seasons; wear sunglasses and a 
wide-brimmed hat when outdoor to reduce pollen getting into eyes.
	– Keep pets out of the bedroom to reduce pet dander allergen in the bedding.
	
l Non-AR is caused by smoke, chemicals or other irritating environmental conditions 
which may provoke non-AR. Hormonal changes, physical defects of the nose (such as 
deviated septum) and the overuse of nasal drops may also cause it.

rebound phenomena – atrophic rhinitis and rhinitis medicamentosa.

impairment. The patient should avoid tasks requiring alertness and skill. These drugs 
can also cause dryness of the mouth and urinary hesitancy.

	In children: 10 mg/kg/dose
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Paracetamol 500 mg 6 hourly for 2–3 days, and then as and when required till 
pain and fever subside
	
	In children: 10 mg/kg 6–8 hourly
	 3.	Bacitracin or Mupirocin ointment applied topically twice daily for 14 days
	 4.	Treatment of community-associated methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) infections 
should be directed by culture and sensitivity test results. Clindamycin, Trimethoprim/
Sulphamethoxazole and Doxycycline are effective against most strains.
Monitoring
Usually improvement in pain, tenderness and inflammation occurs within 
24–48 hours after initiation of treatment. The patient should be monitored regularly. 
If there is flaring of infection in the form of spreading facial cellulitis, then the 
patient should be hospitalized and shifted to systemic intravenous antibiotics. If 
the patient is having recurrent furunculosis, then he or she should be investigated 
for diabetes mellitus. Patients with complications often require hospital admission, 
drainage of the boil and intravenous antibiotics.
Patient education
	
l Do not fidget with the furuncle as this lies in the dangerous area of the face and can 
cause serious complications like cavernous sinus thrombophlebitis due to retrograde 
spread through valveless veins.
	
l Complete antibiotic therapy to avoid risk of developing antimicrobial resistance.
