EPISTAXIS
Epistaxis can be classified according to the location of bleeding in the nasal cavity as 
either anterior or posterior. Anterior bleeding accounts for more than 90% of the cases. 
Anterior bleeds tend to be characterized by a slow, persistent oozing, whereas posterior 
bleeds tend to bleed more profusely carrying a higher risk of airway compromise, 
aspiration of blood and life-threatening haemorrhage. The most important causes of 
epistaxis include trauma in the form of nose picking, hypertension, bleeding disorders, 
nasal mass and acute inflammation.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Bleeding from the nose and mouth
	
l Shock due to excessive loss of blood

The treatment depends on a number of factors such as:
	
l Site and severity of bleeding
	
l Condition of the patient (check for blood pressure; high blood pressure needs to be 
normalized for control of epistaxis)
	
l Identification of a local or systemic cause for the bleeding
	 1.	At the time of initial contact, distinguish the patients who require prompt 
management from the patients who do not. 
	 2.	In cases with active epistaxis, check the vitals of the patient and manage blood loss 
and shock.
	 3.	In the absence of life-threatening bleeding, initiate first-line treatments as in the 
subsequent text prior to transfusion, reversal of anticoagulation or withdrawal 
of anticoagulation/antiplatelet medications for patients on these medications. If 
bleeding actively, pinch the nose (apply firm sustained compression to the lower 
third of the nose, with or without the assistance of the patient or caregiver) for 5 
minutes or longer and position the patient as sitting upright and leaning forward, 
to avoid aspiration of the blood and again check the nose for bleeding. Instruct the 
patient not to swallow or blow the nose. Position the patient in supine (or other) 
lateral position if signs and symptoms of shock are present.
	 4.	For patients in whom bleeding precludes identification of a bleeding site despite 
nasal compression, treat ongoing active bleeding with nasal packing.

Use nasal packing for patients with a suspected bleeding disorder or for 
patients on anticoagulation or antiplatelet medications.
	 5.	Perform anterior rhinoscopy to identify the source of bleeding after removal of any 
blood clot (if present). 
	 6.	Treat patients with an identified site of bleeding with an appropriate intervention, 
which may include one or more of the following: topical vasoconstrictors, nasal 
cautery and moisturizing or lubricating agents.
	
	Note: When nasal cautery is chosen for treatment, anesthetize the bleeding site and 
restrict application of cautery only to the active or suspected site(s) of bleeding.
	
	For details see Bleeding Disorders in Chapter 4.
Recurrent epistaxis
	
l Instruct the patient to minimize the recurrence of bleeding, including limiting local 
trauma (no nose blowing or picking) and applying nasal hydration with saline mist 
or ointments and increasing ambient humidity with a cool mist vaporizer to reduce 
mucosal irritation. If minor bleeding recurs, instruct the patient (or parent) to pinch 
the nostrils together for 5–30 minutes non-stop as above. Identify the cause and treat 
accordingly.
	
l In patients with recurrent nasal bleeding, despite prior treatment with packing 
or cautery or in patients with recurrent unilateral nasal bleeding, perform nasal 
endoscopy to identify the site of bleeding and perform further management.
	
l Refer to ENT specialist for evaluation of candidacy for surgical arterial ligation, 
angiography and/or endovascular embolization for patients with persistent or 
recurrent bleeding not controlled by packing or nasal cauterization.
	
l Refer to a specialist for assessment of the presence of nasal telangiectasias and/or 
oral mucosal telangiectasias in patients who have a history of recurrent bilateral 
nosebleeds or a family history of recurrent nosebleeds to diagnose hereditary 
haemorrhagic telangiectasia syndrome (HHT).
Patient education
	
l Patients, especially children, must be advised against nose picking.
	
l As first aid, explain how to pinch the nose tightly and apply ice pack over the nose, 
while waiting for proper medical attention.

It is the acute inflammation of the palatine tonsils, generally bacterial in aetiology.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Pain in the throat aggravated on swallowing and congestion of the tonsils and the 
anterior pillars/posterior pharyngeal wall
	
l Fever and malaise
	
l Enlarged and tender jugulodigastric lymph nodes

Plenty of oral fluids, rest and warm saline gargles

1.	Cap. Amoxycillin 500 mg 8 hourly
	
	In children: 50 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for 7 days
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Azithromycin 12 mg/kg once daily (maximum 500 mg) for 5 days
	
	In children: 50 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for 5 days
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Roxithromycin 150 mg twice daily for 5 days
	
	In children weighing 6–40 kg: 5–8 mg/kg daily
	
	In case of severe infection, Cap. Amoxycillin 250/500 mg + Clavulanic acid 
125 mg 8 hourly for 5–7 days
	 2.	Tab. Paracetamol 8–10 mg/kg 6–8 hourly and then as and when required, till 
fever subsides
	
		
Refer to an ENT surgeon if the child has frequent attacks of acute tonsillitis or 
has chronic hypertrophic tonsillitis for consideration for tonsillectomy.
PERITONSILLAR ABSCESS
Peritonsillar abscess or collection of pus in the peritonsillar space, is the most common 
deep infection of the head and neck and is caused by a combination of aerobic 
and anaerobic bacteria. The infection can cause significant airway obstruction in 
children. The most common aerobic organism associated with peritonsillar abscess 
is Streptococcus pyogenes (group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus). The most 
common anaerobic organism is Fusobacterium. Early diagnosis of the abscess 
allows appropriate treatment to begin before the abscess spreads into the surrounding 
anatomic structures.

SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Unilateral severe throat pain, odynophagia, hot potato voice, muffled and thick 
speech, foul breath, ipsilateral earache on the same side as abscess and decreased 
mouth opening are present.
	
l On examination, erythematous, swollen tonsil with uvular deviation to the 
opposite side, purulent exudate on tonsils, drooling and cervical lymphadenopathy 
are the frequently found signs.
	
l Both abscess and cellulitis have swelling above the affected tonsil, but with abscess 
discrete bulge, with uvular deviation to the opposite side and pronounced trismus.
Treatment (Hospitalize)
	 1.	Hospitalization is advisable as the patient may need intravenous fluids to combat 
dehydration.
	 2.	Incision and drainage of abscess is performed at the point of maximum bulge above 
the upper pole of tonsil (to be done by an ENT surgeon).
	 3.	Inj. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM twice daily for 2–3 days; then switch over to oral 
antibiotics or Ampicillin/Sulbactam 3 g every 6 hours or Penicillin G 10 million 
units every 6 hours. Switch to oral Amoxicillin/Clavulanic acid 1 g twice daily or 
Penicillin V 500 mg four times daily.
	
	In Penicillin-allergic patients or when penicillin is not appropriate, give Inj. 
Clindamycin 600–1200 mg IV infusion or IM injection per day, in 2–4 equally 
divided doses; then switch over when appropriate to Tab. Clindamycin 300 mg 
orally every 6 hours or 600 mg twice daily and for more severe infection 300–450 
mg orally every 6 hours.
	 4.	Inj. Metronidazole 400 mg IV three times daily for 2–3 days and then switch over 
to oral for 5–7 days.
Refer to a higher centre for interval tonsillectomy in case of recurrent peritonsillar 
abscess.
Patient education
	
l Visit emergency room in case of a sore throat and trouble in swallowing, trouble 
in breathing, difficulty in speaking, drooling or any other signs of potential airway 
obstruction.
	
l Arrange follow-up with a doctor or an ENT specialist after treatment for a 
peritonsillar abscess and if the abscess persists as one may need a different antibiotic 
or repeat incision and drainage. In case of recurrent episodes of acute tonsillitis, 
more than four to five annually, the patient must be referred for surgery.
	
l Explain the risk factors and their prevention – do not smoke, maintain good dental 
hygiene and promptly treat oral infections.

ACUTE PAROTITIS
It is an acute bacterial infection of the parotid gland. Usually there is unilateral swelling 
of the parotid gland with potential abscess formation. It can be associated with poor 
dental hygiene, dental caries and dehydration. The most common cause is S. aureus 
(could be MRSA).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Swelling at the angle of the mandible pushing the ear lobule laterally, generally 
unilateral, induration and tenderness of the gland
	
l Purulent saliva may be expressed from the duct opposite the upper second molar

Adequate hydration, good oral hygiene, repeated massage of the gland

1.	Cap. Cloxacillin 20–40 mg/kg in four divided doses for 7 days
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Clindamycin 300 mg twice daily
	 2.	If anaerobic infection is suspected or there is poor dental hygiene, Tab. 
Metronidazole 400 mg 3 times a day added
	 3.	Tab. Paracetamol 8–10 mg/kg thrice daily for 3 days and then as and when 
required, if pain and fever persist
	 4.	Antiseptic mouthwash (containing povidone-iodine 1% or chloroxylenol 1.02%, 
menthol 0.12%, absolute alcohol 60.8%) to be used 3 times a day

In case parotitis is not responding to antibiotics and there is increasing fluctuant 
swelling over the parotid region or development of induration over the gland, incision 
and drainage must be done. The patient should be referred to an otolaryngologist for

FACIAL PARALYSIS
The VII cranial nerve is frequently affected in diseases of the ear. The central causes 
(upper motor neuron type) are brainstem infarction, tumours and multiple sclerosis. The 
peripheral causes are inflammatory (AOM, COM or herpes zoster oticus), traumatic 
(accidental or iatrogenic), neoplastic or idiopathic (as in Bell’s palsy or Melkersson-
Rosenthal syndrome) and due to systemic diseases such as diabetes mellitus, 
sarcoidosis and demyelinating diseases. Bell’s palsy is described below.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l It is an acute (onset in less than 72 hours), idiopathic, unilateral, lower motor 
paralysis of the facial nerve. The minimum diagnostic criteria for the Bell’s palsy 
are: 
	– Paralysis or paresis of one side of the facial muscles
	– Absence of any central nervous system disease
	– Absence of signs of any ear disease
	– Absence of cerebellopontine angle disease

Treat the underlying cause of the lesion. Surgical intervention is often indicated in 
peripheral causes like AOM, COM and tumours. All such patients must be referred to 
an ENT surgeon.
Pharmacological (idiopathic paralysis of the facial nerve – new-onset Bell’s 
palsy presenting within 72 hours of symptom onset)
The aim of treatment in the acute phase of Bell’s palsy is to increase the speed of 
recovery and to prevent corneal complications.
	 1.	In patients with incomplete eye closure, eye-protective measures (eye patching 
and frequent application of lubricating drops during the day and an eye ointment 
at night) should be used.
	 2.	Tab. Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day is given in single or two divided doses for 1 week 
(maximum 60 mg/day). Review after 1 week. To increase the probability of recovery, 
oral steroids should be started within 72 hours of symptom onset, if possible.

666    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
	If clinical improvement is present, taper steroids over 4–5 days. If there is no 
clinical improvement, continue for another week before tapering the dose.
	 3.	Acyclovir or Valacyclovir is given combined with corticosteroids in patients with 
severe to complete paresis.
Notes:
	
l Acyclovir or Valacyclovir should not be used alone.
	
l Exercise physiotherapy for acute Bell’s palsy of any severity and use of 
electrostimulation are not recommended. However, they may be recommended for 
patients with persistent weakness.
Most patients with Bell’s palsy have complete motor function recovery within 
6 months without treatment. About one-third of patients may have incomplete recovery 
and residual effect. Poor prognostic factors are old age, hypertension, diabetes 
mellitus, impairment of taste and complete facial weakness. Residual effects include 
post-paralytic hemi-facial spasm, co-contracting muscles, synkinesis and sweating 
while eating or during physical exertion.
Patient education
	
l Wear an eye pad over the affected eye or use lubricant eyedrops to avoid exposure 
keratitis.

RED EYE
This is a common condition. It is divided into non-painful and painful red eye. 
Non-painful red eye is caused by conjunctivitis, lid abnormalities, e.g. trichiasis, 
entropion, blepharitis, meibomitis, ectropion, lagophthalmos, molluscum contagiosum, 
episcleritis (foreign body sensation/grittiness), subconjunctival haemorrhage, inflamed 
pinguecula and pterygium.
Painful red eye is caused by acute attack of primary angle-closure glaucoma, 
phacomorphic glaucoma, corneal ulcer/keratitis, acute anterior uveitis, scleritis and 
endophthalmitis; it may be associated with circumcorneal congestion (ciliary injection).
Conjunctivitis may be classified into:
	 I.	Infective conjunctivitis caused by bacterial, chlamydial or viral microorganisms
	 II.	Allergic conjunctivitis
NON-PAINFUL RED EYE
I. INFECTIVE CONJUNCTIVITIS
A. Bacterial Conjunctivitis
Bacterial conjunctivitis manifests as acute mucopurulent, purulent, angular and 
membranous conjunctivitis.
Acute mucopurulent conjunctivitis
Common aetiological microorganisms are S. aureus, S. epidermidis, Haemophilus 
aegyptius (Koch–Weeks bacillus), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus viridans 
and Streptococcus pyogenes.

Appropriate antibiotic should be selected based on culture sensitivity reports. 
Acute purulent bacterial conjunctivitis
Acute purulent conjunctivitis can affect newborn babies, adolescents and adults. The 
most fulminant form of purulent conjunctivitis occurs due to N. gonorrhoeae. It is 
characterized by severe lid oedema, erythema, chemosis, thick purulent discharge, 
preauricular lymphadenopathy and frequent corneal involvement.
Treatment (adults)
A dual treatment regimen consisting of the following:
	 1.	Inj. Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM injection once + Azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose

	Or
	
	Tab. Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
	 2.	In patients with Cephalosporin allergy, Azithromycin 2 g orally in a single dose
	 3.	In case of corneal involvement, hospitalize and switch to Inj. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV 
every 12–24 hours in place of IM Ceftriaxone. The duration of treatment depends

Ophthalmia neonatorum
It is also called conjunctivitis of the newborn and neonatal conjunctivitis, and occurs 
during the first 28 days of life. It may be due to gonococcal or non-gonococcal bacteria. 
In the latter type, herpes simplex II and Chlamydia are the aetiological agents in 80% 
of the cases. The infection is acquired from the maternal birth canal.
SALIENT FEATURES
Complications like corneal blindness, cataract, nystagmus, endophthalmitis or 
panophthalmitis and metastatic stomatitis and arthritis can occur.

Hospitalize and evaluate for systemic involvement.

Irrigate the conjunctival sac hourly with warm normal saline before antibiotic 
instillation until the discharge is eliminated; wipe away the discharge with moistened 
cotton wool.
Pharmacological (gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum)
	 1.	Systemic treatment in full-term babies with normal birth weight after sensitivity 
testing
	
	Inj. Ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg (maximum 125 mg) as a single IM/IV dose
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Cefotaxime 100 mg/kg IM/IV as a single injection
	 2.	If corneal involvement (see the section ‘Corneal Ulcer)
	 3.	Bacitracin/Erythromycin eye ointment 2–4 hourly
	 4.	Mother also to be treated with systemic therapy
	 5.	Chlamydial infection treated simultaneously as it may also coexist

Pharmacological (non-gonococcal neonatorum)
This is a milder disease occurring within 5–14 days after birth. It is caused by 
chlamydial, bacterial or herpetic infection.
	 1.	For bacterial causes, Tobramycin or Ciprofloxacin Or Gatifloxacin 0.3% eyedrops 
Or Bacitracin eye ointment 4 times a day for 2 weeks
	 2.	If chlamydial infection is suspected:
	
	Tab. Erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day orally in 4 divided doses for 14 days along with 
Erythromycin ointment topically 4 times a day
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Azithromycin 20 mg/kg orally for 3 days
	
	Note: As other Chlamydia-associated infections such as pneumonia and otitis 
media can accompany inclusion conjunctivitis in the newborn, topical treatment is 
not adequate.
	 3.	If extensive conjunctival or corneal involvement is present, also treat the parents, 
primarily the mother. If there is no response after 1 week of therapy, refer for an 
appropriate culture and sensitivity testing to a tertiary care level.
Antenatal care 
Prophylaxis: Screening of high-risk pregnant women (pregnant women with vaginal 
discharge, dysuria, STI such as syphilis, genital herpes, etc.; multiple sexual partners, 
sexual contact with a partner with an unspecified STI) and treatment of maternal 
urogenital infections during pregnancy and sexual partner
Pharmacological treatment (gonorrhoea in pregnant women)
	 1.	Inj. Procaine penicillin 4.8 million IV/IM with 1 g oral probenecid
	 2.	In Penicillin-resistant cases, Inj. Spectinomycin 4 g in 2 divided doses IM single 
injection in the gluteal region

Tab. Azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose
Or 
Tab. Erythromycin 500 mg base 4 times per day for 7 days
Or

erythromycin is preferred)
Test pregnant woman for cure 3 weeks after treatment for chlamydial infection and re-
screen 3–4 months after completion of antibiotic therapy. Screen all women who are 25 
years or younger or at an increased risk of sexually transmitted diseases for chlamydial

B. Chlamydial Conjunctivitis – Trachoma
Trachoma is a chronic bilateral cicatrizing follicular keratoconjunctivitis caused by 
Chlamydia trachomatis and is the leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l At least two of the following signs are present: superior tarsal follicles, limbal 
follicles (Herbert’s pits), typical conjunctival scarring and vascular pannus.
	
l Diagnosis is confirmed by conjunctival cytology.

Key to treatment is SAFE (surgery for entropion/trichiasis, antibiotics, facial cleanliness 
and environment change such as control of disease-spreading flies and access to clean 
water) strategy.
Active trachoma
	 1.	Cap. Azithromycin 1 g single dose in adults 
	
	In children: 20 mg/kg single dose (maximum 1000 mg)
	
	Or
	
	Cap. Doxycycline 100 mg 2 times a day for 2 weeks
	
	(Caution: Contraindicated in children, pregnant women and nursing mothers)
	
	In children weighing less than or equal to 45 kg: Erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day PO 
divided into 4 doses daily for 14 days

	Or
	
	Sulphacetamide 20% eyedrops 3–4 times for 6 weeks
	
	Or
	
	Ciprofloxacin 0.3% ophthalmic solution 4 times a day and ciprofloxacin 0.3% eye 
ointment at night for 8 weeks
Refer all patients with trichiasis to an eye specialist as soon as possible.
Surgical treatment
Perform eyelid surgery for correction of trichiasis and entropion to prevent corneal 
blindness. Do not remove eyelashes (epilation) except as a temporary measure while 
waiting for surgery as eyelashes may cause further damage when they regrow.
Patient education
	
l Infection spreads through personal contact (via hands, clothes or bedding) and by 
flies that have been in contact with discharge from the eyes or nose of an infected 
person. With repeated episodes of infection over many years, the eyelashes may 
be drawn in so that they rub on the surface of the eye, with pain, discomfort and 
permanent damage to the cornea
	
l Treat the whole family/household contacts even if only one child has active trachoma
	
l Antibiotic treatment of cases and community members should be completed within 
2 weeks of screening
	
l Screen annually for trichiasis
	
l Improve ocular hygiene – facial cleanliness in children
	
l Advise for environmental improvement – eliminating flies, provision of adequate 
running water supply and latrines, etc
	
l Surgery does not always prevent trichiasis in the future as the remaining scar tissue 
may contract and turn other eyelashes inwards. Emphasize on annual post-surgery 
review to detect further trichiasis

C. Viral Conjunctivitis
Viral conjunctivitis often occurs in epidemics. It includes the following entities: 
epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, pharyngoconjunctival fever, acute haemorrhagic 
conjunctivitis and Newcastle conjunctivitis.

676    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Itching, burning, tearing, gritty sensation, recent history of upper respiratory 
infection or contact with a patient with conjunctivitis; starts in one eye, involves 
the fellow eye a few days later
	
l Conjunctival congestion, chemosis, watery discharge, conjunctival haemorrhages, 
preauricular lymphadenopathy and swollen lids
	
l Vision unaffected; photophobia uncommon

l Avoid patching; use dark goggles; avoid close contact with other persons and 
swimming for 2 weeks. The doctor must wash his/her hands after examination of 
such patient and instruments should be disinfected after each use. 
	
l Apply cool compresses.
	
l Emphasize on hand hygiene.

It is usually a self-limiting illness. Antiviral agents are not effective. Corticosteroids are 
contraindicated; however, these are used if vision is threatened.
	 1.	Secondary infection prevented by antibiotic eyedrops (as in mucopurulent 
conjunctivitis)
	 2.	Naphazoline 0.05% Or Zinc sulphate 0.125% eyedrops 1 drop 4 times a day
	 3.	Carboxymethylcellulose 0.5% eye drops Or Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose 
(HPMC) 1 drop 4 times a day
	 4.	Removal of symptomatic pseudomembranes or membranes
	
	Refer to an ophthalmologist if the patient’s condition deteriorates or vision 
is affected or there is no response in 7–10 days. Topical steroids loteprednol/
fluorometholone are indicated for specific corneal involvement under supervision 
of an ophthalmologist.
Patient education
Explain to the patient that it is highly contagious; therefore, he/she should not share 
towels, handkerchief and other objects with other persons.

II. CONJUNCTIVAL ALLERGIC DISORDERS
Conjunctival allergic disorders include acute allergic conjunctivitis (hay fever 
conjunctivitis – seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, perennial allergic conjunctivitis), 
atopic keratoconjunctivitis, vernal keratoconjunctivitis, giant papillary conjunctivitis, 
phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis, conjunctivitis medicamentosa, etc.
A. Acute allergic conjunctivitis (hay fever conjunctivitis)
It is a recurrent, bilateral type I, IgE-mediated hypersensitivity to a variety of 
exogenous air-borne allergens such as pollens, animal dander, dust and moulds, and 
may be seasonal or perennial (chronic or acute type).

Avoid exposure to the allergen or minimize exposure to the allergen, if possible; 
perform dilution of the allergen by frequent washing with clean water and by 
instillation of tear substitutes and cold compresses to the eye. Wear protective goggles 
outdoors.

1.	Topical combination of antihistamine (Antazoline 0.5% or Pheniramine) and 
vasoconstrictor (Naphazoline hydrochloride 0.05%) eyedrops 4 times a day till 
resolution of symptoms
	 2.	Disodium cromoglycate 4% eyedrops 2 times a day Or 2% eyedrops 4 times a day 
till resolution of symptoms
	
	Or
	
	Ketorolac tromethamine 0.5% eyedrops 4 times a day till resolution of symptoms
	
	Or
	
	Olopatadine eyedrops 0.1% twice a day, or 0.2% once daily
	
	(Caution: Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated as a first-line therapy. If 
required, they should be prescribed only by an ophthalmologist in low concentra­
tions for a limited period only.)
	 3.	If severe, administer Tab. Cetirizine hydrochloride 10 mg Or Levocetirizine 5 mg 
once a day for the duration of acute symptoms (in children, 5 mg once a day)
	 4.	If severe, mild topical steroids Loteprednol 0.2% Or Fluorometholone 0.1% 4 times 
a day for 1–2 weeks
	 5.	If uncontrolled, Prednisolone sodium phosphate 1% eyedrops or Dexamethasone 
0.1% or Betamethasone 0.1% 4 times a day for 2 days, twice daily for 4 days, 
followed by once daily for the next 3 days and then discontinue

Patient education
	
l Symptomatic therapy and avoidance of allergen as far as possible or minimization 
of exposure to allergens is the mainstay of the therapy.
	
l Wear protective goggles outdoors. 
	
l Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated as a first-line therapy. Do not 
self-medicate. If required, they should be applied only on prescription of an 
ophthalmologist.
	
l Apply cool compresses.
B. Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis
It is characterized by the presence of red nodule at bulbar conjunctiva, most often 
at the nasal limbus of one eye. It is a cell-mediated type (type IV) conjunctival 
hypersensitivity to tubercular protein; the commonest endogenous allergen and others 
include staphylococcal antigens, worm infestations, fungal antigens and idiopathic.
Topical treatment
	 1.	Dexamethasone 0.1% eyedrops Or Betamethasone 0.1% eyedrops or loteprednol 
0.2% eyedrops under supervision
	 2.	Moxifloxacin 0.5% Or Gentamicin 0.3%, Or Ciprofloxacin 0.3% eyedrops 4 times 
a day for 7 days
	 3.	If cornea is involved (see the section ‘Corneal Ulcer’)
	 4.	Any systemic cause to be ruled out and treated accordingly, especially if recurrent 
or bilateral keratoconjunctivitis
Spring catarrh (vernal keratoconjunctivitis)
It is a bilateral, recurrent papillary conjunctivitis occurring in a warm climate due to 
hypersensitivity to exogenous allergens.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Itching, ropy discharge, gelatinous thickening at the limbus and papillae 
(cobblestones) in the upper palpebral conjunctiva
Non-pharmacological treatment
	
l Avoidance of allergen, wind and rubbing of the eye; tear substitutes (barrier 
function, diluting allergen, washing away allergen); wearing glasses or goggles; air 
conditioning with appropriate filters

Naphazoline 0.05%, Zinc sulphate 0.12%, Antazoline hydrochloride 0.5%, 
Chlorpheniramine 0.01% 4 times a day

HERPES ZOSTER OPHTHALMICUS (HZO)
Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is another neurotrophic virus that has a predilection for the 
ophthalmic division of the trigeminal dermatome most frequently affecting the nasociliary 
branch. The human herpesvirus 3 (HHV-3) is also known as VZV. Primary infection 
usually occurs before age 10 years, manifesting clinically as chickenpox (varicella). The 
virus then establishes a latent state in the sensory ganglia. In circumstances of diminished 
cell-mediated immunity, physical trauma, surgery, severe intercurrent illness, radiation 
therapy and corticosteroids, the virus may reactivate and spread to the corresponding 
dermatome to generate the characteristic unilateral vesicular exanthem (shingles). Ocular 
zoster can affect any part of the eye from the conjunctiva to the optic nerve. Cranial nerve 
palsies involving the third (most common), fourth and sixth nerves may occur rarely. 
Complications can occur months or years after the acute phase.
Risk of ocular involvement: Hutchinson’s sign (involvement of the skin at the tip, side 
and root of the nose [supplied by the nasociliary nerve] strongly correlates with ocular

680    Standard Treatment Guidelines
involvement); elderly in fifth and seventh decades and patients with AIDS tend to have 
a severe disease at an earlier age.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Symptoms include pain and altered sensation of the forehead on one side; rash 
affecting the forehead and upper eyelid appears a day to a week later; general 
malaise, headache and fever occur, followed by ocular symptoms – discomfort, 
discharge, redness, pain, photophobia and diminution of vision. 
	
l Signs  include unilateral painful erythematous maculopapular rash in the 
distribution of ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve commonly on the 
forehead and upper eyelid, and painful, red, vesicular rash, progressing to 
crusting after 2–3 weeks; resolution often involves scarring and periorbital 
oedema, and can affect any of the ocular or adnexal tissues.
	
l Associated ocular features include mucopurulent conjunctivitis (common), 
associated with vesicles on the lid margin; these usually resolve within 1 week; 
epithelial keratitis (early sign, within 2 days) involves pseudo-dendrites without 
terminal knobs, scleritis, nummular keratitis, interstitial keratitis, disciform keratitis, 
neurotrophic keratitis, cranial nerve palsies, optic neuritis and glaucoma. Acute 
keratitis can occur up to 1 month following the onset of dermatitis. Chronic/relapsing 
keratitis can occur up to several months following the initial HZO infection.
	
l Associated feature includes post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) characterized by varying 
degrees of constant or intermittent pain in the distribution of the affected dermatome.

l Rest and general supportive measures (reassurance, support at home, good diet, 
plenty of fluids); avoidance of contact with elderly or pregnant individuals, also 
babies and children not previously exposed to VZV (who are non-immune) or 
immunodeficient patients
	
l Mechanical cleansing and cool compresses

Treatment with oral antivirals as below begun within 72 hours of the onset of rash can 
reduce the severity of the disease, speed resolution of skin lesions, and reduce viral 
shedding and any long-term complications:
	 1.	Tab. Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times a day for 7–10 days
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Famciclovir 500 mg 3 times a day for 7 days
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Valacyclovir 1000 mg 3 times a day for 7 days
	
	If severe disease, Inj. Acyclovir 5–10 mg/kg IV 3 times a day for 5 days
	 2.	Topical antiviral for ocular involvement and Acyclovir 3% ointment.

	 3.	Systemic steroids should be given under antiviral cover to treat associated inflammatory 
conditions like uveitis and optic neuritis cranial nerve palsy. (Caution: Their use may 
increase the risk of ocular complications such as mucous plaques and keratitis).
	 4.	Topical corticosteroids may be necessary for treating uncontrolled inflammation. Taper 
corticosteroids gradually to a level that minimizes the risk of rebound inflammation.
	 5.	Prophylactic antibiotic can be given to prevent bacterial infection. 
	 6.	Anti-glaucoma drugs for herpetic trabeculitis.
	 7.	Neurotrophic keratitis is treated with artificial tears, punctal plugs and patching.
	 8.	Topical cycloplegics help to prevent ciliary spasm associated with herpes zoster 
inflammatory disease.
	 9.	Acute pain control is achieved by local care and oral analgesics. (Caution: Topical 
anaesthetics should never be prescribed because of their corneal toxicity.)
	10.	The pain associated with post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN), in most cases, 
resolves spontaneously but may last for months to years. PHN can be treated 
with analgesics, tricyclic antidepressants or anticonvulsants (Gabapentin, 
Carbamazepine). Start therapy at a low dose and titrate upward until pain relief 
occurs or adverse effects become intolerable.
	11.	Refer to Chapter 14 for treatment of skin lesions.
Provide urgent referral to an ophthalmologist in case of deeper cornea involvement, 
untreated disciform keratitis (can lead to scarring), neurotrophic ulceration (can lead to 
perforation), anterior uveitis or raised intraocular pressure (IOP).
Patient education
	
l Avoid contact with at-risk people such as pregnant women and people with weak 
immune systems to prevent spreading the VZV.
	
l It is highly contagious and a person with shingles can pass the VZV to anyone who is 
not immune to chickenpox. This usually occurs through direct contact with the oozing 
blisters. Keep the rash clean and covered. Scabs on blisters are not contagious.
	
l Good immunity helps in prevention of recurrence.
	
l Most cases of shingles clear up within 2–3 weeks. However, shingles pain continues 
long after the blisters have cleared and may persist up to 2 or more weeks.
	
l Punctal occlusion, artificial tears, bandage contact lenses, tarsorrhaphy, eyelid 
reconstructive surgery and conjunctival flaps may be required for the treatment of 
the various HZO complications. Tarsorrhaphy is especially useful in recalcitrant 
cases of neurotrophic keratitis.
	
l Vaccination with varicella vaccine for prevention: All children should receive two 
doses of the chickenpox vaccine, also known as a varicella immunization. Adults who 
are 50 years old or older should get a shingles vaccine (varicella-zoster) immunization.

RHINOSPORIDIOSIS OCULI (OCULAR RHINO)
Rhinosporidiosis is caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi. The disease spreads from 
animal hosts to humans by taking bath in the same pond in which cattle take bath. 
The spores of this disease spread through the polluted water and reach the eyes, 
nose, mouth, urethra and anus and grow there slowly. Children are more affected. 
Chhattisgarh has a high prevalence rate of this disease. The nose and nasopharynx 
are the most commonly involved in more than 70% of reported cases, with ocular 
manifestations accounting for 15% of cases.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Clinical presentation of rhinosporidiosis depends on the location of the lesion 
and is typically found in mucosal membranes. The second most common site of 
ocular lesions is the conjunctiva and lacrimal sac.
	
l The ocular rhino presents as a polypoidal and vascular mass commonly affecting 
the conjunctiva (soft, pink, fern petal–like growth of the conjunctiva with grey, 
white spots studded on the surface), lacrimal sac, sclera and eyelids. It can mimic 
a granuloma/papilloma or a burst chalazion.
	
l Lacrimal sac involvement presents with soft fluctuant swelling in the region of the 
lacrimal sac with a history of epistaxis or blood-stained discharge from the punctum. 
	
l More uncommon sites include the lip, palate, maxillary antrum, uvula, epiglottis, 
larynx, trachea, bronchus, ear, vulva, penis, rectum and scalp. In the rare occasion 
of a disseminated infection, the limbs, trunks, viscera and brain can be involved, 
with brain involvement often leading to fatalities.
	
l Diagnosis is mostly clinical by typical appearance. Definitive diagnosis of 
rhinosporidiosis depends on histological examination with immunohistochemistry 
primarily conducted through excisional biopsy, scraping of superficial lesions or 
fine needle aspiration.
Treatment (refer to an eye surgeon)
There is no definite medical treatment.
Surgical treatment
It involves surgical excision of the conjunctival mass and dacryocystectomy with 
cauterization of the lacrimal passages for lacrimal sac lesions. Presurgical dapsone as 
an adjuvant drug to surgery is effective in disseminated rhino.
Patient education
	
l Primary prevention is to avoid swimming in stagnant water, particularly in warm, 
tropical climates or endemic regions. Avoid using the ponds used by cattle for taking 
bath.
	
l If possible, make a separate pond for the use of cattle.

PAINFUL RED EYE
Painful red eye can result from various underlying conditions, each with distinct 
characteristics and management approaches.
	
l Acute infection with localized pain/tenderness without visual loss: 
Dacryoadenitis/dacryocystitis, lid abscess, cellulitis, hordeolum 
	
l Acute inflammation with diffuse pain/tenderness with mild visual 
loss: Conjunctivitis, keratitis, scleritis, anterior uveitis, orbital cellulitis 
	
l Acute inflammation with profound visual loss: Acute congestive glaucoma and 
secondary glaucoma, endophthalmitis
All painful red eye or visual loss should be referred immediately to a tertiary care 
level or an ophthalmologist.
GLAUCOMA
Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy which manifests as typical visual field defects 
(nerve fibre bundle defects), the aetiology of which is in some way related to IOP.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The classical triads of increased IOP, optic nerve head cupping and visual field 
changes are always present and are signs of progress of the disease and are the 
benchmark for assessing the response to therapy.
	
l Glaucoma comprises various types, including primary open-angle glaucoma, 
characterized by gradual optic nerve damage; angle-closure glaucoma, featuring 
sudden increases in IOP due to blocked drainage angles; and normal-tension 
glaucoma, where optic nerve damage occurs despite normal eye pressure levels.
	
l The width of the angle of the anterior chamber further differentiates the glaucoma 
into open and closed angle varieties.
CONGENITAL GLAUCOMA/BUPHTHALMOS
Each type of glaucoma requires specific management approaches tailored to effectively 
preserve vision, as outlined below.

	 3.	 Sudasinghe T. The regional sero-epidemiology of rhinosporidiosis in Sri Lankan humans and 
animals. Acta Trop. 2011;120:72–81.
PAINFUL RED EYE
Painful red eye can result from various underlying conditions, each with distinct 
characteristics and management approaches.
	
l Acute infection with localized pain/tenderness without visual loss: 
Dacryoadenitis/dacryocystitis, lid abscess, cellulitis, hordeolum 
	
l Acute inflammation with diffuse pain/tenderness with mild visual 
loss: Conjunctivitis, keratitis, scleritis, anterior uveitis, orbital cellulitis 
	
l Acute inflammation with profound visual loss: Acute congestive glaucoma and 
secondary glaucoma, endophthalmitis
All painful red eye or visual loss should be referred immediately to a tertiary care 
level or an ophthalmologist.
GLAUCOMA
Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy which manifests as typical visual field defects 
(nerve fibre bundle defects), the aetiology of which is in some way related to IOP.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The classical triads of increased IOP, optic nerve head cupping and visual field 
changes are always present and are signs of progress of the disease and are the 
benchmark for assessing the response to therapy.
	
l Glaucoma comprises various types, including primary open-angle glaucoma, 
characterized by gradual optic nerve damage; angle-closure glaucoma, featuring 
sudden increases in IOP due to blocked drainage angles; and normal-tension 
glaucoma, where optic nerve damage occurs despite normal eye pressure levels.
	
l The width of the angle of the anterior chamber further differentiates the glaucoma 
into open and closed angle varieties.
CONGENITAL GLAUCOMA/BUPHTHALMOS
Each type of glaucoma requires specific management approaches tailored to effectively 
preserve vision, as outlined below.

Chapter 13  Eye Diseases    683
References

image/a-typical-case-of-rhinosporidiosis [accessed January 14, 2024]. 
	 2.	 Ghosh AK, De Sarkar A, Bhaduri G, Datta A, Das A, Bandyopadhyay A. Ocular rhinosporidiosis. 
J Indian Med Assoc. 2004;102(12):732–764. 
	 3.	 Sudasinghe T. The regional sero-epidemiology of rhinosporidiosis in Sri Lankan humans and 
animals. Acta Trop. 2011;120:72–81.

characteristics and management approaches.
	
l Acute infection with localized pain/tenderness without visual loss: 
Dacryoadenitis/dacryocystitis, lid abscess, cellulitis, hordeolum 
	
l Acute inflammation with diffuse pain/tenderness with mild visual 
loss: Conjunctivitis, keratitis, scleritis, anterior uveitis, orbital cellulitis 
	
l Acute inflammation with profound visual loss: Acute congestive glaucoma and 
secondary glaucoma, endophthalmitis
All painful red eye or visual loss should be referred immediately to a tertiary care 
level or an ophthalmologist.

Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy which manifests as typical visual field defects

l The classical triads of increased IOP, optic nerve head cupping and visual field 
changes are always present and are signs of progress of the disease and are the 
benchmark for assessing the response to therapy.
	
l Glaucoma comprises various types, including primary open-angle glaucoma, 
characterized by gradual optic nerve damage; angle-closure glaucoma, featuring

l The width of the angle of the anterior chamber further differentiates the glaucoma 
into open and closed angle varieties.
