Each type of glaucoma requires specific management approaches tailored to effectively 
preserve vision, as outlined below.

684    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The classic triad of manifestations, any one of which should arouse suspicion 
of glaucoma in an infant or a young child, includes epiphora, photophobia, 
blepharospasm and an enlarged cornea with haziness within the first few years.
	
l IOP is usually normal as sclera in children distends leading to increased corneal 
diameter.
Pharmacological treatment
The aim is to control IOP till definitive treatment, i.e. surgery, is performed.
	 1.	Timolol drops 0.25–0.5% eyedrops 1 drop instilled at 12-hourly interval
	
	Or
	
	Betaxolol 0.25–0.5% eyedrops 1 drop instilled at 12-hourly interval 
	 2.	Dorzolamide 1 drop instilled at 12-hourly interval
	 3.	Brimonidine strictly contraindicated in patients 2 years old or younger
	 4.	Tab. Acetazolamide 12 mg/kg in 3–4 divided doses.
Surgical treatment
Surgical treatment at a tertiary care centre includes goniotomy and trabeculotomy or 
trabeculotomy with trabeculectomy as well as glaucoma drainage devices. Monitor 
corneal diameter, IOP, disc changes and refraction periodically.
Secondary childhood glaucoma
It is secondary to certain developmental anomalies, which need to be treated along 
with the glaucoma.
Patient education
	
l It is a slowly progressive disease, usually amenable to surgery. Regular lifelong 
follow-up is a must for early detection of any failure/complications.
	
l The eye is vulnerable to trauma and thus contact sports may be restricted in these 
children.
	
l Screening of any child, especially the one having siblings, who has a large cornea, 
photophobia or excessive watering of the eyes should be done.
ANGLE-CLOSURE GLAUCOMA – ACUTE
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Acute pain, redness and blurring of vision in the affected eye, and halos around lights 
along with headache and vomiting in some cases may occur.
	
l Signs include a red eye with corneal oedema, hazy cornea, shallow anterior 
chamber and vertical oval dilated pupils with a high IOP.

Chapter 13  Eye Diseases    685
	
l Chronic angle-closure glaucoma ensues when repeated subacute attack leads 
to peripheral synechiae, zipping up of the angle and persistent rise of IOP with 
subsequent optic atrophy. 
	
l IOP is raised due to pupillary block.
Pharmacological treatment
	 1.	Inj. Mannitol 20%, 1.5–2 g/kg, IV infusion over half an hour
	
	Or
	
	Glycerol 50%, 1–1.5 g/kg in 50% solution orally, mixed with cold lemon or orange 
juice in 3–4 divided doses
	
	(Caution: It can cause hyperglycaemia in patients with diabetes. Do not drink 
water for 1 hour after ingesting the tablet; contraindications include dehydration 
or cardiac decompensation.)
	 2.	Pilocarpine 2% eyedrops every 15 minutes for 1 hour and thereafter 6 hourly 
started after IOP has been lowered by hyperosmotics as above
	 3.	Tab. Acetazolamide 500 mg stat followed by 250 mg every 6 hours and maintained 
till the definitive treatment of laser peripheral iridotomy relieves the pupillary block
	 4.	Timolol 0.5% eyedrops 2 times a day (if pressure is still high) to be continued till 
surgery
	
	Or
	
	Betaxolol 0.5% eyedrops 2 times a day (preferred in patients with asthma and 
patients with cardiac conduction defects) 
	 5.	Add, if required topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, alpha-2 adrenergic and 
prostaglandin analogues to control IOP.
	
	(Caution: All mydriatics/cycloplegic drugs which dilate the pupils are contraindicated.)
Monitoring: Once the IOP falls to early 20s by the treatment listed above – usually 
in a day or so – evaluate it by gonioscopy, disc cupping and visual field charting. 
Definitive treatment is iridotomy by laser or surgery depending on the facilities 
available. Prophylactic laser peripheral iridotomy should be performed on the fellow 
eyes as soon as possible.
	
l IOP is the most significant and titrable response. The disease can recur after a successful 
iridotomy so the patient should be under follow-up at 6-monthly intervals at least.
Patient education
	
l Do not ignore headache and chronic ache in the eyes and report to the eye specialist 
if coloured halos appear around light.
	
l Pilocarpine can induce myopia, increase inflammation and cause accommodative 
spasm in the young patient and miosis in an older patient who has concomitant 
cataract leading to diminished vision.
	
l Topical beta-blockers need to be used with caution in chronic obstructive pulmonary 
disease, myasthenia gravis, cardiac arrhythmias, diabetes mellitus, etc.

condition: Angle-Closure Glaucoma – Chronic 686 Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma
text:
686    Standard Treatment Guidelines
ANGLE-CLOSURE GLAUCOMA – CHRONIC
IOP is raised due to progressive angle closure or by repeated intermittent subacute 
attacks secondary to pupillary block. The condition is commonly asymptomatic until 
significant visual loss has occurred. The presentation is thus more akin to open-angle 
glaucoma. The clinical course resembles that of open-angle glaucoma in its lack of 
symptoms, modest elevation of IOP, progressive glaucomatous optic nerve damage and 
characteristic visual field loss. 
On gonioscopy, permanent peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) is present in chronic 
angle-closure glaucoma.

condition: Angle-Closure Glaucoma – Chronic 686 Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma
text:
1.	Timolol 0.25–0.5% or betaxolol 0.25–0.5% eyedrops 2 times a day usually required 
lifelong
	 2.	Brimonidine 0.2% eye drops 2 times a day
	 3.	Dorzolamide 2% eye drops 3 times a day
	 4.	Latanoprost 0.005% once at night time
Surgical treatment
Laser or surgical peripheral iridotomy is done to eliminate any element of pupillary 
block in the affected as well as the fellow eye. If the glaucoma is still uncontrolled on 
maximal tolerable medical therapy (i.e. two topical antiglaucoma medications), then 
glaucoma filtering surgery or trabeculectomy should be performed.
Repeat gonioscopy periodically as progressive angle closure can occur even with 
a patent peripheral iridectomy. An iridectomy with or without long-term use of ocular 
hypotensive medication will control the disease for most patients with chronic angle-closure 
glaucoma. Others may require subsequent filtering surgery or goniosynechialysis.
Patient education
Since the disease is asymptomatic, do not ignore non-specific headache or eye ache.
PRIMARY OPEN-ANGLE GLAUCOMA
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The IOP is usually greater than 21 mmHg with associated nerve head cupping 
and visual fields defects.
	
l The condition is usually asymptomatic; however, some complain of frequent 
change in spectacles and mild ache of the eyes.
	
l Gonioscopically, the angle of the anterior chamber (AC) is widely open.

condition: Angle-Closure Glaucoma – Chronic 686 Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma
text:
1.	Timolol 0.25–0.5% or Betaxolol 0.25–0.5% eyedrops 1 drop 12 hourly and the morning 
dose as early on waking as possible (suppresses aqueous humour production)
	 2.	Latanoprost 0.005% eyedrops given only once at bedtime (increases aqueous 
outflow) (Caution: Maintain constant cold chain; heat-stable preparation is also 
available.) 
Or 
Bimatoprost 0.03% eyedrops once at bedtime (does not require cold chain)
Or 
Travoprost 0.004% eyedrops once at bedtime (does not require cold chain)
	 3.	Brimonidine tartrate 0.2% twice daily (also increases uveoscleral outflow and 
confers neuroprotection)
If initial therapy fails, refer to a higher centre and substitute/add another 
agent preferably belonging to a different group. If the patient is not controlled 
on two topical drugs, then consider alternative treatment with either laser 
trabeculoplasty or glaucoma filtering surgery.
Check IOP and optic nerve head every 3 months and visual field at 6-monthly intervals.
Patient education
	
l Pilocarpine can cause accommodative spasm and induce myopia leading to brow 
ache and a need to readjust reading spectacles of the patient.
	
l Avoid instillation of more than 1 drop of the drug or double doses in case morning 
dose is missed.
	
l Most drugs, especially beta-blockers, cause burning and stinging sensation on 
instillation. Chronic use can lead to dry eyes and tear supplements may be required.
	
l Explain to patients about punctual occlusion, i.e. pressing the medial end of the 
lower lid, to increase drug and cornea contact time.
	
l In patients with diabetes, do not give timolol eyedrops as they can mask the warning 
symptoms of hypoglycaemia. Give cautiously in asthma, myasthenia gravis and 
cardiac arrhythmia.
	
l Avoid a sedentary lifestyle.
	
l Perform annual screening of high-risk individuals, i.e. high myopia, large cups more 
than 0.5:1 or asymmetry in cups of more than 0.2, or any person with a positive 
family history of glaucoma, or aged >35 years for IOP and fundus examination.
Lens-Induced Glaucoma
Lens-induced glaucoma occurs secondary to the cataractous lens either by leakage of lens 
protein or by lens intumescence. In addition to medically lowering the IOP, the cataractous 
lens needs to be removed, under steroid cover, to suppress the inflammatory element.

688    Standard Treatment Guidelines
References
	 1.	 AAO PPP Glaucoma Panel, Hoskins Centre for Quality Eye Care. Primary Angle Closure PPP 
– 2020. https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/primary-angle-closure-disease-
ppp [accessed January 14, 2024].
	 2.	 American Academy of Ophthalmology. Angle-Closure Glaucoma. 2013, https://www. aao.org/
munnerlyn-laser-surgery-centre/angleclosure-glaucoma-19 [accessed January 14, 2024]. 
	 3.	 Allingham, Ramji, Fredman, Moroi, Shafranov, Shields (eds), In: Shields Textbook of Glaucoma. 
6th ed. Lippincott William & Wilkins; 2012.
	 4.	 Salmon JF, Sharma T. Chronic angle closure. Ophthalmology. 2005;112(10):1844. 
CORNEAL ULCER (ULCERATIVE KERATITIS)
Corneal ulcer is defined as superficial suppurative inflammation occurring in the eyes 
with some predisposing factors. It may be classified as follows: (i) bacterial corneal 
ulcer, (ii) fungal corneal ulcer (mycotic keratitis), (iii) viral corneal ulcer (herpetic 
keratitis) and (iv) acanthamoeba keratitis. Corneal ulcers frequently occur in the eyes 
with some predisposing factors.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Pain, redness, excessive tearing, photophobia, sticky discharge, swollen lids and 
blurred vision, blepharospasm, ciliary congestion, corneal haziness, infiltration 
of the cornea, ulcer/abscess in the cornea
	
l Decreased corneal sensitivity, hypopyon, iritis, secondary glaucoma and superficial 
corneal vascularization; corneal ulcer stained green with fluorescein 2%
	
l Complications: Corneal thinning, ectasia, descemetocoele, secondary glaucoma, 
perforation and its sequelae including endophthalmitis or panophthalmitis. 
Treatment (to be managed by an ophthalmologist)
Perform corneal scrapings from the base and edges of the ulcer to make smears for 
Gram, KOH and Giemsa stains and culture and sensitivity testing. Initiate therapy based 
on clinical picture and findings obtained on smears of corneal scrapings. As a first-line 
therapy, broad-spectrum antibiotics are started in all cases unless there is a high index 
of clinical suspicion of another form of infection or another form of infection is 
confirmed by scrapings. The treatment is modified according to the clinical response 
and result of culture and sensitivity of microorganisms.
A. Bacterial corneal ulcer

l Avoid patching.
	
l Use protective eyewear. Maintain proper ocular hygiene by regular cleaning of 
discharge twice a day.
	
l Remove contributory factors, e.g. trichiasis, foreign body, entropion and dacryocystitis.

Chapter 13  Eye Diseases    689
	
l Removal of necrotic tissue increases the efficacy of antibiotics.
	
l Prevention and treatment of complications – secondary glaucoma should be detected 
and treated adequately.

Start empirical therapy with broad-spectrum antibiotics and refer to an ophthalmologist.
	
l In a non–contact lenses wearer with a low risk of visual loss, Moxifloxacin or 
Gatifloxacin or Ciprofloxacin or polymyxin B eyedrops 1–2 hourly while awake
	
l In a contact lenses wearer with a low risk of visual loss, Moxifloxacin or 
Gatifloxacin eyedrops + Tobramycin or Polymyxin B 1–2 hourly while awake and/
or ointment Ciprofloxacin or Tobramycin 1–4 times a day
	
l In cases with doubtful risk of visual loss, Moxifloxacin or Gatifloxacin eyedrops 
plus Tobramycin or Polymyxin B, every 5 minutes for 5 times, then every 
30 minutes till midnight, and then 1 hourly
	
l In patients with a high risk of visual loss (ulcer size >1.5–2 mm), combination of 
two drugs
	
l Definitive therapy is started based on the culture and sensitivity of microorganisms.
	 Hospital admission is necessary for sight-threatening/impending perforation/non-
compliant patient or not able to follow-up daily.
	
	1.  Fortified Cefazoline 5% eyedrops (50 mg/mL) (mix 5 mL of distilled water in 
250 mg of Cefazoline solution) 
	
	Note: Prepare solution using aseptic technique and Vancomycin 5% 
(25 mg/mL) eyedrops instilled 1 drop every 30 minutes or 1 hourly round the 
clock for at least 24 hours
	
	2.  Topical fortified Gentamicin (mix 2 mL 80 mg injectable solution of 
Gentamicin in one vial of commercially available 0.3% 4 mL Gentamicin 
eyedrop solution) 
	
	Note: Prepare solution should be prepared fresh using aseptic technique or Tobra­
mycin 14 mg/mL (1.4%), instilled 1 drop every 0.5–1 hour for the first 24 hours
	
		
Frequency of administration is reduced according to the response and 
continued for 2–3 weeks. If compliance with frequency of topical instillation 
as above is not possible:
	
Cefazolin 100 mg and Gentamicin 20 mg subconjunctival injection after 
anaesthetizing the conjunctiva
	
Or
	
May use fortified Tobramycin 14 mg/mL solution in place of Gentamicin. 
For suspected methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), Vancomycin and for 
Pseudomonas, fortified Ceftazidime may be added
3.	Atropine sulphate 1% eyedrops/ointment to be applied 2 or 3 times per day 
4.	Tear substitutes 3–4 times daily
5.	Tab. Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
6.	Tab. Vitamin C once daily

690    Standard Treatment Guidelines
7.	Tab. Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily or Tab. Ofloxacin 200 mg once daily 
for 5–7 days for Pseudomonas infection and severe cases.
8.	Parenteral antibiotics indicated in perforated corneal ulcer, impending 
perforation, corneal ulcer following perforating injury and infections caused 
by Neisseria or Haemophilus microorganism
Note: Corticosteroids are contraindicated in corneal ulcers. If associated with secondary 
glaucoma, see the section ‘Glaucoma’.
Refer to an ophthalmologist at a higher centre in case of no improvement in signs 
and symptoms after 48 hours or whole cornea being hazy, large ulcer, severe ocular 
trauma, other ocular structures affected or intractable pain, and impending perforation/
perforated ulcer.
Non-healing ulcer
(Caution: Corticosteroids are contraindicated.) 
	
l Avoid corneal injury by protective eyewear. 
	
l Avoid self-medication and traditional remedies such as cow’s urine, honey, juice, 
milk and kajal. 
	
l Prompt visit for eye checkup on experiencing a foreign body falling into the eye.
Surgical procedure
	
l Conjunctival flap, amniotic membrane graft, therapeutic or tectonic keratoplasty, 
cyanoacrylate glue with bandage contact lens
B. Fungal corneal ulcer (mycotic keratitis)
Mycotic keratitis usually develops 2–3 weeks following a corneal injury with an 
organic or vegetative matter. The common fungi causing fungal keratitis in order of 
frequency are Fusarium, Aspergillus, Candida and Curvularia.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Severe signs, less symptoms, dry, rough or cheesy appearance with feathery 
margins, satellite lesions, immune ring, endothelial plaque, thick immobile 
infected hypopyon

The management approach to fungal keratitis involves topical antifungal agents such as 
Natamycin or Voriconazole, along with frequent corneal debridement to remove fungal 
elements. In severe cases or those resistant to medical therapy, surgical intervention 
such as corneal transplantation may be necessary. Early diagnosis and prompt initiation 
of appropriate antifungal treatment are crucial for optimizing outcomes.
	 1.	Natamycin 5% suspension 1–2 hourly for the first 24–48 hours and then 4–6 hourly 
for 2–3 weeks after resolution

Chapter 13  Eye Diseases    691
	
	And/or
	 2.	1% eyedrops 1 hourly if the desired response is not seen with a single agent
	
	Or
	
	Amphotericin B 0.15–0.25% formulation prepared in distilled water every 
15–30 minutes for 24–48 hours, and then 1–2 hourly continued for 2–3 weeks or till 
resolution of keratitis
	 3.	In case of immunocompromised patients, spreading ulcer, perforation or impending 
perforation:
	
	Cap./Tab. Fluconazole 200 mg 2 times a day for 2–3 weeks
	 4.	Since superadded bacterial infection is common, Moxifloxacin or Tobramycin 
eyedrops added (see the section ‘Bacterial Conjunctivitis’)
	 5.	Atropine 1% eyedrops/ointment 3 times a day
	 6.	Tear substitutes 3–4 times a day
	 7.	Regular debridement of the necrotic tissue to be done by an ophthalmologist
	 8.	Antiglaucoma treatment if required
Surgical treatment
It includes subconjunctival/intrastromal/intracameral antifungal injections, conjunctival 
flap and therapeutic keratoplasty.
C. Viral corneal ulcer (herpes simplex keratitis)
It is characterized by unilateral or bilateral recurrent attacks of keratitis in the form of 
infections, epithelial keratitis, stromal keratitis, endothelialitis, etc. The attack is often 
precipitated by trivial trauma, fever, cold, emotional stress, menstruation, etc.
Treatment (epithelial keratitis)
	 1.	Acyclovir eye ointment 3% 5 times a day for 2–3 weeks or Tab. Acyclovir 400 mg 
5 times a day for 10 days or Ganciclovir ophthalmic gel 0.15% 5 times a day till 
healing of ulcer, followed by 3 times a day for 7 days
	 2.	Topical Homatropine 2% or Cyclopentolate 0.5% eyedrops 2 times a day
	 3.	Broad-spectrum antibiotic as in the treatment of mucopurulent conjunctivitis till 
ulcer heals
	 4.	Artificial tear substitutes 3–4 times a day (Caution: Steroids are contraindicated.)
	 5.	Healing starts in 2–5 days and completes in 2 weeks. In case the ulcer does not heal 
in 2 weeks, is neuroparalytic or is resistant to acyclovir, refer to an ophthalmologist. 
Also refer to an ophthalmologist if more than two recurrences occur in a year and give 
Tab. Acyclovir 400 mg 2 times a day for 3–6 months for prevention of recurrence.
Treatment (Stromal keratitis)

1.	Mild disease
	
	Fluorometholone 0.1% Or Loteprednol etabonate ophthalmic suspension 0.2–0.5% 
4 times daily (Caution: Shake the bottle well before use. Do not use for longer 
than 14 days.)
	
	For milder disease, lower concentration of 0.12% Prednisolone Or 1:10 dilution 
Dexamethasone 0.1% eyedrops 4 times a day, tapered slowly to once daily or once 
a week before stopping
	
	Moderate-to-severe disease
	
	Dexamethasone 0.1% Or Prednisolone 1% eyedrops every 3 hours, tapered 
gradually on the basis of clinical response and continued till lesions heal
	
	(Caution: Avoid corticosteroids in the presence of epithelial ulceration.)
	 2.	Tab. acyclovir 400 mg 5 times a day Or prophylactic acyclovir eye ointment 
5 times a day to be continued as long as steroids and tapered with corticosteroids 
to prophylactic doses
	 3.	Homatropine 2% eyedrops 1 drop 3 times a day; in severe cases, atropine 1% 
eyedrops 1 drop 2 times a day
	 4.	Artificial tears 3–4 times a day
Mixed epithelial and stromal keratitis
First treat epithelial and then treat stromal keratitis as per the protocol mentioned above.
Patient education
	
l To report to an ophthalmologist in every case of eye redness, pain or diminution 
of vision
	
l Regular follow-up at 6-monthly intervals since viral keratitis is known to recur
References
	 1.	 Viral diseases of the cornea and external eye. In: Albert DM, Jakobiec FA, Miller JW (eds), 
Albert and Jakobiec’s Principles and Practice of Ophthalmology. 3rd ed. Philadelphia, PA: WB 
Saunders Co; 2008, pp. 637–704.
	 2.	 American Academy of Ophthalmology. External Disease and Cornea. Section 8. Published after 
collaborative review with the European Board of Ophthalmology Sub Committee. 2013–2014. 
	 3.	 World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia. Guidelines for the Management 
of Corneal Ulcer at Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Care Health Facilities in the South-East 
Asia Region. WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia; 2004, https://iris.who.int/bitstream/
handle/10665/205174/B3516.pdf?sequence=1 [accessed January 14, 2024].
CATARACT
Cataract refers to the opacification of crystalline lens at any age. The most common is 
senile cataract.

Chapter 13  Eye Diseases    693
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Gradual painless progressive diminution of vision occurs in one or both eyes.
	
l There occur excessive glare, monocular diplopia or polyopia, coloured halos 
around lights, diurnal variation in vision, change in colour values and fixed black 
spots before eyes.
	
l Ocular examination reveals greyish white or whitish lenticular opacity on torch 
light examinations depending on the stage of cataractogenesis, i.e. immature, 
mature or hypermature. Detailed evaluation of cataract changes and fundus 
examination is done after dilating the pupils using distant direct ophthalmoscopy, 
slit-lamp examination, direct ophthalmoscopy, etc.

Till date, no proven drug treatment exists to delay, prevent or reverse the development 
of senile cataract. Definitive treatment of senile cataract is lens extraction. Indications 
of lens extraction are visual handicap, interference in patient activities due to poor 
vision or glare disability even if cataract is immature. In mature and hypermature 
cataract, urgent lens extraction is done to prevent further complications such as 
glaucoma, iritis or displacement of lens.
Optical treatment
In early cataract, decreased vision may be improved by accurate refraction and 
prescribing corrective spectacles.
Surgical treatment
Indicated:
	
l To improve visual function in patients with symptomatic visual disability
	
l As surgical therapy for ocular disease (e.g. lens-related glaucoma or uveitis)
	
l To facilitate management of ocular disease (e.g. to allow a view of the fundus to 
monitor or treat diabetic retinopathy [DR] or glaucoma)
The choice of the procedure depends on the patient, the type of cataract, the 
availability of proper instruments and equipment and the degree to which the surgeon 
is comfortable and proficient in performing standard extracapsular cataract extraction 
(ECCE), phacoemulsification or non-phaco small incision surgery. Posterior chamber 
intraocular lens placed inside the capsular bag is the preferred modality. Newer technique 
includes femtosecond laser-assisted phacoemulsification, which is very costly. New 
generation cataract lenses, known as premium intraocular lenses (IOLs), not only correct 
astigmatism but also provide enhanced near and distance vision, reducing reliance on 
glasses after surgery. These lenses improve patients’ visual freedom and quality of life, 
offering options such as multifocal, toric, and extended depth of focus (EDOF) lenses.

condition: Dry Eyes Syndrome and Computer Vision Syndrome
text:
694    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Postoperative treatment
	 1.	Ciprofloxacin 0.3% eyedrops 4 times a day Or Moxifloxacin 0.3% eyedrops 1 drop 
6 hourly for 7 days
	 2.	Prednisolone acetate 1% Or Dexamethasone 0.1% eyedrops 1 drop 2 hourly to 4 
times a day depending on the inflammation with tapering over 4–6 weeks with 
declining frequency every week
	 3.	Lubricating eyedrops/mydriatics as per the operative procedure and advice of 
the surgeon
	 4.	Tab. Ibuprofen 400 mg 3 times a day after meals for pain relief
Patient education
	
l Diabetes mellitus and high body mass index are additional risk factors for the 
development of cataract. 
	
l Do not wait for maturation of cataract for undergoing cataract operation as 
complications may develop. Secondary glaucoma and other complications may 
develop if total cataract remains unoperated for a long time.
	
l Visual rehabilitation in the early postoperative period is faster in small-incision 
cataract surgery.
	
l Emphasize on personal hygiene and avoid rubbing, trauma and splashing of the eyes, 
dust, smoke and sunlight for 3 weeks. Wear protective dark glasses outdoors. Wash 
the head after 3 weeks.
	
l Schedule postoperative follow-up visits on days 2, 7, 15, 30 and 45. If necessary, 
schedule more frequent postoperative visits.
	
l Ensure frequent instillation of eyedrops as advised.
	
l Nd:YAG laser is used for posterior capsulotomy which is required to improve vision 
in a large percent of patients >1–3 years after cataract surgery with intraocular lens 
implantation.
References
	 1.	 Preoperative evaluation of the cataract patient. In: Albert DM, Jakobiec FA, Miller JW (eds), 
Albert and Jakobiec’s Principles and Practice of Ophthalmology. 3rd ed. Philadelphia, PA: WB 
Saunders Co; 2008, pp. 1415–1420.
	 2.	 Extracapsular cataract extraction. In: Albert DM, Jakobiec FA, Miller JW (eds), Albert and 
Jakobiec’s Principles and Practice of Ophthalmology. 3rd ed. Philadelphia, PA: WB Saunders 
Co; 2008, pp. 1431–1439.
	 3.	 Phacoemulsification. In: Albert DM, Jakobiec FA, Miller JW (eds), Albert and Jakobiec’s Principles 
and Practice of Ophthalmology. 3rd ed. Philadelphia, PA: WB Saunders Co; 2008, pp. 1441–1463.
DRY EYES SYNDROME AND COMPUTER 
VISION SYNDROME
It represents a diverse group of conditions characterized by symptoms of ocular discomfort 
and is associated with decreased tear production and/or abnormally rapid tear film 
evaporation. Abnormality in precorneal tear film results in ocular surface damage and dry 
eyes and affects 15% of elderly, especially females, and 20–30% of contact lens wearers. 
Dry eye may compromise results of corneal, cataract and refractive surgery.

condition: Dry Eyes Syndrome and Computer Vision Syndrome
text:
Chapter 13  Eye Diseases    695
Common causes for dry eyes syndrome 
Environmental: Excessive heat, air-conditioning and prolonged computer use
Systemic: Ageing and menopause; side effect of antihistamines, birth control pills, 
diuretics, psychotropic drugs, steroids, etc.; diseases like Sjögren's syndrome, 
rheumatoid arthritis and collagen vascular diseases
Local: Abnormality of the lacrimal gland, eyelids, ocular surface and lacrimal drainage 
system; topical medications and contact lens use
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Symptoms usually precede signs. Symptoms are ocular irritation and pain, 
dryness, grittiness, foreign body sensation, itching, burning, photophobia, 
redness, excessive tearing and blurring of vision. 
	
l Signs are conjunctival congestion, decreased tear, meniscus, irregular corneal 
surface and debris in the tear film.
	
l The condition also presents as corneal epithelial keratitis, fine or coarse, 
fluorescein/rose bengal staining and inflammation of the ocular surface in 
advanced cases. In severe cases, mucous plaques, corneal filaments, epithelial 
defects, secondary infections, and thinning and perforation of the cornea can 
occur. There may be associated blepharitis, meibomianitis and eyelid abnormality.
	
l Various tests for dry eyes include Schirmer’s test, break-up time, conjunctival 
cytology and tear osmolarity. 
	
l In severe cases, complications like persistent epitheliopathy, sterile corneal 
ulcerations and secondary microbial infections can occur.

Lack of correlation between signs and symptoms makes it difficult to diagnose 
mild-to-moderate forms of dry eyes.

condition: Dry Eyes Syndrome and Computer Vision Syndrome
text:
In mild cases, apply hot compresses and perform eyelid massage. Wear protective 
goggles outdoors. 
Avoid continuously watching monitors (computer/TV/mobile); take a break every 
20 minutes to look 20 feet away for 20 seconds (20–20–20 rule). 
Avoid direct fan/AC air on eyes.

Mild dry eyes
Artificial tear substitutes with preservatives up to four times a day (Methylcellulose 
0.5–1%, HPMC, Polyvinyl alcohol [1.4%], Polyvinyl pyrrolidone [3–5%])

696    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Moderate dry eyes
	 1.	Artificial tears without preservatives 4 times to 1 hourly a day (Carboxymethyl 
cellulose 0.05 and 0.1%)
	 2.	Lubricating eye ointment, HPMC gel at bedtime
	 3.	In case of excessive mucin secretions, 10% Acetylcysteine eyedrops 1–2 drops into 
the affected eye 3–4 times daily
	 4.	Topical Cyclosporine A 0.05% eyedrops twice a day
	
	Refer to an ophthalmologist for reversible occlusion and lower punctum (plugs).
Severe dry eyes
Follow (1)–(4) same as in moderate cases as above with increased frequency with eye 
pad/bandage contact lens. Artificial tears with glycerine and electrolyte can also be used 
for hydration and healthy corneal epithelium.
	
l Topical Prednisolone 1% or Dexamethasone 0.1% eyedrops, tapered over 4 weeks
	
l Sodium hyaluronate 0.1% eyedrops 3–4 times a day
Other therapies may include oral flaxseed oil, oral omega-3 fatty acids, autologous 
serum tears, topical vitamin A, bandage contact lens or a scleral lens.
Surgical treatment
	
l Reversible inferior punctal occlusion (punctal plugs)/permanent occlusion
	
l Tarsorrhaphy (lateral and medial), conjunctival/mucous membrane grafting, parotid 
duct transplantation, amniotic membrane transplant, stem cell transplant
References
	 1.	 Cornea. In: Bagheri N, Wajda BN (eds), The Wills Eye Manual. 7th ed. Philadelphia, PA: Wolters 
Kluwer; 2017, pp. 118–122.
	 2.	 AAO PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee, Hoskins Centre for Quality Eye Care. Dry Eye 
Syndrome Preferred Practice Pattern (PPP) – 2018. American Academy of Ophthalmology. https://
www.aao.org/preferred-practice-pattern/dry-eye-syndrome-ppp-2018 [accessed January 14, 2024]. 
	 3.	 American Academy of Ophthalmology. Basic and Clinical Science Course, Section 8, External 
Diseases and Cornea. 2007–2008, pp. 61–80. 
	 4.	 Ocular surface disease [Section 6]. In: Foster SC, Azar DT, Dohlman CH (eds), Smolin and 
Throft’s The Cornea, Scientific Foundations and Clinical Practice. 4th ed. 2005, pp. 573–646.
REFRACTIVE ERRORS
Refractive errors (ametropia) are the optical defects of the eye in which the parallel 
rays of light entering the eye do not come to focus on the fovea centralis. Ametropia 
includes myopia, hypermetropia and astigmatism. Astigmatism may be combined with 
myopia or hypermetropia.
SALIENT FEATURES
Refractive errors are characterized by blurred vision, subnormal vision, eye strain 
or asthenopia, headache, tearing, latent or manifest strabismus, etc.

No pharmacological treatment is available for ametropia.
Optical and surgical
	
l Accurate retinoscopy and corrective spectacles or contact lenses
	
l Keratorefractive surgery
Patient education
If spectacles are not used, the patient may develop amblyopia. Young patients (aged 
20 years and older) opting for laser correction should wait till the refraction is stable 
for at least 1 year.
Refer to an ophthalmologist for high-end pathological myopia for funduscopy and 
low vision/blind rehabilitation.
Reference
	 1.	 Prescription of spectacles. Albert DM, Jakobiec FA, Miller JW (eds), Albert and Jakobiec’s 
Principles and Practice of Ophthalmology. 3rd ed. Philadelphia, PA: WB Saunders Co; 2008, 
pp. 5269–5274.
STRABISMUS (SQUINT)
Any child presenting with strabismus should have the following conditions ruled out:
	
l Refractive error – refraction should be done under full cycloplegia, i.e. Atropine 
ointment 1% 3 times a day for 3 days especially if younger than 5 years and 
Homatropine for those aged 6–18 years prior to performing retinoscopy. If any 
refractive error is present, that should be fully corrected by spectacles for at least 
3–6 months, before performing definitive surgical therapy for strabismus.
	
l Any opacity in the media, e.g. cataract, corneal opacity and retinoblastoma should 
be corrected.
	
l Amblyopia element whether induced by strabismus or vice versa should be treated 
with occlusion therapy or other modality before treating strabismus.
	
l Important differential diagnosis of pseudostrabismus must be kept in mind.

Correct the refractive error or associated cataract, corneal opacity, etc. Perform fusion 
exercises for intermittent exotropia and other orthoptic exercises.
Surgical
Definitive therapy is surgical realignment of the axis once other associated features 
have been treated by surgery on extraocular muscles.

698    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Patient education
	
l Functional improvement in strabismus is best between 3 and 5 years of age.
	
l It is a misconception that squinting is spontaneously corrected as the child grows; 
therefore, treatment of strabismus should not be delayed.
References
	 1.	 Concomitant strabismus. In: Albert DM, Jakobiec FA, Miller JW (eds), Albert and Jakobiec’s 
Principles and Practice of Ophthalmology. 3rd ed. Philadelphia, PA: WB Saunders Co; 2008, 
pp. 4333–4343.
	 2.	 Paediatrics. In: Bagheri N, Wajda BN (eds), The Wills Eye Manual. 7th ed. Philadelphia, PA: 
Wolters Kluwer; 2017, pp. 325–328.
IRIDOCYCLITIS (ANTERIOR UVEITIS)
Uveitis is defined as inflammation of the uveal tract, i.e. iris, ciliary body and choroid. 
Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body constitutes iridocyclitis or anterior uveitis. 
Anterior uveitis (AU) is termed “acute” when the inflammation lasts less than 
6 weeks and “chronic” when it lasts longer. Chronic forms of anterior uveitis are more 
insidious, and the patient may be asymptomatic. Regular eye examinations provide the 
opportunity to screen for chronic anterior uveitis. The acute nature of anterior uveitis 
in most cases leads the patient to seek care, resulting in early detection of the disease.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Acute anterior uveitis is characterized by painful red eye, diffuse periorbital 
pain, photophobia, blurred vision and excessive tearing. There is no purulent or 
mucopurulent discharge.
	
l Ocular examination reveals ciliary injection, normal or deep anterior chamber, 
small irregular pupil, posterior synechia, media opacities, tenderness of the 
eyeball and variable decrease in vision.
	
l Slit lamp biomicroscopy is essential for diagnosis and monitoring the treatment. 
Slit lamp examination in active cases reveals marked flare and cells in the anterior 
chamber and fine keratic precipitates at the back of the cornea. Posterior segment 
involvement and changes in intraocular pressure may occur in anterior uveitis.
	
l The condition needs extensive systemic workup. Important differential diagnosis 
includes acute conjunctivitis and acute congestive glaucoma.
Treatment (refer immediately to an ophthalmologist)
Red flag signs
	
l AU is diagnosed by excluding posterior ocular involvement (vitreous, retina, choroid). 
	
l Advise exercise caution for endophthalmitis in cases with a history of intraocular surgery.
	
l Be vigilant for metastatic endophthalmitis, such as Klebsiella endophthalmitis, and 
inquire about recent fevers or sepsis.

Chapter 13  Eye Diseases    699
	
l Be cautious about infectious keratitis, as steroids may reveal underlying herpes 
simplex epithelial disease.
	
l Watch out for masquerade syndrome, including malignancy or intraocular foreign body.
	
l In chronic angle-closure glaucoma, iris ischaemia can manifest as anterior chamber 
cells.

1.	Dexamethasone 0.1% eyedrops or Prednisolone acetate 1% eyedrops 1–2 hourly, 
tapered gradually on the basis of slit-lamp evidence of anterior chamber activity; 
if topical steroids required for long term, switch over to Loteprednol 0.5% or 
fluoromethanol 0.1% to decrease chances of secondary glaucoma
	 2.	Homatropine hydrobromide 2% eyedrop solution in mild to moderate inflammation
	
	Or
	
	Atropine sulphate 1% eye ointment once or thrice a day in severe inflammation
	 3.	If no response (within 7 days), severe anterior uveitis, bilateral involvement and 
panuveitis:
	
	Tab. Prednisolone 1 mg/kg or 40–80 mg/day orally every morning at breakfast or 
on alternate days; tapered gradually depending on satisfactory clinical response 
over 2–4 weeks’ period 
	 4.	Subconjunctival mydricaine injections containing Atropine and Adrenaline along 
with Lignocaine to prevent the formation of permanent posterior synechiae
	 5.	If no response within 1 week or non-compliant, posterior uveitis or severe uveitis:
	
	Periocular corticosteroids – subconjunctival or posterior subtenon injection (preferred)
	
	Methylprednisolone acetate – 20, 40, 80 mg/mL or Triamcinolone acetonide 
(10, 40 mg/mL) 0.5–1.0 mL
	
	(Caution: Contraindication – infectious uveitis, e.g. herpetic or toxoplasmosis, 
known steroid responder, patients with glaucoma or elevated IOP)
	 6.	If no response or development of steroid complications, immunosuppressive 
therapy given under supervision of an ophthalmologist
	 7.	Close monitoring of IOP and treatment appropriately; if elevated, Timolol maleate 
0.5% eyedrops 2 times a day and/or Acetazolamide 250 mg 4 times a day 6 hourly; 
Pilocarpine avoided
	 8.	Tab. Ibuprofen 400 mg 3 times a day
	 9.	Identify specific cause and manage accordingly (syphilis, tuberculosis, herpes 
simplex, herpes zoster, toxoplasmosis, etc.)

l The initial follow-up of patients with anterior uveitis should be scheduled between 
1 and 7 days, depending on severity. The evaluation should include the following

700    Standard Treatment Guidelines
procedures: visual acuity, IOP measurement, slit-lamp examination, assessment of 
cells and flare, ophthalmoscopy and evaluation of response to therapy.
	
l After the initial workup, the number and frequency of follow-up visits vary. If 
at follow-up, the anterior chamber reaction is improving, the medicines may be 
continued or reduced, depending on the severity of the initial reaction.
	
l Cycloplegics may be discontinued when the cellular reaction has subsided and 
flare is absent. Steroids should be continued until the cellular reaction is minimal 
or absent. Steroids should be withdrawn slowly (tapered). During tapering, observe 
the patient for signs of increased inflammation. 
Surgical treatment
Surgical treatment is required for various complications of anterior uveitis.
Follow-up: Chronic anterior uveitis may require long-term use of low-dose topical 
steroids (e.g. 0.125% Prednisolone every other day). In steroid responder (i.e. increased 
IOP), concurrent treatment with a beta-blocker is advised unless contraindicated. Once 
the patient's condition stabilizes, follow-up should be done every 1–6 months.
Patient education
	
l Explain that recurrent/chronic nature of the disease may interfere with vision, 
particularly in complicated cataract and steroid-induced glaucoma.
	
l Patients with a history of uveitis, juvenile rheumatic arthritis and ankylosing 
spondylitis should be instructed to report immediately to an ophthalmologist even 
if there is mild diminution of vision.
	
l Recurrent episodes of anterior uveitis and subsequent therapy may lead to various 
complications particularly complicated cataract and steroid-induced glaucoma.
	
l Possible side effects or toxic effects of long-term topical periocular and systemic 
corticosteroid therapy should be explained.
References
	 1.	 Uveitis. In: Bagheri N, Wajda BN (eds), The Wills Eye Manual. 7th ed. Philadelphia, PA: Wolters 
Kluwer; 2017, pp. 601–610. 
	 2.	 Uveitis and other intraocular inflammations. In: Yanoff M, Duker JS (eds), Ophthalmology. 5th 
ed. Edinburgh: Elsevier; 2019, pp. 865–871.
	 3.	 Harthan JS, Opitz DL, Fromstein SR, Morettin CE. Diagnosis and treatment of anterior uveitis: 
optometric management. Clin Optom (Auckl). 2016;8:23–35.
ORBITAL CELLULITIS
Suppurative inflammation of adipose and soft tissues of the orbit is termed as orbital 
cellulitis. It occurs more frequently in children than in adults. Periorbital and orbital 
cellulitis represent distinct clinical conditions, presenting with overlapping features that 
can pose challenges in differentiation.
Orbital cellulitis involves an infection within the orbit, specifically postseptal 
structures located posterior to the orbital septum. The majority of cases (more than

Chapter 13  Eye Diseases    701
80%) are associated with local sinus disease, particularly ethmoid sinus. Other 
causes include extension of infection from dental abscess; ear, face and lid infection; 
panophthalmitis; dacryocystitis; dacryoadenitis; postoperative to any facial or ocular 
surgery; perforating injury; and haematogenous spread. On the other hand, periorbital 
cellulitis pertains to an infection affecting the eyelids and surrounding skin without 
involving the orbit, designated as preseptal structures anterior to the orbital septum. 
Notably, neither infection involves the globe.
SALIENT FEATURES
There occur marked unilateral axial irreducible proptosis, restricted and painful 
ocular motility, lid oedema, chemosis of the conjunctiva and constitutional 
symptoms such as fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, malaise and prostration.
Common organisms
	
l Adult: Staphylococcus species, Streptococcus species, Bacteroides species
	
l Children: Haemophilus influenzae
	
l Following trauma: Gram-negative rods
	
l Dental abscess: Mixed, aggressive aerobes and anaerobes
	
l Immunocompromised patients (diabetes, chemotherapy, HIV infection): Fungi 
including Mucor and Aspergillus
Treatment (refer immediately to an ophthalmologist and hospitalize)
Orbital cellulitis is an emergency with serious complications including intracranial 
infection, cavernous sinus thrombosis and vision loss.
	 1.	Immediate CT/MRI scan of the head and orbits to see the extent of cellulitis as well 
as rule out intracranial involvement
	 2.	Immediate consultation with ENT and ophthalmology specialists and paediatrician 
in case orbital cellulitis suspected in children, if moderate to severe periorbital 
cellulitis present, or no improvement or deterioration after 24–48 hours of therapy 
	 3.	Investigations: WBC count, CRP, blood culture, microbiology swab (conjunctiva, 
nasopharynx, external wounds)

Give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics to cover Gram-positive, Gram-negative 
and anaerobic organisms initially, and then switch to narrower-spectrum antibiotics as 
per report of culture and sensitivity. If clinical condition of the patient improves, then 
switch to oral medication (total duration 10–14 days).
	 1.	Inj. Ampicillin + Sulbactam 3 g IV 6 hourly in adults
	
	In children: 300 mg/kg/day in 2–3 four divided doses (maximum daily dose 12 g)
	
	Or

702    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
	Inj. Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV 8 hourly in adults
	
	In children: 240 mg of Piperacillin component/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses 
(maximum daily dose 18 g Piperacillin)
	 2.	In suspected MRSA or in those with suspected meningitis, add Inj. Vancomycin 
IV at 15 mg/kg every 12–24 hours in adults with normal renal function
	
	In children: 40 mg/kg/day in two or three divided doses (maximum daily dose of 2 g)
	
	For adults who are allergic to Penicillin, Vancomycin as above plus Ceftriaxone 
2 g IV daily 
	
	And
	
	Inj. Metronidazole 500 mg IV 8 hourly
	
	For Vancomycin allergy, Clindamycin 600–900 mg IV every 8 hours
	
	In children: 20–40 mg/kg/day IV 6–8 hourly
	 3.	Oxymetazoline 0.05% nasal drops 2–3 drops in each nostril 2 times a day, in 
children: 0.025%
	 4.	Add, if required, nasal corticosteroid spray to quicken the resolution of sinusitis
	 5.	Moxifloxacin or bacitracin ointment 4 times a day for corneal exposure and chemosis
	 6.	Lubricating eyedrops/artificial tears 1–2 hourly or antibiotic eye ointment 5 times 
a day to prevent exposure keratopathy
	 7.	Symptomatic therapy for pain: antipyretics and analgesics in usual doses
Note: The use of systemic corticosteroids in the management of orbital cellulitis remains 
controversial. If systemic corticosteroids are considered, it is probably safest to wait for 24–
48 hours until an adequate intravenous antibiotic loading dose has been given (3–4 doses).
Fungal infection
Parenteral antifungal therapy along with surgical debridement of paranasal sinuses:
Inj. Amphotericin B deoxycholate: Test dose of 1 mg IV infused over 20–30 
minutes and loading dose of 0.25–0.5 mg/kg IV infused over 2–6 hours followed by 
maintenance dose of 0.25–1 mg/kg IV every day or up to 1.5 mg/kg IV once daily (may 
increase gradually by 0.25-mg increments/day). Reconstitute by dissolving the contents 
of a 50-mg vial of Amphotericin B in powder form in 5% dextrose.
Note: All the patients must be carefully monitored at least daily for vision, fundus, 
corneal exposure, ocular motility, pupillary reaction, corneal sensations, proptosis and 
systemic status including CNS function.
Surgical treatment
	 1.	If the orbit is tight, an optic neuropathy is present or the IOP is severely elevated, 
immediate canthotomy/cantholysis may be needed.
	 2.	Surgical drainage is indicated if orbital abscess forms based on clinical features, 
USG and CT scan findings; if there is poor response or no response to the IV 
antibiotic therapy; or if there is a threat to ocular function.
	 3.	Perform tarsorrhaphy or Frost suture to prevent exposure keratopathy.
	 4.	Perform sinusotomy or craniotomy for pus in paranasal sinus or brain abscess 
respectively.

Chapter 13  Eye Diseases    703
Patient education
	
l Any ear, sinus or dental infection, especially in children, should be treated promptly.
	
l Any child presenting with unexplained lid oedema or cellulitis should be 
immediately referred to an ophthalmologist.
References
	 1.	 Infectious processes of the orbit. In: Albert DM, Jakobiec FA, Miller JW (eds), Albert and 
Jakobiec’s Principles and Practice of Ophthalmology. 3rd ed. Philadelphia, PA: WB Saunders 
Co; 2008, pp. 2961–2975.
	 2.	 Infectious orbital disease. In: Bagheri N, Wajda BN (eds), The Wills Eye Manual. 7th ed. 
Philadelphia, PA: Wolters Kluwer; 2017, pp. 285–290.
	 3.	 Orbital cellulitis. UpToDate. January 17, 2023, https://www.uptodate.com/contents/orbital-
cellulitis [accessed January 14, 2024].
SUDDEN PAINLESS VISUAL LOSS
Sudden visual loss is a common complaint with variable presentations among patients 
of different ages. The differential diagnoses of sudden vision loss are vast. In general, 
monocular vision loss usually indicates an ocular problem. Binocular vision loss is 
usually cerebral in origin. Common ocular conditions are optic neuritis, massive vitreous 
haemorrhage, Eales’ disease, diabetic/hypertensive retinopathy, occlusion of central 
retinal artery/vein, toxic amblyopia due to spurious alcohol poisoning, massive retinal 
detachment (RD), central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) and macular oedema.
Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is the single most important ocular 
emergency and needs treatment urgently.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Eye is normal externally but there occur episodic transient visual obscuration or 
sudden profound painless severe loss of vision, reduced visual evoked potential (VEP), 
abnormal reaction of the pupil, cherry red spot and pale disc in the fundus in CRAO.
	
l A marked abnormality in pupil is relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) 
fundus in which there occurs optic disc oedema with flame-shaped haemorrhages 
in papillitis/neuroretinitis and normal disc in retrobulbar neuritis.
	
l In central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), there occur massive retinal and pre-
retinal haemorrhages, disc oedema and venous engorgement.
Treatment (refer immediately to an ophthalmologist)
	
l Rule out malingering – the patient may or may not respond to pharmacological 
therapy or may even recover spontaneously. 
	
l In multiple sclerosis, a proven case may benefit with the following: Inj. 
Methylprednisolone for 3 days followed by an oral steroid.
	
l CRAO may benefit with immediate IOP lowering – pressure on globe, paracentesis 
and Tab. Acetazolamide 500 mg stat followed by 250 mg every 6 hours.
	
l Assess cardiology, lipid, coagulation profile, etc., to prevent recurrence or other eye 
involvement. For management of specific problems, see below.

704    Standard Treatment Guidelines
ENDOPHTHALMITIS
Endophthalmitis is of two types: (i) exogenous endophthalmitis caused by the direct 
inoculation of infecting agent through breach in the continuity of ocular coats, e.g. 
postoperative and post-traumatic; and (ii) endogenous endophthalmitis resulting due 
to haematogenous spread of infective agents. Depending on the aetiology of infectious 
agents, both these categories may be bacterial or fungal.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There is a history of eye surgery, penetrating injury, fever, infection or 
predisposing systemic diseases leading to metastatic endophthalmitis.
	
l There occur marked visual loss, ocular pain, headache, ocular discharge, 
photophobia, intense redness and lid swelling.
	
l Ocular examination reveals conjunctival and ciliary congestion, and profound 
decrease in vision even up to perception of light with accurate or inaccurate 
projection of rays. Corneal oedema, hypopyon, signs of uveitis, reduction in 
intraocular pressure and exudation in the vitreous leading to reduced or absent 
fundus reflex are the other associated features. The clinical picture is variable 
depending on the route of entry, infectious process and duration of the disease.
Treatment (refer immediately to an ophthalmologist as an emergency)
Postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis

1.	Intravitreal injection of antibiotics after drawing 0.3 mL vitreous tap for laboratory 
diagnosis – Inj. Vancomycin hydrochloride 1 mg in 0.1 mL plus Inj. Ceftazidime 
2 mg in 0.1 mL or Inj. Amikacin sulphate 0.4 mg in 0.1 mL
	 2.	Subconjunctival injection Vancomycin 25 mg/0.5 mL plus Ceftazidime 
100 mg/ 0.5 mL plus Dexamethasone 0.25 mg/0.5 mL
	 3.	Vancomycin eyedrops 50 mg/mL plus Amikacin eyedrops 15 mg/mL 1 drop every 
6 hours
	 4.	Homatropine 2% eyedrops 3 times a day Or Atropine 1% eyedrops 3 times a day (do 
not administer in extremes of age) Or Atropine 1% eye ointment 2 times a day
	 5.	Prednisolone acetate 1% eyedrops Or Dexamethasone Or Betamethasone 0.1% 
eyedrops every 6 hours
	 6.	Tab. Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day in a single morning dose after 24–48 hours of antibiotic 
use and continue for 10–14 days (Caution: Contraindicated in fungal infection)
	 7.	Parenteral antibiotics (Vancomycin plus Cefazoline) given as a supportive therapy in 
some cases
	 8.	Antibiotic changed according to vitreous culture and sensitivity if required
Surgical treatment
Vitrectomy – pars plana vitrectomy is indicated if visual acuity is limited to light 
perception or if there is poor response to above-mentioned treatment in 48 hours.

Chapter 13  Eye Diseases    705
Vitrectomy may also be required in the resolved phase of endophthalmitis for vitreous 
opacification/membranes.
Treatment for traumatic endophthalmitis

1.	Hospitalize the patient and administer immunization for tetanus
	 2.	Inj. Vancomycin 1 g IV infused over 1 hour every 12 hours
	 3.	Inj. Gentamicin 2 mg/kg every 12 hours
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Ceftazidime 2 g IV every 12 hours
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV/day
	 4.	Should consider Clindamycin in all cases until B. cereus infection has been excluded
	
	Inj. Clindamycin 600–900 mg IV every 8 hours
	
	In children, 20–40 mg/kg/day IV 6–8 hourly
	
	Continue antibiotics for 7–10 days
	 5.	Topical fortified eyedrops, subconjunctival injection, intravitreal injection and 
cycloplegic drops as in cases of postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis
Surgical treatment
	
l Repair the ruptured eyeball at the earliest.
	
l Pars plana vitrectomy – indications are similar to those of postoperative bacterial 
endophthalmitis. In severe cases, vitrectomy should be strongly considered.
Fungal endophthalmitis
Exogenous fungal infections may occur postoperatively or secondary to trauma. 
Endogenous fungal endophthalmitis should be treated as an emergency treatment.

1.	Vitrectomy to debulk the vitreous of fungi
	 2.	Intravitreal Amphotericin B 5–10 mcg/0.1 mL Or Voriconazole 50–100 mcg/0.1 mL
	 3.	Inj. Amphotericin B 0.5–1.5 mg/kg/day slow infusion over 2–6 hours (50-mg vial 
in powder form and is dissolved in 5% dextrose) for 10–14 days
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Fluconazole 400 mg loading dose followed by 200 mg daily (total dose should 
not exceed 600 mg/day)
	
	In children, 12 mg/kg loading dose followed by 6 mg/kg/day 
	
	Or 
	
	Tab. Voriconazole 6 mg/kg for 2 doses followed by 4 mg/kg twice a day
	 4.	Homatropine 2% eyedrops 4 times a day or atropine 1% eye ointment 2 times a day
	
	(Caution: Avoid steroids.)

706    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Patient education
	
l All patients with open globe injury must contact an ophthalmologist after getting 
initial treatment.
	
l Cataract-operated cases should never ignore pain, tearing, photophobia and decrease 
in vision in the operated eye and must consult the ophthalmologist at the earliest.
References
	 1.	 Infectious endophthalmitis. In: Yanoff M, Duker JS (eds), Ophthalmology. 5th ed. Edinburgh: 
Elsevier; 2019, pp. 865–871.
	 2.	 American Academy of Ophthalmology. Endogenous endophthalmitis: diagnosis and treatment. 
EyeNet Magazine. June 2016, https://www.aao.org/eyenet/article/endogenous-endophthalmitis-
diagnosis-treatment [accessed January 14, 2024].
	 3.	 Fungal infections and the eye. Albert DM, Jakobiec FA, Miller JW (eds), Albert and Jakobiec’s 
Principles and Practice of Ophthalmology. 3rd ed. Philadelphia, PA: WB Saunders Co; 2008, pp. 
4717–4749.
	 4.	 Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study Group. Results of the endophthalmitis vitrectomy. Arch 
Ophthalmol. 1995;113:1479–1496.
OPTIC NEURITIS
Optic neuritis includes papillitis (inflammation of the optic disc), retrobulbar neuritis 
(inflammation of the retro-ocular portion of the optic nerve) and neuroretinitis when 
both the optic disc and the retina are inflamed. The chief causes of optic neuritis 
are demyelinating diseases (usually multiple sclerosis), systemic viral/bacterial 
infections, autoimmune diseases and secondary to ocular inflammations, e.g. uveitis, 
endophthalmitis and orbital cellulitis. MRI of the brain to detect multiple white matter 
lesions should be done for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occur unilateral or bilateral sudden severe visual loss, ipsilateral eye pain, 
markedly impaired colour vision, visual obscurations in bright light and episodic 
transient visual obscuration on physical exertion, hot bath, hot weather, fatigue, etc. 
	
l Profound decrease in visual acuity, dyschromatopsia, central or paracentral 
scotoma, tenderness of the globe near superior rectus insertion and reduced 
visually evoked response are seen.
	
l There is marked abnormality in pupillary response to light reflex (sluggish or 
afferent pupil defect).
	
l Fundus examination reveals optic disc oedema with or without flame-shaped 
retinal haemorrhages in papillitis and neuroretinitis and a normal fundus in 
retrobulbar neuritis.
Treatment (refer immediately to an ophthalmologist)
	 1.	MRI brain and orbit with optic nerve sections should be ordered. Visual evoked 
potential (VEP) can aid in diagnosis.

Chapter 13  Eye Diseases    707
	 2.	In demyelinating optic neuritis, give Inj. Methylprednisolone 1 g/day 
(or 15 mg/kg/day) IV in 2–4 divided doses, or single dose for 3 days followed by 
Tab. prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day orally for 11 days, tapered by 20 mg on day 12 and 
then 10 mg/day on days 13 and 15. Methylprednisolone should be given under 
monitoring in the hospital. 
	 3.	In the case of proven infective aetiology, administer appropriate systemic antibiotic 
to eliminate the focus of infection.
(Caution: Oral Prednisolone alone is not recommended.)
Patient education
	
l Explain about recurrent nature of the disease and that permanent visual loss can occur.
	
l Explain that there is a risk of developing multiple sclerosis.
	
l Avoid factors provoking transient visual obscurations like physical exertion, hot 
bath, hot weather, stress, anxiety and anger.

DIABETIC RETINOPATHY
DR is the microangiopathy of retinal vasculature occurring in long-standing diabetes 
mellitus resulting in structural damage to the neural retina. It is classified into non-
proliferative DR and proliferative DR; diabetic macular oedema (DME) may be present 
at any of these stages.

l Early diagnosis, proper diabetic control, diet change and exercise, careful follow-up
	
l Fundus photography, fluorescein angiography and timely laser photocoagulation or 
vitrectomy surgery or both

l No effect of antiplatelets on DR
	
l Good diabetic and hypertensive control

	Intravitreal injections of ranibizumab or bevacizumab at monthly intervals for 3

and required frequently) 
	 2.	Monitoring to be done by vision and OCT macula
	 3.	In cases of non-resolving DME, can try intravitreal Aflibercept

l Explain the importance of yearly fundus examination and strict control of diabetes

not seeing properly and then bring it with them for eye examination.

RETINAL DETACHMENT
RD is defined as separation of the sensory retina from retinal pigment epithelium. It 
may be localized, or the entire retina may be involved. RD involving the macula results 
in profound visual loss. RDs are of three types: (i) rhegmatogenous RD, (ii) exudative 
RD and (iii) tractional RD.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Rhegmatogenous RD is caused by the formation of a hole/tear in the retina. Clinical 
features include symptoms of flashes of light, sudden shower of black spots and 
veiled visions, and loss of central vision if the macula is also detached. The diagnosis 
is made by examination of the fundus by distant direct ophthalmoscopy and direct 
and indirect ophthalmoscopy. The detached retina appears grey with oscillating folds.
	
l Tractional RD is caused by gliotic bands on the retina.
	
l Exudative RD is caused by collection of serous fluid between the neurosensory 
retina and the retinal pigment epithelium.
Treatment (to be treated by an ophthalmologist)

There is no pharmacological therapy which can prevent, delay or cure rhegmatogenous 
RD. Exudative RD due to inflammatory conditions such as panuveitis (Vogt–Koyanagi–
Harada syndrome (VKH), sympathetic ophthalmitis) or posterior scleritis is treated with 
systemic corticosteroid and/or pulsed methylprednisolone therapy as described in the 
treatment of uveitis and optic neuritis. 
Refer patients who are refractory to corticosteroids or in whom serious 
steroid-induced complications develop to a tertiary care hospital for treatment with 
immunosuppressive drugs.
Surgical treatment for rhegmatogenous RD
Treatment of choice is reattachment surgery involving: 
Sealing of retinal break by creating aseptic chorioretinitis using cryotherapy or laser 
photocoagulation

710    Standard Treatment Guidelines
And/or
Scleral buckling
Or
Vitreoretinal surgery with internal tamponade using gases or silicone oil
Patient education
	
l Patients with high myopia, family history of RD, post-cataract surgery and past 
episodes of chorioretinal inflammation should be warned of the premonitory signs 
of impending RD (sudden onset of floaters, flashes of light and sudden obscuration 
of one field of vision). In such cases, they should immediately undergo a dilated 
fundus examination by indirect ophthalmoscopy by an ophthalmologist.
	
l Explain to these patients not to indulge in contact sports.
	
l Educate patients on the need to maintain near-normal glucose levels and near-normal 
blood pressure as well as the need to exercise, good serum lipid level control and 
follow-up screening examinations in patients with DM but without DR.

Skin Diseases
SKIN AND SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS
Skin and soft-tissue infections (SSTIs), also referred to as skin and skin structure 
infections, represent a group of infections that are diverse in their clinical presentations 
and degrees of severity. They are generally classified into two categories: purulent 
infections (e.g. furuncles, carbuncles, abscesses) and non-purulent infections (e.g. 
erysipelas, cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis). The majority of SSTIs are caused by bacteria 
and are referred to as acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSIs) and 
their management is given below. Some cases are caused by viruses – most notably, 
varicella zoster virus (VZV), which is the causative organism of chickenpox and shingles 
(management given separately in following section). Complicated skin and soft-tissue 
infections (cSSTIs) representing the severe form of infectious disease involves deeper 
soft tissues. Involvement of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) further 
complicates cSSTI with increased hospitalization, health care costs and overall mortality.
PURULENT INFECTIONS
Superficial bacterial infections of the skin caused by purulent organisms are called 
pyoderma. These are classified as primary and secondary pyoderma (superimposed on 
other dermatoses and traumatic or post-surgical wounds). Gram-positive organisms 
including S. aureus and Streptococci are commonly implicated.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Superficial infections can involve the skin or the hair follicle. Skin involvement 
present as impetigo contagiosa, bullous impetigo and ecthyma.
	
l Impetigo is a highly contagious superficial pyoderma of the skin, seen commonly 
in infants and small children; glomerulonephritis can occur as a complication 
(Fig. 14.1).
	
l Hair follicle involvement can lead to folliculitis, furunculosis or carbuncle 
(Figs. 14.2a and 14.2b). Clinically, a suppurative lesion of a hair follicle can be 
observed. A group of adjacent furuncles with subcutaneous involvement and 
multiple discharging sinuses is seen in a carbuncle. Diabetes is an important 
predisposing factor.

714    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Oral antibiotics
Cloxacillin – 500 mg 6 hourly; children: 50–100 mg/kg/day 6 hourly.
Cephalexin – adults and children >15 years: 250 to 500 mg PO 4 times daily; children 
≤15 years: 25 to 50 mg/kg/ day PO divided into 3 to 4 times.
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole – adults: 1 to 2 DS tablet(s) PO twice daily; children: 
8–12 mg/kg/day of Trimethoprim divided into 4 doses IV or 2 doses PO.
Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid – adults and children ≥40 kg: 875 mg of Amoxicillin PO 
twice; children <40 kg: 25 mg/kg/day of Amoxicillin PO divided into 2 doses.
Ceftriaxone – adults: 1 g IV daily; children: 50–75 mg/kg/day IV divided into 1–2 doses.
Cefazolin – adults: 1 g IV three times daily; children: 50 mg/kg/day IV divided into 3 doses. 
Nafcillin – adults: 1–2 g IV six times daily; children: 100–150 mg/kg/day divided into 
4 doses.
Vancomycin – adults: 30 mg/kg/day divided into 2 doses; children: 40 mg/kg/day 
divided into 4 doses.
Linezolid – adults and children ≥12 years: 600 mg IV/PO twice daily; children 
<12 years: 10 mg/ kg/day IV/PO twice daily.
Piperacillin + Tazobactam – adults and children >40 kg: 3.375 g IV three or four times 
daily; children ≤40 kg: 100 mg/kg of Piperacillin IV three times daily.
Clindamycin – adults: 300–450 mg PO four times daily; adults: 600 mg IV three times 
daily; children: 20–40 mg/kg/day IV/PO divided into 3 doses.
CELLULITIS AND ERYSIPELAS
Cellulitis and erysipelas are non-purulent infections, usually caused by streptococcal 
or staphylococcal infections of the subcutaneous tissues resulting from contamination 
of minor wounds.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Erysipelas is a superficial variant of cellulitis caused primarily by group 
A streptococci which presents as a tender, erythematous, indurated plaque 
with edges or frank cellulitis which is an infection of the deep dermis and 
subcutaneous tissue that manifests as areas of erythema, swelling, warmth 
and tenderness (Figs 14.4 and 14.5) with/without constitutional symptoms and 
regional lymphadenopathy. Potentially fatal systemic toxaemia may supervene 
in patients who remain untreated.
	
l Blood cultures are not routinely indicated due to low yield (positive in 
<5%). Blood cultures indicated for extensive cellulitis, special populations 
(immunosuppressed, severe post-surgical wounds, etc.) and those severely ill. 
Raised ASO in serial titre in group A streptococcal infection with ASO. Imaging 
is helpful in some cases.

Chapter 14  Skin Diseases    715
	
l Ultrasound is used to rule out deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in cases of scrotal 
swelling. A CT scan may be necessary if there is suspicion of a deeper infection, 
such as necrotizing fasciitis or pyomyositis. However, a negative CT scan does 
not completely rule out necrotizing fasciitis, so surgical consultation should be 
obtained for further evaluation.
	
l Recurrent cellulitis or erysipelas can result in chronic changes in affected skin 
and lymphatics.
	
l Lymphoedema, alcoholism, diabetes mellitus, intravenous drug abuse and 
peripheral vascular disease are all risk factors for cellulitis. 
	
l Pain out of proportion to the clinical signs, in particular, if accompanied by a 
history of rapid progression should prompt consideration of a necrotising fasciitis.

Figure 14.5.  Ill-defined red raised lesion of erysipelas.

l Treatment involves incision, drainage, surgical debridement, broad-spectrum 
antibiotic therapy and supportive care depending on severity and presence or absence 
of systemic features, i.e. high-grade fever and symptoms of endotoxic shock. 
	
l See Figure 14.3 for the general approach to the management of acute bacterial skin 
and skin structure infections. Superficial and small abscesses respond to drainage 
and rarely necessitate antibiotic therapy. 
	
l Cellulitis follows a gradual resolution pattern in its natural course. Fever and 
inflammation commonly persist within the initial 72 hours of treatment. Effective 
management involves limb elevation, ongoing administration of narrow-spectrum 
antimicrobial therapy and addressing comorbid conditions that may worsen 
cellulitis (such as oedema, diabetes and vascular disease).
	
l Immunocompromised individuals should receive prompt treatment, including 
antimicrobial coverage for potential atypical organisms. Patients with complicated 
infections, such as suspected necrotizing fasciitis and gangrene, need comprehensive 
empiric antibiotic treatment, inpatient care and consultation with a surgical specialist 
for debridement. 
	
l Outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy (OPAT) including ambulatory care can 
be considered suitable for patients in need of intravenous treatment. Regular daily 
assessment and an early transition to oral therapies are advisable.
	
l For individuals experiencing repeated episodes of cellulitis, it is essential to identify 
and address risk factors, and, when necessary, administer prophylactic measures.
Necrotising Fasciitis
The affected area may exhibit erythema, oedema, warmth and a shiny appearance, 
and be extremely tender. Delayed diagnosis can lead to skin breakdown and the 
development of frank cutaneous gangrene. In cases of compartment syndrome, surgical 
emergency fasciotomy is necessary. 
Antibiotic Stewardship Practice Points
In determining the optimal management of a patient with a skin or soft tissue infection 
(SSTI), following points must be considered: 
	
l Determine first whether the infection is purulent or non-purulent, and second 
whether the infection is mild, moderate, or severe. 
	
l Most purulent infections are treated with incision and drainage (I & D) first, 
followed by administration of oral antibiotics directed against Methicillin Resistant 
Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) in moderate cases and intravenous antibiotics 
directed against MRSA in severe cases. 
	
l Employ non-pharmacologic therapy particularly cleansing and irrigation and incision 
and drainage whenever possible. Non-pharmacologic therapy is sufficient alone 
without antibiotics to treat mild purulent infections. 
	
l Most non-purulent infections are treated with oral antibiotics directed against group A 
β-haemolytic Streptococcus (GAS) in mild cases and intravenous antibiotics directed

Chapter 14  Skin Diseases    717
against GAS in moderate cases. Severe non-purulent infections are treated with 
surgical debridement and intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics that cover MRSA. 
	
l Select antibiotics based on host factors such as type of SSTIs, extent and severity of 
the infection, risk factors for MRSA, and comorbid conditions. Also consider safety 
concerns – allergies, hepatic and renal functions and drug interaction concerns. 
	
l Monitor for cessation of the spread of the infection and for the reduction of 
inflammation within 48–72 hours after antibiotic administration. Otherwise, 
re-evaluate the diagnosis and/or the antibiotic regimen. If patient responds, de-
escalate antibiotics – switch from IV to oral or narrower spectrum antibiotic.
	
l Educate patients presenting with diabetic foot infections (DFIs) about the importance 
of achieving optimal glycaemic control and keeping the feet clean and dry to prevent 
foot ulcers and subsequent infections. Most DFIs require surgical interventions ranging 
from debridement to resection and amputation. Most DFIs also require wound care, 
including debridement to remove necrotic tissue, off-loading to redistribute pressure 
off the wound and appropriate dressings to allow for moist wound healing. Bed rest 
and leg elevation are recommended initially to decrease swelling and oedema.
Patient education
	
l Poor hygiene, the sharing of personal items, physical contact and crowded living 
conditions facilitate the spread of contagious infections such as furuncles, carbuncles 
and impetigo. 
	
l Peripheral vascular disease and pre-existing skin diseases increase the risk of 
erysipelas and cellulitis. 
	
l Educate patients presenting with diabetic foot infections (DFIs) about the importance 
of achieving optimal glycaemic control and keeping the feet clean and dry to prevent 
foot ulcers and subsequent infections.
	
l Poorly controlled diabetes often leads to DFI. Traumatic events such as cuts and 
bites, and injection drug use result in wounds that increase the risk of skin infections 
and abscesses.

LEPROSY
Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous disease affecting skin and nerves caused by 
Mycobacterium leprae. Mode of spread is by respiratory droplet infection and close 
personal contact.
SALIENT FEATURES 
	
l At least one of the following cardinal signs must be present to diagnose leprosy: 
	1.	 Hypopigmented or reddish skin lesions with definite sensory deficit
	2.	 Involvement of the peripheral nerves, as demonstrated by definite thickening 
with/without loss of sensation and/or weakness of the corresponding muscles 
of hands, feet or eyes, supplied by that nerve
	3.	 Demonstration of M. leprae in the skin smear 
		
The first two cardinal signs can be identified by clinical examination alone, 
while the third can be confirmed by examination of the slit skin smear.
	
l Leprosy may be classified as paucibacillary (PB): Patient with less than 
five hypoaesthetic, hypopigmented lesions (including localized single nerve) 
(Fig. 14.6) and multibacillary (MB): Patient with five or more lesions including 
skin and nerves or more than one nerve trunk involvement.

number of lesions, bacillary index and number of nerves involved tends to increase.
	
l Baseline investigations before starting drugs include: haemogram, LFT, slit skin 
smear (if available), chest X-ray and tests to rule out G6PD deficiency.

l Complicated leprosy with or without drug reactions should be referred to a tertiary 
care centre.

l If the treatment is interrupted for less than 3 months at a stretch, recommence 
regimen where it was left off to complete the full course. Review in detail for 
persisting disease at the end of therapy.

nodosum leprosum). If untreated, it may cause disability.

CUTANEOUS TUBERCULOSIS
Cutaneous tuberculosis affects skin and/or mucosa with or without underlying 
systemic involvement. Skin tuberculosis may be indicated by clinical features and 
typical histological findings, but the only absolute criterion is the demonstration of 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis in either tissue culture from skin biopsy or cytological 
smear, or the demonstration of mycobacterial DNA by PCR (Nucleic Acid 
Amplification Test or NAAT). A strongly positive Mantoux reaction of >15 mm in 
diameter, a positive IFN-γ release assay and response to anti-tuberculosis therapy also 
point towards the diagnosis of cutaneous TB.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Commonly cutaneous tuberculosis presents as several types (Table 14.2), 
however, following clinical disease entities are commonly seen:
	– Lupus vulgaris: Granulomatous lesion with marginal activation central 
clearing and atrophy (Fig. 14.8a).
	– Scrofuloderma: Granulomatous ulcer with fibrosis, atrophy, sinus formation 
and deeper structure involvement as the focus of suppuration (Fig. 14.8b and c).
	– Tuberculosis verrucosa cutis: Verrucous plaque with or without atrophy.
Confirm the diagnosis of cutaneous tuberculosis with investigations such as 
histological examination of skin biopsy for TB granulomas, positive culture of 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB), or microscopy for acid-fast bacilli (AFBs) from 
skin biopsy. In cases where the histology findings are equivocal, but there is a strongly 
positive Mantoux test, further evaluation is warranted. If laboratory facilities are not 
available, refer the patient to a higher centre for confirmation of the diagnosis before 
starting antitubercular therapy. The patient needs to be evaluated in detail for co-
existent systemic focus of tuberculosis.
Screen the patients for underlying immunosuppression, particularly if extensive or 
multifocal disease is present.

SCABIES
A common skin infestation caused by arthropod mite (Sarcoptes scabiei) and 
transmitted by close personal contact after an incubation period of 3–4 weeks.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Nocturnal itching, excoriated papules, papulovesicles, burrows and excoriation, 
lesions seen on interdigital clefts of hands, wrist, axillary folds, breasts, 
periumbilical region, medial side of thigh and genitals (in males) (Fig. 14.9). 
	
l Burrows are pathognomonic and a family/contact history of similar complaints 
invariably present. 
	
l Common complications are secondary pyoderma, eczematization and 
glomerulonephritis (post-streptococcal).
Figure 14.9.  Lesions of scabies with secondary bacterial infection in the interdigital web spaces and 
over genitals in a male child.

Maintenance of adequate personal hygiene by daily bath with soap and water.

Secondary bacterial infection, when present, should be treated with antibiotics before 
specific antiscabetic therapy.

1. Specific therapy
A. For children (>2 months), adults, pregnant and lactating mothers
Permethrin cream 5% to be applied generously, after bath, at bedtime, covering entire 
surface of the body below neck (except face). In infants and neonates, head and neck 
to be also included (tip to toe application). Minimum contact period 8–12 hours; to be 
washed off next morning. Second application to be applied 1 week later.
Or
Lindane 1% lotion or cream. Rinsed off after 6 hours; contraindicated in pregnant 
women and infants.
Or
Benzyl benzoate 25% ointment. Rinsed off after 24 hours.
Or
Crotamiton 10% ointment. Rinsed off after 24 hours, then reapplied for 24 hours.
Or
Precipitated sulphur 2–10% precipitate in petrolatum base. Rinsed off after 24 hours, 
then reapplied every 24 hours for the next 2 days (with a bath taken between each 
application) 
In patients who failed treatment with or who cannot tolerate topical medications:
For children >15 kg or 5 years and adults (except pregnant and lactating 
mothers)
Tab. Ivermectin 12 mg single dose given on day 1 and day 7.
In children: 200 mcg/kg single dose given on day 1 and day 7.
Note: GBHC is not preferred as its repeated topical application or accidental ingestion 
may lead to adverse neurological effects such as seizures.
2. Supportive therapy
Tab. Cetirizine 10 mg Or Levocetirizine 5 mg at night for 10–15 days.
In children: Cetirizine 2.5–5 mg/kg/day single dose Or Levocetirizine 1.25–2.5 mg 
once daily for 2 weeks.
Or
Tab. Pheniramine maleate 25 mg 3 times a day for 10–15 days.
In children: 0.5 mg/kg/day divided in 3 doses.
Follow up after 1 week. If problematic itching persists, a topical anti-pruritic such 
as crotamiton either alone or in combination with hydrocortisone may be advised after 
ensuring adequacy of antiscabetic treatment.
Patient education
	
l Disinfestation of bedding and clothing by ordinary laundering and/or sun exposure 
is required. All clothes and bedding must be washed at high temperature (>50°C) or 
must be kept in a plastic bag for up to 72 h.

l Itching will persist for a few days but usually resolves within 1–2 weeks. The

PEDICULOSIS (LICE INFESTATION)
Two species of lice are obligate parasites in man namely: (i) Pediculus hominis which 
has two variants: (a) Pediculus humanus capitis, the head louse; (b) Pediculus humanus 
corporis, the body louse and (ii) Pthirus pubis (the pubic louse).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Severe itching, frequently followed by secondary bacterial infection with regional 
lymphadenopathy and eczematization, resulting in matting of hair. Also known as 
plica polonica. On examination, one can see nits that are firmly attached to hair 
shaft within 6 mm from the scalp skin.
	
l Transmission occurs by head-to-head contact, sharing of combs and caps, infested 
clothing of bedding and poor personal hygiene; transmission of pubic lice is by 
sexual contact.
	
l Blue grey maculae (maculae cerulea) of altered blood may be seen at the site of 
louse bite/feed.

l Infested clothing and bedding should be washed properly in hot water and dried in 
sunlight. Clothes should be ironed from inside with special attention to seam line.
	
l In pubic lice infestation, sex partner should be treated as well, and a search for other 
sexually transmitted infections (STI) should be undertaken.

1. Specific therapy
1% Permethrin in surfactant rinse, single 1-hour application on the affected area.

Chapter 14  Skin Diseases    727
Or
Lotion GBHC 1% to be applied on scalp (in head louse infestation), whole body 
including pubic region, thighs, buttocks (in pubic and body lice infestation) for a period 
of 12 hours to be washed off later on.
For scalp lice repeat application after 1 week after surviving eggs have hatched.
2. Supportive therapy
If persistent itching,
Tab. Cetirizine 10 mg once daily at night for 7 days.
In children (2–6 years): 5 mg; (>6 years) 10 mg once daily.
Or
Tab. Pheniramine maleate 25 mg three times a day for 7 days.
In children: 0.5 mg/kg/day in three divided doses.
3. Treatment of the secondary infection 
Any suspected bacterial infection should be treated with anti-staphylococcal antibiotic, 
preferably first-generation Cephalosporin (Cephalexin: adult dose 0.25–1 g 6–8 hourly; 
in children 25–100 mg/kg/day) and further antibiotic therapy should be tailored as per 
microbiological studies.
Patient education
	
l All clothing, towels, bed linens, upholstery used by an infested child within 2 days 
prior to diagnosis should be washed in hot water at about 50°C, or machine dried at 
the highest heat setting, for at least 30 minutes and sun dried.
	
l In case of pubic lice, shave the area, if possible, and ensure adequate personal 
hygiene.
	
l Daily bath with soap and water and change of clothing. To remove nits with the help 
of a fine toothed comb. Other family members and schoolmates, if infested, have to 
be treated simultaneously.
