MYIASIS (MAGGOTS)
Myiasis is the infestation of body tissues of man and animals by the larvae of Diptera 
(two-winged flies). Clinically myiasis can be classified according to the part of the body

728    Standard Treatment Guidelines
affected: cutaneous myiasis, wound myiasis and furuncular myiasis (larvae penetrate 
and develop within the skin); nasopharyngeal myiasis, intestinal and urogenital myiasis.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The eggs or larva (maggots) can be seen in large numbers in the denuded or raw 
lesions. 
	
l In the furuncular form, boil-like lesions develop gradually over a few days; each 
lesion has a central punctum, which discharges serosanguineous fluid. Posterior 
end of the larva is usually visible in the punctum.
	
l Regional lymphadenopathy, mild constitutional symptoms and eosinophilia may 
be present.
	
l Wound myiasis occurs when fly larvae infest open wounds in a living host.
	
l Mucous membranes (e.g. oral, nasal, and vaginal membranes) and body cavity 
openings (e.g. in or around the ears and eye socket) can also be affected.

1.	Treatment of secondary bacterial infection as in treatment of cellulitis and 
erysipelas (see Bacterial Skin Infections).
	 2.	For furuncular myiasis a surgical incision is made and the larva is then removed 
with forceps, taking care so as to avoid damaging the larva, as retained parts can 
lead to a severe inflammatory reaction. 
	 3.	Sometimes, the punctum needs to be enlarged by cruciate incisions in furuncular 
myiasis. Manual removal followed by irrigation is used to treat wound myiasis. 
	 4.	Liquid paraffin and turpentine oil application is followed by gentle removal of the 
larva with the help of forceps.
Patient education
Explain to the patient about personal hygiene and also explain about the proper care of 
the wound (not to allow flies to sit on raw/open wound).

ONYCHOMYCOSIS
Invasion of the nail plate by Dermatophytes, Scytalidium or other non-dermatophyte 
moulds is called onychomycosis (Tinea unguium). Invasion of nail plate by Candida 
is regarded as candidal onychomycosis. Distal lateral subungual onychomycosis is the 
most common type where the fungus enters via the distal subungual and lateral nail

Chapter 14  Skin Diseases    729
groove and presents as onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis. The commonest 
causative species is T. rubrum followed by T. mentagrophytes.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The nail plate may appear to be discoloured (yellow, green or black), disfigured 
or, in extreme cases, might be totally destroyed. The nail folds may also show 
swelling and redness indicative of paronychia (Fig. 14.10).
	
l Other causes of nail plate involvement should be ruled out, e.g. psoriasis, eczema, 
alopecia areata, lichen planus.

It is prudent to determine the type of organism causing onychomycosis by nail 
scraping microscopy using potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount and/or culture. Rule 
out immunosuppression, HIV, diabetes mellitus.
Topical therapy
Indicated for <50% distal nail involvement, or 3–4 nails involved and in children
	 1.	Amorolfine 5% nail lacquer applied to the nail once weekly
	 2.	Ciclopirox 8% solution daily application over and above the previous application; 
remove once weekly
	
	Or
	
	Efinaconazole 10% solution-once daily application for 1–2 months
Systemic therapy
Tab. Terbinafine 250 mg once a day for 6 weeks for finger nails and 12 weeks for toe 
nails Or 250 mg twice daily for 1 week/month for 3 pulses

Or

month (pulse) – 2 pulses for fingernails and 3 pulses for toe-nails.
In children (>12 years): 5 mg/kg/day for 3 months.

In children: 10–20 mg/kg twice daily as above.
For candidal onychomycosis, Tab Fluconazole 150 mg once a week for 3–6 months for

CANDIDIASIS
Candidiasis is an infection with protean clinical manifestations, caused by Candida 
species that are also part of normal skin/mucosal flora. The infections are usually 
confined to the skin, nails, mucous membrane (Fig. 14.11) and gastrointestinal tract but 
can be systemic and affect multiple internal organs. Various mechanical, nutritional, 
physiological, systemic and iatrogenic factors predispose to Candida infection. 
Figure 14.11.  Violaceous lesions of lichen planus of tongue with secondary candidal infection. 
Scraping in 10% KOH reveals pseudo-hyphae or budding yeast cells.

Chapter 14  Skin Diseases    731
SALIENT FEATURES
Cutaneous candidiasis
	
l Intertrigo is the most common clinical presentation of candidiasis on glabrous 
skin.
	
l Common locations for the infection include the genitourinary, perineal, axillary, 
gluteal, interdigital and submammary areas and between the folds of skin of the 
abdominal wall.
	
l Pruritus and erythematous macerated areas of skin with satellite vesicopustules 
are characteristic features.
Candidal paronychia
	
l It is common in individuals whose hands are chronically involved in wet work, 
e.g. housewives, bakers, fishermen and paan vendors.
	
l Redness, swelling and tenderness of the paronychial area with prominent retraction 
of cuticle towards the proximal nailbed. Occasionally, pus can be expressed from 
beneath this area. The nails might also be infected and discoloured. 
Oral candidiasis
See Acute Oropharyngo-Oesophageal Candidiasis in Chapter 6.

l To keep the affected area dry and clean.
	
l Maintain oral hygiene – Chlorhexidine mouth wash thrice daily after each meal.
Pharmacological (Candidal paronychia)
Cap. Fluconazole 3–6 mg/kg (maximum 150 mg) orally once a week depending on the 
area affected for 4–6 weeks. In case nail plate is also involved, treat as onychomycosis.
Or
Cap. Itraconazole 200 mg once daily for 7 days.
Note: Griseofulvin is not effective in Candida infection.
Pharmacological (mucocutaneous candidiasis) 
Topical 1% Clotrimazole/2% Miconazole nitrate or 1% Ciclopirox cream gel or lotion 
twice daily for 14 days. 
Treatments of oral candidiasis, vaginal and vulvovaginal candidiasis and balanitis 
or balanoposthitis are discussed in respective sections below. Extensive candidiasis 
resulting in internal organ involvement is an AIDS defining infection (see section on 
AIDS and Opportunistic Infections in Chapter 7).

TINEA CAPITIS
Ringworm of the scalp in which the essential feature is invasion of hair shafts by a 
dermatophyte fungus. School-going children (mostly prepubertal) are most commonly 
affected.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Presentation is variable depending on the types of hair invasion, level of host 
resistance and degree of inflammatory host response.
	
l Grey scaly patches appear as patches of partial alopecia, often oval or circular in 
shape with fine scaling. Green fluorescence under the Wood’s lamp is usual in 
Microsporum infection (Fig. 14.12a).
	
l Kerion is a painful inflammatory condition, seen as hair follicles discharging pus, 
thick crusting and matting of adjacent hair (Fig. 14.12b).
	
l Black-dot variety (relatively non-inflammatory type) of patchy alopecia – seen as 
black dots occur as the affected hair breaks at the surface of the scalp.
	
l Favus: Yellowish, cup-shaped crusts known as scutula. Adjacent crusts enlarge 
to become confluent and form a mass of yellow crusting.
	
l Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstration of spores and hyphae in KOH wet 
mount preparation of affected hair and/or brilliant green fluorescence in Wood’s 
lamp examination.

SUPERFICIAL FUNGAL INFECTIONS 
It has attained an alarming magnitude in India, in last 6–7 years with sudden increase 
in its incidence and prevalence. Today, superficial fungal infections constitute about 
1/3rd of all outpatient visits.
The following changes in manifestation have been observed: 
	
l Unusually extensive diseases with or without co-morbidity 
	
l Poor/partial response to conventional topical and systemic antifungals in standard 
dosing 
	
l Treatment failure: Topical, systemic and combination
	
l Need for unusually long treatment duration; more than 6–8 weeks
	
l Quick recurrences/relapses/reinfection after stopping treatment
	
l Presents with atypical morphology/uncommon sites of involvement
	
l Involves many family members at the same time
	
l Involve all age groups including infants and young children
	
l Emergence of resistance to the commonly used systemic antifungal drugs
	
l Both chronic and recurrent dermatophytosis are called ‘Recalcitrant dermatophytosis’ 
Atypical clinical presentation/T. incognito or unusual morphology
Morphology is modified due to application of topical super potent or potent steroid 
with or without antifungals.
	
l T. pseudoimbricata: This clinically manifests as ring-inside-ring or waves or rings

l Scalp involvement: Extension of facial lesion to involve scalp hair even in adults 
(Fig. 14.14c).
	
l Diffuse scaly lesions: Every suspected scaly lesion with defined margins and with 
or without central clearing should be tested for fungal infection.

l In addition to systemic and topical antifungal treatment (see T. cruris and 
T. corporis), general measures are important.
	
l Daily bath and adequate drying of the skin with special attention to flexural areas

l Avoid using tight occlusive or body-hugging synthetic clothing

l Wash infected clothing separately

DIAPER DERMATITIS
It is a very common problem in small infants. It is induced by the occlusion of the areas 
covered by impermeable diapers, often triggered by an episode of diarrhoea. Prolonged 
contact with urine leads to an irritant contact reaction which presents with erythema 
(Fig. 14.15). Erosions may develop if the area remains untreated. The buttocks and 
other convexities of the thighs are involved, while the skin folds are typically spared.

1.	Area to be kept dry.
	 2.	Barrier creams and emollients such as white soft paraffin cream must be used to 
restore the disrupted epidermis.
	 3.	In case of severe inflammation, hydrocortisone 1% cream may be used for very 
short periods of time.
	 4.	Zinc oxide paste (petroleum jelly 50%, zinc oxide 50%) may prevent skin irritation 
due to diarrhoea.
	 5.	Recalcitrant cases to be referred to a specialist.
Parent education
	
l Avoid impermeable diapers
	
l Keep the skin dry
	
l Avoid use of topical antiseptics and medicated soaps

ECZEMA AND DERMATITIS
Eczema is an ‘inflammatory skin reaction characterized by itching, redness, scaling and 
clustered papulovesicles, induced by wide range of external or internal factors acting 
singly or in combination’.
Customarily the eczemas are divided into:
	
l Endogenous (constitutional): Atopic dermatitis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, lichen 
simplex chronicus (LSC) and
	
l Exogenous (environmental): Contact allergic dermatitis, primary irritant dermatitis, 
photosensitive eczema, etc.
SALIENT FEATURES
Itching and vesicular eruptions on erythematous skin with erosion and exudation 
in acute cases (Fig. 14.16) or thickening, accentuated skin markings, fissuring with 
pigmentation (described as lichenification) in chronic cases.
Figure 14.16.  Acute eczematous lesions of atopic dermatitis.

A definitive diagnosis of the type of eczema is mandatory as different varieties of 
eczema require different management strategies. However, at primary healthcare 
level, the aim is to provide relief of symptoms and signs, appropriate to the stage of 
dermatitis, and subsequent referral to a tertiary care centre for diagnosis and appropriate 
management strategy.
1. Local treatment
In acute exudative eczema: soak with dilute potassium permanganate solution 
(1:10,000) and 0.25% silver nitrate solution or 0.8% aluminium subacetate solution.
In long-standing situations:
Acute/subacute – appropriate topical steroid (Table 14.3) in lotion/gel or cream base 
for 2–4 weeks.
Chronic long-standing and/or lichenified lesions – appropriate topical steroid 
(Table 14.2) in ointment/emollient base for 2–4 weeks.
2. Systemic treatment
Tab. Cetirizine 10 mg Or Levocetirizine 5 mg at bedtime till symptoms subsides.

MILIARIA (PRICKLY HEAT)
Miliaria is caused by obstruction or disruption of the sweat gland duct during hot and 
humid summer seasons or in patients with recurrent/chronic high-grade fever, resulting 
in a leakage of sweat into the epidermis (miliaria crystallina and miliaria rubra) or 
dermis (miliaria profunda).

Chapter 14  Skin Diseases    741
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l In miliaria crystallina, the obstruction is superficial, producing multiple small 
clear fluid containing vesicles without erythema. 
	
l In miliaria rubra, the later changes include keratinization of the intraepidermal 
part of the sweat duct and it presents as erythematous, itchy, papules commonly 
over the trunk, neck, axilla and groin. 
	
l Miliaria profunda is associated with rupture of the sweat duct at the level of the 
dermal-epidermal junction leading to skin coloured non-itchy papules.
	
l Itching and stinging provoke scratching which may lead to secondary infection; 
also known as periporitis (multiple staphylococcal abscesses). Eczematization 
can also occur.

l Avoid causal factors like heat and occlusion due to oils, creams, cosmetics, etc.
	
l Cool baths and aeration.
Pharmacological (Miliaria rubra)
	 1.	Emollients like anhydrous lanolin or Calamine lotion applied locally over the 
affected areas.
	 2.	Menthol 0.5% in aqueous cream or mild topical steroids may be added.
	 3.	In case of secondary infection, topical antibiotics (see section on Bacterial Skin 
Infections).
	 4.	For relief of itching, Tab. Levocetirizine 5 mg Or Cetirizine 10 mg once daily Or 
Pheniramine 25 mg three times a day.
	 5.	Tab. Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid) 500 mg twice daily aids in the recovery of the 
sweat ducts.
Patient education
	
l Frequent cool baths and aeration
	
l To stay in cool environment to minimize the body’s need to sweat
	
l No oil application over scalp and body

Blackwell; 2016, pp. 94.1–18.

ACNE VULGARIS
Chronic inflammatory condition of the pilosebaceous glands of the face, neck and 
upper back. Usually occurs in adolescents and young adults. Acne can be secondary to 
mechanical friction/occlusion, detergents/chemicals, ultraviolet exposure, occupational, 
associated hirsutism/virilism exogenous, other climate/factor and drugs, namely, 
steroids topical or systemic, INH, Rifampicin, Phenytoin, lithium, halogenated drugs – 
bromides/chlorides, and use of cosmetics/oils/petroleum/cream applications.
SALIENT FEATURES
Two types of lesions are seen clinically such as non-inflammatory (comedones: 
blackheads or white heads) and inflammatory: pustules, nodules, cysts and abscesses 
(Fig. 14.17). The lesions commonly resolve with post-inflammatory macules, pigment 
changes and scarring.

Washing/cleaning of face to keep skin non-sticky, dry and dirt free; shampooing to 
keep scalp non-greasy.

Non-inflammatory acne. Retinoic acid cream/gel (0.025%; 0.05%) usually applied 
once a day – at bedtime or alternate day. A therapeutic response appears characterized

by redness and scaling within 3–6 weeks. Treatment is usually continued for at least 
3 months.
(Caution: Not to apply near/into eye/mouth; contraindicated in pregnancy and 
lactation) 
Gel Retinoic acid, if not tolerated may be substituted by Adapalene 0.1% gel (usage 
and precautions same as above).
Or
Cream/gel Azelaic acid 20% applied once or twice a day after facewash.
Inflammatory acne. Inflammatory acne treatment may need to be combined with 
treatment for non-inflammatory acne.
Mild cases. Topical retinoid therapy as above
Or
Clindamycin gel 1% to be applied twice a day (or more) for 4–6 weeks.
Or
Erythromycin gel/lotion 2%; 4% (safe in pregnancy) to be applied twice a day (or more) 
for 4–6 weeks. Begin with the lower strength.
Or
Benzoyl peroxide gel 2.5%, 5% (safe in pregnancy) to be applied to clean skin initially 
once daily on alternate days then twice a day (or more) for 4–6 weeks.
Moderate-to-severe cases should be referred to a specialist preferably without 
treating with systemic antibiotics.
	 1.	Alternate Topical retinoid therapy as given earlier Or Adapalene 0.1% gel (usage 
and precautions same as above). Note: Same drug should not be used topically as 
well as systematically as there is no extra-therapeutic benefit.
	 2.	In case of papulopustular acne, Cap. Doxycycline 50–100 mg once daily for 
4–12 weeks. The dosage can be reduced in accordance with the clinical response 
and discontinued.
	
	Or

	Or

	Treatment may need to be continued for up to 6 months. Severe and unresponsive

Patient education
	
l Redness and scaling with retinoic acid may be seen as a part of a therapeutic 
response. Gels are less irritating. Lasting benefit only after long duration use of 
comedolytic agents, usually for more than 6 months. Concentration and frequency 
of application can be adjusted to minimize problematic side effects.
	
l Avoid oil application on the scalp and wash scalp on alternate days.

ALOPECIA AREATA
Alopecia areata is presumed to be an immunologically mediated disorder characterized 
by non-scarring patchy loss of hair (Fig. 14.18). It presents with single or multiple skin 
coloured, smooth, oval to circular patches of alopecia over the scalp or any other hairy 
parts of the body depending on the extent of involvement.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l In two-thirds of the cases, partial or complete re-growth of hair occurs within 5 years.
	
l In up to 80% of patients with limited patchy hair loss, the condition is of short 
duration (<1 year); rule out other causes on patchy non-cicatricial alopecia such 
as tinea capitis, trichotillomania and syphilis.
Figure 14.18.  Alopecia areata – multiple, circumscribed patches of hair loss.

For patients with less than 50% scalp involvement
	 1.	Intralesional Triamcinolone 10 mg/mL 0.2–0.5 mL per patch every 4–6 weeks (to 
be treated by a specialist) except for children <10 years of age.

PITYROSPORUM INFECTIONS OF THE SKIN
Tinea versicolor and Pityriasis capitis (Dandruff)
Tinea versicolor is an infection of the skin caused by the dimorphic fungus – 
Malassezia furfur. Pityriasis capitis (Dandruff) is caused by Pityrosporum ovale.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Tinea versicolor is characterized by superficial, scaly, hypo- or hyperpigmented, 
irregular perifollicular macules, most often occurring on the trunk and proximal 
extremities (Fig. 14.19).
	
l Pityriasis capitis (dandruff) presents as diffuse itchy lesions over the scalp 
with hair loss; may be associated with erythema, scaly lesions over eyebrows, 
eyelashes and nasolabial fold.

746    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Figure 14.19.  Hypopigmented discrete and coalescing macules of tinea versicolor over upper back. 
KOH scraping from the lesion reveals both hyphae and spores (spaghetti and meatball appearance).

1.	Topical therapy
	
	Topical 2.5% Selenium sulphide lotion/shampoo applied liberally to affected areas 
for 7–10 minutes prior to rinsing, 3–4 times per week.
	
Or
	
Topical Ketoconazole 2% lotion, apply once for 15 minutes before taking bath on 
affected areas daily till controlled and then reduced to 2–3 times per week,
	
Or
	
Topical Miconazole 2% cream apply twice daily for several weeks.
	
Or
	
Topical Clotrimazole 1% cream.
	 2.	Systemic therapy in case of patients with extensive disease, frequent recurrences, 
or for whom topical agents have failed
	
Tab. Fluconazole 400 mg as a single dose Or Tab. Fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 
4–6 weeks Or Cap. Itraconazole 200–400 mg once daily for 3–7 days may be given 
to prevent early relapse.
Patient education
	
l Avoid oil application
	
l Frequent head wash and comb after each head wash
	
l Recurrence is common and regular application of any of the topical agents helps to 
reduce high rates of recurrence 
	
l Although it does not leave any permanent scar or pigmentary changes, skin tone may 
take several months to return to normal

PITYRIASIS ALBA (PATCHY HYPOCHROMIA)
Pityriasis alba affects over 80% children; its aetiology is obscure, although an 
association with atopy has been suggested. The lesions appear as ill-defined 
hypopigmented macules, most commonly over the face, with a slight scaly surface. It 
should be differentiated from other causes of hypopigmented macules such as vitiligo 
(which is depigmented) and indeterminate Hansen’s (an intermediate stage before 
tuberculoid tuberculoid Hansen’s sets in).

1.	Emollients such as white paraffin should be applied twice daily for 4–6 weeks.
	 2.	Hydrocortisone 17-butyrate cream 0.1%, or Mometasone furoate 0.1% cream to 
be applied twice daily on the affected skin until symptoms resolve in patients with 
symptoms of itching, or persistent lesions.
CHICKENPOX OR VARICELLA
Varicella is the primary infection caused by Varicella zoster virus (VZV). It is highly 
infectious and is transmitted by droplet infection (Fig. 14.20).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The incubation period is about 14 days. Disease starts with fever followed by a 
morbilliform erythematous rash, followed by formation of papules which rapidly 
become clear, tense vesicles. This is followed by conversion into pustules on an 
erythematous base.
	
l Lesions appear on the trunk, then spread centripetally to involve face, scalp and 
limbs with the presence of lesions in different stages at various sites. Reactivation 
of disease results in herpes zoster or shingles.
Figure 14.20.  Polymorphic (vesicular, pustular and crusted) lesions with surrounding erythema of 
chickenpox.

HERPES ZOSTER (SHINGLES)
Herpes zoster occurs due to reactivation of VZV which lies dormant in sensory nerve 
root ganglion following primary infection as chickenpox.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Grouped vesicular lesions on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution 
with severe localized pain (Fig. 14.21).
	
l The thoracic segment and trigeminal nerve area are more commonly involved; 
involvement of ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve (eruptions in the 
ophthalmic area including tip of nose) may lead to corneal ulcers and scarring. 
	
l Post-herpetic neuralgia defined as persistence of pain for more than 1 month after 
healing of zoster, motor nerve involvement leading to paralysis of facial muscles, 
ocular muscles and bladder can occur. 
	
l Lesions in immunocompromised and HIV patients may involve multiple 
dermatomes and course of the disease is painful and prolonged.

Rest and isolation alone in case of mild disease in an otherwise healthy person.
Pharmacological supportive therapy
	 1.	Tab. Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day till resolution of symptoms
	
	In children: 10 mg/kg/day.

	 2.	Tab. Cetirizine 5 mg once a day till resolution of symptoms
	
	In children: 0.5 mg/kg/day every 8 hours. 
	 3.	Calamine lotion topically till resolution of symptoms. 
Pharmacological definitive therapy
In painful zoster infections in adults and at any age in facial zoster and in the 
immunocompromised, treatment should be started as early as possible, preferably 
within the first 1 or 2 days. The recommended treatments include:
Tab. Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times a day for 5–7 days.
In children: 80 mg/kg/day in 5 divided doses.
Or
Tab. Famciclovir 250–500 mg three times a day or 750 once daily for 7 days
Or
Tab. Valaciclovir 1 g thrice daily for 7 days.
Refer immediately to a tertiary care hospital in case of hearing defect and facial palsy,

Inj. Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV 8 hourly for 5–7 days.

HERPES SIMPLEX
Herpes simplex is the commonest infection caused by DNA virus, human Herpesvirus 
(HSV). Type 1 is classically associated with facial infections and type 2 is typically 
genital. Following primary infection, virus remains latent in sensory nerve ganglia 
and its reactivation under various circumstances is responsible for recurrent episodes. 
Transmission occurs by direct contact or droplets from infected secretions. Incubation 
period is 4–5 days. Diagnosis is supported by Tzanck smear made from a vesicle. On 
Giemsa staining, it shows multinucleated giant cells and ballooning degeneration of 
keratinocytes. 
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Grouped vesicular lesions on erythematous base are present on lips (herpes 
labialis, Fig. 14.22) or tongue, palate and buccal mucous membranes (herpetic 
gingivostomatitis) or anywhere else on the body. 
	
l The primary episode is painful and associated with regional tender 
lymphadenopathy. Recurrent episodes are relatively asymptomatic.
	
l Complications include disseminated herpes simplex in debilitated and 
immunosuppressed patients, herpetic encephalitis or meningitis, eczema 
herpeticum in patients with atopic dermatitis and erythema multiforme.

750    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Figure 14.22.  Grouped, vesicular lesions over erythematous background in herpes labialis.

Supportive therapy in herpes labialis
Identify and avoid precipitating factors in recurrent herpes labialis like sun exposure, 
febrile illness and alcohol intake. 
Specific therapy in herpes labialis
	 1. 	Mild case is self-limiting (5–7 days) and no specific therapy is required.
	 2. 	Moderate-to-severe cases, Tab. Acyclovir 200 mg 5 times a day for 7 days.
Prophylaxis (recurrent episodes more than 6 per year, refer to a specialist)
Tab. Acyclovir 400–800 mg a day for 6–9 months and, in addition, to supportive therapy.
Patient education
	
l It is an infectious condition transmitted by direct contact/droplet infection. 
Therefore, the patient should avoid contact until all the lesions get crusted. 
	
l Herpes simplex 2 is transmitted via sexual route, so the patient should take proper 
precautions (see section on Genital Ulcers).

LICHEN PLANUS
Lichen planus is a symptom complex of itching and self-limited eruptions which can 
involve the glabrous skin, mucous membrane, hair and nails. The natural history is 
variable with a usual course of 9–18 months. Oral and hypertrophic lesions run chronic 
course. Diagnosis is usually clinical; however, it should be confirmed by a specialist. 
Drugs causing lichenoid eruptions are Captopril, Allopurinol, beta-blockers, gold, 
Tetracycline, Arsenic, Penicillamine, NSAIDs, INH, Chloroquine, Carbamazepine, 
Sulphonylureas.

VITILIGO
Vitiligo is a pigmentation disorder characterized by depigmented macules (Fig. 14.27) 
which develop as a result of the immune-mediated destruction of melanocytes with both 
humoral and cell-mediated immunity playing a role. Family history may be present 
in up to 20% of patients. An association with other autoimmune diseases including 
hyperthyroidism, adrenocortical insufficiency, alopecia areata and pernicious anaemia 
has been described.

classified as universal vitiligo which carries a bad prognosis. Koebnerization is 
commonly seen in vitiligo.

MELASMA
Melasma usually occurs in dark skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick skin type IV–VI). 
The pathogenesis is complex and involves interplay of many factors such as ultraviolet 
radiation and visible light exposure, genetic predisposition, cosmetics, hormonal 
factors such as thyroid disorder, patients on hormone replacement therapy, drugs and 
pregnancy. Melasma of pregnancy usually resolves in few months after delivery but, 
otherwise, spontaneous remission is rare.

psychosocial impact of dyspigmentation of melasma has to be considered. 
	
l Melasma Area and Severity Index (MASI) is a validated scale which helps to 
measure the facial hyperpigmentation extent.

1.	Sun avoidance and broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF of at least 30 which covers 
UVA, (Minimum PA+++) UVB and Visible Light Or Blend of inorganic (with iron 
oxide/zinc oxide) and organic sunscreen may be used.
	
	Sunscreen to be applied liberally (teaspoon rule), every 2–3 hours, after sweating or 
swimming and even when indoors, since infrared rays contribute to its pathogenesis.

Albinism is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder. Patients are at risk of skin

childhood.

Urticaria (hives) is a non-specific vascular response to a wide variety of stimuli. Acute 
urticaria presents with erythematous wheals, which may be associated with swelling of 
loose connective tissue (angio-oedema) affecting lips, face, scrotum, larynx and trachea.

Soothing applications – cold water sponging and clearance of airway in case of 
laryngeal oedema.

according to response and tolerance. 
Or 
Tab. Hydroxyzine 10–25 mg three times a day. 
In severe cases, antihistaminics can be started intravenously and once controlled, 
patient is maintained on oral preparations as above.

	 1.	Inj. Epinephrine in 0.5–1.0 mL of 1:1000 IM. Patients with severe airway obstruction

DERMATOLOGICAL EMERGENCIES
A quick assessment of the condition of the patient can be made by assessing whether 
eruptions involve large areas of skin or blisters and erosions present or does patient 
appear ill?
Serious emergencies involve blisters and erosions covering large areas of skin 
with toxic symptoms like fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea and dehydration. These 
patients require urgent referral to a specialist centre.
Three broad groups are:
Group I. Extensive blistering and erosions – pemphigus, toxic epidermal necrolysis, 
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Group II. Extensive skin involvement without blisters – erythroderma, viral 
exanthems, drug rashes
Group III. Localized skin lesions – cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis

Group I 
To be treated at a tertiary care level [pemphigus, toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), 
Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)]
TOXIC EPIDERMAL NECROLYSIS (TEN) AND STEVENS-
JOHNSON SYNDROME (SJS)
These are severe mucocutaneous reactions, most commonly to drugs and are 
characterized by epithelial sloughing. It can be frequently associated with systemic 
complications and can result in multiorgan failure and death, thus carrying an 
appreciable mortality rate. Severity of the process ranges from SJS (<10% BSA 
involvement of epidermal detachment) to SJS-TEN overlap (10–30% BSA) to the most 
severe variety – TEN with >30% BSA involvement.
PEMPHIGUS VULGARIS
The immunobullous disorders are characterized by antibody-mediated autoimmune 
destruction. In the pemphigoid group, there is destruction of the hemidesmosomes and 
elements of the basement membrane zone. In the pemphigus group, antibodies target 
structural components of the desmosomes. These processes result in blistering of the 
skin and mucosae.
Pemphigus vulgaris presents with oral mucosal erosions in 50–70% cases followed 
by the development of vesicles on the skin which disrupt with trivial trauma to leave 
behind painful erosions with marginal extension and little tendency to heal on their own.

Lower abdominal pain syndrome
Lower abdomen pain is caused by staying microbes that colonize the cervix or vagina 
which spontaneously ascend to endometrium, fallopian tubes and adjacent peritoneum.

Majority of the cases are STI with Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae

C h a p t e r   15
Obstetrics and Gynaecology
NORMAL AND HIGH-RISK PREGNANCY
Pregnancy is a transient physiological state during a woman’s reproductive years, and it 
requires important considerations regarding diet, lifestyle and drug therapies to achieve 
a good maternal and foetal outcome with minimal morbidity and mortality. Antenatal 
care (ANC) is a coordinated approach to medical care and psychosocial support that 
optimally begins before conception and extends throughout the antepartum period.
The aims of ANC are:
	
l To screen high-risk cases, predict, prevent, detect and manage medical and 
obstetrical complications at the earliest 
	
l To educate mothers about the physiology of pregnancy and labour
	
l To counsel about breastfeeding and contraception
	
l To promote institutional delivery to reduce maternal and perinatal morbidity and 
mortality
The objective is to ensure a normal pregnancy with the delivery of a healthy baby 
from a healthy mother. The woman should be instructed regarding:
	 1.	Diet: Pre-pregnancy caloric requirements depend on the physical work done by the 
woman. The increased requirement of 350 kcal for the pregnant state should be made 
available by diet. A pregnancy diet should be light, nutritious, easily digestible and rich 
in proteins, vitamins and minerals. The diet should consist of at least 0.5 L (if not 1 L) 
of milk, plenty of green leafy vegetables (one katori serving in each meal) and fruits 
as available, in addition to the normal Indian diet consisting of a balanced cereals and 
pulses combination. Foods rich in iron like green vegetables and jaggery and protein-
rich foods like nuts should be stressed upon. Fat consumption can be predominantly of 
animal source so as to take care of vitamins A and D.
	 2.	Exercise: Any exercise the woman is accustomed to prior to pregnancy can be 
continued but not to the point of fatigue. Antenatal exercises done under medical 
supervision are useful in pregnancy. No new exercise should be initiated during 
pregnancy. Sedentary women should be allowed only walking. Women with multiple 
pregnancy and complications like heart disease, hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, 
intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), history of preterm labour, antepartum 
haemorrhage (APH) and threatened abortion should practice isometric exercises.

786    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Regular moderate ambulation in pregnancy reduces the risk of thromboembolism. In 
healthy pregnant and postpartum women, at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-
intensity aerobic activity (i.e. equivalent to brisk walking) spread throughout the 
week and should be adjusted as medically indicated. Patients prescribed prolonged 
bed rest or restricted physical activity are at risk of venous thromboembolism, bone 
demineralization and deconditioning.
	 3.	Clothing: It should be non-constricting. 
	 4.	Travel: Most common obstetric emergencies occur in the first and third trimesters. 
Travel by vehicles having jerks should be avoided, especially in the first and 
last 6 weeks of pregnancy. Occasional travelling in a pressurized aircraft is 
safe up to 36 weeks. Check specific airline requirements with the individual 
carrier. Prolonged sitting should be avoided due to venous stasis and risk of 
thromboembolism (should walk about after every 2 hours).
	 5.	Employment: Jobs requiring prolonged standing (>8 hours/day) are associated 
with a risk of preterm delivery.
	 6.	ANC visits: Eight visits in a normal pregnancy are preferred but there should 
be a minimum of four ANC visits as per Government of India recommendations 
(first as soon as pregnancy is detected; second between 24 and 28 weeks; third 
at 32 weeks; and fourth at 36–37 weeks). The scheduled eight visits should be as 
follows: first trimester – contact 1, up to 12 weeks; second trimester – contact 2, 
20 weeks, contact 3, 26 weeks; third trimester – contact 4, 30 weeks, contact 5, 34 
weeks, contact 6, 36 weeks, contact 7, 38 weeks, contact 8, 40 weeks; return for 
delivery at 41 weeks if not given birth. ANC visits in high-risk pregnancies are 
individualized on a case-to-case basis.
	 7.	Clinical workup during each antenatal visit: Blood pressure (BP), weight gain, 
oedema feet, pallor, and cardiovascular, respiratory and breast examinations are 
done in every visit. Symphysio-fundal height, presentation, foetal heart rate(s) 
(FHR), amniotic fluid volume, inquiry about daily foetal movement charting 
(DFMC) and pelvic assessment are done at 37 weeks. Per speculum examination 
of the cervix and vagina should be performed at the first visit. Per vaginum 
examination should be done in the first visit in the first trimester or early second 
trimester in the absence of ultrasound.
	 8.	Lab workup during pregnancy is shown in Table 15.1.
	 9.	Rh-ve women (with Rh+ve husband) need to be monitored on similar lines with 
additional testing using indirect Coombs’ test (ICT) at 1 and 28 weeks. Anti-D 
immunoglobulin 300 mcg IM is recommended in ICT-negative patients at 28 weeks 
of pregnancy and postpartum if the baby is Rh+ve and neonatal direct Coombs’ test 
is negative. ICT +ve patients should be managed only at centres with facilities for 
amniocentesis and/or cordocentesis, amniotic fluid optical density estimation and 
intrauterine foetal transfusions.
	10.	Medication safety: Women with a history of neural tube defects should receive 
Tab. Folic acid 5 mg/day, at least, before conception, and continue till 12 weeks of 
gestation. All other women should receive 400 mcg/day in the first trimester.

	11.	Dose of Iron (60–100 mg elemental iron) and Folic acid 0.5 mg (Tab. Iron 
folic acid) once daily after 12 weeks onwards is continued throughout pregnancy 
and thereafter for 3 months postpartum. It may be given in the first trimester if 
the patient is not having vomiting. Note: Do not withhold iron supplements in 
pregnant women with sickle cell and those who are thalassaemia carriers, with no 
signs and symptoms of iron overload. Iron supplementation should be done as per 
ferritin levels in these patients.
	12.	Calcium supplement: Tab. Calcium supplementation 1000–1500 mg in 2 divided 
doses along with Vitamin D 500 IU daily from 16 weeks onwards to prevent 
gestational hypertension. (Caution: Separate the administration of Iron at least 
2 hours apart from calcium carbonate, milk or milk products.)
	13.	Immunization: Live vaccines are generally contraindicated in pregnancy. These 
include MMR, varicella and BCG vaccines. Toxoids, immunoglobulins and 
inactivated vaccines can safely be given in pregnancy. However, unless there is 
any immediate concern, it is better to postpone the administration till the second 
trimester when the organogenesis is completed. Immunize all pregnant women with 
2 doses of Tetanus and Diphtheria vaccine (Td). The first dose is given just after 
the first trimester or as soon as the woman registers for ANC, whichever is later. 
The second dose is given 1 month after the first dose but at least 1 month before the 
expected date of delivery (EDD). Td-booster is given if pregnancy occurs within 
3 years of the last pregnancy and 2 Td doses were received. Give immunoglobulins 
along with Td to a woman in labour if she has not previously received tetanus vaccine. 
If the woman is fully immunized, no further doses are necessary in pregnancy. 
Tdap should be administered between 27 and 36 weeks of pregnancy to maximize 
passive antibody transfer to the foetus and it replaces 1 dose of Td. However, Tdap 
vaccine can be given at any time during gestation if required for epidemic or wound 
management. In case of a pandemic, the influenza vaccine can be given earlier to 
protect the mother. Whenever indicated, pneumococcal, meningococcal, hepatitis A 
and B, rabies and inactivated (parenteral) typhoid vaccines should be administered.
	
	Note: Breastfeeding is not a contraindication to any vaccination including live 
vaccines because most of the viruses have not been found in the breast milk. 
However, yellow fever vaccine should be avoided in lactating mothers.
HIGH-RISK PREGNANCIES
Refer all high-risk pregnancy cases to a higher centre with a referral letter (Table 15.2). 
These include:
	
l Short statured (<145 cm), age less than 18 years, fifth child and above (grand multi 
para), elderly primigravida (age >35 years), previous pregnancy complications bad 
obstetric history (recurrent abortions, previous intrauterine foetal death, perinatal 
death or early neonatal death), IUGR, hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, history of 
prolonged/obstructed labour, prior history of preterm labour or pre-labour rupture of 
membranes, previous history of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), retained placenta,

790    Standard Treatment Guidelines
previous history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), previous caesarean section 
(CS)/instrumental delivery, previous history of congenital or chromosomal anomalies
	
l Current pregnancy complications: Multiple pregnancy, insufficient weight gain, 
malpresentation, Rh iso-immunization, APH, IUGR, hypertensive disorder of 
pregnancy, GDM, poly/oligohydramnios, unsatisfactory progress of labour and 
associated medical disorders – heart disease, overt diabetes mellitus, chronic 
hypertension, epilepsy, haemoglobinopathies; antepartum foetal assessment 
performed with weekly non-stress test (NST), biophysical profile (BPP), modified 
BPP after 28 weeks and other advice as per specific risk factors.
Patient education
	
l Determine whether there are important taboos about foods which are nutritionally 
important for good health. Advise the woman against these taboos.
	
l Advise the woman on how to prepare for institutional delivery, when to go, what to 
bring and where to go in emergency.
	
l Explain the danger signals when she should report to the health centre immediately, 
day or night, without waiting such as vaginal bleeding, convulsions, severe 
headaches with blurred vision, severe abdominal pain, fast or difficult breathing, 
escape of fluid from the vagina or change in frequency or intensity of foetal 
movements, persistent vomiting or decreased urine output. She should report to the 
health centre as soon as possible if any of the following symptoms appears: swelling 
on the face or hands, abdominal pain, fever, dysuria and feeling ill.
	
l Explain about black staining of stools due to oral iron, therefore, not to worry about it. 
	
l Iron and calcium supplements should be taken at different times of the day or at 
least 2 hours apart. 
	
l Discuss birth spacing after delivery and counsel on the importance of family 
planning and decide upon a mode of contraception during the antenatal period itself. 
Give advice on correct and consistent use of condoms for dual protection from 
sexually transmitted infections or HIV (for details on methods of contraception, see 
Contraceptives below).
	
l Sexual intercourse should be avoided in case of threatened abortion/preterm labour, 
and during the last 4 weeks of pregnancy.
	
l Bowel: Constipation, fissures and haemorrhoids are common during pregnancy and 
should be treated with fluids, bulk laxatives and stool softeners. 
	
l Smoking, alcoholism and drugs of abuse are contraindicated. Caffeine is best avoided. 
	
l DFMC: After 28 weeks, the woman should keep foetal movement count.
	
l Follow-up visits: These are planned every 4 weeks till 28 weeks, every 2 weeks till 
36 weeks and weekly thereafter.

LABOUR AND ITS MANAGEMENT
Normal Labour
Normal labour is defined as labour which starts spontaneously at term, with the foetus 
in the vertex position, and terminates naturally without artificial aid or complications. 
It is a retrospective diagnosis.
Diagnosis of labour
	
l Painful uterine contractions at regular intervals with increasing intensity and 
frequency and stages of labour (Table 15.3)
	
l Progressive cervical dilatation and effacement (in primigravidae, first effacement 
and then dilatation are seen; in multipara, effacement and dilatation take place 
simultaneously)
	
l Formation of bag of membranes
	
l Show (passage of blood-stained thick mucous plug)
When the patient reports to the hospital with labour pains, examination should be 
conducted by a doctor on duty and risk category should be assigned (Tables 15.2 and 15.3).

l Foetal heart monitoring should be done by intermittent auscultation with the help of

l FHR should be counted for 60 seconds following contraction (normal FHR is 
110–160 beats/min).

and at the following intervals:

l Add 5 units Inj. Oxytocin in 1000 mL or 2.5 units in 500 mL Ringer’s lactate (RL)/
Normal saline (NS) and start at 16 drops/min.

SECOND STAGE OF LABOUR
	
l Shift the patient to the delivery table.
	
l Inform the paediatrician. Ensure that all delivery equipment and supplies, including 
newborn resuscitation equipment, are available, and the place of delivery is clean 
and warm (25°C).
	
l Allow the patient in any position whichever is preferred by her.
	
l Observe standard precautions – personal protection equipment.
	
l Clean and drape the parts.
	
l Monitor FHR every 5 minutes; half-hourly for pulse, and frequency, intensity and 
duration of uterine contractions; and hourly for temperature and BP. Per vaginum 
examination hourly. Infiltrate the perineum with local anaesthetic agent if episiotomy 
is planned.
	
l The woman is encouraged to bear down.
–  The duration of active first stage (from 5 cm to full cervical dilatation) usually 
does not extend beyond 12 hours in the first labour, and usually does not 
extend beyond 10 hours in subsequent labour. Assess the progress of labour, 
rate of descent 1 cm/h in primigravida and 2 cm/h in multigravida, and rotation 
of sutures. Prolonged second stage occurs if rate of descent is >1 hour in 
multigravida and >2 hours in primigravida.
	
l PV examination is performed at 30- to 60-minute interval in primigravida and 15- to 
30-minute interval in a multipara to assess the progress of labour. If there is normal 
descent and rotation, proceed for vaginal delivery with restrictive use of episiotomy. 
If there is protracted descent or malrotation, reassess for caput/moulding and exclude 
CPD. Reassess after 1 hour. If arrest of descent or CPD is present, plan for instrumental 
vaginal delivery or LSCS. Episiotomy is given if required (see Episiotomy given in the 
following text).
	
l Conduction of delivery: To control birth of the head, keep the baby’s head flexed 
and gently support the perineum as the head delivers. Routine suction of the mouth 
and pharynx is not indicated. Examine the neck for the cord. The loose cord is 
slipped over and the tight cord is divided in between two large artery forceps. If 
there is no tight cord around the neck, delayed cord clamping must be practiced 
(at least 1 minute after delivery). Delivery of the shoulders is done after restitution 
and external rotation of the head. After moving slightly to the right side, the head is 
held firmly but with care in between two hands, left above the right, and the head is 
depressed downwards to deliver the anterior shoulder. Carrying the head upwards 
towards the mother's abdomen will affect delivery of the posterior shoulder and the 
trunk. The anterior shoulder should be delivered first.
	
l Administer Oxytocin 10 units IM after delivery of the baby to prevent PPH. 
(Caution: Store at 15–30°C.)
	
l Clamp and cut the umbilical cord after cessation of cord pulsation. Perform 
early clamping only if there is foetal distress and Rh incompatibility or maternal 
resuscitation is required.

800    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Newborn care 
	 1.	The baby should be delivered on the abdomen of the mother and dried there to 
maintain skin-to-skin contact. The mother and the baby must not be separated for 
1 hour after delivery if the baby has normal spontaneous breathing. Breastfeeding 
should be started as soon as possible.
	 2.	Ensure establishment of respiration in the baby or institute resuscitation, if required 
(for details, see Newborn section in Chapter 19).
	
l Shift the baby on a clean tray covered with dry linen and cover with a clean and 
dry towel only after 1 hour of birth. 
	
l Record APGAR (‘appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, and respiration’) rating 
at 1 and 5 minutes. The cord is clamped with a disposable cord clamp or ligated 
with sterilized silk tie keeping a stump of 2–3 cm long.
	
l Examine the baby for any structural anomaly. 
	
l Identification tape is tied on the wrist of both the mother and the baby. Keep the 
baby immediately with the mother to maintain skin-to-skin contact. 
	
l Do NOT either bath the baby with soap and water or clean the baby with oil.
	
l Give Inj. Vitamin K (1 mg if birth weight >1000 g; 0.5 mg if birth weight 
<1000 g; IM on the anterolateral thigh on the right side) and birth dose of 
Hepatitis B vaccine (0.5 mL IM on the anterolateral thigh on the left side).
THIRD STAGE OF LABOUR
Active management of third stage of labour (AMTSL) consists of:
	 1.	Immediate administration of a uterotonic drug. 
	 2.	Controlled cord traction (CCT). 
	 3.	Inj. Oxytocin 10 IU IM given immediately after delivery of the baby.
	 4.	Deliver the placenta by CCT when the uterus is well contracted.
	 5.	Keep one hand on the hardened uterus and apply counter-traction just above the 
symphysis pubis.
	 6.	Apply gentle traction on the cord.
	 7.	Check and ensure completeness of the placenta on its delivery.
	 8.	Examine the placenta for completeness of cotyledons and membranes, three-vessel 
cord, site of cord insertion or presence of retroplacental clot or haemorrhage.
	 9.	Uterine massage only if uterus is relaxed by mother with one hand on her own, till 
uterus is contracted and feels hard. Palpate the uterus every 15 minutes and repeat 
massage as needed during the first 2 hours. Monitor that the uterus does not relax 
after the massage is stopped.
	10.	Examine the woman for any tears and repair if any. Stitch the episiotomy.
	11.	Check vital signs immediately, then every 15 minutes for the first 2 hours, and then 
every 30 minutes for 1 hour and every 1 hour for 3 hours. Examine the condition 
of the uterus and look for contraction and retraction of the uterus.
	12.	Inspect the vulva for any bleeding.
	13.	Repair perineal tear/episiotomy as described later.
	14.	Ensure breastfeeding immediately.

Prevent uterine inversion by:
	
l Practicing AMTSL during labour in all women and by the following Don'ts: 
	– Do not pull the cord in the absence of uterine contraction.
	– Do not exert fundal pressure to deliver the placenta.
	– Do not pull the cord in placenta accreta.
	
l Anticipate complications like haemorrhage, shock, sudden death and referral to a 
higher facility without delay.
Counsel for postplacental or postpartum IUCD insertion (see Contraceptives given 
in the following text).
FOURTH STAGE OF LABOUR
This starts an hour or two after delivery when the tone of the uterus is re-established 
as the uterus contracts again, expelling any remaining contents. These contractions 
are hastened by breastfeeding, which stimulates production of the hormone oxytocin.
Referral to higher centre during labour and postpartum period and responding to 
the following problems during labour and delivery: Assess facilities and expertise 
available and appropriate timely referral if:
	
l FHR <120 or >160 beats/min
	
l Prolapsed cord
	
l Breech presentation
	
l Shoulder dystocia
	
l Morbidly adherent placenta
	
l Inversion of the uterus
	
l Suspected rupture of the uterus
	
l Multiple births
	
l Other complications – severe anaemia, cardiac failure
During the referral process, continue on-going measures like IV fluids, indwelling 
catheter and uterine massage. Escalate doses of Oxytocin (till 100 units is reached, in 
cases of atonic PPH and retained placenta). Vaginal pack in traumatic PPH must be 
instituted simultaneously.

Episiotomy (incision of the perineum)
It should not be performed routinely.
Applied selectively for: Breech, forceps or vacuum delivery, occiput posterior 
positions, rigid perineum, scarred perineum and shoulder dystocia
Timing of episiotomy: At crowning of the head (in vertex presentation) or at climbing 
of breech (in breech presentation) during a contraction when the perineum is at the 
maximum stretch
Procedure
	
l Clean the area with an antiseptic solution.
	
l Infiltrate beneath the vaginal mucosa, beneath the skin and deeply into the perineal 
muscle using 10 mL of 1% lignocaine.

l Check at the incision site for the effect of local anaesthetics by pinching with forceps 
before giving incision.
	
l Perform episiotomy at crowning. Place two fingers between the baby’s head and the 
perineum and cut 3–4 cm of the perineum in the mediolateral direction.
	
l After delivery of the baby and placenta, carefully examine for extensions of tears.
	
l Repair the episiotomy with Polyglactin Rapide 2–0 suture (chromic catgut if 
Polyglactin Rapide is not available). Close the vaginal mucosa with continuous 
suture starting 1 cm above the apex. Perineal muscles are approximated using 
interrupted sutures. The skin is closed with subcuticular (or mattress) sutures.
Care of episiotomy
	
l Perineal hygiene: The area should be cleaned by the patient with antiseptic solution 
or soap and water after urination and defaecation. Advise sitz bath. Avoid sitting with 
crossed legs to avoid episiotomy site gaping.
	
l Analgesics are prescribed for allaying pain.
CAESAREAN SECTION
Lower Segment Caesarean Section
It is an operative procedure in which the foetus after the end of the 28th week is 
delivered through an incision on the abdominal and uterine wall. When an incision is 
made in the lower segment of the uterus, it is called lower segment CS. Indications for 
CS are depicted in Table 15.4.
Preoperative preparation
	
l Informed written consent for the procedure, anaesthesia and blood transfusion should 
be obtained.
	
l Withhold pre-medicative sedation.

l A scalpel is used to make a 3-cm transverse incision on the lower segment of the

Closing the uterine incision
	
l The corners of the uterine incision are grasped with Green-Armytage or sponge-
holding forceps.
	
l The lower segment margins should be grasped and made sure that they are separated 
from the bladder.
	
l A thorough examination is done to look carefully for any extension of the uterine 
incision.
	
l If an extension is present, it should be repaired first.
	
l The uterus is closed in two layers. The first layer, consisting of deeper layers of 
the myometrium, is closed by continuous sutures with no. 1 chromic catgut or 
polyglactin mounted on curved atraumatic needle. The second layer, consisting of 
the rest of the myometrium, is closed by continuous sutures using the same suture 
material burying the first layer beneath it. The peritoneal flaps may be opposed by 
continuous inverting sutures to prevent any raw surface. Non-closure of visceral and 
parietal peritoneum is preferred.
	
l If there is any further bleeding from the incision site, it should be dealt with by 
reinforcement of figure-of-eight sutures.

Postoperative care
	
l The patient should be observed meticulously for at least 6–8 hours.
	
l Periodic check-up of pulse, BP and vaginal bleeding is mandatory.
	
l 2.5–3 L of IV fluid should be given in the form of RL, 5% dextrose and 0.9% NS 
over 24 hours.
	
l Inj. Oxytocin 20 units/L should continue for at least 6–8 hours following CS.
	
l Prophylactic antibiotics (single dose 60 minutes prior to incision; for details, see 
Perisurgical prophylaxis in Chapter 18). Analgesics and Ranitidine are given on an 
as-required basis parenterally initially and then orally.
	
l Oral fluids should be given on the second day and a light solid diet should be started 
from the third day.
	
l The stitches should be removed on the sixth day.
	
l The patient should be discharged following the removal of stitches if otherwise fit. 
She should be asked for postnatal check-up after 2 weeks.
	
l The baby should be put to breast within 1 hour of delivery and exclusive 
breastfeeding should be continued up to 6 months.
POSTPARTUM CARE
Puerperium begins as soon as the placenta is expelled and lasts for approximately 
6 weeks (immediate within 24 hours, early up to 7 days and remote 6 weeks).
	
l Ask the mother for heavy bleeding, bowel and urinary problems and breast 
engorgement. Observe pallor, pulse, BP and temperature 4 hourly; check uterine 
involution and foul-smelling discharge. Encourage the mother to pass urine

following delivery as soon as convenient. Advise her to always have someone near 
her for the first 24 hours to respond to any change in her condition.
	
l Stress on early ambulation.
	
l Advise the mother to have an adequate balanced diet rich in calories, proteins, fat, 
plenty of fluids, minerals and vitamins, rest and sleep.
	
l Advise her to maintain hygiene and use sanitary napkins, and explain the importance 
of hand washing to prevent infection of the mother and baby.
	
l Advise the mother to wash the perineum twice daily and after urination and 
defaecation. Ask her not to insert anything into the vagina.
	
l Care of bowel: The problem of constipation is less because of early ambulation and 
liberalizations of the dietary intake. A mild laxative such as isabgol husk 2 teaspoons 
may be given at bedtime if needed.
	
l Advise the mother to avoid sexual intercourse until the perineal wound heals, 
preferably for 4–6 weeks.
	
l Counsel for birth spacing and family planning (for details, see Contraception in the 
following text). Maternal–infant bonding (rooming-in) should start within the first 
few moments after birth. The baby should be kept on bed with the mother.
	
l Immunization
	 1.	 Administer anti-D immunoglobulin to non-immunized Rh- negative mother with 
Rh- positive baby (see ANC given earlier).
	 2.	 Booster dose of tetanus toxoid should be given at the time of discharge if it is 
not given during pregnancy.
	
l Advise on routine postpartum care visits – first visit within the first week, preferably 
within 2–3 days, second visit between 7 and 14 days and third visit at 4–6 weeks, or 
earlier if problems are present – fever, urinary tract infection (UTI), perineal infection, 
hypertension, urinary incontinence, severe anaemia, postpartum blues or HIV positive. 
	
l Continue iron and calcium supplementation for at least 6 months.
	
l Advise postpartum exercises to reduce the risk of puerperal venous thrombosis, to 
prevent backache and to prevent genital prolapse and stress incontinence of urine. 
These should be taught to each and every woman after delivery. Physical activity 
should be resumed without delay.
Counsel on exclusive breastfeeding 
	
l Start breastfeeding within half an hour of birth and as early as possible after CS. 
Do not give any other food or drink before starting breastfeed. Counsel on correct 
positioning during breastfeeding and nipple care (cleaned and kept dry after feeding 
is over) and explain about burping after each feed. 
	
l Babies should be exclusively breastfed for the first 6 months of life. 
	
l Breast milk contains exactly the nutrients a baby needs, is easily digested and 
protects the baby against infection.
	
l Breastfeeding problems 
	– Antenatal period: Identification of inverted nipples; correction by gently applying 
pressure over the nipple from the base of the areola in horizontal and vertical 
directions

810    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	– Puerperal period
	
■Crack nipple: Maintain local cleanliness before and after each breastfeed; if 
severe, the mother can use a breast pump and the infant is fed with expressed milk. 
Provide breast support, express breast milk and advise feeding in proper position.
	
■Mastitis is a tender, reddened breast 3–4 weeks after delivery. Treatment is 
with antibiotics (Cap. Amoxicillin 500 mg 6 hourly for 10 days). Prevention 
is by proper positioning of the baby and good attachment of the baby’s mouth 
to the breast.
	
■Breast abscess is a firm, acutely tender breast with erythema (for details, see 
‘Breast Abscess’ in Chapter 18). Refer to a higher health facility for drainage 
of abscess.
	
	
In all the above-mentioned conditions, encourage breastfeeding. Support 
breasts with binder/brassiere.

Others
	
l Slight degree of uterine descent with cystocele, stress incontinence and relaxed 
perineum are the common findings and can be cured by effective pelvic floor 
exercises. However, if the prolapse is marked, appropriate surgery should be done 
after 3 months.
	
l If any of the danger signs is present, refer to a higher centre.
	
l Reassure in case of heavy bleeding in the first menses after uneventful delivery, 
especially in non-lactating women. If bleeding persists following childbirth, rule out 
retained bits of placenta, get ultrasound examination done and manage accordingly.
	
l In case of leucorrhoea, rule out puerperial sepsis and manage accordingly.
POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE
PPH is excessive blood loss from the genital tract after delivery of the foetus exceeding 
500 mL or any amount of blood loss which leads to deterioration of the general 
maternal condition (however, in a woman with anaemia, blood loss less than 500 mL 
can lead to PPH and deterioration of maternal condition) or any amount of blood loss 
which leads to deterioration of maternal condition.
PPH requires prompt and effective management, failing which it may result 
in complications such as hypovolaemic shock resulting in multiorgan failure like 
coagulation failure, renal failure, hepatic failure and adult respiratory distress 
syndrome, and may also result in maternal death.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Primary PPH, i.e. bleeding within 24 hours of delivery, is commonly due to 
atonic uterus (90% of cases) or cervical/vaginal tears (traumatic PPH). It can also 
be due to occult uterine inversion, uterine rupture or coagulation defect.
	
l Degree of PPH: Mild PPH – blood loss 500–1000 mL, no clinical shock; major 
PPH – blood loss >1000 mL and continuing bleeding; severe PPH – blood loss 
>2000 mL or clinical shock.
	
l Secondary PPH is abnormal bleeding occurring between 24 hours and 6 weeks of 
delivery due to sepsis, retained placental bits, or placental polyp, and choriocarcinoma.

l Perform AMTSL in all deliveries for PPH prevention. Prevention of uterine atony is 
key to reduce PPH. Identify at-risk patients with of uterine atony leading to PPH. These

812    Standard Treatment Guidelines
include grand multiparae, case with overdistended uterus commonly due to multifoetal 
pregnancy, polyhydramnios and large baby, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, anaemia, 
APH, obstructed labour, prolonged labour, pregnancy with fibroid, prior induction/
augmentation with Oxytocin, malformed uterus, precipitate labour, intrauterine device 
(IUD), history of previous third-stage complications and jaundice in pregnancy.
	
l Deliver these patients in a hospital with facilities for blood transfusion, under skilful 
supervision, or refer to a tertiary care hospital.
	
l Prompt resuscitative measures and cause-directed management depending on degree 
of blood loss are the mainstay of the treatment. Methods to measure blood loss such 
as blood collection drape, calibrated jug and standard absorptive cloths for early and 
accurate estimation of blood loss can be used.
	
l Make use of the golden hour (first hour after beginning of severe PPH) to ensure 
the best chance of survival.
	
l Early decision for operative corrective measures should be taken by a senior 
obstetrician before irreversible shock or dilutional coagulopathy (80% of blood 
replaced by fluids while awaiting blood/blood fractions) sets in.
	
l A patient with untreated severe PPH may collapse within 2 hours. Loss of more than 
40% of total blood volume is life threatening. In traumatic PPH, the uterus is contracted, 
and the type of bleeding is variable in amount, continuous and bright red in colour.
	 In atonic PPH, the uterus is soft and flabby. The bleeding is usually dark 
coloured and large in amount coming out in intermittent gushes coinciding with 
uterine relaxation. Sometimes, both atonic and traumatic causes may co-exist 
particularly following instrumental vaginal deliveries. In inversion of the uterus, the 
uterus is not felt per abdomen with a protruding vaginal mass and the patient in shock.
	
l Monitor PR, BP, RR and urine output. While resuscitative measures are underway, a 
thorough clinical examination is made to ascertain the cause of PPH, and definitive 
treatment is planned accordingly. 
Atonic PPH

l Perform early detection and management of anaemia (blood loss of 200–250 mL can 
be fatal in patients with anaemia) and other risk factors, and develop complication 
readiness plans.
	
l Prevent dehydration as it may slow contractions and prolong labour.
	
l Prevent prolonged labour by monitoring labour using the partogram (if active 
labour lasts for more than 12 hours, refer to a facility that can provide a C-section 
if needed).
	
l Encourage the woman to pass urine frequently to avoid having a full bladder.
	
l Do not speed up labour by pushing on the uterus to expel the baby.
	
l Avoid pushing when the cervix is not completely dilated.
	
l Reduce cervical, vaginal and perineal trauma by avoiding routine use of forceps and 
restricting use of episiotomy.
	
l Perform early detection and rapid treatment of haemorrhage

l Perform AMTSL by shortening the third stage of labour and reducing blood loss by 
facilitating delivery of the placenta with oxytocin 10 units IM or IV immediately 
after delivery of the baby after ruling out a twin pregnancy, leading to effective 
uterine contractions and prevention of PPH by avoiding uterine atony.
Active management
	 1.	Shout for help.
	 2.	Urgently mobilize and involve all available medical personnel.
	 3.	Quick evaluation of the general condition of the woman is made (pulse, BP, 
respiration and airway).
	 4.	If the patient is in shock, treatment is started immediately. Even if signs of shock 
are not present, it should be kept in mind that the patient’s condition may worsen 
any time. Early fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids is essential for the 
management of shock.
	 5.	Massage the uterus carefully (see below) to stimulate contraction and retraction to 
reduce blood loss as well as to expel blood and blood clots. Blood clots trapped in 
the uterus inhibit effective uterine contraction.
	 6.	Fix a wide-bore IV cannula 18G to a large vein and IV fluids with Inj. Oxytocin 
infusion. 
	 7.	Send blood for Rh typing (if not already done) and for cross-matching of 
requisition of blood.
	 8.	Catheterize the urinary bladder as a full bladder inhibits uterine contraction.
	 9.	Check the placenta and membrane for completeness or for missed cotyledons.
	10.	Examine the cervix, vagina and perineum (episiotomy wound and lacerations). 
The para-urethral region should be done and repaired as and when required.
	11.	If the uterus is atonic and fails to contract, continue uterine massage (see below).
	12.	Oxytocic drugs can be given together or sequentially. Oxytocin infusion (40 units 
in 500 mL RL/NS at 125 mL/min) is given. (Caution: Limit fluid containing 
oxytocin to maximum 3 L; it requires stringent handling and storage conditions.) 
If the uterus contracts and bleeding is controlled, continue oxytocin infusion 20 IU 
in 1 L of NS/RL. Keep close observation.
	13.	Assess need for blood requirement and transfuse as early as necessary.
	14.	If bleeding continues, examine the placenta thoroughly again. If there are signs of 
retained placental fragments, they must be removed.
	15.	Assess the status of coagulation using a bedside clotting test. Failure of a clot to 
form after 7 minutes or a soft clot that breaks down easily suggests coagulopathy. 
Coagulopathy may occur in abruption placentae, jaundice in pregnancy, 
thrombocytopenic purpura, HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, 
low platelet count) or IUD.
	16.	Observe for uterine tone. In case of an atonic uterus, perform bimanual uterine 
massage. Bimanual compression reduces the blood loss before medical or 
mechanical methods stop the excessive blood loss.
	17.	If the uterus remains atonic, continue uterine massage and Inj. Oxytocin infusion, 
and add Inj. Methylergometrine maleate 0.2 mg IV or IM; this may be repeated 
IM 2–4 hourly (maximum 5 doses 1 mg/24 hours). (Caution: It is contraindicated

814    Standard Treatment Guidelines
in heart disease, hypertension and Rh-negative pregnancy; and requires stringent 
handling and storage conditions.) Inj. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 15 minutes.
	18.	If the uterus remains atonic and bleeding is not controlled, 15-methyl PGF2α 
250 mcg by deep IM is given, which may be repeated every 15–90 minutes up to 
a maximum of 2 mg (8 doses). (Caution: It is contraindicated in bronchial asthma 
and epilepsy.)
	19.	Tab. Misoprostol 800 mcg per rectum or 600 mcg per oral or sublingually acts 
within 9–12 minutes after administration. (Caution: Administer with caution in 
patients with epilepsy; it may cause shivering, nausea and elevated temperature. 
Do not repeat for at least 2 hours after an earlier dose.)
	20.	If the uterus remains atonic, apply bimanual uterine compression by placing the 
right-hand fist in the anterior fornix and pressure is given against the anterior wall 
of the uterus. The left hand is pressed deeply into the abdomen behind the uterus 
and pressure is applied to the posterior wall of the uterus so as to keep the uterus 
pressed in between both hands.
	21.	If bleeding continues, ask the assistant to compress the aorta by giving downward 
pressure just above the umbilicus slightly to the left. If pressure is adequate, the 
femoral pulse will not be palpable. The use of intrauterine balloon tamponade 
is recommended for women not responding to uterotonics. This procedure can 
potentially avoid surgery and is appropriate while awaiting transfer to a higher-
level facility.
	22.	If bleeding continues in spite of all this, shift the patient to the operating theatre for 
surgical management (Table 15.5).

PUERPERIUM PYREXIA AND SEPSIS
It refers to a rise of temperature reaching 100.4°F (38°C) or more on two separate 
occasions 24 hours apart within the first 10 days following delivery, excluding the 
first 24 hours after delivery. Causes of puerperal sepsis are UTI, mastitis, infection 
of CS wound, pulmonary infection, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, endometritis and 
endomyometritis. Predisposing risk factors are malnutrition, anaemia, prolonged 
rupture of membranes >18 hours, repeated vaginal examination, dehydration and 
ketoacidosis during labour, traumatic operative delivery, haemorrhage – antepartum 
or postpartum, retained bits of placental tissue or membranes, placenta praevia and 
caesarean delivery.

Perineal wound: If sepsis is present, remove stitches to drain pus. Dress the wound with 
hot compress and mild antiseptic lotion followed by application of antiseptic ointment.
Retained placental bits: Retained placental bits of a diameter of more than 3 cm 
should be removed. Perform surgical evacuation after antibiotic coverage for 24 hours.
Pelvic thrombophlebitis: Treat with Heparin IV for 7–10 days along with antibiotics.
Pelvic abscess: Drain by colpotomy.
Pelvic or generalized peritonitis and pyoperitoneum: Maintaining electrolyte 
balance by IV fluids along with appropriate antibiotic therapy usually controls 
peritonitis. But in unresponsive cases, laparotomy is indicated. If no pathology is found, 
drainage of pus may be effective. Hysterectomy is indicated in cases with rupture, 
perforation, multiple abscess, gangrenous uterus or gas gangrene infection. Ruptured 
tubo-ovarian abscess should be removed.
Septic shock: Management includes fluid and electrolyte balance, respiratory supports, 
circulatory support with noradrenaline, dopamine or dobutamine, infection control 
with intensive antibiotic therapy, surgical removal of septic foci, specific treatment like 
dialysis for renal failure, etc. Surviving Sepsis Bundle should be followed within the 
first hour of reporting to the facility (Fig. 15.3).
The Surviving Sepsis Bundle Hour-1:
	 1.	Measure lactate level. Re-measure if initial lactate is >2 mmol/L.
	 2.	Obtain blood cultures prior to administration of antibiotics.
	 3.	Administer empirical antibiotics, and then modify therapy after culture and 
sensitivity report and de-escalate after 48–72 hours.

PREGNANCY WITH COVID-19
Pregnant women do not have an increased susceptibility to COVID-19 virus compared 
with non-pregnant women. Pregnant women with COVID-19 infection, especially those 
who develop pneumonia, appear to have an increased frequency of preterm delivery, pre-
eclampsia and caesarean delivery for abnormal FHR tracings, which is likely related to 
severe maternal illness. Vertical transmission (transmission from the mother to the baby 
antenatally or intrapartum) is probable, although the proportion of pregnancies affected 
and the significance to the neonate are yet to be determined. At present, there is no 
evidence of vaginal secretions or breast milk being tested positive for COVID-19. There 
are currently no data suggesting an increased risk of miscarriage or early pregnancy loss 
in relation to COVID-19 and its teratogenicity.
ANC care during COVID-19 pandemic
Routine ANC, tailored to minimum, is scheduled at 12, 20, 28 and 36 weeks of gestation 
at the discretion of the maternal care provider, unless they meet the self-isolation 
criteria. In high-risk pregnancy, visits have to be individualized according to the high-

Chapter 15  Obstetrics and Gynaecology    821
risk factors. Telehealth visits are encouraged. Intrapartum services should be provided 
in a way that is safe, with reference to minimum staffing requirements and the ability 
to provide emergency obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal care where indicated. Three 
demarcated zones, each housing all the needed equipment and services (wards, labour 
rooms, operation theatres, neonatal resuscitation areas and mother and neonatal intensive 
care unit [ICU]), are required for the management of healthy, suspected and confirmed 
COVID-19 mothers. Triage every pregnant woman at entry and allot into one of the zones 
depending on the presentation. When an outpatient office visit occurs, all patients and 
health care workers must follow standard precautions and wear PPE as appropriate for 
the area and wear a triple-layered surgical mask; one asymptomatic partner is allowed. 
All women should be screened for COVID-19 and at 38 weeks of pregnancy and should 
be isolated by using the ICMR guidelines for non-pregnant adults.
Approach towards management of pregnant women with COVID-19
Figure 15.4 depicts the management of pregnancy and labour in patients with 
COVID-19. (For details of COVID-19 diagnosis and management, see the section 
‘Influenza-Like Illness (ILI)/Severe Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI)/COVID-19’ 
in Chapter 5.) Do not delay obstetric management in order to test for COVID-19. 
Reduce elective procedures like induction of labour for indications that are not 
strictly necessary, routine growth scans not for a strict guidance-based indication and 
routine investigations to minimum at the discretion of the care provider. If ultrasound 
equipment is used, it should be decontaminated after use.
COVID-related medical management
Use of Remdesivir and Ivermectin should be as per the guidance of the government 
from time to time. Hydroxychloroquine crosses the placenta. Investigational drugs for 
COVID-19 that are known to be teratogenic include Ribavirin and Baricitinib.
Pregnancy complications and medications
Antenatal betamethasone: Antenatal Betamethasone as indicated can be given 
between 24 0/7 and 33 6/7 weeks of gestation in patients at a high risk of preterm birth 
(PTB) within 7 days and in pregnant patients with suspected or confirmed COVID-19. 
However, do not administer Betamethasone at 34 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks of gestation who 
are at risk of PTB within 7 days for pregnant patients with suspected or confirmed 
COVID-19; the benefits to the neonate are less clear.
Low-dose Aspirin: Individualize decision to give low-dose Aspirin when indicated 
for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis in those with suspected or confirmed COVID-19. 
(Caution: Continuing pre-eclampsia prophylaxis is likely not worthwhile in severely 
or critically ill patients or those near term.)
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs): may be used when indicated. 
However, there are anecdotal reports of experiencing severe disease with the use of 
Ibuprofen early in the course of infection.

Antenatal care
•	 Routine antenatal care, tailored to minimum, at the discretion of the maternal care provider at 12, 20, 28 and 
36 weeks of gestation, unless they meet current self-isolation criteria.
•	 For symptomatic patients, defer appointments until 7 days after the start of symptoms, unless severe symptoms 
(aside from persistent cough). Monitor foetal kick count.
•	 Use own transport for visit to hospital or call 108, informing the ambulance staff about her status.
•	 Refer for antenatal ultrasound for foetal growth surveillance after 14 days following the resolution of acute illness.
Intrapartum care
•	 Assessment of severity of COVID-19 symptoms by a multidisciplinary team including an infectious diseases or 
medical specialist.
•	 Delivery should be preferably at tertiary care centre or a district hospital.
•	 Maternal observations – temperature, respiratory rate and oxygen saturations every hour.
•	 Confirmation of the onset of labour, as per standard care.
•	 Electronic foetal monitoring using cardiotocograph (CTG). If facilities for continuous electronic foetal monitoring 
are not available, manual monitoring should be done by frequent auscultation of FHR as indicated for high-risk 
pregnancy using full PPE.
Care in labour
•	 Hourly oxygen saturation during labour
•	 Aim to keep oxygen saturation >94%, titrate oxygen therapy accordingly
•	 If signs of sepsis, investigate and treat as per guidance on sepsis in pregnancy, but also consider active COVID-19 
as a cause of sepsis and investigate according to guidance
•	 Continuous electronic foetal monitoring in labour (as above)
•	 Mode of delivery individualized guided by the obstetrics indication and cardiorespiratory stability and saturation of 
the mother
•	 Epidural analgesia, if required in labour to women with suspected/confirmed COVID-19 to minimize the need for 
general anaesthesia if urgent delivery is needed

Management of patients with COVID-19 admitted to critical care
•	 Hourly observations, monitoring both the absolute values and the trends. 
•	 Titrate oxygen to keep saturations >94%. 
•	 Hourly RR looking for the rate and trends. Start or increase oxygen if RR increases. 
•	 Radiographic investigations (chest X-ray and CT of the chest using abdominal shield as per protocol) as for the 
non-pregnant adult. Do not delay due to foetal concerns.
•	 ECG, CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA), ECHO and full sepsis screening as appropriate to rule out differential diagnoses. 
•	 Steroids and anticoagulant therapy are indicated in moderate and severe cases. Use of Remdesivir, Ivermectin, as 
per guidelines issued by the government from time to time. Consider bacterial infection if the WBC count is raised 
(lymphocytes usually normal or low with COVID-19) and commence antibiotics. 
•	 Apply caution with IV fluid management. Try boluses in volumes of 250–500 mL and then assess for fluid overload 
before proceeding with further fluid resuscitation. 
•	 Individualize frequency and suitability of FHR monitoring taking into consideration the gestational age of the foetus 
and the maternal condition. Delivery is indicated for maternal indication. If a patient with severe COVID is unable to 
maintain oxygen saturation by non-invasive methods. Urgent delivery is indicated for foetal reasons, birth should 
be expedited as normal, as long as the maternal condition is stable.
