Tocolysis: Tocolysis is contraindicated in following the general principles of avoiding 
such an intervention with systemic disease. Individualize decision on tocolysis 
depending on the degree of clinical severity of the infection. If there is pulmonary 
involvement, avoid beta-mimetic agents. 
Magnesium sulphate: In women with respiratory compromise, the use of magnesium 
sulphate for maternal seizure prophylaxis and/or neonatal neuroprotection should be 
decided on a case-by-case basis since the drug may further depress respiration. Seek 
consultation with maternal–foetal medicine and pulmonary/critical care specialists.
Maternal oxygen saturation (SaO2): Maintain at ≥95% during pregnancy, which is 
in excess of the oxygen delivery needs of the mother. If SaO2 falls below 95%, obtain 
an arterial blood gas and maintain maternal PaO2 >70 mmHg for a favourable oxygen 
diffusion gradient from the maternal to the foetal side of the placenta with oxygen therapy.

In the ICU, consider prone/semi-prone position in severely ill pregnant patients 
with COVID-19. General supportive care of the critically ill patient with COVID-19 
pneumonia is similar to that of patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome due 
to other causes. In moderate to severe disease, unfractionated Heparin is generally 
preferred in pregnant women (for details, see ‘Influenza-Like Illness (ILI)/Severe Acute 
Respiratory Infection (SARI)/COVID-19’ in Chapter 5). 
Precautions during labour, delivery and neonatal care
Timing of delivery in infected women: COVID-19 alone is not an indication for 
pregnancy termination or delivery. The timing and mode of delivery should be 
individualized. Early delivery may be warranted if the pregnant women is critically ill. 
There is no beneficiary evidence of delivery via CS; hence, the mode of delivery should 
be based on the progression of labour and obstetric decisions. 
Maternal observations, especially the oxygen saturation (maintain >94%), should 
be monitored throughout labour. Administer intravenous fluids with caution. A decision 
for shortening the second stage of labour can be considered and a low threshold should 
be kept, and escalate management if any signs of decompensation develop.
Management of labour and delivery
	 1.	Prehospital notification of possible infection is given to the facility.

Chapter 15  Obstetrics and Gynaecology    825
	 2.	All women must be screened for symptoms and signs of COVID-19: history and 
examination for fever and/or new cough, shortness of breath, sore throat, muscle 
aches, rhinorrhoea/nasal congestion and anosmia.
	 3.	Perform testing of pregnant women with suspected COVID-19 at admission or who 
develop symptoms of COVID-19 during admission. 
	 4.	The evaluation and diagnosis of women admitted to labour and delivery with 
suspected COVID-19 are similar to that of other patients admitted to the hospital 
with suspected disease. 
	 5.	Use of personal protective equipment during examination: All health care workers 
with person-to-person contact and the patient should wear a triple-layer surgical 
mask, under the assumption that every patient and health care colleague might be 
infected with COVID-19.
	 6.	Cleaning and maintenance of facilities and medical equipment should be done with 
adequate PPE to the health care worker. One percent Sodium hypochlorite solution 
with contact time of 30 minutes can be used.
Care of COVID-19-positive in-patients
	 1.	Use of personal protective equipment during labour and delivery: All health care 
workers with person-to-person contact should wear a triple-layer surgical mask and 
appropriate PPE.
	 2.	Pregnant COVID-19 in-patients should be cared for in specially equipped rooms in 
antepartum, intrapartum and postpartum COVID-19-only units, halls or hospitals. 
	 3.	Patients with suspected or confirmed COVID-19 should wear a surgical mask, 
including during labour and delivery. 
Analgesia and anaesthesia
	
l In patients with known or suspected COVID-19, neuraxial anaesthetics 
(Bupivacaine 0.0625–0.1% with 2 mcg/mL, Fentanyl or Ropivacaine 0.08–0.1% 
with 2 mcg/mL Fentanyl for epidural) can be administered as indicated. They 
have several advantages in labouring patients in terms of good analgesia reducing 
cardiopulmonary stress from pain and anxiety, and in case an emergency caesarean 
is required, they obviate the need for GA. GA is an aerosol-generating procedure 
increasing the risk of transmission of infection.
	
l Use of nitrous oxide for labour analgesia in these patients is not recommended 
because of insufficient data about cleaning, filtering and potential aerosolization 
of nitrous oxide systems. Limit the use of intravenous, patient-controlled analgesia 
because of the risk of respiratory depression. All staff should don a PPE with a 
fluid-resistant surgical mask (FRSM) and eye protection.
	
l If GA is administered, preoxygenate the patient for 5 minutes with 100% oxygen 
and perform rapid sequence induction (RSI) to avoid manual ventilation of the 
patient’s lungs. Use a video-laryngoscope to improve intubation success and avoid 
awake fibreoptic intubations, to avoid aerosolization. Follow all personal protective 
measures. Place a high-efficiency hydrophobic filter between the facemask and

826    Standard Treatment Guidelines
the breathing circuit or between the facemask and the reservoir bag to avoid 
contaminating the atmosphere. 
	
l Full PPE including a filtering face piece level 3 (FFP3) mask should be worn by 
all involved health care providers before commencing GA for a caesarean delivery.
Labour management 
Management of labour is not altered in women giving birth with confirmed or suspected 
COVID-19; in addition, the following precautions to be taken:
	 1.	Limit person-to-person contact and time in the labour unit and hospital, as safely 
feasible. 
	 2.	For patients who require cervical ripening, consider outpatient mechanical ripening 
with a balloon catheter as an option. For in-patient cervical ripening, using two 
methods (e.g. mechanical and misoprostol or mechanical and oxytocin) decreases 
the time from induction to delivery, compared with using one agent only. 
	 3.	Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has not been 
detected in vaginal secretions or amniotic fluid, so rupture of foetal membranes 
and internal FHR monitoring may be performed for usual indications, but data are 
limited. It should be noted that labour, and particularly pushing, often causes loss 
of faeces, which can contain the virus and spread the infection. Delayed pushing 
in the second stage should not be routinely advocated.
	 4.	Regarding timing of cord clamping, there is no consensus – delayed cord clamping 
provided there is no other contraindication.
	 5.	Abandon the practice of oxygen therapy for foetal resuscitation; the nasal cannula 
and face mask used are in contact with the maternal respiratory tract and secretions, 
so handling of such equipment increases contamination/exposure between the 
patient and the provider.
Foetal Monitoring
The need for and frequency of foetal monitoring depends on the gestational age, 
stability of maternal vital signs, other maternal comorbidities, and discussions with 
the patient and her family considering the possibility of increased risks of stillbirth 
and perinatal morbidities in the absence of testing as well as the possible risks from 
increased contact with health care personnel performing this testing. For hospitalized 
patients, a Bluetooth-enabled external foetal monitor can transmit the FHR tracing to 
the obstetric provider. The monitor can be used continuously in unstable hospitalized 
patients in whom caesarean delivery would be performed for a persistent non-reassuring 
FHR pattern.
Intrapartum and postpartum fever: COVID-19 infection should be part of 
the differential diagnosis of intrapartum and postpartum fever, particularly when 
accompanied by respiratory symptoms and reduced oxygenation. Such patients should 
be tested for COVID, along with evaluation for common causes of intrapartum and 
postpartum infection (e.g. chorioamnionitis, endometritis).

Follow-up of pregnant women who recover from COVID-19 
An ultrasound to assess foetal growth is reasonable a few weeks following maternal 
recovery, especially in patients who had severe illness. Very limited COVID-19-specific 
data on foetal growth are available. Foetal growth restriction was reported in two of 
three pregnancies complicated by SARS and who delivered 5 and 7 weeks after the 
onset of illness. The placenta showed areas of foetal thrombotic vasculopathy, which 
may have been caused by SARS-related coagulopathy or placental hypoxia during the 
acute maternal illness.
Postpartum care/breastfeeding
Infant evaluation
	
l Mothers with suspected COVID-19 and unknown test results (either pending 
or not tested): Infants born to such women are not COVID-19 suspect.
	
l Mothers with known COVID-19: Test these infants within 14 days of delivery 
or up to 28 days after birth as they are COVID-19 suspects, and isolate from 
other healthy infants, and they should be cared for according to infection control 
precautions for patients with confirmed or suspected COVID-19. 
Mother–baby contact 
	 1.	Room-in stable neonates exposed to COVID-19 infection from mothers or other 
relatives with their mothers and be exclusively breast-fed. A healthy, willing, 
asymptomatic family member, COVID-19 negative, may be allowed in the room 
to provide support for breastfeeding and helping in taking care of the neonate. 
Temporary separation (not rooming-in and avoiding skin-to-skin contact) can be 
stressful for mothers; disrupt breastfeeding; and have negative effects on newborn 
stress, feeding and bonding).
	 2.	If mother–baby separation is implemented because of sickness of the mother or 
neonate or the neonate is being fed with expressed breast milk of the mother by a 
nurse or a trained family member who has not been in contact with the mother or 
other suspected/proven case, the following should be considered:
	
l Infant COVID-19 suspects should be isolated from other healthy infants and 
cared for accordingly.
	
l If another healthy family member is providing infant care (e.g. diapering, bathing, 
feeding), he/she should use appropriate personal protective equipment (healthy 
family members should wear a gown, gloves, face mask and eye protection).
	 3.	If separation is indicated (the mother is on transmission-based precautions) but not 
implemented, other measures may be utilized to reduce potential mother-to-infant 
transmission and include:
	
l Physical barriers (e.g. a curtain between the mother and the newborn) can be 
constructed, and the newborn can be kept ≥6 feet away from the mother.
	
l The mother can wear a face mask and practice hand hygiene when in close 
contact with her infant, particularly when feeding.

828    Standard Treatment Guidelines
After hospital discharge
Discharge if COVID test is negative and maternal and foetal/neonatal condition is 
stable. A mother with COVID-19 infection should maintain a distance of at least 6 feet 
from the newborn and use a mask and hand hygiene for newborn care until (i) she is 
afebrile for 72 hours without the use of antipyretics and (ii) at least 7 days have passed 
since symptoms first appeared. (For details see Neonate discharge in Chapter 19.)
Breastfeeding and formula feeding: Continue breastfeeding as no virus in the maternal 
milk of infected patients has been found. However, follow all droplet precautions during 
breastfeeding as transmission could occur through close contact during breastfeeding. 
In case the mother and the baby are separated, feed the infant with expressed 
breast milk by another healthy caregiver until the mother has recovered or has been 
proven uninfected, provided that the other caregiver is healthy and follows hygiene 
precautions. The mother should use strict handwashing before pumping and wear a 
mask during pumping. Use a dedicated breast pump. Strict adherence to sterilization 
guidelines is recommended for women bottle feeding with formula or expressed milk.
Analgesia: Acetaminophen as the preferred analgesic agent in the lowest effective 
dose may be used when clinically indicated for postpartum pain. (Caution: There are 
anecdotal reports of possibly experiencing severe disease with the use of ibuprofen 
early in the course of infection.)
Postpartum hospital visit 
	 1.	Modify or reduce postpartum outpatient care to reduce the risk of inadvertent 
exposure. If telehealth is available, perform early postpartum assessments, 
including wound and BP checks, with telehealth followed by a comprehensive 
postpartum visit at 12 weeks, especially in patients with comorbidities.
	 2.	Screen and provide support to all postpartum patients for postpartum depression 
4–8 weeks after delivery by using self-report, 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal 
Depression Scale and anxiety. 
Contraception
	 1.	Permanent and reversible contraception: Permanent contraception (tubal 
sterilization) does not add significant additional time or risk when performed at an 
uncomplicated caesarean birth and thus should be performed if planned. 
	 2.	Defer permanent contraception after a vaginal birth as it is an elective procedure.
	 3.	If a reversible contraceptive method is desired, provide an alternative form of 
contraception (e.g. immediate postpartum long-acting reversible contraception or 
depot medroxyprogesterone acetate) to avoid additional outpatient postpartum visits.

EARLY PREGNANCY COMPLICATIONS
NAUSEA AND VOMITING IN PREGNANCY
Nausea and vomiting of mild-to-moderate intensity are especially common complaints 
from early pregnancy until about 16 weeks. In few cases, they may progress to 
hyperemesis.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l It is a common complaint on rising in the morning but sometimes occurs at other 
times of the day; vomitus is usually small and clear and does not produce any 
impairment of health or restrict the normal activities of the pregnant woman. 
	
l Hyperemesis gravidarum is the most severe form of nausea and persistent 
vomiting leading to weight loss (>5% of prepregnancy weight) and ketosis. 
There are usually signs of dehydration with postural hypotension and tachycardia. 
Hyperemesis gravidarum may cause volume depletion, electrolytes and acid–base 
imbalances, nutritional deficiencies and even death.
	
l Diagnosis is by exclusion of medical and surgical causes of vomiting like liver 
or GIT disorders, pyelonephritis and diabetes mellitus, and molar (and multiple) 
pregnancy should be ruled out in all cases of hyperemesis by ultrasound.

The treatment goals are to:
	
l Reduce symptoms through changes in diet/environment and by medication
	
l Correct consequences or complications of nausea and vomiting (e.g. fluid depletion, 
hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis)
	
l Minimize the maternal and foetal effects of maternal nausea and vomiting and their 
treatment
	
l Look for a medical or a surgical cause and treat accordingly. If no identifiable cause 
is found, treat as given next.

Provide reassurance and advice to take frequent small, dry carbohydrate–rich meals and 
avoid triggers, and advice about diet and avoidance of fatty or spicy foods, especially 
avoidance of large volume of drinks in the morning. Meals and snacks should be eaten 
slowly and in small amounts every 1–2 hours to avoid a full stomach.
A. Moderate cases

Tab. Doxylamine succinate 10 mg + Pyridoxine HCl 10 mg Or Tab. Promethazine 
10 mg 1–2 tablets Or Ondansetron 4–8 mg Or Metoclopramide 10 mg Or 
Domperidone 10 mg at bedtime. If required, one more tablet can be added in the 
morning and afternoon.
B. Excessive vomiting, especially after first trimester (inability to retain anything 
orally): Hospitalize and treat as hyperemesis gravidarum.
C. Hyperemesis gravidarum: There occurs excessive vomiting resulting in metabolic 
acidosis with signs of dehydration (dry tongue, loss of skin turgor, oliguria).
	 1.	Admit all cases in the hospital away from a stressful home environment. 
	 2.	Stop oral intake of fluids and nutrition and start RL or dextrose saline slowly. 
	 3.	Monitor PR, BP, RR and temperature. Perform investigations – CBC, LFT, RFT 
and fT3/fT4/TSH.
	 4.	Check serum electrolytes and urinary ketones at admission and 4 hourly until 
become negative for ketones. 
	 5.	Provide emotional support and psychiatric referral, if required.
	 6.	Perform USG for foetal well-being and to rule out multiple or molar pregnancy and 
liver disorders.
	 7.	Provide antiemetics as above, if required.
Once the vomiting stops and dehydration is corrected, discharge after 24 hours.
In prolonged vomiting
	 1.	Tab. Thiamine 25–50 mg 3 times a day (if orally tolerated). If vomiting is not 
controlled, consider fluid and electrolyte replacement in 6–8 hours.

Chapter 15  Obstetrics and Gynaecology    831
	 2.	Inj. Metoclopramide 10 mg IV or IM 8 hourly.
	 3.	Tab. Pantoprazole 40 mg orally once daily or parenterally 40 mg IV once a day, 
given over at least 2 minutes or over 15 minutes. 
	 4.	If not controlled, Inj. Promethazine chloride 25–50 mg IM or IV 8 hourly.
	
	Or 
	
	Inj. Chlorpromazine 25–50 mg IM 4–6 hourly.
	
	Once vomiting is controlled for 24 hours, oral intake is gradually started. If well 
tolerated, then only IV fluids are omitted. First, dry carbohydrate foods are given 
in the form of small meals at frequent intervals. Gradually, a full diet is introduced. 
In prolonged and severe disease, parenteral nutrition may be necessary.
	
	If well tolerated for 48 hours, the patient can be discharged from the hospital with 
dietary advice, reassurance and continuation of Tab. Doxylamine succinate 10 mg 
+ Tab. Pyridoxine HCl 1–2 tablets at bedtime for 5–7 days or longer depending on 
the response and continue prenatal care.
Monitoring and follow-up
Assess for complications – stress ulcers in the stomach, Mallory–Weiss syndrome, 
jaundice, convulsions, coma and renal failure.
In some refractory severe cases of hyperemesis gravidarum, if maternal survival is 
threatened or if hyperemesis gravidarum is causing severe physical and psychological 
burden, consider termination of the pregnancy.
Patient education
	
l Adjust timing of medication in relation to the time of sickness.
	
l Women with nausea should eat before or as soon as they feel hungry to avoid an 
empty stomach, which can aggravate nausea. A snack before getting out of bed in 
the morning can be helpful.
	
l Women should try to become aware of, and avoid, environmental triggers and 
foods which might provoke their nausea and vomiting. Fluids are better tolerated if 
cold, clear and carbonated or sour (e.g. ginger ale, lemonade) and if taken in small 
amounts between meals.
	
l Taking prenatal vitamins before bed with a snack instead of in the morning or on an 
empty stomach may also be helpful.
	
l Avoid supplements containing iron until symptoms resolve, as iron causes gastric 
irritation and can provoke nausea and vomiting.
	
l This is a benign disorder and gets relieved by 14–16 weeks of pregnancy.

pregnancy. J Obstet Gynaecol Can. 2016;38(12):1127–1137.

l Increased abortions are seen with increasing parity and maternal age. 
	
l Recurrent abortions – two or more consecutive abortions should be investigated

l Effective contraception should be initiated soon after abortion as ovulation can occur 
as early as 2–3 weeks after an abortion.

l Bed rest, reassurance, avoiding constipation, coital abstinence

1.	Inj. Pethidine 50 mg + Promethazine 25 mg for those who have pain and are 
anxious.
	 2.	Tab. Folic acid 5 mg daily. 
	 3.	Monitor for the continuation of pregnancy after confirming cardiac activity by 
USG. Discharge the patient 48 hours after bleeding stops. Continue prenatal care.

l Reporting immediately if bleeding recurs.
	
l Continuing bed rest for at least 2 weeks
	
l Abstinence till at least two follow-up visits in the next 4 weeks when normal

l High-fibre diet to avoid constipation
	
l Need of follow-up after 2 weeks for foetal growth by clinical and/or USG parameters

	– Reassurance, if no living child
	– Need for contraceptive: Can be started immediately after evacuation
	– When to resume coitus: After 4 weeks, if no complications
	– When to attempt conception: After at least 6 months

SEPTIC ABORTION
Any abortion associated with fever and signs of pelvic or generalized sepsis is 
considered septic abortion. It usually results from induced abortions done by untrained 
practitioners using non-sterile techniques, especially in settings where induced abortion 
is illegal, but sepsis may follow spontaneous and elective abortions.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Fever, tachycardia, abdominal distension and tenderness, pelvic tenderness 
and purulent vaginal discharge typically appear within 24–48 hours after an 
abortion. In severe cases, there may be endotoxic shock and end-organ failure.
	
l Complications like injury to viscera like uterus and bowel, internal or external 
haemorrhage, peritonitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, renal failure, 
hepatic failure, endotoxic shock and tetanus can occur.
	
l Investigations include CBC, ABO group and Rh type, serum electrolytes, LFT, 
KFT, coagulation profile, high vaginal and endocervical swab for culture, urine 
culture, blood culture and arterial blood gas. USG is done to confirm or exclude 
retained products of conception, foreign body, intra-abdominal collection and 
uterine/bowel/bladder injury, X-ray abdomen (erect) is done if there is suspicion 
of gut perforation.
Treatment (to be managed at a tertiary care level)
Treatment is intensive antibiotic therapy plus uterine evacuation as soon as possible. 
Initiate treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of suspicion of severe 
sepsis, with or without septic shock after drawing samples for culture and sensitivity. 
Modify antibiotic regimen based on culture results.

1.	IV fluids for correction of electrolyte imbalance (see the section ‘Shock’ in 
Chapter 2). 
	 2.	Oxygen by facemask in severe cases. In cases of adult respiratory distress 
syndrome, intubation and ventilatory support is required, and hydrotherapy, if 
required. 
	 3.	If BP is not controlled with fluid replacement, start Epinephrine through central 
line in dose 0.05–1.5 mcg/kg/min if there is evidence of hypoperfusion and target 
a MAP of 65 mmHg and dose titrated according to clinical and haemodynamic 
response (for details, see Shock and Septicaemia in Chapter 2).

836    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 4.	In case of shock, acidosis is corrected by IV Sodium bicarbonate 50–100 mEq in 
NS. 
	 5.	Empirical antibiotics should be started after taking samples for blood culture and 
other microbiology samples for culture and sensitivity:
	
	Inj. Piperacillin–Tazobactam 4.5 g IV over 30 minutes as a loading dose, and then 
after 4 hours 3.375 g IV over 4 hours and every 8 hours Or in critically ill patients, 
Inj. Imipenem IV 1 g every 6 hours Or Inj. Meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours 
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Clindamycin 900 mg IV 8 hourly plus Inj. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours
	
	Note: Continue the above-mentioned antibiotic therapy until culture sensitivity 
results provide an indication for changing the initial antibiotic regimens or the 
patient does not respond to therapy. Monitor pulse, temperature, BP, RR, urine 
output and serum electrolytes.
	
	In severe cases, CVP and ABG monitoring is required. Therapeutic goals are to 
maintain MAP >65 mmHg, urine output >30 mL/min, arterial PO2 >60 mmHg and 
CVP 6–12 cm H2O.
	 6.	Search and eliminate the source of sepsis.
	
	 A.	 Uterine evacuation: If the patient’s condition is stable within 1 hour of 
antibiotic therapy, evacuation of the uterus by suction or ovum forceps to 
remove infected products. If general condition is low at admission, evacuation 
after 6–8 hours of antibiotic therapy and treat hypovolaemia.
	
	 B.	 Laparotomy in case of injury to the uterus, suspected injury to the gut, presence 
of foreign body in the abdomen as evidenced by X-ray or felt through the 
fornix, and peritonitis.
	
	 	
Or
	
	 	
Colpotomy in cases of pelvic abscess.

ECTOPIC PREGNANCY
Treatment of ectopic pregnancy should be undertaken at a secondary/tertiary care level set-
up. Laparoscopic surgery or laparotomy is done in all cases of ectopic pregnancies except in 
a few selected cases that are highly compliant and reliable and fulfil the following criteria:
	
l Unruptured ectopic pregnancy in a haemodynamically stable patient 
	
l Gestational sac size <3.5 cm in the greatest diameter

Chapter 15  Obstetrics and Gynaecology    837
	
l Serum hCG titre <1000 mIU/mL
	
l Absence of foetal cardiac activity

Refer to a higher centre if ectopic pregnancy is suspected or diagnosed.
Expectant management (for unruptured ectopic pregnancy, gestational sac 
<3.5 cm and low or falling β-hCG <1000 mIU/mL, no pain, no/minimal 
fluid in pouch of Douglas (POD), cardiac activity present, haemodynamically 
stable)
	 1.	Hospitalize the patient.
	 2.	Obtain pre-treatment hCG titres, haemogram, and liver and renal function tests.
	 3.	Repeat hCG titres every 48–72 hours until <20 mIU/mL, and then weekly till 
negative. If β-hCG negative, transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS) is done to see 
resolution of ectopic pregnancy.
Medical management (unruptured haemodynamically stable, cardiac activity 
present, no contraindications to methotrexate, gestational sac <3.5 cm and 
β-hCG <5000 mIU/mL)
Check β-hCG, TVS, haemogram, RFT, LFT, ABO typing and Anti-D in Rh negative
	
l Day 1: Inj. Methotrexate 50 mg/m2 body surface area IM
	
l Day 4: β-hCG
	
l Day 7: β-hCG decline >15%, and then weekly β-hCG titres till negative; if <15%, 
repeat methotrexate
Note: Absolute contraindications to Methotrexate are haemodynamically unstable, 
ruptured ectopic pregnancy, unable to comply with medical management follow-up, 
breastfeeding, immunodeficiency, alcoholism, alcoholic liver disease or chronic liver 
disease, pre-existing blood dyscrasias, sensitive to methotrexate, active pulmonary 
disease, peptic ulcer disease, and hepatic, renal or hematological disorder. Relative 
contraindications are gestational sac >3.5 cm and with embryonic cardiac motion. 
In case of persistent or increasing β-hCG, medical or surgical treatment is given as 
mentioned above.
All other cases should be managed by laparoscopic salpingectomy and the specimen 
should be sent for confirmation by histopathological examination. Laparotomy should 
be done in cases of haemorrhagic shock. Salpingotomy is performed in case of small 
gestational sac <2 cm and located in the distal third of the fallopian tube.
Patient education
	
l Resolution of ectopic pregnancy may take up to 6 weeks. 
	
l A total of 5–10% of cases require surgery despite medical therapy.

838    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Signs and symptoms of tubal rupture such as vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, 
weakness, dizziness or syncope must be reported promptly. 
	
l Patients should refrain from alcohol and folic acid–containing vitamins during this 
period. 
	
l Sexual intercourse should be avoided during therapy and at least 3 months of 
conception interval.

MEDICAL TERMINATION OF PREGNANCY (MTP)
The Government of India has legalized MTP up to 20 weeks of gestation by the MTP 
Act (1971). The MTP (Amendment) Act (2021) amends the Act to increase the upper 
limit for termination from 20 to 24 weeks for certain categories of women, removes 
this limit in the case of substantial foetal abnormalities and constitutes Medical Boards 
at the state level. Under this Act, pregnancy can be terminated under the clauses given 
next by registered persons in registered places only.

1.	Damage to the life of the pregnant woman 
	 2.	Grave injury to the physical or mental health of the pregnant woman 
	 3.	Pregnancy caused by rape 
	 4.	Substantial risk that if the child was born, he/she would suffer from such physical 
or mental abnormalities as to be seriously handicapped
	 5.	Failure of any contraceptive method or device
Key provisions of the MTP Amendment Act (2021)
	 1.	Termination due to failure of contraceptive method or device: Under the Act, a 
pregnancy may be terminated up to 20 weeks in the case of failure of contraceptive 
method or device. 
	 2.	Opinion needed for termination of pregnancy
	 a.	 Opinion of one registered medical practitioner (RMP) for termination of 
pregnancy up to 20 weeks of gestation
	 b.	 Opinion of two RMPs for termination of pregnancy of 20–24 weeks of gestation.
	 c.	 The opinion of the state-level medical board essential for a pregnancy to be 
terminated after 24 weeks in case of substantial foetal abnormalities
	 3.	Upper gestation limit for special categories: The Act increases the upper gestation 
limit from 20 to 24 weeks for special categories of women, including survivors 
of rape, victims of incest and other vulnerable women (differently abled women, 
minors, among others). 
	 4.	Confidentiality: The ‘name and other particulars of a woman whose pregnancy has 
been terminated shall not be revealed’, except to a person authorized in any law

Chapter 15  Obstetrics and Gynaecology    839
that is currently in force. There will be a fine and/or imprisonment of 1 year in case 
of breach of women’s confidentiality.
	 5.	The necessary consent form as laid out in the Act should be duly filled in and 
signed. Opinion of one RMP is mandatory for MTP up to 20 weeks and two RMPs 
for some categories of pregnant women from 20 to 24 weeks as per the MTP 
(Amendment) Act (2021).
	 6.	Maintain admission register and record particulars of the women who receive 
medical abortion drugs and report as per the MTP Act.
First-trimester MTP methods
Uncomplicated incomplete abortion (both induced and spontaneous) can be managed 
with MVA or electric vacuum aspiration (EVA) or with oral, sublingual or vaginal 
medical abortion (preferred).
	
l After checking eligibility (gestation age, Hb, ABO grouping and Rh typing), 
counselling and consent (mandatory as per Form C of the MTP Act), MTP can 
be done up to 49 days’ amenorrhoea after proper counselling and excluding 
contraindications (previous allergic reaction, inherited porphyria, chronic adrenal 
failure and known/suspected ectopic pregnancy). It is not mandatory to perform 
ultrasound (USG) before MTP. USG may be performed for dating a pregnancy 
with irregular cycles, lactation amenorrhoea, clinical discrepancy or uncertainty in 
examination and to exclude an ectopic gestation before a MTP.
	
l In case of Rh negative, there is no need of Inj. Anti-D in medical or surgical abortion 
till 12 weeks.
	
l Refer to Table 15.8 depicting the medical management of abortion and post-
abortal contraception. In the event that vomiting ensues within 30 minutes of oral 
misoprostol, the medication should be repeated. The woman generally aborts in the 
next 4–8 hours. Successful abortion may be confirmed by pelvic examination, pelvic 
ultrasound or a repeat hCG measurement. (Note: Low hCG levels can be detectable 
for up to 4 weeks after successful expulsion.) Follow-up is needed only in the event 
of a problem or excessive bleeding. If ongoing symptoms of pregnancy are reported 
and/or there has only been minimal or no bleeding after taking the medications as 
directed, suspect ongoing pregnancy and evaluate further by pelvic examination 
(demonstrating a growing uterus) or an ultrasound scan (demonstrating an ongoing 
pregnancy). Do not use endometrial thickness as an indicator for this purpose.
	
l In case of partial or incomplete evacuation (prolonged or intermittent heavy episodes 
of bleeding, usually lasting for more than 2 weeks) and if retained products are seen 
on USG, surgical removal of retained products is done. Consider antibiotic cover 
and the possible need of blood transfusion. 
	
l For initiation of contraception, an ultrasound is not needed. Non-IUD methods can 
be started immediately. IUDs can be inserted whenever the medical abortion has 
been deemed successful. Due to the risk of teratogenesis, surgical termination of a 
pregnancy in case of failed medical management is recommended.

840    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Surgical method (in case of uncomplicated incomplete abortion): Suction and 
evacuation can be done only in centres approved under the MTP Act. MVA can be 
done in all PHCs.
Note: Adequate disinfection of the instruments used for performing the termination of 
pregnancy and maintaining the adequate levels of cleanliness are vital to preventing 
post-abortion infection. Antibiotics (oral) should be given for non-life-threatening 
infections and IV antibiotics for life-threatening infections. Warning signs are purulent/
foul-smelling vaginal discharge, fever with chills, giddiness with syncopal attacks and 
severe abdominal pain. Perisurgical single-dose ampicillin, amoxicillin, cephalosporins 
or doxycycline are all effective given 60 minutes prior to the surgical abortion 
procedure to reduce the risk of post-procedural infection.
Patient education
	
l Details of the method and the small risk of complications should be explained. 
	
l Medical methods fail in around 5% of cases and these will require surgical curettage. 
	
l Patients should be motivated for concurrent contraception, and option of all available 
methods, both temporary and permanent, should be discussed prior to abortion. 
However, acceptance of a contraceptive method must never be a precondition for 
providing an abortion.
Second-trimester MTP methods (between 13 and 20 weeks)
	
l For MTP after 24 weeks of gestation in case of substantial foetal abnormality, 
permission of the Medical Board is required.
	
l It should be conducted in secondary and tertiary care level. None of the second 
trimester methods is 100% safe and effective. Misoprostol 400 mcg oral, sublingual 
or vaginal 2–4 hours is given before the procedure for pre-procedure priming of the 
cervix. For the second trimester MTP, medical methods are preferred (Table 15.9).
	
l Methods are usually combined so as to increase the success rate and to shorten 
induction–abortion interval. Most commonly, extra-amniotic ethacridine is combined 
with oxytocin or a combination of mifepristone and misoprostol by various routes.

MEDICAL DISORDERS COMPLICATING PREGNANCY
ANAEMIA IN PREGNANCY
Prevalence of anaemia in pregnancy in India is 80% and that of severe anaemia is 
10–15%. Causes of anaemia in pregnancy are the same as those encountered in the non-
pregnant state. However, iron-deficiency anaemia is the commonest cause in pregnancy. 
In about 40–50% of cases, there is an associated folic acid deficiency.
Anaemia in pregnancy is defined as haemoglobin concentration of less than 11 g/dL 
and haematocrit of less than 33%. It is further classified depending on Hb levels as 
mild (10–11 g/dL), moderate (7–10 g/dL), severe (<7 g/dL) and very severe (<4 g/dL).

after 1–2 weeks. Reticulocyte response is observed in 5–10 days (increases to 5–6%) 
and rise in Hb/haematocrit in 2–3 weeks. The concentration is expected to rise at the

non-compliance, defective absorption, continuing loss, associated deficiencies and

Total dose of iron to be given is calculated using the following formulae:
2.4 × weight (in kg) × deficit Hb (target Hb – actual Hb) + 500 mg
(Caution: Oral iron is suspended at least 24 hours prior to parenteral therapy to

Supplement with protein and multivitamin after parenteral iron.

Management of patients with anaemia during labour
	 1.	Propped-up position, oxygen therapy, restriction of fluids

MEGALOBLASTIC ANAEMIA IN PREGNANCY
Megaloblastic anaemia is one of the acquired nutritional anaemias that may complicate 
pregnancy. The two most common causes are deficiencies of folic acid or vitamin B12; 
however, most often it is secondary to folic acid deficiency as folate requirements are 
increased during gestation. It is referred to as pernicious anaemia when deficiency of 
Vitamin B12 is due to its malabsorption in the intestine. Other causes include alcohol 
abuse, chemotherapy, leukaemia, hypothyroidism, certain medications (metformin, ARV, 
phenytoin, valproic acid, sulphasalazine, triamterene) and some genetic conditions.

URINARY TRACT INFECTION IN PREGNANCY
UTIs are among the most common bacterial infections during pregnancy. Hormonal 
and mechanical changes during pregnancy increase the risk of urinary stasis and 
vesicoureteral reflux. These changes, along with an already short urethra and difficulty 
with hygiene due to a distended pregnant belly, increase the frequency of UTIs in 
pregnant women.

Chapter 15  Obstetrics and Gynaecology    845
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l UTIs present as cystitis or acute pyelonephritis.
	
l Fever >38°C with chills, burning and frequent micturition with abdominal pain 
is the typical presentation.
	
l UTI represents a spectrum, from asymptomatic bacteriuria to symptomatic acute 
cystitis, to the most serious, pyelonephritis. 
	
l UTI in pregnancy can cause abortion and pre-term delivery.
	
l Investigations include urine microscopic examination, culture and sensitivity, 
and positive urinalysis result in symptomatic patients, and is confirmed by urine 
culture showing 100,000 CFU/mL or more. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is clinically 
significant at colony counts of 100,000 CFU/mL (105 CFU/mL) or higher. Lower 
colony counts may represent contamination from the vulva or vagina and do not 
require treatment (for details, see ‘Urinary Tract Infections’ in Chapter 10).
Treatment (acute cystitis)
Tab. Nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals 100 mg orally 3–4 times a day for 
5–7 days (Caution: Nitrofurantoin should be avoided after 34-weeks of pregnancy due 
to risk of RBC haemolysis in G6PD-deficient foetuses.)
Or
Cap. Amoxicillin 500 mg orally thrice daily for 5–7 days 
Or
Tab. Cephalexin 500 mg orally twice daily for 3–7 days
Or
Tab. Cefuroxime 250 mg orally twice daily for 3–7 days
Note: Norfloxacin, Ciprofloxacin, Ofloxacin and Nalidixic acid are contraindicated 
in pregnancy.
If not controlled, refer to a higher centre (with a referral slip with all details of the 
investigations and treatment given).
Inj. Cefotaxime 1 g 12 hourly IM/IV for 5–7 days
Or
Inj. Ceftriaxone 1 g daily deep IM or IV given over 5 minutes
Note: Amoxicillin–clavulanate should not be used as a first-line agent in the third 
trimester due to the associated risk of necrotizing enterocolitis in the foetus.
If symptoms recur, repeat urine culture 1–2 weeks after completing the treatment for 
acute cystitis. After treating a recurrent acute infection, initiate antimicrobial urinary 
suppression for the remainder of the pregnancy, preferably using a lower single daily 
dose of an antibacterial drug to which the bacterium isolated was susceptible. 
For details, see ‘Urinary Tract Infections’ in Chapter 10.

HYPERTENSIVE DISORDERS OF PREGNANCY
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy include chronic hypertension (hypertension before 
20 weeks of gestation), gestational hypertension (development of new hypertension 
after 20 weeks of gestation without proteinuria), pre-eclampsia–eclampsia (gestational 
hypertension with or without proteinuria or associated with end-organ damage) and 
pre-eclampsia superimposed on chronic hypertension. White-coat hypertension refers 
to elevated clinic (≥140/90 mm Hg) BP, but normal BP measured at home or work 
(<135/85 mm Hg); it is not an entirely benign condition and conveys an increased risk for 
pre-eclampsia. Masked hypertension is another form of hypertension, more difficult to 
diagnose, characterized by BP that is normal at a clinic visit but elevated at other times, 
most typically diagnosed by 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM) or automated 
home BP monitoring. See Figure 15.5 for differential diagnosis among hypertensive 
disorders in pregnant women. Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy may cause maternal 
and foetal morbidity, and they remain a leading cause of maternal mortality.

PRE-ECLAMPSIA
Pre-eclampsia is one of the most common causes of maternal and perinatal morbidity 
and mortality. It affects around 5–8% of all pregnancies. Pre-eclampsia is principally 
a syndrome of signs occurring more frequently in primigravida. When superimposed 
with convulsions, it is termed eclampsia. Other high-risk factors are multiple pregnancy, 
hydramnios and molar pregnancy.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Hypertension (BP >140/90 mmHg recorded on at least two occasions at least 4 
hours apart or single reading of ≥160/110 mmHg) with or without proteinuria 
and/or non-dependent oedema developing after 20 weeks of gestation in a 
previously normotensive non-proteinuric patient.
	
l Pre-eclampsia definition criteria (Table 15.10): Proteinuria is optimally assessed 
by screening with automated dipstick urinalysis and then, if positive, quantifying 
with a urine protein/creatinine ratio. A ratio ≥30 mg/mmol (0.3 mg/dL) is 
abnormal (Table 15.11). Proteinuria is not mandatory for a diagnosis of pre-
eclampsia. (Trace, 0.1 g/L; 1+, 0.3 g/L; 2+, 1 g/L; 3+, 3 g/L; 4+, 10 g/L.) 
Oedema is excluded from the diagnostic criteria unless pathological. However, 
the presence of pitting oedema over the ankles after 12 hours of rest and/or rapid 
gain in weight of >0.5 kg/week or >2 kg/month may be early features.
	
l Signs of severe pre-eclampsia are BP >160/110 mmHg or higher diastolic on two 
occasions at least 4 hours apart in a woman on bed rest, 24-hour urinary proteins, 
5 g or more of protein or 3+ or greater on urine dipstick testing of two random 
urine samples collected at least 4 hours apart.
	
l Features of imminent eclampsia are severe headache, visual disturbance, 
epigastric or right hypochondriac pain, oliguria (urine output <500 mL/24 hours), 
pulmonary oedema or cyanosis.
	
l Evaluate biochemical parameters: elevated serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL 
or a doubling of baseline, thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100,000/µL), 
microangiopathic haemolysis and raised liver enzymes. 
	
l Complications of severe pre-eclampsia include the following: HELLP 
syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelet count), eclampsia, 
cerebrovascular haemorrhage, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, abruptio 
placentae, IUGR and intrauterine death of foetus.

Hospitalize all cases. Severe BP (>160/110 mmHg) requires urgent treatment in a 
monitored setting. Definitive therapy is to terminate pregnancy. The choice between 
immediate delivery and expectant management depends on:
	 1.	Severity of disease 
	 2.	Condition of the mother and foetus 
	 3.	POG

848    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Obtain blood tests: Hb, grouping, Rh typing, total plate count (TPC), serum urea, 
creatinine, uric acid, LFT (S. bilirubin, SGOT, SGPT, LDH), coagulation profile (PT, 
aPTT, plasma fibrinogen [in selected cases]), urine (routine and microscopic) and 
obstetric USG.
A. Gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia without severe features (outpatient 
expectant management, if pregnancy <37 weeks, no foetal or maternal compromise 
and no proteinuria)
	 1.	Advise complete bed rest preferably in the left lateral position and regular diet 
adequate in proteins and calories with omission of extra table salt.
	 2.	Advise follow-up every week. At each visit:
	
l Check BP, urine for protein, weight and generalized body oedema.
	
l Exclude and counsel about symptoms of severe pre-eclampsia.
	
l Monitor foetal growth; ask the woman about foetal movements; check FHR. 
Perform USG weekly.

1.  Proteinuria 
2.  Other maternal organ dysfunction, including:

l If all observations remain stable, continue follow-up. Book the woman for 
delivery at the PHC/hospital at term (do not allow to cross the EDD).
	
l Refer to a higher centre if BP >150/100 mmHg, GA <30 weeks and foetal 
affection (IUGR, oligohydramnios).
Mild pre-eclampsia (BP >140/90 but <160/100 mmHg)
Follow-up twice a week. Refer and admit at a secondary or tertiary care centre 
if significant proteinuria, pregnancy <32 weeks, unreliable patient, platelets <1 
lakh, elevated urine albumin, deranged uterine or umbilical artery Doppler, foetal 
compromise (IUGR, oligohydramnios). Consider delivery at 37 weeks.
Once 37 weeks are attained or any indication for termination appears, termination 
of pregnancy is done depending on:
	
l Bishop score
	
l Pelvic assessment
	
l Foetal status
In an unfavourable cervix, cervical priming is done with prostaglandin (PGE2 gel) 
or intracervical extra-amniotic Foley's catheter with a balloon of 30 mL NS. In a 
favourable cervix, labour induction is done by oxytocin and ARM.
Gestational age more than 37 weeks
If there is no foetal compromise, assess the cervix, pelvis and foetal presentation. If all 
are favourable, induction should be done. If the cervix is unfavourable but other factors 
are favourable, then ripen the cervix and then induce.
Note: CS should be done for obstetric indications only.
Patient education
	
l Encourage additional period of rest.
	
l Advise no salt restriction but encourage the practice of no extra salt.
	
l The patient undergoing ambulatory treatment should be warned of symptoms of 
worsening disease evidenced by:
	– Gross swelling of the body
	– Oliguria, anuria
	– Headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain
	– Hospitalization if these symptoms appear
	
l Explain the importance of regular ANC as severe pre-eclampsia can supervene 
without any symptoms. Instruct the patient to report immediately in case of ominous 
symptoms such as persistent severe headache, visual disturbances (diminished 
vision, double vision or blindness), epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting and oliguria.
	
l Vitamin C or vitamin E to prevent pre-eclampsia is not recommended.

850    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Pre-eclampsia with severe features
Anti-hypertensive treatment is started if there is persistent BP >140/90 mmHg, and 
if the patient is already on an ACEI or ARB, change to the anti-hypertensive given 
next. The aim of treatment is to achieve a BP less than 140/90 mmHg or equal to 
135/85 mmHg.
	 1.	Tab. Labetalol 100 mg 3 times a day. Some patients may require 1200–2400 mg 
orally per day (titration increments should not exceed 200 mg orally 2 times a day). 
	 2.	If BP is not controlled with the above, add:
	
	Tab. Nifedipine retard 5–10 mg 8 hourly (maximum 60–120 mg/day) (Caution: 
Do not give nifedipine by sublingual route.)
	
	Note: ARBs and ACEIs are foetotoxic; thus are contraindicated in pregnancy.
	 3.	Low-dose aspirin 75–150 mg/day, 12 weeks onwards, if there is a previous history 
of pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, pre-existing vascular disease, 
autoimmune disease or APLA syndrome, type 1 or 2 diabetes or pre-existing 
kidney disease (see Gestosis score) and continue till the birth of the baby.
Monitoring
	
l Daily monitoring of weight gain, BP, urine albumin, urine output
	
l Weekly lab investigations – haemogram with platelet count, liver and kidney 
function tests, especially serum uric acid, fundoscopy
	
l Clotting profile in case of non-severe pre-eclampsia and gestational hypertension 
not necessary if the platelet count is normal
	
l Foetal monitoring by clinical and USG growth assessment, daily foetal movement 
count, NST twice weekly and biophysical score weekly, Doppler studies in IUGR
Definitive management
Termination of pregnancy by labour induction/CS is done in the following conditions:
Gestational age 37 weeks, foetal compromise like severe growth retardation, 
oligohydramnios, abnormal NST or biophysical score, maternal compromise like 
development of features of severe pre-eclampsia, onset of labour, rupture of membrane 
or bleeding. A decision to deliver should not be based on the amount of proteinuria or 
change in the amount of proteinuria.
Refer all cases of severe pre-eclampsia to a higher centre with telephonic message 
to the receiving centre in case:
	
l If CS and blood transfusion facilities are not available (but before transfer, give 
loading dose of Inj. Magnesium sulphate and antihypertensive, if needed)
	
l HELLP syndrome
	
l Acute renal failure or oliguria which persists for more than 48 hours after delivery
	
l In preterm or IUGR foetus when neonatal facilities are not adequate

B. Hypertensive emergency/crisis in pregnancy
	
l Acute-onset, persistent (lasting 15 minutes or more), severe systolic (≥160 mmHg) or 
severe diastolic hypertension (≥110 mmHg) or both in pregnant or postpartum women
Treatment (at PHC)
General measures: Keep the patient in a quiet room in bed and position on the left side.
Start treatment immediately
	 1.	Cap. Nifedipine 10 mg orally (not sublingually), can be repeated after 
30–60 minutes. Maximum dose 20 mg 4 hourly
	 2.	Prophylactic anticonvulsant Inj. Magnesium Sulphate loading dose 4 g diluted 
to 20% (8 mL drug with 12 mL NS) to be given slowly IV in 15 minutes. 5 g IM 
(50%) in each buttock (total 10 g). If recurrent fits after 30 minutes of loading dose, 
repeat 2 g 20% (4 mL drug with 6 mL NS) slow IV in 5 minutes.
Refer to a CHC/higher centre once stable with a trained staff and record of 
treatment with a telephonic message to the referral centre. However, if the woman is 
in the late first stage or second stage of labour, conduct the delivery and start medical 
treatment, stabilize and only then refer the woman for further management, if needed, 
along with a trained staff. 
Severe pre-eclampsia/hypertensive emergency (at referral hospital; 
tertiary care centre preferred)
	
l Observation in the ICU for 24 hours 
	
l Assessment of maternal and foetal conditions; BP monitoring 2–4 hourly; hourly 
urine output monitoring; watching for signs and symptoms of impending eclampsia 
and foetal distress
	
l Lab investigations: Haemogram with platelet count, liver and kidney function tests, 
urinary proteins, coagulation profile, fundus examination, obstetric ultrasound with 
biophysical profile scoring (BPS)
	
l Patient kept nil orally and in impending eclampsia cases, can give intravenous fluids 
like RL at a rate of 60 mL/h (maximum 125 mL/h).

Immediate management
Goals of treatment are the following: gradual lowering of BP to target BP 
≤150/90–100 mmHg (NOT to normalize) and decreasing proteinuria.
	 1.	Tab. Nifedipine 10 mg orally can be repeated after 30–60 minutes (maximum dose 
20 mg 4 hourly). (Caution: Side effects include tachycardia, headache, flushing 
and aggravation of angina. Rapid fall in BP can cause foetal distress. Nifedipine 
should NOT be given sublingually to a woman with hypertension.)
	
	Step-up: If BP is not controlled with oral treatment (>160/110 mmHg), then IV 
drugs are started with intensive monitoring.

852    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
		
Inj. Labetalol 20 mg IV bolus over 2-minute period, followed by second bolus 
40 mg after 10 minutes; if BP not controlled, then third bolus 80 mg after further 
10 minutes or until the desired effect is reached (maximum up to 220 mg). Or IV 
infusion – add 200 mg in NS so as to make total 200 mL infusion (1 mg/mL); start 
at 20 mg/h (20 mL/h) (5–6 drops/min), double every 20 minutes until the desired 
effect is reached (BP ≤150/90–100 mm of Hg), and give maintenance dose 40 mg/h 
(10–12 drops/min).
	
	If an injection is not available, give Tab. Labetalol 200 mg orally and it can be 
repeated in 30 minutes if an appropriate improvement is not observed.
	
	Or
	
	If labetalol is not available or not effective, Inj. Hydralazine 5 mg IV every 
30 minutes, maximum dose 30 mg.
	 2.	Maintenance therapy: After initial control of acute hypertension, start oral 
maintenance therapy with antihypertensives as described in management of mild 
pre-eclampsia given earlier.
	 3.	Prophylactic anticonvulsants in women with severe pre-eclampsia especially in 
cases with signs and symptoms of impending eclampsia. Pritchard regimen: Loading 
dose is Magnesium sulphate 4 g IV as 20% solution over 15 minutes (only in patients 
with eclampsia/impending eclampsia) and simultaneously 10 g intramuscular as 
(50%) solution (5 g in each buttock), 10 mL (5 g) in each buttock (total of 14 g) 
followed by second dose 5 g in alternate buttocks every 4 hours for maintenance. 
(Caution: Magnesium sulphate is contraindicated in myasthenia gravis and impaired 
renal function. Side effects are respiratory depression and neuromuscular depression 
in mothers.) Discontinue after 24 hours once BP is lowered and provide expectant 
management as planned.
	
	Monitor patients before each dose as below and suspend or postpone the use of 
Magnesium sulphate if any of the following is present:
	
l RR <16/min (respiratory depression)
	
l Absent patellar reflex (muscle paresis)
	
l Urine output <30 mL/h in preceding 4 hours (impaired renal function) or 100 
mL in last 4 hours
Management of magnesium sulphate toxicity
	(a)	 If urine output <30 mL/h:
	
l Withhold magnesium sulphate.
	
l Administer RL infusion 1 L infusion over 8 hours.
	
l Monitor for pulmonary oedema.
	(b)	 If respiratory arrest occurs:
	
l Perform assisted ventilation.
	
l Administer Calcium gluconate 1 g (10% of 10 mL) IV slowly over 10 minutes.
	 4.	Corticosteroids for foetal lung maturation: In all women with pre-eclampsia 
delivering before 34 completed weeks, give Inj. Dexamethasone 6 mg 12 hourly 4 
doses or 2 doses of Inj. Betamethasone 12 mg IM 24 hours apart in women. Note: Do 
not use dexamethasone or betamethasone for the treatment of HELLP syndrome.

	After initial evaluation and stabilization of the patient, further management is 
decided depending on foetal maturity and maternal response.
Expectant management: It is considered if pregnancy is between 24 and 34 weeks and 
hypertension controlled with maximum of two drugs, urine output is normal, laboratory 
investigations are normal and there is no foetal compromise. The patient should be 
hospitalized till delivery.
Manage as mentioned in the mild pre-eclampsia with antihypertensives, bed rest and 
more frequent maternal and foetal monitoring.
Definitive management of termination of pregnancy if:
	
l Pregnancy beyond 34 weeks: Stabilize maternal condition and terminate pregnancy.
	
l Pregnancy less than 24 weeks: Stabilize maternal condition and terminate pregnancy. 
	
l Patient on expectant management develops the following features: Uncontrolled 
hypertension despite maximum dose of two antihypertensive drugs, eclampsia, 
raised liver enzyme >2 times with right upper quadrant pain and tenderness, 
pulmonary oedema, platelet <1 lakh/mm3, creatinine >1 mg/dL over baseline, 
persistent headache, vomiting and visual disturbance suggestive of impending 
eclampsia, papilloedema and foetal compromise.
Postpartum care
	 1.	Provide high-dependency care as clinically indicated minimum for 24 hours. 
	 2.	Measure BP at least four times a day; closely monitor for 48 hours; BP must be 
measured up to third to fifth days.
	 3.	Continue antihypertensive treatment if BP >150/100 mmHg.
	 4.	Use labetalol, nifedipine, enalapril, captopril, atenolol and metoprolol. Do not use 
ARB, amlodipine and ACEIs other than enalapril and captopril.
	 5.	Reduce antihypertensives if BP <130/80 mmHg for 48 hours.
	 6.	Maintain close attention to fluid balance. 
	 7.	Instruct postnatal breastfeeding mothers to avoid diuretics. 
	 8.	Consider postpartum thromboprophylaxis. 
	 9.	Measure platelet count, transaminases and serum creatinine 48–72 hours after birth.
	10.	Continue prophylactic anticonvulsant till 24 hours postpartum.
Patient education
	
l Emphasize the need for follow-up visit 1 week after discharge and again after 
6 weeks postpartum for reclassification, necessary investigations and antihypertensive 
treatment if required. 
	
l Advise on the need for preconception counselling in cases of chronic hypertension. 
	
l Advise on the need of close antepartum monitoring in the next pregnancy. Advise 
regarding prophylactic low-dose aspirin (150 mg) started early in pregnancy.
	
l Report immediately if alarming symptoms such as headache, nausea, oliguria and 
visual disturbances are present.

854    Standard Treatment Guidelines
ECLAMPSIA
Eclampsia is a life-threatening complication of severe pre-eclampsia, also called 
toxaemia of pregnancy. It occurs during or after the 20th week of gestation or in the 
postpartum period.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occur generalized convulsions associated with signs of pre-eclampsia 
during pregnancy, labour or within 7 days of delivery and not caused by epilepsy 
or other convulsive disorders. Key warning signs of developing eclampsia in a 
woman diagnosed with pre-eclampsia are severe headaches, blurred or double 
vision or epigastric pain.
	
l Patient may develop acute left ventricular failure, cerebral haemorrhage, renal 
tubular necrosis, DIC, foetal distress, abruptio placentae, foetal death and even 
maternal death can occur.
Treatment (to be managed at a tertiary care level)
Principles of management are control and prevention of recurrence of convulsion and 
control of hypertension. Treat any complication that arises and deliver safely as soon as 
possible. Continue anticonvulsant therapy 24 hours after delivery or last fit whichever 
is later.
Refer patients with eclampsia and ensure that a trained staff member accompanies 
the patient during transfer. Maintain a record of treatment and send a telephonic 
message to the referral unit, ensuring availability of a mouth gag and oxygen, and 
placing the patient in the left lateral position.
Non-pharmacological (during seizures)
	
l Place the patient in left lateral position in a separate quiet room with padded rails 
on the sides of the bed. Secure and maintain the airway. Use mouth gag or airway 
to prevent tongue biting/tongue falling back. Intubate if the patient is deeply 
unconscious or there is poor arterial blood gases, extensive laryngeal oedema and 
extreme restlessness.
	
l Perform suction to remove oropharyngeal secretions. 
	
l Provide oxygen by facemask at 6–8 L/min.
	
l Set up IV access and start IV fluids – RL at 60 mL/h; catheterize with an indwelling 
catheter.
	
l Monitor heart rate and respiration, BP and urine input/output hourly. 
	
l Perform the following laboratory investigations: haemogram with platelet count, liver 
and kidney function tests, urinary proteins, coagulation profile, serum electrolytes 
and fundus examination.
	
l Foetal assessment includes DFMC, daily NST and USG.

	 2.	Fluid management (RL 1–1.5 mL/kg/h or 80 mL/h) should be closely monitored

factors need invasive monitoring, continuous frusemide or renal dose dopamine

	 3.	Antihypertensives: These are given as described in ‘Pre-eclampsia’ above. 
The aim is to gradually lower the BP to 140–150/90–100 mmHg. Monitor BP 
every 15 minutes. Cap. Nifedipine 5–10 mg is given orally. Repeat 10 mg every 
30–60 minutes till adequate response is seen. 
Definitive management is termination of pregnancy irrespective of foetal maturity. 
Termination is by labour induction and vaginal delivery if good prospects are seen 
within 24 hours or CS in case of an unfavourable cervix not responding to priming or 
worsening maternal or foetal condition.
Indications of CS are the following: all deeply unconscious patients unless delivery is 
imminent, uncooperative patient due to restlessness, foetal distress, failed induction or 
any other obstetric indication, if vaginal delivery is unlikely to occur within 6–8 hours 
from the onset of the first eclamptic seizure or eclamptic seizures are not controlled in 
6–8 hours and other obstetric indications.

856    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Care after delivery
	
l Patients with eclampsia and severe pre-eclampsia need intensive monitoring for at 
least the initial 72 hours. 
	
l Continue anticonvulsant till 24 hours after delivery or fit, whichever occurs later. 
	
l Gradually decrease the dose of antihypertensives. 
	
l The patient is discharged after 10–14 days of delivery or earlier if BP is controlled 
without antihypertensives. 
	
l Follow up after 6 weeks for re-evaluation.
Patient education
	
l Delivery is the only definitive treatment. Underlying disease remains till delivery 
and complications can arise despite control of BP on treatment. 
	
l Symptoms of severe pre-eclampsia like headache, vomiting, epigastric pain, 
decreased urine output and blurring of vision should be immediately reported. 
	
l There is a need for prolonged hospitalization. 
	
l Advise early booking in the next pregnancy as there is 25–30% risk of recurrence. 
	
l Prophylactic measures like low-dose aspirin can be started in early pregnancy. 
	
l There is a need for re-evaluation at 6 weeks postpartum for reclassification and 
investigations of hypertension and a need for long-term antihypertensives. 
	
l There is a high risk of development of chronic hypertension in later life.

PREGNANCY WITH HEART DISEASE
Organic heart disease in pregnancy is commonly due to rheumatic heart disease 
followed by congenital heart disease. Rheumatic valvular lesion predominantly includes 
mitral stenosis (80%). Marked haemodynamic changes in pregnancy have profound 
effects on heart disease. Cardiac failure occurs during pregnancy around 30 weeks, 
during labour and soon following delivery.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occur severe or progressive dyspnoea, progressive orthopnoea, paroxysmal 
nocturnal dyspnoea, haemoptysis, syncope with exertion or chest pain related to 
effort or emotions.
	
l Signs are murmur – pansystolic, late systolic, loud ejection systolic and diastolic 
associated with a thrill.
	
l Echocardiography is diagnostic.
Treatment (refer to a tertiary care centre as soon as diagnosis made)
If the woman comes in cardiac failure to PHC or CHC:
	 1.	Oxygen
	 2.	Propped-up position
	 3.	Inj. Frusemide 40–80 mg IV 
	 4.	Shifted to a tertiary care centre once stable, preferably with a trained person
Depending on the limitation of physical activity, the patient is classified into 
classes I–IV of the New York Heart Association (NYHA) (Table 15.12) and managed 
according to the NYHA class irrespective of the aetiology of the heart disease.

Indications for MTP before 12 weeks are primary pulmonary hypertension, 
Eisenmenger’s syndrome and pulmonary veno-occlusive diseases. Relative indications 
are history of heart failure in a previous pregnancy or NYHA class 3 or 4 in the present

l Frequent antenatal visits. Ask for shortness of breath, orthopnoea, wheezing, 
palpitation and weight gain, and check for basal rales, hepatomegaly and 
dependent oedema.
	
l Reassign NYHA grade at every visit.
	
l In congenital heart disease, perform USG for foetal anomaly at 11–13 and 18–22 
weeks and foetal echocardiography at 22–24 weeks.
	
l Rest for 10 hours each night and 1–2 hours after each meal. Light housework and 
walking without climbing stairs are permitted. No heavy work is allowed. 
	
l Avoid extra salt intake.
	
l Detect and treat the risk factors, e.g. infections (urinary, dental, respiratory tract), 
anaemia, hypertension, arrhythmias and hypothyroidism.
	
l Elective admission to hospital: 
Grade I: At 38 weeks
Grade II: At 28 weeks
Grade III and grade IV: As soon as pregnancy is diagnosed, should keep the 
patient in the hospital throughout the pregnancy
	
l Emergency admission to the hospital is done in case of any deterioration of 
functional status, pregnancy complication, onset of cough, dyspnoea, chest pain, 
crepts or tachyarrhythmias.

DIABETES IN PREGNANCY
Pregnancy can be complicated by pre-existing insulin-dependent or non-insulin-
dependent diabetes or GDM. GDM is defined as the carbohydrate intolerance of 
variable severity with onset or first recognition during pregnancy.
Screen all pregnant women. Risk assessment for GDM should be undertaken at 
the first prenatal visit. Figure 15.9 depicts the diagnostic algorithm and management of 
GDM. If 2-hour postprandial is ≥120, it is called decreased gestational glucose tolerance 
(DGGT) and if 2-hour postprandial is >140 mg/dL, it is called GDM. A fasting plasma 
glucose level >126 mg/dL or a casual glucose > 200 mg/dL meets the threshold for 
the diagnosis of diabetes, i.e. overt DM, if confirmed on a subsequent day, and precludes 
the need for any glucose challenge.

All pregnancies in females with diabetes should be managed at a referral facility/tertiary 
care centre. GDM can be easily controlled by diet (medical nutrition therapy [MNT]) 
and exercise. Only in few women in whom blood sugar is not controlled by diet and 
physical exercise, oral antidiabetic (metformin) or insulin injections are required.

Medical nutrition therapy (MNT): Complex carbohydrates should provide about 
35–45% of the total calories, proteins 20–25% (10 g extra intake of protein) and fat 
35–40% which should be well distributed throughout the day. A high-fibre diet is 
beneficial with 30–50 g fibre daily. Total diet should be distributed in three major meals 
and three mid-meal snacks. Total daily calorie intake should be 30 kcal/kg current 
pregnancy body weight if the patient’s current weight is 80–120% of the ideal pre-
pregnancy weight. In case current weight is <80% or >120% of the ideal pre-pregnancy 
weight, then calorie intake is 35–40 kcal/kg current pregnancy weight or 25 kcal/kg 
current pregnancy weight respectively. Total daily calorie intake should be 30–35 kcal/
kg current pregnancy weight; if the woman’s weight is more than 150% of the ideal 
body weight, then caloric intake is 15 kcal. An extra 250–400 kcal can be taken in the 
second and third trimesters.

864    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Monitoring of glycaemic control:
	
l Monitor fasting blood sugar (FBS) and 2-hour postprandial blood sugar (PPBS). 
Perform first follow-up after 2 weeks of starting diabetic diet and subsequent 
follow-up till 28 weeks once in a month, from 28 to 32 weeks every 2 weeks, and 
after 32 weeks every week till delivery. In high-risk pregnancies, frequency of 
monitoring may be intensified by self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG). For 
details, see ‘Diabetes Mellitus’ in Chapter 11.
	
l Glycosylated Hb (HbA1c) should be done in the first trimester. The A1c target in 
pregnancy is <6% if this can be achieved without significant hypoglycaemia, but 
the target may be relaxed to <7% if necessary to prevent hypoglycaemia. Value of 
9% or above indicates poor glycaemic control and carries a higher risk of congenital 
malformation; MTP may be offered after proper evaluation. 
	
l Glycaemic goals in patients on diabetic diet are fasting venous <95 mg/dL; 1-hour 
postprandial <140 mg/dL and 2-hour postprandial <120 mg/dL. If 50% values are 
deranged, then start insulin along with diabetic diet.
Antepartum foetal monitoring
Ultrasound assessment of foetal gestational age should be done as early as possible. 
Routine anomaly scan is done at 9–11 weeks and then at 18–22 weeks and foetal 
ECHO at 24–26 weeks of gestation. Assessment of asymmetric foetal growth is done 
by ultrasonography, particularly in the early third trimester. Thereafter, routine obstetric 
scan is done once a month, especially to detect macrosomia and polyhydramnios.

Hospitalize in case of excessive vomiting; infections; maternal complications such 
as hypertension, retinopathy and nephropathy; foetal compromise like macrosomia 
or intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR); or poor diabetic control. Congenital foetal 
anomalies are directly related to glycaemic control in the first trimester only. Good 
glyaemic control during organogenesis reduces the rate of congenital malformations.
A. Antenatal management: Initial evaluation should include blood sugar, KFT and 
fundoscopy.
(a) Pre-existing diabetes
	 1.	If the patient is on oral hypoglycaemics and his/her disease is controlled, switch to 
insulin therapy as soon as pregnancy is diagnosed. Metformin and glyburide can 
be continued. (Caution: Both cross the placenta to the foetus but teratogenesis is 
not reported; however, long-term effects are under investigation.) Other oral and 
non-insulin injectable glucose-lowering medications lack long-term safety data. 
Discontinue Metformin by the end of the first trimester, when used to treat PCOS 
and induce ovulation. Do not use Metformin in women with hypertension or pre-
eclampsia or who are at risk for intrauterine growth retardation.
	 2.	Inj Insulin: 0.6–0.8 unit/kg in the first trimester, 0.7–0.9 unit/kg in the second 
trimester and 0.8–1.2 units/kg in the third trimester. Figure 15.10 depicts insulin 
therapy algorithm in gestational diabetes.

	 3.	Usually, a combination of intermediate-acting and regular insulin in proportion 
of 2:1 is given. Two-thirds of the total requirement is given in the morning before 
breakfast and one-third is given at night with regular insulin before dinner and 
intermediate at bedtime. Dose adjustment is done to maintain blood sugar level 
between fasting <90 mg/dL and postprandial <120 mg/dL. Sampling of blood 
should be done initially fasting, pre- and post-breakfast, pre- and post-lunch, pre- 
and post-dinner, and 2 AM regularly till controlled and then daily monitoring by 
fasting and postmeal sugars.
(b) GDM
	 1.	General management is the same as outlined above. 
	 2.	Reassess after 2 weeks of diet control. If FBS >90 mg/dL and 2-hour PPBS is 
>120 mg/dL, start insulin therapy. Regular insulin, if required, may be given before 
breakfast, before lunch and before dinner or a combination of regular and long-
acting insulin can be given before breakfast and dinner. Hypoglycaemia should 
be avoided. Start insulin from smaller doses. The initial dose of NPH (Neutral 
Protamine Hagedorn) insulin could be as low as 4 units and dose adjusted by 
follow-up blood sugar every fourth day.
	 3.	If fasting plasma sugar is >120 mg/dL, insulin is usually required for control. 
Regular insulin is adjusted to normalize post-breakfast glucose and intermediate-
acting insulin for post-lunch glucose control. If evening or fasting glucose is 
elevated, a second daily injection is added. If both are elevated, a mixture of 
intermediate and regular insulin before dinner is added. If only fasting is elevated, 
add intermediate-acting insulin at bedtime.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Regular Insulin 3 times a day before each main meal which can be combined 
with 1 dose of intermediate-acting insulin at bedtime in case there is fasting 
hyperglycaemia.
	(c)	Overt DM: Overt DM is said to be present if any of the following findings are 
recorded: random blood sugar or 2-hour PPBS >200 mg/dL, FBS >126 mg/dL and 
HbA1c >6.5%.
	
	Start insulin directly with MNT in consultation with endocrinologists. There is 
an increased incidence of pre-eclampsia (25%) in patients with GDM. Low-dose 
aspirin 75/81 mg daily reduces pre-eclampsia and small-for-gestational-age baby 
by improving uteroplacental circulation.
	
	Blood sugar target: Target blood sugar is to achieve plasma blood sugar levels 
fasting <90 mg/dL, before lunch, dinner and bedtime snack, if 60–105 mg/dL; after 
meals (2 hours) <120 mg/dL; and from 2.00 to 6 AM >60 mg/dL. When levels are 
high, daily monitoring with insulin dose adjustment is required.
	
	Once control is achieved, the patient can be managed at home with weekly blood 
sugar profile.

Chapter 15  Obstetrics and Gynaecology    867
Antepartum monitoring
	 1.	Urine glucose monitoring is not useful in GDM.
	 2.	Maternal surveillance includes BP and urine protein monitoring to detect 
hypertensive disorders.
B. Time for delivery and management during labour: In uncomplicated cases 
on MNT with good glycaemic control, pregnancy can be continued till the EDD. In 
patients on Metformin or Insulin, delivery is planned at 38–40 completed weeks unless 
glycaemic control is poor or another indication for delivery is present. In the presence 
of complications or foetal compromise, pregnancy is terminated earlier, but requires 
balancing in view of increased risk of neonatal morbidity or mortality associated with 
early delivery and the increased risk of stillbirth associated with expected management. 
Unless otherwise indicated, elective CS is performed if estimated foetal weight is >4 kg.
Labour is managed with intensive monitoring. Blood sugars are monitored 3–4 hourly; 
the aim is to keep blood sugars between 100 and 120 mg/dL, using the sliding scale 
method with regular insulin. If glucose level <70 mg/dL, start 5% Dextrose infusion. 
During labour, be prepared for shoulder dystocia and early cord clamping.
C.  Immediate neonatal care for baby of mother with GDM
	
l A paediatrician experienced in resuscitation of the newborn should be present during 
delivery. Avoid hypothermia in the newborn, and encourage early breastfeeding to 
prevent hypoglycaemia and observe for 24 hours. 
	
l Monitor newborn for hypoglycaemia starting at 1 hour of birth and continue 
every 4 hours (prior to the next feed) till four stable glucose values are obtained. 
The cut-off capillary blood glucose for hypoglycaemia is <45 mg/dL in normal-
birth-weight newborn and <54 mg/dL in case of IUGR to initiate treatment. 
Evaluate for other neonatal complications like respiratory distress, convulsions and 
hyperbilirubinaemia. Conduct physical examination to exclude congenital anomalies.
D.  Follow-up of GDM in postpartum period
Monitor maternal blood glucose level after delivery and 24-hour postpartum, and if found 
to be high, check again on follow-up after 6–12 weeks of delivery by glucose tolerance test 
(GTT) and reclassify as outside of pregnancy. If found normal, repeat GTT after 6 months 
and every year to determine return of glucose intolerance or progression. In patients with 
GDM and chronic hypertension BP, the target is 120–160 systolic/80–105 diastolic.
For other details, see ‘Diabetes Mellitus’ in Chapter 11.
Patient education
	
l In all patients of childbearing age with known type 1 or type 2 diabetes, good 
blood sugar control should be achieved in the preconception period/next delivery 
and throughout pregnancy to avoid high risk of congenital anomalies. Prepare 
a contraceptive plan to prevent pregnancy until glycaemic targets are achieved. 
Provide Folic acid supplement (400 mcg routine) prior to conception and throughout 
pregnancy. Review and provide counselling on the use of nicotine products, alcohol 
and recreational drugs, including marijuana. Emphasize monitoring for glycaemic

control and complications (retinopathy) in every trimester and for 1 year postpartum 
as these patients are at risk of developing subsequent diabetes.
	
l Provide comprehensive diabetes self-management education. Strict adherence to 
dietary advice and insulin therapy is essential throughout pregnancy. As insulin 
requirements change throughout pregnancy, frequent blood sugar monitoring is 
required throughout pregnancy. 
	
l Patient on insulin therapy should be told about symptoms of hypoglycaemia like 
palpitations, sweating and dizziness and their management. 
	
l Counsel women with GDM about the increased risk of recurrence in subsequent 
pregnancies and risk of developing frank diabetes later.
	
l Contraceptive advice – combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) and IUDs are 
preferably avoided. Barrier methods, progestogen-only pills/implants/injectables or 
sterilization can be offered.

PREGNANCY
PRETERM LABOUR
The onset of labour pains in pregnant women after 24 weeks and before 37 weeks of 
gestation associated with progressive dilatation and effacement of the cervix is known 
as preterm labour. Subcategories of PTB are based on gestational age: extremely 
preterm (<28 weeks), very preterm (28 to <32 weeks) and moderate to late preterm 
(32 to <37 weeks). Preterm babies are prone to serious illness or death during the 
neonatal period, and preterm labour is the single largest leading cause of neonatal death 
and the second leading cause of deaths among children younger than 5 years. Without 
appropriate treatment, survivors are at an increased risk of lifelong disability and poor 
quality of life (QOL).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occur uterine contractions of duration of 30 seconds or more, with two to 
three contractions per 10 minutes accompanied by cervical dilatation (>2 cm) and 
effacement (>80%) with or without leaking or bleeding per vaginum.

l Risk factors include low socioeconomic status, heavy manual labour, extremes of 
age (younger than 20 years and older than 40 years), previous history of abortion or 
preterm delivery, cervical or vaginal infection, multiple pregnancy or over-distended 
uterus, cervical incompetence or other uterine malformations, cervical length on TVS 
≤25 mm, hypoxic conditions like anaemia, heart disease, pre-eclampsia, IUGR, foetal 
congenital malformations and antepartum haemorrhage in the present pregnancy.

condition: Obstetric Disorders Complicating Pregnancy Preterm Labour
text:
l Screen women for high-risk preterm delivery and treat correctable cause, if any. 
Treat infections, if present. Advise coital abstinence, avoiding smoking and avoiding 
strenuous exercise. 
	
l Perform antepartum foetal surveillance as per high-risk pregnancy protocol. Perform 
serial ultrasound examination for cervical length (CL), funneling of the cervix and 
bulging of the membrane in the endocervical canal. Perform prophylactic cervical 
cerclage only if there is documented cervical incompetence. Foetal fibronectin (fFN) 
test is done between 24 and 34 weeks. It is not informative if done with ruptured 
membranes, bleeding, cervical cerclage in situ and gestation <24 or >34 weeks 
(normal value >50 ng/mL).
	
l Educate about warning signs for preterm labour – menstrual-like cramps, low 
dull backache, pressure (feels like the baby is pushing down), increase in vaginal 
discharge, leaking and uterine contractions <10 minutes apart even if painless.
	
l Admit patients with a low risk of delivery for observation (no evidence of cervical 
changes, negative fFN, cervix length <20 mm); offer analgesia. Reassess after 
2 hours. If there are no/irregular infrequent contractions and no cervical changes, 
discharge and follow-up as an outpatient after 7 days.
Established preterm labour
	 1.	Recommend hospitalization with complete bed rest, preferably in a centre with 
neonatal ICU.
	 2.	Perform the following laboratory investigations: haemogram, urine culture and 
endocervical swab for culture and sensitivity, C-reactive protein and USG for foetal 
well-being. Assess cervical dilatation by sterile digital vaginal examination unless 
it is contraindicated by ruptured membranes and suspected placenta praevia.
	 3.	Tocolytic treatments (acute and maintenance treatments) are not recommended for 
women at risk of imminent PTB for the purpose of improving newborn outcomes. 
They are needed for the first 48 hours only to allow for the action of steroids; 
transfer to a tertiary care facility if necessary.
	
		
Immediate tocolysis is performed in pregnancies <34 weeks, if membranes are 
intact and labour is not advanced (cervical dilatation <4 cm), those needing transfer to 
a hospital for neonatal intensive care, those who have not yet completed a full course 
of corticosteroids and there is no indication for immediate delivery. Note: Vaginal
