bleeding, placental abruption or intrauterine infection is not a contraindication 
for tocolysis.
	
	Cap. Nifedipine 20 mg orally loading dose is given; repeat after 30 minutes if 
contraction persists, followed by 10–20 mg every 4–8 hours until contractions 
cease or for up to 48 hours. (Caution: Do not administer along with magnesium 
sulphate; it is contraindicated in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes [PPROM], 
chorioamnionitis, placenta abruption, maternal hypotension [<90/50 mmHg] and 
cardiac disease. Use with caution in renal disease; maternal side effects include 
flushing, headache, nausea, dizziness and hypotension.)
	
	If nifedipine is contraindicated, though very expensive, consider after 
cost-effectiveness analysis Inj. Atosiban 6.75 mg IV over 1 minute vial followed by 
an infusion of 18 mg/h for 3 hours and then 6 mg/h for up to 45 hours (to a maximum 
of 330 mg) in 0.9% NS. The duration of treatment is 48 hours. 
Monitoring during tocolysis
Monitor pulse, BP and cessation of uterine contractions. 
If PR >120/min and BP <90/50 mmHg, stop tocolysis. 
Monitoring in magnesium sulphate therapy is as outlined in Eclampsia above. 
Monitor for the onset of chorioamnionitis (fever, maternal or foetal tachycardia, 
uterine tenderness, foul-smelling liquor, leucocytosis).
	 4.	Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is given in eligible women at 24–34 weeks of 
maturity; when PTB is considered imminent within 7 days of starting treatment, 
including within the first 24 hours, and PPROM and no clinical signs of infection are 
present, steroids are given for foetal lung maturity.
	
	Inj. Dexamethasone 6 mg IM 4 doses 12 hours apart or 12 mg IM 2 doses 
12 hours apart.
	
	(Caution: It is contraindicated if clinical or laboratory evidence of chorioamnionitis 
is present. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is not recommended in women 
undergoing planned CS at late preterm gestations [34–36+6 weeks]). 
	 5.	Cap. Ampicillin 500 mg Or Erythromycin 500 mg 4 times a day for 5–7 days, only if 
there is premature rupture of membranes (PROM) and no clinical signs of infection. 
Routine antibiotics are not recommended in patients with intact amniotic membranes 
and no clinical signs of infection. Prenatal Co-amoxiclav is also not recommended.
	
		
Patients may be discharged after 1 week of tocolysis followed by regular 
antenatal surveillance.
	 6.	Progesterone supplementation is restricted to women with a singleton pregnancy 
and a history of spontaneous PTB with a shortened cervix ≤20 mm at ≤24 
weeks on transvaginal sonography in the mid-trimester. In singletons without 
prior spontaneous preterm birth (SPTB) but CL ≤20 mm at ≤24 weeks, vaginal 
progesterone 200 mg suppository daily is given from diagnosis of short CL until 
36 weeks. In singletons with prior spontaneous PTB 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone 
caproate (17-OHPC), 250 mg/weekly IM is given preferably starting at 
16–20 weeks until 36 weeks.

	Note: Neither vaginal progesterone nor 17-OHPC is recommended as a preventive 
agent in singleton gestations with no prior PTB, unknown CL, preterm labour and 
preterm premature rupture of membranes, and for asymptomatic women with a 
positive cervicovaginal fFN screen result and multiple pregnancy. In these women 
with prior PTB, if the transvaginal ultrasound CL shortens to <25 mm at <24 
weeks, cervical cerclage may be offered.
	 7.	Role of cervical cerclage: Cervical cerclage is not routinely recommended; it is 
useful only in documented short, cervical insufficiency. 
	 8.	When gestational age <32 weeks at any time from immediately prior to birth up 
to 24 hours prior to anticipated birth, imminent PTB (cervix ≥4 cm) or planned 
PTB for foetal or maternal indications (pre-eclampsia), Inj. Magnesium sulphate 4 
g loading dose IV over 30 minutes followed by 1 g/h till delivery or maximum up 
to 24 hours whichever came first. (Caution: Do not combine with nifedipine.)
Indications for immediate delivery
These include advanced labour, major foetal malformation, ineffective tocolysis, 
chorioamnionitis, other maternal or foetal indications for delivery, foetal death, 
pregnancy >34 weeks with attained lung maturity and foetal distress.
	 1.	The mode of delivery is decided as per obstetric indications.
	 2.	Careful foetal monitoring is required throughout labour in women in established 
pre-term labour if group B Streptococcus (GBS) is found on high vaginal swab 
(HVS) or mid-stream urine (MSU) or they have had a previously affected baby.
	 3.	Inj. Penicillin G 5 million units IV initial dose, and then 2.5 million units IV every 
4 hours till delivery Or Inj. Ampicillin 2 g IV initial dose, and then 1 g IV every 
8 hours till delivery is given. 
	
	If penicillin allergic, give Inj. Cefazolin 2 g IV initial dose, and then 1 g IV every 
8 hours till delivery. If at a high risk for anaphylaxis, give Inj. Clindamycin 900 mg 
IV every 8 hours till delivery Or Inj. Erythromycin 500 mg IV every 6 hours until 
delivery Or Inj. Vancomycin 1 g IV every 12 hours till delivery.
	 4.	Avoid using the ventouse at less than 36 weeks. 
	 5.	Ensure that the neonatal team is present for delivery.
	 6.	Perform early cord clamping to prevent hypervolaemia, polycythaemia and 
neonatal jaundice.
	 7.	If there is any sign of hypoxia, CS is better, but the foetus should have a fairly good 
chance of survival depending on the neonatal care facility.
Newborn interventions
	
l Ensure availability of adequate childbirth care (including resuscitation, thermal care, 
feeding support, infection treatment and safe oxygen use). Provide kangaroo mother 
care for the routine care of newborns weighing 2000 g or less at birth, as soon as the 
newborns are clinically stable.
	
l Unstable newborns weighing 2000 g or less at birth, or stable newborns weighing 
less than 2000 g who cannot be given kangaroo mother care, should be cared for in a

during stabilization and transfer of preterm newborns to specialized neonatal care 
wards, wrapping in plastic bags/wraps may be considered as an alternative to prevent 
hypothermia.
	
l Start continuous positive airway pressure therapy for newborns with respiratory 
distress syndrome as soon as the diagnosis of respiratory distress syndrome is made. 
	
l Start surfactant replacement therapy for intubated and ventilated newborns with 
respiratory distress syndrome early (within the first 2 hours after birth). However, 
prophylactic administration in preterm newborns before the onset of respiratory 
distress is not recommended. 
	
l Start oxygen therapy with 30% oxygen or air (if blended oxygen is not available), 
rather than with 100% oxygen. Use progressively higher concentrations of oxygen 
only if the neonates's heart rate remains <60 beats/min after 30 seconds of adequate 
ventilation with 30% oxygen or air. 
Patient education
	
l Advise the patient to restrict physical activity after discharge. 
	
l Advise sexual abstinence till at least 34 weeks of gestation. 
	
l Explain the risk of recurrence in subsequent pregnancy, and therefore the need for 
early booking and prophylactic measures in the next pregnancy.

ANTEPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE
APH is defined as bleeding from the genital tract after 20 weeks of pregnancy and 
before completion of the second stage of labour. It is a major cause of maternal 
morbidity, mortality and perinatal loss. APH is due to placental cause (placenta praevia, 
abruptio placentae) in as high as 70% of cases, and in 25–30% of cases, the cause may 
remain undetermined. Placenta praevia is more common among multiparous women. 
The higher the order of pregnancy, the more is the chance of placenta praevia. Abruptio 
placentae is more common among primigravida women; however, it may be seen in 
multipara also. It is usually associated with hypertensive disorders in pregnancy.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Clinical presentation varies depending on the severity of blood loss 
(Table 15.13) and cause of bleeding (Table 15.14). In mild haemorrhage, there 
may be no maternal or foetal compromise, while massive haemorrhage can lead to 
hypovolaemic shock, coagulation failure, renal failure and foetal distress and may 
result in maternal and foetal death. In case of silent abruption, classic features of 
abdominal pain and tense and tender uterus may be absent in posterior placenta.

the suspected diagnosis of placenta praevia at 20 weeks of gestation by abdominal 
scan and by transvaginal scan, and then a repeat scan at 36 weeks to look for 
placental migration.

Antenatal management of placenta praevia
The aim is to prevent premature births.
	 1.	Prevent and treat anaemia in placenta praevia.
	 2.	Counsel regarding the risk of preterm delivery and haemorrhage.
	 3.	Investigate and manage warning bleeding.
	 4.	Rule out adherent placenta in known case of placenta praevia with previous CS.

A. Massive haemorrhage
The resuscitative measures given next are started immediately in massive haemorrhage. 
Simultaneously prepare the patient for termination of pregnancy by vaginal/CS

1.	Establish intravenous line (one or two 14/16-gauge cannula)
	 a.	Draw 20 mL blood for cross-match, haemogram and coagulation profile.

	 2.	Head down tilt, keep the patient warm. 
	 3.	Provide oxygen by mask at 8 L/min.
	 4.	Empty the bladder (Foley’s catheter for urine output). Maintain input and output chart.
	 5.	In haemodynamically unstable patients, perform initial resuscitation and stabilization 
with crystalloids and colloids and blood replacement therapy. Immediate transfusion 
of packed cells is done regardless of initial vital signs and initial haemoglobin.
a.	 Give enough blood and crystalloids to maintain a haematocrit at least 30% and 
urine output at least 30 mL/h.
b.	Always obtain DIC profile; if present, administer fresh frozen plasma or

c.	 There is no place of heparin in obstetric haemorrhage.
d.	Avoid surgical procedures if possible in the presence of existing or impending

	 6.	Rule out vasa praevia, placental separation and other causes of bleeding.
	 7.	Perform the following laboratory tests: Hb, grouping, Rh typing, cross-matching, 
bedside coagulation profile and urine for protein and sugar.
	 8.	Perform USG to assess gestational age, BPP, presentation and estimated foetal 
weight, and exclude associated abruption and congenital anomalies.
	 9.	Monitor vital signs. Perform further obstetric management as per establishment of 
diagnosis and take decision about delivery or expectant management.

Expectant management
In a case of placenta praevia without maternal and foetal compromise, expectant 
management is planned if pregnancy is less than 37 weeks and the patient is not having 
active bleeding and labour pains and there is no congenital anomaly in the foetus.

a.	 Indications for CS are the following: any time in gestation if severe bleeding/

For induction, ARM is done followed by oxytocin infusion. Oxytocin infusion is

Criteria for outpatient management
These include 72 hours of in-patient observation without vaginal bleeding, stable 
serial haematocrit ≥35%, reactive NST at time of discharge, 24-hour transport facility 
available, compliance with bed rest at home and weekly clinical follow-up until 
delivery including serial Hb and USG.

POST-TERM PREGNANCY
Postdated/post-term pregnancy is defined as pregnancy reached or continued beyond 
2 weeks of EDD, i.e. 42 completed weeks or ≥294 days from the first day of last 
menstrual period (EDD plus 14 days) while late-term gestation is defined as one occurring 
after 41 completed weeks. Maternal risks of post-term pregnancy include an increased 
frequency of labour abnormalities and sequelae of failed labour induction and foetal 
macrosomia, third- and fourth-degree perineal lacerations and PPH. Foetal risks of post-
term pregnancies include an increased risk of stillbirth, macrosomia, which increases the 
likelihood of operative vaginal deliveries, caesarean deliveries and shoulder dystocia, as 
well as neonatal seizures, meconium aspiration syndrome and low 5-minute Apgar scores.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Diagnosis of prolonged pregnancy is based on correct menstrual history and 
obstetric examination (fundal height; abdominal girth – static or diminished; 
foetal head – hard, fixed or engaged; amount of liquor – diminished; palpation – 
feeling of full of foetus) and internal examination (feeling of hard skull bones of 
the foetus through the cervix or fornices).
	
l Perform USG for estimation of gestational age, amniotic fluid volume, placental 
grading, foetal biometry, estimated foetal weight and congenital anomalies.
Treatment (all cases to be managed at a higher centre)
Women with post-term gestations who have an unfavourable cervix can either undergo 
labour induction or be managed expectantly with foetal monitoring (Fig. 15.12).
The exact timing of induction (between 41 and 42 weeks of gestation) is decided 
considering clinician and patient preferences and local circumstances.
Patient education
	
l Accurate determination of gestational age is essential for accurate diagnosis and 
appropriate management of late-term and post-term pregnancies. 
	
l If there is a difference of greater than 5 days between gestational age date using 
the last menstrual period and first-trimester ultrasound (preferably between 11 and 
14 weeks), the estimated date of delivery should be adjusted as per the ultrasound. 
On second-trimester ultrasound, if there is a difference of greater than 10 days, the 
estimated date of delivery should be adjusted as per the second-trimester ultrasound. 
When there has been both a first- and a second-trimester ultrasound, the gestational 
age should be determined by the earliest ultrasound.

CONTRACEPTION
A method or a system which allows intercourse and yet prevents conception is called a 
contraceptive method. This contraception may be temporary when the effect lasts only 
till the couple uses the method, but the fertility returns after the use is discontinued. 
The permanent contraceptive methods are surgical and are aimed to achieve sterility 
after a surgical procedure.
A couple in the reproductive age group who desires contraception should be 
provided information about all the available methods of contraception and should 
be counselled and helped so as to choose a method most suitable for that couple. 
Various contraceptive methods available are:
I. Temporary methods
A.	 Hormonal contraceptives
	– COCPs
	– Injectable hormonal contraceptives (DMPA and NET-EN)
	– Progesterone-only pill (ketodesogestrel)
B.	 Non-hormonal contraceptive pills
	– Centchroman
C.	 Intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD)
	– Multiload 280 and Multiload 375
	– CuT 380A
	– LNG IUD (Mirena)
D.	 Barrier methods
	– Male condoms
	– Vaginal diaphragms with spermicidal jelly
	– Contraceptive sponge
II. Permanent methods
A.	 Female sterilization
	– Postpartum sterilization
	– Interval ligation (laparoscopic or minilap ligation)
	– Ligation concurrent with MTP
B.	 Male sterilization
	– Vasectomy (traditional or non-scalpel)
I. Temporary contraceptive methods
A. Hormonal contraceptive pills
(i) Combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs)
Any of the low-dose COCPs containing 30 mcg Ethinyloestradiol and a Progestin 
(0.3 mg Norgestrel or 0.15 mg Levonorgestrel or 0.15 mg Desogestrel) can be 
prescribed. One tablet should be taken daily with meals at a consistent time. It should 
be started on day 5 of the menstrual cycle. Abstinence or barrier method should be used 
for 5 days. Pills should be taken for 3 weeks followed by 1 week of pill-free interval 
during which placebo tablets should be taken if the pack contains 28 tablets.

Contraindications
COCPs are contraindicated in cases with current or history of:
	
l Thromboembolic disease, cerebrovascular disease, coronary artery disease
	
l Complicated valvular heart disease
	
l Active liver disease
	
l Current or past breast cancer 
	
l Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding 
	
l Pregnancy 
	
l Heavy smokers older than 35 years
	
l Migraine with neurological symptoms 
	
l Diabetes >20 years or with vascular disease 
	
l Current gallbladder disease 
	
l Uncontrolled hypertension (BP >160/100)
Note: Oral contraceptives should not be taken during the first 6 months postpartum by 
breastfeeding females and the first 3 weeks postpartum by non-breastfeeding females. 
Pills can be started immediately after spontaneous or induced abortion. They can be 
used with caution in cases with controlled hypertension, diabetes, migraine without 
neurological symptoms and non-smokers with age more than 35 years without any 
other medical illness.
Follow-up: The first follow-up should be within 3 months and then annually. Follow-
up involves history, BP, urinalysis, breast examination, liver palpation and pelvic 
examination.
Patient education
Common side effects are nausea, vomiting, GI upset, breast changes, weight gain, acne, 
breakthrough bleeding, amenorrhoea, rash and vaginal candidiasis. Side effects usually 
decrease after 2–3 months of use.

C. Emergency contraception
Emergency contraception (EC) is not a regular FP method and is not an abortifacient 
and is intended for ‘emergency use’ alone. Emergency contraceptive pills (ECP) are not 
effective once the process of implantation of fertilized ovum has begun.
Indications: All the hormonal OCPs (combined as well as single) in varying doses 
and IUCDs can be used for EC after a voluntary sexual act without contraceptive 
protection; incorrect or inconsistent use of regular contraceptive methods – failure to 
take oral contraceptives for more than 3 days and being late for contraceptive injection; 
contraceptive failure or mishaps: miscalculation of an infertile period; failed coitus 
interruptus; expulsion of an intrauterine device and/or in case of slippage/leakage/
breakage of condom; and in the event of sexual assault. 
	 1.	The first dose of ECP should be taken within 72 hours (more effective if used 
within 12–24 hours) following unprotected sex. Failure of EC to prevent pregnancy 
beyond the time frame of efficacy window (72–120 hours) following unprotected 
intercourse limits its use in clients who usually report later than this interval. The 
calculation of 72 hours or 3 days should start from the first unprotected penetrative 
vaginal intercourse the woman has had during that particular menstrual cycle.
	
	Any of the following can be used:
	
	Levonorgestrel (LNG) 0.75 mg single dose of 1 tablet of 1.5 mg or 2 tablets of 
0.75 mg each. Or 2 doses of 1 tablet 0.75 mg each, 12 hours apart. Or
	
	COCPs containing 50 mcg Ethinyloestradiol with 0.3 mg Norgestrel 4 tablets 
12 hourly for 2 doses.
	
	Or
	
	Low-dose COCPs containing 30 mcg Ethinyloestradiol with 0.3 mg Norgestrel 4 
tablets 12 hourly for 2 doses.
	
	Note: Side effects are similar to those with OCP as seen in the first weeks of 
starting OCPs and last for 1–2 days. Overall, ECPs are well tolerated. Some women 
may experience nausea and vomiting with ECPs.
	 2.	IUCD insertion is done within 5 days of unprotected act provided there is no 
evidence of pelvic infection or rape.

l Explain side effects of ECP which include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, fatigue, 
headache, lower abdominal pain, breast tenderness and vaginal bleeding. 
	
l ECP must be used under medical supervision. 
	
l EC is not a regular FP method and is not an abortifacient and is intended for 
‘emergency use’ alone. It decreases the risk of pregnancy by 70–90%. The earlier it 
is taken, the better is the success rate. EC does not protect against subsequent acts 
of coitus (except IUCD).
	
l If vomiting occurs within 2 hours of the dose, it must be repeated.

D. Intrauterine contraceptive devices
Any of the devices mentioned next can be inserted inside the uterus by trained health 
personnel at a healthcare facility under aseptic conditions after obtaining informed 
consent. IUCD should be inserted during or shortly after menstruation during the 
follicular phase of menstruation. The CuT 380A can be inserted immediately after 
delivery with counselling and informed consent (post-placental IUCD [PPIUCD]) 
within 10 minutes after expulsion of the placenta following vaginal delivery on the 
same delivery table; intra-caesarean insertion is done after removal of the placenta and 
before closure of the uterine incision or within 48 hours after delivery, or post-abortion, 
if there is no infection, bleeding or any other contraindication. The IUCD should not 
be inserted from 48 hours to 6 weeks following delivery because there is an increased 
risk of infection and expulsion. It can be inserted within 5 days of unprotected coitus. 
These devices need to be changed after the duration of their lifespan (Table 15.15). 
Post-abortal IUCD can be inserted following MTP with surgical or medical method and 
spontaneous or medically managed complete abortion.
	
l Advise the client to report any increase in vaginal bleeding or uterine cramping.
	
l Manage vaginal haemorrhage related to uterine atony as per the standard procedure 
(immediate PPIUCD does not increase the risk of uterine atony).
	
l If severe uterine cramping occurs and persists after PPIUCD insertion, conduct a 
speculum or bimanual examination to check for partial or complete expulsion.
	
l If the woman complains of fever, perform a full clinical evaluation and manage 
infection accordingly.

	 1.	Displacement of IUCD
–	 It can be visualized in the cervix or upper vagina after placement.
–	 Remove IUCD with sterile forceps and reinsert the same IUCD if not 
contaminated with all aseptic precautions. If IUCD has been contaminated, 
discard it and use a new IUCD.
	 2.	Uterine perforation 
–	 It occurs rarely.
–	 Signs and symptoms of perforation are sudden loss of resistance to inserting 
instruments during insertions, unexplained pain and uterine depth greater than 
estimated. 
–	 If suspected, stop the procedure and gently remove instruments and IUCD.
–	 Keep the client at rest, start IV drip and observe vital signs and abdominal 
tenderness, guarding and rigidity.
–	 It there is severe abdominal pain, any change in vital signs or peritoneal signs, 
refer for emergency surgical intervention.
–	 Administer prophylactic antibiotics.
Follow-up: The first follow-up should be after the next menstrual period to check for 
complications and to rule out expulsion. After that, perform follow-up as and when 
required.
Contraindications
	
l Pregnancy, postpartum 48 hours to 6 weeks, septic abortion, distorted uterine cavity, 
uterine fibroids, current or past history (within 3 months) of PID or STD, increased 
risk of STD, AIDS, pelvic tuberculosis, unexplained vaginal bleeding, trophoblastic 
disease, genital tract malignancy
Patient education
	
l Give a card mentioning the type of IUCD inserted and date, along with month and 
year when IUCD needs to be replaced/removed and contact phone number if she 
has any problems with IUCD.
	
l Common side effects are increased menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhoea. These 
decrease after initial 2–3 months.
	
l Spontaneous expulsion can happen in some cases; a new IUCD can be reinserted.
	
l At 6 weeks postpartum, the IUCD strings can be felt by some women. If bothersome, 
the string can be cut short.
	
l Return for removal of the IUCD at any time she wants pregnancy and she will have 
an almost immediate return of fertility.
	
l IUCD offers no protection from HIV or other STDs, so report if abnormal vaginal 
discharge occurs.
	
l Failure rates are 0.5–3%. Ectopic pregnancy can still occur. Report if there is missed 
period or persistent irregular or heavy bleeding accompanied by severe pain in the 
abdomen.

888    Standard Treatment Guidelines
E. Barrier methods
These are inexpensive, available over-the-counter and coitus-dependent methods. Male 
condoms, vaginal diaphragm, spermicidal jellies and vaginal sponge can be used.
Male condoms
Any of the available condoms can be used. For each act of coitus, a new condom should 
be used. If the condom breaks or if there is spillage or leakage during intercourse, the 
woman should contact a clinician within 72 hours and emergency contraception (EC) 
should be provided to her.
Contraindication: The only contraindication is in cases with severe allergy to latex 
rubber.
Vaginal diaphragm
It is available in different sizes. Proper size should be checked by a clinician by 
pelvic examination. It should be inserted only 2 hours before intercourse. About 
a tablespoonful of spermicidal cream or jelly should be placed in the dome of the 
diaphragm prior to insertion. It should be left in place for approximately 6 hours (but 
not >24 hours) after coitus. Additional spermicide should be placed in the vagina before 
each additional episode of sexual intercourse, without removing the diaphragm. After 
removal, wash with soap and water, rinse and dry.
Follow-up: It is performed annually to assess proper fitting of the diaphragm.
Contraceptive sponge
Contraceptive sponge contains spermicidal agent such as Nonoxynol 9. It should be 
removed at least 6 hours after sexual intercourse. The maximal wear time is 30 hours.
Patient education
	
l Barrier methods provide protection against STDs and PID. Only condoms have been 
proven to prevent HIV infection. 
	
l Other advantages are prevention of diseases like PID and carcinoma cervix. 
	
l It can be used soon after delivery. 
	
l There are no hormonal side effects. 
	
l Side effects like vaginal dryness, itching, irritation and allergic reactions can occur. 
	
l Failure rates are very high; condoms, 14%; diaphragm with spermicidal jelly, 20%; 
sponge, 28% (highest) have been reported.
II. Permanent contraceptive methods
There is no strict age limit for permanent methods, but they are typically recommended 
for individuals who have completed their family planning goals.
In practice, these methods are often performed after the age of 30 or after the birth 
of the second child. However, decisions regarding permanent methods should be 
made based on individual circumstances, health and informed consent. Permanent 
contraception is provided by sterilization operation in male or female partners.

The client must make informed decision voluntarily and must give consent on the 
consent form for sterilization. 
A. Female sterilization
Sterilization can be done by laparoscopic ligation for interval ligation and by 
mini-laparotomy for first trimester abortions or tubectomy.
Timing
	
l Interval sterilization: Within 7 days after the menstrual period is over or after 
6 weeks postpartum
	
l Postpartum sterilization: After delivery till 7 days but preferably within 48 hours
	
l MTP: Concurrently
	
l Spontaneous abortion: Concurrently but under antibiotic cover and in the absence 
of infection and anaemia
Contraindications
There are no absolute contraindications. Relative contraindications are psychiatric 
disorder, acute febrile illness, jaundice, Hb <8 g/dL, chronic systemic disease, 
malignancy, bleeding disorder and severe nutritional deficiency. Postpartum sterilization 
is contraindicated in puerperal sepsis or fever, severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, 
premature rupture of membrane >24 hours, severe APH or PPH, and genital tract trauma.
Note: Post-abortal sterilization is contraindicated in sepsis, fever, haemorrhage, severe 
trauma, uterine perforation and acute haematometra.
Follow-up: The first follow-up should be done 7 days after the surgery for wound 
examination and stitch removal if required. The second follow-up is recommended after 
1 month or after next menstrual period, whichever is earlier. Subsequent follow-ups are 
done if the client develops any complication or has a query.
B. Male sterilization
Contraindications
There are no absolute contraindications. Relative contraindications include psychiatric 
and physical illness, local genital conditions, including large varicocele, hydrocele, 
inguinal hernia, filariasis, cryptorchidism, previous scrotal surgery and intrascrotal mass.
Follow-up: The first follow-up is done after 7 days of surgery for wound examination 
and stitch removal. The second follow-up is done after 3 months with semen analysis.
Subsequent follow-ups are done if required in case of any complication or queries.
Patient education
	
l It is a safe and simple procedure.
	
l It is a permanent method to prevent future pregnancies.
	
l It does not affect sexual pleasure, ability or performance.
	
l It has a small chance of failure even if performed under optimum circumstances.

20 ejaculations or for a period of 3 months.
	
l Sterilization does not provide protection against reproductive tract infections/STDs 
or HIV/AIDS.
	
l Failure rates with female sterilization are <0.5% and with male sterilization <0.1%.

PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE
PID is a spectrum of infections involving female upper genital tract, i.e. cervix, uterus, 
tubes, ovaries and pelvic peritoneum. The disease may have an acute or chronic 
presentation. Most cases of acute PID are the result of polymicrobial infection. The 
commonest cause is sexually transmitted diseases and other causes are post-abortal and 
puerperal sepsis, operative procedures like dilatation and curettage, endometrial biopsy 
and insertion of IUD.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l PID is diagnosed if lower abdominal pain and if one or more of the following 
minimum clinical criteria are present on pelvic examination: cervical motion 
tenderness, uterine tenderness and adnexal tenderness. One or more of the 
following additional criteria include tubo-ovarian mass, fever, cervical discharge 
and leucocytosis. 
	
l In severe cases, the patient may be toxic with high-grade fever, vomiting, dehydration 
and abdominal distension.

Treatment (acute PID)
The patient can be treated as an outpatient or in-patient depending on the severity of 
clinical features.
I. Outpatient treatment
	 1.	Patients with mild to moderately severe PID with slight pain and tenderness 
without toxic features like high-grade fever, vomiting and abdominal distension 
can be managed as outdoor patients as according to presenting symptoms, signs, 
clinical conditions and causative organisms. For details, see Chapter 14.
	 2.	Follow-up is done after 2–3 days of initiation of therapy; the patient is re-evaluated 
for clinical response. If there is poor response, the patient should be admitted for 
intravenous antibiotics.
See also ‘Sexually Transmitted Infection (Syndromic Approach)’ in Chapter 14.
II. Indoor treatment
	
l Hospitalize if diagnosis is uncertain and surgical emergencies such as appendicitis 
and ectopic pregnancy cannot be ruled out; the patient has tubo-ovarian abscess, 
pregnancy, severe illness or nausea and vomiting; the patient is HIV positive or 
unable to follow or tolerate an outpatient regimen; or outpatient therapy has failed.
	
l Advise bed rest and hydrotherapy if the patient is febrile. IV fluids are given in cases 
of vomiting and dehydration and correction of electrolyte imbalance.
	
l Investigate and obtain haemogram with ESR, LFT, KFT, serum electrolytes, blood 
culture, endocervical swab culture and ultrasonography, if adnexal mass is present.
	
l Monitor by clinical condition, vital monitoring, signs and symptoms of pelvic 
abscess and peritonitis.

Either of the following regimens may be instituted at the earliest without waiting for 
culture reports:
A. Regimen A
	 1.	Inj. Cefoxitin 2 g IV every 6 hours for 2–4 days
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Cefotetan 2 g IV every 12 hours
	 2.	Inj. Doxycycline 100 mg IV or orally every 12 hours
	 3.	Inj. Metronidazole 500 mg IV 8 hourly

B. Regimen B
	 1.	Inj. Clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours
	 2.	Inj. Gentamicin 2 mg/kg IV followed by 1.5 mg/kg every 8 hours
	 3.	Inj. Metronidazole 500 mg IV 8 hourly
	 4.	In case of severe pain, Inj. Diclofenac sodium 75 mg deep IM 8 hourly
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Paracetamol 1 g as and when required

and pelvic tenderness, improvement in constitutional symptoms). After this, 
Doxycycline 100 mg 2 times a day orally or Clindamycin 450 mg oral 4 times a

	Inj. Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM in a single dose Plus Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice

Follow-up: Clinical improvement (defervescence; reduction in direct or rebound 
abdominal tenderness; and reduction in uterine, adnexal and cervical motion

Consider further diagnostic tests/laparoscopy if symptoms do not improve or worsen 
within 72 hours. Different procedures may be required in the following situations:
	
l Colpotomy for drainage of midline pelvic abscess
	
l Dilatation and evacuation of septic products of conception in post-abortal sepsis
	
l Laparotomy in cases of pyoperitoneum, resistant peritonitis, intestinal obstruction,

l Evaluate, test and presumptively treat the sexual male partner if he have had a

l Inj. Ceftriaxone 125 mg IM followed by oral Doxycycline 100 mg 2 times a day for

Removal of intrauterine device
If PID occurs with an IUD in place, treat the PID using appropriate antibiotics. 
Removal of the IUD does not provide any additional benefit.
Note: Do not remove IUD if the woman wishes to continue its use. However, remove 
it after commencing antimicrobials if the patient does not want to keep the IUD. After 
removal of the IUD, contraceptive counselling is necessary. 
Treatment (chronic PID)
Chronic PID can also be caused by pelvic tuberculosis which requires medical treatment 
first. Treatment of chronic PID is surgical. The type of surgery is decided considering 
pathological lesion, patient’s age and desire for child bearing. Definitive surgery is total 
abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy but in young females, 
conservative surgery is preferred. Injection Placenta extract and pelvic diathermy may help.
Treatment (pelvic tuberculosis)
Primary treatment is medical therapy with antitubercular drugs for 6 months (for 
details, see ‘Tuberculosis’ in Chapter 1). 
Indications of surgery are primary unresponsiveness, persistence or enlargement 
of adnexal mass after 4–6 months of treatment, and persistence or recurrence of pelvic 
pain on treatment. Definitive surgery is total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral 
salpingo-oophorectomy.
Patient education
	
l Emphasize behavioural and contraceptive methods to prevent the acquisition 
of STDs. 
	
l Patients must be encouraged to complete the recommended antibiotic treatment for 
the full course, i.e. 14 days. 
	
l Advise sexual abstinence until complete treatment. The sexual partner of the patient 
diagnosed with PID must be treated to prevent reinfection.

DYSMENORRHOEA
It is defined as painful menstruation of sufficient magnitude so as to incapacitate 
day-to-day activities. There is no identifiable pelvic pathology in primary 
dysmenorrhoea (incidence 15–20%), and in secondary (congestive) dysmenorrhoea, 
pain occurs in the presence of pelvic pathology. Common causes include fibroids, 
adenomyosis, PID, endometriosis, ovarian cyst or tumours, IUCD and STI.

l There occurs crampy pain over the lower back, above the suprapubic region and 
pelvic bone.
	
l Some have severe pain in their back and in thighs.
	
l It usually starts a day before menstruation and is relieved gradually over 1–3 days 
with the flow of menstrual blood.
	
l Other symptoms include nausea, diarrhoea, fatigue, headache and fever. Severity 
ranges from intermittent, mild to disabling.
	
l Diagnosis is clinical, per abdomen, per vaginum examination and pelvic US 
laparoscopy.

l Improvement in general health and psychotherapy; usual activities including sports 
to be continued; exercise, acupuncture, sleep relaxation techniques

In patients with persistent dysmenorrhea despite medical therapy with NSAIDs 
and/or oral contraceptives, consider Laparoscopy for diagnosis and therapeutic purpose.

PREMENSTRUAL SYNDROME (PMS)
PMS is a cyclic recurrence of physical, psychological or behavioural symptoms that 
appear after ovulation and resolve after the onset of menstruation. It requires treatment 
when the symptoms are severe enough to interfere with the woman’s lifestyle, 
relationships and occupational functioning.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Common somatic symptoms include feeling of bloating, body aches, breast 
tenderness, headache, food cravings and poor concentration. Emotional 
symptoms include emotional hypersensitivity, depression, irritability, mood 
swings, anxiety, tension, fear of loss of control and confusion. The degree and 
type of symptoms can vary significantly from woman to woman.
	
l Diagnosis is confirmed by excluding the concomitant medical or psychiatric 
disorders with which it may be confused (depending on the symptoms).

Lifestyle advice should be offered to all women as the first line of treatment.
	
l Daily charting of symptoms for 2 months
	
l Dietary modifications like increasing complex carbohydrate meals; reducing or 
eliminating – especially in the luteal phase – salts, chocolate, caffeine and alcohol; 
and consuming several small meals per day
	
l Moderate regular aerobic exercise like brisk walk 1–2 miles/day for 4–5 days/week
	
l Stress management courses/counselling

1.	Tab. Pyridoxine 100 mg/day for 10–14 days (during luteal phase) (maximum daily 
dose is 150 mg)
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Evening primrose oil 500 mg 3 times a day
	 2.	In case of headache or premenstrual dysmenorrhoea, NSAIDs like mefenamic acid 
500 mg 3 times a day for the duration of symptoms till the onset of menstruation

	Tab. Spironolactone 100 mg/day
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Bromocriptine 1.25–5 mg/day in the luteal phase for mastalgia
	
	(Caution: Common side effects are nausea and vomiting. Tablets can be given

	 4.	Tab. Fluoxetine 5–20 mg/day 2 weeks before the symptoms or throughout the

	Low-dose COCPs, 1 pill daily from 5th to 25th day of the cycle.
	
	Or

POLYCYSTIC OVARIAN SYNDROME (PCOS)
PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in 5–10% of reproductive-age-group 
women worldwide. Although its exact aetiology is unclear, it emerges from a complex 
interaction of genetic and environmental traits. PCOS is characterized clinically 
by oligomenorrhoea and hyperandrogenism, as well as the frequent presence of 
associated risk factors for cardiovascular disease, including obesity, glucose intolerance,

Chapter 15  Obstetrics and Gynaecology    897
dyslipidaemia and obstructive sleep apnoea. Broadly four phenotypes have been 
identified: phenotype A with androgen excess + ovulatory dysfunction + polycystic 
ovarian morphology; phenotype B with androgen excess + ovulatory dysfunction; 
phenotype C with androgen excess + polycystic ovarian morphology; phenotype D 
with ovulatory dysfunction + polycystic ovarian morphology.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Using the Rotterdam criteria, diagnosis requires the presence of at least two 
of the following three findings: hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction and 
polycystic ovaries. However, in adolescents, if clinical or biochemical features 
of hyperandrogenism and anovulation are present, demonstration of polycystic 
ovaries on USG is not essential for diagnosis of this condition. Delay work-up 
in adolescents with oligomenorrhoea for 2 years as anovulation is common after 
menarche. In adolescents, diagnosis is based on the presence of clinical and/or 
biochemical hyperandrogenaemia.
	
l Menstrual dysfunction: The menstrual irregularity typically begins in the peripubertal 
period, and menarche may be delayed. The menstrual pattern is typically one of 
oligomenorrhoea (fewer than nine menstrual periods in a year) and, less often, 
amenorrhoea (no menstrual periods for 3 or more consecutive months). Women with 
PCOS often experience more regular cycles after age 40 years.
	
l Hyperandrogenism can be diagnosed clinically by the presence of excessive 
acne, androgenic alopecia, acanthosis nigricans or hirsutism (terminal hair in a 
male-pattern distribution); or by hyperandrogenaemia. However, measurement 
of androgen levels is helpful on rare occasions when an androgen-secreting 
tumour is suspected (i.e. when a patient has marked virilization or rapid onset of 
symptoms associated with PCOS).
	
l A polycystic ovary is defined as an ovary containing 20 or more follicles per 
ovary when 8 mm Hz USG probe is used, each measuring 2–9 mm in diameter. 
String of pearls appearance (peripheral distribution of follicles) or an ovary 
that has a volume of greater than 10 mL ensuring no corpora lutea, cysts or 
dominant follicles are present on transvaginal ultrasonography. If corpus luteum 
or dominant follicle is seen. the scan should be repeated in the next cycle. On 
transabdominal USG, ovarian volume ≥10 mL on either ovary. In patients with 
irregular menstrual cycles and hyperandrogenism and in patients with <8 years 
after menarche, an ovarian ultrasound is not necessary for PCOS diagnosis.
	
l Insulin resistance prevalence is 50–75% with acanthosis nigricans and obesity. 
Insulin resistance is the root cause of obesity.
	
l Depending on presentation and appearance of symptoms, exclude pregnancy, 
thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinaemia and non-classical congenital adrenal 
hyperplasia and endometrial cancer.

l Lifestyle changes, including diet, exercise, weight loss and cessation of smoking, 
are the first line of treatment for improvement of long-term outcomes and should 
precede and accompany pharmacological treatment. 
	
l Screen and address metabolic complications in all patients including BP evaluation, 
a lipid panel, a 2-hour oral GTT, and obstructive sleep apnoea.

The goals for treatment depend on the presenting complaint and the profile of 
the patient with PCOS. Treatment should be individualized depending on the 
age, reproductive needs and main complaints, and it may be directed towards 
treating infertility, regulating menses for endometrial protection and controlling 
hyperandrogenic features, including hirsutism and acne.
First-line therapy for patients who are unable to achieve adequate control with 
lifestyle interventions on the patient’s presentation and desire for pregnancy includes:
I.	
In case pregnancy or ovulation induction not desired for menstrual abnormalities 
and hirsutism/acne, and for adolescents, COCPs, patches, vaginal ring containing 
Ethinyloestradiol 20–30 mcg combined with a progestin such as Norethindrone 
or Norethindrone acetate, progestins (Desogestrel, Cyproterone acetate, and 
Drospirenone). (Caution: Avoid 35 mcg Ethinyloestradiol plus Cyproterone acetate 
preparations. Avoid preparations that have Norgestrel and Levonorgestrel because 
of their androgenic activity. There is also an increased risk of thrombotic events in 
women with obesity, thrombophilias, past history of thromboembolism, etc.)
	
For menstrual irregularities in sexually mature adolescents who choose not to or 
cannot take COCP, intermittent Progestin therapy as below:
	
Tab. Micronized progesterone 100–200 mg given orally at bedtime 
	
Or
	
Tab. Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) 10 mg given orally at bedtime for 
7–10 days out of each month or cycle
	
Or
	
Inj. DMPA 150 mg intramuscularly every 3 months 
	
Withdrawal bleeding can be expected to occur within a few days of cessation of the 
course of progestin administration. (Caution: Side effects include mood symptoms 
[depression], bloating and breast soreness. Oral progestin is NOT a means of 
contraception.)
	
In the case of endometrial hyperplasia, progesterone derivatives, progestin-
containing oral contraceptives or the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system 
(Mirena) may be given.

Chapter 15  Obstetrics and Gynaecology    899
	
Menstrual abnormalities usually can be controlled within 1–2 months of starting 
COCP treatment and androgen levels are normalized within 18–21 days. In those 
who respond to or tolerate COCP, continue for a few years, and then induce a 
withdrawal bleed at least every 3–4 months. If there is no withdrawal bleeding 
or abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), rule out endometrial hyperplasia with 
transvaginal ultrasound. In PCOS, an endometrial thickness of less than 7 mm 
is unlikely to be hyperplasia. For heavy menstrual bleeding, a higher dose may 
be required, and once active bleeding is controlled, therapy with cyclic COCP or 
progestin should be started to prevent recurrence of AUB.
II.	 For metabolic/glycaemic abnormalities and for improving menstrual irregularities, 
in adolescents and if unable to tolerate COCP, in addition to lifestyle modification, 
give:
	
Tab. Metformin 500 mg daily to be taken before the evening meal to minimize 
nausea; increase the dose gradually to 1000–2000 mg daily in 2 divided doses or 
delayed-release preparation in once-daily dose. A minimum of 3-month therapy 
is required. (Caution: It is contraindicated in patients with impaired hepatic or 
renal function, alcoholism or cardiopulmonary insufficiency and can cause lactic 
acidosis; obtain metabolic panel as a baseline.)
III.	In women pursuing pregnancy/infertility, for ovulation induction:
	
Tab. Letrozole 2.5 mg once daily third to eighth days of cycle combined with 
intrauterine insemination (IUI)
	
Or
	
Tab. Clomiphene citrate in the lowest effective dose (50–150 mg daily) for 5 days 
beginning on cycle days 2–5
	
Note: Refer to a specialist in case there is uncontrollable menstrual irregularity 
despite COCP therapy or women are infertile with clomiphene citrate–resistant 
PCOS. Metformin may be added if there is no response. 
IV.	 Hirsutism may require at least 6 months of treatment before improvement begins 
with COCP. If 6 months or more of COCP treatment has failed to adequately 
improve symptoms or the symptoms are still poorly tolerated and there is failure 
of cosmetic measures (such as shaving, bleaching, depilatory agents), Topical 
Eflornithine hydrochloride cream for reduction of unwanted facial hair may be 
used. It takes approximately 6–8 weeks to see clinical effect. It needs to be used 
repeatedly and indefinitely to prevent regrowth. 
	
Or
	
In combination with COCP, fourth-generation progesterones, like Drospirenone, are 
preferred Or Tab. Spironolactone 50−100 mg daily or 2 divided doses Or Flutamide 
250 mg twice daily (Caution: hepatotoxicity and higher cost) Or Finasteride 5 mg 
daily. Approximately 9–12 months of therapy is required to achieve the maximal 
effect, because of the long growth cycles of sexual hair follicles. It may continue

900    Standard Treatment Guidelines
as long as the patient wishes to maintain her improvement in hirsutism or the dose 
is reduced gradually after 1 year of therapy for maintenance therapy as efficacious.
	
Additional permanent treatment methods such as electrolysis, lasers or intense 
pulsed light can be added depending on the patient’s preference, cost of cosmetic 
measure, tolerance of discomfort/pain and risks.
	
The treatment of acne is the same as in patients without PCOS and is discussed 
separately in Chapter 14.
Long-term monitoring
	 1.	Screen and treat metabolic abnormalities (type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, 
hypertension) and CVD risk at the time of initial diagnosis. Hypertension should 
be treated; however, lipid-lowering treatment is not recommended routinely and 
should be prescribed only by a specialist.
	 2.	Women with PCOS who conceive are at an increased risk for GDM, pre-eclampsia, 
caesarean delivery, and preterm and post-term delivery. In addition, their newborns 
are at an increased risk of being large for gestational age.
	 3.	Regularly follow patients for early detection and management of endometrial, 
breast and ovarian cancer due to increased risk of developing endometrial and 
breast cancer in PCOS.
Patient education
	
l Inform patients about the possible long-term risks to health and need for screening, 
treatment and regular follow-up. Educate patients about lifestyle changes, including 
diet, exercise and weight loss for improvement of long-term outcomes.
	
l Emphasize that weight loss can improve metabolic risk, restore ovulatory cycles and 
possibly improve live birth rates, and is the first-line intervention for most women.

ABNORMAL UTERINE BLEEDING
AUB is defined as any woman who experiences a change in her previously established 
menstrual pattern or whose lifestyle is adversely affected or any bleeding from the 
genital tract which is a deviation from the normal in frequency, cyclicity or quantity and 
occurs in the absence of pregnancy (Table 15.16). Acute AUB may occur spontaneously 
or within the context of chronic AUB (AUB present for most of the previous 6 months).

902    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Severe acute bleeding
Outpatient management
	 1.	Tab. Conjugated equine oestrogen 2.5 mg PO 4 times a day
	 2.	Tab. Tranexamic acid 500 mg 3 times a day for 5 days
	 3.	Tab. Mefenamic acid 500 mg 3 times a day
	 4.	If no response after 2–4 doses of conjugated oestrogen or if severe bleeding 
(>1 pad/h) continues, Dilation and Curettage (D&C)
	 5.	After severe bleeding stops, switch to combined oral contraceptives (COC) 1 pill 4 
times a day for 4 days, then 3 times for 3 days, and then 2 times for 2 days, followed 
by once daily for 3 weeks, then 1 week off, and then cyclically for at least 3 months)
	 6.	High-dose Progesterone (Norethisterone acetate) 10 mg 3 times a day for 4 days 
followed by 5 mg 2 times a day for 3 days, and then 10 mg once daily for 14 days
In-patient management in case of profuse active bleeding or moderate-to-
severe anaemia or orthostatic hypotension
	 1.	Inj. Conjugated equine oestrogen 25 mg IV every 4 hours for 24 hours. (Caution: 
Use with caution in patients with cardiovascular or thromboembolic risk factors.)
	 2.	Inj. Tranexamic acid 1 g loading dose followed by 500 mg IV 8 hourly for 5 days. 
(Caution: Use with caution in patients with a history of thrombosis, and carefully 
consider concomitant administration of COCs.) 
	 3.	High-dose progesterone (Norethisterone acetate) 10 mg 3 times a day for 4 days 
followed by 5 mg 2 times a day for 3 days, and then 10 mg once daily for 14 days
	 4.	Transfuse packed RBC if Hb <7.5 g/dL.
	 5.	Simultaneous with IV Conjugated oestrogen, start OCPs as in outpatient 
management.
	 6.	D&C if no response to the above-mentioned medical management.
Menorrhagia
	 1.	Obtain TSH, haemoglobin, platelets, TVS/saline infusion sonography (SIS) if 
anatomic cause suspected (e.g. large uterus on pelvic examination).
	 2.	If age >35 years or high risk for endometrial carcinoma, obtain endometrial biopsy.
	 3.	Tab. Tranexamic acid 500 mg 3 times a day.
	 4.	Tab. Mefenamic acid 500 mg 3 times a day.

904    Standard Treatment Guidelines
In-patient management 
	 1.	Inj. Tranexamic acid 1 g loading dose followed by 500 mg IV 8 hourly. (Caution: 
Use with caution in patients with a history of thrombosis, and carefully consider 
concomitant administration of COCs.)
	 2.	Cyclic OCPs for at least 3 months.
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Mefenamic acid 250–500 mg 3 times a day.
	
	Or
	
	If OCPs contraindicated, MPA 10 mg starting on day 14 of cycle, take 14 days, off 
14 days, and then repeat for at least 3 months.
	
	Or 
	
	Levonorgestrel (LNG IUD).
	 3.	If the response is inadequate, do TVS/SIS.
–	 If polyps/submucous myomas, consider hysteroscopic resection, uterine artery 
embolization, endometrial ablation and hysterectomy.
–	 If endometrial hyperplasia, do endometrial sampling.
–	 If suspected adenomyosis, consider MRI. For treatment, consider progestin 
therapy, LNG IUD, leuprolide or hysterectomy (definitive treatment).
	 4.	If TVS normal or abnormality not amenable to conservative procedure, 
consider endometrial ablation and hysterectomy if child-bearing is complete. If 
child-bearing, maintain menstrual calendar.
Treatment (chronic AUB – not actively bleeding)
	 1.	Iron therapy: Elemental iron maximum 60 mg 3 times a day depending on the 
degree of anaemia.
	 2.	Levonorgestrel intrauterine system Or OCs (monthly or extended cycles), progestin 
therapy (oral or intramuscular), Or Tranexamic acid, and NSAIDs. If a patient is 
receiving IV conjugated equine oestrogen, add progestin or transition to OCs. 
(Caution: Do not use unopposed oestrogen for long-term treatment for chronic 
AUB. Histopathological diagnosis is must before starting hormonal therapy in all 
cases except puberty menorrhagia.)

Follow-up is done after 1, 3 and 6 months of therapy. Treatment is stopped after 3–6 months. 
If symptoms recur, medical treatment should be continued or surgery can be offered.
Role of surgery – endometrial curettage
	
l In case of acute bleeding in a haemodynamically unstable patient, quickly control the 
bleeding. 
	
l In acute episode, if bleeding does not decrease significantly in 12–24 hours with medical 
treatment, then re-evaluation is mandatory and surgical curettage should be done. 
	
l If age is >35 years, premenstrual dilatation and curettage for endometrial histology 
is a must to rule out endometrial pathology.

Chapter 15  Obstetrics and Gynaecology    905
Definitive therapy
If medical therapy is not effective, then endometrial ablation or hysterectomy should 
be performed.
Patient education
	
l In majority of patients, medical management cures the problem. 
	
l Common side effects of high-dose oestrogens are nausea, vomiting, headache, 
depression and fluid retention. High-dose oestrogens are contraindicated in liver 
disease, history of thromboembolic disorder, cardiovascular disease and oestrogen-
dependent neoplasm.
	
l Common side effects of progestogens are depression, fluid retention, fatigue, 
insomnia, dizziness, nausea and breast tenderness. 
	
l Common side effects are acne, weight gain, fluid retention and hoarseness of voice.
	
l Emphasize maintaining a menstrual calendar.
	
l Emphasize correction of anaemia and good healthy diet.
	
l Explain about optimizing weight.
	
l Perform evaluation, counselling and management of breakthrough bleeding or 
IUCD-related bleeding.
	
l Provide information about medical management of DUB and uterine ablative 
surgeries.
	
l Explain the risk of endometrial cancer.

MENOPAUSE
Permanent cessation of menses for 1 year is known as menopause for which there are 
no obvious pathological and physiological causes. It usually occurs between 40 and 
50 years, mean age being 48 years. Perimenopause is the period immediately before and 
up to 1 year after the final menstrual period (FMP). It may last for 3–5 years. Long-term 
consequences due to decreased oestrogens can increase the risk of ischaemic heart disease 
due to adverse effects on lipid profile and pathological fractures due to osteoporosis.

906    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Perimenopause is characterized by irregular menstrual cycles, endocrine changes 
and symptoms such as hot flushes, night sweats, palpitations, vaginal dryness, 
itching, atrophy of the breast and skin, urethral syndrome, stress incontinence, 
mood changes (like anxiety, irritability, depression), insomnia and joint pains 
that may affect a woman’s QOL. It may be considered as a biological marker for 
chronic disease.
	
l Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), earlier called premature menopause, is 
amenorrhoea due to loss of ovarian function before the age of 40 years.
	
l Diagnosis is always clinical; markers for diagnosis of menopause are preferably 
restricted for use in special situations. FSH >10 IU/L indicates declining 
ovarian function. FSH levels >20 IU/L are diagnostic of ovarian insufficiency 
in the perimenopausal age group with vasomotor symptoms (VMS), even in the 
absence of cessation of menstruation. FSH level >40 IU/L done at least 4 weeks 
apart confirms menopause or impending menopause and is associated with low 
oestradiol levels. Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) becomes undetectable, inhibin 
levels fall, and antral follicular count and ovarian volume decrease at menopause.

Menopause requires no medical treatment. Management of menopause focuses on 
relieving signs and symptoms, and requires a holistic approach to diagnose the latent 
and overt non-communicable diseases (NCD). Evaluate age-related factors (CVD; 
skeletal and muscle health; breast, cervical and endometrial cancer), lifestyle and 
socioeconomic status, and treat accordingly.

l Advise the patient to have a balanced diet with fruits, vegetables and semi-skimmed 
milk adequate in vitamins and minerals. Recommend a reduction or avoidance of 
smoking and alcohol consumption.
	
l Exercise: Recommend aerobic exercise (such as walking or swimming) for 
20–30 minutes every day.
	
l Pelvic floor muscle exercises called Kegel exercises can improve some forms of 
urinary incontinence.

1.	Tab. Calcium 1500 mg daily along with Vitamin D3 supplementation (1500–2000 
IU/day).
	 2.	Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in primary ovarian insufficiency, early 
menopause and induced menopause that follows bilateral oophorectomy or 
iatrogenic ablation of ovarian function as below. Rule out contraindications to

Chapter 15  Obstetrics and Gynaecology    907
HRT, namely present endometrial/breast cancer, acute phase myocardial infarction, 
undiagnosed breast lump/abnormal vaginal bleeding and acute liver disease.
	 3.	Hypertension and diabetes, if present, should be controlled before HRT is prescribed.
Conventional HRT
Single therapy with oestrogens
Conjugated equine oestrogen 0.625–1.25 mg.
Or
Oestriol 1–2 mg is given daily 1–25th day every month or daily without any break. If 
symptoms recur during the drug-free period, then give continuous therapy.
Or
Transdermal oestradiol patch 50 or 100 mcg/day applied twice a week away from the 
breast, preferably on the shaved skin of the buttock, thigh or legs (limiting factor is 
local skin reactions).
Note: Transdermal oestradiol patch is preferred in case of gallbladder disease, 
hypertriglyceridaemia, history of thromboembolism, poorly controlled hypertension, 
recent myocardial infarction, vascular diseases, migraine, chronic hepatic dysfunction 
and malabsorption syndrome.
Combined therapy with oestrogens and progestin in women with intact uterus
	 a.	Oestrogen therapy as above. 
	 b.	Progestogen: MPA 5–10 mg Or Dihydrogesterone 10–20 mg or Norethisterone 
2.5 mg) Or 200 mg micronized Progesterone is added from 13th to 25th days in 
cyclic sequential regimen. 
Note: If withdrawal bleeding is not acceptable, then give continuous combined 
treatment (0.625 mg conjugated equine oestrogen + 2.5 mg Medroxyprogesterone 
acetate Or 1 mg micronized oestrogen + 100 mg micronized progesterone).
If conventional HRT is contraindicated
Tab. Tibolone 2.5 mg/day (Caution: Major side effects are weight gain, oedema, breast 
tenderness, GIT symptoms and vaginal bleeding.)
In symptomatic elderly women with atrophic vaginitis and other urogenital symptoms 
who do not desire long-term HRT, Oestriol cream daily application of 0.5 g delivering 
0.5 mg of oestriol for 3 weeks followed by twice-weekly application for 3–4 weeks
Response to treatment and follow-up
	
l Key indicator of response to therapy is improvement in symptoms. Follow-up is 
done at 2–3 months, and then at 6-monthly intervals. Yearly mammography, Pap 
smear, pelvic USG and serum oestradiol are advisable.
	
l Short-term treatment is advocated for acute symptoms and oestrogen use for 
long-term benefits is controversial.

908    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Patient education
	
l Explain to the patients that the following side effects due to oestrogens can occur: 
fluid retention, breast tenderness, nipple sensitivity, nausea, headache and leg 
cramps. Side effects due to progestogens are fluid retention, breast tenderness, 
oedema, headache, acne, PMS, abdominal cramps and vaginal bleeding.
	
l Follow-up visits for 2–3 months and then at 6-monthly intervals are necessary.
References
	 1.	 Meeta M, Digumarti L, Agarwal N, Vaze N, Shah R, Malik S. Clinical practice guidelines 
on menopause: an executive summary and recommendations: Indian Menopause Society 
2019–2020. J Midlife Health. 2020;11(2):55–95.
	 2.	 The menopause & related problems. In: Kumar S, Padubidri VG, and Daftary SN (eds), Shaw’s 
Gynaecology. 17th ed. Elsevier; 2018, pp. 86–98.
POSTMENOPAUSAL BLEEDING
Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) is bleeding that occurs after menopause has been 
established for at least 1 year. It is different from infrequent, irregular periods that occur 
around the time of menopause. Any vaginal bleeding that occurs 6 months after the last 
period (presumed menopause) should be investigated.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Obese women and women taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT) are more 
likely to experience postmenopausal bleeding.
	
l Vaginal atrophy is the most common cause of bleeding from the lower reproductive 
tract. Lesions and cracks on the vulva may also bleed. Sometimes bleeding occurs 
after intercourse. Bleeding can occur with or without an associated infection.
	
l Bleeding from the upper reproductive system can be caused by hormone 
replacements, atrophic endometritis, endometrial cancer (5–10%), endometrial 
polyps, cervical cancer, cervical lesions, uterine tumours, ovarian cancer or 
oestrogen-secreting tumours in other parts of the body. 
	
l Diagnosis is confirmed by hysteroscopy, endometrial or cervical biopsy. Non-
invasive tests include saline infusion sonography (SIS), a refinement of vaginal probe 
ultrasound.
	
l Endometrial sampling and endocervical curettage are often necessary for 
definitive diagnosis.

Treatment depends on the cause (Table 15.18).

C h a p t e r   16
Psychiatric Conditions
SCHIZOPHRENIA AND ACUTE PSYCHOTIC DISORDER
Psychosis is characterized by the presence of hallucinations, delusions, severe 
behaviour abnormality (either extreme agitation and excitement or marked psychomotor 
retardation or catatonic behaviour) or disorganized thinking process. It can be further 
categorized into different types, e.g. schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorders, delusional 
disorders, acute psychosis and substance-induced psychotic disorder. Schizophrenic 
disorders are considered as severe and persistent. The illness tends to be chronic. The 
onset is insidious and symptom onset can span over few months to years. Patients may 
present to a general physician when they develop a physical or behavioural problem.
Acute psychotic disorder is usually defined as any psychotic disorder with an acute 
onset (less than 2 weeks) with complete recovery within 2–3 months.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l A change in personality and behaviour in the form of remaining quiet and 
socially withdrawn, gradual decline in socio-occupational performance or 
person exhibiting socially disorganized behaviour (abusive, aggressive, violent, 
destructive, roaming aimlessly)
	
l Catatonic symptoms: Maintaining odd postures for long time, mutism, 
ambivalency, staring, and neglect of personal care
	
l Talking irrelevantly, suspiciousness, fearfulness, thoughts of being harmed or 
controlled by some external agencies
	
l Muttering to self, laughing, smiling or crying without any obvious reason
	
l Hearing voices, muttering or talking to self or with imaginary figures
	
l Along with the cardinal symptoms of psychosis mentioned above, cognitive and 
marked psychosocial dysfunction may also be present, which begins usually in 
late adolescence

condition: Psychotic and Mood Disorders Schizophrenia and Acute Psychotic Disorder
text:
l A patient with psychosis can be managed on an outpatient or in-patient basis 
depending on the severity. The initial treatment as given below may be started on an 
outpatient basis. Preferably, the patient should be referred to a psychiatrist.

condition: Psychotic and Mood Disorders Schizophrenia and Acute Psychotic Disorder
text:
Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    911
	
l Common indications to consider inpatient care include suicidal behaviour, severe 
agitation or violence, refusal to eat or drink, inability to care for self or catatonia.
	
l The various treatment options for schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders 
include antipsychotic medications (typical/atypical antipsychotic), electroconvulsive 
therapy (ECT), adjunctive medications like Benzodiazepines, mood stabilizers and 
psychosocial interventions. The initial treatment can be started by any medical 
professional; however, a psychiatrist’s opinion must be taken in case of difficulty in 
management or if the patient does not respond to primary treatment.

Psychoeducation: Educating the family about nature of illness, need of treatment, etc.

condition: Psychotic and Mood Disorders Schizophrenia and Acute Psychotic Disorder
text:
Goals of treatment in patients with psychosis
	
l Prevent harm to self and others
	
l Control disturbing behaviour
	
l Reduce the severity of psychosis and associated symptoms, viz. agitation, 
aggression, negative symptoms and affective symptoms
	
l Determine and address the factors that led to the occurrence of the acute episode, 
especially if history of substance use (e.g. cannabis, stimulants)
	
l Facilitate a rapid return to the best level of functioning
	
l Develop alliance with the patient and family
	
l Formulate short- and long-term treatment plan
	
l Connect the patients with appropriate aftercare in the community
Approach to treatment
	
l Choice of medication depends on the availability of medications, cost and side 
effect profile. Other factors include prior response to treatment, experience of side 
effects (if there is past history of treatment) and patients’ preference for a particular 
medication including the route of administration.
	
l Antipsychotic medications form the mainstay of the treatment. These include 
atypical antipsychotics (Risperidone, Quetiapine, Olanzapine, Aripiprazole) and 
typical antipsychotics (Haloperidol, Trifluoperazine, Chlorpromazine). During each 
visit, all patients should undergo monitoring for signs and symptoms of metabolic 
syndrome (in the case of atypical antipsychotics) and extrapyramidal symptoms 
(EPS) for those receiving typical antipsychotics.
Treatment can be started as below:
Atypical antipsychotics
Tab. Risperidone 2 mg/day, gradually increased to 4 mg/day in 2 divided doses over 
2–4 days. Further dose up-titration can be done with 2 mg every 1–2 weeks depending 
on tolerability and clinical response. The usual therapeutic dose is 4–8 mg/day.
Or
Tab. Olanzapine 5 mg/day as a single night-time dose; can be gradually increased 
up to 20 mg/day over 2–3 weeks depending on response and tolerability. The usual

condition: Psychotic and Mood Disorders Schizophrenia and Acute Psychotic Disorder
text:
912    Standard Treatment Guidelines
therapeutic dose is 10–20 mg/day. (Caution: Olanzapine has a high potential to cause 
metabolic syndrome [weight gain, hyperlipidaemia and precipitate diabetes mellitus]. 
Hence, patients require weight monitoring every month and lipid and blood sugar 
monitoring every 6 months; avoid in patients with diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia 
and obesity).
Or
Tab. Quetiapine 25 mg twice a day on the first day, 75–100 mg in 2 divided doses on 
days 2–3, 150–200 mg in 2 divided doses on days 4–5 and 200–400 mg on days 6–7, 
can increase up to maximum dose of 900 mg/day over 2–3 weeks depending on the 
response and tolerability. Slow-release (SR) preparations are available in strengths 
of 50, 100, 200 and 300 mg; the patient can be shifted to SR preparations after 2–3 
weeks. The usual dose is 400–600 mg/day. (Caution: It causes sedation; consider a less 
sedating alternative, if sedation causes significant distress to the patient.)
Or
Tab. Aripiprazole 5–30 mg/day once daily; started at 5 mg/day and increased gradually 
over intervals of 1–2 weeks.
Note: Risperidone, Olanzapine and Quetiapine have been associated with weight gain 
when used for a long period. Patients should be encouraged for lifestyle modification 
like regular physical exercise and diet control.
Typical antispychotics
Tab. Haloperidol 5 mg/day, increase by 5 mg every 3–4 days in 2–3 divided doses 
depending on tolerability and response (up to 20 mg/day) over 2–3 weeks, and then 
30 mg/day (in 2–3 divided doses) over 2–3 weeks depending on the clinical response 
and tolerability (Antipsychotics may cause mild-to-moderate side effects like sedation, 
slowness of movements, EPS such as changes in facial expression and gait, rigidity, 
excessive salivation, akathisia, dryness of the mouth and constipation. The patient usually 
develops tolerance to these over a few weeks.)
If the patient develops EPS, add:
Tab. Trihexyphenidyl 2 mg once in morning and once in afternoon (attempts to taper 
be made after 3 months); the usual dose is 2–8 mg/day. For detailed management of 
EPS see below.
Specific circumstances
Acute agitation or violent behaviour
Inj. Haloperidol 5–10 mg IM + Inj. Promethazine chloride 25–50 mg IM stat. The dose 
can be decided depending on weight, level of agitation and previous history of EPS. 
Or
Inj. Lorazepam 2–4 mg IM, if Haloperidol and Promethazine are not available or are 
contraindicated; adjust the dose depending on the level of agitation.

	 For sleep disturbance (insomnia)

condition: Psychotic and Mood Disorders Schizophrenia and Acute Psychotic Disorder
text:
l Follow-up is required weekly for the first 2–3 weeks. Once the symptoms stabilize, 
the frequency of follow-ups may be gradually reduced to once in a fortnight to 
once in 1–3 months. Improvement in symptoms is usually seen within a week. 
However, it may take few weeks to months for the full response to come. Evaluate 
patients for potential side effects on every follow-up. For acute psychotic disorder, 
continue treatment for 6–9 months and medicines should be tapered off gradually 
over 1–2 months.
	
l For the first episode of schizophrenia, if the patient is in remission, continue 
treatment for 1–2 years. In patients with multiple episodes or exacerbations, continue 
treatment for 5 years or more after the last episode. In patients with multiple 
episodes of aggression and of suicide attempts, treatment should be given lifelong.
	
l For patients not compliant to medication and with a history of relapse, depot 
antipsychotics can be considered:
Inj. Fluphenazine decanoate 25–50 mg deep IM by Z technique in the gluteal region 
every 15 days.
Or
Inj. Haloperidol decanoate 50–100 mg deep IM by Z technique in the gluteal region 
and repeat every month.
Notes:
	
l Atypical antipsychotic depot injections (Risperidone and Paliperidone) are available 
in the market but are expensive; therefore, decision to put the patient on a particular 
depot preparation should be taken by a psychiatrist considering cost-effectiveness. 
Depot preparation of Risperidone is given once in 2 weeks, and Olanzapine and 
Paliperidone depot preparations once in a month.
	
l Treatment-resistant cases, patients with catatonic symptoms or those with a high 
suicide risk should be referred to a psychiatrist for clozapine since it requires vital 
parameter monitoring along with blood count monitoring on a regular basis. Patients 
with catatonic symptoms or suicide risk may need modified ECT to be given by a 
psychiatrist in inpatient setting under general anaesthesia.
Patient/Family education
	
l Both the patient and the caregivers should be educated that schizophrenia is a 
psychiatric illness, which can be effectively treated by medicines. The family should 
be advised to be supportive and not to criticize the patient. Try to maintain low 
expressed emotion family environment.
	
l Sensitize the patient and family members to the common side effects that might 
occur. If the patient develops spasm of a part of the body like the neck or extremities

914    Standard Treatment Guidelines
or high-grade fever or alterations in the sensorium, or/and rigidity in extremities, 
immediately contact the treating doctor or the psychiatrist.
	
l Antipsychotics are often associated with weight gain. Encourage the patient for 
lifestyle modification like avoidance of fats. Encourage high-fibre diet and regular 
physical activity.
	
l Treatment should not be stopped abruptly without the advice of the treating psychiatrist.

Substance Use Disorders. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023.
	 2.	 Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines. Hoboken, NJ: John 
Wiley & Sons Ltd; December 2021.

Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer; 2021.

Oxford University Press; 2018.
