schizophrenia. Indian J Psychiatry. 2017;59(Suppl 1):S34–S50.
	 6.	 Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide. 5th ed. 2014.
BIPOLAR AFFECTIVE DISORDER
Bipolar affective disorder (BPAD) is a serious mental illness. It is an affective disorder; 
there is either mania (elevated mood) or depression (depressed mood) in a persistent 
and pervasive manner. It is an episodic illness with complete recovery between 
subsequent episodes. The illness is characterized by episodes of mania and depression 
or mania alone with intervening periods of normalcy. Patients may present to a 
physician in a new episode or when they develop a physical or behavioural problem, 
while on treatment with a psychiatrist.
SALIENT FEATURES
Episodes of mania are characterized by the following:
	
l Elevated, expansive or irritable mood, inflated self-esteem, or grandiosity, 
decreased need for sleep, overtalkativeness, overactivity, increased sociability, 
interfering behaviour and excessive involvement in pleasurable activities that 
have a potential of harmful consequences (buying sprees, sexual indiscretions). 
	
l Symptoms should be present for a minimum duration of 1 week for a diagnosis 
of mania to be made (for details about depressive episodes, see the section 
‘Depression’).

Treatment for a patient in current episode of mania can be done on an outpatient or an 
inpatient basis. Inpatient setting should be considered for patients with severe agitation

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    915
or violence, suicidality or catatonia. Such patients should be referred to a psychiatrist 
after initiating primary treatment. 
	
l The goal of treatment is to treat the current episode and provide prophylaxis since 
the episodes tend to recur. Prophylaxis is usually indicated if there are more than 
2–3 episodes in the previous 4–5 years.
	
l In patients of with BPAD already on treatment, the same may be continued.
	
l The treatment modalities in a case of mania include mood stabilizers (Valproate, 
Lithium, Carbamazepine, Oxcarbazepine), antipsychotics (preferably atypical 
antipsychotics) and ECT. However, mood stabilizers remain the mainstay of treatment.
Newly diagnosed case of mania
In a newly diagnosed case of mania, treatment can be started with either a mood 
stabilizer or an atypical antipsychotic.
Mood stabilizers
Tab. Valproic acid 500 mg/day; it can be increased over 1–2 weeks to 1000–
1500 mg/day depending on the response and tolerability. (Caution: Avoid in patients 
with hepatic dysfunction, pregnant females or young females [risk of PCOS]).
Or
Tab. Lithium carbonate 600–800 mg in divided doses. It should be used only under 
strict supervision of a Psychiatrist. (Caution: Before starting Lithium, pre-lithium 
workup should be done which includes baseline urea, creatinine and thyroid function 
test. Measure serum lithium levels [fasting 30 minutes before the next scheduled dose] 
on the sixth day after starting Lithium; reassess every 3–4 months [therapeutic levels 
are between 0.6 and 1.2 mEq/L levels]. Assess renal function every 6 months.)
Note: In case the patient develops toxicity or has high-grade fever, diarrhoea or 
vomiting, stop Lithium as dehydration can precipitate lithium toxicity (for details of 
lithium toxicity, see psychiatric emergencies.
Antipsychotics
In a newly diagnosed case of mania, treatment can be started as below:
Tab. Risperidone 1 mg/day gradually increased to 2–4 mg/day in 2 divided doses over 
2–4 days, which can be further increased depending on tolerability and clinical response 
(usual therapeutic dose 4–8 mg/day, although most patients are likely to respond at 4 
mg/day)
Or
Tab. Olanzapine 5 mg/day as a single night-time dose; can be gradually increased 
up to 20 mg/day over 2–3 weeks depending on response and tolerability. The usual 
therapeutic dose is 10–20 mg/day. (Caution: Olanzapine has a potential to cause 
hyperlipidaemia and precipitate diabetes mellitus. Avoid in patients with diabetes 
mellitus, dyslipidaemia and obesity. Monitor lipid and blood sugar every 6 months.)

916    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Or
Tab. Quetiapine, as in schizophrenia
Or
Tab. Haloperidol 5 mg/day, which can be increased up to 20 mg/day (in 2 divided 
doses) over 2–3 weeks depending on the response and tolerability
Or
Tab. Sodium valproate Or Divalproex (combination of sodium valproate and valproic 
acid) 500 mg/day; can be increased over 1–2 weeks to 1000–1500 mg/day depending 
on response and tolerability
Or
Tab. Lithium carbonate (mood stabilizers), to be used only under strict psychiatric 
supervision
In dysphoric mania, mild episodes, monotherapy with lithium, divalproex or olanzapine 
as above
Note: Risperidone and Olanzapine have been associated with weight gain when used 
for a long period. Encourage patients for lifestyle modification like regular physical 
exercise and diet control.
If the patient develops EPS, see above and psychiatric emergencies.
For sleep disturbance (insomnia)
Tab. Lorazepam 1–2 mg Or Clonazepam 0.25–1 mg at bedtime may be given in the 
initial period (usually for 10–15 days, to be tapered off thereafter). 
In case of acute excitement or violent behaviour, the patient may be given:
Inj. Haloperidol 5–10 mg IM Stat. And Inj. Promethazine chloride 25–50 mg IM 
Or
Inj. Lorazepam 2 mg IM. The injection can be repeated after 8 hours (For details, see 
psychiatric emergencies.)
Improvement starts within 1 week. The treatment may need to be given for a period of 
3–6 months, usually at least for 3–4 months after the patient becomes asymptomatic. 
If there is no improvement in a week, the patient should be referred to a psychiatrist. 
Current episode of depression
The line of treatment is similar to that as described in the section ‘Depression’. 
However, the patients with bipolar depression should always be prescribed a mood 
stabilizer along with the antidepressant. Most antidepressants if given alone in a patient 
with bipolar disorder without cover of mood stabilizer have a strong potential to cause 
switch to mania.

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    917
Prophylactic treatment
Tab. Lithium carbonate 900–1500 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses (Caution: It should be 
given only by a psychiatrist. Regularly monitor serum lithium levels. The patient must 
discontinue lithium carbonate therapy and contact his/her physician if clinical signs 
of lithium toxicity such as diarrhoea, vomiting, tremors, mild ataxia, drowsiness or 
muscular weakness occur. Also explain not to take other medicines without consulting 
the doctor.) 
Or
In rapid cyclers (>5 episodes/year), Tab. Sodium valproate or divalproex 500–1500 mg/day 
in 2–3 divided doses
Once dose is stabilized, both Lithium and Valproate can be given as a single dose 
depending on feasibility, tolerability and the patient’s choice.

Follow-up is required weekly for the first 2 weeks. Once the symptoms stabilize, the 
frequency of follow-ups may be gradually reduced to once in a fortnight to once in 
1–3 months. Patients should be evaluated for potential side effects on every follow-up.
Patients on lithium
	
l As mentioned above, regular monitoring of serum levels is needed.
	
l The patient should be advised to maintain adequate hydration (at least 3–4 L of 
water).
	
l If a patient develops acute gastrointestinal infections (diarrhoea, fever, vomiting) or 
any condition which can cause potential dehydration, maintain adequate hydration 
and stop lithium if supratherapeutic levels are present. Restart Lithium once the 
patient is medically fit.
	
l In case a patient develops the signs and symptoms of Lithium toxicity (diarrhoea, 
vomiting, tremors, mild ataxia, drowsiness or muscular weakness), stop Lithium and 
refer him/her immediately to a psychiatrist. For details, see Psychiatric emergencies.
	
l Avoid medications like diuretics, ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs. Avoid lithium in 
patients with renal dysfunction, pregnant females (especially during first trimester) 
or patients with dermatological illnesses.
	
l Liver function test and blood cell counts should be performed at baseline and once 
in 6 months in patients on carbamazepine and sodium valproate. 
Note: Prophylactic treatment should be given only under psychiatric supervision. 
Prophylaxis is required generally after 2–3 episodes. Prophylactic treatment may 
continue for 1–2 years in case of first episode of mania, 3 years in case of second 
episode of mania and lifelong in case of more than three episodes.
Patient education
	
l Provide general guidelines about the illness and medications similar to those for 
schizophrenia.

918    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Emphasize on recurrent course of illness and not to get too much worried on recurrences. 
	
l Relapses can be treated as successfully as the first episode. 
	
l When on lithium, advise to take plenty of fluids, especially during summer, and not 
to restrict salt. 
	
l If the patient develops fever, vomiting or diarrhoea while on lithium, reduce the dose 
of lithium to half and contact the physician or the psychiatrist immediately.

Cambridge University Press; 2014.

DEPRESSION
Depression is one of the commonest psychiatric disorders. It is the fourth leading cause 
of disability worldwide. Most patients present to a mental health professional referred 
by physicians, having medically unexplained physical symptoms (e.g. headache, body 
pain and other vague symptoms); they usually have underlying depression.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Persistent and pervasive sadness of mood, loss of pleasure in activities, which one 
enjoyed earlier, generalized lack of interest; anxiety often associated and some 
patients may present with irritability
	
l Lack of energy, slowness of thought, decreased concentration and efficiency
	
l Lack of sleep, appetite and libido
	
l Ideas of insufficiency, inadequacy and worthlessness, unexplained ideas of guilt, 
death wishes, suicidal ideas, history of suicidal attempt
	
l Disruption of social and occupational functioning
	
l Symptoms present for a minimum period of 2 weeks in persistent manner for a 
diagnosis of depression to be made (hypothyroidism may co-exist)

Treatment can be done on an outpatient or an inpatient basis. Common indications to 
consider inpatient setting include suicidal ideas or attempts, catatonia, refusal to eat or 
severe malnutrition.

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    919

l Provide cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT; to be given by a psychiatrist/clinical 
psychologist).
	
l For pregnant or lactating females experiencing mild to moderate depression, 
interventions may include counselling, reassurance, psychological support and 
encouragement.

In patients with severe depression, presence of risk of harm to self (suicidality, poor oral 
intake) or prominent psychosocial dysfunction, start pharmacotherapy.
There are various classes of antidepressants; commonly used are selective serotonin 
response inhibitors (SSRI), serotonin–norepinephrine response inhibitors (SNRI), 
tricyclic antidepressant (TCA), and noradrenaline and specific serotonin antidepressant 
(NaSSA). Due to safety and side effect profile, SSRI forms the first line of treatment. 
Other antidepressants can also be initiated on first contact.
Antidepressants exhibit a delay in onset of action. It takes about 2–3 weeks after 
initiation of the medication for its antidepressant effect to begin.
SSRI
Cap. Fluoxetine 20–60 mg/day as a single dose in morning with food; starting with 
20 mg/day which can be increased up to 60 mg/day in increments of 20 mg after 
5–6 weeks depending on response and tolerability.
Or
Tab. Sertraline 50–200 mg/day as a single dose in morning with food; starting with 
50 mg/day which can be increased up to 200 mg/day after 2–3 weeks in increments of 
50 mg depending on response and tolerability.
Or
Tab. Escitalopram 10–20 mg/day as a single dose in morning with food; starting with 5 mg/
day which can be increased to 10 mg/day over 2–3 weeks, and further up to 20 mg/day after 
5–6 weeks in case of non-response (most patients would respond at 10 mg/day)
Or
Tab. Paroxetine 12.5–60 mg/day; increase dose by 12.5 mg/day every 2–3 weeks 
depending on tolerability and response.
(Caution: SSRI can cause severe gastric distress [heartburn] and nausea; hence, it 
should never be taken on an empty stomach. Do not increase the dose until gastric 
distress settles down. SSRI, at times, can also cause paradoxical worsening of 
anxiety symptoms when initiated. The dose increment in such cases should be even 
more gradual. SSRI can also lead to paradoxical insomnia; hence, it should be better 
prescribed in the morning. In case the patient complains of sedation, the same can be 
shifted to night-time dose. Other side effects of SSRIs are agitation, headache, tremors, 
delayed ejaculation, erectile dysfunction and loss of appetite.)

920    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SNRI
Tab. Venlafaxine 75 mg/day, can be increased to 150 mg/day in two divided doses 
over 1–2 weeks; further increased to 225 mg/day after 5–6 weeks in case of inadequate 
response; extended-release preparations given as a single dose Or Desvenlafaxine 
50–100 mg single dose daily
Or
Tab. Mirtazapine 15–45 mg/day as a single night-time dose starting with 
15 mg/day which can be increased up to 45 mg/day in increments of 15 mg after 
5–6 weeks depending on clinical response and tolerability (Caution: Side effects 
include sedation, giddiness, increased appetite and weight gain. It can be used as a 
sedative in low doses where Benzodiazepines are contraindicated.)
TCA
Tab. Imipramine 75–150 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses; to be started at 25 mg twice a 
day, and increased by 25 mg every third day till 150 mg/day depending on the clinical 
response and tolerability
Or
Tab. Amitriptyline 25–200 mg/day; start with 25 mg/day, and then increase the dose 
to 50 mg/day over the next 4–5 days; the dose can be further increased by 25 mg/day 
every 2–3 weeks till a maximum dose of 200 mg/day.
Note: TCAs should be mostly given at night time as they have a high potential for 
sedation. Start with a low dose. Side effects include sedation, anticholinergic side 
effects (blurring of vision, giddiness, postural hypotension, weight gain) and other 
life-threatening side effects like epilepsy, heart disease, glaucoma and benign prostatic 
enlargement. TCAs should be avoided in patients with epilepsy, heart disease, glaucoma 
and benign prostatic enlargement. Due to their effect on noradrenaline, TCAs can also 
be considered in patients with excessive bodily complaints.
Special circumstances
Comorbid anxiety and insomnia
In the initial phase of treatment of depression, patients may present with severe anxiety and 
sleep disturbance, and may need additional antianxiety medication for anxiety as well as 
for insomnia, more so since SSRIs also have a tendency to cause restlessness in the initial 
phase of treatment. Hence, it is advisable to provide a cover for anxiety by administering
Tab. Lorazepam 2–6 mg Or Tab. Clonazepam 0.5–2 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses.
Suicidality
	 1.	Patients expressing passive death wishes should be started on antidepressants and 
should be observed closely. In case patients experience active ideas to harm themselves 
or any suicidal attempt, refer them immediately to a psychiatrist for admission.
	 2.	ECT is a very effective modality of treatment in patients with suicidality, hence 
can be started by a psychiatrist after due consent of the patient and relatives along 
with antidepressant cover.

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    921
(For details, see psychiatric emergencies.)
Assessment of response to treatment
	 1.	Antidepressant medication begins to improve sleep, appetite and anxiety feelings 
within about 1 week. Feelings of depression may take from 2 to 4 weeks to 
improve. By about 12 weeks, most of the patients substantially improve. Observe 
closely patients with suicidal tendencies during this period. If there is no response 
to treatment in 5–6 weeks, check compliance and reconfirm diagnosis. If compliant 
with medication, increase the dose, change antidepressant, augment with another 
SSRI or antidepressant from another class or refer to a psychiatrist at this stage. 
Refer to a psychiatrist earlier if the patient is non-responsive to medical treatment 
or is becoming a threat to himself/herself or to the society.
	 2.	For the first episode of depression, continue treatment for 6–9 months. The dose 
may be tapered off over a period of 6–8 weeks. However, if symptoms recur 
during this period, continue for another 3–4 months. In case of multiple episodes 
of depression, treatment may need to be continued indefinitely.
	 3.	In cases of bipolar depression, patients while on antidepressants may have a sudden 
switch to mania. In such cases, stop antidepressants immediately, and refer the 
patient to a psychiatrist. Refer depression with suicidal intent or attempt patients 
for ECT to a psychiatrist.
Patient education
	
l Explain the nature of illness, consequences of untreated depression, suicidal risk, 
need of adequate doses for adequate duration and other supportive measures.
	
l Explain to the patient and caregiver about expected delay in therapeutic response as 
it takes time to appear but side effects may appear earlier. Initially, follow-up visits 
should be made every 2–3 weeks until the patient starts reporting improvement 
after which the duration of follow-up can be increased to once a month. Common 
side effects of TCAs are dry mouth, constipation, postural hypotension (giddiness), 
blurred vision, sweating, palpitation, tremors, delayed micturition, sedation, erectile 
dysfunction, etc.
	
l Common side effects of SSRIs are agitation, headache, nausea or heartburn, tremors, 
delayed ejaculation, erectile dysfunction and loss of appetite.
	
l Mirtazapine causes sedation, giddiness and increased appetite and weight gain.
	
l Advise the patient to avoid driving or operating machinery if he/she is drowsy.
	
l Advise the patient to avoid alcohol during treatment, as it may cause oversedation 
and dizziness.
	
l Explain to the patient not to stop medicines abruptly as it may lead to 
discontinuation syndrome.
References
	 1.	 Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) Guideline for Mental, Neurological and 
Substance Use Disorders. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023.
	 2.	 Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines. John Wiley & Sons 
Ltd; December 2021.

MENTAL AND BEHAVIOURAL PROBLEMS IN CHILDREN
Psychological and behavioural problems are quite common in children. The behavioural 
problems in children can be neurodevelopmental like intellectual disability/mental 
retardation, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or autism spectrum 
disorder (ASD). These illnesses usually present themselves at an early age of onset. 
Certain conditions develop at later ages like anxiety spectrum, depressive disorders, 
psychotic illness, substance use disorders and obsessive-compulsive disorders. These 
disorders are not age specific. These disorders are intense, pervasive and interfere with 
the child’s functioning.
Some of these problems have been enlisted below and children exhibiting such 
problems would need a detailed assessment. An early intervention would be helpful 
to prevent functional decline in a child. The child with complaints as below may be 
referred to a psychiatrist, paediatrician or clinical psychologist for further assessment 
and treatment:
	
l Frequent mood swings
	
l Social isolation (avoiding friends and 
family)
	
l Anger and rage attacks
	
l Abusing drugs
	
l Spending excessive time in bathroom 
or room alone
	
l Engaging in any sort of repetitive 
behaviours
	
l Talking to self/muttering
	
l Not doing the activities he/she used to 
enjoy
	
l Worrying constantly
	
l Lacking energy or motivation
	
l Poor appetite
	
l Having sleep difficulties
	
l Academic decline
	
l Rebelling against authority
	
l Hitting or bullying other children
	
l Damaging other people’s property
	
l Not concerned with his/her appearance
	
l Obsessed with his/her weight
	
l Attempting to injure himself/herself 
or others
Refer children to a psychiatrist in the following situations:
	
l Suicidal thoughts/attempts
	
l Exhibiting verbal, physical or sexual aggression
	
l Suspected drug abuse
	
l Not eating, poor self-care
	
l Child presenting with seizure

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    923
Management of some common psychiatric conditions encountered in children is given 
in the following sections.
Parent/Patient education
	
l Parental counselling; learning to anticipate the situations in which behavioural 
problems appear and plan ahead so as to minimize disruption
	
l Encouraging parents to screen the peer relationships of the child so as to protect the 
vulnerable child
	
l Recognizing the attention difficulties of the child and tailoring the work expectations 
by reducing the length and complexity of assignments
	
l A coordinated effort at both home and school
	
l Referring to a psychiatrist, or a higher centre for treatment and management

health services. Paediatrics. 2004;113:1839.
	 2.	 Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Centre for Mental

Adolescents: A Guide for Child-Serving Organizations. U.S. Department of Health and Human

	 3.	 Pennsylvania Department of Public Welfare, Office of Mental Health and Substance Abuse

	 4.	 National Institute of Mental Health. Mental Health Medications. U.S. Department of Health and 
Human Services. Available at Mental Health Medications – National Institute of Mental Health

DEPRESSION IN CHILDREN
Depression in children is not uncommon; however, the presentation may vary. The 
predominant mood is often irritable. Diagnosis is made on the same criteria as in adult 
depression. Depression should be suspected in a child presenting with decline in school 
performance; withdrawal from peers; increased conflict with peers, siblings, parents 
and other adults; crying spells; change in eating habits, especially binge eating and 
increased carbohydrate craving; and irritability. Children may be anxious and tearful 
and may also present with somatic symptoms.
Treatment is mainly supportive. Pharmacological treatment is generally not 
encouraged. Fluoxetine (SSRI) is the only drug which is FDA approved for treatment 
of children with depression. Fluoxetine and escitalopram (SSRI) are drugs which are 
approved for treatment of depression in adolescents if depression is severe. Duration 
of treatment is as described in adult depression.

ATTENTION-DEFICIT/HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER (ADHD)
ADHD is one of the commonest psychiatric disorders in children, seen more often in 
boys. It is a neurodevelopmental disorder which causes significant impairment in social, 
academic and occupational functioning.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There is a persistent pattern of hyperactivity or inattention (more frequent and 
severe than typical of children at a similar level of development). 
	
l Hyperactivity and impulsivity can present in the following manner: appears 
fidgety, tapping hands and feet, always on the go, leaves seat in the middle of 
the class, runs about or climbs in situations in which it is inappropriate, talks 
excessively, difficulty waiting for his/her turn, and interrupts or intrudes on others.
	
l Onset is usually before 12 years of age. 
	
l Symptoms have to be present for at least 6 months which are inconsistent to the 
developmental level and negatively impact socio-occupational and academic 
activities.
Treatment (To be treated by a psychiatrist)

1.	Environmental modification: Changes in the environment should be made to reduce 
stimulation for the child. Such modifications include:
	
l Making a structure and routine in the child’s life (e.g. a timetable for the entire 
day may introduce some regularity in the child’s life)
	
l Structuring the physical environment (e.g. keeping a place for everything, using 
verbal and visual cues for everything)
	
l Minimizing distractions while studying or doing other activities requiring 
sustained attention
	 2.	Parent training intervention
	
l Parent training involves psychoeducation about the illness.
	
l Explain to them about maintaining good communication, and giving clear, 
specific, and short instructions.
	
l Encourage parents to maintain persistence and patience with the schedule and 
training.
	
l Advise them to reduce critical commenting, teach the child to anticipate situations 
and allow behavioural problems to appear, and plan ahead to minimize disruptions.

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    925
	
l Encourage parents to screen peer relationships of the child to protect the 
vulnerable child.
	
l Ask the parents to tailor the work expectations by the child, reducing the length 
and complexity of assignments as per the attentional deficits of the child.
	
l Advise them to involve the school and teachers and have a coordinated effort 
at home and at school in tailoring their approach to the child and giving special 
considerations to the child like one-on-one sessions and giving extra time to the 
child to complete class work. 
	 3.	Coordinated effort at both home and school
	 4.	Cognitive training and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)

Tab. Methylphenidate 2.5–5 mg twice a day after meals at 8 AM and 12 noon after 
meals; can be increased up to 10–15 mg/day (0.3–2.0 mg/kg/day). The maximum dose 
is 60 mg/day, to be given under strict psychiatric supervision; available as 5- and 10-mg 
tablets. It should not be given in the evening as it is a stimulant and would cause the 
child to be awake and energetic.
Or
Tab. Atomoxetine 0.5 mg/kg/day and increased after a minimum of 3 days to 1.2 mg/kg/
day, given as a single or two divided doses (morning and afternoon); available in strengths 
of 10- and 18-mg tablets/capsules. 
(Caution: Common side effects include headache, insomnia, nausea, vomiting, 
decreased appetite and abdominal pain.)
Note: Basic assessments that should be done before starting a medication include 
weight, height, ECG, pulse and blood pressure. These should also be assessed at every 
follow-up.
Patient Education
Advise the patient to stop Methylphenidate and immediately call the doctor if any of 
the serious side effects are observed such as fast, pounding or uneven heartbeats; fever, 
sore throat and headache with a severe blistering, peeling, red skin rash; aggression, 
restlessness, hallucinations, unusual behaviour or motor tics; easy bruising, purple spots 
on the skin; or dangerously high blood pressure (severe headache, blurred vision, buzzing 
in the ears, anxiety, confusion, chest pain, shortness of breath, uneven heartbeats, seizure).

MENTAL RETARDATION (MR)/INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY
It is a developmental disorder associated with delayed intellectual development with 
onset in childhood. It is defined as an intellectual functioning level (as measured by 
standard test for intelligence quotient [IQ]) that is well below average and causes 
significant limitations in daily living skills and adoptive functioning. As many as 1 out 
of every 100 children in the country has MR. Children with MR present with delayed 
developmental milestones (motor, speech and language and social). Persons with MR 
usually have deficits in social, adaptive and functional skills to a variable degree.

l By most definitions, it is more accurately considered a disability rather than a 
disease. Currently, there is no ‘treatment’ for an established disability, although with 
appropriate support and teaching, most individuals can learn to do many things.
	
l People with MR benefit through various approaches like teaching them basic life 
skills and social skills. The basic goal of management is to make the individual/child 
independent in most of the activities. Educating family members and caregivers 
about the illness and addressing their burden as caregivers is also very important.
	
l People with developmental disabilities learn throughout their lives and can obtain 
many new skills even late in life with the help of their families, caregivers, 
clinicians and the people who coordinate the efforts of all of these people.
	
l Although there is no specific medication for ‘MR’, many people with developmental 
disabilities develop medical complications and may take several medications. There 
are specific programmes that people with developmental disabilities can take part in 
wherein they learn basic life skills. These ‘goals’ may take a much longer amount 
of time for them to accomplish but the ultimate goal is independence. This may 
be anything from independence in basic personal care (like tooth brushing) to an 
independent living.
	
l Disability certificates are issued by a specialty medical board at the district level 
or medical college level.
	
l People with MR can also present with significant behavioural problems like 
aggression, irritability or crying spells. In such cases, low-dose Tab. Risperidone 
0.5–2 mg/day, Olanzapine 2.5–5 mg/day or fluoxetine can be initiated to address 
the behavioural problems.

MIXED ANXIETY DEPRESSION
It is one of the commonest psychiatric disorders seen in general clinical practice 
presenting with anxiety and depressive symptoms.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Presence of both anxiety and depressive symptoms
	
l Anxiety and depressive symptoms not sufficient enough to meet criteria for 
anxiety or depressive disorder, respectively
	
l Symptoms of autonomic hyperactivity like palpitations, tremors, dry mouth and 
stomach churning

This includes psychological support, encouragement, relaxation exercises, yoga and 
meditation. Non-pharmacological management is the mainstay of treatment in mixed 
anxiety depression.

Antidepressants can be avoided unless the symptoms are severe or fulfil the 
criteria for an independent episode of either depression or anxiety. A short course 
of benzodiazepines for 2–3 weeks may suffice.
	 1.	Tab. Lorazepam 1–4 mg/day Or Tab. Alprazolam 0.5–1.5 mg/day Or Tab. 
Clonazepam 0.5–1.0 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses.
	
	Treatment should be started at the lowest dose, which can be increased up to 
the maximum dose to achieve a therapeutic response, but attempt should be to 
keep it at the minimal possible level. Do not give Benzodiazepines for more than 
2–4 weeks because of abuse potential and development of tolerance to it.
	 2.	If there is no response or satisfactory improvement and medication is needed for a 
longer time, an antidepressant can be added. The dosages and duration are similar 
to those discussed in the section ‘Depression’.
Patient education
	
l It is a mild illness, although symptoms may last for a long time. Lifestyle changes 
like stress management, regular physical exercise and avoiding overwork often help 
in reducing symptoms.

GENERALIZED ANXIETY DISORDER
It is one of the common psychiatric disorders in general clinical practices. It is more 
common in women than in men. Patients often present in primary care with symptoms 
of sympathetic overactivity, vague aches or pains, sleep disturbance, forgetfulness or 
worrying too much.
The symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), as described below, are 
present for several months for at least several weeks at a time.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Apprehension about the future, feeling on the edge, worrying something might 
go wrong, persistent anxiety, present all the time but intensity seems to be out of 
proportion to reality
	
l Motor tension – restlessness, inability to relax, trembling, shakiness
	
l Apprehension, worries of future, irritability, sleeplessness
	
l Autonomic overactivity – palpitations, sweating, dry mouth, increased frequency 
of micturition, abdominal distress
	
l May be accompanied with irritability, insomnia, significant socio-occupational 
dysfunction

l Supportive psychotherapy – reassurance, psychological support, encouragement
	
l Psycho-education regarding illness and various treatment strategies
	
l Anxiety management – progressive muscular relaxation, deep breathing exercises, 
meditation, yoga, etc.
	
l Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) – to be done by a trained psychotherapist

Treatment strategies for GAD include Benzodiazepines and antidepressants. 
Tab. Lorazepam 1–4 mg/day Or Tab. Clonazepam 0.5–1.0 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses.

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    929
Treatment should be started at the lowest dose, which can be increased up to the 
maximum dose to achieve a therapeutic response, but attempt should be to keep it at 
the minimal possible level. Mean duration of treatment with Benzodiazepine should 
be around 4–6 weeks, and then tapered and stopped as there is a risk of dependence. 
Benzodiazepines can also be given on an as-and-when-needed basis (SOS)
SSRI
If the patient fails to respond to Benzodiazepines as above or requires treatment for a 
longer duration, antidepressants should be considered. 
Tab. Sertraline 50–200 mg/day as a single dose in morning with food; starting with 25 
mg/day which can be increased up to 200 mg/day after 5–6 weeks in increments of 
50 mg in case of non-response. Most patients may not require more than 50 mg/day.
Or
Cap. Fluoxetine 20–60 mg/day as a single dose in morning with food; starting with 
10 mg/day which can be increased to 20–60 mg/day in increments of 20 mg after 5–6 weeks 
in case of non-response. Most patients may not require more than 20 mg/day.
Or
Tab. Escitalopram 10–20 mg/day as a single dose in morning with food; starting 
with 5 mg/day which can be increased up to 20 mg/day after 5–6 weeks in case of 
non-response. Most patients may not require more than 10 mg/day.
Or
Tab. Paroxetine 12.5–50 mg/day in a single dose in the morning with food; starting with 
12.5 mg/day with increments of 12.5 mg/day after 2–3 weeks in case of non-response.
(Caution: SSRIs may exacerbate anxiety symptoms in the first few days; usually a low 
dose is required for anxiety disorders.)
Or
Tab. Buspirone 15–60 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses. It is effective in 60–80% of patients 
especially in reducing the cognitive symptoms. It takes 2–3 weeks to show its effect.
Beta-blockers
Tab. Propranolol 20–40 mg/day in 2 divided doses, given especially if the predominant 
symptoms are those of sympathetic overactivity. (Caution: To be avoided in patients 
with a history of chronic obstructive airway disease and bronchial asthma)
Note: SSRIs should be used if the patient needs treatment for a longer period. Both 
SSRIs and benzodiazepines can be started together. Benzodiazepines can be withdrawn 
over 2–4 weeks as the SSRIs take over the effect. In another approach, buspirone may 
be combined with Benzodiazepines initially as it shows its effect after 2–3 weeks after 
which Benzodiazepines may be gradually withdrawn.

PANIC DISORDER
Panic disorder is a common psychiatric disorder, presenting often in primary care or 
general medical emergency settings. The patients are likely to be misdiagnosed as 
having acute cardiorespiratory problem. It is described as an episodic illness, in which 
episodes often last from a few seconds to a few hours.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patient presents with discrete episodes of sudden-onset feeling of intense fear, 
discomfort or anxiety; autonomic disturbances like palpitations, chest pain, 
choking sensations, dizziness and feelings of unreality; and feeling of impending 
doom characterized by intense fear of dying, losing control or something bad 
about to happen.
	
l The condition is not associated with situational trigger and occurs out of the blue. 
	
l Onset and remission of individual attacks are spontaneous.
	
l In between episodes, anticipatory anxiety of recurrence of episodes or persistent 
fear of going alone might occur.
	
l Diagnosis is usually made when several attacks have occurred in the previous 
month. It is often associated with agoraphobia – fear of places from where escape 
may be difficult in case of development of anxiety symptoms.

Treatment can be divided into treatment of acute attack and long-term plan. Both strategies 
include starting either pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy or a combination of both.

condition: Social Phobia or Social Anxiety Disorder
text:
Acute attack 
The modalities of treatment remain like those discussed for GAD. However, for a 
person suffering an acute panic attack, mouth-dissolving, short-acting Benzodiazepines 
(Clonazepam 0.5–1 mg, Alprazolam 0.25–1 mg or Lorazepam 1–2 mg) can be given stat.
Patients having recurrent episodes, those not responding adequately to as-and-when-
required medications or those having significant socio-occupational decline due to 
panic attacks can be started on antidepressant drugs (SSRI, SNRI, TCA). Drugs and 
dosages remain similar to those in the treatment of GAD.
Response may take 2–3 weeks to begin and 8–12 weeks to stabilize. Treatment needs 
to be given for a minimal period of 8–12 months. Medicines should be tapered off 
thereafter slowly over a period of 6–8 weeks. If the patient does not show any response 
in 6 weeks, refer to a psychiatrist.
Patient education
	
l Provide general reassurance about benign nature of symptoms and spontaneous 
recovery of individual attacks.
	
l Advise the patient not to avoid the anxiety-provoking situations, and try to face them.
	
l Ask the patient to perform breathing exercises.

SOCIAL PHOBIA OR SOCIAL ANXIETY DISORDER
Social phobias often start in adolescence and are centred around fears of scrutiny by 
other people in comparatively small groups rather than in crowds. They are equally 
common in both the sexes.

OBSESSIVE COMPULSIVE DISORDER
Obsessive compulsive disorder is characterized by thoughts and actions which are 
repetitive in nature and involuntary. These thoughts and acts become a great source of 
anxiety for the patients. Obsessions are defined as repetitive, unwanted thoughts, urges 
or images which interfere with all aspects of daily life. They are said to be ego-dystonic 
and cause severe anxiety. Compulsions are defined as repetitive actions (physical or 
mental) which are performed as a result of underlying obsessions. These acts are mostly 
performed to reduce the underlying anxiety arising due to obsessions. Illness usually 
begins in adolescent or early adult life and the majority of patients have a chronic 
waxing and waning course. 
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Recurrent obsessional thoughts may present in the form of repetitive ideas, 
images or impulses (e.g. constantly thinking that the door has been left unlocked). 
	
l These are perceived as senseless by the sufferer, who feels distressed and tries to 
resist them unsuccessfully.
	
l Compulsive acts are repetitive behaviour which are not enjoyable and do not result 
in the completion of inherently useful tasks such as cleaning compulsions (repeated 
hand washing, repeated bathing, spending more time washing clothes, utensils, 
cleaning the house), checking compulsions (constantly going back to check the door

934    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 lock, checking work for mistakes, spelling errors), counting compulsions (counting a 
particular set of numbers repeatedly), repeating compulsions (re-repeating sentences, 
rewriting, repeating certain acts) and ordering and re-arranging.
	
l These significantly interfere with the person’s normal routine, occupational 
(or academic) functioning or usual social activities or relationship.

l Psychoeducation, reassurance, support
	
l CBT (to be given by a psychiatrist/clinical psychologist)
	
l Exposure and response prevention (to be given by a psychiatrist/clinical psychologist)
Psychoeducation
	
l Explain regarding the nature of illness and treatment strategies, and that the duration 
of treatment is going to be prolonged.
	
l Explain the association between obsessions, compulsions and the distress felt by 
the patient.
	
l The course and outcome of the illness should be explained properly. The need for 
treatment (psychotherapy and/or pharmacotherapy) should be emphasized.
	
l Educate the family about the nature of illness, explaining to them not to blame the 
patient for his/her acts and thoughts. Address critical commenting.

SSRI form the mainstay of pharmacological intervention. However, other drugs with 
serotonergic preponderance (Venlafaxine, Clomipramine) can also be given. The 
dosing in obsessive compulsive disorder is usually higher than that for patients with 
depression. The dose of medications should be increased to the maximum doses by 
4–6 weeks depending on tolerability. An adequate trial is considered when medications 
are given at the maximum dose possible for at least 12 weeks.
SSRI
Tab. Sertraline 150–200 mg/day as a single dose in morning with food; starting with 
50 mg/day which can be increased up to 200 mg/day after 5–6 weeks in increments 
of 50 mg in case of non-response
Or
Cap. Fluoxetine 60–80 mg/day as a single dose in morning with food; starting with 
10 mg/day which can be increased to 20–60 mg/day in increments of 20 mg after 
5–6 weeks in case of non-response
Or
Tab. Escitalopram 20–30 mg/day as a single dose in morning with food; starting 
with 5 mg/day which can be increased up to 30 mg/day after 5–6 weeks in case of 
non-response

(Caution: SSRIs may exacerbate anxiety symptoms in the first few days; usually a 
low dose is required for anxiety disorders. Side effects include gastrointestinal distress, 
nausea, headache, nervousness, anorexia, restlessness and sexual side effects.)
Or
Tab. Clomipramine 75–150 mg/day in single or divided doses; to be started with 25 mg 
twice a day, increased by 25 mg/day every third day till 150 mg/day (to be avoided in 
patients with epilepsy, heart diseases, glaucoma and benign prostate hypertrophy)
In the initial 2–4 weeks of treatment, one may need to add Benzodiazepines like 
Diazepam, Lorazepam or Alprazolam if anxiety symptoms are troublesome. These can 
be given in doses as described in the section ‘Generalized Anxiety Disorder’.
Anxiety and distress are the first symptoms to respond. Obsessive and compulsive 
symptoms respond later. Doses of SSRIs required are often higher than in depression 
and response is slower than in depression. If no response is seen within 6–8 weeks, the 
patient should be referred to a psychiatrist.
Patient education
	
l Reassure the patient that although disease is distressing and disabling, it is treatable.
	
l The drug takes about 2 weeks for its therapeutic response to manifest.
	
l Side effects may appear before the onset of therapeutic response. Common 
side effects of Clomipramine are dry mouth, constipation, postural hypotension 
(giddiness), blurred vision and sedation. Side effects of Fluoxetine and other SSRIs 
include gastrointestinal distress, nausea, headache, nervousness, anorexia, restlessness 
and sexual side effects. The patient usually adapts to these side effects with time.
	
l Advise the patient that treatment may continue for a long time. He/she should not 
leave drugs without medical advice.
	
l In case of any untoward effects of drugs, he/she must immediately get in touch with 
his/her clinician.
	
l The patient must continue all his/her regular activities as far as possible.
	
l Yoga, meditation and physical exercises are useful measures along with drug therapy.

for obsessive-compulsive disorder. Indian J Psychiatry. 2017;59(Suppl. 1):S74–S90.
	 6.	 Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide. 5th ed. 2014.

936    Standard Treatment Guidelines
ACUTE STRESS DISORDER
Acute stress disorder follows immediately after a stressful event of exceptional nature. 
The stressor can be an overwhelming traumatic event like a serious threat to life, 
security or one’s physical integrity. The symptoms last only for a short period varying 
from few hours to days.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l To make a diagnosis of acute stress disorder, an immediate and temporally related 
stressor should be associated with the onset of symptoms.
	
l Symptoms include marked symptoms of anxiety and increased arousal. An initial 
state of daze is followed by depression, anxiety, anger, despair, overactivity and 
withdrawal.
	
l The clinical picture often changes rapidly with a mixture of the above-mentioned 
symptoms.
	
l In case the stressor persists and is irreversible in nature, symptoms reduce within 
1–3 days.
	
l Nature of stressor commonly includes overwhelming traumatic experience (e.g. 
natural catastrophe, accident, battle, criminal assault, rape, multiple bereavement 
or domestic fire).

l Addressing the individual’s requirements for medical care, rest, nutrition and control 
of injury-related pain and establish a safe environment
	
l Detailed recollection of the traumatic event – psychological debriefing
	
l General support, reassurance and assistance with coping resources

l There is no significant role of medications.
	
l In cases of extreme anxiety, give Tab. Lorazepam 1 mg Or Clonazepam 0.25 mg on 
as-and-when-required basis and increase the dose, if necessary, to 2–4 mg/day or 
0.5–1.0 mg/day, respectively, in divided doses; in elderly (or debilitated), use half 
the adult dose if anxiety symptoms or the distress is uncontrollable.
	 If insomnia is troublesome, Tab. Lorazepam 5–15 mg may be given at bedtime. 
Medication needs to be given only for a few days.
Patient/Family education
Reassure and educate the patient and the family that the symptoms are short lasting and 
the patient would recover fully within a short time.

POST-TRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER (PTSD)
PTSD was first reported after the Vietnam War, but later similar syndrome has been 
seen in the victims of natural disasters, major accidents and personal injuries like rape 
or mugging. Prevalence of PTSD may be as high as 50–80% following the traumatic 
event.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Symptoms follow a major traumatic event of life-threatening or catastrophic 
nature (natural or man-made disasters) after a delay.
	
l Symptoms generally occur within 6 months of the event. Symptoms of PTSD are 
divided into four clusters.
	
l The patient has intrusive and recurrent memories of the trauma which involve 
repeated reliving of trauma in the form of flashbacks, nightmares, intrusive 
recollections of the event and avoidance of stimuli related to trauma.
	
l There occur emotional numbness, and/or negative changes in mood or cognitions 
pertaining to the trauma, unresponsiveness and detachment from other people.
	
l Autonomic hyperarousal and hypervigilance on exposure are seen.
Treatment (to be treated by a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist)
A trauma-focused psychological therapy is preferred. Special training is required to carry 
out psychological interventions in such patients. Few modalities are mentioned below.

l Emotional support, reassurance
	
l Behaviour therapy with focus on exposure and desensitization
	
l CBT

Do not routinely use drug treatments as first-line treatment for PTSD, although SSRIs 
like Fluoxetine, Sertraline, Escitalopram, Venlafaxine or Mirtazapine are given when 
symptoms of depression or anxiety are disabling. Dosage is similar as in anxiety

938    Standard Treatment Guidelines
disorders and depression. Duration of treatment may vary from 6 months to a year 
depending on the response.
Patient education
	
l Patient and family members should be educated regarding the nature of the illness.
	
l Correlation between the traumatic event and the symptoms should be explained.
	
l The need to start psychotherapy should be emphasized and that PTSD usually is seen 
after a period of few months.
	
l The patient often relives the trauma in the form of nightmares, flashbacks or 
recollection of the event.
	
l One should contact one’s doctor if he/she develops such symptoms after a major 
traumatic event.
References
	 1.	 Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines. John Wiley & Sons 
Ltd; December 2021.
	 2.	 Sadock BJ, Sadock VA, Ruiz P. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry. 12th ed. Wolters 
Kluwer: Philadelphia; 2021.
	 3.	 Harrison P, Cowen P, Burns T, Fazel M. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry. 7th ed. Oxford: 
Oxford University Press; 2018.
INSOMNIA
Insomnia is one of the commonest complaints in psychiatric, medical and general 
clinical practice. It can be primary or secondary in nature. Primary insomnia usually 
refers to sleep problems with no underlying cause. Secondary insomnia is usually when 
sleep disturbances are a result of an underlying cause. Common causes include a recent 
stress, psychiatric illnesses like depression and anxiety disorders, pain in any body part 
or substance abuse.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Insomnia can be sleep-onset insomnia (difficulty in initiating sleep) or sleep 
maintenance insomnia (frequent awakenings from sleep, early morning insomnia 
or non-restorative sleep). In the elderly, the physiological reduction in the number 
of hours of sleep does not amount to insomnia. If the patient is distressed by 
decreased sleep, treatment may be given to increase the duration of sleep. 
	
l Stressful situation leading to insomnia or the symptoms of the causative illness 
can be elicited on careful enquiry. Duration of symptoms may vary from few days 
to many months or years depending on the cause.

Treat the underlying cause. In both primary insomnia (in which no cause is identifiable) 
and insomnia due to other causes, management includes introducing good sleep hygiene 
and/or medications for a short period, if required.

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    939
Sleep hygiene
	
l Set a consistent schedule: Go to bed at a set time each night and get up at the same 
time each morning. Avoid daytime naps. Limit daily in-bed time to the usual amount 
present before the sleep disturbance.
	
l Avoid large meals near bedtime; eat at regular times daily. Take no stimulant medication 
or food beverages (caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, etc.) especially in the evenings.
	
l Perform mild-to-moderate physical exercise in the morning.
	
l Relax before going to bed: a warm bath, reading or another relaxing routine can 
make it easier to fall sleep. Avoid evening stimulation: Substitute television by radio.
	
l Do not lie in bed awake: If you cannot get to sleep after about 20 minutes in bed, do 
not just lie in bed. Do something else, like reading, watching television or listening 
to music, until you feel tired.
	
l Practice evening relaxation routines, such as progressive muscular relaxation or 
meditation.
	
l Maintain comfortable sleeping conditions: Avoid extreme temperatures.

Tab. Zolpidem 5–10 mg at bedtime
Or
Tab. Lorazepam 1–2 mg or Clonazepam 0.25–0.5 mg at bedtime
Precautions
	
l Medication should be given 0.5–1 hour before the usual time of going to bed. 
	
l Medications should be prescribed at the lower dose for a period of 5–7 days. 
	
l Benzodiazepines have a risk of abuse potential if taken for more than 3 weeks. 
Diazepam and Nitrazepam carry a risk of dependence and should be avoided.
	
l Zolpidem also has dependence potential and therefore long-term use should be 
discouraged.
Patient education
	
l Stress on basic principles of sleep hygiene as above. 
	
l The patient should avoid exceeding the prescribed dose and should not take 
medicines beyond the prescribed period. 
	
l Sometimes these drugs can lead to sedation during daytime. In such case, reduce the 
dose to half and contact the doctor. 
	
l Diazepam and nitrazepam carry a risk of dependence.
References
	 1.	 Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines. John Wiley & Sons 
Ltd; December 2021.

ALCOHOL USE DISORDER
Dependence is defined as a pattern of use of any substance (e.g. alcohol) in which the 
substance takes on a much higher priority than other behaviours.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Craving, compulsion to drink, difficulties in controlling alcohol consumption, 
withdrawal symptoms
	
l Tolerance (increasing amount required to achieve the same effect)
	
l Progressive neglect of alternative pleasures or interests and persisting despite 
clear evidence of overtly harmful consequences and withdrawal state 
	
l Withdrawal symptoms: tremor, tachycardia, anxiety, sleep disturbance, nausea, 
vomiting, hallucination, generalized seizure and delirium in severe cases

condition: Substance Use Disorders Alcohol Use Disorder
text:
I. Detoxification (Treatment of the withdrawal state and associated problems)
Detoxification can be done in an outpatient or inpatient setting. Outpatient treatment is 
preferred when the withdrawal state is uncomplicated.
	 1.	Tab. Chlordiazepoxide 10–50 mg 4 times a day, depending on severity of 
dependence
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Diazepam 5–20 mg 4 times a day
	 2.	Inj. Thiamine 100–300 mg IM in divided doses in patients who have a greater 
severity of withdrawal or those who are in delirium tremens or cannot take orally 
(once the patient can take orally or is out of delirium, switch to oral Thiamine)
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Thiamine orally along with oral multivitamins and Tab. Folate 1 mg
	
	Once the patient is well sedated and stable, the dosage should be decreased 
20% per day over a maximum period of 2 weeks. The patient should be monitored 
during this period for the appearance of the signs of delirium.
	
	For elderly patients or in the presence of significant liver disease, Tab. Oxazepam 
15 mg Or Tab. Lorazepam 2–4 mg every 6 hours should be started.
	 3.	Inpatient treatment is advised when withdrawal state is associated with seizures, 
delirium or emesis, fluid and electrolyte disturbance, medical conditions like 
pneumonia or surgical problem (e.g. head trauma), hallucinatory behaviour, 
suicidal risk and previous history of delirium tremens.

condition: Substance Use Disorders Alcohol Use Disorder
text:
Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    941
Note: The vital signs and withdrawal symptoms should be monitored 2–4 hourly. Once 
the patient is stable, the dose should be gradually tapered off (20% per day) over a 
period of 7–10 days.
Treatment of dependence with complications
Basic treatment is as described above, but the patient needs to be hospitalized. 
Guidelines are as below:
	 1.	Fluid and electrolyte disturbance should be corrected, especially if there is 
vomiting or fever.
	 2.	Seizures: Rum fits (appearing within 24 hours of abstinence) can be treated 
with Inj. Diazepam 10 mg Or Inj. Lorazepam 2 mg IV stat, especially when 
seizures are repeated. Prophylactic treatment is not recommended for true alcohol 
withdrawal fits.
	 3.	Delirium tremens: The patient should be preferably treated in an intensive care 
unit.
	 a.	An intravenous line should be started immediately and Inj. Thiamine 100 mg 
administered IV, or IM. Thiamine along with multivitamin should be continued 
parenterally till normal diet is resumed. Later, oral thiamine should be continued 
for at least 3–4 months.
	 b.	Dextrose and saline IV should be given at a rate adequate to replace fluid losses 
and maintain blood pressure.
	 c.	Hyperthermia should be managed with cold sponge.
	
	Tab. Paracetamol 500 mg 4 times a day may be used in the absence of any 
hepatic dysfunction.
	 d.	Inj. Diazepam 10 mg should be given slowly IV and should be repeated every 
15–20 minutes till sedation is achieved.
	 e.	Physical restraint may be necessary if the patient is combative.
	 f.	Associated medical and surgical problems should be simultaneously investigated 
and treated appropriately.
II. Long-term treatment (To be treated by a psychiatrist)
The goal of this treatment is to help the patient maintain long-term abstinence.

Individual counselling and family support should be planned along with 
pharmacotherapy. After remission, the patient should be encouraged to join self-help 
groups like Alcoholics Anonymous.

condition: Substance Use Disorders Alcohol Use Disorder
text:
Deterrents like Disulfiram or anticraving agents like Naltrexone or Acamprosate are 
used for long-term treatment of alcohol dependence.
Tab. Disulfiram 250 mg a day may be used if the patient desires enforced sobriety and 
has remained alcohol-free for at least 7–10 days.

condition: Substance Use Disorders Alcohol Use Disorder
text:
942    Standard Treatment Guidelines
(Caution:
	
l Disulfiram should be started after taking proper consent from the patient. The patient 
should be explained in detail regarding the benefits and side effects of disulfiram 
including possibility of life-threatening disulfiram–ethanol reaction (DER). 
	
l Patients taking disulfiram develop an extremely unpleasant reaction (DER) on 
intake of even small amounts (e.g. 7 mL) of alcohol. The reaction occurs due to 
accumulation of acetaldehyde and includes flushing, headache, throbbing in the 
head, dyspnoea, hyperventilation, tachycardia, hypotension, sweating and confusion. 
	
l In the event of DER, fall in BP should be controlled on a priority basis. If DER is mild, 
assurance and oral fluids suffice. In case of moderate or severe DER, IV fluids are 
required and some patients may even need dopamine infusion. 
	
l Generally, DER does not occur in the first week of disulfiram use and if alcohol 
is consumed after 5–7 days of stopping disulfiram, but can occur up to 2 weeks 
after stopping Disulfiram.
	
l Disulfiram should be continued for several months to establish a long-term pattern 
of sobriety.)
Or
Tab. Naltrexone 50 mg orally once daily may be used.
(Caution: Baseline hepatic functions should be assessed and monitored once a 
month while on Naltrexone treatment. The drug is usually continued for a period of 
6 months. However, it may have to be withdrawn in the presence of significant liver 
disease [i.e. several-fold increase in the serum levels of transaminases].)
Or 
Tab. Acamprosate (333 mg) 1–2 g/day in 3 divided doses. There is no optimum 
duration of therapy but benefit beyond 12 months has not been demonstrated. 
(Caution: It is contraindicated in severe renal and hepatic failure; reduce dosage in 
moderate renal impairment; monitor renal and liver function regularly.)
Patient education
	
l The patient should be told about the nature of illness, course and treatment 
modalities available through individual sessions. 
	
l Warn the patients about the risk of relapse and encourage them to seek treatment at 
the earliest. Educate patients about relapse prevention by identifying and handling 
high-risk situations, drink refusal skills and assertiveness, handling negative mood 
states, managing anger and following a healthy lifestyle.
	
l Engage family support, listen to family members, counsel them to change their 
negative responses and provide support to the patient in recovering from addiction.
	
l Inform about the self-help groups, where persons recovering from substance 
dependence offer mutual support to recover, like Alcoholics Anonymous.
	
l Emphasize on regular follow-up and use reminders to monitor both the health 
condition and substance use and retaining the patient in treatment as it is a chronic, 
relapsing condition.

OPIOID DEPENDENCE SYNDROME
Opioid dependence is a complex health condition that often requires long-term 
treatment and care because of significant associated health, psychological and social 
impairment. The essential components of an effective treatment system include focus 
on both detoxification with subsequent abstinence-oriented treatment and substitution 
maintenance treatment followed by rehabilitation by improving social functioning. 
Commonly abused opioids include codeine, fentanyl, heroin, morphine, opium, 
methadone, oxycodone and hydrocodone taken as inhalational form, smoking or through 
IV route. Screening tools like CRAFFT and ASSIST help in screening substance use 
(including cannabis) and related problems in primary and general medical care settings.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Craving (strong compulsion to take an opioid)
	
l Difficulties in controlling opioid consumption – taking substance at any time, 
unable to stop or consuming a moderate amount of an opioid
	
l Tolerance (increasing amount required to achieve the same effect over time)
	
l Progressive neglect of alternative pleasures or interests
	
l Opioid withdrawal symptoms: aches and pains, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, 
yawning, tachycardia, piloerection, vomiting, loose motions, sleep disturbance 
and spontaneous ejaculation; persisting with drinking despite clear evidence of 
overtly harmful consequences (the patient continues to take the substance through 
IV route despite developing HIV/AIDS)
	
l Signs suggestive of chronic drug use: poor self-care, poor dentition, parasitic 
skin infections, malnutrition, new or old marks of injections on the arms or legs 
(presence of HIV/AIDS, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, tuberculosis and skin infections at 
injection sites should alert the physician and chronic drug use possibility explored)
Treatment (to be treated by a psychiatrist or at a de-addiction centre)
The essential components of an effective treatment system include:
	 1.	Detoxification with subsequent abstinence-oriented treatment

944    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 2.	Substitution maintenance treatment with buprenorphine
	 3.	Rehabilitation by improving social functioning

Withdrawal symptoms may need to be treated symptomatically as follows: 
	 1.	Hypnotics (e.g. Zolpidem, long-acting benzodiazepines) for sleep disturbance
	 2.	NSAIDs for aches and pains
	 3.	Antidiarrhoeals for loose motions
	 4.	Antiemetics for nausea and vomiting
	 5.	Fluid and electrolyte balance for electrolyte imbalance
	 6.	Managing associated physical and mental disorders simultaneously
	 7.	Manage certain withdrawal symptoms like insomnia, restlessness and mild body 
aches symptomatically which may persist as above and with non-pharmacological 
interventions like relaxation therapy even after 3 weeks.
	 8.	If withdrawal symptoms are severe enough and are not effectively controlled 
with symptomatic management, Tab. Buprenorphine Or Tramadol can be used for 
detoxification. The starting dose is decided according to the amount of opioid used 
by the patient in 24 hours. Subsequent doses need to be adjusted according to the 
severity of withdrawal symptoms, which usually peak during third to seventh days 
of withdrawal.
	
	Tab. Buprenorphine 1.2–4.0 mg/day orally in 4–6 divided doses
	
	Or
	
	Cap. Dextropropoxyphene 50–100 mg thrice a day; Available as 25-mg tablet
	 9.	In case the patient has persistent tachycardia or hypertension, Tab. Clonidine 
100–200 mcg 3–4 times a day (Caution: Monitor BP before each dose; skip dose 
if BP is <90/60.)
Tapering off of the medication can be started from the third day onwards, depending on 
the response. Usually, detoxification medicines are required for days.
Long-term treatment

Individual counselling, family support and encouraging the patient to join the self-help 
groups are also important to help him/her maintain long-term abstinence. However, 
opiate dependence is a highly relapsing disorder and prolonged inpatient stay in settings 
that also provide rehabilitative inputs may be required in some cases.
Pharmacological (to be treated by a psychiatrist)
Opioid substitution therapy (OST) with Buprenorphine or Methadone. These drugs 
are available only through OST centres accredited by the National AIDS Control 
Organisation (NACO) or the designated deaddiction centres.

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    945
To reduce craving, Tab. Naltrexone 50 mg/day orally is used for 6–12 months and 
thereby to help the patient maintain long-term abstinence. Before starting Naltrexone, 
ensure that there is no opioid use in the last 7 days. (Caution: Assess baseline hepatic 
functions and monitor once a month while on naltrexone treatment. Do NOT use in 
patients with liver failure or acute hepatitis. There is a risk of fatal overdose in patients 
who use opioids more than 24 hours after their last dose of naltrexone, due to rapid 
loss of opioid tolerance.)
Anticraving drugs 
Tab. Disulfiram 250–500 mg/day in inpatient setting (for details, see the section 
‘Alcohol Use Disorder’). Continue long-term therapy with anticraving drugs to 
establish long-term abstinence.
Patient education
	
l Explain to the patient about the nature of illness, course and treatment modalities 
available through individual sessions. 
	
l Arrange collaboration with various other service organizations (schools, NGOs, 
District Mental Health Programmes).
See also the subsection ‘Patient Education’ in the section ‘Alcohol Use Disorder’.

CANNABIS USE DISORDER
Cannabis use disorder and cannabis-related disorders include problems that are 
associated with substances derived from cannabis plant. These plant extracts are 
known by various names across cultures. In India, cannabis and its products are 
commonly known as ‘Bhang’, ‘Ganja’, ‘Sulfa’ and ‘Hashish.’ Cannabis use is known 
to precipitate schizophrenia in individuals with vulnerability and is also associated 
with anxiety and depression. Screening tools like CRAFFT and ASSIST help in 
screening substance use (including cannabis) and related problems in primary and 
general medical care settings.

946    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l A patient with cannabis intoxication presents with conjunctival suffusion (red 
eyes), increased appetite, dry mouth and tachycardia.
	
l Craving – strong compulsion to take cannabis – is present.
	
l There are difficulties in controlling cannabis consumption – taking substance at 
any time, unable to stop or consuming a moderate amount of cannabis.
	
l Tolerance (increasing amount required to achieve the same effect) is seen.
	
l There occurs progressive neglect of alternative pleasures or interests. Cannabis can 
precipitate certain psychiatric disorders, especially schizophrenia. A few signs and 
symptoms might help in recognizing the same such as recent deterioration in school 
grades, behavioural changes, change of friends, lack of interaction with family, 
increasing isolation, changes in eating pattern, delinquent behaviour, secretiveness 
in acts and possessions, memory impairment, increased need for money but on what 
spent not apparent, stealing money and problems with law (rash driving).
	
l Cannabis intoxication symptoms are conjunctival suffusion (red eyes), increased 
appetite, dry mouth and tachycardia.
	
l Cannabis withdrawal symptoms are precipitated usually within 1 week of 
cessation of heavy and prolonged use of cannabis. They are irritability, anxiety, 
sleep difficulties, restlessness, decreased appetite and depressed mood.

In case of suspicion of cannabis use and in high-risk cases, screen urine for 
tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). Clinical correlation is required because concomitant use 
of certain medications may lead to false-positivity tests.

l It is the first line of management of cannabis dependence. Educating the user about 
the harms of cannabis use should be done either individually or in a group setup. 
	
l Refer to a psychiatrist or a clinical psychologist for motivational enhancement treatment 
(MET) to increase self-control, help the patient identify risk factors and situations which 
perpetuate cannabis use and bring about rapid and internally motivated change. 
	
l Principles of engaging an adolescent are reassurance about confidentiality, being 
non-judgemental and screening for mental health problems, while discussing whole 
life rather than only substance. Family needs to be educated about the problem and 
should be supportive. 
	
l Simple behavioural strategies such as rewarding the patient for having a negative 
urine test are helpful.

Symptoms of cannabis intoxication and withdrawal are mostly transient, mild and 
self-limiting. Reassurance and supportive care are usually sufficient. Place the patient 
in a calm, cool, quiet atmosphere with optimal lighting.

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    947
Cannabis intoxication
In case of severe, distressing anxiety symptoms or unmanageable, disruptive psychotic 
symptoms, give a short-acting Benzodiazepine.
	 1.	Tab. Alprazolam 0.5–1.5 mg/day Or Tab. Clonazepam 0.5–1.0 mg/day in 2–3 
divided doses 
	
	AND
	
	In case of severe anxiety with autonomic features (tachycardia, sweating, dilated 
pupils), Tab. Propranolol 40–80 mg/day for 1–2 days 
	 2.	In case of psychotic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations), low-dose antipsychotic,
	
	Tab. Quetiapine 25–50 mg/day Or Tab. Olanzapine 2.5–5 mg/day
Cannabis withdrawal syndrome
In patients with severe and distressing withdrawal symptoms:
Tab. Chlordiazepoxide 10–40 mg 4 times a day, depending on severity of dependence 
for 7 days
Or 
Tab. Diazepam 5–20 mg 4 times a day for 7 days 
In case of insomnia, add:
Tab. Zolpidem 5–10 mg at night
Or
Tab. Baclofen 40 mg/day 
The duration of treatment is around 7 days.
Cannabis dependence
	
l Complete abstinence and psychosocial support remain key to the treatment. The 
patient may need hospitalization for abstinence, or regular contact is required in 
outpatients with frequent use of urine drug screens. However, interpretation of urine 
drug testing for cannabis is challenging because of the persistence of metabolites for 
4–5 days after a single use and for 1 month after chronic daily use.
	
l If there are associated anxiety, depressive or behavioural symptoms, antianxiety, 
antidepressant or low-dose antipsychotics are indicated.
	
l The patient should be referred to a psychiatrist. 
	
l No medication has been approved; all medications are empirical with no particular 
recommendations for any specific medication. In combination with psychosocial 
interventions, potential options include: Tab. Buspirone up to 60 mg/day or Baclofen 
40–60 mg/day or Fluoxetine 20–40 mg. The usual duration of treatment is 3–12 months.
	
l Refer patients to a tertiary care centre in case of severe cannabis dependence, 
comorbid psychiatric diagnosis with risk of harm to self/others, comorbid serious 
medical conditions, adolescents, elderly or pregnant patients and highly disturbed 
family environment.

948    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Patient/family education
	
l Inform the patient and family about the ill-effects of cannabis and the tell-tale signs 
of possible cannabis use and that the patient be brought to a specialist if the patient 
is suspected of abusing cannabis.
	
l Identify certain family and environmental factors that may increase the risk for 
cannabis use. Generally, the crucial periods of risk for drug use and abuse occur 
during key life transitions, such as moving from elementary school to middle school 
or association with drug-abusing peers, particularly in youth.
	
l Explain about harm reduction strategies and education about cannabis withdrawal 
syndrome. Family communication and cohesion are protective, as these families are 
often more supportive and adolescents are reinforced for adaptive coping behaviour. 
Additionally, the feeling of being cared for and connected to parents or guardians 
protects adolescents from substance use.
See also the subsection ‘Patient Education’ in ‘Alcohol Use Disorder’.
References
	 1.	 Sazegar P. Cannabis essentials: tools for clinical practice. Am Fam Physician. 2021;104(6):598–
608.
	 2.	 Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India. Standard Treatment Guidelines for 
the Management of Substance Use Disorders and Behavioural Addiction. 2020. https://main.
mohfw.gov.in/sites/default/files/boolbehavioural.pdf [accessed March 15, 2024].
NICOTINE DEPENDENCE
Nicotine dependence is a major public health problem. Nicotine is abused in the form 
of tobacco, smoked in bidis, cigarettes and hooka, and chewed as such or in pan masala.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Most tobacco users smoke or use smokeless tobacco on a daily basis.
	
l Indicators of dependence include the time from waking to first use. About 15% 
of the dependent smokers light up within 5 minutes of waking, while almost half 
smoke within the first half hour of the day.
	
l Typical physical symptoms following cessation or reduction of nicotine intake 
include craving for nicotine, irritability, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, 
restlessness, sleep disturbances, decreased heart rate, and increased appetite or 
weight gain.

l Progressively lowering the number of cigarettes smoked or tobacco sachets 
used daily
	
l Using past quit experience
	
l Setting a quit date

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    949
	
l Throwing away items such as ashtrays the night before the quit day dawns, 
preferably as a ceremonial gesture
	
l Advising the patient that starting from the quit date, total abstinence is essential
	
l Helping the patient identify each of the environmental conditions that most likely 
lead to tobacco use and then developing a course of behaviour that avoids those 
conditions or prevents them from occurring
	
l Suggesting that the patient develop an alternate plan to having a cigarette during the 
morning toilet, smoking after a meal and smoking to manage stress at work or in 
traffic, being in an argument, and so on
	
l The five Ds to handle urges:
	– Delay until the urge passes. It usually takes 3–5 minutes.
	– Distract yourself. Call a friend or go for a walk. 
	– Drink a glass of water.
	– Deep breaths – Relax! Close your eyes and take 10 slow, deep breaths.
	– Discuss your feelings with someone close to you.

Nicotine gum, one piece of 2 mg gum/h for light smokers and 4 mg gum for highly 
nicotine-dependent smokers.
Note: One piece of gum should be chewed slowly at one time until a peppery taste or 
tingling of gums occurs. Chewing can be stopped here and the gum is kept between the 
gums and the cheek. The process is repeated over 30 minutes. One should not eat or 
drink anything 15 minutes prior to and during the use of the gum. Absorption of nicotine 
in the buccal mucosa is decreased by an acidic environment. Therefore, patients should 
not use beverages (e.g. coffee, soda, juice) immediately before, during or after nicotine 
gum. The duration of treatment is 4–6 weeks. The gum is weaned off subsequently by 
tapering the frequency and strength of the gum over 2–3 months or less.
Or
Tab. Bupropion treatment is started 1–2 weeks before the quit date. The usual dose 
is 300 mg/day given in 2 divided doses. It is started as 150 mg as a single daily 
dose in the morning and increased to 150 mg twice a day on the fourth day. This is 
continued for 7–12 weeks after the quit date and maintenance therapy may go on for 
6 months.
Or
Tab. Varenicline 1–2 mg/day.
(Caution: It is important that patients continue to receive counselling and support 
throughout treatment with Bupropion and Varenicline and for a period of time 
thereafter. Adverse effects include feelings of agitation or restlessness that decrease in 
1–2 weeks after starting medication. Insomnia, gastrointestinal upset, appetite suppression 
and weight loss, headache and lowering of seizure threshold also have been reported.)
Patient education
The patient should be sensitized to the ill-effects of tobacco use.
