PSYCHIATRIC EMERGENCIES
Psychiatric emergencies are defined as an acute disturbance of thought, behaviour 
or mood which if left untreated might cause the patients to incur harm to themselves 
or others.
Psychiatric emergencies can be classified as follows:
	
l Major (causing threat to life): Suicidal patients, extremely agitated patients
	
l Minor (causing severe incapacitation but no imminent threat to life): Grief, 
rape, panic attacks
	
l Medical emergencies in psychiatry: Delirium tremens (DT), delirium due to 
general medical conditions, neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), serotonin 
syndrome (SS), psychiatric drug overdose.
PATIENTS WITH A SUICIDE RISK
All the patients who have either expressed an active will to die or considered possible 
plans or techniques for the same (suicidal ideations), have threatened to harm 
themselves (suicidal threat) or have attempted to harm themselves with the intent to 
die (suicide attempt) need immediate psychiatric intervention.
Suicidal ideas or attempts can happen due to underlying psychiatric illness, 
e.g. depression, adjustment disorders, personality disorder, psychosis, especially 
schizophrenia, or under intoxication of any substance (alcohol, cannabis, etc.). They 
can also occur in patients with chronic medical illnesses which impair the quality of 
life significantly like stroke, movement disorders and cancers.
Assessment of a patient with suicide risk
Screen all patients for the imminent risk of suicide and refer patients with active 
ideations or recent attempts preferably to a psychiatrist and treated in an inpatient set-up.
The following points would help in the assessment:
	 1.	Therapeutic alliance and rapport building: Build a good rapport with the patient 
and work towards building a therapeutic alliance. In doing so, it helps the patient 
to express himself/herself freely and feel heard, and helps in the formation of a

condition: Psychiatric Emergencies Patients with a Suicide Risk
text:
Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    951
comprehensive management plan. Patient, empathetic listening and having a non-
judgemental attitude towards the patient are important for the same.
	 2.	Psychiatric evaluation: Elicit a thorough history and examination of the mental 
status of the patient as most self-harm episodes have an underlying psychiatric or 
psychological illness, and treat the underlying cause.
	 3.	Assessing risk factors: Identify risk factors that increase the probability of a 
suicide attempt in a person expressing suicidal thoughts, and accordingly perform 
risk stratification. Risk factors include:
	
l Past history of attempted suicide (the strongest predictor of suicide intent)
	
l Currently harbouring hopeless ideas
	
l Family history of suicide
	
l Presence of psychiatric illness or chronic medical illness
	
l Recent stressor
	
l Unstable social environment and poor social support
	 4.	Identifying warning signs: Look for warning signs that a person with an 
underlying psychiatric or psychological illness might express and not overtly 
express any ideas. These signs can be either verbal or behavioural.
	
l Verbal signs: Expressing hopelessness for the future, feeling of being a burden 
on others, loss of purpose in life
	
l Behavioural signs: Withdrawing themselves from family and society, making 
arrangements or getting affairs in order, increasing substance use, dramatic 
changes in mood, increase in impulsive behaviours or a person suffering from 
psychosis with command hallucinations
	 5.	Assessing risk for a suicide attempt 
	
l Suicidal thoughts can be either passive death wishes (a person wishes that his/
her life would end but does not express any plans or intent to die) or suicidal 
ideations (a person actively expresses wish to die, has either made plans or 
thought about means and ways to end life), or a person might present with a 
recent suicide attempt.
	
l For a person expressing suicidal ideas, intensity and frequency of such thoughts 
in the last 48 hours should be enquired. He/she should also be asked whether 
he/she has thought of ways or planned an attempt for suicide; details regarding 
the same should be gathered.
	
l In case of recent or even past events, assessment of intentionality of the attempt 
(intent to die, preparations or plans made before the attempt) and lethality of 
the attempt (method of suicide, risk of death if the chosen method would have 
been successful) should be thoroughly examined.

condition: Psychiatric Emergencies Patients with a Suicide Risk
text:
Medical stabilization should be priority in case of a patient who comes with a recent 
suicide attempt. Provide necessary first aid to the patient or refer him/her to the 
emergency department for the same.
	 1.	Once the patient is medically stable, perform a thorough assessment of the patient 
as above, ascertain the risk of suicide and identify the underlying illness.

condition: Psychiatric Emergencies Patients with a Suicide Risk
text:
952    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 2.	Treatment is specifically directed at the cause, if identifiable. A few measures 
should be taken for the patient irrespective of the cause, including:
	
l Ensure that the patient is in a safe supervised environment and should always 
be accompanied by someone and should not be left alone. Perform 24-hour 
observation with suicide precautions as next.
	
l Refer the patient to a psychiatrist immediately after ensuring the following steps:
	– Involve family members and explain to them about the seriousness of the 
problem. They should be actively included in management.
	– Offer psychological support. Reassure the patient and do not criticize.
	– Remove all dangerous or potentially dangerous objects such as knife, blade, 
sharp-edged objects, rope, dupatta and medication supply from the immediate 
vicinity of the patient. Cut off access to any potentially harmful object.
	 3.	In the case of a violent or agitated patient with a risk of self-harm, give acute 
sedation with Lorazepam or a combination of Haloperidol and Promethazine IM. In 
case of non-availability of injectables, oral Clonazepam or Lorazepam can also be 
given. (Caution: It is contraindicated in patients with depression or CNS depression 
due to alcohol.)
	 4.	Refer the patient to a psychiatrist or higher centre along with detailed case notes 
including details of suicide assessment, previous psychiatric history and treatment 
received.
In a psychiatry setting
	 1.	Hospitalize acutely suicidal patients, requiring medical management of an attempt, 
when more intensive psychiatric management is required, or when no suitable 
caregivers/support people are available.
	 2.	In case of refusal, clearly document reasons for not admitting in the person’s file.
	 3.	Provide a safe environment.
	 4.	Conduct thorough psychiatric evaluation.
	 5.	Assess past suicidal behaviour, including intent of self-injurious acts.
	 6.	Identify specific psychiatric signs and symptoms.
	 7.	Treat the underlying disorder (depression, psychosis, mania, etc.).
	 8.	Certain medications (like Lithium and Clozapine) and treatment options (like 
electroconvulsive therapy [ECT]) should be considered as first-line treatment if the 
patient has persistent suicidal ideas or intent following any diagnosed psychiatric 
disorder but not due to adjustment disorder.
	 9.	Identify the current psychosocial situation and nature of crisis and individual 
strengths and vulnerability.
	10.	Specifically inquire about suicide thoughts and plans.
	11.	Reassess mental status regularly.
	12.	Follow closely over the week after discharge.
Patient/family education
	
l Family should be advised to follow a supportive approach towards the patient and 
not criticize.
	
l Suicidal attempt is indicative of distress and needs treatment of the causative illness.

DELIRIUM TREMENS
Delirium tremens (DT) is a severe form of alcohol withdrawal. It can occur due to 
sudden cessation of alcohol use after continuous consumption for days on end or even 
after sudden reduction of the dose of alcohol consumed.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l It is characterized by the presence of delirium (rapid onset, fluctuating course of 
disturbances in consciousness, psychomotor activity, attention and sleep) and severe 
alcohol withdrawal (tremors, autonomic instability and temporal correlation with the 
last dose of alcohol):
	– Tremulousness of the whole body
	– Acute confusional state which is characterized by unawareness of a person, time 
and place
	– Acute agitation
	– Hallucinatory behaviour
	– Autonomic disturbances like fluctuations in blood pressure, tachycardia, diaphoresis
	
l Complications of DT: The usual duration of DT extends from 3–4 to 7 days. 
Prolonged delirium can increase the chances of further complications and mortality 
due to cardiac arrhythmias; risk of seizures; poor oral intake leading to electrolyte 
abnormalities, Wernicke’s encephalopathy and Korsakoff’s psychosis; risk of head 
injury due to increased chances of fall; aspiration pneumonitis; etc.

1.	It is a psychiatric emergency. The patient should preferably be treated in an intensive care 
unit.
	 2.	Strict vital monitoring and input output charting should be done. Establish intravenous 
access and send blood investigations including:
	
l Complete blood count to rule out infection as a cause for delirium or comorbid 
condition
	
l Serum electrolytes to rule out dyselectrolytaemia as a cause for delirium or 
comorbid condition (due to poor oral intake, a person in DT can develop 
hyponatremia and hypokalaemia)

954    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Random blood sugar to rule out hypoglycaemia
	
l Liver function test (chronic alcoholics can have alcoholic liver disease and at 
times might also have hepatic encephalopathy)
	
l ECG to rule out any arrhythmias or cardiac abnormalities
	 3.	Inj. Thiamine 100 mg IV or IM stat and twice a day parenterally for 5 days 
along with multivitamins until normal diet is resumed. Continue oral Thiamine 
100 mg/day for at least 3–4 months.
	 4.	IV Dextrose should be given only after or along with Thiamine to avoid Wernicke’s 
encephalopathy as in chronic alcohol intake, there is a depletion in thiamine levels.
	 5.	Administer IV fluids Dextrose or Normal saline at a rate adequate to replace fluid 
losses and maintain blood pressure.
	 6.	Benzodiazepines form the mainstay of the treatment. In case of liver dysfunction, 
shorter-acting benzodiazepines (Lorazepam) are preferred, and in the absence of 
liver dysfunction, longer-acting agents like Diazepam and Chlordiazepoxide can 
be given.
	 7.	In patients who are not able to take orally or have severe DT, Inj. Lorazepam 2–4 
mg slow IV 3–4 times a day.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Diazepam 10–20 mg 3–4 times a day. Stop benzodiazepines in case the 
patient becomes drowsy. (Caution: Monitor vitals strictly. A high dose can lead to 
hypotension and respiratory depression.)
	 8.	Manage hyperthermia with cold sponge or Tab. Paracetamol 500 mg 4 times a day 
in the absence of any hepatic dysfunction.
	 9.	Investigate and treat any associated medical and surgical problems.

PATIENTS WITH ACUTE AGITATION
Agitation is defined as an excessive motor (physical) or verbal activity or emotional 
excitement. It can have psychiatric or even medical aetiologies. Psychiatric causes 
of agitation include psychosis and schizophrenia, acute manic excitement, substance 
intoxication, DT and delirium due to other causes, and dementia. Medical causes of

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    955
agitation include head injury; CNS infections; stroke; encephalopathy; delirium due to 
medical conditions like electrolyte imbalance, infections, stroke, trauma or metastasis; 
seizures; and postictal confusion.

1.	Assess and evaluate the cause of agitation. Most of the times agitation reduces once 
the management of the underlying cause is initiated.
	 2.	Ensure the safety and protection of the patient, caregivers, doctors and staff during 
examination of an acutely agitated patient.
	 3.	Take measures like removing all objects which can be used as potential weapons; 
attempt to de-escalate the individual, speaking in a calm, non-provocative voice; 
and provide adequate security in case the patient becomes violent.
	 4.	In case a patient does not respond to verbal de-escalation and continues to pose a 
risk to the people and the immediate surroundings, give:
	
	Tab. Lorazepam 2 mg or Tab. Clonazepam 1–2 mg. If the patient refuses to accept 
medications orally, administer by parenteral route.
	
	Inj. Haloperidol 5–10 mg with Inj. Promethazine 25–50 mg IM or Inj. Lorazepam 
2–4 mg IM. Monitor vitals every 2 hours.
	 5.	Refer the patient after initial management to a psychiatrist or a mental health 
establishment.

liaison psychiatry. Indian J Psychiatry. 2022;64(Suppl. 2):S484–S498.

PATIENTS WITH EXTRAPYRAMIDAL SYNDROME (EPS)
EPS is a set of neurological signs and symptoms which occur as a reaction to 
antipsychotic medications. Usually, geriatric age group, higher dosages or fast titration 
of antipsychotic medications are risk factors which increase propensity to EPS. 
Different types of EPS include drug-induced parkinsonism, acute dystonia, akathisia 
and tardive dyskinesia.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Symptoms of drug-induced parkinsonism include resting tremors, bradykinesia, 
posturing of limbs, cogwheel rigidity and masked facies.
	
l These symptoms usually occur from 7 to 14 days after starting antipsychotics.

1.	Stop or reduce the dose of the offending agent. If possible, consider switching to a 
drug with less EPS potential (Olanzapine, Quetiapine, Aripiprazole),
	 2.	In case stopping or changing the drug is not possible, consider adding an 
anticholinergic agent. Tab. Trihexyphenidyl 2 mg and if required dose gradually 
increased to 8 mg in divided doses or Tab. Benzhexol 5–10 mg in divided doses.
	 3.	Evaluate anticholinergic side effects on every follow-up.
ACUTE DYSTONIA
An acute dystonic reaction is characterized by involuntary contractions of muscles of the 
extremities, face, neck, abdomen, pelvis or larynx. The contractions can be either sustained 
or intermittent and can lead to abnormal movements or postures. Some examples of 
dystonia include blepharospasm, oculogyric crisis, animus (failure of normal relaxation of 
pelvic floor muscles during attempted defecation) and torticollis. Dystonia involving the 
laryngeal muscles is a medical emergency and can lead to death due to asphyxia.

1.	Inj. Promethazine 25–50 mg IM stat, and then switch to oral Tab. Promethazine 
25 mg 3 times a day.
	 2.	Stop or reduce the dose of the offending agent. If possible, consider switching to a 
drug with less EPS potential (Olanzapine, Quetiapine, Aripiprazole).
AKATHISIA
It is defined as a subjective feeling of restlessness and mental unease. It usually presents 
with increased motor activity and observable motor restlessness; the patient keeps on 
moving around or paces up and down, and is unable to sit still for a long time. High 
dosage of antipsychotics, antipsychotic polypharmacy and rapid dose titration are a few 
risk factors. Most typical antipsychotics and atypical antipsychotics Aripiprazole and 
Lurasidone have a higher potential to cause akathisia.

1.	Reduce or stop the offending agent. If possible, consider switching to a drug with 
less EPS potential (Olanzapine, Quetiapine)
	 2.	Tab. Propranolol 20–80 mg/day in divided doses. (Caution: Avoid beta-blockers 
in patients with bronchial asthma, bradycardia and hypotension.)

NEUROLEPTIC MALIGNANT SYNDROME
NMS is a potentially life-threatening condition which usually occurs as an idiosyncratic 
reaction to antipsychotic medications. A few risk factors leading to NMS include 
sudden increase or decrease in the dose, high dose of antipsychotic, polypharmacy, 
dehydration, physical restraint and older age group.
Patients with NMS are at an increased risk of morbidity due to renal failure and 
disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) secondary to rhabdomyolysis, deep 
venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism due to dehydration and immobilization. 
Patients may also develop aspiration pneumonia because of difficulty swallowing and 
an altered mental status.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patients with NMS present in a toxic state. As per Levenson’s criteria, at least three 
major or two major and four minor symptom criteria must be present to make a 
clinical diagnosis of NMS.
	– Major criteria: Hyperpyrexia, lead pipe rigidity, elevated creatinine phosphokinase 
(CPK) level
	– Minor criteria: Tachycardia (>25% above baseline), abnormal arterial pressure 
(systolic or diastolic pressure >25% above baseline or fluctuation of either systolic 
pressure >25 mmHg or diastolic pressure >20 mmHg), altered consciousness, 
diaphoresis, leucocytosis
	
l All patients with the above presentation should undergo baseline investigations 
including complete blood count, CPK levels, kidney function tests and liver function 
tests. CPK levels >1000 UI/L and leucocytosis are the commonly found abnormalities.
	
l Presence of hyperthermia, rigidity and elevated CPK levels >1000 IU/L in a patient 
indicates a high probability of NMS.

Refer all patients with a strong suspicion for NMS to a higher centre preferably with 
an intensive care setting for management.
	 1.	Stop the offending drug immediately.
	 2.	Keep the patient in a comfortable and cool environment with the room temperature 
around 21–23°C.
	 3.	Treat hyperthermia using cooling blankets or ice packs.
	 4.	Perform blood investigations like haemogram, liver function and kidney function 
tests, arterial blood gas (ABG) and CPK levels.

958    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 5.	Monitor vitals – pulse, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and respiratory rate.
	 6.	Start IV fluids round the clock. Maintain aggressive hydration to prevent renal damage.
	 7.	Manage any metabolic abnormality, if exists. In case of metabolic acidosis, start 
the patient on Sodium bicarbonate.
	 8.	In case of labile arterial pressure, start calcium channel blockers.
	 9.	In more severe cases:
	
	Tab. Bromocriptine 2.5 mg 3 times a day orally or via nasogastric tube, increased 
further by 2.5 mg/day up to a dose of 45 mg/day.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Dantrolene 1–2.5 mg/kg IV bolus followed by 1 mg/kg every 6 hours up 
to a maximum dose of 10 mg/kg/day. Once the patient is stabilized, switch to 
oral Dantrolene 50–200 mg/day in less severe cases. (Caution: Due to a risk of 
hepatoxicity, discontinue Dantrolene once symptoms begin to resolve.)

LITHIUM TOXICITY
Lithium is considered as a first-line agent for the treatment of bipolar disorders. It also 
finds its use in patients suffering from major depressive disorders and patients with high 
impulsivity and suicidality. Lithium toxicity is defined as lithium levels >1.5 mEq/L.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Depending on the levels of lithium in the body, toxicity can be divided into:
	– Mild (1.5–2.5 mEq/L): Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, lethargy, fine tremors, 
fatigue, ataxia, bradycardia, T-wave changes
	– Moderate (2.5–3.5 mEq/L): Coarse tremors, dysarthria, seizure, confusion, 
agitation, delirium, tachycardia, hypertonia, renal failure
	– Severe (>3.5 mEq/L): Coma, stupor, seizures, hyperthermia, hypotension, renal 
failure
Before starting the patient on Lithium, it is imperative to get baseline kidney and 
thyroid function tests, and electrocardiogram. As Lithium has a narrow therapeutic

Chapter 16  Psychiatric Conditions    959
range (0.6–1.2 mEq/L), Lithium level estimation should be done regularly, and 
thereafter on the sixth day before the next scheduled dose; measure Lithium level every 
time the dose is adjusted and 3–6 months after stabilizing the dose.

Lithium toxicity is a psychiatric emergency. If not managed timely or in moderate to 
severe cases, renal damage and/or permanent neurological damage including death can 
occur. Refer all patients with suspected Lithium toxicity to a higher centre, preferably 
with an intensive care unit set-up.
	 1.	Stop Lithium immediately if Lithium toxicity is suspected.
	 2.	Secure IV line; send sample for Lithium level estimation, serum Urea and serum 
Creatinine immediately, and get an ECG to rule out any arrhythmias.
	 3.	Forced diuresis with isotonic fluids like 0.9% Normal saline or Ringer’s lactate. 
Loop diuretics like Furosemide and Torsemide can also be used to cause diuresis. 
(Caution: Avoid ACE inhibitors, Thiazide diuretics or NSAIDs.)
	 4.	Monitor vitals and urine output.
	 5.	Monitor Lithium levels 12 hourly; they should show a falling trend.
	 6.	In case of levels >3 mEq/L or if symptoms of Lithium toxicity are very severe 
irrespective of the levels, the patient should be started on peritoneal or haemodialysis.

[Internet]. Treasure Island, FL: StatPearls Publishing; 2023, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/
NBK519062/ [accessed December 16, 2023].
	 2.	 Kamal ZM, Dutta S, Rahman S, et al. Therapeutic application of lithium in bipolar disorders: a 
brief review. Cureus. 2022;14(9):e29332.

Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer; 2021.

VALPROATE TOXICITY
Sodium valproate or Valproic acid is a commonly used antiepileptic agent. It also finds 
its use in psychiatry as a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorders and disorders with poor 
impulse control, and for affective symptoms and marked agitation in schizophrenia 
and other psychoses. Common side effects include gastritis, nausea, lethargy, 
tremors, hepatotoxicity and alopecia. Therapeutic levels of Valproate range from 50 
to 100 mg/L. Many side effects are mostly dose related and increase in severity and 
frequency at plasma levels >100 mg/L. Central nervous system side effects usually 
appear at levels greater than 180 mg/dL.

960    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patients with Valproate toxicity can present with the following symptoms: nausea 
and vomiting, coarse tremors, ataxia, drowsiness, confusion or delirious picture, 
and coma.
	
l Complications are dose related, reversible hepatotoxicity, cerebral oedema 
leading to brain herniation, prolonged CNS depression, coma and Valproate-
related hyperammonaemic encephalopathy presenting as drowsiness and acute 
confusion.

1.	Stop Sodium valproate if Valproate toxicity is suspected in any patient.
	 2.	Manage in an intensive care unit.
	 3.	Management is mostly conservative and supportive in nature.
	 4.	Maintain airway, breathing and circulation.
	 5.	Establish intravenous access immediately.
	 6.	Collect blood samples for:
	
l Serum Valproate levels to rule out toxicity
	
l Complete blood count to rule out thrombocytopenia
	
l Liver function tests (raised transaminases can indicate hepatotoxicity)
	
l Serum Ammonia to rule out Valproate-induced hyperammonaemia as it can 
cause encephalopathy which presents as delirium
	
l Random blood glucose (hypoglycaemia can present as coma, delirium or 
drowsiness; it can also occur as a comorbid condition along with valproate toxicity)
	
l Serum electrolytes and ABG to rule out any electrolyte abnormalities or 
metabolic abnormalities which can occur as a consequence of altered mental 
status
	
l ECG to rule out Valproate-induced conduction abnormalities

OSTEOARTHRITIS (OA) OF THE KNEE
Osteoarthritis of the knee is a chronic joint disorder seen in elderly people in which 
there is progressive softening and disintegration of articular cartilage.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Presenting symptoms include pain, stiffness after rest, difficulty in climbing stairs, 
difficulty in getting up from squatting position, grating sensations and off-and-on 
episodes of flare and swelling. Erythema and palpable warmth are possible but rare. 
Varus/valgus/deformity and/or fixed flexion contracture occur in severe cases.
	
l Classical radiological triad is seen on anteroposterior weight-bearing radiograph – 
joint space narrowing (JSN), peripheral osteophyte formation and subchondral 
sclerosis. The Kellgren–Lawrence (KL) grading scheme is used for diagnosis of 
radiographic OA: KL grade 0, no radiographic features; KL grade 1, doubtful 
joint narrowing and possible osteophytic lipping; KL grade 2, presence of definite 
osteophytes and possible JSN; KL grade 3, multiple osteophytes, definite JSN, 
possible bony deformity; and KL grade 4, large osteophytes, marked JSN, severe 
sclerosis and definite bony deformity.
	
l Ultrasound is useful for anterior knee pain with suspected tendinopathy or 
associated bursitis. MRI is useful for persistent undiagnosed knee joint pain, 
meniscal tears and loose bodies.

The goal is alleviation of pain and improvement of functional status. Optimally, patients 
should receive a combination of non-pharmacological and pharmacological treatment.

l Evaluate the ability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs) and instruct in joint 
protection techniques.
	
l Supportive adjunctive therapy is essential to improve functional adaptation and to 
diminish pain.

Chapter 17  Bone and Joint Diseases    963
	
l Self-management programmes and patient education programmes are strongly 
recommended to improve pain and function.
	
l Advise supervised/unsupervised exercise and/or aquatic balance exercise, and 
supervised yoga exercises for knee and hip OA.
	
l Use western toilets and avoid squatting. Avoid sitting in crossed-leg position. 
	
l Perform supervised isometric quadriceps strengthening exercises (all vigorous 
exercises should be avoided in an acutely swollen/painful knee) depending on 
individual need, circumstances and self-motivation. 
	
l Participate in neuromuscular training (balance, agility and coordination) programmes 
in combination with traditional exercises to improve performance-based function 
and walking speed.
	
l Sustained weight loss in obese or overweight patients is beneficial for enhancing 
pain and function.
	
l Apply local heat or cold fomentation.
	
l Use suitable footwear; however, lateral wedge insoles are not recommended.
	
l Assistive devices, such as a cane (to be held in the hand contralateral to the more 
painful side) or a walker, may be recommended for patients experiencing significant 
impact on ambulation, joint stability or pain due to disease affecting one or more 
joints.
	
l Use braces to improve function, reduce pain and improve quality of life.
	
l There is limited evidence for supplements like turmeric, ginger extract, glucosamine, 
chondroitin and vitamin D in reducing pain and improving function in mild-to-
moderate knee OA.
	
l There is limited evidence that laser treatment, acupuncture, manual therapy, 
percutaneous electric nerve stimulation, pulsed electromagnetic field therapy or 
extracorporeal shock wave therapy may improve pain and function.

may be required before there is prolonged and established functional limitation and 
severe pain.
	 Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is indicated for severe knee osteoarthritis when 
conservative measures fail to alleviate pain and disability, leading to significant 
functional impairment, decreased quality of life and interference with daily 
activities such as walking, climbing stairs and standing for extended periods. 
Prosthesis survival rates are high, with approximately 90% still functional after 10 
years, making it an effective long-term solution for addressing knee arthritis and 
restoring mobility.
	
l Arthroscopy with lavage and/or debridement is not recommended. Arthroscopic 
partial meniscectomy can be used for treatment of meniscal tears in patients with 
concomitant mild-to-moderate OA who have failed physical therapy or other non-
surgical treatment.

improve function. High tibial osteotomy could be considered to enhance pain relief 
and function in appropriately selected patients with unicompartmental OA of the 
knee. Patient-specific factors such as age, sex, smoking, obesity and comorbidities 
should not be barriers to referral for joint surgery.
Patient education
	
l There is no curative pharmacological agent for OA of the knee, and the disease is 
irreversible.
	
l Non-pharmacological treatment has a major role to play in treatment.
	
l Avoid activities which exacerbate pain like sitting cross-legged or squatting on the 
floor.
	
l Opt for ramps instead of stairs whenever possible. When navigating stairs, utilize 
the stronger leg to step up and the weaker leg to step down.
	
l Do not perform vigorous exercises with an acutely inflamed knee.
	
l Take minimal possible medications that provide symptomatic relief and wait for 
1–2 weeks for the drug to show its effect.
	
l Topical applications do not penetrate into the joint through the skin directly.
	
l Intra-articular steroid injections give only temporary relief and the risks of repeated 
intra-articular injections far outweigh their advantages.
	
l Report back if there are recurrent effusions in the knee or systemic symptoms. The 
former may be caused by mechanical disorder along with OA of the knee like loose 
body or meniscal tear. The latter situation could be caused by diseases of the knee 
other than OA.

RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS (RA) 
RA is characterized by persistent inflammatory synovitis (usually involving small 
and large peripheral joints in symmetrical fashion) associated with morning stiffness 
causing cartilage destruction and bone erosion leading to changes in joint integrity 
(Fig. 17.1). RA symptoms develop gradually. The onset, severity and specific symptoms 
of this condition can vary greatly from person to person. Symptoms may present 
continuously or resolve completely or there may be alternating periods of bothersome 
symptoms and complete resolution.

Early recognition and treatment improve the rate of clinical response and is important 
in achieving control of disease and prevention of joint injury and disability, particularly 
in patients with serious disease and/or poor prognostic factors. However, in patients 
with early disease, the joint manifestations are often difficult to distinguish from other 
forms of inflammatory polyarthritis. The more distinctive signs of RA, such as joint 
erosion, rheumatoid nodules and other extra-articular manifestations, are seen primarily 
in patients with long-standing, poorly controlled disease but are frequently absent on 
initial presentation. Most patients with moderately to severely active RA will require 
sustained therapy and adjustments in their treatment regimen over months to years to 
achieve treatment goals. Treatment must be individualized, based on physicians’ and 
patients’ preference, and medical contraindications.

l Encourage physical and occupational therapy for relieving pain, reducing 
inflammation and preserving joint structure and function. In acute pain, advise rest 
and splint.
	
l Improve general fitness and encourage regular exercises directed at maintaining 
muscle strength and joint flexibility without exacerbating joint inflammation.
	
l A variety of orthotics (splints, functional insoles and therapeutic footwear) and 
assistive devices (cane, walker) can be helpful in supporting and aligning deformed 
joints to reduce pain and improve function.
	
l A tailored hand exercise programme and care by podiatrist may be useful.

968    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Education and counselling play a crucial role in fostering an understanding of the 
nature of RA and in developing effective coping mechanisms for managing the 
challenges associated with this condition.
	
l There is no strong evidence supporting the efficacy of a specific diet or any 
complementary therapies for long-term benefits in managing this condition.
Pharmacological (Fig. 17.1)
Refer to a specialist (physician) at a higher centre. Begin disease-modifying antirheumatic 
drug (DMARD) early in the disease following the treat to target therapy approach:
	 1.	For DMARD-naive patients with established disease, first-line treatment with 
conventional DMARD (cDMARD) is monotherapy with oral MTX, Leflunomide 
or Sulfasalazine as soon as possible and ideally within 3 months of onset of 
persistent symptoms (Fig. 17.1). Prediction of response to a particular DMARD is 
not possible. It takes 4–6 weeks to show its effect.
	 2.	Hydroxychloroquine may be used as an alternative to oral MTX, Leflunomide or 
Sulfasalazine for mild palindromic disease.
	 3.	Escalate dose as tolerated. Consider short-term bridging treatment with 
glucocorticoids (oral, intramuscular or intra-articular) when starting a new 
cDMARD. 
	 4.	Add additional cDMARDs (oral MTX, Leflunomide, Sulfasalazine or 
Hydroxychloroquine) in combination as a step-up strategy when the treatment target 
(remission or low disease activity) has not been achieved despite dose escalation.
	 5.	Glucocorticoids (Prednisolone) can be used for a short period of time (bridging 
therapy) when a person is starting a new DMARD, intended to improve symptoms 
while waiting for the new DMARD to take effect (which can take 2–3 months).
	 6.	Consider oral NSAIDs (including traditional NSAIDs and COX II selective 
inhibitors) when control of pain or stiffness is inadequate considering the potential 
gastrointestinal, liver and cardio-renal toxicity and the person's risk factors, 
including age and pregnancy. 
	 7.	When treating symptoms of RA with oral NSAIDs, use the lowest effective dose 
for the shortest possible time and a PPI, and review risk factors for adverse events 
regularly.
	 8.	In acute inflammation, any of the NSAIDs as given in the section 'Osteoarthritis 
(OA) of the Knee' may be given except paracetamol. The anti-inflammatory action 
of the NSAIDs may take 2–4 weeks to become evident.
	 9.	Reduce NSAID dosages in the elderly and in patients with impaired renal function. 
Concomitant use of more than one NSAID only increases toxicity and has no 
additional benefit. Patients not responding to one NSAID may still show a good 
response to another.
	10.	Topical applications containing Salicylates, Capsaicin, Nicotinates, menthol, 
camphor and NSAIDs in various combinations may provide symptomatic relief.
	11.	Re-evaluate every 3–5 weeks for effectiveness of therapy (degree of improvement 
in the number and extent of actively inflamed joints) and side effects.

Doses of the DMARD are as follows:
Tab. MTX 7.5–15 mg is given every week as single dose. Concomitant folic acid 5 mg/
week as single dose 12 hours before or after MTX reduces side effects. (Caution: There 
may be nausea, mouth sores, liver damage, increases in incidence of chest infection,

GOUT
Gout is a disease related to deposition of uric acid, classically in the joints, soft tissues 
(termed tophi), or kidney interstitium and/or uric acid nephrolithiasis. The natural 
history of gout has three stages: asymptomatic hyperuricaemia, acute intermittent gout 
and chronic gouty arthritis. Ninety percent of gout occurs in men between the ages of 
30 and 50 years. It is uncommon in premenopausal women.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Presenting symptoms include sudden onset of severe pain, erythema, and swelling 
and disability of a single joint, usually MTP (metatarsophalangeal) joint of the 
great toe (podagra). Other common sites are the ankle, knee, shoulder and wrist. 
These symptoms may be accompanied by pruritus, fever and desquamation of 
the skin overlying the affected joint. 
	
l Acute attacks peak within the first 12 hours and last 5–7 days.
	
l It is precipitated by alcohol binges, dehydration, trauma, surgery and certain drugs. 
Risk factors include genetics, obesity, chronic kidney disease and hypertension.
	
l It can also occur as chronic gouty arthritis or chronic tophaceous gout with 
deposition of uric acid crystals in connective tissue as tophi (commonly at the 
great toe base, fingers, wrists, hands, olecranon bursa and Achilles tendon).
	
l Serum uric acid (>6 mg/dL), ESR, leucocyte count (may be ≥15,000/μL) and 
joint radiographs show punched-out joint erosions with overhanging edges (rat-
bite lesions). The diagnosis of gout is clinical, and X-rays are often not useful in 
making a diagnosis. Consider joint aspiration and microscopy of synovial fluid 
if a diagnosis of gout remains uncertain or unconfirmed.

Thorough history and physical examination and assessment of severity of attacks

l Weight control, healthy diet, hydration, exercise, and smoking and alcohol cessation, and 
avoiding high-protein diet, red meat, Niacin and Thiazides (if thiazide or loop diuretics 
are being used to treat hypertension, consider alternative antihypertensive agents)
	
l Joint rest and ice packs as adjuncts to therapy

Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia does not require treatment.
In an acute attack of gout, initiate therapy within 24 hours of onset. Continue ongoing 
pharmacotherapy without interruption, until the acute attack of gout completely resolves.

treat a gout flare unless NSAIDs, colchicine and corticosteroids are contraindicated, 
not tolerated or ineffective. Refer the person to a rheumatologist before prescribing 
an IL-1 inhibitor.

Chronic gout
In patients with recurrent gout (≥2 episodes per year), chronic gouty arthritis, tophi or 
radiographic changes of gout, delay starting urate-lowering therapy until 1–2 weeks 
after the signs of inflammation have resolved with the target to achieve a uric acid 
level <6 mg/dL. Allopurinol or Febuxostat is the first-line treatment taking into account 
the person's comorbidities and preferences. Avoid Febuxostat in major cardiovascular 
diseases (such as previous myocardial infarction or stroke, or unstable angina).
	 1.	Tab. Allopurinol 50–300 mg/day, starting with low dose, and titrating the dose 
upwards gradually every 2–5 weeks to achieve target serum uric acid level 
≤6 mg/dL; doses greater than 300 mg daily given in divided doses (maximum dose 
of 900 mg in severe disease); should start patients with chronic kidney disease 
(CKD) of stage 4 or higher at 50 mg/day or 100 mg alternate days (Caution: Rash 
is the most common adverse event. In case of Allopurinol toxicity, or intolerance 
in patients with normal renal function, give Tab. Sulphinpyrazone 200–800 mg/
day in divided doses. Good hydration is required, and it is not indicated in patients 
with a history of uric acid kidney stones.)
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Febuxostat 40 mg (equivalent to 300 mg/day of Allopurinol) to 80 mg/day (no 
dose reduction is required in CKD)
	 2.	Prophylactic therapy with low-dose colchicine or low-dose NSAIDs to prevent 
acute gout flares in patients on urate-lowering therapy, Tab. Colchicine 0.5 mg 
twice a day for 6–12 months after starting Allopurinol (Caution: In patients with 
renal impairment, adjust dosage and limit course to 6 months.)
Note: Although not all patients with elevated serum urate levels have gout symptoms or 
recurrent gout attacks; some patients with urate levels below the commonly identified 
threshold of 6 mg/dL may have symptoms. However, maintaining serum urate 
<6 mg/dL reduces acute gout attacks and subsequent joint damage.
Follow-up:
	
l If serum urate is <6 mg/dL and there have been no gout attacks for 1 year, reduce 
Allopurinol by 100 mg. Re-check serum urate 6 monthly and lower Allopurinol 
dose further if urate remains <6 mg/dL; however, indefinite urate-lowering therapy 
is required if there are two or more gout attacks, tophi or renal stones.
	
l Refer the patient to a rheumatologist if acute gout attack fails to resolve within 
14 days when treated as above, there are uncontrolled recurrent gout attacks despite 
use of Allopurinol 900 mg daily or Sulphinpyrazone, there are uncontrolled recurrent 
attacks when serum urate >6 mg/dL, and there is intolerance of Allopurinol and 
Sulphinpyrazone.
	
l Patients with urolithiasis should be assessed by a urologist.
Patient education
	
l Explain therapeutic objectives to patients. Tell them that both pharmacological and 
non-pharmacological treatment are needed to optimally treat gout.

976    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Patient education
	
l Back care is essentially a functional restoration programme whose goal is not pain 
relief but restoration of function. Activities of daily life and job may predispose to 
faulty back posture leading to injury to the back. 
	
l Plan back rehabilitation programme on an individual basis and educate patients 
about the structure and function of the back and that there may not be a cure for 
their condition, but they can learn skills such that they can lead a meaningful and 
enjoyable life.
	
l Lifestyle modifications:
Reduce weight in overweight patients.
Tobacco cessation: Tobacco is a risk factor for low back ache and disc degeneration.
No or limited alcohol intake: Alcohol abuse leads to reduced muscle strength and 
less ability to perceive tissue damage.
Exercise: Exercise is the keystone to treatment of low back pain. Adequate 
flexibility is believed to prevent excessive stress to the lower lumbar spine. Patients 
who are not physically fit may be more likely to have low back pain. Both flexor and 
extensor group muscles should be strengthened for optimum fitness.
	 Stress reduction, psychotherapy and cognitive restructuring
	
l Posture care: Poor posture leads to stress on spinal joints which leads to pain. 
Prevention encompasses all posture care in activities of daily life.
General: Whenever possible, sit down.
Do not reach.
Do not lift weights above the head.
Do not stoop.
Do not move furniture by pulling it in front of you.
Do not push windows up.
Do not get overtired.
Do not maintain any one position for a prolonged period.
Sleeping: The mattress should be firm. Sleep on your sides with your hip and knee 
bent. Do not sleep on your stomach. 
Sitting: Take care of the back while sitting by using a well-designed fully adjustable 
chair to provide plenty of support to the lower back. If the chair is uncomfortable, 
use a rolled-up towel or small pillow to support the back. When sitting for long 
periods, sit down with the knees higher than the hip. The best way to do this is to 
sit with the foot on a foot stool. While driving, sit as close to the steering wheel as 
possible, thereby flexing the hip and knees.
Getting up from sitting position: It is important not to arch the back on the act of 
getting up from sitting. Keep your back straight and use your hand for support, if 
necessary.
Standing: The best way to stand is like a barman’s posture. Always keep one foot 
on a raised surface. Never maintain a stooped forward position when standing.

Lifting: Never bend over to lift something off the ground with the knees straight. 
When lifting something off the floor, bend the hip and knee keeping the spine 
straight. Hold the object as near to the body as possible, and then get up keeping the 
spine straight. Never hold anything weighing more than 8 kg more than 2 feet from 
the body. Never lift anything weighing more than 9 kg above the shoulder level.
Household chores: Always avoid a stooped position.
	
l Refer to a higher centre in case of severe pain that disturbs sleep/is not responding 
to conservative treatment for more than 2 weeks/is associated with severe restriction 
of neck or back movements or sciatic pain or constitutional symptoms/displays 
neurological symptoms – bladder or bowel involvement with back pain.

An injury to a ligament(s), by sudden unnatural or excessive movement of a joint, is 
termed a sprain. Symptoms are pain, swelling and discoloration of the skin, especially 
bruising and impaired joint function.

no joint instability
	
l Moderate or grade II sprains: Pain, oedema, ecchymosis, joint tenderness with 
some loss of joint motion but no joint instability 
	
l Severe or grade III sprains: Gross instability of the joint with complete tearing of 
all fibres, marked swelling and severe pain

l Check sensation and circulation distal to the injury. Obtain X-rays of the involved 
region to rule out a fracture. Stress X-rays may show abnormal opening of the joint 
in a grade III sprain.
	
l RICE therapy consists of a combination of rest, ice, compression and elevation.
	
l After initial treatment, various methods to treat sprain can be classified into three 
main groups:
	– Conservative or conventional, which includes immobilization with cast/splint

ANKLE SPRAIN
Epidemiological data have shown that 80% of individuals will suffer an ankle sprain 
during their lifetime. There are three types of ankle sprain patterns, namely, lateral, 
syndesmotic and medial. Ankle sprains involve the lateral ligament group (85%), 
because it is less resistant to load, so it is easier to injure compared with the others 
ligament groups. The lateral ankle ligament comprises the anterior talofibular ligament 
(ATFL), the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) and the posterior talofibular ligament 
(PTFL). The ATFL is the most vulnerable, and its damage results in anteroposterior 
instability, while CFL involvement leads to inversion instability.

l Acute injuries should be immediately treated within the initial 48–72 hours and the 
most used treatment protocol is the RICE regimen (rest, ice, compression, elevation). 
	
l NSAIDs and paracetamol are equivalent in reducing pain at a 3-day follow-up. There 
is no statistically significant differences in pain relief between NSAIDs and opioids.
	
l After the initial treatment, various methods to treat sprain can be classified into three 
main groups: 
	 1.	 Conservative or conventional, which includes immobilization with cast/splint 
or other types of external support, which allow at most partial joint mobility,

980    Standard Treatment Guidelines
combined with standard non-supervised exercises, application of ice and partial 
weight-bearing.
	 2.	 Functional, which is a combination of an external device that supports the ankle 
with a rehabilitation programme that includes early joint mobilization with 
external supports like tapes, elastic bandages and braces in order to protect the 
joint from the risk of re-injury, as well as coordination training
	 3.	 Surgical treatment: The surgical treatment of an acute ankle sprain typically 
involves the primary repair of torn ligaments through suturing. Surgery is 
recommended only in cases where patients exhibit persistent symptoms, such as 
chronic ankle joint instability, and do not respond to other forms of treatment.
Note: Compared with conventional immobilization, early functional treatment allows 
earlier return to sport and to work, while there is no substantial difference concerning 
instability and re-injury rate. Functional treatment has better results considering time 
to return to pre-injury activities, swelling reduction, joint stiffness and subjective and 
objective joint instability without any differences for recurrence or pain. Use of braces 
during the functional treatment has better objective functional outcome scores.
Rehabilitation: Restoring ankle dorsiflexion and preventing joint stiffness are crucial 
objectives in rehabilitation programmes, as the reduction in range of motion poses 
a risk for recurring sprains and persistent joint instability. Various interventions and 
rehabilitation programmes are suggested, encompassing proprioceptive training, 
coordination exercises, strength training, functional workouts and manual mobilization.
	
l Motor control is pivotal in walking and maintaining posture; however, after an ankle 
sprain, lower limb muscle activation patterns may become disrupted. Therefore, 
neuromuscular training, especially utilizing the wobble balance board during the 
subacute phase, can enhance proprioception and help prevent re-injury.
Patient education
	
l Do not massage the area and also no hot fomentation in acute stage; it will increase 
the swelling. Avoid application of lime (chuna) on local area.
	
l Give rest to the injured area until the pain subsides (usually 7–10 days for mild 
sprains and 3–5 weeks for severe sprains).
	
l Avoid activities that cause pain or swelling.
	
l Practice moderation in physical activities.
	
l If the pain and swelling decreases within 48 hours after a sprain, move the affected 
joint in all directions.
	
l Avoid high-heeled shoes (for ankle sprains).

OSTEOPOROSIS
Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disorder characterized by low bone mass, 
micro-architectural defect in bone and increased risk of fracture. WHO has defined 
osteoporosis as bone marrow density ≥2.5 standard deviation or more below the 
young normal mean by Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA/DEXA) scan. Risk 
factors for osteoporosis are female sex, age >60 years, family history of osteoporosis, 
Caucasian origin, early menopause, low BMI, smoking, sedentary lifestyle and long-
term (≥3 months) corticosteroid use. It is important to consider secondary causes of 
osteoporosis including drugs.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l It is an asymptomatic disease, and it is characterized by increased fractures at 
the hip, vertebrae, distal radius, proximal humerus and pelvis. Loss of height 
and kyphosis in elderly is one of the clinical manifestations of asymptomatic 
osteoporosis.
	
l Fracture is the real-time clinical manifestation of osteoporosis; it increases 
dramatically with ageing and is more frequent in women than in men.
	
l Conventional radiographs should not be used for the diagnosis or exclusion of 
osteoporosis. Refer for DEXA/DXA scan when plain films are interpreted as 
severe osteopenia. Bone mineral density (BMD) should be measured by DEXA 
scan performed on two sites, preferably anteroposterior spine and hip.
	
l Biochemical markers of bone turnover have no role in the diagnosis or in 
the selection of patients for BMD measurement. The T-score of DEXA scan 
compares the BMD with that of a 30-year old adult of the same gender. A T-score 
that is ≤2.5 is diagnostic, a T-score between –1.0 and –2.5 is osteopenia, and a 
T-score of –1.0 or higher is normal.
	
l Low risk includes no history of hip or spine fracture, a BMD T-score at both the 
hip and the spine above –1.0, and a 10-year probability of a hip fracture <3% or 
a 10-year probability of a major osteoporosis-related fracture <20%. 
	
l Moderate risk includes no history of hip or spine fracture, a BMD T-score at both 
the hip and the spine above –2.5, and a 10-year probability of a hip fracture <3% 
or a 10-year probability of a major osteoporosis-related fracture <20%.

982    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l High risk includes a history of hip or spine fracture, a BMD T-score at both 
the hip and the spine ≤2.5 and, a 10-year probability of a hip fracture >3% or a 
10-year probability of a major osteoporosis-related fracture >20%.
	
l Very high risk includes multiple spine fractures and a BMD T-score at both the 
hip and the spine ≤2.5. 
	
l Fracture risk is expressed as absolute risk (IOF [International Osteoporosis 
Foundation], WHO); FRAX tool computes the 10-year probability of a major 
osteoporotic fracture.
	
l For assessment of fracture risk in post-menopausal women and men older than 
50 years:
	– A FRAX assessment is required in those with clinical risk factors for fragility 
fracture.
	– BMD should be measured in those with intermediate fracture risk by FRAX to 
refine 10-year risk, and in high and very high fracture risk by FRAX to guide 
the drug choice and provide baseline for BMD monitoring.

The goals of treatment are:
	
l Reduction in the incidence of fractures
	
l Alleviation of fracture-related morbidity
	
l Prevention of subsequent fractures

1.	Adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D intake or supplements and balanced diet, 
especially in post-menopausal women, and DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop 
Hypertension) diet to control hypertension
	 2.	Regular weight bearing and balance exercises
	 3.	Fall prevention by use of assistive devices like walking sticks or walker, and use of 
proper fitting shoes, handrails, non-slippery mats in washroom, hip pads to dampen 
the impact of fall and proper electrical lighting
	 4.	Avoidance of smoking and excessive alcohol and caffeine

The approach to treatment is as follows:
	 1.	Bisphosphonates reduce the risk of fractures in post-menopausal females diagnosed 
with primary osteoporosis.
	 2.	In patients who experience adverse effects with or contraindications to 
bisphosphonates, Denosumab (RANK ligand inhibitor) is recommended only as a 
second-line treatment. (Caution: Denosumab's anti-resorptive effects are reversible 
on stopping, leading to a temporary spike in bone turnover. This is linked to bone 
loss and an elevated risk of multiple vertebral fractures, raising concerns.)
	
	On discontinuation of Denosumab, add bisphosphonate like Zoledronate or 
alternative therapy.

	 4.	Treatment with teriparatide should always be followed by anti-resorptive agents to 
prevent bone density decline and loss of fracture efficacy. 
	 5.	Individualize the decision to initiate bisphosphonate, based on individual factors 
for females older than 65 years with low bone mass (osteopenia), aiming to reduce

osteoporosis and where bisphosphonates are not suitable (kidney, liver derangement), 
give Inj. Teriparatide (recombinant human PTH 1–34) 20 mcg subcutaneously 
daily injections for 18–24 months. After completion of the course, continue with 
anti-resorptive osteoporosis therapies as above.
(Caution: Side effects are leg cramps, dizziness and potential osteosarcoma.)
Or
In case of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis in men and women at high risk of fracture 
or those who have failed or are intolerant to other available osteoporosis therapy, give 
Inj. Denosumab, pre-filled 1-mL (60 mg) syringe subcutaneously once in every 6 months 
or give Romosozumab. (Caution: It lowers calcium; hence, supplement with daily 
calcium and vitamin D; it is avoided in immunosuppressed patients and contraindicated 
in pregnancy.) The effect of the drug lasts up to 6 months and usually another dose 
would be required for at least a year after completion of treatment with Denosumab as 
bone mineral density (BMD) returns to pre-treatment levels within 18 months. 
For pain of osteoporotic fracture in both the acute and the chronic phase, conventional 
analgesics should be used regularly rather than on demand (see the section 
‘Osteoarthritis [OA] of the knee’).
Note: Following the treatment with Teriparatide or Romosozumab (24 or 12 months, 
respectively), initiate treatment with Alendronate, Zoledronate or Denosumab 
without delay. Raloxifene may be considered as an option for follow-on treatment 
after an anabolic drug in women. When other anti-resorptive and anabolic treatments 
are contraindicated or not tolerated, Strontium ranelate can be used to treat post-
menopausal women with osteoporosis and men with severe osteoporosis, considering 
the risk–benefit in relation to cardiovascular and thromboembolic events. Initiation by 
a specialist is advised.
Monitoring and duration of therapy
	
l Perform comprehensive risk assessment after the initial 3–5 years’ treatment period 
on bisphosphonates and address them accordingly.
	
l Assess compliance regularly and at least annually.
	
l For post-menopausal women with a high risk of fracture, prioritize bisphosphonates 
as the initial therapeutic option. 
	
l Regularly reassess fracture risk after 3–5 years of bisphosphonate treatment.
	
l Following reassessment, recommend a ‘bisphosphonate holiday’ for women with 
low-to-moderate fracture risk who are currently on bisphosphonates.
	
l Consider anabolic therapy (such as teriparatide) for women with a very high risk of 
fractures, including those with multiple fractures. 
	
l Ensure that all women receiving osteoporosis therapies, excluding anabolic therapy, 
incorporate calcium and vitamin D into their diet or through supplements.

Chapter 17  Bone and Joint Diseases    985
	
l Monitor BMD in high-risk individuals with low BMD every 1–3 years. Repeat 
vertebral imaging if there is documented height loss, new back pain, postural change 
or suspicious finding on chest X-ray following the last (or first) vertebral imaging 
test. 
	
l In high-risk patients on bisphosphonates, review treatment including renal function 
evaluation every 5 years.
Patient education
	
l Emphasize on prevention of osteoporosis with lifestyle changes, adequate dietary 
intake of calcium and regular exercise. Based on the initial condition of the patient, 
provide a complete exercise recommendation that includes weight-bearing aerobic 
activities for the skeleton, postural training, progressive resistance training for muscle 
and bone strengthening, stretching for tight soft tissues and joints and balance training.
	
l Perform early identification of symptoms of one or more fractured vertebrae – 
loss of height, persistent back pain and a stooping (bent forward) posture. People 
older than 50 years are at the greatest risk of developing osteoporosis and having 
related fractures. Accurate height measurement yearly is a critical determinant of 
osteoporosis treatment efficacy.
	
l Explain measures to help prevent from falling and breaking a bone and check home 
for hazards such as uneven rugs, trailing wires and slippery floors. Remove loose 
wires; use non-skid mats; install handrails in bathrooms, halls and long stairways; 
and light hallways, stairwells and entrances. Encourage patients who are predisposed 
to falling to wear sturdy, low-heeled shoes and hip protectors; keep all items within 
reach and avoid using step stools.
	
l Avoid long-term immobilization and recommend partial bed rest (with periodic 
sitting and ambulating) only when required and for the shortest periods possible. 
	
l Advise patients to avoid forward bending and exercising with the trunk in flexion, 
especially in combination with twisting.
	
l If treatment is started, repeat DEXA scanning on a regular basis may be suggested 
to look at how effective the treatment is.

986    Standard Treatment Guidelines
ACUTE PYOGENIC OSTEOMYELITIS
Acute osteomyelitis is an acute infection of the bone commonly seen in children 
younger than 10 years. It is rare in adults unless they are immunocompromised or 
taking steroids.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Presenting features include pain over the limb (localized pain), fever, swelling 
and inability to use the limb. Tenderness over the metaphyseal area of the bone, 
local rise of temperature and restriction of range of movement of the adjacent 
joints are seen. TLC, ESR and CRP are raised. Blood culture is positive for 
pyogenic organisms.
	
l Diagnosis is considered if any of the following two criteria are present: classic 
symptoms of localized pain, fever (with or without chills and rigours), swelling 
in the metaphyseal area, warmth and limited range of motion of the adjacent 
joint; pus aspirated from the bone; positive bone or blood culture for pyogenic 
organisms; and radiographic changes typical of acute osteomyelitis (soft-tissue 
swelling, periosteal reaction, lytic areas in the metaphysis).

Approach to diagnosis and management
	
l Imaging may not always be necessary for diagnosis confirmation, as X-ray changes 
typically manifest 7–10 days post illness onset. However, if a child's response to 
medical treatment is inadequate within 24–48 hours, or if signs suggest potential 
surgical intervention, MRI may be utilized to precisely assess infection location 
or explore alternative diagnoses like malignancy. In cases of suspected Acute 
Hematogenous Osteomyelitis (AHO) with accompanying joint effusion or concerns 
of infection spread, ultrasound can aid in diagnostic clarification for further action.
	
l Invasive diagnostic procedures should be considered to obtain aspirates and/
or biopsy specimens from bone or purulent fluid collections for microbiological 
analysis, including aerobic bacterial culture and Gram staining.
	
l Prior to administering antimicrobial therapy, draw blood cultures and surgical 
samples to ascertain the microbiological diagnosis for optimal selection of 
antimicrobial agents in terms of choice of antibiotic and duration of therapy. In 
instances where there is a delay in invasive diagnostics but patients exhibit severe 
symptoms or rapidly progressing infections, immediate empirical antimicrobial 
therapy should commence. Ideally, surgical samples should be obtained within 
24–48 hours post initiation of antibiotic treatment.
	
l Choose empirical antimicrobial therapy targeting community-acquired methicillin-
resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA), guided by local susceptibility 
data and patient history, particularly regarding prior CA-MRSA infections and 
colonization. In certain scenarios, additional empirical antimicrobial coverage may

Chapter 17  Bone and Joint Diseases    987
be necessary for pathogens other than S. aureus, such as Kingella kingae in younger 
patients or those with underlying haemoglobinopathies at higher risk for Salmonella 
spp. infection.
	
l In cases of a child presenting with sepsis or exhibiting rapidly progressive 
infection, or in clinically stable children with substantial abscesses (>2 cm), prompt 
debridement of infected bone and associated abscesses is advised upon diagnosis, 
rather than relying solely on medical therapy. If aspiration yields pus from bone 
or acute osteomyelitis is suspected in adults, patients with diabetes, children 
on hemodialysis, intravenous drug users, children with orthopedic implants, or 
immunocompromised hosts, referral to an orthopedic surgeon is recommended.
	
l For children requiring surgical intervention, routine use of surgical-site antimicrobial 
agents (instilled or implanted) is not recommended.
	
l When dealing with confirmed AHO, selecting a definitive antibiotic regimen should 
prioritize effectiveness against the identified pathogen or most likely pathogen, while 
aiming for the narrowest spectrum, lowest adverse effects and best host tolerance. 
Treatment response should be assessed through sequential monitoring of CRP levels 
and serial clinical evaluations, including assessment of febrile response, pain and 
musculoskeletal function.
	
l Children responding well to initial intravenous antibiotic therapy can be transitioned 
to an oral antibiotic regimen if feasible and well tolerated. If oral therapy is not 
suitable, outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy (OPAT) can be considered 
to shorten hospital stays, with the selection of OPAT setting dependent on local 
resource availability. The optimal duration of therapy typically spans 3–4 weeks 
for uncomplicated courses of AHO caused by methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus 
aureus (MSSA), although longer durations may be necessary for cases involving 
MRSA, other pathogens, or complicated courses.
	
l End-of-therapy imaging studies like plain X-rays or MRI are generally unnecessary 
for uncomplicated AHO cases but are recommended for children with complicated 
AHO or involvement of the growth plate (physis).
	
l In instances of primary treatment failure or early or late recurrence of AHO, 
reassessment of the antimicrobial regimen's adequacy (spectrum, dosage, penetration 
to infection site and adherence) and consideration of surgical intervention for 
therapeutic or diagnostic purposes are warranted before broadening the antimicrobial 
spectrum or restarting therapy. Additionally, reassessment of the AHO diagnosis may 
be necessary, especially in culture-negative cases.
	
l Children identified as at risk for long-term adverse outcomes in AHO should 
undergo specialist follow-up for at least 1 year.

l Advise rest, splintage to the part (plaster slab/ traction), elevation of the limb and 
sponging for fever.
	
l If aspiration is positive for pus, drain the pus (must be performed by an orthopaedic 
surgeon) and send for culture and sensitivity.

988    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Other indications for surgical interventions include drainage of subperiosteal or soft-
tissue abscesses, contiguous foci of infection, excision of sequestra (i.e. devitalized 
bone) and failure to improve after 48–72 hours of antimicrobial therapy.
	
l Postoperative duration of splintage depends on the extent of damage to the bone. The 
usual duration is 4–6 weeks. Gradually mobilize the limb and permit gradual weight 
bearing thereafter. In case of extensive destruction, bone might require support for 
a few months.

Immediately start with intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics with or without 
surgical decompression depending on the most likely organism present after drawing 
sample for culture and sensitivity. The commonest bacterial pathogen is S. aureus 
(40–80% of cases). Change antibiotic depending on culture report or response to 
therapy.
	 1.	Inj. Cloxacillin 50–100 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses
	 2.	Inj. Gentamicin 5–7.5 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses or Inj. Amikacin 15 mg/kg/
day in 2–3 divided doses, if resistant to Pseudomonas aeruginosa
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 1–2 weeks (maximum dose 
2 g/day)
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Cefotaxime 100–200 mg/kg/day by IV infusion or IM or IV in 2–4 divided 
doses
	
	Or
	
	If the patient is hypersensitive to Penicillins and Cephalosporins: Inj. Clindamycin 
40 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses
	
	Or
	
	If MRSA suspected, Inj. Vancomycin by IV infusion 500 mg over at least 
60 minutes every 6 hours or 1 g over at least 100 minutes every 12 hours; neonates 
up to 1 week, 15 mg/kg initially, and then 10 mg/kg every 12 hours; infants 
1–4 weeks, 15 mg/kg initially, and then 10 mg/kg every 8 hours; children older 
than 1 month, 10 mg/kg every 6 hours
	
	Continue intravenous administration of antibiotics till favourable clinical response is 
achieved (1–2 weeks), and then switch to oral antibiotics. The choice of oral antibiotic 
largely depends on culture and sensitivity report. The total duration of antibiotic(s) 
administration ranges at least 3–4 weeks of intravenous/oral antibiotics.
	 3.	Oral/Inj. Paracetamol for fever (see section on Fever in Chapter 1)
Patient education
	
l Antibiotic therapy may be required for a few weeks depending on the response.
	
l Plaster (or any other splintage) might be required for prolonged periods.
	
l Do not make the child walk (in case of lower limb bone involvement) unless 
permitted.

ACUTE SEPTIC ARTHRITIS
Acute septic arthritis is inflammation of a joint caused by pyogenic microorganisms, 
usually seen in children younger than 10 years. Septic arthritis is usually 
monomicrobial. The key to early diagnosis and favourable outcome remains a high 
index of suspicion since delay in diagnosis leads to permanent damage to the joint. Hip 
and knee joints are the commonest joints to be affected.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occur inability to move the affected joint, refusal to walk or limp, hip pain 
referred to the knee, acute local signs of inflammation (warm and painful joint 
with effusion) and clinical signs of sepsis (fever, malaise); however, more than 
two-thirds of infants with septic arthritis are afebrile. 
	
l Neonates present with pseudoparalysis of extremities, discomfort while changing 
the diaper and unhappy or out of sorts but rarely appear to be ill or moribund. 
	
l Ultrasound examination of the suspected septic hip joint greatly aids in diagnosis.

Refer the patient immediately to an orthopaedic surgeon. Treatment of septic arthritis 
is shown in Figure 17.2. (Also see the section ‘Acute Pyogenic Arthritis.’)
Non-pharmacological and surgical
	
l Keep the joint in a position of comfort.
	
l Collect synovial fluid and blood cultures prior to administration of antibiotics. If 
synovial fluid cannot be obtained with closed needle aspiration, the joint should be 
aspirated under radiographic guidance. Certain joints (such as the hip or sacroiliac 
joint) may require surgical arthrotomy for aspiration.
	
l Before commencing antibiotic treatment for suspected septic arthritis, send synovial 
fluid for Gram stain, bacterial culture (in a sterile tube, ideally with an EDTA or 
blood culture bottle) and white blood cell counts with differential and assessment for 
crystals (monosodium urate and calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition crystals).
	
l If aspirate is purulent, perform drainage of the joint on an emergency basis (needle 
aspiration, arthroscopic drainage or arthrotomy).

990    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Drain the joint even if the joint aspiration is doubtful in the presence of a strong 
clinical suspicion because the risks of negative arthrotomy are far too less than not 
draining an infected joint having pus. The latter situation may be disastrous for the 
joint resulting in lifelong permanent disability for the patient. Patients with severe 
infection may require repeated aspirations or arthroscopic irrigations. 
	
l After drainage, splint the joint with a POP slab or skin traction to relieve pain and 
prevent contractures till the patient is afebrile and pain free and the joint is clinically

1.	The initial empirical antibiotic therapy coverage should include S. aureus and 
Streptococcus species. The choice of antibiotics, duration of the therapy and 
monitoring of the therapy are the same as mentioned in the section on acute 
pyogenic osteomyelitis as above.
	 2.	Oral antibiotics demonstrate comparable efficacy to intravenous antibiotics in the 
treatment of septic arthritis.
	 3.	Septic arthritis caused by MRSA requires drainage or debridement, along with 
14 days of intravenous antibiotics followed by oral antibiotics, completing a 3- to

	Note: Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended for preventing joint infection 
in patients with joint replacements undergoing routine outpatient dental, urological 
or gastrointestinal procedures.
