condition: Medical Care of the Surgical Patient
text:
C h a p t e r   18
Surgery
MEDICAL CARE OF THE SURGICAL PATIENT
Preoperative assessment of the patient 
For achieving the desired optimum results in a surgical patient, apart from evaluating 
the nature and extent of the diseases and choice of surgery from available options, the 
assessment of the patient for his/her ability to withstand the stress of surgery and anaesthesia 
is very important. The factors that must be considered in preoperative assessment are: 
	
l The disease (and its extent) for which the surgery is planned
	
l The condition of the patient and his/her organ systems
	
l The relative urgency of the surgery
	
l The type of surgery and its alternatives
	
l The relative morbidity and mortality of the disease
	
l The relative morbidity and mortality of the surgical procedure
All these factors are interdependent and this assessment is the most fundamental 
task to be performed in a surgical patient. The best person to undertake this task is 
the surgeon himself/herself. Surgeon may, at times, need the help of a physician, 
cardiologist or anaesthetist to take the right decision. The preoperative assessment 
should also include discussion on drugs being taken by the patient and documentation 
of known allergies. 
Informed consent
Informed consent should be taken in the language understood by the patient after a 
detailed discussion by the surgeon (or his/her responsible assistant) with the patient 
and his/her close relatives informing them about the nature of the procedure planned, 
benefits expected, risks involved and possible alternatives, giving full opportunity to 
them to ask questions and clear doubts. If there is a need to change the procedure while 
surgery is underway, a member of the surgical team should take revised consent after 
explaining the need to change procedure and document it.
Preoperative preparation
	
l Routine investigations: haemoglobin, total leucocyte count, differential leucocyte 
count, coagulation profile, urine routine examination and, in patients older than 
30 years, chest X-ray and ECG.

condition: Medical Care of the Surgical Patient
text:
Chapter 18  Surgery    993
	
l Special and specific investigations depending on the nature of the procedure planned 
and the physical condition of the patient for evaluating fitness for surgery. 
	
l Lipstick, nail polish and other cosmetics, which may mask cyanosis and interfere 
with pulse oximetry, should be removed. 
	
l Dentures, spectacles, contact lenses, artificial limbs, artificial eyes, hearing aid and 
jewelery, cash and mobile phones should be removed before shifting the patient to 
the operation theatre. 
	
l Withhold feeds before surgery depending on the age of the patient and nature of 
anaesthesia and surgery planned. 
	
l Bathing – if possible, the patient should take a proper bath with soap or antiseptic 
agent on the day prior to and on the morning of surgery giving special attention to 
the operative area. He/she should wear only clean hospital clothing.
	
l Perioperative glycaemic control with target glucose level <200 mg/dL in patients 
with or without diabetes should be achieved.
	
l Surgical site should be marked. In patients undergoing any surgical procedure, hair 
either should NOT be removed or, if absolutely necessary, should be removed only 
with a clipper. Shaving is strongly discouraged at all times, whether preoperatively or 
in the operating room. It results in damage to the skin and leads to abrasions that may 
not be visible. If the skin is to be shaved, it is best done immediately before surgery. 
	
l Elicit history of allergic reactions to any chemical solutions.
	
l While scrubbing, one should work away from the operative site. Visibly soiled skin 
should be washed with soap and water before using surgical scrub.
	
l Surgical safety checklist should be filled in by the surgeon, anaesthesiologist and 
nursing personnel.
	
l Preoperative prophylaxis should be given as per Institutional antibiotic policy.
	
l Administer pre-anaesthesia medication as per policy. Normothermia should be 
maintained. Warming devices should be used in the operating room and during the 
surgical procedure for warming of the patient’s body with the purpose of reducing 
surgical site infection (SSI).
Skin preparation for surgery 
Preoperative surgical antisepsis aims at blocking infection into surgical wound and 
consists of hand washing and gloving along with application of antiseptic to the surgical 
site.
Alcohol (70% ethyl or isopropyl alcohol): Alcohol-based antiseptic solutions based on 
chlorhexidine gluconate for surgical site skin preparation should be used in patients 
undergoing surgical procedures. Alcohol is 95% effective against Gram-negative and 
Gram-positive bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi and viruses. It is not completely effective 
against spores. All traces of alcohol should be dry before drapes are put. Alcohol is 
never used on mucous membranes and open wounds as it may cause desiccation.
Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis (SAP): It should be administered 60–120 minutes 
before surgical incision depending on the half-life of the antibiotic used. (For details, 
see ‘Perisurgical Antibiotic Prophylaxis’ in the following text.)

condition: Medical Care of the Surgical Patient
text:
994    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Drug treatment: Examples include antihypertensives, IV fluids, anticoagulants and 
vitamin K, where relevant.
Non-drug treatment: Examples include rectal washouts, vaginal douches and stomach 
wash, where relevant.
Handling of medicolegal cases
First aid has to be provided in all cases who report in an emergency state. After 
stabilizing the patient, he/she should be properly guided and helped in shifting to the 
appropriate centre.
In case that we decide to treat, we must:
	
l Send an information, in duplicate, to the police. 
	
l Prepare a medicolegal report. 
	
l Preserve and seal clothes, etc.
	
l Preserve fluid and stain samples where indicated. 
	
l Respond to information sought by the police. 
	
l Arrange to take dying declaration, where indicated. 
	
l Preserve all X-rays and patient records. 
	
l Respond to court summons. 
	
l In case of death, hand over the body to the police. 
	
l In case of discharge/referral, need to inform the police.
Care during transfer
This would depend on a number of factors like nature, the patient’s condition, reasons 
for referral, readiness of the referral centre to accept the patient and whether the transfer 
is an emergency or elective.
Emergency transfer
	
l Identify the degree of emergency. 
	
l Adopt resuscitative measures in serious patients with management of shock, oxygen, 
etc. 
	
l Transfer in a well-equipped ambulance to a referral centre with prior intimation and 
confirmation of the readiness at the referral centre (see relevant section for specific 
care during transport in Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in Chapter 2).
	
l Doctor or paramedical staff should accompany the sick patient if required.
Referral slip
It should contain information on:
	
l Condition of the patient when first seen
	
l Diagnosis and resuscitative measures taken
	
l Reasons for referral
	
l Where referred
	
l Precautions advised during transportation
	
l Any other information (e.g. any staff or equipment sent along with any 
communication given to the referral centre or specialist concerned)

Chapter 18  Surgery    995
References
	 1.	 Preoperative care including the high-risk surgical patient. In: O’Connell PR, McCaskie A, Sayers 
RD (eds), Baileys & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery. 28th ed. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, 
Taylor & Francis Group; 2023, pp. 285–298.
	 2.	 Bashaw MA, Keister KJ. Perioperative strategies for surgical site infection prevention. AORN 
J. 2019;109(1):68–78.
	 3.	 Preoperative and postoperative management. In: Zinner MJ, Ashley SW, Hines OJ (eds), 
Maingot’s Abdominal Operations. 13th ed. New York: McGraw Hill Medical; 2018, pp. 8–121.
POSTOPERATIVE CARE
Postoperative pain relief
Postoperative pain is associated with all surgical procedures. This varies according 
to the surgical procedure. Severe pain can prolong gastrointestinal ileus and urinary 
retention, impair respiratory movements producing atelectasis and predispose to deep 
vein thrombosis due to immobilization.
Various methods to alleviate postoperative pain are NSAIDs, opioids (intramuscular, 
transdermal or transmucosal), patient-controlled analgesia, local infiltration of anaes­
thetic drugs, epidural analgesia and intrapleural analgesia. The method used depends 
on the site and the magnitude of surgery done, severity of pain, whether the patient is 
allowed orally, and facilities and expertise available. It is necessary to give analgesics 
by intramuscular or intravenous route in the immediate postoperative period and till 
the patient is able to accept orally.
Commonly used agents are:
Inj. Diclofenac sodium 75 mg 6–8 hourly
Or
Inj. Pentazocine (30 mg/mL) 30–60 mg IM/IV repeated 3–4 hourly
Or
Inj. Tramadol (50 mg/mL) IM/IV 4–6 hourly
Or
Inj. Morphine (15 mg/mL) 10–15 mg, can be repeated 4–6 times
In tertiary care centres, epidural analgesia, intravenous patient-controlled analgesia 
and intrapleural analgesia can be used under expert care. When the patient is able to 
accept orally:
Tab. Paracetamol 500 mg 3–4 times a day
Or
Tab. Ibuprofen 400–600 mg 8 hourly
Postoperative nausea and vomiting
Postoperative nausea and vomiting lead to significant morbidity and prolonged 
hospitalization. They have an incidence of 20–30% after abdominal surgery. Predisposing 
factors are diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, gastro-
oesophageal reflux, emergency surgery and use of certain anaesthetic drugs and opioids.

Bowel obstruction (mechanical or paralytic ileus) should be ruled out as a cause of 
vomiting by proper examination and investigations, if it is associated with abdominal 
distension and fever and occurs beyond the third postoperative day.
Nausea and vomiting are managed with bed rest, intravenous fluids, analgesics to 
relieve postoperative pain and nasogastric decompression.

Inj. Metoclopramide (5 mg/mL) 10 mg IM/IV 1–3 times daily or as and when needed
Or
Inj. Ondansetron (2 mg/mL) 4–8 mg slow IV or IM
In children: 100 mcg/kg (maximum 4 mg/day) by slow IV or IM
Or
Inj. Promethazine (25 mg/mL) 2 mL IV as and when needed

Common causes and treatment according to time period include: 
Within 48 hours (inflammatory response to surgical trauma, drug reactions and 
transfusion reactions): Usually, no laboratory investigations are required. Fever 
is managed with cold sponging and antipyretics such as Paracetamol (injectable/
oral forms). Fulminant infection of surgical wound with group A Streptococcus and 
Clostridium perfringens can give rise to fever in this period, so the wound should be 
evaluated for signs of infection.
Days 2–5: Patients with thoracic and upper abdominal surgeries are more prone to 
develop basal atelectasis. Perform chest physiotherapy under supervision to facilitate 
expectoration of sputum and give Paracetamol. Investigate with a chest radiograph in 
case of failure of improvement with chest physiotherapy and antipyretics.
Days 3–5: Evaluate the wound for signs of surgical site infection (SSI) (redness, 
induration, tenderness and purulent discharge) to identify the cause of fever. If signs 
of infection are evident, open one or more sutures and drain out the infected material. 
Send wound discharge for culture of pathogenic organisms. Frequent daily evaluation 
of the wound is necessary to monitor response to treatment. Empirical broad-spectrum 
antibiotic coverage may be provided till the culture report is available.
Day 5: All indwelling catheters (central line, Foley catheter, IV cannula, nasogastric 
tube) should be taken out unless demanded by the patient’s condition. If the presence of 
catheter is essential, then it should be replaced with a new one and the site of placement 
may be changed particularly in case of IV catheters. In case of urinary catheters, clean 
the preputial skin and the external urinary meatus daily with soap and water. Send blood 
and urine culture as and when necessary and choose antibiotics accordingly. Manage 
chest infection with chest physiotherapy, steam inhalation and suitable antibiotics. If 
chest X-ray demonstrates the presence of pleural effusion in a patient having respiratory 
difficulty, then thoracocentesis may be attempted.

Postoperative pneumonia
Pulmonary disorders remain the most frequent postoperative problem and 10–15% of 
patients are considered to have clinically significant chest complication after surgery 
under general anaesthesia.
Factors predisposing to increased chest complications are smoking, obesity, 
chronic restrictive and obstructive lung disease, prolonged general anaesthesia and 
presence of nasogastric tube. Postoperative pneumonia is caused by pathogens such as 
Pseudomonas, Serratia, Klebsiella, Proteus and Streptococcus.

998    Standard Treatment Guidelines
PERISURGICAL ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS
SSIs are the most common health care–associated infections (HAI)/nosocomial infections in 
surgical patients accounting for prolonged hospital stay, mortality and increased cost of care.
Prophylaxis is the measure taken to prevent an infection and can be characterized 
as primary prophylaxis (prevention of an initial infection), secondary prophylaxis 
(prevention of recurrence or reactivation of a pre-existing infection) or eradication 
(elimination of a colonized organism to prevent the development of an infection). 
Primary perioperative prophylaxis consists of a mainly antimicrobial prophylaxis 
that may be beneficial in surgical procedures associated with a high rate of infection 
(i.e. clean-contaminated or contaminated procedures) and in certain clean procedures 
in which there are severe consequences of infection (e.g. prosthetic implants) even if 
infection is unlikely (Table 18.1).
Note: SAP is an adjunct to, not a substitute for, a good surgical technique. Antibiotic 
prophylaxis is one component of an effective policy for the control of hospital-acquired 
infection which includes attention to basic infection control strategies, the surgical 
technique, the duration of the procedure, hospital and operating room environments, 
instrument sterilization issues, preoperative preparation (e.g. surgical scrub, skin 
antisepsis, appropriate hair removal), perioperative management (normothermia and 
glycaemic control) and the underlying medical condition of the patient.

Development of local guidelines
Local guidelines serve as a framework for local development or modification after 
discussion with clinicians and management. These guidelines should be developed 
in conjunction with the Drugs and Therapeutics, and Antibiotic and Protocol 
Development Committees. Responsibility for prophylaxis in each unit should be 
clearly assigned. Guideline implementation should be supported by a programme of 
continuing education.
Choice of antibiotic
Antibiotic selection is based on the organism most commonly causing wound infection 
in the specific procedure, pharmacological characteristics (Pk/Pd) of the ideal agent, the 
safety profile and the patient’s medication allergies, and cost of the antibiotic agent. In 
certain gastrointestinal procedures, oral and intravenous administration of agents with 
activity against Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria as well as mechanical preparation 
of the bowel is warranted. 
Antimicrobial agents with the narrowest spectrum of activity are required 
for efficacy in preventing infection and the chosen antibiotics must reflect local, 
disease-specific information about the common pathogens and their antimicrobial 
susceptibility. Cefazolin provides adequate coverage for most types of procedures. 
Table 18.2 depicts the prophylactic regimen for operations at risk. A past history 
of a serious adverse event should preclude administration of a particular antibiotic 
like penicillin.
Note: Routine use of vancomycin prophylaxis is not recommended for any procedure. 
Consider vancomycin prophylaxis for patients with known MRSA colonization or at 
high risk for MRSA colonization (e.g. patients with recent hospitalization, nursing home 
residents, patients on haemodialysis).
Colonization and resistance
Longer administration of surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis and use of multiple 
antimicrobials can alter individual and institutional bacterial flora, leading to changes 
in colonization rates and increased bacterial resistance. Surgical prophylaxis can also 
predispose patients to Clostridium difficile–associated colitis.
In general, postoperative antibiotic administration is not recommended.

Factors associated with increased risk of infection are:
Systemic factors: Diabetes, corticosteroid use, obesity, extremes of age, malnutrition, 
recent surgery, massive transfusion, multiple (three or more) preoperative comorbid 
medical diagnoses. 
Local factors: Foreign body, electrocautery, injection with epinephrine, wound drains,

Preoperative and/or intraoperative measures for the purpose of 
preventing SSI
	
l Warming devices should be used in the operating room and during the surgical 
procedure for warming of the patient’s body.
	
l Protocols for intensive perioperative blood glucose control should be used for 
both patients with diabetes and adult patients without diabetes undergoing surgical 
procedures.
	
l Goal-directed fluid therapy should be used intraoperatively. 
	
l Surgical hand preparation should be performed by scrubbing with either using a 
suitable antimicrobial soap and water or using a suitable alcohol-based handrub 
before donning sterile gloves.
	
l Either sterile disposable non-woven or sterile reusable woven drapes and surgical 
gowns can be used during surgical operation. 
	
l Antibiotic incisional wound irrigation should not be used. Consider the use of 
irrigation of the incisional wound with an aqueous povidone–iodine solution 
before closure for the purpose of preventing SSI, particularly in clean and clean-
contaminated wounds. There is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against 
saline irrigation of incisional wounds for the purpose of preventing SSI. 
	
l Preoperative oral antibiotics combined with mechanical bowel preparation (MBP) 
should be used to reduce the risk of SSI in adult patients undergoing elective 
colorectal surgery. 
	
l Treat known patients with nasal carriage of Staphylococcus aureus undergoing other 
types of surgery with perioperative intranasal applications of mupirocin 2% ointment 
with or without a combination of chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) body wash. 
	
l Do not discontinue immunosuppressive medication prior to surgery.
	
l Give oral or enteral multiple nutrient–enhanced nutritional formulas for the purpose 
of preventing SSI in underweight patients who undergo major surgical operations.
	
l Adult patients undergoing general anaesthesia with tracheal intubation for surgical 
procedures should receive an 80% fraction of inspired oxygen intraoperatively and, 
if feasible, in the immediate postoperative period for 2–6 hours.
	
l Prophylactic negative pressure wound therapy may be used primarily on closed 
surgical incisions in high-risk wounds and taking resources into account. Triclosan-
coated sutures may be used, independent of the type of surgery. 
	
l Laminar airflow ventilation systems should not be used to reduce the risk of SSI for 
patients undergoing total arthroplasty surgery.

1004    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Postoperative wound management 
Do not apply antimicrobial agents to surgical incision for prevention of SSI. Cover 
postoperative wounds with occlusive dressings.
Postoperative wound care
	
l Do not prolong SAP after completion of the operation. Perioperative surgical 
antibiotic prophylaxis should not be continued due to the presence of a wound drain 
for the purpose of preventing SSI. Remove the wound drain when clinically indicated. 
	
l Antimicrobial sealants should not be used after surgical site skin preparation.
	
l Plastic adhesive incise drapes with or without antimicrobial properties should not 
be used. 
	
l Consider the use of wound protector devices in clean-contaminated, contaminated 
and dirty abdominal surgical procedures. 
	
l Advanced dressing of any type should not be used over a standard dressing on 
primarily closed surgical wounds.
	
l Apply occlusive dressings within 2 hours of wounding and these should be left on for 
at least 24 hours for optimal healing to occur for acute wounds. Occlusive dressings 
should never be used on infected wounds. Dressing changes can be performed once 
or twice daily. If other types of occlusives are used, the timing of the dressing changes 
will vary between 1 and 7 days, depending on the wound characteristics.

Wound infections are classified as:

WOUND CARE
Wounds can be classified as acute or chronic and further as arterial, venous, trophic, 
malignant, etc. (Table 18.4). Acute wounds heal uneventfully within an expected time 
frame, e.g. burns. For the purpose of guidelines, chronic wound can be defined as an ulcer 
present at least for 6 weeks. Chronic wounds include non-healing or infected surgical or 
traumatic wounds, venous ulcers, pressure ulcers, diabetic foot ulcers and ischaemic ulcers.

Open wound can be clean wound, clean contaminated wound, contaminated wound 
and dirty wound. Management of open wounds depends on the size and depth of 
involvement and the extent of undermining, the appearance of the wound surface 
(necrotic or viable), amount and characteristic(s) of wound exudate and status of the 
periwound tissues (pigmented, scarred, atrophic, cellulitic). Meticulous wound care 
includes adequate cleansing, debridement, oedema control in infected and acute wound, 
and prevention of ischaemia, in addition to maintaining a clean wound environment 
and keeping the bacterial count as low as possible.

1008    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Acute wounds
The overall objectives in caring for wounds that are incompletely clotted are to 
minimize unnecessary blood loss and to avoid the formation of a haematoma.
	 1.	Irrigate gently with copious quantities of sterile water or normal saline. Debris 
and necrotic tissue should be removed without damaging healthy tissue. Sharp 
mechanical debridement may be necessary to expose viable tissue for large areas 
of fibrinous exudates or eschar. Chemical debridement is useful for those areas that 
are difficult to access by sharp debridement. 
	
	Chemical debridement of the wounds may be done using topical agents – 
antiseptics (Chlorhexidine, Povidone–iodine, alcohol, Hydrogen peroxide, 
Triclosan) and antibacterials (Silver sulphadiazine, Neomycin, Polymyxin, 
Bacitracin, Mupirocin). When debridement is complete, dressings can be applied.
	 2.	Healing of acute clean wound is further facilitated by closure. Alternatively, closure 
can be delayed for several days to allow infection to clear.
Note: Wound healing is impaired by malnutrition, oedema, bacterial contamination, 
ischaemia, smoking and immunosuppressants.
Chronic wounds (ulcers)
Identify and treat the predisposing factors, e.g. diabetes mellitus, uraemia, jaundice, 
peripheral arterial or venous disease, severe anaemia, protein deficiency, rheumatoid 
arthritis, systemic vasculitis, Cushing’s syndrome and conditions requiring systemic 
steroid therapy and chemotherapy.

l Encourage daily or twice-a-day bath; the patient should avoid walking barefoot or 
with slippers and should be encouraged to wear shoes and socks.
	
l Patients with leg ulcer should reduce standing or excessive walking. In leg ulcer 
due to chronic venous insufficiency or oedema, patients should be advised to wear 
elastic stockings, elevate the leg and foot end of the bed while asleep and perform 
some leg exercises to activate the calf muscle pump.

Identify the microorganism and treat accordingly. Tubercular ulcer is treated with 
antitubercular drug (ATT; 2HRZE + 7HR) for at least 9 months (for details, see the 
section ‘Tuberculosis’ in Chapter 1).
Surgical treatment
	 1.	Perform surgical debridement in ulcers associated with necrotic tissue or slough. 
Debridement removes non-viable tissue, pathogens (biofilm), contaminants and 
foreign (or other) material and also drains areas of infection. It is important that 
debridement includes the base of the wound as well as the wound perimeter. 
Chronic wounds may require serial debridement in the operating room to 
sufficiently prepare the wound bed.

debridement to help direct antimicrobial therapy. Clean the wound with 
physiological normal saline or sterile water only (antiseptics delay wound healing). 
	 3.	Daily dressing: Gauze adheres to the wound bed, and it may remove viable tissue 
from the wound surface on removal resulting in delayed wound healing. Some of 
the commonly used dressings are:
	
l Occlusive (moisture-retentive) dressings with sterile paraffin gauze in case of 
clean and shallow ulcers without any pus discharge or other features of infection 
(occlusive dressings have barrier properties that enable to prolong the presence of 
moisture and wound fluid in the wound bed)
	
l Hydrocolloid gel in case of wound with slough (such as bed sores)
	
l Calcium alginate dressing for bleeding wounds and wounds with a cavity
Refer patients with chronic leg ulcer to general surgeons with experience in 
peripheral vascular problems for surgical treatment or to a vascular surgeon.
Patient education
	
l To prevent ulcers in future, explain about the care of the leg and wearing socks, shoes 
(especially in patients with diabetes) and compression stocking in case of varicose 
vein. 
	
l Maintain good personal hygiene (daily bath) and after bath the healed scar area 
should be massaged with an emollient cream such as Lanolin or some other suitable 
oil to keep the scar tissue soft and supple and prevent further breakdown. 
	
l Regularly perform calf muscle activating exercises and leg elevation, and avoid 
prolonged period of standing or sitting with legs down.
	
l In case of patients with diabetes, control of diabetes is necessary.

FROSTBITE
Frostbite is a severe, localized cold-induced injury due to freezing of tissue. Immersion 
foot (also referred to as trench foot) is a non-freezing cold injury (NFCI) that may also

1010    Standard Treatment Guidelines
cause tissue loss and long-term sequelae. Milder forms of injury include frostnip and 
chilblains (pernio). Chilblains are most common in young women, but both sexes and 
all age ranges may be affected. Frostbite is well documented in the military and in 
countries with extreme temperatures. It is also seen particularly in those who partake 
in winter sports such as skiing, hiking, mountain and ice climbing. Risk factors include 
smoking; previous cold injury; exposure of the hands and arms to vibration; exhaustion; 
dehydration; malnutrition; comorbidities such as peripheral vascular disease (PVD), 
diabetes or mental illness; and people taking beta-blockers.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Frostnip refers to cold-induced, localized paraesthesias that resolve with 
rewarming. There is no permanent tissue damage. Frostnip is distinct from 
frostbite but may precede it.
	
l Pernio, or chilblains, is characterized by localized inflammatory lesions 
(oedematous, often reddish or purple, and may be very painful or pruritic) 
resulting from acute or repetitive exposure to damp cold above the freezing point.
	 Areas most frequently affected by frostbite include the ears, nose, cheeks, chin, 
fingers and toes. Permanent damage from chilblains (pernio) is uncommon, with 
symptoms and signs generally resolving within 2–3 weeks.
	
l Immersion foot (or trench foot) involves injury to the sympathetic nerves and 
vasculature of the feet.
Severity classification
Depending on the depth of the tissue involvement, frostbite is classified into four 
degrees of severity, in a similar fashion to the classification of burns:
	
l First-degree frostbite: It is very superficial and is characterized by a central area 
of pallor and anaesthesia of the skin surrounded by oedema.
	
l Second-degree frostbite: It consists of large blisters containing clear fluid 
surrounded by oedema and erythema, developing within 24 hours and extending to 
or nearly to the tips of digits. The blisters may form an eschar, which later sloughs 
off, revealing healthy granulation tissue. There is no tissue loss.
	
l Third-degree frostbite: The injury is deeper and the blisters are smaller, 
haemorrhagic and more proximal. The skin forms a black eschar in 1 to several 
weeks.
	
l Fourth-degree frostbite: It extends to muscle and bone, and involves complete 
tissue necrosis. Mummification occurs in 4–10 days.

Pre-hospital care
	
l Get the patient to a warm environment as soon as possible. Whenever possible, pad 
or splint the affected area to minimize injury en route.

Chapter 18  Surgery    1011
	
l Remove wet clothing and boots (consider problems of replacement if swelling 
occurs), and replace wet gloves and socks with dry ones.
	
l Remove jewelry from the affected digits or other extraneous material from the 
body part early as significant swelling can be expected post-thaw, and vascular 
compromise may occur with tight rings.
	
l Do not rub frostbitten areas in an attempt to rewarm them as it can cause further 
tissue damage. 
	
l If sensation returns, help to mitigate risks (e.g. add a layer and change to warmer or 
dryer socks or boots) and the patient can continue to walk. If there is no return of 
sensation, move the injured to the nearest warm shelter (hut or base camp) and seek 
medical treatment. If at high altitude (>4000 m), supplementary oxygen should be 
considered.
	
l Avoid walking on frostbitten feet; this can increase tissue damage. If walking is 
necessary for evacuation, do not rewarm the feet before walking.
	
l Do not rewarm frostbitten tissue if there is a possibility of refreezing before reaching 
definitive care. Tissue that thaws and then refreezes results in more extensive tissue 
damage. Field rewarming should be undertaken only if the frozen part can be kept 
thawed and warm until the victim arrives at definitive care.
	
l If pre-hospital warming is attempted, options include placing the affected area in 
warm (not hot) water or warming it using body heat (e.g. placing frostbitten extremity 
in the armpit/abdomen or groin for 10 minutes) and then replacing the boots/gloves.
	
l Avoid the use of stoves or fires, heat lamps, heating pads and radiators to rewarm 
frostbitten tissue. Such tissue may be insensate, and burns can result. 
Hospital-based management
Undertake full assessment and management of underlying unstable comorbidities, 
trauma or hypothermia before frostbitten extremities are treated. 
	 I.	Correct underlying moderate or severe hypothermia (<32°C) to bring core 
temperature above 35°C before initiating frostbite warming. Mild hypothermia 
(32°C and 35°C) may be treated concurrently with the frostbite injury. Early signs 
of hypothermia include shivering, cold and pale skin, slurred speech, fast breathing, 
tiredness and confusion. Small babies look bright red and have cold skin and very 
low energy. If their temperature drops to 32°C or lower, shivering stops completely, 
and they become unconscious. 
	 II.	Maintain appropriate hydration with oral fluids if the patient is alert and has no 
gastrointestinal symptoms. In case of nausea or vomiting or having an altered mental 
status, IV normal saline in small boluses. Warm intravenous fluids before infusion.
	III.	Management of frostbite extremities involves rapid rewarming, wound care, efforts 
to enhance tissue viability and prevention of complications. 
1.	 Rapidly rewarm frostbitten tissue in warm (not hot) water at 37–39°C (98.6–
102.2°F) in water bath until it can be assessed for the presence of haemorrhagic 
blisters or cyanosis. Remove jewelry from the affected digits early if not 
removed earlier. Gentle active motion of the extremity while rewarming may

1012    Standard Treatment Guidelines
help but avoid trauma to the injured area against the container walls during 
treatment. Note: Dry heat is not recommended as it is difficult to regulate.
	
Thawing is usually complete when the tissue is red or purple and soft to the 
touch. The time period for optimal rewarming varies from 15–30 minutes up 
to 1 hour. Rewarming of frostbitten tissue may be painful requiring appropriate 
analgesia.
2.	 Wound care: Keep wounds open immediately following water bath or 
whirlpool treatment and allow them to dry before applying any dressing. Then 
apply bulky sterile non-adherent dressing to the affected area using aseptic 
technique. Insert pledgets (e.g. sterile cotton) between digits to prevent tissue 
maceration during demarcation. Avoid occlusive dressing. Protect lower 
extremity wounds with a cradle and upper extremity wounds with sterile 
sheets. Topical aloe vera, applied with dressing changes, is beneficial only for 
superficially injured areas. 
3.	 Blister: Drain by needle aspiration, debride and bandage large clear/cloudy 
non-haemorrhagic bullae that interfere with movement, such as those over 
joints. Leave haemorrhagic blisters alone. Haemorrhagic bullae of comparable 
size and location are drained by aspiration but are NOT debrided. Other minor 
bullae should be left intact. For deep injuries, no surgical debridement should 
be planned until imaging is performed.
4.	 Elevation to reduce oedema, and daily hydrotherapy to improve range of 
motion. Splinting may be required to prevent contracture formation. 
	
Avoid ambulation on the thawed lower extremity (unless only distal toes are 
affected).
5.	 Tab. Ibuprofen 400–600 mg every 12 hours Or Aspirin 325 mg daily orally.
6.	 Tetanus prophylaxis: Tetanus Toxoid vaccine, 2 doses 1 month apart
7.	 Infection prophylaxis: Post-thaw daily or twice-daily warm whirlpool 
treatments to reduce bacterial colonization. Routine use of prophylactic 
antibiotics is not recommended. Avoid topical antibiotics. Parenteral antibiotics 
should be given at the earliest sign of infection covering Staphylococcus, 
Streptococcus and Pseudomonas species.
8.	 At 24 hours post-insult after rewarming, assess and document severity of the 
tissue involvement and grade lesions for comparison after therapy (photograph 
or diagram of the affected extremity). Then, at day 2, a technetium-99 triple-
phase bone scan should be performed on the more severe injuries. Grades 2–4 
injuries require hospitalization and full investigation as they are associated 
with an increased risk of amputation and long-term sequelae.
9.	 In severe injury (Grade 3/4) presenting within 24 hours at high risk for life-
altering amputation (e.g. multiple digits, proximal amputation), without 
contraindications, recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA), Or 
Alteplase 0.15 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes Or Tenecteplase (though costlier). 
After treatment with rtPA is completed, begin treatment with Inj. Enoxaparin 
1 mg/kg subcutaneously, given twice daily for 14 days.

Chapter 18  Surgery    1013
10.	 In severe frostbite (Grade 3/4) presenting after 24 hours, Inj. Iloprost 
0.5 ng/kg/min IV infusion, increased every 30 minutes by 0.5 ng/kg/min, to 
a maximum of 2 ng/kg/min. If the patient develops headache or hypotension, 
decrease the dose by 0.5 ng/kg/min. The infusion is given for 6 hours/day for 
5 days at the maximum tolerable rate, up to 2 ng/kg/min.
Note: Hyperbaric oxygen, pentoxifylline, heparin without thrombolysis and others are 
unproven therapies.
Refer for early surgical consultation preferably with an orthopaedic surgeon with 
experience managing frostbite for long-term wound care, including hydrotherapy, 
repeated tissue debridement, escharotomy, fasciotomy and possibly delayed amputation. 
Patient education
	
l Timely pre-hospital and definitive hospital management are important to minimize 
final tissue loss and maximize functionality of the affected limb. Severe frostbite 
injuries presenting within 24 hours of the injury can be salvaged with treatment with 
either thrombolytic agent or Iloprost.
	
l Explain the following preventive measures to the patient/caregiver which include 
minimizing predisposing factors, paying attention to weather forecasts, dressing 
appropriately for the weather and having an emergency plan when venturing to 
remote regions:
	– Avoid alcohol consumption, smoking and exposure to water or metal surfaces. 
Alcohol makes the person fall asleep in the cold, a common cause of frostbite 
and loss of heat at a faster rate, and smoking makes the person more vulnerable 
to the effects of the cold.
	– Maintain adequate calorie intake and hydration.
	– In the setting of extreme cold temperature and high winds, plan for unexpected 
weather. Frostbite can develop in a matter of minutes. 
	– Appropriate multiple thin layers of warm, loose-fitting clothing to protect skin 
from moisture, wind and cold include a hat, face protection, eye protection under 
extreme conditions, mittens (as opposed to gloves), warm and water-resistant 
shoes and several layers of loose-fitting clothes. Avoiding perspiration or wet 
extremities. Change wet clothing as soon as feasible.
	– Small chemical heat packs may be placed in gloves or shoes but should be used 
with caution to avoid burns through direct contact with the skin. 
	– Perform “cold checks” in case of extremity numbness or pain or if concerned that 
frostbite may be developing. Recognize frostnip or superficial frostbite before it 
becomes more serious and minimize the duration of cold exposure.
	– Emollients do not protect against frostbite. 
	– Individuals travelling to remote areas or driving in icy conditions should, prior 
to departure, make sure to keep a warm blanket and some spare clothes, inform 
others of their anticipated route and carry adequate emergency supplies in case 
they become stranded.
	– Persons frequently exposed to cold environments should be aware of common 
frostbite symptoms and signs and should withdraw to warm shelter as soon as

1014    Standard Treatment Guidelines
these are noticed. The extremity at risk for frostbite (e.g. numb, poor dexterity, 
pale colour) should be warmed with adjacent body heat from the person or a 
companion, in the axilla or on the abdomen.

VARICOSE VEINS
Chronic venous disease of the lower limb is one of the most common conditions 
affecting the adults. Varicose veins, the most common complaint, represent one end of 
the spectrum of venous disease which extends through increasing degrees of venous 
incompetence and may result in leg ulceration in the most severe cases.
Basle study venous classification
Varicosities:
	(i)	Telangiectasia/hyphen webs (spider veins): Intradermal varicose veins that are 
small and rarely symptomatic
	(ii)	Reticular veins: Subcutaneous veins that begin at the tributaries of the trunk veins
	(iii)	Trunk veins: Varicose veins of the greater/lesser saphenous system and its named 
tributaries
These are the veins which are caused by incompetence of the valves connecting 
superficial and deep venous systems. This leads to regurgitation of blood from 
the high-pressure deep venous system to the superficial venous system. To accommodate 
this extra blood, the superficial veins dilate, elongate and become tortuous; these are known 
as varicose veins. These require surgical correction. Secondary varicose veins, especially 
after deep venous thrombosis, require conservative therapy with elastic stockings.
Chronic venous insufficiency:
	(i)	Dilated subcutaneous veins 
	(ii)	Hyperpigmented/depigmented areas 
	(iii)	Open/healed ulcer
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Varicose veins refer to any dilated, tortuous, elongated vein regardless of size.
	
l Duplex ultrasonography is confirmatory and also helps in localization of 
perforators and at times saphenopopliteal opening which is of immense help in 
the performance of operation.
	
l Evaluation of the deep venous system is a must in a patient with a history or 
clinical examination suggestive of deep venous thrombosis (leg oedema, present 
or past ulcer).

l Carefully examine the lower limb for saphenofemoral reflux, varices and perforators 
in the thigh and manifestations of venous incompetence in the calf and foot. 
	
l Reassure and use of elastic compression stockings and elevation of the limb.
	
l Definitive treatment includes injection sclerotherapy or surgical treatment.
Surgical
Surgery is contemplated in the case of patent deep venous system and competent valves. 
Saphenofemoral incompetence is treated with flush ligation at the saphenofemoral 
junction and stripping up to just below the knee. Perforator incompetence is treated with 
radical perforator ligation by either open or endoscopic method.
Postoperative management
	 1.	Perform graduated compression bandaging immediately following stripping or 
avulsion of veins. Replace bandages with compression stocking after 2 days. 
	 2.	Elevate the limb and encourage the patient to walk with compression stockings 
after first change of dressing 48 hours after the operation.
	 3.	Control postoperative pain with dextropropoxyphene or NSAIDs.
Patient education
	
l Emphasize do’s: leg exercise, leg elevation, wearing stockings, early ambulation and 
drinking 4–5 L of fluids in a day. 
	
l Avoid hot bath, exposure to extremes of temperature, pregnancy, contraceptive pills 
and oestrogens, and long journeys (flight).
	
l Teach the patient leg exercises – frequent movements of the toes and heels, 
Sarvangasan or Shirshasan, and elevation of the foot end of the bed about 6 inches 
by putting a block of wood or 2 bricks under the foot end of the bed.
	
l Avoid prolonged standing or dangling the legs down.

PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASES
Peripheral arterial disease (PAD), also known as PVD, develops most commonly as 
a result of atherosclerosis or hardening of the arteries. The clogged arteries cause 
decreased blood flow to the legs, which can result in pain when walking and eventually 
gangrene and amputation. Those with PAD are at an increased risk for heart disease, 
aortic aneurysms and stroke. PAD is also a marker for diabetes, hypertension and other

1016    Standard Treatment Guidelines
conditions. Causes of gangrene are trauma, infection (gas gangrene, non-clostridial 
gangrene), physical agents causing necrosis (heat, cold, chemicals [strong acids or 
alkali], radiation and electrical injury) or systemic (Raynaud’s disease, ergot poisoning, 
syphilis, embolism of artery, thrombosis, thromboangiitis obliterans and diabetes).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Pain on muscular activity of the limb and pain in lower limbs on walking for a 
certain distance (intermittent claudication) and routine physical activity causing 
pain in upper limbs (the severity of intermittent claudication varies widely, from 
mild discomfort to debilitating pain)
	
l Cold legs/feet or pallor of the limb, especially hands and fingers in case of upper 
limb and sole and toes in case of the lower limb, enhanced on elevation of the limb
	
l Numbness, tingling and weakness in the lower legs and feet; feeble or absent 
pulses like radial/ulnar pulse at the wrist or pedal pulse at the ankle; painful 
ulcers in the limb more commonly at the digits or sole of the foot; evidence of 
pre-gangrene – hyperaesthesia, pallor, oedema, ulceration and rest pain
	
l Evidence of gangrene – blackening of the toes/foot/fingertips; history of 
amputation of a part or whole of a limb in the past
	
l A 6-minute walk test and colour Duplex scan for assessing arterial flow in major 
arteries of the affected limb and opposite limb for comparison and detection of 
concomitant disease; an ankle brachial systolic blood pressure index (ABPI; 
normal 1–1.40) (value less than 0.8 indicates arterial insufficiency and less than 
0.5 indicates severe ischaemia); computed tomographic angiography (CTA) of 
the extremities to diagnose anatomic location and presence of significant stenosis 
in patients with lower extremity PAD.

Perform vascular review of symptoms to assess walking impairment, claudication, 
ischaemic rest pain and/or the presence of non-healing wounds, and comprehensive 
pulse examination (superficial temporal, carotid, radial, ulnar, brachial, axillary, femoral, 
popliteal, anterior and posterior tibial arteries at the ankle and dorsalis pedis on the 
dorsum of the foot); perform simultaneous examination with both hands for comparison 
of the pulses of the two sides. Do NOT palpate carotid arteries together as this may 
lead to vagal stimulation and profound bradycardia and syncope. In individuals older 
than 50 years, ask for a family history of a first-order relative with an abdominal aortic 
aneurysm (AAA) and palpate the abdomen for any pulsatile swelling in the midline due 
to a large aneurysm of the abdominal aorta. Auscultation of the abdomen in the midline 
may reveal a ‘bruit’ due to stenosis of the abdominal aorta or its major branch.
Moist gangrene or severe infection in the limb (urgent admission)
	 1.	Inj. Amoxicillin 500 mg IV 6 hourly Plus Inj. Cloxacillin 500 mg IV 6 hourly 
	
	Or Inj. Amoxycillin-clavulanic acid 1000 mg/200 mg every 8 hours

Chapter 18  Surgery    1017
	 2.	Inj. Metronidazole 500 mg 8 hourly IV infusion 
	 3.	Inj. Unfractionated Heparin bolus of 80 units/kg followed by infusion of 
18 units/kg adjusted to activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) of 1.5–2 times 
control for at least 5 days
	
	Or 
	
	Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), dose depending on product and adjusted 
for renal insufficiency for at least 5 days
	 4.	Inj. Tetanus toxoid 0.5 mL IM if not given in past 6 months
Refer or consult a vascular surgeon for definitive management.
Acute limb ischaemia and a salvageable extremity should undergo an emergency 
evaluation to define the anatomic level of occlusion and prompt endovascular or 
surgical revascularization.
	 1.	Balloon angioplasty when possible as the initial procedure to improve distal blood 
flow or bypass surgery when an autogenous vein conduit is available
	 2.	Catheter-based thrombolysis 
	 3.	Mechanical thrombectomy devices, which can be used as adjunctive therapy
	 4.	Tab. Aspirin 75 mg/day or Clopidogrel 75 mg/day in case of symptomatic 
atherosclerotic lower extremity PAD to reduce the risk of MI, stroke and vascular 
death and to asymptomatic individuals with an ankle-brachial index (ABI) less than 
or equal to 0.90.
Intermittent claudication
	 1.	Identification and treatment of the underlying cause; lifestyle change; smoking 
cessation; daily exercise within tolerable level for the patient and limb care to avoid 
trauma; diet restriction to reduce blood lipid levels (for treatment of hypertension, 
diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidaemia, see respective sections)
	 2.	Supervised exercise training to be performed for a minimum of 30–45 minutes in 
sessions performed at least 3 times per week for a minimum of 12 weeks.
	 3.	Tab. Aspirin or Clopidogrel 75 mg/day.
	 4.	Therapeutic trial in patients with lifestyle-limiting claudication. Tab. Cilostazol 
100 mg orally 2 times per day.
Note: The effectiveness of the therapeutic use of homocysteine-lowering drugs – 
folic acid and vitamin B12 supplements in individuals with lower extremity PAD 
and homocysteine levels greater than 14 mmol/L – is not well established. The 
clinical effectiveness of pentoxifylline, l-arginine and Ginkgo biloba as therapy 
for claudication is marginal and not well established. Vitamin E and chelation (e.g. 
ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) are not recommended as a treatment for patients with 
intermittent claudication and may have harmful adverse effects.
Refer patients with a vocational or lifestyle-limiting disability due to intermittent 
claudication to a vascular surgeon for endovascular procedures.

Patient education
	
l Do not ignore leg pain, numbness or other symptoms, and dismiss them as a normal 
part of aging.
	
l Screening is required for peripheral artery disease, if older than 70 years, older 
than 50 years with a history of diabetes or smoking, and younger than 50 years, but 
having diabetes and other peripheral artery disease risk factors such as obesity or 
high blood pressure, walking impairment, claudication, and/or non-healing ulcers.
	
l Emphasize proper foot care, including use of appropriate footwear, chiropody/
podiatric medicine, daily foot inspection, skin cleansing and use of topical 
moisturizing creams, and address urgently skin lesions and ulcerations in all patients 
with diabetes and lower extremity PAD.
	
l To instruct to get evaluation done in patients at risk of critical limb ischaemia (CLI) 
at least twice annually by a vascular specialist owing to the relatively high incidence 
of recurrence and an individual with diabetes or any individual with diabetes and 
known lower extremity PAD with ABI <0.4 should undergo regular inspection of 
the feet to detect objective signs of CLI.

CERVICAL LYMPHADENOPATHY 
An enlarged cervical lymph node is the commonest cause of lump in the neck. Cervical 
lymph nodes may become enlarged as a result of inflammation or neoplastic process 
(Table 18.5). Enlargement of the cervical lymph nodes commonly occurs with viral 
infections. Lymph node of >2 cm in paediatric patients is considered abnormal. Acute 
bacterial adenitis is caused by S. aureus or group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus 
pyogenes). A site of entry may be found, e.g. mouth or scalp. Anaerobic bacteria may be 
associated with dental disease in older children. Tuberculosis is one of the commonest 
causes of cervical lymphadenopathy, and non-tender nodes persist for more than 2 weeks 
and with associated systemic symptoms of fever, malaise and weight loss.

Detailed history and examination are essential to pinpoint specific aetiology. Majority 
of the lymph nodes are reactive to viral infections of the upper respiratory tract and, 
therefore, do not require any treatment.

Treatment (tubercular lymphadenopathy)
	 1.	Start antitubercular therapy (see ‘Tuberculosis’ in Chapter 1). 
	 2.	Assess response to ATT at 3–4 months
	
l Resolution of LN with settling of systemic symptoms.
	
l Delayed response (paradoxical reaction)- increase in LN size or new signs of

	 3.	In case of isolated Mantoux test positivity without suggestive findings on FNAC,

	 4.	BCG lymphadenitis typically occurs in children under 2 years of age and presents

l It is important to note that NAAT or acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear positivity

l For small-sized lymphadenitis, a ‘wait and watch’ approach is often recommended.
	
l If the lymphadenitis is large and suppurative, repeated aspiration or rarely 
incision and drainage may be required for management.

factor of malignancy. A biopsy is done to establish the diagnosis. Depending on the

Chapter 18  Surgery    1021
ABSCESS
An abscess is a tender mass normally surrounded by an erythematous area varying 
from pink to deep red. Abscesses are caused by infection of sebaceous/sweat glands/
lymph nodes leading to inflammation and pus formations. Some common conditions 
predisposing the abscess formations are immunosuppression, chronic steroid, 
chemotherapy, diabetes, cancer, AIDS, sickle cell disease, leukaemia, etc. Some other 
contributory factors are exposure to dirty environments, exposure to persons with 
certain types of skin infections, poor hygiene and poor circulation.
Abscesses can develop in many parts of the body. Common sites include armpits 
(axillary abscess) and inner thigh (groin), rectal area (perirectal abscess), gluteal 
abscess, external vaginal area (Bartholin's abscess), breast abscess, liver (hepatic 
abscess), lungs, neck, face, teeth (dental abscess) and tonsils (peritonsillar abscess).
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The common symptoms are a painful, compressible mass that is red, warm to 
touch and tender. Fluctuation is a classical feature but usually a late presentation. 
Sometimes, abscesses progress as a pointing sign and can see the material inside 
which spontaneously ruptures.
	
l The infection can spread to the tissues under the skin and even into the 
bloodstream and the patient may develop fever and feel sick.
	
l Differentiate an abscess from a cyst. Both are fluid-filled swelling, but an abscess 
is infected usually with a sign of inflammations while a cyst is not. However, a 
cyst can become infected and turn into an abscess.
	
l Rule out a cold abscess by the absence of local inflammatory features. 
	
l Most of the time, the diagnosis of an abscess is clinical and quite evident. The 
role of ultrasound is only when the diagnosis of an abscess is doubtful in case of 
a deep-seated abscess such as intermuscular abscess and intra-abdominal abscess.

Surgical
Incision and drainage (by the Hilton method) under local anaesthesia (or general 
anaesthesia in case of large abscess):
	
l Clean the abscess site with antibiotic lotion (povidone–iodine 5%) and shaving of 
hairs (if hairy). 
	
l Infiltrate local anaesthesia after skin test (0.5% plain lignocaine).
	
l Make an incision through most of the width of the abscess. Incision is given on the 
most dependent part or fluctuant part of the abscess.
	
l Break all loculi and septa with the finger gently or by sinus forceps to drain all pus. 
Take care not to open the normal deep plane.
	
l Send the purulent material/swab for culture and sensitivity while awaiting the final 
report; antibiotic may be started, if required.

1022    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Irrigate the cavity with normal saline, particularly in a deep-seated abscess.
	
l Pack the abscess cavity with gauze soaked with povidone–iodine 5% lotion and 
dressing is now done. Remove the pack after 48 hours.
	
l Limb elevation above the heart level facilitates wound healing as well as pain relief 
in case of any wound of extremities.
Special precautions
	
l Evaluate the patient more thoroughly before incision and drainage in case of an 
abscess along the spinal column, neck and chest and in typical areas where a 
tuberculous cold abscess could be present. 
	
l In case of swelling in the popliteal area, rule out the possibility of popliteal aneurysm.
	
l A large abscess in the lower quadrants of the abdomen may indicate lesions inside 
the peritoneal cavity.
	
l Peri-rectal abscesses require a fair-sized, crucial (cross-shaped) incision to prevent 
development of fistula-in-ano.
	
l Signs of an abscess near the ends of bones, particularly in children, may signify 
acute osteomyelitis and should be referred to a hospital.
	
l In case of tender swelling below the inguinal ligament, particularly in a female, rule out 
the possibility of an obstructed femoral hernia before carrying out incision and drainage.
	
l Drainage of a peritonsillar abscess and abscess of the oropharynx and retropharynx 
must be done with adequate precautions and ensuring availability of endotracheal 
intubation, suction and other facilities (for details, see respective sections).

The role of antibiotics is limited to before the formation of an abscess, i.e. the stage of 
cellulitis/erythematous/induration. Once an abscess is formed, do not give antibiotics 
before incision and drainage, else antibioma would form. In case an abscess forms despite 
antibiotic, it indicates that either bacteria are not sensitive or antibiotic is given in underdose.
If features of persistent inflammation and systemic signs of infection are present, give 
antibiotics with broad-spectrum coverage, specially Gram-positive coverage, at least 
for 5 days as follows:
	 1.	Tab. Amoxicillin 500 mg + Clavulanic acid 125 mg 8 hourly Or Cefuroxime axetil 
250–500 mg twice daily or Tab. Roxithromycin 150 mg twice a day
	 2.	Tab. Metronidazole 400 mg 8 hourly for 5–7 days
	 3.	Tab. Ibuprofen 400 mg 3 times a day after food for 3 days
Refer in case of a deep abscess involving vital structures of the body such as the neck, 
axilla, popliteal fossa and groin and an abscess which requires drainage under general 
anaesthesia such as an ischiorectal abscess and large breast abscess. 
Patient education 
	
l Perform daily dressing of the abscess cavity with hydrogen peroxide and povidone–
iodine 5% lotion.
	
l Maintain cleanliness of the wound.

Chapter 18  Surgery    1023
BREAST ABSCESS
A breast abscess can develop de novo (i.e. primary; no inciting disease) or it can occur 
as a complication of another disease process (i.e. secondary) such as periductal mastitis, 
skin infection over the breast or granulomatous lobular mastitis. It is more common in 
lactating women probably because of breastfeeding and poor breast hygiene. It may 
be associated with duct ectasia. The breast abscess may be superficial and deep. It is 
usually caused by S. aureus and anaerobic streptococci.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Patients with a primary breast abscess present with localized, painful 
inflammation of the breast associated with fever and malaise, along with a 
fluctuant, tender, palpable mass.
	
l The time course is variable; mastitis and abscess may present concurrently, or an 
abscess may develop 5–28 days following treatment for mastitis.
	
l The diagnosis is established with ultrasonography demonstrating a fluid collection 
and may also be used for guided aspiration of the collection.

Surgical
	 1.	Superficial abscess: Perform incision and drainage with local anaesthesia. Incision is 
made radially near the nipple and areola so as to minimize the ductal injuries. In case 
of an abscess elsewhere over the breast, the incision is given along the Langer’s line.
	 2.	In case USG of the breast shows fluid collection, perform guided needle aspiration. 
Two to three aspirations are sufficient in many cases, although larger collections 
may require up to six aspirations.
	 3.	Deep abscess: The incision and drainage (under general anaesthesia preferred) 
is given along the Langer’s line. Abscess cavity is reached with scissors/artery 
forceps following the principle of Hilton technique. In case of problematic 
drainage, dependent drainage is ensured by giving counter-incision over the lower 
part of the breast. The dead space can be obliterated to reduce the healing time by 
giving large stitches which are tied over large gauge pieces.
Large abscesses require operation under intercostal block or general anaesthesia.

Provide rest and support to the breast and continue breastfeeding from both the breasts 
and manual emptying of the breast; however, in case of a larger abscess, shift to bottle 
feeding temporarily.

1.	If there are features of persistent inflammation and systemic signs of infection, 
antibiotics with broad-spectrum coverage, especially Gram-positive coverage as 
above in the section ‘Abscess’, should be instituted for at least 5 days.
	 2.	Tab. Ibuprofen 400 mg as and when required.

1024    Standard Treatment Guidelines
In some cases, suppression of lactation with hormones may be required if the mother 
finds breastfeeding too painful.
Patient education
	
l In case of lactational infection, explain to the patient to maintain good hygiene 
and to continue breastfeeding from both the sides unless it is a large abscess and 
very painful. Milk drainage (by either breastfeeding or pumping) is important for 
resolution of infection and relief of discomfort. 
	
l Advise on timely weaning of the infant.

THYROID SWELLING
Thyroid swelling forms one of the most important differentials for swelling in front of 
the neck. The differential diagnoses of thyroid swelling are benign goitre, intrathyroid 
cysts, thyroiditis, and benign and malignant tumours. Simple goitre is an enlarged 
thyroid gland and occurs commonly around puberty in girls due to iodine deficiency. 
Malignancy should be suspected in case of extremes of age, male sex, rapidly growing 
swelling, persisting pain, dysphagia, recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, hardness and fixity 
of the thyroid gland and presence of one or more palpable neck nodes. FNAC, isotope 
scan and ultrasonography are helpful in differentiating the causes of thyroid swelling.

diagnosis:

10–15 mg 4 times a day and propranolol 20 mg 3 times a day). Fully discuss the 
potential complications with the patients – mentioning the risk to the parathyroid gland 
and recurrent laryngeal nerve.

1026    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Complications:
	
l The most immediate life-threatening complication is haemorrhage under deep cervical 
fascia, which can lead to acute asphyxia. Management includes reopening of the suture 
line, drainage of the haematoma and re-exploration for control of bleeders. Damage to 
recurrent laryngeal nerve can lead to respiratory distress (bilateral recurrent laryngeal 
nerve) and hoarseness of voice. Parathyroid damage leads to hypocalcaemia.
	
l Symptomatic hypocalcaemia (positive Chvostek’s or Trousseau’s sign or corrected 
serum calcium level <8 mg/dL) is treated with 10% calcium gluconate intravenously. If 
hypocalcaemia persists, oral calcium supplement and synthetic Vitamin D are necessary.
	
l Late complications include recurrent thyrotoxicosis (Graves’ disease), hypothyroidism 
and recurrence of malignancy at the local site or in the lymph nodes in the neck.
The patients operated for nodular goitre might require long-term thyroxine 
therapy. Patients operated for well-differentiated carcinoma of the thyroid will require 
postoperative thyroid scan and ablation of residual thyroid with radioiodine. 
If ablation of the thyroid is complete, follow-up of these patients is with thyroglobulin 
every 6 months and rising titres of thyroglobulin are an indication of radioactive scan. 
Since ablation of the thyroid is complete, these patients will require lifelong thyroxine. 
Radioiodine therapy is indicated in follicular, papillary and mixed carcinoma. 
Following total thyroidectomy, a total-body radioactive isotope scan should be arranged 
4 weeks after the operation. During this period, l-thyroxine therapy should be withheld. 
If radioactive scan shows residual thyroid tissue or metastatic deposit, then further 
dose of radioiodine should be given to ablate these. Following isotope scan, high-dose 
L-thyroxine (0.2–0.3 mg) should be started and continued for life. Radioactive iodine 
has no role in residual/metastatic medullary carcinoma. Treatment approach to Hurthle 
cell neoplasm is similar to that to follicular neoplasm.

Patients should be followed at 3-monthly intervals for the initial 2 years and 
6 monthly intervals for the next 3 years and then at yearly intervals for life. On each 
follow-up visit, the patient should be examined for any local or nodal recurrence in the 
neck; a chest X-ray should be done to exclude pulmonary deposit and clinical features 
of thyroid toxicity are noted and dose of L-thyroxine regulated.
Patient education
Thyroid problems often run in families and if family members are unwell, they should 
be encouraged to consult whether thyroid testing is warranted.

ACUTE ABDOMEN
Abdominal pain can occur due to a variety of medical and surgical causes. It is 
important to elicit a detailed clinical history and perform abdominal examination to 
determine the cause of pain. In very severe cases, it may be necessary to give treatment 
before proper history can be obtained or examination is allowed by the patient.
Causes of acute abdomen
Abdominal causes
	 1.	Inflammation of the peritoneum due to bacterial or chemical contamination; 
perforation of the appendix or bowel, ulcer, pancreatitis or pelvic inflammatory 
disease
	 2.	Mechanical obstruction of hollow viscera – intestinal obstruction, ureteric 
obstruction due to stone or other causes and obstruction of the biliary tree
	 3.	Vascular disturbances – vascular rupture, embolism or thrombosis, torsion 
of pedicle
	 4.	Abdominal wall injury or infection in the muscles; referred pain in case of 
pneumonia, angina, spine-radiculitis and torsion of the testis
Metabolic causes
	 1.	Insect bite, lead poisoning, uraemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, porphyria and other 
allergic causes
Neurogenic causes
	 1.	Organic – tabes dorsalis, herpes zoster, neuralgia
	 2.	Functional
Approach to the patient with acute abdomen
	 1.	In view of the variety of causes, it is absolutely essential to elicit an orderly detailed 
history about the nature of pain and perform a sequential examination (Fig. 18.3). 
Narcotics or analgesics should be withheld till the provisional diagnosis is made 
after a comprehensive clinical examination. 
	 2.	A proper history can provide more valuable information than the investigations. 
The features of the history that must be elicited are site, time and nature of onset, 
severity, nature of pain, progression, duration, relieving factors, exacerbating 
factors and radiation. History of GI complaints like vomiting, constipation, 
haematemesis, melaena and urinary complaints should be obtained. 
	 3.	Examination of the patient with respect to facies, posture in the bed and respiration can 
help in localizing the cause and nature of pain. The abdominal examination should be 
thorough but extremely gentle starting from the non-tender area. Points to be noted are 
area of maximum tenderness, guarding, rebound tenderness, bowel sounds, obliteration 
of liver dullness and presence of any associated mass or free fluid in the abdomen.

orifices, peripheral pulsations, genitalia, bowel sounds and rectal and/or vaginal 
examination. 
	 5.	Laboratory investigations depend on the suspected cause of pain and include 
haemogram, kidney function tests, liver function tests, serum or urinary amylase 
AXR, abdominal X-ray; CECT, contrast-enhanced computed tomography; CT, computed tomography; CXR, chest 
X-ray; FAST, focused assessment with sonography in trauma; LLQ, left lower quadrant; LUQ, left upper quadrant;

APPENDICITIS
Appendicitis is the commonest cause of acute abdomen and may appear as catarrhal 
appendicitis or as obstructive appendicitis and sometimes it may present as an 
appendicular lump or appendicular abscess or as burst appendix with peritonitis.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l There occurs acute central abdominal pain followed by nausea, vomiting and fever, 
with the pain, after a variable period, shifting to the right lower abdomen, localized 
tenderness maximum at the McBurney’s point, rebound tenderness and guarding in 
the right iliac fossa. 
	
l An inflammatory lump is seen in the right lower abdomen or signs of peritonitis 
occur.
	
l Polymorphonuclear leucocytosis and ultrasonographic appearances may help to 
corroborate the clinical diagnosis. 
	
l Investigations are primarily undertaken to exclude other conditions like ectopic 
gestation in females or ureteric calculus.

The definitive treatment is appendicectomy and the sooner, the better. It can be 
performed laparoscopically if facilities and expertise are available. Surgery should 
be delayed if the patient is moribund with advanced peritonitis in which case the 
conservative measures will need to be supplemented by measures to make him/her 
fit for operation. An interval appendicectomy (after 4–6 weeks of relief of acute 
symptoms) should be performed where a lump has formed, an attack has already 
resolved or circumstances make surgery not feasible.

Stop oral feeding.
Pharmacological (expectant management)
	 1.	Intravenous fluids to maintain hydration. Requirement of fluids would be more if 
the patient has peritonitis and sepsis.
	 2.	Inj. Ciprofloxacin infusion (100 mg/50 mL) 100 mL twice a day for 5 days. 
	
	Or 
	
	Inj. Ceftriaxone 1 g 12 hourly.
	 3.	Inj. Gentamicin (40 mg/mL) 80 mg IV 8 hourly.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Amikacin (500 mg/2 mL) 2 mL IV twice a day.

1032    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 4.	Inj. Metronidazole infusion (500 mg/100 mL) 100 mL IV 8 hourly.
	 5.	Inj. Diclofenac sodium (25 mg/mL) 50 mL IM as and when required.
	
	(Caution: Purgation, enema and abdominal massage are contraindicated.)
Assessment of response:
Pain subsides first, followed by relaxation of the abdomen and control of fever. 
Tenderness disappears later. Polymorphonuclear leucocytosis tends to settle down. 
Failure of signs and symptoms to subside or the appearance of new signs and symptoms 
during expectant treatment calls for surgical intervention.
Postoperative management
	
l Oral feeding is started when the abdomen is soft, the patient has passed flatus/stools 
and bowel sounds have appeared. Start with liquids, gradually permitting semisolid 
and solid diet over a period of 2–3 days.
	
l Antibiotics should continue for 5 days or more if the condition demands in 
case of a perforated or gangrenous appendix. Initially, antibiotics are given by parenteral 
route and later switched to oral route when the patient starts tolerating semisolid diet.
	
l The patient is discharged usually between the third and the fifth postoperative days 
if he/she is comfortable, ambulatory, tolerating semisolid or solid food, afebrile and 
having a healthy wound.
	
l Sutures are removed around the seventh postoperative day.
Patient education
	
l Normal routine physical work can be permitted in 2–7 days (2–3 days after 
laparoscopic appendicectomy).
	
l Moderate physical work is permitted after 4–6 weeks (2 weeks after laparoscopic 
appendicectomy).
	
l Heavy physical work is permitted after 2–3 months (4–6 weeks after laparoscopic 
appendicectomy).

CHOLELITHIASIS
Most patients with cholelithiasis have stones/calculi exclusively in the gallbladder, but 
15% of patients, in addition, have common bile duct (CBD) stones.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Most patients are asymptomatic; some patients present with dyspepsia or vague 
epigastric pain. The remaining patients may present with recurrent biliary colic or 
with acute cholecystitis or with symptoms of CBD disease or gallstone or pancreatitis.
	
l Obesity, fertility and diabetes are known to increase the chances of gallstone formation. 
	
l Diagnosis is made clinically and confirmed by ultrasonography.

Low-fat diet with no spices
Definitive treatment is cholecystectomy in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients 
with diabetes or other immunocompromising conditions –a– solitary large stone or 
multiple small stones with wide cystic duct or porcelain gallbladder or anxious patients. 
If the patient comes after 48 hours, manage conservatively and cholecystectomy after 
6–8 weeks.
Expectant management: In case of acute cholecystitis, empyema gallbladder and 
stones in the CBD, the patient should be kept nil orally and administered maintenance 
IV fluids (for details, see ‘Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance and Replacement 
[in Adults]’ in Chapter 2 and in Children in Chapter 19).

	Or
	
	a. Inj. Ampicillin (500 mg/mL) 1 mL IV 6 hourly.
	
	b. Inj. Cloxacillin (500 mg/mL) 1 mL IV 6 hourly.
	
	Or
	
	a. Inj. Ciprofloxacin (infusion (100 mg/50 mL) 100 mL IV twice a day.
	
	b. Inj. Amikacin (500 mg/2 mL) 2 mL twice a day.
	 3.	In case anaerobic bacterial infection is suspected or anticipated, give: 
	
	Inj. Metronidazole (500 mg/100 mL) 100 mL IV 8 hourly.
	 4.	Inj. Diclofenac sodium (25 mg/mL) 2–3 mL IM as and when required or 6 hourly.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Pentazocine lactate (30 mg/mL) 1 mL as and when required.
	 5.	In patients having obstructive jaundice, add Inj. Vitamin K (10 mg/mL) 1 mL IM 
once or twice a day till prothrombin time reaches a satisfactory level.
Antibiotics are usually stopped after 5–7 days unless the patient has evidence of 
persistent infection or has an indwelling tube (e.g. T-tube).
Patient education
	
l Fatty and fried meals should be avoided for 3 months.
	
l Ambulation as early as possible is encouraged.
	
l If T-tube has been placed, it should be removed after 2–3 weeks after ensuring 
that the CBD is patent and non-dilated, and there is free flow of contrast into the 
duodenum during T-tube cholangiography.
