Prevention of infection
	 1.	Always clean hands with soap and water and wear sterile gloves, if available, 
before conducting the birth of the baby and while examining babies during the first 
few days of life. 
	 2.	Tie umbilical cord using two ligatures or a disposable clamp. Apply cord clamp or 
ligature at least 2 or 3 cm beyond the base of the cord.
	 3.	The surface for conducting delivery and placing the baby after birth must be clean. 
	 4.	Do not apply any medication/substance to the cord or eyes after birth. Leave stump 
uncovered and dry.
	 5.	Do not give prelacteal feeds. 
	 6.	Give exclusive breastfeeding from birth.
Care of the umbilical stump
	 1.	Umbilical stump should be inspected after 2–4 hours of birth. Bleeding may occur 
at this time due to shrinkage of cord and loosening of the ligature.
	 2.	The cord must be left open without any dressing. Do not apply any medication on 
the cord.
	 3.	The cord usually falls after 4–10 days.
	 4.	Inspect the stump for any discharge or infection and kept clean and dry till 
complete healing takes place.
Exclusive breastfeeding
Advise mothers to:
	 1.	Start breastfeeding within 1 hour of normal birth and as early as possible after 
caesarean section. Do not separate mother from the child.
	 2.	Not to give any prelacteal feeds such as honey, water, jaggery, honey, etc. 
	 3.	Give breastfeeds to baby on semi-demand as often as the child wants day and night, 
at least eight times in 24 hours.
	 4.	Give the baby exclusive breastfeeding for at least the first 6 months of life. However, 
there may be situations where it may not be possible to provide human milk, i.e. 
maternal death, severe maternal illness and documented lactational inadequacy. 
	 5.	Not to give water to the baby during period of exclusive breastfeeding. Do not 
introduce ghutti, gripe water, honey or animal or powdered milk. Give complementary 
foods from 6 months of age. Continue breastfeeding up to 2 years of age or beyond. 
Care of eyes
Routinely, no eye care is required. If the eyes are sticky, frequently clean eyes using 
sterile cotton swabs soaked in normal saline or by instillation of antibiotic eye drops 
every 2–4 hours (for details of Ophthalmia neonatorum, see Chapter 13).
Early identification of high-risk newborns
Babies born to mothers with eclampsia, antepartum haemorrhage, diabetes, etc., are 
considered as high-risk newborns and delivery should be conducted at a centre where 
all facilities for the care of the newborn are available. The following examination at

1066    Standard Treatment Guidelines
birth or during the first few days would help detect high-risk babies need of immediate 
referral to an appropriate health facility which has adequate newborn care.
	 1.	Weigh baby. Babies with birth weights <2000 g are at increased risk of morbidity 
and mortality and need careful assessment by a physician trained in child health. 
	 2.	Examine for major malformations. Most major and life-threatening 
malformations such as neural tube defects, oesophageal and anal atresia, 
diaphragmatic hernia, etc. can be detected at birth by careful examination. Some 
important clues to an underlying malformation are non-passage of meconium at 
24 hours of age or non-passage of urine at 48 hours after birth. 
	 3.	Sucking, activity and cry. Newborn infants who have poor sucking, are less active 
than normal and have a weak cry are very ill and need immediate referral. 
	 4.	Respiratory distress. Babies who have a respiratory rate of >60 bpm (counted 
for at least 1 minute and persisting on repeat count) or have severe subcostal 
retractions have respiratory distress and need immediate referral. 
	 5.	Identification of severe jaundice. Yellow staining of the skin within 24 hours of 
age or involving the palms and soles at any age is considered severe jaundice and 
requires immediate referral for further evaluation and management.
	 6.	Screen infants at birth or by 1 month of age, diagnose for hearing loss by 3 months 
of age and initiate early intervention services by 6 months of age. 
Immunization
All newborns delivered at a health facility should be given BCG, zero dose of oral polio 
vaccine and birth dose of Hepatitis B within 24 hours of birth. All COVID positive 
(symptomatic or asymptomatic) babies should receive hepatitis B vaccine immediately 
after or within 24 hours of birth, and BCG and zero dose OPV at discharge (OPV within 
15 days of birth) (for details, see Immunization in the following text).
COMMON CLINICAL PROBLEMS IN NEWBORNS
There are several phenomena after birth that are normal, and mothers only need 
reassurance. These include the following:
Persistent epiphora (watering of eyes). Some neonates may develop persistent epiphora 
(watering) due to blockage of nasolacrimal duct by epithelial debris. Advise mother to 
massage the nasolacrimal duct area (by massaging the either side of the nose adjacent to 
the medial canthus) five to eight times daily, each time before she feeds the baby. Avoid 
the use of kajal as it may transmit infections or may even cause lead poisoning. 
Weight loss of 6–8% (10–12% in preterm infants) in the first few days of life is 
normal and most infants regain their birth weight by 10–14 days. Delayed feeding 
and unsatisfactory feeding schedule may be associated with excessive weight loss. An 
adequately fed baby passes urine at least five to six times in a day while many babies 
pass urine (even stools) after each feed during the first 3 months of life. The average 
daily weight gain in term babies is around 30 g per day.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1067
Mastitis neonatorum. Engorgement of breasts occurs in term babies of both sexes on 
the third or fourth day and may last for days or even weeks which is due to persistence 
of maternal hormones for some time. Do not do local massage, fomentation and 
expression of milk. Reassure mother that this regresses on its own.
Mucoid vaginal secretions. Most female babies have a thin, greyish, mucoid, vaginal 
secretion, which should not be mistaken for purulent discharge.
Hymenal tags. Mucosal tags at the margin of hymen are seen in two-third of 
female infants.
Vaginal bleeding. Vaginal bleeding may occur in female babies about 3–5 days after 
birth because of withdrawal of maternal hormones. The bleeding is mild and lasts for 
2–4 days. Additional vitamin K is unnecessary. 
Milia, Epstein pearls, Mongolian spots, capillary nevi, etc. There are a few 
developmental variants which may be present. The mother needs to be reassured.
Red rashes on the skin may be seen at 2–3 days of life. These are normal and disappear 
spontaneously after 2–3 days without any specific treatment. 
Peeling skin. Dry skin with peeling and exaggerated transverse sole creases is seen in 
all post-term and some term babies. 
Subconjunctival haemorrhage. Semilunar arcs of subconjuctival haemorrhage is a 
common finding in normal babies. The blood gets reabsorbed after a few days without 
leaving any pigmentation.
Sucking callosities. The presence of these button-like, cornified plaques over the centre 
of upper lip has no significance.
Tongue tie. It may be in the form of a fibrous frenulum with a notch at the tip of the 
tongue. This does not interfere with sucking or later speech development.
Nonretractable prepuce. The prepuce is normally non-retractable in all male newborn 
babies and should not be diagnosed as phimosis. The urethral opening is often 
pinpointed and is visualized with difficulty. The mother should be advised against 
forcibly retracting the foreskin.
Umbilical hernia. Umbilical hernia may manifest after the age of 2 weeks or later. 
Most of these disappear spontaneously by 1 or 2 years of age.
Regurgitation of feeds and vomiting. Unlike vomiting, non-projectile expulsion 
of stomach contents without force (regurgitation) is normal and simply needs advice 
regarding feeding technique.
Bowel disorders. No medication should be prescribed for passage of stools after 
each feed (exaggerated gastrocolic reflex) as this is normal in some babies. From 3rd 
to 14th day many exclusively breastfed babies frequently pass golden yellow, sticky, 
semi-loose/loose stools (10–15 times/day) without illness/dehydration. These are 
transitional stools and require no medication. Some normal breast fed babies may pass 
stools infrequently (once every few days). This is not constipation. Formula-fed babies 
generally have more formed stools.

1068    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Delayed passage of urine. Non-passage of urine by 48 hours after birth may suggest 
urinary tract anomalies. Such babies need to be investigated. Crying before passing 
urine is normal.
Jitteriness is abnormal only when it is excessive or persists even during feeding and 
then it may suggest hypoglycaemia or hypocalcaemia.
Dehydration fever. Transitory moderate fever (up to 38.5°C) usually during the second 
or third day of life in summer months in an active baby who sucks well is normal and 
responds to lowering the environmental temperature.
Watch closely for the following danger signs:
	
l Bleeding from any site
	
l Appearance of jaundice within 24 hours of age or yellow staining of palms or soles
	
l Failure to pass meconium within 24 hours or urine within 48 hours.
	
l Persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, poor feeding, undue lethargy or excessive 
crying, drooling of saliva or chocking during feeding, respiratory difficulty, apneic 
attacks or cyanosis, sudden rise or fall in body temperature, seizures and evidence 
of superficial infections such as conjunctivitis, pustules, umbilical sepsis, oral 
thrush, etc.

Follow each baby in the well baby clinic for assessment of growth and development, 
early diagnosis and management of illnesses and health education of parents. It is 
preferable that every baby is seen and assessed by a health worker at each immunization 
visit. 
Excessive crying. Most babies cry when either they are hungry or are having 
discomfort such as due to full bladder before passing urine, wet napkin, nose block, 
etc. Excessive inconsolable crying or high-pitched crying is indicative of meningitis or 
any other painful inflammatory conditions.
Umbilical sepsis. If there is pus discharge not extending to periumbilical skin, apply 
10% Gentian violet or Povidone Iodine locally twice a day. However, if there 
is periumbilical erythema or induration administer syrup erythromycin 40 mg/kg/day 
in three to four divided doses. If the newborn has any other high-risk factor, refer to a 
higher centre.
Umbilical granuloma. A red flesh-like nodule at the base of umbilical cord can be 
managed by cautery with silver nitrate or application of common salt for 3–4 days.
For breast-related problems, see Chapter 15.
LOW BIRTH WEIGHT BABIES
Nearly 75% neonatal deaths and 50% infant deaths occur among the low birth weight 
(LBW) babies. Even after recovery from neonatal complications, some LBW babies 
may remain more prone to malnutrition, recurrent infections and neurodevelopmental 
handicap.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1069
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Low birth weight (LBW) baby is the one who weighs less than 2500 g at birth, 
very low birth weight (VLBW) if <1500 g and extremely low birth weight 
(ELBW) <1000 g.
	
l Preterm newborns are classified on the basis of completed gestation period as:
	 (i)	 Extremely preterm: Less than 28 weeks
	(ii)	 Very preterm: 28 to <32 weeks
	(iii)	 Late and moderate preterms: 32 to <37 weeks
	
l LBW may result from either prematurity (gestational age <37 weeks) or intrauterine 
growth retardation (IUGR), which is also called small-for-date (SFD) baby.

Indications for hospitalization are as follows:
Birth weight of less than 1800 g; gestational age of less than 34 weeks, neonate who is 
not able to take feeds from the breast or by cup (katori) and spoon (irrespective of birth 
weight and gestation), and a sick neonate (irrespective of birth weight and gestation).
	 1.	Keep the LBW babies warm: Room temperature should be kept between 28°C and 
30°C. Following methods may be used:
	– Maternal-baby skin-to-skin contact (Kangaroo mother care [KMC]). The 
timing of initiation of KMC depends on the birth weight and stability of the 
infant. Initiate KMC immediately if the baby is more than 1800 up to less than 
2500 g and stable at birth. More than 1200 and up to less than 1800 g with 
serious morbidities may take days before KMC can be initiated. Transfer to 
a specialized centre, if possible. Best transported in skin to skin contact with 
mother/family member (if transport incubator not available). For infants with a 
birth weight less than 1200 g, KMC may take several days or even weeks to 
initiate, depending on the infant’s stability and medical condition.
	– Duration of KMC should be gradually increased based on the tolerance of infant. 
	– Place the naked baby between the mother’s breasts in an upright position. The 
head should be turned to one side and in a slightly extended position to keep 
the airway open and for allowing eye-to-eye contact between the mother and 
her infant. The hips should be flexed and abducted in a ‘frog’ position; the 
arms should also be flexed. The infant’s abdomen should be at the level of the 
mother’s epigastrium. Mother’s breathing stimulates the infant, thus reducing 
the occurrence of apnoea. Support the infant from the bottom with a sling/
binder. Wrap baby and mother with a shawl. Cover the baby’s head with a 
cap. The mother carrying an infant in the KMC position can walk, stand, sit 
or engage in different activities. If comfortable, the mother can sleep with 
the infant in kangaroo position in a reclined or semirecumbent position. The 
duration of each KMC session should be gradually increased for as long as 
the mother can comfortably provide KMC. The infants in KMC need to be

1070    Standard Treatment Guidelines
removed from skin-to-skin contact only for changing diapers and clinical 
assessment according to hospital schedules.
	
Note: Don’ts of Kangaroo Mother Care
§	 Do not bathe till the infant weighs 2500 g; sponging may be done
§	 Do not handle infant too frequently
§	 Do not give bottle feed
§	 Do not allow infants to be in contact with sick people
	– Discontinue KMC when gestation reaches term, or the weight is around 2500 g
	– Proper clothing – cap, woolen sweaters, socks and mittens
	– Blankets
	– Overhead radiant warmer
	– Incubator
	 2.	Breast milk is the ideal feed for all infants, including those with LBW. Offer 
breastfeeding frequently, ideally every 2 hours, and on demand. Ensuring continued 
frequent feeding at night is also important for the well-being and growth of LBW infants. 
	 3.	Nutritional supplements as under:
	
	For very LBW (<1500 g) infants 
	– Calcium 120–140 mg/kg/day once the infant reaches 100 mL/kg/day of feeds 
till term gestation (i.e. 40 weeks’ postmenstrual age)
	– Phosphorus 60–90 mg/kg/day once the infant reaches 100 mL/kg/day of feeds 
till term gestation (i.e. 40 weeks’ postmenstrual age) 
	– Vitamin D 800 IU/day once the infant is on 100 mL/kg/day of feeds till 
6 months of age or beyond based on the current national/IAP guidelines 
	– Iron 2–4 mg/kg/day from 2 weeks of age till 6 months of age or beyond based 
on the current national/IAP guidelines 
	
	For other LBW (1500–2499 g) infants
	– Vitamin D 400 IU/day once the infant is on full enteral feeds starting at 
6 months of age or beyond based on the current national/IAP guidelines 
	– Iron 2–3 mg/kg/day from 6–8 weeks of age till 6 months of age or beyond based 
on the current national/IAP guidelines.
	
	Nutrition guidelines to provide fluids and nutrients to LBW babies are given in 
Table 19.1. LBW infants should be preferably given 10–15 mL/kg per day of enteral 
feeds (minimal enteral nutrition), preferably expressed breast milk, starting from the 
first day of life, with the remaining fluid requirement met by intravenous fluids.
	
	Ensure adequacy of nutrition by monitoring frequency of urine (8–12 times 
per day) and weight gain (15–20 g per day).
	 4.	Vitamin K 1.0 mg (0.5 mg for babies less than 1000 g) IM after birth (i.e. the 
first hour by which infant should be in skin-to-skin contact with the mother and 
breastfeeding is initiated) if not given earlier.
	 5.	Multivitamin drops 0.3 mL/day from 2 weeks of age.
Early detection of sickness by periodic evaluation. Refer to higher centre in 
the presence of any one or more of the following signs: lethargy, refusal to feed, 
hypothermia, respiratory distress, grunt, apnoea, abnormal weight gain pattern,

jaundice over soles and palms, abdominal distension, feed intolerance, cyanosis, pallor, 
sclerema, seizures and bleeding.
Monitoring 
	
l Monitor growth of LBW for weight (daily), head circumference (weekly) and length 
(weekly or fortnightly) during their stay in SNCU. Serial growth monitoring to be 
done by intergrowth chart for preterm babies.
	
l If the infant has inadequate weight gain, check the amount of intake, assess attachment 
(if taking direct breastfeeding), spluttering/spillage (if on paladai/cup/spoon feeds), look 
for nipple and breast problems in the mother and complications, if any such as cold 
stress, sepsis, oral thrush, anaemia and late metabolic acidosis and treat accordingly.
Discharge
	
l LBW babies can be discharged from hospital when they are feeding from breast or 
breast and cup, gaining weight for three consecutive days, no signs of illness, able 
to maintain normal body temperature when roomed-in with mother and mother is 
confident of taking care of the baby.
	
l For immunization of LBW babies, see section on Immunization. If the LBW baby is 
not sick, the vaccination schedule is the same as for the normal babies. A sick LBW 
baby, however, should receive immunization only on recovery.

NEONATAL JAUNDICE
More than 50% of normal newborns and 80% of preterm infants experience some 
degree of jaundice. Jaundice can be physiological or pathological. 
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Jaundice is a common physical finding (manifesting as yellowness of the skin 
of the face when the serum bilirubin level exceeds 5 mg/dL) during first week of life.
	
l As the degree of jaundice increases, there is a cephalopedal progression of 
jaundice. For extent of jaundice, see Figure 19.2. 
	
l More than 90% of all neonatal jaundice is physiological and does not need 
any specific therapy. It is recognized by its characteristic timetable: jaundice 
appears between 24 and 72 hours of age, its maximum intensity (peak serum 
bilirubin always below 15 mg/dL) is seen on the 4th to 5th day of life and usually 
disappears before 14 days of life.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1073
	
l About 5% of newborn babies develop pathological jaundice. It should 
be considered a medical emergency as it may cause bilirubin encephalopathy or 
kernicterus when unconjugated bilirubin exceeds 20 mg/dL (term baby) or lower 
levels (preterm babies). 
	
l Pathological jaundice is recognized by ANY of following features: gestational 
age under 38 weeks, a previous sibling with neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia requiring 
phototherapy, visible jaundice in the first 24 hours of life, visible jaundice at 
discharge, blood group incompatibility, high prevalence of G6PD deficiency, 
primipara mother and weight loss at discharge >3% per 24 hours of age or >7% 
cumulative weight loss and persistence of jaundice beyond 8 days in term baby and 
beyond 2 weeks of age in preterm baby or signs of underlying illness.

Screening and assessment of jaundice
	
l Assess all newborns for jaundice every 12 hours, especially in the initial 3–5 days. 
Monitoring for severe neonatal jaundice may be needed till the end of the first 
week of postnatal life, especially in neonates who are at a high risk of developing 
significant pathological jaundice as above.
	
l Examine the naked baby in bright natural light. Alternatively, the baby can be 
examined in white, fluorescent light. Make sure there is no yellow/off white 
background. Examine blanched skin and gums or sclera. Visual assessment has 
reasonable accuracy, particularly when total serum bilirubin (TSB) is less than 
12–14 mg/dL. Absence of jaundice on visual inspection reliably excludes the 
jaundice. Note carefully the depth of jaundice (degree of yellowness) as it is an 
important indicator of the level of jaundice, and it does not figure out in Kramer’s 
rule (Fig. 19.2). A deep yellow staining (even in the absence of yellow soles or 
palms) is often associated with severe jaundice. Estimate TSB in such circumstances.
	
l Evaluate all newborns with visible jaundice with transcutaneous bilirubin (TcB) or TSB. 
If transcutaneous bilirubinometer is available, use it in babies with a gestational age of 
35 weeks or more and a postnatal age of more than 24 hours. Observe trends in TcB 
values and if it indicates a bilirubin level greater than 14 mg/dL, check serum bilirubin.
Measure serum bilirubin if:
	
l Jaundice in the first 24 hours
	
l Beyond 24 hours: If on visual assessment or by transcutaneous bilirubinometry, TSB 
is likely to be more than 12–14 mg/dL or approaching phototherapy range or beyond
	
l If unsure about visual assessment
	
l During phototherapy, for monitoring progress and after phototherapy to check for 
rebound in select cases (such as those with haemolytic jaundice)
Serious jaundice (if any one of following): 
	
l Presence of visible jaundice in the first 24 hours 
	
l Yellow palms and soles anytime

Treatment of pathological jaundice is usually phototherapy and exchange transfusion. 
Figures 19.3 and 19.4 provide guidelines for initiating phototherapy or exchange 
transfusion in babies, respectively. The risk factors for hyperbilirubinemia are gestation 
below 38 weeks, albumin below 3.0 g/dL, isoimmune haemolytic disease, G6PD 
deficiency or other haemolytic diseases, sepsis and clinical instability in the previous 
24 hours. Table 19.3 provides guidelines for initiating phototherapy and exchange 
transfusion in LBW babies.
1. Phototherapy 
Total serum bilirubin levels only are taken to decide the need to start phototherapy. 
If the plotted bilirubin value is above the selected intervention line, the baby should 
be started on phototherapy. In such babies, also check the exchange transfusion chart 
(Fig. 19.4) as some of the babies may need exchange transfusion; if needed refer 
immediately to a health facility with facility for exchange transfusion. If below the 
intervention line, observe and monitor bilirubin 12–24 hourly. In case the baby has 
direct bilirubin levels (>20% of total bilirubin), phototherapy is not indicated as baby 
can develop bronze baby syndrome due to porphyria deposition under the skin.

Most preterm babies are placed under phototherapy, when their serum bilirubin 
approaches 10–12 mg/dL, and term babies are given phototherapy when their serum 
bilirubin approaches 15 mg/dL.
During phototherapy, the naked infant (with covered eyes and nappy for genitalia) 
is kept about 45 cm below the phototherapy unit with light-emitting diode (LED) 
or fibreoptic or fluorescent lamps or tubes or bulbs. (Caution: Rash, overheating, 
dehydration and diarrhoea are the most common side effects of phototherapy.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1077
Encourage frequent breastfeeding during phototherapy. Unless there is evidence of 
dehydration, supplementing breastfeeding or providing IV fluids is unnecessary. 
Although direct sunlight decreases TSB concentrations, there are practical difficulties 
involved in safely exposing infants to the sun, either inside or outside.)
Note: Many babies while undergoing phototherapy may pass greenish-yellow stools 
which by themselves are not harmful as long as baby is active. Phototherapy does not 
have to be continuous and can be interrupted for feeding, clinical procedures and to 
allow maternal bonding. 
Intensive phototherapy 
Intensive phototherapy is needed for neonates nearing exchange transfusion threshold. 
Phototherapy can be intensified by adding another light source or increasing the 
irradiance of the initial light source used. Double-surface phototherapy can be used for 
severe jaundice. Guidance for escalation of care is shown in Figure 19.5.
Note: Assessment of the severity of jaundice by looking at the skin is unreliable. 
Estimate serum bilirubin 12–24 hourly to monitor response to therapy depending on 
the age of the child, the presence of hyperbilirubinemia neurotoxicity risk factors, the 
TSB concentration, and the TSB trajectory. Phototherapy may be discontinued when the 
serum bilirubin level falls below 13–14 mg/dL. The decision to continue phototherapy 
is determined by finding a balance between exposing the infant to phototherapy, 
separating mothers and infants, and the aim of preventing a rebound increase in TSB 
levels after the phototherapy treatment. Rebound hyperbilirubinemia is defined as a 
TSB concentration that reaches the phototherapy threshold for the infant’s age within 
72 to 96 hours of discontinuing phototherapy.
Failure of phototherapy. Failure of phototherapy may be considered in infants with 
serum bilirubin in the exchange or pre-exchange zone, if there is no decline in bilirubin 
of 1–2 mg/dL after 4–6 hours and/or bilirubin levels do not reach below the exchange 
transfusion level despite intensive phototherapy. 
2. Exchange transfusion should be promptly performed if infant shows signs of acute 
bilirubin encephalopathy (e.g. hypertonia, arching, retrocollis, opisthotonos, high-
pitched cry, or recurrent apnea). or if TSB is ≥25 mg/dL, above the recommended age 
and risk specific cut-off for TSB (Fig. 19.5).
Exchange transfusion should be done by central or peripheral route, aiming to 
replace double the baby’s blood volume, and should be performed by skilled personnel 
in a well-equipped centre.
Note: No role of phenobarbitone, tin-mesoporphyrin, agar, albumin, charcoal, 
Cholestyramine, clofibrate, glycerine, chinese herbs, homeopathy, acupuncture, 
Riboflavin or manna in management of hyperbilirubinaemia.
3. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) can be administered at a dose of 0.5–1 g/kg 
over 2 hours in isoimmune hemolytic disease when the TSB reaches or exceeds the 
escalation-of-care set point. The dose can be repeated in 12 hours if necessary.

Neonates with hyperbilirubinaemia follow-up should be done considering the gestational 
age at discharge, physical examination findings, presence of hyperbilirubinaemia risk 
factors, feeding adequacy, weight changes and family support when deciding when to 
repeat bilirubin measurements within the 4 to 24-hour time window.
	 1.	If bilirubin levels are between 2–3.4 mg/dL or 3.5–5.4 mg/dL within 1–2 days, 
repeat measurements are warranted. For bilirubin levels of 5.5–6.9 mg/dL in those 
discharged <72 hours, follow-up within 2 days is recommended, with clinical 
judgement guiding further actions.
	 2.	Conduct periodic developmental screening until school age, including assessments 
of early language milestones. 
	 3.	Those who exhibited signs of encephalopathy or underwent exchange transfusion 
should have a sensorineural hearing assessment via brainstem-evoked audiometry 
before reaching 6 months of age.
	 4.	Other follow-up, including vaccination, growth monitoring and feeding practices, 
can continue as for a normal neonate.
Prolonged jaundice. If jaundice persists beyond 2 weeks or 21 days in preterm infants 
and if baby’s stool is pale and urine is dark, refer the baby to a specialized centre for 
further evaluation and management of obstructive jaundice.
Parent education
	
l Provide education including an explanation of jaundice; the need to monitor infants 
for jaundice, dehydration and lethargy; signs of ineffective feeding, fussiness and 
illness; and an assessment of understanding of these issues and the recommended 
follow-up. Encourage all women to breastfeed 8–12 times a day and to wake the 
baby for feeds, if necessary. Breastfeeding is considered adequate, if the infant 
passes urine 6–8 times in 24 hours, sleeps for 2–3 hours after feeds and gains weight 
adequately after initial 7–10 days.
	
l Provide lactation/feeding support to mothers whose baby is visibly jaundiced. 
Supplementation is recommended only for dehydrated newborns and where weight 
loss from birth is >10%. Expressed breast milk is the preferred supplementation. 
	
l Routine supplementation with intravenous fluids, honey or dextrose water for 
newborns with jaundice is not recommended.
	
l Do not interrupt breastfeeding or breast milk for any jaundice. Provide reassurance that 
breastfeeding, nappy changing, and cuddles can usually continue during phototherapy.

There are now a number of vaccines available for childhood immunization. However, 
there are those which are considered essential for all children because the infections 
which they protect against are important national causes of childhood morbidity and 
mortality (Tables 19.4 and 19.5). Figure 19.6 shows vaccine schedule as per National

General Instructions
	
l Vaccination at birth implies as early as possible within 24 hours after birth or, at the

l Recommended age in weeks/months/years implies completed weeks/months/years.
	
l Screen for contraindications and precautions prior to administering any vaccine(s).
	
l Use recommended schedule to determine vaccines needed based on age, medical 
condition and risk factors. 
	
l Ensure proper storage of vaccines, maintaining the cold chain to preserve potency. 
Safeguarding potency is a collective responsibility spanning from manufacturing to 
administration. 
	
l Check each vaccine and diluent vial carefully for damage or contamination prior 
to use. Diluents have diverse compositions, so only use the diluent specified by the 
manufacturer for the particular vaccine and presentation. 
	
l Implement measures to store Look-Alike Sound-Alike (LASA) vaccines safely to 
avoid errors.

vaccines, they should be given either in the same session or on the same clinic day

Severe allergy or anaphylaxis or anaphylaxis-like reaction occurs rarely. Do not

l Anaphylaxis is a severe reaction and usually begins within minutes of vaccine 
administration. Early warning signs of anaphylaxis are localized swelling, erythema 
and urticaria around the injection site progressing to whole body and upper and/or 
lower respiratory tract obstruction (painless swelling of face and mouth, flushed, nasal 
congestion sneezing, tears, hoarseness, nausea, vomiting, difficult breathing, abdominal 
pain, wheezing, noisy, difficult breathing), collapse, low blood pressure, irregular weak 
pulse. In general the more severe the reaction, the more rapid the onset of anaphylaxis. 
Anaphylaxis Management
Management of anaphylactic reaction is as follows:
	 1.	Put the patient in recovery position and ensure patent airway
	 2.	Assess heart rate and respiratory rate and begin CPR, if necessary
	 3.	Administer Adrenaline (1:1000 solution) 0.01 mL/kg/dose (maximum 0.5 mL) deep 
IM in anterolateral thigh in the opposite limb. (If weight is unknown, approximate 
dose is <2 y 0.0625 mL; >2–5 y 0.125 mL; 6–11 y 0.25 mL; >11 y 0.5 mL). In very 
mild cases, adrenaline can be given subcutaneously. (Caution: Ensure Adrenaline 
is in-dated; discard if brown tinge)
	 4.	Set up IV access
	 5.	If the patient is conscious after adrenaline, lay patient flat and elevate legs, if tolerated
	 6.	Give oxygen
	 7.	Call for professional help and ambulance or any other available mode of transport. 
NEVER leave the patient alone

Reporting of Adverse Events following Immunization (AEFI)
Timely reporting aids in prompt investigation and intervention. Report all serious 
AEFI, signals and events associated with a newly introduced vaccine, AEFI that may 
have been caused by an immunization error, significant events of unexplained cause 
occurring within 30 days after vaccination and events causing significant parental or 
community concern. Report to appropriate authorities as per the Operational Guidelines 
for Surveillance and Response to AEFI (2024). 
Any healthcare provider (public or private) who comes across any AEFI has the 
responsibility to inform the district health authorities (District Immunization/RCH 
Officer) either directly or through a government medical officer. Serious/severe AEFIs are 
immediately notified to the Medical Officer of nearest government PHC, CHC and/or the 
District Immunization Officer (DIO) by quickest means of communication, e.g. telephone, 
SMS, WhatsApp, email, messenger, etc. Minor events are recorded in AEFI registers. All 
notified serious/severe AEFI should be documented on a Case reporting form (CRF) and 
submitted to SAFE-VAC, a web based application, as soon as possible within 24 hours. In 
addition, routine reporting, by keeping AEFI registers to continue. All ANMs of a block 
or planning unit should record all AEFIs (serious, severe and minor) informed to them 
from their respective areas on weekly basis and document them in an AEFI register. The 
MO I/C of the block or planning unit (PHCs, CHCs, etc.) should analyze the information 
regularly to look for any pattern or preventable programme errors.
AEFIs are further classified as per the following criterion:
Common minor AEFIs: Local reaction, fever and systemic symptoms can result 
as part of the immune response. In addition, some of the vaccines’ components 
(e.g. adjuvant, stabilizers or preservatives) can lead to reactions.
Severe AEFIs and serious AEFIs: AEFIs will be considered serious if they 
result in death, require hospitalization, result in persistent or significant disability/
incapacity or if a cluster (two or more cases) of AEFIs occur in a geographical 
area. An AEFI will be considered severe if it is not minor but does not result in 
death, hospitalization, or disability. “Severe” is used to describe the intensity of 
a specific event (as in mild, moderate, or severe). The event itself, however, may 
be of relatively minor medical significance. 
Furthermore, AEFI can be classified according to the cause, such as an AEFI could 
be caused by quality defects in the vaccine, or vaccine product related reaction or 
immunization error related reaction, immunization related stress or co-incidental event.

Immunization error-related reactions are caused by inappropriate vaccine handling, 
prescribing, or administration, and are thus preventable in nature. Factors/causes 
contributing to vaccine errors include the following:
	
l Transmission of infection by contaminated multidose vial or reuse of disposable 
syringes and needles
	
l Reconstitution errors/wrong vaccine preparation using incorrect diluent or expired 
vaccine 
	
l Use of reconstituted vaccine beyond stipulated time (e.g. 4 h for BCG and measles 
and 2 h for JE) or in subsequent sessions
	
l Injection administered at incorrect site: BCG given subcutaneously (SC), rabies, or 
hepatitis B vaccine given SC or DPT administered SC 
	
l Improper storage and transport of vaccine: Vaccines frozen during storage and 
administered can give rise to sterile abscess. These vaccines are also ineffective.
	
l Wrong patient (e.g. vaccine DPT2 given to a patient with a history of convulsions 
with DPT1) 
	
l Contraindication is ignored: Live vaccine administered to an immunosuppressed subject
	
l Immunization anxiety-related reaction: An AEFI arising from anxiety about the 
immunization, e.g. vasovagal syncope in an adolescent following vaccination. The 
anxiety may spread to community too, at times
	
l Coincidental event: An AEFI that is caused by something other than the vaccine 
product, immunization error, or immunization anxiety, e.g. fever after vaccination 
(temporal association) and malarial parasite isolated from blood.
Immunization in special circumstances
	 1.	Immunization in preterm infants: In general, all vaccines may be administered 
as per schedule according to the chronological age irrespective of birth weight or 
period of gestation. Very LBW/preterm babies can be given immunization if they 
are stable otherwise.
	 2.	Children receiving corticosteroids: Children receiving oral corticosteroids in high 
doses (Prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day) for more than 14 days should not receive live 
virus vaccines until the steroid has been discontinued for at least 1 month. Killed 
vaccines are safe but may not be completely effective in such situations. Patients on 
topical or inhaled steroids should not be denied their age-appropriate vaccine. Avoid 
live vaccines during therapy with immunosuppressants other than corticosteroids 
unless benefits outweigh risks. OPV should not be given to household contacts 
(<6 years age) of children on chemotherapy during routine immunization/pulse polio 
days to decrease any inadvertent risk from shedding of vaccine virus.
	 3.	Children with asplenia or hyposplenia (resulting from sickle cell anaemia or 
radiation therapy) or awaiting splenectomy: Immunization with pneumococcal 
(both conjugate and polysaccharide), Hib, typhoid and meningococcal vaccine 
should be given in addition to routine vaccination. In elective splenectomy, initiate 
vaccination with these 2 weeks prior to splenectomy. In emergency splenectomy, 
vaccinate 2 weeks after splenectomy. All live vaccines may be safely given.

1090    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 4.	Vaccination in children with HIV infection: Children infected with HIV are 
vulnerable to severe, recurrent or unusual infections by vaccine preventable 
pathogens. Immune response may be suboptimal as it depends on the degree of 
immunodeficiency at that point of time. Vaccination is usually safe and effective 
early in infancy before HIV infection causes severe immune suppression. Immunity 
to measles, tetanus and hepatitis B wanes faster than other antigens. Live vaccines 
are recommended in asymptomatic HIV-infected children except BCG and OPV. 
However, in the symptomatic child, all live vaccines are forbidden but at times 
measles/MMR/varicella vaccines may be considered on individual merit (if CD4+ 
count >15%). Yellow fever vaccine is contraindicated in both asymptomatic and 
symptomatic children. Post vaccination regular monitoring of seroconversion is 
desirable for killed vaccines in an HIV-infected child. 
	 5.	Minor illness: For example, fever, diarrhoea, respiratory infections and 
malnutrition should not be construed as contraindications to immunization.

CEREBRAL PALSY
Cerebral palsy is a group of non-progressive neurological condition affecting body 
movements and posture, caused by injury to the developing brain. Overall, cerebral 
Table 19.7.  (Continued)

1092    Standard Treatment Guidelines
palsy represents a heterogeneous clinical syndrome rather than a single disease. 
Although considered non-progressive, the clinical manifestations may change over 
time with interplay of brain maturity, muscle strength and coordination, bone length, 
formation of secondary deformities and contractures as the child grows older. Cerebral 
palsy is related to brain damage, so there are several associated problems in such 
individuals. Intellectual disabilities, learning difficulties, visual, hearing or speech 
impairment, seizures, and imperfect sensory prehension may additionally impair their 
physical and functional capabilities.
SALIENT FEATURES
The clinical manifestation in cerebral palsy depends on its type: 
	
l Spastic: Predominant type with hypertonia, hyperreflexia, clonus and spasticity as 
the key features. Depending upon the body region involved, the spastic type may 
be differentiated into broad categories of hemiplegia, diplegia or quadriplegia.
	
l Athetoid (extrapyramidal or dyskinetic): Characteristics are uncontrollable and 
writhing movements of certain body parts, involuntary contractions leading to limb 
positioning in fixed postures, and can also involve muscles in the oropharyngeal 
region, leading to feeding difficulties and speech abnormalities.
	
l Ataxic: Loss of balance and tremors accompany voluntary movements. Usually 
presents with generalized hypotonia. 
	
l Mixed type: Symptoms of more than one type of cerebral palsy.

l Evaluate for other neurological deficits (mental sub-normality, learning disability, 
hearing, vision, squint, seizures, speech and swallowing difficulties), severity of all 
deficits and presence of complications (contractures, dislocation, demineralization, etc.).
	
l Functional evaluation is done using Gross Motor Function Classification Scale 
(GMFCS), a 5-level classification. It is based on self-initiated movements, with 
emphasis on sitting, transfers and mobility. The classification takes into account the 
need for hand-held mobility devices (such as walkers, crutches, or canes) or wheeled 
mobility, and quality of movement. 
	
l Multidisciplinary management is done by a team comprising of paediatrician, 
orthopaedic surgeon, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, clinical psychologist, 
etc. The associated conditions require direct medical and therapeutic interventions 
from other medical specialties. 
	
l The goal is to maximize person’s independence, self-reliability and community 
engagement. Early diagnosis and intervention are important.
Non-invasive 
Physiotherapy 
To achieve mobility and functional independence – gait and balance training, muscle 
strengthening and stretching, functional positioning and posture correction, etc. after

taking into account the unique physical capabilities as well as limitations, the cognitive 
maturity and age of the patient. Parents need to be instructed under supervision a series 
of exercises designed to prevent the development of contractures.
Occupational therapy 
	
l For improving the existing abilities of the individual, his/her adaptation to the 
environment and bring out the best possible functional performance – specific 
techniques such as constraint induced manual therapy to promote use of affected part 
by restraining the unaffected part and sensory integration therapy (ability to receive, 
interpret and act on stimulations or inputs received through sensory receptors). 
	
l There is an increasing use of robotic devices for assisted movements and 
rehabilitation of both upper and lower limbs in cerebral palsy. 
Speech and language interventions by speech specialist
Augmentative (related to developing and enhancing any of the speech capabilities 
the individual possesses) and alternative (replaces the speech completely, e.g. use of 
facial expressions, gestures, etc.). The speech specialist also facilitates feeding and 
swallowing interventions in individuals with such disabilities.
Psychological support: Psychological support is provided to help individuals with 
cerebral palsy cope with cognitive, behavioral, emotional, and psychosocial limitations. 
These support sessions can be planned individually or in groups based on the specific 
needs of the individual.
Eating, drinking and swallowing difficulties 
Develop an individualized plan taking into account the understanding, knowledge 
and skills of parents, caregivers for children and young people with cerebral palsy for 
managing eating, drinking and swallowing difficulties. 
Special education: Special educators help them using the appropriate teaching method 
suiting the physical and learning abilities of individuals with cerebral palsy.

Treat appropriately for muscle spasticity, athetosis and seizures (for details see 
Chapter 9). Associated disorders need treatment at the same time when spasticity 
treatment is in progress. 
For dystonia Tab. Trihexyphenidyl with 0.25–2 mg twice or thrice daily; dose gradually 
titrated depending upon the clinical response; can be used to control generalized dystonia. 
(Caution: Avoid during fever to reduce the risk of of malignant hyperthermia.) 
Or
Tab. Baclofen can be used for generalized dystonia and/or spasticity. Start with lower 
dose of 1–2 mg in children >12 years and 5 mg in older children. The dose can be 
gradually titrated once or twice per week to achieve maintenance dose of up to 10 mg in

1094    Standard Treatment Guidelines
2–5 years, and 15 mg in older children. (Caution: Monitor for sedation and respiratory 
depression at higher doses). It may not be effective in all the cases. In selected cases 
associated with diffuse spasticity, intrathecal baclofen (ITB) pump has shown some 
beneficial effects.
Few patients with severe painful dystonias may also require drugs like Gabapentin, 
benzodiazepines like Clobazam and Clonidine.
Intramuscular botulinum toxin A injections can be considered in select patients with 
localized or segmental spasticity, when administered by experienced healthcare 
professionals, to reduce spasticity in local muscle groups. 
Surgical (Invasive)
Surgical interventions to improve the overall mobility, range of motion and body 
alignment in cerebral palsy individuals after reduction in spasticity only: osteotomies 
for correction of bone deformities and restoring alignment; for enhancing range of 
motion – release of contractures, muscle/tendon transfers, muscle/tendon lengthening 
and selective dorsal rhizotomy spinal surgery for reducing spasticity and judicious use 
of orthotic splints and assistive devices (e.g. Rollator) can also help improve function.
Parent/Patient education
	
l Cerebral palsy is a static encephalopathy and occurs due to the damage (insult/
injury) to developing (maturing) brain (embryo to 5 years). Various risk factors 
present in mother and father of a child having cerebral palsy, e.g. repeated abortions, 
malnourishment, drug abuse, young age, poor prenatal care etc.
	
l Awareness, early diagnosis and intervention is associated with better outcomes. 
Suspect and seek assistance in child with development delays – if a baby remains dull 
most of the time and has less movements of limbs and head and/or cannot move the 
limb in a purposeful manner, instead it just goes in an unorderly manner (usually in 
one particular direction only), thumb in palm and/or persistent fisting beyond 2 months 
of age; reduced head circumference; retarded growth, delayed social smile, abnormal 
turning of neck and head; asymmetry of body posture, movement and reflexes.
	
l Rehabilitation for children with special needs consists of frequent sessions of 
physiotherapy, occupational therapy, cognitive therapy, and special education. These 
interventions aim to improve the quality of life of children and should be provided 
by a multidisciplinary team of experts. Family education and involvement are also 
crucial components of the rehabilitation process. 
	
l Provide information about prognosis at some stage that the child may not improve 
further and may have harmful spasticity, ataxia or movement disorders. Certain 
cases, especially those who have been overlooked or neglected, may develop 
contractures, dislocations, etc.

FLUID AND ELECTROLYTES
Babies requiring IV fluid therapy
	
l Babies with lethargy and refusal to feed
	
l Moderate to severe breathing difficulty
	
l Babies with shock
	
l Neonates with severe asphyxia
	
l Abdominal distension with bilious or blood-stained vomiting
Fluid and electrolyte therapy is divided into three phases:
	 1.	Correction of pre-existing deficits. The losses, via renal or extra-renal route, should 
be estimated and corrected as soon as possible; for example, rehydration therapy 
for diarrhoeal dehydration.
	 2.	Provision of maintenance requirements for normal metabolism.
	 3.	Correction of ongoing losses. These may occur via the gastrointestinal tract 
through losses (as in diarrhoea, vomiting, etc.) or removal (suction, aspiration, 
etc.). Replacement of such losses should be similar in type and amount to the fluid 
being lost.
Out of these three phases, we shall discuss the maintenance requirements here. 
Correction of pre-existing deficits and correction of ongoing losses shall be discussed, 
wherever relevant (see section on Diarrhoea).
Maintenance requirements in children
A guideline for estimating daily fluid and electrolytes requirement in a normal 
child under normal conditions is: water, 100 mL/100 kcal/day; sodium, 1–3 mEq/ 
100 kcal/day; potassium, 1–2 mEq/100 kcal/day. Hence, the fluid requirement based 
on caloric requirement for different weight groups can be calculated as follows:

Conditions that increase fluid requirement

1098    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 1.	Anaemia due to decreased RBC production: It may be due to:
	
l Deficiency of one or more of haematopoietic nutrients, i.e. iron, folic acid, 
and vitamin B12. Deficiency of other nutrients such as copper, protein, etc., is 
uncommon.
	
l Bone marrow infiltration due to abnormal cells as in acute and chronic 
leukaemia, disseminated malignant diseases, myelofibrosis, etc.
	
l Bone marrow aplasia – congenital and acquired aplastic anaemia (severe and 
moderately severe) and pure red cells aplasia such as Diamond-Blackfan 
syndrome, transient erythroblastopenia of childhood.
	 2.	Anaemia due to increased RBC destruction: Haemolytic anaemia. Commonest 
haemolytic anaemia seen in this part of the country is thalassaemia major. Others 
include sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, haemolytic 
anaemia, malaria, etc.
	 3.	Anaemia due to excessive blood loss: Usually in such cases, the site of bleeding is 
obvious. For example, massive oesophageal variceal bleeding, rectal polyps, etc. In 
cases like ankylostomiasis, Meckel diverticulum, etc., there may be only occult bleed.
Clinical approach in a child with anaemia
Careful history and physical examination provide useful clues towards the likely cause 
of anaemia, thereby guiding the most appropriate laboratory tests required to avoid 
unnecessary expenses in diagnosis, for example,
	
l Nutritional iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) is uncommon below 6 months of age in 
a term-born child with normal birth weight. IDA is more common in infants and 
children who are on predominant milk-based diet despite adequate complementary 
nutrition (predominant milk based diet).
	
l Most children with beta thalassemia major are normal at birth and usually start 
becoming anaemic between 6 and 18 months of age. (For details see chapter 4 on 
Blood Disorders).
	
l Constitutional aplastic anaemia (Fanconi pancytopenia) presents between 5 and 
10 years, whereas congenital pure red cell aplasia can manifest in the first few months. 
	
l Megaloblastic anaemia occurs in infants and toddlers, preschool children with 
prolonged exclusive breastfeeding by undernourished mothers. 
	
l Presence of splenomegaly and hepatomegaly suggests the diagnosis of either 
haemolytic anaemia or leukaemia (usually there is associated lymphadenopathy) or 
anaemia of chronic infection/inflammation. 
	
l Presence of petechial and/or purpuric spots is suggestive of concomitant thrombo­
cytopenia and points towards the diagnosis of acute leukaemia, aplastic anaemia or 
megaloblastic anaemia.

Initial investigations to be carried out in cases of anaemia – estimation of Hb%, 
TLC, DLC and platelet count, examination of peripheral blood smear for RBC size 
and shapes, anisopoikilocytosis, presence of immature cells and haemoparasites,

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1099
reticulocyte count. Currently, most of the laboratories use electronic cell counters for 
haematological investigations which give additional useful information such as MCV, 
MCH, MCHC, etc.
The following important information can be gathered from the above investigations:
	
l Type of anaemia on the basis of cell size, such as microcytic (MCV < 80 fl), 
normocytic and macrocytic (MCV > 90 fl), and on the basis of Hb content, 
i.e. hypochromic or normochromic.
	
l Associated thrombocytopenia and/or neutropenia (bicytopenia or pancytopenia) is 
suggestive of aplastic anaemia, megaloblastic anaemia, bone marrow infiltration 
due to leukaemia, etc. 
	
l Increased, normal or decreased reticulocyte count is suggestive whether anaemia is 
due to increased destruction or decreased production of RBCs.
The following section describes the differential diagnosis of cases of anaemia 
according to preliminary investigation results. 
1. Microcytic hypochromic anaemia 
Two important causes are:
	 i.	In iron deficiency anemia (IDA), the reticulocyte count is typically normal or 
mildly elevated. 
	 ii.	In beta thalassemia major, the reticulocyte count is typically elevated and 
can range from 4% to 6% or higher. Peripheral smear also shows target cells 
and numerous nucleated RBCs. Elevated foetal haemoglobin (HbF) on blood 
electrophoresis confirms the diagnosis. Lead poisoning, pyridoxine-responsive 
anaemia, sideroblastic anaemia and copper deficiency are rare causes of microcytic 
hypochromic anemia. (For details, see Chapter 4.)
2. Macrocytic normochromic anaemia 
	 i.	Megaloblastic anaemia of B12 and folate deficiency is common and may have 
associated neutropenia and/or thrombocytopenia. The reticulocyte count is usually 
low. Bone marrow examination reveals megaloblastic changes. 
	 ii.	Other causes of macrocytic anaemia are liver diseases, hypothyroidism, thiamine 
deficiency and some inborn errors of metabolism.
3. Normocytic normochromic anaemia 
This group comprises a large number of causes:
	 i.	Congenital or acquired aplastic anaemia – usually have macrocytic anaemia 
or pancytopenia and decreased reticulocyte count. Bone marrow aspiration 
or biopsy is confirmatory. 
	 ii.	Bone marrow infiltration such as leukaemia and other neoplasms, storage disorders, 
myelofibrosis, etc. Diagnosis is confirmed by bone marrow examination.
	iii.	Haemolytic anaemia – such as immune haemolysis, hereditary spherocytosis, 
G6PD deficiency, etc. Reticulocyte count is increased. 
	iv.	Anaemia resulting from acute blood loss.
See also Anaemia in Chapter 1 and Anaemia in Pregnancy in Chapter 15.

1100    Standard Treatment Guidelines
IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA (IDA)
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Iron deficiency anaemia commonly occurs in children due to nutritional 
deficiency. However, IDA is uncommon in term breastfed children but 
prematurity, perinatal blood loss or cow milk feeding may lead to IDA in infancy.
	
l It is characterized by pallor, irritability, pica and absence of organomegaly and 
lymphadenopathy (10–15% may have mild splenomegaly).

After the period of exclusive breastfeeding (6 months), cereal-based diet should be 
added. Encourage green leafy vegetables and fruits.

Severe anaemia (Hb <6 g/dL)
Blood transfusion to all children with Hb ≤4 g/dL and children with Hb 4–6 g/dL with 
any of the following: dehydration, shock, impaired consciousness, heart failure, fast 
breathing, very high parasitaemia (malaria) (>10% of RBCs)
	 1.	Give packed cell transfusion, usually 10 mL/kg usually given over 4–6 hours 
while monitoring for signs of heart failure. One unit increases haemoglobin 1 g/
dL without active bleeding or haemolysis. In states of acute blood loss like trauma, 
whole blood 20 mL/kg may be given over 3–4 hours under close monitoring 
if packed cells are not readily available (for details, see Appendix XIII). The 
hematocrit rise after whole blood transfusion is less than packed cell transfusion. 
	 2.	Inj. Frusemide (1 mg/kg/dose) may be administered if there is evidence of 
cardiovascular overload.
Mild anaemia
Initiation of therapy. Oral ferrous salts (sulphate, gluconate, etc.) are the preferred 
therapeutic iron preparation.
Syr./Drops/Tab. Ferrous Sulphate/Ferrous gluconate/Ferrous fumarate 
2–3 mg/kg/day of elemental iron in two to three divided doses to be given between 
meals for 8–12 weeks after normal Hb concentration for age is achieved. (Caution: 
Milk or milk products, tea or any other calcium preparation should particularly be 
avoided 1 hour before or after the drug.)
Note: Usual iron preparations have 35–50 mg elemental iron per 5 mL of syrup or 
per mL of drops. Elemental content of various ferrous salts is Ferrous sulphate 20%, 
Ferrous gluconate 12%, Ferrous fumarate 33% and Colloidal iron 50%. Older children 
who can take tablets be given Iron-Folic acid tablets and Tab Vitamin B12.
Response to therapy. Decreased irritability and improved appetite is seen in 
12–24 hours. Reticulocytosis is seen within 2–3 days and rise in Hb is noticeable by 
5th-7th day. Rate of rise of Hb is 0.25–0.4 g/dL/day (daily or even weekly estimation 
of Hb% is not required). Usually, normal Hb levels are obtained by about 8–12 weeks.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1101
If the response is inadequate, check for the prescribed dose, compliance, presence 
of diarrhoea and/or malabsorption, infections (particularly urinary tract infection 
and tuberculosis), occult blood loss or β-thalassaemia trait which may have been 
misdiagnosed as IDA. In case of no improvement in Hb levels after 3 months, refer the 
child to FRU/district hospital for further investigations.
Modification or step-up therapy. The response after parenteral iron is not rapid as 
oral iron. Parenteral iron therapy is not preferred in children. However, it is necessary 
if there is interference to absorption of oral iron, chronic diarrhoea or malabsorption, 
occult bleeding from GIT when oral iron therapy may not maintain desired Hb. 
Parenteral iron therapy may also be used in severely anaemic child not likely to take 
oral therapy because of socioeconomic reasons.
Patient/Parent education
	
l IDA occurs generally due to dietary deficiency of iron. Once the diet is modified, 
the patient should stick to that diet.
	1.	IFA supplementation programme: In children (6 months to 5 years) 20 mg 
elemental iron Plus Folic acid 100 mcg biweekly; 6–10 years 45 mg elemental 
iron plus Folic acid 400 mcg weekly; adolescents (10–19 years) weekly dose of 
100 mg elemental iron plus Folic acid 500 mcg weekly.
	2.	Age-specific deworming for children 12 months and above. In adolescents, 
bi-annual deworming.
	
l Iron medicine should be taken between meals and never along with milk/milk 
products or tea. 
	
l Intake of iron medicine usually causes harmless black discolouration of the teeth 
and stools. The teeth discolouration can be prevented by rinsing the mouth with 
water after doses.
	
l Increase in Hb levels with iron therapy will take approximately 5–7 days and about 
12 weeks for desired normal Hb level to be achieved.

PROTEIN ENERGY MALNUTRITION (PEM)
Nutritional marasmus and kwashiorkor are two extreme forms of malnutrition. Such 
extreme forms are rare; most cases suffer from mild and moderate nutritional deficit.

1102    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Milder forms may just present with failure to thrive, i.e. decreased rate of weight gain. 
	
l Marasmus is characterized by gross wasting of muscle and subcutaneous tissues 
resulting in emaciation, marked stunting and no oedema. 
	
l Markedly retarded growth, psychomotor changes and oedema of dependent parts 
are the three essential clinical features of kwashiorkor.
	
l Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) is defined by very low weight-for-height/
length (WFH) (Z score below 3SD), and/or a mid-upper arm circumference 
(MUAC) <115 mm and/or bilateral oedema and/or presence of visible wasting. 
SAM increases significantly the risk of death in children under 5 years of age and 
increases the case fatality rate in children suffering from diarrhoea and pneumonia.
	
l PEM is usually associated with:
	– Anaemia due to iron, protein, vitamin B12 or folic acid deficiency 
	– Xerophthalmia due to vitamin A deficiency and 
	– Other micronutrient deficiencies including magnesium, copper, zinc, vitamins 
B, C, D and K
If any of the following medical complications, refer immediately to Nutritional 
Rehabilitation centre (NRC):
	
l Poor appetite, visible severe wasting, oedema of both feet
	
l Severe palmar pallor, any sick young infant (<2 months old), lethargy, drowsiness, 
unconsciousness, continually irritable and restless, any respiratory distress, signs 
suggesting severe dehydration in a child with diarrhoea, hypothermia/fever, 
extensive skin/eye involvement.

1104    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Indian Academy of Paediatrics (IAP) takes a weight of more than 80% of expected 
for age as normal. Grades of malnutrition are: Grade I (71–80%), Grade II (61–70%), 
Grade III (51–60%) and Grade IV (≤50%) weight of expected value for that age. 
Alphabet k is post-fixed in the presence of oedema.

1.	Mild-to-moderate undernutrition. Mild and moderately undernourished children 
are best treated in their own home surroundings. Domiciliary treatment of 
malnourished children by their mother is economical, offers in-built advantage 
of practical health education and is associated with minimal recurrence risk.
	 2.	The parents should be advised to increase the food intake of the child by all available 
means. The child should receive an adequate amount of calories and protein in the 
diet, which should be prepared from the locally available, inexpensive foods.
	 3.	The child should be kept under surveillance by using a growth chart and effort 
should be made so that he does not slip down to severe malnutrition. Carry out 
appetite tests at each visit, particularly for those who do not gain weight steadily.
Severe malnutrition
Severely wasted children, those with oedema need hospitalization. Other indications 
for admission in an undernourished child are persistent vomiting, severe dehydration, 
severe diarrhoea, fever, hypothermia, shock, systemic infection, child not alert, very 
weak, apathetic, unconscious, convulsions, severe anaemia, jaundice, bleeding, age 
less than 6 months, or persistent loss of appetite. Admit the child, if any other general 
sign that a clinician thinks requires admission for further assessment or care or if the 
caregiver is unable to take care of the child at home. Those with severe stunting alone 
may be managed in the community. Hospital management of severe malnutrition is 
summarized in Table 19.12. Initial treatment involves managing complications. The 
aim is to treat complications and stabilize the child.
There are 10 essential steps in two phases – an initial stabilization phase and a 
longer rehabilitation phase (Fig. 19.7). The focus of initial management is to prevent 
death while stabilizing the child.

1108    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Important things NOT to do 
	
l Do not give IV fluids routinely. IV fluids can easily cause fluid overload and heart 
failure. Only give IV fluids to children with signs of shock. Oral feeds/fluids can be 
safely given through nasogastric tube in a lethargic child instead of IV fluids.
	
l Do not give diuretics to treat oedema. The oedema will go away with proper feeding. 
Giving diuretics will worsen child’s electrolyte imbalance and may cause death.
	
l Do not give high-protein formula. Almost all severely malnourished children have 
infections, impaired liver and intestinal function. Because of these problems, they 
are unable to tolerate even the usual amount of dietary protein.
	
l Do not give iron during the stabilization phase. Add iron only after the child has 
been on catch-up formula for 2 days (usually during week 2). Giving iron early in 
treatment has been associated with free radical generation and may interfere with 
the body’s immune mechanisms against proliferating bacteria.
Treat other associated conditions
Malaria, tuberculosis (see respective section), suspect HIV if child has also other 
problems like persistent diarrhoea, oral thrush, pneumonia, parotid swelling or 
generalized lymphadenopathy. Investigate and follow HIV guidelines.
Persistent diarrhoea: Diarrhoea is common in severe malnutrition but with cautious 
refeeding, it should subside during the first week. In the rehabilitation phase, the poorly 
formed loose stools are not a cause for concern provided the child’s weight gain is 
satisfactory. If the child has persistent diarrhoea, screen for non-intestinal infections

Discharge criteria: For all infants and children, it is 15% weight gain and no signs of illness. 
Child has good appetite, no oedema, consistent weight gain (>5 g/kg/day for 3 consecutive days),

NUTRITIONAL RICKETS
Rickets is defective mineralization of growing skeleton caused by deficiency of 
vitamin D characterized by skeletal deformities like genu valgum/genu varum, 
broadening of wrists, susceptibility to fractures, weakness, hypotonia and disturbances 
in growth. Most often it is nutritional (lack of exposure to sunlight and inadequate 
dietary intake) and occurs between 2 months and 2 years of age. Radiological picture 
shows that epiphyseal growth plate is increased in thickness, cupped with hazy 
metaphyseal borders. Serum calcium is generally normal or low, phosphate is low or 
normal and alkaline phosphatase is raised in nutritional rickets.

l Encourage the child to play outdoors/increase exposure to sunlight.
	
l Enhance dietary sources of vitamin D – dairy products, egg and fish liver oil.

1.	Vitamin D 60,000 IU bi-weekly for 5 doses in children (12 months to 18 years) 
followed by 400–600 IU daily as maintenance dose. Daily dose is preferred.

Vitamin D (2000 IU/day) is recommended for treatment of nutritional rickets and 
symptomatic vitamin D deficiency in infants, 3000 IU/day or its equivalent in 
weekly/monthly bolus doses may be given in children older than 1 year. The above 
therapy should be given for a minimum of 12 weeks. 
	 2.	Repeat X-ray wrist after 4 weeks. If the response is positive, i.e. healing line of 
rickets is seen on X-ray, continue oral vitamin D 400–600 IU/day for another 
6 weeks. If no response to therapy after 4 weeks refer to a higher centre for 
evaluation of non-nutritional rickets.
	
	Note: Use of intramuscular Vitamin D is not recommended for routine use unless 
in cases of suspected malabsorption or severe malnutrition where compliance to 
weekly doses and follow-up is questionable. 
	 3.	Calcium intake of 50–-75 mg/kg/day (not exceeding 500 mg/day) must be ensured either 
through diet or supplementation in combination with vitamin D in <12 years old).

l Discourage early cessation of breastfeeding. 
	
l Consumption of dairy products, green leafy vegetables which are rich in calcium 
should be emphasized. Vitamin D intake from food products is limited unless fortified.
	
l Exposure to sunlight is beneficial for a child with rickets. 
	
l No special type of oil is required for massage. 
	
l Most of the deformities improve in the due course of time.

PICA
Pica involves repeated and chronic ingestion of non-nutrient substances including 
mud, plaster, paint, earth, clay, etc. Most of the time, it is self-limiting and represents 
manifestations of family disorganization, poor supervision and affectional neglect.

l Pica below 2 years does not need any intervention.
	
l Children with pica are at an increased risk of lead poisoning, iron deficiency, 
bezoars, and parasitic infections. They should be investigated for these problems 
and if present, treated suitably.
	
l Education, guidance and counselling of the family.
	
l The child has to be kept occupied in other tasks and provided with environmental 
stimulation.

BREATH HOLDING SPELLS
Paroxysmal self-limiting events occur in up to 5% of healthy children and are rare prior 
to 6 months of age, peak at about 2 years of age and abate by 5 years of age.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Child starts crying (precipitated by an upsetting event such as anger, fear or injury) 
and then holds breath in expiration followed by a colour change (blue or pale). 
	
l Spell may resolve spontaneously, or the child may lose consciousness and 
may have convulsions. Normal breathing and alertness are resumed within a minute.

Reassurance. Explain that attacks are harmless and always abort by itself.
Immediate measures
	 1.	Prevent injury during the episode. Assist the child to the floor and have him lie flat.
	 2.	If loss of consciousness occurs, place the patient on the side to protect against aspiration.
	 3.	Maintain patent oral airway but do not start CPR.
	 4.	Do not shake the baby, splash water or put anything in the mouth.
Long-term measures
There are NO prophylactic medications. Treat iron deficiency if associated.
Refer to a higher centre
	
l If the child is less than 3 months or unconsciousness lasts for more than 1 minute.
	
l If attacks are too frequent or seizure disorder or cyanotic spell is suspected.
Parent education 
	
l Avoid precipitating factors such as exhaustion, hunger or injury. Do not give toys or 
tasks beyond the child’s abilities and try to distract.
	
l Avoid excessive rules and restrictions. Try to remove unnecessary frustrations.

PRIMARY NOCTURNAL ENURESIS
Primary nocturnal enuresis should be regarded as a variation in the development of 
normal bladder control. The most common cause in primary enuresis is inappropriate

1114    Standard Treatment Guidelines
toilet training. Three common aetiological factors are: sleep arousal disorder (the child 
is not awakened by the sensation of a full bladder), bladder factors (low nocturnal 
bladder capacity and/or an overactive bladder, emptying reflexes are not inhibited 
during sleep), or nocturnal polyuria (reduced ADH). Constipation may be an additional 
aggravating condition. Psychological causes may be found in secondary nocturnal 
enuresis and 3% children have organic pathology such as obstructive uropathy or UTI.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Primary nocturnal enuresis is the recurrent involuntary passage of urine during 
sleep by a child aged 5 years or older, who has never achieved consistent night-
time dryness. Primary nocturnal enuresis two sub-types – without daytime 
symptoms and with daytime symptoms (urgency, frequency, or daytime wetting). 
	
l In primary nocturnal enuresis, the child has never been dry at night while in 
secondary nocturnal enuresis child has been continent for at least 6 months before 
the child begins to wet again. 
	
l Children are labelled enuretic in case of regular (more than twice per week for 
3 consecutive months) wetting persists beyond the age of 5 years.

Non-pharmacological (Effective in 30% cases)
	
l Rule out organic causes. Restrict fluid intake and avoid caffeinated beverages in 
the evening.
	
l Bladder exercises:
	
(i)	 Hold urine as long as possible during the day. 
	 (ii)	 Practice repeated starting and stopping the stream at the toilet bowl.
	 (iii)	 Practice getting up from bed and going to the bathroom at bedtime before sleep.

Indicated only in children >7 years of age where sufficient trial of non-pharmacological 
management has failed or if the child is having social problems due to it or rapid-onset 
improvement is needed. 
Tab. Desmopressin 0.1–0.5 mg at bedtime. 
Or
Tab. Imipramine: 6–8 years (25 mg), 9–12 years (50 mg), >12 years (75 mg) once a 
day at bedtime. Success rate 30–60%, relapse rate 90%.
Assessment of response: The child has achieved 14 consecutive dry nights or a 90% 
improvement in the number of wet nights per week. Partial response: the child’s 
symptoms have improved but 14 consecutive dry nights or a 90% improvement in the 
number of wet nights per week has not been achieved.

WHEEZY CHILD
Wheezing is a clinical symptom present in asthma and other illnesses including 
bronchiolitis and other viral infections, foreign body inhalation, tuberculosis, pneumonia,

1116    Standard Treatment Guidelines
cystic fibrosis, immune deficiency, bronchomalacia, hypersensitivity pneumonia and 
conditions compressing the airways. The most common cause of recurrent wheezing in 
the first 5 years of life is viral infection and thereafter asthma. Sometimes children with 
pneumonia present with wheeze. The differential diagnosis of wheezing in a child under 
5 is detailed in Table 19.15. Wheezing in asthma is recurrent, gets worse in night and 
after exercise, seasonal and may be associated with other allergic illnesses like atopic 
dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, etc. (for details, see section on Bronchial Asthma in Chapter 
1). Asthma is usually a diagnosis of older age (>6 y) but may be diagnosed even in 
children younger than 5 years. However, viral infections associated wheeze is the most 
common cause of wheezing in a younger child (<5 y). Absence of family history and 
personal history of atopy with gradual decrease in frequency of episodes is seen in such 
transient wheezers who grow out of their wheezing episodes. Clinical features suggestive 
of other cause of wheezing are: neonatal onset, associated with difficulty in feeding, 
choking or vomiting, localized findings in chest or abnormality in cardiovascular system. 
The use of terminology like multi-trigger wheeze, transient wheeze and episodic 
viral wheeze was for diagnosis and better management of affected children. It may be 
difficult to classify all children with wheezing into one of these categories, including 
asthma. Therefore, a ‘symptom-based approach’ may be used to predict the probability 
of asthma in a younger child with wheezing. For example, a young child with 
wheezing which may occur 2–3 times a year and lasts <10 days/episode with symptom 
free between episodes is less likely to have asthma. In contrast, a young child with 
prolonged (>10 days) wheezing after a viral episode with intermittent cough or heavy 
breathing between episodes is more likely to evolve into asthma even when he/she may 
not be a persistent/late onset wheezer.
