Acute wheeze
Mild acute first or recurrent wheeze does not require any specific treatment. Children 
who are feeding well and do not have respiratory distress can be sent home on 
symptomatic treatment for fever and nasal block. However, parents must be explained 
the red flag signs so that they can bring the child immediately to hospital in case 
respiratory distress becomes severe and child is unable to feed.
Severe wheeze (Admit in emergency)
1. Severe bronchiolitis

Child should be nursed in a comfortable position, maybe in mother's lap. Monitoring 
should be frequent.

1.	Oxygen: A child in severe respiratory distress or SpO2 less than 92% requires 
oxygen in a non-threatening way. The oxygen Blow-by method (where oxygen is 
administered right in front of nostril or mouth) may be better than mask or hood if 
these make the child irritable.
	 2.	Intravenous fluids: Most of these children with severe distress cannot feed. Child 
should be kept well hydrated with intravenous fluids and under/over hydration 
should be avoided.
	 3.	There is an unpredictable response to bronchodilators in young wheezers. However, 
a trial of bronchodilators is given to children admitted with severe disease.
	
	Nebulized Adrenaline (0.1 mL to 0.5 mL/kg maximum 5 mL) is preferred in 
bronchiolitis. If there is response, it may be repeated on as and when basis. Frequency 
of nebulization is reduced, and oxygen is withdrawn when the child starts improving.
	 4.	There is no role of antibiotics and chest physiotherapy. No cough syrups or 
sedatives should be given.
2. Acute severe wheeze in recurrent wheeze
	 1.	It is treated the same way as bronchiolitis, except Salbutamol nebulization or MDI 
(100 μg/puff) with spacer may be used as bronchodilator in recurrent wheezer.
	
	Generally, 3 doses of Salbutamol given one every 20 minutes (0.15 mg/kg/dose 
Salbutamol add normal saline to make it 3 mL every dose). One dose of nebulization 
is equivalent to 4–5 doses given by MDI with spacer. 
	 2.	Very occasionally steroids may be required to treat very severe acute episode, 
particularly in a multi-trigger wheezer. Systemic steroids are preferred over inhaled 
in such situations. Tab. Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (or in equivalent dose any other 
steroid) may be used for a short course of 3–5 days.

1118    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Prophylaxis in recurrent wheezing

Protect from environmental triggers like dust, smoke, perfumes, deodorants, repellents, etc. 
Parents should be advised to follow these instructions irrespective of severity of disease.

If episodes are mild and infrequent, no prophylaxis is required. Each episode is treated 
as discussed above. However, prophylaxis to prevent recurrence may be needed if 
episodes are frequent (more than or once a month) and severe.
Prophylaxis in severe and frequent multi-trigger wheeze (MTW)
Inhaled corticosteroids (MDI Budesonide with spacer). If child shows a decrease in 
severity and frequency of episodes, stop treatment. If there is recurrence after stopping 
intermittent inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), a decision to give long-term ICS may be taken.
A multi-trigger wheezer with severe recurrent episodes and a family history of 
atopy or asthma may be labelled as asthma and treated accordingly.
Prophylaxis in severe and frequent episodic viral wheeze (EVW)
Intermittent Montelukast (Sachet) 4 mg/day, given for a week or so beginning with the 
onset of episode may be useful but may be less effective than ICS. Trial of ICS may 
be given as in MTW and followed up in the same way with decision for long-term 
depending on the response. For treatment of asthma, see Chapter 1.
ACUTE BRONCHIOLITIS
Acute bronchiolitis is an acute respiratory tract infection commonly caused by viral 
pathogens. The commonest aetiological agent is Respiratory syncytial virus. Other 
viruses include rhinovirus, parainfluenza, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus 
and bocavirus. Mycoplasma is more frequently implicated in older children with 
bronchiolitis. Bronchiolitis commonly occurs in infants under 6 months of age. Peak 
occurrence is during winter and early spring.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Coryzal prodrome lasting 1–3 days, followed by persistent cough and either 
tachypnoea or chest recession (or both) and either wheeze or crackles on chest 
auscultation (or both). Associated fever, usually below 39°C, occurs in around 
30% of cases along with poor feeding (typically after 3–5 days of illness). With 
increasing severity of illness, there may be lower chest indrawing, excessive 
crying due to hypoxaemia, cyanosis and respiratory failure. Young infants with 
this disease (in particular those under 6 weeks of age) may present with apnoea 
without other clinical signs. Fever occurs in around 30% of cases, usually less 
than 39°C. There may be a history of viral upper respiratory infections in other 
family members in the recent past.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1119
	
l The chest may appear hyperexpanded and may be hyper-resonant to percussion. 
Wheezes and fine crackles may be heard throughout the lungs.
	
l Mild disease is characterized by rapid respiration, no chest indrawing, no problem in 
feeding, no clinical evidence of hypoxaemia and oxygen saturation is more than 92%.
	
l Severe disease is characterized by chest indrawing, difficulty in feeding, clinical 
evidence of hypoxaemia, lethargy, convulsion, oxygen saturation <92%.
	
l Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment, considering age, seasonal patterns, typical 
presentation and physical examination. Blood tests and radiological imaging are 
generally unnecessary. However, in severe cases, investigations may be warranted 
to rule out alternate diagnoses like bacterial pneumonia, congenital heart disease, 
or sepsis. These may include arterial blood gas analysis, complete blood count, 
C-reactive protein, serum electrolytes and chest radiography. Assessing lactate 
dehydrogenase (LDH) concentration in nasal wash fluid is suggested for gauging 
bronchiolitis severity. While viral identification does not significantly impact 
management, in hospitals, tests like antigen detection, immunofluorescence, 
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and culture of respiratory secretions can be 
conducted to curb antibiotic misuse and prevent nosocomial transmission.

Immediately refer babies and children with bronchiolitis for emergency ICU care, if 
they have any of the following:
	
l Apnoea (observed or reported), baby or child looks seriously unwell, severe 
respiratory distress (grunting, marked chest recession, or a respiratory rate of over 
70 breaths/minute), central cyanosis, convulsions, altered sensorium.
	
l Babies and children with bronchiolitis to be admitted to hospital if they have 
any of the following: a respiratory rate of over 60 breaths/minute, difficulty with 
breastfeeding or inadequate oral fluid intake (50–75% of usual volume, taking into 
account of risk factors) and persistent oxygen saturation of <92%, when breathing air.

l For associated nasal block, normal saline drops in both nostrils as and when 
required, especially before feeds and use of home remedies (ginger, honey, tulsi) for 
control of cough and plenty of liquids orally.
	
l For hospitalized patients, elevation at 30–40 degrees and neck slightly extended.
	
l To be nursed in a comfortable environment.
	
l Ensure adequate hydration by allowing small aliquots of oral or nasogastric fluids 
or intravenous fluids if the child is not able to take orally.
	
l Hand washing and standard precautions should be practiced while nursing children 
with bronchiolitis.

Treatment of mild disease (ambulatory treatment at home)
No antibiotics.
Syr. Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg 4–6 hourly for fever (for details, see section on Fever 
in Chapter 1).

1120    Standard Treatment Guidelines
If the patient shows overall improvement with no evidence of chest indrawing, cyanosis 
and difficulty in feeding, continue treatment as above. If there is partial improvement, 
the patient should be called again after 2 days or earlier if patient deteriorates for 
reassessment.
If there is no improvement or deterioration at any time during the illness, the patient 
should be treated as a severe disease.
Severe disease.
	 1.	Humidified oxygen administration is recommended for babies under 6 weeks or 
children of any age with underlying health conditions if their oxygen saturation is 
less than 90% as monitored with pulse oximetry and persistently less than 92%. 
This can be administered via an oxygen hood or nasal catheter. 
	
	Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) in case of impending respiratory failure. 
	
	Note: Avoid routinely conducting upper airway suctioning unless infants or 
children exhibit respiratory distress, feeding challenges due to upper airway 
secretions, or present with apnoea.
	 2.	Give fluids by nasogastric or orogastric tube in babies and children with 
bronchiolitis if they cannot take enough fluid by mouth. Intravenous (isotonic) 
fluids, if the child is not able to feed. Avoid use of hypotonic fluids as they may 
increase the risk of hyponatraemia. 
	 3.	Drugs with questionable value might reduce need for admission or length of 
hospital stay in bronchiolitis cases, but broad consensus is lacking such as 
nebulization with adrenaline (epinephrine) as a potential rescue medication 
(inconsistent and short-lived improvement) or hypertonic saline (3%) may be 
administered for trial in hospitalized children. They are not routinely recommended 
for use in bronchiolitis but may be repeated, if there is a good clinical response to 
wheezing. 
	
	Adrenaline inhalation 0.3 mg/kg by nebulizer after dissolving the solution in 3 mL 
saline can be repeated every 4–6 hourly as required. 
	
	Or
	
	3%/7% hypertonic saline inhalation as and when needed.
	
	Note: No role of antibiotics, steroids [oral or inhaled], Ipratropium, Ribavirin

sulphate (IV or inhaled; do not use sedatives
	
	Or
	
	Salbutamol inhalation (0.15 mg/kg dissolved in 3 mL solution)

	 4.	Syr. Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg/dose may be given 4–6 hourly. 
	
Monitoring and assessment of response: Monitor improvement in respiratory rate, 
lower chest indrawing, difficulty in feeding, excessive crying, cyanosis and oxygen 
saturation, if available, every 4–6 hours till there is significant improvement. If a 
child does not improve/deteriorate, look for underlying heart disease, i.e. myocarditis/
congenital heart disease and get an X-ray chest and look for massive collapse of lung/

Discharge criteria
No supplemental oxygen for 10 hours; had minimal or no chest recession and is feeding 
adequately without the need for intravenous fluids and has consistently maintained 
SpO2 >94%.
Patient education
Provide key safety information for parents and carers as how to recognize developing 
‘red flag’ symptoms:
	
l Worsening work of breathing (grunting, nasal flaring, marked chest recession)
	
l Fluid intake is 50–75% of normal or no wet nappy for 12 hours
	
l Apnoea or cyanosis
	
l Exhaustion (e.g. not responding normally to social cues, wakes only with prolonged 
stimulation)
	
l How to get an appropriate medical help if any red flag symptoms develop

Pneumonia is commonly caused by infectious agents, e.g. viruses, bacteria and 
mycoplasma. Viruses alone or combined with bacteria are responsible for majority of 
the cases. In developing countries, bacterial pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. 
influenzae) may be more common. The comparison of pneumonia types: viral, bacterial

l On the basis of clinical features, pneumonia can be classified as mild to very 
severe disease.
No pneumonia: Cough and cold; no fast breathing and no indicators of severe 
pneumonia.
Pneumonia: Fast breathing, e.g. age below 2 months ≥60 RR/min;

Severe/very severe pneumonia: General danger signs: central cyanosis, or

investigations such as complete blood count (CBC), blood culture, chest X-ray,

recommended. Molecular methods like multiplex reverse transcription polymerase 
chain reaction (RT-PCR) and BioFire can also be used. Monitoring CRP, 
procalcitonin, and CBC levels can provide insight into the response to treatment.

1128    Standard Treatment Guidelines
ORAL THRUSH (ORAL CANDIDIASIS)
Oral candidiasis may be seen as early as 7–10 days of age (peak 4th week of life) 
uncommon after 12 months of age, when it is secondary to broad-spectrum antibiotic 
treatment. Chronic/recurrent oral candidiasis is seen in hypoparathyroidism, Addison’s 
disease, autoimmune disorders, immunodeficiency, AIDS, myelosuppressive therapy 
and severe malnutrition.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Thick white patches in the oral mucosa may spread to involve the lips, buccal mucosa, 
tongue and palate. The lesions are difficult to scrape off and this differentiates them 
from milk. After scraping, there is an erythematous base and some bleeding. 
	
l Asymptomatic or may cause pain in the mouth, discomfort, anorexia and 
decreased feeding. Rarely may cause aspiration pneumonia. Patients are often 
asymptomatic and present no interference with eating. However, oesophagitis 
due to Candida infection may manifest with chest pain and poor feeding. Oral 
candidiasis may be associated with diaper candidiasis, so it is always important 
to check for diaper rash when thrush is present. 
	
l Diagnosis is confirmed by the fact that on removing the plaques, punctate areas 
of bleeding are seen on the undersurface.

Correction of faulty sterilization technique of bottle; best to avoid bottle feeding. In 
nursing mothers, the breast may be a reservoir for the yeast, so applying a topical 
antifungal between feeds to the breast may help eradicate the infection.

Nystatin (100,000 units/mL) oral suspension 1 mL applied to each side of mouth every 
4 hours directly to the lesions with a swab. Application may be continued for 10–14 days.
Or
Clotrimazole 1% cream, gel or lotion, oral application 3–4 times/day after feeding for 
5–7 days.
Or
Miconazole gel 25 mg 4 times a day for 5–7 days.
Gentian violet 1% aqueous solution one or two times a day, for 5–7 days (can stain tissues 
and clothes) if resistant to Nystatin, but is messy to use and should not be swallowed. 
Treatment is administered for 7 days and should be continued for 48 hours after lesions 
have resolved. If symptoms persist, continue treatment to complete a full 14-day course.
In resistant to topical therapy/chronic cases (in immunocompromised children ≥12 
months and moderate/severe thrush in all children ≥12 months) 
Syp. Fluconazole 3–6 mg/kg PO once daily for 2 weeks.

Warning
Resistant/recurrent/chronic thrush in a child with no obvious predisposing factor/source 
of infection look for underlying endocrinopathy/immune disorder, AIDS and malnutrition.
Patient/Parent education
Emphasize on breastfeeding, care/hygiene of the nipple and treatment of vaginal 
candidiasis in an expectant mother. Counsel parents not to use feeding bottle. 
	
l If the baby is bottle-feeding, sterilize teats and bottles after each use.
	
l If the mother is breastfeeding, clean the nipples gently between feeds.
	
l Sterilize dummies and teething rings regularly.
	
l If the baby gets nappy rash, make sure to treat it properly.
	
l Use antibiotics only when necessary.
	
l If the child has asthma, make sure they wash their mouth with water after asthma 
preventer medications.
	
l If the child has diabetes, try to keep their blood sugar level within its target range.
	
l Wash clothing at 60°C to kill fungus.

CONSTIPATION
Constipation is defined as the passage of hard stools that are difficult to pass irrespective of 
frequency. However, passage of stool less than twice a week is considered as constipation. 
Genuine hard stools may result from inadequate milk intake, hunger stools, use of over-
strength artificial feeds and low roughage diet. While fewer than 5% of children with 
constipation have a definitive organic cause, the vast majority have no proven cause 
and are labeled as having functional constipation. Organic causes of constipation may 
include imperforate anus, meconium plug, low intestinal obstruction, neonatal small 
colon syndrome, Hirschsprung’s disease, cystic fibrosis or hypothyroidism.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Fretfulness, poor appetite, intermittent abdominal pain, distension. Retentive 
posturing occurs with urge to defaecate, relieved after going to the toilet, 
overflow soilage may appear.
	
l There may be a history of recurrent UTI. Weight gain may be impaired.
	
l Evaluate additional factors such as stool consistency, presence of associated pain 
or difficulty during defecation, the existence of associated fissures and soiling of 
underwear before assigning the label of constipation. Faecal soiling of underwear 
and persistent faecal odour may suggest an organic cause of constipation rather 
than a functional cause. Abdomen is often distended and tympanic to percussion. 
Faecal masses palpable above pubis and in left colon, rarely entire colon is filled 
with firm mass; on rectal examination, hard stools are palpable in ampulla.

1130    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Warning signs for non-functional constipation requiring further work-up: 
	
l Constipation starting in neonatal age 
	
l Delayed passage of meconium > 48 h
	
l Family history of Hirschsprung’s disease 
	
l Blood in stools without anal fissures 
	
l Perianal fistula or anal scars
	
l Fever or weight loss with constipation
	
l Tuft of hair on spine or sacral dimple
	
l Urinary incontinence, dribbling, weakness in lower limbs
	
l Fear during anal inspection 
If a surgical cause is suspected, investigate and treat accordingly. The diagnosis of functional 
constipation may be considered in the absence of above-mentioned red flag signs and when 
any of the two or more criteria are fulfilled: 
	
l Stool frequency ≤2 per week 
	
l History of hard and painful bowel movements 
	
l History of retention of stools 
	
l Large diameter stool obstructing the Indian pots 
	
l Faecal incontinence
	
l Per abdomen or per rectum examination reveals faecal mass
Treatment (functional constipation)
The main objective of medical management is to dislodge the faecal mass, overcome 
withholding behaviour and promote regular bowel habits.

l Dietary modification: Ensure adequate fluid intake in diet. In infants, breast milk 
should continue as it is less likely to cause constipation than cow’s milk, can add 
extra sugar in cow’s milk if child is not breastfed.
	
l Add fibre to cereals (wheat bran, oat, corn), pulses, vegetables, salads and fruits and 
isabgol. A rough formula for amount of fibre (g) needed per day is (age in years + 5) 
or 0.5 g/kg/day.
	
l Behavioural modification.
	– Toilet training to achieve regular evacuation. Child is instructed to use bathroom after 
breakfast or dinner to take advantage of meal stimulated increase in colonic motility.
	– Maintain a calendar to record stooling.
	– Positive reinforcement (reward/appreciation) for successful toileting 
(no punishment for failure).
Follow up with regular contact with child and parent for 2–3 years.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1131

1.	Medical management includes disimpaction and maintenance therapy. 
	
	Disimpaction (to clear the gut of all hard faecal mass): Polyethylene glycol (PEG) 
1.5–2 g/kg/day in two divided doses for 3–6 days. PEG is available as a powder which 
should be dissolved in 120–240 mL of water or juice and given over 20 minutes. Do 
not double the dose of drug if the previous dose was missed. (Caution: Children may 
complain of bloating, nausea or abdominal cramps.) Advise the patient to consult the 
doctor, if the patient develops vomiting or diarrhea after PEG. 
	
	Or
	
	Enema may be tried as an alternate agent as saline enema 6 mL/kg once or twice 
per day or as sodium phosphate enemas 2.5 mL/kg (maximum 133 mL).
	
	Maintenance: Pharmacological agents may be used as maintenance therapy only 
after successful disimpaction has been achieved. Both osmotic and stimulant 
laxatives can be used. PEG and lactulose are osmotic laxatives and are preferred 
over stimulant laxatives in children. PEG is the first choice of drug which can be 
administered as 0.5–1 g/kg/day in two divided doses.
	
	In older children who are hospitalized, slow disimpaction can be done over 
2–3 days by giving PEG with electrolytes orally 25 mL/kg/h up to 1,000 mL/h until 
clear stool comes.
	
	Note: PEG cannot be used in children under 1 year of age. 
	
	Lactulose <1 year: 2.5 mL; 1 to <5 years: 2.5–10 mL; 5–20 years: 5–20 mL twice 
a day. Both PEG and lactulose should not be used together. 
	
	Stimulant laxatives like Bisacodyl and sodium picosulphate (2.5–10 mg per day 
up to 4 years; 2.5–20 mg per day from 4–18 years) should be used only as rescue 
therapy for acute constipation. Stimulant laxatives should not be used beyond 
2–3 days. 
	
	Bisacodyl 5 mg/day in children 3–10 years of age and 10 mg/day in 10–18 years old. 
	
	Assessment of response: Effective treatment is characterized by consistent and 
painless bowel movements, successful toilet training and the absence of fecal soiling 
or blood in stools. Utilizing a stool diary as a monitoring tool can enhance compliance 
with the treatment plan. Avoid abrupt stopping of the laxatives. Taper maintenance 
therapy and stop when the child is symptom-free for 2–3 months and continue over 
a period of 2–3 months to prevent chances of recurrence. Most common cause of 
failure is short-term treatment and suboptimal doses. In cases of a relapse of acute 
constipation during maintenance therapy in children, stimulant laxatives like Senna 
and Bisacodyl can be used as a short-term rescue therapy for 2–3 days.
	 2.	In severe cases with faecal soiling, in the initial stages: bowel cleaning/
disimpaction may be required with enemas 1–2/day or suppositories 1–2/day.
	 3.	In very severe cases with multiple faecoliths, failed medical treatment, mental 
retardation, etc., surgical disimpaction may be done.

Patient/Parent education
	
l The parents should be empowered to titrate the medication against the child’s stools.
	
l Explain the importance of dietary modifications.
	
l Treatment should not be abandoned early after recovery.
	
l Bowel training should have only positive reinforcements. Negative reinforcement 
should be avoided at all costs.
See also Constipation in Chapter 6.

RECURRENT ABDOMINAL PAIN OF CHILDHOOD (RAP)
Three or more bouts of abdominal pain occurring over a period of not less than 
3 months and severe enough to interfere with child’s normal activities. It is most 
common in the age group of 5–15 years and in 90% of cases it is functional.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Paroxysmal means the child appears well in between the episodes or sometimes 
dull continuous ache may be present 
	
l Mostly periumbilical, epigastric or suprapubic
	
l Episodes last for generally less than 1 hour
	
l Not related temporally to activity, meals, and stress or bowel habits
	
l Rarely awakened from sleep
	
l Normal physical examination and growth 
	
l Warning signs pointing towards organic pain
	– Well-localized pain away from midline (Apley’s law – farther the pain from 
midline, more likely to be organic) 
	– Repeated vomiting
	– Pain awakening the patient from sleep
	– Radiation to shoulder, back, scapula, lower extremities
	– Age less than 6 years
	– Associated fever, arthralgias, rash, rectal bleeding
	– Consistent sleepiness following pain attacks 
	– Intermittent faecal incontinence

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1133
	– Weight loss or growth deceleration 
	– Recurrent isolated episodes of pain that come suddenly and last for several 
minutes to few days 
	
l In case of any warning sign, patients should be investigated accordingly, otherwise 
treat as functional. However, basic investigations, e.g. urine, stool, CBC, erythrocyte 
sedimentation rate, CRP level. Mantoux and ultrasound examination might be done. 
	
l Pregnancy testing and screening for sexually transmitted infections should be 
considered in adolescents or if there are concerns about sexual abuse. 
	
l Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is generally not required.

l Treat organic cause if found. 
	
l Environmental intervention to avoid painful stress; change in parent reaction to 
avoid secondary gain. Common psychogenic factors responsible for RAP are 
complaint modelling (parents with abdominal pain), school phobia, learning 
problems, anxious overachiever, ridicule by peers, teacher incompatibility, attention 
seeking (attention withdrawal after an illness, over busy parents, single child, 
sibling rivalry, eating time conflict, forceful toilet training), family psychopathology 
(parental conflict, single parent). 
	
l Visits to doctor and placebos often help. 
	
l Child is asked to maintain pain chart (help in assessment of improvement as well 
as aetiology). 
	
l If required, help from a psychologist may be taken.

1.	Reassurance of the parents and child.
	 2.	Constipation if present may be treated.
Note: Routine use of antispasmodics, antidepressants, acid suppressants and prokinetics 
is not recommended.
Patient/Parent education
	
l Explain the outline of the work up and treatment for the child before starting 
treatment. Doing so after negative work up makes family feel that the physician 
is making excuses. Explain that the cause of RAP in most children is non-organic. 
	
l Discovery of cause may lessen the family’s concern but may not alleviate the symptoms. 
There is no way to be certain that abdominal pain is because of an identified disease 
entity. Pain may continue and its persistence does not mean serious organic disease.

ACUTE DIARRHOEA
Acute diarrhoea is defined as passage of three loose stools per day for a duration of 
less than 7 days, and increased fluidity or volume of stools. It is commonly caused by 
Rotavirus, E. coli, V. cholerae, Giardia or parenteral infections and invasive diarrhoea 
by Shigella, Salmonella and E. histolytica.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Clinical features of diarrhoea are frequent stools, vomiting, fever and dehydration. 
	
l Dehydration is categorized into some dehydration and severe dehydration 
(Table 19.18). Investigations in acute diarrhoea may be done if there are 
indications (Table 19.19).
	
l Dysentery is diarrhoea presenting with loose frequent stools containing visible 
blood. It is usually associated with fever, abdominal cramps and rectal pain. Most 
episodes in children are due to Shigella but can be caused by Salmonella, E. coli, 
C. jejuni and infrequently by E. histolytica.

1. Low osmolarity oral rehydration solution (ORS) in some dehydration.

Amoebic dysentery
Young children should not be routinely treated for amoebiasis as it is an infrequent 
cause of bloody diarrhoea in children. Amoebiasis should be considered only if two 
different antibiotics usually effective for Shigella have been given sequentially without 
showing signs of clinical improvement, or if a microscopic examination of fresh stool 
done in a reliable laboratory shows trophozoites of E. histolytica containing RBCs.

1 tablet for older children.
(Also see Chapter 6.)
Systemic infections
Systemic infections are to be treated by appropriate antibiotics. Rule out meningitis, upper 
respiratory infection (URI) and dyselectrolytaemia and give ORS in sips.

l There is not much role of antiemetics in a child with vomiting. If vomiting persists,

mg/kg) or Domperidone (0.5 mg/kg) may be tried before giving intravenous fluids. 
	
l Binding agents, e.g. Kaolin/pectin, etc., are not useful. 
	
l Following drugs are contraindicated: Antimotility agents, e.g. Loperamide,

Keep record of vitals, e.g. pulse, BP, CFT, respiratory rate (1 hourly) and temperature (6 
hourly). Monitor for improvement or worsening of signs of dehydration. Record urine 
output and stool frequency and consistency.

l Admit, if PEM grade III or age <3 months (as higher chances of complications, e.g.

l Investigate for lactose intolerance, incipient infections, e.g. urinary tract infection

l Exclude parenchymal renal failure if child has not passed urine after hydration. 
Give a fluid challenge (20 mL/kg of normal saline) followed by Frusemide injection 
(1–2 mg/kg). If urine is still not passed, consider parenchymal renal failure and 
manage accordingly.

l Give information on natural course of diarrhoea to avoid dissatisfaction and

consistency usually improves by 3–7 days.
	
l Explain that most of the complications in diarrhoea are because of dehydration and 
thus ORS is the mainstay of therapy. 
	
l Explain preparation of ORS and method of administration. 
	
l In case of dysentery, diarrhoea takes 2–3 days to cease after disappearance of blood. 
	
l Nutritional advice as mentioned earlier in the non-pharmacological section.
	
l Education about food and water hygiene.
	
l Rota virus vaccine is available (for details, see Immunization given earlier). 
Vaccination should be strictly as per schedule. Postpone vaccination in infants with 
acute gastroenteritis as it might compromise the efficacy of the vaccine.
	
l Consider risks versus benefits before vaccination for infants with chronic 
gastrointestinal disease, gut malformations, previous intussusception and 
immunocompromised infants.

ACUTE VIRAL HEPATITIS
Acute viral hepatitis is defined as inflammation of liver caused by a number of 
hepatotropic viruses like Hepatitis A, B, C, D, E viruses, etc. Commonest causes for 
infective hepatitis among children are Hepatitis A virus followed by Hepatitis E. Both 
of these are transmitted by faeco-oral route. Hepatitis B and C virus infections are more 
common in children requiring blood products for certain chronic illnesses. Mother-to-
child transmission of these viruses at birth is very rare.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1139
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The illness may vary from asymptomatic infection, anicteric hepatitis to icterus 
and sometimes may even lead to acute liver failure (ALF) as fulminant hepatitis. 
	
l Prodrome constituted by fever, malaise, nausea, emesis, anorexia and abdominal 
discomfort may precede the appearance of jaundice. It may go unnoticed or 
may be severe mimicking malaria or typhoid fever. Acute hepatitis must first be 
differentiated from other disorders that cause similar symptoms.
	
l LFT along with viral serology testing for HAV IgM and HEV IgM.
	
l Acute hepatitis if there is jaundice or elevated total bilirubin levels ≥3.0 mg/dL, 
or elevated serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels >200 IU/L.
	
l In case prolonged course then measure prothrombin/international normalized 
ratio (PT/INR).

l Rest if the patient feels exhausted or fatigued (forced rest does not help and does not 
shorten the time to recovery).
	
l Regular small frequent meals with high caloric content. High carbohydrate diets are 
acceptable but should be hygienic. Traditionally, sugarcane juice is used as home 
therapy though it has no established benefit. 
	
l Maintain adequate hydration in case of vomiting and avoid fatty meals.

There is no specific treatment for simple acute viral hepatitis. Uncomplicated cases 
can be treated at home.
	 1.	If patient has frequent vomiting, Syr./Tab. Metoclopramide 0.1 mg/kg/dose can be 
given as and when required but not to be repeated before 6 hours. 
	 2.	Usually, fever abates after jaundice appears. Occasionally if the situation requires, 
Paracetamol may be used sparingly (see section on Fever in Chapter 1).
Note: Persistent high-grade fever suggests alternative diagnosis. Hospitalization 
is required only in clinically severe illness, e.g. alteration in sleep pattern, altered 
behaviour, abnormal movements, persistent vomiting, dehydration, decreased urinary 
output, bleeding from any site or any other complication.
Patient education
	
l Continue breastfeeding or other regular feeding. 
	
l Observe carefully for any danger signs listed above. 
	
l Usually a self-limiting disease, and fever subsides after the jaundice is evident 
clinically. Most patients start recovering in 7–14 days’ time. Total duration of illness 
is 3 weeks.

1140    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Hepatitis A and B are two different diseases. Vaccination with hepatitis B vaccine 
does not protect against hepatitis A (see Immunization for details).
	
l Hepatitis A spreads through contaminated food and water and close person-to-person 
contact. See Immunization for details for vaccination against Hepatitis A.
	
l Raw or insufficiently cooked food (fruits, vegetables, salads) or cooked food handled 
by an infected individual can be the source of hepatitis A infection.
See also Jaundice and Acute Viral Hepatitis in Adults in Chapter 1 and Appendix II.

CHICKENPOX OR VARICELLA
Varicella is the primary infection caused by Varicella-zoster virus. It is highly infectious 
and is transmitted by droplet infection. The incubation period is about 14 days.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Begins as crops of small red papules over the trunk appearing within 1 day 
of fever and systemic symptoms which quickly develop into clear, often oval 
vesicles on an erythematous base. Contents become cloudy in about 24 hours 
and then scab. Many such crops may appear for 3–4 days. The initial exanthem 
is intensely pruritic macules that evolve through papular stage. 
	
l Bacterial superinfection, thrombocytopenia, arthritis, hepatitis, encephalitis or 
meningitis can complicate the disease. 
	
l The disease is severe in adolescents and adults as well as immune compromised 
individual. Reactivation disease results in herpes zoster or shingles (for details, 
see Skin section in Chapter 14).

l Itching is bothersome and scratching effect may be minimized by making the patient 
wear mittens, daily change of clothes and good personal hygiene may decrease the 
risk of secondary infection.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1141
Pharmacological symptomatic therapy
	 1.	For management of fever (see Fever in Chapter 1), Aspirin and other salicylates 
are contraindicated due to risk of Reye’s syndrome and should not be used. 
	 2.	Local anti-pruritic agents like Calamine lotion may alleviate itching. If itching is 
not relieved with the above, Tab. Pheniramine 25 mg two times a day.
	
	In children: Syr. 0.5 mg/kg/day every 8 hours
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Cetirizine 10 mg once a day
	
	In children (2–6 years): 5 mg; (>6 years) 10 mg once a day. 
	 3.	In case of immunocompromised children on long-term treatment with steroids, 
those on anti-cancer drugs or other immunosuppressive therapy, HIV positive 
patients, children older than 12 years of age and those with chronic cutaneous or 
pulmonary disorders who are at increased risk of severe disease, oral Acyclovir if 
started within few hours (<24 h) of the onset of rash may decrease the duration, 
magnitude of fever as well as the number of skin lesions. 
	
	Tab. Acyclovir 20 mg/kg/ day is given 6 hourly for 5 days.
	 4.	In case the patient is severely immunocompromised, viral encephalitis or severe 
disease in adults, Inj. Acyclovir should be started as soon as possible in all cases 
at the dose of 10 mg/kg 8 hourly IV for 7 days.
Note: Acyclovir not recommended routinely for a healthy child.
Assessment of response to therapy
	
l Most cases will stop having fever after the initial 3–4 days when new crops of 
vesicle stop appearing. The vesicles normally heal by scabbing in about a week’s 
time. Persistence of fever may suggest secondary infection.
	
l The disease can be complicated by secondary bacterial infection of skin lesion, 
thrombocytopenia, pneumonia – particularly in adolescents and adults, Reye’s 
syndrome, postinfectious encephalitis and if any of these develop they should be 
treated appropriately.
	
l Post-exposure prophylaxis with VZIG (Varicella Zoster Immunoglobulin) 
is recommended in susceptible individuals with significant contact with 
varicella/herpes zoster who are at high risk for severe disease – severely 
immunocompromised, neonates born to mothers who develop varicella 5 days before 
or 2 days after delivery, neonates born at <28 weeks of gestation/or birth weight 
<1000 g or pregnant women. 
	
l Inj. VZIG 0.2–1 mL/kg diluted in normal saline over 1 hour IV to be given as soon 
as possible but not later than 96 hours following exposure. 
	 Note: VZIG is very expensive. If unaffordable/not available, give IVIG 200 mg/kg Or 
Tab. Acyclovir 80 mg/kg/day for 7–10 days beginning from the 7th day of the exposure.
Patient/Parent education
	
l The disease commonly is self-limiting in healthy children. Child should be excluded 
from day care or school till after 6th day of the rash or till scabs are formed.

1142    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Do not use over-the-counter fever medicines as they may contain aspirin or other 
salicylates. 
	
l Potent vaccine is available for protection against the disease and is recommended 
for all healthy children with no prior history of varicella, especially in children 
belonging to certain high-risk groups (for details, see Immunization).

MEASLES
Measles is an acute viral disease of childhood, associated with high rates of morbidity 
and mortality. It directly or indirectly contributes to 7% of the under five deaths in the 
developing world.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, an erythematous maculopapular rash 
appearing on the 4th day of the illness and a pathognomonic enanthem (Koplik 
spots) characterize it. 
	
l Rash starts from behind the ears, along the hairline, involve the face and then the 
trunk and the limbs. The rash fades over about 7 days in the same progression 
as it evolved. 
	
l Fever usually subsides after the appearance of the rash unless there is some 
complications such as otitis media, bronchopneumonia, laryngotracheobronchitis 
(croup) and diarrhoea. Acute encephalitis, which frequently results in permanent 
brain damage, occurs in approximately 1 in every 1000 cases. 
	
l Another cause of persistence of fever could be flaring up of Koch’s.

l The patient should be isolated from other susceptible individuals, particularly 
unimmunized children for at least 4 days after the appearance of the rash.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1143
	
l Bed rest is usually required, and sponging may be required for febrile patients. 
	
l Small frequent feeds and plenty of oral fluids should be continued.

No specific antiviral treatment is available.
	 1.	Fever is managed with oral Paracetamol (see the section on Fever in Chapter 1). 
	 2.	If there is persistent coryza or nasal itching which is disturbing the child, Syr. 
Promethazine 1 mg/kg/day in 3–4 divided doses can be used.
Treatment of other co-existing problems
	 1.	Syr. Vitamin A 100,000 IU/mL orally for 2 consecutive days; 1 mL for 6–12 
mo and 2 mL in 12 months to 5 years. A third dose may be given 4 weeks later, 
particularly if there are manifesting signs of vitamin A deficiency. Alternately, 
capsule vitamin A (50,000 IU) can be used as an oral preparation. 
	 2.	Treat secondary bacterial infection appropriately like bronchopneumonia and/or 
gastrointestinal infection.
Patient/Parent education
	
l The disease leads to marked anorexia and also often precipitates PEM and other 
deficiencies. Regular frequent feeds must continue. Extra meals should be added to 
provide for increased requirement during convalescence.
	
l The disease usually lasts 10–12 days and the maximum risk of infectivity is 
5 days prior to and 4 days after the appearance of rash. The rash usually heals by 
desquamation and often leaves some hyperpigmented stains on the body which 
disappears over weeks subsequently. 
	
l The parents must report to the hospital in case the child develops any of the 
following warning signs: 
	– Stiff neck, facial twitching or convulsions (seizures), extreme drowsiness, loss of 
consciousness or altered behaviour. 
	– Rapid and or laboured breathing, difficulty in feeding, cyanosis. 
	– Significant dehydration as evident by sunken eyes or fontanelles, loss of skin 
turgor, dryness of tongue or lack of tears, etc. 
	– Blood in stools.
	
l Vaccination against measles is recommended at 9 months of life and a subsequent 
dose with MMR is mandated at 12 through 18 months of age. Catch up 
vaccination beyond 12 months should be MMR. There is no role of giving measles 
vaccination to a child who has already suffered from the disease. 
	
l Measles vaccine can be administered to unimmunized infants aged 6 months through 
5 years during outbreaks. Revaccinate these children with two doses of measles 
vaccine, first dose at 12 through 15 months and at least 4 weeks after the previous 
dose, and the second dose at 4 through 6 years of age.
	
l In case any other susceptible child (unimmunized child below 5 year) has been in contact 
with the patient of measles then it may be worthwhile to immunize this individual.

1144    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Measles vaccine is useful, if used early it can prevent or decrease the severity of the 
disease in the secondary contacts (see Immunization for details).
	
l All children aged 9 months to 5 years should receive an additional dose of MR 
vaccine under the MR campaign of Government of India irrespective of previous 
immunization status.

MUMPS
Mumps is a disease caused by a virus that can infect many parts of the body, especially 
the parotid salivary glands.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The parotid glands become increasingly swollen and painful over a period of 
1–3 days. There is often a fever of up to 103°F (39.4°C), with headache and loss 
of appetite, vomiting, aches 1–2 days prior to parotid swelling.
	
l Mumps can also involve the brain, pancreas and other organs. The involvement 
of these organs signifies a severe disease and there is usually a recrudescence of 
high fever in such situations in addition to organ specific symptoms. 
	
l Meningoencephalitis is the most common complication (250/100,000 cases). 
Other complications are orchitis, epididymitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis, thyroiditis, 
myocarditis, deafness, optic neuritis and arthritis.

l Child should be encouraged to drink plenty of fluids. Water, decaffeinated soft drinks 
and tea are better tolerated than acidic fruit juices (like orange juice, grape fruit juice 
or lemonade) that make parotid pain worse. 
	
l Either warm or cold packs, whichever feels better, may be used to soothe the swollen 
parotid glands.

1.	Most cases are treated symptomatically on OPD basis.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1145
	 2.	Fever when troublesome may be brought down using non-aspirin fever medications 
such as Paracetamol (10–15 mg/kg/day SOS or every 4–6 hours). These medicines 
will also help relieve pain in the swollen parotid glands.
	
	(Caution: Aspirin is contraindicated in children with viral illnesses due to risk of 
Reye’s syndrome.) 
	 3.	Being a viral illness, antibiotics have no role. There is no specific therapy available. 
	 4.	Patients with abdominal pain, testicular swellings or signs of raised intracranial 
tension need to be admitted in the hospital.
Patient/Parent education
	
l Parents should be explained about the warning signs, such as. 
	– In boys, watch for high fever, with pain and swelling of the testicles. 
	– Watch for abdominal pain that can mean involvement of the pancreas in either 
sex or involvement of the ovaries in girls. 
	– Severe headache, stiff neck, convulsions (seizures), extreme drowsiness, etc., 
suggest CNS involvement and need for admission to a tertiary level centre. 
	– Recurrence of high-grade fever (above 101oF/38.3oC) often heralds onset of the 
above complication and can be used as an early referral sign.
	
l Children usually recover from mumps in about 10–12 days. The first attack of 
mumps almost always gives lifelong protection against another; therefore, such 
children do not benefit from any immunization later.
	
l Mumps can be prevented by a vaccine which can be given as part of the 
mumps-measles-rubella (MMR) vaccine given at the age of 12 through 18 months, 
and the second dose before age 4 years, provided at least 4 weeks have elapsed since 
the first dose. Catch-up vaccination should ensure that all school-aged children and 
adolescents have received two doses of the MMR vaccine. The minimum interval 
between the two doses is 4 weeks. Give one dose if previously vaccinated with one 
dose (for details, see Immunization).

ACUTE FLACCID PARALYSIS (AFP)
A case of AFP is defined as any child aged <15 years, with acute onset of flaccid paralysis 
without any obvious cause (e.g. severe trauma or electrolyte imbalance like hypokalaemia). 
AFP is a notifiable disease, and all cases must be reported immediately to Nodal Officer

1146    Standard Treatment Guidelines
(Continued)
and District Surveillance Officer, NPSP Unit, Directorate of Family Welfare. India has 
shifted to the virological system of case classification, i.e. within 90 days of paralysis 
onset, all cases should undergo final classification as confirmed polio, non-polio AFP or 
compatible with poliomyelitis. India has been declared polio free by WHO.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The paralysis is of acute onset (<4 weeks) and the affected limb(s) are flaccid 
(floppy or limp). If the AFP is due to polio, then sensation is never affected. 
Other important differentials to be considered in cases with AFP are detailed 
in Table 19.20. This includes possible illness due to Guillain-Barré syndrome, 
transverse myelitis, traumatic neuritis, viral infections caused by other 
enteroviruses, toxins and tumours. With the eradication of polio, Guillain-Barré 
syndrome has become the major AFP. Seasonal occurrence of Guillain-Barré 
syndrome, often coinciding with a spurt of viral fever, are also observed. Isolated 
facial paralysis is not included.
	
l Pseudo paralysis due to pain in congenital syphilis, osteomyelitis, abscess, scurvy, 
unrecognized trauma leading to contusions, slipped epiphysis or fractures, etc., 
can also mimic AFP.

An AFP case is ‘confirmed’ as polio only by the isolation of wild poliovirus from any stool specimen.
An AFP case is classified as ‘non-polio AFP’ if wild poliovirus is not isolated from adequate stool* specimens.
If stool specimens are inadequate, final classification of the AFP case as either non-polio AFP or compatible with 
polio will depend on the results of 60 days follow-up examination. If the 60 days follow-up examination shows no 
residual weakness, the case is classified as non-polio AFP. The final classification of the case as ‘compatible’ or 
discarded as ‘non-polio AFP’ is determined by the National Expert Review Committee (ERC) which meets every 
month in New Delhi to review all such cases.
*Adequate stool: Two specimens collected within 14 days of paralysis onset and at least 24 hours apart; each 
specimen must be of adequate volume (8–10 g) and arrive at a WHO-accredited laboratory in good condition 
(i.e. no desiccation, no leakage, with adequate documentation and evidence that the cold chain was maintained.)

Treatment for acute POLIO like illness 
All cases should be treated as below except patients with isolated single lower 
limb involvement and reporting after 4 days of onset of paralysis and currently not 
progressing for more than 48 hours.
Table 19.20.  (Continued)

l Complete bed rest and correct positioning of the affected limbs in the optimal 
position as follows:
Hip – slight flexion, knee – 5° flexion, foot – 90° with support against the soles. 
Both legs should be supported from the lateral sides with pillows or rolled towels or 
salt/sand packs to prevent rotation. When pain subsides, passive movements of the 
joints for about 10 minutes, 2–3 times a day. 
	
l Warm water fomentation using hot packs with soaked towels wrapped around the 
affected parts for about 10 minutes, 2–3 times a day help in relieving pain. 
	
l If transient urinary retention occurs, alternate hot and cold compresses over the 
suprapubic region.
(Caution: No massage or intramuscular injections as it may further precipitate paralysis. 
Watch for progression, particularly for the involvement of the respiratory muscles.)

There is no specific drug therapy for polio. For fever and pain, use Paracetamol or 
Ibuprofen (see section on Fever in Chapter 1). Referral to a tertiary care centre with a 
ventilatory support facility if there is progression of paralysis, respiratory distress, bulbar 
involvement, paralysis of upper limbs which is <3 days old (there is a higher risk of 
diaphragmatic involvement in such cases), marked drowsiness or any other complication.
Patient/Parent education
	
l No dietary restrictions; however, continue breastfeeding or other regular feeding. 
	
l Paralysis progresses usually for about 4–7 days after onset. Recovery may start 
thereafter over days to weeks with little recovery of strength after 6 months of 
illness. A regular physiotherapy facilitates recovery of muscles.
Note: Post-polio residual paralysis should be referred to an appropriate center for 
rehabilitative services.
	
l January 2020 marks the 9 years since the last case of polio was reported in India. 
However, Polio infection circulation is still endemic in two countries, namely 
Afghanistan and Pakistan. All travellers to and from these countries (irrespective of 
gender and age and not restricted to children but even adults) MUST get vaccinated 
with single dose of OPV at least 4 weeks before their actual departure to or arrival 
from these countries. This adult dose needs to be repeated after 1 year if further 
travel or stay is anticipated.

PERTUSSIS (WHOOPING COUGH)
Whooping cough is caused by Bordetella pertussis and can have long-term poor effects 
on health.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Beginning as a mild upper respiratory tract infection (catarrhal stage), can progress to 
severe paroxysms of cough, often with a characteristic whoop, followed by vomiting. 
	
l The child runs out of breath with bulging eyes, flushed face, lacrimation, salivation, 
protrusion of tongue and distension of the neck veins, etc. Such episodes are 
exhausting and precipitated by yawning, sneezing, eating or even suggestion.
	
l The diagnosis is mainly clinical supported by lymphocytic leucocytosis (total count 
15,000–1,00,000 cells/microlitre) on the CBC.

1.	Syr./Tab. Azithromycin 10 mg/kg for 5 days (maximum 500 mg/day) Or 
Clarithromycin 15 mg/kg/day for 7 days Or Erythromycin 40–50 mg/kg/day in four 
divided doses orally for 14 days initiated early in the coryzal phase of the disease, 
i.e. first week of the illness. Beyond the first week, antibiotics only reduce the 
infectivity of the index case. Individuals are non-infectious 5 days after initiating 
antibiotics. Spontaneous clearance of the organism occurs by the 4th week in most 
individuals. Once the paroxysms start, no antimicrobials have any benefit except 
for eradication of any secondary pulmonary infection.
	
	In patients allergic to macrolides (only in infants above 2 months), Cotrimoxazole 
8 mg/kg/day of Trimethoprim in two doses for 14 days.
	 2.	In patients with severe coughing paroxysms, Salbutamol 1–2 mg/kg/day in three 
to four divided doses for a week or so may be tried. 
	
	Note: Antihistaminics and corticosteroids do not reduce the cough of pertussis.
	 3.	Admit all neonates and young infants with severe paroxysms that interfere 
with feeding and presence of complications such as bacterial pneumonia, 
encephalopathy or CNS haemorrhage for intravenous fluids and oxygen therapy. 
Exercise contact and droplet precautions till 5 days after antibiotic therapy has been 
started in all admitted patients.
Supportive therapy
	 1.	Oxygen therapy is required in severe cases with respiratory distress 
	 2.	Hydration should be maintained with intravenous or oral fluids in adequate 
amounts (cough suppressants are usually not helpful)

1150    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 3.	Maintain nutrition
	 4.	Avoidance of factors that provoke coughing such as passive smoking, biofuel, 
smoke, etc
Management of contacts
	
l Pertussis is a highly transmissible illness with secondary attack rates up to 80% in 
susceptible household contacts who are exposed to the index case during the period 
of infectiousness (first 4 weeks of the illness, maximum infectivity in 1st week).
	
l Restrict post-exposure prophylaxis to high-risk groups such as neonates, 
unimmunized or partially immunized young infants and individuals with other 
comorbidities. All other contacts should be placed on surveillance and antibiotics 
started at the first respiratory symptom. The same regimes as used for therapy are 
effective for prophylaxis.
Patient/Parent education
	
l Explain the need to continue feeding during the prolonged period of cough, adequate 
hydration and nutrition to prevent onset of malnutrition. 
	
l Antibiotic therapy must be continued for full course to prevent relapse of the disease, 
even if they may not be providing any relief in the symptoms. 
	
l All contacts under 7 years of age must be given antibiotics. 
	
l Contact the doctor immediately, if the patient develops listlessness, apnoea or 
seizures. This is particularly common in infants below 6 months.
	
l Immunization against pertussis is available as triple antigen (DPT) or as Pentavalent 
(with additional Hib and Hepatitis B) and three primary doses are routinely advised 
for all infants followed by a booster after 1.5 and 4.5 years after the primary 
immunization. The primary immunization is expected to reduce the disease burden 
by two-thirds. (For details, see Immunization.)

CARDIAC FAILURE
Cardiac failure is defined as a state in which the heart cannot deliver an adequate 
cardiac output to meet the metabolic needs of the body. Clinical presentation is 
dependent on age and degree of cardiac reserve. Common causes according to age of 
presentation are:
	
l Neonate: Severe anaemia, heart block, congenital heart disease, e.g. hypoplastic left 
heart, coarctation, left-to-right shunt and large mixing cardiac defects.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1151
	
l Infant: Left-to-right shunt, supraventricular tachycardia.
	
l Children: Rheumatic fever, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, acute hypertension, 
e.g. acute glomerulonephritis.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Exertional dyspnoea, poor weight gain, feeding difficulties, breathing too fast 
and better when upright, persistent cough and wheezing, excessive perspiration 
and irritability, puffiness of face and pedal oedema. 
	
l Tachypnoea, tachycardia, small volume pulse, peripheral cyanosis, pedal/facial/ 
sacral oedema, hepatomegaly, raised JVP (appreciated well in older children), 
gallop rhythm, cardiomegaly and failure to thrive.
	
l Chest radiography is a first-line investigation in children with suspected HF. 
Assess electrolytes (Na+, K+, Cl–, Ca2+), glucose, acid-base status, urea and 
creatinine, hepatic transaminases, thyroid hormone levels, and a complete blood 
count at the initial presentation of HF and repeat as needed to assess ongoing 
clinical status. 
	
l Perform 12-lead electrocardiography (ECG) at the time of presentation with HF, 
to exclude features of congenital or ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia and pre-
excitation. 
	
l All patients with symptoms consistent with HF should undergo echocardiography 
at, or as soon as possible after, the initial presentation. 
	
l Identify and treat the underlying cause.

l Restricted activity and bed rest with upright posture depending on cardiac reserve.
	
l In severe CHF, dietary modifications in infants by increasing calories per feed. 
Breastfeed supplementation, nasogastric feed to avoid the exertion of active feeding.
	
l No added salt in diet and fluid restriction. Monitor weight and fluid balance 
(input/output) charting.
	
l Tepid water sponging in case of fever.

Treat anaemia with iron and/or packed cells as and when indicated. The algorithm for

	Tab. Spironolactone 1–3 mg/kg/day in two divided doses. 
	 3.	In cases with regurgitant cardiac lesions like severe MR where reduction in after 
load is required
	
	Tab. Captopril 0.25 test dose build up doses from 1.5–3 mg/kg/day in three divided 
doses.
	
	Or
	
	Tab. Enalapril 0.08–0.5 mg/kg/dose 12–24 hourly (maximum 1 mg/kg/day).
	 4.	Patients with hypotension and low cardiac output should be referred to a higher 
centre for further management with
	
	Inj. Dopamine infusion (40 mg/mL) 10 mcg/kg/min prepared in normal saline or 
5% dextrose. Correct hypovolaemia before infusion is started and BP during the 
infusion.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Dobutamine infusion 10–20 mcg/kg/min. Both the drugs can be used 
simultaneously to have added response because of different mechanism of actions.
	
	Or

l Decreased salt intake should be emphasized.

DIABETES MELLITUS (DM)
Most of the cases of DM in children are of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (Type 1) 
and have hyperglycaemia with glucosuria. Type 2 diabetes mellitus is also being diagnosed 
in children and adolescents associated with obesity or metabolic syndrome. These children 
usually have a strong family history of type 2 diabetes. A few forms of monogenic diabetes 
like maturity-onset-DM of the young (MODY) can also be seen in few paediatric patients.

1154    Standard Treatment Guidelines
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l While some cases present with classical symptoms of polyphagia, polydipsia, 
polyuria and weight loss, many children at the onset present in the state of 
diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
	
l A minority of cases, while asymptomatic, are detected to have glucosuria and 
hyperglycaemia.
	
l Diagnosis of DM is made by demonstration of hyperglycaemia (random 
plasma glucose more than 200 mg/dL). Table 19.21 shows the cut-off levels 
of plasma glucose used for diagnosis of DM, while doing an oral glucose 
tolerance test (GTT) which involves administering a glucose dose of 1.75 g/kg 
of ideal body weight (maximum 75 g). Baseline HbA1c provides the estimate of 
duration of hyperglycaemia and also the effectiveness of the subsequent therapy. 
The routine use of autoantibodies (anti-insulin, GAD, islet cell) in diagnosis of 
type 1 diabetes is not recommended.
	
l Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) may be the first presentation of type 1 diabetes 
in a child. It may also be a dreaded acute complication in previously diagnosed 
children with type 1 diabetes when associated with poor compliance to 
insulin therapy or during acute sickness. The symptoms are non-specific like 
dehydration, lethargy, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and altered sensorium. 
	
l The biochemical hallmarks of type 1 diabetes ketoacidosis are as follows:
	 Hyperglycaemia (>200 mg/dL) 
	 Acidosis (venous pH <7.3 or serum bicarbonate <15 mmol/L)
	 Ketosis (blood ß-hydroxybutyrate ≥3 mmol/L) or moderate to large ketonuria

(high triglyceride and/or low-high-density lipoprotein [HDL]), and hypertension.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1155

Treatment goals are as follows:
	
l Maintain a good ‘time in range’ (70% and above), defined as percentage of time the 
blood glucose values lie in target range of 70–180 mg/dL 
	
l Prevention of acute complications such as diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and 
hypoglycemia
	
l Prevention of long-term complications and achieving good quality of life
	
l Achieve normal growth and development
Mainstay of treatment are as follows: 
	 1.	Medical nutrition therapy (MNT): There is not a specific diet for diabetes; 
however, it is advisable for children to embrace a healthy eating regimen 
with restricted consumption of snacks, sweeteners and high-glycaemic index 
carbohydrates. Promote intake of complex carbohydrates with low glycaemic index 
food (lower risk of postprandial hyperglycaemia). Calorie mixture should have 
55% carbohydrates, 30% fat and 15% proteins. Calorie intake should be split as 
20% breakfast, 20% lunch, 30% dinner and 10% each for 3 snacks at mid morning, 
mid afternoon and evening. Reduce fats derived from animal sources and replace 
with fats of vegetable origin. Encourage frequent small meals with homemade 
fluids during acute illness to avoid ketoacidosis. Following ‘the plate method’ 
is recommended, with one-third of the plate comprising high-quality, high-fiber 
rich carbohydrates, another third consisting of fruits and vegetables and the final 
third comprising protein. Calculating the carbohydrate content as ‘carb count’ aids 
in adjusting insulin therapy. One carbohydrate exchange is equivalent to 15 g of 
carbohydrates. 
	
	Regularity of eating pattern is very important so that diet and insulin dosing is 
synchronized. Things to avoid in diabetes management include the following:
	
l Refrain from constant grazing and irregular meal timings
	
l Avoid prolonged periods of fasting
	
l Do not skip meals before engaging in exercise or physical activity
	
l Steer clear of consuming sugar-sweetened beverages and caffeinated drinks
	
l Limit the intake of extra salt, particularly from sources like papads, baked goods 
and processed foods
	
l Exercise caution with diet-free and sugar-free products, especially those with 
high fat content despite lower sugar levels
	
l Minimize eating out
	 2.	Physical activity: Maintaining optimal metabolic control requires the incorporation 
of a consistent fitness and physical activity routine. Parents should play a crucial 
role in motivating their children to adopt a simple fitness regimen, including 
activities like walking, running, dancing, using stairs regularly and playing in open 
spaces. While children with diabetes can engage in various sports, they should 
be educated to check their blood glucose levels before exercising. If their blood 
glucose is low, it is advisable to consume a snack to prevent hypoglycemia.

1156    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 3.	Glucose monitoring: Blood glucose monitoring is a crucial element in diabetes 
management. BG should be monitored daily using glucometer by each patient. 
	 4.	Insulin therapy: Insulin therapy should be initiated soon after the diagnosis 
of diabetes in children. The preferred insulin therapy involves multiple daily 
injections with a basal-bolus regimen. Explain to patients and parents about the 
nature and prognosis of the disease and need for lifelong insulin replacement and 
need for daily monitoring of blood glucose as well as good follow-up plan to screen 
for complications of diabetes. Children should participate in helping parents in 
administration of insulin.

Insulin therapy: The regimen is personalized to accommodate the child’s meal and 
activity patterns for convenience. 
	
l Subcutaneous insulin is administered as a combination of long-acting and short- 
acting insulin. In children, use of premixed insulins is not recommended. 
	
l Total insulin dose is calculated based on weight and age. The dose is 0.5–0.7 U/
kg/day in a younger child (<10 years), 0.5–0.7 U/kg/day in a prepubertal child and 
0.8–1.2 U/kg/day in a peripubertal child. 
	
l Both Neutral Protamine Hagedorn (NPH)/regular insulin and insulin analogues can 
be used depending on cost considerations, feasibility and accessibility. Premixed 
twice daily insulin, are unsuitable for use in children and adolescents. Regular, rapid, 
or ultra-rapid-acting insulin is administered preprandially, timed according to the 
onset and peak of action. 
A.	In a split-mix regimen, insulin is administered as follows: NPH insulin and fast-
acting (regular) insulin in the ratio of 2–3:1. Two-thirds of total daily dose is injected 
as NPH and one-third as regular insulin. Both NPH and regular can be mixed in 
the same syringe with higher dose (2/3rd dose) in morning before breakfast than in 
the evening before dinner (1/3rd dose). Older children (>2 years old) may need an 
additional dose of only regular insulin in the afternoon before lunch. For example, 
if the total dose of insulin in a 32-kg child is 30 units, amount of NPH to be given 
is 20 units (2/3rd) which is divided as 14 units and 6 units for breakfast and dinner, 
respectively. The remaining 1/3rd is given as regular insulin equally spaced three 
times before meals as 3 units each time. 
B.	Basal-bolus regime, long-acting insulin like glargine, is used in 40–50% of total 
insulin requirement as once or twice daily injection. The bolus dose is generally 
given as regular insulin or insulin analog (lispro, aspart) divided three times before 
breakfast, lunch and dinner (i.e. before every major meal). For example, in the same 
child weighing 30 kg, the physician may start with 28–30 U units of total daily 
insulin. Inj. Glargine 12 U and regular insulin 5 U or 6 U premeal three times a day. 
	
l Blood glucose levels are monitored before each meal and the dose of insulin adjusted 
accordingly. Blood glucose levels should ideally be 80 mg/dL fasting and 140 mg/dL 
after meals (acceptable range between 80 and 240 mg/dL). Early morning 3 AM 
blood glucose level should be more than 70 mg/dL. Individualize dose of insulin 
based on blood glucose charting to avoid hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia.

treat as hypoglycaemia as mentioned below. 
	
l Any increase or decrease in insulin dose is by 10–15%. Generally, not more than 
5–6 units. 
	
l Avoid changing basal insulin doses frequently. Insist on uniform timing of basal 
insulin injection daily – this may be preferred in the morning for younger children.
	
l After initial stabilization, newly diagnosed cases may have gradual decline in insulin 
requirement even up to 0.5 units/kg/day. This may persist for several weeks to 
several months (honeymoon phase).
	
l Decrease total dose of insulin by 10% at the time of discharge from hospital as the 
increased activity at home will decrease the insulin requirement. 
	
l Insulin can be administered through various means, including syringes, pens, or 
advanced technology such as insulin pumps.
	
l Insulin syringes: Use U-100 syringes with U-100 vials (100 units of insulin/mL) 
and U-40 syringes with U-40 vials (40 units of insulin/mL). Attached needles are 
typically 6 or 8 mm long. Regular and NPH insulin are commonly available in 40 
IU/mL strength, while insulin analogues are usually found as 100 IU/mL.
	
l Patients should be instructed to verify the strength of the insulin vial before usage.
	
l Insulin pen: These pens come in reusable or disposable options (the latter being 
more expensive). Typically, they have 1-unit increments (0.5 unit increments may 
also be available). Insulin pens are portable and convenient, and the pen needles are 
usually 4, 5, or 6 mm long.
	
l Insulin pump: An insulin pump delivers short-acting or regular insulin through 
a battery-operated pump continuously over 24 hours, ensuring a basal supply. For 
mealtime, additional boluses of insulin can be administered using the same device.

1158    Standard Treatment Guidelines
The insulin is directed through a flexible catheter and a cannula directly into the 
subcutaneous fat over the abdomen or gluteal area. While effective, insulin pumps 
are expensive and require operational expertise.
	
l Insulin storage: Once in use, opened vial/cartridge of insulin can be stored at room 
temperature for 4 weeks or at 4–8°C in the refrigerator (middle shelf) for 3 months. It 
should never be frozen or exposed to direct sunlight. In hot climates where a refrigerator 
is unavailable, insulin may be stored in clay pots using the double pot method. 
	
l Insulin Injection: Children over 8 years of age can self-inject insulin, while parents 
typically handle the task for younger children. Insulin is injected subcutaneously in 
the anterolateral thigh or the anterior abdominal wall, leaving out 2 inches from all 
sides of the navel. The deltoid region is not ideal for children. Regularly rotating 
injection sites to prevent lipohypertrophy is crucial. Proper disposal of lancets and 
sharps should be taught to all patients and their families.
	
l Glucose monitoring: Blood glucose monitoring is crucial element in diabetes 
management. BG should be monitored daily using glucometer by each patient. 
	
l Encourage individuals receiving multiple dose insulin or insulin pump therapy to 
perform self monitoring of blood sugar (SMBG): prior to meals and snacks; occasionally 
after meals (postprandially), at bedtime, prior to exercise, when low blood glucose 
suspected to confirm hypoglycaemia and to monitor recovery and during intercurrent 
illness to prevent hyperglycaemic crises; and prior to critical tasks, such as driving. 
	
l Periodically blood glucose estimation at 3–4 AM is required to detect early morning 
hypoglycaemia. 
	
l An effective blood glucose log should document premeal and 2-hour postmeal 
values at least three times a day. Regularly evaluate SMBG technique, results and the 
patient’s ability to use the data to adjust therapy. 
	
l Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) may be useful among children, teens and 
younger adults. CGMS glucose monitoring provides real-time readings or recorded 
data revealing fluctuations, including hypo- and hyperglycemia, which might go 
unnoticed with timed finger-prick checks. The sensors lasts 5 -14 days and needs 
calibration using finger-prick values from a glucometer. The CGMS log facilitates the 
calculation of “time-in-range,” defined as the percentage of time the blood glucose 
remains between 70 and 180 mg/dL. An optimal value is 70% or higher. CGM may be 
a useful supplement to SMBG among individuals with hypoglycaemic unawareness 
(neuroglycopaenia occurring before autonomic activation with reduced awareness 
about hypoglycaemia) or frequent hypoglycaemia.
	
l Monitor urine ketones during episodes of uncontrolled hyperglycaemia, insulin 
deficiency, intercurrent illness and impending ketoacidosis especially with 
abdominal pains, vomiting, drowsiness or rapid breathing or when persistent blood 
glucose levels > 250 mg/dL are present.
	
l Glycaemic targets for children and adolescents: Consider a risk-benefit assessment, 
including hypoglycaemia risk, when individualizing glycaemic targets for children 
and adolescents with type 1 diabetes.
	
l Glycosylated haemoglobin (HBA1C) target <7.0% (estimation once every 3 
months). A lower HBA1C target (<6.5%) is reasonable if it can be achieved without

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1159
excessive hypoglycaemia. Children below 6 years are unable to recognize symptoms 
of hypoglycaemia; thus, they are at increased risk of adverse neurologic outcomes. 
	– Plasma glucose before meals (pre-prandial): 70–130 mg/dL. Plasma glucose 
postmeal: 90–180 mg/dL.
	– Plasma glucose at bedtime and overnight: 80–140 mg/dL.
	
If the child is taking basal-bolus therapy, measure postprandial glucose when there is 
a discrepancy between pre-prandial glucose values and HBA1C levels and reassess 
preprandial insulin doses.
Hypoglycaemia
Hypoglycaemia is defined as a fall in blood glucose levels <70 mg/dL which poses 
danger to the child. It is the most common acute complication in children and is more 
dangerous than hyperglycaemia as hypoglycaemia can cause sudden unconsciousness and 
convulsions. Children may complain of palpitations, sweating (adrenergic symptoms), 
confusion, headache, lethargy (neuroglycopenic symptoms) and irritability or tantrums. 
	 1.	Educate parents and the child about the risk factors for hypoglycaemia like missing 
meals, excessive insulin dose, concomitant alcohol administration, sleep and 
exercise. Younger children are at a higher risk for hypoglycaemia as titration of 
insulin dose with meal amount may be highly variable. 
	 2.	Hypoglycaemia is an emergency. 
	 3.	Administer easy-to-dissolve sugar like Glucon-D instead of fatty substances like 
ice-cream, chocolates, etc. The dose of sugar is 9 g in a child <30 kg and 15 g in 
an older child. Blood glucose should be checked with a glucometer 15 minutes 
after glucose administration which should increase to >100 mg/dL. Administer the 
short-/fast-acting insulin in reduced dose (10%) followed by the meal. 
	 4.	In case of severe hypoglycaemia (<54 mg/dL) administer Inj. Glucagon 1 mg for 
children >25 kg and 0.5 mg for children <25 kg) intramuscular or subcutaneous 
(for details, also see Chapter 11).
Sick day management
	
l Do not omit insulin
	
l When unwell frequent random BG and ketone (urine or blood) monitoring is needed, 
usually 2–3 hourly. Top-up insulin is often needed
	
l Calculate total daily dose (TDD) based on ketone bodies level 
	
l If BG < 80 mg/dL, regular insulin should be omitted. Instead, frequent feeds in small 
quantities should be given with BG monitoring every 2–3 hours. Basal insulin should 
be given. If urine ketones are positive, basal insulin can be reduced by 30%.
	
l Hospitalize: If the child is drowsy, vomiting more than three times, not tolerating 
oral feeds, develops fast breathing, and has significant abdominal pain. 
Ketoacidosis (See below)
Prevention of complications
Urine for protein with a random spot urine sample for Albumin-to-creatinine ratio 
(ACR) with a 5-year diabetes duration. Measure eGFR at initial evaluation and then

1160    Standard Treatment Guidelines
based on age, diabetes duration and treatment. It should be done once every year in a 
5-year diabetes duration.
Retinopathy: Initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination at age ≥10 years or post-
puberty onset (whichever occurs first) in children with diabetes for a duration of 3–5 years.
Neuropathy: Annual comprehensive foot exam at age ≥10 years or post-puberty onset 
(whichever occurs first) in children with diabetes for a duration of 3–5 years.
Hypertension: Measure BP at every visit; confirm elevated BP at separate visit; high-
normal BP or hypertension (SBP or DBP consistently >90th percentile and ≥95th 
percentile for age, gender, and height respectively); confirm BP on 3 separate days. 
Treat accordingly. BP target: consistently <90th percentile for age, gender and height.
Dyslipidaemia: Obtain a fasting lipid profile in children aged ≥10 years soon after 
diagnosis and if abnormal repeat annually. If LDL-C <100 mg/dL, repeat lipid panel 
every 3–5 years. Serum cholesterol should be less than 200 mg/dL, LDL less than 
130 mg/dL and triglycerides less than 140 mg/dL.
Thyroid function tests should be done once every year to detect concomitant 
hypothyroidism.
Patient/Parent education
	
l Patient/parents should be taught self-diabetic care which should include:
	– Technique of measuring insulin in the syringe 
	– Importance of drawing insulin always in the same sequence (usually regular 
insulin first) so that same type of insulin is left over in the dead space of the 
syringe
	– Explain technique of subcutaneous injections and importance of rotating injection 
sites – arms, thighs (upper and lower), buttocks and abdomen
	– Blood sugar monitoring, maintaining the records of treatment and sugar levels 
	– Adherence to diet. Adjusting bolus insulin doses as per the carbohydrate content 
and quality 
	– Regular exercise 
	– Recognizing the symptoms of hypoglycaemia and its home management
	
l Give instructions for identification and management of intercurrent illnesses 
periodically to avoid complications of ketoacidosis, dehydration, uncontrolled or 
symptomatic hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia. 
	
l More frequent blood glucose (at least every 3–4 hours including through the night 
and sometimes every 1–2 hours) and ketone (urine or blood) monitoring during 
intercurrent illness. Blood keton meters are available as point-of-care devices that 
measure ketones using fingerpick like a glucometer.
	
l Monitor and maintain salt and water balance as hyperglycaemia, fever, excessive 
glycosuria and ketonuria all contribute to increased fluid losses.
	
l Educate parents/patients to NEVER completely stop insulin even if the child is 
ill and not eating. Even in the fasting state, some insulin is still required for basal 
metabolic needs, which may go up during an acute illness situation so that more 
frequent monitoring of BG and ketones is required.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1161
	
l Vomiting in a child or adolescent with diabetes is considered as a sign of insulin deficiency 
until proven otherwise. Other causes include food poisoning or low blood glucose. 
	
l Provide routine vaccinations for children and adults with diabetes according to 
age-related recommendations. Influenza vaccine annually in all patients with 
diabetes aged ≥6 months and pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine in all patients 
with diabetes aged ≥2 years.

SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Mild DKA – if venous pH is between 7.2 and 7.3 or serum bicarbonate is between 
10 and 15 mmol/L. 
	
l Moderate DKA – if venous pH <7.2 and serum bicarbonate <10 mmol/L. Severe 
if venous pH <7.1 or serum bicarbonate <5 mmol/L.
Treatment (to be managed in intensive care/critical care unit) 
	
l Draw blood samples for baseline – blood glucose, gas analysis, serum electrolyte, 
blood ketones, renal function tests and screening tests for infection 
	
l Monitor the following parameters hourly to two-hourly: vitals, fluid intake, urine 
output, sensorium, capillary glucose, serum electrolytes, blood and/or urinary 
ketones and insulin infusion

l Correct dehydration slowly over 24–48 hours. Intravenous fluids should replace the 
deficit and add the maintenance fluid for 24–48 hours and given as crystalloids (0.45 
or 0.9% NS, Ringer’s lactate or plasmaLyte). Weight-based fluid calculation in DKA is

in the first hour. 
	
l In case of mild DKA and child is taking orally, then give subcutaneous insulin and 
encourage oral hydration for resolution of mild DKA.
