HYPOTHYROIDISM
Hypothyroidism is characterized by decrease in the function of the thyroid glands. 
Most cases in children are due to congenital hypothyroidism causes such as aplasia, 
hypoplasia or ectopia of thyroid gland. Common causes of acquired hypothyroidism 
are iodine deficiency, lymphocytic thyroiditis and following irradiation of cervical 
region for malignant disorders. Diagnostic studies and treatment are same as that for 
congenital hypothyroidism. Universal newborn screening is recommended for all live 
births to detect congenital hypothyroidism at birth.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Congenital hypothyroidism is difficult to diagnose in neonatal period as the symptoms 
and signs may not be fully developed. However, prolongation of physiological 
jaundice and feeding difficulty in the form of sluggishness and choking during 
feeding occurs. Infants cry less, sleep more and have constipation, abdominal 
protuberance and umbilical hernia. Infants with these features should be screened by 
thyroid function tests to avoid delay in diagnosis. Gradually, the features of physical 
and mental retardation become more obvious which can be severe. 
	
l Newborn screening can be performed using cord blood or heel-prick sample or 
venous blood (after 48 hours of birth) to detect raised TSH levels. The diagnosis 
is confirmed based on demonstration of low serum T4 with raised TSH on a 
repeat sample. Serum T3 levels may be normal and are not useful for diagnosis. 
A TSH level of >20 mIU/mL mandates an urgent repeat blood sample and need 
to start treatment as soon as possible. 
	
l Radionuclide scans can be helpful in identifying the cause of congenital 
hypothyroidism, but treatment should not be delayed pending the results of these 
scans or thyroid ultrasonography.

Initiation of therapy. L-thyroxine (Tab. 25, 37.5, 50, 62.5, 75, 100 and 125 mcg).
Initial dose in neonatal period is 10–15 mcg/kg/day (usually 37.5–50 mcg per day), 
given as a single daily dose half an hour before the first feed in the morning. The tablet 
can be crushed and mixed in expressed breast milk or any other liquid for small infants. 
Treatment should be started immediately if TSH in newborn screening is more than 
80 mIU/mL without waiting for a second repeat blood sample.
Note: Treatment is required lifelong, and the requirement keeps changing with 
increasing age. In later part of infancy, dose decreases to 5–6 mcg/kg/day and then to 
3–4 mcg/kg/day in children to an adult dose of 2 mcg/kg/day.
Assessment of response 
	
l Early response is evident in the initial few weeks and consists of symptomatic 
improvement in alertness, relief of constipation, improvement in appetite and

1164    Standard Treatment Guidelines
feeding. Increased linear growth and osseous maturation is seen over the next 
few months.
	
l Follow clinically every month for 6 months, then every 3 months until 2 years. 
Recurrence of symptoms such as lethargy, constipation and weight gain suggests 
undertreatment, while diarrhea, palpitations, increased appetite, and weight loss 
suggest overdosing. 
	
l Periodic check on thyroid function tests is needed (3–6 monthly). Serum T4 level 
should be maintained in upper normal range and TSH levels suppressed to normal. 
	
l After a few months of starting therapy, sometimes features suggestive of raised 
intracranial tension such as headache and vomiting may appear. The patient should 
be immediately admitted and treated.

URINARY TRACT INFECTION (UTI)
UTI is a common bacterial infection in infants and children. One per cent boys and 
3–5% of girls under 14 years develop UTI. The risk of UTI is higher in children with 
congenital urinary tract anomalies, chronic diarrhoea and malnutrition. Delay in 
diagnosis and treatment can lead to irreversible and long-term damage to the developing 
kidneys. It may result in renal scarring, hypertension and renal insufficiency.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Symptoms are non-specific. In neonates, it presents as a part of sepsis, while in 
infants and young children, symptoms can include fever, diarrhoea, vomiting, 
pain and poor weight gain. Older children may have burning, micturition, 
urgency, frequency, flank pain, turbid urine and recent onset enuresis. Adolescents 
may have symptoms restricted to the lower tract, and fever may not be present.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1165
	
l Diagnosis is confirmed by growth of significant number of organisms of a 
single species in the urine while a provisional diagnosis of UTI can be made on 
urinalysis, i.e. significant pyuria (>10 leucocytes/mm3 in fresh uncentrifuged 
sample, or >5 leucocytes per high power field in a centrifuged sample) and rapid 
dipstick tests (leucocyte esterase and nitrite) (Table 19.24).
	
l Recurrent UTI seen commonly in girls is defined as the recurrence of symptoms with 
significant bacteriuria in patients who have recovered clinically following treatment.
Optimal urine sample collection for UTI diagnosis in young neonates, infants and 
older children
Toilet-trained children: The most preferred method for urine collection is midstream 
urine collection using the clean catch method. This approach is noninvasive and 
practical. Before collecting the midstream urine sample, it is important to ensure proper 
cleaning of the genital area with soap and water.
Non-toilet trained children: For this group, either simple urethral catheterization or 
suprapubic aspiration is recommended.
Note: In neonates, infants and older children, urine samples should never be collected 
from a urobag or minicom. Instead, the preferred method is to use a urine collection bag 
adhered to the perineum for infants or a sterile, cotton wool-tipped swab for neonates. 
Process the urine sample as soon as possible, ideally within 30 minutes of collection, 
to prevent contamination and ensure accurate results.

Definitions
Significant bacteriuria: Colony count of >105/mL of a single species in a midstream 
clean catch sample.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: Presence of significant bacteriuria in a child with no symptoms.
Recurrent UTI: Second episode of UTI.
Complicated UTI: Presence of fever >39°C, systemic toxicity, persistent vomiting, 
dehydration, renal angle tenderness and raised creatinine.
Simple UTI: UTI with low-grade fever, dysuria, frequency, urgency but none of the 
symptoms of complicated UTI.

Maintain adequate hydration and encourage liberal fluid intake to alleviate dysuria
Note: Routine alkalinization of urine is not necessary.

Therapy should be started after obtaining urine culture depending on patient’s age, 
degree of toxicity, state of hydration, ability to retain oral intake and the likelihood 
of compliance with medication. The treatment may be modified once the result of 
antimicrobial sensitivity is available. 
Complicated UTI and/or age less than 3 months (Hospitalized)
Intravenous therapy with broad-spectrum third-generation cephalosporins for the first 2–3 
days, followed by oral antibiotics once the clinical condition improves (patient is afebrile 
and stable after 48 hours) and these are continued for 10–14 days. IV therapy is preferred 
to oral drugs for children younger than 3 months and those with suspected urosepsis.
	 1.	Inj. Cefotaxime 100–150 mg/kg/day IV in 3–4 divided doses.
	
	Or
	
	Inj. Ceftriaxone 75–100 mg/kg/day IV in 1–2 divided doses.
	
	Further modification in antibiotic regimen can be done as per culture sensitivity 
reports.
	 2.	Add amikacin or gentamicin in a child with urosepsis who does not improve within 
24–48 hours of single empirical agent.
	
	Inj. Gentamicin 5–6 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses. 
If age more than 3 months empirical therapy with third-generation Cephalosporin as 
above. In a child with normal renal function, a single daily dose of Inj. Gentamicin can be 
given in place of Cephalosporins. Alternate IV antibiotics may be used as guided by the 
culture sensitivity report. Patients can be switched to oral antibiotics once they are stable.
Uncomplicated UTI and age >3 months
Give oral antibiotics as below for a period of 3–5 days. The choice of antibiotics can 
be revised as per culture sensitivity reports if there is no relief with empirical therapy. 
Adolescents with cystitis may be treated for a shorter duration of antibiotics lasting 3 days.
Syr. Cefixime 8–10 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (as gram-negative organisms are the 
most common causes of UTI)

Monitoring
	
l An abdominal ultrasound examination and repeat urine culture are necessary in 
patients who fail to show clinical response (reduction of fever and toxicity) within 
48 hours of initial treatment. Abdominal ultrasound is also indicated in children with 
UTI younger than 5 years of age to detect congenital abnormalities of renal tract.
	
l The aim of evaluation after UTI is to identify patients at high risk of renal damage, 
mainly those >1 year of age and those with vesicourethral reflux (VUR) or urinary 
tract obstruction. Patients with recurrent UTI and/or vesicoureteric reflux should be 
evaluated for bowel bladder dysfunction. 
	
l Recurrent UTI may be suspected if there are two or more episodes of upper UTI 
(acute pyelonephritis), or one episode of upper UTI (pyelonephritis) and one 
episode of lower UTI (cystitis), or three or more episodes of cystitis in a child over 
an undefined period of observation. This differs from adults, where frequency is 
determined on an annual rate.
	
l Ultrasound of the kidney, ureter, and bladder is recommended for all children with 
UTI.
	
l A micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) is indicated in children with abnormal 
kidney ultrasound, recurrent UTI, or in children below 2 years of age with non-E. 
coli UTI. MCU should not be performed during the acute stages; ideally, wait for 
4–6 weeks after UTI.
	
l A dimercaptosuccinic acid scan (DMSA scan) is recommended in children with 
recurrent UTI and high-grade vesicoureteral reflux (grade 3–5). DMSA should not 
be performed in acute stages.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria (significant bacteria count in the absence of 
symptoms of UTI) 
Asymptomatic bacteriuria does not require any treatment as it does not cause renal 
injury. The presence of asymptomatic bacteriuria in a patient previously treated for UTI 
should not be considered as recurrent UTI.
Circumcision reduces the risk of recurrent UTI in infant boys.
Long-term follow-up
	
l Assess renal function once a year in a child who had severe complicated UTI or 
recurrent UTI; Watch for proteinuria after successful treatment of UTI, it may be 
associated with pyelonephritic renal scarring and would need medical intervention. 
	
l Monitor physical growth and blood pressure every 6–12 months, through 
adolescence. 
	
l Urinalysis for proteinuria, serum creatinine and ultrasound examination for renal 
growth should be done annually. 
	
l Further follow-up and monitoring Aim for symptomatic improvement, complete and 
sustained resolution of fever and return of normal well being. 
	– Document normal urine analysis at the end of treatment of current UTI. 
	– Do not repeat urine culture unless there is a new UTI/breakthrough UTI. 
	– Urine analysis during further febrile episodes in the presence of a known risk 
factor for UTI. 
	– Watch for proteinuria after successful treatment of UTI, it may be associated with 
pyelonephritic renal scarring and would need medical intervention.
	
l UTI can be effectively managed by primary care physician; however, refer to 
a paediatric nephrologist if recurrent UTIs, UTI associated with bowel-bladder 
dysfunction, VUR, underlying urologic or renal abnormality and children with renal 
scar, deranged renal function, hypertension. 
Patient education
	
l Emphasize on adequate fluid intake and frequent voiding and avoid constipation. 
	
l Provide toilet training in children with VUR and encourage volitional low pressure 
voiding with complete bladder emptying and double voiding.
	
l Screening of siblings and offspring is required in case of vesicourethral reflux 
detected by ultrasound. Further imaging is required if ultrasonography is abnormal.

ACUTE GLOMERULONEPHRITIS 
(POST-STREPTOCOCCAL)
It follows streptococcal infection of throat or skin by 1–2 weeks. Complications like 
congestive heart failure or encephalopathy may occur in a few patients. Diagnosis is 
clinical with urine showing RBCs, WBCs and mild proteinuria. Serum C3 levels are low. 
Serum Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titres are elevated in most patients of post-streptococcal 
glomerulonephritis (PSGN) (up to 90%). Disease is self-limiting and generally resolves 
in 1 month; however, microscopic urinary changes may persist up to 1 year.
SALIENT FEATURE
Sudden onset of gross haematuria, proteinuria, oedema, hypertension, oliguria and 
other features of renal insufficiency.

Child should be admitted for monitoring and treatment if complications occur.

l Routine activity need not be restricted unless features of acute renal failure or severe 
hypertension occur. 
	
l Fluids and sodium intake is restricted like in acute renal failure.

There is no specific treatment.
Treatment of hypertension
	 1.	Inj. Frusemide 1–2 mg/kg/day in two divided doses till oliguria and fluid retention 
lasts.
	 2.	Cap. Nifedipine 0.25 mg/kg orally 4–6 hourly. 
	 3.	Inj. Procaine penicillin 4 lakh units once daily if evidence of sore throat or skin infection.
Monitoring and follow-up
	
l Regular weight record, strict intake-output chart, blood pressure recording should 
be done regularly.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1171
	
l Refer to a higher centre if hypertension, haematuria or renal failure do not show an 
improving trend within 48 hours of conservative therapy. In such cases, work-up for 
underlying systemic nephritis may be needed.
Patient/Parent education
	
l Parents should be explained the natural course. More than 95% recover within 
2–4 weeks. Only a few patients may end up with chronic renal insufficiency.

NEPHROTIC SYNDROME (NS)
Nephrotic syndrome is an important chronic disorder in children. It can be primary 
(idiopathic) or secondary (SLE, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, amyloidosis, etc). About 
90% of children with idiopathic nephrotic syndrome have ‘minimal lesion’ on renal 
histology and respond promptly to corticosteroids and are classified as ‘steroid 
sensitive’. Approximately three-fourths of patients have one or more relapses. Steroid 
toxicity and frequent serious infections complicate such cases.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia (S. albumin <3.0 g/dL), and oedema. 
Dipstick or heat coagulation of urine shows 3+/4+ proteinuria. Spot protein/
creatinine ratio >2 or urine protein excretion >40 mg/m2/h (on a timed sample), 
24-hour urine protein >3.5 g. Estimation of blood levels of antistreptolysin O 
and C3 in patients with gross or persistent microscopic haematuria to rule out 
glomerulonephritis.
	
l Investigations which help in diagnosis and management are urine analysis, blood 
counts, serum cholesterol, serum proteins, blood urea, serum creatinine, urine 
culture, X-ray chest, Mantoux, HBsAg.
Definitions useful for guiding treatment are as follows: 
Remission: Urine albumin nil or trace (spot urine protein to creatinine ratio (Up/Uc) 
<0.2 mg/mg) for three consecutive early morning specimens.
Relapse: Urine protein (>3+ (Up/Uc >2 mg/mg)) for three consecutive early morning 
specimen having been in remission previously.
Partial relapse: Urine protein 1+/2+ (dipstick), Up/Uc between 0.2 and 2, or 24-hour 
urine protein 4–40 mg/m2/day; serum albumin ≥3.0 g/dL; and absence of oedema.
Frequent relapses: Two or more relapses in the initial 6 months, or more than three 
relapses in any 12 months.

1172    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Steroid dependence: Two consecutive relapses when on alternate day steroids or within 
14 days of its discontinuation.
Steroid resistance: Absence of remission despite therapy with 4 weeks of daily 
prednisolone in a dose of 2 mg/kg per day.
Complicated relapse: Relapse associated with life-threatening complications: (i) 
hypovolaemia requiring inpatient care, (ii) severe infection (peritonitis, cellulitis and 
meningitis), or (iii) thrombosis.
Congenital nephrotic syndrome: Onset of nephrotic syndrome within the first 3 months 
of life.

Goals of treatment
	
l At the initial stage of the disease, the objectives include confirming diagnosis, 
excluding secondary causes, and assessing for potential complications.
	
l Kidney biopsy is reserved for specific situations (as detailed in Table 19.27), while 
genetic studies may be warranted in certain cases of initial steroid resistance, such as 
infancy onset, familial history of steroid resistance, extrarenal or syndromic features, 
lack of response to calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) and prior to kidney transplantation.
	
l Relapses are addressed with oral Prednisolone, initially at a dosage of 2 mg/kg (60 mg/
m2) daily until urine protein is trace or absent for three consecutive days, followed by 
1.5 mg/kg (40 mg/m2) every other day for 4 weeks. Subsequent treatment strategies are 
tailored according to the patient’s clinical progress. Infrequent relapses are managed 
with Prednisolone for 4–6 weeks, following the aforementioned regimen.
	
l Patients with nephrotic syndrome necessitate vigilant monitoring, early detection and 
prompt management of complications arising from the disease or its treatment. The 
management strategy primarily aims to minimize relapse frequency while mitigating 
adverse effects associated with immunosuppressive medications. Collaboration with 
a paediatric nephrologist is advised for such cases.
Long-term alternate day Prednisolone therapy
Initiate therapy at a dose of 0.5–0.7 mg/kg on alternate days for a duration of 9–12 
months. During episodes of fever or upper respiratory tract infections, Prednisolone 
may be administered daily at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg (15 mg/m2) for 5–7 days to prevent 
infection-induced relapses.
Close monitoring for steroid toxicity, including obesity, diminished stature, impaired 
glucose tolerance, cataracts, elevated intraocular pressure and osteoporosis, is essential 
during therapy. Avoid repeated courses of prolonged Prednisolone treatment. Patients 
experiencing ongoing relapses despite alternate-day Prednisolone or exhibiting signs 
of steroid toxicity should be evaluated for steroid-sparing therapies.
Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome
Refer steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome to a paediatric nephrologist as it presents 
a management challenge due to the unpredictable response to immunosuppression,

NEONATAL SEIZURES
Seizures in newborns are among the most identifiable and prevalent manifestations 
of neurological disease during the neonatal period. The incidence increases with 
decreasing gestational age and birth weight, being most prevalent in very low birth 
weight (VLBW) infants. Neonatal seizures are often acute symptomatic due to 
underlying brain insults. Focal clonic multifocal clonic, and focal tonic seizures 
are usually accompanied by ictal EEG activity while subtle, generalized tonic and 
myoclonic episodes may be non-epileptic as they are not associated with electrographic 
ictal activity. True seizures are often accompanied by open eyes. Differentiate between 
non-epileptic phenomena like jitteriness and benign sleep myoclonus. 
Jitteriness can be provoked by stimulation and aborted by gentle restraint and is 
not accompanied by autonomic changes (tachycardia, increased BP, etc.) or abnormal 
eye movements.
Features of spasms due to tetanus include involuntary contraction of muscles, 
often with fists persistently and tightly clenched, trismus (lockjaw), opisthotonus 
(arched back), triggered by stimuli such as touch, light, or sound. The baby is conscious 
throughout, often crying in pain.
Serum glucose, electrolytes, calcium and magnesium must be done in all. CSF 
studies and culture must be done in all except when the diagnosis is definite, e.g. 
hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy. A portable 60-minute EEG by a trained technician 
and interpreter is useful in recognizing subclinical seizures, epileptic encephalopathies

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1177
and prognosis. A cranial ultrasound is the minimum imaging required, but an in-house 
MRI with diffusion tensor imaging is the modality of choice done immediately for 
aetiology and at 3–6 months for prognosis.

Management should be done as per Figure 19.13. Try to discontinue all medications 
at discharge if neurological examination is normal. There is no need to taper the 
anticonvulsants. Continue oral phenobarbitone and/or phenytoin till discharge or up to 
3 months (especially in those with an abnormal neurologic examination). (Caution: Do 
not use bolus doses of diazepam or midazolam for control of convulsions in neonates. 
Valproate should also not be used in neonates for risk of side effects. Levetiracetam 
may be used as an alternate drug in refractory neonatal seizures).
Monitoring 
Monitor EEG if available. If the patient is on Phenobarbitone maintenance, consider 
obtaining a trough level if available. Always attempt to wean to one drug for 
maintenance therapy.
Weaning of all antiseizure medicines (ASMs)
Try to discontinue all medicines at the time of discharge if seizure free for 48–72 
hours depending on neurological examination, cause of seizures and EEG pattern. 
If neurological examination, feeding and tone assessment is normal, stop ASMs. If 
feeding and tone assessment is not normal, continue ASMs. If reassessment of feeding 
and tone assessment at 1 month of age and EEG is normal taper ASMs over 2 weeks. 
If abnormal reassess at 3 months of age.
ACUTE SYMPTOMATIC SEIZURES
A seizure occurring within a week of an acute brain insult (trauma, infection, toxic, 
metabolic or vascular insult) is called an acute symptomatic seizure. The future risk of 
unprovoked seizures is only 3–10%.
	
l Serum calcium, magnesium, electrolytes and glucose should be estimated for all 
children. Lumbar puncture should be done in febrile infants and in those with 
suspected meningoencephalitis. A plain CT scan is indicated in traumatic brain injury 
and a contrast-enhanced CT scan is indicated in children above 2 years, especially 
those presenting with convulsive seizures, focal seizures, cluster of seizure or focal 
neurological deficits to rule out granuloma.
	
l In a hypocalcaemic breastfed infant, an underlying Vitamin D deficiency state in the 
child and in the feeding mothers should be corrected. AEDs are required in the acute 
phase and can be withdrawn in a week in acute traumatic brain injury or in 3 months in 
illnesses with parenchymal involvement (e.g. CNS tuberculosis or pyogenic meningitis 
with parenchymal involvement). (For AED details, see Epilepsy in Chapter 1.)

FEBRILE SEIZURES
Febrile seizures are brief (2–5 min), generalized tonic-clonic and self-limited seizures 
followed by a brief post-ictal period of drowsiness, in an otherwise healthy, febrile child 
(temperature >38.4 C or 101°F) of 6 months to 6 years of age, without any evidence 
of underlying neurological disease. They are the most common seizure disorder during 
childhood, with a uniformly excellent prognosis. They occur rarely before 6 months 
and after 5 years of age. The peak age of onset is approximately 14–18 months of 
age, found in 3–4% of young children. There is a strong family history of febrile 
convulsions in siblings and parents, suggesting a genetic predisposition. Except for the 
cases at high risk, simple febrile seizures rarely develop into epilepsy. 
Definitions 
	
l Febrile status epilepticus: Febrile seizure lasting for 30 minutes or more. 
	
l Febrile seizure plus: Febrile seizures that continue past the usual age where they are 
expected to resolve (6 years) and/or accompanied by afebrile generalized (tonic-
clonic, atonic, myoclonic, myoclonic-atonic, or absence) or focal seizures. 
	
l Genetic epilepsy with febrile seizure plus (GEFS+): Febrile seizures plus with a 
family history of febrile seizures, febrile seizures plus, or afebrile seizures like 
generalized tonic clonic, myoclonic, absence atonic and focal seizures.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Febrile seizures usually occur when the temperature is rising rapidly to generally 
39°C (102°F) or more of core temperature. They are of two types: 
	
(i)	 Typical (simple) febrile seizure occurs on day 1 of fever, does not last for 
more than 10 minutes; generalized tonic-clonic; generally, not more than one 
episode within 24 hours. 
	
(ii)	 Atypical or complex febrile seizure may persist for more than 15 minutes; 
it could be focal in nature; more than one episode of seizure in 24 hours; 
associated with abnormal neurological findings or deficits. An organic cause 
such as an infectious or toxic process should be considered and investigated. 
Late onset febrile seizures, persistent febrile seizures, generalized epilepsy 
and febrile seizure plus (GEFS+) and febrile status epilepticus (FSE) are part 
of the spectrum of febrile seizures.
	
l Lumbar puncture: A lumbar puncture with examination of CSF is essential 
to rule out possibility of meningitis in cases with first episode of febrile 
seizures in children less than 1 year of age. Infants who are not vaccinated 
with Pneumococcal and Hib vaccine. CSF analysis is not needed in all cases of 
complex febrile seizures but should be done in febrile status epilepticus. 
	
l Neuroimaging (MRI) should be done in those with complex febrile seizures with 
prolonged or focal features. No follow-up imaging is needed in those with normal 
imaging at initial screening.

1180    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l EEG has no role in case of simple febrile seizures. However, in cases with 
atypical febrile seizure or in a child with high risk for developing epilepsy, it 
may be helpful. 
	
l High risk for developing epilepsy includes a positive family history of epilepsy, initial 
febrile convulsion prior to 9 months of age, a prolonged or atypical febrile seizure, 
delayed developmental milestones and an abnormal neurological examination.

Most febrile seizures are brief and would be over by the time a child is brought to 
the doctor or a health facility. Management includes definitive diagnosis, restraint in 
investigations, treatment of an acute episode, prophylaxis for future episodes and family 
counselling. The role of defervescence in preventing febrile seizures is questionable.
Out-of-hospital treatment
Rectal liquid Diazepam (0.5 mg/kg) or buccal Midazolam (0.3 mg/kg) for acute 
termination of seizures that last for 2 minutes or more.

Clear the airway, semiprone lateral position and oxygen therapy.

It is a safe and effective method of prophylaxis but does not reduce the risk of future 
epilepsy. It is not indicated in the first episode of febrile seizures, may be offered if 
recurrent simple febrile seizures and parental anxiety. 
Tab Clobazam 0.5–1.0 mg/kg for 2–3 days in two divided doses during fever or Tab/
Syr for up to 3 days, to be discontinued after 3 days.
Intermittent prophylaxis (during febrile illness)
It is a safe and effective method of prophylaxis but does not reduce the risk of future epilepsy. 
Tab Clobazam 0.75 mg/kg for 2–3 days in 2 divided doses during fever or Tab/Syr. 
Diazepam 0.3 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours (1 mg/kg/day) for 2–3 days of febrile illness started 
on the day of onset of fever. Dose can be adjusted if oversedation or ataxia noted.
Continuous prophylaxis
Febrile status, complex and recurrent febrile seizures (>6/year in spite of intermittent 
prophylaxis) may need EEG, neuroimaging and continuous prophylaxis with AED. 
Sodium valproate may be used in infants and older children respectively for 1–2 years 
of seizure free period. Carbamazepine and phenytoin are not useful. 
Patient/Parent education
	
l The parents and caretaker should be assured of the benign nature of the disease and 
should be told that no neurological deficit or mental retardation occurs as a result 
of simple febrile seizure.

l Routine immunization as per schedule should be followed. After DPT vaccination,

Similarly after measles vaccination, oral Paracetamol in the same dose can be 
started on the 4th day from the day of vaccination and given for 3–4 days to avoid

NEUROCYSTICERCOSIS
Neurocysticercosis (NCC) is the disease produced by invasion of the CNS by the 
cystic stage (cysticercus) of pork-tapeworm (Taenia solium) and is a common cause 
of seizures worldwide. It is the most common parasitic cause of CNS disease and is 
prevalent in every continent except Antarctica. In humans, the disease is acquired by 
ingestion of contaminated food or water with the eggs of T. solium. NCC is an easily 
treatable entity if diagnosed in time and appropriate management is done.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The clinical features depend upon site and number of cysts in the CNS and the 
inflammatory response of the CNS. It can present as a ‘silent’ case on one hand 
to encephalitis-like symptoms. On the other hand any neurologic, cognitive 
or personality disorder in an individual from an endemic area may represent 
neurocysticercosis. However, seizures, either focal or generalized, remain the 
most common form of presentation.
	
l Less common are meningeal irritation, hydrocephalus or increased intracranial 
tension. Decreased visual acuity may be seen in ocular cysticercosis. In spinal 
neurocysticercosis, patients present with evidence of cord compression, nerve 
root pain, transverse myelitis or meningitis.
	
l On neuroimaging studies (CT and MRI), the presence of an eccentric scolex 
in a cystic lesion is pathognomic of an NCC. Cystic lesions with or without

1182    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	 enhancement and calcifications are the commonest findings. Serological tests 
are not recommended for diagnosis and management of children with NCC as a 
positive serological test (EITB, ELISA and dot-blot assay) supports the diagnosis 
of NCC but a negative test does not exclude it. Routine screening of family 
members of children with NCC is not recommended. 
	
l Peripheral eosinophilia is seen in approximately a third of NCC cases. There is 
no role of routine testing of CSF samples. In cysticercal meningitis, CSF shows 
moderate pleocytosis (mostly mononuclear cells, rarely >300 cells per mm3), 
increased protein (50–300 mg/dL) and low glucose levels; hypoglycorrhachia is 
associated with a poor prognosis.

Treatment must be individualized in terms of number and location of lesions, as 
well as based on the viability of the parasites within the nervous system. Growth of 
a parenchymal cysticercus may be life-threatening though is not a common event. 
Actively manage a growing parasite with antiparasitic drugs. Manage hydrocephalus 
or intracranial hypertension on first priority basis, if present.

1.	In live NCC cysts and transitional NCC granuloma, Tab. Albendazole 15 mg/kg/day 
in two doses per day for 14 days, taken with fatty meals.
	
	(Caution: Cysticidal drugs are absolutely contraindicated in ophthalmic lesions; 
perform fundoscopy before use of cysticidal drugs; monitor patients carefully for 
development of raised ICP.) No role for antiparasitic agents in patients with only 
calcified lesions, because the cysts are already dead. 
	
	Albendazole 15 mg/kg/day may be combined with Praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day for 
10–14 days in case of more than two viable cysts.
	 2.	Tab. Prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day started 2–3 days prior to cysticidal drugs and 
continued for 5–7 days to reduce the risk of cerebral oedema at the time of cyst 
breakdown.
	
	In cysticercal encephalitis. Inj. Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg/day (maximum 16 mg/
day) IV or pulse Methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day, maximum 1,000 mg/day) for 
3–5 days followed by tapering may be used.
	 3.	In case of seizures, anticonvulsants such as Carbamazepine or Phenytoin should 
be initiated and continued in appropriate doses. 
	
	Note: There is no role of routine prophylaxis with antiseizure medications (ASMs) 
in children with NCC.
Follow up
	
l Perform a follow-up contrast-enhanced CT scan or contrast-enhanced MRI 6 months 
after the initial scan.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1183
	
l If the follow-up scan indicates the resolution of the lesion, the antiseizure 
medications (ASMs) can be gradually tapered and stopped. 
	
l In the case of a calcified lesion, continue ASMs for a seizure-free interval of 2 years.
	
l If the lesion persists, consider retreatment with Albendazole or a combination of 
Albendazole and Praziquantel. (for details, see section on Epilepsy and Status 
Epilepticus).
Surgical treatment
There is no role of major surgical procedures except for some cases with 
extraparenchymal NCC. Surgical intervention such as endoscopic removal may be 
required in intraventricular and subarachnoid NCC, ventriculoperitoneal shunting for 
hydrocephalus and excision of giant symptomatic cysts that fail to respond to medical 
therapy or intraocular cysts.
	 1.	A ventricular shunt must be placed if there is evidence of hydrocephalus. This 
should precede medical treatment. 
	 2.	Surgical intervention is also required for removal of a large solitary cyst for 
decompression, removal of mobile cysts causing ventricular obstruction and some 
cases that fail to respond to medical therapy (spillage of cyst contents is not seen 
in these cases as is seen in cases of echinococcosis). Surgical decompression is 
the only treatment recommended for intraventricular cysts and cysticidal therapy 
should not be co-administered. 
	 3.	Ocular cysticercosis should be treated surgically only; enucleation is frequently 
required.
Patient/Parent education
	
l Neurocysticercosis is a preventable parasitic infection caused by larval cysts. 
Humans become infected after consuming under-cooked food or unpeeled fruits and 
vegetables, especially pork, or water contaminated with tapeworm eggs, or through 
poor hygiene practices. Food safety, improved sanitation and hygiene are all crucial 
to preventing the transmission of T. solium. Thorough cooking of food, especially 
pork, kills the parasite.
	
l All members of a family of an index case of cysticercosis should be examined for 
the presence of eggs or signs of disease and treated if necessary.

ACUTE ENCEPHALITIS SYNDROME
Acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) is a clinical syndrome where a person presents with 
fever and alteration in mental status with symptoms like confusion, delirium, coma with/
without seizures. Infections (such as viral, bacterial, fungal, parasitic, spirochetal) are the 
most common causes of AES with other causes being drugs, chemical and toxins. In patients 
with AES, both infectious and non-infectious forms may coexist. For instance, a patient with 
viral encephalitis might exhibit associated metabolic abnormalities such as hyponatremia, 
liver dysfunction, or kidney dysfunction. Encephalopathy arises from metabolic alterations 
and toxic etiologies, while encephalitis results from viral, bacterial, or fungal infections. 
Clinical features are somewhat similar, with the distinction between encephalopathy and 
encephalitis relying on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings. Encephalitis is characterized 
by elevated protein and cells in the CSF, whereas CSF is normal in encephalopathy or 
non-infectious AES. Although there can be exceptions, fever, focal seizures and focal 
signs are more common in encephalitis compared to encephalopathy. Geographical and 
seasonal clustering, along with other epidemiological characteristics, play a crucial role in 
clinical decision making. The recent AES reported from few parts in India was associated 
with consumption of lychees (seasonal fruit) which had caused significant fatalities in 
children (known locally as Chamki fever). It was postulated that the deaths had occurred 
by concurrent hypoglycaemia in the affected children. The toxins present in unripe lychee 
fruits namely methylene cyclopropyl acetic acid and hypoglycin A, carried a high risk for 
hypoglycaemia. The risk of mortality was highest in malnourished children. 
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Clinical diagnosis of a state of altered mental state (mental confusion, 
disorientation, delirium, coma) with fever with/without seizures which may result 
from both infective and non-infective causes. 
	
l Diagnostic work-up includes microbiological tests for confirming the aetiological 
agent by cerebrospinal fluid analysis, neuroimaging and supportive blood tests.

The diagnosis and management of infection-associated encephalitis have been 
discussed separately below under acute meningoencephalitis.
Supportive treatment is the mainstay of therapy and should be started immediately 
without confirmed aetiological agent.
	 1.	Maintain airway, breathing and circulation. 
	 2.	Check and correct any metabolic abnormality like hypoglycaemia and 
electrolytes – serum sodium, potassium and calcium. 
	 3.	Correct hypoglycaemia by IV bolus of 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose in an unconscious 
child. Alternately, administer 10% dextrose solution through nasogastric tube, if a 
child is not in shock. Recheck plasma glucose in 10–15 minutes.

ACUTE MENINGOENCEPHALITIS
Acute meningoencephalitis is an acute inflammatory process involving meninges 
and brain tissue due to infectious causes. The common aetiological agents are viruses 
and bacteria. Children of any age may be affected.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Fever, headache, vomiting, irritability, altered state of consciousness, signs of 
meningeal irritation and seizures. 
	
l The primary purpose of investigations is to confirm the diagnosis and identify the 
causal pathogen. This may include 
	– Blood culture, CBC, CRP, Procalcitonin
	– CSF analysis (Gram stain, acid-fast bacilli [AFB] stain and culture)
	– Other CSF tests: Multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (e.g. BioFire for 
rapid PCR-based detection of common viral and bacterial pathogens), latex 
particle agglutination (LPA), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
	– MRI is preferred over CT scan when clinical settings and resources permit, 
as MRI provides better soft-tissue resolution and can help identify certain 
pathogens or complications more effectively
	
l CSF examination differentiates the viral from bacterial cause of acute 
meningoencephalitis (Table 19.28).

Until a bacterial cause is excluded, empirical parenteral antibiotic therapy should

TUBERCULOUS MENINGITIS
Tuberculous meningitis is the inflammation of meninges due to lympho-haematogenous 
spread of the primary infections of tuberculosis to the meninges, found in about 0.3% of 
untreated primary infection in children. It is the most dangerous form of extrapulmonary 
tuberculosis. Seventy percent of the cases are found in children less than 5 years of age.

Chapter 19  Paediatric Conditions    1189
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l The clinical progression of tubercular meningitis (TBM) may be rapid or gradual. 
The signs and symptoms progress slowly over several weeks and can be divided 
into three stages: 
	– The 1st stage, which typically lasts 1–2 weeks, is characterized by non-specific 
symptoms, such as fever, headache, irritability, drowsiness and malaise. Focal 
neurologic signs are absent. 
	– The 2nd stage usually begins more abruptly. The most common features 
are lethargy, neck-rigidity, seizures, positive Kernig or Brudzinski signs, 
hypertonia, vomiting, cranial nerve palsies and other focal neurologic signs. 
	– The 3rd stage is marked by coma, hemiplegia or paraplegia, hypertension, 
decerebrate posturing, deterioration of vital signs and eventually death.
	
l Complications: Survivors may have motor deficits, cranial nerve deficits, mental 
retardation, learning disabilities, seizures, hydrocephalus, blindness, deafness and 
diabetes insipidus. 
	
l The diagnosis is made by analysis of CSF on lumbar puncture, which shows 
lymphocytic leucocytosis with elevated protein and a low sugar.
	
l In adults and children with signs and symptoms of TB meningitis, Xpert MTB/
RIF or Xpert Ultra should be used in CSF as an initial diagnostic test for TB 
meningitis rather than smear microscopy/culture.
	
l Demonstration of AFB in CSF confirms the diagnosis, but the yield is very 
poor. Culture of CSF shows growth of M. tuberculosis, but takes too much time. 
Positive tuberculin skin test corroborates the diagnosis but may be negative in 
severely malnourished/disseminated disease. 20–50% of children have a normal 
chest radiograph others may show primary disease. CT scan or MRI of brain may 
be normal during early stages of the disease. Later it can show exudates in the 
basal cisterns of brain, periventricular ooze and hydrocephalus. Some may even 
show tuberculomas. 
	
l Also test for COVID-19.

Treatment consists of proper supportive care, including non-pharmacological treatment, 
specific antitubercular therapy, treatment of increased intracranial tension and, if 
required, surgical treatment.

l Nutrition: After initial stabilization, nutritional rehabilitation should be done as given 
in section on PEM 
	
l Skin care and prevention of bedsores 
	
l To take care of bowel and bladder
	
l Physiotherapy and occupational therapy should be instituted early to prevent 
deformities and contractures

1.	Appropriate fluid therapy to correct dehydration due to frequent vomiting and 
decreased oral intake. 
	 2.	Treatment of SIADH. Fluid restriction to 3/4th or 2/3rd of maintenance. Treatment 
for raised intracranial tension. 
	 3.	Inj. Dexamethasone: 0.15 mg/kg IV 6 hourly followed by Tab. Prednisolone 
1.5 mg/kg/day when the patient is fit to take orally through mouth or nasogastric 
tube. Steroids at this dose should be given for 4 weeks and tapered over another 
2 weeks. A total of 6–8 weeks’ therapy with steroid is recommended. 
	 4.	Inj. Mannitol 20% 5 mL/kg IV over 10–15 minutes followed by 3 mL/kg every 
6 hours for 48 hours.
	 5.	Glycerol 1 mL/kg/dose every 6–8 hours, diluted in orange juice or water, given 
through feeding tube for 3–4 weeks depending on the presence of hydrocephalus 
and clinical response.
	 6.	Tab. Acetazolamide 50 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for 3–4 weeks depending

TRAUMATIC INJURIES
Traumatic injuries can occur at any age but most commonly they are seen at the 
age of 2–5 years and from 7 to 12 years. These injuries may result from automobile 
accidents, sports mishaps or falls (e.g. in elderly and in epilepsy) leading to either loss, 
mobility, intrusion, extrusion of deciduous or permanent dentition. While dealing with 
dental and maxillofacial injuries, the medicolegal aspect may be borne in mind for 
future evidence in honourable courts/insurance claims.
Luxation injuries form 30–40% of all the dental injuries and cause trauma to 
supporting structures of teeth ranging from minor crushing of the periodontal ligament 
and neurovascular supply of the pulp to total displacement of the teeth. They are usually 
caused by sudden impact such as a blow fall or striking a hard object.
In concussion, tooth has normal mobility, undisplaced and tender to percussion 
due to oedema and haemorrhage in the periodontal ligament. In subluxation, teeth has 
increased mobility and sensitive to percussion. In lateral luxation, trauma displaces the 
tooth lingually, buccally, medially or distally, i.e. out of its normal position away and 
from its long axis. In extrusive luxation, the tooth is displaced from the socket along 
its long axis in a coronal direction and the tooth is very mobile.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Signs and symptoms include pain, swelling, bleeding, facial asymmetry, inability 
and difficulty to chew or occlude teeth properly and restriction in mouth opening.

1.	Rule out root fracture by taking intraoral periapical radiographs in different 
angulations. Radiograph of lip can be done to rule out the presence of fracture 
fragment of tooth/foreign body.
	 2.	Relieve the occlusion by selective grinding of opposing teeth.
	 3.	Immobilize the injured tooth by repositioning and fixation of teeth.
	 4.	Reposition laterally luxated teeth under local anaesthesia.
	
 	For repositioning of extruded tooth, a slow and steady pressure is required to 
displace the coagulum formed between the root apex and the floor of the socket.

Note: Repositioning is done under local anaesthesia using finger or forceps pressure 
and stabilize the tooth using passive and flexible splint for a period of 2 weeks.
TOOTH LUXATION
It refers to a tooth being displaced in its socket (extruded/intruded or mobile) or 
dislocated/avulsed (tooth being knocked out of its socket). An avulsed permanent tooth 
needs to be replaced as soon as possible in its socket for a better prognosis.
In intrusive luxation, tooth is forced into its socket in an apical direction. It may 
exhibit a shortened or partially submerged appearance in the socket compared to 
adjacent teeth, and there might be reduced or absent tooth mobility, indicative of 
ankylosis. Additionally, on percussion, a metallic sound may be heard.

Teeth with incomplete root formation
	 1.	Allow eruption without intervention
	 2.	If no movement within 4 weeks, initiate orthodontic repositioning.
	 3.	If the tooth is intruded more than 7 mm, reposition surgically or orthodontically.
Teeth with complete root formation
	 1.	Allow eruption without intervention if the tooth is intruded less than 3 mm. If there 
is no movement within 8 weeks, reposition surgically or orthodontically before 
ankylosis develops.
	 2.	If the tooth is intruded 3–7 mm, reposition surgically or orthodontically.
	 3.	If the tooth is intruded beyond 7 mm, reposition surgically.
	 4.	Given the likelihood of pulp necrosis in teeth with complete root formation, it is 
recommended to initiate root canal therapy, incorporating a temporary filling with 
calcium hydroxide, approximately 2–3 weeks after repositioning.
	 5.	Once an intruded tooth has been repositioned surgically or orthodontically, stabilize 
with a flexible splint for 4 weeks.

l Propolis: Potent antimicrobial, antioxidant anti-inflammatory agent. It is a better 
transport media than Hank’s balanced salt solution (HBSS) and milk.
	
l Hank’s solution: This pH-preserving fluid is best used with a trauma-reducing 
suspension apparatus.
	
l Milk: Shown to maintain vitality of periodontal ligament cells for 3 hours, milk is 
relatively bacteria-free with pH and osmolarity compatible with vital cells.
	
l Saline: This is isotonic and sterile.
	
l Coconut water: It is rich in amino acids, vitamins and minerals which help in 
nourishing cells and maintaining viability.
	
l Saliva: This keeps the tooth moist; however, it is not ideal because of incompatible 
osmolarity, pH and presence of bacteria.
	
l Contact lens solution: It is a sterile formulation with moisturizing properties, 
making it convenient for lens wearers.
	
l Water: This is the least desirable transport medium because it results in hypotonic 
rapid cell lysis.

MAXILLOFACIAL INJURY
This includes fracture of the jaw bones (maxilla, mandible, zygomatic and other facial 
bones) with or without displacement, deviation or dislocation. Le Fort I, II or III are 
the terms used to describe fractures that involve the jaw.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Symptoms include bruising, swelling, pain and tenderness over the fracture site. 
There may be numbness, cuts, bleeding, facial deformity, malocclusion (feeling 
that the teeth do not fit together correctly), misalignment of teeth, and lost or 
loosened teeth.
	
l Pain may be experienced when biting down. Movement of the jaw may cause 
muscle spasm or produce a grinding sound. 
	
l There may be associated wounds of the face or mouth or dental injuries. There 
may also be bruising under the tongue or a cut in the ear canal due to the 
backward movement of the broken jaw.
	
l Individuals who suffer facial trauma severe enough to fracture the maxilla or 
mandible may be unconscious or unable to speak.

Given the potential life-threatening nature of injuries associated with severe facial 
trauma, it is crucial to prioritize resuscitation, thoroughly assess all injuries and stabilize 
the individual.
	 1.	Check and provide a patent airway, and maintain ventilation and circulation. In 
case of major trauma, see the section ‘Trauma’ in Chapter 2.
	 2.	Secure airway: Remove blood clot, foreign bodies or broken dentures, and clear 
the airway; immobilize the jaw and stabilize the tongue; pull the maxilla placing 
two fingers at the back of the palate forward and upward and stabilize the dental 
arch by temporary stabilization using Erich Bar and stainless steel wiring.
	 3.	Bleeding: Control bleeding with pressure pack. Usually, intraoral bleeding stops 
with proper reduction of the bones in most cases.
	 4.	Provide stabilization of the fracture by bandages (Barrel and Barton) or with 
interdental wiring.
	 5.	Undertake a detailed history and examination findings with investigations 
(radiological imaging) and document them for medicolegal purposes.
	
	Obtain a clear description of the events (mechanism of injury, including 
the magnitude, location and direction of impact) leading up to the trauma from 
the individual or witnesses. Also determine if there was loss of consciousness or 
any changes in mental status, vision, hearing or occlusion. A complete medical 
history may be obtained, including medical conditions (especially any underlying 
bone disease, neoplasia, arthritis or temporomandibular joint [TMJ] dysfunction), 
medications, allergies and occupation. 
	
	Refer to an oral maxillofacial surgeon or an oral health practice in a hospital. 
Isolated injury
In case of an isolated injury, obtain a dental X-ray before surgery. If additional 
information is needed, obtain CT scan in both the axial and the coronal planes. Perform 
chest radiography to rule out the aspiration of teeth or other dental hardware.
	 1.	For pain, NSAIDs and local anaesthetics as required. 
	 2.	In patients with midface fractures, give prophylactic antibiotics.
	 3.	Tetanus immunization status should be verified and updated as needed. 
	 4.	Apply ice or cold packs to the injured area of jaw (15–20 minutes each hour while 
awake to reduce swelling) at least 3–4 times a day for 2 days after injury or surgery. 
The ice to be placed in a small plastic bag, with a towel between the ice and the 
skin. After 48 hours, warm packs may be applied to decrease the bruising.
	 5.	Raise head end.
Definitive management
The ultimate goal of treatment is to reestablish occlusion. The mode of therapy for 
any type of jaw fracture is determined by the individual’s age and general health as 
well as the position, stability and severity of the fracture. The individual’s dental and 
periodontal status, the availability of materials and instrumentation for repair, the

availability of dental consultation, and the skill and experience of the surgeon are 
also important.
Refer to a higher centre in case of displaced fractures, deviated occlusion, bi-jaw 
fractures, and Le forte I, II, III level fractures.
Mandibular fractures
Patients with minimally displaced fractures and children are amenable to conservative 
therapy. Dressings help relieve the discomfort of the fracture. Minimal occlusal load is 
recommended when this mode of therapy is used. The goals of treatment include anatomic 
reduction of fracture segments, restoration of occlusion and avoidance of complications.
Closed or open reduction may be used, depending on the individual circumstances. 
Fractures of maxilla or mandible with unaltered occlusion
	 1.	Jaws are immobilized for 1–8 weeks through maxillo-mandibular fixation (MMF) 
where the jaws are lined up and arch bars (like braces) are put in place and wired, 
or rubber banded to keep the jaws shut allowing healing in a correct manner. 
(Caution: Never do a MMF in patients with epilepsy, head injury, asthma or 
compromised airways.)
	 2.	Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) surgery may be needed for certain 
types of fractures and more severe fractures. 
	 3.	If the individual has dentures and they are not broken, the dentures may be used 
to reduce a mandibular fracture. The dentures act as a splint, and with the use of 
circumferential mandibular wires, they can stabilize the fracture. The upper and 
lower dentures can be wired together to maintain MMF. If the individual lacks teeth 
(edentulous) but has no dentures, a Gunning-type splint can be fabricated and used 
in the same manner as dentures.
Maxillary fractures
Certain types of Le Fort I fractures can be treated with MMF. Many Le Fort fractures 
require more complex surgical treatment for optimal results.
Patient/parent education
	
l Diet: Diet progression involves transitioning from clear liquids to full liquids, and 
eventually to the Wired Jaw Diet, i.e. blenderized foods, which may require thinning 
with a small amount of water or milk.
	
l The appropriate time to return to work following a traumatic facial injury depends 
on the nature and extent of the injury and on the individual’s job requirements. 
Restrictions may include avoiding activities that require talking for more than 
1 hour per day.
	
l Prevent jaw fractures by avoiding trauma to the chin and lower face as follows:
–	Always use seat belts and shoulder harnesses while riding in a car, even if the car 
is equipped with airbags. Buckling up protects facial bones and upper body from 
dashboard impacts and other injuries.

TEMPOROMANDIBULAR JOINT DISORDER (TMD)
TMD is a major cause of non-dental pain in the orofacial region. It is a collective 
term for a group of musculoskeletal and neuromuscular conditions which includes 
several clinical signs and symptoms involving the muscles of mastication, the 
temporomandibular joint (TMJ) and the associated structures. TMD is classified as 
intra-articular or extra-articular. It affects up to 15% of adults, with a peak incidence 
at 20–40 years of age. The aetiology of TMD is multifactorial and includes biological, 
environmental, social, emotional and cognitive triggers.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Common symptoms include jaw pain or dysfunction often associated with jaw 
movement (e.g. opening and closing the mouth, chewing), ear ache, headache and 
facial pain. Pain in front of the ear without ENT causes is mostly of TMJ origin. 
	
l The diagnosis of TMD is based largely on history and physical examination – findings 
of abnormal mandibular movement, decreased range of motion, tenderness of 
masticatory muscles, pain with dynamic loading, signs of bruxism and neck 
or shoulder muscle tenderness. A clicking, crepitus or locking of the TMJ may 
accompany joint dysfunction.

1.	In case of recent trauma, dislocation, malocclusion, dental infection or abscess, refer 
to a dentist or oral maxillofacial surgeon for standard or panoramic radiography. 
Perform CT to assess bone abnormalities such as ankylosis, dysplasias, growth 
abnormalities, fractures and osseous tumours. Imaging should also be considered 
in patients who have failed to respond to conservative TMD treatment.
	 2.	In case of abnormal cranial nerve findings, evaluate for other causes. 
	 3.	Most TMJ symptoms resolve over time.

l Jaw rest, soft diet, moist warm compression and passive stretching exercises. 
	
l Biofeedback and cognitive behaviour therapy for pain management in patients with 
symptomatic TMD. Counsel these patients for behaviour modifications such as stress 
reduction, sleep hygiene, elimination of parafunctional habits (e.g. teeth grinding, 
pencil or ice chewing, teeth clenching) and avoidance of extreme mandibular 
movement (e.g. excessive opening during yawning, toothbrushing and flossing).
	
l Physical therapy options such as ultrasound, iontophoresis, electrotherapy, or low-
level laser therapy. 
	
l Acupuncture (6–8 sessions of 15–30 minutes duration) for myofascial TMD.

1.	NSAIDs (naproxen, piroxicam) are first-line agents typically used for 10–14 days 
for initial treatment of acute pain.
	 2.	Muscle relaxants can be prescribed with NSAIDs if there is evidence of a muscular 
component to TMD.
	 3.	For chronic TMD pain, a trial of tricyclic antidepressants, such as amitriptyline, 
desipramine and nortriptyline, may be considered.
	 4.	Use of benzodiazepines is limited to 2–4 weeks in the initial phase of treatment. 
Longer-acting agents with anticonvulsant properties (i.e. diazepam, clonazepam, 
gabapentin) may provide more benefit than shorter-acting agents.
	 5.	Opioids are not recommended and, if prescribed, should be used for a short 
period in case of severe pain for patients in whom non-opiate therapies have been 
ineffective. 
Occlusal splints and adjustments 
Occlusal splints in select patients with severe bruxism and nocturnal clenching to 
alleviate or prevent degenerative forces placed on the TMJ, articular disk and dentition. 
Patient education
	
l The exact cause of a TMJ disorder is often difficult to determine. Pain may be due 
to a combination of factors, such as genetics, arthritis or jaw injury or habitual 
clenching and grinding of teeth. 
	
l Pain and discomfort are temporary and can be relieved with self-managed care by 
changing eating habits (cut food into small pieces or soft food, avoid too much 
chewing and stop chewing gum), jaw muscle exercises or nonsurgical treatments.

TEMPOROMANDIBULAR JOINT (TMJ) DISLOCATION
The common causes of TMJ dislocation include extreme opening of the mouth, as 
may occur during eating, yawning, laughing, singing, vomiting or prolonged dental 
treatment and less often after trauma. In addition, iatrogenic dislocation may occur 
during anaesthesia induction and upper endoscopy. Risk factors include an anatomic 
mismatch between the fossa and the articular eminence, weakness of the capsule and 
temporomandibular ligaments and torn ligaments. Patients who have had one episode 
of dislocation are predisposed to recurrence.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Acute TMJ dislocation is characterized by a wide-open mouth that is unable to 
close. The condyle moves anterior to the articular eminence making a hollow in 
front of the ear. 
	
l Painful spasm of the muscle of mastication.

Wrist pivot reduction
This procedure is used to realign displaced wrist bones with an aim to restore function, 
relieve pain and promote healing in the affected wrist joint, facilitating the patient’s 
recovery and return to normal activities. In this technique, the clinician grasps the 
mandible bilaterally by placing his/her thumbs in the menton region of the mandible and 
resting the other fingers of both hands on the occlusal surfaces of the mandibular teeth. 
Then with an upward force directed at the menton and a downward force on the teeth, 
the clinician’s wrist will pivot towards the patient and allow the condyles to reduce.
Patient education
	
l After the joint is relocated, a soft or liquid diet is recommended for several days to 
minimize jaw movement and stress. Explain to the patients to avoid foods that are 
hard to chew, such as tough meats, carrots, hard candies or ice cubes, and be careful 
not to open their mouths too widely.
	
l TMJ dislocation can continue to happen in people with loose TMJ ligaments. 
	
l Limit the range of motion of the jaws (e.g. by placing their fist under their chin 
during yawning to keep from opening of the mouth too wide).

HALITOSIS
There are various physiological and pathological causes of halitosis or bad breath which 
may be extraoral or intraoral. In adults, chronic periodontal disease is a major cause of 
halitosis. Other causes include local conditions such as poor oral hygiene, extensive 
caries, gingivitis, healing extraction wounds and necrotic tissues from ulcerations. 
Stagnation of saliva associated with food debris, excessive smoking, especially cigar, 
dentures can also cause a type of halitosis known as ‘denture breath’. Halitosis can 
be due to systemic factors of pathological origin such as diabetes, uraemia or kidney 
failure. Some drugs may also cause bad breath such as antihistamines, amphetamines, 
tranquillizers, diuretics and atropine-like drugs which reduce saliva production and 
therefore decrease the self-cleansing ability of the oral cavity.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Diagnosis is established by a medical history, if any, clinical and laboratory 
examination with halimeter sulphide monitor.
	
l Organoleptic measurement is the most reliable and practical procedure. It is 
a sensory test scored on the basis of the examiner’s perception of a subject’s 
oral malodour. Organoleptic measurement can be carried out by sniffing the 
patient’s breath and grading the level of halitosis from 0 (no appreciable odour) 
to 5 (extremely foul odour). Assessment of oral halitosis should be carried out on 
two or three occasions for a reasonably accurate diagnosis.

l Home remedies include parsley, cloves, guava peels and egg shells or chewing gum. 
	
l Drink plenty of fluids; eat fresh, fibrous vegetables; and rinse the mouth after eating 
or consuming milk products, fish and meat.
	
l Avoid coffee, smoking, drugs and foods that might be responsible for halitosis.

The management of halitosis depends largely on the cause and assesses treatment needs 
of a patient.
	 1.	Explain halitosis and give instructions for oral hygiene (support and reinforcement 
of a patient’s own self-care for further improvement of his/her oral hygiene). 
	 2.	Physiological halitosis, oral halitosis and pseudo-halitosis to be treated by a dentist. 
	
	This involves the mechanical reduction of intraoral nutrients and microorganisms 
through procedures such as scaling, root planing, and oral hygiene instructions. 
Alternatively, chemical reduction of oral microorganisms can be achieved using 
mouthwashes containing chlorhexidine, cetylpyridinium chloride, and zinc chloride.

1202    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
	Note: Penicillins, Metronidazole, Ciprofloxacin and Tinidazole are commonly used 
antimicrobials/antibiotics for systemic causes (periodontitis) of halitosis, but not 
for intraoral causes (periodontitis) of halitosis.
	 3.	In case of extraoral pathologic halitosis or halitophobia, refer to a physician or 
medical specialist such as a psychiatrist or psychologist.

TOOTH HYPERSENSITIVITY
The term tooth hypersensitivity, or dentinal sensitivity, is often used interchangeably 
to describe a clinical condition of an exaggerated response to an exogenous stimulus 
(thermal, tactile, osmotic or chemical). This occurs when the protective layer of enamel 
gets thinner or lost or when gums recession occurs exposing the underlying dentin. The 
incidence is 8–30% of adult population between 20 and 40 years of age.
Common reasons for gingival recession are inadequately attached gingivae, 
prominent roots, toothbrush abrasion, oral habits resulting in gingival laceration, i.e. 
traumatic tooth picking, eating hard foods, excessive consumption of carbonated drinks, 
psychogenic grinding of teeth (bruxism), faulty brushing technique, excessive flossing, 
gingival recession secondary to specific diseases, i.e. necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis 
(NUG) and crown preparation.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Dentin hypersensitivity is defined as sharp, short pain arising from exposed 
dentin in response to stimuli typically thermal, chemical, tactile or osmotic, which 
cannot be ascribed to any other dental defect or pathology.
	
l Hypersensitivity is most commonly noted on buccal cervical zones of permanent 
teeth. Although all tooth types may be affected, canines and premolars in either 
jaw are the most frequently involved.

l Educate patients about diet and oral hygiene using soft brush, and pea size amount 
of toothpaste. Apply sensitive toothpaste after brushing. 
	
l Dentifrices like toothpaste and mouthwashes (having strontium chloride 10%/
potassium nitrate 5%/sodium fluoride 2%) available over-the-counter for at least

Note: Mouthwash not to be used for children up to 6 years of age.
(See below in Patient education section.)

	 1.	Varnishes (5% Sodium fluoride coating resin) are applied topically on affected

	 2.	Thin film of varnish is applied to cover open tubules for a temporary relief. For

	Refer to an endodontic surgeon for root canal treatment with the crown if partial

Patient education

and vegetables in diet. A written diet history should be obtained for patients with dentinal 
hypersensitivity. Caution about brushing teeth soon after ingestion of citrus fruits. 
	
l Maintain good oral hygiene.
	
l Advise on toothbrushing technique and plaque control to prevent further loss of 
dentin, and hence hypersensitivity. 
	
l Avoid over-brushing, overuse of dentifrice, excess flossing and inappropriate use 
of toothpicks.

TOOTHACHE
The causes of pain associated with tooth and gums are: 
	 1. 	Pulpal causes: Caries, abrasion, attrition, erosion (exposure of dentin due to acidic 
erosion), trauma to the tooth (injuries leading to a cracked or fractured tooth) 
(Table 20.1).
	 2.	Periodontal causes
	 3.	Non-dental causes: Maxillary sinusitis, trigeminal neuralgia and psychological 
disorders
History and examination
When investigating acute dental pain, the history should focus on the pain’s: location, 
type, frequency and duration, onset, exacerbation and remission (e.g. response to heat 
or cold), severity and area of radiation.

IMPACTED TEETH
When a tooth fails to erupt in the oral cavity beyond its chronological eruption age. It 
happens when tooth size is bigger than the dental arch size as an evolutionary process.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Pain, trismus, swelling, pus discharge and inability to occlude or chew.

1.	Prophylactic removal of third molars is avoided unless for orthodontic or planned 
for orthognathic surgery. 
	 2.	Surgical removal of impacted third molars should be limited to patients with 
associated pathology. Such pathology includes unrestorable caries, severe 
periodontitis, cellulitis, abscess and osteomyelitis, internal/external resorption of 
the tooth or adjacent teeth, fracture of tooth, increased follicular space including 
cyst /tumour, tooth/teeth impending surgery or reconstructive jaw surgery and 
when a tooth is involved in or within the field of tumour resection or infected 
mandibular fracture.
	 3.	In case of pericoronitis (localized inflammation of the overlying gums), antibiotics 
are generally not indicated; instead, management typically involves implementing 
oral hygiene measures. However, in cases of recurrent pericoronitis (more than 
two or three occurrences), or if the symptomatic tooth has not erupted beyond 
its chronological age, the recommended course of action is the removal of the 
impacted tooth.

1206    Standard Treatment Guidelines
POST DENTAL PROCEDURE COMPLICATIONS
Swelling and pain
Swelling is common after certain dental procedures, particularly after extraction and 
periodontal surgery. Holding an ice pack to the cheek can prevent much of the swelling. 
Ice therapy can be used for the first 18 hours. Cold compress should be held on the 
cheek for a 25-minute period every hour or two. If swelling persists or increases after 3 
days or if pain is severe, an infection may have developed, refer the patient to a dentist.
Pain after a dental procedure can be moderate to severe. Pain relievers can be 
prescribed.
Bleeding 
Bleeding from an extraction socket is the most common postoperative haemorrhage. 
While minor bleeding is normal immediately after the procedure, persistent or heavy 
bleeding warrants attention. Bleeding may be continuation of primary, reactionary 
(occurring within 48 hours of the operation when the effect of vasoconstrictor in local 
anaesthesia wears off and there is reactive hyperaemia), or secondary haemorrhage 
(a rare complication of tooth extraction which may be due to infection which destroys 
the blood clot. It starts about 7 days after operation). Bleeding may also be due to some 
local causes like trauma, laceration, friable granulation tissue, clot dislodgment, certain 
medical conditions like haemophilia, or the use of anticoagulant medications, infection, 
violent exercise, application of heat, coughing or may be due to some systemic causes.

l Patients experiencing excessive bleeding should follow post-extraction care 
instructions provided by the dentist, which may include biting on gauze, avoiding 
strenuous activities, and refraining from certain foods.
	
l Generalized oozing from the soft tissues usually can be arrested by manual 
pressure or a gauze pack placed over the area by using roll of cotton, gauze or 
clean handkerchief or black tea bag; apply it over the socket and bite firmly for 
30–45 minutes.
	
l Do not spit out.
	
l Do not take hot fluids.
	
l Avoid use of alcohol and smoking.
	
l If bleeding persists, seek prompt dental attention to prevent complications and 
ensure proper healing.
FAINTING ON DENTAL CHAIR (SYNCOPE)
Most patients reach the point of fainting due to fear and it usually happens as local 
anaesthesia is applied. Postural hypotension usually results when suddenly getting up 
from a lying or seated position.

DENTAL CARIES
This is a multifactorial infectious disease affecting the enamel of the tooth. If left 
untreated, it can affect the dentine and pulp. Decalcification of enamel occurs as a result 
of acid production by bacteria in dental plaque. Factors contributing to this process 
include the consumption of excessive sugary foods and refined carbohydrate beverages, 
inadequate oral hygiene practices and genetically soft (immature) enamel, all of which 
can contribute to the development of caries.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Dental caries appears as chalky white, brown or black discoloration, cavities 
in the tooth, usually painless in the beginning and on progression may cause 
increased sensitivity to hot, cold or sweet and sour foods and intense pain.

Examine for stage of caries and treat accordingly.
	 1.	In non-cavitated lesion and low-risk patients with good oral hygiene practices, no 
treatment is required. Caries prevention measures should be advised.
 2. Cavitated lesions require restoration when cavity has not encroached pulp; refer to 
a dentist for
	– Root canal treatment for painful tooth with or without periapical abscess
	– Extraction, if tooth cannot be restored
	 3.	For pain, give Tab. paracetamol 500 mg in adults (in children, 10 mg/kg) as and 
when required, and every 6 hours or ibuprofen 400 mg or diclofenac 50 mg on an 
as-and-when-required basis.
Caries risk assessment
	
l For patients with active caries: Follow-up visit every 3 months and to check the 
progression of white spot on the teeth

causing the gums to separate from the teeth.

l Perform oral prophylaxis as above with the aim to control or eliminate gingivitis

PERIODONTITIS
It is an inflammatory and degenerative condition of the soft and bony tissues supporting 
the teeth. Causes include poor oral hygiene, crowding of teeth, use of tobacco in any 
form, poor diet and compromised body immunity. 
Periodontitis is of two types:
	 1.	Destructive periodontal disease: If gingivitis is allowed to continue unchecked over 
a period of time, there is progressive loss of gingival tissues, loosening attachment 
(loose tooth) and loss of alveolar bone. If treatment is not sought, teeth start falling 
within months to years.
	 2.	Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis or periodontitis (also called trench mouth or 
Vincent’s angina with severe ulceration): This type of periodontitis causes necrosis 
of gums and soft tissues.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Red, swollen, painful gums, bleeding from gums either spontaneously or on 
eating something hard, difficulty in chewing food, pockets containing pus 
discharge from gum on pressing, elongated and/or loosening of teeth, recession 
of gums, and small lesions and ulcers on gums.
	
l There is slowly progressive destruction of periodontium, leading to loss of 
periodontal attachment and presence of periodontal pocket.
	
l Diagnosis: Perform probing to elicit bleeding, measure pocket depth and attachment 
levels to detect subgingival calculus; testing teeth for mobility and vitality; and 
radiographic evaluation.

l Initial phase: Aim is to control or eliminate gingivitis and arrest any further progression 
of periodontal disease by the removal of plaque and other contributory factors.
	
l Corrective therapy like scaling, root planing and periodontal surgery is performed.
	
l Maintenance phase: Provide motivation and guidance to maintain good oral hygiene.

Advise oral hygiene even if bleeding gums are present (brushing twice daily with a 
super soft toothbrush for at least 2 minutes). Refer to a dentist for oral prophylaxis for 
thorough scaling and root planing.
(See also the section ‘General Measures for Good Oral Hygiene’.)

ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS IN ORAL HEALTH CARE
Numerous medical conditions predispose patients to bacteraemia-induced infections. 
However, it is not possible to predict when a susceptible patient will develop an

condition: Antibiotic Prophylaxis in Oral Health Care
text:
Chapter 20  Dental Conditions    1215
infection. Thus, prophylactic antibiotics are recommended when these patients undergo 
procedures that are at risk for producing bacteraemia. Bacteraemia, bacteria in the 
bloodstream, is anticipated following invasive dental procedures. Infective endocarditis 
(IE) is an uncommon but life-threatening complication resulting from bacteraemia. 
Only a limited number of bacterial species have been implicated in resultant 
postoperative infections. The viridans group streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus, 
Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, Serratia and Candida are some of the microorganisms 
implicated with IE. IE prophylaxis for dental procedures is recommended only 
for patients with underlying cardiac conditions associated with the highest risk of 
adverse outcome (presence of a cardiac prosthetic valve, transcatheter implantation 
of prosthetic valves, cardiac valve repair with devices (such as annuloplasty rings or 
clips) and left ventricular assist devices or implantable heart devices and in children 
with cyanotic congenital heart disease or repaired congenital heart disease with residual 
defects, persisting leakage and cardiac transplantation recipients who develop cardiac 
valvulopathy for the following dental procedures:
	
l Dental extractions
	
l Periodontal procedures including surgery, scaling and root planing, probing and 
recall maintenance
	
l Dental implant placement and reimplantation of avulsed teeth
	
l Endodontic (root canal) instrumentation or surgery only beyond the apex
Antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated in all dental procedures that involve 
manipulation of gingival tissue or the periapical region of teeth or perforation of the 
oral mucosa. Antibiotic prophylaxis is NOT recommended for the following dental 
procedures:
	
l Routine anaesthetic injections through non-infected tissue
	
l Taking dental radiographs 
	
l Placement of removable prosthodontic or orthodontic appliances
	
l Adjustment of orthodontic appliances
	
l Placement of orthodontic brackets
	
l Shedding of deciduous teeth
	
l Bleeding from trauma to the lips or oral mucosa
	
l Scaling
Antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures is Not generally suggested for patients 
with the following underlying conditions or devices:
	
l Implantable electronic devices such as a pacemaker or similar devices
	
l Septal defect closure devices when complete closure is achieved
	
l Peripheral vascular grafts and patches, including those used for haemodialysis
	
l Coronary artery stents or other vascular stents
	
l CNS ventriculoatrial shunts
	
l Vena cava filters
	
l Pledgets
