ORAL POTENTIALLY MALIGNANT DISORDERS (OPMD)
OPMDs are defined as ‘any oral mucosal abnormality that is associated with 
a statistically increased risk of developing oral cancer’. The terms pre-cancer, 
premalignant and precursor lesions are often used to broadly describe clinical 
presentations with the potential to become cancerous. Among oral diseases, oral cancer 
is a critical health issue and global public health burden due to its life-threatening 
potential. A rise in the incidences of oral cancer is anticipated in the coming decades.
Lesions with dysplastic features have been categorized under OPMDs, such as 
oral leucoplakia, erythroplakia, oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF), and proliferative 
verrucous leucoplakia, and are assumed to have a high risk of malignancy. Early 
diagnosis, prevention and treatment of OPMDs are needed to prevent their malignant

Chapter 20  Dental Conditions    1217
transformation into oral cancer. These lesions are caused by tobacco use, gutka, betel 
nut chewing and exposure to human papillomavirus.
In case of suspicious lesions, perform vital tissue staining with tolonium chloride 
and a diagnostic biopsy for any mucosal lesion that persists for more than 14 days after 
obvious irritants have been removed to confirm the diagnosis.
For details, see section Screening for cancers in Chapter 8.
Oral leucoplakia: This is a clinical condition characterized by white patches that are 
not easily scrubbed off and cannot be diagnosed as any other definite oral lesions. It 
has a malignant potentiality from 3% to 11% of the cases.
Erythroplakia: It appears same as leucoplakia with speckled areas of redness 
and/or ulcers. Though far less common than leucoplakia, erythroplakia is much 
more prone to show signs of dysplasia or malignancy at the time of diagnosis. Such 
lesions have a flat, macular, velvety appearance and may be speckled with white spots 
representing foci of keratosis.
OSMF: This is a chronic disorder characterized by fibrosis of the oral mucosal 
lining with gradual unnoticed closure of the oral opening with a feeling of tightness; 
appearance of white bands in the buccal mucosa, lip, faucial pillars and floor of the 
mouth; and burning sensation of the mouth, more so with spicy food.

1.	Abstinence from gutka, betel nut chewing 
	 2.	Jaw exercises to promote opening of the mouth 
	 3.	Antioxidants, intralesional injection of Triamcinolone, placental extracts and 
hyaluronidase 
Refer for surgical excision of the fibrous bands.
Oral lichen planus: It appears as localized or diffuse thread-like interlacing bluish white 
ulcers, mostly on the buccal mucosa, tongue and alveolar mucosa. Oral lichen planus 
is often asymptomatic. The patient may experience varying degrees of discomfort, 
exacerbated by eating spicy or acidic foods. Co-morbidities include hypertension, 
diabetes mellitus and anxiety disorder.
General approach to management of OPMD is as follows: 
	 1.	Early diagnosis, biopsy being the gold standard
	 2.	Tobacco cessation
	 3.	Oral hygiene
	 4.	Diet counselling
	 5.	Symptomatic treatment for pain with topical drugs
	 6.	Anxiety and stress reduction
	 7.	Local and intralesional use of steroids
	 8.	Treat secondary infection with antibiotics
	 9.	Long-term follow-up
Some of the commonly encountered problems in oral mucosa are described in 
detail in the subsequent sections.

1218    Standard Treatment Guidelines
MOUTH ULCERS
These are generally due to trauma, infection (bacterial, viral or fungal), neutropenia or 
malignancy related. The common ones are trauma, aphthous or viral ulcers.
Trauma ulcers: Any sharp pointed tooth, fractured tooth or a denture or an injury will 
result in an ulcer in any part of the oral cavity.
Aphthous ulcers: These are recurrent ulcers of non-viral origin that occur on the 
movable surfaces of the oral cavity. Size is variable but may have a rim of erythema 
with yellow base, and later becoming greyish hue. They are classified as minor, major 
or herpetiform in clinical presentation. The minor is <1 cm, and the major 1–3 cm in 
diameter. The herpetiform comes in multiple crops of 1–3 cm. Although the cause 
is unknown, systemic conditions associated with aphthous ulcer include Behçet’s 
syndrome, HIV and vitamin deficiency states (vitamin B group, folic acid). Behçet’s 
disease is a more severe and generalized form involving the eye, skin and genitalia.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l A prodromal phase marked with tingling of the oral mucosa
	
l Painful ulcers
	
l Crater like soft-tissue ulcer with a yellowish base
	
l Tenderness
	
l Usually heal in 7–10 days but reappear in the oral cavity

1.	Take a proper history and carry out a detailed clinical examination to ascertain 
cause and treat accordingly.
	 2.	Control pain.
	 3.	Control stress.
	 4.	Prevent secondary infection with proper oral hygiene instructions.
	 5.	Prescribe vitamin B complex.
	
	Refer to an oral health practice if the ulcer does NOT heal in 2 weeks’ time, as this 
could be a malignancy. (See also Oral Ulcers in Chapter 6.)
ORAL CANDIDIASIS OR THRUSH
This fungal infection is caused by Candida species of the oral cavity and is usually seen 
in children, full or partial denture wearers or immunocompromised persons. Common 
causes are poor oral hygiene, malnutrition, prolonged use of antibiotics, use of steroid 
inhalers and alcohol abuse, and is also seen in patients with diabetes mellitus, HIV/
AIDS, leukaemia, cancer, asthma and viral infections.

SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Painful sores and blisters in the oral cavity
	
l Whitish plaque in the oral cavity (soft tissues), which can be scrapped
	
l Fever, enlarged and tender lymph nodes in the neck

l Advice on good oral hygiene with toothbrush and mouthwash
	
l Diet counselling and hydration
	
l Treating and eliminating the cause
	
l Prescribing analgesics (topical) for pain relief and antifungal agents (consider 
antibiotics if secondary infection is present)
(See also oral ulcers in Chapter 6.)
LEUCOPLAKIA
Leucoplakia is a predominantly white or grey lesion of the oral mucosa that cannot 
be clinicopathologically characterized as any other definable lesion. These patches 
can occur at any time in life, but it these are most common in senior adults. Causes 
of leucoplakia can include irritation from rough teeth, fillings or crowns or ill-fitting 
dentures that rub against the cheek or gum, chronic smoking, pipe smoking, or other 
tobacco use, sun exposure to the lips, HIV or AIDS. Leucoplakia is the most common 
premalignant or ‘potentially malignant’ lesion of the oral mucosa.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Appearance of solitary or multiple white lesions, with a uniform, flat and thin 
appearance developed slowly over weeks to months on any site of the oral cavity 
(buccal mucosa, alveolar mucosa, floor of the mouth, tongue, lips and palate). 
These lesions may become thick and slightly raised, and may eventually take on 
a hardened and rough texture. These are usually painless, but may be sensitive to 
touch, heat, spicy foods or other irritants.
	
l Homogeneous leucoplakia exhibits shallow cracks and has a smooth, wrinkled or 
corrugated surface with a consistent texture throughout and is usually asymptomatic. 
	
l Non-homogeneous leucoplakia exhibits predominant white or white-and-
red lesions that may be irregularly flat, nodular or exophytic and are often 
associated with mild complaints of localized pain or discomfort. In general, 
non-homogeneous leucoplakia has a higher malignant transformation risk, but 
oral carcinoma may develop from any leucoplakia.
	
l Proliferative verrucous leucoplakia is an aggressive type of leucoplakia that 
almost invariably develops into malignancy. 
	
l Definitive clinical diagnosis is obtained by lack of changes after eliminating 
suspected aetiological factors during a follow-up period of 2–4 weeks 
(in some cases the time may be longer) and proven histopathologically by biopsy.

1.	Eliminate the possible aetiological factors, i.e. irritation by any roughened tooth, 
trauma, Candida, etc. It usually clears in a few weeks or months after the source 
of irritation is removed.
	 2.	Advise complete cessation of tobacco. 
	 3.	In dysplastic leucoplakia, plan treatment and follow-up according to histological 
grade. In cases with epithelial dysplasia, perform complete surgical removal 
(leaving free-lesion borders). Other options include cryosurgery, laser surgery 
and electrocautery.
For hairy leucoplakia, refer to an ART centre (see Chapter 7 for details).

The malignant transformation rate of oral leucoplakia varies from 0% to 33%. Overall, 
3–8% of leucoplakias develop malignant transformation in an average follow-up 
period of 5 years. Some leucoplakias show an increased recurrence rate (proliferative 
verrucous leucoplakia). Regular check-up of these patients is essential, probably every 
3, 6 and then 12 months, in both treated and untreated patients.
Note: Photodynamic therapy, the carotenoids beta-carotene and lycopene and systemic 
retinoic acid (vitamin A) have demonstrated limited effectiveness in speeding up 
the resolution of oral leucoplakia. The systemic side effects of retinoic acid reduce the 
risk–benefit ratio for this indication considerably.
Patient education
	
l There is no known therapy to prevent the development of oral leucoplakia. Early 
diagnosis and treatment of leucoplakia can reduce the high rates of oral cancer, 
morbidity and mortality. Prolonged and close follow-up care is essential, but the 
prognosis may still be poor.
	
l Healthy lifestyle and the abstinence of tobacco are the best way for prevention.
	
l Fresh fruits and vegetables may have a protective effect in the primary prevention 
of oral cancer and precancer.

ORAL LICHEN PLANUS
The diagnosis of oral lichen planus is initially based on the clinical presentation 
of bilateral white patches with or without ulcers or blisters. In case of an atypical

Chapter 20  Dental Conditions    1221
presentation, atrophic or ulcerating biopsy and histopathological examination of the 
affected tissue may be needed to exclude another disease that may mimic oral lichen 
planus (e.g. discoid lupus erythematosus and epithelial dysplasia). Haematological/
immunological investigations are not routinely indicated but should be undertaken 
where clinically appropriate.

l Reassurance in case of asymptomatic non-ulcerative lichen planus; explanation 
of the nature of the condition, including its aetiology, clinical features, treatment, 
follow-up and prognosis
	
l Advice on avoidance of risk factors such as tobacco and alcohol
	
l Dietary advice regarding intake of fresh fruit and vegetables
	
l Emphasize the importance of maintaining good oral hygiene

Symptomatic non-ulcerative lichen planus: Topical anaesthetic and/or barrier 
agents for symptomatic relief of pain such as 2% lidocaine gel on painful areas Or 
Benzydamine hydrochloride (0.15%) spray or mouth rinse.
Atrophic/ulcerative oral lichen planus: Topical corticosteroid preparations – 
Clobetasol ointment (0.05%) applied to painful areas 3–4 times daily Or Triamcinolone 
Or Fluticasone cream (0.05%) applied to painful sites 3–4 times daily Or Soluble 
prednisolone tablets 5 mg dissolved in 15 mL of water and used as a mouth rinse 
3–4 times daily Or Betamethasone sodium phosphate (500 mcg dissolved in 10–15 mL 
of water) used as a mouth rinse up to 4 times daily Or Fluticasone propionate spray 
(50 mcg per puff) directed to affected areas up to 3–4 times daily or Beclomethasone 
spray (100 mcg per puff) sprayed 3–4 times daily on affected sites.
In case of associated candidiasis, administer appropriate topical antifungal 
preparations. If localized lesion(s), consider lichenoid reaction to amalgam. In 
severe, symptomatic atrophic/ulcerative oral lichen planus, unresponsive to topical 
measures, give systemic prednisolone, short reducing dose maintenance with topical 
corticosteroids plus antifungals as appropriate.
For details, see Lichen Planus in Chapter 14.
Patient education
	
l Oral lichen planus may typically persist for many years. 
	
l Counsel patients particularly for avoidance of tobacco and alcohol, maintaining a 
diet rich in vitamins A, C and E, and maintaining good oral hygiene with regular 
dental care.
	
l Advise all patients to undergo periodic follow-up for any visual changes to the 
lesion site by their general dental practitioner. Isolated areas of increasing whiteness, 
speckling (areas of redness and whiteness) or solitary ulceration unlikely to reflect 
local trauma require further specialist opinion and possible biopsy.

TEETHING/CARE OF TEETH IN CHILDREN
Teething is the appearance of teeth through the gums in the oral cavity of infants and 
young children. The deciduous dentition starts erupting at 6 months of age till 6 years. 
The shedding of deciduous teeth starts at 6 years of age and permanent teeth start 
appearing till 12 years of age, making this period a mixed dentition stage. Deciduous 
teeth are susceptible to dental caries due to lack of oral care or breastfeeding, or due to 
nursing bottle or breastfeeding when the child is sleeping.
SALIENT FEATURES
	
l Fretfulness, biting or chewing on hard objects
	
l Drooling, which precedes teething, swelling and tenderness of gums
	
l Refusing food and sleeping concern
	
l Teething is not a cause of severe or systemic symptoms, such as high fever or 
diarrhoea.

l Teething is a normal physiological process: simple self-care measures are recommended.

Chapter 20  Dental Conditions    1223
	
l Gentle massage on the gums or biting on clean objects (e.g. teething rings) relieves 
the symptoms.
	
l Parents or caregivers should be advised to start cleaning the gums in infants with a 
soft wet cloth wrapped around the index finger, at least twice daily.
	
l They should start brushing the child’s teeth as they start to appear with a soft brush, 
and slowly add the toothpaste when the child can learn to spit.
	
l Provide diet counselling with restriction of sugary food intake particularly between 
meals.
	
l Avoid giving milk in a bottle when the child is sleeping.
	
l Visit a dentist as the first teeth start to appear and every 6 months.
	
l Perform enameloplasty, pit and fissure sealant, topical fluoride application, diet 
counselling as above; pulpotomy, pulpectomy or extraction as required.
	
l Patients with crowding in the mixed dentition period should be planned for serial 
extraction.
	
l In selected cases, space maintainer should be planned to prevent crowding or 
malocclusion in the permanent dentition.
GOOD ORAL HYGIENE
Toothbrushing is extremely important for cleaning teeth, massage of the surrounding 
gums and maintaining oral hygiene. Regular brushing keeps the tooth surface free of 
plaque, which is a soft material that gets deposited on the tooth surface and is the cause 
of dental caries and periodontal problems.
	
l Select the right quality of toothbrush which should be short and soft and have 
uniformly trimmed bristles.
	
l Brush teeth at least twice a day for 2–3 minutes particularly at night before going 
to sleep and floss daily.
	
l Use the right technique of toothbrushing and NEVER use force while brushing. 
	
l Eat healthy food such as fruits, vegetables and gram products (especially whole grain 
and dairy products during meals and snacks).
	
l Avoid eating in between meals. If it cannot be avoided, rinse your mouth or 
preferably brush your teeth.
	
l Limit sugar intake, and if one chooses to consume sugar, it is preferable to do so 
during meal times rather than indulging in between snacks. Frequent consumption 
of foods high in sugar, such as toffees, cookies, cake and sweetened beverages, 
increases the risk for tooth decay. Avoid frequent consumption of foods that easily 
adhere to the tooth surface such as candy.
	
l Rinse every night with an alcohol-free over-the-counter fluoridated mouth rinse.
	
l Do not smoke or chew tobacco.
	
l Ensure regular dental check-up at 6-monthly intervals and restoration of all active 
decay as soon as possible.

Oral hygiene measures in patients undergoing chemotherapy and 
radiotherapy
	
l Emphasize on good oral hygiene from the onset of chemotherapy. 
	
l Commercially available mouthwashes like hydrogen peroxide can be harmful and 
should be discontinued. 
	
l Encourage patients to drink plenty of water and other fluids with the exception of 
diversities such as coffee or tea. 
	
l During and following radiotherapy, the teeth may become hypersensitive. Apply 
fluoride gel topically.
	
l Radiation therapy of the head and neck can cause trismus. To minimize the effect of 
radiation in the muscles around the face and muscles of mastications, place a mouth 
block during external beam radiation. Advise the patient to perform daily stretching 
exercises at least 3–4 times daily.
	
l Avoid wearing dentures during the first 6 months after completion of the radiotherapy.
	
l Prevention is the most effective technique used to avoid haemorrhage. When the 
platelet count is low (<20,000/mm3), even toothbrushing can be traumatic. Cleaning 
of the mouth should be carried out with a disposable sponge, a sterile piece of gauge 
or a cotton swab with chlorhexidine 0.12% or povidone–iodine rinse.
TOOTHBRUSHING TECHNIQUE
	 1.	Place bristles along the gumline at a 45° angle.
	 2.	Bristles should contact both the tooth surface and the gumline. 
	 3.	Maintain a 45° angle with bristles contacting the tooth surface and gumline. 
	 4.	Gently brush using back, forth and rolling motion along all of the outer and inner 
tooth surfaces.
	 5.	Tilt the brush vertically behind the front teeth. 
	 6.	Make several up-and-down strokes using the front half of the brush.
	 7.	Place the brush against the biting surface of the teeth and use a gentle back-and-
forth scrubbing motion.
	 8.	Brush the tongue from back to front to remove odour-producing bacteria.

Appendix  I
Local Anaesthetics
Local anaesthesia is given for a variety of procedures, and many safe and effective topical 
anaesthetic agents are now available with a low risk of adverse events. Key points to be 
considered before giving local anaesthetics are careful patient assessment, the importance 
of having an overall understanding of the local agent being used, recommended 
monitoring requirements and potential adverse events, including life-threatening events.
Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) remains a serious adverse event despite 
advances in prevention, detection and treatment. Such events range across a continuum 
from mild subjective prodromal symptoms to seizure, cardiac arrest and/or death. A 
variety of factors influence the likelihood and severity of LAST including individual 
patient risk factors, concurrent medications, location and technique of block, specific 
local anaesthetic compound, total local anaesthetic dose (the product of concentration 
and volume), timeliness of detection and adequacy of treatment.
While LAST occurrences are rare and can still happen despite proper technique, 
education and preparedness, it is imperative to have a thorough comprehension of the 
best practices related to the administration of local anesthesia to ensure patient safety.
Principal adverse effects
	
l Cardiovascular: Hypotension, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest 
	
l Pulmonary: Respiratory impairment and arrest 
	
l CNS (may be subtle, atypical or absent): Agitation, confusion, drowsiness, 
muscle twitching, seizures, non-specific tinnitus, blurred vision, metallic taste, 
circumoral numbness 
	
l Allergic: Urticaria, angioneurotic oedema, anaphylactoid reaction 
	
l Epidural/caudal/spinal anaesthesia: Hypotension, urinary retention, lower 
extremity weakness and paralysis, loss of sphincter control, headache, backache, 
cranial nerve palsies, slowing of labour
	
l Sedation may abolish the patient’s ability to recognize or report LAST-related 
symptoms. Consider LAST in any patient with altered mental status, neurological signs 
and symptoms of cardiovascular instability (HR, BP, ECG) after regional anaesthetic.
Risk factors for LAST
	 1.	Patient characteristics 
	
l Extremes of age – younger than 16 years or older than 60 years 
	
l Low muscle mass – particularly with neonates, infants and the debilitated 
elderly

l Female > male 
	
l Comorbidities – cardiac disease, especially arrhythmias, conduction 
abnormalities, ischaemia and congestive heart failure; liver disease; metabolic 
disease, especially diabetes mellitus, isovaleric acidaemia, mitochondrial disease 
and carnitine deficiency; CNS diseases; low plasma protein binding – liver 
disease, malnourishment, infants, pregnancy
	 2.	Local anaesthetic characteristics 
	
l Bupivacaine has a lower safety margin and resuscitation is more difficult in the 
event of LAST, but local anaesthetics such as ropivacaine and lidocaine still 
account for a significant proportion of LAST events. 
	
l Block site, total local anaesthetic dose, test dosing and patient comorbidities are 
more predictive of high plasma levels of local anaesthetic than are body weight 
or body mass index. 
	
l Local anaesthetic infusions are particularly problematic after 1–4 days and in 
patients with small body mass. 
	
l Seizure is up to five times more likely after peripheral nerve block (PNB) than 
after epidural block.
	 3.	Practice setting
	
l Up to 20% of LAST cases occur outside of the hospital setting. 
	
l Non-anaesthesiologists are involved in up to 50% of LAST cases.
Strategies to prevent LAST
	 1.	Use the lowest effective dose of local anaesthetic (dose = volume × concentration). 
	 2.	Use incremental injection of local anaesthetics – administer 3–5 mL aliquots, 
pausing 15–30 seconds between each injection while observing for symptoms of 
toxicity between each injection. 
	 3.	Avoid epidural, caudal or intrathecal injection in patients with hypovolaemic shock, 
sepsis or coagulopathy and if there is infection at the injection site. 
	 4.	Identify at-risk patients prior to using local anaesthetics.
	 5.	Aspirate the needle or catheter before each injection for blood in syringe or tubing 
(there is an ~2% false-negative rate for this diagnostic intervention). Toxic plasma 
levels (from accidental intravascular injection) may cause cardiopulmonary 
collapse and seizures. 
	 6.	Intravenous access is essential during major regional block.
	 7.	Toxicity is additive in nature; therefore, adjust accordingly local anaesthetic re-
dosing and/or administration by different perioperative providers. 
	 8.	Use a test dose/pharmacological marker for identifying intravascular injection:
	
l Intravascular injection of epinephrine 10–15 mcg/mL in adults produces a 
≥10 beat heart rate increase or a ≥15 mmHg systolic blood pressure increase 
in the absence of β-blockade, active labour, advanced age or general/neuraxial 
anaesthesia. 
	
l Intravascular injection of epinephrine 0.5 mcg/kg in children produces a 
≥15 mmHg increase in systolic blood pressure.

l Appropriate subtoxic doses of local anaesthetic can produce subjective 
symptoms of mild systemic toxicity (auditory changes, excitation, metallic taste, 
etc.) in unpremedicated patients. 
	
l Fentanyl 100 mcg produces sedation if injected intravascularly in labouring patients. 
	 9.	The risk of LAST associated with truncal blocks may be reduced by using lower 
concentrations of local anaesthetics, dosing on lean body weight, adjunctive 
epinephrine and observation for at least 30–45 minutes after the block.
	10.	Monitor the patient during and after completing the injection. Clinical toxicity can 
be delayed 30 minutes or longer. Patients receiving liposomal bupivacaine (LB) 
should receive the same level of vigilance afforded to any patient receiving a local 
anaesthetic. 
	11.	Include local anaesthetic dosing parameters and at-risk patient concerns as part of 
the pre-incisional surgical pause. 
The pharmacological treatment of LAST is different from that of other cardiac 
arrest scenarios.
Management of LAST
	 1.	Stop injecting local anaesthetic.
	 2.	Get help and call for the LAST Rescue Kit (1 L lipid emulsion 20%; several large 
syringes and needles, IV set, LAST management checklist).
	 3.	Alert the nearest cardiopulmonary resuscitation team – resuscitation may be 
prolonged.
	 4.	Airway management: Ventilate with 100% oxygen/avoid hyperventilation/advanced 
airway device, if necessary. Prevent hypoxia and acidosis, as both potentiate LAST. 
	
	Note: LAST resuscitation is different from ACLS. One may have to perform CPR 
for a prolonged time.
	 5.	Control seizures: Diazepam is preferred. Propofol or thiopental should be used with 
caution; succinylcholine will terminate tonic–clonic muscle activity, but not CNS 
electrical activity).
	 6.	Manage arrhythmias and provide cardiovascular support
	
	One may have to perform CPR for a prolonged time. Administer amiodarone 
as first-line antiarrhythmic (usual doses as per ACLS); avoid lidocaine and other 
sodium channel blockers.
	
	Notes:	
	
	
l Reduce individual epinephrine boluses to ≤1 mcg/kg as standard dose of 
epinephrine (1 mg) can impair resuscitation from LAST and reduce the efficacy 
of lipid rescue.
	
l Avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers or other local 
anaesthetics.
	 7.	Consider lipid emulsion therapy at the first sign of a serious LAST event – lipid 
emulsion 20% (>70 kg) 100 mL bolus rapidly over 2–3 minutes Or infusion 
200–250 mL over 15–20 minutes; if (<70 kg) bolus 1.5 mL/kg rapidly over 
2–3 minutes or ~0.25 mL/kg/min infusion over 15–20 minutes. If the patient

remains unstable, repeat bolus once or twice. (Caution: Do not exceed 12 mL/kg 
lipid emulsion [particularly important in the small adult or child].) Continue 
infusion for at least 10 minutes after haemodynamic stability is achieved.
	 8.	Propofol is not a substitute for 20% lipid emulsion. If only propofol is available, 
avoid large doses of propofol, especially in haemodynamically unstable patients.
	 9.	Transfer the patient to a monitored setting.
	10.	Prolonged monitoring is required for at least 4–6 hours after a cardiovascular event 
Or at least 2 hours after a limited CNS event. If LAST event is short lived and 
without any signs of cardiovascular instability after monitoring for ~30 minutes, 
one may proceed with surgery.

Ropivacaine
Ropivacaine is a long-acting amide local anaesthetic. It has a few properties that 
make it unique. Ropivacaine is less lipophilic than other local anaesthetics, such as 
bupivacaine, and is less likely to penetrate large, myelinated motor fibres. The S(−) 
enantiomer has significantly less cardiotoxicity and neurotoxicity.

Proparacaine
Paracaine (Proparacaine 0.5%) is used as a topical agent in ophthalmic surgery. 
Proparacaine hydrochloride ophthalmic solution is a rapidly acting topical anaesthetic, 
with induced anaesthesia lasting approximately 10–20 minutes.
Eutectic mixture of local anaesthetics (EMLA) cream is utilized for skin 
anaesthesia prior to cannulation in paediatric patients. It comprises an equal-weight 
eutectic mixture of lidocaine and prilocaine; it is formulated as a 5% emulsion, with 
2.5% of each component. Its applications encompass the prevention of pain associated 
with intravenous catheter insertion, blood sampling, superficial surgical procedures and 
the topical anaesthesia of leg ulcers for cleansing or debridement. Additionally, it finds 
use in numbing the skin before tattooing, electrolysis and laser hair removal.

Appendix  II
Infection Prevention and Control: 
Basic Components
Health care–associated infections (HAI) are one of the most common adverse events 
in delivery of care and a major public health problem with an impact on morbidity, 
mortality and quality of life. Some common HAIs are bloodstream infections, urinary 
tract infection, pneumonia, surgical site infection (SSI) and gastrointestinal infections. 
Infection prevention and control (IPC) refers to measures taken up to prevent and control 
transmission of infections in health care settings. Effective IPC is central to providing 
high-quality health care for patients and a safe working environment for those who work 
in health care settings. Prevention of infections reduces the need to use antibiotics and 
thereby development of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). IPC is implemented through 
the multidisciplinary IPC committee in health care facilities (HCFs).
Basic components of IPC are:
	 I.	Standard precautions are the basics of IPC and should be observed for ALL 
patients.
	 II.	Transmission-based precautions, also called additional precautions, are required 
for suspected or known infectious patients.
	III.	Bundle approach is followed for prevention and control of HAI.
	IV.	Surveillance of HAI is done to assess the burden, monitor trends and develop 
evidence-based polices to contain infections and address AMR and patient safety.
I. STANDARD PRECAUTIONS 
Standard precautions are the minimum infection prevention practices that apply to ALL 
patient care, regardless of suspected or confirmed infection status of the patient, in any 
setting where health care is delivered. Standard precautions include:
1. Hand hygiene
Hand hygiene is the most important measure to prevent the spread of infections among 
patients and health care workers (HCWs). Perform hand hygiene (hand washing or hand 
rubbing using hand sanitizer).
	
l Hand washing (40–60 seconds): Wet hands and apply soap; scrub all surfaces; rinse 
hands and dry thoroughly with a single-use towel; use the towel to turn off faucet. 
	
l Hand rubbing (20–30 seconds): Apply enough alcohol-based (70%) hand rub 
product to cover all areas of the hands; rub hands until dry.

Appendix II  Infection Prevention and Control: Basic Components    1233
Use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled (e.g. blood, body fluids), or after 
caring for patients with gastroenteritis; otherwise, an alcohol-based hand rub may be 
used.
Moments of hand hygiene
	 i.	Before and after any direct patient contact and between patients, whether gloves 
are worn or not
	 ii.	Before putting on gloves and again immediately after removing gloves
	iii.	Before handling an invasive device
	iv.	After touching blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, non-intact skin and 
contaminated items, even if gloves are worn
	 v.	During patient care, when moving from one body site to other (always move from 
a clean body site to a contaminated site)
	vi.	After contact with inanimate objects in the immediate vicinity of the patient
Ensure availability of hand-washing facilities with clean running water and hand 
hygiene products (soap, alcohol-based hand rub and clean single-use towels,) at the 
point of care.
2. Use of personal protective equipment (PPE)
Use gloves, masks, foot cover, protective eye wear, face shields and protective clothing 
(e.g. reusable or disposable gown, jacket, laboratory coat) as appropriate depending on 
the risk assessment.
Gloves: There are three types of gloves: 
	 i.	Clean, non-sterile gloves: Wear when touching blood, body fluids, secretions, 
excretions, mucous membranes, non-intact skin or other potentially infectious 
materials (OPIMs) like intravenous line insertion and removal, discontinuation 
of venous lines, pelvic/vaginal examination, suctioning non-closed systems, 
endotracheal tubes, or touching mucous membranes or non-intact skin; and for 
handling items visibly soiled with blood, body ﬂuids, secretions or excretions 
like emptying emesis basins, handling/cleaning instruments, handling waste and 
cleaning spills of body fluids.
	 ii.	Sterile, single-use gloves should be used for aseptic procedures, e.g. surgical 
procedure, vaginal delivery, invasive radiological procedure, central line access, 
preparing total parenteral nutrition and chemotherapeutic drugs.
	iii.	Heavy duty/utility gloves should be used for decontamination of large equipment, 
cleaning of ﬂoors, walls and HCF furniture such as beds. These gloves can be 
reused after cleaning but must be discarded if cracked, torn or punctured, or when 
their ability to function as a barrier is compromised.
	
	Gloves are not indicated (except for contact precautions) where there is no 
potential for exposure to blood or body fluids, or contaminated environment.
	
l Direct patient exposure: Taking blood pressure, temperature and pulse; 
performing SC and IM injections; bathing and dressing the patient; transporting 
the patient; caring for eyes and ears (without secretions); any vascular line 
manipulation in absence of blood leakage

1234    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Indirect patient exposure: Using the telephone; writing in the patient chart; 
giving oral medications; distributing or collecting patient dietary trays; 
removing and replacing linen for patient bed; placing non-invasive ventilation 
equipment and oxygen cannula; moving patient furniture
Facial protection (eyes, nose and mouth)
Masks are worn where appropriate to protect the mucous membranes of the nose and 
mouth during procedures and patient care activities likely to generate droplets and 
splashes or sprays of blood, body ﬂuids, secretions and excretions. Masks should fully 
cover the nose and mouth and prevent ﬂuid penetration. Triple-layer surgical masks ﬁtted 
tightly to the face should be worn and discarded immediately after use. Mask should be 
discarded after 6 hours of continuous use and earlier if it gets wet or dirty with secretions.
Respirators are required for pathogens transmitted by airborne route (e.g. 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox) or while performing aerosol-
generating procedures in patients with flu, pneumonia or severe acute respiratory 
infections (SARI). Some types are particulate filtering respirators (N95), half- or full-
face elastomeric respirators and powered air-purifying respirators (PAPR).
Eye protection (eye visor, goggles) is required to protect the eyes. These should ﬁt 
snuggly over and around the eyes. Personal prescription glasses are not a substitute 
for goggles.
Face shield is required to protect mucous membranes of the eyes, nose and mouth 
during activities that are likely to generate splashes or sprays of blood, body fluids, 
secretions and excretions. The face shield should cover the forehead, extend below the 
chin and wrap around the side of the face.
Gown: A clean non-sterile apron or gown is generally adequate to protect the skin and 
prevent soiling of clothing during procedures and/or patient care activities that are 
likely to bring contact with blood, body substances, secretions or excretions (except 
sweat). Remove the soiled gown as soon as possible and perform hand hygiene. A 
ﬂuid-resistant apron or gown should be worn when procedures are likely to generate 
splashing or sprays of blood or body substances and there is a risk that clothing may 
become contaminated with blood and body substances. Gowns and aprons preferably 
must be changed between patients. Reusable gowns can be laundered and sterilized as 
required before reuse.
Footwear: Closed footwear, which can be easily cleaned and disinfected, must be used 
whenever work processes or environments could cause foot injuries or spillage of blood 
or body ﬂuids. Personal footwear should be changed when entering clean areas such 
as OTs, labour rooms and ICU. Shoe covers may be used over street shoes to protect 
clean areas from soil and dirt brought in by shoes.
Hair covers: Long hair must be secured with a rubber band and hair cover worn to 
protect the hair and to protect the patient from falling hair.
PPE selection, sequence of donning and doffing: PPE must be worn after risk 
assessment. Full PPE is required when providing direct care to highly infectious 
patients such as SARS-CoV-2-infected patients and Ebola virus.

Risk of acquiring infection is much more while doffing compared with that while 
donning. For donning PPE, wear rubber boots or shoe cover, move to a clean area and do 
hand hygiene followed by gown or apron, face mask or respirator, face shield or goggles, 
cap and gloves. For removing PPE (doffing), ask for some assistance and remove the 
gloves followed by apron or gown; do hand hygiene; remove the face shield or goggles, 
mask and gloves; and then do hand hygiene. Hand hygiene is always the final step after 
removing and disposing of PPE.
3. Respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette
The control of spread of pathogens from the source is key to avoid transmission. Cough 
etiquettes include:
	 i.	Covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing 
	 ii.	Use and proper disposal of tissue paper in a closed container (no-touch receptacles)
	iii.	Hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions 
	iv.	Triage and fast tracking of patients with cough and cold 
	 v.	Spatial separation (1–2 m) of persons with acute febrile respiratory symptoms or 
to place these patients in a separate area while waiting for care 
	vi.	Providing masks to coughing patients and other symptomatic persons when they 
enter the health care setting
4. Environmental cleaning
Use adequate procedures for the routine cleaning requirements as per different zones 
with neutral detergent and disinfection of environmental and other frequently touched 
surfaces.
5. Sharp safety
There should be careful handling of sharp instruments and prevention of needlestick 
and injuries from other sharp instruments. Use care when handling needles, scalpels 
and other sharp instruments or devices; cleaning used instruments; and disposing of 
used needles and other sharp instruments. 
	 i.	Engineering and work practice controls are the primary methods to reduce 
exposures to blood and OPIM from sharp instruments and needles. Engineering 
controls include self-sheathing anaesthetic needles, safety scalpels, needleless IV 
ports, etc. 
	 ii.	Work practice controls such as: 
a.	 NOT recapping needles (if need to recap, use one-handed scoop technique for 
recapping needles between uses and before disposal)
b.	Not bending or breaking needles before disposal
c.	 Not passing a syringe with an unsheathed needle by hand 
d.	Removing burs before disassembling the hand piece from the dental unit and 
using instruments in place of fingers for tissue retraction or palpation during 
suturing and administration of anaesthesia

1236    Standard Treatment Guidelines
e.	 Disposal of all used syringes and needles, scalpel blades and other sharp items 
in an appropriate puncture-resistant container located close to the area where 
they are used
6. Safe injection practices
For prevention of transmission of infectious diseases between one patient and another, 
or between a patient and HCWs during preparation and administration of parenteral 
(e.g. intravenous or intramuscular injection) medications:
	 i.	Prepare injections using aseptic technique in a clean area.
	 ii.	Disinfect the rubber septum on a medication vial with alcohol before piercing.
	iii.	Do not use needles or syringes for more than one patient (this includes 
manufactured prefilled syringes and other devices such as insulin pens).
	iv.	Medication containers (single-dose and multidose vials, ampoules and bags) are 
entered with a new needle and new syringe, even when obtaining additional doses 
for the same patient.
	 v.	Use single-dose vials for parenteral medications when possible.
	vi.	Do not use single-dose (single-use) medication vials, ampoules and bags or bottles 
of intravenous solution for more than one patient.
	vii.	Do not combine the leftover contents of single-use vials for later use. Do not store 
it for future use on the same patient.
	viii.	Handling of multidose vial: The following apply, if multidose vials are used:
a.	 Dedicate multidose vials to a single patient whenever possible.
b.	 If multidose vials will be used for more than one patient, they should be restricted 
to a centralized medication area and should not enter the immediate patient 
treatment area (e.g. dental operatory) to prevent inadvertent contamination.
c.	 If a multidose vial enters the immediate patient treatment area, it should be 
dedicated for single-patient use and discarded immediately after use.
d.	Date multidose vials when first opened and discard within 28 days, unless the 
manufacturer specifies a shorter or longer date for that opened vial.
e.	 Disinfect the rubber septum on a medication vial with alcohol before piercing.
f.	 Do not leave the needle in the septum. Use a separate needle and syringe for 
entering the vial.
Best practices in intravenous infusion care and management
	 i.	Do not use fluid infusion or administration sets (e.g. IV bags, tubing, connections) 
for more than one patient and replace the administration set every 24 hours or 
earlier if infusion set may have been compromised.
	 ii.	Avoid looping IV tubing; use protective caps on the tubing ends instead.
	iii.	When preparing IV bags, do so on a flat, stable surface; it is unsafe to prepare them 
while hanging on an IV pole.
	iv.	Date and initial all IV bags and tubing upon initiation and change according to 
organizational guidelines to ensure accountability and prevent IV fluids from 
hanging for more than 24 hours.

7. Aseptic techniques
Handling of patients using aseptic technique during procedures, i.e. using practices 
and procedures to prevent contamination from pathogens during procedures such as 
performing surgical procedures, performing biopsies, dressing surgical wounds or burns, 
suturing wounds, inserting a urinary catheter, wound drain, intravenous line, or chest 
tube, administering injections, using instruments to conduct a vaginal examination and 
delivering babies, involves applying the strictest rules to minimize the risk of infection. 
Handle equipment/linen soiled with blood, body fluids, secretions and excretions in a 
manner that prevents skin and mucous membrane exposures, contamination of clothing 
and transfer of pathogens to other patients or the environment.
8. Safe waste disposal
Ensure that waste disposal is done as close to the point of generation as possible in 
accordance with prevailing regulations (Bio-Medical Waste Handling Rules, 2016, and 
Amendments thereof). Discard all the waste contaminated with blood, body fluids, 
secretions and excretions, human tissues, masks and apron (if linen) in yellow bins; all 
contaminated plastic waste in red bags (except blood bags; to be discarded in yellow 
bags); and sharps in puncture-proof containers (separate for needles and broken glass). 
All laboratory waste should be pretreated before handing over to biomedical waste 
collection agency. Waste generated from COVID-19 facilities should be clearly labelled 
as COVID-19 waste and segregated in double-colour-coded plastic liners as per existing 
rules and transported in separate covered trolleys to separate storage room away from 
other biomedical waste. Leftover food item from patients with COVID-19 should be 
discarded as general municipal waste in green liners.
Incident reporting: Report any incident of sharp or needlestick injury or inappropriate 
waste disposal immediately and perform appropriate management of accidental 
occupational exposure to blood and body fluids.

1238    Standard Treatment Guidelines
9. Spill management
All spills of blood and body fluids should be treated with freshly prepared 1% sodium 
hypochlorite or bleaching solution for a contact time of 20 minutes. In large spills 
(>30 mL), use 10% sodium hypochlorite or bleaching solution.
10. Cleaning, sterilization and disinfection
Clean, disinfect and reprocess reusable equipment appropriately before use on another 
patient. Patient care items (e.g. dental instruments, devices and equipment) are 
categorized as critical, semi-critical or non-critical, depending on the potential risk for 
infection associated with their intended use.
Critical items are those which penetrate the skin or mucous membrane, or enter the 
sterile tissue or vascular system, e.g. surgical instruments and implants. These items can 
be single-use sterile products or before use on each patient should be treated with steam 
sterilization, dry heat, hydrogen peroxide (gas plasma), ethylene oxide or chemical 
sterilant (with contact time varying from 3 to 12 hours depending on concentration, 
temperature and pH of chemical disinfectant used). 
Dental handpieces and associated attachments, including low-speed motors and 
reusable prophylaxis angles, should always be heat sterilized between patients and not 
high-level or surface disinfected.
Semi-critical items are those which come in contact with non-intact skin or intact 
mucous membrane without penetration, e.g. laryngoscopes, endoscopes, anaesthesia 
equipment, respiratory therapy equipment, anaesthesia breathing circuits, mouth 
mirrors, amalgam condensers, reusable dental impression trays and digital radiography 
sensors. It is preferable to sterilize semi-critical items using heat if they are heat-tolerant 
rather than using high-level disinfection. If semi-critical items are heat sensitive, use 
high-level disinfection with chemicals like glutaraldehyde, ortho-phthalaldehyde, 
hydrogen peroxide and peracetic acid or hypochlorite (with contact time varying from 
10 to 45 minutes).
Non-critical patient care items are those which are in contact with the intact skin 
and have no contact with the mucous membrane and pose the least risk of infection 
transmission, e.g. ECG electrodes, radiograph head/cone, blood pressure cuff and 
facebow. These items need not be transported to a central processing area. These 
require cleaning and decontamination if visibly soiled, and disinfected regularly such 
as after use on each patient or daily with low-level disinfection. Stethoscope should be 
cleaned with detergent and water and dried or wiped with 70% alcohol. BP cuff can be 
soaked and washed. It should be dried completely before reinserting or use disposable 
disinfecting wipe for disinfecting cuff and tubing. Protecting these surfaces with 
disposable barriers might be a preferred alternative.
Respiratory therapy equipment/devices (mechanical ventilator, panels, trolleys, 
support arm, high-flow nasal cannula, oxygen concentrators, non-invasive ventilation 
devices, ultrasonic nebulizers): Surface disinfection is done with 70% alcohol-based

disinfectants. Heat moisture exchange filters used with humidifiers and non-invasive 
ventilations should be changed daily. Always fill humidifiers and oxygen reservoirs 
with sterile water and discard leftover water whenever water level reaches below 
lower-level marking. Refill with sterile water after thorough cleaning of humidifier with 
detergent and water followed by alcohol disinfection (autoclave daily, if autoclavable). 
Always aspirate 1% sodium hypochlorite solution in suction tubes after doing suction. 
Discard aspirates from suction bottles every 6 hours and clean suction bottles with hot 
water and detergent.
General use items (bed pan, crockery, cutlery, bowls, eating utensils): The combination 
of hot water and detergents is sufficient to decontaminate and keep these items dry. 
There should be no sharing of eating utensils and drinking vessels consistent with 
principles of good personal hygiene and for the purpose of preventing transmission of 
infections. 
Furniture should be cleaned with damp dust with detergent/phenol; mattresses and 
pillows should be covered with impermeable covers; wash covers with detergent and 
keep dry and disinfect with phenol/2% Lysol.
Cleaning, disinfection, sterilization process
Cleaning to remove debris and organic contamination from instruments should always 
occur before disinfection or sterilization. If blood, saliva and other contamination are 
not removed, these materials can shield microorganisms and potentially compromise 
the disinfection or sterilization process. Automated cleaning equipment (e.g. ultrasonic 
cleaner, washer-disinfector) should be used to remove debris to improve cleaning 
effectiveness and decrease worker exposure to blood. 
After cleaning, dried instruments should be inspected, wrapped, packaged or placed 
into container systems before heat sterilization. Packages should be labelled to show 
the sterilizer used, the cycle or load number, the date of sterilization and, if applicable, 
the expiration date. This information can help in retrieving processed items in the event 
of an instrument processing/sterilization failure.
Sterilization monitoring should be done and recorded using physical, chemical and 
biological indicators.
Physical (sterilizer gauges, pressure, temperature and exposure time) and chemical 
(indicator tapes, strips) indicator monitoring should be performed daily to detect 
procedural errors and autoclave malfunctions. Double indicator strips should be used 
with one outside and one inside every package for immediate inspection and to verify 
that the steam has penetrated the package respectively. Biological indicators (e.g. killing 
of highly resistant microorganisms such as Geobacillus or Bacillus species) or spore 
tests should be done at frequency considered appropriate depending on sterilization load 
and purpose (to be tested with every load of implants). Failure of any of the controls 
is an indication for recall and resterilization. Maintain accurate records to document 
that cycle parameters have been met and establish accountability. In addition, if there 
is a problem with a sterilizer (e.g. unchanged chemical indicator, positive spore test),

documentation helps to determine whether an instrument recall is necessary in case of 
equipment malfunctions.
11. Safe handling of textiles and laundry
Handle, transport and process used soiled linen separately from unsoiled linen. 
Place contaminated textiles and fabrics into leakproof bags and securely tie before 
transporting for washing. Treat soiled linen including those of patients with COVID-19 
with 0.5% hypochlorite before mixing with unsoiled linen. Do not sort or rinse 
contaminated laundry at the location where contamination occurred. Treat linen in a 
manner which prevents skin and mucous membrane exposures and contamination of 
clothing. Handle contaminated laundry with a minimum of agitation to avoid transfer of 
pathogens to other patients and/or the environment. Surgical drapes and reusable gowns 
must be sterilized before use with steam autoclaving after laundering.
II. TRANSMISSION-BASED PRECAUTIONS
Transmission-based precautions, also called additional precautions or isolation 
precautions, are second tier of infection prevention required for patients with known 
or suspected infectious disease. Transmission-based precautions include:
	 1.	Contact precautions are used for patients with clinical disease/syndrome or 
infectious aetiologies capable of transmission by close contact – direct or indirect 
through fomites (e.g. faecal incontinence, large draining wounds, conjunctivitis, 
scabies, impetigo, Clostridium difficile, multidrug-resistant organisms, SARI 
including COVID-19).
	 2.	Droplet precautions are used for patients with clinical disease/syndrome or 
infectious aetiologies capable of transmission by respiratory droplets (>5 µm) 
generated by a patient while coughing, sneezing or talking (e.g. flu, pneumonia, 
SARI including COVID-19, whooping cough, mumps, meningitis, pharyngitis, 
doing high-risk procedures like sputum induction, aerosolized administration of 
medications, bronchoscopy).
	 3.	Airborne precautions are used for patients with clinical disease/syndrome or 
infectious aetiologies capable of transmission by the airborne route (<5 µm), 
e.g. aerosol-generating procedures (i.e. open suctioning of the respiratory tract, 
intubation, bronchoscopy, cardiopulmonary resuscitation) in patients with 
suspected or confirmed COVID-19, and patients in closed non-ventilated spaces 
infected with tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox and disseminated herpes zoster.
	 4.	Triage at entry: Have a dedicated area for triage of infectious patients separating 
them from other non-infective patients. Apply standard precautions based on risk 
assessment (hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene and appropriate use of PPE). Universal 
triple-layer surgical masking is followed in case of community or cluster transmission 
of respiratory infections (SARI including COVID-19). Avoid direct contact as much as 
possible by using infrared thermometers, glass/plexiglass screen and kiosks. Maintain 
a distance of at least 1–2 m between patients and provide surgical masks to coughing 
patients. Perform hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions.

Adjunctive measures
Important adjunctive measures that are not considered primary components of 
programmes to prevent transmission of infectious agents, but improve the effectiveness 
of such programmes, include:
	 1.	Antimicrobial management programmes (see Antimicrobial Stewardship)
	 2.	Post-exposure chemoprophylaxis with antiviral or antibacterial agents
	 3.	Vaccines used for both pre- and post-exposure prevention (such as measles, 
varicella, hepatitis B, COVID-19, tetanus vaccine)
	 4.	Screening and restricting visitors with signs of transmissible infections especially 
during community outbreaks of infectious diseases and for high-risk patient units 
(visitors have been identified as the source of several types of HAIs [e.g. pertussis, 
M. tuberculosis, influenza and other respiratory viruses]
	 5.	Use of barrier precautions by visitors when appropriate
	 6.	Restricting susceptible health care personnel from entering the room of patients 
known or suspected to have measles, chickenpox, disseminated zoster or smallpox 
if other immune health care personnel are available

III. BUNDLE CARE APPROACH
Care bundles include a set of evidence-based measures that need to be implemented 
together to show a signiﬁcant improvement in patient care. Together they have a 
greater effect on the outcome than the isolated implementation of individual measures. 
Adherence to bundles helps to deliver consistent and reliable patient care.
Care bundles that have shown signiﬁcant impact on the prevention of HAI include 
sets of:
	
l Bundles for the prevention of central line–associated bloodstream infections 
(CLABSIs)
	
l Bundle for the prevention of catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs)
	
l Bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)
	
l Bundle for the prevention of SSI
IV. SURVEILLANCE
Surveillance of HAIs is a basic requirement for organizing and maintaining an effective 
IPC programme and to substantially reduce morbidity and mortality. Surveillance 
should be a part of clinical diagnosis and treatment of patients with suspected infection. 
Unnecessary sampling for culture/testing of patients without clinical signs and 
symptoms/environment is not required. Surveillance should be conducted by infection 
control personnel in an active, laboratory-based (in liaison with the ward), prospective, 
priority-directed manner for calculation of risk-adjusted incidence rates. Some of the 
common types of surveillance are:
	
l Active and passive surveillance 
	– Active surveillance: It involves systematic collection of data by a designated 
trained hospital infection control professional/nurse. Information is accumulated 
by using a variety of data sources within and beyond the wards. 
	– Passive surveillance: It consists of reporting of any occurrence of suspected 
HAI by clinicians or nurses. Both active and passive surveillance should be 
complementary to each other so as not to miss any case.
	
l Process and outcome surveillance: Process surveillance is an audit of a practice or 
process of IPC such as hand hygiene or care bundles, use of multidose vials and safe 
injection practice. Outcome surveillance aims to detect an HAI event such as device-
associated infection, SSI, morbidity and mortality. HCFs with limited resources and 
minimal trained staff should carry out the basic process and outcome surveillance.

Appendix II  Infection Prevention and Control: Basic Components    1247
	
l Clinical/patient-based surveillance: This involves counting of HAIs, assessing risk 
factors, and monitoring patient care procedures and practices for adherence to the 
principles of IPC. This also requires ward rounds and discussion with caregivers.
	
l Laboratory-based surveillance: This surveillance is based solely on the ﬁndings of 
laboratory studies of clinical specimens. The microbiology laboratory also carries 
out studies on patterns of AMR for common isolates and new or emerging pathogens 
and patterns of resistance. This information is reported to the Hospital Infection 
Control Committee (HICC) and various clinical units of the HCF.
	
l Priority-directed and comprehensive surveillance: Priority-directed surveillance, 
also called targeted, focused or surveillance by objectives, focuses on speciﬁc events, 
processes, organisms and/or patient populations. On the other hand, comprehensive 
surveillance is resource-intensive, and involves continuous monitoring of all patients 
for all HAI events and/or processes.

Appendix  III
Drugs and Pregnancy
Use of medications during pregnancy requires a careful assessment of risks and benefits 
for them. Physiology of pregnancy affects the pharmacokinetics of medications used. 
Also, certain medications can easily cross the placenta to reach the foetus and cause 
foetal malformations. Although some medications are considered safe during pregnancy, 
the effects of other medications on the foetus are unknown. Around half of the pregnancies 
are unplanned. Therefore, risks of any prescription medications should be evaluated in all 
women of reproductive age. Medication during pregnancy may be necessary in coughs 
and colds, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, etc., requiring episodic treatment, or to continue 
treatment in pre-existing illnesses such as epilepsy, depression or hypertension. In 
maternal epilepsy, depression or hypertension, risk of not taking medication may 
prove to be serious than the risk associated with taking them. While total avoidance of 
pharmacological treatment in pregnancy is practically not possible, benefit and the risk 
to baby should be weighed in all cases. During the first trimester, teratogenic effects are 
frequent with a higher risk from third to 11th weeks of gestation. During the second 
and third trimesters, drugs may affect the growth and functional development of the 
foetus or have toxic effect on the foetal tissues. Drugs administered shortly before term 
or during labour may have adverse effect on the mother or on the neonate.
Five categories (A, B, C, D, X) which indicate the potential of systemically absorbed 
drugs causing birth defects were established by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), 
United States. The pregnancy category of a medication assesses the risk of foetal injury 
if the pharmaceutical is used as directed by the mother during pregnancy. It does not 
account for any risks posed by pharmaceutical agents or their metabolites in breast milk. 
FDA pregnancy risk categories
Category A 
Controlled studies in women have failed to demonstrate a risk to the foetus in the first 
trimester and there is no evidence of risk in later trimesters. Medications in this class 
are considered safe to use in pregnancy, e.g. vitamins, folic acid and levothyroxine.
Category B
Animal reproduction studies have not demonstrated a foetal risk but there are no 
controlled studies in pregnant women OR animal studies have demonstrated risk 
to the foetus that was not confirmed in controlled studies in pregnant women in 
the first trimester and there is no evidence of a risk in later trimesters. Medications 
in this class are generally considered safe, e.g. acetaminophen, amoxicillin, 
ondansetron, metoclopramide, cephalosporins, metronidazole.
(Continued)

Appendix III  Drugs and Pregnancy    1249
Category C
Studies in animals have revealed adverse effects on the foetus and there are no 
controlled studies in women, or studies in women and animals are not available. 
Drugs from this class can be given to pregnant women if the benefit to the mother 
outweighs the risk to the foetus, e.g. promethazine, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, 
sertraline, diltiazem, beta-blockers, sumatriptan, spironolactone, fluroquinolones, 
clarithromycin.
Category D
Evidence of human foetal risk has been documented, but the benefits to the mother 
may be acceptable despite the risk to the foetus. Drugs in this class may be used 
in pregnancy if the benefits to the mother outweigh the risk to the foetus (i.e. a 
life-threatening situation or a serious disease for which safer medication cannot 
be used or are not efficacious), e.g. aspirin (third trimester), paroxetine, phenytoin, 
aminoglycosides, valproic acid, ACE inhibitors, ARBs.
Category X
Studies in animals or humans have demonstrated teratogenic effects. The risk to the 
foetus clearly outweighs any potential benefit to the mother. Drugs in this category 
are contraindicated in pregnancy, e.g. thalidomide, isotretinoin, warfarin, ergometrine.

1250    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Common medicines that can be used safely during pregnancy
•	 Acetaminophen and low-dose ibuprofen for pain relief
•	 Prenatal vitamins for proper nutrition
•	 Iron supplements to prevent anaemia
•	 Some antibiotics for treating infections – penicillins, cephalosporins
•	 Antacids for heartburn relief
Basic principles to be followed while medication use in pregnancy
1.	 Withdraw all unnecessary medications 3–6 months before conception (in those women who are 
at the risk of conceiving or who wish to become pregnant).
2.	 Go for non-pharmacological measures, if possible. 
3.	 Medicines should be prescribed only in case of compelling indication. They are best avoided in 
the first trimester, if at all possible. Assess benefit versus risk.
4.	 Advise patient not to take any over-the-counter medication without consultation while pregnant.
5.	 Choice of a medicine should be done based on data on best safety profile over the years. 
Category A is considered the safest category and Category X is absolutely contraindicated in 
pregnancy.
6.	 Medicines should be prescribed in small doses and for short duration.
7.	 Counsel pregnant women to stop all social drugs such as caffeine, alcohol, smoking. Inform 
them about the risk of using these substances during pregnancy.
Micronutrient supplements with vitamins and minerals before, during and after 
pregnancy are safe. Some of the categories of commonly used medicines considered 
relatively safe during pregnancy are shown in Table 1. Table 2 depicts medicines that 
have been proved to be harmful to the foetus, and so their use during pregnancy is 
contraindicated.

1256    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Vaccines during pregnancy
Immunization is as effective in women who are pregnant as in those who are not (Table 3).
Table 3.  Vaccines during pregnancy.
Influenza vaccine 
Recommended for all pregnant women in the second or 
third trimester during influenza season.
Tetanus, tetanus-diphtheria-
pertussis (Tdap) vaccine
Tetanus vaccine – 2 doses during pregnancy; immunization: 
Immunize all pregnant women with 2 doses of Tetanus toxoid 
(Td). The first dose is given just after the first trimester or as soon 
as the woman registers for antenatal check-up (ANC), whichever 
is later. The second dose is given 1 month after the first dose but 
at least 1 month before EDD. Give Td to a woman in labour if 
she has not previously received tetanus vaccine. Fully immunized 
– no further doses are necessary in pregnancy. Influenza 
vaccination is recommended during pregnancy for mothers from 
26 weeks onwards. Tdap vaccine may be given to all pregnant 
patients during each pregnancy, as early in the 27–36 weeks of 
gestation as possible. In case of a pandemic, the influenza vaccine 
can be given earlier to protect the mother.

Vaccine for measles, mumps, 
poliomyelitis or cholera, 
hepatitis A, hepatitis B, 
plague, rabies, typhoid or 
vaccine for yellow fever
Potential but unknown risks; may be given during pregnancy, if 
risk of infection is substantial. Should be reserved for situations 
in which the woman or foetus is at significant risk of exposure 
to a hazardous infection and risk of adverse effects from the 
vaccine is low.
Live attenuated vaccines
Vaccine for German measles 
(rubella) 
Potential infection of the placenta and developing foetus; no 
defects in neonates have been attributed to rubella vaccine, 
and women vaccinated inadvertently during early pregnancy 
need not be advised to terminate pregnancy based solely on 
theoretical risk from the vaccine.

(varicella)

placenta and developing foetus; risk is highest between 13 and

Appendix  IV
Drug Use in Lactating Mother
Many mothers need to use drugs during breastfeeding for some medical condition. 
Almost all drugs are able to enter breast milk and therefore carry a risk to breastfed 
infants. While prescribing a drug to a lactating mother, factors such as the dose received 
via breast milk, pharmacokinetics and effect of the drug in the suckling infant need to 
be taken into consideration. Most drugs are considered ‘safe’ during breastfeeding in 
low therapeutic doses.
Factors affecting drug transfer into breast milk
Transfer of drugs into breast milk is influenced by protein binding, lipid solubility and 
ionization. Nearly all drugs transfer into breast milk to some extent except heparin and 
insulin which are too large to cross biological membranes. The infant almost invariably 
receives no benefit from this form of exposure.
	
l Transfer is greatest in the presence of low maternal plasma protein binding and high 
lipid solubility. In addition, milk is slightly more acidic than plasma (pH of milk is 
approximately 7.2 and that of plasma is 7.4), allowing weakly basic drugs to transfer 
more readily into breast milk.
	
l Infants have a severely limited glomerular filtration rate and creatinine clearance 
approximately one-third in comparison to adults; this impairment is greater in 
premature infants.
	
l The hepatic metabolism process, especially phase 1 oxidation and phase 2 
glucuronidation, is impaired in neonates.
	
l Drugs more susceptible to first-pass metabolism have a higher oral bioavailability, 
resulting in accumulation and toxicity.
	
l Decision for the breast-feed while the mother is on drug therapy is done by overall 
assessment of benefits and risks.
	
l The amount of a drug ingested by breastfeeding is difficult to assess.
Guidelines for prescribing drugs during breastfeeding
	
l Choose the lowest effective dose of the drug. Suspend breastfeeding (and use and 
bottle-feeding) for drugs with known potential toxicity, such as cytotoxic drugs and 
radiopharmaceuticals, or in cases of prolonged toxic drug therapies.
	
l Avoid drugs like aminoglycosides, thyrostatics, chloramphenicol, tetracycline 
immunosuppressants, cytostatics and sedatives.

1258    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Select alternative routes or products to have minimal systemic exposure to the 
mother, e.g. choose a high-fibre diet or fibre laxative over a stimulant laxative.
	
l Select drugs with a short half-life to minimize drug secretion and exposure in breast 
milk, e.g. paroxetine and sertraline over fluoxetine.
	
l If a drug is needed:
	– Suspend breastfeeding for drugs with known potential toxicity, such as cytotoxic 
drugs and radiopharmaceuticals. 
	– Do not breast-feed in cases of prolong toxic drug therapies. In such cases, infant 
exposure may be decreased by alternating breast- and bottle-feeding.
	– Time of drug intake versus breastfeeding: Breast-feed before the next scheduled 
dose to minimize the drug concentration to the lowest level. A drug re-enters 
the blood circulation from the mammary gland followed by fall in the blood 
concentration of the drug.

condition: Appendix V: Drug Use in Patients with Hepatic Impairment
text:
Appendix  V
Drug Use in Patients with 
Hepatic Impairment
There are complex interactions between the drug and the liver function. Alteration in 
responses of drugs in liver disease can be due to all or some of the following reasons:
	
l The hepatobiliary system plays an important role in metabolism, activation, 
excretion and interaction between the drug and the body. More than 50% of 
cytochrome enzymes essential for drug metabolism are found in liver cells. 
	
l Moderate to severe hepatic cell impairment has to be present for significant 
alteration in the response of drugs as the liver has a large cellular reserve for the 
maintenance of hepatocellular activity.
	
l Impaired liver function results in reduced metabolism of drugs and increases 
accumulation of drug in the body to the toxic level at a normal dose.
	
l Dose of drug with low bioavailability has to be reduced in patients with hepatic 
impairment as bioavailability increases and hepatic clearance decreases in such patients. 
	
l There is alteration of volume of distribution of drugs due to oedema/ascites. 
Oedema and ascites in chronic liver disease may be exacerbated by drugs that cause 
fluid retention, e.g. NSAIDs – acetylsalicylic acid, ibuprofen, dexamethasone and 
prednisolone. In contrast, a decreased therapeutic effect may also be noted in patients 
with cirrhosis with β-adrenoceptor antagonists and certain diuretics. On the other 
hand, loading dose of these drugs may have to be increased if rapid peak level is 
required. Increased volume of distribution results in increased elimination half-life. 
The most prevalent causes of cirrhosis are chronic alcohol use disorder, viral hepatitis 
B (HBV) and C (HCV) infection, and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).
	
l Patients with cirrhosis have often impaired renal function resulting in hepatorenal 
syndrome which leads to accumulation of drug and its metabolite. Dosage of the 
drug needs to be carefully adjusted in such cases.
	
l Risk factors that may predispose patients to drug-induced liver disease include 
gender (it tends to be more common in females), age, genetics, concurrent diseases 
(obesity, diabetes, co-infection with HIV) and polypharmacy. 
	
l Withdrawal of the drug generally results in resolution of the liver disease, although 
this is not always the case.
	
l Overt clinical complications (portal hypertension, bleeding varices, jaundice, 
ascites, variceal haemorrhage and hepatic encephalopathy) are seen when the liver 
is damaged to the point that it cannot function adequately.

condition: Appendix V: Drug Use in Patients with Hepatic Impairment
text:
1262    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Routine liver function tests do not reflect actual liver function but are rather markers 
of liver cellular damage. Hepatic dysfunction is less overt and may not be apparent 
until much of the functioning liver is lost.
	
l Transaminases (AST and ALT) are significantly increased in acute liver disease; 
in cirrhosis, the increase may not necessarily be seen due to massive reduction in 
functioning hepatocytes, leading to a false ‘normal’ result.
	
l Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT): It is elevated by a high alcohol intake and 
enzyme-inducing drugs (e.g. Rifampicin, Phenytoin).
	
l Alkaline phosphatase (ALP): Increased level can indicate biliary damage and 
cirrhosis; extrahepatic causes of increased ALP include malignancy and bone disease 
(e.g. Paget’s disease).
	
l Child–Pugh scoring system may be used to assess the severity of hepatic impairment.
Prescribing principles to minimize the risk of liver injury from medications
1.	 Prescribe drugs to a minimum. 
2.	 Prefer drugs that do not need hepatic metabolism for elimination. 
3.	 Give the lowest effective dose of a drug.
4.	 The oral route is generally preferred in patients with liver disease. Assess for the potential 
presence of rectal varices and the increased risk of bleeding for rectal route of administration.
5.	 Avoid modified-release or long-acting preparations as they can accumulate. 
6.	 Avoid prodrugs that need hepatic metabolism for activation and hepatotoxic drugs. 
7.	 Ask the patients to bring a list of all prescription and non-prescription medications including 
herbs, vitamins and supplements and review medications regularly and discontinue 
medicines with potential to cause hepatic impairment or medicines which should be avoided.
8.	 If the patient is taking several medications, make sure that the ingredients are not same; 
explain the risk of taking an accidental overdose.
9.	 Explore whether the patient drinks a significant amount of alcohol daily; avoid or restrict the 
use of drugs having potential interaction, e.g. acetaminophen and metronidazole.
10.	 Select appropriate antibiotics considering altered pharmacokinetics as bacterial infection is 
one of the most frequent complications in patients with cirrhosis. 
11.	 Consult with hepatologist before starting new medications in case of advanced liver disease 
(e.g. liver cirrhosis).
Drug-induced liver injury (DILI)
DILI usually involves and is precipitated by toxic drug or its metabolite that either 
elicits an immune response or directly affects the biochemistry of the cell. It is 
classified as intrinsic (or direct) versus idiosyncratic. Intrinsic DILI is dose-related 
and occurs in a large proportion of individuals exposed to the drug (predictable) and its 
onset is within a short time span (hours to days). Idiosyncratic DILI is not dose-related 
and occurs only in a small proportion of exposed individuals.
Potential idiosyncratic reactions, and their causative medicines include:
	
l Acute liver failure: Allopurinol, Aspirin, Cyclophosphamide, NSAIDs
	
l Cholestasis: Warfarin, Azathioprine, Carbimazole, oral contraceptive pills, Flucloxacillin
	
l Fibrosis and cirrhosis: Methotrexate
	
l Acute hepatitis: Phenytoin, Isoniazid

condition: Appendix VI: Drug Use in Patients with Renal Impairment
text:
Appendix  VI
Drug Use in Patients 
with Renal Impairment
Safe medications in kidney disease involve determination of renal function and 
consideration of changes in drug pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics 
(PD) as kidney function declines. Patients with kidney disease often suffer from 
multimorbidity, including diabetes, hypertension and heart failure, because of 
being on multiple medicines prescribed by a range of prescribers who often do not 
coordinate treatments. They are also susceptible to further kidney injury and metabolic 
derangements from medications, which can worsen the disease. Additionally, drug 
dosing errors are common in patients with renal impairment and can cause adverse 
effects or ineffective therapy and thus poor outcomes. Negative consequences 
associated with medication in chronic kidney disease (CKD) can be categorized into 
events that result in harm to the kidneys, such as acute kidney injury (AKI), hastened 
decline in kidney function and progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). 
Additionally, there are other metabolic complications, such as hyperkalaemia, 
hypercalcaemia, hypoglycaemia and bleeding. Ensuring the safe utilization of 
medications in CKD entails a multifaceted approach. This includes assessing kidney 
function, taking into account alterations in drug PK and PD with declining kidney 
function, and using prudent strategies in the administration of therapies to address 
uraemic complications and other concurrent health conditions.
Guidelines and drug safety points while prescribing and de-prescribing in renal impairment.
•	 Drug prescription should be kept to minimum. Known nephrotoxic drugs should be avoided in 
all patients with renal disease. 
•	 Exercise caution while prescribing medicines with narrow therapeutic index.
•	 Some medicines – angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs), angiotensin receptor 
blockers (ARBs), statins and sodium–glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) – inhibitors may 
reduce cardiovascular disease risk and/or reduce CKD progression. However, carefully 
consider the likelihood of benefits.
•	 Both hyperkalaemia and hypokalaemia are safety concerns for patients with CKD, as they can 
lead to altered cardiac electroconduction, arrhythmias and sudden death.
•	 Adhere to prescription guidelines. Altered drug PK/PD profiles in CKD may warrant dosage 
modification or drug discontinuation. Several drug classes and selected agents that may 
require dose adjustment or de-prescription in CKD are given below. NSAIDs and proton pump 
inhibitors are priority medicines for de-prescribing in CKD because of potential adverse effects.
(Continued)

•	 Renal function test should be done to determine the glomerular filtration rate or creatinine 
clearance before starting and during the period of treatment and adjust the dose as necessary.
•	 Known nephrotoxic drugs should be avoided in all patients with renal disease. 
•	 The dosage regime in patients with renal impairment is aimed to achieve similar amount 
of drug in the body either by increase of dosage intervals without changing the dose or by 
reduction of the dose without changing the frequency.
