condition: Appendix VII: Drug Use in Glucose- 6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency
text:
Appendix  VII
Drug Use in Glucose-6-Phosphate
Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency
G6PD deficiency, a hereditary predisposition to haemolysis, is the commonest red cell 
enzymopathy in humans and has an X-linked inheritance seen predominantly in males. 
Homozygotes and heterozygotes can be symptomatic, although the disease typically is 
more severe in persons who are homozygous for the deficiency. This X-linked inherited 
disorder most commonly affects persons of African, Asian, Mediterranean or Middle-
Eastern descent.
	
l It causes a spectrum of diseases including neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia, acute 
haemolysis and chronic haemolysis, and an absence of clinical symptoms. Acute 
haemolysis is caused by exposure to an oxidative stressor in the form of an 
infection, oxidative drug or fava beans; therefore, treatment is mainly avoidance 
of the stressors. Drugs are not themselves substrates for the G6PD enzyme, but 
the enzyme deficiency predisposes individuals to haemolysis when some drugs are 
administered. G6PD-deficient erythrocytes are thus more susceptible to drug-induced 
lysis, which can manifest clinically as acute haemolytic anaemia. Furthermore, 
oxidation of haemoglobin iron results in the formation of methaemoglobin, and 
methaemoglobinaemia may accompany anaemia in G6PD deficiency. Oxidative drugs 
ingested by a woman who is breastfeeding may be transmitted in breast milk and can 
cause acute haemolysis in a G6PD-deficient child.
	
l Acute haemolysis is self-limited, but in rare instances it can be severe enough to 
warrant a blood transfusion. 
	
l Neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia may require treatment with phototherapy or exchange 
transfusion to prevent kernicterus. The variant that causes chronic haemolysis is 
uncommon because it is related to sporadic gene mutation rather than to the more 
common inherited gene mutation. 
	
l Haemolysis typically occurs 24–72 hours after ingestion, with resolution within 
4–7 days.

condition: Appendix VII: Drug Use in Glucose- 6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency
text:
l During episodes of acute haemolysis, individuals may experience severe anaemia, 
elevated reticulocyte counts and indirect hyperbilirubinaemia. Essential diagnostic 
measures include a complete blood count (CBC), reticulocyte count and thorough

condition: Appendix VII: Drug Use in Glucose- 6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency
text:
1270    Standard Treatment Guidelines
peripheral smear evaluation. Enzyme assays for G6PD enzyme activity are done to 
confirm deficiency. The following key indicators must be considered:
	
–
Anaemia characterized by a 3- to 4-g/dL decrease in Hb
	
–
The anaemia presents as normocytic, normochromic, with a neutrophilic response 
observed.
	
–
Marked anisopoikilocytosis and an elevated red blood cell distribution width 
(RDW) may be evident.
	
–
Microspherocytes, ‘bite’ cells, ‘blister cells’ and Heinz bodies are observed.
	
–
Serum haptoglobin levels are reduced, and urine haemoglobin tests positive. 
Management and prevention 
The main treatment for G6PD deficiency is avoidance of oxidative stressors. 
Screen neonates for G6PD deficiency especially when family history, ethnic or 
geographic origin, or the timing of the appearance of neonatal jaundice suggests the 
possibility of G6PD deficiency.
Prevention of ADRs in G6PD deficiency
Individuals with G6PD deficiency may experience haemolytic anaemia triggered by 
specific antibiotics and anti-inflammatory drugs. The variability in drug reactions 
among individuals is attributed to inherited differences in drug metabolism and genetic 
variations in G6PD deficiency. The risks and severity of haemolysis are typically dose-
related. The interplay between genetic factors and drug exposure underscores the need 
for personalized and cautious prescribing practices in patients with G6PD deficiency to 
minimize the potential for haemolytic reactions. For details of the drugs to be avoided, 
see the subsequent text.
Where feasible, all patients should be tested for G6PD deficiency before 
administering primaquine for treatment of malaria. If testing is not available, patients 
receiving primaquine should be monitored closely, and patients should be instructed 
to stop taking primaquine if signs or symptoms of haemolytic anaemia appear (e.g. 
weakness or pallor, or if their urine becomes red or black). 
Discontinue the offending oxidative stressor, most commonly a medication. 
	
l Most patients recover spontaneously and require monitoring. 
	
l If the anaemia is very severe (preexisting anaemia, or if rapid decline in Hb), 
then a packed cell transfusion can be lifesaving. 
	
l If Hb <7 g/dL, consider packed cell transfusion.
	
l If there are no signs of haemoglobinuria, packed cell transfusion is not required; 
monitor closely for 48 hours.
Consider comorbidities, haemodynamic stability and the patient’s previous 
haemolytic experience to decide management.
	
l Oxygen and fluids are critical during acute crisis.
	
l Acute kidney injury may be due to hypovolaemic shock or haemoglobinuria. 
Renal function usually recovers with time.

condition: Appendix VIII: Managing Adverse Drug Reactions
text:
Any drug that is capable of producing beneficial therapeutic effects can also cause 
unwanted ‘adverse’ effects. Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are common and 
constitute an important patient safety challenge. A significant proportion of patients 
in the community experience ADRs which complicate treatment, result in poor 
compliance and delay cure besides admissions to hospital. Hospitalized patients 
frequently experience ADRs that complicate and prolong their stay. Many of these 
ADRs are preventable if greater care is taken. The underreporting of ADRs remains 
the largest barrier to health care professionals in identifying an ADR when it presents. 
Major barriers to reporting ADR involve information systems, lack of information 
and available resources, unawareness of the importance of reporting, difficulties in 
diagnosing the ADR, the assumption that the ADR is unimportant or minor, uncertainty 
about how and to whom to report it, and fear of the ramifications of reporting.
Definitions
An adverse drug event (ADE) is defined as any untoward medical occurrence that 
may be present during treatment with a medicine, but which does not necessarily have 
a causal relationship with this treatment.
ADR is response to a drug that is noxious and unintended and occurs at doses 
normally used in patients for prophylaxis diagnosis or therapy of a disease. It does not 
include therapeutic failures, overdose, drug abuse, non-compliance and medication 
errors. Drug withdrawal, drug abuse syndromes, accidental poisoning and drug 
overdose complications should not be defined as ADRs.
A serious adverse event or serious ADR is any untoward medical occurrence that 
at any dose results in death, is life-threatening, requires hospitalization or prolongation 
of existing hospitalization, results in persistent or significant disability/incapacity, and 
results in congenital anomaly/birth defect.
Classification of ADRs
ADRs can be categorized in a number of ways (e.g. duration, incidence/frequency, 
severity, types of ADRs, location and body systems affected).

condition: Appendix VIII: Managing Adverse Drug Reactions
text:
1276    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Identification of ADRs and their management
All drugs have the potential for ADRs; therefore, medicines should be prescribed 
considering the risk of ADR and benefits of medicine. ADRs contribute adversely 
to patient safety. Patient safety requires early identification of ADRs, appropriate 
management and prevention to support both information exchange and the reporting 
and analysis of patient safety data. 
	 1.	Distinguish ADRs from ADEs: An ADR is a type of ADE whose cause can be 
directly attributed to a drug and its physiological properties. ADRs occur despite 
appropriate prescribing and dosing, whereas ADEs may also be associated with 
inappropriate use of the drug or errors or other confounders that occur during drug 
therapy but are not necessarily caused by the pharmacology of the drug itself. A 
causal relationship is suspected for an ADR but is not required for an ADE.
	 2.	Temporal relationship of ADRs: Symptoms that occur soon after a drug is taken 
are often easily connected with the use of a drug. A patient’s new or worsening 
symptom may be the first sign of an ADR. Symptoms and signs may manifest 
soon after the first dose or only after chronic use. Assessing the timing between 
administration of the drug and development of the reaction is an important step in 
identifying an ADR and determining causality. The next step is to identify patterns 
in ADR symptoms and classification of an ADR when it presents as above.
	 3.	Detect populations at risk of ADR and apply pharmacovigilance principles 
to prevent ADRs: Many factors can increase the likelihood of an ADR. They 
include hereditary factors, certain diseases, multiple comorbid conditions and 
medications, very young or old age, pregnancy, breastfeeding, prior history of 
ADRs, dose and duration of exposure.
	 4.	Management: It includes withdrawal of the drug if it can be safely stopped, or if 
the event is life-threatening or intolerable, and administration of specific treatment 
of its effects. Assess whether there is any reasonable alternative and whether 
medicine is medically necessary. The offending medicine may be continued if the 
problem is mild and expected to resolve over time.
	 5.	Devise methods for ADR detection and surveillance methods: Surveillance 
methods can detect reactions and prove associations. Perform intensive monitoring 
‘triggers’ by review of medication charts and medical records of patients admitted 
in the hospital.
	
l A ‘Trigger Tool’ is an easy-to-use method for accurately identifying adverse 
events (harm) and measuring the rate of ADEs over time. 
	
l Trigger Tool review: It includes chart review, via automated or manual 
processes, to detect ‘triggers’ that may be representative of an ADE or ADR. 
The trigger is investigated to determine whether an ADE occurred (e.g. if an 
INR of >6 is the trigger, the chart is then reviewed for any evidence of bleeding 
to determine whether an adverse event has occurred, although an elevated INR 
in itself is not an adverse event). Other common laboratory tests and reports of 
predetermined threshold changes in laboratory values (critical value) can assist 
in identifying an ADR, for example, laboratory monitoring of liver function tests

before and after prescribing statins. A new order for a serum drug level may 
alert the practitioner to investigate whether an ADR caused by drug toxicity or 
treatment failure is occurring.
	
l Medication order screening is done for any abrupt, unexpected discontinuation 
of a drug or a substantial dosage increase or reduction. 
	
l Trigger medications: These include medications commonly used to treat 
ADRs, such as antidotes and reversal agents, e.g. Naloxone, Flumazenil, 
Diphenhydramine, 50% glucose, antiemetics, vitamin K, sodium polystyrene 
sulphonate, corticosteroids or antidiarrheals may be a sign that a practitioner 
is treating an ADR. However, administration of a trigger medication does not 
always indicate that patient harm occurred.
	
l Daily review of multidisciplinary notes in a patient’s chart, e.g. notes pertaining 
to oversedation, lethargy and falls, may be the sign of an ADR caused by an 
analgesic, a sedative or a muscle relaxant. Reports of a rash in a patient’s 
progress notes may be indicative of an ADR and should be investigated for a 
drug-related cause, such as an allergic reaction.
	 6.	Reporting of ADRs: Pharmacovigilance (or drug safety) is the practice of 
monitoring the effects of medical drugs after they have been licensed for use. India 
has a national Pharmacovigilance Programme (PvPI). Every hospital should have 
the special PV cell to monitor and report the ADR. Reporting helps in identifying 
a causal relationship between the drug and the adverse reaction, if one exists. Dial 
toll free helpline number 1800 180 3024 to report ADRs. Mail the filled ADR 
reporting form directly to pvpi@ipcindia.net or pvpi.ipcindia@gmail.com. 
	
l All suspected adverse reactions to medicines and vaccines (adverse event 
following immunization [AEFI) should be reported as soon as possible because 
over-reporting is always better than under-reporting (ADR form available at 
cdsco.nic.in).
	
l All health professionals should report ADRs, especially ADRs to newly 
marketed drugs or new drugs added to the hospital formulary, all serious 
reactions and interactions (expected or not), ADRs which are not clearly stated 
in the package insert, unusual or interesting ADRs, an observed increase in the 
frequency of a given reaction, ADRs in a special field of interest such as drug 
abuse, ADRs in pregnancy and during lactation, ADRs in children and ADRs 
occurring from overdose or medication error or unusual lack of efficacy or when 
suspected pharmaceutical defects are observed or any product quality problems.
	 7.	Prevention: Prevention of ADRs requires familiarity with the drug and potential 
reactions to it. 
	
l Use fewest drugs, whenever possible. Carefully select drugs and initial 
dose especially in very young and elderly. If patients develop non-specific 
symptoms, ADRs should always be considered before beginning symptomatic 
treatment. Keep ADRs in the differential diagnosis.
	
l Use drug that you know well; do not change therapy from known drugs to 
unfamiliar ones without good reasons.

potential drug interactions; analysis should be repeated whenever drugs are

l Identify drugs and patients at high risk for being involved in ADRs. Take 
extra care to prescribe drugs known to exhibit a large variety of interactions 
and ADRs such as anticoagulants, hypoglycaemics, drugs affecting the CNS 
and antibiotics.
	
l Maintain an accurate patient’s medication list. Review all the drugs used by 
your patients regularly, especially non-prescription drugs.
	
l Beware of the interaction of drugs with certain foodstuffs, alcohol and even 
household remedies.
	
l If ADR is suspected, consider stopping/dose reduction and notify the ADR 
using the adverse event form.
	
l Counsel patients on expected ADRs, their management, and when and where 
to report ADRs.

condition: Appendix IX: Safe Use of Radiological Contrast Media
text:
Various forms of contrast media have been used to improve medical imaging. Iodinated 
and gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCA) are used in most radiology practices. 
Like all other pharmaceuticals; however, these agents are not completely devoid of 
risk. Adverse side effects from the administration of contrast media vary from minor 
physiological disturbances to rare severe life-threatening situations. Therefore, it is 
critical for faculty and staff to know how reactions to contrast agents manifest and how 
to treat them promptly.
Preparation for prompt treatment of contrast media reactions must include 
preparation for the entire spectrum of potential adverse events and include prearranged 
response planning with availability of appropriately trained personnel, equipment and 
medications. For any diagnostic procedure, the referring physician and radiologist 
should consider the risk-to-benefit profile of the proposed contrast material–enhanced 
examination and potential imaging alternatives that would provide the same or better 
diagnostic information and confirm a valid clinical indication. Obtain consent for the 
injection of iodinated contrast material as per requirements.
Contrast media commonly used in conventional radiology are:
	 1.	Barium sulphate: It is a well-established and preferential oral agent for the 
examination of the gastrointestinal radiographic and fluoroscopic examinations. 
It causes image contrast due to its property of high attenuation of X-rays. It is 
available as paste, suspensions (of varying densities) and powder (for making paste 
and dilute suspension).
	
l It is used in various forms and amounts depending on the study in investigating 
various conditions of the gastrointestinal tract.
	
l Various investigations include barium swallow, upper GI studies, follow-through, 
enteroclysis, enema and oral contrast in CT scans.
	
l It is used in single- and double-contrast studies. Double-contrast studies also use 
other agents such as water, air and methyl cellulose.
	
	Contraindications, side effects and special precautions
	
l Barium sulphate is contraindicated in perforation of the GI tract – can cause 
severe peritonitis.
	
l Constipation may occur after oral or rectal barium sulphate. Adequate hydration 
should be maintained.
	
l Rarely impaction, obstruction, appendicitis, cramping or diarrhoea may occur. 
Accidental venous intravasation can lead to the formation of emboli.
Appendix  IX
Safe Use of Radiological Contrast Media

text:
1280    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Barium sulphate may be retained for years in closed cavities.
	
l ECG abnormalities may occur during barium sulphate enemas.
	
l Accidental aspiration into the lungs can lead to pneumonitis or granuloma 
formation.
	
l Hypersensitivity reactions can occur due to the additives used in the formulation.
	 2.	Iodine-based contrast media (water-soluble): They are the mainstay contrast 
agents for use in radiographic, fluoroscopic, angiographic and CT imaging. 
They are a versatile group of agents used for intravenous, oral and other routes 
of administration, such as urethral and intra-articular. Iodine has a higher atomic 
number as compared with the different tissues of the body. This property creates 
image contrast due to differential photoelectric absorption.
	
	Ionic contrast media/high-osmolality contrast media (HOCM): These include 
Sodium and Meglumine diatrizoate and iothalamate. There is a high incidence 
of adverse reactions in intravascular and intrathecal administration. Their use is 
limited to gastrointestinal and cystourethral administration.
	
	Non-ionic contrast media/low-osmolality contrast media (LOCM): These are 
monomeric (Iohexol, Ioversol, Iopamidol) and dimeric (Iotrolan, Iodixanol). They 
are available in various iodine concentrations from 240 to 370 mg/mL, in 10, 20, 
40, 50 and 100 mL.
	
l There is a broad range of indications in the form of intravascular and 
intracavitary routes.
	
l Intravascular includes intravenous pyelogram (IVP), venography, angiography 
contrast-enhanced CT scans, etc.
	
l Intracavitary includes hysterosalpingography (HSG), micturating cystourethro­
gram, fistulogram, etc.
	
l Dose varies from each investigation and case-to-case basis.
	
l In general, non-ionic media are better tolerated than ionic media and more non-
ionic contrast can be used.
	
l Non-ionic media should be preferred for intravascular use whenever possible.
MRI Contrast Media
Gadolinium is the main component of the contrast material commonly used in magnetic 
resonance imaging (MRI) examinations. Gadolinium molecules alter the magnetic 
properties of nearby water molecules and shorten the T1 relaxation time in the voxels in 
which they are present. So, they appear bright on T1-weighted images, thereby resulting 
in enhancement of MRI image. Intravascular and interstitial enhancement are the two 
mechanisms that alone or in combination cause enhancement of underlying tissue after 
contrast administration. The most common route of administration is intravenous.
They are divided into four groups depending on whether the carrier ligand is linear 
or macrocyclic:
	 1.	Linear–ionic: Gadopentetate dimeglumine, gadobenate dimeglumine, gadoxetic 
acid disodium salt
	 2.	Linear–non-ionic: Gadodiamide, gadoversetamide

Appendix IX  Safe Use of Radiological Contrast Media    1281
	 3.	Macrocyclic–ionic: Gadoterate meglumine
	 4.	Macrocyclic–non-ionic: Gadoteridol, gadobutrol
Contraindications and adverse reactions to gadolinium
	 1.	It is contraindicated in patients with acute or chronic renal disease (GFR <30 mL/
min) or patients with renal failure, as they may develop nephrogenic systemic 
fibrosis (NSF).
	 2.	Allergic reactions to GBCA are rare and are more likely to occur in patients with a 
history of hypersensitivity to gadolinium-based or iodinated contrast media, known 
allergy or bronchial asthma.
	 3.	Traces of gadolinium deposits may be deposited in dentate nucleus of the 
cerebellum and globus pallidus.
	 4.	A lower risk of NSF and lower gadolinium deposition is seen with macrocyclic 
agents.
Ultrasound Contrast Media
Intravenous injection of contrast-containing microbubbles of gas which oscillate 
when exposed to ultrasound beam affects ultrasound background scatter with resultant 
increase in intravascular contrast.
Ultrasound contrast media are categorized according to gas present in microbubble 
shell as those containing sulphur hexafluoride gas, octafluoropropane, air or perflexane gas.
Advantages
	
l Ultrasound contrast media are used for evaluation of vascularity of various organs 
of the body.
	
l They are useful in lesion characterization.
	
l Since they are excreted through the lung, they can be used in patients with kidney 
disease and those with allergy to iodinated contrast media.
	
l They allow dynamic and repeat examinations.
	
l They do not involve radiation, so are safer.
Disadvantages
	
l The circulation residence time is low as they are taken up by the immune system, 
liver or spleen.
	
l Ultrasound produces more heat, so frequent monitoring is required.
Acute Adverse Reactions
Both allergic- and chemotoxic-type (physiological) reactions are associated with 
the dose and molecular toxicity of each radiological contrast agent in addition to 
its physiological characteristics. Radiologists should consider screening for the 
predisposing factors that increase the risk for reaction, both allergic-like and non-
allergic reactions.
Risk factors for acute adverse reactions to contrast agents
	
l Previous reactions to iodinated contrast agents

to diabetic nephropathy, dehydration, congestive heart failure, concurrent 
administration of nephrotoxic drugs (e.g. non-steroidal anti-inflammatory

Strategies to reduce risk of contrast-induced nephrotoxicity (CIN) and 
nephrogenic systemic fibrosis
	 1.	Identify patients at risk (those dependent on dialysis, with severe chronic renal 
failure without dialysis, or with acute renal failure).
	 2.	Consider alternative diagnostic study, such as CT or ultrasonography.
	 3.	Avoid use of gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) whenever possible; if 
use of GBCA is unavoidable, use group 2 agent (e.g. Gadopiclenol) followed by 
prompt dialysis, but only if the patient is already undergoing dialysis.
	 4.	Use the lowest possible dose of GBCA. Do not re-administer GBCA for several 
days to 1 week after the initial dose.
Other Special Precautions
	
l They are contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to a particular 
contrast agent. Special precautions should be taken in patients with a history of 
allergy, asthma, atopy, dermatitis and urticaria; previous generalized contrast 
medium reaction; etc. Patients with physiological reactions do not require 
premedication in the future, whereas those with allergic reactions may need 
premedication with steroids. Premedication to avoid or minimize possible allergic

reactions may be considered. There is no cross-reactivity between different 
classes of contrast medium. For example, a prior reaction to gadolinium-based 
contrast medium does not predict a future reaction to iodinated contrast medium, 
or vice versa, more than any other unrelated allergy. Distinguishing allergic from 
physiological reactions is important because patients with physiological reactions do 
not require premedication in the future, whereas those with allergic reactions may 
need premedication with steroids. Test dose before injection of the full dose is not 
completely reliable; the patient should be kept under observation for 30–60 minutes 
following injection.
	
l Antihistamines should be given by a separate injection to avoid precipitation.
	
l Patients on adrenergic β-blockers are more prone to severe adverse effects to contrast 
media.
	
l An interval of at least 48 hours should be allowed before studies are repeated, 
especially in patients with reduced renal function.
	
l Preparatory dehydration is not necessary and may be dangerous in infants, young 
children, the elderly, patients with multiple myeloma and patients with azotaemia 
(especially those with polyuria, oliguria, diabetes, advanced vascular disease or 
pre-existing dehydration).
	
l Special precaution should be taken in patients with cerebral thrombosis or embolism, 
primary or metastatic cerebral lesions, subarachnoid haemorrhage, increased 
intracranial pressure, arterial spasm, transient ischaemic attacks and in any condition 
when the blood–brain barrier is breached or the transit time of the contrast material 
is prolonged.
	
l The results of protein-bound iodine and radioactive iodine uptake studies will 
not reflect thyroid functions for at least 16 days following the administration of 
iodinated contrast media.
	
l Avoid in patients known or suspected to have phaeochromocytoma.
	
l Contrast media by IV route can promote the phenomenon of sickling in individuals 
homozygous for sickle cell disease.
	
l Safety of contrast media for use in pregnancy has not been determined; the benefit 
to the patient should be carefully weighed against the possible risk to the foetus.
	
l Since contrast media are known to be excreted in breast milk, nursing should be 
stopped and alternate feeding substituted for 24–48 hours following administration.
Management of Physiological and Allergic Reactions to Contrast Media
Reactions occur at random and are generally unpredictable. Most of the patients recover 
when properly treated.
Timing of reaction occurrence: Most reactions occur in the first hour after 
administration, and many occur within the first 5 minutes. Late adverse reactions may 
occur rarely between 1 hour and 1 week after injection of iodinated contrast agents. 
Delayed reactions are more common in young adults, women and patients with a 
history of allergy.

condition: Appendix IX: Safe Use of Radiological Contrast Media
text:
Appendix  X
Serological Markers
Inflammation, both acute and chronic, is an important pathophysiological component of 
many diseases. Knowledge about blood/serum biomarkers of inflammation is important 
not only for diagnosis but also for monitoring response to therapy. Although these 
markers are non-specific, and are not diagnostic for any particular condition, they may 
help to identify a generalized inflammatory state along with other tests and aid in the 
differential diagnosis. For example, in some diseases, serial measurements of C-reactive 
protein (CRP) also may be of prognostic value. Some of the more commonly used 
inflammatory markers include those given next.
Blood counts (e.g. white blood cell count, red blood cell count, 
haemoglobin count)
Neutrophilia is defined as a higher neutrophil count in the blood than the normal reference 
range of absolute neutrophil count (i.e. >8000 cells/mm3). It is a marker of inflammation, 
associated with severe acure respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), myocardial injury with 
raised enzymes and clinical cardiac dysfunction. Peripheral smear can show neutrophils 
with toxic granules, Pelger–Huët abnormality and/or myeloid precursors.
Lymphopenia is defined as decreased absolute lymphocyte count (ALC; i.e. 
<1000/mm3). It is a common haematological abnormality in viral infections like HIV 
and COVID-19. In COVID, it is considered as a marker of severity of cytokine storm, 
ICU stay, severity of ARDS and mortality. Peripheral smear can show atypical, reactive 
lymphocytes.
Lymphocytosis can occur as the body’s normal response to an infection or 
inflammation. ALC is normally maintained in a range of fewer than 4000 lymphocytes/
µL. Elevation of the lymphocyte count above this level can be harmless and temporary 
or can occur in any viral or bacterial infection, autoimmune disorder associated with 
inflammation or some haematopoietic malignancies.
Neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (NLR) is the most well-established inflammatory 
marker that reflects systemic inflammatory response. NLR is derived from absolute 
neutrophil and lymphocyte counts, and can be used to gauge the severity of 
inflammation and, also, prognosticate: if <3.5, mild disease; and if >3.5, moderate to 
severe disease. The normal NLR is 1–2. NLR is influenced in many conditions like

condition: Appendix IX: Safe Use of Radiological Contrast Media
text:
Appendix X  Serological Markers    1289
coronary heart disease, stroke, diabetes, obesity, psychiatric diagnosis, cancer of solid 
organs, anaemia and stress. It can be used as a reliable and cheap indicator of prognosis 
of solid tumours.
Platelet to lymphocyte ratio (PLR) is being increasingly used as an informative 
marker to reveal shifts in platelet and lymphocyte counts due to acute inflammatory and 
prothrombotic states. Shifts in PLR are particularly helpful in evaluating the severity 
of systemic inflammation and predicting infections and other comorbidities, especially 
in inflammatory rheumatic diseases. The shifts in PLR are particularly helpful when 
evaluated with other parameters like NLR.
The normal range of PLR varies between 90 and 210.
Platelets are within normal limits in most patients. Thrombocytopenia mainly 
occurs in cases of dengue. Thrombocytosis is rare and can be seen in cases of iron-
deficiency anaemia with superadded infection or bleeding. RBC parameters remain 
unaffected.
C-reactive protein (CRP)
CRP is one of the most widely studied and utilized biomarkers of inflammation. It 
is produced by the liver in response to proinflammatory cytokines and its levels rise 
rapidly during acute inflammation. High-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) is particularly 
valuable in assessing low-grade chronic inflammation associated with conditions 
like cardiovascular disease. CRP levels may be used to contribute to the diagnosis or 
monitor inflammation in many acute or chronic conditions, including:
	
l Infections from bacteria or viruses
	
l Inflammatory bowel disease, disorders of the intestines that include Crohn’s 
disease and ulcerative colitis
	
l Autoimmune disorders, such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis
	
l Lung diseases, such as asthma
Interpretation of CRP levels is done as follows:
	
l Less than 0.3 mg/dL: Normal (level seen in most healthy adults)
	
l 0.3–1.0 mg/dL: Normal or minor elevation (can be seen in obesity, pregnancy, 
depression, diabetes, common cold, gingivitis, periodontitis, sedentary lifestyle, 
cigarette smoking and genetic polymorphisms)
	
l 1–10.0 mg/dL: Moderate elevation (systemic inflammation such as in rheumatoid 
arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or other autoimmune diseases, 
malignancies, myocardial infarction, pancreatitis, bronchitis)
	
l More than 10.0 mg/dL: Marked elevation (acute bacterial infections, viral 
infections, systemic vasculitis, major trauma)
	
l More than 50.0 mg/dL: Severe elevation (acute bacterial infections)
CRP levels have been used to monitor the efficacy of treatment as the levels fall 
quickly once the cause of inflammation has resolved. They usually decrease during the 
first 48 hours if treatment is adequate; increases in CRP concentrations during the first

condition: Appendix IX: Safe Use of Radiological Contrast Media
text:
1290    Standard Treatment Guidelines
48 hours suggest inadequate therapy. Waiting for at least 24 hours is recommended 
before repeating CRP measurements, except in neonates, in whom testing is 
recommended after 18–24 hours. While interpreting CRP levels, one must be aware 
of interfering factors. NSAIDs, statins and magnesium supplementation are known to 
falsely reduce CRP levels while trauma may falsely elevate the levels.
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
ESR measures the rate at which red blood cells settle in a tube of blood. Elevated 
ESR is a non-specific indicator of inflammation, influenced by factors such as 
fibrinogen and immunoglobulins. Though non-specific, it is useful for monitoring and 
follow-up of inflammatory activity. It is used as a ‘sickness indicator’ because of its 
reproducibility and low cost. However, it is neither sensitive nor specific as a general 
screening test. Elevated ESR may occur in multiple clinical settings and should not 
be interpreted as stand-alone laboratory value. The only role which elevated ESR 
level can play is to heighten the practitioner’s index of suspicion of the potential for 
underlying illness and, also, follow-up of treatment. Along with other tests, it can help 
diagnose or monitor conditions associated with inflammation, e.g. infection, arthritis, 
vasculitis or inflammatory bowel disease. An ESR may also be used to monitor an 
existing condition.
Normal values of ESR are 0–15 mm/h in men and 0–20 mm/h in women.
Procalcitonin (PCT)
Procalcitonin is a precursor of the hormone calcitonin, and its levels rise in response 
to bacterial infections. Widely used in distinguishing bacterial from viral infections, it 
aids in antibiotic decision making. The main indication for PCT measurement is to aid 
in the diagnosis of bacterial infection and as a marker to guide antibiotic therapy. The 
normal value of procalcitonin is <0.05 ng/mL. PCT levels greater than 0.5 or 0.1 ng/mL 
are often considered suggestive of bacterial infection. Generally, a higher PCT level is 
often associated with bacterial infections, while lower levels are more indicative of viral 
infections or non-infectious inflammatory conditions. PCT levels aid in the diagnosis 
of sepsis, with increased PCT levels having a high positive predictive value and normal 
levels a high negative predictive value.
Calprotectin
Calprotectin is a calcium- and zinc-binding protein found within neutrophils. It is 
used as an inflammatory marker since it rises in parallel with disease activity in 
conditions such as systemic inflammatory diseases, infection and atherosclerosis. 
Tests are available to measure it in blood and stool. Faecal calprotectin is especially 
used in monitoring inflammatory bowel disease. Its role is limited to gastrointestinal 
inflammation that too does not provide information about the cause of inflammation. 
Other limitations include non-specificity, false positives and negatives, and variable 
sensitivity and specificity besides cost and accessibility issues.

condition: Appendix IX: Safe Use of Radiological Contrast Media
text:
Appendix X  Serological Markers    1291
Ferritin
Ferritin, first discovered as an iron storage protein, has emerged as a biomarker not 
only in iron-related disorders but also in inflammatory diseases, or diseases in which 
inflammation has a central role. It is unclear whether serum ferritin reflects or causes 
inflammation, or whether it is involved in an inflammatory cycle. Since serum ferritin 
arises from damaged cells, it can be taken to be a marker of cellular damage. Though 
considered an acute phase reactant, it should not be interpreted in isolation.
In addition to this homeostatic role, ferritin plays a key role in inflammatory 
pathology also. Though not specific to any disease, ferritin levels can be used as 
both a biomarker of disease progress and prognosis and a target for therapeutic 
intervention. Combining ferritin measurements with other iron-related markers and 
clinical information helps provide a more comprehensive understanding of a patient’s 
iron status.
The normal range for ferritin in blood serum is 24–336 ng/mL for adult males and 
24–307 ng/mL for adult females.
Lactate
Lactate, a byproduct of anaerobic metabolism, serves as a valuable marker in assessing 
the severity of infection. During infections, especially those leading to sepsis, cells may 
experience oxygen deprivation, prompting an increase in lactate production. Elevated 
lactate levels indicate tissue hypoperfusion and can be indicative of a compromised 
circulatory system. Monitoring lactate levels is crucial in critical care settings as it helps 
in gauging the severity of infection, assess the effectiveness of treatment and guide 
interventions to improve tissue oxygenation and overall patient outcomes. Elevated 
lactate levels are associated with an increased risk of organ dysfunction and mortality in 
severe infections. Interpretation of lactate levels should always be done in conjunction 
with a comprehensive clinical assessment and other laboratory tests to determine the 
underlying cause.
The normal range for serum lactate may vary depending on the laboratory and 
method but is considered to be 0.5–2.0 mmol/L or 4.5–18 mg/dL.
Interleukins (ILs)
ILs are a family of cytokines involved in cell communication during immune responses. 
Most commonly they are released from macrophages, mast cells and endothelial cells. 
Different ILs (IL-1, IL 2, IL4, IL-10) serve distinct functions. IL-6 is the key mediator, 
assessing inflammation and immune system activity. It is associated with acute-phase 
reactions and is elevated in various inflammatory conditions, either acute or chronic. 
This includes situations such as infection, trauma, burns and cancers. It is secreted 
by monocytes and macrophages in response to inflammatory stimuli. Elevated levels 
of IL-6 are indicative of worsening clinical features in patients at risk for severe 
COVID-19, including respiratory failure, the need for mechanical ventilation/intubation 
and mortality.

condition: Appendix IX: Safe Use of Radiological Contrast Media
text:
1292    Standard Treatment Guidelines
The use of ILs has limitations as their specificity is often limited, as elevated levels 
may be associated with various conditions, and can fluctuate rapidly, and a single 
measurement may not accurately represent the dynamic nature of immune responses. 
Moreover, variations in assay techniques and the lack of standardized reference ranges 
can affect result interpretation. While ILs are indicative of inflammation, they do not 
provide insights into the underlying cause.
The normal value of IL-6 is <7 pg/mL (in children, it can be up to 15 pg/mL). In 
moderate infections, it is 15–100 pg/mL. In severe infections, it may be raised up to 
100–500 pg/mL (>500 pg/mL is critical).
Coagulation-related parameters
The coagulation system is closely intertwined with the immune response, and 
its activation is part of the host defence mechanism against invading pathogens. 
Coagulation-related parameters play a dual role in infections by aiding the immune 
response through inflammation-induced fibrinogen elevation and contributing to host 
defence via platelet activation. However, severe infections may lead to dysregulated 
coagulation, causing disseminated intravascular coagulation and microvascular 
thrombosis. Monitoring these parameters like D-dimer helps assess infection severity, 
guiding clinical interventions:
	
l Thrombocytopenia (normal 1.5–4.5 lakh/mm3)
	
l Elevated D-dimer (normal <250 ng/mL)
	
l Elevated fibrinogen (normal 2.0–4.0 g/L) (however, in the late stages, thrombolysis 
may decrease fibrinogen levels and increase fibrin degradation products)
	
l Increased fibrin degradation products levels (normal 1.25–10 mcg/mL)
	
l Prolonged prothrombin time (normal 11–13 seconds)
	
l Prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) (normal 26–35 seconds)
D-Dimer
D-dimer is a biomarker used to assess and monitor the presence of blood clot formation 
and breakdown in the body. Elevated D-dimer levels indicate increased fibrinolysis, 
suggesting the recent formation or degradation of blood clots. While it is a sensitive 
marker for various medical conditions, including deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary 
embolism and disseminated intravascular coagulation, D-dimer is not specific to any 
particular disease and requires interpretation in the context of clinical findings.
Tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α)
TNF-α is a proinflammatory cytokine that plays a central role in the initiation and 
amplification of the inflammatory cascade. Elevated levels of TNF-α are observed 
in chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory 
bowel disease. TNF-α is responsible for increased microbicidal activity of leucocytes. 
Measurement of TNF-α often requires invasive procedures, such as collecting tissue 
samples or obtaining synovial fluid in the case of joint disorders. This can limit its

condition: Appendix IX: Safe Use of Radiological Contrast Media
text:
Appendix X  Serological Markers    1293
practicality for routine monitoring, especially in certain clinical settings. TNF-α levels 
can vary significantly over time and even within the course of a day. This lack of 
specificity limits its diagnostic value for identifying a particular disease.
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
LDH is a key enzyme in the glycolytic pathway and a cytoplasmic enzyme found in 
most organs; it has been linked to inflammation response and cell damage. LDH is a 
non-specific marker used in assessing a range of conditions, including infections, cancers 
and cardiovascular events, but its diagnostic value depends on the specific clinical 
context and additional laboratory findings. Elevated LDH is a negative prognostic 
marker (normal range 0–250 units/L). Its lack of specificity, tissue source ambiguity, 
susceptibility to interference and dynamic nature limit its diagnostic precision.
Other biochemistry parameters
In the presence of infection, particularly in severe cases or systemic conditions, 
the liver’s synthetic function may be compromised, leading to albumin production. 
Simultaneously, the release of AST and ALT into the bloodstream can occur due to 
liver cell damage.
	
l Decreased Albumin
	
l Increased Aspartate aminotransferase (SGOT one to two times the upper limit 
of normal)
	
l Increased Alanine aminotransferase (SGPT one to two times the upper limit of 
normal)
These inflammatory parameters help to rapidly identify severity of infection, hence 
facilitating the early initiation of effective treatment. In addition, these inflammatory 
parameters could be used to predict the transition from mild to severe/critical infections.
The above are just a few examples where serological markers of inflammation, if 
used intelligently, can facilitate clinical practice. Newer markers are emerging rapidly, 
and one must be prudent in their usage. Some of these are being used in research to 
develop therapeutic strategies.
Other newer serological markers
Measuring bradykinin, histamine, serotonin, leukotrienes, chemokines, lysosomal 
enzymes, nitric oxide, platelet-activating factor, thrombin markers, etc., is not routinely 
performed in day-to-day clinical practice; certain situations warrant their assessment. 
These markers are commonly utilized in specialized settings, such as research studies 
or specific clinical contexts. For example, in allergy and immunology clinics, histamine 
and leukotrienes might be measured to diagnose and manage allergic conditions. 
Additionally, assessing these markers can provide insights into inflammatory and 
vascular processes, aiding in the diagnosis and monitoring of certain diseases, such 
as vasculitis or inflammatory disorders. However, their routine use in general clinical

condition: Appendix IX: Safe Use of Radiological Contrast Media
text:
1294    Standard Treatment Guidelines
practice is limited due to factors like cost, technical complexity and the availability of 
more practical diagnostic approaches.
Key points
Most of the above-mentioned serological biomarkers are non-specific tools that should 
always be used in conjunction with the patient’s overall clinical picture and other 
diagnostic results.
Some examples where they can be used to aid in the diagnosis, monitor treatment 
response or, even, prognosticate are:
	
l Certain suspected inflammatory disorders (e.g. ESR is useful for giant cell arteritis 
and CRP for neonatal sepsis)
	
l Distinguish between inflammatory and non-inflammatory diseases (e.g. osteoarthritis 
vs. rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease vs. irritable bowel syndrome)
	
l Manage certain antibiotic therapies (e.g. PCT measurements can be used to support 
shortening the duration of antimicrobial therapy)
	
l Predict recovery (e.g. PCT levels can be used to predict 28-day cumulative mortality 
risk for patients diagnosed with sepsis)
It cannot be emphasized enough that although it is important to be aware of 
serological markers of inflammation, one must be clear about their practical application 
in a particular clinical scenario before ordering for the laboratory test.

condition: Appendix X: Serological Markers 1288 Appendix XI: Oxygen Therapy
text:
Oxygen is an essential part of resuscitation and patient stabilization in critical illness 
and saves lives when used judiciously in the treatment of hypoxaemia. However, 
oxygen is often used inappropriately, and the dangers of over-oxygenation are 
not recognized. Oxygen does not relieve dyspnoea in the absence of hypoxaemia. 
Dyspnoea can occur for many reasons other than cardiorespiratory disease, including 
metabolic acidosis, anxiety and pain, and treatment with oxygen is not indicated in 
these cases. Both hypoxaemia and hyperoxaemia are harmful. Hyperoxaemia can 
cause coronary vasoconstriction. High-flow oxygen is commonly used in intensive 
therapy units (ITU) and hyperoxaemia in these settings can lead to adverse outcomes. 
Inappropriate oxygen use in patients at risk of type 2 respiratory failure (T2RF) can 
result in life-threatening hypercapnia (respiratory acidosis, organ dysfunction, coma and 
death). The goal of oxygen delivery is to maintain targeted oxygen saturation (SpO2) 
levels through the provision of supplemental oxygen in a safe and effective way which 
is well tolerated to:
	
l Relieve hypoxaemia and maintain adequate oxygenation of tissues and vital organs, 
as assessed by SpO2/SaO2 monitoring and clinical signs
	
l Prevent excessive carbon dioxide (CO2) accumulation, i.e. selection of the 
appropriate flow rate and delivery device
	
l Ensure adequate clearance of secretions and limit the adverse events of hypothermia 
and insensible water loss by use of optimal humidification (dependent on mode of 
oxygen delivery)
Indications for oxygen therapy
Oxygen is used as a medical treatment in both chronic and acute cases, and can be used 
in hospital, pre-hospital or entirely out of hospital, dependent on the needs of the patient 
and the advice of the medical professional. 
	 1.	Use in acute conditions
	
	In the pre-hospital environment, high-flow oxygen is definitively indicated for 
use in resuscitation, major trauma, anaphylaxis, major haemorrhage, shock, active 
convulsions and hypothermia or for any other injury or illness causing hypoxaemia 
such as COVID-19. 
	
		
The oxygen flow should be moderated to achieve target oxygen saturation 
levels, based on pulse oximetry (with a target level of 92–98% in most patients, or 
88–92% in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [COPD] or patient-
Appendix  XI
Oxygen Therapy

condition: Appendix X: Serological Markers 1288 Appendix XI: Oxygen Therapy
text:
1296    Standard Treatment Guidelines
specific target range for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure). The aim of 
the supplemental oxygen is to improve oxygenation; it does not treat the underlying 
causes of hypoxaemia; therefore, the underlying cause must be diagnosed and 
treated as a matter of urgency. The oxygen saturation should be checked by pulse 
oximetry, ‘the fifth vital’ in all breathless and acutely ill patients, and recorded.
	 2.	Use in chronic conditions
	
	It is commonly used in patients with COPD with PaO2 ≤55 mmHg or SaO2 ≤88%, 
and in case of chronic bronchitis or emphysema, who may require additional 
oxygen to breathe either during a temporary worsening of their condition or 
throughout the day and night. 
	 3.	It is used in the treatment of an acute or emergency situation in which hypoxaemia 
or hypoxia is suspected, and if the patient is in respiratory distress manifested by:
	
l Dyspnoea, tachypnoea, bradypnoea, apnoea
	
l Pallor, cyanosis
	
l Lethargy or restlessness
	
l Use of accessory muscles: nasal flaring, intercostal or sternal recession, tracheal tug
	 4.	It is used as a short-term therapy, e.g. post-anaesthetic or surgical procedure.
	 5.	It is used in palliative care.
Oxygen therapy indications
1.	 Critical illness requiring high levels of 
supplemental oxygen
Give 15 L/min via a reservoir mask and once stable, 
reduce oxygen to aim for a saturation range of 
94–98%. If patient at risk of type 2 respiratory failure 
(T2RF), aim for the same initial saturation as all 
other critically ill groups pending ABG.
2.	 Serious illness requiring moderate 
amounts of oxygen if the patient is 
hypoxic
Initially give 2–6 L/min via nasal cannulae or 
5–10 L/min via face mask, aiming for a saturation 
range of 94–98%. If saturation cannot be maintained 
or initial saturation is <85%, use a reservoir mask with 
10–15 L/min. If at risk of T2RF, aim for saturation 
of 88–92%, adjusting to 94–98% if the ABGs show 
normal carbon dioxide.* Repeat ABG after 30–60 min.
3.	 COPD/other conditions at risk of 
T2RF requiring low-dose/controlled 
oxygen
Before ABG, use a 28% Venturi mask (4 L/min), 
aiming for a saturation range of 88–92%, adjusting 
to 94–98% if the ABGs show normal carbon 
dioxide.* Repeat ABG after 30–60 min. If the patient 
has an oxygen alert card, aim for the target range 
specific to him/her. If the patient is hypercapnic and 
acidotic, despite 30 min of appropriate treatment and 
oxygenation, consider non-invasive ventilation.
4.	 Conditions for which the patient 
should be closely monitored but 
oxygen is not required unless hypoxic
If hypoxaemia develops, follow recommendations as 
per serious illness (point 2 above).
ABG, arterial blood gas; COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
*Unless there is a history of previous hypercapnic respiratory failure requiring non-invasive or invasive ventilation, 
in which case the target saturation should remain at 88–92%; if no diagnosis is known but the patient is older than 
50 years and a long-term smoker with chronic dyspnoea, treat as presumed COPD.

condition: Appendix X: Serological Markers 1288 Appendix XI: Oxygen Therapy
text:
Appendix XI  Oxygen Therapy    1297
Oxygen therapy in COVID-19
Medical oxygen is an essential medicine in the treatment of COVID-19 and saves lives.
Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure
Severe illnesses in COVID-19 typically occur approximately 1 week after the onset of 
symptoms. The most common symptom is dyspnoea and hypoxaemia. Fifteen percent 
of individuals with COVID-19 develop moderate to severe disease and require 
supplemental oxygen. These patients require close monitoring for worsening respiratory 
status as some patients may progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). 
	
l Oxygen delivery can be increased by using a non-rebreathing mask and prone 
positioning. In adults with COVID-19 and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, 
conventional oxygen therapy may be insufficient to meet the oxygen needs of the 
patient. Options for providing enhanced respiratory support include high-flow nasal 
cannula (HFNC), non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV), intubation and 
invasive mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). 
HFNC is preferred over NIPPV. 
	
l NIPPV may generate aerosol spread of SARS-CoV2 and thus increase transmission 
of nosocomial infection. 
	
l Patients with fatigue and at risk for exhaustion, because of respiratory distress, 
will require invasive ventilation. In invasively ventilated patients with COVID-19, 
positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) level on the ventilator is important to reduce 
the fatality rate.
	
l High flow nasal oxygen (HFNO), continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or 
non-invasive ventilation (NIV) in severe COVID-19 should be used only in selected 
patients with hypoxaemic respiratory failure.
Asymptomatic and mild COVID-19
Patients with asymptomatic and mild COVID-19 should undertake a 6-minute walk test 
to assess cardiopulmonary exercise tolerance and unmask hypoxia. For this test, the 
patient with pulse oximeter attached to his/her finger is asked to walk in the confines 
of the room for 6 minutes continuously. 
6-Minute walk test
	
l The test is positive if there is any drop in saturation below 94%, an absolute drop 
of more than 3–5% or feeling of being unwell (light-headed, short of breath) while 
performing the test or at the end of 6 minutes. 
	
l Patients with positive 6-minute walk test may progress to become hypoxic and 
hence early admission to hospital (for observation and oxygen supplementation) is 
recommended. 
	
l The test can be repeated every 6–8 hours of monitoring in the home setting. 
	
l It should not be done in patients older than 70 years, those with uncontrolled asthma 
and pregnant patients.

condition: Appendix X: Serological Markers 1288 Appendix XI: Oxygen Therapy
text:
1298    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Proning 
To improve breathing and oxygen saturation, in patients undergoing home care with 
SpO2 below 94%, advise awake proning (30–120 minutes in prone position followed 
by 30–120 minutes in left lateral decubitus, right lateral decubitus and upright sitting 
position). Criteria to be fulfilled for awake proning are normal mental status and able 
to self-prone or change position with minimal assistance. Avoid proning in patients 
with haemodynamic instability and situations in which close monitoring is not possible.
Oxygen delivery systems
All hospitals coping with patients with COVID-19 have to ensure the availability of 
supplemental oxygen. There are three main types of oxygen delivery systems: 
	 1.	Compressed gas 
	 2.	Liquid oxygen in cryogenic containers
	 3.	Oxygen concentrators for medical use 
Considerations for the selection of oxygen source include, but are not limited to, 
factors such as: 
	
l Size and weight of the device 
	
l Storage capacity 
	
l Cost and the ability to fill the device
Oxygen cylinders
Oxygen cylinders provide pressurized oxygen and require pressure regulators and 
flow metres to deliver oxygen safely to the patient. However, leakage from ill-fitting 
adapters and frequent replacement when high oxygen flows are needed are the limiting 
factors.
Oxygen concentrators
	
l Oxygen concentrators are a portable, battery-operated and cost-effective device, 
good for hospital and home use. They are used in patients suffering from chronic 
and acute breathing disorders requiring oxygen support. In moderate cases of 
COVID-19, when the patient experiences a drop in oxygen levels below 90%, where 
the oxygen requirement is a maximum of 5 L/min while waiting for arrangement 
of a bed at hospitals or on oxygen cylinders along with proning, the goal of oxygen 
therapy is to achieve a saturation level of 94%; once the patient has 93–94% oxygen 
level, the oxygen therapy may be discontinued. 
	 Note: While using an oxygen concentrator, the patient should be well hydrated 
and doors and windows should be kept open. There are two types of concentrators 
– continuous flow and pulse dose. Continuous flow concentrators keep supplying 
the same flow of oxygen every minute if they are not turned off. The pulse dose 
concentrators release oxygen on detecting inhalation.
	
l While procuring oxygen concentrators, the oxygen purity indicator (OPI) should be 
>90% and capacity of oxygen concentrator (minimum continuous flow of 5 L/min

condition: Appendix X: Serological Markers 1288 Appendix XI: Oxygen Therapy
text:
Appendix XI  Oxygen Therapy    1299
at 90% oxygen concentration is required with one oxygen outlet). Supplying 90% 
of oxygen concentration is mandatory. 
	
l Weight of the oxygen concentrator machine indicates the oxygen production capacity 
(heavier normally implies a greater capacity.)
	
a.	Small 5-to 10-kg concentrators are suitable for COPD (with output of 90% 
oxygen at 1–2 LPM)
	
	90%–30% or ( 1 LPM, 2 LPM) means that 90% oxygen is available only at 1 or 
2 LPM flow, respectively, and on higher flows, oxygen drops to 30%.
	
b.	Medium (15–19 kg) concentrators give an output of 90% oxygen at flows from 1 to 
5 LPM; they are suited for patients with COVID with mild to moderate disease.
	
c.	Large (20 kg and above) concentrators, suitable for critical patients and patients 
with COVID, give an output of 90% oxygen from 1 to 10 LPM flow; they can 
be used for two patients. 
	
l Cryogenically produced liquid oxygen is generated off-site (not at a medical 
facility). Large bulk liquid oxygen tanks at a medical facility are refilled periodically 
by a truck from a supplier. The liquid oxygen tank supplies a centrally piped system 
throughout the health facility by self-vaporization and for which a power supply is 
not required. However, external supply chain mechanisms, transport and storage 
due to the risks associated with higher pressures are the limiting factors. The liquid 
oxygen tank needs extra care in more extreme environments. Oxygen cylinders 
should be kept ready as a backup supply. Centralized, piped oxygen systems deliver 
pressurized oxygen through wall outlets close to the ICU bed. The systems are 
usually fed by a large liquid oxygen tank or large oxygen cylinders.
	
l The typical flow metre range for medical oxygen is between 0 and 15 L/min up to 
25 L/min. Flow rate in young infants up to 2 months is 0.5–1 L/min, and in those 
aged 2 months to 5 years is 1–2 L/min. 
Oxygen flow systems
Oxygen is preferably administered by non-rebreathing systems outside the operating 
room. There are mainly two types of non-rebreathing oxygen delivery systems:
	 1.	Fixed performance high-flow system: It predetermines room air entrainment to 
achieve the desired flow and fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2). Venturi devices 
are the most commonly used high-flow oxygen devices for unintubated patients. 
Variation in orifice or entrainment port size will change FiO2, whereas variation 
of oxygen flow rate will determine the total volume of gas provided by the device. 
FiO2 values of 0.24–0.40 are readily provided by these masks.
	 2.	Variable performance low-flow system: Air entrainment varies to meet the 
patients’ inspiratory flow requirements.
  Oxygen delivery method selected depends on:
	
l Age of the patient 
	
l Oxygen requirements/therapeutic goals 
	
l Patient tolerance to selected interface 
	
l Humidification needs

condition: Appendix X: Serological Markers 1288 Appendix XI: Oxygen Therapy
text:
1300    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Devices for delivery of oxygen
	 1.	A nasal cannula (NC) comfortably provides oxygen at low-flow rates, 2–6 L/min, 
delivering a concentration of 24–40%. A catheter (8 FG in children) should be 
inserted to a depth equal to the distance between the side of the nostril and the inner 
margin of the eyebrow. Keep the catheter clear of mucus. In case a nasogastric tube 
is required for feeding, insert it through the same nostril as the oxygen catheter and 
the other nostril should be kept clear of all obstructions including mucus.
	 2.	Nasal prongs are designed to lie just within nostrils. They are preferred over nasal 
catheter in young infants and children with severe croup or pertussis as catheter 
can provoke paroxysms of coughing. 
	
	Care and considerations of child with simple nasal prongs
	
	Position the nasal prongs along the patient’s cheek and secure the nasal prongs on 
the patient’s face with adhesive tape.
	
l Position the tubing over the ears and secure behind the patient’s head. Ensure 
that straps and tubing are away from the patient’s neck to prevent risk of airway 
obstruction.
	
l Check the nasal prongs and tubing for patency, kinks or twists at any point in 
the tubing and clear or change the prongs if necessary.
	
l Check the nares for patency – clear with suction as required.
	
l Change the adhesive tape weekly or more frequently as required.
	 3.	Simple face mask: It covers the nose and mouth with side-to-side perforations 
which allow room air entrance when placed over the patient’s nose and mouth. 
Oxygen is delivered at a high flow rate (5–6 L/min) to avoid accumulation of 
carbon dioxide. The mask interferes with feeding and many infants may refuse but 
it is a good device to achieve oxygenation in severely distressed patients and in 
emergency situations when high-flow rate oxygen is required. 
	 4.	Mask with reservoir bag: A partial rebreathing mask is a simple face mask with an 
attached reservoir bag; it provides oxygen at 40–80% or even higher at 5–10 L/min.
	 5.	Non-rebreather masks with one-way valve system which prevents exhaled gases 
mixing with fresh gas flow draw oxygen from an attached reservoir bag, with 
one-way valves that direct exhaled air out of the mask. When properly fitted and 
used at flow rates of 10–15 L/min or higher, they deliver close to 100% oxygen. 
The delivered FiO2 of this system is 60–80%, depending on the oxygen flow and 
breathing. This type of mask is indicated for acute medical emergencies.
	 6.	Demand valves or oxygen resuscitators deliver oxygen only when the patient 
inhales, or, in the case of an apnoeic (non-breathing) victim, the caregiver presses a 
button on the mask; these are useful in emergency situations when a limited supply 
of oxygen is available and there is a delay in transporting the patient to higher 
care. Care must be taken not to overinflate the patient’s lungs, and some systems 
use safety valves to help prevent this. These systems may not be appropriate for 
unconscious patients or those in respiratory distress.
Monitoring of a patient on oxygen therapy: Monitor closely to identify and correct 
any problem in delivery of oxygen and for signs of improvement.
	
l Monitor the position of prongs/catheter and blockade by mucus.

condition: Appendix X: Serological Markers 1288 Appendix XI: Oxygen Therapy
text:
Appendix XI  Oxygen Therapy    1301
	
l Check the oxygen flow rate and connections.
	
l Monitor the heart rate (HR) and respiratory rate (RR), and signs of respiratory distress. 
Increase in HR and RR suggests a need for increasing FiO2 and other measures.
	
l Perform pulse oximetry every 6–8 hours to record in all patients as the ‘fifth vital sign’.
	
l Assess with arterial blood gases (ABGs), if indicated as below.
	
l Maintain oxygen saturation (>90%) by pulse oximeter.
  Check blood gases in the following situations:
	
l ABG analysis should be performed before oxygen therapy, if possible, in all 
critically ill patients. For critically ill patients or those with shock or hypotension 
(systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg), the initial blood gas measurement should be 
obtained from an arterial sample.
	
l ABG analysis should be performed for any patient with risk factors for hypercapnic 
respiratory failure who develops acute breathlessness, deteriorating oxygen 
saturation, drowsiness or other symptoms of carbon dioxide retention (unexplained 
confusion and agitation).
	
l ABGs should be measured or oximetry done within 2 hours of starting oxygen 
therapy and FiO2 adjusted accordingly. (An adequate response is defined as PaO2 
>7.8 kPa or SaO2 >90%.)
	
l ABG analysis should be performed for patients with hypoxaemia at risk of 
arrhythmias or respiratory failure or metabolic acidosis (such as patients with 
diabetes) and monitor continuously by oximetry.
	
l ABG analysis should be performed in case there is an unexpected or inappropriate 
fall in SpO2 below 94% or fall of >3% in saturation or increasing breathlessness in a 
patient with previously stable chronic hypoxaemia (e.g., severe COPD). (Allowance 
should be made for transient dips in saturation to 90% or less in normal individuals 
during sleep.)
	
l ABG analysis should be performed for patients who were mostly stable previously 
but have now deteriorated clinically and require increased FiO2 to maintain a 
constant oxygen saturation.
	
l In the acute stage, response should be assessed daily by ABG analysis or oximetry 
and FiO2 adjusted accordingly.
Potential complications of oxygen use 
Carbon dioxide (CO2) narcosis: This occurs in patients who have chronic respiratory 
obstruction or respiratory insufficiency which results in hypercapnia (i.e. raised 
PaCO2). Oxygen in these patients can reduce their respiratory drive, causing respiratory 
depression and a further rise in PaCO2 resulting in increased CO2 levels in the blood 
and CO2 narcosis.
Monitoring of SpO2 or SaO2 informs of oxygenation only. Therefore, beware of the 
use of high FiO2 in the presence of reduced minute ventilation.
Pulmonary atelectasis (pulmonary oxygen toxicity): High concentrations of oxygen 
(>60%) may damage the alveolar membrane when inhaled for more than 48 hours 
resulting in pathological lung changes.

condition: Appendix X: Serological Markers 1288 Appendix XI: Oxygen Therapy
text:
1302    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Retrolental fibroplasia (retinopathy of prematurity): An alteration of the normal 
retinal vascular development, mainly affecting premature neonates (<32 weeks' 
gestation or 1250 g birth weight), can lead to visual impairment and blindness.
Note: Never give oxygen in paraquat poisoning unless the patients are suffering from 
severe respiratory distress or respiratory arrest, as this can increase the toxicity. Oxygen 
therapy is not recommended for patients who have suffered pulmonary fibrosis or other 
lung damage resulting from bleomycin treatment. 
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Supplemental high levels of oxygen cause ventilation–perfusion imbalance reducing 
respiratory drive to the point of precipitating respiratory failure and eventual death; 
therefore, care needs to be exercised in patients with COPD, such as emphysema, 
especially in those known to retain carbon dioxide (T2RF). However, the risk of the 
loss of respiratory drive is far outweighed by the risks of withholding emergency 
oxygen, and, therefore, emergency administration of oxygen is never contraindicated. 
Transfer from field care to definitive care, where oxygen use can be carefully 
calibrated, should occur long before significant reductions to the respiratory drive.
Precautions 
Oxygen is a drug, and use outside of an emergency situation should be prescribed by 
a medical practitioner only. Oxygen therapy should be closely monitored and assessed 
at regular intervals.
	
l Both hypoxaemia and hyperoxaemia are harmful. Supplemental oxygen relieves 
hypoxaemia but does not improve ventilation or treat the underlying cause of the 
hypoxaemia. Monitoring of SpO2 indicates oxygenation not ventilation. Therefore, 
beware of the use of high FiO2 in the presence of reduced minute ventilation.
	
l Many children in the recovery phase of acute respiratory illnesses are characterized 
by ventilation/perfusion mismatch (e.g. asthma, bronchiolitis and pneumonia) and 
can be managed with SpO2 in the low 90s as long as they are clinically improving, 
are feeding well and do not have obvious respiratory distress.
	
l Normal SpO2 values may be found despite rising blood carbon dioxide levels 
(hypercapnia). High oxygen concentrations have the potential to mask signs and 
symptoms of hypercapnia.
	
l Therapeutic procedures and handling may increase the child’s oxygen consumption 
and lead to worsening hypoxaemia.
	
l Children with cyanotic congenital heart disease normally have SpO2 between 
60% and 90% in room air. Increasing SpO2 >90% with supplemental oxygen is 
not recommended due to risk of overcirculation to the pulmonary system while 
adversely decreasing systemic circulation. However, in emergency situations with 
increasing cyanosis, supplemental oxygen should be administered to maintain their 
normal level of SpO2.

condition: Appendix X: Serological Markers 1288 Appendix XI: Oxygen Therapy
text:
Appendix XI  Oxygen Therapy    1303
WEANING OXYGEN/STOPPING OXYGEN
Oxygen should be stopped when arterial oxygenation is adequate with the patient 
breathing room air (PaO2 >8 kPa, SaO2 >90%). In patients without arterial hypoxaemia 
but at risk of tissue hypoxia, oxygen should be stopped when the acid–base state and 
clinical assessment of vital organ function are consistent with resolution of tissue 
hypoxia.
In children, unless clinically contraindicated, an attempt to wean oxygen therapy 
should be attempted at least once per shift if the child appears clinically well, all vital 
signs are in normal limits, there is no or mild respiratory distress, the child is taking 
adequate amounts orally and is alert, and his/her colour is pink and behaviour is normal.
	 1.	Cease oxygen therapy entirely and maintain line of sight for approximately 
5 minutes.
	 2.	If SpO2 falls below 92%, or specific target as per relevant clinical guideline, or 
as ordered by medical staff, re-commence oxygen therapy at the lowest flow rate 
necessary to maintain target SpO2.
	 3.	Perform continuous pulse oximetry for 30 minutes post-cessation of oxygen 
therapy.
	 4.	If oxygen wean is successful, perform vital sign observation and intermittent SpO2 
monitoring 30 minutes later, and then hourly for 2 hours.
References
	 1.	 Oxygen Delivery. Clinical Guidelines (Nursing). https://www.rch.org.au/rchcpg/hospital_
clinical_guideline_index/Oxygen_delivery/ [accessed January 4, 2024].
	 2.	 Dondorp AM, Hayat M, Aryal D, Beane A, Schultz MJ. Respiratory support in COVID-19 
patients, with a focus on resource-limited settings. Am J Trop Med Hyg. 2020;102(6):1191–1197. 
	 3.	 WHO. COVID-19 Technical Specifications for Procurement of Oxygen Therapy and Monitoring 
Devices. WHO/2020-nCoV/MedDev/TS/O2T.V1 17. June 2020. https://www.who.int/docs/
default-source/medical-devices/tech-specs-o2-therapy-monitoring-final-draft.pdf [accessed 
March 12, 2024].
	 4.	 O’Driscoll BR, Howard LS, Earis J, Mak V. British Thoracic Society guideline for oxygen use 
in adults in healthcare and emergency settings. BMJ Open Respir Res. 2017;4:e000170.

condition: Appendix XII: Clinically Important Drug–Drug Interactions
text:
Appendix  XII
Clinically Important Drug–Drug 
Interactions
A clinically relevant drug–drug interaction (DDI) occurs when the effectiveness or 
toxicity of one medication is altered by prior administration or co-administration of 
another medicine. The potential for clinically important DDIs can often be predicted 
based on the drug properties, method of drug administration and patient-specific 
parameters. DDIs are one of the commonest causes of ADRs. Identifying the most 
important and clinically relevant drug interactions is essential to patient safety.
Drug interactions can be categorized into four groups:
	 I.	Interactions of drugs with other drugs (DDIs)
	 II.	Drugs with food (drug–food interactions)
	III.	Drug with disease condition (drug–disease interactions)
	IV.	Drug with laboratory investigation (drug–laboratory interactions)
I. DRUG–DRUG INTERACTIONS
There are three possible outcomes when DDIs occur:
	 1.	One drug may intensify the effects of the other: Aspirin (antiplatelet) given together 
with warfarin/coumarin (anticoagulant) increases chances of bleeding; antihistamines 
increase the sedative effects of barbiturates, tranquilizers, alcohol and pain relievers.
	 2.	One drug may reduce the effects of the other: Beta-blockers used with terbutaline.
	 3.	The combination may produce a new response not seen when either drug is given 
alone: Alcohol and disulfiram (Antabuse) when taken together may result in many 
unpleasant and dangerous responses.
Mechanism of drug interactions
Interactions can be pharmacodynamic or pharmacokinetic. Some drug interactions are 
due to a combination of mechanisms.
1. Pharmacodynamic drug interactions: These are relatively predictable if the actions 
of the medicine are known. Pharmacodynamic interactions are those in which drugs 
influence each other’s effects directly. These involve the additive effect of similar 
medicines, or a cancelling effect, for example:
	
l Increasing risk of hypotension with two antihypertensives
	
l Antagonism – beta-blockers used with terbutaline
