2. Pharmacokinetic drug interactions: Pharmacokinetic interactions are more 
complex and usually involve interference with (ADME principle):
	
l Absorption: Drugs, food and drinks can alter the absorption of drugs. This is one 
important site of drug interaction, e.g.
	– Antacids and oral iron preparations block absorption of Quinolones, Tetracycline 
and Azithromycin.
	– Iron supplements and calcium chelate in the stomach, instead of being absorbed 
into the bloodstream.
	– When Ampicillin and Omeprazole are taken with food, their absorption is reduced.
	– Ampicillin or Amoxicillin taken with allopurinolmay result in increased skin rash.
	– Omeprazole, Lansoprazole and H2-antagonists decrease the absorption of 
Ketoconazole and Delavirdine.
	
l Distribution: The drug moves from bloodstream into various fluids and tissues 
or it may get bound to plasma proteins. One drug may displace another drug from 
these sites.

condition: Appendix XII: Clinically Important Drug–Drug Interactions
text:
1306    Standard Treatment Guidelines
	
l Metabolism: Most drugs are metabolized in the liver. The liver has many enzymes 
that metabolize the drugs and these enzymes can be induced or inhibited by drugs, 
thus causing increase or decrease in metabolism of other drugs:
	– INH inhibits metabolism of Carbamazepine on one hand, but induces the metabolism 
of oral contraceptives on the other hand, resulting in contraception failure.
	
l Excretion: Drugs are excreted primarily by kidneys. One drug may decrease or 
increase the excretion of drugs. A change in blood concentration causes a change in 
the drug’s effect. If the concentration increases, there may be more adverse effects, 
or if the concentration decreases, there may be lack of therapeutic response.
	– INH inhibits Diazepam excretion leading to enhanced Diazepam response. 
Furosemide enhances lithium toxicity.
3. Pharmaceutical interactions (in vitro interaction): These can be classified as those 
interactions that occur prior to systemic administration, for example, incompatibility 
between two drugs mixed in an IV fluid. These interactions can be physical (e.g. with 
a visible precipitate) or chemical with no visible sign of a problem. For example: 
	
l Ketamine is incompatible with barbiturate and diazepam.
	
l Do not combine thiopentone and suxamethonium.
	
l Do not combine protamine zinc sulphate and soluble insulin.
	
l Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose solutions.
	
l Amphotericin precipitates in saline.
	
l Gentamicin is physically/chemically incompatible with most beta-lactams, resulting 
in loss of antibiotic effect.
4. Unknown mechanisms: Not all interactions can be predicted based on readily 
recognizable mechanism. Be wary of new combinations for which literature is sparse 
or non-existent.
II. DRUG–FOOD INTERACTIONS
Drug–food interactions occur when drugs react with foods, dietary supplements or 
beverages (including alcohol). Some drugs may interfere with the body’s ability to 
absorb nutrients. In the same way, certain herbs and food can lessen or increase the 
impact of a drug.
	
l Consumption of alcoholic drinks while on the antimicrobial metronidazole will 
cause skin flushing, nausea, headache and palpitations. Alcohol enhances the 
hypoglycaemic effect of antidiabetic medication, and the hypotensive effect of many 
antihypertensive drugs. Tobacco can also diminish the effectiveness of medications 
by increasing drug metabolism. Caffeine, which is found in tea, coffee, soft drinks 
and chocolate and some medications, can increase the risk of theophylline toxicity. 
Green leafy vegetables like broccoli, spinach and watercress interact with warfarin 
because the high vitamin K content of these foods counters the effect of Warfarin.
	
l Grapefruit juice enhances the effect of drugs like Simvastatin, Nifedipine and 
Cyclosporine.
	
l Dairy products reduce the absorption of biphosphonates, oral iron, Levothyroxine 
and certain antibiotics (Ciprofloxacin and Tetracycline).

condition: Appendix XII: Clinically Important Drug–Drug Interactions
text:
Appendix XII  Clinically Important Drug–Drug Interactions    1307
III. DRUG–DISEASE INTERACTION
Drug–disease interactions occur when a drug worsens or exacerbates an existing 
medical condition. Conditions that place patients at high risk for drug interactions 
include kidney or liver disease, diabetes, asthma, cardiac problems, epilepsy and high 
or low blood pressure. Drug–disease interactions are more common among the elderly, 
who tend to have more concomitant diseases. Some examples are:
	
l Nasal decongestants containing pseudoephedrine should be avoided in patients with 
hypertension as it increases blood pressure.
	
l NSAIDs may cause airway constriction in patients with asthma.
	
l NSAIDs can decrease the effectiveness of antihypertensive medications.
IV. DRUG–LABORATORY INTERACTIONS
Some drugs alter the test specimen, or directly interfere with the test reagents. For 
example, Cephalosporins may alter urine glucose and ketone tests. Daptomycin and 
Telavancin can falsely prolong or elevate prothrombin time and the international 
normalized ratio. Acetaminophen, Lisinopril, Albuterol and Atenolol, as well as red 
wine, have been reported to cause falsely high sugar on continuous glucose monitors 
(CGMs). Since drug–laboratory test interactions during new drug development are 
not required for drug approval, the absence of a drug–laboratory test interaction in the 
prescribing information does not preclude the existence of a yet unreported interaction.
Risk factors for drug interactions 
The risk and severity of drug interactions depend on different factors including the number 
of prescribed medications, duration of treatment, patient's age and stage of the disease.
High-risk patients 
	
l Patients on multiple drugs (higher the number of drugs, greater is the risk of drug 
interactions; polytherapy may determine the ‘prescribing cascade’, which occurs 
when an ADR is misunderstood, and new potentially unnecessary drugs are 
administered; therefore, the patient is at risk to develop further ADRs)
	
l Very young and very old patients (the elderly are more prone to drug interactions 
as they are more sensitive to some pharmacodynamic effects and also tend to be on 
multiple drugs; similarly, children are more vulnerable to the occurrence of potential 
DDIs by changes in absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion)
	
l Patients with comorbidities and impaired pathways of drug elimination such as renal 
or hepatic impairment
	
l Multiple prescribers or pharmacies
	
l Infrequent monitoring or non-compliance
High-risk drugs
These include drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, e.g. Warfarin, Carbamazepine, 
Phenytoin, Theophylline and Digoxin.

condition: Appendix XII: Clinically Important Drug–Drug Interactions
text:
1308    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Minimization of drug–drug interactions
DDIs are usually preventable and are responsible for a large number of hospital 
admissions as a result of medically important, sometimes serious or even fatal adverse 
events and partial or complete abolishment of treatment efficacy. 
	
l Differentiate between a pharmacokinetic and a pharmacodynamic DDI.
	
l Stratify the severity and potential outcomes of a DDI based on a patient scenario.
	
l Develop a plan to manage a DDI, including safe therapeutic alternatives and monitoring.
Strategies for reducing the risk of drug–drug interactions
	
l Minimize the number of drugs prescribed.
	
l Keep a short list of top DDIs handy.
	
l Focus on high-risk patients and focus on high-risk drugs. Complete a thorough drug 
history, including illicit drugs and over-the-counter drugs, especially when starting 
a medication, adding a new medication and stopping a medication.
	
l Perform risk assessment – as to how common the interaction is. How severe will the 
interaction be, if it occurs? Is it a dose-related interaction?
	
l Use an alternative drug or adjust the dosage when an inducer of metabolism is added 
to or deleted from the patient's regimen.
	
l Adjust the dosages of medications when indicated and timing of administration to 
minimize interference with absorption, e.g. iron and calcium.
	
l Monitor for early signs of adverse reactions and toxicity when combinations of toxic 
agents cannot be avoided.
	
l For test results that do not correspond with the clinical picture, obtain confirmatory 
tests by an alternate assay method, if available, and suspect DDI.
	
l Electronic prescribing systems that can alert the user early on to potential 
interactions and can assist with drug selection and dosage are helpful.
	
l Educate about possible drug interactions when a reaction or potential adverse effect 
can be anticipated.

condition: Appendix XIII: The Clinical Use of Blood and Blood Safety
text:
Appendix  XIII
The Clinical Use of Blood 
and Blood Safety
Timely access to safe and quality blood and blood components is an important step of 
patient management. Rational use involves using the right product, in the right dose 
and on the right time to reduce unnecessary and unsafe transfusions and to improve 
patient outcomes and safety along with minimizing the risk of adverse events including 
transfusion reactions and transmission of infections such as HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, 
syphilis, malaria and other diseases. Before transfusion of blood, clinicians must weigh 
the pros and cons of blood transfusion. Transfusion should be done only when benefit 
outweighs the risk associated with transfusion. Blood and its products must be stored at 
their indicated temperature and conditions; otherwise, they can become contaminated.
Blood and blood products should be procured from licensed blood banks only and 
should be collected from a remunerated voluntary blood donor only. Each unit should 
be screened for transfusion-transmitted infection (TTI) markers as recommended (HIV 
I and II, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis and malaria) by the Drugs Control Act (1940). 
Each unit must be tested for TTI markers as recommended (HIV I and II, hepatitis B, 
hepatitis C, syphilis and malaria) by the Drugs Control Act (1940). Each unit must have 
a sticker indicating negative TTI markers and have a valid expiry. Each unit must report 
the patient's blood group along with the label.
The key principle of clinical transfusion practice
Transfusion is only one part of the patient’s management. The decision to transfuse 
blood or blood products should always be based on a careful assessment of the patient 
by clinical parameters and supported by laboratory parameters and this assessment 
is necessary to save life or prevent significant morbidity. It should also be based on 
knowledge of the resources available for managing patients and the safety of the 
blood and blood products available. Transfusion guidelines should be developed 
by each hospital and must be approved by the Hospital Transfusion Committee and 
should include:
	
l Clinical and laboratory investigations must support indications for the use of blood 
product. Possibilities of alternatives to transfusion must be explored before blood 
transfusion. It should not be used as volume expander or for wound healing, etc. 
Intravenous fluids like crystalloids and colloids must be used.

condition: Appendix XIII: The Clinical Use of Blood and Blood Safety

Appendix XIII  The Clinical Use of Blood and Blood Safety    1313
	
l Labeling should be present on available blood products and alternatives to 
transfusion: dosage, storage conditions, risk of transfusion-transmissible infection, 
means of administration, contraindications and precautions.
	
l Standard blood request form should provide full information about the patient and 
the need for transfusion supported by laboratory parameters.
	
l Maximum Surgical Blood Ordering Schedule (MSBOS) should be followed as a guide 
to the number of units of blood and blood products that should normally be requested 
for each type of operation, with guidance on its adaptation when required.
	
l Development and implementation of standard operating procedures for 
transfusion protocol must be prepared at the hospital level. 
	
l Training of health staff must be done for monitoring immediate and delayed 
transfusion reactions.
	
l Monitoring and evaluation at the hospital level should be done.
	
l The details of transfusion record must be kept in the patient's record file along with 
the cross-match report.
	
l Each and every reaction must be reported to the blood bank for investigation and 
uploading on haemovigilance website ("https://nib.gov.in/haemovigilance/HvPI_
website/HvPI_index.html"Haemovigilance Programme Of India (HvPI) (nib.gov.in). 
The key points of rational use of blood
	
l Judicious use of blood and blood components should be done. The motto is never 
to transfuse unless it is worth the risk. RBC transfusion is not routinely indicated 
for pharmacologically treatable anaemia such as iron-deficiency anaemia and 
vitamin B12- or folate-deficiency anaemia.
	
l Whole blood has a very limited use in clinical practice to replace red cells in acute 
bleeding when there is also a need to correct hypovolaemia.
	
l Preference for ‘fresh blood’ is another totally misguided practice. Avoid use of fresh 
blood because of increased risk of transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease 
(GVHD) and TTIs. 
	
l Single-unit whole blood transfusion has no significant therapeutic benefit. 
Discourage single-unit/fresh blood use.
	
l The preparation of blood components allows a single blood donation to provide 
treatment for three to four patients, and also avoids the transfusion of elements of the 
whole blood that the patient may not require, thus minimizing transfusion reactions. 
One unit of blood can be separated into 1 unit of fresh frozen plasma (FFP), 1 unit of 
packed red blood cells (PRBC) and 1 unit of random donor unit of platelets.
	
l Plasma can transmit most of the infections present in whole blood and there are very 
few indications for its transfusion. Plasma derivatives (human albumin, coagulation 
factor concentrates, immunoglobulins) are prepared under a pharmaceutical 
manufacturing process from large volumes of plasma comprising many individual 
blood donations. They must be tested to minimize the risks of transmitting infection. 
	
l Recombinant factors VIII and IX and immunoglobulins prepared by recombinant 
DNA technology are often favoured because of no risk of transmitting infectious 
agents to the patient.

l Use of autologous blood is safest and pre-surgical haemodilution in elective surgery 
helps in conserving blood.
	
l Advantages of single donor platelets (SDP) over random donor platelets (RDP) are:
	– There is reduced donor exposure which further reduces the risk of alloimmuni­
zation and incidence of transfusion-transmitted diseases. It yields a leucocyte-
reduced product, thus reduces non-febrile haemolytic transfusion reactions in 
recipients.
	– It provides the full effective dose. 
	– A platelet donor can donate every 72 hours.

*Refrigerator preferably should be an approved blood bank refrigerator, ideally fitted with a temperature recording device and 
temperature deviation alarm.
†Unrefrigerated whole blood less than 24 hours old is labelled as fresh whole blood (FWB). Intracellular pathogens 
(cytomegalovirus [CMV], human T cell lymphotropic viruses [HTLV]), Treponema and malarial parasite survive in fresh blood 
leucocytes, thus increase the risk of transfusion-transmitted infections. Due to the presence of viable lymphocytes, there are more 
chances of transfusion reaction (TA graft-versus-host disease [GVHD]).
‡In stable non-bleeding patients, platelets are withheld till counts of 10,000/microlitre. Do not use platelets in patients with 
autoimmune thrombocytopenia and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura except for life-threatening bleeding. (See also Chapter 4.)
Doses
PRBC: The decision to transfuse should be based on clinical assessment of the patient 
and not on the laboratory parameters. The physiological adaptation to acute or chronic 
anaemia should be considered. The decision for dosage depends on the baseline 
haematocrit, the desired rise and the cardiorespiratory status of the patient. In neonates, 
the dose is 10–15 mL/kg.
In chronic anaemia, every hospital should decide a trigger value of haemoglobin 
and should strictly follow it. 
Platelets
	
l Adults: One Single Donor Platelet (SDP) prepared from a donor using platelet apheresis 
equipment. Perform a platelet count on the recipient after 1 hour of transfusion. Repeat 
SDP transfusion can be done after 24 hours if the platelet count is low. 
	
l If SDP is not available, Random Donor Platelets (RDP) can be transfused. The dose 
for RDP is 1 unit per 10 kg of body weight, so a 60 kg patient will need six RDP 
units. The increase in platelet count with one SDP is about 30,000–35,000 mm3, 
whereas 1 unit of RDP increases by 6,000–8,000/mm3. Preferably, platelets from a 
compatible blood group should be transfused, but in emergencies, cross-matching 
across blood groups can be done.
	
l Neonates: Transfuse 10 mL of platelet concentrate (RDP) per kg of body weight.
Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP): Transfuse 15 mL per kg of body weight.
Cryoprecipitate: Transfuse 1 unit per 10 kg of body weight.
Compatible blood groups for blood components
	
l Red cell transfusion should always be ABO and RhD compatible with the recipient 
and cross-matched to confirm compatibility before transfusion.
	
l Whole blood transfusion should always be group specific. 
	
l ABO identical platelets are the components of choice, except in emergency.
	
l FFP must be ABO compatible.
	
l Cryoprecipitate can be given across ABO barrier.
(Continued)

1316    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Safe administration of blood or blood components
Errors in requesting, supply and administration of blood/components can lead to serious 
adverse reactions. Follow all the steps given next precisely:
	 1.	Pre-transfusion blood sample collection (3–5 mL in PLAIN vial) and correct 
labelling at bedside is the responsibility of the medical officer in-charge of the 
ward, and must NEVER be delegated to nurses or medical students. Check and 
confirm the patient’s identity.
	 2.	Request should be sent only on Blood Requisition Form, properly filled with details 
of clinical diagnosis, indication for transfusion, number of units of blood product 
required, urgency, time and date of submission, history of transfusion and reactions, 
if any, obstetric history in females, etc.
	 3.	Obtain informed consent for transfusion from the recipients, get it countersigned 
by the treating clinician and document it. 
	 4.	Collecting blood products prior to transfusion: Bring written documentation to 
identify the patient and check that the following details on the compatibility label 
attached to the blood pack exactly match the details on the patient’s documentation: 
patient’s family name and given name, patient’s hospital reference number, 
patient’s ward, operating room or clinic, and patient’s ABO and Rh D group and 
record in the blood collection register.
	 5.	Maintain cold chain during transport of blood to ward/another hospital in 
temperature-controlled devices.
	 6.	Perform final bedside checks for identification of the recipient before transfusion 
by checking name and registration number, compatibility report and label on the 
blood pack to prevent any identification error and transfusion reaction. Blood unit 
pack should be visually inspected and checked for expiry date. Do not use pack 
if there is any evidence of signs of deterioration such as leakage, unusual colour 
or signs of haemolysis which may be the only warning that the blood contains 
bacterial contamination and may cause a severe or fatal reaction when transfused.
	 7.	Transfusion of blood/components and concurrent fluids and medications: Blood 
should be transfused only by a separate IV line using disposable sterile blood 
transfusion set with an appropriate filter. It should be changed at least 12-hourly 
during blood component infusion or after every 4 units of blood if given within 
12-hour period in warm climate. Use fresh blood administration set or platelet set 
primed with saline to infuse platelet concentrates. Only normal saline, 4% albumin 
and ABO-compatible plasma can be given concurrently through the same IV device 
as red cell transfusion. (Caution: NEVER give electrolyte and colloid solutions 
containing calcium with blood cell components collected in anticoagulant- 
containing citrate as they may cause clotting of the infusion line. Do NOT use 5% 
dextrose and do NOT add medication to the blood bag or the transfusion line.)
	 8.	Monitor vitals: Pulse, BP, temperature, respiration rate, fluid balance (oral and 
IV intake, urinary output) and signs of the potential complications of transfusion

text:
1318    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Transfusion reaction
Transfusion reaction can occur in spite of all relevant laboratory tests. The severity of the 
reaction varies from being relatively mild to more severe, and at times can be fatal. Acute 
reaction present with fever/chills, hypotension/tachycardia, cola-coloured urine, nausea, 
vomiting, pain in the flanks/back/abdomen/chest, etc. Delayed reaction may present 5–10 
days post-transfusion with fever, anaemia, jaundice, increased bleeding tendency and 
thrombocytopenia. GVHD and transfusion-transmitted diseases can present late.
Documentation in the case file is essential for future reference and should include 
recipient consent for transfusion, name and type of blood/components, unit number, 
the blood transfusion compatibility report, date and time of transfusion, pre- and post-
transfusion vital signs, volume transfused, any adverse event and identification of 
bedside transfusion staff.
Management of transfusion reaction
	 1.	If an acute transfusion reaction occurs, first look for any discrepancy in the blood 
pack labels and the patient’s identity; stop transfusion immediately. 
	 2.	In an unconscious or anaesthetized patient, hypotension and uncontrolled bleeding 
may be the only signs of an incompatible transfusion. 
	 3.	In a conscious patient undergoing a severe haemolytic transfusion reaction, signs 
and symptoms may appear very quickly – within minutes of infusing only 5–10 mL 
of blood. Close observation at the start of the infusion of each unit is essential.
	 4.	Document transfusion reaction and report as per the hospital protocol and national 
guidelines for haemovigilance.
Category 1: Mild (localized cutaneous reactions: urticaria, rash, pruritis)
	 1.	Slow the transfusion – the symptoms usually subside if the transfusion is slowed 
and antihistamine is given. 
	 2.	Give an antihistamine: Inj. Chlorpheniramine 0.1 mg/kg by IM injection. 
	 3.	Continue the transfusion at the normal rate if there is no progression of symptoms 
after 30 minutes. 
	 4.	If there is no clinical improvement within 30 minutes or if signs and symptoms 
worsen, treat as Category 2.
Category 2: Moderately severe (urticaria, rigours, fever, pruritis, restlessness, 
tachycardia, palpitations, headache)
	 1.	Stop the transfusion. Replace the infusion set and keep the IV line open with 
normal saline. 
	 2.	Notify the doctor responsible for the patient and the blood bank immediately. 
	 3.	Send blood unit with infusion set, freshly collected urine and new blood samples 
(one clotted and one anticoagulated) from the vein opposite the infusion site 
with appropriate request form to the blood bank and laboratory for investigations 
(as below). 
	 4.	Administer antihistamine IM (Inj. Chlorpheniramine 0.1 mg/kg or equivalent) and 
oral or rectal antipyretic (Paracetamol 10 mg/kg: 500 mg to 1 g in adults). Avoid 
aspirin in patients with thrombocytopenia.

condition: Appendix XIII: The Clinical Use of Blood and Blood Safety
text:
Appendix XIII  The Clinical Use of Blood and Blood Safety    1319
	 5.	Give IV corticosteroids and bronchodilators if there are anaphylactoid features (e.g. 
bronchospasm, stridor). 
	 6.	Collect urine for the next 24 hours for evidence of haemolysis and send to the 
laboratory. 
	 7.	If clinical improvement occurs, restart transfusion slowly with the new blood unit 
and observe carefully. 
	 8.	If there is no clinical improvement within 15 minutes or if signs and symptoms 
worsen, treat as Category 3. 
Category 3: Life-threatening (rigors, fever, restlessness, respiratory distress, 
headache, loin/back pain, chest pain, hypotension [fall of ≥20% in systolic 
BP], tachycardia [rise of ≥20% in heart rate], haemoglobinuria [red urine], 
unexplained bleeding [DIC])
	 1.	Stop the transfusion. Replace the infusion set and keep the IV line open with 
normal saline. Infuse normal saline (initially 20–30 mL/kg) to maintain systolic 
BP. If the patient is hypotensive, give over 5 minutes and elevate the patient’s legs. 
	 2.	Maintain airway and give high-flow oxygen by mask. 
	 3.	Give Adrenaline (as 1:1000 solution) 0.01 mg/kg body weight by slow 
intramuscular injection.
	 4.	Give IV corticosteroids and bronchodilators if there are anaphylactoid features (e.g. 
bronchospasm, stridor). 
	 5.	Give diuretic: Frusemide 1 mg/kg IV or equivalent. 
	 6.	Notify the doctor responsible for the patient and the blood bank immediately. 
	 7.	Send blood unit with infusion set, fresh urine sample and new blood samples 
(one clotted and one anticoagulated) from the vein opposite the infusion site 
with appropriate request form to the blood bank and laboratory for investigations 
(as below). 
	 8.	Check a fresh urine specimen visually for signs of haemoglobinuria (red or pink 
urine). 
	 9.	Start a 24-hour urine collection and fluid balance chart and record all intake and 
output. Maintain fluid balance. 
	10.	Assess for bleeding from puncture sites or wounds. If there is clinical or laboratory 
evidence of DIC (see Chapter 4 for details), give platelets (adult: 5–6 units) 
and either cryoprecipitate (adults: 12 units) or FFP (adults: 3 units). Use virally 
inactivated plasma coagulation products, wherever possible. 
	11.	Reassess. If the patient is hypotensive, give further saline 20–30 mL/kg over 
5 minutes. Give inotrope, if available.
	12.	If urine output is falling or there is laboratory evidence of acute renal failure (rising 
K+, urea, creatinine), maintain fluid balance accurately and give further frusemide, 
if required. Consider dopamine infusion, if available. Seek expert help: the patient 
may need renal dialysis. 
	13.	If bacteraemia is suspected (rigours, fever, collapse, no evidence of a haemolytic 
reaction), start broad-spectrum antibiotics IV to cover Pseudomonas and Gram positives.

1320    Standard Treatment Guidelines
Investigating the acute transfusion reaction 
	 1.	Immediately report all acute transfusion reactions, with the exception of mild 
hypersensitivity (Category 1), to the doctor responsible for the patient and to the 
blood bank that supplied the blood. 
	
		
If you suspect that the patient is having a severe life-threatening reaction, 
seek help immediately from the duty anaesthetist, emergency team or whoever is 
available and skilled to assist.
	 2.	Record the following information on the patient’s notes: 
	
l Type of transfusion reaction
	
l Length of time after the start of transfusion that the reaction occurred
	
l Volume, type and pack numbers of the blood products transfused
	 3.	Take the following samples and send them to the blood bank for laboratory 
investigations:
	
l Immediate post-transfusion blood samples (one clotted and one anticoagulated: 
EDTA/Sequestrene) from the vein opposite the infusion site for: 
–	Full blood count, coagulation screen, direct antiglobulin test, urea, creatinine, 
electrolytes 
–	Blood culture in a special blood culture bottle
	
l Blood unit and giving set containing red cell and plasma residues from the 
transfused donor blood
	
l First specimen of the patient’s urine following the reaction
	
l Patient’s 24-hour urine sample
	 4.	Complete a transfusion reaction report form.
Prevention of febrile reaction
Febrile reactions are quite common, but fever is associated with other adverse reactions 
to transfusion; therefore, exclude other causes, particularly acute haemolysis and 
bacterial contamination, and the patient’s underlying conditions (e.g. malaria) before 
arriving at a diagnosis of a febrile reaction. 
If the patient is a regular transfusion recipient or has had two or more febrile non-
haemolytic reactions in the past: 
	 1.	Give an antipyretic 1 hour before starting the transfusion: e.g. paracetamol 
10–15 mg/kg orally. Do not use aspirin in a patient with thrombocytopenia. 
	 2.	Repeat the antipyretic 3 hours after the start of transfusion. 
	 3.	Transfuse slowly, where possible: 
	
l Whole blood and red cells: 3–4 hours per unit 
	
l Platelet concentrates: Up to 2 hours per concentrate
	 4.	Keep the patient warm. 
	 5.	If this fails to control the febrile reaction and further transfusion is needed, use buffy 
coat-removed or filtered red cells or platelet concentrates to remove the leucocytes.
Delayed complications
Appropriate tests should be done to detect the cause of reaction which may appear after 
a week and result in delayed haemolysis or unexplained fall in haemoglobin. A record 
should be maintained in the patient’s medical file.

Appendix XIII  The Clinical Use of Blood and Blood Safety    1321
Evaluate cases of suspected transfusion-transmitted disease. If confirmed, the 
involved blood unit must be identified in the report. Attempt should be made to recall 
the donor for retesting and counselling. Other recipients who received components from 
the suspected blood unit should also be investigated.
All reported cases of unexplained acute liver dysfunction occurring between 
2 weeks and 6 months after the transfusion of blood or components should be 
investigated as possible post-transfusion hepatitis. The donor of the implicated unit 
should be informed, counselled and permanently deferred.
Monitoring and evaluation
A transfusion committee should be established in each hospital to implement the policy 
and guidelines and monitor the use of blood and blood products at the local level.
The monitoring system should cover: 
	
l The safety, adequacy and reliability of the supply of blood, blood products and 
alternatives to transfusion
	
l The traceability of all blood and blood products, from blood collection to transfusion
	
l Compliance with the national/state/hospital guidelines on transfusion and reporting 
and the impact on prescribing practice
	
l Patterns of blood usage and clinical transfusion practice within hospitals and 
between similar hospitals at regional, provincial and district levels

Appendix  XIV
Critical/Panic Laboratory Value
A critical or panic laboratory value refers to a result that falls significantly outside the 
normal reference range and poses an immediate threat to a patient’s health, therefore 
requires immediate attention of the health care provider. Rapid communication and 
appropriate interventions are essential in managing these critical values to provide the 
best possible care and outcome for the patient. Critical values can be identified for 
various laboratory tests, including blood tests, imaging studies and other diagnostic 
procedures.
	 1.	Specific thresholds for critical values are based on clinical guidelines and 
laboratory standards. When a critical value is identified, the laboratory immediately 
notifies the health care team, through a designated and secure communication 
system. This prompt communication ensures that health care providers are aware 
of the critical result so that swift action is taken to address the patient’s condition 
such as adjusting medications, administering emergency treatments or performing 
urgent procedures. The goal is to stabilize the patient and address the underlying 
issue that led to the critical result.
	 2.	Examples of critical laboratory values include extremely low levels of 
haemoglobin, markedly elevated or low blood glucose levels, abnormal electrolyte 
concentrations or critical results from imaging studies such as a CT scan. These 
values often indicate a life-threatening situation, and health care providers must 
respond rapidly to prevent further harm to the patient.
	 3.	It is important for health care providers to have established protocols and 
procedures for managing critical laboratory values to ensure a timely and 
coordinated response. Effective communication within the health care team is 
crucial, and follow-up actions, documentation and monitoring of the patient’s 
response are integral parts of the process.
	 4.	Every hospital should identify its major critical alerts and laboratories should 
prioritize communicating them effectively to the clinical team.

Notes:
•	Please be aware that variations in normal values may exist across different books and references.
•	For microbiological tests, critical alert is alerting the clinicians of a possible infective aetiology based on 
presumptive suspicion of infection before the final (confirmed) results are available. The suspicion of any 
microorganism on microscopy, rapid card tests or colony morphology should be communicated for modification 
in the empirical therapy much before the initiation of targeted therapy so that mortality can be prevented in 
serious infective syndromes such as pneumococcal meningitis or melioidosis.
All attempts should be made to reduce the communication time of all the culture-
positive, molecular test reports to clinicians for a prompt action in a clinically useful 
time frame. Early and rapid communication of negative reports is equally important in 
microbiology for changing the empirical treatment and investigation of the other causes.
